Trump announces Greenland security deal with Denmark
The US will effectively control Greenland’s security under an agreement reached with Denmark and the self-governing Arctic territory, President Donald Trump has announced.
Trump has long argued that the US should acquire Greenland from Denmark because of the island’s strategic position and the need to counter Russian and Chinese influence in the Arctic. His demands sparked outrage in Copenhagen and further strained relations with America’s NATO allies in Europe.
In a Truth Social post on Friday, Trump said the agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns.”
“At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America,” he added.
“Additionally, from now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.”
Trump promised that the US would be “very protective” of Greenland, describing the deal as “a dream come true for the United States of America.”

Exclusives
Military
Russia is using inaccurate missiles that can miss by hundreds of meters to attack Ukrainian cities — and plans to scale them up. Russia is increasingly using RM48U missiles originally designed as air-defense training targets to attack Ukraine. Their large margin of error makes them especially dangerous when fired at Ukrainian cities, where they can strike civilian areas far from any intended targets.
One machine handles 52% of a Russian oil plant—Ukrainian drones just hit it. Satellite images show Ukrainian FP-1 drones hit the crude unit that handles 52% of Russia's TANECO refinery, 1,200 km from Ukraine.
Drones hit Rostov-on-Don for the second straight night—OSINT monitors say the military airbase was likely the target again. The local authorities confirmed more than 50 drones downed overnight but said nothing about the airfield where Ukraine reportedly destroyed three aircraft and three helicopters the previous night.
Ukraine's snipers didn't vanish in the drone war—their job changed beyond recognition. Up to 154 pounds on their backs, weeks at one position, a thermal scope always running—modern sniping is far more watching than shooting.
Russia was sure the terrain made this village impossible to take—Ukraine walked in anyway. Days of reconnaissance, drone strikes, and artillery went into the 66th Brigade's push on Serednie. When the village fell, Russian channels called the liberation footage an AI fake.
Russian e-commerce will lose $4.8 billion to the drone campaign against its warehouses, analysts estimate. Analysts cut a whole year's growth forecast for Russian online retail by a fifth, and blamed the strikes alone.
Russia kills captain of Tanzanian-flagged ship in latest attack on civilian shipping in Black Sea. Russia has repeatedly attacked civilian shipping around Ukraine's Black Sea ports, putting international crews and maritime trade at risk.
No missiles intercepted again: Russia strikes Kyiv water infrastructure amid warnings of harsher winter attacks. Russia also struck residential areas in Odesa and Zaporizhzhia, injuring civilians and damaging homes and other civilian infrastructure.
Ukraine strikes two Russian S-400 launchers in Bryansk. The same systems were used to attack Kyiv overnight. Ukraine is increasingly targeting systems Russia uses to launch missiles at its cities as Kyiv faces shortages of high-end interceptors.
A fifth of Russian refining sits idle, and the sector's earnings still grew. The money is being made on prices and state compensation rather than on the volumes the front line actually needs.
One pincer stalled a year ago, the other has just been broken near Kostiantynivka—Russia's ring will not close, Ukrainian commander says. Frontal assaults on fortified cities cost far more men and time than closing a ring behind them would have.
Intelligence and technology
Russia paid a recruit to vandalize London mosques and make it look like a homegrown hate crime. A Ukrainian man has pleaded guilty to the attacks. Direct Action UK, a fake British far-right group, then circulated images of the graffiti.
Stop arming Ukraine or we shut down your defense firms, pro-Kremlin group tells Latvia, Poland, and Portugal. Latvia's security service has opened a terrorism case and jailed one suspect, with the group's deadline set for 7 October.
Ukraine kept this strike drone secret for two years—its maker says it has destroyed more than 350 Russian systems. Ukraine's RAM-2X had been hunting Russian air defense systems and ballistic missile launchers, and the silence ended only when wrecked drones reached Russian hands.
International
Russia plans "accidental" drone strikes on NATO countries, Tusk says. Tusk said the tactic could be used to test whether NATO would act if an attack on one of its members could be presented as a mistake.
EU pledges €3.3 billion for Ukraine, von der Leyen says "more is coming" as Russia's escalating air war makes life in Ukrainian cities increasingly difficult. The new funding comes as Ukraine appeals for more air defense to counter increasingly complex Russian attacks, including advanced missile and drone strikes on Kyiv.
Belarus holds military drills around the Suwalki Gap, NATO's only land link to the Baltics. Minsk says troops are guarding infrastructure, manning checkpoints, and practicing against saboteurs and drones. It has not disclosed the total number of personnel involved.
Poland to provide Ukraine with scarce F-16 missiles to shoot down jet-powered drones — "What Ukraine needs right now." The aid package will also include aviation equipment, Poland's deputy defense minister says.
Fire temporarily shuts part of Slovak ammunition plant amid plans to triple capacity. The company operating the factory plans to triple its annual capacity of roughly 100,000 shell bodies and holds a seven-year agreement to supply EU states.
The EU has billions in unspent defense funds. It wants to use them for projects with Ukraine. The plan could bring more Ukrainian defense companies into Europe's growing defense industry.
Humanitarian and social impact
Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid. More than 6,000 people, including around 200 children, may remain trapped in the Russian-occupied city, where civilians lack food, water and medicine and some are risking mined fields to escape.
Russia's war has devastated Donetsk Oblast, with losses already exceeding $26 billion. The preliminary estimate covers destroyed industry, energy infrastructure, agriculture, transport, and other sectors, while much of the damage remains impossible to assess.
Ukraine receives 252 bodies as repatriation remains one of the few functioning channels with Russia. The repatriation of bodies gives families of missing Ukrainians a chance to identify their loved ones and finally bury them.
From the frontline to a rehab center: a rescued dog from Pokrovsk now helps wounded Ukrainians on the other side of the country. A rescued puppy from Pokrovsk now has an unusual volunteer role: visiting wounded Ukrainians at a rehabilitation center in Lviv.
Political and legal developments
Kyiv's arms industry wants to kill the export fee. Parliament just refused to route that money to the army. Ukraine's arms makers want the 20-30% export fee scrapped as Europe's defense market opens—while parliament won't route the cash to the army.
The US House just passed the first major Russia oil sanctions in two years—one signature stands between them and law. Named for the late Senator Lindsey Graham, it clears the way for tariffs of up to 100% on China, India, and the other top buyers of Russian energy.

BreakingTrump claims US Greenland security deal, China reportedly among adversaries being kept out
US president says Washington will expand its military presence on the island; sources report the restrictions include China
US President Donald Trump said on Friday that the United States had reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland giving Washington permanent authority over security on the Arctic island and requiring American approval for military activity or sensitive investment by US adversaries.
The US would immediately begin developing a large military presence on the island, Trump said, adding that Washington would work with Greenlanders on its development and construction. He said the agreement had no end date and would come at no cost to US taxpayers.
Fox News Digital reported that the restrictions cover China and Russia, citing a senior US official. The official said the deal grants the US permanent access, basing and overflight rights and allows it to establish additional military installations.

US warns allies of missile delivery delays due to shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:45:36 UTC
06:45:36 KST

US warns allies of missile delivery delays due to shortage
The US has warned allies to expect delays of as much as five years in key weapons deliveries as it rebuilds its own depleted munitions stocks.
Multiple European nations are expecting deliveries of key missile and air defence capabilities to be pushed back as a result of the US military exhausting its own arsenal in the Iran war, officials said.
Germany has asked the US to speed up delivery of the long-range Tomahawk cruise missile and the ground-based Typhon launcher, but depleted US stocks of the powerful weapon means its manufacturer, RTX Corp’s Raytheon, is unlikely to fulfil the order in the next five years.
Two other officials said some Eastern European nations also reliant on US weapons systems have experienced delays since soon after the US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb 28.
The Defense Department didn’t immediately return a call seeking comment.
The Pentagon’s decision to prioritise its own stockpiles is also straining Ukraine’s push for the US to send it more Patriot air defence interceptors ahead of what is expected to be a difficult winter for the war-torn nation. The issue of Ukraine’s badly needed air defense will be a key topic at next week’s United Nations meetings in New York.
President Donald Trump earlier this week told reporters that he’s talking to Ukraine about either sending them a “far less sophisticated version” of the Patriot system, or granting licences for Europeans to build the weapons.
The US is estimated to have used more than half of its most advanced Patriot missile variants, a third of its Tomahawk missiles and almost half of its precision strike missiles and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, interceptors in Iran. The Congressional Budget Office said the US had probably used as much as two-thirds of its inventory of missile defence interceptors since June 2025.
The military fired so many munitions at Iranian targets during the first few months of the war that it “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” Pentagon officials acknowledged to its inspector general.
Officials are now working to stockpile critical components and selected munitions, as well as streamline production lead times, the watchdog office said in a report released this week.
Defence firms are ramping up production, with Lockheed Martin Corp working to increase annual capacity from around 600 to 2,000 of the most advanced PAC-3 MSE, or Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement.
The stockpile shortages aren’t just impacting the US and Europe. In April the US told Japan its Tomahawk deliveries would be delayed by as much as two years. Saudi Arabia has also urged allies, including the US, to provide military support to help counter attacks from the Houthis in Yemen. Washington has not said if it will provide extra assistance.
Still, the US continues to deliver weapons bought by European allies for Ukraine through NATO and European Union initiatives, the people said.
Europe’s main concern is that the US continues to provide Ukraine with battlefield support.
European leaders plan to lobby Trump on providing Ukraine with more Patriots next week as world leaders attend United Nations meetings. EU officials also hope to push the US to grant European nations licences to build their own Patriots that could eventually be provided to Kyiv. BLOOMBERG

UN chief urges Security Council to reset peacekeeping operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:42:15 UTC
06:42:15 KST

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday urged the Security Council to overhaul the way UN peacekeeping operations are deployed and supported, calling for a renewed focus on political solutions, stronger partnerships with host countries and more adaptable missions.
Addressing a Security Council debate in New York on UN peacekeeping operations, Guterres said the changing nature of armed conflicts had exposed limitations in the way peacekeeping mandates are designed and implemented.
“For nearly 10 years, I have seen what peacekeepers can do when the Security Council stands behind them – and what they endure when it is divided,” Guterres said.
“We do not lack tools. What we lack, all too often, is the political space to use them,” he added.
Guterres said the need to adapt peace operations is at the center of a review requested under the Pact for the Future, arguing that peacekeeping must respond to a significantly different international security environment.
“Peacekeeping is, above all, a political instrument,” he said. “It is deployed to support political solutions – never as a substitute for them.”
He said that for decades, UN peacekeepers were primarily deployed to help parties to civil wars implement comprehensive peace agreements.
But such agreements are now rarer, harder to reach and more fragile, according to the secretary-general.
“Most of our missions now operate where peace remains elusive,” he said.
Guterres said the environment in which peacekeepers operate has changed rapidly.
“Peacekeepers are attacked. Civilians are targeted. International law is violated with a mounting sense of impunity,” he said. 
'Peacemaking before peacekeeping'
He outlined five broad priorities for what he described as a “reset” of UN peacekeeping.
The first priority, he said, should be putting peacemaking first.
“Let me be clear: peacekeeping operations should be deployed only when a peace agreement, or at least a robust ceasefire, is in place,” Guterres said.
He acknowledged that peacekeepers can help preserve peace but argued that they cannot create lasting peace in the absence of a political settlement.
“We cannot keep peace where there is no peace to keep,” he said.
Guterres identified a new partnership with host states as his second priority.
“Peace cannot be imported,” he said. “It must be built from within – by the national actors, who hold the key.”
He called for host governments to be consulted when mandates are established and renewed, while also ensuring that other parties to conflicts and civil society are heard.
His third priority was to ensure that peacekeeping mandates are designed for the circumstances in which missions actually operate.
“Protection built into missions’ mandates from the outset – in how they are planned, mandated and resourced – so that when civilians are threatened, peacekeepers can act decisively,” he said.
Guterres' fourth priority was to empower peacekeeping missions with greater operational flexibility and adequate resources.
The UN chief identified stronger cooperation among the UN, regional organizations and host countries as his fifth priority.
“No organization can address today’s conflicts alone,” he said.
Guterres also drew a distinction between peacekeeping and peace enforcement.
He reiterated that UN peacekeeping operations should be deployed only where a peace agreement or robust ceasefire exists.
“When circumstances require, we need peace enforcing, not peacekeeping,” he said.
Guterres concluded by emphasizing that the effectiveness of UN peacekeeping ultimately depends on political unity among Security Council members.
“Unity is built – through effort, engagement and compromise,” he said.
“That is, first and foremost, the work of this Council.”
He said no mandate, budget or technology could replace political unity among council members.

Putin Transfers Nestlé, Auchan Stakes to $177 Moscow Firm With One Employee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:36:47 UTC
06:36:47 KST

- Category
- World
Putin Transfers Nestlé, Auchan Stakes to $177 Moscow Firm With One Employee
Russia placed the local businesses of Swiss food giant Nestle and French supermarket chain Auchan under temporary administration on September 17, explicitly linking the move to European military support for Ukraine.
Bloomberg reported the seizure on the same day, describing it as the largest takeover of foreign corporate assets inside Russia since at least 2024.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov grounded the decision in the two companies' European origins. "One of the factors taken into account when making this decision was that this is an unfriendly country," he told reporters on September 18, according to Bloomberg.
He added that the country involved ranked among those most actively engaged in military action against Russia.
The Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, issued the decree late on September 17, ordering stakes in the firms' Russian operations transferred to a company called AO L.E.V. Menedzhment, the outlet reported.
Registry data cited by Bloomberg showed the manager was registered in Moscow in 2024 with a charter capital of about $177 and a single employee, carrying little public profile before the order.
Nestle has operated in Russia since the 1990s, running six plants that employ more than 7,000 people, according to Bloomberg. Russia accounts for roughly 2% of the company's global sales, worth about $2.5 billion a year.
Auchan opened its first Russian store in 2002 and now runs 230 supermarkets and hypermarkets across the country, the report noted. Nestle shares fell as much as 1.9% on September 18, touching a three-month low before paring losses.
Nestle stated on September 18 that it had noted the decree and was weighing its options, Bloomberg reported. The company vowed to take "all necessary steps to protect its rights" and ensure continuity for its employees.
Auchan Retail Russia requested clarification of the order and pledged a fuller response once it obtained more information, the outlet added. The Swiss government was expected to comment later on September 18.
Russia has taken over dozens of foreign holdings since 2023, when it created a temporary management mechanism for assets tied to "unfriendly" countries, according to Bloomberg. The local units of Fortum, Danone, and Carlsberg were among them.
Danone and Carlsberg briefly recovered their assets before being forced to sell to Russian buyers at steep discounts. In August, Putin signed a law allowing courts to block departing foreign investors from buying back what they had sold.
The order extends a run of Kremlin seizures targeting Western firms that stayed in the country. 
In July, a decree placed the Russian operations of Dutch paint maker Akzo Nobel under a state-linked manager, following earlier takeovers of Danish insulation firm Rockwool and Polish-American packaging producer CanPack.
Days later, Reckitt, a British company, accepted a post-tax loss of about $232 million to offload its Russian hygiene unit under strict exit rules. That sale formed part of a wider exodus, with roughly 62% of Western firms holding major Russian assets having left since 2022.

How a New Trump Administration Rule Could Restrict Access to Green Cards—and Confront Immigrants With a Tough Choice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:35:45 UTC
06:35:45 KST

President Donald Trump’s Administration is rolling out a new rule that experts predict will make it more difficult for immigrants to get green cards if they access public assistance programs, such as Medicaid and food stamps—and could deter those hoping to obtain the status from enrolling in public benefits.
The rule, which goes into effect on Friday, updates a policy dating back to the 19th century that the U.S. has long used to prohibit immigrants who are believed to be likely to become a “public charge” from getting green cards.
Trump’s Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has argued that the change “is restoring the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves,” adding that it is “reaffirming the requirement of self-reliance, protecting public resources, and ending policies that encouraged dependency on hard-working American taxpayers.”
The rule marks the latest move in Trump’s efforts to sharply restrict both illegal and legal immigration. The President enacted a similar change during his first Administration, but the effort was subjected to court challenges and ultimately rescinded by his successor, Joe Biden.
The new rule has already been challenged in court by a coalition of more than a dozen states, including New York and California. It’s unclear at this point how the ongoing litigation will affect the rollout of the rule.
Here’s what to know about the new rule and how it could affect immigrants.
What is the “public charge” rule?
With its new policy, the Trump Administration is implementing a change to what’s known as the “public charge” rule, a policy first established under the Immigration Act of 1882. Since then, one factor that the U.S. government has considered when reviewing green card applications is whether the applicant is likely to become dependent on government assistance.
Historically, officials reviewing these types of applications have only taken into account cash benefit programs—for instance, Supplemental Security Income from Social Security—as “public benefits” that could lead to an immigrant being deemed a “public charge” and having their green card application denied. They have usually not deemed non-cash public benefits, such as Medicaid and food stamps, as programs that would disqualify an immigrant from obtaining permanent resident status.
During his first term in the White House, Trump tried to expand the programs that could result in an immigrant being deemed a “public charge,” but a federal judge ruled that the policy had to be vacated, saying it had “numerous unexplained flaws” that made it “arbitrary and capricious.”
When former President Joe Biden was in office, he officially rescinded Trump’s rule and stipulated that non-cash benefits would not result in an immigrant being considered a “public charge.”
How is the Trump Administration’s new policy different from the long-standing “public charge” rule?
In July, the Trump Administration revealed that it was revoking the Biden-era policy and was rolling out a change similar to the one that faced legal challeges during Trump’s first term. Under the new rule, officials reviewing green card applications are able to consider a broader scope of public benefit programs. The Trump Administration has noted that the new “public charge” rule does not apply to some immigrants—for instance, refugees.
The guidance, though, is vague—it doesn’t include a full list of the benefits that can be taken into consideration, saying only that immigration officers will be “using good judgment and discretion” and will be “making individualized, fact-specific public charge inadmissibility determinations, based on a totality of the alien’s circumstances.”
“Now, the officers who are reviewing and adjudicating these cases have much more discretion in how they make that determination—whether they believe the person is likely to become a public charge,” says Melissa Shepard, the legal services director at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center. “The difference now is that it’s a much broader analysis, whereas before it was a little more limited.”
Adriana Cadena, the executive director of the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition, says she worries that, because the new policy is so broad, it “opens the door for abuses by immigration officials” during the green card application process.
“It’s going from having guidance and clarity and understanding to opening the door to any kinds of programs,” she says.
How could the Trump Administration’s new rule affect immigrants?
Immigration experts say that the new policy could result in more green card applications being rejected, as well as cause many immigrants to delay seeking permanent resident status.
Charles Kuck, an immigration lawyer and former national president of the American immigration Lawyers Association, says that he expects there will be “massive numbers of denials” of green card applications as this new policy is rolled out. He adds that he and his colleagues have heard from some of their clients that they plan to wait until after Trump leaves the White House before filing their green card applications.
People who do not have permanent resident status in the U.S. are not eligible for many public assistance programs, but experts also warn that the new rule could result in immigrants disenrolling from public benefit programs that they or their children are eligible for because they are afraid of potentially harming their chances of obtaining a green card in the future.
Experts are additionally concerned that the Trump Administration’s new rule opens the door to immigration officials taking into account whether a green card applicant’s family member used a public benefit. The new rule stipulates that “if there is evidence in the record the alien’s family members whom the alien is legally obligated to support receive means-tested public benefits based on the alien’s income falling below the designated threshold, DHS would consider that fact.”
Kuck says he fears that this could lead to a situation where, for example, if a green card applicant’s child who is a U.S. citizen receives a public benefit, such as a free school lunch program, that could lead to their parent’s application being denied.
According to Shepard, it’s not yet clear how exactly the new policy will be applied in practice because it is so broad and gives immigration officers “so much discretion.” But she says she believes the change will cause people to be “a lot more cautious” and potentially fearful to access public assistance programs.
Cadena says the new rule is “forcing families to choose between either being able to adjust their status in the future or be able to have access to essential programs like food and child care.”
“In the current environment that we are in, where immigrant family safety is constantly being threatened, immigrant families … want to be able to keep their families together,” Cadena says. “And if keeping their child enrolled in an important program like Medicaid is going to threaten that, then they would more than likely disenroll their children from these programs.”
DHS has previously estimated that the rollout of the “public charge” change could lead to more than 950,000 people disenrolling from or choosing not to enroll in public assistance programs.
The change is the latest action the Trump Administration has taken to restrict immigration, including ramping up efforts to limit several legal pathways to immigration and proposing raising the fees associated with applying for citizenship.
“This is just one small factor or small piece of the entire immigration system, I think, that is under attack,” Shepard says.

Trump says son reimbursed Russian oligarch who funded wedding celebrations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:34:00 UTC
06:34:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sept. 18 that his son, Donald Trump Jr., told him he would reimburse Russian businessman Umar Kremlev after Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward celebrations surrounding Trump Jr.'s wedding earlier this year.
"When I heard the story, I asked him, and he said, 'I'm paying him back, Dad,' and that was a while ago," Trump told reporters. "With all of that being said, I understand that Don's paid him back."
The comments came days after investigative outlet ProPublica reported that Kremlev, a Russian businessman with close ties to President Vladimir Putin, covered hundreds of thousands of dollars in expenses connected to Trump Jr.'s wedding celebrations in the Bahamas in May. The reported expenses included renting a private island where guests stayed and a reception was held, as well as a fireworks display.
Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Trump, subsequently acknowledged Kremlev's role in the celebrations. In a statement posted to Instagram, they said Kremlev, whom they described as a friend, had hosted two nights of festivities after their private wedding as a gift. They rejected suggestions that the arrangement had a political motive.
Kremlev has headed the International Boxing Association (IBA) since 2020 and has developed close ties with the Kremlin. Putin awarded him Russia's Order of Friendship earlier this year, and Kremlev traveled to China as part of a Russian business delegation during a visit by Putin shortly before the wedding celebrations.
Under Kremlev, the IBA received major financial backing from Russian state-owned energy company Gazprom, which became the organization's general partner in 2021. The sponsorship agreement expired at the end of 2022.
The International Olympic Committee withdrew its recognition of the IBA in 2023 after years of disputes over the organization's governance, finances, and sporting integrity.
Ukraine has also imposed sanctions on Kremlev. Ukrainian authorities have targeted a number of Russian figures over their support for Moscow and links to the Russian state since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.
The revelations have also prompted scrutiny in Congress. Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, opened an investigation into Trump Jr.'s relationship with Kremlev and requested records related to the payments, saying they raised national security and public corruption concerns.
After the ProPublica report was published, Trump said in a White House statement that he had "no idea who Umar is" and had "never heard of him."

US President Donald Trump said Friday that his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week will include “a lot of different deals,” adding that the two leaders will have a "very good meeting."
“President Xi and I have a good relationship,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’re going to have a lot of different deals here ... We’re going to have a very good meeting.”

Trump also said that the US and China carry out espionage against each other.
“Somebody said: ‘Oh, they spy on us.’ And I said: ‘Maybe they do, but we spy on them, too’,” he explained, adding that he would not disclose classified information.

Saudi civil defense authorities issued emergency alerts Friday in seven areas, warning residents of an unspecified threat and urging them to follow instructions sent through the national early warning platform.

Why the Outcome of Russia's First Parliamentary Elections in Years Is All But Assured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:18:06 UTC
06:18:06 KST

Russia is just one day into three-day elections that will determine the makeup of the lower house of the country’s parliament, the State Duma. But the outcome of the vote has been all but guaranteed since before the first ballots were cast.
The elections, the first parliamentary vote the country has held since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, are widely expected to result in the Kremlin-aligned United Russia party maintaining its overwhelming dominance in the Duma.
The party currently holds 310 of the 450 seats in the chamber, giving it a supermajority and the power to make major legislative decisions without the input of other parties. It needs to keep at least 300 seats to retain that supermajority.
Four other political parties are also expected to be represented in the Duma following the election, all of which generally vote in line with United Russia and support the war in Ukraine. They are the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia, the A Just Russia party, and the New People party.
Democracy watchdogs and foreign governments have denounced Russia’s elections as being neither free nor fair. Russian officials have rejected such claims in the past, saying that the country carries out its voting process in line with the law.
But experts tell TIME that the Russian government exerts its influence in ways that all but predetermine the results of elections and ensure that President Vladimir Putin and United Russia maintain control.
And this year’s vote, says David Szakonyi, an expert on Russia and election fraud who is professor at George Washington University, is “occurring in the most repressive political environment in Russia's post-Soviet history.”
Here's what experts have to say about how the Kremlin ensures elections result in its desired outcome—and why it continues to hold them.
Restricting opposition
The Kremlin uses multiple levers to influence elections on the government level, at the polls, and in daily civilian life, according to Szakonyi.
“Without a doubt, the most powerful tool” in the Kremlin’s arsenal, Szakonyi says, is limiting which candidates appear on the ballot in the first place.
In the case of the ongoing parliamentary vote, the one anti-war party that was registered by the Central Election Commission, the Yabloko party, was prohibited from participating in the election by Russia’s Supreme Court. The high court ordered that the party be removed from the ballot last month in response to a lawsuit from the pro-Kremlin Rodina party that accused the Yabloko party, which has garnered support from young Russians and those opposed to the war in Ukraine, of copyright infringement, receiving foreign funding, and extremism.
Szakoni says that the Kremlin has the ability to “harness the judicial system to pass rulings” such as the Supreme Court’s decision against the Yabloko party, which it uses as a “legal veneer” that shields the influence of Putin’s government over the ballot.
This screening of anti-war and other opposition parties, he says, comes months in advance of elections, creating a list of candidates that includes little or no meaningful opposition at all.
The Kremlin has also labeled opposition figures who oppose the war as “foreign agents,” a designation that prevents them from holding public office. In other instances, opposition leaders and activists such as Alexei Navalny have been prosecuted and imprisoned. Still others have fled the country.
The vote count
Experts tell TIME that the Russian government has also exercised its influence more directly on vote counts to achieve its desired election results.
“Historically,” Szakonyi says, Russian electoral officials have “intervened regularly to deliver votes to the ruling party and take them away from competitors.”
In the past, this was done via “crude ballot box stuffing,” he says; now, he asserts it is also performed by altering the results of online votes.
Online voting is used in more than a third of Russia’s regions, which Szakonyi asserts puts more power in the government’s hands since it eliminates the physical tally represented by paper ballots.
“The way that the electronic votes are being counted is almost completely a black box for the rest of society,” he says.
Regina Smyth, an expert on Russia and authoritarian regimes who is a professor at Indiana University, says that “falsification,” or the practice of altering the number of votes that are counted, occurs at precinct election commissions, of which there are over 90,000, all across Russia, that she says are “mostly staffed by loyalists, and they will simply report false numbers.”
There is also fraud, Smyth alleges, in “mobile voting,” when officials deliver and pick up ballots from people in their homes who are, for example, disabled or ill and unable to vote otherwise.
‘Implicit threat’
On a deeper level, an “implicit threat” stemming from the Russian government sways countless votes each election cycle, Szakonyi contends.
“Many Russian voters do not have the autonomy to cast an independent vote. They work for the state,” he says. He argues that many university students, healthcare workers, and teachers, whose livelihoods depend on state-run organizations, belong to a “block of captive, vulnerable voters” who fear prosecution by the Kremlin more than they value the influence of their ballot.
Voting is also taking place this year in Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine: in Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014, and in the Luhansk, Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
“In the occupied territories of Ukraine, where the elections are being held in these illegally occupied territories, soldiers, heavily armed soldiers, travel from house to house coercing people to vote,” Smyth tells TIME.
A lack of independent election oversight
On top of the various methods the Kremlin allegedly uses to achieve the voting results it wants, there are slim to no oversight mechanisms in place to document election interference in the country.
Golos, which was the only independent election watchdog within Russia, shuttered in 2025 following years of governmental pressure after its chairman was found guilty of working with an "undesirable organization" and imprisoned in a penal colony.
Szakonyi describes Golos’ loss as the “biggest blow toward any type of accountability” for the Kremlin, saying it was “the biggest tool that civil society had to identify, uncover, and publicize the fraud that was basically happening in every single electoral cycle.”
Russia has also refused to invite international election monitors from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), the world’s largest regional security organization, to observe this year’s elections.
Maria Telalian, director of the OSCE’s election-monitoring office, the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, said in a statement last month that the decision not to invite any OSCE monitors was “deeply regrettable, particularly as it continues a pattern of not implementing the commitments that every OSCE participating State has undertaken towards its own citizens and the international community.”
The ongoing vote marks the third nationwide election in Russia to take place without OSCE observation. Russia previously imposed severe limits on OSCE election observation in 2021 that the organization said made monitoring that year’s parliamentary elections in the country impossible. It did not invite the group’s monitors to the 2024 presidential election at all.
So why is Russia holding elections at all?
Despite the results of the parliamentary elections being all but determined, they carry a symbolic weight crucial to Putin’s legitimacy in the public eye and his desire to continue the war against Ukraine, experts tell TIME.
“There's lots of reasons to have elections. First and foremost, the Russian population expects elections,” Szakonyi says. “Putin's legitimacy depends on his ability to win election votes to the presidency and have his ruling party win on a regular interval, and demonstrate that they're popular and that their policies are in demand from the citizenry.”
During an address in which Putin urged Russians to vote days before the elections began, the leader said that “your choice and resolve will show once again that millions of people stand behind our fighters” and that “participating in the elections is our shared contribution to Russia’s victory.”
“This is a way for him to theoretically show that the Russian population is united behind his war and wants to continue fighting, and that Russia has had this referendum and will continue to push harder,” Szakonyi says.

US military estimates Iran war cost at $43.6 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:07:35 UTC
06:07:35 KST

Breadcrumb
US military estimates Iran war cost at $43.6 billion
The US military's price tag for the Iran war has grown to $43.6 billion as of 3 September, according to a new estimate provided this week to lawmakers.
The figure from US Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched by the United States and Israel on 28 February.
A Congressional Budget Office report released Tuesday said the war had cost $38 billion through 1 August and will continue to rack up expenses of around $3 billion a month depending on the conflict's intensity.
The new breakdown, seen by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Punchbowl News, also showed the continued use of expensive munitions by American forces.
Weapons costs jumped by more than $6 billion in just over a month, from $21.7 billion listed in the CBO report to $28.1 billion in US Central Command’s estimate.
The financial cost is just one measure of the impact of the Iran war, which also is affecting oil prices and the stock market and has led to deaths and injuries of American troops.
The political costs will be calculated in November's midterm congressional elections, with Republicans facing increasing headwinds from the war's unpopularity.
The US military's one-page breakdown to Congress includes costs for operating warships, planes and bases as well as for equipment losses and medical support for troops.
Casualties tallied by the Pentagon have included 18 dead and more than 830 wounded, according to the Defense Casualty Analysis System.
The report does not include damage to US bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released Monday said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
In the new report to Congress, the figure for munitions was by far the largest, constituting well over half of all costs. The advanced weapons that have been in the most demand are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army's Patriot and THAAD systems.
The diminished stockpiles also have caused alarm in Europe, where U.S. and NATO officials have told the AP that there is a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors.
Saudi Arabia also is running low on interceptors and has turned to regional and Western allies for assistance as its standoff with Houthi rebels in Yemen drags on.
(The Associated Press)

Where thinking beats mugging up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:06:54 UTC
06:06:54 KST

(Top row, R-L): AM/NS India CSR head Vikas Yadvendu, Uttar Pradesh deputy CM Brajesh Pathak, Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka, and DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar with some of the winners of Times Critical Thinking Championship in Delhi
(Top row, R-L): AM/NS India CSR head Vikas Yadvendu, Uttar Pradesh deputy CM Brajesh Pathak, Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka, and DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar with some of the winners of Times Critical Thinking Championship in Delhi
(Top row, R-L): AM/NS India CSR head Vikas Yadvendu, Uttar Pradesh deputy CM Brajesh Pathak, Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka, and DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar with some of the winners of Times Critical Thinking Championship in Delhi
NEW DELHI: Hands hovered over buzzers as students listened intently to each question, ready to hit the button before their competitors. Every few moments, a buzzer broke the silence and another answer was put to the test. But points were not won through recall alone, as the questions pushed students to reason, judge, analyse and think beyond the obvious.The questions came thick and fast. "If a meteor crashes on the Moon and an astronaut is 1,000km away, when will they hear the sound?" A student quickly buzzed in with the answer: they wouldn't - sound cannot travel through the vacuum of space.Then came a word puzzle: "Which word becomes shorter when you add two letters to it?" Buzzers went off again. The answer was "short" - add "er" and it becomes "shorter".That was the scene at the auditorium of DPS RK Puram on Friday as students went head to head in the semi-final and final rounds of the AM/NS India Times Critical Thinking Championship 2026, conceived and conducted by Times Foundation. The Nav Ratna prize distribution ceremony was held soon after, during which chief guest Brajesh Pathak, deputy chief minister of Uttar Pradesh, handed over certificates to the winners.
Pathak, who spoke of the "immense effort" involved in reaching so many schools and students, urged participants to never stop asking questions. "Human beings are not machines meant to follow the same routine. We have the ability to think, understand and show the world a new direction," he said.The championship has been designed to encourage students to move beyond rote memorisation and develop the ability to question, analyse information and arrive at conclusions independently. The students who reached Friday's rounds had already made their way through a much larger field. From thousands of participants, 140 were shortlisted for written and oral assessments. The field was then narrowed to 36 students for the buzzer rounds, with nine winners emerging. The gathering included their parents, DPS teachers and other representatives."Critical thinking is very important for the younger generation because students need to learn to ask questions, reason and analyse before reaching conclusions. We see this initiative not as a one-off event but as a long-term process," said Vikas Yadvendu, head, CSR, AM/NS India.Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka said, "Critical thinking is the need of the hour. With young people exposed to so much information through social media, they can sometimes lose sight of their own judgement or be misled. So, such initiatives are important."DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar said, "This initiative encourages children to think, reason and analyse. Over 10 lakh students have participated across languages, and next year, we aim to reach one crore."Over the past six months, TCTC reached more than one million students from over 20,000 schools, spanning Grades III to XII across 28 states and eight Union Territories, with the programme conducted in 14 languages.
But amid those numbers were students from different corners of the country, each with their own interpretation of what it meant to think critically.Bhanvi, a Class V student from Kerala, summed it up simply: "Critical thinking is not agreeing with something just because everyone thinks it is right. Don't always listen to others. Use your own mind." Aaryahi Hazarika, a Class IV student from Assam, said it helped people find solutions carefully, while Sarah from Kashmir described it as the ability to "think out of the box". Divisha, a Class IV student of DPS East of Kailash, described it as "finding solutions by thinking with our own minds" rather than blindly following others.
Meghna Dhulia is an Assistant News Editor at The Times of India, bringing over a decade of experience in journalism. She specialises in education reporting, covering both foundational and higher education with a clear, insightful lens. Her work sheds light on critical issues shaping the future—ranging from policy impact and systemic challenges to compelling human stories from the field. Her experience also extends to the news desk, where she has overseen editorial workflows, ensuring readers receive balanced, reliable and impactful news.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story Has Nothing New to Say About Female Rage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:06:45 UTC
06:06:45 KST

This article discusses the full season of Netflix’s Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story
Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story is about female rage and repression. That isn’t my personal interpretation of the latest installment of Ian Brennan and Ryan Murphy’s Netflix true-crime anthology. It’s the talking point that the show’s makers have been leading with, in publicity materials and in multiple interviews. These are fine themes for the first season of Monster with a female subject, even if they’re not exactly unique within a post-Big-Little-Lies, #MeToo-informed TV landscape where so many dramas aimed at women double as amplifiers for gendered frustrations. The well of misogyny isn’t in danger of running dry anytime soon. But if we must keep diving into it, each descent should at least leave us with some new insight or nuance.
Lizzie Borden, now streaming, fails to clear even that bar. Perhaps the least historically accurate Monster yet—and that’s saying something—the season uses the infamous tale of a Fall River, Mass. woman who probably hacked her wealthy father and stepmother to death with an axe in 1892 as a conduit to just about every plague on womankind you can imagine, past, present, and perennial. Rape. Domestic violence. Pregnancy and childbirth. Housework. Menstrual maladies. Pressure to marry. The premium put on physical beauty. The perils of sex work. Confinement in the home and subjugation to male relatives. By tying together Lizzie’s story with the legends of supposed forerunner Elizabeth Báthory and descendent Aileen Wuornos, Brennan, who wrote every episode, suggests a simplistic kinship between all female killers.
There’s no use fretting over the extremely purposeful anachronisms and inaccuracies in this retelling, which plays as fast and loose with the Borden family as that classic nursery rhyme. With 26-year-old Ella Beatty starring as a dreamy, blank-screen Lizzie, who ages from 32 to her 60s by the end of the season, and Charlie Hunnam and Rebecca Hall cast as parents who were really a couple of decades the actors’ seniors, everyone is much younger and prettier than their real-life counterparts. And more shocking, in some ways, than the hyperspeed double murder reenactment that opens the premiere, is what immediately follows it: a flashback to four months earlier, when Lizzie scares off a suitor by passing a bucket of menstrual blood on the white sofa where they’re sitting. As it turns out, what the fictionalized Bordens refer to as her “lady time” had some relevance to the actual case. But Lizzie Borden is such a massive remix, mingling facts with half-truths and rumors and fabrications, it barely matters which detail is which.
Because its source material is not especially extensive—one double homicide, as opposed to the lengthy and lurid sagas of most past Monster subjects—the show is forced to stretch. The series is padded with Fall River horror scenes that either never happened (the oyster poisoning that leads to so much operatic barfing) or didn’t transpire remotely the way they’re shown (the murder of Bertha Manchester, played by Linda Reiter). Brennan also adds queer love to Lizzie’s life, in the form of the family’s maid, Bridget Sullivan, who they really did call Maggie, after a former servant. He is far from the first to investigate this angle; the 2018 film Lizzie, to take just one example, is also built around a romance, between Chloë Sevigny’s Lizzie and Kristen Stewart’s Bridget.
Monster is, however, the first dramatization to make such imaginative use of the character. Phantom Thread breakout Vicky Krieps, who played ‘Bitch of Buchenwald’ Ilse Koch in Monster’s Ed Gein season, is a conspicuously Germanic Irish maid, with an ahistorical shag haircut dyed a series of shades reminiscent of, by turns, Wuornos and Ziggy Stardust. She has picked up skills in everything from cooking and cleaning to pharmacology in the course of her global travels. It’s no mystery why the awkward, sheltered Lizzie, who craves a bigger life, is enchanted by this glamorous, androgynous outsider. Maggie is easily the best part of the season, thanks in no small part to Krieps’ at once humane and otherworldly performance.
She’s also the unstuck-in-time character who first connects Lizzie to murderesses from other eras. As Maggie reads from a French book about Báthory, a 16th century Hungarian noblewoman said to have killed hundreds of young women and bathed in their blood in pursuit of eternal youth, we see Krieps—with hair and makeup straight out of the goth club—as the so-called Blood Countess. The Runaways’ anthem of teen-girl rebellion “Cherry Bomb” blares. And Lizzie is electrified by the story. She feels a kinship with Báthory. Never mind that killing your cruel parents to free yourself and massacring a village’s worth of peasant girls because La Mer has yet to be invented are about as different as murder motives get. The fact that each woman is acting in response to some form of sexism is, I guess, supposed to bridge that gulf.
It takes almost half the season for the third member of the deadly trio, played by Murphyverse MVP Sarah Paulson, to show up. Often framed as America’s first female serial killer, Wuornos, a Florida sex worker who killed seven johns between 1989 and 1990, is, in this telling, as inspired by Lizzie as Lizzie is by Báthory. Her presence, and her unsuccessful attempt to claim in court that she acted in self-defense against rape, allows the show to take on—and force us to watch—sexual violence. I’m not sure it needed to be shoehorned into the rare true-crime drama where it doesn’t have an obvious place. Brennan also connects Aileen’s well-documented queerness with the speculative relationship between Lizzie and Maggie. On a pilgrimage to the Borden home, now a bed and breakfast, Aileen and her girlfriend (Jessie Lee) have public sex. A fantasy sequence has the two couples dancing side-by-side in Lizzie’s sacred garden shed. But it’s never clear what Monster is trying to say about lesbians and murder, and this is a case where ambiguity leaves space to insert some pretty dark assumptions.
The outcomes for each of the three female killers are as different as their motivations. Lizzie is acquitted and buys a mansion with her inheritance, presumably because sexist men can’t conceive of a woman committing such physical murders—and because she learns to correctly perform femininity, crying and fainting at appropriate moments, during the trial. Despite wrenching testimony, coarse, unfeminine Aileen is convicted and executed. This might lead you to conclude that privilege and falling in line with patriarchal expectations are what it takes for a woman to get away with murder. But then there’s the rich, powerful, and apparently quite appearance-obsessed Báthory. Our last glimpse of the countess is as a rotting corpse, bricked up in her castle for her sins. So what is really being said here?
Not much, as far as I can tell. Lizzie Borden certainly makes a strong case that women have always been repressed, that rage is the obvious product of that repression, and that liberation is the only antidote. (Of course we get a scene in the finale where Lizzie celebrates suffrage.) But if you didn’t know that, it’s probably also news to you that water is wet and the pope is Catholic. The show’s obsession with women’s bodies as the sites of unending horrors reminds me of House of the Dragon’s repeated depictions of traumatic childbirth. It’s as though viewers are expected to go in completely ignorant of basic hardships afflicting half the human population and must see them reproduced over and over again in gory detail to be enlightened, much less empathetic. And in that case, I suppose it’s also necessary to render interchangeable three notorious women defined by actions rooted in a near-universal form of rage.
But theirs are old stories, already told and retold in every conceivable media, and often, effectively, by women. Wuornos was, of course, most famously portrayed by Charlize Theron, in writer-director Patty Jenkins’ career-making, Oscar-winning 2003 film also titled Monster. Isabelle Huppert stars as Báthory in The Blood Countess, a new feature by German experimental cinema legend Ulrike Ottinger, which is earning praise on the festival circuit for its strangeness and sense of humor. Meanwhile, on TV, creator Liz Meriwether just gave us Furious—another story of female rage, female repression, and yes, even a (fictional) female serial killer. While Krieps is mesmerizing in Monster and frequent Murphy production designer Matthew Flood Ferguson has outdone himself with lavishly suffocating Gilded Age interiors, Furious is the superior show because it takes “being a woman is hard” as the given it is rather than as the endpoint of many repetitive episodes. It has dark, lived-in comedy and real stakes, posing the question of what can realistically be done about systemic misogyny and the anger over it that stains women’s lives.
“All your books are written by men,” Maggie scolds Lizzie in Monster’s season premiere. When you consider how heavily male the creative team behind Lizzie Borden is (executive producer Max Winkler directed six episodes and Sarah Adina Smith, two), this kind of has to be a self-aware line. But whether it’s intended as a wry apology or a small joke, I couldn’t tell you.

Farmers warn of food security impact from visa changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:06:38 UTC
06:06:38 KST

Farmers fear Working Holiday Maker visa changes will cause worker shortages and food insecurity
In short:
The federal government has outlined an overhaul of the Working Holiday Maker visa system, capping the number of renewed applications after one year in the country.
The agricultural industry warns this could limit production and negatively impact Australia's food security.
Farmers fear the changes could lead to worker shortages during peak harvest seasons.
Agricultural industries warn changes to working holiday visa migration policy could threaten crops and Australia's food security.
On Thursday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke outlined Labor's migration policy, including an overhaul of the Working Holiday Maker visa system.
Farmers are coming into the Christmas harvest of popular fruits such as mangoes, lychees, berries and cherries, as well as the summer grain season.
While the industry is concerned they will not be able to find enough workers to pick crops to get them to market, the "one bright light" is that agriculture will be added to the skilled worker visa list.
Less incentive to go bush
Across the country, agriculture employs more than 250,000 workers each year according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Figures from the 2021 census showed people from cultural and linguistically diverse backgrounds made up 13 per cent of the agricultural workforce.
Backpackers on Working Holiday Maker visas wanting to stay for another year need to work 88 days in regional or remote parts of Australia.
Under the changes, visa holders would also have to enter a ballot, with the number of places capped at 45,000 — down from the 57,000 who qualified this year.
The number of places will be capped further to 5,000 for those seeking a third year, down from 31,000 this year.
Queensland Farmers' Federation chief executive Kylie Porter feared a lottery-type system would not be attractive to visa holders.
"What we're doing is we're placing at risk Australia's food security over an issue which could be resolved in a way that's far more amenable to those regional and rural communities across Australia," she said.
"Christmas harvest periods are intense, and we absolutely rely on that workforce to be able to complete those harvests."
Kaya Barry is a senior lecturer at Griffith University who received an Australian Research Council fellowship to explore the contributions of seasonal migrants in Queensland's agricultural industry.
Dr Barry said larger farms secured most of their workers through the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme and Labor's policy change would have a greater impact on smaller operations.
"For smaller farms, particularly the family-run stuff … they can't guarantee the seasonal work is there year-round, and that's where the backpackers have filled those shortages," she said.
Dr Barry said PALM workers would not be able to replace backpacker labour on farms.
"It's really important to have highly mobile workers who are willing to just come and do two or three weeks and then move on to the next place and follow that harvest trail around the country," she said.
Dr Barry said it was also not feasible to rely on an Australian workforce.
"We don't have enough people living in regional and rural Australia to do all that work."
Industry needs workers now
Prior to Labor's policy announcement, the federal government had paused working holiday visa applications coming from 24 out of 29 countries.
Mr Burke said the time frame for processing these visas would now take three months; previously, it had taken days.
Head of Citrus Australia, Nathan Hancock, said the current backlog of processing applications is putting pressure on all industries.
"People have been waiting three to four months for their applications to be approved. In many of these industries, harvest is about to start in two weeks," he said.
"This just creates more angst and more concern for all of those industries that would normally rely on workers at this time."
With berry harvest underway in New South Wales and gearing up in Victoria and Tasmania, Berries Australia CEO Rachel Mackenzie warned workforce shortages could lead to wasted crops.
"You may have periods where you need quite a lot more workers than other periods … we need those backpackers to assist with surge capacity and be a complement to the existing PALM workers," she said.
"For some growers [fewer workers] might mean that they have to finish their season early, it may mean that they can't get their crops picked in time."
'One bright light'
The industry has welcomed the addition of agriculture to the skilled worker visa, with Mr Hancock calling it the "one bright light in all of this".
"It is positive to see that agriculture will be added to the [skilled worker] visa," he said.
But Mr Hancock is calling for more clarity on these changes, including specifically which types of workers will be added to the skilled worker visa.
"Hopefully that does, in my case, go down to horticulture … fingers crossed."

Germany receives first F-35 jet from US as NATO boosts military spending
Germany received the first of nearly three dozen F-35 stealth warplanes it ordered four years ago from Lockheed Martin.
Germany has received its first F-35A Lightning II fighter jet, as the country accelerates a major military buildup and increases defence spending amid a broader push by European NATO members to strengthen their armed forces.
The delivery on Friday is part of Germany’s effort to fulfil NATO nuclear-sharing duties and modernise its military after decades of relatively low defence spending.
Lockheed Martin formally presented the aircraft to the German government during a ceremony at its production facility in Fort Worth, Texas, attended by German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius.
“This is the beginning of a new era for the German Air Force: the new F-35A fighter jet is the world’s most advanced combat aircraft,” Pistorius said in a statement. “It is characterised by its stealth capabilities, close integration with other platforms, and exceptionally powerful sensor technology.”
Germany ordered 35 F-35As in 2022, the year Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. The aircraft are intended to replace Germany’s ageing Tornado fleet.
The Trump administration has long pressured Europe to spend more on defence, allowing Washington to focus on other challenges such as countering China.
European countries, including Germany, are ramping up military budgets as a result, agreeing in 2025 to Trump’s demand to devote five percent of GDP to security-related spending by 2035.

Zelensky’s endgame, Houthi dominance, German decline: RT stories that shaped the week

Zelensky’s endgame, Houthi dominance, German decline: RT stories that shaped the week
Zelensky’s state of corruption devours itself
In what’s become a recurring moment in Ukraine, another one of Vladimir Zelensky’s top officials fled the country this week amid a metastasizing corruption scandal. Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, who resigned last week after Ukraine’s Western-backed anti-corruption agencies discovered his cybercrime chief was running a protection racket for scam call centers, left Ukraine on Sunday night bound for Paris, according to Ukrainian media.
Kravchenko, who was personally appointed by Zelensky, has denied any wrongdoing, and accused the anti-corruption agencies, NABU and SAPO, of operating bribery and protection schemes of their own. He claims he’s got evidence of “concentration of undue influence” within the agencies, which he plans to show to Zelensky’s Western sponsors.
Whether or not they’ll listen is another story. Yulia Mendel, a former communications aide to Zelensky, has spoken out about the mire of corruption in Kiev for months, to no avail. Mendel was scheduled to speak at the European Parliament on Wednesday, at an event promoting “diplomacy instead of escalation,” but found herself barred from the building upon arrival, days after Zelensky personally sanctioned her.

Merz nears his end
With his officials falling one by one to corruption scandals and his political rivals smelling blood in the water, Zelensky likely senses his endgame playing out, Russian foreign policy expert Alexander Bobrov wrote for RT on Tuesday. If there’s anyone who knows the feeling, it’s German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Merz canceled his planned trip to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, after his Christian Democrats’ humiliating loss to the right-wing AfD in state elections earlier this month, Reuters reported on Tuesday. The chancellor’s approval rating has plummeted to 10%, and half of the German public expects him out of office by the year’s end.
Merz has made steep and unpopular welfare cuts to finance Germany’s ambitious rearmament program, as the country’s economy continues to flatline – thanks largely to Berlin’s self-imposed embargo on Russian oil and gas imports. All of this has played into the hands of the AfD, which has promised an end to “all war-prolonging support measures” for Ukraine, and the deportation of Ukrainian migrants.
Merz’s Christian Democrats are on track for another wipeout in state elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin this weekend. By Sunday night, the chancellor’s departure could be a done deal.
Total Houthi dominance
Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, better known as the Houthis, scored some major tactical and strategic victories this week. After a lightning advance along the country’s Red Sea coast last week, the group launched missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia’s main oil port of Yanbu, and the Saudi airbase of Khamis Mushait.
The effects of the Houthi campaign were immediately visible at the petrol pumps in Europe. With Saudi Arabia cutting exports, the Houthis have asserted their position as arbiters of global fuel prices. US President Donald Trump reportedly refused to intervene on behalf of his Saudi allies, meaning the Houthis have forced Riyadh into a lose-lose choice: admit defeat so oil flows can resume, or keep fighting and bear responsibility for a global energy crisis.
In a further humiliation for the Kingdom, the Houthis claimed on Wednesday to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet using “a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile.” The group claimed three shootdowns of Saudi jets in 2017 and 2018, but Wednesday’s victory was the first backed by video footage.
War crimes sentence for the West’s Kosovo proxy
As the Saudis desperately search for allies against the Houthis, former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) commander Hashim Thaci learned first-hand where an alliance with the West leads: to a prison cell.
Thaci was advised and armed by NATO during the KLA’s brutal secession campaign against Yugoslavia in the 1990s, a campaign that led to NATO bombing Belgrade for 78 days on behalf of the ethnic Albanian militia. Despite serving as prime minister, then president, of the self-proclaimed nation of Kosovo with the West’s blessing, Thaci’s past caught up with him on Wednesday when a war crimes tribunal in The Hague sentenced him to 25 years behind bars for the murder of 96 political opponents and the kidnapping and torture of hundreds of others.
Thaci was defended in court by some of his former NATO backers, and scores of Albanians rioted on the streets of The Hague when the verdict was handed down.
RT explored the case against Thaci in detail back in February, and examined just how far NATO and the Atlanticist institutions in The Hague would go to protect him. As it turned out, Thaci should have listened when Henry Kissinger warned: “It may be dangerous to be America’s enemy, but to be America’s friend is fatal.”

Piddington’s case for secession is no less watertight than Kosovo’s. Let’s see if NATO sends in the bombers…
NATO 3.0 marches towards war
Joking aside, NATO evidently has its hands full these days preparing for a cataclysmic war with Russia. The bloc’s Military Committee – tasked with turning political statements into war-gamed plans – met in Copenhagen on Friday, with talks scheduled to run until Saturday afternoon.
RT looked at the ‘NATO 3.0’ doctrine taking shape at the meeting. Under this one-sided rebalancing of the bloc, Europe assumes the cost and risk of NATO’s looming confrontation with Russia, while the US insulates itself from the consequences. Russia has given the Europeans ample warning, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stating this week that “if Europe, which talks daily about preparing for war against Russia, attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short.”
This hasn’t stopped the French and the Germans preparing hospitals and filling blood banks for a “mass casualty” clash in eastern Europe. The Poles and the Baltic states are eagerly going along with these preparations, despite standing to lose the most. Slovakia’s Robert Fico, however, isn’t marching in lockstep with his neighbors.
“I am deeply concerned that they are merely looking for a pretext for a major conflict between NATO and Russia,” he said on Thursday, before skipping a meeting with Zelensky in Kiev. “The situation has never been as serious and tense regarding the possibility of a pan-European war conflict as it is now.”
What to watch out for
We’ll be watching what – if anything – concrete emerges from NATO’s Copenhagen meeting on Saturday, before switching our attention to Germany where another AfD landslide could deal a death blow to Merz’s chancellorship.
You will find up-to-date reporting on the results of Russia’s Duma elections once exit polls are released on Sunday, with a concrete picture emerging overnight and into Monday.
Across the Atlantic, the NYPD are already preparing to shut down roads as world leaders descend on New York for the 81st UN General Assembly. The assembly kicks off on Tuesday, and we expect the conflicts in Europe and the Middle East will top the agenda.
Watch out for Trump’s opening speech on Tuesday, followed by Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Zelensky on Wednesday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will deliver his address on Thursday, with Lavrov taking the lectern on Saturday.

US military puts Iran war cost at $43.6B in latest estimate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:00:37 UTC
06:00:37 KST

The US military's price tag for the war on Iran has grown to $43.6 billion as of September 3, according to a new estimate provided this week to lawmakers.
The figure from US Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched by the United States and Israel on February 28.
A Congressional Budget Office report released on Tuesday said the war had cost $38 billion through August 1 and will continue to rack up expenses of around $3 billion a month depending on the conflict's intensity.
The new breakdown on Friday, seen by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Punchbowl News, also showed the continued use of expensive munitions by American forces.
Weapons costs jumped by more than $6 billion in just over a month, from $21.7 billion listed in the CBO report to $28.1 billion in US Central Command’s estimate.
The financial cost is just one measure of the impact of the Iran war, which also is affecting oil prices and the stock market and has led to deaths and injuries of American troops.
Death toll and midterms
The political costs will be calculated in November's midterm congressional elections, with Republicans facing increasing headwinds from the war's unpopularity.
The US military's one-page breakdown to Congress includes costs for operating warships, planes and bases as well as for equipment losses and medical support for troops.
Casualties tallied by the Pentagon have included 18 dead and more than 830 wounded, according to the Defense Casualty Analysis System.
The report does not include damage to US bases in the Middle East, which Tehran has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones.
A report from the Pentagon inspector general released on Monday said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
In the new report to Congress, the figure for munitions was by far the largest, constituting well over half of all costs.
The advanced weapons that have been in the most demand are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army's Patriot and THAAD systems.
The diminished stockpiles also have caused alarm in Europe, where US and NATO officials have told the AP that there is a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors.

US Treasury’s Bessent plans to discuss AI and rare earths with China’s He, source says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:59:25 UTC
05:59:25 KST

US Treasury’s Bessent plans to discuss AI and rare earths with China’s He, source says
WASHINGTON - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent plans to discuss AI, trade, rare earths and economic issues when he meets with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York City this weekend, according to a source familiar with his plans.
The discussions are significant because the US and China are the two major forces driving development of advanced AI tools and the global adoption of the technology. Rare earths play a crucial role in the manufacturing of technology.
Bessent and He will meet ahead of a summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept 24 in Washington.
The Associated Press first reported the US plans.
Bessent said in a statement that he expects the discussions to cover “both open- and closed-weight models.” Open-weight models are AI systems with publicly accessible core elements. Users can download and fine-tune them for specific tasks.
Chinese open-weight models are becoming more popular with US companies because they can be cheaper than so-called closed-weight AI tools, such as those developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and other US companies.
Chinese AI models have even been used by the US government. Reuters reported on Sept 17 that a US government website employed an AI model from a Chinese company to allow users to search proposed federal regulations even though the FBI accused the model’s developer, Alibaba, of “malicious” copying of Anthropic’s technology.
“The United States remains the leader in AI. And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems,” Bessent said in his statement regarding the China talks.
The Treasury secretary has recently called for the US and China to agree on AI “guardrails” aimed at keeping powerful models out of the hands of malign non-state actors.
Questioned on AI safety at a House of Representatives Financial Services Committee hearing on Sept 15, he said it was up to US AI firms to decide whether to slow down their development, but argued they should be held liable for what they build and generate as a safety measure.
Details about the meetings in New York, which are expected to explore possible areas for Trump and Xi to agree on, have been scant. The source said that the meetings could extend to Sept 21 on a technical or “working” level.
Other key topics for Bessent and He to discuss include potential extension of a tariff truce that expires on Nov 10, and improving flows of Chinese-produced rare-earth magnets and critical minerals that China had severely curtailed in 2025.
The truce capped tariffs imposed during Trump’s second term in office at about 20 per cent. The Supreme Court later struck down Trump’s tariffs invoked under a national emergencies law, but his administration has been rebuilding them under new authorities.
In May, China pledged to increase purchases of US agriculture products and at least 200 Boeing aircraft, but details on those transactions have yet to emerge. REUTERS

Venezuelan government, opposition continue 2nd round of US-backed dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:57:06 UTC
05:57:06 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Venezuela's government and opposition continued a second round of US-backed dialogue Friday, with political guarantees, freedom of expression, political prisoners, and judicial reform among the issues expected to be discussed.
“We are here with great responsibility to give the Venezuelan people a consolidation of a path toward democracy,” opposition negotiator Dinorah Figuera said ahead of the talks.
The meeting is being held at the Melia Caracas hotel, where the delegations began the second round Thursday. No statements to the media were scheduled during the talks.
The sides have not disclosed details of the discussions, but the opposition said the second phase would address civil and political guarantees and freedom of expression.
The first round ended with two agreements, including one focused on the renewal of Venezuela's Supreme Court.
The parties also agreed to seek the recovery of Venezuelan assets held at the Bank of England to assist victims of the earthquakes that struck the country in June.
Venezuela and the opposition are now close to an agreement on the transfer of about $4 billion in gold reserves held at the Bank of England to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, according to reports.
Figuera said earlier this week that the opposition delegation would continue discussions on the reinstitutionalization of the Supreme Court, including procedures for nominating new judges.
She also said the talks would address conditions for a future electoral process, while calling for the release of political prisoners.
The dialogue resumed after Venezuelan authorities announced the lifting of restrictions on several news websites, including local and international media outlets that had been blocked for years.
The opposition delegation does not include prominent opposition leaders Maria Corina Machado and Edmundo Gonzalez Urrutia.
The talks are being held under interim President Delcy Rodriguez following the capture of former President Nicolas Maduro in a US operation on Jan. 3.
