UK court clears woman of voicing support for Hamas in university speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:55:57 UTC
05:55:57 KST

UK court clears woman of voicing support for Hamas in university speech
Sarah Cotte said her comments were not in support of Hamas, but in support of Palestinians’ right to resist.
A London court has cleared a British woman of supporting Palestinian group Hamas in a speech she gave outside her university in 2023.
The jury at the Central Criminal Court, more commonly known as the Old Bailey, on Friday found Sarah Cotte, 22, not guilty of expressing support for the group that’s designated a “terrorist” organisation under UK law.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Andy Burnham apology for Labour stance on Gaza: Is UK’s position shifting?
- list 2 of 3The British state has recast protest as terrorism
- list 3 of 3UK charities, protest groups: Israeli ban threat ‘will not intimidate us’
Public prosecutors had alleged that Cotte voiced support for Hamas two days after the group led the deadly attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023.
During a speech she gave outside the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) in London at the time, she expressed “unconditional solidarity” with the Palestinian resistance, the court was told. Prosecutors claimed this was a “thinly veiled reference” to Hamas.
Cotte repeatedly rejected attempts to equate the two, telling the court: “I don’t support Hamas and I have never supported Hamas. I was supporting the right to resist.”
Speaking to Al Jazeera after the verdict on Friday, Cotte said the court’s decision was a “testament to how people are feeling about British support for Zionism”.
“I never condemned the right to armed struggle in Palestine,” Cotte said. “I didn’t let them corner me and make this a conversation about what Zionists want to talk about.”
Instead, she said, “I used it as a platform to talk about what I thought was important, which was the Palestinian struggle, British support for Zionism and our rights as people of conscience.”
Hamas was officially proscribed in its entirety by the UK government in late 2021, when its political wing was also banned. Its military wing, the Qassam Brigades, has been proscribed since 2001. Those found guilty of supporting such groups can face up to 14 years in prison.
On the final day of the week-long trial on Friday, Cotte again denied expressing support for Hamas during her speech at SOAS while she was a student there and argued that she had only expressed support for Palestinians’ “right to resist”.
“I think that the killing of civilians is always a tragedy. At the same time, I don’t think it is a surprise,” she told jurors about her comments regarding Hamas’s October 7 attack.
“I think saying it is understandable and agreeing with it is two different things, so I think it is understandable and could be justified,” she explained.
“I don’t think it’s my role to impose conditions on the Palestinian people and their struggle,” Cotte added.
In comments to Al Jazeera after the verdict, she said: “This victory will re-energise the whole of the solidarity movement … We stand with the Palestinian people and their right to be agents in their struggle for freedom.”
Responding to the not guilty verdict, Anas Mustapha, head of Public Advocacy at CAGE International, said the ruling showed that “ordinary people will not accept the criminalisation of speech in support of the Palestinian right to resist occupation.”
“Sarah Cotte has been found not guilty, and we are delighted for her, her family, and everyone who stood alongside her through more than two and a half years of investigation and court proceedings,” Mustapha said.
Cotte gave the speech on October 9, 2023. She was arrested over it on January 31, 2024. An earlier trial found her not guilty of a second charge of expressing support for Hamas in a WhatsApp group chat.

Putin says Russia needs to expand, update its aircraft fleet, airport infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:55:09 UTC
05:55:09 KST

Burc Eruygur
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Friday that his country needs to expand and update its aircraft fleet, as well as domestic airport infrastructure.
Speaking via videoconference at a signing ceremony for an agreement between Russian flag carrier Aeroflot and state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec for 90 MC-21 aircraft, Putin said projects to build new terminal buildings and upgrade airfield and border infrastructure have been successfully completed in several regions.
Putin said a developed aviation network is crucial for Russia to connect its territories and ensure accessibility to remote regions, including those in the Arctic, Siberia, and the Far East.
“Naturally, modern airports also provide a boost to regional economies, fostering growth in trade, business activity, and, of course, tourism. They also ensure higher service quality and faster passenger processing.
“With this in mind, we are systematically upgrading airport infrastructure,” Putin said, adding that 20 runways and 26 terminal complexes nationwide have been commissioned since 2021.
Putin further said that new terminals have been opened in a number of cities, including Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Khabarovsk, Magadan, Novosibirsk, and Cheboksary, stating this work is being carried out through a combination of state funding and private sector investment.
“We will continue to provide all necessary support to investors,” Putin went on to say, adding that at least 75 airports in the country are slated for modernization by 2030, or over a third of Russia’s entire airport network.
The president also underlined the need to expand and renew Russia’s aircraft fleet, describing the issue as one of “fundamental importance.”
He called the contract for supplying the 90 MC-21 aircraft to Aeroflot a “highly significant step in this direction,” saying that it will provide a substantial workload for aircraft manufacturers, as well as their suppliers and contractors.
“I expect the contract to be executed strictly in line with the established schedule, without delays or disruptions,” Putin added.
According to Rostec, the delivery of the 90 MC-21 aircraft to Aeroflot is scheduled for the years 2029-2032 and is the largest such contract in the history of Russian civil aviation.
"The agreement includes not only the delivery of the aircraft, but also flight simulators, training for pilots and ground personnel, as well as technical support for the aircraft," it noted.

US warns allies of weapons delivery delays due to stocks depleted by Iran war: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:53:09 UTC
05:53:09 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The US has warned its allies to expect delays of up to five years in deliveries of key weapons as Washington works to replenish munitions stocks depleted during its war with Iran, Bloomberg reported Friday.
Several European countries are facing delays in receiving missile and air defense systems, while Germany has asked Washington to accelerate deliveries of Tomahawk cruise missiles and Typhon launchers. However, shortages of the weapons mean Raytheon, a unit of the RTX Corp., may not be able to fulfill the order within five years, according to the report.
The shortages are also affecting Ukraine, which has sought additional Patriot air defense interceptors ahead of an expected difficult winter. President Donald Trump has said Washington was discussing either providing Ukraine with a less advanced version of the Patriot system or allowing European countries to manufacture the weapons under license.
In the conflict with Iran, now in its seventh month, the US is estimated to have used more than half of its advanced Patriot missile variants, about one-third of its Tomahawk missiles, and nearly half of its precision strike missiles and THAAD interceptors.
Pentagon officials have acknowledged that heavy weapons use has created strategic inventory shortfalls and exposed production bottlenecks. Defense companies are now increasing output, including Lockheed Martin, which plans to raise annual production of PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors from about 600 to 2,000.
European leaders are expected to press Trump next week for additional Patriot support for Ukraine during meetings at the UN in New York. EU officials also hope to secure US licenses allowing European countries to produce Patriots for Kyiv.

OpenAI’s Sam Altman to brief UN Security Council next week
UNITED NATIONS - OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman will brief the United Nations Security Council next week during the annual gathering of world leaders in New York for the UN General Assembly, an OpenAI spokesperson said on Sept 18.
The 15-member Security Council is due to meet on Sept 23 on artificial intelligence and international security, just weeks after several AI industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the increasingly powerful technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and slip beyond human control.
“Sam Altman will brief an open UN Security Council meeting in person next week,” an OpenAI spokesperson told Reuters. “His remarks are expected to focus on the steps OpenAI is taking to ensure AI is safe and benefits people globally, along with the need for international coordination and shared safety standards.”
The UN Security Council, which is charged with maintaining international peace and security, met for the first time on the risks of artificial intelligence in 2023, when China said the technology should not become a “runaway horse” and the United States warned against its use to censor or repress people.
Altman has been warning about the risks well before the current AI boom.
In a 2015 essay titled Machine Intelligence, part 1, he said the “development of superhuman machine intelligence is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity”. REUTERS

Russia seizes assets of Nestle, French firms over West’s Ukraine support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:35:45 UTC
05:35:45 KST

Russia seizes assets of Nestle, French firms over West’s Ukraine support
WARSAW - The Russian authorities have seized the businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestle and three French groups, a move the Kremlin defended on Sept 18 as a justified measure against firms representing “unfriendly countries” that back Ukraine.
A decree signed by President Vladimir Putin transferred the Russian operations of Nestle, French retailer Auchan and the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain, now known as Lemana Pro, to a company called LEV Management.
The decree, issued late Sept 17, also covers the Russian subsidiaries of French logistics group FM Logistic.
France late Sept 18 called on the Russian authorities to “reverse this decision”.
Investigative outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe reported that LEV Management was created only at the end of 2025, and is headed by a Russian interior ministry general. It had no known business activity.
It was the latest move by Russia against Western firms in response to a barrage of sanctions over its war against Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
Most Western companies quickly sold their Russian operations and holdings after the Ukraine invasion, or at least isolated them, as sanctions have made trading in most goods difficult.
Others remained, citing concerns for their employees or citizen’s well-being, but often sharply scaling back their operations.
Russia has since made it difficult for firms to leave, requiring presidential authorisation for deals, or seizing the assets outright.
Assets at risk
In a short statement, Nestle said it was “committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees”.
“The company is assessing the situation and its options,” it added.
Nestle has six factories and Russia and employs around 7,000 people, mainly for coffee, pet care, infant nutrition and confectionary products, a spokesperson said.
Jean-Philippe Bertschy of the Swiss investment bank Vontobel said he expected the financial impact to Nestle would be small “given Russia’s limited contribution to group sales”.
He said Russia now accounted for just over one percent of the group’s sales, down from around two percent before the Ukraine war.
It has suspended “the vast majority of sales, non-essential imports, advertising and capital investment”, he said, while continuing to supply essential food items.
“This practice has historically often been a precursor to a forced sale or effective expropriation of operations in the market,” said analysts at the brokerage Jeffries.
“This was the case already for Danone and Carlsberg for example in 2023,” they wrote, estimating that a write-off of Nestle’s Russia business, including money it had not been able to repatriate, could cost the Swiss firm around one billion francs (S$1.5 billion).
Nestle shares dropped 2.6 per cent on the Zurich stock exchange on Sept 18.
Auchan and Leroy Merlin are both controlled by France’s Mulliez family, which also owns the Decathlon sports retailer.
Auchan’s Russian subsidiary said on Sept 18 that it had requested “clarifications” from the authorities over Putin’s decree.
The French foreign and economy ministries said in a joint statement late on Sept 17 that France “condemns” the move, and urged Moscow to go back on its decision.
Auchan’s subsidiary is one of Russia’s main retailers, with 241 stores in the country, including 62 hypermarkets, and over 33,000 employees according to its website.
“Once the corresponding information has been received, we will be able to provide more detailed comments,” Auchan Retail Russia said a statement to Russian news agencies.
The latest seizure echoes a string of other forced asset transfers, including Moscow’s 2023 takeover of Danone’s Russian business, which was later sold to a nephew of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov. AFP

jesus mari lazkano traces changing landscapes through painting and animated film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:35:39 UTC
05:35:39 KST

Six paintings and animated film examine landscapes in transition
On September 11, Basque Luxury Studio in San Sebastián, Spain, opened ‘Azken Natura,’ a solo exhibition by Jesus Mari Lazkano. The exhibition brings together six medium- and large-scale paintings made between 2021 and 2026, alongside a screening of the short film ‘Natura Fugit,’ created by Lazkano in collaboration with production companies Dibulitoon and Art Frame. The 22-minute film premiered in 2025 at the San Sebastián International Film Festival. Developed over four years, the project involved nearly 3,000 drawings by Lazkano depicting the melting of the Alpine glacier Mer de Glace. The drawings were assembled into an animated short that extends the artist’s pictorial approach into moving image.
At Basque Luxury Studio, the film is presented alongside six works from ‘The Last Ice,’ a body of work focused on Lazkano’s representation of nature. Five of the works are acrylic paintings on canvas, while the sixth is a pastel and colored-pencil drawing on paper. Together, the pieces examine the landscape as a changing physical environment and question the ways in which nature is approached and used. The paintings depict landscape, reality, and the surrounding environment as spaces undergoing significant change. The works consider a future in which familiar landscapes may no longer exist in their current form, connecting Lazkano’s visual language with wider discussions around human impact on the environment.
‘Azken Natura’ uses visual art to frame environmental change
From the perspective of visual art, ‘Azken Natura’ addresses the relationship between environmental change and the sustainability of human actions. While these issues are commonly discussed through scientific, political, and social frameworks, the exhibition focuses on the communicative and emotional dimensions of the subject. Painting and animation become tools for translating environmental data and physical change into visual forms that can enter public and cultural discussion. The exhibition also considers the role of visual culture during periods of broader change. As new environmental concerns reshape social and cultural perspectives, artists contribute images and visual references through which these shifts can be understood and represented. ‘Azken Natura’ establishes this visual framework through a combination of large-scale painting, drawing, and animation.
‘Azken Natura’ is the eighth exhibition organized by Basque Luxury over the past decade. As part of its program promoting local culture, the company has previously organized solo exhibitions dedicated to Alfredo Bikondoa, Iñigo Manterola, Víctor Goikoetxea, Miguel Balliache, José Zugasti, and Jose Luis Zumeta. The current exhibition presents the work of Jesus Mari Lazkano, one of the prominent contemporary artists on the Basque cultural scene. ‘Azken Natura’ remains open to the public through September 2028.

US appeals court rejects Trump policy allowing swift deportations to third countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:33:26 UTC
05:33:26 KST

US appeals court rejects Trump policy allowing swift deportations to third countries
BOSTON, Sept 18 - A US federal appeals court rejected on Friday a policy adopted by President Donald Trump's administration that allows authorities to rapidly deport migrants to countries other than their own without giving them a chance to raise safety concerns.
Ruling in a case that is likely headed to the Supreme Court, a three-judge panel of the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld a February decision by a lower-court judge that declared the Department of Homeland Security's policy unlawful.
The ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by migrants subject to deportation orders that has become a key test of what due process protections the government must provide before removing people to countries with which they have no connection.
"This decision confirms that due process and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented by putting someone on a plane to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings," Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said
Under Trump, the administration has entered into a series of agreements that have allowed it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, in many cases Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.
The Trump administration is expected to appeal. Earlier in the same case, the administration twice convinced the Supreme Court to lift a preliminary injunction protecting migrants' due process rights, clearing the way for eight men to be deported to South Sudan.
DHS had no immediate comment.
Under the third-country deportation program, DHS adopted a policy in March 2025 that would allow migrants to be sent to such countries if immigration authorities have credible diplomatic assurances they will not be persecuted or tortured there.
The policy called for only minimal notice before a migrant could be sent to a third country that had not given the State Department such assurances.
THIRD COUNTRY DEPORTATIONS
US District Judge Brian Murphy, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, set aside the policy and concluded that it failed to protect migrants' due process rights and could lead to their swift deportation to unfamiliar and potentially dangerous countries, without notice.
On appeal, the Trump administration contended that Murphy's order if left intact would usurp its authority to execute potentially thousands of valid orders of deportation to third countries.
But US Circuit Judge Seth Aframe, writing for Friday's panel, said Murphy adopted a "sensible" interpretation of the immigration law requiring migrants be given a "meaningful" chance to raise any concerns before they are deported.
"DHS's proposed interpretation would deny access to that protection to a substantial swath of noncitizens who are sent to third countries with no notice of their destination," Aframe wrote. "We decline to adopt such an interpretation."
The panel included two Biden appointees, including Aframe, and a judge appointed by a Republican president.
However, the 1st Circuit overturned one part of Murphy's ruling on procedural grounds. That part of the ruling concerned whether the government must first try to deport migrants to countries they have ties to before sending them to third countries. REUTERS

Air Force Set Up a Depot in UK During Epic Fury for Faster Battle Repairs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:33:06 UTC
05:33:06 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Air Force depots are not typically meant for quick repair jobs—aircraft can stay in depot for weeks and months getting repairs—but during Operation Epic Fury, the service moved some of its stateside heavy maintenance capability forward to fix battle-damaged aircraft closer to the fight.
As the war with Iran stretched from its projected timeline of weeks into several months, Air Force leaders were forced to adapt its aircraft maintenance strategy for a prolonged conflict.
The service relies on three maintenance depots at Hill Air Force Base, Utah; Robins Air Force Base, Ga.; and Tinker Air Force Base, Okla.—to conduct major maintenance overhauls and inspections on fighters, bombers, airlifters, and other aircraft.
During Epic Fury, barrages of Iranian missile and drone attacks on U.S. forces operating out of Middle East resulted in levels of battle damage that normally would have required the aircraft to be transported back stateside for repairs.
Instead, Air Force Materiel Command temporarily surged a depot capability to RAF Mildenhall in the United Kingdom so damaged aircraft could be patched up and sent back into combat, AFMC Commander Lt. Gen. Linda Hurry told an audience this week at AFA’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber conference.
“Most people think of depots as Tinker, Robbins, and Hill; well, it doesn’t need to be just there,” Hurry said. “We knew you needed a capability out at Mildenhall … what if we push that forward?”
“That’s what we’ve been asking all of our Airmen—how do we do things smarter? How do we deliver capability faster? It doesn’t have to be 7,000 miles away.”
Air Mobility Command’s new boss, Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley, said Hurry’s move paid off, describing how the depot operation quickly repaired damaged aerial refueling booms on KC-135 Stratotankers.
“I think we turned 30 [booms] instead of bringing them all the way back to the states,” Tulley said, adding it was a great example of “generating readiness in contact.”
Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink and Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach made readiness a defining priority soon after taking their jobs last year. The intense pace of operations against Iran will stress that focus, with much of the fleet likely to need heavy maintenance overhauls to reset.
The Air Force’s proposed 2027 budget includes $4.2 billion for the Consolidated Sustainment Activity Group, which is responsible for managing spare parts.
“We absolutely need additional funding for spares,” Hurry said, adding “right now, we have a $14 billion hole in supply.”
“I know we’re not going to get it all at once, … but once we get even a penny, we have to be ready to execute it,” Hurry said. That will mean securing long-term contracts to inject stability into the supply chain.
“The other thing is, we’re looking for is multiple sources of supply; gone are the days of monopolies. We can’t just have one person producing the one critical part,” Hurry said. “I need five of you producing them because if we get down to the crunch, we’re going to have to have a healthy shelf so that we can fight globally.”
Meanwhile, Hurry said AFMC has started using artificial intelligence tools to improve forecasting accuracy. “We’re using all sorts of things to try to make sure we better understand where the needs are and where we can position those critical assets globally around the world,” she said.
Additive manufacturing is another tool AFMC has started to use to “reverse engineer some of the parts that we need,” she added.
But technology alone isn’t enough, she said, adding that “process improvement” can solve a lot of challenges.
“Quite frankly, if we can understand the process and break it down into constraint and mitigate that constrain, the collective throughput of the entire system goes so much better,” Hurry said. “That’s exactly what’s going on in the depot. That’s exactly what we did when we surged operations for [Epic Fury].”

====================================================================================================

Generals vs. Netanyahu: Israel’s election is turning into a real political war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:31:39 UTC
05:31:39 KST

Israel's Oct. 27 Knesset election will feature 38 electoral lists to choose from set against the background of an ongoing war with Iran in a nation on the brink of civil strife. Most of all, however, the vote will be a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. As politicians divvy up parliamentary seats that they have yet to win, polls offer neither the right-wing bloc nor the opposition “camp of change” an easy path to victory. In Israel’s convoluted electoral system, the outcome will depend not only on the top parties’ popularity, but also on the willingness of radical, Arab, and ultra-Orthodox groups to compromise when the politicking moves to the coalition-forming stage.
Echoes of the war
Israel's upcoming election will be the first since the series of wars that followed the massacre carried out by the Hamas terrorist group on October 7, 2023. Despite ceasefires in Gaza and Lebanon and the end of active hostilities with Iran, the war is not over for Israel. IDF soldiers remain in Gaza and Lebanon, the military remains on heightened alert over Iran, and tensions remain high in Judea and Samaria (the West Bank). Netanyahu’s promised “total victory” (at least over Hamas and Lebanon’s Hezbollah) has not been achieved, even if both groups have suffered heavy losses.
Against this backdrop, one of the key questions ahead of the election is whether Benjamin Netanyahu can remain in power after the security failure that led to the October 7 tragedy. The campaign has raised questions about the responsibility of the political leadership and security agencies for the Hamas attack, the military’s condition and readiness, the aims and results of the recent wave of wars, and the issue of extending mandatory military service to students at ultra-Orthodox yeshivas.
Netanyahu argues that the army and intelligence chiefs failed to warn him of the impending attack, instead portraying Hamas as a contained force. At the same time, the prime minister says he should be judged by the results of the subsequent wars, which led to the elimination of much of the leadership of Hamas and Hezbollah, the killing of Iran’s top military commanders, and strikes against Iran’s nuclear program.
Netanyahu's main rivals – Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Lieberman, and Yair Golan – hold the government politically responsible for the catastrophe and are calling for a state commission of inquiry into the events before, during, and after October 7. They also accuse Netanyahu’s government of damaging Israel’s international standing and weakening its support in the West, including in the United States.
Still, the issue of October 7 stands out. Haaretz recently reported that roughly 10 days before the Hamas attacks, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed had warned Netanyahu of a major attack being planned by Yahya Sinwar, who was then leading Hamas in Gaza. According to the newspaper, however, the prime minister did not pass the information on to the heads of the security agencies. Netanyahu’s office called the report “an absolute lie,” saying no such conversation ever took place. Eisenkot, Bennett, Lieberman, and Golan issued a joint statement demanding an immediate and comprehensive investigation and promising to establish a state commission under the next government. Bennett himself said that he knew Netanyahu had received the warning. The following day, the prime minister instructed his lawyers to prepare a lawsuit against the newspaper and the authors of the report.
The events of October 7 feature not only in politicians’ statements but have also shaped electoral lists of major parties, virtually all of which include veterans of the recent wars, relatives of those killed or taken hostage, and activists from organizations that emerged after the Hamas attack. Just hours before registration closed, Netanyahu announced that Talik Gvili, the mother of police officer Ran Gvili — who was killed fighting terrorists on the morning of October 7, and whose body was then taken to Gaza — would join the Likud list, taking ninth place. Reservist Elisha Medan, who lost both legs fighting in the Gaza Strip, took 15th place, while attorney Itzik Buncel, the father of soldier Amit Buncel, who was killed in Gaza in December 2023, took 29th.
Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) party, gave second place on his party's list to Rafi Ben-Shitrit, the former mayor of Beit She’an. His son Elroy was also killed on October 7.
Ben-Shitrit is one of the founders of the October Council, which brings together families of those killed or taken hostage, survivors of the attack, and reservists. The organization is campaigning for a state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7. In August 2026, it published a report on the persistence among the political leadership and security establishment of the belief that Hamas could be contained.
Sharon Sharabi took sixth place on the Yisrael Beiteinu list. His brother Yossi was taken hostage from Kibbutz Be’eri on October 7 and died in captivity, while another brother, Eli, was released after 491 days in Gaza. Sharon Sharabi became one of the most prominent figures in the campaign to free the hostages.
The events of October 7 have also become part of the political biographies of leaders of several parties. On the morning of October 7, Yair Golan, a reserve major general and leader of the left-wing Democrats party, went south on his own initiative, evacuating people from the fighting. Ofer Winter, a reserve brigadier general and leader of the right-wing Amha Israel party, likewise made his own way to the Gaza border, joined soldiers near Kibbutz Be’eri, and took part in the fighting.
The Reservists party, which submitted a joint list with Yaron Zelicha’s Economic Party, is led by reserve Lt. Col. Yoaz Hendel. After the war began, he returned to active duty and fought in the Gaza Strip, later forming and commanding the Be’eri reserve battalion. Reservist Shlomi Demari, who lost his brother on October 7, took seventh place on the joint list.
On the “Together” (Beyahad) joint list of Bennett and Lapid, sixth place went to reserve Major General Noam Tibon, who on the morning of October 7 traveled south from Tel Aviv, helping Nova festival survivors and wounded soldiers along the way. He took part in the fighting before reaching Nahal Oz, where he evacuated his son, daughter-in-law, and two granddaughters from a besieged home.
Netanyahu’s main rival in the race for prime minister is Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot, a reserve lieutenant general and former IDF chief of staff. During the war, he lost his son Gal and nephew Maor Cohen Eisenkot, who were killed in the Gaza Strip.
Netanyahu’s main rival – Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot, a reserve lieutenant general and former IDF chief of staff
Even the ultra-Orthodox Shas party, which has consistently opposed mandatory military service for yeshiva students, placed reserve officer Dror Amos sixth on its list.
Other major fault lines in the campaign include judicial reform, the future of the Gaza Strip and Judea and Samaria, and the related question of establishing a Palestinian state. Equally contentious is the debate over Israel’s very character: the balance between its Jewish and democratic identities, the relationship between religion and state, and whether the country needs a constitution. These issues divide not only Netanyahu’s supporters and opponents but also the parties within each camp. Reaching compromise will be difficult. First though, the people will have their say.
How Israel’s elections work
The first poll conducted after the party lists closed and published by the Walla news portal on Sept. 9 shows how heavily the outcome depends on parties that are currently hovering around the electoral threshold of 3.5%. According to the poll, Eisenkot’s Yashar would win 25 seats, Likud 21, the joint Bennett-Lapid list 14, and Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu and Golan’s Democrats nine each. Winter’s Amha Israel, with exactly 3.5% of the vote, would clear the threshold and win four seats, while the joint Hendel-Zelicha list, at 2.8%, would fall short. The parties in the current coalition, together with Winter, would have 51 seats, the Zionist opposition parties 57, and the Arab parties 12. Neither camp would have the 61 seats needed for a majority, although the figures could still shift in either direction as the campaign progresses.
Israel is a single nationwide constituency, with all 120 Knesset seats allocated proportionally among party lists according to the number of votes they receive. Votes cast for lists that do not clear 3.5% are not transferred to any other party but are excluded from the calculations. As a result, the share of seats won by parties that clear the threshold increases, meaning the number of small parties falling just short of the threshold can change the balance of power between the camps.
Israeli voters do not vote for a prime minister but for a party list. After the results are announced, the president consults with all factions that have entered the Knesset, each of which says whom it recommends be tasked with forming a government. The president then gives the mandate to the Knesset member whom he or she believes has the best chance of forming a government capable of winning the body's confidence.
The first candidate is given 28 days, after which the president can extend the period by another 14 days. If the attempt fails, the mandate can be given to another member of Knesset. If all the subsequent options provided by law are exhausted, the Knesset is dissolved and new elections are held – as has happened more than once under Netanyahu. To take office, the incoming prime minister must present the cabinet and its main policy priorities to the Knesset and win a vote of confidence.
The leader of the largest party does not automatically become prime minister. After the 2009 election, for example, Tzipi Livni’s Kadima won 28 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud won 27. However, most right-wing and religious factions backed Netanyahu, and President Shimon Peres asked him to form the government. Netanyahu assembled a coalition, while Livni, who led the largest faction, remained in the opposition.
Another precedent was set in 2021. After Netanyahu failed to form a government, the mandate was given to Yair Lapid, leader of Yesh Atid. Lapid assembled a coalition of eight parties, ranging from the right-wing Yamina to the left-wing Labor and Meretz and even including the Islamist Ra’am, and he agreed with Yamina leader Naftali Bennett on a rotation arrangement. Bennett became prime minister first, even though his party was one of the smallest in the coalition, with just six seats. The new government won the confidence vote 60 to 59, with one abstention.
The law does not require 61 members to vote in favor of a government for it to be approved. It is enough to receive more votes in favor than against. This makes it possible to form a minority government – a cabinet formed by parties with fewer than 61 seats that relies on the support or abstention of other factions during confidence votes.
Under the numbers recorded in the Walla poll, Netanyahu’s Zionist opponents could theoretically try to form a minority government with the external support or neutrality of the Arab parties. But such a scenario would require the agreement not only of the Arab factions but also of potential coalition partners, and some of those parties refuse to rely on Arab votes. Another possible route would be to redraw the boundaries of the current camps and bring in some parties that had belonged to the opposing bloc before the election.
Netanyahu’s opponents could try to form a minority government with the support or neutrality of Arab parties
Failure to reach an agreement could lead to another election. After the April 2019 vote, Netanyahu was five seats short of a coalition majority. Yisrael Beiteinu party leader Avigdor Lieberman controlled five seats but was unwilling to join a government that planned to concede to the demands of religious parties by amending the law on ultra-Orthodox military service. No compromise was reached, and the Knesset voted to dissolve itself.
After the September 2019 election, neither Netanyahu nor Benny Gantz managed to form a government. A third election was held in March 2020, after which they formed a rotation-based national unity government. It collapsed after the state budget failed to pass, and in March 2021, Israelis went to the polls for a fourth time in less than two years. That cycle ended with the formation of the Bennett-Lapid government.
The threat of another election after the October vote remains, but it is only one possible scenario. The polls are still volatile, and the balance of power could shift in response to both external events and domestic political crises. At the very least, some parties hovering around the electoral threshold may withdraw before election day to prevent votes for their party from being lost to the larger political camp they associate with.
Israel’s political camps
The division of Israeli politics into right and left predates the state itself, emerging within the Yishuv – the Jewish population of Mandatory Palestine and its self-governing institutions. On one side was the socialist Labor Zionist movement, which dominated the leadership of the Yishuv and the of Israel for decades.
Its main political heir was the Labor Party, which later merged with Meretz to form today’s Democrats. On the other was Vladimir Jabotinsky’s Revisionist movement, which advocated a tougher struggle for a Jewish state and laid claim to the entire historic Land of Israel. It gave rise to Menachem Begin’s Herut party, which became the foundation of Likud, established in 1973.
After the 1967 Six-Day War, one of the central issues in Israeli politics became the future of the territories captured during the fighting – the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Golan Heights. The UN and most countries consider them occupied territories (Sinai was returned to Egypt under a peace treaty).
Broadly speaking, the right favored maintaining Israeli control over the territories and expanding Jewish settlements, while the left supported territorial compromise in exchange for peace. But the divide was never absolute. It was right-wing Prime Minister Menachem Begin who agreed to return the entire Sinai to Egypt under the 1979 peace treaty, while Ariel Sharon’s government carried out a unilateral disengagement in 2005, withdrawing Israeli forces and dismantling all Jewish settlements in the Gaza Strip and four settlements in the northern West Bank.
After Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization signed the Oslo Accords in the 1990s, the Palestinian Authority was established and granted limited self-government in the Gaza Strip and parts of the West Bank. The political divide increasingly focused on whether to establish or prevent a Palestinian state, its possible borders, the status of Jerusalem, the fate of the settlements, and the risks of transferring territory to Palestinian control.
Religion and state became another major political divide. In Israel, “liberal” does not neatly correspond either to the right-left divide over the Palestinian issue or to economic liberalism. The left-wing Democrats, centrist parties, and some secular right-wing politicians describe themselves as liberal, and they are united by support for individual and civil liberties, civil marriage, the operation of public transportation and businesses on Saturdays, and equal obligations to the state. Thus Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, which is right-wing on security and the Palestinian issue, can be closer on religion-state questions to the Democrats and the secular center than to the ultra-Orthodox and religious Zionist parties in the right-wing bloc.
Parties that describe themselves as centrist occupy a space between the traditional camps. They generally seek to combine a tough approach to security with a willingness to compromise politically, and a secular, liberal agenda with a rejection of a left-wing identity. But Israel’s center is not a single ideological movement. At different times, the label has been applied to parties with substantially different platforms, often built around a particular leader or a demand to replace the existing political elite.
Since 2019, another divide has become firmly entrenched in Israeli politics – one between Netanyahu’s supporters and the parties seeking to remove him from power. It overlaps with the traditional right-left divide but does not coincide with it: right-wing politicians Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman have been among Netanyahu’s opponents, while ultra-Orthodox parties and representatives of the religious Zionist right have remained his staunch allies.
The split emerged alongside Netanyahu’s criminal prosecution. In November 2019, he was indicted on charges of fraud, bribery, and breach of trust. Netanyahu denies the charges and has called the investigations politically motivated.
Israeli law does not require a prime minister to resign automatically after being indicted, and he can remain in office while on trial. By contrast, under Supreme Court rulings, a minister or deputy minister who is not prime minister must step down after being charged with a serious offense. An ordinary Knesset member, however, is likewise not automatically required to give up their seat.
Netanyahu’s opponents have argued that the criminal cases gave him an additional personal incentive to remain prime minister — and to use his power to pursue changes to the judicial and law-enforcement systems. Netanyahu denies this.
His trial began in May 2020. He gave evidence from December 2024 through June 2026. After 98 hearings, his testimony was completed. The defense must now present its other witnesses, after which the sides will move to closing arguments. No verdict has been issued, and Netanyahu retains the presumption of innocence. In June 2026, the judges again recommended that prosecutors drop the bribery charge. The prosecution did not withdraw it, however, and proceedings on the remaining charges continue.
The series of elections from 2019 to 2021 showed that attitudes toward Netanyahu can override the importance of ideological proximity between parties. In 2021, right-wing, centrist, and left-wing parties joined with the Islamist Ra’am to form a coalition whose main common goal was to replace the prime minister.
Attitudes toward Netanyahu can outweigh ideological proximity between parties
Bennett assumed the role first. A former director general of the Yesha Council, he opposed a Palestinian state and supported extending Israeli sovereignty to parts of the occupied territories. Before the election, he pledged neither to make Yair Lapid prime minister under a rotation deal nor to form a government dependent on Ra’am. But he later broke both promises before subsequently insisting that his views on security and the Palestinian issue had not changed and that his decision was driven by the need to end the political crisis.
The judicial overhaul pursued by Netanyahu’s government since 2023 has deepened the divide. Supporters argued that the changes were needed in order to limit the Supreme Court’s influence over decisions by elected authorities. Opponents saw them as an attempt to weaken independent judicial review and the system of checks and balances. The dispute over Netanyahu and his criminal cases was thus joined by a fundamental disagreement over the powers of the government, the Knesset, and the Supreme Court.
In election polls, parties are generally grouped into the Netanyahu bloc, the Zionist parties seeking to replace the government, and the Arab lists, which are counted separately. These are not unified ideological camps but potential coalition groupings. Within each, disagreements persist over the Palestinian issue, the judiciary, the relationship between religion and state, and obligations of military service.
Polls place Netanyahu’s Likud, the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties, Itamar Ben-Gvir's far-right Otzma Yehudit, and the joint Religious Zionism-Zehut list of Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin in the Netanyahu bloc. Ofer Winter’s right-wing Amha Israel is also counted as a member, and its leader has said he belongs to the right-wing camp and will recommend only Netanyahu for prime minister. At the same time, Winter has refused to join forces with politicians he holds responsible for the October 7 security failure.
However, this bloc cannot be treated as a ready-made future coalition. The ultra-Orthodox parties have made their participation in government conditional on the passage of a law regulating the status of yeshiva students and allowing many of them to avoid military service. The dispute over the legislation has already triggered a crisis in their relations with Likud. Winter, by contrast, is demanding that before the government is formed a law be passed that, in his words, will “put an end to draft evasion” and require all young Israelis to serve in the military or otherwise contribute to the state. In short, their mutual support for Netanyahu is not enough to resolve the fundamental conflict between the incumbent prime minister's potential post-election coalition partners.
Ahead of the 2022 vote, Netanyahu succeeded in uniting three competing right-wing lists – Religious Zionism, Otzma Yehudit, and Avi Maoz’s Noam – so they could clear the electoral threshold together. This time, it proved impossible to create a single list of Likud’s potential right-wing partners, although Smotrich did reach an agreement with Feiglin. Depending on the poll, the Smotrich-Feiglin and Winter lists either clear the threshold by a narrow margin or fall just short. Maoz’s separate list fails to clear the threshold and therefore also acts to siphon votes from other right-wing parties.
New alliances are no longer possible now that the lists have closed, but individual parties can still withdraw from the race. Netanyahu is therefore likely to continue pressuring parties and candidates hovering around the threshold.
Polls place Eisenkot’s Yashar, the joint Naftali Bennett-Yair Lapid list, Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, and Yair Golan’s Democrats among the Zionist parties opposed to the current government. Eisenkot refers to these four parties as the “camp of change,” but their commitments vary. Bennett and Lieberman have explicitly said they will not join a Netanyahu government. Golan has consistently called for Netanyahu’s removal. And Eisenkot is demanding a change of government and is himself seeking the prime minister’s post, even if he has not made an equally categorical commitment never to join a coalition with Netanyahu.
There are also significant differences within the camp opposed to Netanyahu. Bennett and Lieberman remain unmistakably right-wing on security and the Palestinian issue, while the Democrats represent the left. Yisrael Beiteinu calls for mandatory military or civilian service for all citizens and rules out a government dependent on ultra-Orthodox or Arab parties. Some center-right politicians are unwilling to work with the Democrats. As a result, there is still no agreement on what kind of government Netanyahu’s opponents should form should they be given the opportunity.
Separate from these four parties is Benny Gantz’s Blue and White. After the 2023 Hamas attack, Gantz’s State Camp bloc reached as many as 35 seats in some polls, putting it in contention to become the country’s largest political force. But Eisenkot and other partners subsequently left the bloc, and what remained of Gantz’s party fell well below the electoral threshold. The “camp of change” is therefore urging Gantz to withdraw, fearing that votes cast for him will be wasted. He has so far said he will continue his campaign.
Pollsters usually count the Arab lists – the Hadash-Ta’al-Balad United List and Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am – separately. They could join a coalition, support a government from outside, abstain in the confidence vote, or remain in opposition. Each option depends not only on the Arab parties themselves but also on whether the Zionist factions are willing to accept their support. Ra’am was already part of the Bennett-Lapid coalition in 2021–22, but since October 7, some right-wing parties have ruled out any government dependent on Arab lawmakers.
Outside the two main camps is the joint Reservists-Economic Party list of Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelicha – provided it clears the electoral threshold. Hendel says he will not give Netanyahu the votes he needs to form a narrow coalition, but at the same time, he is open to joining a broad government with Netanyahu provided that it is backed by 70–80 members of Zionist parties. He also rules out joining a cabinet dependent on Arab or ultra-Orthodox factions.
Both Netanyahu and his opponents are now calling for a “broad Zionist government,” but there is no agreement on what it should look like. Such a coalition would clearly exclude the Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties, but questions remain. Some are open to serving in a government with Netanyahu, while others would work with Likud only after a change of the party's leader. Some would also refuse to sit in the same government with the Democrats, Otzma Yehudit, and Religious Zionism.
The main contenders
Coalition arithmetic does not answer the campaign’s central question: who will head the next government? In one of the latest polls asking voters who is best suited to serve as prime minister (conducted by the Kantar Institute for the public broadcaster Kan and published on September 6), 38% of respondents chose Eisenkot over Netanyahu, while 35% chose the incumbent. When asked to choose between Netanyahu and Bennett, the incumbent led 37% to 32%, while in a head-to-head matchup between Eisenkot and Bennett, the former IDF chief of staff led 36% to 17%. The results vary depending on the pair presented, but at the time of the poll, Eisenkot was the only candidate ahead of Netanyahu in a head-to-head comparison.
Benjamin Netanyahu: Likud’s indispensable leader
Benjamin Netanyahu is 76. He first became prime minister in 1996, later serving as foreign and finance minister before returning to the premiership in 2009 and remaining in office until 2021. At the end of 2022, Netanyahu formed another government. He has served as Israel’s prime minister longer than anyone else.
Likud has entered the current election once again as a party built around a single undisputed leader. Netanyahu is seeking only to retain the premiership. And the party is fielding no alternative candidate.
The allocation of other cabinet posts will depend on the coalition’s makeup. Netanyahu will have to negotiate both with his current partners, who want to retain influence over security, finance, and religious affairs, and with centrist parties if he opts to form a broader government.
Gadi Eisenkot: the general who became Netanyahu’s main challenger
Gadi Eisenkot is 66. He served in the military for 41 years, commanding the Judea and Samaria Division and Northern Command, heading the Operations Directorate, serving as deputy chief of staff, and serving as chief of staff from 2015 to 2019.
Eisenkot entered politics ahead of the 2022 election as part of Benny Gantz’s State Camp. After October 7, he became a minister without portfolio and joined the narrow war cabinet formed at the time. In June 2024, he left the government with Gantz. In 2025, he left the State Camp, resigned his Knesset seat, and later founded the Yashar party.
Eisenkot is running for prime minister. His party is also seeking the education portfolio and the post of minister for the reconstruction and development of the north and south.
Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid: together again
Naftali Bennett is 54. An entrepreneur and former special forces officer, he began his political career in Netanyahu’s circle. He later served as director general of the Yesha Council and led the religious Zionist Jewish Home party. Bennett went on to serve as economy, education, and defense minister before becoming prime minister in 2021 with just six Knesset seats, leading a coalition of right-wing, centrist, and left-wing parties that included Ra’am.
Yair Lapid is 62. A former television host, he founded the centrist Yesh Atid party in 2012 and later served as finance and foreign minister. Under the 2021 coalition agreement, Bennett and Lapid agreed to rotate the premiership: Bennett would serve first, and after the Knesset was dissolved early in summer 2022, Lapid briefly became prime minister.
They are running together in this election on the Beyahad joint list, which Bennett leads. He is also its candidate for prime minister.
Avigdor Lieberman: “Now it’s my turn”
Avigdor Lieberman is 68. Born in Chisinau, he began his political career in Likud and served as director general of the Prime Minister’s Office under Netanyahu. In 1999, he founded Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home), initially as a party aimed at new immigrants. Today, only four of the top 10 candidates on his list are Russian speakers, including Lieberman himself.
Lieberman has served as foreign, defense, and finance minister, as well as chair of the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee.
Although Yisrael Beiteinu is polling at around nine seats, Lieberman has not abandoned his ambition to become prime minister. At the same time, the party has already named its candidate for one of the key security posts. Lieberman has designated lawmaker Hamad Amar, a member of the Druze community, reserve officer, and former minister in the Finance Ministry, as its choice for national security minister. Yisrael Beiteinu is thus seeking the ministry currently headed by Ben-Gvir, which oversees the police and the fight against crime.
Yair Golan: the general leading the left
Yair Golan is 64. A reserve major general, he commanded the Northern Command and Home Front Command and served as deputy chief of staff from 2014 to 2017. He entered politics in 2019 alongside former Prime Minister Ehud Barak and formally joined the far-left Meretz party in December 2020. Under the Bennett-Lapid government, he served as deputy economy minister. In 2024, Golan was elected leader of the Labor Party and subsequently merged it with Meretz to form today’s Democrats.
Golan is not seeking the premiership, but the Democrats have already identified several ministries they plan to seek. Golan said the party would demand the Education and Justice portfolios: Education to strengthen public education and tie school funding to the teaching of core subjects, and Justice to repeal provisions of the judicial overhaul enacted by the current government and restore the powers of legal advisers.
Golan has also named the Defense, National Security, and Communications ministries among the portfolios the party wants. The Democrats’ demands overlap with those of other potential coalition partners: Yisrael Beiteinu and Ra’am have already put forward their own candidates for national security minister, while Eisenkot has promised the education portfolio to a member of his party.
Benny Gantz: from frontrunner to fighting for survival
Benny Gantz is 67. He served as chief of staff from 2011 to 2015 and founded the Israel Resilience Party (Hosen LeYisrael) ahead of the 2019 election, which became the foundation of the Blue and White alliance. Gantz has served as speaker of the Knesset and defense minister. In 2020, he agreed to join Netanyahu’s government under a rotation deal for the premiership. However, the government collapsed before the premiership was due to pass to him. After October 7, Gantz again joined Netanyahu’s government, leaving it in June 2024.
In January 2024, Gantz’s State Camp, which then included Eisenkot and Gideon Sa’ar’s New Hope party, was polling at as many as 35 seats. Sa’ar and Eisenkot later left the alliance. In the current election, Gantz is running his own Blue and White list, which is unlikely to clear the electoral threshold.
Ofer Winter: a new challenger on the right
Ofer Winter is 55. A reserve brigadier general, he commanded the Duvdevan special forces unit, the Givati Brigade, and the 98th Division, and served as military secretary to the defense minister and chief of staff of the Central Command. He left active duty in 2024. In August 2026, Winter announced the formation of Amha Israel, a party targeting right-wing voters dissatisfied with both the government and the army’s previous leadership.
Second on the list is Arab Christian Yousef Haddad, a former Golani Brigade soldier and commander who was seriously wounded during the Second Lebanon War and later became one of Israel’s best-known international advocates. He hopes to become the first Arab to serve in Israel’s political-security cabinet and is seeking the public diplomacy portfolio.
Winter has pledged to recommend only Netanyahu for prime minister, but has set a condition for joining the government: before it is formed, a law must be passed requiring all young citizens to serve in the military or otherwise contribute to the state. Winter has not publicly demanded the Defense Ministry or another security portfolio for himself. Haddad, for his part, said the party would not join a government led by Eisenkot.
Partners with strings attached
Beyond the candidates for prime minister, the makeup of the next government will be determined by the parties controlling the final handful of seats needed to form a majority. The collection of potential kingmakers includes far-right parties, ultra-Orthodox factions, and Arab lists alike.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich: rivals on the far right
Itamar Ben-Gvir is 50. He leads the far-right Otzma Yehudit party and has served as national security minister, with authority over the police, since late 2022. Before entering the Knesset, Ben-Gvir was an activist in Kach, a movement banned in Israel, and a lawyer for people accused of nationalist offenses. In 2007, a court convicted him of incitement to racism and supporting a terrorist organization. He later sought to distance himself from some of his earlier views but retained a platform calling for the annexation of Judea and Samaria, the expansion of settlements, harsher conditions for Palestinian prisoners, and the widespread arming of civilians.
In the run-up to this election, Ben-Gvir has added another coalition demand, unveiling a seven-year plan for the “voluntary emigration” of Gaza residents and saying that in the next government, Otzma Yehudit will demand the creation of a separate Ministry of Emigration.
On Sept. 9, the party also petitioned the Central Elections Committee to bar Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, from running, arguing that the party rejects Israel’s character as a Jewish state and supports armed struggle against it. The committee has yet to consider the claims, and its decision can in any case be appealed to the Supreme Court.
Bezalel Smotrich is 46. The leader of Religious Zionism serves as finance minister and also as a minister in the Defense Ministry, where he oversees matters related to the Civil Administration and settlement development in Judea and Samaria. Smotrich opposes a Palestinian state and supports extending Israeli sovereignty over the West Bank. His supporters see settlement expansion as the party’s main promise fulfilled, while opponents accuse him of effectively annexing the territories without a formal government decision.
Smotrich is running jointly with the Zehut party of 64-year-old Moshe Feiglin, who holds second place on the list. Feiglin is a former Likud lawmaker and the founder of a movement opposed to the Oslo Accords. His platform combines territorial annexation and an expanded Jewish presence on the Temple Mount with liberal economic policies, less government regulation, and cannabis legalization.
The ultra-Orthodox: allies who can no longer be taken at their word
Shas is an ultra-Orthodox party whose full name translates as “World Sephardi Union – Guardians of the Torah.” It was established primarily to represent religious Jews from the Middle East and North Africa. Aryeh Deri remains Shas’s political leader, but the party makes key decisions after consulting the Council of Torah Sages, a group of the most influential Sephardi rabbis.
United Torah Judaism represents the Ashkenazi ultra-Orthodox community. For the first time since 1992, it is running under that name as an alliance of three, rather than two, formally independent parties: Degel HaTorah (representing the Lithuanian stream), the Hasidic Agudat Yisrael, and the new Homat Torat Yisrael (“Bulwark of Israel’s Torah”). Degel HaTorah’s Yaakov Asher heads the list, and Agudat Yisrael representative Yitzhak Goldknopf is second. Here too, lawmakers answer to rabbinical councils and the leaders of the largest Hasidic communities.
The emergence of a third party within United Torah Judaism stems from an internal dispute in Agudat Yisrael. Representatives of several Hasidic groups accused the Gur community, the alliance’s largest, of wielding too much influence over the allocation of seats and budgets. The creation of Homat Torat Yisrael gives the dissenters their own party funding and the option of eventually breaking away from the joint list. For now though, they describe the move as technical and remain within United Torah Judaism.
The main grievance Shas and United Torah Judaism share with Netanyahu is that his government has failed to pass the promised law regulating yeshiva students’ exemption from military service. Following a Supreme Court ruling, the state must draft them under the existing law and halt funding to institutions whose students evade the draft. The Haredi parties want to preserve the special status of Torah study and limit penalties against yeshiva students who choose not to serve.
The decision to join a future coalition will be made not only by Deri, Asher, or Goldknopf, but above all by the parties’ rabbinical leadership. Shas representatives have floated the idea of refusing to join Netanyahu’s next government until an agreed law is passed, but Deri has made no final commitment. United Torah Judaism has put it more bluntly: it will not join a coalition that fails to resolve the status of yeshiva students. Their traditional alliance with Likud therefore does not guarantee unconditional support for Netanyahu after the election.
The traditional Haredi parties also face a new challenger in this election: the Ha-Tzibur Ha-Haredi (“Haredi Public”) list, led by Beit Shemesh Deputy Mayor Moti Leitner, which is aimed primarily at working Haredim and others who feel unrepresented by Shas and United Torah Judaism. American-born Haredim are seen as a potential source of support, as they are more likely to combine a religious lifestyle with solid jobs and secular education. The party advocates teaching math and English, expanding employment, and drafting those who are not actually engaged in Torah study: “Those who do not study must serve.”
Two women are among the list’s top six candidates. This sharply distinguishes the new party from Shas and United Torah Judaism, which do not include women on their lists. Leitner presents the party as an alternative to the existing Haredi leadership, accusing it of perpetuating poverty, opposing secular education, and protecting draft exemptions even for those who do not study at yeshivas. At the same time, Ha-Tzibur Ha-Haredi retains its ultra-Orthodox identity and says it is committed to protecting the right to full-time Torah study. The party may nevertheless fail to clear the electoral threshold.
Two Arab paths
Two major Arab lists are running in the election. The first is a joint list of three parties – Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad. It is headed by Hadash’s Yousef Jabareen, followed by Ta’al leader Ahmad Tibi in second place and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh in third.
Hadash is an Arab-Jewish left-wing bloc centered on the Communist Party of Israel. Ta’al is a secular Arab party built around Tibi. Balad represents the Palestinian national movement and calls for transforming Israel from a Jewish state into a “state of all its citizens.” In the 2022 election, Hadash and Ta’al won five seats, while Balad, which ran separately, failed to clear the threshold.
The second list is Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am, an Islamist Arab party and the parliamentary arm of the Islamic Movement’s southern branch in Israel. The movement split in 1996 over participation in elections, with the northern branch rejecting Israel’s state institutions (it was banned in 2015) while the southern branch chose parliamentary politics and remained legal. In 2021, Ra’am became the first independent Arab party to join a governing coalition, entering the Bennett-Lapid government. Its leader, Mansour Abbas, focused negotiations on funding for Arab municipalities, fighting crime, improving infrastructure, and gaining recognition for Bedouin villages.
In August 2026, Abbas said that Arab parties had been forced to accept the state’s Jewish character as a reality in order to participate in elections. Avi Maoz, followed by Ben-Gvir, then called for Ra’am to be barred from the vote. Otzma Yehudit also cites alleged ties between the Islamic Movement-affiliated Aid 48 foundation and organizations linked to Hamas, but Ben-Gvir’s main concern is that Ra’am could provide the seats needed to form a governing coalition made up of Netanyahu’s opponents.
A notable feature of the current Ra’am list is the second-place candidacy of former Deputy Minister for Internal Security Yoav Segalovich, a retired police major general and the first Jewish candidate in Ra’am’s history. Under the Bennett-Lapid government, he coordinated the fight against crime in the Arab sector.
Ra’am is seeking to return to pragmatic cooperation with Zionist parties. The United List includes both supporters of backing a government from outside to replace Netanyahu and opponents of any coalition that continues military operations and the occupation of Palestinian territories. That is why pollsters count Arab seats separately: it is impossible to know in advance whether Arab lawmakers will join the government, support it from outside, abstain in the confidence vote, or remain in opposition.
Either way, the sheer diversity of party lists and campaign platforms shows how deeply divided Israeli society has become. Yet whoever wins the election and whatever government emerges, there is little reason to expect the country’s internal crisis to end. According to a study published in June 2026 by the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI), 55% of Israelis consider internal polarization and divisions the country’s greatest existential threat – more serious than Iran’s nuclear program or the Palestinian conflict. Six in 10 respondents see a real danger of bloodshed and physical violence within Israel, potentially escalating into civil war.
55% of Israelis consider internal polarization and divisions the country’s greatest existential threat
The next government will therefore have to do more than decide how to wage the war and shape the country’s postwar future. It will also have to govern a deeply divided society in which a significant share of citizens no longer see their political opponents as rivals but as a threat to the country’s future.

US probes possible espionage after F-35 parts diverted to Hong Kong: Report

Berk Kutay Gokmen
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Sensitive F-35 fighter jet technology was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong this summer, prompting a congressional inquiry and concerns that China could gain access to components of the highly classified weapons system, Politico reported Friday.
A shipment of F-35 parts being sent from Australia to the US for repairs was rerouted while crossing the Pacific, according to the report. The Pentagon reportedly confirmed that some components had gone missing.
Anadolu separately contacted the Pentagon seeking confirmation and further details about the incident but had not received a response at the time of publication.
According to Politico, the parts were being transported by an intermediary for F-35 manufacturer Lockheed Martin but ultimately arrived in Hong Kong. It remains unclear why they were diverted or who currently possesses them, the report said.
The incident prompted ongoing briefings for congressional staff serving on key national security committees. State Department and Pentagon officials began briefing staff in June, with further briefings expected, it added.
Among the shipment’s contents was an F-35 canopy, which covers the cockpit and incorporates stealth technology available only to the US and its allies, according to the report. If obtained by an adversary, the components could potentially be studied and reverse-engineered.
The Pentagon’s F-35 Joint Program Office said it was “aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components.”
The office said it is working with US authorities and industry partners “to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence.”
Because Hong Kong is a Chinese special administrative region, the diversion potentially placed the equipment within Beijing’s sphere of influence, according to the report.
China has also conducted espionage targeting classified Pentagon programs, including the F-35, the report said.
“It’s no secret that China has been aggressively trying to get F-35 data through electronic espionage, among other means,” J.J. Gertler, a former House Armed Services Committee staff member, was quoted as saying.
“But even if they already had specifications or other data about the part, possessing a real one can give them even more to go on and can verify or refine whatever they already had learned.”

Planning a trip overseas soon? Be prepared to pay more to fly

In its Domestic Airline Competition in Australia report, it also revealed just how concentrated the market is locally.

If global central banks sneeze, will the RBA catch the same cold?
Well, the reality is the Reserve Bank was already lifting official interest rates earlier this year before many other global central banks, because Australia was experiencing inflationary pressures before the war in the Middle East started.

It blames three things: a change in tune from global central banks which are now lifting rates; higher oil prices stemming from the war in the Middle East; and large investments in artificial intelligence.
And while higher interest rates aren’t good for borrowers, it’ll benefit savers depending on just how aggressive the banks are to attract deposits.

Bathla's books show company was $736m out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:28:56 UTC
05:28:56 KST

Inside the mammoth task that could keep Bathla in administration for another year
In short:
Administrators of the Bathla Group have been given up to another year to run the voluntary administration.
The ABC understands the company bank accounts had not been reconciled for some time and may contain about $736 million of overstated inter-company receivables and payables.
What's next?
Administrator Teneo has secured $4.7 million in initial funding and is continuing talks with lenders about longer-term support.
Administrators of the Bathla Group have been given up to another year to run the voluntary administration, as they try to secure longer-term funding and work through a sprawling portfolio of property projects and creditor claims.
The NSW Supreme Court on Friday extended the convening period for the administration until September 13, 2027.
But the order does not mean the administration, or Bathla's construction operations, are funded for another 12 months.
Rather, it gives administrators Teneo more time before they are required to convene the second meeting of creditors, where creditors would ultimately be asked to decide the future of the companies.
Why administrators sought another year
The ABC understands the administrators sought the 12-month period because they considered anything shorter inadequate, given the scale of the task ahead.
That includes assessing hundreds of individual projects, working through the group's financial records and, ultimately, providing creditors with enough information to make decisions about the future of the companies.
“We have taken a cautious approach to the time frame to ensure there is sufficient time to progress and complete projects in an orderly way,” Teneo's head of financial advisory Stephen Longley said.
But the ability to keep construction projects moving remains dependent on funding.
"The extension gives us the time needed to progress projects towards completion but that outcome remains dependent on securing further lender support to maintain critical central functions at Bathla," Mr Longley said.
"Locking in this funding is therefore an immediate priority and discussions are continuing."
Longer-term funding still not secured
Teneo has secured $4.7 million in initial funding and is continuing talks with lenders over longer-term support for active construction projects and the shared costs of keeping Bathla's operations running.
Six lenders are currently providing the initial funding, while discussions are ongoing with other financiers that could potentially join the arrangement.
The funding talks come as administrators continue to work out the financial position of the group.
There are about $3.4 billion in currently known consolidated creditor claims.
That includes approximately $3.08 billion claimed by secured lenders and $145 million owed to the Australian Taxation Office.
It is also understood it includes about $48 million to private lenders and $110 million to other unsecured creditors, subject to ongoing reconciliation.
Untangling Bathla's financial records
The ABC understands Teneo's review to date has found the group's bank accounts had not been reconciled for some time, while its records may contain about $736 million in overstated inter-company receivables and payables, subject to reconciliation.
Key planning, design and construction information is also understood to be spread across different systems, staff email accounts, network drives and hard-copy records, rather than held in a single central repository, and reviewing these books could take many months.
A preliminary review has identified about 219 current projects carrying approximately $3.13 billion in debt, against a preliminary total value of about $4.87 billion, with figures subject to ongoing review.
Hundreds of properties face different outcomes
The ABC understands about $400 million worth of completed property is currently for sale or under contract.
It is expected that sale proceeds would initially be applied against secured lending, with any further amounts available to the individual Bathla companies, dependent on the outcome of those sales.
Across projects under construction, about a quarter of the lots are already subject to pre-sale contracts, while three-quarters remain available for sale.
It is understood administrators' preliminary assessment also identified about 167 undeveloped sites forming part of Bathla's land bank.
About 30 per cent are expected to be marketed for sale in their existing condition, while the strategy for the remaining 70 per cent is yet to be determined.

Poland issues air attack warning for eastern regions near Ukraine border
Air raid sirens sounded in major eastern Polish cities and military aircraft were scrambled on Thursday as authorities issued an urgent air attack warning for regions bordering Ukraine.
Poland's Government Security Centre (RCB) broadcast an emergency mobile alert to residents across the eastern and south-eastern Lubelskie and Podkarpackie provinces. The warning ordered civilians to immediately find a safe place, follow emergency services' instructions, and await further official updates. The security alert remains in effect until further notice.
Local authorities confirmed that air raid sirens were activated in the regional capitals of Lublin and Rzeszow shortly after the broadcast.
Lieutenant Colonel Jacek Goryszewski, spokesperson for Poland's Armed Forces Operational Command (DORSZ), confirmed that military radar tracked the fast-moving unmanned aerial vehicle heading directly towards Polish territory."We are still verifying data from our systems, but initial indications suggest the drone either struck its target or was neutralised four kilometres on the other side of the border, inside Ukraine," Goryszewski told PAP.
He added that the exceptional speed of the jet-powered drone necessitated the immediate scrambling of Polish and allied fighter aircraft to protect domestic airspace.
The Polish Air Navigation Services Agency (PANSA) announced on X that airports in Rzeszow and Lublin had halted all flights to grant total freedom of movement to military aircraft operating in the area. Rzeszow-Jasionka Airport serves as a vital international logistics hub for Western aid entering Ukraine.
The emergency measures followed an earlier statement from DORSZ which announced that Polish and allied military aircraft had commenced operations in domestic airspace. The deployment was triggered by massive Russian strikes using jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles targeting western Ukraine.
Military officials said that the deployment is a preventative measure aimed at securing and protecting Polish airspace, particularly in areas adjacent to the threatened border zones. The Operational Command added that it is actively monitoring the situation and that all response forces remain on high alert for immediate reaction.
Early on Thursday afternoon, DORSZ confirmed that military aviation operations were concluded after Russian drone strikes targeting western Ukraine subsided.
"No violation of Polish airspace was recorded," the Command wrote on X. The resolution allowed PANSA to fully resume commercial and civilian flight operations at Lublin and Rzeszow airports.
Simultaneously, RCB officially lifted the air attack warning.
Military officials said that while the immediate threat has passed, forces continue to monitor the border region closely as part of ongoing preventative defence measures. (PAP)
