Democrats lead in polls, Republicans pour in millions. Can money turn US midterms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:21:02 UTC
03:21:02 KST

Washington, DC — Voting in the US midterm elections has started 46 days before Election Day, with Democrats ahead in the polls and Republicans ahead in ad spending.
Campaigns are calling it the home stretch.
David Levine, a law professor at the University of California, doubts the money will matter much. “I think that in this year, large amounts of PAC (Political Action Committee) money may not be all that effective,” he told TRT World.
Voters “get saturated with advertisements,” and “the marginal returns will be minimal in most places.”
Early voting opened in Virginia on Friday, and voters in Idaho, Minnesota and South Dakota can cast absentee ballots in person.
Republican candidates and groups have reserved more than $557 million in advertising in the nine most competitive Senate races, against $343 million for Democrats, according to an NPR analysis of data from the tracking firm AdImpact.
Three Trump-aligned groups, among them the MAGA Inc. super PAC, added more than $150 million in reservations over the past two weeks.
A super PAC can raise unlimited sums as long as it acts independently of a campaign.
The US Supreme Court also opened more room for party spending in June, ruling 6-3 that limits on how much a party can spend in coordination with its candidates violate the First Amendment.
The polls point the other way.
A Marquette Law School survey released on Wednesday found 54 percent of likely voters backing a Democrat for Congress and 41 percent a Republican.
President Donald Trump’s approval hovers around 37 percent.
Prices over ads
The reason sits in the checkout line.
Marquette found inflation and the cost of living the top concern for 37 percent of Americans, and only 19 percent approve of Trump’s handling of it.
Grocery bills are higher than six months ago, say 81 percent. Gasoline prices have climbed since the war with Iran began on February 28, say 80 percent.
Levine ties those prices to Trump’s tariffs and the war with Iran, and says many voters have already made up their minds.
“A late surge in advertising may not move the needle,” he says, especially if the ads try to convince voters that things are wonderful while gas station signs say otherwise.
Votes already cast
Levine expects a big surge in early and mail voting from people “eager to express their opposition to administration policies.”
Voters excited by candidates such as Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, may be among the first at the polls. That blunts late advertising, he says, “because those votes will already have been cast.”
The US Senate has 100 members. Republicans currently hold 53 seats and Democrats hold 47, counting two independents who vote with them.
Democrats need a net gain of four for a majority. At 50-50, Vice President JD Vance would break ties for Republicans.
The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, lists seven Senate races as toss-ups: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. Five are Republican-held.
On Tuesday, Cook moved New Hampshire, where Democratic Representative Chris Pappas faces former senator John Sununu, from lean Democratic to toss-up.
Texas pits Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, against Democratic state Representative James Talarico. Ohio has Senator Jon Husted against former Senator Sherrod Brown.
In Maine, Senator Susan Collins is seeking a sixth term against Troy Jackson, a former state Senate president.
Democrats must win in several states Trump carried in 2024, including Texas, Ohio, Alaska, and Iowa, while holding Georgia, Michigan, and New Hampshire.
The House is the shorter climb: Republicans hold 218 seats to the Democrats’ 214, with one independent and two vacancies.
Experts say redistricting does not change national generic-ballot polls. It changes how those votes turn into House seats.
Mid-decade maps in Texas, California, Florida, Ohio and several other states moved about 35 million people into new districts and gave Republicans a net structural estimated edge of roughly two to six seats versus the 2024 map.
Texas and Florida added Republican-leaning seats; California offset much of that with Democratic-leaning seats.
Democrats therefore need a larger popular-vote margin than a bare majority to take the House, though current leads of seven to eight points still put them ahead in most forecasts.
Other factors that can still move the numbers in the next six weeks include gas prices and inflation data, developments in the Iran war, the makeup of early and mail voters, candidate-level events in toss-up Senate and House races, and turnout gaps among younger voters, Hispanics, and independents.
Late-cycle tightening or polling error also remain possible.
David N. Gibbs, a professor of history at the University of Arizona, expects the usual midterm penalty for the party in the White House.
Republicans, he says, “will almost certainly continue this trend and will lose Congressional seats.”
He points to a “poor state of the economy” and warns that “the Republican losses in Congress could be even greater than current polls suggest.”

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China registered robust growth in foreign direct investment (FDI) in high-tech industries during the first eight months of the year, despite a decline in overall inflows, official data showed on Friday.
During this period, FDI in high-tech industries surged 35.1 percent to 200.26 billion yuan (about 29.66 billion U.S. dollars), accounting for 41.7 percent of the national total, a rise of 12.4 percentage points from a year earlier, the Ministry of Commerce said.
A total of 42,582 new foreign-invested enterprises were set up, an increase of 0.3 percent year on year, while FDI in actual use came in at 479.95 billion yuan, down 5.3 percent from the previous year.
By sector, the manufacturing industry attracted 119.55 billion yuan in FDI, while the service sector drew 350.42 billion yuan.
Specifically, FDI in R&D and design services, services for the commercialization of sci-tech achievements, and electronic and telecommunications equipment manufacturing jumped 74 percent, 64.2 percent and 41.9 percent, respectively.
The rising ability to attract foreign investment in high-tech industries reflects a fundamental shift in the factors driving China's appeal to global capital -- from "cost-driven" to "innovation-driven," said Zhang Xiaotao, director of the International Investment Research Center at the Central University of Finance and Economics.
Zhang attributed this increasing appeal to high-caliber R&D talent, complete industrial supporting facilities and efficient supply chains, as well as China's efforts in cultivating emerging industries.
According to a national conference on advanced manufacturing held in Beijing on Wednesday and Thursday, China must treat the development of advanced manufacturing as a major strategic task, and press steadily to boost its strength in manufacturing.
Next-generation intelligent manufacturing should serve as the primary direction, with greater emphasis on digital and intelligent empowerment, high-end manufacturing and self-reliance, green and low-carbon development, and cross-sector integration, it added.
Additionally, in June, China unveiled a 15-measure action plan to stabilize and optimize foreign investment utilization, focusing on expanding market access, streamlining investment procedures, boosting investment promotion, strengthening services and safeguards for foreign investors, and improving foreign capital management.
A new version of the Catalog of Encouraged Industries for Foreign Investment, which took effect on Feb. 1 this year, aims to steer more foreign capital into advanced manufacturing, modern services, high-tech industries, energy conservation and environmental protection, as well as into the central, western and northeastern regions of the country.
During the first eight months of 2026, actual investment from France, Switzerland and the Republic of Korea (ROK) grew by 39.2 percent, 16.7 percent and 16.5 percent, respectively, with investment via free ports included in these calculations.
This year has seen frequent investment moves by foreign companies in China's high-end manufacturing sector. Semiconductor equipment maker STI from the ROK is building a semiconductor manufacturing base in Guangzhou in south China, with a total investment of approximately 12.4 billion yuan, while German automotive parts giant Schaeffler is pouring an additional 1 billion yuan into a humanoid robotics factory in east China's Jiangsu Province.
Chen Jianwei, a professor at the University of International Business and Economics, said that multinationals are confirming the irreplaceable position of the Chinese market in the global value chain with substantial investment.
"It is expected that the proportion of foreign investment in high-tech industries will continue to rise, with R&D centers and regional headquarters accelerating their aggregation in China," he added. ■

====================================================================================================

News Analysis: Regional tensions put Saudi oil exports under pressure, rattle global energy markets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
02:17:22 CST
03:17:22 KST

RIYADH, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Escalating tensions across the Middle East are increasingly weighing on Saudi Arabia, one of the world's largest oil exporters.
As the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict continues to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, growing hostilities between Yemen's Houthi group and Saudi Arabia are also threatening Riyadh's oil export routes through the Red Sea, putting mounting pressure on Saudi Arabia's oil sector.
EASTERN ROUTE: HORMUZ TRAFFIC REMAINS SUBDUED
Like other major oil-exporting countries in the region, Saudi Arabia has traditionally shipped its crude oil from eastern ports into the Gulf and then through the Strait of Hormuz to international markets.
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), an average of about 20 million barrels per day of crude oil and petroleum products passed through the Strait of Hormuz in 2025, accounting for roughly one quarter of global seaborne oil trade.
Since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran in February, Iran has effectively restricted traffic through the strait. The vital route remains far from normal to this day.
Recent data from maritime analytics firm Kpler highlights that only a handful of commodity-carrying vessels pass through the waterway daily, with a complete absence of Very Large Crude Carriers and Liquefied Natural Gas tankers on multiple days.
To mitigate the impact of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia had begun exploring alternative export routes, including the East-West Pipeline, which transports oil to Yanbu Port on the Red Sea coast of western Saudi Arabia for shipment through the Red Sea.
WESTERN ROUTE: A "SAFETY VALVE" BECOMES A RISK POINT
However, Saudi Arabia's alternative western route for oil exports has also come under increasing constraints as the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement has intensified.
Accusing Saudi Arabia of violating areas under their control in Yemen, the Houthis announced on July 20 a maritime ban on Saudi vessels transiting the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The group subsequently claimed to have carried out attacks on Saudi vessels passing through the strait.
As the conflict between the two sides intensified, the Houthis began launching attacks against targets inside Saudi Arabia, including oil facilities.
The Saudi Ministry of Energy said on Sept. 11 that the East-West pipeline had come under multiple attacks in the Riyadh and Madinah regions, causing injuries. The pipeline was subsequently shut down as a precaution.
Analysts noted that the pipeline had previously served as a strategic "safety valve" for Saudi Arabia but had itself become a vulnerable point in the oil supply chain.
As of Sept. 16, Saudi authorities had not announced an official timetable for restarting the pipeline.
U.S. officials have suggested that flows could resume within "days," while Reuters reported that full repairs might take five to six weeks. Goldman Sachs said market estimates for the repair period ranged from a relatively quick recovery to as long as about eight weeks.
The more significant impact of such attacks was their effect on confidence in global oil markets. Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia could alter investors' assessments of the severity and duration of the conflict.
LONG-LASTING REPERCUSSIONS
Pressure on both of Saudi Arabia's major crude export routes has already begun to spill over into physical oil trading.
At the same time, the inventory "buffer" that has helped the global crude market absorb supply shocks is being eroded, shifting market attention toward when the entire supply chain, from oil fields and pipelines to storage facilities, ports and international shipping lanes, can return to stability.
IEA data showed that global observed oil inventories fell by another 95 million barrels in August. Since the end of February, inventories have declined by a cumulative 507 million barrels, equivalent to an average draw of roughly 2.8 million barrels per day.
Adam Ritchie, chief economist at Shell Trading, said in Oslo on Wednesday that since the escalation of the Middle East conflict, the global market had lost about 1.6 billion barrels of crude oil and condensates as well as roughly 36 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas supplies.
Rising transportation costs are adding to the pressure.
Paul Bradshaw, a director at Emirates National Oil Company, said that cargo insurance costs for some vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz had risen to 5 to 6 percent of cargo value, while additional war-risk premiums could reach as high as 10 percent.
Anders Opedal, chief executive officer of Norwegian energy company Equinor, said that if Middle Eastern supplies remain disrupted for an extended period, tighter energy markets and sharp price volatility could persist longer. ■

First-ever orthodontic treatment restores giant panda's normal bite in China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
02:17:10 CST
03:17:10 KST

CHENGDU, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese specialists have successfully corrected a giant panda's crooked jaw using an orthodontic technique adapted from human treatment, in the first such procedure performed on this species.
The treatment, jointly carried out by the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding and West China Hospital of Stomatology, restored the panda's ability to bite and chew normally. Related research was published in July in The Angle Orthodontist, a leading international orthodontic journal.
Beixia, a male giant panda born in 2022, suffered a jaw injury shortly after birth. By around three months old, his lower jaw had begun to deviate to the left, causing milk to leak from his mouth and raising concerns that he could eventually struggle to chew bamboo, which posed a serious threat to his survival.
With Beixia's jaw still developing, veterinarians and orthodontists decided to use the panda's natural growth potential to correct the asymmetry. They digitally scanned his mouth and designed a customized fixed appliance, with three orthodontic elastic bands to apply gentle traction and guide the jaw toward more symmetrical growth.
Long Hu, an orthodontist at West China Hospital of Stomatology, said it was the first time a growth-modification technique used in human orthodontics had been applied to a giant panda.
"Little was known about jaw development in giant pandas, but for Beixia's health, we decided to take on the challenge," Long said.
The treatment lasted about six months. The bands were removed before each feeding and put back afterward. At first, Beixia would push at them with his tongue or paw at his mouth, requiring caregivers to watch closely to prevent the bands from coming loose or being swallowed.
Follow-up examinations showed that Beixia's jaw deviation had largely been corrected, and normal sucking, chewing and swallowing functions had been restored. Now four years old, he can eat normally and remains active and playful.
The treatment reflects increasingly refined veterinary care for China's captive giant panda population, which reached 808 by the end of 2025.
The panda base also plans to establish more systematic oral health records for giant pandas and further advance research and clinical applications in panda dentistry.
"What we aim for is not simply an increase in numbers, but a steady, sustainable, high-quality growth of the panda population," said Wu Honglin, deputy director of the Shenshuping base of the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda. ■

China's trade in goods rose 17.6 percent year on year to 34.8 trillion yuan (about 5.15 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first eight months of 2026, with exports up 14.6 percent and imports increasing by 22 percent.
Zhang said China's foreign trade has shown stronger momentum in innovation and continued structural upgrading this year, trends also reflected at the Canton Fair.
Among the exhibitors, more than 11,000 are high-quality enterprises, including those that use specialized and sophisticated technologies to produce novel and unique products and those that hold leading positions in specific manufacturing segments, Zhang noted.
Roughly 64 percent of exhibitors use new technologies such as the industrial internet and artificial intelligence (AI), while new and green products will account for 23.2 percent and 26 percent of exhibits, respectively, with both shares reaching record highs.
This year's fair will further enhance its digital and intelligent operations by integrating technologies like AI and big data throughout the exhibition process, said Zhang.
It will introduce 22 smart application scenarios and 16 AI applications for the first time, and will be the first in China's exhibition industry to provide booth-level navigation across the entire venue and augmented reality displays of booth information.
Foreign trade companies are increasingly shifting from simply securing orders and selling products to building business systems and improving services. This year's fair will for the first time cover 10 categories of producer services in its trade services section, and 36.5 percent of exhibitors have shifted to a "product plus service" model, Zhang revealed.
More than 210,000 overseas buyers have so far completed pre-registration for this year's fair, with more expected to register as the opening date approaches.
This year marks the 70th anniversary of the Canton Fair, which has expanded from 9,600 square meters of exhibition space and 1,200 buyers at its inaugural session to 1.55 million square meters and around 310,000 buyers today.
The changing mix of products at the fair reflects the evolution of China's industrial structure. Agricultural and specialty products, handicrafts, textiles and light industrial goods featured prominently in its earlier years, before mechanical and electrical products became the fair's largest product category for the first time at its 86th session in 1999.
Today, the fair features products ranging from consumer electronics to new energy storage products, embodied intelligence products and smart medical equipment, with many cutting-edge Chinese-made products making their debuts at the event.
The Canton Fair has also served as a platform for Chinese foreign trade companies to enter and expand in international markets. From 1965 to 1979, annual exports generated through the fair accounted for more than 30 percent of China's total exports, exceeding 50 percent in some years, Zhang said.
Today, participating companies account for approximately 5 percent of China's foreign trade enterprises but contribute 16 percent of the country's general trade exports, according to Zhang.
Beyond securing orders, the fair also brings together the latest global market demand, consumer preferences, industry trends, product standards and application scenarios, Zhang said. ■

South Sudan remains central to one of the region's largest displacement crises, with more than 2.3 million South Sudanese living as refugees in neighboring countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, and Sudan, according to the UNHCR. ■

Fact Check: False video alleges Berlin votes destroyed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:15:00 UTC
03:15:00 KST

Fact Check: False video alleges Berlin votes destroyed
September 18, 2026
Berliners will vote in state and district elections on September 20. In the days leading up to the vote, a video circulated on social media that allegedly shows a man opening postal voting envelopes and destroying ballots cast for the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD).
DW Fact check reviewed more than a dozen posts sharing the footage. The posts use similar captions, presenting the video as evidence of election fraud in Germany. Several have amassed hundreds of thousands of views on X.
How widely has the video spread? And is its reach driven by genuine public interest? Or is something else boosting its visibility? DW Fact check investigated the video and the accounts sharing it.
Claim: A video shows a man destroying AfD ballots in Berlin with a carpet knife.
One post sharing the footage claims:
"A video circulating in Berlin shows a man opening mail-in voting envelopes and destroying ballots marked for the AfD, while ballots for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU are left intact. The footage appeared days after the AfD's landslide victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Berlin holds its state election on September 20."
The post had received about 327,000 views when DW Fact Check reviewed it on September 18.
DW Fact check: False
At first glance, the ballot paper appears authentic. Its names and layout match those of the official ballot paper for the Spandau 2 constituency in western Berlin, which is publicly available online. However, there are several inconsistencies in the documents shown in the video.
Berlin's state returning officer, Stephan Bröchler, told DW that the documents shown in the video are not authentic election papers from Berlin.
Bröchler said the envelopes shown in the video did not match the official ones used for this election. Bröchler also noted that the way the envelopes are sealed appears suspicious.
According to official guidelines issued by Berlin's election authorities, postal voters receive a voting package containing a "Wahlschein," or a voter declaration that needs to be signed, plus two envelopes and the ballot papers for the elections. For the September 20 vote, Berliners receive two ballot papers: a grey-and-blue ballot for the election to the city-state House of Representatives and an orange ballot for their District Assembly.
In the video, however, the documents do not correspond to the official postal voting package. The person in the video opens a red envelope and removes a white envelope. The signed voter declaration is missing. Without it, a mail-in ballot would be invalid.
The person then takes out only the grey-and-blue ballot paper for the Berlin House of Representatives from the white envelope.
Although voters may choose to vote in only one of the two elections, it would be unusual for three envelopes in succession to contain only one ballot paper. However, the footage does not clearly show whether the second envelope is really empty.
Another detail raises doubts about the video's authenticity: In the background, large grey bins allegedly containing postal ballots are marked with a version of Berlin's coat of arms featuring the Berlin bear.
Bröchler said such features were not used by Berlin's election authorities.
"Marking the ballot boxes with a Berlin bear is also unknown and uncommon here," he said.
Bröchler's conclusion is clear: "It can be ruled out that any actual Berlin election documents are involved. The video is clearly intended to discredit postal voting."
Has the video really gone viral?
One of the accounts that shared the video has previously come under scrutiny. An investigation by the Lithuania-based research organization Debunk linked the account to the so-called "Sprinter" network, a group of X accounts. The researchers identified what they described as signs of coordinated and inauthentic activity, including unusually high posting volumes, frequent account renaming and evidence of purchased followers. Debunk said the network was used to amplify pro-Kremlin narratives.
DW Fact check reviewed more than 15 other posts sharing the footage, many of them using nearly identical captions. Together, the posts had accumulated more than 3.2 million views by the time DW Fact check examined them.
The accounts sharing the video also showed several suspicious characteristics. Almost all of the 15 accounts examined exhibited at least one sign of potentially inauthentic behavior, including rapid follower growth, frequent username changes or limited evidence of normal user engagement.
One account, which presented itself as an independent media company based in West Asia, had more than 43,000 followers despite having been created only in April 2026. During that period, the account changed its username nine times.
On their own, these characteristics do not prove that the accounts are coordinated or that the video's engagement was entirely artificially generated. They do, however, show that the video's apparent reach should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of widespread, organic discussion on X.
A pattern seen before
The video resembles other false election-related claims that have circulated about Germany in recent months.
Ahead of the September 6 election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, DW Fact check examined a video that similarly purported to show AfD postal ballots being destroyed. The claim was false.
Among other inconsistencies, all three crossed-out ballots shown in the footage carried the same name on the signed voter declaration. The envelopes had already been opened, and the ballots lacked a hole punch required for use with voting templates designed for blind and visually impaired voters.
DW Fact check has also investigated and debunked numerous other false claims targeting Germany's postal voting system.
Julia Smirnova, who investigates influence operations as a researcher at the Berlin-based Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), told DW that these similarities, together with the way the new video is being disseminated, indicate that it is "highly likely" to be part of the Storm-1516 influence operation.
German security authorities and researchers have attributed Storm-1516 to Russia.
The operation has previously used fabricated videos, forged documents and purported eyewitness accounts to spread false narratives about elections and other political issues.
In February 2025, Germany's Interior Ministry said it had indications that two fake videos alleging manipulation of AfD ballots were connected to the Storm 1516 campaign, citing similarities in their content and distribution.

====================================================================================================

‘Leave no one behind’: how IDF paratroopers abducted Jordanian Legionnaires to free a comrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:12:33 UTC
03:12:33 KST

Long before “leave no one behind” became one of the most enduring ideas associated with the IDF, a wounded paratrooper lying alone beyond the armistice line helped create one of the stories behind that ethos.
His name was Yitzhak Gibli, better known to his comrades as “Little Gibli.” After he was wounded during a 1954 reprisal raid and captured by Jordan, some of the best-known figures of Israel’s early military history began planning a remarkable series of operations with one objective: seize enough Jordanian soldiers and police officers to help bring their comrade home.
The episode became part of the Paratroopers Brigade’s mythology, a story involving a dangerous raid, a soldier who demanded that his friends abandon him to save themselves, covert abduction plans and, ultimately, a prisoner exchange.
‘Little’ only in name
Gibli was born in Egypt in 1930. His mother died when he was young, his father became ill and he grew up in difficult circumstances. At 16, he falsified his age and joined the Palmach. After the War of Independence, he served in Unit 101 and later the IDF’s 890th Paratroopers Battalion.
The nickname “Little Gibli” was used to distinguish him from Binyamin Gibli, who headed Military Intelligence at the time. His fellow soldiers, however, described a fighter who was anything but slight in character. He volunteered readily and regarded figures including Ariel Sharon, Meir Har-Zion and Aharon Davidi as his military family.
On June 27, 1954, infiltrators from Jordan killed Meir Reiner near Ra’anana. The following day, seven soldiers from the 890th Battalion set out on a reprisal operation against an Arab Legion camp near the village of Azzun, east of Qalqilya.
The mission was codenamed Baruch 1. According to operational documents, its goal was to kill three to five Legion soldiers.
Gibli left the bedside of his sick father to take part. In an interview published in the IDF magazine Bamahane in 1963, he recalled that his father asked him to return quickly and bring him fruit. It was the last request his father made of him.
‘Leave me here’
The force crossed the armistice line and came under fire. The paratroopers charged the position, entered the camp and killed two guards. During the firefight, Gibli was struck in the head and leg.
His comrades treated his wounds and carried him for about 1.5 kilometers. But as Jordanian forces drew closer, it became clear that continuing to carry him could put the entire group at risk.
Gibli told them to leave him beside the road.
According to his later account, he even kicked at his comrades with his healthy leg until they agreed.
They removed his rifle and grenades, reasoning that a wounded, unarmed soldier had a better chance of surviving capture. The men embraced him and continued their withdrawal.
Ariel Sharon’s subsequent debrief recorded the decision in stark terms: the wounded soldier had been carried until it was no longer possible to take him farther.
Gibli would later receive a military commendation for continuing to fight after he was wounded and for insisting that his comrades leave him rather than endanger themselves. In 1973, the citation was converted into the Medal of Courage, one of the IDF’s highest decorations.
Singing to be captured
Left alone, Gibli smoked a cigarette, listened to jackals and thought about his father.
Fearing he might bleed to death before anyone found him, he began singing a Palmach song in an attempt to attract attention.
Soon he heard voices approaching.
Gibli later said roughly a dozen Jordanian Legionnaires rushed toward him. He shouted in Arabic that he was unarmed, but one soldier shot him again. A Jordanian officer stopped the incident, and Gibli was taken to a hospital before being transferred to prison in Zarqa.
The version initially presented to the Israeli public was that an IDF force had crossed the border by mistake.
Behind closed doors, Prime Minister Moshe Sharett and Defense Minister Pinhas Lavon knew what had happened. Four days after the raid, Lavon praised the fighters at a Cabinet meeting, including the decision to leave the wounded Gibli behind.
At the same time, the military began searching for a way to get him back.
‘Gibli Yitzhak to freedom’
The effort was given a name: GIL, a Hebrew acronym for “Gibli Yitzhak to freedom.”
Around that mission gathered men who would become some of the best-known names in Israeli military history, among them Sharon, Har-Zion, Davidi, Rehavam Ze’evi, Motta Gur and Saadia Elkayam.
The idea was straightforward: if Jordan held one Israeli paratrooper, Israel would acquire enough Jordanian Legionnaires and police officers to create bargaining power for his release.
An order for GIL 1, issued by Ze’evi on July 6, called for Jordanian officers and soldiers to be lured into Israeli territory and captured without gunfire.
One plan involved announcing that two Arab infiltrators had been caught and would be returned through UN officers and Israeli police. Sharon was to disguise himself as a UN officer, while other soldiers would pose as police. An IDF jeep was even painted white.
Accounts later differed over whether the attempted deception succeeded or merely aroused the suspicions of a Jordanian officer. What is clear from the surviving documentation is that the plan was drawn up.
GIL 2 followed on July 29. This time, the written objective was explicit: force the Arab Legion to return the captive Israeli soldier by abducting a Legionnaire or policeman from the Rumana area and bringing him back alive.
The order warned of the possibility of a diplomatic complication and described the operation as “semi-military.”
At the end of August came GIL 3, near Khirbet Sikha. Again, the soldiers were instructed not to open fire and not to cross the armistice line.
According to documentation published years later, Israel eventually held as many as 10 Jordanians who were intended to strengthen its hand in negotiations.
Bringing Gibli home
Eventually, the strategy produced the desired result.
Gibli was released in a prisoner exchange following efforts led by then-IDF chief of staff Moshe Dayan. In return, the Jordanians held by Israel were sent back to the kingdom.
Gibli crossed into Israel through Jerusalem’s Mandelbaum Gate and was welcomed with a celebration in an orchard near Bnei Brak.
Dayan awarded him a commendation, which was later converted into the Medal of Courage.
Gibli died in November 2008 at age 78.

Found Associations explores the café as a material ecosystem
For Paris Design Week 2026, four Latvian designers and artists partnered with Kalve Coffee to explore the café as a small-scale material ecosystem, where by-products generated through everyday consumption become starting points for new forms of production. The project brings together biodesign and circular economy principles through a connected chain of material experiments, turning the café into both a source of materials and a laboratory for their transformation. Three substances generated through the café’s daily operation, used coffee grounds, dirty water, and excess foamed milk, move through a series of treatment and production stages. The output of one experiment becomes the input for the next, creating a continuous chain in which materials change their function and form.
continuous material chain links consumption and production
The connections between the individual processes form the central structure of Found Associations. Instead of presenting the materials as separate experiments, the project links them through a sequence in which each process provides material for the next. Low-tech techniques are combined with laboratory-based methods, demonstrating different approaches to transforming the by-products of café consumption. The exhibition’s title, Found Associations, refers to the need to create new interpretations when working with excess materials. The project considers not only their visual and sensory qualities, but also the language traditionally used to describe discarded materials. By looking beyond the familiar category of ‘waste,’ the designers examine how these substances can acquire different functions and material identities.
Found Associations presents the café as an experimental model of circular economy, connecting consumption directly with production. Coffee grounds become a filter, milk becomes an adhesive, and water becomes a spatial material, establishing the café itself as a setting for continuous material experimentation and new associations.

Ukraine’s ‘Operation Vivaldi’ pushed Russian forces back around Lyman in the Donbas. Now both armies are massing troops for the next battles farther south.
Unknown

2026-09-18
18:10:03 UTC

Ukraine’s ‘Operation Vivaldi’ pushed Russian forces back around Lyman in the Donbas. Now both armies are massing troops for the next battles farther south.
Andriy Biletsky, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, said this week that his units are successfully carrying out Operation “Vivaldi.” The first of its four phases, he said, is nearing completion: Russian units near the town of Lyman, which had been trying to push through to the Siverskyi Donets River opposite Sloviansk, have been driven back across the Chornyi Zherebets River, a tributary of the Siverskyi Donets. Judging by published footage, the situation for Russian forces has indeed deteriorated as a result of a Ukrainian offensive that has lasted several months. There is still no confirmation, however, that Ukrainian forces have pushed the Russians back across the Chornyi Zherebets.
Meduza has condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine from the very start, and we are committed to reporting objectively on a war we firmly oppose. Join Meduza in its mission to challenge the Kremlin’s censorship with the truth. Donate today.
Lyman
- Russian troops — the 20th Army — crossed the Chornyi Zherebets near Makiivka in early 2025, and that summer the 25th Army crossed farther south, near Torske. Since then, the two armies have been trying to break through to Lyman from the north and east. In early summer 2026, they assaulted the town and failed. That was the high point of the Russian offensive. 20th Army assault troops were spotted on the outskirts of Sviatohirsk, penetrated 10–12 kilometers behind Ukrainian lines as far as the Oskil River, and even crossed the Siverskyi Donets with a small force near Pryshyb, east of Sviatohirsk, while the 25th Army entered Lyman and tried to fight its way through to the crossings south of the town.
- But that was also the moment the 3rd Corps launched its counteroffensive. By July, Russian troops had been driven out of Lyman except for its southeastern edge. Ukrainian forces then went on the offensive in other sectors: against the 20th Army’s northern flank near Karpivka and Ridkodub, against its southern flank near Yarova, and from the “pocket” near Stavky against the junction between the 20th and 25th Armies.
- In early September, Russian President Vladimir Putin unexpectedly said Russian forces had captured Sviatohirsk. He could not have picked a worse moment: that was precisely when 20th Army troops were falling back from the forests east of Sviatohirsk and elsewhere along the front.
- By the time Biletsky spoke, published footage had confirmed Ukrainian advances near Yarova and Novoselivka; from the Ridkodub and Karpivka area to the village of Serednie; and from the “pocket” at Stavky and from Lyman, advancing behind the 20th Army’s lines around Kolodiazi and as far as the outskirts of Zarichne on the Chornyi Zherebets River.
- Russia’s 25th Army, meanwhile, still holds positions near Lyman. Whether it also still holds Zelena Dolyna and Shandryholove is unclear. No visual confirmation has emerged that Ukrainian forces have reached the Chornyi Zherebets or crossed it, as some unofficial Ukrainian sources claim.
- Biletsky did not describe the plans for the next phases of the offensive. A few weeks ago, he was given a new post: he now commands not only the corps but also the newly created “Center” operational-tactical group, which is meant to defend Sloviansk and neighboring Kramatorsk against a Russian advance from the north and east.
- Ukrainian forces may well try to use counterattacks to halt a Russian advance that poses a far greater operational threat: the push along the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets toward Mykolaivka and in the area of the Siverskyi Donets–Donbas canal toward the eastern outskirts of Druzhkivka and the southern outskirts of Kramatorsk. In recent days, Ukrainian units reinforced by the 46th Airmobile Brigade, which previously fought where the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Donetsk regions meet, and by at least one assault regiment, have been trying to counterattack near Rai-Oleksandrivka, southeast of Mykolaivka.
The Russian offensive on Druzhkivka and Dobropillia
- The Russian command appears to have realized that the troops advancing on the Sloviansk–Kramatorsk urban area cannot succeed with the forces they have. The Russian force trying to break through to Druzhkivka from the west along the Kazennyi Torets River has been reinforced with units of the 90th Tank Division and the 41st Combined Arms Army, which had spent more than a year fighting where the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Donetsk regions meet — including against Ukraine’s 46th Brigade, which has also been transferred to the center of the Donbas.
- The reinforced Russian force pushed several kilometers toward the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk road and advanced to the outskirts of Druzhkivka.
- Some of the troops that had been attacking in the sector between Dobropillia and Druzhkivka, meanwhile, were given a new task: to increase the pressure on Dobropillia from the east. Another Russian force launched an offensive aimed at outflanking Dobropillia from the southwest. So far, though, these Russian attacks have not produced any decisive gains.
- Both sides are clearly preparing for a fall and winter campaign and for heavy fighting southwest and southeast of Kramatorsk, and they are massing forces in the central Donbas accordingly.
Orikhiv and Mala Tokmachka
- Russian forces have captured Mala Tokmachka, a village that became a meme more for its name than for its operational significance. To document the capture, the Russian command arranged extensive aerial filming showing troops raising Russian flags throughout the village. Yet judging by footage published by the Ukrainian military, the front has already moved several kilometers northwest of Mala Tokmachka.
- Mala Tokmachka fell not because of the efforts of Russia’s 70th Motorized Rifle Regiment, which had been fighting for it for years, but because of the rapid advance of neighboring units. Russian troops from the “Dnepr” Group of Forces pushed through Novodanylivka to the outskirts of Orikhiv — a local Ukrainian stronghold that anchors Ukraine’s entire defense in the central Zaporizhzhia region. Another large Russian formation, the “Vostok” Group of Forces, advancing from the direction of Huliaipole, reached the Orikhiv–Novomykolaivka road despite months of Ukrainian counterattacks, getting behind Ukraine’s 118th Mechanized Brigade, which had been defending Mala Tokmachka. After that, the village became impossible to hold.
- The Ukrainian position around Orikhiv keeps deteriorating. The Russian command has committed forces from one of its air assault divisions southwest of the town, with the clear intention of outflanking it from the west as well. That division had previously been deployed on the bank of the Dnipro south of Zaporizhzhia, near the settlement of Stepnohirsk. Ukrainian forces counterattacked at Stepnohirsk and in the surrounding area over the summer. Even then, there was speculation that this had become possible because the Russian paratroopers had left for an unidentified sector of the front. Now they have “surfaced” near Orikhiv, just as Russian forces are mounting a decisive push on the town.

Russia systematically uses cognitive tools not only against Ukraine but also against its allies, Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said at the Cognitive Influence and Resilience Forum.

According to the minister, Russia systematically uses cognitive tools not only against Ukraine but also against its allies. The aggressor state flexibly adapts hostile narratives to the specific characteristics of particular societies. In particular, it exploits political divisions in Europe and the United States, manipulates historical memories of colonialism and the Soviet legacy in Africa, Asia, and the Middle East, as well as distrust of the West in Latin American countries.

Cognitive influence, the minister noted, is also aimed at emotional exhaustion and spreading fear. According to the head of the foreign ministry, over the years of full-scale war, Ukraine has gained significant experience in countering cognitive threats and, at the same time, has shifted to proactive measures – in particular, in shaping its own international positioning.
"We have changed the perception of our state. The world recognizes Ukraine's new role – as a security partner. Not a supplicant, but a provider of security," the minister said.
Sybiha said an important component of a state's cognitive capacity is its ability to engage with foreign societies, build trust, and shape its own agenda. Ukrainian diplomacy plays a special role in this. According to the foreign minister, diplomatic missions operate directly within the environments where decisions regarding Ukraine are made. They serve as a platform for setting the agenda, building trust, engaging with foreign societies, and representing Ukraine abroad.
"A modern diplomatic mission is no longer merely a channel for conveying an official position. It is the state's sensory organ, which must understand the local environment and promptly identify changes, risks, and opportunities. That is precisely why developing the cognitive capacity of diplomacy is not merely a matter of communications. It is a matter of our ability to understand the world in which we operate and to effectively defend Ukrainian interests," the minister said.
He also highlighted the strategic importance of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' updated Communications Strategy for 2026-2030. The document establishes external communications not merely as a tool for informing the public, but as an integral component of national resilience. The strategy introduces the concept of cognitive influence into professional discourse and envisions a coordinating role for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the field of external communication.
Finally, Sybiha emphasized the need for proactive and asymmetric measures in cognitive confrontation – primarily the use of creative approaches and ridiculing the aggressor.

====================================================================================================

Israel tore itself apart on Yom Kippur - then October 7 reminded us of our collective 'we'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:06:29 UTC
03:06:29 KST

It is a Yom Kippur that will long be etched in Israel’s collective memory.
No, not October 1973, when two Arab armies staged a savage surprise attack on the holiest day of the Jewish calendar, triggering the 19-day Yom Kippur War that cost the lives of 2,691 soldiers. That this day will always be etched in the Jewish consciousness goes without saying.
There is another one as well: the Yom Kippur of 2023, just 13 days before the brutal surprise attack of October 7 – on Simchat Torah.
The Yom Kippur when Israel turned against itself
That was the Yom Kippur when Jews were pitted against Jews over the erection of a makeshift mechitza (partition) in Tel Aviv’s Dizengoff Square and other public spaces throughout the country.
Prayer books were thrown into the Dizengoff fountain, tallitot (prayer shawls) were thrown to the ground, and the somber Kol Nidre service was disrupted by the sound of shrill whistles and secular protesters shouting “Shame, shame.”
Scuffles broke out between those who came to pray and those who came to protest Orthodox prayer in a public space, in contravention of a High Court ruling.
Some wept at the scene; others wept when they saw pictures of it days later.
Had we lost it?
Yom Kippur 2023 will be remembered as a symbol of a nation at the brink – unwilling to compromise and intolerant of one another. It was also a Yom Kippur that Hamas head Yahya Sinwar saw, and he could only have been encouraged by the spectacle of Israel tearing itself apart.
To an enemy waiting to pounce, a nation whose citizens were at one another’s throats must have looked like a nation incapable of rallying together against a mortal threat.
Yet it did.
That Yom Kippur will always stand as tragic proof that when we tear ourselves apart from within – and there is no greater manifestation of that than physically fighting over a mechitza on Yom Kippur – we leave ourselves dangerously exposed to enemies from without. So obsessed with finding fault in one another, we ignored the wolf at the gates.
The High Holy Days are times of reflection and introspection, of looking inward, correcting one’s path, and mending one’s own faults. The anger and hatred that burst forth on that Yom Kippur came from finding fault not with oneself but with one’s neighbor and from having neither the patience nor the tolerance to hear the other side out.
If ever there were a day meant to disabuse us of our own infallibility, it is Yom Kippur.
“We have sinned, we have acted treacherously, we have robbed, we have spoken slander,” Jews say over and over on this day, followed by the recitation of a long litany of sins: “For the sin we have sinned before You under duress or of free will and for the sin we have sinned before You in hardness of heart.”
And on and on and on – a testament to our infinite fallibility.
Yet on that Yom Kippur of 2023, and throughout the angry days, weeks, and months that preceded it, each of the warring camps in the judicial reform debate was convinced of its own infallibility and the absolute righteousness of its cause – a certainty that brooked no room for compromise and allowed little, if any, understanding of the fears and concerns of the other side.
And it led to machzorim being tossed into water fountains and tallitot strewn on the ground. And much, much worse.
October 7 reminded Israel that there is only ‘we’
SOME WILL say that we learned nothing, that Israeli society has completely failed to internalize the lesson, and that we are right back at one another’s throats just as we were then.
The same certitudes. The same absence of doubt. The same absolutism. The same portrayal of ideological rivals as enemies.
But that is not the whole picture.
This impression is caused, to a certain extent, by the fact that we are in an election season. Elections the world over do not exactly bring out the best in people; on the contrary, they amplify their worst instincts. They create a political incentive to sow divisions, pit “them” against “us,” and paint every policy debate in catastrophic colors.
That is exactly what some politicians on both sides are doing now. It is to be expected. But during an election campaign, the bitter, divisive rhetoric of leaders does not necessarily reflect the sentiments of those they hope to lead – or the quieter, more measured mood of the country.
October 7 did change things.
It forced a recognition that however deeply we differ, our fate is shared.
Today – as always – political debates are fierce, and the shrillest voices attract the most attention. But beneath the noise lies a basic understanding that our political rivals are not our enemies and that the real threat remains beyond our borders.
Israel’s airwaves over the last three years have been tragically filled with interviews with wounded soldiers, bereaved wives, mothers, and fathers, released hostages, and relatives of hostages who never made it home alive.
Across those heart-wrenching interviews, one recurring theme emerges: A nation whose sons and daughters – religious and secular, from the Right and the Left – sleep together in the same tent in Syria, fight together in the same tank in Lebanon, patrol together in the same jeep in the West Bank, and clear the same tunnels in Gaza should be able to find a way to live together in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv without tearing itself apart.
We should be worthy of their sacrifice, goes the standard response to those stories of heroism and selflessness.
Those soldiers are the antithesis of the “us vs them” attitude so prevalent on that Yom Kippur three years ago.
Instead, they embody the collective “we” that runs throughout the Yom Kippur liturgy: “We have sinned, we have betrayed, we have robbed…”
The liturgy, like those stories, leaves no room for “us” and “them.”
There is only “we.”

Authorities imposed an overnight curfew in Nigeria's central city of Minna on Friday after security forces opened fire as hundreds of people took to the streets to protest against the deaths of 37 detainees in the custody of a paramilitary force.
The victims - many of whom were children - were found dead on Thursday in the cells of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which had raided suspected illegal gold mines and locked up dozens of miners in the city, the capital of Niger State.
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ordered an investigation into the deaths after his government earlier suspended some senior officials. But anger over the incident led to clashes overnight and into Friday.
As the start of curfew approached at 6 p.m. (1700 GMT), security forces had restored order to the streets of Minna. They had earlier fired live rounds as protesters - some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles - called for justice. A Reuters witness saw one body on the ground.
"We are not thieves. We are simply seeking a way to make a living by mining," Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters.
Some protesters had tried to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighborhood.
Niger State Governor Umar Bago said many of the dead were children, aged 14 to 18, who had been working in the mines instead of going to school. "There are issues of illegal mining, and it is taking a toll on our children," he said.
Investigation promised, bodies already buried
The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on September 15 to 16 in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. It initially said a suspected disease outbreak may have been involved in their deaths, but later said the cause of death had not been established and would be determined by medical examinations.
Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo ordered the immediate suspension of Niger State's NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of a full investigation.
"It is an unfortunate incident; however, a full investigation will be conducted while the commandant under whose watch this happened remains suspended," the Interior Ministry said in a statement.
The victims were buried late on Thursday in accordance with Islamic tradition, raising questions about if or how authorities would carry out further forensic examinations to determine the cause of death.
'We will not forgive them'
The mother of one of the detainees, Shafa'atu Suleiman, told Reuters outside the hospital on Thursday that she had visited her son Abdullahi in detention and found him in a cramped NSCDC cell, before later learning that he had died.
Officials had refused to allow relatives to deliver food to the detainees and demanded 100,000 naira ($75) for them to be freed, she said.
"This is injustice. We will not forgive them."
NSCDC officials did not respond to multiple requests for comment on her accusations.
Nigeria has tried for years to curb unauthorized mining at thousands of informal sites that operate across the country. The authorities say illegal mining damages the environment and leads to losses of government revenue.

Judging by his spread on the top floor of the building, curated by Ronny Carny, the prize was well-earned. He clearly has a penchant for color – striking, bright, rich hues at that – and is adept at presenting them in compelling ways.
Indeed, the Osnat Mozes Painting Prize committee members noted Rosenberg’s ability to explore the formal transformations of painting with deep sensitivity, precision, and a playful approach.
Notwithstanding the seemingly free-flowing line of aesthetic attack, Rosenberg says his approach to the visual bottom line takes on plenty of corporeal, definitively tactile elements en route.
“These works may give the impression of being very organized and tight, and my works look very graphic and neat. But my method is much wilder. In my studio, and in my life, I feel there is a lot of room for playing around with material, unfettered ideas, working outside in gardening and welding, and things that come from very different worlds.”
That, indeed, provides fascinating insight into the person behind the exhibited end product, and some of the subtext to his cerebral roaming.
“All of that brings me ideas I can use in my work, at home and in my studio,” Rosenberg explains. Each to his own, naturally, and, as they say, if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.
There is very little of the recognizable real world – as we generally know it – in Rosenberg’s paintings. That said, the images don’t require much clarification. There are grid shapes, excerpts of what appear to be latticed windows, and the odd meandering worm-like design that could reference anything going on.
Yet it doesn’t come across as overly abstract. Everything seems to be rooted in a user-friendly, readily accessible world. That makes the works even more alluring and attractive, even without the compelling color, form combos, and intriguing layering.
The Osnat Mozes award jurors also succinctly discerned that Rosenberg’s works “focus heavily on the relationship between the flat surface of a canvas and its capacity to generate visual illusions, balancing serious, painstaking inquiry with self-aware humor.”
Rosenberg goes along with the yin-yang observation of his creative machinations and what they deliver on his canvases.
“I don’t always search for an image,” he notes. “Often, what is more important to me is the confluence between the materials and the colors, the contrasts.”
That much is obvious from his collection at Artists’ House, with the former coming through in his use of rust in a couple of works. That adds substance and a softly abrasive dimension to the otherwise smooth outer layer, as well as enriching the palette purview, per se.
There is something of a balancing act across all the works of various ilks. Seemingly disparate color fusions produce an oxymoronic effect rather than dissonance; clearly defined shapes and shades reconcile with comfort, as do the straight-laced and tongue-in-cheek parts, and the stratified and more two-dimensional aesthetics.
Existential themes
It comes as no surprise to learn that October 7, 2023, themes, and subsequent regional altercations, feature prominently in the work of some of the artists in the season opener.
The violence and repeated existential threats that appear to be our lot in this part of the world are core to Orit Livne’s portfolio.
A cluster of postcard-sized paintings form part of her War Diary venture: “There were originally 40, corresponding to the 40 days of the war with Iran,” she explains. Her modestly proportioned slot on the middle floor at Artists’ House allowed room for just half of her thematic output.
“I started on this on the first day of that war,” she adds. It was very much a here-and-now project. “The plan was to make one small painting each day, to complete it and not touch it again. Then I’d do another one [on the morrow].”
Livne strays into spiritual realms when I ask about the numerical element: “The children of Israel wandered in the desert for 40 years, and the standard duration of quarantine is 40 days. Suddenly, 40 became an important number, with depth and meaning.”
She might have added that on his first ascent up Mount Sinai, Moses spent 40 days and 40 nights on the peak as God passed the Ten Commandments to humankind.
The small works start with a layer of oil paint, after which Livne erases parts with rags soaked in turpentine.
That process of reduction spawned imaginary scenes that gradually gave way to a more visually brighter view, suggesting a glimmer of better things to come shimmering just over the horizon.
Diminishing the initial color application, for Livne, follows a philosophical take on life: “For me, erasure and reduction are a very important procedure. It is a sort of anti-material approach.”
Her threesome on the upper floor, gleaned from her far larger Meanwhile series, follows the same technique: applying a top layer and painstakingly chipping away at it to produce unexpected nuances of form and shade.
As you spend time with the red-hued works, you begin to discern fetching floral shapes that emerge from the backdrop.
For this venture, Livne also used thinned paint that underscores the diminishing dynamic and conversely helps delineate the spectral figures of the flowers.
The images have a dream-like quality that seems to draw on the past and allude to fading memory.
Innocence reclaimed
On a far brighter, tender, life-affirming note, Julia Aronson’s Horizon drawing series takes us back to where we all began, and the most innocent and trusting phase of our existence on terra firma.
Her set takes a minute or two to work out, as the drawings initially conjure up thoughts of gently undulating terrain or something far more abstract.
The thematic scene gradually emerges as you note a baby’s head, from very close up, and the juxtaposition of the soft, pillowy flesh belonging to two human entities.
The infant’s mouth is secured to its mother’s nipple as it latches onto its only source of life-giving nutrition. It is the most intimate of pairings, as they bask in a symbiosis of complete dependence and unconditional loving communion.
“That is my last baby,” says the 46-year-old mother of three. “I am not going to have any more children, so I wanted to document it.” She managed that with gusto and abundant maternal love.
Many artistic presentations warrant a zoom-in, zoom-out viewing tactic to appreciate the technical minutiae that make up the whole. Horizon takes that to a completely different level.
The snapshot of babe and breast recurs across the group of drawings, from different angles and perspectives. If you take a more graphic approach, you may home in on the dispassionate details.
That, of course, is an important aspect of the aesthetic composition, but the spectator experience is immeasurably enhanced when you note that a small shaded spot is, in fact, a baby’s nostril.
There is a paradoxically fragmented continuum to the aligned frames that pull you this way and that as you try to work out the lay of the land – in real geomorphological terms – as your brain tries to balance the figurative and the nebulous.
There is more in the way of uncompromising parental safeguarding and love going on in Elkana Levi’s oil painting triad.
Palette-wise, all three are dominated by shades of brown and olive green, a testament to the fact that he has spent much of the past three years in reserve military duty.
Levi pulls nary a punch in conveying the reality of his ludicrously imbalanced lifestyle, trying to find the time and emotional wherewithal to glean some comfort from his quotidian – supposedly normal – life between donning his khaki uniform, slinging his rifle across his shoulder, and heading off for yet another stint on the frontlines.
Noah’s Ark proffers a particularly touching scene in which Levi depicts himself in soldier garb, palpably at the end of his emotional and physical wits, slumped in a rocking chair.
He holds a toy Noah’s ark in one hand and a paintbrush in the other, with his infant daughter resting in his lap.
He looks exhausted, bewildered, and discombobulated by the never-ending seesaw logistics of his life, and appears to be unsure about what he should be doing away from the army.
Should he make the most of his downtime by getting back to his creative pursuit, or should he be doing his best to compensate his child for the long periods when she had to make do without her dad?
The constant disruptions to his personal life are also clearly displayed, albeit in a more abstract form, in another canvas he calls Still Life in Respite, which shows a crumpled plastic bag filled with sweaty, dusty uniforms.
And the large Untitled Soldier scene depicts a soldier bending over to tie his bootlaces. His rear end, unabashedly displayed front and center, evokes something almost post-human and conveys an air of despondency spawned by prolonged presence on the battlefield.
The paintings come from Levi’s self-explanatory series called Art in Respite. By definition, it has a documentary nature.
“When I paint realistic works, I document the moment I get back home – with my emotions and what I bring back from the army.”
It is a jarring point in time, and forms part of – in a probably unintentional curatorial juxtaposition with Livne’s postcard set – a wartime journal.
“I can see how I was at the time of each painting,” Levi says. “In that way I can also follow my own growth and development.”
Diverse yet unified
Nitsan Ben-Zimra’s installation-fashioned collection on the ground floor comprises diverse objects, aesthetics, and textures, yet imparts a feeling of continuity and cohesion.
The 30-year-old multidisciplinary artist makes optimal, intelligent use of the two rooms at her disposal in her We’ve Moved arrangement, displayed in a very physical structural sense.
A diminutive needle-and-plaster set fuses what looks like an unfurled roll of cloth, with needles tidily inserted, with the white plaster of the wall on which it is mounted.
The seamless edifice-artwork synthesis reappears in the second room where a metal plate, which has been subjected to some industrial-leaning treatment, with ostensibly peeling wallpaper or some other similar peripheral material, gives the impression of a substratum emerging as the whitewashed wall surface decays.
That is quite an optical trick, and Ben-Zimra is clearly blessed with sensitive and capable hands, as well as an eye for visual potential wherever she looks.
The large monochromatic ultra-blurry photograph which faces the so-called wall peeling item feeds off nocturnal urban sentiments and aesthetics the vast majority of us would miss – or dismiss – as uninteresting or even downright ugly.
The artistic bottom line is the result of a somewhat convoluted process: printing the image on thermal paper before transferring it to a much larger format, which heightens the grainy, fuzzy quality of the image, adding mystery and intrigue while accentuating the manifold linear mélange.
The works, which also include a long piece of rope hung vertically on one of the walls that tapers toward the floor, and a distinctly defunct office desk propped up at an improbable angle with drawers that can never be opened, straddle the fine line between reality and fantasy, and original purpose and reinvention.
All in all, that’s not a bad start to the Artists’ House new season and one which bodes well, at least in an artistic sense, for our continued existence in this part of the world.
The exhibitions close on November 7.
For more information: www.art.org.il

Yom Kippur 2026: The Jewish people are chosen - but not because they are better - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:06:05 UTC
03:06:05 KST

The High Holy Day prayer book contains many beautiful prayers that express basic Jewish values. I would like to discuss the prayer Ata Behartanu, which appears in the Amida of every service on the High Holy Days. It contains a concept that has been repeatedly misunderstood throughout the ages.
“You have chosen us among all peoples, loving us, wanting us. You have exalted us among all nations, making us holy through your commandments, drawing us close to Your service, and calling us by Your great and holy name.”
Indeed, this basic Jewish concept of the chosen people is found in many other places in the liturgy. Whoever is given an aliyah to the Torah recites the blessing “…Who has chosen us from among all the peoples,” and in the Shabbat and festival kiddush we say “…For you have chosen us and sanctified us from among all peoples.”
This concept did not originate in the siddur (prayer book). It’s already found in the Torah. Thus, we read, for example, in Exodus 19:5-6: “Now therefore if you… keep my covenant, then you shall be my own treasure from among all peoples… and you shall be unto me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.”
This idea is reiterated in Deuteronomy (7:6): “For you are a holy people unto the Lord your God: the Lord your God has chosen you to be his own treasure out of all the peoples that are on the face of the earth.”
Why the 'Chosen People' concept is attacked by so many non-Jews
Before we continue, let us turn for a moment to the detractors of the chosen people concept.
William Norman Ewer is reputed to have said: “How odd of God to choose the Jews,” and in 1939 Arnold Toynbee attacked this concept at length in his book A Study of History.
Indeed, the chosen people concept was also attacked by many Jews.
In 1911, Yosef Hayim Brenner wrote in his book Mikan Umikan: “With keen and passionate pleasure I would blot out from the prayer book of the Jew of our day ‘ki vanu vaharta,’ ‘You have chosen us,’ in every shape and form.”
In 1945, Rabbi Mordecai Kaplan carried out Brenner’s wish. In the Reconstructionist Sabbath Prayer Book, the blessing before the Torah was changed from “who has chosen us” to “who has brought us close to His service.”
On the other hand, there are some Jews today who understand this concept in the opposite direction. They think that because God chose us, we are better than non-Jews and may therefore mistreat them.
I believe that all these groups misunderstood the concept. To understand this concept, we must examine the verb “bahar,” meaning “to choose,” in the Tanach. It normally refers to God choosing a person or place for a specific task.
For example, in Deuteronomy (18:5), the priests are chosen to stand before God and serve him forever. In I Kings 8:16, God says that he chose King David to lead the Jewish people. In that same verse, God says that he chose Jerusalem to build the Temple there. And in Deuteronomy we are repeatedly told that God will choose a place to make His name dwell there.
Thus it is with the chosen people concept.
The four tasks Jews were chosen to carry out
THE JEWISH people were chosen for four specific tasks:
The first task is described in Isaiah 43 (v. 10, 12, 21): “You are my witnesses, says the Lord, and my servant whom I have chosen. That you may know and believe me and understand that I am He… The people which I formed for myself, that they might tell of my praise.” In other words, God chose us to teach the world about monotheism.
The second task of the chosen people is to observe the Torah and the mitzvot. As we read in Psalms (105:42-45): “For He remembered His holy word unto Abraham… and He brought forth His people with joy [from Egypt], His chosen ones with singing… that they might keep His statutes and observe his laws.”
The third task is described in Genesis 18:19. God chose Abraham “that he may command his children… to keep the way of the Lord, to do righteousness and justice.” When Jews lead the struggle for social justice, they are fulfilling this task.
The final task is described, once again, in Isaiah (49:3, 6): “And [God] said unto me: You are my servant Israel, in whom I will be glorified… I have also made you a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach the ends of the earth.”
Thus far we have seen that the Jewish people was chosen for four very specific tasks. Critics might still say that we wrote this in our Bible because we thought we were better than everyone else, while Jewish chauvinists might say that this proves that we are better than everyone else. My answer would be that the Torah itself tells us the opposite.
As we read in Deuteronomy (7:7-8): “It is not because you are the most numerous of peoples that the Lord set His heart on you and chose you – indeed, you are the smallest of peoples; but it was because the Lord loved you and kept the oath He made to your fathers that the Lord freed you with a mighty hand… from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.”
Until now, we have described a one-way process. God chose us to fulfill certain tasks, and our role was totally passive. But beginning with the Revelation at Mount Sinai, the Jewish people reciprocated – it chose God’s covenant, and it chose to do the mitzvot.
As we read in Exodus 19:8: “And the people replied together saying: everything which God said – we shall do.” And in Exodus 24:7, “Everything that God said, we shall do and we shall obey.”
This idea was expanded in the famous midrash that describes God as offering the Torah to all the nations of the Earth and each refused because they rejected one specific mitzvah, until God “came to Israel and said: Will you accept the Torah? They said: yes, yes! ‘Everything that God said, we shall do and we shall obey’” (Lamentations Rabbah, parasha 3, ed. Buber, fol. 62a).
That is why Israel Zangwill wrote 100 years ago: “A Chosen People is really a choosing people.” And Leon Roth replied to Ewer’s “how odd of God to choose the Jews” with, “It’s not so odd, the Jews chose God!”
Let us summarize what we have learned:
As we recite Ata Behartanu many times during the High Holy Days, let us remember that we were chosen out of God’s love, not because of our own special characteristics. And we have four tasks: to teach the world that there is one God; to observe His Torah and commandments; to do justice; and to be a light unto the nations.
I hope and pray that we and our leaders will take these tasks to heart in the year ahead.
The writer, a Conservative rabbi, is president emeritus of The Schechter Institutes in Jerusalem, where he serves as a professor of Talmud and Jewish law.

"Throughout the entire war, I haven't criticized anyone… But today I want to "thank" the former Chief of the General Staff and his electronic warfare chief for the fact that, over the past year, no one in the Ukrainian Armed Forces has systematically worked on technologies to counter mesh modems, and no one has shielded the capital with electronic warfare measures, while watching the enemy develop this technology. A mesh network is a decentralized computer network topology in which nodes connect directly to one another and act as switches. A large number of nodes creates multiple possible paths for data transmission, and one of the key properties of such a network is self-healing. At the same time, although a mesh network is more resilient than a centralized one, it is also vulnerable.
Later, Beskrestnov added in the comments: "As soon as I saw a mesh modem in the UAV, I bought two, tried to overload them with what I had, confirmed that it was possible, and shared my experience. From that moment on, we should have started conducting electronic warfare against mesh networks. A year ago."
