Saudi Aramco has told at least two European refining customers they will receive no crude oil next month following an attack on the kingdom’s key East-West pipeline, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
European refiners typically buy Saudi crude under contracts guaranteeing monthly supplies, but Aramco has informed customers that deliveries planned for next month will not proceed, according to the report.
Saudi Arabia had earlier warned European customers that some cargoes would be cancelled after drone attacks damaged three pumping stations, forcing the shutdown of the pipeline and disrupting oil loadings at the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
The disruption has prompted refiners to seek alternatives. Poland’s Orlen, for example, has bought North Sea crude to replace disrupted Saudi imports, according to traders cited by Reuters.
Reuters could not independently verify the Bloomberg report. Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Aramco is working to partially restart the pipeline within days and restore it to full capacity within six weeks, Bloomberg reported.
The company has also increased crude exports through the Gulf using ship-to-ship transfers off Oman’s Sohar port to offset reduced shipments through the Red Sea.
France calls for G7 energy meeting
The disruption comes as crude prices have risen about 20 percent this month amid the US-Iran conflict and fighting involving Houthi forces in Yemen.
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Friday that France would convene a G7 meeting on energy in the coming weeks to strengthen cooperation and discuss options for releasing strategic reserves.
“In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues,” Macron said.
The meeting would also provide an opportunity “to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves”, he added.
Macron said the surge in fuel prices was “not the result of government decisions” but a consequence of the geopolitical situation. He said existing support measures would be reviewed and adjusted to help households.
“Before spending vast sums of money, which is taxpayers’ money and would ultimately translate either into a higher deficit or higher taxes, we must above all remain focused on addressing the root causes,” Macron said.

Russia Increasingly Targeting Ukraine’s Railways, Threatening Economic, Social Security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:45:41 UTC
01:45:41 KST

Russia has continued to expand its campaign against Ukraine’s railway network, systematically targeting infrastructure that has become a lifeline for civilian travel and vital cargo transport as Ukrainian airspace remains closed.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 500 locomotives, with over half of those losses recorded over these eight months alone, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Tuesday, Sept. 15.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Currently, Ukraine’s state-owned railways are currently losing 37 to 40 locomotives a month, Politico reported.
“Strikes on Ukraine’s border crossings disrupt the delivery of foreign military aid through key transport and logistics hubs used by the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU,)” Russia’s Ministry of Defense said on Tuesday, claiming responsibility for a drone strike on the Yahodyn international border crossing in Volyn Oblast.
Russian drone tactics keep evolving
Russia increasingly relies on jet-powered drones, including the “Geran”-type, to conduct strikes on railway targets.
Such drones are more difficult to intercept due to their speed, which can reach up to 400-600 kilometers per hour (roughly 250-370 miles per hour).
Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, chairman of the management board at Ukrzaliznytsia – Ukraine’s state-owned railway operator – said Russia intensified its attacks on passenger trains after obtaining mesh-network antennas last fall.
EU Allocates €100B for Ukraine in 2028-34 Budget Plan
The technology enables drones to relay signals to one another or to connect to ground-based transmitters, allowing Russian operators to control them in real time and strike moving targets.
Russia has reportedly used these transmitters in occupied parts of Ukraine, as well as in Belarus.
On Sept. 13, Russian forces struck the Yahodyn railway station in Ukraine’s Volyn region, just four kilometers (roughly two miles) from the Polish border, in what may have been a deliberate strike on a train carrying diplomats.
The passengers included former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and European security advisers.
“The latest strikes near the Polish border show that their additional goal is to increase risks for our foreign guests, partners, diplomats, politicians and reporters... Russians want them also to be scared to travel to Ukraine,” Pertsovskyi told Politico.
Railway remains a lifeline
“Ukraine’s railway keeps the country moving,” Sybiha said, stressing that continued support from the country’s partners was needed to prevent a humanitarian crisis.
Ukraine’s dependence on rail has grown sharply due to civilian flights not operating in the country.
The railway remains central to evacuation of civilians from frontline areas, carrying humanitarian and commercial cargo, and moving grain and other critical goods across the country.
The same dependence makes it a strategically important target for Russia, as the railway remains central to Ukraine’s economic and social security.
“Russians aim to isolate our frontline communities, sow panic and fear among the already exhausted locals, paralyze the economy,” Pertsovskyi said.
According to Mykola Kalashnyk, Ukraine’s Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport, Russia has attacked Ukraine’s railway infrastructure at least 1,534 since the beginning of 2026.
The attacks have taken a toll on railway personnel. At least 52 employees of Ukrzaliznytsia have been killed on duty, and 317 others have been injured.
Each new locomotive costs about €5 million (roughly $5.7 million), but the pace of Russia’s destruction is outstripping Ukraine’s available financial resources, Pertsovskyi told Politico.
“We have reliable partners helping us with this, such as the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the World Bank,” he said.
Rather than the standard 1,435-millimeter (approximately 56 inches) gauge used across most European countries, Ukraine uses a 1,520 millimeter (roughly 60 inches), limiting the pool of stock that allies could transfer to Ukraine.
According to Politico, only the Baltic states and Finland use compatible equipment.
Sybiha has called on Ukraine’s partners to urgently assist the country in finding locomotives compatible with its rail gauge, while Lithuania separately pledged to send Ukraine new locomotives.
Meanwhile, Ukrzaliznytsia is developing contingency plans to protect passengers and preserve service when routes are interrupted by Russian attacks.
“We have various operational plans to balance safety, but we are certainly not considering a scenario where we stop,” Pertsovskyi said.
“Just as our country does not contemplate giving up the fight, the railway, naturally, does not contemplate halting its operations,” he continued.
Beyond the railways, Russia is also striking passenger buses.
On Thursday, a first-person-view (FPV) drone struck a passenger bus near a public transport stop in Zaporizhzhia’s Kosmichnyi district, injuring eight people.
A Russian drone struck a bus carrying passengers in the Nikopol district, killing five and injuring at least seven people on Wednesday.
Separately on Wednesday, Russian forces also attacked a Kyiv-Mykolaiv passenger train.

The Guardian view on youth unemployment: too few jobs in too many places | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:45:29 UTC
01:45:29 KST

The ideas that Neets (young people not in education, employment or training) simply aren’t trying hard enough to find a job, or don’t want one, are “myths,” Alan Milburn wrote in his interim report on the subject earlier this year – “sometimes cruel ones”. Although 84% of Neets say they want to work, their prospects are unfairly limited by where they live. Rotherham has one suitable vacancy for every 22 young adults. The Cotswolds has one for every four. For too many young people, particularly those in deprived parts of Britain, there simply aren’t enough jobs.
This is the finding from an index published last week by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), which ranked British towns according to the availability of jobs for young people. Like so many features of Britain’s Neet crisis, from poor mental health to school drop-out rates, the index is a map of disadvantage. At the top are affluent towns in southern England that account for nine in 10 of the areas with the highest numbers of vacancies. At the bottom are places such as Inverclyde and East Renfrewshire, where young people might once have followed their parents into manufacturing and industry. Deindustrialisation destroyed those jobs, and such places never recovered.
Given that half of the rise in Neets aged 18 to 24 since 2019 is due to changes in the labour market, jobs are a good place for the government to focus. In 2024, the Starmer government launched a “youth guarantee,” including a pilot jobs programme that provides six months’ paid work to 18 to 24-year-olds who have been receiving universal credit for 18 months. This was a positive step, but 18 months is far too long for young people to wait for support, and almost half of Neets don’t claim benefits, so aren’t eligible for this scheme.
The IPPR has called for the creation of a new “youth contract”, comprising short-term placements for all people at risk of becoming Neet in areas where jobs are scarce, more apprenticeships at the smaller firms that dominate Britain’s labour market, and more dedicated work coaches. These would all be improvements to the status quo. But if today’s young people are to find employment that will sustain them into adulthood, the government will need an industrial strategy capable of creating long-term opportunities in places where few exist.
The devolution of vocational training to local authorities, which are better placed to understand the demands of regional labour markets than Whitehall civil servants, is welcome. But ministers will need a dose of realism about where “good” jobs will come from. Andy Burnham’s talk of “reindustrialising” regions resembles a Westminster pipe dream. As manufacturing has developed, it has lost the ability to reliably create widespread employment. Even in the US and China, where governments have generously subsidised industry, manufacturing jobs continue to fall as a share of total employment.
As the economist Dani Rodrik recently observed in an essay collection about reindustrialisation, much of Britain’s future employment won’t be in manufacturing or high-productivity service sectors, but in industries such as retail, hospitality and care. If Mr Burnham wants to create “good growth in every postcode”, his government must transform the conditions of work in these industries so they provide gainful employment – and opportunities for today’s young people to build future careers.

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:59 UTC
01:38:59 KST

Sitting down with a cup of coffee is one of life’s simple pleasures. However, many people are not fully aware of the actual differences between different types of coffee beyond their names. For example, what exactly is espresso? Although the name may sound like “express,” it is more closely related to the Italian idea of coffee being “pressed out” under pressure. That, however, is only part of the story. What makes this more confusing is that all espresso is coffee, but not all coffee is espresso.
The differences largely come down to the type of roast and how the beans are ground and brewed. Espresso is the most concentrated form of coffee, made by forcing hot water through finely ground beans under high pressure. As a result, more flavor is extracted in a short time, creating a bold and concentrated drink. Espresso often carries hints of chocolate, caramel, or nuts. It also forms the base of many popular coffee drinks, including lattes, cappuccinos, and macchiatos.
Espresso lovers appreciate it for its strong flavor, thick texture, and distinctive crema — the thick, golden-brown layer of foam that forms on top of a freshly brewed shot. It adds a velvety texture and a slight bitterness that many enjoy. Since espresso takes only about 20 to 30 seconds to brew and is usually served in a 25- to 30- milliliter portion, it is ideal for those in a hurry. Even so, some people prefer to sip it slowly, showing that coffee is as much about personal experience as it is about preparation.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
坐下來喝一杯咖啡是人生中簡單的樂趣之一。然而，除了名稱之外，很多人並不完全了解不同咖啡種類之間的實際差異。例如，義式濃縮咖啡（espresso）究竟是什麼？雖然這個名字可能聽起來很像「快速（express）」，但它其實與義大利語中在壓力下「被擠出」的咖啡概念更為相關。然而，那只說對了一部分。更讓人感到困惑的是，所有的濃縮咖啡都是咖啡，但並非所有的咖啡都是濃縮咖啡。
這些差異主要在於烘焙種類，以及如何研磨與沖煮咖啡豆。濃縮咖啡是咖啡最濃縮的形式，它是透過高壓方式強行將熱水沖過磨成細粉的咖啡豆萃取而成。因此，在短時間內能萃取出更多風味，形成口感強烈且濃郁的飲品。濃縮咖啡通常帶有一點巧克力、焦糖或堅果的風味。它同時也是許多熱門咖啡飲品的基底，包括拿鐵、卡布奇諾以及瑪奇朵。
濃縮咖啡的愛好者喜愛它濃烈的風味、醇厚口感，以及獨特的咖脂（在新鮮萃取的濃縮咖啡上方形成的那層濃厚、金褐色的泡沫）。它增添了絲絨般的口感，以及許多人喜愛的微苦風味。由於濃縮咖啡只需約二十至三十秒即可沖煮完成，且通常以二十五至三十毫升的分量供應，因此非常適合趕時間的人。即便如此，有些人仍喜歡慢慢啜飲，這說明了咖啡的重點不只在於製作過程，更關乎個人的體驗感。
What Did You Learn?
1. What does the author mean by saying “all espresso is coffee, but not all coffee is espresso” in the first paragraph of the Day 1 passage?
(A) Espresso is one type of coffee, but coffee includes various types.
(B) Espresso and regular coffee are unrelated, but both are widely consumed.
(C) Espresso is made in a special way, while coffee is prepared in many ways.
(D) Espresso contains all kinds of ingredients, while coffee includes only one type.
2. Which feature of espresso helps create its smooth texture and slight bitterness?
(A) The coarse grounds used during brewing.
(B) The crema that forms on top of the drink.
(C) The paper filter that removes fine particles.
(D) The long brewing time that extracts flavors slowly.
答案：1. A 2. B
Words in Use
1. confusing a. 令人困惑的
The instructions were so confusing that Bill had to read them several times. 說明內容太令人困惑，比爾不得不讀好幾遍。
2. largely adv. 大部分
Andy’s success was largely due to his persistence.
安迪的成功主要歸功於他的堅持。
3. concentrated a. 濃縮的
The company produces concentrated fruit extracts that are used in a variety of beverages.
這家公司生產濃縮果汁萃取液，用於各種飲品中。
4. finely adv. 細緻地
The chef finely chopped the onions for the soup.
廚師把洋蔥切得非常細來做湯。
5. extract vt. 萃取，提煉
Scientists extract useful substances from plants to create new medicines.
科學家從植物中萃取有用物質來製作新藥。
Practical Phrases
1. be aware of. . . 了解∕知道……
Amy should be aware of the rules before joining the contest. 艾咪在參加比賽前應該要知道規則。

Many health problems are related to long-term stress and a lack of proper rest.
許多健康問題與長期壓力以及缺乏適當休息有關。

For Daniel, success comes down to daily practice.

This chair is ideal for those who sit for long hours at work. 這張椅子很適合需要長時間坐著工作的人。

Emma answered the question in a hurry, so she made a small mistake. 艾瑪匆忙作答，因此犯了一個小錯。

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday inspected joint precision missile live-fire drills at the Jioupeng Base (九鵬基地) in Pingtung County, where multiple types of attack drones took part in joint combat exercises for the first time.
The three-day drills, which concluded yesterday, featured indigenous Hsiung Feng III anti-ship missile systems, Tien Kung III surface-to-air missile systems and US M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems, footage released by the Presidential Office showed.
The drills were the first time multiple types of attack drones had been incorporated into joint combat exercises, Lai told military personnel.
Photo: AP via the Presidential Office
“The coordinated use of uncrewed vehicles and conventional weapons showed that the military is accelerating efforts to strengthen its overall combat capabilities,” Lai said. “It also demonstrated to the people and the international community that the armed forces have confidence in their ability to defend national sovereignty and fulfill their responsibility to maintain regional peace and stability.”
Units carried out joint air defense, counterstrike, sea-air coordination, coastal strikes and nearshore defense operations during the drills, he said, praising the personnel for their performance.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of National Defense said a Chinese military drone flew from Taiwan’s southwestern airspace to waters off Taitung between 12:05am and 6am yesterday morning to monitor the exercise.
As the timing coincided with Lai’s inspection of the exercise, the military closely monitored the drone and deployed aircraft, naval vessels and land-based missile systems, it said.
Lai has made defense modernization a key part of his agenda, given the rising threat from China, including by developing drones and spending more on defense, something US President Donald Trump has repeatedly pressed allies to do.
Lai yesterday was accompanied on his visit by Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄), other senior security officials and Ocean Affairs Council Minister Kuan Bi-ling (管碧玲), whose agency runs the Coast Guard Administration (CGA).
The government has been working to better integrate the CGA into overall defense planning, as it would have an auxiliary role to the navy in case of a war.
During the main annual war games last month, a coast guard ship was fitted with anti-ship missiles.
Separately yesterday, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰), while inspecting plans for the construction of new facilities for the Matsu Coast Guard Patrol Team, announced that in addition to improving compensation for six categories of CGA personnel, the government would also improve the agency’s equipment.
Next year, one 1,000-tonne patrol frigate, three 100-tonne patrol boats and six 35-tonne patrol boats would be deployed for maritime patrol and security operations, he said.
The government has also allocated NT$1.93 billion (US$60.68 million) to build a 2,000-tonne ocean-going patrol vessel, as well as NT$140 million to enhance special operations equipment, to improve the effectiveness of efforts to combat smuggling and human trafficking operations, he said.

US approves 48 F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia

01:38:58 KST

The US has approved a US$24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth warplanes to Saudi Arabia, the US Department of State said on Thursday, the kingdom’s latest major arms purchase since the start of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia has long sought to buy F-35s, but officials from Israel has voiced concern about their sale to Riyadh despite a push for the kingdom to normalize relations.
“The proposed sale will improve Saudi Arabia’s capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense, and improving interoperability with US forces,” the department said. “[It] will also augment Saudi Arabia’s operational aircraft and enhance its air-to-air, and air-to-ground self-defense capability.”
Photo: AFP
The Saudi Arabian embassy in Washington praised the transaction, saying it “reflects the strength and enduring nature” of the relationship with the US.
The security cooperation between the two countries “has contributed to regional stability, strengthened our collective defense capabilities, and advanced our shared security interests,” it added.
Saudi Arabia has been repeatedly targeted with drone and missile strikes by Tehran’s forces since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in February, and has also been hit by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Yemen’s civil war had been dormant for years, but fighting between Houthis and the internationally recognized, Riyadh-backed government reignited in July, with the rebels declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
Washington has not directly entered the conflict, but a US official said earlier this week that a US military task force is working to enhance intelligence sharing and planning assistance for Saudi Arabian forces.
The department has notified the US Congress about the proposed sale, which would require the approval of US lawmakers. It did not provide a time frame for the delivery of the jets.
The F-35 sale “will not alter the military balance in the region,” it said.
The US has so far only allowed the sales of F-35s to its closest allies, including a number of NATO allies and Israel.
The F-35 sale is the latest in a series of major arms buys by Saudi Arabia this year.
The department announced the approval of a US$5 billion sale of more than 10,000 bombs to Riyadh earlier this month.
Washington also signed off on the sale of 60 tank engines and related equipment to Saudi Arabia at a cost of US$750 million this month, and a US$1.96 billion deal in July for the kingdom to buy guidance sections that can convert rockets into precision weapons.

Fed staff should have known Silicon Valley Bank was vulnerable, new report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:56 UTC
01:38:56 KST

An outside review of the Federal Reserve's oversight of the failure of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023 has found the Fed's staff "knew, or should have known," that the bank was vulnerable prior to the crisis, Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said Friday.
Bowman's announcement of the report's findings immediately escalated political tensions around the Fed. The White House said the report implicated Fed Governor Michael Barr, who was appointed by President Joe Biden in 2022 and held Bowman's job as the Fed's top bank regulator during the banking crisis in 2023 that led to Silicon Valley Bank's failure.
Trump said this week the Fed's board is "hostile" after Chairman Kevin Warsh joined a unanimous vote of the Federal Open Market Committee to raise interest rates. Some in the Fed community have worried the report, which was being publicly undertaken, would be used as a pretext to push Barr off the board. Neither Trump nor Warsh made any immediate announcements to that effect.
The Fed's Board of Governors declined to comment on the report, beyond Bowman's comments. She announced the initial results of the review, by the consulting firm Starling Advisory Group, in a speech in London.
Starling didn't immediately respond to questions about whether it would release the full report. Bowman described the consulting firm's work as an initial report, but didn't say when or whether the public might see the full results of the inquiry.
Silicon Valley Bank experienced a run in March 2023 after the bank announced it had sold securities at a $1.8 billion loss and needed to raise more capital. The bank's large holdings of U.S. Treasurys had lost value after the Fed began raising interest rates.
The bank's customers included tech startups and venture capital firms. Many kept large sums on deposit at the bank, above the $250,000 threshold for deposit insurance. When the bank showed signs of strain, customers immediately sought to withdraw their funds, prompting a dramatic, fast-moving run on the bank.
The bank's deposits were "94 percent uninsured and concentrated in venture capital–backed technology companies," Bowman said the review found.
After the run, the heads of the Fed, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Treasury Department issued a joint statement saying they would insure all deposits in the bank, even those above the FDIC's $250,000 limit.
Barr was assigned to review of the episode in April 2023. The Fed's staff conducted an investigation that found its bank supervisors were overcautious in responding to the episode.
The new review largely concurs, according to Bowman's description. The outside firm found Fed supervisors knew, or should have known, about the risks in advance, Bowman said. The report does not identify Barr by name and instead attributes the failures to supervisory staff.
Barr stepped down from the supervisory position in February 2025 to allow President Donald Trump to select a new top regulator for the Fed. The president picked Bowman, who was confirmed by the Senate for that role.
Barr told the newsletter Capitol Account in July that he had agreed to cooperate with the new review.
White House spokesman Kush Desai charged that Barr "failed to do his job throughout this debacle, and then put out a report widely regarded as politicized and self-serving absolving himself of any blame. Everyday Americans, investors, and financial markets deserve competence and accountability in a Federal Reserve that keeps its eye on the ball."
A spokesperson for the Fed did not immediately respond to an email seeking a response to Bowman's comments and whether the Fed might release the Starling report itself.
Barr's review in 2023 had found the Fed had shifted its regulatory standards following a 2018 law. That change effectively reduced the Fed's standards, Barr said, and prompted "a less assertive supervisory approach."
The new outside review disagreed, Bowman said. "The delays in supervisory action were not caused by the regulatory tailoring mandate," she said.
Bowman has already begun a sweeping overhaul of the Fed's bank-oversight practices. She has said she plans to reduce the ranks of the Fed's supervision and regulation division by about 30%. An update to the Fed's staff page showed a dozen senior staff had left the division by early September, though some new staff had been added and others may be hired going forward.
The new review was a waste of taxpayer money, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, of Massachusetts, who is the ranking Democrat on the Senate banking committee, said in a statement following Bowman's comments.
"It's an embarrassing attempt to re-write history designed to pave the way for more dangerous deregulation that will lead to the next Silicon Valley Bank disaster," Warren said.
— Megan Cassella and Jeff Cox contributed to this report.

President attends quake drill in Taitung County
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:38:54 UTC
01:38:54 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday inspected a large-scale earthquake disaster response drill in eastern Taiwan that involved more than 150 international search-and-rescue and medical personnel.
“Disasters know no borders,” Lai said in remarks after the inspection, stressing the importance of conducting joint drills in peacetime to establish common procedures and coordination so that countries can mount more effective rescue operations when disasters strike.
The three-day event in Taitung County from Wednesday through yesterday was part of National Disaster Prevention Day exercises.
Photo: Liu Jen-wei, Taipei Times
Yesterday’s drill — simulating a magnitude 7.3 earthquake in the southern section of the East Longitudinal Valley — involved personnel from 11 countries.
American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene, Canadian Trade Office in Taipei Executive Director Marie-Louise Hannan and Swedish Representative to Taiwan Carl Michael Grans were among the foreign representatives at yesterday’s drill.
A “semi-notified, unscripted” format was used as participants responded to simulated damage to critical infrastructure and disruptions to external assistance.
The drill incorporated lessons from Typhoon Danas and the Mataian River (馬太鞍溪) barrier lake disaster in Hualien County last year, including arrangements for backup communications, as well as evacuations and shelters.
The government has expanded international disaster-response cooperation in the past few years, including cooperation between Taiwan and Germany on disaster prevention, humanitarian assistance and joint rescue operations, Lai said.
More than 177,000 people have been trained as disaster preparedness personnel, up from about 100,000 last year, he said.

Australia tightens visa rules, to detain tourists who overstay, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:53 UTC
01:38:53 KST

Australia will detain tourists who overstay visas to send a message of deterrence under new rules aimed at reducing levels of migration, a minister said yesterday.
Australia’s ruling Labor party has denied it is tightening visa rules in response to the rise of the far-right One Nation, which has become one of the country’s most popular parties this year with pledges to drastically slash migration.
Under reforms announced on Thursday, Australia would stop family members accompanying students, introduce ballots for working holiday makers and crack down on overstayers.
Photo: Reuters
Tourists would be put in immigration detention to reduce the level of visa overstayers, which has risen to 77,000, Australian Assistant Minister for Immigration Matt Thistlethwaite said.
“Once the word gets around, ‘Hey, I overstayed on my tourist visa for a couple of weeks, I got picked up and I spent a couple of weeks in immigration detention, it’s not a nice place, I’m going home.’ Once that gets around, then we think that obviously that deterrence will ensure that people abide by the conditions,” he said.
People who do not have the right to remain in Australia would face a “consequence” and be removed, he added.
Since 2015, Australia’s immigration detention centers have swelled with people with criminal convictions awaiting deportation after a policy change that saw mandatory cancelation of permanent visas for certain criminal offenses.
Australian Minister for Immigration and Citizenship Tony Burke, announcing the new policy on Thursday, said the government would open 250 beds and add 100 compliance officers to house the visa overstayers in different facilities.
Australian Tourism Industry Council CEO Erin McLeod said talk of detaining tourists was not good for Australia’s image.
“I don’t think it does our reputation as a welcoming destination any good and can become quite damaging — tourism is an important part of the Australian economy,” she said.
The council represents thousands of small tourism businesses.
Refugee Council of Australia director of policy Rebecca Eckard said the move raised safety and legal concerns.
“It is being framed as punitive to change behavior. The use of punitive detention is not permitted under Australia’s immigration act,” she said.
“There has been a major problem with immigration detention,” she added, pointing to concerns raised by the government ombudsman over insufficient staffing and healthcare access.

Tang Prize laureates honored ahead of today’s lectures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:52 UTC
01:38:52 KST

The six recipients of the seventh Tang Prize were honored at a ceremony in Taipei yesterday, ahead of a full day of lectures today featuring their award-winning work.
Five of the six laureates attended the ceremony at the Taipei Performing Arts Center to receive their awards in person. Steven A. Rosenberg, one of three recipients in the biopharmaceutical science category, was unable to travel to Taiwan, according to the Tang Prize Foundation.
During the ceremony, Tang Prize Selection Committee convener Wong Chi-huey (翁啟惠), a former president of Academia Sinica, and the chairs of the four category selection panels introduced the laureates and outlined their major contributions.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
The six recipients were announced by the prize’s selection committees in mid-June.
They are scheduled to deliver lectures at the Taipei Bioinnovation Park throughout Saturday, discussing the research and ideas they have developed over their careers.
American atmospheric chemist Susan Solomon received the Tang Prize in Sustainable Development for research that helped establish chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, as the primary cause of the expanding hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica.
Her work explained the chemical reactions behind ozone depletion and provided a scientific basis for global efforts to phase out CFCs under the Montreal Protocol.
The Tang Prize in Biopharmaceutical Science was jointly awarded to Rosenberg, Michel Sadelain and Carl H. June for developing cancer treatments that harness patients’ own immune cells.
Their work on tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies helped pioneer “living drugs,” in which immune cells are collected, enhanced or genetically modified, and returned to patients to attack cancer.
Chinese historian Ge Zhaoguang (葛兆光) received the Tang Prize in Sinology for his research on Chinese intellectual, cultural and religious history.
His influential studies exploring the question “What is China?” have challenged conventional historical perspectives and introduced new approaches to the study of China.
Yale University constitutional scholar Bruce Ackerman received the Tang Prize in Rule of Law for his work on constitutional government, judicial review and democratic institutions.
His ideas include “dualist democracy,” which distinguishes routine government decision-making from rare periods of broad public mobilization that bring about fundamental constitutional change.
The Tang Prize is a biennial award established in 2012 by Taiwanese entrepreneur Samuel Yin (尹衍樑) to recognize significant contributions in four fields: sustainable development, biopharmaceutical science, sinology and rule of law.

Rowing champions voice Brisbane venue concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Prominent Australian rowing figures have criticized the approval of Rockhampton’s crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River as the venue for the sport at the Brisbane Olympics, arguing the course would require extensive investment and leave little lasting legacy.
Worries about the venue initially focused on the 500 crocodiles that live in and around the river, but there are also concerns about the impact of river current on the fairness of competition and the lack of accommodation in the city of 80,000.
However, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli announced in state parliament on Thursday that an independent technical review had found the course capable of hosting fair rowing and canoeing competitions in 2032.
Photo: AP
Experienced coaches and former elite rowers remain unconvinced that a venue about 600km north of the host city is the best option.
“Without a massive infrastructure spend, it’s just going to be like a country regatta with Olympic athletes,” said former world championship medalist Andrew Butler, who has coached rowing for 17 years, including on the Fitzroy River.
“Why are you taking it 700km away from a multi-sport event when it’s obviously not to a better venue?”
Three-times Olympic champion Drew Ginn said he had concerns that water depth, river characteristics and the potential for flooding could all impact the competition.
“I row on a river in Melbourne. I love rowing on it, love training on it, but I’d never want to compete at the Olympic Games on it,” he said.
“If you have flowing and moving water, that is completely unfair,” Ginn said.
“One lane over another lane can be dramatically different. Imagine if [a flood] happens the week of the competition. Races get cancelled or the venue has to be moved,” he said.
“There’s never been a national championships held there, there’s a reason for that. It feels like it’s a gamble that the Queensland government’s taking,” he added.
Ginn also called for the technical review to be made public.
“If there’s good evidence for it and good data for it, then you should be able to make it transparent,” he said.
In a statement issued by Brisbane 2032 organizers on Thursday, World Rowing President Jean-Christophe Rolland was quoted as saying the venue could deliver fair competition, but unusually the body did not issue its own statement nor the report.
There was no immediate response from World Rowing to a request for comment on the technical endorsement.
In a short statement, Rowing Australia “acknowledged” the completion of the technical review while making it clear neither it nor Rowing Queensland had played any part in the process.
John Driessen, an Olympic rowing coach and former elite rower who has coached on the Fitzroy River, echoed Butler and Ginn’s concerns over the legacy of the venue.
“I’ve coached at Fitzroy and it worked really well. But turning it into an Olympic-class course, I would have thought would be quite expensive and difficult,” he said.
“There’d be a lot of money going into a spot where there’s no real guarantee that it would benefit the state of Queensland in the future.”
However, Driessen said he did not think the Fitzroy River course would necessarily lead to unfair competition.
“It’s quite a shallow course,” he said. “If they’re going to maintain the basic principles of a rowing course with depth and lack of flow, then I think it would be a challenge to achieve that. I’m not sure that if the course was run at Rockhampton, it would be that unfair in terms of lanes,” he added.
Driessen said hosting the Olympic rowing at Moreton Bay just north of Brisbane, the site favored by Rowing Queensland, was a “no-brainer” and “the simple answer.”
Butler favored the original plan to stage the rowing on flat water at Wyaralong Dam some 86km southwest of Brisbane, describing it as “probably the best course I’ve rowed on in Queensland.”
“Investment there would be an absolute legacy ticket,” said the twice Australian champion.
However, Crisafulli is determined that regional cities around Queensland should be able to share in the Olympic experience and has previously denounced critics as “elitist.”
“I thought the Olympics was a sporting event,” Butler said.

EDITORIAL: Protecting the participating society
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Taiwan ranked seventh worldwide for civil participation in The Global State of Democracy 2026: Democracy in an Age of Conflict report published on Tuesday by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance. The Stockholm-based intergovernmental organization, which has more than 30 member states, evaluates four characteristics of democracies: representation, rights, rule of law and participation.
Taiwan ranked far above its neighbors in the “participation” category, with South Korea 36th and Japan 60th. The category measures voter turnout and the strength of civil society, as well as participation in political and nonpolitical organizations.
Taiwan was up five places from a year earlier in “representation,” down one place in “rule of law” and unchanged in the other two. With 57 percent of the countries assessed declining in at least one measure of democratic performance, maintaining a high standard is no small feat. Yet one look at Taiwan’s history demonstrates why its ranking is not surprising.
Although the nation’s democracy is relatively young, it has been built upon decades of ordinary people taking action for social and political change. During the 1970s and 1980s, the dangwai (黨外, “outside the party”) movement challenged the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) political monopoly under martial law and pushed for greater political freedoms. Rights advocates, journalists, lawyers and ordinary citizens organized in spite of the risks, helping lay the groundwork for political liberalization.
In 1990, three years after martial law was lifted, thousands of students demanded the dissolution of the aging National Assembly, the repeal of the temporary provisions governing the country and a timetable for political liberalization. The rally, known as the Wild Lily student movement, accelerated constitutional reforms, including the retirement of the “10,000-year congress” and the introduction of direct presidential elections in 1996.
The tendency of Taiwanese society to organize and demand change did not end with democratization. In 2011, Japan’s Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear crisis gave new momentum to the anti-nuclear movement, prompting thousands to protest construction of the Fourth Nuclear Power Plant in New Taipei City’s Gongliao District (貢寮) and call for a reassessment of nuclear energy policy. Three years later, students and civic groups of the Sunflower movement occupied the Legislative Yuan over the government’s handling of a cross-strait trade agreement.
Last year, civic groups mobilized volunteers to collect signatures and trigger recall votes against KMT legislators. While all 24 recall votes failed, they drew an average turnout of more than 56 percent — much higher than the turnout typically seen in recall elections — demonstrating that voters on both sides of the political divide were motivated to take part.
Taiwan’s record of participation is not limited to politics. When devastating floods affected more than 1,600 homes in Hualien County’s Guangfu Township (光復) last year, tens of thousands of volunteers traveled from across the nation to help clear mud and debris, distribute food and supplies and assist residents in rebuilding their homes.
The same spirit is visible in nationwide urban resilience and air-defense drills, which have increasingly involved cooperation between local governments, businesses and residents. Whether disaster response or crisis preparedness, the efforts reflect a broad willingness among the public to take care of their communities.
Behind the long-standing culture of participation is a broader sense that society is something worth investing in and improving.
A 2021 Pew Research Center survey of 17 advanced economies asked people what made their lives meaningful, fulfilling and satisfying. While most cited factors such as family, jobs and material well-being, Taiwan was the only nation in which “society” ranked as the top source of meaning. It was also the only nation that ranked “freedom” in the top five.
Taiwanese pointed to the convenience and safety of daily life, affordable healthcare and the freedom provided by the nation’s democracy and rule of law. One woman said that she felt “fortunate to live in Taiwan, especially in the aspect of public health, democracy, and the rule of law and human rights, because it is very free.”
However, as much as Taiwanese value their free, safe and democratic society, they must also understand that it is not self-sustaining. It must be cultivated — especially as younger generations would face new challenges amid a rapidly changing political, technological and international landscape.
Taiwan’s ranking in the democracy report is much more than an impressive number. It represents decades of ordinary people dedicating their time to organize, volunteer, vote, protest and generate systemic change. That is something Taiwan should be proud of — and something worth protecting.
Taiwan’s domestic political situation is following recognizable political rhythms, while the international environment surrounding Taiwan is undergoing a major transformation. Within Taiwan, there are ongoing battles between the legislative and executive branches over the budget, and between cities and the central government over resources. Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

Green manufacturing in Vietnam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Taiwanese companies have been part of Vietnam’s manufacturing landscape since the 1990s. They have established a presence across sectors including electronics, textiles and materials.
However, the conditions for manufacturing are changing. Vietnam is pushing toward net zero emissions by 2050, while global companies are placing greater environmental demands on their suppliers.
For Vietnam, the green transition is becoming part of a broader challenge: How to remain competitive as the requirements of global manufacturing change.
That shift is important to Taiwanese companies already operating in Vietnam. Many supply global brands whose environmental requirements are becoming stricter. Apple, for example, requires its entire direct manufacturing supply chain to use 100 percent renewable electricity for Apple production before 2030. Last year, more than 20 gigawatts of renewable energy procured by suppliers and online in Apple’s supply chain generated more than 38 million megawatt-hours of clean energy.
Requirements like those do not stop at the headquarters of global brands. They reach the factories producing their components and products. For Taiwanese manufacturers in Vietnam, reducing emissions is gradually becoming a part of doing business. A competitive manufacturing location is no longer judged only by labor costs, infrastructure or access to markets. The availability of cleaner electricity is becoming part of the equation.
Vietnam is moving in that direction. Its revised Power Development Plan VIII, approved in April last year, targets renewable energy, excluding hydropower, at 28 to 36 percent of the power mix by 2030. The plan also places emphasis on developing the power system and grid to meet rising demand. Vietnam has also introduced a direct power purchase mechanism, allowing large electricity users to buy power directly from renewable-energy generators. The framework was updated in June.
However, for Taiwanese manufacturers, green electricity is only part of the issue: The power also has to be reliable. Vietnam’s electricity shortages in 2023 exposed the vulnerability of its rapidly expanding industrial base. In 2024, authorities asked major manufacturers in northern Vietnam, including Foxconn, to voluntarily reduce electricity use by 30 percent during periods of high demand. The request was precautionary rather than mandatory, but it highlighted a problem that matters to manufacturers operating in global supply chains: An interruption in electricity can quickly become an interruption in production.
This is where the interests of Vietnam and Taiwanese manufacturers begin to overlap. Vietnam needs to expand cleaner energy while making its electricity system more reliable. Taiwanese companies need a production base that can meet the environmental expectations of global customers without compromising the stability of their operations.
Some companies are already responding. Foxconn and Brookfield in June announced that they would jointly develop up to 1 gigawatt of utility-scale wind, solar and battery capacity in Vietnam, supported by long-term power-purchase agreements. The significance is not simply the size of the proposed investment. It points to a broader shift: Manufacturers are becoming more interested in the energy infrastructure around their factories, not just the factories themselves.
The same trend can be seen elsewhere in Taiwan’s manufacturing presence. Far Eastern New Century has been expanding renewable-energy use across its production network, including operations in Vietnam. Taiwanese manufacturer Je Hong Textile is developing a new factory in Vietnam focused on environmentally friendly fabrics, with features including wastewater treatment, LEED Gold standards and planned solar generation. Tainan Enterprises has also operated a LEED Gold-certified facility in Vietnam since 2017.
These examples do not mean that every Taiwanese factory in Vietnam is already green or that the transition will be easy — companies face different costs, technologies and regulatory conditions — but they show that Vietnam already has an established group of Taiwanese manufacturers with reasons to invest in cleaner production. That creates an opportunity to deepen the economic relationship.
Taiwan-Vietnam ties have long been shaped by trade, investment and manufacturing. The “China Plus One” strategy — avoiding a reliance solely on manufacturing and sourcing in China — has added to Vietnam’s importance as companies diversify production beyond China.
However, the next stage does not necessarily have to mean simply building more factories. Vietnam itself wants to attract investment that brings greater technology and value, while moving toward higher-value and more complex activities within global value chains. The World Bank has identified this as an important part of Vietnam’s longer-term development path.
Renewable electricity alone will not move Vietnam up the value chain. What it can do is help create the industrial conditions that increasingly matter to international manufacturers: cleaner production, more reliable power and the ability to meet tougher environmental standards. For Taiwanese companies, that makes Vietnam’s energy transition increasingly relevant to their own competitiveness. For Vietnam, it offers a way to improve an industrial base that is already closely connected to global production.
The foundations are already there. Taiwanese companies have spent decades building factories and production networks in Vietnam. Vietnam is now changing what it expects from its industrial economy. The next chapter of Taiwan-Vietnam economic cooperation might be less about how many factories are built and more about the conditions the factories operate in: cleaner energy, reliable electricity and an industrial environment that can meet increasingly demanding international standards.
For Vietnam, the task is to make the industrial base it has built over the decades greener and more competitive, while becoming better positioned in higher-value parts of global value chains.
Tran Thi Mong Tuyen is a research fellow at the Pacific Forum, a Rotary Scholar and a doctoral candidate at National Chengchi University. She is also a former fellow at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and a visiting academic at National Taiwan University.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung ruled out sending troops to the Strait of Hormuz to join the US war against Iran, despite pressure from US President Donald Trump, as Lee fights to reverse hemorrhaging public support and get his policy agenda back on track.
Lee has seen his approval ratings plunge in the past two months, hitting a fresh record low of 37 percent in a poll released yesterday — down from a high of 67 percent earlier this year. He faces strong domestic opposition to sending troops to the Middle East.
“There will be no involvement or intervention in the war,” Lee said during a snap news conference aimed at shoring up public support. “We will not deploy troops or military assets for that purpose. We have adhered to that principle so far, and that principle will remain unchanged.”
Photo: Bloomberg
The remarks were Seoul’s clearest message yet on deploying troops or military assets to the Middle East after Trump ramped up pressure on the US ally over its lack of support for the war with Iran.
South Korea is reviewing ways to help ensure safe passage through the strait by expanding the operations of its naval unit already deployed near the area, Lee said.
While the comments might please Lee’s base domestically, they might further fuel tension with key security partner Washington, Zeitgeist Institute director Eom Kyeong-young said.
“Just imagine how the US would feel hearing that,” Eom said, adding that more diplomatic language could have been helpful.
“He seemed to make those remarks with his core supporters in mind, but they looked problematic coming from a president,” Eom added.
At home, many South Koreans have soured on Lee over the economy. Even as the global artificial intelligence build-out reaps record profits for chip giants SK Hynix Inc and Samsung Electronics Co, voters are seeing little impact on their lives, with surveys highlighting growing discontent on issues such as Seoul’s high property prices.
Lee apologized “to the people who continue to struggle through their daily lives in difficult circumstances.”
He said he was “taken aback by what seemed to be a sudden wave of disappointment and concern from the public,” but added that “the people are always right.”
Lee ordered a sweeping reshuffle of his cabinet weeks ago, changing out his finance, defense and justice ministers among others, with his top policy adviser Kim Yong-beom stepping down.
The reset and shift in messaging have failed to boost Lee’s approval ratings.
“This is a crisis of trust. Voters are at a point where they don’t believe what he says, no matter what he says,” Eom said.
Lee has also been struggling to balance Seoul’s all-important relationship with security ally Washington, which stations about 28,500 soldiers in the South in part to help protect it from the nuclear-armed North.
Trump canceled long-planned joint military drills with Seoul last month, citing his friendship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Seoul’s purported refusal to help with Iran.

01:38:49 KST

At National Cheng Kung University, researchers began with magnets from discarded electric-vehicle motors supplied by a local recycler. They dissolved a one-gram sample and tested how to separate dysprosium, a valuable rare-earth metal, from neodymium and praseodymium.
A 2022 paper in Materials, by Chen Wei-sheng (陳偉聖), Jian Guo-cai (簡國財) and Lee Cheng-han (李政翰), demonstrated selective extraction. It also identified unfinished work, including multistage processing and regenerating the extraction liquid. The experiment established a technical foundation, without claiming an industrial business.
The government wants to turn such expertise into a more secure source of industrial materials. Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) announced in February a pilot production line within three years. Officials have separately set a 2030 goal of producing domestically half of an anticipated annual rare-earth requirement of about 2,000 tonnes.
Photo: AFP
Taiwan’s opening in a “non-red” (less dependent on China) supply chain, lies in specialized refining and recycling. Imported feedstock, a kind of raw material, could supplement recovered magnets. The commercial task is to turn that material into consistent products manufacturers want to buy.
FROM SEPARATION TO SALE
China’s dominance makes that work urgent. It accounted for 91 percent of refined magnet rare earths and 94 percent of sintered permanent-magnet production in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
Photo: Reuters
The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) has reported progress beyond separating individual elements. The institute told the Central News Agency (CNA) in November last year that researchers could produce rare-earth oxides and metals at 99.9 percent purity from resources containing about 5 percent rare earths. They had also formulated neodymium-iron-boron alloy and were testing materials with companies and universities.
ITRI planned technology transfer to industry this year. It also reported adapting waste-acid and wastewater-recycling techniques to reduce the processing burden. Continuous operation would still have to establish consistent quality and environmental performance at an acceptable cost.
An oxide, a metal and a finished magnet serve different customers. A purity figure alone cannot establish whether the output suits a particular application. Buyers need the appropriate composition and consistent performance, as well as sufficient volume.
Taiwan already has magnet manufacturers. Taigene Metal (台全金屬) describes a longstanding business producing rare-earth and ferrite magnets, with a factory in Taoyuan. Such manufacturers offer potential customers for local refiners, provided the new material meets their specifications.
Leo Chang (張永撙), vice president of UWin Nanotech, draws a similar distinction. His company’s precious-metal recovery technologies operate commercially. Its rare-earth recycling applications remain under development.
“From our perspective, Taiwan’s main constraint is not necessarily technical capability, but rather feedstock availability and overall economics,” he told the Taipei Times.
His proposed starting point is concentrated, valuable waste such as end-of-life permanent magnets. Recovering rare earths indiscriminately from discarded electronics would incur substantial collection and dismantling costs.
CAN THIS FEED THE PLANTS?
Published economic research supports examining each waste stream separately. An AIChE Journal study this year by Chris Laliwala of Carnegie Mellon University and colleagues modeled recovery from discarded permanent magnets. Electric-vehicle and hybrid-vehicle magnets could support profitable recovery under the study’s assumptions. Its hard-disk-drive case could not, partly because available feedstock was insufficient.
Those US-based calculations cannot establish Taiwanese costs. They show why a recycler needs a realistic collection forecast before choosing a processing line. A large electronics industry does not automatically provide enough accessible, suitable magnets.
The government’s search for primary material continues alongside recycling. Kung in July said officials would visit California and Colorado next month to assess deposits. The purpose was to establish whether those resources matched Taiwan’s requirements. He also described contacts with Australia and Canada. These were sourcing assessments, not confirmed deliveries.
Taiwan could therefore combine selected recycled material with imported feedstock. The right combination depends on which elements customers need and the form in which they purchase them. An aggregate tonnage target cannot answer those questions.
Public policy already extends beyond the laboratory. The Industrial Development Administration last month told CNA that the government was supporting upstream refining and downstream applications. Research subsidies would help diversify material sources and develop substitutes or technologies requiring smaller quantities.
The Resource Circulation Promotion Act (資源循環推動法), promulgated in June, adds a demand-side instrument. Article 32 requires public bodies to prioritize designated environmental and circular products and services. Product categories and assessment procedures depend on implementing rules.
Chang argues that public purchasing could attract private investment by creating demand for recovered materials. Subsidies may also help overcome limited scale. The law supplies a framework; manufacturers and public purchasers still need contracts covering suitable products.
A ROLE BEYOND TAIWAN
Chang sees an export opportunity in the processing itself. Taiwan could supply equipment and engineering to regional recycling facilities near the waste, instead of importing large quantities of discarded products.
“In this way, Taiwan could become a technology and processing partner rather than simply a destination for imported waste,” he said.
That could generate business abroad. Securing materials for Taiwanese factories would require additional supply agreements: selling equipment overseas does not itself reserve the resulting output for Taiwan.
Kristy Hsu (徐遵慈), of the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research, proposes a framework for such cooperation in an essay she supplied in response to questions. Her contribution to the Center for Strategic and International Studies’ Taiwan and the Pacific links Australia’s resources with Taiwan’s manufacturing capabilities and US technology, capital and markets.
She calls for permanent coordination and a trusted supplier network, extending the existing Taiwan-US economic dialogue. Her proposal addresses how partners could organize cooperation; it does not document an operating rare-earth venture.
ITRI declined an interview for this article. The economics ministry had not answered questions about the pilot’s products and timetable. Public sources reviewed do not establish its current saleable output, a complete commercial financing package or committed buyers.
Taiwan has a credible technical opening. Its success will depend on connecting specialized refiners to existing manufacturers and overseas suppliers. For a machinery company, the practical result would be repeat deliveries of the right material at an agreed price. That is the industrial capacity the pilot must help build.
Romain Blachier is an associate researcher at the Fondation Jean-Jaures, president of the Association France-Formosa, a lecturer in geopolitics and a renewable-energy professional.

For a small nation, Taiwan has an unusually long list of territorial disputes. In part or in whole, it has disputes over the Spratly Islands (Nansha Islands, 南沙群島) with Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei. It also has another territorial dispute with Vietnam over the Paracel Islands, and with Japan over the Senkaku Islands (Diaoyutai Islands, 釣魚台). Of course, the biggest territorial disputes are with the People’s Republic of China (PRC), which not only claims all of the above, but also Pratas Island (Dongsha, 東沙島), Kinmen, Penghu and all of Taiwan itself. Baby orangutans in India expose scale of trafficking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:47 UTC
01:38:47 KST

Five baby orangutans abandoned in an Indian forest have exposed a “massive” exotic wildlife trade, with traffickers smuggling increasingly rare species into the country, experts said.
They warn of a growing multimillion dollar trade in endangered animals, including apes smuggled through war-torn Myanmar to feed demand among wealthy Indians seeking exotic status symbols to flaunt on social media.
“There have been several instances of exotic wild animals being found or seized across the country,” Humane World for Animals India director Sumanth Bindumadhav said. “The scale is massive.”
Photo: AFP / Odisha Forest Department
Critically endangered orangutans are native only to Indonesia’s Sumatra island and Borneo, which it shares with Malaysia and Brunei.
Yet the five tiny orangutans were found by rangers in Balasore, India.
Aged about one-and-a-half years old, they are being cared for at a zoo.
Indonesia has requested their return.
Humane World in a June report detailed what it called a “rising trade in exotic wildlife,” demonstrated by a “steep increase in seizures” that reflected a “surge in illegal trade.”
The report estimated India’s exotic pet market to be about US$42.6 million in 2024.
Orangutans and gibbons, small apes, were being “increasingly trafficked into India” from Southeast Asia’s rainforests, it added.
A senior official at India’s Wildlife Crime Control Bureau said “thousands of social media influencers” were promoting exotic species as pets online, fueling demand among followers.
“It is a huge market,” the official said on condition of anonymity. “Rich people keep them in their homes.”
Under a government voluntary disclosure scheme, more than 40,000 people had registered exotic animals by February 2021, government data showed.
The figure is likely only a fraction of those in private hands, analysts said.
“The true scale of it is actually quite frightening,” Bindumadhav said.
Former India head of global anti-wildlife-trade group TRAFFIC Shekhar Kumar Niraj said the surge in trafficking was also linked to a “rising number” of animals held in private hands.
“Private zoos have violated laws at a very alarming scale across the country,” Niraj said. “Primates are very popular in zoos because they are very intelligent, like to interact with humans, the kind of thing zoos want.”
The World Wide Fund for Nature-India said it documented 56 seizures involving about 4,000 exotic animals in 2022 alone.

Asian Games issues mount at opening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:43 UTC
01:38:43 KST

The Asian Games in Japan on Friday faced more accusations of poor organization with a world champion gymnast “totally exhausted,” the public drafted in to rescue stranded athletes and South Korea lodging a complaint about a Japanese warlord.
The continent’s premier sporting spectacle opens in Nagoya and Aichi prefecture today, but the build-up has been soured by several issues.
That includes a shortage of rooms for the more than 17,000 athletes and officials — a bigger number than the Olympics.
Photo: Reuters
Some teams have also criticized the quality of the accommodation, including beds that are too short.
To save money there is no athletes’ village, organizers instead putting competitors in hotels, temporary cabins and on a cruise ship.
Organizers say that the accommodation is safe, cost-effective and comfortable.
Chinese gymnast Zhang Boheng, who won two silver medals at the Paris Olympics and has two world championship titles to his name, said he and some of his teammates were left waiting for six hours after landing on Wednesday.
“I’m totally exhausted,” he said in a video published on Thursday and shared widely on Chinese social media.
“I didn’t expect that after breakfast at 7:00am the next time I could eat would be close to 7:00pm,” the 26-year-old said.
He said the wait was caused by registration and paperwork, before heading to the cruise ship where 4,000 Games participants are to be housed in Nagoya’s port area.
However, when they arrived at the ship, he said heavy rain prevented them from boarding.
“A whole day was basically wasted like this,” added Zhang.
“In the end we really couldn’t take it any more so we decided to book rooms at a hotel to rest.”
The video has since been taken down, but Chinese state media said that other Chinese athletes also faced travel delays upon arrival.
Beijing’s consulate in Nagoya contacted Chinese citizens in the area to give the badminton team lifts after issues with a shuttle bus and a shortage of public transport tickets, Xinhua reported.
Chinese social media users applauded athletes, including table tennis star Sun Yingsha, for stretching and exercising at the airport.
The hashtag “Asian Games absurd” has since been viewed more than 94 million times on Weibo.
India’s team had similar delays at the airport.
“There was an issue in getting accreditation for athletes at the airport during immigration. There were long queues with a lot of other nations there,” India’s chef de mission and Indian Olympic Association treasurer Sahdev Yadav said.
“But these things happen and we have got everything sorted,” he said, adding that “these are all teething problems and our focus is now on performance.”
South Korea’s Yonhap news agency reported that some of the country’s athletes waited at the airport for more than five hours on Thursday.
“We are aware of the situation including reports that athletes have had to wait for hours and we are doing our best to handle it,” a Korean Sport and Olympic Committee (KSOC) official said.
Also yesterday, the KSOC said it had filed a complaint with Games organizers for featuring a Japanese warlord at a welcoming ceremony.
The event on Tuesday included a person dressed as Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who led Japan’s invasions of Korea in 1592 to 1598, and the ceremony prompted a backlash in South Korea. Historical issues are sensitive between South Korea and Japan, with Hideyoshi’s invasion a significant episode in Korean history and Korea under Japanese colonial rule from 1910 to 1945.
There was no immediate response from the Olympic Council of Asia or the local organizing committee.

Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) expects to sell twice as many chips in the coming year, fueled by the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) across different industries.
AI is of great benefit to a variety of sectors, Huang told reporters on the sidelines of an event convened by King Charles III in Scotland on Thursday. Nvidia is the top seller of AI accelerators, chips used to develop and run AI models.
Huang is maintaining his bullish stance at a time when concerns are growing about AI. Industry leaders have discussed slowing down development of the technology over fears that it might be potentially dangerous. Huang said that companies need to take responsibility and make sure their AI software and services are safe before releasing them.
Photo: AP
Last month, Nvidia projected sales growth of 70 percent in its next fiscal year. It said at the time that revenue could double if the company had enough supply to meet surging demand.
King Charles III convened technology leaders and other influential figures for a summit focused on the mounting risks of AI, a topic that has captivated the globe this week. While the executives there did not publicly commit to any changes, some addressed the safety concerns directly.
“Those of us building AI must test systems rigorously,” Huang said in brief remarks at the royal event on Thursday. “When a product is not safe enough, we should hold it back.”
Joining Huang in Scotland were OpenAI’s chief financial officer Sarah Friar and Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis. Anthropic PBC public affairs chief Tino Cuellar also joined the AI forum at Dumfries House, along with leaders from other technology companies, nonprofits and educational institutions, including Beijing’s Tsinghua University.
“Those in our world who value our humanity and its vital moral component are anxiously seeking your reassurance that we will not lose control of our destiny,” the King said in his opening remarks. The gathering was designed to discuss how the technology could be “harnessed in ways to benefit society and the natural world,” Buckingham Palace said in a statement.
The event is timely. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei triggered a global debate about the escalating risks of AI in a weekend essay calling for a slowdown in frontier model development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed with the essay’s conclusions, while Hassabis described it as the “right path forward.” Meanwhile, Nvidia’s Huang disagreed with a slowdown or further regulation. Over the past week, two AI researchers quit Google DeepMind and Anthropic, claiming that the technology could be lethal.
Those concerns have caused jitters among lawmakers and the wider public internationally.
At the summit, King Charles posed two key questions: “First, how can we harness the benefits of AI, with safety at its heart. And, second, how can we build international cooperation and consensus to achieve this, so no nation is left behind — and the future of mankind protected?”

Reframing the Trump-Xi meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:42 UTC
01:38:42 KST

Prior to next week’s expected meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), reports have emerged that Beijing has sought to use Xi’s visit to the US as leverage in hopes that Washington would delay new arms sales to Taiwan. Some in US policy circles have also called for the withdrawal of US military personnel assisting with training in Taiwan.
Familiar questions that arose prior to the previous Trump-Xi meeting have resurfaced. Would Trump make concessions to Xi regarding Taiwan? Would the US revert to its policy of strategic ambiguity? Would Taiwan become a bargaining chip in US-China negotiations?
Focusing attention on “how much the US would concede on Taiwan” before the meeting even takes place essentially amounts to allowing Beijing to set the agenda — for US-China relations to remain stable, the Taiwan issue must remain on the table.
This is a noteworthy aspect of Beijing’s recent diplomatic maneuvers. China has once again been repeatedly emphasizing that Taiwan is “the core of the core” of its interests, while attempting to persuade Washington to accept a particular causal argument: US-China relations are unstable because the US and Taiwan have grown too close.
After Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim’s (蕭美琴) visit to Italy last week, Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs Wang Yi (王毅) demanded that France refrain from holding any official exchanges with Taiwan. From Beijing’s perspective, reducing tensions in the Taiwan Strait must always begin with altering the behavior of others.
However, the party that has been steadily increasing military pressure in the Taiwan Strait is not the US, nor is it Taiwan. Beijing the one in the driver’s seat when it comes to military exercises, coast guard activities and “gray zone” operations in the Strait.
Similarly, the recent efforts of the US, Japan and European countries to reduce their supply-chain reliance on China were not requested by Taiwan — rather, the moves are the result of individual countries reassessing the risks of economic coercion and security threats.
If Taiwan is on the agenda at the meeting next week, rather than repeatedly asking what Trump might trade Taiwan in exchange for, the more important question should be to ask Xi what China is prepared to contribute to achieve regional peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait.
The issue also involves how Taiwan views itself. Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) has put forward the idea of a “symbiotic partnership” between the US and Taiwan, addressing everything from trade and investment to industrial ecosystems. Taking this line of thinking a step further, what Taiwan and the US should really seek to establish is a greater shared understanding of regional risks. Having dealt with China for decades, Taiwan has firsthand experience with Beijing’s decisionmaking, “united front” tactics and “gray zone” operations. That experience could allow Taiwan to play a more proactive role as the US, Japan and Europe re-evaluate their China policies.
Dialogue between US and Chinese leaders could reduce the risk of conflict, which would not necessarily be a bad thing for Taiwan, but “stability” should not mean asking the US to reduce arms sales, Taiwan to scale back its international activities or other countries to limit their interactions with Taiwan.
If Beijing truly hopes that the Trump-Xi meeting would bring stability to the Taiwan Strait, the outside world should also observe whether China reduces military activities around Taiwan, scales back its “gray zone” activities and stops its coast guard for law enforcement as a pretext to alter the “status quo” in the Taiwan Strait.
What needs to be addressed is not the “Taiwan issue,” but China.
Wang Hung-jen is a professor in National Cheng Kung University’s Department of Political Science.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

Scientists discover a new wild cat in more than century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:39 UTC
01:38:39 KST

Scientists have discovered a new species of wild cat for the first time in more than a century, a Bolivian researcher said on Thursday.
The tilcayo tiger cat, a small feline with a spotted, leopard-like coat, was identified in the mountainous Yungas region near La Paz, Bolivia.
Locals who saw the creature in the Bolivian Andes had mistaken it for an ordinary house cat, said biologist and National Geographic explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who was part of the research team that studied them.
Photo: National Geographic via Reuters
The nickname “tilcayo” given to the animal by locals inspired its new scientific designation: Leopardus tilcayo.
Nogales-Ascarrunz lauded the discovery as a “remarkable event, because a new wild cat species hasn’t been described in 100 years.”
The cat is the first new feline discovered since the Uruguayan pampas cat in 1923.
The tilcayo is slightly smaller than a domestic cat, measuring about 45cm, with rounded ears.
A pair of tilcayos — the only such creatures found so far — have undergone whole genome sequencing, Nogales-Ascarrunz said, referring to a type of in-depth genetic testing.
A male tilcayo is living at an animal shelter in Yungas, after it was handed over by a family who had taken it in.
A female was rescued and released into the wild after being attacked by locals.
“So far, it’s only been detected in Bolivia,” the explorer said.
They were classified as vulnerable to extinction, but their small numbers meant they could soon be considered “at much greater risk” of dying out, she said.

BOJ raises rates in split decision amid US pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:38 UTC
01:38:38 KST

The Bank of Japan (BOJ) raised its benchmark interest rate in a split decision showing dissent within the board as it confronts mounting inflation risks and unusually explicit calls for further policy normalization from Washington.
The BOJ lifted its policy rate by a quarter point to 1.25 percent yesterday at the end of a two-day meeting, according to its statement, in a move predicted by all economists surveyed by Bloomberg.
Japan’s currency slipped about 1 percent to ￥157.54 against the dollar during Governor Kazuo Ueda’s post-decision briefing, even after he said the BOJ needed to avoid letting prices deviate above target and harming the economy.
Photo: Bloomberg
“The stage for setting policy has changed,” Ueda said. When asked if back-to-back hikes or larger moves were possible, he said the BOJ would not rule out any particular policy options in advance of board meetings.
The lack of more hawkish language in the statement also offered little reason for investors to make bullish bets on Japan’s currency, especially after the Federal Reserve firmed up its views following its rate increase with a unanimous vote earlier this week.
“The key point was that two board members voted against the decision. I believe that the market took that as dovish relative to what had been priced in,” Daiwa Securities senior economist Kento Minami said. “On the other hand, the BOJ’s assessment of the economy, prices and financial conditions remains hawkish. You can see that they see the need of a faster pace of rate hikes than before.”
Japan’s exporter-heavy Nikkei 225 stock gauge rose 1.4 percent as the yen weakened. The broader Topix index edged lower, weighed down by as financial stocks.
Markets outside Japan took the BOJ decision in stride. The two-year Treasury yield held a small rise after the decision, while most G10 currencies except for the yen traded in a narrow range.
The rate hike, coming just three months after the BOJ’s previous increase, marks the shortest interval between rate hikes since 1990, when the central bank’s rapid policy tightening played a key role in bursting Japan’s asset bubble. It was the sixth rate increase under Ueda — the most by any BOJ chief in at least half a century — and came after a wave of pressure from US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent to push up rates.
The BOJ’s accelerated pace of hikes also comes after a shift in the global backdrop for monetary policy as authorities address the fallout from the Iran war. The Fed underscored the change with its Wednesday move and the European Central Bank raised rates last week for the second time this year.
“The Bank of Japan’s decision Friday to raise rates again so soon after its last move in June suggests political and diplomatic pressure to stem the yen’s slide helped drive the tightening — rather than inflation concerns alone. The yen’s mild drop on the news underlined the dovish surprise relative to expectations in the market [but not our own],” economist Taro Kimura said.
In a meeting with Ueda last month, Bessent “expressed strong support” for Japan’s decisive steps to address the weakening of the yen, the Department of the Treasury said.
While the yen weakened against the dollar after yesterday’s decision, it remains stronger than in July after coordinated intervention by the US and Japan at the end of that month helped push it further from the about 40-year low of ￥163.99 set on July 23.
