Macron hosts Carney on trip to outpost off Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:36 UTC
01:38:36 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron today embarks on a rare and symbolic visit to a remote French territory in the North Atlantic, hosting Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at a time of growing tensions with Washington.
The three-day visit to Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a three-island archipelago of less than 6,000 people just 25km off Newfoundland, would be the first by a French president in more than a decade.
The trip to France’s only remaining possession in North America, a vestige of the huge territories Paris once controlled in what is now Canada and the US, carries immense symbolic resonance.
Photo: AFP
Macron insists that US President Donald Trump’s second mandate has served to prove his point that Europe needs to be more sovereign, especially on security.
Against the background of an intensifying spat with Trump who has even threatened to annex Canada, Carney has welcomed a proposal for his country to become the EU’s first “associate member.”
He is due to join Macron tomorrow as the first Canadian premier to visit the territory. The last visit by a French head of state was by Francois Hollande in 2014.
The archipelago is one of several strategically-located French overseas territories that span the globe.
“Saint Pierre and Miquelon is not some insignificant remnant of empire to be managed piecemeal. It is France and Europe in North America,” said French Senator Annick Girardin, a former overseas territories minister.
Trump, who has repeatedly described Canada as the “51st” US state and dismissed its premier as “governor Carney,” earlier this month posted an image with a map of North America in which areas including Canada were colored in with the US flag.
Carney has in turn described his nation as “the most European of non-European countries.”
The joint visit would underscore that Canada and France countries share “the same values of freedom, democracy, the rule of law and respect for the sovereignty of nations,” the French presidential palace said.
“In a world marked by the return of power politics, geopolitical tensions and new forms of dependency, France and Canada share a common ambition: to work together, and with all countries that share these values, to strengthen their capacity to make decisions and act independently,” the Elysee said.
Carney’s office quoted him as saying that “Canada and France share more than a border. We share a history, common values, and a resolute commitment to building a more secure and prosperous world. In an uncertain world, President Macron and I understand the importance of this relationship”.

Prized Mexican relic returns on loan, two centuries on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:36 UTC
01:38:36 KST

A cherished 16th-century Mexican manuscript that tells the history of the Aztecs in pictograms on Thursday went on display in Mexico City, nearly two centuries after it was whisked off to France.
The Codex Azcatitlan recounts the history of the Aztec civilization, from the creation of the Aztec Empire to its fall during the Spanish conquest, which ushered in Christianity.
Mexico has been demanding for years that France return it, but so far France has refused.
Photo: AFP
Members of an indigenous group that has campaigned for its restitution reacted ecstatically to seeing two folios from the precious document on display inside a glass case at the National Museum of Anthropology.
“They hid our history from us, they stole it!” Emilia Mendoza of the Hnahnu community said at the opening of the exhibition. “This is a battle won, a first step toward the restitution of these books that reside in other countries.”
Speaking at the inauguration, Mexican Secretary of Foreign Affairs Roberto Velasco said the exhibition was about “reuniting a population with its [collective] memory.”
The pictograms “represent our history, the written voice of our ancestors and the deep root of our identity,” he said.
Written shortly after the arrival of the Spanish in the 16th century, the codex, or manuscript, is considered one of the most important accounts of Aztec culture.
It narrates the migration from Aztlan, the mythical birthplace of Aztec civilization, to the promised land of Tenochtitlan, the forerunner of Mexico City.
Scenes rendered in vibrant reds, blues, greens and yellows depict warriors in feathered headdresses and ritual acts in pyramid temples.
France’s National Library, which has maintained possession of it for more than a century, loaned it to Mexico to commemorate 200 years of relations between the two countries.
Mexico, which has launched a push to recover colonial-era cultural objects held outside the country, wants France to go further and hand it back.
Since 2018, more than 16,200 items have been repatriated from various countries, the National Institute of Anthropology and History said last year.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum pressed French President Emmanuel Macron to return the Codex Azcatitlan and another precious manuscript, the Codex Borbonicus, the latter’s visit to Mexico last year.
“If it’s from Mexico, why isn’t it in Mexico?” ethnohistorian Karen Trejo wondered at the exhibition opening.
The manuscript, which fills 25 sheets of parchment that were imported from Europe in the 16th century, was donated to the National Library of France in 1898 by the widow of the Franco-Mexican collector Eugene Goupil.
It was brought to France half a century earlier by Joseph Marius Alexis Aubin, a French researcher specializing in indigenous US cultures.
It is one of two major volumes illustrating indigenous Aztec life that have been kept in France, along with the Codex Borbonicus, which represents divinatory and solar calendars.
The Codex Borbonicus is kept at the library of the French National Assembly.

Ex-cyber official indicted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:35 UTC
01:38:35 KST

The Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office yesterday indicted a former official of the National Institute of Cyber Security’s research and acquisition center for allegedly hacking into a classified institute database.
Hsu Hsih-chung (許世璋), a former deputy director of the center, and three of his subordinates are accused of breaking into the institute’s database to obtain classified information, the office said.
The defendants face charges over alleged contraventions of cybersecurity and digital privacy rules in the Criminal Code and the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法), it said.
Photo: Hsu Tzu-ling, Taipei Times
Hsu allegedly built an unauthorized crawler to access administrative information, bypassing the organization’s budget management system, which he believed to be inefficient, the indictment said.
Using the crawler, Hsu and his accomplices compromised the institute’s internal budget documents, as well as national identification and National Health Insurance numbers of institute employees, among other privileged information, it said.
In January 2024, Hsu inadvertently discovered a back door into the institute’s human resource system and obtained personal data of all of the employees, which he allegedly shared with the three codefendants, it said.
Believing that the organization’s project budget management system was inadequate, Hsu in March last year asked the institute to adopt a new system, but his proposal was rejected, prosecutors said.
Hsu allegedly told subordinate Peng Ming-chun (彭敏君) to bypass the internal system’s authorization mechanisms by exploiting the loophole he had previously identified in handling the center’s budget documents, the office said.
Hsu allegedly instructed Ting Po-feng (丁柏楓) to design a crawler capable of extracting internal documents without authorization, a task Peng facilitated by advising Ting on a programing language and other technical matters, it said.
Ting discovered that any document could be accessed by entering the document’s serial number on the enterprise information portal, enabling him to design the crawler Hsu had specified, it said.
Ting saved the institute’s entire payroll in his private cloud storage and internal documents on a personally owned computer, it said.
Ting regularly used Microsoft Azure to summarize confidential budget documents, including budgets and timelines, which he saved into a folder shared with the other defendants, the indictment said.
Hsu and his accomplices used the crawler and illegally obtained data to establish an alternate budget platform on the Internet, from which he managed the center’s funding, it said.
The institute in May last year banned virtual private networks from accessing the internal system, prompting Hsu to order subordinate Lee Yu-hsuan (李昱勳) to use the latter’s personal laptop as the crawler’s relay, it said.
Given that there is no evidence that the defendants leaked information to a third party, the office said it sought a reduced sentence for the defendants on account of mitigating circumstances, the indictment said.
The crawler on average accessed the internal system once every 2.6 systems for a total of 207,938 times by March, or 85 percent of all traffic to the institute’s network by employees, it said.

ITRI touts technological collaboration with the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:31 UTC
01:38:31 KST

The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) is spearheading Taiwan’s drive to enhance technological collaboration with the US, Japan and Europe in critical fields, institute president Chang Pei-zen (張培仁) said in an interview with the Chinese-language Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times) published yesterday.
Global relationships in technology are valuable to Taiwan’s development of uncrewed systems, critical minerals and optical communications, Chang said.
The institute is also cooperating with the private sector to spur industry upgrades across the economy, he said.
Photo: Yu An-ting, Taipei Times
It played a key role in Taiwan-US collaboration in the Green UAS cybersecurity and supply chain compliance certification program, he said.
The US had expected that it would take 11 months to transfer the certification to Taiwan, but the ITRI’s contribution allowed the process to be completed in five months, he said.
The institute with the Ministry of Economic Affairs’ assistance is also facilitating the development of technology to refine critical minerals, aimed at meeting 50 percent of domestic demand for rare earths by 2030, he said.
The ITRI has established experimental assembly lines for that project on site, which would be scaled up as the program goes forward, Chang said.
The institute is also working closely with Japanese private-sector partners to develop high-efficiency converters for use in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers in exchange for transferring base stations and private networks to Japan, he said.
The cooperation is helping Taiwanese and Japanese enterprises work together to integrate optical communication components and systems, he said.
The institute has a decades-long relationship with Lithuania’s laser industry, which produces the emitters for Taiwan’s laser sector, Chang said.
France and the Netherlands are partners in the ITRI’s bid to develop copackaged optics, an emergent technology believed to have tremendous value to AI data centers, he said.
The institute is also cooperating with European satellite manufacturers to improve Taiwan’s telecommunications capabilities and working with the UK to develop 3D printing tech that could be used in multi-band base station antennas, he said.
Asked about unevenness in technology upgrades in the Taiwanese economy, Chang said sectors “closer to wind” would naturally be faster to adapt to new technologies.
The ITRI is not only helping the nation’s strategic industries to stay on the cutting edge of global developments, but also promoting the distribution of technologies in small and medium-sized industries and traditional industries, he said.
The integration of Taiwanese plastic injection molding and precision machining into semiconductor supply chains is a success story for the ITRI’s efforts to upgrade the nation’s economy, he said.
The institute is mulling changing its strategy of developing, transferring and applying new technologies in sequence, Chang said.
Instead, it is starting the technological research and development process by first interviewing end-users about their needs, as the institute has been doing with robotics, he said.
Every new technology the institute develops in connection with the sector begins with interviewing 10 or more enterprises in the industry, which greatly facilitates the process of translating technology into a commercial product, Chang said.
The ITRI is taking part in the government’s “hundred industries” initiative to help distribute AI technology to traditional industries and small businesses, as the institute carries out its own digitization, he said.

====================================================================================================

To understand the threat to our real democracy, watch Putin’s fake one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:30 UTC
01:38:30 KST

Millions of people are participating in Russia’s three-day elections to choose a new parliament. The purpose of the exercise is to maintain Russian President Vladimir Putin’s authority over the political process, which means his party, United Russia, would retain control of the Duma.
That much is settled before the polls opened yesterday, although the scale of the government’s victory would not be declared until the votes are counted. A portion of seats is available for other “systemic parties” that function as Kremlin licensed-opposition, padding out the pretence of pluralism. They serve as pressure valves for public frustration and parliamentary proxies when rival factions within the ruling elite want to nudge Kremlin policy in one direction or another.
The Kremlin likes to minimize the difference between United Russia’s official tally and a number that would plausibly reflect public attitudes to the regime. If the gap is too wide, achieved by fraud too blatant, it conveys insecurity in the Kremlin. Putin’s power does not depend on endorsement by ordinary Russians, but his authority is sustained by the illusion that he listens and cares. An egregiously stolen election would prove that he does not.
Illustration: Kevin Sheu
Everyone knows the result is fixed, but it would breach a social contract if the fiction became too absurd. Electoral verisimilitude is harder than usual to pull off this time because of war fatigue. No one can pretend any more that the “special military operation” in Ukraine has gone to plan. It was supposed to take weeks and is now in its fifth year. There have been about 1.5 million Russian casualties.
A shortage of volunteers stirs fear that another mobilization of unwilling army reserves is in the works. Putin has denied that any such draft is required. That he needs to offer public reassurance at all amounts to recognition that progress on the front has stalled and the mood at home has soured.
Ukrainian drone and missile strikes have made the war visible and economically palpable thousands of kilometers away from the frontline. The veil of state propaganda cannot be drawn across plumes of smoke rising from oil refineries and lines at gasoline pumps.
There are no accurate opinion polls in an authoritarian state. Russians are disinclined to share their private thoughts with strangers on the phone, especially when denigrating the armed forces is a criminal offense.
A more reliable indicator of growing dissent is the increased rate of its repression. Last month, Yabloko, an inconsequential liberal party, was barred from the elections on a preposterous trumped-up technicality. The real objection was the party’s campaign slogan — “For peace and freedom.”
Yabloko had previously been tolerated as an irrelevant vintage party from the pre-Putin era, not exactly tame, but unthreatening; not worth the risk of aggrandizement by political martyrdom. That calculus changed with signs that voters were drifting toward the only available anti-war banner. It was not a big movement, but enough to persuade the authorities that denying the party representation after the ballot could be messier than blocking it in advance.
If banning the opposition depresses turnout, all the better. The Kremlin appears to have accepted that a sincere show of enthusiasm for the status quo is unavailable. A boring, low-key election, telling a story of submission and stability, is the next best thing.
Such is the perverse craft of “managed democracy” — the mechanics of running gangster authoritarianism through a notionally liberal constitution. It requires a mix of performative coercion, tactical concession and confected consent. The economic spoils of corruption have to be dispensed widely enough to feed a quiescent elite. There has to be enough theater of public participation to legitimize the regime. However, genuine freedom must also be discredited as the path of chaos.
That has been an easy line to sell to Russians who recall post-Soviet democratization as a time of rampant gangsterism, surrendered superpower status and national immiseration. Putin is a product of that era and the embodied backlash against it. He transferred the engines of oligarchic capitalist self-enrichment to the reconstituted chassis of a Soviet-style state. He made himself an avatar for imperial nostalgia and an exhausted population’s craving for order. He promised to express the national interest more efficiently as its sole incarnation than any raucous, divided parliament ever could.
That offer has less appeal in established democracies, where political pluralism and the rule of law have deeper roots, but it has an audience. The core proposition — a strong leader to avenge a once great country’s humiliation by — has twice carried Donald Trump to the White House. His ratings have plummeted, but he can still count on credulous adulation from as many as one in three Americans.
What is the equivalent number in Britain? The leading product in this market is Reform UK, which now polls at about 23 percent, level with Labour. Nigel Farage’s position has slipped this year as his personal and party finances have come under scrutiny, but his core supporters are untroubled by the whiff of grubby lucre. For some, convinced that the whole system is a rotten sham, scandal around Reform UK’s receipt of multimillion-dollar donations positively burnishes the brand. It proves that Farage is a baller, capable of beating the “establishment” parties at their own game — a gamble that the savvy, loadsamoney crypto crowd are backing.
The deep cynicism feeding that judgement is a vital element in the chemical compound that corrodes democracy. I remember it as the most pungent feature of Russian politics when I lived in Moscow, watching the 1990s experiment in democracy fail.
It is the demoralized conviction that no politician would ever be motivated by a spirit of public service. The only categories are weak and strong; suckers and players. To succeed, a nation needs to be led by a strong player. Constitutions and laws are just parts of the toolkit for exercising power. The liberal view that holds them sacred as a system for holding governments to account is the mark of a sucker.
Farage does not put it quite like that. He did tell his party conference last week that an incoming Reform government would declare a “national emergency” to enact a radical agenda within the first 100 days and tolerate no objection from parliament, the courts or Whitehall. No one can say they were not warned.
It is not an explicitly anti-democratic agenda, but it never is with populists in opposition. No one wins elections by promising to cancel future ballots and, as the Russian experience shows, once power has been secured, the well-managed poll is a valuable mechanism for consolidating control.
There is a process of hollowing-out that comes first. It is a relentless corrosion of trust in independent institutions and the sluicing of public debate with caustic cynicism. It is the stirring of disillusionment and frustration into nihilistic rage against the system; sowing division and amplifying despair to make authoritarian rule sound like release from political paralysis.
Russia was lost down that road long ago. British democracy is thankfully more robust, more culturally embedded. Or so we hope. Resilience is not immunity. The Putin model of venal cynicism that dresses authoritarian kleptocracy in a call for national redemption will not declare its motives in an election campaign. The democratic fightback cannot wait until that election to see how far the poison has spread.
Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist.

Within Taiwan, there are ongoing battles between the legislative and executive branches over the budget, and between cities and the central government over resources. Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

Local media headlines and political pundits have picked up his supporters’ slogan “ocean current” (洋流) — a play on the last character of Shen’s name, which literally means “ocean” (洋), and the character (流), which can mean “current,” “flow” or “trend” — to

Yet the carefully crafted 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration (NDD), the longest BRICS declaration so far, reveals a subtle, but important shift. BRICS is moving from a loose grouping toward a more substantive platform for the global south, giving developing countries greater voice and bargaining space

Are you outraged by Sydney Sweeney — again? More fool you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:28 UTC
01:38:28 KST

Would it be insanely unfashionable to defend Sydney Sweeney?
You may or may not have heard that the Euphoria star has done an ad for a sports betting site. Sorry, I think we still have to call them “sports prediction markets” in the US, which only recently popped its legalized sports betting cherry, and is behaving like a complete teenage boy about the whole thing.
Anyway, among other poses, the ad features a naked Sweeney holding a couple of footballs over her breasts, which are — and I feel she would want us to acknowledge this — seriously among the very best in Hollywood. Maybe THE best. Listen, it is what it is. Life would be very boring if we could not say so with a twinkle.
Forgive me. Life is, in fact, very, very boring, because yet another Sweeney-advertising-centered firestorm has been ignited by this ad. (Last year, some lunatic genuinely suggested her “good jeans” American Eagle ad was something to do with white supremacy and eugenics.)
Her latest product endorsement has drawn the ire of a cascade of female athletes, who have described it variously as demeaning women’s sport, sexualized representation of athletes and “a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, [and] every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is — teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity.”
Come on. With respect, I just do not think it is a kick in the face for any of those things. Not to be a crazed optimist, but the great thing about where women’s sport has got to today is that it feels a whole lot bigger and stronger and more compelling than whether Sweeney did or did not get her tits out for a gambling ad. I cannot help feeling it would have been cooler for women’s sport to simply not even mention the naked gambling ad at all. And, if it had to, maybe focus on the gambling bit rather than the woman advertising it. I have not definitively run the numbers on this, but instinct tells me that gambling wrecks a lot more lives than Sweeney.
Honestly, not everyone has to be the same and on-message, and I could not be more convinced that Sweeney adds to the gaiety of the nations. I love it that she is out there in the culture, pissing off reflexively judgmental people who ignore so many bigger issues, but have really strong views on sexy ad campaigns. And even slightly sexist ones. I truly loved it when, after one controversy or another a couple of years ago, Sweeney posted a picture of herself in a sweatshirt reading: “SORRY FOR HAVING GREAT TITS AND CORRECT OPINIONS.” (Would also like to know where you buy this sweatshirt, etc.)
That she has emerged as such a frequent culture wars punching bag says so much more about the predictable, playable nature of her serial detractors than it does about her. Why can’t they just face it — Sydney’s gonna Sweeney. None of it feels like that big of a deal in the grand scheme of things.
Or rather, it does to some. After another ad campaign last year, some fashion analyst gasped to the New York Times: “It seems like she’s not embarrassed or ashamed promoting all of these different projects.”
Hmm. Always great to see women implying other women should be feeling shame for hideous crimes like being a face of both Miu Miu AND Armani Beauty. The previous year, a columnist had described Sweeney as “problematic yet unashamed,” which, ironically, I found somewhat problematic. Have to say, I am a big fan of women not being made to feel shame unless whatever they have done is really quite bad.
Indeed, it was after a veteran female producer and film studies professor publicly dismissed her as not pretty and bad at acting that Sweeney gave a reactive interview in which she observed of Hollywood: “This entire industry, all people say is ‘women empowering other women’. None of it’s happening. All of it is fake and a front for all the other shit that they say behind everyone’s back.”
Amazing. Because where is the lie? Inevitably, it was her who got branded unsisterly for saying it.
A few months later, non-insult was added to non-injury once it emerged that Sweeney was dating the considerably older former Taylor Swift foe/Justin Bieber manager Scooter Braun, who is a sort of music industry vampire, but not in a hot way.
I saw someone who obviously fancied Sweeney lamenting this romance as “like a 19-year-old wonderkid signing for Al-Nassr,” which is a fun joke and about the level of sseriousness with which we should treat other people’s dating choices. Don’t worry about it, guys! It is not like you have to have sex with Scooter Braun. She is doing it for you — relax.
Ultimately, I always feel somewhat compelled to defend Sydney’s right to do whatever stupid things she feels like in her 20s, safe — if not sound — in the knowledge that she will be forced to spend her entire 30s and probably her entire 40s atoning for every single one of them in every single interview, where every single reporter will just really want her to express shame and/or personal growth. It is all such an endlessly dreary bore. There must be less repressed and joyless things to do with our time.
While we spend far too long figuring those out, I do hope Sweeney finds a way to continue apparently not giving a shit — and that everyone else considers they might have more fun if they took a leaf out of her book from time to time.

Taiwan welcomes delegates for launch of global disaster alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:27 UTC
01:38:27 KST

Taiwan welcomed disaster management officials and experts from around the world yesterday ahead of the launch of a new international alliance aimed at strengthening disaster preparedness and response.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) and Minister of the Interior Liu Shyh-fang (劉世芳) jointly hosted a dinner in Taipei for delegates to the World Alliance for Disaster Management (WADM), ahead of its official launch today.
The WADM will bring together governments, emergency response agencies, businesses, academic institutions and civil society groups to cooperate throughout the disaster management cycle, Lin said.
Photo: CNA
The alliance will facilitate professional training, information sharing, capacity building, joint exercises and practical exchanges in disaster prevention, early warning, emergency response and post-disaster recovery, he added.
“Disasters and risks know no borders, and we need to work together to build resilience to these challenges,” Lin said.
The WADM builds on President William Lai’s (賴清德) vision of turning the National Fire Agency Training Center in Nantou County into a major disaster response training hub for the Indo-Pacific, he added.
Liu said Taiwan’s experience of receiving international assistance after the deadly 1999 Jiji earthquake underscored the importance of cross-border disaster cooperation.
Taiwan now conducts large-scale earthquake response drills annually and is prepared to offer international partners high-standard professional training at the Nantou center, she said.
This year’s exercises included search-and-rescue teams from the United Kingdom, Germany, South Korea, Turkey, the Philippines, Timor-Leste and Fiji, as well as disaster medical teams from Australia and Japan, Liu said.
Palau Vice President Raynold Oilouch said at the dinner that his country was proud to be a founding member of the WADM.
Palau is vulnerable to typhoons, tsunamis and droughts and is currently experiencing its driest conditions in more than two decades, he said.
Oilouch said the expertise brought together through the WADM could provide valuable guidance as Palau prepares for what could become a catastrophic drought.
Delegates are scheduled to visit the National Fire Agency Training Center tomorrow.

Groups urge review of owl habitat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:26 UTC
01:38:26 KST

Environmental advocates yesterday protested the selection of the site for the Shalun Science Park project, urging the environmental impact assessment committee to prioritize eastern grass-owl conservation over industrial development.
The site is located at the Shalun Farm (沙崙農場) in Tainan’s Gueiren District (歸仁), Government Watch Alliance executive director Hsu Hsin-hsin (許心欣) said ahead of the committee’s meeting, adding that the farm is owned by state-run Taiwan Sugar Corp (Taisugar).
It was selected by the National Science and Technology Council’s Southern Taiwan Science Park Bureau specifically for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) to build 11 fabs, she said.
Photo courtesy of the Tainan Wild Bird Society
While the bureau chose the site mainly because of the convenience of Taisugar exclusively owning the property, the 507-hectare plot is home to critically endangered eastern grass-owls, as well as 36 other endangered or valuable bird species, Hsu said.
TSMC in 2023 announced in its Biodiversity Statement upholding the AR3T biodiversity conservation principle, she said.
The AR3T principle refers to “avoid, reduce, restore, regenerate and transform” in conjunction with biodiversity conservation practices.
Hsu said TSMC failed to prioritize avoidance of critical natural habitats in line with the principle, as it plans to build fabs on an eastern grass-owl ecological hotspot.
Taiwan Hsinchu Foundation chairman Sam Lin (林聖崇) called on TSMC to use brownfield instead of farmland or undeveloped land.
For example, petrochemical industrial parks such as the Linyuan Industrial Park would be an ideal alternative site, particularly as the petrochemical industry is shrinking and transforming, he said.
The brownfields left in petrochemical industrial parks can be redeveloped and continue to support high-tech industries such as semiconductors, he added.
Lin also called for setting up a water resource collaboration platform for the project to prevent competition for water between the agricultural and industrial sectors.
Alliance national land conservation director Chen Chi-chung (陳祺忠) said that the critical bird habitats are south of the high-speed rail’s Taiana station’s special zone.
The government refused to move the project site northward to fully preserve the habitats because the northern fields are owned by private agricultural operators, he said.
Private land would be more difficult to obtain, Chen said, urging the government not to sacrifice natural habitats for industrial development.
The issue of eastern grass-owl conservation was discussed at the project’s scoping meeting held at the Ministry of Environment in Taipei yesterday.
The meeting adjourned at about 6pm yesterday and is to continue in two weeks’ time.

Tale of infidelity inspires arts festival in Tainan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:25 UTC
01:38:25 KST

The grassroots-organized Tainan Zhamei Arts Festival began yesterday and is to run through Tuesday, featuring five days of traditional Taiwanese opera performances, banquets and cultural activities.
The event initially began as an online joke, with netizens satirically suggesting the city host the traditional opera The Case of Executing Chen Shimei (鍘美案), in which Judge Bao (包公) — a Song Dynasty official renowned for his moral uprightness — executes an allegedly unfaithful husband.
It was inspired by the daughter of former president Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁), who accused her ex-husband of having an affair.
Photo: Screen grab from the festival’s Facebook page
In an online post last month, Chen Hsing-yu (陳幸妤), known locally as the “daughter of Tainan,” revealed that she was divorced. She accused her ex-husband of neglecting the family for years, having an inappropriate relationship with a clinic nurse and even withholding NT$23 million (US$723,089) in education funds set aside for their three sons.
In a show of public sympathy for Chen Hsing-yu, the organizing team raised tens of millions in New Taiwan dollars in less than a month by calling on members of the public to sponsor banquet tables and soliciting sponsorship from various sectors, turning an online joke into a large-scale cultural event.
It has become an example of a grassroots organization in Tainan and is to celebrate traditional opera culture, banquet culture and charity.
All five evenings are to feature performances centered around themes of betrayal, infidelity and retribution, including different renditions of the story of Judge Bao.
The event begins at 5pm and ends at 9pm each night at the Anyi parking lot in Tainan’s Anping District (安平), with free entry for the first two days and seating on a first-come, first-served basis, although visitors may bring their own chairs and picnic mats.
Tomorrow and on Monday and Tuesday, the event would host traditional Taiwanese banquet dinners, known as bando (辦桌) with opera performances.
All 750 banquet tables available across the three evenings have sold out for NT$16,800 each.
Last night’s performances started with the Goodoo Puppet Troupe, which performs Taiwanese hand puppetry, or budaixi (布袋戲), followed by singer Huang Fei (黃妃).
Tonight would see the Luo Yu-cong Opera Troupe take to the stage with a show incorporating traditional folk performances, war drums and performances by local students.
The Sun Kailin Opera Troupe is to perform tomorrow night and the Chunmei Opera Troupe on Monday. The Shiu Kim Taiwanese Opera Troupe are to give the closing performance on Tuesday, featuring well-known actress Lu Hsueh-feng (呂雪鳳).

Health promotion agency urges caution on overeating at Mid-Autumn Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:25 UTC
01:38:25 KST

With the Mid-Autumn Festival falling on Friday next week, the Health Promotion Administration (HPA) cautioned that festive gatherings featuring mooncakes, barbecues, drinks and snacks can easily lead to excessive calorie intake.
People should adjust portion sizes and food choices, while incorporating vegetables, fruits and whole grains into meals to maintain a balanced diet and healthy weight, HPA Director-General Shen Ching-fen (沈靜芬) said.
A traditional 180g lotus seed paste mooncake with pine nuts contains about 720 calories, equivalent to approximately 2.5 bowls of white rice, the agency said.
Photo: Tsai Shu-yuan, Taipei Times
People are advised to check nutrition labels and compare calorie, sugar and fat content before purchasing mooncakes, it said.
Mooncakes can also be cut into smaller portions and shared with family and friends to regulate calorie intake, while unsweetened tea or water is recommended over sugary drinks, it said.
For holiday barbecues, the agency advised following three main principles: lower calories, avoiding charred food and minimizing smoke exposure.
The primary hazard when grilling is charred food, as high-temperature cooking can generate heterocyclic amines, while meat juices, fat or sauces dripping onto open flames produce polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, it said.
Avoid direct contact between food and open flames, limit exposure to high heat and turn food regularly during cooking, it said, adding that burnt portions should be discarded before eating.
People are also encouraged to adopt a “more vegetables, less meat” approach, choosing moderate amounts of fish and chicken while increasing servings of vegetables such as green or bell peppers and other food like mushrooms and baby corn, it said.
Processed foods including sausages, bacon and meatballs should be limited, it added.
Barbecue sauce should be applied sparingly to reduce sugar and sodium intake, while natural seasonings such as scallions, garlic and pepper can be used to enhance flavor, it said.
Another commonly overlooked hazard is smoke, the agency said.
Barbecue fumes can increase concentrations of air pollutants such as PM2.5, potentially irritating the eyes and respiratory system, it said.
The HPA recommended choosing well-ventilated outdoor locations and avoiding indoor spaces or poorly ventilated balconies.
Barbecue and seating areas should be separated when possible, and people should avoid remaining downwind of smoke for extended periods, it said.
Those tending the grill should also take regular breaks, while vulnerable groups should exercise additional caution, it added.
Separately, a doctor at Lian An Wellness Center said that people with gallstones should be especially careful during the holiday.
High-fat foods can stimulate gallbladder contractions, potentially causing gallstones to shift and block bile ducts, triggering pain, said Yang Jian-hua (楊建華), director of the center’s ultrasound room.
People with gallstones should avoid consuming large quantities of high-fat foods, such as mooncakes, salted egg yolk pastries and barbecue dishes within a short period of time, he said.
While people should avoid overeating, skipping meals can also increase the risk of gallstones, he said.
Prolonged fasting reduces gallbladder contractions and bile release, allowing bile to remain in the gallbladder for extended periods and increasing the likelihood of sludge, sediment and gallstone formation, he said.
About one in every 13 people was found to have gallstones, according to the center’s analysis of more than 35,000 health examination records last year.
As gallstones often produce no obvious symptoms, many cases are discovered only during routine health examinations or abdominal ultrasound scans, it said.
People with a family history of gallstones, middle-aged or older women, women who have given birth multiple times, people who are overweight or those undergoing rapid weight loss, as well as those with chronic diseases such as diabetes or liver disease, face a higher risk, Yang said.
Maintaining gallbladder health does not require eliminating dietary fats entirely, but rather maintaining regular meals, controlling overall fat intake and avoiding prolonged fasting or rapid weight loss, he said.

Two chimps escape through unsecured doors: Taipei Zoo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:21 UTC
01:38:21 KST

Two chimpanzees escaped from their enclosure on Thursday because staff did not properly secure two doors, Taipei Zoo said yesterday.
The chimpanzee enclosure is separated from the zoo’s public areas by a double-door access corridor, Taipei Zoo spokesman Tsao Hsien-shao (曹先紹) told a news conference.
However, a caretaker had forgotten to engage the slide bolt on the door between the corridor and the enclosure, allowing the two animals to force it open, Tsao said.
Photo courtesy of Taipei Zoo
The chimpanzees forced open the access corridor’s exit door, which had been left unlocked by workers carrying out construction in the area, he said.
The zoo will review its management guidelines, improve employee training and supervision, and increase inspections, he added.
At 4:55pm on Thursday, a 44-year-old male chimp named Hsiao Chiang (小強) and an 11-year-old male named Wa Chih (娃智) escaped from their enclosure, prompting zoo management to activate an emergency response plan, Taipei Zoo said.
At about 5pm, the area around the breached enclosure was sealed off and nearby visitors were evacuated, while veterinary staff prepared to tranquilize and capture the escaped animals, it said.
Hsiao Chiang remained near the chimpanzee enclosure and visited the area for the female chimpanzees before being tranquilized with a dart at 5:28pm, the zoo said.
Wa Chih moved to the giraffe exhibition area before heading to a tree near the lion enclosure, where zoo staff administered a tranquilizer dart, but Wa Chih removed it, it said.
Zoo staff administered a second dart, the zoo said.
The second dart subdued Wa Chih at 5:40pm, it said.
The two chimpanzees were taken to the zoo’s Animal Medical Center for examination and returned to their indoor enclosures after waking at about 8pm.
Taipei Zoo Animal Section head Wu Li-hsin (吳立信) said that almost 50 staff and several barricades were deployed in the capture of the chimpanzees.
In the event of an animal escape, Tsao said that keeping a safe distance is key.
Another way visitors can help is by reporting any sightings of escaped animals to the zoo, he said.

US committed to First Island Chain deterrence: MAC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:19 UTC
01:38:19 KST

The US remains committed to maintaining deterrence along the First Island Chain, Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) said yesterday.
Taiwan remained in close communication with the US, Shen said, adding that messages received by Taipei indicated that maintaining deterrence along the First Island Chain remained a US policy priority.
He made the remarks to reporters on the sidelines of a seminar held in Taipei by National Chengchi University’s Institute of International Relations on developments in China and the country’s outlook since the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) 20th National Congress in 2022.
Taiwan should closely watch whether US President Donald Trump and his team reiterate that Washington’s Taiwan policy remains unchanged during a second meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) on Thursday next week, Shen said.
His comments came after former National Security Council secretary-general Su Chi (蘇起) on Thursday said that risks in the Taiwan Strait were rising due to changes in US security commitments to Taiwan, and Beijing’s growing sense of urgency over Taiwan.
The likelihood of Washington announcing new arms sales to Taiwan was “very, very low,” Su said, adding that Beijing would react strongly to such a move before or after the Trump-Xi meeting.
Taiwan should not rely solely on external powers for its security and should consider political measures to reduce cross-strait tensions, Su said.
“I am not as pessimistic as Su Chi,” Shen said.
Asked about Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung’s (林佳龍) statement that Taiwan and the US should “jointly manage China,” Shen said the phrase referred to managing risks rather than China itself.
“Jointly managing China means jointly managing risks. It does not mean managing mainland China,” he said.
Taiwan has the resolve and capabilities to work with Washington to preserve peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait by deterring Beijing from using force to alter the “status quo,” Shen said.
Regarding the upcoming fifth plenary session of the CCP’s 20th Central Committee, Shen said that the MAC had prepared for various scenarios and would update its assessment of personnel changes as developments unfold.
“The more important event is next year’s 21st National Congress,” Shen said.
Major personnel decisions, including those concerning Xi’s tenure, could be settled then, Shen added.

Center-local disconnect hurts KMT campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:16 UTC
01:38:16 KST

Wei Ping-cheng (魏平政), the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) candidate for Changhua County commissioner in November’s local elections, on Sept. 6 officially opened his campaign headquarters with a major rally. KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) and Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) attended the event, demonstrating the firm support of party leadership and neighboring KMT-governed local governments.
However, conspicuously absent was Changhua County Commissioner Wang Hui-mei (王惠美), who sent flowers in her place.
Meanwhile, the position of campaign headquarters director-general remains vacant.
Behind the fanfare, the rally highlighted deeper challenges facing the KMT in managing the handover of power in the county and its candidate-nomination process.
There is an institutional and communication disconnect that leads to anxiety over policy continuity. Judging from Wang’s public expression of frustration and news of political trouble in the region, the impasse seems to reflect a structural contradiction common in Taiwan’s party politics. They arise when a party’s central electoral machinery and a local administration differ over the timing of nominations or their preferred candidates. A lack of careful and thorough communication easily results in resentment.
For an incumbent local leader, their record in office and the continuity of local development projects are their greatest political assets. For the party leadership, the priority is to consider the overall strategic picture. When the two sides differ, a situation can emerge in which the party leadership is eager to push ahead, while the local government prefers to hang back.
Wang’s absence and the flowers she sent might have been a political statement by a local leader confronted with an unfavorable successor.
Another issue in the handover process is focus on replicating victories and the need for reforms that go beyond sloganeering.
At the rally, senior KMT figures harked back to the party’s comeback victory in the county eight years ago, seeking to replicate a winning formula.
However, victory in elections depends on adapting to changing circumstances.
Focusing on successes can boost morale, but it does not automatically secure votes. As a key electoral battleground, Changhua County has a complex voter base and deeply entrenched local factions. Motivational rhetoric or appeals to the broader political picture are unlikely to bridge divisions at the grassroots level. The real task is to bring together views from competing camps, factions and supporters around the greatest common denominator.
A third challenge is to resolve differences.
Wei has demonstrated flexibility and a willingness to seek broad support, which is the right approach to breaking a deadlock.
However, rebuilding political trust requires time and sincerity.
If the KMT’s leadership and its Changhua County campaign team fail to substantively address the concerns of the local administration and establish channels for dialogue, the plan to “unite to win” could face serious obstacles.
Bringing local political forces back into the fold and paving the way for a smooth handover of governance will be the deciding factors in whether the KMT can retain its hold on power in Changhua County.
Wei Chi-hung is president of the Taiwan International Cultural and Educational Public Interest Association.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader
Taiwan’s domestic political situation is following recognizable political rhythms, while the international environment surrounding Taiwan is undergoing a major transformation. Within Taiwan, there are ongoing battles between the legislative and executive branches over the budget, and between cities and the central government over resources. Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

China did not lose face: President Xi Jinping (習近平) was an honored guest in India, was endorsed as the chair of BRICS for next year, and China is to host the next summit. Yet the carefully crafted 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration (NDD), the longest BRICS declaration so far, reveals a subtle, but important shift. US holds off tariffs until Xi summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:16 UTC
01:38:16 KST

The US is expected to hold off announcing new tariffs on China and other trading partners until after next week’s summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and US President Donald Trump, according to people familiar with the matter, a delay that could preserve such a threat as leverage in the negotiations.
While the reason for the postponement is unclear, Trump has repeatedly used tariff warnings to press trading partners for concessions. The administration had intended to release a trade report on alleged excess capacity before the meeting that would recommend a 7.5 percent tariff on Chinese goods, Bloomberg previously reported.
It is also uncertain whether the final tariff rate would change from the previously expected level, which would restore Trump’s second-term duties on China to about 20 percent, which Beijing has previously said is consistent with its trade truce with Washington.
Photo: Bloomberg
US and Chinese negotiators are set to meet over the weekend to discuss any agreements ahead of Xi’s state visit. The trip would be Xi’s first to the US since 2023, when he met former president Joe Biden during a visit that included attending the APEC summit in San Francisco.
In March, the Trump administration launched an investigation into more than a dozen major trading partners under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 over excess capacity concerns. Those expected levies, along with already-implemented duties related to forced labor, are set to eventually bring rates closer to Trump’s country-specific tariffs that were overturned by the Supreme Court earlier this year.
The Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House did not respond to requests for comment. Inside US Trade first reported the delay.
China has previously signaled that it could take action if US tariffs exceed prevailing levels when the trade truce was struck.
“Capacity issues should be viewed in a comprehensive and fair manner, and should not be used as a pretext for protectionism,” Huang Ling, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Commerce, said late last month. “We will continue to closely follow and comprehensively assess subsequent US moves, and reserve the right to take all necessary measures.”
“A key question for the US team is how much it might be willing and able to leverage tariff threats to push China for stronger import and export commitments. Chinese exporters’ resilience to Washington’s hefty tariffs through 2025 is likely to blunt that leverage,” economist Nicole Gorton-Caratelli said.

Ministry freezes electricity rates until December meet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:15 UTC
01:38:15 KST

The Ministry of Economic Affairs yesterday said it would delay setting new electricity rates until its meeting in December, in a bid to help curb increases in consumer prices.
Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) proposed raising electricity rates by about 12.83 percent to NT$4.2675 per kilowatt-hour, reflecting increases in energy costs, Deputy Minister of Economic Affairs Lai Chien-hsin (賴建信) told a news conference after wrapping up the electricity price review committee’s meeting.
The average electricity rate would remain unchanged at NT$3.78 per kilowatt-hour from next month until the next review, Lai said.
Photo: CNA
Seeking a Cabinet-backed subsidy of NT$71.1 billion (US$2.24 billion) to help Taipower absorb the fuel price surges from March through last month would be the ministry’s priority, Lai said.
Taipower is expected to lose NT$71.1 billion this year, he said, adding that the company could have been profitable this year, if the Middle East conflict did not occur.
Taipower posted a profit of NT$76.1 billion last year, giving it some leeway to absorb the electricity rate freeze, Taipower president Kuo Tien-ho (郭天合) said.
“As neighboring countries have relied on supplementary budgets and subsidies to mitigate the impact from the Middle East conflict, the committee decided to support to seek government funding first to ease Taipower’s financial burden,” Lai said.
The NT$71.1 billion subsidy, if approved by the legislature, would significantly improve Taipower’s financial situation and help ease the pressure for further electricity rate hikes, Lai added.
Taipower is facing mounting financial pressure, as it has accumulated losses of more than NT$400 billion due to absorbing high global crude oil prices instead of passing costs to consumers for the past few years, Kuo said.
Taipower lost NT$21.4 billion in the first seven months of this year, bringing its accumulated losses to NT$372.2 billion, he added.
General Chamber of Commerce of the Republic of China chairman Paul Hsu (許舒博), a member of the electricity price review committee, said he did not support a blanket freeze on electricity rates.
“We hope electricity rates can be frozen for households and small and medium-sized traditional industries, while high-tech industries should see moderate [price] adjustment,” Hsu said.
A mild increase would have a relatively limited effect on high-tech companies, Hsu added.
The committee discussed the possibility of hiking electricity rates for heavy power users such as artificial intelligence (AI) data centers and semiconductor companies, but no consensus was reached, Lai said.
Increases in electricity demand from AI and semiconductor companies should not push up rates for all users, he said.
However, electricity pricing cannot predetermine that specific industries should bear the additional costs, he added.
Industries’ electricity use patterns, growth prospects, international competitiveness and the impact on consumer prices would be reviewed by a working group and discussed further in December, he said.

As the domestic influenza epidemic enters its peak season and continues to escalate, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) yesterday announced that publicly funded influenza antiviral drugs for seven eligible groups have been extended to Oct. 31, allowing those who develop flu-like symptoms to receive the medication without undergoing a rapid influenza test.
The CDC has extended the expanded use of flu antiviral drugs to seven groups: healthcare and influenza-prevention personnel; residents and staff at nursing homes, long-term care facilities and similar institutions; kindergarten and daycare workers and home-based caregivers; students from kindergarten through high school, vocational high school and the first three years of junior colleges; people who live with or care for those at high risk of severe influenza; livestock and poultry farmers, zoo workers and animal disease-prevention personnel; and personnel in densely populated areas such as military camps where clusters are likely to occur.
The state-funded antiviral medicines are Tamiflu and Eraflu, both oseltamivir drugs, and have been distributed to about 4,000 contracted medical institutions nationwide, the CDC said.
Photo: Taipei Times
People who meet the eligibility requirements and develop flu-like symptoms do not need to take a rapid influenza test beforehand. Doctors can prescribe the drugs based on the patient’s condition and their clinical judgement, the CDC said.
The necessity of administering free antiviral drugs and the timing of treatment are also to be determined by doctors, it said.
The CDC said that influenza can cause serious complications and urged people to seek medical attention as soon as possible if they develop symptoms such as rapid breathing, difficulty breathing, cyanosis, bloody sputum, chest pain, altered consciousness or low blood pressure.
The CDC advised people to wash their hands frequently, practice good cough etiquette and wear a mask when they have respiratory symptoms.
Students with flu-like symptoms should seek medical attention and get plenty of rest, returning to school only after they have recovered to prevent the virus from spreading among classmates.

====================================================================================================

Zinc deficiency could be cause of hair loss: doctor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:13 UTC
01:38:13 KST

About 30 percent of people seeking medical attention for hair loss have a zinc deficiency, a dermatologist said on Monday.
Some people can improve their condition in as little as six weeks by eating zinc-rich foods such as oysters and pumpkin seeds, said Ko Wei-li (柯偉立), head of the dermatology section at Cheng Ching Hospital in Taichung
Citing an example, Ko said that blood tests found a severe zinc deficiency was the primary cause of sudden and rapid hair loss in a 37-year-old male patient whose hair was thinning at the crown and temples.
Photo: Huang Hsu-lei, Taipei Times
The man, an office worker of average height and weight, had been concerned he was developing male-pattern baldness, as his father is completely bald, Ko said.
However, tests revealed that his blood zinc level was 85 percent of the lower limit of the normal range, he added.
After six weeks of adding more zinc to his diet, including oysters, beef and pumpkin seeds, under the guidance of a nutritionist, most of his hair had grown back and his zinc levels had returned to a healthy range, he said.
Zinc deficiencies are often caused by improper dieting or long-term consumption of foods low in zinc, though a small number of patients have conditions that cause the deficiency, such as chronic diarrhea, he said.
About 90 percent of the structure of human hair is protein, or keratin, Ko said.
A zinc deficiency can affect the synthesis of hair keratin, causing slower growth, thinning hair strands and more fragile hair that is prone to breakage, the doctor said.
People concerned about zinc deficiency and hair loss should not take supplements on their own, but should first undergo testing at a qualified medical facility and discuss a suitable zinc supplementation plan with a doctor and a nutritionist, he said.

Russians vote as Ukraine war drags on for fifth year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:12 UTC
01:38:12 KST

Russians yesterday began voting in a tightly controlled three-day election that is set to tighten Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 26-year grip on power, in the country’s fifth year of war with Ukraine.
It is Russia’s first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in February 2022. Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organized voting in occupied Ukraine.
The EU slammed the elections, saying “repression” had been used to eradicate opponents, while a Council of Europe body denounced the vote as “fake.”
Photo: AP
While few Russians doubt Putin’s United Russia party would cruise to victory again, the vote offers a gauge of public support for the war. Putin has ruled Russia since 1999 and his party has dominated politics since the early 2000s. Moscow has banned criticism of the Ukraine campaign, and elections under Putin rarely produce surprises. Putin had called on Russians to vote to show they back Moscow’s troops and to deliver an “answer to those who want to weaken Russia.”
The Kremlin published footage of the 73-year-old president voting online — rare footage of the longtime leader. On Moscow’s streets, several voters said they wanted the war in Ukraine to end — but on Russia’s terms, backing Putin’s goals.
Rail worker Sergei Korenets said he would back United Russia, voting for “stability” — echoing Putin’s main slogan.
Asked whether four-and-a-half years of war amounts to “stability,” Korenets said: “Of course, I want all this [the war] to end as quickly as possible.”
Despite sweeping Western sanctions, Russia’s economy has not collapsed and life in the capital remains relatively normal even as Moscow bombards Ukrainian cities daily.
United Russia faces only parties that broadly back Putin’s policies and the war: the Communist Party, the nationalist LDPR, A Just Russia and New People.
Yabloko, which called for an end to the fighting, was barred from running shortly before the vote. One of its main figures, Lev Shlosberg, was imprisoned for criticizing the war.
Russia has since 2022 introduced Soviet-style censorship and jailed war critics.
“I am fully for the special military operation,” Lyubov said.
“NATO cannot be at our borders,” she added, repeating one of Putin’s arguments for launching the war.
However, she criticized some social policies, upset by Putin raising the pension age several years ago, saying she wanted a “return to the Soviet economic system.”
Older voters are among Putin’s strongest supporters, although many complain about living standards.
Putin’s political opponents have mostly been driven into exile ,and his main opponent, Alexei Navalny, died in an arctic prison in 2024.
Russia’s exiled opposition has urged anti-Kremlin Russians not to boycott the elections, but instead vote “against Putin’s party.”
Navalny’s widow, Yulia Navalnaya, called on anti-war Russians to cast their ballots at noon tomorrow.
Yabloko disagrees, saying that it was better not to vote.
“You are suggesting that we once again go, like sheep, dancing to their tune, and vote for those who have caused the deaths of people in Russia and Ukraine?” party chairman Nikolay Rybakov said.

UK police brace for soccer brawls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:08 UTC
01:38:08 KST

Police are on red alert as the English Championship braces for the renewal of two bitter feuds when Millwall face West Ham and Wolves meet West Brom this weekend.
Leaders West Ham travel to the Den tomorrow for the first “Dockers Derby” against London rivals Millwall in 14 years.
Wolves host fourth-placed West Brom in the Black Country derby on Sunday — two years after their last meeting was marred by a bloody battle in the stands.
Photo: AFP
Millwall and West Ham have an especially gory history, with one supporter of each club killed in sickening clashes in 1976 and 1986.
Those horrific incidents came at the height of the hooliganism era that blighted English soccer.
However, the enmity, born a century ago in London’s docks, has lost none of its ferocity in the past few years.
In 2009, a Millwall supporter was stabbed outside West Ham’s former home at Upton Park before a stormy League Cup tie that culminated in several pitch invasions, prompting then-minister of sports Gerry Sutcliffe to label the incidents “a disgrace to football.”
West Ham were fined ￡115,000 (US$153,000) for failing to prevent their fans entering the pitch, while several supporters were convicted of violent disorder.
Separated by just over 10km across the River Thames, the 100th showdown between the Lions and the Irons would play out against a backdrop of high security across south-east London.
Social media have been rife with threats between rival fans in the build-up to tomorrow’s game.
“We want fans to enjoy the match safely and have worked with both clubs to help this happen,” the Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
“A Section 35 dispersal order will be in place, allowing officers to remove anyone causing disorder,” it said.
Adding to the tension around the fixture, some Millwall fans would be housed in the same stand as the 1,774 West Ham supporters in a sell-out crowd of about 19,000 at the Den.
Strict segregation would be in place to keep the rivals apart.
Millwall have not beaten West Ham since 2004 and Lions boss Alex Neil hopes the hostile atmosphere can help his team stun Nuno Espirito Santo’s men.
“It should be a brilliant atmosphere. It means a lot to our fans and everybody connected with both clubs,” Neil said.
Just 24 hours after Millwall face West Ham, an equally explosive clash is to take place in the west midlands.
The first league meeting between Wolves and West Brom in five years comes after a FA Cup tie in 2024 was scarred by crowd trouble. Wolves’ 2-0 win at the Hawthorns two years ago was halted for 38 minutes after fans clashed in the stands, with police assaulted, missiles thrown and flares set off.
There were 43 arrests, with 12 sentenced and five given permanent bans.
In a joint statement, Wolves and Albion said supporters can “expect enhanced stewarding, policing, robust ticketing controls and additional safety measures” on Sunday.
Wolves and Albion emphasized the punishments dished out for the 2024 clashes show “disorder, violence and criminal behavior carry significant consequences and will continue to be dealt with robustly.”
All four clubs will hope the weekend’s derbies pass off far more peacefully than some of their previous encounters.

Restoration work at Mataian yields fruit: official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:05 UTC
01:38:05 KST

Up to 224 hectares of a farmland damaged by last year’s Mataian River (馬太鞍溪) barrier lake overflow in Hualien County has been restored and planted with dryland crops, with a specialty product made from the post-disaster crops, soy milk blended with millet, launched in Taipei yesterday.
The post-disaster recovery efforts were led by the Ministry of Agriculture and implemented mainly by the Hualien District Agricultural Research and Extension Station in collaboration with agricultural authorities and local agricultural workers.
Station Crop Environment Section chief Tsai Yi-chen (蔡依真) said disaster-stricken farmlands amounted to nearly 774 hectares, of which 383 hectares were lightly to moderately affected with a mud buildup of 50cm or less.
Photo: CNA
Such moderately affected fields have the potential to restore their soil fertility through soil improvement methods, Tsai said, adding that test results showed that the mud is free of heavy metal.
They were initially uncultivable due to damaged soil structure, poor soil drainage and post-disaster debris accumulation, she said.
The station used excavators and plows to help remove debris and turn the soil to depths of up to 70cm, Tsai said.
It also applied organic fertilizers or planted green manure crops for up to three months to restore the farmland’s fertility, she said.
The station has collaborated with the Taiwan Agricultural Research Institute on growing cherry radishes, kale and buckwheat, and trail planting at the Mapulong Farm and Pangcah Farm in the county’s Guangfu Township (光復) from November last year, Tsai said.
Most other restored farmlands were planted with dryland crops such as soybean, millet, sorghum or corn, she said.
The soil improvement methods have boosted local soil fertility, Tsai said.
For example, the corn cultivated on restored fields grew stronger and weighed up to 262g per ear of corn, much higher than those planted on fields without using organic fertilizers, at 39g per ear, she said.
Up to 224 hectares of the affected land has been restored and cultivated with dryland crops, she added.
Deputy Minister of Agriculture Huang Chao-chin (黃昭欽) said the region used to focus on rice production prior to the disaster.
However, irrigation water has become more difficult to obtain due to the enhanced flood prevention works after the disaster, he said.
With the Irrigation Agency’s efforts to drill wells and divert water, dryland crop cultivation has become feasible for the region, Huang said, adding that sales channels and markets must be adjusted accordingly.
To help promote the crops, the ministry’s Resources Sustainability Department formulated environmental, social and governance (ESG) projects, and invited corporate participation in post-disaster recovery, he said.
The station said the ESG projects include corporate investments in post-disaster cultivation training, organic fertilizer procurement, agricultural machinery donations, millet soy milk purchases, charity meal services and indigenous crop cultivation.

An F-16 fighter jet crashed in the United States: the pilot ejected, two police officers were hospitalized
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
19:37:30 EEST
01:37:30 KST

An F-16 fighter jet crashed in the United States: the pilot ejected, two police officers were hospitalized
Kyiv • UNN
The aircraft crashed during a training flight in Grand Traverse County. The pilot survived, while two sheriff's employees were hospitalized with injuries.
In the U.S. state of Michigan, an F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jet belonging to the 149th Fighter Wing of the Texas Air National Guard crashed. The pilot managed to eject and survived. Following the crash, there was a threat of a toxic-substance leak in the area where the aircraft went down, and two sheriff’s office employees were hospitalized. CBS News reports, as reported by UNN.
Details
The crash occurred on September 17 at approximately 1:52 p.m. local time in Grand Traverse County, near the city of Traverse City in northern Michigan. According to the U.S. military, the F-16 was conducting a training flight from the Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center. The aircraft belonged to the 149th Fighter Wing of the Texas Air National Guard, based at Joint Base San Antonio–Lackland.
The pilot was the only person on board. He ejected before the aircraft struck the ground. He was found near the crash site and taken to Munson Medical Center in Traverse City. According to local authorities, the pilot was conscious and able to communicate with law enforcement officers. His condition was assessed as stable. The pilot’s name has not yet been released.
After the fighter jet crashed, a fire broke out at the site and several explosions were heard. Due to a possible hazardous-substance leak, residents within approximately one mile of the crash site were initially urged to remain indoors and were later evacuated.
In addition, medical personnel reported a risk of exposure to hydrazine—a toxic substance used in the F-16’s emergency power unit. A decontamination center was set up at a local hospital for people who may have come into contact with the substance.
As of the morning of September 18, two employees of the Grand Traverse County Sheriff’s Office remained hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening. Other people who sought medical assistance had been discharged.
The cause of the crash has not yet been officially determined. At the same time, recordings of communications between the pilots and air traffic controllers suggest that the aircraft may have struck a bird before crashing. Military officials emphasize that this version has not yet been confirmed and is being examined as part of the investigation.
The 149th Fighter Wing was in Michigan as part of Operation Northern Cactus exercises, during which the military practiced relocating personnel and equipment and conducting flights from unfamiliar sites. Following the crash, some of the planned F-16 flights in the area were canceled. The investigation into the cause of the fighter jet’s crash is ongoing.
Recall
In August 2026, a Turkish Air Force F-16 crashed in Yalova during a training flight. The pilot ejected and survived.

Explosion near a Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center in Lviv region: detainees suspected of terrorism; two more improvised explosive devices found in one of their homes
Kyiv • UNN
Two residents of Lviv region are suspected of a terrorist attack near the Stryi Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center, where a serviceman was seriously wounded. Two more IEDs were found in one of their homes.
Two men detained after explosives were detonated near a Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center (TCC) in Lviv region have been notified of suspicion of committing a terrorist attack. According to the Security Service of Ukraine, law enforcement officers found two more improvised explosive devices at the residence of one of the suspects, reports UNN.
Details
The counterintelligence department of the Security Service and the National Police, "following hot on the trail," detained two residents of Lviv region who committed a terrorist attack near the administrative building of the Stryi District TCC on September 17 this year.
The investigation established that the suspects threw an improvised explosive device (IED) onto the territory of the military enlistment office. As a result of the incident, a serviceman at the restricted-access facility was injured.
To carry out the terrorist attack, the perpetrators drove up to the district TCC building in their own car; one of the assailants threw an improvised bomb through the vehicle's window onto a parking area near the military enlistment office, and they hurriedly left the scene.
Later, during an inspection of the explosive device by a TCC serviceman, the IED detonated, seriously injuring him.
According to the investigation, the detainees were two residents of Mykolaivskyi District, Lviv region, aged 48 and 41.
During a search at the residence of one of the suspects, law enforcement officers found two more improvised explosive devices. They were seized and sent for the relevant examinations.
Investigators from the Security Service notified the suspects of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 258 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (committing a terrorist act by a group of persons acting under a prior conspiracy).
The investigation is ongoing to establish all the circumstances of the crime, including the terrorists' possible involvement in cooperation with Russian special services.
Recall
In Mykolaiv, Lviv region, an explosion occurred near a TCC building; a serviceman was injured and hospitalized.

BRUSSELS — Top European officials are increasingly alarmed that Russia could stage drone or missile attacks against NATO countries as Moscow steps up its hybrid campaign across the continent.
The warnings underscore a growing sense of anxiety in Europe amid fast-proliferating incidents of airspace violations and sabotage attempts in recent months. NATO allies have repeatedly said they see the attacks as pressure from the Kremlin to reduce their support for Ukraine but have muted their response over fears of escalation.
French President Emmanuel Macron summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting on Friday to talk about Ukraine, Iran and the growing energy crisis.
He called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented” as he announced a new critical infrastructure protection plan, adding: “In recent weeks … the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and France has intensified.”
Guillaume Lacroix, leader of the Radical Party of the Left, left the meeting saying: “At the age of 50, I have rarely felt such vertigo.”
“It is no coincidence that the Polish prime minister is speaking out so strongly,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said Friday. “We need to take that warning very seriously … we must consistently demonstrate that we do not accept this and that we will take action if necessary.”
On Thursday, Finnish President Alexander Stubb told his country it was “worth mentally preparing for something to happen” including sabotage and Russian drones.
Advertisement
Moscow is also ramping up its bellicose rhetoric ahead of Russia's legislative election this weekend that is widely expected to keep President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party in power.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov this week warned Europe it would face a “very short” war if NATO allies attempted to attack the country.
“Russia has stepped up the pace of its activities — we need to remain vigilant,” said one senior European defense official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “This may be seen as a manifestation of a broader trend ... we have seen similar warnings before, and there may well be more to come.”
So far, the latest incidents haven't prompted any additional multilateral responses, a second senior European defense official said. But “we are monitoring closely,” they added.
U.S. intelligence reports in August warned that Moscow was planning a limited assault on a NATO country in the coming years. CIA Director John Ratcliffe warned Russian officials in Moscow late last month not to escalate conflict with NATO allies, in particular Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, in response to Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Yet it remains unclear whether the latest warnings are based on fresh intelligence.
On Friday, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said Vilnius had “the same intelligence” as Tusk “about a possible foreign-flag operation” but suggested that dated back to July.
“I see the public statements of politicians about this as part of a coordinated campaign to warn Russia not to make stupid decisions and not to try to do something thinking that it will not reach [NATO’s mutual defense clause] Article 5 and will not be washed away,” he said.
Allies have not formally been briefed on any new intelligence inside NATO, according to two alliance diplomats, and NATO has so far not changed its threat assessment.
“At this time, we see no imminent threat of attack,” said a NATO official speaking on behalf of the organization, adding: “But we cannot not be naive or complacent, and we must make sure NATO remains strong in the years ahead.”
Advertisement
Ed Arnold, a former NATO official and adviser at the D Group consultancy, said the warnings could also be designed to raise public awareness of threats and to “pre-bunk” false flag attacks before they take place.
A senior NATO military official said that Russia may be lashing out because of its difficulties in defeating Ukraine. “It therefore may incorrectly perceive the only way out is through increasing its hybrid campaign — that’s a losing proposition, because we are ready to respond.”
Between January and August, there were 100 officially attributed hybrid incidents across Europe compared to 60 during the same period last year, according to the Ukraine-based Sahaidachnyi Security Center think tank — with a particularly sharp rise in airspace violations.
A senior NATO official said the real number was “easily 200 plus” not counting cyberattacks — of which there are “thousands” each month against the military alliance’s Brussels headquarters alone. “Numbers are up, severity is up, [Russia’s] risk appetite is up,” they said.
