Artists in Gaza have painted a mural of Macklemore wrapped in a Palestinian flag on a huge slab of concrete in the ruins of Gaza City, after the US rapper was kicked off Ed Sheeran's upcoming tour for calling for a "Free Palestine."
The mural, on a slab that leans against ruined buildings surrounded by rubble, depicts the "Thrift Shop" rapper raising a fist in the air.
"Thank you for using your voice for Palestine," it reads.
"We wanted to send a message to thank rapper Macklemore in this simple way," said Anne Redwan, 26, who designed and painted the mural with fellow artist Qusai al-Helo.
"As an artist living under siege here in Gaza, we are waiting for support from anyone who can see (the) persecution we live under," she told Reuters. "We can paint murals bigger than this to express our feelings."
Macklemore, who has long supported Palestinian causes, was cut from British pop star Sheeran's musical lineup over remarks on stage criticizing Israel's military assault in Gaza, which was launched after Hamas-led fighters attacked Israel in October 2023.
Macklemore removed from tour dates amid pushback

Nearly a year after a ceasefire ended major fighting in Gaza, reconstruction has yet to begin. Most buildings have been destroyed, and more than two million residents are confined to around a third of the enclave's territory, mostly in tents or crowded rooms in damaged buildings among the ruins.

Gaza aid donations emerge amid Sheeran, Macklemore fallout

Kraft, in turn, said Sheeran had told him he would donate $2 million for aid in the region, and had asked him to match the pledge. Sheeran has not commented on any donations. Macklemore's donation drew a matching $1 million pledge from Ms Rachel, a popular children's TV personality.
Aid agency officials said the boost in celebrity attention could help bring more support to Gaza, where nearly all residents rely on aid for food, water, medical care and shelter.
"But what's really most important is that people who have been so generous keep fighting over a sustained time," said Toby Fricker, a local official with UNICEF. "That's why we really call for sustained support, not one-off peaks, but sustained."

Hussein Murtaja, who runs a Gaza humanitarian group that provides mental health support to children, said Macklemore's solidarity matters more than the money he donated.
"When artists of this stature, with this many followers or fans, all come to know more about the cause, and support reaching a political solution, support achieving peace for the people of Gaza... That means a great deal to us."

====================================================================================================

Meet the second-generation Israeli farmer and reservist who grows tomatoes on the Egyptian border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:34:59 UTC
01:34:59 KST

As Israel’s largest regional council, Ramat HaNegev is home to approximately 10,500 residents spread across communities, kibbutzim, and farms covering 22% of Israel’s landmass.
Few choose to live in the remote Negev highlands, especially in the Nitzana region of the council, which has five small, remote agricultural communities near the Egyptian border, including Kadesh Barnea (officially known as Nitzanei Sinai), which is only 300 meters away.
But nearly four years ago, Noam Efrat, 33, chose to return to his roots and raise his own family in Kadesh Barnea. He handles the bright red, deliciously sweet cherry tomatoes from his family’s farm carefully before they are transported and sold in boutique shops in Tel Aviv.
An isolated moshav of 87 families, Noam, his wife, Noa, and their young son, Negev, enjoy the quiet that defines the desert landscape. The young family moved to the south from Metula in 2022.
Working on his father’s cherry tomato farm today, Efrat recalled that, as a teenager, he dreamed of living as far away as possible from the Egyptian border community.
“I didn’t think as a teenager that I would end up working on my father’s farm as an adult. When you live in a rural area, you just want to escape and see the world,” Efrat told the Jerusalem Post Magazine in a recent interview.
While his childhood was filled with the freedom of roaming sand dunes with friends and learning to grow and take care of tomatoes in his family’s greenhouses, Efrat believed that life was waiting to happen in the fast-paced cities. After completing his army service, Efrat chose to live in central Israel.
“I lived in Florentin in Tel Aviv, but after a while, I understood that I did not like city life, so I moved to Metula in the north,” he said.
Efrat studied for a combined degree in computers and environmental sciences and met his wife at Tel Hai College.
Eventually, the couple moved back to Kadesh Barnea, and Efrat continued to his master’s degree in agroinformatics at Ben-Gurion University’s Sde Boker campus in Midreshet Ben-Gurion.
AS A TOMATO farmer who has also served over 300 days in IDF reserve duty since October 7, Efrat wakes up each day at 5:30 a.m. and drives five minutes away to his family’s meshek (farm).
“The advantage is the short distance to work and no traffic along the way,” he said of living in Kadesh Barnea. “After two hours of early morning work, I get home by 8 so that I can take my son, Negev, to daycare, and then go back to work again until noon.”
In the afternoon, Efrat returns to work in the greenhouses when it is less hot. “Our schedules are determined by the hours of sunlight – the moment the sun sets and it gets dark, we head back home.”
Efrat said that living in Kadesh Barnea as a farmer is living the dream. But both his parents, Iftach and Celia, had no background in farming when they first moved from Beersheba to Kadesh Barnea over 30 years ago.
Efrat’s mother, Celia, had made aliyah from São Paulo, Brazil. “She didn’t know that there were areas in the world as quiet as Kadesh Barnea, let alone in Israel. She had lived all her life in the city,” he recalled with a smile. “This quiet of the Negev desert was a bit of a shock for her.”
Today, in addition to agricultural opportunities, residents of the Nitzana region also work in local tourism and education, and some even travel an hour to Beersheba for work. The Nitzana region is also known for its ancient Nabataean and Byzantine archeological and historical sites.
Farmers experimented with growing different vegetables
When Efrat’s parents moved to the Nitzana region in 1995, the only employment opportunities were agricultural: “So my father learned how to grow cherry tomatoes, which was popular at the time. Farmers today mostly grow cucumbers, wine grapes, peppers, and salicornia (a succulent edible plant also known as sea asparagus).”
Efrat also pointed out that over time, the farmers in his region experimented with growing different vegetables: “At first it wasn’t known if tomatoes could grow well in the Negev desert. In fact, tomatoes grow amazingly in greenhouses thanks to the desert temperatures. The cool desert nights really help with their growth.”
In addition, the Nitzana region depends on brackish geothermal desert groundwater, as well as desalinated water, for agriculture and farming. The brackish water originates from local water sources around the Kadesh Barnea area. Water doesn’t have to be transported from far away, which saves money.
“The salinated water actually makes for sweeter cherry tomatoes,” added Efrat.
Tomato knowledge farming extends into another area
BUT EFRAT’S vast knowledge in Negev tomato farming also extends to another area: the history of the Nitzana region. Besides working on the family’s tomato farm, Efrat also helps run a project called Gesher L’Dorot (A Bridge for Generations), which documents the history and development of the Nitzana region.
Efrat and several other locals are working to set up a digital archive that will be accessible online and include interviews with the original pioneers of the communities as well as photographs, videos, timelines, and other media documentation of the people who helped make this remote region thrive.
“The idea for this archive began when I was living in the north, in Kibbutz Hagoshrim. I had an academic scholarship and one of the requirements was that I visit a senior citizen in the kibbutz once a week. His name was Itzhak, and he was one of founders of the kibbutz, and he was also very active with the kibbutz archive,” explained Efrat.
“I thought that it was amazing that I could visit the Kibbutz Hagoshrim’s website and gain access to a wealth of information and photos about its history. It made me realize that I knew very little about the history of my own home and community, just the date of Kadesh Barnea’s establishment.”
The original community of Kadesh Barnea, named after the site where the Israelis camped and from where Moses sent out the 12 spies to scout the Land of Israel in the Bible, was established in Sinai in the 1970s.
When the moshav was dismantled following the Egypt-Israel peace treaty, the original garin (group) of the founders wanted to remain together. They moved around several times in the Ramat HaNegev regional council, first settling in Nitzana, then Ashalim, and finally settling along the Egyptian border in 1986.
Efrat explained that the original residents wanted to continue to use the name Kadesh Barnea for their new community, but a government committee in charge of naming cities and small communities refused, citing that there was only one Kadesh Barnea and th at it had been in Sinai. So while Nitzanei Sinai became the official postal address, the residents continue to use Kadesh Barnea as the community’s name to this day.
“Thanks to the Gesher L’Dorot project, I really got to know the elderly founders of the communities in the Nitzana region,” said Efrat. “It was a great opportunity to interview people in Ezuz, Be’er Milka, Nitzana, Kmehin, and of course my home community of Kadesh Barnea.”
WHILE THE BEAUTY and wholesome lifestyle of the western Negev is striking, Efrat does not overlook the challenges of living in the Nitzana region. Following the construction of Israel’s hi-tech border fence, dozens of drones fly over from Egypt to Israel, sometimes even dozens a day, carrying ammunition, drugs, and weapons, like M16 rifles, to Bedouin cartels in the south.
“There are drones and arms smuggling coming from the Egyptian border,” he noted. “Although this is considered a peaceful border, there are tensions because of the smuggling.”
Another challenge is access to quality medical care.
“Our son Negev was born with a hearing disability. He needed specialized medical care and medical checkups that were not available to us in the south or in Beer Sheva,” explained Efrat. “We had to do Negev’s ear surgery in Jerusalem, where he was able to get the medical care he needed. You have to be prepared for a lot of time on the road if you’re in this kind of situation.”
But despite the challenges, Efrat and his wife are content raising Negev in Kadesh Barnea with grandparents Iftach and Celia next door.
“All the traveling I did when I was younger to get as far away as possible from my moshav made me understand and appreciate how much I needed to get back home. We’re happy here,” Efrat concluded.■
The writer lives with her family in Midreshet Ben-Gurion in Ramat HaNegev, where she works as an English teacher and writes in her free time. She made aliyah from Calais, Maine, in 2004.

Trump touts plan for new U.S. base as Poland warns of risks from Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18

Trump touts plan for new U.S. base in Poland as NATO ally's leader warns of "real risk" from Russia
Berlin — The U.S. has made "major progress" on plans to establish a permanent U.S. Army base in Poland, President Trump said Thursday in a social media post.
"If this goes ahead, the location will be announced very soon," Mr. Trump said in his Truth Social post, which was shared by the White House on X. He said the new base would be a "historic step" for the U.S.-Poland alliance.
Poland's government is likely to welcome the rhetoric as concern mounts over the possible spread of Russia's ongoing full-scale war on neighboring Ukraine to NATO territory.
A "real risk" of Russia's war on Ukraine spreading?
Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke in Poland's parliament, hours before Mr. Trump's post, of a "real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the [NATO] eastern flank and even cause destruction."
Citing unspecified intelligence, Tusk said Russia could portray such an incident — of which there are already numerous examples — even if it is deliberate, as an accident in a bid to erode NATO's willingness to mount a joint response.
Tusk also referred to a new generation of jet-powered attack drones that Russia has been using to attack Ukraine. Compared to the propeller-driven weapons used for more than four years, the newer drones fly faster and at higher altitudes, making them more difficult to intercept.
Russia is also increasingly targeting Ukrainian infrastructure near the Polish border, Tusk said.
On Sunday, a Russian drone struck a passenger train inside Ukraine carrying foreign dignitaries on a visit, including senior European officials and former CIA Director David Petraeus, forcing them to evacuate just a few miles from the border with Poland.
"Maybe they didn't know that some Americans had been there, or maybe, oppositely, they knew, because I don't trust them," Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CBS News in an exclusive interview this week.
"I think that they knew," Zelenskyy added, calling it part of a Russian strategy to intimidate himself and other foreign leaders.
Another drone struck a truck at a nearby gas station. The drone impacts forced Poland's border guards to temporarily suspend cross-border traffic, evacuate people from vehicles and enhance security.
Poland hardens its border
Poland has also boosted its military preparedness. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said Tuesday that soldiers from an engineering regiment were reinforcing border guard infrastructure along the Polish-Ukrainian frontier.
According to the Polish Armed Forces, the measures include the installation of Hesco bastions — wire and mesh structures filled with sand or gravel that are easy to set up as protective barriers — along with new observation and guard posts.
Similar work has been confirmed at three border crossings, in Dorohusk, Medyka and Korczowa. The total number of additional Polish soldiers sent to the border has not been made public. Officials have said the measures should not be considered a general military mobilization or large-scale buildup, as they are intended specifically to reinforce and secure border infrastructure.
But Poland, and its European NATO allies, along with Ukraine and Russia, know a U.S. troop deployment — especially a permanent one — would be a step up in NATO's fortifications of its eastern flank.
Trump administration's "confusing" NATO stance
Mr. Trump's post on Thursday, in which he lauded "our Great U.S./Polish Alliance," was the latest twist in his administration's evolving plans and messaging around U.S. troop deployments that have kept close European allies guessing.
In May, Vice President JD Vance accused media outlets of "overreacting" to an announcement that a planned deployment of 4,000 U.S. forces to Poland had been canceled. Two days later, Mr. Trump announced that the deployment was not only going ahead, but that it would involve 5,000 troops.
"All's well that ends well," Poland's Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said at the time.
His Swedish counterpart, Maria Malmer Stenergard, called the U.S. position on joint defense under the nearly 80-year-old NATO alliance, "confusing indeed, and not always easy to navigate."
The roughly 10,000 U.S. forces currently stationed in Poland are there largely on a rotational basis.
In June, Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz said the U.S. military was considering Poland's proposal to establish a permanent base, but that no final decision had been made.
Separately, the Pentagon has been conducting a broader review of U.S. troop deployments across Europe. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, in announcing the review in June, said the "era of freeriding" by America's NATO allies was over, accusing them of "shameful" inaction during the Iran war.
Kosiniak-Kamysz has named Poznań and Wrocław as potential locations for an American base, but no final location has been announced.

China drafts guidelines to strengthen online protection for minors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
00:34:56 CST
01:34:56 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Cyberspace Administration of China has drafted a set of guidelines to ensure healthy and safe internet use by minors, laying out a series of regulations for relevant service providers.
The draft was made public on Friday and is open to public comment until Oct. 17.
The draft encourages the research, development and manufacture of smart terminal products specifically designed for minors and tailored to the laws and characteristics of their physical and mental development, as well as internet technologies and services conducive to the healthy growth of minors.
Minors shall not be exposed to online social networking services with strangers, virtual intimate relationship services, and online services that induce addiction in minors or are detrimental to their physical and mental health, the draft reads.
Internet services for minors under 16, such as online social networking services and artificial intelligence services that may affect minors' cognition, can only be provided through a minor mode, according to the draft.
It also clarifies the functions of the minor mode, which include identifying online information detrimental to minors' physical and mental health, protecting minors' personal information rights and interests, preventing minors from becoming addicted to the internet, and facilitating guardians in fulfilling their guardianship responsibilities.
As of December 2025, China had more than 200 million internet users aged 6 to 19, the 57th Statistical Report on China's Internet Development revealed.
With the increasingly evident impact of social media on minors' mental well-being, behavior and safety, a growing number of countries and regions have recently started to explore ways to raise the legal threshold for minors' use of social media platforms, said Wang Zhiqin, deputy director of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology.
The draft proposes a model with Chinese characteristics for protecting minors online, representing a positive response to the global trend toward strengthening online protection for minors, Wang said. ■

Stringent ‘red entry’ clause in land revenue record proposed to curb farm fires in Delhi-NCR and adjoining areas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:34:12 UTC
01:34:12 KST

NEW DELHI: Seeking to make rules to act against stubble burning cases more stringent, the Centre has proposed to mark land revenue records of erring farmers with a ‘red entry’ for a period of 15 months that may potentially be much more consequential than just an existing fine.The rules, once finalised, will be applicable in Delhi, Punjab, Haryana and National Capital Region (NCR) of Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. Stubble burning episodes in these areas lead to a substantial increase in the level of air pollution in Delhi-NCR every winter.Though the draft rules to this effect, notified by the Union environment ministry, have not spelt out the consequences of the ‘red entry’ mark in the land revenue record, officials hinted that they may potentially disallow farmers to sell their lands and stop them from availing benefits of govt schemes. They may even include restrictions on getting registered for selling their produce at minimum support price (MSP) at designated ‘mandis’ for a certain period.The proposed rules, which will be finalised after analysing stakeholders’ comments and suggestions, have a provision to extend the ‘red entry’ tag for a further period of 15 months if any subsequent incident of stubble burning is found on that land or the erring farmers fail to pay environmental compensation (fine) within the first tag period.
The existing rules, framed in April 2023 and amended to increase quantum of fine in Nov 2024, have the provision for ‘red entry’ till the penalty by the erring farmer is made, but the draft of the new rules proposes land record-based compliance mechanism by introducing the continuation of the tag for 15 months and its further extension for the next 15 months in case of repeat incidents of stubble burning.Stakeholders are expected to send their comments and suggestions to the ministry within 60 days. The draft was published on Wednesday.The proposed new rules retain the existing quantum of penalty provisions whereby the farmers having an area of land of less than two acres will have to pay an environmental compensation (fine) of Rs 5,000 per incident; those having an area of land of two acres or more but less than five acres need to pay Rs 10,000 per incident; and the farmer having an area of land of more than five acres will have to pay Rs 30,000 per incident as a penalty.
The fine collected under the rule will be deposited in the account of the respective State Pollution Control Board or Pollution Control Committee.The draft proposes that the collected amount will be utilised for various activities including subsidising residue management technologies such as in-situ crop residue management equipment and machinery; incentivising crop diversification programmes; and supporting development and operation of biomass utilisation and storage infrastructure among others in Delhi-NCR and adjoining areas.

Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

====================================================================================================

Three words from Kevin Warsh have Wall Street wondering how far the Fed will go with rate hikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:33:43 UTC
01:33:43 KST

With a few carefully chosen words, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh both explained this week's decision to hike interest rates and raised vexing questions about what comes next.
Warsh described Wednesday's decision to lift the central bank's benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point not specifically as a tightening of policy but rather as removing "a dose of accommodation." Further, he said the move was possible because of a U.S. economy that appears to have "strengthened" and financial conditions that have become less restrictive.
While the language may sound like central bank semantics, it gets to the heart of what markets are debating now: How far will the Warsh Fed go if it has only removed a "dose" of help, and what are the guidelines it will be using to formulate policy?
The phrase was "the one stand-out hawkish element" of Warsh's post-meeting commentary to the press, Krishna Guha, head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI, said in a client note.
"This was not a mistake; it was a phrase he repeated several times and looked very much a deliberate choice to frame policy in this way," Guha added, noting that "the framing is substantively different to that used by the Fed in recent years, and raises the possibility of a more open-ended approach to the number of hikes that might be required."
That framework has included a calibration of where policy should sit relative to the so-called neutral rate, one that neither boosts nor holds back growth. By extension, benchmark rates that sit well above the neutral rate are considered restrictive, while those closer to or below neutral are regarded as accommodative.
What about neutral?
Warsh's framing of the hike as removing "a dose" of accommodation could be seen as the first of multiple steps toward withdrawing support the Fed no longer feels is necessary. The Fed is looking to return inflation to 2%, and policymakers generally consider raising rates as a way to tamp down demand and control price pressures.
"Warsh's framing, if taken literally, raises the possibility that rates might have to keep going up until financial conditions facing the private sector are no longer 'accommodative' — however that is defined," Guha said. "This is a relatively open-ended prospect."
Warsh had the chance to clarify what benchmark he was using to determine how much accommodation remains in policy.
Asked by CNBC's Steve Liesman to explain how far he sees the current rate — in a target range of 3.75%-4% — sitting above neutral, Warsh essentially rejected the framing, in a statement that runs counter to how central bank policy has operated for more than a decade.
Warsh said measuring the benchmark rate relative to neutral is "useful academically. It's a discussion to help us think about policy. Do I think it has any operational effect of decisions that we make today? No, I don't."
The answer helped add a layer of mystery to a Fed chairman already developing a reputation for being cryptic when it comes to how he views the wheels of policy needing to be tuned.
Markets wonder what's next
A round of post-meeting speculation on Wall Street about what's to come has ensued.
One of the initial reactions was pricing in higher odds for another hike when the Fed next meets in October. Goldman Sachs added an October increase to its forecast, as does Bank of America, which also expects another move in December. The market-implied odds of an October increase were near 58% Friday morning, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. A week ago, the probability was 42%.
"The word 'accommodation' means 'stimulus' at the Fed; this comment implies that the current monetary policy stance is meaningfully stimulative," wrote James Egelhof, chief U.S. economist at BNP Paribas Securities.
"With policy starting at a stimulative stance, a strong cyclical impulse, and persistent inflation, we think significant rate increases, perhaps more than the three we expect, may be necessary to stabilize the unemployment rate from below and prevent overheating next year," he added.
Egelhof agreed that the "dose of accommodation" remark was "the most striking feature" of Warsh's abbreviated news conference.
Markets are pricing in the likelihood that the Warsh Fed removes a few more "doses" before it is finished. Futures are implying a fed funds rate of 4.635% near the end of 2027, which would argue for three or four more hikes ahead.
If that's the case, the Fed at the very least will undo many of the FOMC rate cuts approved under Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell, who now sits on the committee as a governor.
The "dose of accommodation" remarks "seemingly helped to underscore this hawkish tone, implying that [the] committee no longer views policy as modestly restrictive," said Jack Janasiewicz, portfolio manager and lead portfolio strategist at Natixis Investment Managers Solutions.
"We remain unconvinced that this is the start of an aggressive new tightening cycle," he said. "Rather, we see this as a removal of the insurance cuts the Fed delivered in the fall of 2025."

====================================================================================================

AI safety debate meets reality at Dreamforce as business leaders say last year's models are enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:31:03 UTC
01:31:03 KST

At Salesforce's annual Dreamforce mega-conference in San Francisco this week, the keynote conversations between CEO Marc Benioff and the heads of Anthropic, OpenAI and Nvidia delved into the raging AI safety debate, with the execs opining on whether model development is moving too fast.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, while on stage with Benioff, urged frontier labs to "run as fast as you can."
But on the grounds of the 50,000-person event, described over a decade ago as the "Super Bowl of software," the discussion was very different. Far from obsessing over the fears of artificial intelligence and whether the rapid advancements of AI models threaten human existence, attendees said they're having trouble even taking advantage of the technology as it exists today.
"It's already hard enough to keep up," said Alec Bronston, who works at Chicago-based retail data company Spins as senior Salesforce director. A potential slowdown would present "a lot of opportunity to just even catch up and get our feet wet," he said.
Dreamforce had a different tone this year, landing in the middle of a dramatic moment in the AI boom. Days before the conference's kickoff, an Anthropic researcher resigned and, on his way out, said the top labs were "gambling with our lives." That led Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman to propose safety initiatives and to push for a slower pace of model development.
In the months leading up to the event, Benioff had been reinforcing Salesforce's role in the AI explosion and batting down the "SaaSpocalypse" narrative, trying to convince investors, customers and employees that AI is an accelerant to its business rather than a threat. Salesforce shares have dropped 8% this year even after a massive pop in August, while other software names like Adobe and Autodesk are down significantly more.
During Salesforce's last earnings call in August, the company unveiled "Claudeforce," a new way for salespeople to access critical data directly from inside Anthropic's Claude chatbot.
On the exposition floor, where companies in the Salesforce ecosystem pay big bucks to tout their software and services, the most highly trafficked booth on Tuesday was Anthropic's. Youthful employees of the AI lab donned oversized white sweaters and carried out demonstrations for passersby.
'Way ahead already'
Salesforce customers and partners at the conference told CNBC that older and cheaper AI models are plenty powerful for everyday sales and customer service work. Many users are still figuring out their AI budgets and determining if their companies are best served using models from Anthropic or OpenAI, or instead opting for cheaper open-source alternatives.
"The frontier models are way ahead already," said Jaya Rohit Vuyyuru, a vice president at consulting firm SummitX. "A lot of the customer base is still getting their feet wet. There's still that gap where the clients can still fulfill and start getting a sense of what agents can do."
Meanwhile, as guests traversed the sprawling Dreamforce campus, or what Salesforce calls the Campground, they interacted with cartoonish corporate mascots, resulting in viral memes on social media. The mascots offered just a slight distraction from the AI chatter that was taking place across the event.
Some attendees said their employers have adopted Salesforce's Agentforce tools, which can respond to customer service questions and sales inquiries. For bots built with Agentforce, Salesforce isn't relying on Anthropic's cutting-edge Claude Fable 5.1 or OpenAI's new GPT-6 Astra, according to a support page on its website.
"The majority of agentic outcomes aren't driven by frontier capabilities," said Tim Sanders, chief innovation officer at software reviewing company G2. "They're driven by last year's AI. It's not that relevant to agentic providers, and certainly not that relevant to SaaS," or software as a service.
Kevin Lee, technology chief at cloud contact center software vendor Nice, said his company doesn't count on high-end models such as Fable for most workloads.
"In large part, with the models that are out there already today, and even one generation behind, they are highly performant and effective at doing the things that our customers need," Lee said. "It's almost like everything beyond this point is icing on the cake."
That's not to undersell the power of AI across the software sector. Many executives say it's been transformational for their business.
Weighing the right model
Electronic signature software developer Docusign, a Dreamforce exhibitor, uses "all the big frontier models as well as some of the open-weight models," said CEO Allan Thygesen.
According to Docusign's website, "larger frontier models are reserved for judgment-intensive work — complex clause analysis, multi-document reasoning, summarization — where general reasoning capability is worth the higher per-call cost."
Frontier models are generally proprietary, preventing users from seeing their data sets or fine-tuning the technology for their own purposes. Open-weight models, by contrast, can be downloaded and run on any infrastructure.
Docusign's home for the three-day event this week was across the street from San Francisco's Moscone Center at the Canopy by Hilton. The company rented out part of the hotel, reserving plenty of quiet meeting space. Thygesen said in an interview there that Docusign uses a technique called model routing to direct each request to the most cost-effective AI system.
It's a tool that Nice and many other companies now use as one major way to keep costs in check while capitalizing on AI.
G2's Sanders said cloud software companies also have to figure out how to play in the new token-based economy, where people pay based on their use of AI and what they demand by way of outputs, rather than on a subscription basis.
Software companies have to adapt both in their use of technology and in how they deliver their own services as customers shift to tokens, Sanders said. A single token represents about three-quarters of a word.
"SaaS up to now has had no variable cost to deliver services," Sanders said. "The profit margin structure changed."
Sanders said that switching from a typical SaaS model to an agentic model could pull down gross margins, or the profit left after accounting for the cost of goods sold, from upwards of 85% to closer to 45%.
There are some companies that want to access the best AI has to offer. Databricks, a data analytics software company with technology for building AI agents, released GPT-6 Astra to all 3,500 of its software developers this week.
"Astra unambiguously out performs our previous highest-end models (Opus 5, Sol 5.6) on highly complex tasks," Patrick Wendell, engineering vice president at Databricks, wrote on X, referring to models from Anthropic and OpenAI, respectively.
Nagarro, a system integrator, is in a very different spot.
Ram Reddy, technology chief for consumer industries at Nagarro, hung around his company's booth this week at Dreamforce. Some who stopped by talked about regulation, following Amodei's chat with Benioff.
But the hottest topic, Reddy said, was Claudeforce and not the future of the frontier. Reddy said that at Nagarro, engineers wait about three months before plugging in the latest models from the AI labs.
"We are not one of those first early adopters jumping at it," he said.
— CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed to this report

Russia’s exiled opposition wants voters at polling stations at noon on the main day of the Duma elections. Its new video borrows from a 1971 American ad against the Vietnam War.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:28:36 UTC
01:28:36 KST

Russia’s exiled opposition wants voters at polling stations at noon on the main day of the Duma elections. Its new video borrows from a 1971 American ad against the Vietnam War.
Actor Nikita Kukushkin, who condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and left the country, has recorded a video supporting the “Noon for a Peaceful Russia” campaign, which Ilya Yashin and several other Russian opposition figures in exile are promoting. They are urging Russians to turn out at polling stations at noon on September 20 — the third and main day of voting in the State Duma elections — as a legal way to register their opposition to the war.
Yashin and Kukushkin posted the video, titled “Ya voyna” (“I Am War”), on their social media accounts on September 18, the first day of the Duma elections. In it, Kukushkin says:
I am war. Help me kill. All you have to do is nothing. Don’t protest. Don’t talk about me. Don’t follow the news. Don’t help the people who have lost their homes. Don’t support the people defending themselves. Say everyone’s to blame. Everyone except the czar. Have a latte at Patriarch’s Ponds. Go to VK Fest. Keep living as though buildings aren’t burning, people aren’t dying, lives aren’t being destroyed around you. Do me a favor: Don’t even think about me. I am war. Help me kill.
He is dressed entirely in black. At the end of the video, a tear runs down his cheek as his face twists into a sinister smile.
The video is an homage to a 1971 American public service ad opposing the Vietnam War. It featured actor Henry Fonda, speaking directly to the camera: “I am war. Help me kill. You don’t have to do anything. Don’t protest. Don’t write your congressman. In fact, do me a favor: Don’t even think about me. I am war. Help me kill.”
The ad was part of the antiwar campaign “Help Unsell the War.” Its name refers to stripping war of its appealing image. Ira Nerken, a 20-year-old Yale student, came up with the campaign after watching a CBS documentary about how the Pentagon used public relations to push its own views on war and peace.
Nerken decided the same methods could make war unpopular. He contacted the head of a New York advertising agency, who recruited hundreds of other advertising professionals to work on the campaign for free. The result was 125 posters and more than 60 antiwar ads, which ran on local U.S. television and radio stations. The major broadcast networks refused to air them.
Time magazine called the “Help Unsell the War” campaign a new and inventive form of antiwar protest, but a somewhat belated one — by 1971, most Americans already opposed the Vietnam War. In 1973, eight years after entering the war, the United States withdrew its troops from Vietnam.
The «Help Unsell the War» campaign has recently drawn renewed attention on social media. Meduza posted about it on its Instagram account.

Zack Polanski requested that the Greens’ ruling executive committee postpone the party’s imminent annual conference so they could focus on the Holborn and St Pancras byelection but was refused.
While party officials say the formal request came from staffers worried about diluting resources by staging a conference a week before Polanski tries to win Keir Starmer’s former Commons seat, the Guardian understands the party leader wanted this to happen.
In the end, the executive committee of the Greens in England and Wales, which has about 25 voting members including Polanski, voted against the plan on Thursday.
The party expects about 3,000 people to attend what would be its biggest gathering, beginning in Brighton on 2 October.
Calling off the event at such short notice would have cost the party a significant sum given it has rented a conference venue, and risked annoying members who have taken time off work and booked travel and hotels.
The byelection, in which Polanski hopes to challenge for a traditionally safe Labour seat, takes place on 8 October, just four days after the conference finishes.
The end of a byelection campaign is traditionally marked by parties trying to canvass as many voters as possible. Having thousands of the Greens’ most active members gathered somewhere else for the final weekend greatly complicates their operation.
Some Greens have also speculated that Polanski would have preferred to fight the byelection before the party votes on a contentious policy motion at its conference, which sets out a motion on Zionism.
Polanski is under pressure to take a stance on the motion, which came top of a members’ vote of policy motions to be debated at the party conference, and is thus almost certain to feature.
The Greens make party policy by member votes at conferences. If passed, the motion would equate Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state in Palestine – with racism and would call for a single Palestinian state. Members who support Zionism would risk being disciplined for racism.
A number of Greens fear passing the motion could alienate Jewish supporters. Polanski, who is Jewish, has not given a public opinion on the issue, but is understood to support a pair of amendments that would tone down the motion.
A Green party spokesperson said: “The party was exploring different ways of allocating our resources effectively while fighting the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. One possible option was to postpone our conference.
“After discussion we remain committed to running an incredibly ambitious Holborn and St Pancras byelection campaign and holding what will be our biggest ever party conference.”

Widespread sexual violence in Ukraine war, most cases tied to Russia, says UN report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Widespread sexual violence in Ukraine war, most cases tied to Russia, says UN report
GENEVA - Russian forces committed widespread sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war in Ukraine, including gang rape and electric shocks to the genitals, while the Ukrainian authorities were also responsible for a smaller number of violations, the UN human rights office said in a report on Sept 18.
The report documented 1,004 verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence between February 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and July 2026.
Of those cases, 89 per cent were attributed to the Russian side, including members of the armed forces, prison service and security agencies, while 11 per cent were linked to Ukraine, including members of the Ukrainian armed forces.
Russia’s permanent diplomatic mission in Geneva declined to comment on the report.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry said in a statement it welcomed the publication of the report, which it said showed the scale of the human rights violations perpetrated by Russia and the measures being taken by Ukraine to prevent such violence and compensate victims.
The statement did not comment directly on the findings of incidents of abuse by Ukrainian forces.
The report cautioned that the findings were not comprehensive because conflict-related sexual violence remains significantly under-reported.
It said Russia’s refusal to grant the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights access to occupied Ukrainian territory, prisoners of war and civilian detainees meant the figures likely underestimate the true scale of the violations.
In occupied areas of Ukraine and within Russia, the Russian authorities carried out sexual violence against Ukrainian prisoners of war and detained civilians at all stages of captivity, including during capture, transfer, interrogation and detention, the report said.
Violations included gang rape, rape, genital mutilation and the use of electric shocks on men’s genitals with a Soviet-era field telephone known as a “tapik”. The findings were based on interviews with victims of sexual violence committed by both sides.
Most victims in detention were men, particularly prisoners of war and detainees, although women and children were also affected, mainly in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
“Sexual violence in conflict is often misunderstood to be mainly affecting women and girls, where in the Ukraine war context, the majority of survivors are men,” Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, said.
“And men and women require different solutions and approaches to their recovery,” she said.
The report concluded that Russia had failed to take steps to prevent, investigate or prosecute sexual violence committed by its personnel and had not engaged with OHCHR’s requests for information.
Russian prisoners of war
In Ukrainian government-controlled territory, nearly half of the violations attributed to the Ukrainian authorities against Russian and third-country prisoners of war and detainees involved threats of sexual violence and beatings to genitals.
OHCHR said it did not document any cases of rape of Russian POWs by Ukrainian forces.
OHCHR said Russian and third-country prisoners of war reported sexual violence in 10 official detention facilities and 55 unofficial or transit locations.
The Ukrainian government had taken some steps to prevent such violations and had cooperated with OHCHR’s requests, although efforts to ensure accountability remained limited, it added.
“I am deeply alarmed by the prevalence of these abhorrent acts documented in our report, and fear that they are almost certainly continuing amid the unceasing violence we are witnessing every day in Ukraine,” said UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk. REUTERS

World Cleanup Day: Small actions can lead to global change  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:17:53 UTC
01:17:53 KST

TALLINN - World Cleanup Day will be celebrated this Sunday, September 20th, with one of its key messages being "Strive for Five" - a call to involve at least 5 percent of the population in a common effort.
The organizers' idea is based on the concept of a social tipping point: if a large enough number of people start acting together, a small shift can evolve into a broader societal change.
In the case of waste, such a change is particularly important because the goal is not only to deal with existing waste but also to reduce waste generation and direct an increasing share of it into recycling.
"In the waste hierarchy, the most important thing is to prevent waste generation - waste that isn't created doesn't need to be collected or managed. At the same time, we must promote the recycling of waste to keep materials in circulation for as long as possible," explained Kaia Oras, a leading expert in environmental statistics at Statistics Estonia.
In 2024, Estonia generated 514,000 tonnes of municipal waste, which is about 7.2 kilograms per person per week. The generation of municipal waste per capita has not decreased in recent years: while 359 kilograms of municipal waste were generated per person in 2015, this figure rose to 375 kilograms in 2024.
"These numbers show that much still needs to be done to reduce waste generation. This requires changes in both consumption and daily choices," said Oras.
Another important goal is to increase recycling. In 2024, 36.4 percent of municipal waste was recycled in Estonia. The target for 2030 is to reach 60 percent, which means there is still a gap of 23.6 percentage points from the current level.
What would happen if 5 percent of the population reduced their waste generation by half?
At the beginning of this year, Estonia had a population of about 1.36 million people. Five percent of the population is approximately 68,000 people. If these individuals were to halve their municipal waste generation, about 12,800 tonnes of municipal waste would be prevented annually. This would account for about 2.5 percent of the total municipal waste generated in Estonia each year. For these 68,000 people, a fifty percent reduction in waste would mean about 3.6 kilograms less municipal waste per person per week - 3.6 kilograms instead of the current 7.2. In total, this would mean about 245 tonnes less municipal waste per week.
"12,800 tonnes is not a very large amount compared to Estonia's total municipal waste generation, but the issue is not just about how much less waste would be produced over a year. What's also important is what such a change could trigger if more and more people started following the same direction," Oras noted.
The idea behind one of World Cleanup Day's main mottos, "Strive for Five," is that change does not have to start with the whole of society at once. Instead, if enough people begin to act in the same direction, the new behavior can spread and become the norm.
"In statistics, we usually see changes when the individual choices of many people have formed a broader trend. Five percent won't solve the waste problem, but it can be enough to give momentum to the change and show that another way is possible," the leading expert explained.
World Cleanup Day is taking place for the ninth time this year, and since 2024, September 20th has been an official UN calendar day. The Estonian initiative "Let's Do It!" ("Teeme Ära"), which began in 2008, has grown into a global movement that has engaged over 139 million people from more than 190 countries and territories over the years.
In addition to traditional cleanup events, special attention is being paid in Estonia this year to the safe collection of small electronics, batteries, and accumulators to increase the recycling of valuable materials and reduce environmental risks. The more specific focus of this year's global World Cleanup Day is on reducing food waste and drawing attention to how more conscious consumption and waste prevention can help create a more resource-efficient and circular economy.

"I am closely monitoring the situation, meeting with the relevant agencies, and speaking with leaders in both Ukraine and the EU. The relevant agencies are constantly monitoring the situation and exchanging information with our allies," Kulbergs states.
He repeatedly reassures the public and promises that if a real threat arises, he will report it immediately.

Latvian researchers conclude their third expedition to Greenland  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:17:36 UTC
01:17:36 KST

RIGA - Geologists from the University of Latvia have returned from their third expedition to Greenland, where they spent a month studying the Fan outlet glacier of the Qaanaaq Ice Cap, LETA was told at the university.
The researchers analyzed the glacier’s thermal structure and determined its surface elevation and ice thickness.
Using ground-penetrating radar, the scientists took measurements over a distance of approximately 35 kilometers. Contrary to previous assumptions, the data obtained indicate that the glacier is composed of cold ice that does not reach the melting point. This was also observed in areas where the ice thickness reaches approximately 300 meters.
During this expedition, the Latvian team also used passive seismic sensors for the first time in Greenland research. The researchers noted that the data collected could help refine the understanding of glacier development and improve predictions of how they will change.
The work was hampered by changeable weather conditions. In August, there were both warm days and very rainy and windy days in northeastern Greenland. Heavy rainfall caused flooding and, in some places, washed away the road between Qaanaaq Airport and the town. The large volume of water also made it difficult to reach the glacier, as glacial meltwater rivers had risen rapidly.
The researchers had to use complicated access routes to reach the retreating edge of the glacier. One of the unusual phenomena observed during the expedition was several-meter-high jets of pressurized glacial water. At the same time, ground-penetrating radar data indicate the presence of tunnels in the lower part of the glacier.
The expedition was supported by the Latvian Council of Science Program for Fundamental and Applied Research Projects.

Bulgaria Deploys Anti-Drone Systems to Protect Critical Infrastructure
Bulgaria will begin deploying anti-drone systems to protect critical infrastructure and increase police patrols around weapons production and storage facilities amid heightened security concerns, Reuters reported on September 18.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said the government had reviewed security measures at critical infrastructure sites and decided to begin equipping them with systems designed to counter drones.
As part of the broader security measures, police have also been instructed to intensify patrols around facilities involved in the production and storage of weapons.
The decision comes days after a fire broke out at a weapons depot operated by Bulgarian arms manufacturer EMCO, raising renewed concerns over the security of the country’s defense facilities, Reuters reported.
EMCO said it believed the fire was the result of sabotage, pointing to more than 10 similar incidents involving Bulgarian defense companies since 2011. The company did not name any potential perpetrators.
EMCO is led by Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev, whose facilities have previously been targeted in attacks that Bulgarian prosecutors attributed to alleged Russian operatives, Reuters reported.
The latest incident follows another fire at a Bulgarian military facility in August. On August 10, a blaze broke out at an ammunition storage site at a military plant in central Bulgaria after a powerful explosion was heard.
The incident occurred near the village of Belitsa in the municipality of Tryavna. Tryavna Mayor Dencho Minev said no one was killed or injured in the explosion and subsequent fire. The blaze was brought under control, while all employees were evacuated from the facility by bus.

RIGA - During a trade mission to Berlin organized by the Latvian Investment and Development Agency (Latvijas Investiciju Un Attistibas Agentura, LIAA), investment projects by German companies and new opportunities for cooperation in Latvia in the fields of energy, defense technology, autonomous mobility, and space technology were promoted, the LIAA informed LETA.
The total planned value of the two most advanced investment projects exceeds EUR 600 million. 54 Latvian companies and organizations participated in the mission, meeting with potential clients, investors, banks, manufacturers, research centers, and medical institutions. The trade mission in Berlin took place from September 14 to 17. The companies represented the information and communication technology, financial technology, life sciences, defense, and dual-use technology sectors.
Summarizing the results of the visit, Economics Minister Viktors Valainis noted that three years of focused work with German partners has already resulted in concrete investment projects totaling more than EUR 600 million. "In Berlin, we discussed the further implementation of a renewable energy project with Notus Energy, and with Dynamit Nobel Defence, we discussed the next steps for the planned defense technology manufacturing facility in Latvia," he said.
During the meeting with the management of Notus Energy, the future implementation of the two companies' renewable energy projects in Latvia was discussed. Attention was focused on practical issues affecting the progress of the projects, including conditions for wind farm development, grid connections, obtaining permits, and the availability of financing.
In talks with the German defense technology company Dynamit Nobel Defence, work continued on the planned production facility in Latvia. The company and the State Defense Corporation signed a memorandum of understanding in February regarding the establishment of the production facility, therefore the Berlin meeting focused on the project's next steps and opportunities to develop the company's other initiatives in Latvia.
According to Valainis, a meeting with Thomas Steffen, State Secretary at the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy, confirmed both countries' interest in expanding economic cooperation. "Our task is to ensure that investor interest translates into production facilities, technologies, and jobs in Latvia, while Latvian companies gain an increasingly strong foothold in the German market," said the minister.
"Latvia and Germany are united by successful economic cooperation and a shared vision of what needs to be done to promote economic growth in both countries and strengthen Europe's competitiveness. The European Union's single market is our greatest advantage, while establishing direct cooperation between companies is an essential prerequisite for successful future development," emphasized German Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy Katherina Reiche and Steffen.
According to the LIAA, the Latvian delegation also met with the company HOLON, which develops fully electric, autonomous passenger minibuses for public transportation and mobility services. The discussions assessed Latvia's potential involvement in the company's European development plans, including the manufacturing of vehicles and their components, the establishment of supply chains, the testing of autonomous mobility, and technology development.
LiveEO, a Berlin-based space technology company that uses satellite imagery and artificial intelligence to monitor power lines, railways, pipelines, and other critical infrastructure, was invited to expand its operations in Daugavpils. The company's subsidiary in Latvia has been operating for four years. In a separate seminar, opportunities for data center development in Latvia were also presented to German companies, said the LIAA.
"This mission demonstrated the results of focused work following the initial meeting. In some investment projects, we are no longer just discussing initial contact - together with investors, we are moving forward with specific next steps so that, once the necessary preparatory work is completed, negotiations can give way to construction equipment," notes Vita Balode-Andrusa, Director of the LIAA's Export and Innovation Services Department.
For other Latvian companies in Berlin, this was the first discussion with a potential partner, and now it is important to turn this contact into the next practical step - arranging a technology trial, initiating supplier qualification, or reaching a contract, said Balode-Andrusa.
Germany is Europe's largest market and is located at the economic heart of the continent, notes Liva Sturmane, head of the Latvian exporters association The Red Jackets. Entering and establishing a foothold in this market often paves the way to other European regions as well. German companies are known for their high standards regarding quality, deadlines, and supplier reliability, therefore successful cooperation with them significantly strengthens a Latvian company's reputation and position in international markets, she said.
In Berlin, the LIAA, the German Association of Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHK), and the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce (AHK) signed a memorandum of understanding. This will provide Latvian companies with access to the knowledge, contacts, and services of the German foreign trade chamber network at 150 locations in more than 90 countries.
As reported, the goal of the visit was to strengthen economic cooperation between Latvia and Germany, promote establishment of new business contacts, and expand opportunities for Latvian companies on the German market.
According to the LIAA, individual programs were created for the information technology, defense, and dual-use technology sectors, which included meetings with potential clients, cooperation partners, and investors. The visit also included tours of German companies, innovation centers, and research institutions.
IT companies participated in artificial intelligence festival "Big Bang AI Festival" and the sixth German-Baltic Digital Summit, as well as visited IT companies, including the Tesla plant in Berlin-Brandenburg and technology company Heidelberg. Defense sector and dual-use technology companies discussed cooperation opportunities in unmanned and anti-drone technologies, robotics, and defense supply chains, and also visited the Marienpark Berlin resilience technology center and German defense technology company Andres Industries AG.
Representatives of the financial technology sector met in Berlin with representatives of the local fintech ecosystem to discuss EU regulations on crypto-asset service providers, access to the German market, and investment opportunities. Meanwhile, representatives of the life sciences sector had the opportunity to visit Campus Berlin-Buch, a major life sciences hub in Berlin, and one of the leading medical technology companies, BIOTRONIK SE & Co. KG.
German businesses, in turn, had the opportunity to learn about the opportunities offered by Latvian companies, with a particular focus on the development of data centers in Latvia.

New Russian Rocket Launch May Support “Rassvet” Network or Military Reconnaissance

New Russian Rocket Launch May Support “Rassvet” Network or Military Reconnaissance
Russia launched a Soyuz-2.1b carrier rocket from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in the Arkhangelsk region on September 17 with a classified payload, defense outlet Militarnyi reported on September 18, citing the Russian Ministry of Defense.
The Russian Defense Ministry announced that stable telemetry was established and onboard systems are functioning normally, though officials declined to disclose the name, quantity, technical specifications, or purpose of the spacecraft.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Citing tracking platform Next Spaceflight, Militarnyi noted that the mission utilized a Fregat-M upper stage. The payload is officially listed as a classified military satellite or part of the “Kosmos” series, though analysts suggest the launch could be tied to the ongoing expansion of Russia’s low-Earth orbit communications system, “Rassvet.”
Russia began deploying the “Rassvet” network—developed by the company Bureau 1440—in March 2026, using the exact same Soyuz-2.1b rocket and Plesetsk launch site to put 16 satellites into orbit. A second batch followed in July. According to Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR), Moscow plans to scale the constellation to 292 satellites by the end of 2027 and up to 924 spacecraft by 2035.
Given the mission’s strict secrecy, the payload may also consist of military hardware, continuing a pattern of covert space deployments this year. On February 5, a Soyuz-2.1b delivered nine objects into orbit—later designated “Kosmos-2600” through “Kosmos-2608"—whose trajectories indicated a reconnaissance function, Militarnyi wrote.
In April, the US Space Force tracked three additional Russian military satellites placed into polar orbits.
The Soyuz-2 rocket family is serially manufactured at the Progress Rocket Space Centre in the city of Samara. Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles have previously struck the facility. Subsequent satellite imagery revealed significant damage to Workshop 106A, the production hall where onboard electronics, guidance systems, and instrument compartments for the Soyuz-2 rockets are assembled.

As Russia intensifies its hybrid warfare in Europe, more serious attacks could occur - Sarts  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:17:13 UTC
01:17:13 KST

RIGA - As Russia intensifies its hybrid warfare in Europe, more serious attacks may be expected, explains Janis Sarts, director of NATO's Center of Excellence for Strategic Communications.
The expert noted on Twitter that reports of Russia's planned attacks on European countries have reappeared in foreign media in recent days.
There is talk of hybrid attacks, which Latvian officials have also warned about. Sarts, however, believes that hybrid attacks is not an accurate description of what is happening.
In his view, this intensification of reports most likely signifies the availability of new intelligence. Since a hybrid war is already underway in Europe, this signals Russia's decision to intensify it - more serious attacks, possible human casualties, and less caution when carrying out attacks, he concludes.
According to Sarts, the intelligence services apparently believe that efforts over the past few months to dissuade Russia from such an escalation have been unsuccessful. "Therefore, we must be prepared for such a turn of events," Sarts emphasizes.
He notes that the decisive factor in how the situation develops - should a larger-scale attack occur - will be how strong and painful the collective response is for Russia.
As reported, the number of Russian hybrid attacks against NATO member states has increased significantly, a high-ranking Alliance official revealed in September.
Last year alone, more than 200 such incidents were recorded, the official said, adding that this figure does not include routine cyberattacks. NATO headquarters, for its part, faces thousands of cyberattacks every month.
The official noted that Russia is attempting to undermine political and practical support for Ukraine and is preparing for a possible further escalation. In particular, Russia is spying on critical infrastructure and supply chains, as well as pre-deploying malware in key industrial control systems.
The Alliance is particularly concerned about changes in the nature of the attacks, the official revealed, explaining that the number of attacks is increasing, their severity is increasing, and the appetite for risk is increasing.
The Alliance is working to strengthen deterrence through military measures and improved protection of critical infrastructure. The Alliance also plans to establish a critical energy infrastructure network to share security information with operators and support joint emergency response exercises, defense against unmanned aerial vehicles, and cybersecurity.
In particularly serious cases, the Alliance's supreme military commander could ask member states to use offensive cyber capabilities, the official noted.
In August, the Constitutional Protection Bureau told LETA that Russia does not currently pose a direct military threat to Latvia, although a number of indicators point to potential long-term plans.
Kaspars Pudans, commander of the National Armed Forces, has also acknowledged that Latvia currently faces no direct military threat; however, the National Armed Forces are prepared for possible hybrid provocations by Russia.

In EU budget negotiations, Latvia will seek additional EUR 7 billion to fortify eastern flank - Kulbergs  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:17:12 UTC
01:17:12 KST

RIGA - Latvia will request an additional EUR 7 billion to strengthen the European Union's (EU) eastern flank during negotiations on the bloc's multiannual budget for 2028-2034, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) told the Saeima European Affairs Committee on Friday.
The prime minister said that under the new EU budget model, funding for cohesion, agriculture, home affairs, and social policy is to be provided within a single funding envelope, while further funding allocations will take place at the national level. The current proposal for Latvia calls for a reduction in overall funding, which Latvia finds unacceptable.
The prime minister noted that Latvia’s request for additional funding is justified by the impact of the geopolitical threat posed by Russia on the economies of the countries on the EU's eastern flank. He cited European Commission (EC) estimates, according to which, due to the geopolitical threat, inflation in member states along the eastern external border has been 3.7 percentage points higher than the EU average, while average gross domestic product (GDP) growth from 2022 to 2023 has been 1.9 percentage points lower than projected for the EU.
According to Kulbergs, when calculating this impact over a seven-year period, Latvia’s economic losses amount to approximately EUR 7.43 billion. Latvia therefore is seeking approximately EUR 7 billion in additional funding during the negotiations. In total, the countries on the EU’s eastern flank are seeking EUR 54 billion.
Kulbergs said that Latvia’s position is also supported by Lithuania and Estonia, and that Finland, Poland, and Romania have expressed their support as well. Following a proposal by the Baltic states, a reference to the eastern flank as a special condition has already been included in the European Council’s conclusions.
The prime minister emphasized that additional funding for Latvia would help cover pressing needs, including in agriculture and the financing of Rail Baltica, which is a critical element from a military standpoint.
At the same time, Kulbergs acknowledged that reaching an agreement on the next EU multiannual budget will be difficult, as the currently proposed budget amount is unacceptable to several EU contributor countries. A general agreement is expected to be reached in December of this year, with the next round of negotiations scheduled for October.
As reported, the European Commission has proposed a budget of approximately EUR 1.76 trillion for the 2028-2034 period, adjusted for inflation at 2025 prices.
The budget, officially known as the multiannual financial framework, requires unanimous approval from all 27 EU member states.
A group of fiscally conservative countries, often referred to as the frugal member states, considers the European Commission’s current proposal for the multiannual budget to be unacceptable.

An investigation by former Deputy Investigatory Powers Commissioner John Goldring found "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct," concluding that one senior officer repeatedly provided false information while another misled colleagues and lied about information he had received.
A panel of three senior judges is now considering whether contempt of court proceedings should be brought against individual MI5 officers or the security service itself, a step the BBC said would be unprecedented.
MI5 said one officer had resigned and another had been suspended pending disciplinary proceedings.
Otty argued against contempt proceedings, citing MI5's apologies and a reform program being carried out under Director General Ken McCallum.

Leaving Schengen/Dublin by 2035 would hurt Swiss economy, weaken security: Gov't report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:16:38 UTC
01:16:38 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Leaving the Schengen/Dublin agreements could cost Switzerland billions by 2035 and weaken its internal security, according to a Federal Council report released Friday.
The government estimated that Swiss gross domestic product could be up to 3.9% lower in 2035 without the agreements, while annual income losses could reach 1,300 Swiss francs (over $1,500) per person.
Without Schengen/Dublin, Switzerland's borders with neighboring countries would become external Schengen borders, requiring significantly expanded border controls.
The number of cross-border workers could fall by up to 60%, particularly affecting the catering and care sectors, while commuters could collectively lose 422,000 hours to border traffic every working day, according to the council.
Tourism could see annual losses of between 320 million and 810 million francs, while additional asylum costs could reach 824 million francs.
This also raises the possibility that up to 170,000 people could relocate to Switzerland.
The government also warned that leaving the arrangements would mean losing access to key European security databases and cooperation mechanisms.
Swiss authorities recorded nearly 40,000 Switzerland-related matches in the Schengen Information System in 2025.
The Federal Council said even significant additional spending could not fully compensate for the security capabilities provided by the agreements.
"The funds that Switzerland could save in the event of the termination of Schengen/Dublin cooperation would not be nearly sufficient to cover the additional costs of the necessary reintroduction of border controls, the operation of its own databases, and the maintenance of internal security," it said. "Even with significant additional financial resources, the level of security that Switzerland achieves thanks to the association could not be fully guaranteed."

Which films are perfect for autumn evenings: TOP 10 movies
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
19:14:56 EEST
01:14:56 KST

Which films are perfect for autumn evenings: TOP 10 movies
Kyiv • UNN
A selection of ten films for cold autumn evenings — from romantic stories to gothic tales, magic, humor, and family dramas.
Autumn is perfect for cozy evenings spent watching movies, so UNN has compiled a top 10 of light films with an autumn atmosphere to brighten up a cold evening.
When Harry Met Sally
Harry and Sally first crossed paths thanks to Harry’s then-girlfriend, who asked him to give Sally a ride. After the trip together, they remained in each other’s memories for a long time, but they did not see each other again until five years later. Harry suggested that Sally have dinner with him, but she declined. Six years later, life brought them together again, this time as neighbors. So, will they end up together?
Good Will Hunting
Will Hunting has exceptional mathematical abilities, but he has not succeeded academically. He looks down on students, yet at the same time does not dare to return to education himself. The reason lies in his inner fears and unwillingness to face difficulties once again. A turning point for the protagonist comes when he meets a young student. This encounter makes him look at his own life differently. The story gradually reveals that behind Will’s confidence lies self-doubt.
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
Autumnal Hogwarts, the enchanted forest, and the adventures of the famous trio create a special mood in this installment of the franchise. Pumpkin juice and the magical world, which is especially suited to cold evenings, add to it. The third film is often associated with a darker atmosphere than the earlier installments of the story. The heroes once again find themselves at the center of new adventures. Dangerous situations and mysteries await them. For a full understanding of the story, it is recommended to start watching from the first film.
The Trouble with Harry
Yes, Harry again! The body of a man named Harry is found in a forest near Vermont. It soon becomes clear that several local residents have reason to believe they may have been involved in his death. As a result, the body changes location several times. Although the situation initially seems grim, it gradually turns into a black comedy. The film combines elements of a thriller and humor.
The Addams Family
Can you already hear those famous snaps to that characteristic little tune? This story is about a family that lives by entirely unusual rules. The film’s atmosphere is shaped by Gothic architecture, distinctive music, and the characters’ gloomy manners. In their world, strange and frightening things are perceived as an ordinary part of life. That is why the monsters here do not seem all that scary. The autumn atmosphere is complemented here by gloomy weather, Gothic elements, humor, and a family story.
Wuthering Heights
The new adaptation reimagines the famous love story based on Emily Brontë’s novel. At the center of the plot are the demanding Catherine and Heathcliff, who has been devoted to her since childhood. Their feelings begin as youthful passion. Over time, this love grows ever stronger and takes on a destructive nature. It is a story about a relationship that goes far beyond light romance amid Wuthering Heights, fog, wind, and Gothic elements.
Dorian Gray
The film transports viewers to Victorian London, where young Dorian is introduced to a world of high-society pleasures and temptations. Lord Henry has a profound influence on the young man, revealing an entirely different life to him. The artist Basil is captivated by Dorian’s remarkable appearance and creates his portrait. Upon seeing the finished painting, the young man makes a wish to remain young forever, and it comes true—but not in the way one might expect. Now the portrait has become his curse… or has it?
Hotel Transylvania
Mavis, Dracula’s daughter, celebrates her 118th birthday, which is a special day for vampires. The celebration is held at a remote hotel, where real monsters gather. Everything changes after the arrival of an American tourist named Jonathan, who comes to the masquerade and does not understand who exactly surrounds him. During his acquaintance with Mavis, the two develop feelings for each other. Now the heroes must figure out whether representatives of such different worlds can be together and how Daddy Dracula will react.
Practical Magic
Strange rumors circulate about the Owens family. People believe that the women from this house have magical abilities and that the men who fall in love with them are destined for an early death. However, the sisters themselves do not seek to use their abilities for evil—instead, they long for ordinary human happiness and mutual love. So, despite their family's reputation, they try to live their own lives. But the old rumors continue to affect their relationships.
Little Women
The plot of the film is based on the novel of the same name by Louisa May Alcott. The events unfold during the American Civil War and focus on the lives of four sisters. Jo dreams of becoming a writer, loves freedom, and is more drawn to the company of boys. Meg is responsible and romantic by nature and envisions a wealthy life for herself. Beth is shy, quiet, and passionate about music. The youngest, Amy, has an artistic temperament and knows how to use her attractiveness to achieve her goals. Despite the closeness between the sisters, each of them follows her own path and tries to find her place in a complicated world.

Russia pulls elite drone unit from northern Donetsk Oblast after losses from Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine's military says
