Saudi Aramco has told at least two European oil refining customers they will receive no Saudi crude shipments next month after an attack on the kingdom’s key East-West pipeline, Bloomberg reported Friday.
The customers typically receive Saudi crude through long-term supply agreements, which provide regular monthly deliveries. People familiar with the matter told Bloomberg that those allocations will not be provided next month.
Saudi Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Saudi Arabia shut down its East-West pipeline last week after drones targeted the facility. The pipeline is expected to resume partial operations within days and return to full capacity within six weeks, according to a person familiar with the situation who spoke on Wednesday.
While oil and security sources previously said two pumping stations were damaged in the attack, a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery identified damage at three stations, sources confirmed in a Reuters report on Thursday.
European refineries that purchase Saudi crude typically receive shipments through Egypt’s Mediterranean port of Sidi Kerir, which is linked to the Red Sea by pipeline infrastructure.
Aramco customers seek alternative oil sources
The disruption has prompted some Aramco customers to seek alternative sources of supply. Poland’s Orlen SA has issued more than 10 tenders since Friday as it looks to secure replacement crude shipments.
European countries belonging to the OECD imported 577,000 barrels per day of Saudi crude in June, according to the International Energy Agency’s monthly Oil Market Report.
The pipeline has provided Saudi Arabia with a vital alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, reducing reliance on a narrow maritime chokepoint through which a significant share of global energy supplies passes.
Any further decline in Saudi crude exports could add pressure to an already strained global energy market, potentially driving higher fuel prices, increasing inflation concerns, and contributing to greater volatility in financial markets.

"Following several visits by Ukrainian delegations to Serbia and vice versa, we have successfully increased trade by 42% during the first half of this year," Vučić said at the Carpathian Eight Summit on Friday.

President Trump, stand with Palestinian democracy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:38:22 UTC
00:38:22 KST

The United States has the sovereign right to deny entry to particular individuals on legitimate security or legal grounds, whether they are Palestinian, Israeli, or of any other nationality. Yet a broad restriction directed at an entire people would be neither wise nor constructive.
Such a policy would silence precisely the Palestinian voices America should want to hear: those who reject violence, seek peaceful engagement, support political reform, and believe that ballots - not bullets - must determine the future of the Palestinian people.
Regarding PA President Mahmoud Abbas specifically, I understand that denying him a visa may be intended to exert pressure on the Palestinian leadership to undertake long-overdue reforms. Yet pressure is effective only when it is paired with a clear, constructive policy that supports democratic change.
Today, the most meaningful opportunity for Palestinian reform is already before us.
Abbas has called legislative elections for November 28 - the first such elections in two decades. Several powerful figures within the Palestinian political establishment are now seeking to postpone or cancel them. Some are reportedly attempting to enlist the US or influential regional countries, including Saudi Arabia, as ones asking to close the democratic door once again.
Washington should not allow its name to be used for this purpose.
Abbas only senior Palestinian leader committed to November 28 election date
Abbas currently stands almost alone among senior Palestinian leaders in keeping the election date. On this issue, he deserves international support. A clear public statement from US President Donald Trump endorsing free, inclusive, and credible Palestinian elections on its determined date, November 28, could be decisive. It could prevent those who fear change from claiming that America demands cancellation or that regional circumstances require it.
If Washington genuinely wants Palestinian reform, it must do more than punish the failures of the existing leadership. It should empower the Palestinian people to choose a new one.
We have already seen the consequences of closing this door.
Palestinian elections scheduled for 2021 were postponed indefinitely. Their cancellation did not create the catastrophe of October 7, 2023, and it would be irresponsible to draw such a simple line of causation. But it deepened the political vacuum, weakened moderate voices, destroyed public confidence, and reinforced Hamas’s argument that change could never be achieved through democratic or peaceful means.
When ballot boxes are closed, extremists offer other boxes - filled with weapons, funerals, and false promises.
We must not repeat that mistake.
A new Palestinian generation is now searching for a different path. Our political movement, Masar Jadid - New Path - was created to answer that demand. In approximately one month, more than 1,200 Palestinians from Jerusalem, Gaza, the West Bank, and the diaspora joined our movement. Most are young. Many are women, students, professionals, academics, entrepreneurs, and people entering political life for the first time.
They are joining because New Path offers ideas rarely stated so clearly in Palestinian politics: democracy, transparency, peaceful transfer of power, an independent judiciary, and one legitimate authority governed by one law and possessing one weapon.
We reject both corruption and extremism. We believe Palestinian interests are better served by dialogue and persuasion than by violence. We support a demilitarized Palestinian state, regional economic integration, and a negotiated two-state solution that provides Palestinians with freedom and dignity while ensuring security for Israelis.
These ideas are attracting support because hundreds of thousands of Palestinians have lost confidence in everything around them but have not yet lost their desire for a better future. They no longer trust the traditional factions. They are tired of being asked to choose between failed government and endless resistance, between stagnation and destruction. They want a third choice: democratic change.
Trump’s recently announced peace initiative has awakened genuine hope that the region may finally move from managing conflict to building a new future. Yet no regional peace architecture can endure if Palestinians remain politically excluded and denied the right to renew their own leadership.
Reconstruction, investment, demilitarization, and regional cooperation all require legitimate Palestinian institutions. Foreign governments cannot impose legitimacy, and aging political elites cannot inherit it indefinitely. It must come from the people.
Trump understands the political power of a mandate from the voters. He also understands that peace requires breaking with failed formulas and confronting entrenched interests. Supporting Palestinian elections would not be a concession to the PA. It would be an investment in a new Palestinian leadership capable of becoming a credible partner for peace.
Trump should therefore state clearly that the US supports holding the November 28 elections on time; that it expects all Palestinian institutions and regional partners to facilitate them; that Jerusalemites and Gazans must be included; and that Washington will judge emerging Palestinian forces by their commitment to democracy, nonviolence, reform, and peace.
Such a declaration could save the election. It could also save lives.
Upcoming Palestinian elections must not be canceled
Canceling elections would tell another generation of Palestinians that peaceful political change is impossible. That message would open the gates of despair and accelerate the next regional earthquake. Supporting elections would send the opposite message: that moderation has allies, peaceful change is possible, and Palestinian society will not remain permanently trapped between authoritarian stagnation and armed extremism.
I continue to believe that Trump can achieve a historic peace in the Middle East - and that the world may one day remember him for doing so. Perhaps such an achievement would even earn the recognition of the Nobel Peace Prize.
But the most meaningful prize would be a generation of Palestinian and Israeli children who grow up knowing politics instead of war, ballots instead of bullets, and hope instead of fear.
Mr. President, do not allow the door to Palestinian democracy to be closed again. Your public support can keep it open - and help change the future of the Middle East.
Samer Sinijlawi is a Palestinian political figure from Jerusalem and the founder and president of Masar Jadid (New Path), a Palestinian political movement advocating democracy, nonviolence, reform, and regional peace.

Haifa International Film Festival brings celebrated cinema and classics to the Carmel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:38:11 UTC
00:38:11 KST

The 42nd Haifa International Film Festival will bring the most celebrated movies from the world’s major festivals to Haifa alongside new Israeli films, documentaries, genre movies, and classics. Originally scheduled for September 26 to October 3 during Sukkot, the organizers added an extra day of screenings on September 25 due to demand.
The festival will open with the Israeli premiere of Avi Nesher’s Our Loves, fresh from its warmly received world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival earlier this month. Nesher will also receive the Haifa festival’s Lifetime Achievement Award for cinematic excellence and his contribution to Israeli culture at the opening-night ceremony, hosted by Lior Ashkenazi.
Our Loves’ narrative begins on October 6, 2023, focusing on several characters who think they are having the worst day of their lives, and blends drama, romance, and comedy as they cope with a situation worse than their worst nightmares.
Artistic director Yaron Shamir has made sure that the international program is extremely strong, featuring many of the most talked-about movies of the year. Danny Boyle, the director of Trainspotting, 28 Days Later, and Slumdog Millionaire, has made a movie set in the cutthroat world of UK tabloid journalism with Ink. The film, which opened the Venice Film Festival, is set in 1969 and dramatizes the transformation of Britain’s Sun newspaper under Rupert Murdoch, played by Guy Pearce.
Olivier Assayas’s The Wizard of the Kremlin spotlights a different kind of political history, starring Paul Dano as Vadim Baranov, an artist and television producer who becomes a political strategist for a rising Vladimir Putin, played by Jude Law. Based on Giuliano da Empoli’s novel, it follows the creation of the political mythology surrounding the Russian leader.
Pierre Salvadori’s 'The Electric Kiss' gives viewers an escape from politics
For viewers who would rather escape politics altogether, Pierre Salvadori’s The Electric Kiss, which opened Cannes this year, offers a Parisian romantic comedy set in 1928 about a grieving painter, a fake psychic, and a series of fraudulent séances.
If you have enjoyed eating Hershey bars, you can now learn the story of the founder of the iconic chocolate company in Hershey: Mark Waters’s biopic about Milton Hershey. Finn Wittrock plays the famous chocolatier, with Alexandra Daddario (who may be the next on-screen Wonder Woman) as his wife.
The Panorama section includes All About Corinne, Marc Fitoussi’s comedy starring Isabelle Huppert as Corinne, an eternal movie extra who dreams of finally getting a substantial role. When she befriends a famous actress, played by Sandrine Kiberlain, she sees a possible route into the inner circle of French cinema. The supporting cast includes Diane Kruger, Anne Marivin, and Emmanuelle Bercot.
Romanian director Tudor Giurgiu’s 3 Days in September tells the story of a heroine whose wedding is wrecked when her fiancé’s mistress appears, sending her fleeing aboard a train and into an all-night journey through an off-season seaside resort. It features a single take lasting more than an hour and shifts between comedy and drama.
Everyone who loves the Big Apple will want to see The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, directed by Noah Segan and starring John Turturro as Harry, an old-school thief trying to survive in the digital age. Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito, and Tatiana Maslany co-star in what is both a crime story and a lament for a city that is changing faster than many of its residents can handle.
Another very different American story is told in The Weight, Padraic McKinley’s Depression-era thriller. Ethan Hawke plays a prisoner offered a chance at freedom by a warden, played by Russell Crowe, if he will help smuggle stolen gold from a remote mine.
One of the most important titles in the Carmel International Competition this year is Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur. The director of Leviathan and Loveless focuses on a successful Russian businessman whose orderly existence begins collapsing in 2022 amid professional, personal, and political pressures. The film won the Grand Prix at Cannes, and additional Haifa screenings have already been added to meet demand.
Also in the competition is François Ozon’s The Stranger, a new adaptation of Albert Camus’s classic novel. Set in French-colonial Algeria in 1938 and starring Benjamin Voisin as Meursault, the film returns to Camus’s story of alienation, murder, and the absurd while giving particular visual weight to the North African setting that forms the novel’s background.
A highlight of the festival will be the Israeli Cinema section, which features Marco Carmel’s much-anticipated Double Panther, based on the true story of Yaakov Elbaz, a criminal recruited by the police to infiltrate the Israeli Black Panthers, a political group that fought for the rights of Mizrahi Jews.
The assignment becomes complicated when Elbaz begins to sympathize with the people he is supposed to betray. Based on police files and archival material that remained confidential for decades, it turns a chapter of Israeli social history into an undercover crime drama, and stars Yaakov Zada-Daniel in the lead role.
Many Waters, written and directed by Imri Matalon, features Lihi Kornowski as a young woman who is paralyzed after an accident in the sea and meets Yosef, played by Alaa Daka, an aide at the rehabilitation center where she receives treatment. An intimate relationship develops between them, but outside pressures threaten it.
The leading director, Nitzan Gilady, passed away earlier this year; his final film, Thou Shalt Love, will be shown. It stars Yael Elkana as Naomi, a 28-year-old haredi (ultra-Orthodox) yoga teacher whose marriage is thrown into crisis when she discovers why her husband failed to appear at an important meeting with their rabbi. Michael Moshonov and Lena Fraifeld co-star.
Tomer Heymann's 'I Want to Tell My Story' is a fresh approach to Holocaust history
Tomer Heymann is one of Israel’s most celebrated documentary filmmakers, and his latest film, I Want to Tell My Story, has an unusual approach to Holocaust history. As Shimon Rothschild approaches his 100th birthday, he reconstructs his own life on a studio set, directing actors portraying relatives who were murdered and restaging episodes including Auschwitz, medical experiments at Sachsenhausen, a death march, and his life after the war. Rather than simply recounting his memories, Rothschild becomes, in effect, the director, which floods him with conflicting emotions.
Uri Levi’s documentary Peace 2030 follows Maoz Inon, whose parents were killed on October 7, and Aziz Abu-Sarah, a Palestinian from Jerusalem who has suffered his own family loss. Together, they embark on an ambitious campaign the achieve Israeli-Palestinian peace by 2030.
Among the Haifa Docs selections is Boaz Dvir’s To Kill a Nazi, an investigation into the extraordinary story of Michel Cojot, a French Jew who sought the truth about his father’s murder at Auschwitz. His pursuit eventually led him to Klaus Barbie in Bolivia and unexpectedly connected him to the events surrounding the Entebbe rescue operation. Jason Alexander of Seinfeld narrates.
Music lovers will want to see Broken English, Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard’s documentary about iconic singer Marianne Faithfull. Made with Faithfull’s participation, it looks back at a six-decade career defined as much by survival and reinvention as by music.
A special Japanese cinema program, From Mishima to Oshima, includes Paul Schrader’s typically unconventional 1985 movie, Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters. Schrader weaves the final day in writer Yukio Mishima’s life with flashbacks and highly stylized dramatizations of his fiction, accompanied by a score by Philip Glass.
The program also includes Kon Ichikawa’s 1958 Conflagration, adapted from Mishima’s novel The Temple of the Golden Pavilion. Its story of an alienated young man whose obsession with the purity and beauty of a Kyoto temple takes a destructive turn remains one of the landmarks of postwar Japanese cinema and literature.
Haifa’s Wildest Nights section offers Hille Norden’s German film Easy Girl, about Nore, an uninhibited young woman who befriends a medical student and gradually reveals her dark past.
Haifa Classics is always a wonderful section, and this year it provides a welcome opportunity to see Barbra Streisand as she was meant to be seen: larger than life, on a movie screen.
The Streisand tribute will include William Wyler’s Funny Girl, the 1968 film that gave Streisand her first movie role, and an Oscar, for her portrayal of vaudeville and Broadway star Fanny Brice, a movie that holds up remarkably well, and features Omar Sharif as her husband, Jewish gambler Nick Arnstein; Gene Kelly’s lavish 1969 musical Hello, Dolly!; and Frank Pierson’s 1976 version of A Star Is Born, in which Streisand stars opposite Kris Kristofferson, with a screenplay by the director and acclaimed authors Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne.
It isn’t the best version of this story, but it will be interesting to see how it holds up after 50 years. Yentl, the classic gender-bending story of shtetl life based on an Isaac Bashevis Singer story, will also be shown.
The Israeli premieres of major new films by Boyle, Assayas, Ozon, Zvyagintsev, and Salvadori, along with a strong Israeli lineup, ambitious documentaries, Japanese masterpieces, and Streisand singing her heart out, make this year’s Haifa International Film Festival an event every cinephile will want to attend.
For more information, go to the website at www.haifaff.co.il/

EU Operation Aspides raised alert level of its ships after Houthi attacks, Kallas says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:38:10 UTC
00:38:10 KST

The European Union's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said on Friday that the EU naval mission in the Red Sea, Operation Aspides, has raised the alert level for its vessels after the situation in the area worsened.
"Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are unacceptable and sabotage the global economy," she said in a post on X.
She added that she had spoken with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al-Saud about diplomatic efforts to end the fighting in Yemen and restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis have expanded their foothold around the Red Sea in recent weeks, capturing several strategically important locations near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Perim Island, which sits at the center of the narrow waterway.
The Iran-backed group has also taken control of the Greater Hanish and Lesser Hanish islands, giving it additional positions from which to observe activity around one of the world's most vital maritime routes.
Houthi positions increase risks for vessels crossing Bab al-Mandab
The Bab al-Mandab remains open to commercial shipping, and the Houthis do not currently have the ability to completely shut down traffic through the strait. Their growing presence in the area, however, gives them better surveillance capabilities and more opportunities to threaten specific vessels.
The strait, which separates the Red Sea from the Gulf of Aden, is only around 18 miles wide at its narrowest point. It serves as a key connection between the Indian Ocean and the Suez Canal, with energy shipments equivalent to roughly 7% of global oil consumption typically passing through the route.
By controlling areas including Mocha, Dhubab, Perim Island, and the Hanish islands, the Houthis have increased their ability to track maritime movement and create uncertainty for commercial operators. Shipping firms and insurers factor these risks into their decisions, sometimes raising costs or avoiding routes altogether when they believe a vessel could become a target.
Houthis use growing foothold to pressure Saudi Arabia
The Houthis have also sought to use their strengthened position to pressure Saudi Arabia, including through attacks targeting the kingdom’s infrastructure and renewed threats against Saudi territory, including remarks involving Mecca.
The situation illustrates the broader impact of the Houthi threat, even without the group fully controlling the maritime passage. The risk of attack alone was enough to influence decisions by shipping companies, insurers, financial institutions, and logistics operators.
Anna Barsky contributed to this report.

A modern-day encounter with Jonah’s ‘leviathan’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:38:01 UTC
00:38:01 KST

A crucial part of the Book of Jonah, which we read during the afternoon service on Yom Kippur, is the big fish that swallowed the prophet.
I think I can understand something of what Jonah felt when that creature approached him, because I once found myself in a somewhat similar situation in the Philippines.
I was so close to a whale that I could have reached out and touched it. Even now I find it hard to believe. I have always been wary of large animals, more than my wife is frightened of cockroaches.
As a child, I read Herman Melville’s masterpiece Moby-Dick, and his descriptions planted a fear of whales deep inside me. From then on, a whale belonged to books, distant oceans, and nightmares. The closest a person like me usually comes to a whale is when, during Sukkot, we add to Birkat Hamazon the verse: “May the Merciful One deem us worthy to dwell beneath the shelter of Leviathan’s hide.”
Years ago, I took my children to SeaWorld in Orlando, where we watched a performance by Shamu, a trained killer whale confined to an enormous pool. He was immense, but he was behind glass, inside a world constructed for him and for the people watching.
So when I was invited to swim and snorkel with whales in the Philippines, I felt like someone accustomed to seeing lions behind bars, suddenly invited to walk through an open safari among free-roaming lions and tigers.
We arrived in Donsol late at night. The next morning I stepped out of my room and found myself on the shore of the ocean. The air was hot and wet. Salt hung in the air, mingling with the heavy, green smell of tropical vegetation. The sea was almost perfectly still, painted by the first light in shades of blue and gray. A few small boats rested offshore. Somewhere deep in the jungle behind us came the calls of birds, and the distant, muffled cries of monkeys.
Everything was too quiet. It was the kind of quiet that makes you feel something is about to happen. There, in that strange and beautiful morning, I prayed Shacharit alone, and studied my Daf Yomi.
'Dive! Go down!': A dark shape, a movement, a spout of water
Later, my companions woke, and we walked down to the pier. I could still smell the sea and hear the small waves tapping against the wooden pilings. None of us yet knew what the creature we were looking for would look like.
We climbed aboard a banca, a long, narrow Filipino boat fitted with bamboo outriggers for stability. Four passengers and three crew members occupied each boat. High on the mast, the spotter scanned the open water. He squinted into the glare, looking for a dark shape, a movement, a spout of water.
When he spotted one, the guide told us to jump.
We slipped into the water wearing the snorkel masks and plastic fins they had provided. We put our faces into the water and saw nothing. The water was extraordinarily clear. For the first two meters, I could see a long way, but the deeper we went, the blue grew darker, then almost black. There was no seabed beneath us. Nothing to orient myself by. Only water. A great deal of water.
Then the guide shouted: “Dive! Go down!”
I dipped less than a meter beneath the surface of the water. And then, from my right, something enormous appeared. A creature the size of a bus.
For a few seconds, my mind simply refused to understand what my eyes were seeing. It did not burst from a storm. No whirlpool, no sudden explosion of water, no warning. It simply emerged from the dark blue, immense and utterly silent.
Its mouth was wide open. Not like the mouth of a fish I knew, but like a vast black opening in the water, something cavernous and bottomless, moving slowly toward us. Its skin was black, scattered with pale markings as large as dinner plates.
I felt the fear before I could even name it. My body stopped responding. I froze. I could not kick. I could not turn. For one terrible moment, I could not even remember to breathe.
The creature kept coming. Slowly. Silently. Something deeply frightening about that silence. It was not attacking. It did not need to. It moved with the absolute confidence of an animal that feared nothing in its world.
And I suddenly understood something that made the fear worse: I was in its world.
It passed directly beneath me, perhaps a meter away. I could see its immense body sliding through the water, so close that every instinct in me screamed to get away. But there was nowhere to go. No ground beneath my feet. No wall. No railing. No boat to climb onto. Nothing. Just blue water between me and the surface, and that enormous black body moving underneath me.
I wanted to swim away. I couldn’t. I wanted to shout. I couldn’t. I was completely, helplessly still.
Only after I climbed back into the boat did I realize that my heart was pounding as though I had just sprinted a kilometer.
And then, with a strange excitement, I thought of Jonah. For the first time in my life, I realized that I had seen with my own eyes something like what he might have seen before the great fish swallowed him. The mouth of our fish was large enough, I thought, to accommodate three people.
There were two differences. It did not swallow me. And the waters of Donsol Bay are far clearer than those of the Mediterranean near Jaffa.
My biblical thoughts were interrupted by the guide shouting that we should prepare for another dive. Another fish had been spotted.
We jumped.
Again came that impossible vision: an enormous head approaching through the water, a black body stippled with white, moving beside us, and my heart beginning to beat faster than I would have liked.
As I watched the great head pass beneath me, I suddenly saw its dorsal fin approaching me directly from the left.
This time fear was not a thought. It was a physical reaction. I swam forward as fast as I could. The fin passed just behind my legs. Water flooded my mask. It entered my nose. I scrambled upward and broke the surface, breathing hard.
'Like a kitchen grater with large teeth rubbing against the skin'
Later we learned that one of our group had not noticed the fin approaching him. It brushed against his abdomen. Had he been half a meter deeper, that enormous fin might have struck and dragged him.
Frightening…
He described the contact as “Like a kitchen grater with large teeth rubbing against the skin.”
The experience of swimming with the whales is called butanding. It is a whale shark, the largest fish in the world. Whale sharks come to Donsol Bay every year between March and July.
Later we saw two more. One rested two or three meters below us, as small as a family SUV. When we approached, it began slowly to move away. This time I was no longer afraid. Something inside me had begun to adjust to the sheer scale of the animal.
I swam above it for almost a minute without touching it. The guide had warned us to “keep your hands to yourselves” (shemirat negi’a), as though he was a mashgiach (supervisor) at a yeshiva.
The whale surged ahead of me, until its enormous body had completely passed beneath me. Then the fish slowed. It seemed almost as if it were playing with me, allowing me to close the distance. I continued swimming above it and diving beside it, and for about a hundred meters we moved together.
I remember the sensation clearly: I was a small man wearing fins and a mask, and beside me was a creature so enormous that it could have crushed me without the slightest intention of doing so. And yet, for those moments, I had the strange feeling that it was comfortable with me too.
Fear gave way to wonder. The experience was overwhelming and unforgettable. In some strange physical sense, I had fulfilled the verse: “There is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein,” from Barchi Nafshi (Psalm 104:26).
Since then, every Yom Kippur, when we listen to the reading of the Book of Jonah, I feel different from the way I felt before that extraordinary encounter with the whale shark, and different from what the congregation beside me is feeling and thinking.
And every Rosh Hodesh, and every holiday, when we recite the Barchi Nafshi, I have a different kavanah, a different intention, than I once did. I now know what a “leviathan” looks like. I know what it feels like when one passes beneath you in deep, silent water. And I know that a verse I have read dozens of times can one day step out of the prayer book, step out of the Bible, and swim directly beneath you.
Yom Kippur will never be quite the same again.
The author is the creator of the JewishTraveler blog.

From Likud to Yisrael Beytenu: The case for a change on the Right - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:37:50 UTC
00:37:50 KST

I joined Likud on the day I received my teudat zehut (ID card). I had not signed a lease yet. I had no bank account, no Hebrew worth speaking, and a mattress on a yeshiva’s floor. But I had the card, and I had the membership form, and I filled out the form first.
If you made aliyah, you understand why. Nobody moves to Israel for the salary. You come because you believe something, and once you are here, you want your belief to have a vote. I came out of Zionism.
But the reason I walked into public life, and the reason I chose that party and not another, had four parts: a free economy that brings prices down instead of managing them; sovereignty in the Land of Israel; victory over our enemies – real victory, not a ceasefire with a countdown; and an army in which every mother’s son serves, because a Jewish state that excuses one community from its own defense has stopped being one people.
Those four things are what I went into politics for, and they are what kept me there through wars, funerals, and the price of cottage cheese. I gave up my seat in the Knesset over the fourth one.
And I have reached a conclusion that took me a long time and cost me most of my political friendships: the party I joined that morning still says all four things, and works, actively and deliberately, to make sure none of them happen.
If you believe in those values, the address has moved to Yisrael Beytenu. Let me show you why, one value at a time, with the record and not with adjectives.
I’ll start with victory, because it is the one that keeps me up at night.
In December 2016, Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman sent a memo to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the chief of staff, and the head of military intelligence.
'severe mistake with far-reaching consequences'
It said that Hamas “plans to move the next conflict into Israel’s territory, with significant, well-trained forces, such as the Nukhba force, into Israeli territory, while conquering an Israeli village, and perhaps several, in the Gaza envelope and taking hostages.”
It said that failing to act was “a severe mistake with far-reaching consequences,” possibly worse than “the results of the Yom Kippur War.”
Read that again. The Nukhba. The villages. The hostages. Seven years before October 7.
He was told the memo was not serious.
Two years later, in November 2018, after 500 rockets were fired on the south, the same cabinet accepted a ceasefire and let Qatari cash cross into Gaza in suitcases. Liberman called it “purely $15 million of terror funding.” He said the government was “feeding a monster” and “buying quiet for a heavy price with no long-term plan.”
Then he did something no one else in that room did: he resigned. He called the deal “a capitulation to terror,” and he walked out of the Defense Ministry rather than put his name on it.
One party wrote the warning and paid for it with a ministry. The other party received the warning, called it unserious, and paid for it with Be’eri and Nir Oz. That is the record. Everything else is noise.
Soverignty. For 15 years, the promise was made at every campaign stop in Efrat and every parlor meeting in Ra’anana. And for 15 years, one man stood between the promise and the vote. Netanyahu blocked the bills his own MKs brought. He took sovereignty off the table in 2020 and called it statesmanship.
Liberman lives in Nokdim. His party left Ariel Sharon’s government over the disengagement when most of the right found reasons to stay. On the land, one party has a slogan and one party has a home address.
The economy. As finance minister, Liberman opened the country to imports, broke the agricultural lobby that had beaten every minister before him, and left a smaller deficit than he found. The coalition that followed paid for its survival with billions in coalition funds for institutions that do not work and do not serve, taken from the families in Modi’in and Beit Shemesh who do both.
That same coalition caved to the lobbies and canceled the reforms that were supposed to lower your prices. Why? Because those lobbies had joined Likud in large numbers, and the party answered to its members before it answered to anyone else. Ze’ev Jabotinsky wrote about the dignity of the free citizen. He did not write about patronage with a Likud stamp.
And lastly, service. In 2019, Liberman refused to enter a government without the draft law passing as written. The country went to a second election over it, and he was mocked for stubbornness. Inside the Likud, I fought the exemption law, lost my seats in committees for it, and finally voted against the exemption laws rather than toe the party line.
On this one issue, there is exactly one party on the Right with a written red line and a record of losing power to keep it.
Some of you are thinking: the Russian party. Yes. We are led by a Russian-speaking oleh who made the most Zionist decision a Jew can make, the same one you made. Half of our top 10 are olim, including me, from Canada.
But we are not only a party for olim. We are a party of all Israelis: a bereaved father from Beit She’an at number two, a Druze veteran, the mayor of Metula, a third of the list religious-Zionist. Secular, religious, and traditional at one table, and everyone at that table serves.

Finland’s first F-35 jets have arrived in the country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:36:46 UTC
00:36:46 KST

- Finland's first two F-35A fighter jets landed at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, 2026, after a ferry flight from Texas.
- Finland plans to field all 64 jets by the end of 2030, reaching initial operational capability in early 2028.
Finland’s first two F-35A fighter jets landed at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, opening the operational phase of a 64-jet purchase meant to replace the Finnish Air Force’s aging F/A-18 Hornet fleet.
The two aircraft, tail numbers JF-510 and JF-512, left Lockheed Martin’s factory in Fort Worth, Texas, on Sept. 15 and made a refueling stop at Lajes Air Base in Portugal’s Azores islands before entering Finnish airspace at 5:21 p.m. local time. They landed at Rovaniemi 24 minutes later, escorted by Finnish F/A-18 Hornets. U.S. Air Force pilots flew the transatlantic ferry flight, a standard arrangement for international transfers involving American military pilots, and Finland’s national roundels were temporarily covered during the trip while the aircraft’s serial numbers and Finnish Air Force tail markings remained visible.
“The F-35 is one of the most significant capability projects in Finland’s defense, and its ambition level is high,” said Gen. Janne Jaakkola, Commander of the Finnish Defence Forces. “The arrival of the first aircraft in Rovaniemi is not an endpoint, but a beginning: we are building the capacity to use the full potential of the aircraft’s performance, as part of Finland’s defense system and as a seamless part of the alliance’s air defense and strike capability.”
Finland’s fleet designation, JF, stands for Joint Fighter, chosen to emphasize the aircraft’s relevance across all branches of the Finnish Defence Forces rather than just the air force. The 64 aircraft will carry sequential numbers from JF-501 to JF-564 as they arrive.
Finland selected the F-35A in December 2021 over Boeing’s Super Hornet, France’s Rafale, the Eurofighter Typhoon and Sweden’s Gripen, in a deal covering the aircraft, weapons, training and sustainment through 2030 valued at roughly 8.4 billion euros, or about $9.5 billion. The purchase followed Finland’s accession to NATO in April 2023, after which the Finnish Air Force began operating as a full alliance member.
“The F-35’s combat capability is in a class of its own,” said Maj. Gen. Timo Herranen, Commander of the Finnish Air Force. “The aircraft’s versatile and advanced sensors enable the detection and identification of new target types, and sensor fusion combines the information produced by the aircraft’s systems to build the pilot’s situational awareness and support decision-making. This information does not stay within a single aircraft; it can be shared with other actors in the networked defense system on land, at sea and in the air.”
The first eight Finnish-built aircraft, from Lockheed Martin’s 17th production lot, remain in the United States, where Finnish pilots and maintenance personnel are completing initial F-35 training at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida and Ebbing Air National Guard Base in Arkansas. Training in the United States is scheduled to continue until early 2028, after which nearly all instruction will shift to Finland, apart from occasional individual courses. Aircraft mechanic training will begin at Rovaniemi later this year, with pilot training starting in January 2027, taught by Finnish instructors who completed their own training in the U.S. and supported by instructors from other F-35 operator nations including the United States, Norway and Denmark.
Base construction is proceeding at four locations. Rovaniemi was ready to receive the first aircraft. Work at the Karelia Air Command’s Rissala base is targeted for substantial completion during 2027 so it can receive its first F-35s in 2028, while the Satakunta Air Command at Pirkkala and the Air Force Academy at Tikkakoski are also undergoing construction to meet the F-35 program’s security and operational requirements.
Col. Tuukka Elonheimo will take over as commander of the Lapland Air Wing on Oct. 1, moving from his post as head of the F-35 Foreign Liaison Office in Washington, D.C., a role he has held since July 2024. The current wing commander, Col. Saku Joukas, will succeed him at that Washington office.
Finland expects to reach initial operational capability in early 2028, when the Lapland Air Wing will fly the F-35 exclusively, and full operational capability by the end of 2030, with deliveries continuing through that year. The Finnish Air Force will operate the F/A-18 Hornet and F-35A in parallel throughout the transition. A formal reception ceremony for invited guests and media is planned for Oct. 1, with President Alexander Stubb, the Defence Forces’ commander-in-chief, in attendance.

frida escobedo studio to take MALBA underground with newly unveiled expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:33:11 UTC
00:33:11 KST

On its 25th anniversary, Malba is preparing to expand beneath Plaza Perú in Buenos Aires, with Frida Escobedo Studio leading a project that will double the museum’s exhibition space. The new architecture moves underground, allowing a substantial extension of the institution while the public square continues across the surface above. Currently in design, the project is expected to open in late 2029 or early 2030.
The expansion introduces new temporary exhibition galleries alongside an auditorium and flexible spaces for public programming. Workshops and storage areas move into the enlarged footprint, while an outdoor courtyard brings open air down into the museum. From the plaza, the intervention is conceived around continuity as Malba gains room beneath the city without giving up the public ground above it.
Frida Escobedo Studio is approaching the project as a reorganization of Malba as much as an addition to it. The existing museum and new underground spaces will be linked through a broader mix of programs, with dedicated areas for exhibitions alongside film, literature, education and other public uses. The architects‘ idea is to loosen the dependence between these activities and the conventional museum route.
An auditorium, for instance, can join the visitor circuit during museum hours or operate independently for a screening later in the evening. The same flexibility extends to educational events and conversations. This gives the expansion a second scale beyond its added square footage, stretching Malba’s activity across more hours and allowing several parts of the institution to function at once.
Frida Escobedo Studio will expand Malba beneath Plaza Perú in Buenos Aires
an expansion fifteen years in the making
Plans to grow Malba beneath Plaza Perú date back to 2011, when the museum first pursued an extension of roughly 3,840 square meters alongside its existing 7,455-square-meter building. Buenos Aires approved the proposal the following year, based on an early scheme by Uruguayan architect Carlos Ott, leaving a thirty-year window for construction to move ahead.
The current commission brings Frida Escobedo Studio into that longer story. Escobedo founded her practice in Mexico City in 2006 and opened its New York office in 2022. Her recent museum work includes the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s new Oscar L. Tang and H.M. Agnes Hsu-Tang Wing in New York, while the studio is also working with Moreau Kusunoki on the renovation of the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

Australia following Canada as EU associate member is ‘pure speculation,’ says Commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:32:48 UTC

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (R) and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese walk through the corridors of Parliament House in Canberra on March 24, 2026. | David Gray/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS ― The European Commission played down the prospect of extending its newly floated “associate membership” concept beyond Canada, at least while Brussels works out the details with Ottawa.
“We have made an announcement that relates to our intention to get closer to our Canadian partners via a process that will possibly go in that direction,” Commission spokesperson Arianna Podestà told reporters in Brussels on Friday. “We will not be speculating about other countries.”
Her comments came as she confirmed that Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will meet Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly next week.
Advertisement
Asked whether the meeting could provide an opportunity to discuss the associate membership idea with Australia, Podestà dismissed the suggestion.
“We have a very strong and close relationship with our Australian partners,” she said. “All the rest is pure speculation, and we’re not going to enter into that.”
Von der Leyen pitched Canada as a potential first EU “associate member” during her State of the Union address on Wednesday. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the ambition behind closer EU-Canada ties but has stopped short of endorsing the proposed status.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola subsequently said countries such as Australia and New Zealand could potentially follow Canada.
But Commission spokesperson Olof Gill stressed that Brussels is currently focused solely on developing the idea with Ottawa.
“What we’re focused on here is putting flesh on the bone on this idea,” Gill said, adding that the Commission is working with member states and Canadian partners to establish what the concept could look like in practice. “All other discussions are subsequent to that.”

China building world’s first mothership for submarine drones, satellite images show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:31:35 UTC
00:31:35 KST

China is building what could become the world’s first mothership capable of carrying and launching giant submarine drones, according to satellite images cited by the Daily Mail.
The vessel was identified under construction at the Hudong-Zhonghua shipyard in Shanghai, a facility where China has previously built large amphibious assault ships. Images taken by U.S. defense intelligence company Vantor show a large red-hulled ship whose unusual design has prompted analysts to suggest it is intended for a new class of underwater warfare.
“The most plausible explanation is that it is a special drone submarine mothership,” H I Sutton, an independent defense analyst specializing in underwater warfare, told Naval News, according to the Daily Mail.
Sutton assessed that the vessel could potentially carry at least four of China’s enormous autonomous submarines and transport them thousands of miles before deploying them at sea.
China is the only country known to have developed uncrewed submarines on such a scale. Their size has prompted analysts to classify them as extra-extra-large uncrewed undersea vehicles, or XXLUUVs.
Two Chinese models, measuring approximately 35 meters and 45 meters, or 115 to 148 feet, were first revealed in January 2025 and have already undergone testing in the South China Sea near Hainan, according to the report.
The vessels are significantly larger than comparable Western designs. The U.S. Navy’s Boeing Orca XLUUV measures about 16 meters, or 51 feet, while Britain’s XV Excalibur is roughly 12 meters, or 39 feet, long.
The Orca has a reported range of up to 6,500 nautical miles and is intended for long-range maritime missions. Britain’s Excalibur began underwater trials in July and is expected to become operational by 2028, with a reported endurance of up to 1,000 miles.
Much less is publicly known about China’s XXLUUVs, including their intended weapons and missions. Sutton said the much larger Chinese submarines could potentially carry heavier payloads than Western underwater drones. The Daily Mail noted that the U.S. system can carry multiple heavyweight torpedoes, suggesting China’s larger vessels may be capable of transporting still greater payloads.
The suspected mothership appears to contain a large internal hangar that analysts believe could house the underwater drones. Its size and configuration, Sutton said, make a civilian or research role less convincing. The ship also appears to have a separate hangar near the bow that could accommodate a helicopter.
Such a platform could substantially extend the operational reach of China’s autonomous submarines. Instead of using much of their range traveling from Chinese ports to distant mission areas, the drones could be carried aboard the mothership and released much closer to their destination.
The project comes as Beijing continues to rapidly expand its naval capabilities. China is already one of the world’s largest producers of warships, and estimates cited by the Daily Mail put its fleet at about 405 vessels, compared with roughly 295 in the U.S. Navy.
Much of that buildup reflects China’s focus on maritime security and its strategic priorities in the western Pacific.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has repeatedly said Beijing intends to bring self-governed Taiwan under Chinese control and has not ruled out the use of force, a position strongly opposed by Taipei. China has also expanded its military presence in the South China Sea, where its sweeping territorial claims are disputed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Brunei and Taiwan.
The precise purpose of the vessel under construction in Shanghai has not been publicly confirmed. But if analysts are correct, it could give China a capability no other navy is currently known to possess: a mobile platform able to transport, launch and potentially recover some of the world’s largest autonomous submarines far from home waters.

Russian parliamentary candidate campaigning under slogan “For Peace” disappears on eve of three-day State Duma vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:28:55 UTC
00:28:55 KST

Yulia Kuznetsova, a State Duma candidate from Russian Ecological Party “The Greens” who was campaigning under the slogan “For Peace,” stopped responding to calls and messages on the evening of Sept. 17, one day before the start of the three-day vote.
Before she disappeared, Kuznetsova denied that she had withdrawn her election observers from polling stations and said that a document purporting to show that she had done so was forged. Nevertheless, when the voting began on the morning of Sept. 18, her observers were removed from Moscow precinct election commissions Nos. 1263, 1273, and 514, based on statements allegedly signed by Kuznetsova, the legal aid project Slovo Zashchite (lit. “A Word for the Defense”) reported. Kuznetsova herself still could not be reached.
The Telegram channel of Slovo Zashchite subsequently published a recording of a conversation with Kuznetsova’s mother, who explained that her daughter had called her and said she had run into problems and had to leave urgently for three days without her phone. Kuznetsova did not say where she had gone. Her mother said she was worried.
Later, a source in Kuznetsova’s campaign team told Slovo Zashchite that she was being held at a police station in Moscow’s Central Administrative District. According to the source, Kuznetsova had relayed to relatives that she was safe and had “gone away for three days so as not to frighten the family.” There has been no direct confirmation of that account from Kuznetsova or her husband.
Nikolai Toropov, head of the Moscow branch of Rassvet (lit. “Dawn”), an unregistered anti-war political movement founded by former presidential hopeful Yekaterina Duntsova, had earlier said that Kuznetsova and her husband were safe. He later withdrew that statement. “There is still no concrete information about their whereabouts,” he wrote, adding that he would publish further updates only after receiving confirmation directly from Kuznetsova or her husband.
An initiative group supporting Duntsova reported that it had drafted an appeal to state prosecutors, encouraging its followers to contact the authorities and demand an investigation into Kuznetsova and her husband’s disappearance.
“We prepared a complaint to the prosecutor’s office asking it to investigate the circumstances of Yulia and her husband Vadim’s disappearance, determine their whereabouts and, if they have been detained, verify that their procedural rights are being respected,” the group wrote on Telegram.
On the evening of Sept. 17, Kuznetsova held a meeting focused on internet freedom with voters in Moscow’s Sokolniki District. Afterward, she told her acquaintances that she was taking a taxi home and was about 15 minutes away, according to the independent channel SotaVision. At about 9 p.m., the phones of Kuznetsova and her husband, Vadim, were switched off. Neither was found at home.
Kuznetsova is running for the State Duma from “The Greens” in Moscow’s Babushkinsky single-member district No. 195. She previously worked on campaigns for opposition politician Boris Nadezhdin, who recently left Russia after suspending his bid to run in the elections amid mounting pressure from the authorities. Alexei Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation and the team of opposition politician Maxim Katz both included her on their lists of recommended candidates for Russian voters to support.

Reform donor Ben Delo loaned £350k to academic later found to have engaged in online bullying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:25:05 UTC
00:25:05 KST

Reform UK’s new mega-donor Ben Delo gave a £350,000 loan to a conservative writer fighting a legal case in which a judge later found she had engaged in online bullying and regrettable conduct with a “whiff of threat and antisemitism”.
Nina Power and her friend, the writer Daniel DC Miller, brought the legal action for defamation against the performance artist Luke Turner, who they had accused of falsely calling them antisemitic. At the same time, Turner brought a counter-claim against the pair accusing them of harassment.
Their libel action failed on the grounds that Turner’s online reach was not big enough to have caused harm to their reputations, while the harassment case also failed on the basis that their conduct was not unlawful.
The loan from Delo to help fund Power’s case before the 2023 trial shines a light on the Reform supporter’s involvement in backing a landmark legal tussle over the boundaries of free speech.
It is understood Delo did not and does not believe Power and Miller held antisemitic views as alleged by Turner, and would never knowingly provide financial or any other support to those who did.
In the case, Miller, who is Jewish, and Power denied promoting fascist or antisemitic views, and said they did not know Turner was Jewish. The judge found there was “no overt antisemitism” displayed by the pair.
But in the counter-claim of harassment, the judge described social media posts by Miller and Power as having “the whiff of threat and antisemitism which they themselves can fairly be held to have created”, although she ruled it was “too occasional, intangible, diffuse and unconsolidated” to have been unlawful.
She said the “radio frequencies of macabre imagery and casualness around antisemitic tropes into which Mr Turner tuned do yield a discernible signal but not one strong enough to be recognised objectively as antisemitic hate speech or a resolved engagement with physical violence sufficient to render this conduct quasi-criminal”.
The judge also said: “Mr Turner evidently had been harassed to a quasi-criminal (or indeed criminal) degree by other people. But what Mr Miller and Ms Power did was not of that order.”
After the failure of the cases, Turner was awarded costs of £1m amounting to 80% of the total, and Power was declared bankrupt. In the course of the bankruptcy proceedings it emerged that Delo had loaned her a sum in the region of £350,000 to help pay her lawyers.
It is understood the loan was made by Delo weeks before the trial started when Power’s conditional fee arrangement with her lawyers collapsed. The loan was made on a commercial basis and secured against the value of a London property she owns, with a repayment schedule.
Delo has been known to be a supporter of the Free Speech Union, run by the Conservative peer Toby Young, and has funded a base known for anti-woke causes.
Power is a former leftwing academic who has written in publications including the Guardian about feminism. She has since described her journey towards being “conservative in the true sense of that word” and wrote a book, What Do Men Want? Masculinity and Its Discontents, in which she argues men have been demonised.
The 2023 high court ruling describes how Miller and Turner were involved in an online incident which emerged from Turner’s involvement in the London arts scene. The artist had risen to prominence thanks to his creative collaborations with the Hollywood actor Shia LaBeouf.
The pair took opposing sides in relation to the London art gallery LD50, which had staged a symposium featuring neo-reactionary speakers and a show advertised online with a quotation from Adolf Hitler, in German gothic font. While Turner described the venue as an alt-Nazi gallery, Miller joined the counter-protest, standing outside LD50 with a placard calling for “the right to openly discuss ideas”.
Miller, who told the court he was of Jewish heritage, is closely associated with the magazine IM-1776, which platforms hard-right views, having previously contributed to the title as an editor and an author. Among the articles published by IM-1776 are pieces celebrating the “Unabomber” Ted Kaczynski and the proto-fascist Italian nationalist Gabriele D’Annunzio.
In the trial, Turner acknowledged he had been wrong to claim Miller was the author of a blog advocating a Hitler-style disability policy.
WhatsApp chats between Miller and Power, disclosed as part of the 2023 trial, did show them dismissing anti-racism as a “psyop”. The term refers to psychological operations used by the military or governments to influence public behaviour.
Power wrote: “The social disapproval for ‘racism’ is a psyop to stop people realising that there *are* alien and fairy races,” and that “black and white were alien races and very different”.
In a later exchange Power brought up Hitler’s autobiographical political manifesto, Mein Kampf, writing “I think … at some point … we need to read Mein Kampf properly …”, adding that she wanted to “understand it”.
In an episode referenced in the judgment, Miller performed at a public event in Athens, delivering a lecture in the persona of the Italian far-right philosopher and antisemite Julius Evola. During the rise of fascism, Evola called for measures to counter “the Jewish menace”. He opposed democracy in favour of a caste-based aristocratic order and was convicted on appeal during the 1950s of trying to revive fascism.
The judge found the pair had between them labelled Turner “low IQ’, ‘sociopathic’, ‘paranoid’, ‘deranged’, ‘obsessive’, ‘paranoid schizophrenic’, ‘dangerously mentally ill’ and so on and on – sometimes accompanied by messages to ‘get help’.” She said in her ruling that Power told her from the witness box that the latter proceeded from genuine and empathetic concern. The judge was unconvinced.
During the trial, Miller and Power denied promoting antisemitic philosophies, describing their interest in the subject as a quest to “critically understand” the issues.
Power and Delo declined to comment. Miller said the story was “based on a systematic distortions of facts”, adding: “I am myself Jewish and proudly Jewish.”

Air France bets on caviar and champagne to lure luxury flyers
Air France is betting big on luxury to keep wealthy travellers spending with lavish servings of caviar and champagne in first-class cabins as soaring fuel costs and disrupted travel patterns squeeze airlines worldwide. The campaign seems to have paid off, with the Paris-based carrier saying that premium bookings and revenue have grown this year despite industry-wide higher fares.
With generous helpings of caviar and champagne, Air France's costly bet on luxury appears to be paying off, helping the Paris-based carrier weather the fallout from the Iran war, Chief Executive Ben Smith told Reuters on Friday.
Airlines worldwide, including parent Air France-KLM , are grappling with soaring jet fuel bills and disrupted travel patterns caused by the nearly seven-month-old Iran war, which has forced some to cut capacity and rein in spending. Air France, meanwhile, is riding things out.
The airline has tapped into the buzz created by the "Emily in Paris" TV show and tourists' enduring fascination with the French capital's fashion, food and hotel scene. It has doubled down on premium offerings, upgrading onboard menus with luxury-branded products and investing heavily in its most lucrative cabins.
"All the luxury brands are based in Paris. We have more Michelin-starred restaurants than anywhere in the world in Paris," Smith said on the sidelines of a London awards show where Air France won best first-class cabin.
Watch moreMeet the French women chefs breaking the mould
"So it is a very specific city. Not only is it gorgeous as a cultural location, but as a luxury city."
Europe's three largest airline groups, including British Airways owner IAG and Lufthansa, have all unveiled redesigned first-class cabins in recent years as they chase growing demand for premium travel, particularly from affluent US passengers.
Smith said Air France's wealthiest customers have not been put off by higher prices. Some former private jet users are even switching to first class, he said, seeking to avoid the scrutiny attached to the higher emissions associated with private flights.
Premium, business and first-class cabins have all delivered growth in bookings and revenue this year, despite Air France raising fares to offset surging fuel costs, Smith said.
Revenue from first-class and premium travel has risen 11 percent, according to company data. Smith also played down concerns that rising inflation in the US could hit premium spending.
"We've raised ticket prices significantly, but no, it's quite solid. It's better than I would have expected," he said.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Barilla is to invest €100 million in the South of Italy and set up a new pasta hub in Foggia in Puglia, the pasta giant said Friday. 
    The Barilla Group is restructuring its industrial operations in Southern Italy by announcing the creation of an integrated pasta hub in Foggia, featuring the construction of a next-generation mill. 
    The project—a €100 million investment taking shape between 2028 and 2030—will create new jobs and establish the Puglian site as one of the group's strategic hubs, delivering improvements in sustainability, logistics, and production efficiency to serve both Italian and international markets.
Consolidating operations at the new Foggia hub will allow the Group to redefine the role of certain production sites in Southern Italy, including through the involvement of industrial partners capable of ensuring operational continuity and supporting future development. 
 
In this context, proposals submitted by Pastificio Liguori S.p.A. to acquire the Marcianise (Caserta) plant, and by Molino Casillo S.p.A. to acquire the mills in Altamura (Bari) and Castelplanio (Ancona), are currently in advanced stages of negotiation. 
 
For both transactions, the Barilla Group considers the preservation of jobs for all affected personnel to be a fundamental prerequisite. 
 
Today, the Barilla Group initiated discussions with trade unions regarding the details of the industrial plan. 
 
Liguori and Casillo have expressed their willingness and commitment to maintaining production continuity at the sites in question, safeguarding local employment and expertise, and ensuring long-term development prospects. 
 
Furthermore, production for the Barilla Group will continue at these same sites under multi-year supply agreements with the acquiring companies.

China-ASEAN Expo opens with focus on CAFTA 3.0, AI, and Pinglu Canal
The expo comes as China and ASEAN begin implementing the upgraded CAFTA 3.0 framework, which aims to facilitate trade, strengthen supply chains and expand cooperation into emerging sectors.
Science and technology authorities and high-tech institutions from countries including Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand have sent delegations to the expo.
China has made significant advances in areas such as AI, electric vehicles and renewable energy, said Destarata Mustafa, counselor for political affairs at the Indonesian Embassy in Beijing. "We hope to expand cooperation with China in these fields."
More than 50 trade and investment promotion activities are being held during the expo, focusing on trade and investment facilitation, regional economic integration, and cross-border industrial and supply chain cooperation.
In the CGTN survey, 84.5% of respondents said deeper China-ASEAN free trade cooperation will inject greater momentum into openness, cooperation and stable growth in the global economy.
China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 opens new areas for cooperation
The expo comes as China and ASEAN begin implementing the upgraded CAFTA 3.0 framework, which aims to facilitate trade, strengthen supply chains and expand cooperation into emerging sectors.
Science and technology authorities and high-tech institutions from countries including Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand have sent delegations to the expo.
China has made significant advances in areas such as AI, electric vehicles and renewable energy, said Destarata Mustafa, counselor for political affairs at the Indonesian Embassy in Beijing. "We hope to expand cooperation with China in these fields."
More than 50 trade and investment promotion activities are being held during the expo, focusing on trade and investment facilitation, regional economic integration, and cross-border industrial and supply chain cooperation.
In the CGTN survey, 84.5% of respondents said deeper China-ASEAN free trade cooperation will inject greater momentum into openness, cooperation and stable growth in the global economy.
AI takes center stage at China-ASEAN Expo
AI is taking a prominent role at this year's expo, with dedicated exhibition areas at the Nanning International Convention and Exhibition Center and the newly established Nanning AI Compound.
The AI exhibition area at the Nanning International Convention and Exhibition Center showcases AI products and technologies covering consumer applications, smart homes, intelligent terminals, robots and embodied intelligence, alongside AI technologies from ASEAN countries.
At the 10,000-square-meter Nanning AI Compound, more than 150 AI companies, including Huawei, iFlytek and Unitree Robotics, are presenting applications across 11 themed sections, focusing on industrial and everyday use.
The venue will also feature an AI-themed market, service robots, robot competitions and performances.
The new exhibition area is also designed to facilitate more targeted cooperation through an intelligent matchmaking system. More than 8,000 pairs of potential cooperation partners have been pre-matched, while nearly 2,000 additional matchmaking sessions are scheduled during the expo. The system has collected around 60 cooperation demand projects from ASEAN countries and matched them with nearly 40 Chinese projects to help companies pursue potential partnerships.
The emphasis on practical applications reflects growing efforts to connect China's AI capabilities with the specific industrial and consumer needs of ASEAN markets.
How Pinglu Canal could strengthen China-ASEAN trade
The newly opened Pinglu Canal has become another highlight of the expo, with a dedicated exhibition area showcasing the 134.2-kilometer waterway and its potential to strengthen regional connectivity.
Connecting the Xijiang River shipping network with the Beibu Gulf, the canal allows vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes to reach the sea directly, creating a more efficient route from China's southwestern hinterland to international markets.
The canal is expected to shorten shipping distances between southwest China and Southeast Asia by more than 560 kilometers, reduce logistics costs by 18% to 30% and save about 5.2 billion yuan (about $775 million) annually.
It also strengthens the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor linking western China with Southeast Asia through railways, roads, waterways and ports.
According to the CGTN survey, 87.6% of respondents said multimodal transport, including river-sea and rail-water transport, when efficiently connected with cross-border industrial and supply chain cooperation, will further facilitate regional trade and investment.
The new connectivity comes as China-ASEAN trade continues to expand. In the first seven months of 2026, trade between the two sides reached $744.41 billion, up 24.7% year on year and accounting for 21.8% of China's total foreign trade.

IPI Demands Justice for Viktoria Roshchyna’s Death in Russian Custody
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:22:03 UTC
00:22:03 KST

- Category
- World
IPI Demands Justice for Viktoria Roshchyna’s Death in Russian Custody
The International Press Institute (IPI) has renewed its call for justice over the death of Ukrainian journalist Victoria Roshchyna and the release of 27 journalists Russia still holds.
The demand was published by the IPI’s official website on September 18.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The statement marked two years since her death and stressed that, of 16 journalists killed while reporting from Ukraine since February 24, 2022, Roshchyna remains the only one to have died in Russian custody during the war.
Roshchyna, a freelance journalist, died on September 19, 2024, after more than a year in Russian captivity. She was 27. After her remains were returned to Ukraine in February 2025, forensic examiners found the body mutilated, with some internal organs removed—possibly to conceal evidence of torture, according to IPI.
The institute noted that Russian authorities have not cooperated with a Ukrainian criminal investigation and refuse to explain how she died or to address allegations that she was tortured.
Those allegations are supported by two separate inquiries. An April 2025 investigation by the Viktoriia Project found numerous signs of torture on the body identified as Roshchyna's. In May 2026, Ukraine's National Police reported that her occipital bone had been broken while she was held at the SIZO No. 2 detention facility in Taganrog, Russia.
Roshchyna disappeared into Russia's secret prison system in August 2023, after traveling to Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia in Ukraine's southeast to investigate war crimes.
Nearly a year passed before Russian authorities confirmed they were holding her on undisclosed charges, and they never disclosed where she had been seized or detained.
She is believed to have died after a transfer to a facility known as SIZO No. 3 in Kizel, possibly while en route to Moscow for a prisoner exchange.
In October 2025, IPI named her a 2025 World Press Freedom Hero for her investigative work on the Russian occupation. She was also posthumously awarded Ukraine's Order of Freedom.
"Victoria Roshchyna paid the ultimate price for her dedication to ensuring the stories of her fellow citizens living under occupation were heard by the world," IPI Executive Director Scott Griffen stated. "IPI will keep demanding justice for Victoria, and we call on the international community to press for the release of every journalist Russia is holding," he added.
As of August 2026, 27 Ukrainian journalists remained imprisoned in Russia, many facing politically motivated charges of "terrorism" or "espionage," according to IPI.
Russian authorities detained about half of them after the full-scale invasion, in some cases filing no public charges and denying the imprisonments outright, leaving the journalists incommunicado.
While Russia and Ukraine regularly exchange prisoners of war, releases of civilians remain far less frequent. Four Ukrainian journalists returned home in June, July, and August 2025, and Russia included no journalists among the 120 civilians it freed in May 2026.
Roshchyna’s death is a stark example of the widespread abuse that occurs within Russia’s detention system.
Earlier reports revealed the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war shortly after capture, and 48 further deaths in custody from torture or denial of medical care have been documented since the invasion began.
More than 95% of interviewed captives have reported torture or ill-treatment. More than 300 detention sites have been identified across Russia and occupied territory, and while 9,716 Ukrainians have been returned since February 2022, thousands remain held incommunicado.

easyJet cabin crew in Portugal plan October and December strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:19:17 UTC
00:19:17 KST

easyJet cabin crew in Portugal voted on Thursday to stage strikes from 2 to 6 October and 19 to 23 December over working conditions and pay.
easyJet cabin crew in Portugal are set to stage two strikes, the first from 2 to 6 October and the second from 19 to 23 December, with the action expected to affect the airline's operations at Lisbon, Porto and Faro airports.
According to the National Union of Civil Aviation Flight Personnel (SNPVAC), around 500 scheduled flights could be grounded during the October strike, excluding any minimum services imposed by the authorities.
The walkout in December could have an even greater impact on the low-cost carrier's operations, as it coincides with the busy Christmas travel period.
easyJet cabin crew held an emergency general meeting this week to discuss working conditions at the airline and decide on further action.
In a statement, SNPVAC said the decision to call the strikes was approved unanimously by the 188 easyJet employees who took part in the meeting. It followed "numerous attempts made by easyJet cabin crew to resolve labour and pay issues, which the company has ignored", the union said.
Among the grievances raised are frequent changes to duty rosters, the alleged breach of the collective labour agreement, unequal treatment of cabin crew and pilots, problems with operational planning and pressure to work overtime because of staff shortages.
The union accuses easyJet of keeping Portuguese crew on "wages below those paid by other airlines operating in Portugal and below those paid by easyJet itself in other countries in the network", where it said salaries fairly reflect the cost of living and the national minimum wage.
SNPVAC also speaks of a "climate of tension and dissatisfaction caused by the long and intolerable deadlock over the various labour disputes" which, it stresses, "has worsened", leading the union to conclude "that easyJet's ultimate aim is to prolong indefinitely the position it has adopted".
In the same statement, the union claims that easyJet "has repeatedly resorted to replacing striking crew members with managers and colleagues from other countries in the network", allowing it to operate flights that would otherwise be cancelled and, according to SNPVAC, effectively undermining the right to strike.
The October strike coincides with the long weekend around Portugal’s Republic Day public holiday on 5 October, which falls on a Monday this year. The December stoppage runs until two days before Christmas, when many people travel for leisure or return home for the festive season.

Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18

00:19:00 KST

Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
September 18, 2026
Billionaire investor and philanthropist Warren Buffett is stepping down as the chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, the holding company said Friday.
Buffett is 96 years old. His son, 71-year-old Howard Buffett, will succeed him in the role as chairman.
'I have never felt better about what comes next'
"I have served Berkshire since 1965," Buffett told shareholders in a message. "Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world. This is not something many people my age can say, and I have never felt better about what comes next."
This comes after Buffett stepped down as the firm's CEO last year, with Greg Abel succeeding him in that position.
"Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values — both worth more than anything on our balance sheet," Buffett said. "Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against."
In a statement of his own, Abel said "the culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian."
How did Buffett lead Berkshire Hathaway?
Buffett purchased textile firm Berkshire Hathaway in 1965 and transformed it into a multinational conglomerate holding company with a worth of over $1 trillion (€871 billion) in terms of market capitalization. Most of the companies worth more than $1 trillion are in the tech sector.
Buffett's investment prowess has led to Berkshire beating the S&P market index in 40 out of the past 60 years.
Berkshire owns whole businesses in sectors such as insurance and energy; the firm also owns restaurant chain Dairy Queen. Moreover, Berkshire invests in companies such as Apple, Coca-Cola, Chevron and Bank of America.
According to Forbes, Buffett is the 10th-richest person in the world today with a net worth of $144.7 billion.
Buffett grew up in Omaha, Nebraska, where Berkshire is also headquartered. Known as the "Oracle of Omaha," Buffett has embraced a folksy public persona and is enamored with American staples such as McDonald's breakfasts, Dairy Queen sundaes and Coca Cola.

Hunter Biden floats conspiracy theory that Israel deliberately allowed Oct. 7 attack
The former US president’s son claimed Israel let the massacre happen to justify its plans for Gaza
Hunter Biden, the son of former US president Joe Biden, floated a conspiracy theory that Israel deliberately allowed the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack to happen as a pretext for carrying out its own plans in Gaza.
Speaking to London’s LBC radio, Biden claimed Israel “knew what was coming” and “allowed it to happen” to pursue a plan that would otherwise never have received a “green light.”
No evidence supported the allegation of deliberate Israeli complicity. Reports that political leaders and security officials ignored warning signs did not establish a conspiracy to let the massacre happen.
Biden cited a disputed Haaretz report alleging that the United Arab Emirates’ leader personally warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about the intentions of Hamas’s Gaza chief Yahya Sinwar. He accused Netanyahu of receiving the warning and doing “absolutely nothing about it.”
Netanyahu denied the newspaper’s account and threatened to sue.
Biden also described the subsequent Gaza war as “akin to genocide,” while acknowledging that the term was “very loaded.” He called Hamas “horrific.”
Israel rejected genocide allegations and said it sought to limit civilian casualties in a war that saw Hamas use civilians as human shields and conduct military operations from homes, hospitals, schools and mosques.
Biden repeatedly criticized Israel during other recent appearances on the podcast circuit. His allegation echoed claims circulated by anti-Israel activists and commentators that Israel permitted the October 7 massacre to justify its military campaign in Gaza.
The Hamas-led attrocity was the single deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust.

MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. Aeroflot and Rostec have signed a contract for the delivery of the second batch of 90 domestically produced MC-21 aircraft, with the air carrier to receive airliners between 2029 and 2032, the Kremlin’s press service reported.
