‘A critical moment’: concern UK is not up to speed in acting on AI risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:57:11 UTC
23:57:11 KST

Towards the end of Keir Starmer’s time in office, his senior ministers, alarmed by the latest developments in artificial intelligence, began drawing up plans for a new AI safety law.
They ordered a review of existing legislation to see what powers they already had, according to those briefed on the plans, and were exploring whether they could force the world’s most advanced technology companies to submit their products for safety testing before launching them.
In the midst of the political chaos that engulfed the former prime minister as he fought to remain in office, however, the plans fell by the wayside.
Now, after two weeks in which the world has been told there is a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans”, and King Charles has warned about its potentially destructive capabilities, the government’s attention has turned again to what to do about AI.
Andy Burnham, Starmer’s successor in Downing Street, has said relatively little about the technology in the past, and in one of his first acts in office he scrapped the department that had been leading the legislative work.
The prime minister’s focus is on more immediate domestic problems. But as he grapples with balancing his first budget and bringing down the cost of living, some fear the threat posed by AI has dropped off the government’s radar.
“The first duty of government is to keep people safe,” said Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the science and technology committee. “The government’s response to an existential threat cannot be to throw its hands up in the air and say there is nothing we can do.”
Risks v potential
Britain has been at the forefront of the debate on AI safety since Starmer’s predecessor, Rishi Sunak, decided to make it one of his top priorities in office.
Amid worries about what super-intelligent tools could do without human involvement, Sunak convened a summit in the UK and persuaded the US, EU, Australia and China to cooperate on AI safety.
Starmer was more bullish about AI’s potential “to increase productivity hugely, to do things differently, to provide a better economy that works in a different way in the future”.
The Guardian has learned that in the former technology department, Emran Mian, the lead civil servant, had plans for AI to replace almost every civil servant in the department when they retired or moved on to a new job.
But at the same time, some in government were keen to remain focused on the risks posed by the technology.
Shortly before Starmer’s departure, Yvette Cooper, then the foreign secretary, told the Guardian she believed AI posed a Hiroshima-style risk to humanity.
Starmer’s government took steps to mitigate the risks Cooper and others had identified. His government allocated £115m in June to fund a response centre to deal with incidents when AI goes rogue and for a new AI biosecurity programme.
Officials in the science department also began reviewing what powers ministers had to compel companies to cooperate with the UK safety regime, and what else they could legislate for.
‘A critical moment’
When Burnham took office earlier this summer, one of his first moves was to abolish the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT).
Kanishka Narayan, the junior minister in charge of AI, was given a promotion and placed in the Cabinet Office, where he continues to oversee the technology but without the logistical support of a dedicated department.
The move alarmed some in the AI industry.
Matt Clifford, the AI investor who had advised Starmer and Sunak, posted on X: “Right now is a critical moment for tech as an economic and national security issue. Tying up our most senior science and tech officials in a [reorganisation] wastes time and energy that’s desperately needed for the actual substance.”
Dame Wendy Hall, a computer scientist who chaired a UK government AI review in 2017, said: “The structure was a bit bloated in DSIT, but the fragmentation we have now has had a much worse impact.”
AI safety rose up the political agenda again over the summer.
In July, OpenAI revealed one of its AI agents had launched an autonomous cyber-attack on Hugging Face, a real company, triggering alarm among technology experts around the world.
Earlier this month, Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher, resigned from his job at Anthropic, claiming the company was “gambling with our lives”. His comments were reposted online by one of his colleagues, Evan Hubinger, who added: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”
Just as these warnings were being made, the Financial Times revealed that Anthropic had launched the latest version of its Claude Mythos tool without submitting it to the UK safety institute first.
Mounting concerns
King Charles intervened this week, convening a meeting of AI executives in Scotland, where he told them: “The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world.”
Public concern is also growing. YouGov said on Friday that just over a third of Britons see AI as the third potential cause of human extinction behind nuclear war and climate breakdown – a figure that more than doubled since last year. Two-thirds think AI has the potential to end human civilisation, a view shared by the Nobel-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, and one in six support a slowdown in AI development.
In parliament, the Labour MP Liam Byrne has asked the head of the safety institute, Henry de Zoete, to testify in front of the business committee he chairs.
De Zoete replied earlier this week, explaining that no one outside the US had been allowed to see Anthropic’s latest product before it launched and insisting that his institute could still monitor such tools after they had been released.
“We have teams of talented AI researchers working on research projects based on both pre-release and post-release testing that are fundamental to the UK’s understanding of AI risk, across chemical-biological, human influence and loss of control,” he said.
Ministers have also begun to comment. Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, told the TUC congress this week there were “clearly huge risks to our national security and society if the right guardrails are not put in place”.
In an article in the Times, Narayan wrote: “Nothing is off the table. Where further regulation, legislation, stronger protections or new powers are needed, we will act.”
Wake-up call
Byrne believes ministers had a wake-up call.
“I think the government is taking it seriously now,” he said. “It has become clear in the last two weeks that perhaps our safety advisers don’t have the power they need to keep us safe.”
This still leaves the question unresolved by successive governments – what can the UK, as a middle-ranking power, do to curb the might of some of the world’s most advanced and fastest-growing technology companies?
For some, the answer is straightforward: regulate and legislate, just as the government would do for any emerging threat.
“The social media companies used to argue that the government is too powerless to act,” said Onwurah. “But there are things the government can do. We could say, for example, that if your frontier model has not gone through the safety institute, we are not going to allow you to sell your commercial models in our country.
“Or, if your AI goes and attacks someone else like happened with Hugging Face, you are legally and financially responsible.”
Many believe that action will only work if it is coordinated with other countries.
“If the US and China do not figure this out, the UK is unlikely to deliver a safe environment on its own,” said Byrne. “But a safety regime which is set and enforced by the UK, Europe, India, Canada and Japan would be robust.”
The former Cabinet Office minister Darren Jones has called on Burnham to put the issue at the top of the agenda when Britain hosts the G20 summit next year. “The AI safety conversation at the moment is around international collaboration on safety testing,” he said. “This is easier to do multilaterally, through treaties or agreements.”
One former government official added: “If together we say we require you to pass your models through our safety institutes – if we did that at a large enough scale, we would be able to stand up to the US government.”
Time to act
Whatever the government decides to do, it may find that now is the best time to do it.
Unusually, many in the industry are themselves calling for stricter regulation.
OpenAI’s head of policy in Europe, Tom Duff Gordon, said this week: “We support stronger UK rules for the handful of companies, including OpenAI, developing the most powerful AI systems.”
One former government official said: “We have strengths in this country when it comes to AI. Our AI industry is third in the world behind the US and China, and we also have considerable convening power with other countries.
“The question for me is whether the new prime minister is alive enough to this problem to take advantage of those strengths.”

Saudi Aramco will not supply European oil refiners with crude in October: Sources
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Saudi Aramco will not supply European oil refiners with crude in October: Sources
NEW YORK – Saudi Aramco told at least two oil refining customers in Europe that they will be allocated no crude in October under long-term agreements after the kingdom’s key pipeline to the Red Sea was attacked, people informed of the decision said.
European customers normally receive Saudi Arabian crude on so-called term contracts, ensuring a steady flow of supply every month. Those deliveries will not take place in October, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public. The decision applies to all European buyers, they said.
Saudi Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment made outside normal working hours.
The absence of Saudi flows in October will heighten the need for European buyers to secure replacements. Already, Poland’s Orlen SA has been hunting for shipments, helping propel the prices of regional oil grades higher. Dated Brent, which is the benchmark for real-world barrels in Europe, topped US$130 this week at one point.
Saudi Arabia was forced to shut its East-West pipeline last week after it was attacked by drones. Aramco is working to partially restart within days and ramp up to full capacity within six weeks, a person familiar with the matter said on Sept 16.
The shutdown has forced Aramco to make the rare move to offer customers in Asia cargoes on a so-called spot basis – agreements for immediate delivery. Once the pipeline restarts, traders will focus on whether Aramco offers refiners in Europe similar terms.
Those supplies to Asia are going through the Persian Gulf, which means Aramco has once again pivoted towards the embattled Strait of Hormuz. The company has sold tens of millions of barrels to customers for collection just outside the waterway this week, a route it had largely shunned during the conflict in the Middle East as regular attacks of ships made the journey risky.
The increased flows towards the Persian Gulf, however, brings little relief to Europe’s refiners. In order to get to buyers in the continent, those shipments would either have to sail through the Red Sea, where Yemen’s Houthi militants have been attacking Saudi ships, or sail almost five weeks around Africa.
European refineries typically lift Saudi crude from Egypt’s Mediterranean port of Sidi Kerir, which is connected to the Red Sea via a pipeline.
European countries in the OECD imported 577,000 barrels a day of crude from Saudi Arabia in June, according to the International Energy Agency. BLOOMBERG

The West won’t fight Russia itself. Eastern Europe may have to
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:55:55 UTC
23:55:55 KST

The West won’t fight Russia itself. Eastern Europe may have to
We have come to regard the countries of Eastern Europe as the most conflict-prone and volatile part of the political landscape surrounding Russia, and there are grounds for this view.
Immediate neighbors often have the most difficult relationships because the more points of contact there are, the more opportunities for friction, and in Russia’s case, geopolitical logic is reinforced by considerable historical experience of invasion, which means Russia has traditionally sought to ensure that no serious threat can emerge from neighboring countries and that its immediate surroundings remain predictable.
This predictability has been secured in different ways over the centuries, sometimes through direct annexation and sometimes through indirect forms of control. Russia’s western neighbors are small in comparison with it, and their policies have often been driven by fear of their much larger neighbor, whether justified or not.
The acute military and political crisis that began in 2022 seems to confirm that stability between Russia and the rest of Eastern Europe shouldn’t be taken for granted, as countries that joined NATO and the EU in the late 20th and early 21st centuries are now pursuing the most intransigent course, seeking not merely to contain Russia but to marginalize it.
Their own capabilities are limited, so they have increasingly used international institutions, above all an increasingly militarized EU, to push larger member states towards a tougher position. A recent example is Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski’s rhetoric concerning the Baltic region and Kaliningrad.
The militarization of Eastern Europe is, in this sense, a continuation of a policy pursued since the 1990s, which rested on the conviction that the expansion of Western military and political institutions was an objective historical process, and that enlargement itself would provide security without ever requiring serious military action.
This assumption was convenient for everyone as the new member states regarded NATO membership as a guarantee of their security, and the veteran members in Western Europe and the US were confident that these guarantees would never actually have to be tested. Nobody seriously expected to fight Russia over the states along its borders.
Let us leave aside for the moment the role NATO expansion played in creating the conditions for the conflict over Ukraine, because whatever one’s interpretation of how we arrived here, the question of military guarantees has now moved from theory to practice.
This creates a fundamental problem for NATO. On the one hand, it can’t simply abandon its security commitments, because if these guarantees cease to be credible, NATO loses much of its purpose. On the other hand, Article 5 of the Washington Treaty is less automatic than is commonly assumed and it doesn’t mechanically send every member of the bloc to war.
Eastern European governments understand this ambiguity. They lack confidence that the larger powers would come to their aid, and history gives them reasons for doubt and encourages some of them to push both Russia and their own allies toward firmer positions.
The objective is to bind the major Western powers ever more tightly to their security, which raises the question: What role would Eastern European countries actually play if a direct military conflict with Russia did occur?
An impartial assessment suggests that they would most likely become both the battlefield and the vanguard, sent into the confrontation ahead of the major Western powers, and elements of this arrangement can already be seen in Ukraine.
Western European societies are neither willing nor prepared to fight Russia themselves, but they have proven to be considerably more comfortable supporting others who are prepared to do so – and Ukraine, for its own reasons, has accepted this role. For the rest of Eastern Europe, however, the calculation is more complicated.
We shall leave aside the Baltic states, where the level of political rhetoric increasingly makes serious discussion difficult, but more established countries with deeper traditions of statehood – Poland, the Czech Republic, and Romania – are perfectly capable of recognizing the danger of being thrown under the bus of military escalation in pursuit of the broader objectives of the European establishment.
This awareness doesn’t necessarily moderate their public rhetoric, but their practical behavior shows a certain degree of caution.
This distinction is becoming increasingly important as military tensions rise. The escalation pursued by Kiev creates a growing possibility of incidents capable of drawing neighboring states more directly into the conflict. For Eastern European countries, encouraging further escalation therefore carries risks, given that they’re likely to bear the immediate consequences of the policies they are advocating.
Until now, Russia has generally assumed that if any European countries eventually contribute to a settlement, they would be the continent’s other major powers, states large and secure enough not to define their policies primarily through fear of Russia.
In a genuine military crisis, however, the logic could turn out to be the reverse, as the countries with the greatest reason to fear an uncontrolled confrontation may also have the greatest interest in preventing one.
Eastern European governments therefore face an increasingly stark contradiction. They want stronger Western guarantees against Russia, and the natural method of obtaining them is to persuade the rest of Europe that the ‘Russian threat’ is immediate and severe, yet the more successful they are in escalating the confrontation, the greater the possibility that their own countries become the front line.
Rationality doesn’t always prevail in international politics, but this doesn’t mean Russia should write off Eastern Europe as a lost cause – because the countries closest to a conflict may ultimately have the strongest reasons to keep it under control.

The Research and Innovation Council has reviewed national strategic choices for RDI and invites a panel of experts to assess the impacts of artificial intelligence
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:53:38 EEST
23:53:38 KST

The Research and Innovation Council has reviewed national strategic choices for RDI and invites a panel of experts to assess the impacts of artificial intelligence
In its meeting, the Research and Innovation Council examined the status of implementation and execution of national strategic choices for RDI. The meeting included expert reviews of the status of the themes of health and wellbeing and defence. The Council has also decided to establish a panel of experts to assess the impact of artificial intelligence on RDI activities.
Last winter, the Council decided on the national strategic choices for RDI policy and activities. They are intended to consolidate resources, clarifies the needs of the administrative branches and operators on where to direct RDI activities, while further reinforcing the message on Finland’s focus points to international partners.
At its 16 September meeting, the Council debriefed the results of this spring’s stakeholder survey on the implementation of the strategic choices. The RDI sector has been largely positive in its reception of the choices. The execution and implementation of the choices has already begun through cooperation between various operators, if at differing speeds. RDI cooperation is growing closer in both the health and defence sectors. There is significant growth potential in both areas, but what remains important is reinforcing RDI activities through public demand, among others.
To ensure successful implementation, there should be a clear division of roles and responsibilities among the actors involved. The Academy of Finland and Business Finland has continued to seek closer cooperation in the different choice areas, and it is their funding that plays a key role in implementing and achieving greater depth in the choices. It remains possible to direct and guide the choices through updates to the multi-year plan for R&D funding in the upcoming government term.
These national strategic choices are:
- data and data-based value creation;
- disruptive technologies;
- health and wellbeing;
- climate, environment and the Arctic dimension; and
- security, resilience and defence.
Calling for a comprehensive vision for the development of artificial intelligence
There is an obvious need to examine the impacts of artificial intelligence on research and innovation activities, technological development and the scientific process. The Council finds that there is a need for a comprehensive, national vision on the direction AI should develop, which should be considered in the preparation of RDI policy decisions.
It is for this purpose that the Council has decided to establish the panel of experts. The panel’s task will be to study and examine the impacts of artificial intelligence of RDI activities, along with the reinforcing effect of artificial investment on the impact of RDI activities. The work of these experts will supplement other ongoing studies into artificial intelligence from the perspective of RDI.
The Council also states that the Ministry of Finance is currently seeking statements on an amendment to the R&D Funding Act. Among other changes, this amendment would allow for the consideration of innovation funding as R&D funding for up to 50 million euros.
Enquiries: Katri Manninen, Special Adviser, tel. 029 5161152, Johanna Moisio, Secretary-General, tel. 0295 160 625

Explainer-How Putin may leverage predictable outcome of Russia's elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:34 UTC
23:53:34 KST

Explainer-How Putin may leverage predictable outcome of Russia's elections
MOSCOW, Sept 18 - Russians are voting in a three-day parliamentary election which is widely expected to see the ruling United Russia party retain its dominance in what is a tightly controlled political system that has excluded most candidates who oppose Moscow's war in Ukraine.
Even though the overall outcome is not in doubt, here are some of the reasons why the vote may be useful to President Vladimir Putin.
A MANDATE FOR MORE WAR?
As president or prime minister for more than a quarter of a century, Putin's grip on Russia has never been tighter. But the war has lasted much longer than many Russians expected and fallout from the conflict is now being felt much more sharply on the home front.
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia itself have escalated, and while civilian casualties are far lower than in Ukraine, they have sharply increased this year. Strikes on oil refineries have caused fuel shortages, while businesses are grappling with drone attacks on their warehouses and polls suggest some Russians are increasingly anxious.
Having framed the election as a test of support for the war, Putin is likely to point to the results to say that most people back his decision to fight on until key war aims are met.
CREATION OF A 'NEW ELITE'
Putin has said that those who fought in Ukraine are "warriors", part of a new "elite" he has promised will have prestigious careers. Should the some 200 veterans standing from a range of parties do well, Putin is expected to point to their success at the ballot box as an example of how Moscow looks after those who risked their lives for the motherland and to show how distinguishing oneself on the battlefield can lead to a high-profile political career. It's a development that could also encourage more people to sign up to fight in Ukraine.
CONTRAST WITH UKRAINE
Putin has repeatedly suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy is illegitimate, pointing to the fact that his five-year term ran out in May 2024 and that Zelenskiy has refused to hold a new election since. Martial law, introduced in Ukraine in 2022, bans any wartime election and the constitution says the president serves until a newly elected one takes office. But Putin - who has faced criticism from Western politicians about Russia's own political system - may use the vote to say that Russia - unlike Ukraine - has stuck to its electoral timetable regardless of the war and is giving people a chance to vote.
SENSE OF NORMALCY
Putin has been keen to show Russians that despite the conflict and everything associated with it they can largely carry on life as before. Increasingly deep and destructive Ukrainian drone strikes have made that harder to achieve in what is the fifth year of the war. But holding a relatively smooth parliamentary election across 11 time zones in what is the world's largest country, whilst also waging war in Ukraine, could help Putin reassure Russians that pre-war traditions are being respected and that life - up to a point - goes on despite the conflict.
MOBILISATION/CENSORSHIP
Putin this month dismissed suggestions by Ukraine and Western media pundits that Russia would carry out a post-election mobilisation to expand the ranks of its army in Ukraine as "nonsense," suggesting it was a malicious suggestion designed to sow panic.
However, domestic and foreign critics of the war fear he could use the outcome of the election to justify such a move, given what Western intelligence agencies say are heavy Russian losses on the battlefield and what they say is Moscow's desire to urgently speed up the pace of its territorial gains with more manpower.
Those same critics fear that the authorities may move ahead with more repressive measures once the election results are in and a pre-election feel-good mood is no longer required.
They point in particular to plans previously floated by the authorities to have mobile service providers charge customers extra for using more than 15 gigabytes of foreign data in a month, a move seen as targeting people who use VPNs or virtual private networks to access websites and apps banned inside Russia. The authorities have given no public indication they intend to imminently resurrect the plan. REUTERS

Your Shoe Size Can Change as You Age. Here's Why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:32 UTC
23:53:32 KST

If you’ve always worn the same size shoe but your sneakers and boots feel tighter now that you’re in, say, your 40s or beyond, you’re not alone. People on TikTok are also sharing their experiences with growing feet as they’re getting older. But do your feet really get bigger with age?
“Yes, but ‘bigger’ is somewhat misleading,” says Dr. Kimberly Koury, an orthopedic surgeon at Atlantic Health. “Adult feet do not continue to grow in the same way they do during childhood. Instead, the shape of the foot can gradually change with age.”
This can happen for a variety of reasons and cause feet to become wider, flatter, and slightly longer, she explains. “Someone may notice that a shoe that fit well when they were younger now feels too tight, even though their actual foot bones have not continued to grow.”
Here’s what to know about why your feet may get bigger with age and what to do about it.
What causes feet to get bigger?
The main reason is that over time, your arch “flattens and spreads,” says Lesly Robinson, a podiatrist and interim dean of the Temple University School of Podiatric Medicine.
This is often due to decreased collagen—the protein that provides strength and elasticity to your skin, muscles, bones, tendons, and ligaments—that naturally happens with age. This can cause the ligaments supporting your arches to become lax, Robinson says. “When the arch falls, the foot both widens and lengthens,” adds Dr. Alexis Dixon, an orthopedic surgeon and foot and ankle specialist in Marina Del Ray, Calif.
Another reason feet may change in shape and size is a foot deformity, like a bunion or hammertoe, which become more prevalent as you get older. A bunion is a bump that forms on the inside of your big toe joint, but it’s not an extra bone growth. Instead, it’s a change in alignment, where the big toe moves toward the other toes, Koury says. “That makes the forefoot wider and can make previously comfortable shoes feel too narrow.” This can also contribute to flattening arches, Robinson says. Hammertoes happen when the tissue of your toes weakens, causing the muscles and tendons to buckle and curve, Dixon says.
Bunions and hammertoes can be genetic or result from wearing tight, narrow shoes over a lifetime, she says. They’re more common for women.
Arthritis is also common in feet and ankles, especially in the big-toe joint, Dixon says. It can cause bone spurs (extra growths of bone tissue) on top of the foot or at the back of the heel, which may rub against your shoe and make it feel too tight.
When do these changes happen, and who’s most affected?
People may notice foot changes starting in their 30s, but there’s no specific age when they happen, says Sindhu Srinivas, a podiatrist in Atlanta.
Age-related foot changes are generally more common for women, Koury says. The hormonal fluctuations in pregnancy and menopause affect collagen, and years of wearing high heels or narrow or ill-fitting shoes may contribute to structural changes in the feet.
People with previous foot injuries, flat feet or bunions (or a family history of these conditions), and a higher body weight are more at risk, Koury adds.
Being overweight puts pressure and stress on the feet, Srinivas says. “Over time, this increased load can contribute to changes in the foot's supporting structures and overall biomechanics.”
How much bigger will your feet get?
The changes happen gradually and can affect your foot’s length, width, and arch height, Srinivas says. But how much bigger your feet can get varies.
A study published in 2016 examined the foot measurements of 68 women aged 20 to over 80. It found that the widths of the balls of the feet increased by 3 to 4 millimeters per decade, while ball circumferences increased by about 5 to 7 millimeters, high-step circumferences 0.4 to 4.8 millimeters, and heel instep circumferences up to 2 millimeters.
“That may sound small, but these changes accumulate over several decades and can become enough to affect shoe fit,” Koury says.
Some people may need a wider shoe, while others might need one a half size larger, Dixon says.
When to see a doctor
If your feet seem to be getting wider or longer and you’re experiencing pain, swelling, numbness, tingling, or difficulty walking or doing other activities, see your doctor, Koury says. Also, talk to your doctor if you’re getting recurrent calluses, blisters, or skin breakdown, or if your bunions, hammertoes, or flatfoot are worsening. Sudden foot changes, especially if they only affect one foot, should also get checked, Srinivas says.
Pay extra attention to your feet if you have diabetes, neuropathy, or circulation problems, as even minor changes in your shoes’ fit can cause more serious problems, Koury says.
Doctors will recommend the best treatment for your feet. This may include orthotics to improve arch support, Robinson says. It’s also possible to modify footwear for bunions or hammertoes, Dixon adds. Physical therapy or exercises may be helpful for some, Koury says. Surgery may be necessary for some foot issues if other treatments don’t help.
How to protect your feet as you age
You can’t necessarily prevent age-related foot changes, but you can take steps to keep your feet healthy as you get older, Koury says.
Most important: wear shoes that fit well. Avoid footwear with narrow toe boxes, which compress your toes (and may cause bunions), and limit high heels, which put stress on the front of the foot and may even cause a deformity, Koury says. Shoes should be supportive and have a wider toe box, Robinson says. “It’s helpful to have your feet measured periodically, including the width, not just the length,” Koury says.
Maintaining a healthy weight can “help reduce unnecessary stress on the tendons, ligaments, and bones,” Sirinivas says.
Regular physical activity strengthens your feet and ankles. Low-impact, weight-bearing activities can maintain foot function and stability, improve balance, and prevent falls, Dixon says. Also try foot exercises, such as standing on one foot while holding onto a counter, or toe scrunches, which involves curling your toes to pick up a washcloth or other object off of the floor.
Treat bunions, flattening feet, or other foot problems as early as possible to avoid problems later, Koury says. “The goal is to accommodate the new foot shape and prevent the changes from becoming painful or functionally limiting.”

Volkswagen recalls over 208,000 vehicles in US over steering defect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:13 UTC
23:53:13 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
German automaker Volkswagen is recalling 208,724 vehicles in the US due to a steering system defect, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).
The recall covers certain 2018 Volkswagen Tiguan, 2018-2019 Volkswagen Atlas and 2019-2021 Audi Q3 models.
One of the bolts attaching the steering rack to the subframe may corrode and break, potentially causing the steering rack housing to fracture, the regulator said.
A broken steering rack housing could result in a loss of steering control, increasing the risk of a crash.
Authorized dealers will replace the right-side mounting bolt on the steering rack free of charge.
Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed on Nov. 10.
The recall was filed under NHTSA campaign number 26V590000, while Volkswagen’s recall codes are 48LG and 48VT.

Red Cross spokesperson: ‘Death and destruction for Palestinians in Gaza continues every day’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:08 UTC
23:53:08 KST

Death and destruction continue to affect Palestinians in Gaza every day despite a decrease in the intensity of hostilities since last year's ceasefire, according to Pat Griffiths, a spokesperson for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
“Let’s be clear: death and destruction for Palestinians in Gaza continues every day. The suffering is real, present and here every day – even when Gaza isn’t in the headlines,” Griffiths told Anadolu.
“Life for Palestinians here is disrupted in ways that are hard to imagine. Children go without education. People go without access to specialist or chronic medical care. Families have lost homes, livelihoods – many are still missing loved ones, not knowing if they are detained or deceased," he said.
Griffiths, who is currently in Gaza City on a weeklong visit, said urgent humanitarian needs remain across the enclave, particularly for food, water, shelter and health care.
“At the ICRC, we adapt our humanitarian response to changing needs and conflict dynamics. But make no mistake: urgent humanitarian needs remain. In terms of food, water, shelter, health, family connection - so much more needs to be done,” she said.
Griffiths said humanitarian access remains one of the biggest challenges facing ICRC teams working in Gaza.
“To help people in need, we need to be able to reach them – wherever they are, including in places of detention. That’s not always possible,” he said.
She said access can be restricted because of security concerns or because those with the authority to grant access do not do so.
“Granting humanitarian access is something that is an obligation for parties to armed conflict and occupying powers. It’s also something this is outside our control as humanitarians,” he said.
“And it’s why working towards improving our humanitarian access is a continuous conversation with those who have influence over it.”
Griffiths added that the problem extends beyond reaching people to ensuring that essential supplies can enter Gaza.
“People still desperately need better access to quality and nutritious food. Hospitals and primary healthcare centres still face shortages of medicines and medical items,” he said.
“Heavy machinery and materials that could be used to safely clear rubble, search for human remains or repair broken water and wastewater systems face restrictions on entry.”
He also pointed to shortages of fuel and engine oil needed to keep generators operating.
“Everyone in Gaza faces challenges in terms of sustained access to electricity, relying on generators that are themselves reliant on enough fuel and engine oil being able to enter so they can function. And there’s not enough fuel and engine oil entering.”
According to Griffiths, shortages are also driving up prices at a time when many displaced Palestinians have lost their homes and livelihoods.
“These shortages in Gaza disrupt essential services and drive prices up. And when people are displaced and lose their homes – they also lose their livelihoods. So, cash is scarce, and people can’t afford what might be available on the market.”
“All of these things make life harder for Palestinians in Gaza right now. It’s why we continue to call for the unrestricted entry and access to those who need it of essential food, goods, medicines and other items.”
She said the ICRC continues to call for international humanitarian law to be upheld in its dialogue with Israeli authorities.
“That’s why, in our dialogue with Israeli authorities, we continue to call for international humanitarian law, which seeks to reduce the suffering of civilians in times of armed conflict, to be upheld.”
“It’s why we continue to call for the political will that is necessary to seek dialogue and sustainable solutions to improve the lives of Palestinians in Gaza. Too many lives are at stake for anything less.”
Impossible choice between tents and unsafe damaged buildings
Griffiths said thousands of Palestinians in Gaza continue to live in tents after being displaced or losing their homes, with many having been forced to move multiple times.
After three years of living in tents through extreme heat and cold, some families are returning to damaged buildings despite the risk of collapse because they have few alternatives.
She recalled the recent collapse of a damaged building in Gaza City where more than 100 people were sheltering. Many were rescued, but others, including children, were killed.
“Choosing between life in a tent … or a building that is damaged and at risk of collapse, just to have a roof over one’s head, is not a choice any family should have to make,” she said.
With winter approaching, Griffiths warned that heavy rain and winds could increase the risk of further collapses and called for heavy machinery to clear rubble and for durable shelter materials to enter Gaza.
'The desire for a normal life'
Despite the destruction and hardship, Griffiths said Palestinians in Gaza continue to express “the desire for a normal life” — to go to school, see friends, work, be with family and return home.
He acknowledged that the ceasefire in October last year reduced the intensity of hostilities and allowed more food and goods into Gaza, but said the humanitarian crisis remains severe.
“Death and destruction for Palestinians in Gaza continues every day,” he said, warning that suffering persists even when Gaza is no longer in the headlines.
Griffiths said Palestinians’ “dreams and hopes” for the future are often missing from international coverage. He also highlighted the kindness and solidarity he has witnessed among people helping their families, communities and even strangers despite years of hardship.
He said the desire for a dignified, normal life reflects the purpose of international humanitarian law: protecting civilians and reducing suffering during conflict.
A Palestinian journalist's poem about freedom
Griffiths recalled a meeting with a Palestinian journalist during a previous visit to Gaza that has remained with her.
“When I was last in Gaza, I met a Palestinian journalist who read to me a poem that he had written,” she said.
“The poem was about a bird that spread its wings and flew. After he finished reading the poem, the journalist told me that he was the bird. He told me that all he wanted to do was to experience the freedom of being able to spread his wings.”
“He was telling me that he wanted to live a life of dignity, with choice and agency.”
Griffiths said the journalist’s aspirations reflected those of many Palestinians in Gaza.
“So many people in Gaza are like him. They have dreams and hopes and fears for their future. They want to spread their wings and live, but they can’t.”

Switzerland adopts new security strategy amid Russia war, rising hybrid threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:01 UTC
23:53:01 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Switzerland's Federal Council on Friday adopted a new national security strategy aimed at preparing the country for an "increasingly unstable" international environment, citing Russia's war against Ukraine, hybrid threats and critical dependencies.
The 2026 Security Policy Strategy establishes three main priorities: strengthening the resilience of the state, economy and society; improving the protection of civilians, institutions and critical infrastructure; and bolstering Switzerland's defense capabilities.
The government said in a statement that the international security situation has become "increasingly unstable and volatile," pointing to intensifying rivalries between major powers, armed conflicts and a weakening international order.
It said there is "still no end in sight" to Russia's war against Ukraine, while cyberattacks, influence operations and other hybrid threats are increasing. Switzerland must also address domestic security risks, natural hazards and pandemics, the statement added.
The strategy contains 10 objectives and 46 measures, prioritizing efforts against what the government considers the most likely threats: hybrid and remote attacks and organized crime within Switzerland.
On defense, the Federal Council said the country must be capable of effectively countering an armed attack, including by establishing the necessary capabilities and cooperation with partner states in advance.
"In view of the current threat situation, the Federal Council had instructed the relevant departments to implement the proposed measures right from the start of the consultation process, and to plan a monitoring system for this purpose," it said.
The State Secretariat for Security Policy will coordinate the work, with the Federal Council due to receive a progress report by the end of 2028.

‘Pray for Gaza’: Is Drake cynically jumping on the bandwagon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:51:33 UTC
23:51:33 KST

Breadcrumb
‘Pray for Gaza’: Is Drake’s new song pro-Palestine, or a publicity stunt?
Canadian rapper and singer Drake, born Aubrey Drake Graham, on Tuesday made headlines again after he premiered his hour-long ‘not so short film’ FOMO, which included an unreleased song titled “Pray for Gaza”
The Genius website, which hosts one of the world’s largest collections of song lyrics and music insights, revealed the lyrics this week.
“I'm a big bad boy in the ends right now, wallah,” Drake says in one verse, using the Arabic-language word for 'by God'.
However, some of the most striking lyrics that have stirred debate are the ones that appear to mention the besieged Gaza enclave.
“Inna di worl, we ah pray for Gaza. Worl' Boss home when I pay with cards. My brand new nickname Baby Gaza. Yuh dun know di killydem crazy, baba. Yeah, Baby Gaza, your opp ma dropped, save the drama,” the lyrics say.
Shahla Omar, freelance culture journalist and The New Arab contributor, describes Drake as an "unserious artist", but doesn't believe the mention of Gaza was an intentional decision to boost his new tracks, as it was likely in the works for a long time.
She noted, however, that Drake and other artists must do more to highlight the plight of Palestinians, considering the scale of their platforms and the impact it would have.
"There are so many musicians today who model themselves on Drake. I think if he were to make more meaningful stances on issues like the genocide in Palestine, at least some of the artists that look up to him would follow suit, less afraid of the repercussions they might face," she said.
"Drake actually has a big tour coming up next year, so it will be interesting to see if he uses that stage to make a stronger expression of solidarity with Palestine than he has so far," she added.
The lyrics have also prompted conversations on social media.
“Drake is using the murder of innocent men, women, and children as a trend to score brownie points with his fanbase, and they’ve all fallen for it,” one person commented on X.
“The suffering and mass extermination of a group of people is now being used as a trendy weapon for social popularity to steer people away from being actual political participants. They would rather stream a Drake song that says “pray for Gaza” than actually do something for Gaza,” another commented.
Calls for a ceasefire
Drake signed an open letter by Artists4Ceasefire in late 2023, urging for a ceasefire after Israel launched a brutal offensive on Gaza, which has since killed over 73,000 people.
In May, Drake also released three albums, with one of them containing lyrics taking aim at music producer DJ Khaled over his silence on Israel’s war on Gaza.
At the time, the lyrics divided opinion, with some praising him for shedding light on the onslaught, while others called him hypocritical for failing to be more vocal on the atrocities taking place.
Some also accused Drake of using alleged war crimes, and what has been determined to be a genocide by leading rights groups, in a song, claiming that he has reduced it to a pop culture moment.
"Your people are still waiting for a ‘Free Palestine,’ but apparently, everything isn't black and white and red and green. I'm seeing everyone's true colours, for real," the song titled 'Make Them Pay' says.
Further questions have now arisen over the Pray For Gaza track, and whether it is indeed a further show of support for Palestinian victims of Israeli occupation, or if it is a reference to singer Vybz Kartel, who popularized "Gaza" as a nickname for Waterford, a neighbourhood in the Jamaican city of Portmore.
"I do think there is an element of bandwagoning here, but Drake is quite a consistent bandwagoner — you can hear it in his frequent switches in musical styles, or the creeping habibification of his lyrics," Omar said.
"I do agree that lyrics like these contribute to a trivialisation of the genocide, whether that trivialisation is intentional or not. We’re seeing it everywhere I think, not just in music. I think that will only get worse the longer this genocide is allowed to continue," she added.
Drake's 'Pray for Gaza' comes amid widespread music-related controversy over the past week, after rapper Macklemore revealed he was removed as a supporting act from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after his call for a “Free Palestine”.
Macklemore said pro-Israel billionaire and Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft told Sheeran he would have to choose between using his stadium and having Macklemore on stage, and that he also pressured other venues to do the same.
Sheeran has faced mounting criticism for what activists said was succumbing to pressure and prioritising money rather than taking an ethical stance on the matter.
Many fans have also dubbed the ordeal a watershed moment in terms of pop culture figures speaking out in support of Palestine.
"To declare yourself an apolitical artist, as Ed Sheeran did in response to the backlash he was facing — we’ve seen in the public roasting he’s gotten since then that such a claim about oneself as an artist simply will not fly anymore. I think there is a growing public understanding that art and politics cannot be separated from each other, and that expressions of solidarity with Palestine are penalised to an absurd extreme," Omar explained.
"I think the cumulative effect of lots of musicians making reference to Palestine and Gaza can build up into something powerful — it’s a kind of immortalisation or time capsule-ing of what the social and political conscience was in a particular moment of time. That includes lyrics and songs that are powerful and poignant, but also the borderline ridiculous," she concluded.

====================================================================================================

Feature: From digital recipes to AI menus, food gets tech touch in Poland
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:51:02 CST
23:51:02 KST

WARSAW, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Following instructions on a screen, chefs from across Poland worked through the steps of making gelato, using a digital tool to balance their recipes as they turned natural ingredients into the frozen dessert.
The demonstration at Warsaw Sweet Tech, a trade fair held from Tuesday to Thursday, brought digital precision into the craft of gelato making.
On the screen, users could fine-tune the recipe's sweetness, fat content and the gelato's firmness, while an automatic balancing function helped calculate the proportions of ingredients.
In the mind of Aleksander Pitura, co-creator of the website myGelato.eu, the goal is to give makers greater freedom to develop their own recipes using natural ingredients, without artificial coloring or flavoring.
For Pitura, the idea grew out of a practical difficulty: making gelato from scratch required knowledge that ready-made mixes did little to teach.
Following instructions on a packet could produce a dessert, he explained, but it did not necessarily help makers understand how to balance ingredients or develop a recipe of their own.
He teamed up with a friend to develop a website that would help gelato makers with those calculations, creating what he described as the first platform of its kind in Poland.
Alongside recipe balancing, the website provides step-by-step production guidance, helping users put their formulations into practice.
That flexibility also matters when recipes cross borders. Pitura said some of his Asian customers preferred less sweetness, requiring formulations to be adjusted for different tastes. His clients include users in Shanghai and Hong Kong.
Innovation in kitchen technology is also changing how food is decorated and presented.
Elsewhere at the fair, Lithuanian family business JetLt showed how a customer's photograph or design could become part of the dessert itself.
The company manufactures flatbed printers that apply edible ink directly to cakes, chocolate and other confectionery, transferring images from a computer onto the treats to give them a personal finishing touch.
The founder's son, representing the company at the fair, said the family began manufacturing the printers in 2016 and had been selling them in Poland for seven years.
At the time production began, he said, theirs was one of only three companies in Europe known to him to be making such printers.
A simple name or logo can take about 30 seconds to print, while a complicated image on a large cake may take up to two minutes, he said. The machines can also decorate several items, such as macarons, in one batch.
For confectioners, the technology offers a way to combine personalized orders with repeatable production. The cake or chocolate still has to be made; printing adds another option for how it is presented.
The family's move into food decoration itself grew out of an earlier craft. The representative recalled his father's work printing on CDs and DVDs before adapting that experience to a very different surface.
"We're always trying something new," he said.
While technology is opening up new possibilities for how food is made and presented, a restaurant's appeal also depends on what happens around the plate.
That part of the experience was the focus of Zuzana AI, a Polish venture exhibiting at the concurrent ProKitchen Expo.
Co-founder Miron Blacerzak said many restaurant QR codes in Poland simply direct diners to static PDF menus, offering little opportunity for interaction.
His team developed a platform designed to turn that familiar code into an interactive assistant. Customers would scan it to open a chat interface, ask for recommendations based on the menu, and then order and pay without installing an app.
For restaurant operators, the system is also designed to answer questions about stock levels and compare the performance of different dishes, connecting the customer-facing service with work behind the scenes.
The project had been under development for three years and was due to launch in about two weeks, Blacerzak said.
The intention, he said, is to help waiters focus on delivering food and making guests feel comfortable, including the small exchanges that can turn a visit into a relationship.
For culinary historian Bogdan Galazka, who holds a doctorate in history from Nicolaus Copernicus University in Torun, Poland, preserving tradition goes hand in hand with embracing the possibilities offered by new technology.
"Modern technology is entering the kitchen, and that is wonderful. A robot waiter can be a pleasant attraction for our guests," he said. "But we must not forget tradition, which safeguards historical and national memory." ■

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Managing economic risks from prolonged geopolitical tensions and disruptions to critical commodities, especially oil and gas products, is at the top of the government's priorities, Malaysia's Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said on Friday.
The renewed conflict in the Middle East, especially over the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, and disruptions to Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure continue to put pressure on the smooth flow of global oil exports, shipping, and energy supply, Akmal said in a televised address.
"The government's priority is to ensure that domestic supply chains continue to function, essential supplies remain sufficient, and global cost pressures do not excessively affect the people's well-being or the continuity of economic activities," he said.
"Under these circumstances, the government will continue to guarantee fuel supply through December 2026 via three approaches: diversifying import sources, optimizing domestic fuel production, and strengthening long-term supply agreements," he said.
Among the diversification measures are sourcing energy from Latin America and Africa and strengthening energy cooperation with Thailand through the signing of a new production-sharing contract and gas sales agreement for a gas field block in the Malaysia-Thailand joint development area, he said.
Akmal also said the government is expanding electricity bill relief for domestic consumers using up to 800 kilowatt-hours per month -- up from 600 kilowatt-hours previously -- to help consumers who are facing rising living costs even as the price of generating power from coal is increasing.
"We must acknowledge that global supply chain disruptions can elevate operating costs, strain businesses, and impact market confidence. However, this situation also opens avenues for us to strengthen national capacity, diversify supply sources, open new markets, and attract high-quality investments," he said. ■

====================================================================================================

Why Putin is placing Nestlé under compulsory administration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:46:22 UTC
23:46:22 KST

Why Putin is placing Nestlé under compulsory administration
Swiss multinational Nestlé is losing control of part of its business in Russia. By presidential decree, two of Nestlé’s subsidiaries have been placed under Russian compulsory administration. Russia correspondent Calum MacKenzie explains the situation.
Why is Putin doing this?
This decision follows a complaint lodged by a Russian company. The company has accused Nestlé of failing to expand its production in Russia and of not exporting anything.
These arguments sound like pretexts. They are not the sort of grounds that would normally lead to the government ordering compulsory administration.
+ Russian supermarket shelves ‘full of Nestlé products’
Past cases of such forced administration have shown that they are usually a precursor to expropriation by the Russian state. Consequently, the expropriated company is often awarded to a figure or company with close ties to the Kremlin.
It stands to reason that such a figure is behind the company’s complaint.
Who could that be?
We do not know. The Russian company that brought charges against Nestlé and demanded compulsory administration is a small firm that hardly anyone had heard of prior to this episode.
But it is worth looking at who is now running the companies that were previously expropriated. These include the Danish brewery group Carlsberg and the French food manufacturer Danone.
In Danone’s case, the company’s Russian operations are now owned by figures associated with the Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov, who is one of Putin’s most loyal governors in the non-ethnic Russian parts of the country.
It is therefore conceivable that Kadyrov was allowed to take over the Russian Danone business as a kind of reward or to keep him loyal. But the Nestlé case is somewhat different in nature.
How does the Nestlé case differ?
In the cases of Danone, Carlsberg and other expropriated firms, the owners were Western companies that wished to leave the Russian market following the start of the war of aggression against Ukraine.
Before they could do so, they were placed under compulsory administration and then expropriated. This gave Western companies in Russia the impression that they would have to expect this ‘punishment’ if they wished to leave the country.
But Nestlé had no plans to withdraw from Russia. It had complied with the regime’s rules. So the compulsory administration now comes as a surprise.
Why the escalation now?
At present, that is still difficult to assess. But a few conclusions can be drawn from the signal this action will send. Western companies still in Russia probably thought they were safe as long as they made no move to leave the country.
That no longer seems to be the case. But leaving the country is now difficult. It would contradict rules that were previously thought applicable.
There is now a situation in which the Kremlin can put Western companies under pressure at will – blackmail them, so to speak – by threatening expropriation.
The situation can be viewed in the context of the Russian economy running into difficulties this year due to the war against Ukraine. The state is therefore looking for new ways to circumvent sanctions and raise money from different sources to plug the budget deficit.

Russian Strikes Damage Zaporizhstal Steel Plant and Kyivstar Facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18

23:46:00 KST

Russian attacks damaged the Zaporizhstal steel plant in Zaporizhzhia and a Kyivstar telecommunications facility in the Kyiv region on Sept. 17, the companies reported.
One worker was injured at the steel plant. Kyivstar reported no casualties or service disruptions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zaporizhstal hit for fourth time in just over a month
Russian forces launched a ballistic missile attack against the Zaporizhstal iron and steel works at dawn on Sept. 17, marking the fourth strike on the facility in a little over a month, Metinvest reported.
Two ballistic missiles damaged production equipment, workshop buildings, utility networks and internal railway infrastructure, according to Metinvest.
Most employees had reached air-raid shelters. One worker who had not reached cover was rescued from the rubble and hospitalized with shrapnel injuries and a concussion. No deaths were reported.
Zaporizhstal halted operations on Aug. 11 following a Russian attack that killed eight workers and injured 28, destroying energy and core processing systems. Subsequent strikes hit the plant on Aug. 27 and Sept. 12, damaging blast furnace, steelmaking, and logistics facilities, as well as injuring four additional employees.
Metinvest said Russia had fired 17 ballistic missiles at Zaporizhstal since August. The group’s chief operating officer, Oleksandr Myronenko, described the repeated strikes on the idled plant as an attempt to prevent repairs and destroy Ukrainian industrial capacity.
Russia Turns Training Missiles Into Deadly Weapons in Ukraine
The plant reported a net loss of Hr. 1.06 billion ($23.7 million) in the first half of 2026, compared with a profit of Hr. 1.37 billion ($30.7 million) a year earlier. Other regional Metinvest facilities are operating at reduced capacity while specialists assess repair timelines.
Founded in 1933, Zaporizhstal is one of the largest metallurgical companies in Ukraine and is part of Rinat Akhmetov’s Metinvest Group. The plant exports steel products to more than 50 countries and has an annual production capacity of 4 million metric tons (4.4 million US tons) of pig iron, 3.6 million metric tons (4 million US tons) of hot-rolled steel and 1.2 million metric tons (1.3 million US tons) of cold-rolled steel.
Kyivstar reports damage but no service disruption
In a separate attack on Sept. 17, Russian strikes damaged a building housing telecommunications equipment belonging to Ukraine’s largest mobile operator, Kyivstar, in the Kyiv region.
Kyivstar said no employees were injured and services continued uninterrupted while technical teams assessed the damage. The strike followed a Sept. 11 drone attack on a Kyivstar office in Kyiv, which damaged engineering facilities but caused no casualties or service outages.
Ukraine’s telecom infrastructure has faced recurring attacks during the war. Kyivstar suffered its most severe disruption in December 2023 when a major Russian cyberattack temporarily cut mobile and internet access for millions of customers.
According to Kyivstar, the company serves 22.4 million mobile customers and 1.1 million fixed-line customers, providing 4G, cloud and cybersecurity services.
Kyivstar and its parent group VEON plan to invest $1 billion in Ukraine’s telecommunications infrastructure through 2027. The company says it has allocated more than Hr. 3.4 billion ($76.1 million) to defense and social projects over the past three years.

A 68-year-old Russian man swam down the Nemunas River from Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave to neighbouring Lithuania to seek asylum, only to be returned to Russia.
A 68-year-old Russian man, who travelled from the Russian Baltic sea enclave of Kaliningrad to Lithuania by river was met by border guards on the riverbank on Thursday afternoon and was sent back without being granted asylum.
“After the swim, he was provided with dry clothing,” Lithuania’s State Border Guard press service told Euronews. “More details about his journey, such as the exact distance covered, the route or how long he was in the water, cannot currently be provided.”
The man allegedly told Lithuanian authorities that he was fleeing Russia because of persecution over his activity on social media, according to the Lrytas news portal.
But after assessing the circumstances, "inconsistent" information provided by the man and “information concerning the threat posed by this person if he were to enter the EU”, Lithuanian authorities decided to return him, a spokesperson for Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service, Giedrius Mišutis, told Lrytas.
It is unusual for people to attempt to enter Lithuania from Russia by swimming across the Nemunas. Nevertheless, Lithuanian border guards continuously monitor the section of the river using technical surveillance equipment, meaning such incidents can be detected and responded to immediately, the service said.
The incident comes as the Baltic state is operating under heightened security pressure along the European Union's eastern frontier: Lithuania borders Belarus, a close Russian ally, as well as Russia’s heavily militarised Kaliningrad exclave.
The country has recorded multiple drone incursions, with the latest being one on Monday, when a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone after it entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus.
Since 2021, Vilnius has also had to contend with what the EU has described as a weaponisation of migration by Belarus and Russia, after thousands of migrants were directed towards the bloc’s eastern borders. This has prompted Lithuania to reinforce surveillance, border infrastructure and staffing along its frontier.

Hungary Says It Can Quit Russian Gas Within a Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:44:00 UTC
23:44:00 KST

Hungary could replace Russian gas with alternative supplies within a year, Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány said on Friday, Sept. 18.
The plan suggests that Budapest may be preparing to reduce Hungary’s heavy reliance on Russian energy, one of the EU’s most persistent national dependencies on Moscow.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Within a year, we will break away from Russian gas,” Kapitány said in an interview with Hungarian outlet Telex.
Kapitány said Hungary’s continued reliance on Russian gas was not caused by an absence of alternative routes. Pipelines enter the landlocked country from several directions, he said, but Russian gas had previously been the most commercially advantageous option.
If the government’s plans proceed as expected, Hungary should be able to secure sufficient gas from non-Russian sources by October 2027 – the EU’s target date for ending Russian gas imports, according to the minister.
Kapitány did not disclose how much Hungary had already reduced its dependence on Russian imports in recent months.
His comments concern Hungary’s ability to replace Russian supplies and do not necessarily mean that Budapest has made a formal decision to terminate its existing contracts with Moscow.
Alternative routes already available
Hungary, particularly under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who shared close ties with the Kremlin, has long argued that its geography and pipeline infrastructure made a rapid break from Russian energy difficult and potentially expensive.
Ukraine Says It Hit Russian Orion Drone Control Station in Crimea
However, Kapitány said the necessary infrastructure already existed and that gas could be brought into the country from several neighboring states.
Hungary’s state-owned energy company MVM has previously signed diversification agreements covering liquefied natural gas delivered through Croatia’s Krk terminal and additional supplies from Western energy companies.
MVM has a long-term contract with Russia’s Gazprom, signed in 2021, for up to 4.5 billion cubic meters of gas annually. Most Russian gas reaches Hungary through the TurkStream pipeline and its extensions across southeastern Europe.
Budapest has repeatedly opposed earlier EU efforts to accelerate the phaseout of Russian energy, warning that an abrupt transition could raise household and industrial energy costs.
Kapitány said Hungary nevertheless had sufficient gas in storage for the coming winter and was not facing an immediate physical supply problem.
Hungary discusses replacing Russian oil
The minister said Hungary also had options for ending its reliance on Russian crude oil.
Budapest has begun negotiations with Croatia over operating the Adria pipeline at full capacity, according to Kapitány. The pipeline connects Hungary with an oil terminal on Croatia’s Adriatic coast and could provide an alternative to Russian crude delivered through the Druzhba pipeline.
Hungary and neighboring Slovakia have continued receiving Russian pipeline oil under exemptions from the EU’s restrictions on Russian crude.
The capacity and commercial terms of the Adria route have repeatedly been disputed by Hungarian and Croatian officials. Replacing Russian oil would therefore require agreements on transit volumes, prices and possible infrastructure upgrades.
Kapitány’s statement marks a notable shift in Budapest’s public messaging, as the government now presents an end to Russian energy dependence as technically achievable, even though the timing and political terms remain unsettled.
The minister also said that a government review of the Russian-built Paks II nuclear power plant project should be completed by the end of 2026.

Record fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:42:08 UTC
23:42:08 KST

European governments have discussed imposing a bloc-wide windfall tax on energy companies, as near-record fuel and gas prices pile pressure on leaders desperate to contain mounting public discontent and the challenge of the far right.
With elections due next year in eight EU countries including France, Italy, Spain and Poland, leaders are scrambling to head off the potential fallout from what analysts have warned could be one of the continent’s biggest energy shocks in decades.
Germany’s finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, called on the European Commission at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday to propose possible ways to tax what he described as the excessive profits of oil companies.
“Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil said, demanding proposals by next month. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.”
Oil futures have climbed back above $100 a barrel, about 50% higher than before the Iran war, as escalating attacks across the Middle East threaten more supply routes. Derivatives markets suggest traders do not expect a near-term drop in prices.
Pump prices have already reached all-time highs across Europe. In Germany, diesel prices surged to a record average of €2.45 a litre on Wednesday, while petrol hit a fresh high of €2.31 a litre, according to Europe’s largest motoring association, ADAC.
Prices are even higher in the Netherlands, where petrol eclipsed last week’s record high to reach €2.73 a litre on Wednesday, with diesel at an average €2.78 a litre. Prices have risen higher still for petrol in Denmark and for diesel in Finland.
Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% higher than a year earlier, while diesel is up 38% and jet fuel costs more than 100% more. Benchmark gas is trading at €81 a megawatt hour, up 150% on a year earlier, with analysts suggesting it could hit €100.
The EU’s economic commissioner, Valdis Dombrovskis, has said the commission has no plans “at this stage” for an EU-wide taxing mechanism, but stressed it was “ready to engage in discussion” and member states were free to impose their own taxes.
Sky-high fuel prices are already a major domestic political issue in France and Italy, both of which next year face crunch elections in which voters’ concerns are likely to be dominated by the soaring cost of living, driven largely by high energy prices.
In Italy, Giorgia Meloni’s ruling rightwing coalition, trailing rivals in the polls, said this week it would scrap road tax for 14.5m cars and motorbikes from next year at a cost of over €2bn, on top of a cut to diesel duty that has already cost €2.8bn.
“We have chosen to redirect a portion of the resources used to address rising fuel prices into a simple, structural measure designed especially for those who use cars and motorcycles every day to work, take their children, or get around,” Meloni said.
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, told ministers he wanted the government’s “full mobilisation” on fuel supply and prices, including efforts to secure supplies internationally by working toward the “peaceful reopening” of the strait of Hormuz.
In the latest of a wave of protests, French fishers blocked access to two ports and a fuel depot in southern France on Thursday over soaring diesel prices that this week rose to €2.37 a litre, just below their record of €2.38.
The fisheries minister, Catherine Chabaud, said the fishers had agreed after six hours of talks to lift the blockades after a promise that those with cashflow issues would be granted zero-interest loans and support measures would to be tied to fuel price changes.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, this week extended emergency fuel subsidies until the end of the year for the agriculture, fishing and construction sectors. But the government is reluctant to step in to cut fuel prices for all.
“Blanket measures that affect everyone – including those who don’t need them – are a false economy,” the country’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, told journalists earlier in the week. “Why? Because ultimately, we’ll have to fund them.”
In August, Spain doubled its diesel tax discount to €0.20 a litre from 1 September after diesel prices jumped by 15.7% in July, while in Germany, the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has promised action “soon” to ease the impact of record fuel prices.
Berlin cut fuel taxes for two months in May, but that lapsed just as renewed clashes in the Middle East began further pushed up oil prices. Merz’s centre-right CDU was this month heavily defeated in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt by the far-right AfD.
Two more state elections this weekend are likely to bring further gains for the far-right party, which has campaigned on a platform of a return to the cheap Russian gas imports Europe largely abandoned after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. The demographic situation in Ukraine has passed the point of no return, Ukrainian economist Alexey Kushch believes.
"Over the past 36 years, Ukraine has lost 50% of its demographic potential. Demographic disintegration began even before the conflict. The conflict accelerated the destruction of the demographic core. Overall, the state of demographics in Ukraine can be characterized as the collapse of the population," the economist wrote on Facebook (banned in Russia; owned by Meta, which is designated as an extremist organization in Russia).
He cited statistics from previous years: "In 1983, the largest number of children were born - nearly 800,000. In 1990, about 750,000 children started going to school in what was then Ukraine. The total number of schoolchildren in the 1990/1991 academic year was 7.13 million. The total number of schools was nearly 22,000. Now, 240,000 children have entered the first grade - 60%. The number of schools has decreased to 12,000, or just under half the previous figure. In total, 3.5 million schoolchildren are currently studying in Ukrainian schools - a reduction of more than half," the expert noted.
"We are definitely past the point of no return. Such losses cannot be recovered. We can only hope for a slowdown of the population's extinction," he concluded.
Since gaining independence in 1991, Ukraine has faced serious demographic problems. According to data from the UN headquarters in Geneva as of autumn 2024, the country's population has decreased by 8 million people since February 2022. In late October 2025, Ella Libanova, Director of the Ukrainian Institute for Demography and Social Studies, reported that research conducted in 2024 showed the country’s population ranged 28 million to 30 million. The last census in Ukraine was held in 2001; at that time, the population stood at 48,457,000.

Three automated bins are being trialled at Shinjuku Station, where more than 2.7 million passengers pass through the wider complex each day. Standing just over one metre tall and moving at a cautious 20 centimetres per second, the machines can stop quickly around passengers. The trial began on 8 September and runs until 20 November on weekdays between 10:00 and 17:00 on the first basement-level paid concourse.
Run by East Japan Railway in the world's busiest rail hub, the project addresses a setting where fixed bins have been reduced for cleanliness and security, and traditional bins are emptied manually more than 10 times a day. The robots follow pre-programmed circular routes between ticket gates to collect general waste and plastic bottles, returning autonomously to a collection point when full.
Designed to assist human workers rather than replace them, Japan Railway is assessing commuter engagement and safe navigation through busy underground areas, using video and sensor data solely for analysis.
While some passengers have welcomed the concept, tourists have been drawn to the devices' large, googly eyes and train-themed livery featuring the station mascot, Shinjukuma.

Putin envoy Dmitriev, AfD prepare meeting on restarting Russian gas supplies to Germany, Reuters reports
Kremlin economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev and the leadership of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party are preparing to meet as early as March to discuss a possible resumption of Russian gas supplies to the EU country, Reuters reported on Sept. 18, citing two undisclosed sources.
The opposition AfD has emerged as Germany's largest party, running on a far-right, anti-immigration platform while calling for cutting assistance to Ukraine and resuming economic cooperation with Russia.
Dmitriev, the CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund who has mediated the U.S.-Russian rapprochement, would meet with AfD co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, a source told Reuters.
Given the AfD's opposition role, the meeting would have little effect on Germany's actual policy but would further underscore the close ties between the far-right party and Moscow.
The party has advocated lifting economic sanctions against Russia and restarting the Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines, which were built to funnel Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea.
Both pipelines were damaged by explosions in September 2022, in what German investigators say was an act of sabotage allegedly orchestrated by a group of seven suspects led by Ukrainian citizen Serhii Kuznietsov. Kyiv has denied any responsibility.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has previously ruled out a future restart of the Nord Stream pipelines.
Before the full-scale war in Ukraine and the subsequent sanctions, Germany sourced over half of its gas imports from Russia. The EU has drastically reduced Russian energy supplies since 2022 and plans to end Russian gas imports completely by next year.
The AfD and Dmitriev's representatives have declined to comment to Reuters on the meeting. Organizers allegedly hoped that U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would also attend, but a U.S. official told the news agency that the American diplomats are unaware of any such meeting.
The summit would happen only if a peace framework between Russia and Ukraine is concluded, and could take place in Israel, the United Arab Emirates, or India, Reuters reported.
