Anthropic quietly sets up biology lab as it ramps AI drug programme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:21:00 UTC
23:21:00 KST

Anthropic quietly sets up biology lab as it ramps AI drug programme
- Anthropic has established a wet biology lab to advance AI-driven drug research, focusing on rare diseases and physical experiments beyond computer simulations.
- The company integrates AI automation with human oversight to accelerate lab work safely, balancing innovation with concerns over AI risks and ethical deployment.
- Anthropic targets drug development for neglected conditions, expanding its resources and partnerships while avoiding direct clinical trials to complement the pharmaceutical industry.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic has quietly set up a laboratory to do physical biology work as it pushes its artificial-intelligence ambitions into the world of drug science.
At a time when fears of AI are gripping the public, the start-up has built a wet lab, or place for physical experiments, in the San Francisco Bay Area, two people familiar with the matter said. Anthropic has said it wants to unlock treatments for rare diseases, and its biology work has gone beyond “in silico” or computer evaluations.
In a Reuters interview on Sept 15, Anthropic’s head of life sciences, Eric Kauderer-Abrams, confirmed the start-up’s wet lab.
“We believe that to do biology, the final test is still and will be for a while in real lab work,” he said. “We absolutely are doing that today, and I would describe our approach as being typical of what you would see in most biotech companies, where there’s some amount of that that we’re doing in our own facilities and some amount of that that we’re working with external partners on.”
A spokesperson later clarified that Anthropic’s lab is not for drug discovery specifically, declining to elaborate.
The move represents a small step toward Anthropic’s enormous ambition to tackle diseases that it thinks the pharmaceutical industry is neglecting – and to do so before staff and the public lose faith that AI justifies erasing jobs and possibly human life, one of the people said. The success of any drug programme it runs is not certain; most drugs fail to pass trials for clinical safety and efficacy.
For Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, the effort is personal. A disease killed his father only a few years before a cure came about, he said in a recent essay. Kauderer-Abrams echoed the sentiment.
“The mission of the company is to develop powerful AI in such a way that benefits the world,” Kauderer-Abrams said. “By far, we see the biggest opportunity for that in the life sciences, and that is motivating everything that we’re doing.”
Balancing ambition with fears of catastrophe
Like other biotech companies, Anthropic is embracing physical automation, said the two people, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The start-up wants to push how its Claude AI can direct robotic units to carry out science experiments with limited human intervention, one of the people said. Still, Anthropic believes that human oversight and involvement are essential for safety, its spokesperson said.
“We’re in the very early innings of using AI to automate the execution of lab work,” said Kauderer-Abrams, “an area that has the potential to bring about meaningful acceleration in so many different processes.”
Anthropic’s race to apply rapidly evolving technology to a biology lab comes at an extraordinary time for the company.
In the past two weeks, some of its researchers warned that AI could lead to human extinction, and Anthropic said it found examples where its systems could have been used towards biological weapons development, which met some scepticism.
Amodei also called for a development slowdown, saying that a future AI more capable than the OpenAI agents that hacked Hugging Face could cause catastrophic damage. At the same time, Anthropic is preparing to go public in a potentially US$2 trillion (S$2.56 trillion) IPO to raise more money for such AI development.
“In our life-science work, we’re always balancing these things,” Kauderer-Abrams said, “making models better in ways that we think will uplift and accelerate developing medicines, and being thoughtful and careful about how we deploy it to limit the risk.”
Procurement ramp-up
Anthropic staked out its intention to start running drug programmes, at a San Francisco event in June. On stage there, Kauderer-Abrams said Anthropic would do pre-clinical work in areas that traditional companies did not find attractive financially.
The company also launched software called Claude Science, and it earlier added Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan to its board and bought the start-up Coefficient Bio for about US$400 million in stock, according to media reports. Anthropic confirmed the acquisition, which will help it build tools for drug development, but it had no comment on the deal price.
Now, Anthropic is bulking up its in-house lab efforts for speed and for first-hand experience in biology, though it outsources work when efficient, Kauderer-Abrams told Reuters.
“There’s some things that we can do much faster in our own hands,” he said, with the goal “to operate at the largest possible scale”.
Anthropic has looked to hire a leader who could ramp up procurement and other operations, it said in a recent LinkedIn job post. Another Anthropic role solicited via Jobera sought an expert on “protein and nucleic acid characterisation,” among other biochemical work. A third Anthropic job listing read: “Our goal is to speed up progress in the life sciences by an order of magnitude.”
Life sciences already represents one of Anthropic’s biggest investment areas by headcount and resources, Kauderer-Abrams said.
Targeting ‘undruggable’ conditions
His view is that AI could fast-track development for conditions previously thought to be “undruggable” – too difficult to treat. The technology could speed up discovery, for instance, of bispecific and trispecific antibodies, complex molecules that can be directed at multiple points on a targeted protein or cell, or hit multiple targets.
The precise diseases Anthropic is addressing and its progress remain unclear. Once a molecule is identified, it can take years to bring a drug to market as it is tested in human trials, a challenge that Anthropic has not taken on. Isomorphic Labs, the drug discovery arm of rival Alphabet, has worked for years to get to the clinic and earlier delayed that goal to the end of 2026.
In its efforts at lab and other industry automation, Anthropic launched the Model Hardware Standard in August, which helps AI operate equipment. A release out of academia called PyLabRobot, unrelated to Anthropic, earlier addressed related though different automation needs.
Anthropic is providing work like the Model Hardware Standard and broader AI services and tools to all manner of top pharmaceutical companies, such as Roche’s Genentech, Bristol Myers Squibb and Novo Nordisk.
At the same time, Anthropic is navigating a trust problem, the two people familiar with its efforts said. Its customers may worry that Anthropic will learn from their competing drug programmes, even as the AI start-up walls off their data from view.
Kauderer-Abrams said that Anthropic, due partly to competition concerns, has set a boundary that it is not running clinical trials for now and is focusing on needs that industry would not address.
“We’re not competing with pharma and biotech companies that make their business in bringing drugs to market,” he said. REUTERS

Rep. Chip Roy doesn't want to regulate AI, but says Congress should have an oversight role

Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, a GOP House hardliner and proponent of limited government, said during a Friday appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" that he feels Congress has an oversight role to play when it comes to artificial intelligence.
But that doesn't necessarily means he thinks the legislature should demand regulation of the technology.
"I don't want to regulate anything," Roy said. "I'm a free market conservative. I'm a limited government conservative."
Instead, Roy said, he'd be in favor of AI CEOs testifying at congressional hearings and explaining what they're doing to address safety concerns.
"There's a perfect role in our federal form of government, our republican form of government, for Congress to have these guys come tell us what they're doing for something that's so pervasive," Roy said.

Other leaders of major AI companies, including OpenAI's Sam Altman and xAI's Elon Musk, endorsed Amodei's sentiment.
At an event this week hosted by the Future of Life Institute, a nonprofit that advocates against large-scale technological risks, Roy joined an unlikely group of his colleagues on stage, including progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, and former White House strategist Steve Bannon.
While there is bipartisan concern at the pace with which AI is developing, there's little consensus on how the federal government should respond. The House left Washington on Wednesday without having taken any major action to address AI safety. The Senate will remain in session for another two weeks, before its members head back to their districts for a pre-election recess.
President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., have both argued the U.S. could lose the AI race to China if it slows its development. Trump went further, calling potential AI threats a "hoax" and opposing regulation. Meanwhile, progressives like Sanders have argued for stricter guardrails and a ban on AI "superintelligence."
Roy, at the Future of Life Institute conference, pushed back on an assertion from Trump that the president should be the lone person making decisions on AI. But he also diverged with his Democratic colleagues and, in his Friday appearance on CNBC, said he wasn't an AI "doomer."
"We have a responsibility to protect our communities and our lives. I want competition and free enterprise to rule the day. I don't want crony capitalism, crony government interference," Roy said.

In the Ternopil region, a young boy has died; his mother and family doctor have been served with notices of suspicion

In the Ternopil region, a young boy has died; his mother and family doctor have been served with notices of suspicion
Kyiv • UNN
The boy died after a prolonged lack of medical supervision. The mother and family doctor were served with notices of suspicion.
In the Ternopil region, a young boy died due to a lack of proper medical supervision; his mother and family doctor have been notified of suspicion, UNN reports, citing the Prosecutor General’s Office.
In the Ternopil region, the mother and family doctor have been notified of suspicion in criminal proceedings concerning the death of a young boy who, according to the investigation, had been without proper medical supervision for a prolonged period
Details
According to the prosecutor’s office, the child was born at the end of May 2021. From July 2021 to March 2023, the mother did not seek the necessary medical assistance or bring her son for preventive examinations, despite existing health problems.
The mother entered into a declaration with a family doctor regarding the child’s medical care. At the same time, according to the investigation, the doctor never personally examined the boy. He entered information into the medical records remotely, based only on the parents’ statements during telephone conversations.
Due to the lack of proper medical supervision, the child’s genetic pathology was not diagnosed in a timely manner.
The boy subsequently died. According to the findings of the investigation, timely detection of the disease, proper treatment, and medical supervision could have prevented his death.
The head of the Kremenets District Prosecutor’s Office notified the 46-year-old mother of suspicion of the malicious failure to fulfill statutory duties regarding childcare, which caused grave consequences (Article 166 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
The family doctor was notified of suspicion of improper performance of professional duties due to a negligent attitude toward them, which caused grave consequences for a minor (Part 2 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).

Surge in fuel prices
The sharp rise in fuel prices was an other issue raised by Emmanuel Macron during the meeting at the Élysée.
According to the president's inner circle, public opinion tends to forget that the international situation is the root cause of the crisis. Emmanuel Macron aimed to remind the candidates for the 2027 presidential election of this.
The rise in prices is "not the result of government decisions", he said.
The blockages in the Strait of Hormuz, in the Gulf, and more recently in the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, in the Red Sea, "have direct consequences for our daily lives", Emmanuel Macron wrote on the social media platform, X.
The French president is calling for the causes of rising petrol prices to be addressed "before spending large sums of money" which he warned would mean "either a bigger deficit or higher taxes".
Macron announced his intention to convene a G7 meeting devoted to energy issues. The meeting, he says, should be held in the coming weeks and will aim in particular to "move towards better coordination on stock levels".

Thousands of migrants surge through Ceuta as Spain moves them to new tent camp | Watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:17:22 UTC
23:17:22 KST

Thousands of migrants surged through the streets of Ceuta on Friday as Spanish authorities began moving people who had been sleeping on beaches and in public spaces to a new temporary camp at the port of the Spanish enclave in North Africa.
Video from the operation showed large groups running through the streets, cheering and shouting as police attempted to manage the transfer. Spanish media reported tense moments as crowds pressed toward the new facility, while Euronews reported that officers fired warning shots into the air as they struggled to control the movement of people.
The operation began early Friday morning and involved hundreds of police and security personnel. The new port facility has space for about 1,700 people and provides tents, beds, showers, toilets and food. EFE reported that more than 3,000 migrants were moved from the Benítez and Trampolín beaches during the operation, meaning the camp cannot accommodate everyone still in the city.
A city still reeling from the July crossing
The latest scenes come more than six weeks after an unprecedented mass crossing from Morocco into Ceuta on July 30 and 31. Spanish authorities say more than 72,000 people entered the enclave during those two days, a number approaching Ceuta’s own population.
Most have since left or been returned, but thousands remain. Ceuta’s local government estimated earlier this week that at least 13,000 migrants were still in the city, while Spain’s central government said Friday that security forces now put the figure at between 9,000 and 10,000.
Many had been sleeping on beaches or in makeshift encampments while Madrid and the local authorities argued over how to house them. The central government moved ahead with the port facility despite political tensions over the response to the crisis.
Pressure mounts on Sánchez
The crisis has become a major political challenge for Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, with protests in Ceuta and elsewhere in Spain accusing his government of mishandling the influx and allowing the enclave’s security and public services to become overwhelmed.
Sánchez has rejected accusations that his government ignored the danger, while acknowledging that authorities did not anticipate the scale of the influx. Declassified documents released this month showed, however, that Spain’s National Intelligence Center, or CNI, warned the government delegation in Ceuta and Moroccan intelligence on July 29 about organized calls on social media for people to enter the enclave by sea and over the border fence the following day.
The documents included messages referring to social media groups with large followings that were openly discussing attempts to cross into Ceuta during Morocco’s Throne Day celebrations. Sánchez has argued that while authorities had indications of possible attempts, they were not warned that an influx on such an extraordinary scale was imminent.
Sánchez has also accused networks linked to Russia and Israel, along with what he called an international far-right movement, of spreading and amplifying disinformation surrounding the Ceuta crisis. He cited research by the European Union’s foreign policy service, though he did not publicly provide detailed evidence tying the campaigns directly to either government. Israel and Russia have denied involvement.
The dispute comes as questions over Ceuta’s future have again surfaced in relations between Spain and Morocco. Sánchez told parliament this month that Ceuta and the nearby enclave of Melilla “have been Spanish for centuries” and said Madrid’s commitment to Spanish sovereignty over both cities remained absolute.
For Ceuta, however, the immediate problem remains much more practical: thousands of migrants are still in the small enclave, the new port camp has only a fraction of the beds required, and Madrid has acknowledged that additional accommodation will have to be found.

The world's 20 best airlines for 2026 have been announced – with only six in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:16:45 UTC
23:16:45 KST

There were wins for Air France, Turkish Airlines and Vueling in individual categories, but Europe struggled to match the haul of awards picked up by carriers from Asia and the Middle East
European airlines have been largely pushed down the pecking order in this year’s World Airline Awards, with Asian and Middle Eastern carriers dominating the top 10.
Singapore Airlines took the overall title, followed by Qatar Airways and Cathay Pacific, while Turkish Airlines was the highest-ranked European carrier in fifth place.
Just six European airlines made the top 20, with Air France, Lufthansa, Iberia, Virgin Atlantic and Swiss International Air Lines joining Turkish Airlines.
The 2026 World Airline Awards were announced at a gala ceremony in London hosted by air transport rating organisation Skytrax.
Known as “the Oscars of the aviation industry”, the awards have been running since 1999 and, according to Skytrax’s CEO Edward Plaisted, “highlights the level of product and service excellence they are providing to customers”.
More than 300 airlines were assessed in the ranking and, although Europe’s operators didn’t blow the competition away in the main category, they did have a decent showing in others.
European airlines triumph in some categories – and fall down in others
Air France did particularly well, scooping awards for the world’s best first class, the world’s best first class lounge dining, and the world’s best first class comfort amenities, as well as being given the nod as the best airline in Western Europe.
Spanish-headquartered Vueling won the award for the best low-cost airline in Europe, a category which also saw the inclusion of Germany’s Eurowings, Spain’s Iberia Express and Volotea and Dutch Transavia.
Meanwhile, Turkish Airlines took a trio of awards, scooping gongs for the best airline in Europe, the world’s best business class catering and the best airline in Southern Europe.
“Being recognised as ‘Europe’s best airline’ for the 11th time and ranking first in two other categories is a great source of pride for us as the Turkish Airlines family,” Murat Şeker, Turkish Airlines chairman of the board, said.
In other categories, Iberia won the award for the best airline staff service in Europe, while LOT Polish Airlines received the award as the best airline in Central Europe.
All European airlines were absent from the world’s best cabin crew category, which was topped by Cathay Pacific Airways, and only Greece’s Aegean Airlines made the top 10 of the world’s best regional airlines category, coming in fourth place.
Qatar Airways loses its top spot
In the overall ranking, Qatar Airways, a nine-time winner of the world’s best airline title, dropped to second spot behind Singapore Airlines.
Nevertheless, the Doha-based operator did manage to scoop four top awards, including the world’s best business class airline – the 13th time the airline has received this accolade – and the best airline in the Middle East.
It also received the first-ever award for the World’s Best Onboard Wi-Fi. That category was introduced this year to recognise the importance of fast and free onboard connectivity for many modern travellers.

Transport Administration to install thermal cameras to count road users
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Transport Administration to install thermal cameras to count road users
The Transport Administration is installing thermal cameras along major highways to collect data on when, at what speed, and what types of vehicles are traveling there.
The agency plans to procure counting devices that will help determine traffic volumes on different road sections. It estimates that designing, purchasing, and installing the equipment will cost around €740,000.
Pedestrians and cyclists will also be counted, but the agency stresses that all data will be anonymous and the devices will not take photos or record license plates.
Arno‑Marko Miller, a traffic‑monitoring equipment expert at the Transport Administration, told ERR that for vehicles, the system will collect data on date, time, speed, vehicle length, direction of travel, vehicle class, headway, and lane detection.
"For pedestrians and cyclists, the system will collect data on date, time, speed, direction, and user type," he added.
All data must be anonymous
Vehicles will be divided into three classes: passenger cars and vans, trucks and buses, and trucks with trailers.
"All data must be anonymous — the devices will not take photos, record video, or capture license plates," Miller emphasized.
In the first phase, 15 thermal cameras will be installed on the Tallinn–Narva highway, 18 on the Tallinn–Tartu–Võru–Luhamaa highway, 12 on the Jõhvi–Tartu–Valga road, and ten on the Tallinn–Pärnu–Ikla road. Additional units will be placed on the Riia roundabout connector road, the Mõigu connector road, and several other sections.
In the second phase, installations will include 15 devices on the Pärnu–Rakvere–Sõmeru road, ten on the Tallinn ring road, six on the Tallinn–Paldiski road, and five on the Ääsmäe–Haapsalu–Rohuküla road. Cameras will be mounted on metal poles or frames.
The collected data will be used in analyses and annual traffic‑count reports, which support road design, construction, maintenance, traffic‑safety planning, budget allocation, and the development of guidelines and documentation.
Procurement requirements specify that the devices must include integrated AI‑based detection and classification capabilities with updatable models. They may not connect outside the Transport Administration's private network, and they must not store images.
Cyclist traffic has never been counted this way before
Mobility expert Kadi Pihlak said that the permanent counting system will, for the first time, provide long‑term, standardized data on pedestrian and cyclist volumes and how they change over time.
"Pedestrian and cyclist movements along state roads have never been counted with thermal cameras before," Pihlak noted.
The data will help assess seasonality, trends in walking and cycling, and the impact of traffic‑management measures, new infrastructure, improved winter maintenance, and the opening or closing of destinations. It will also help prioritize which pedestrian and cycling paths should be maintained or repaired first.
"Creating a counting system is an important step toward better understanding walking and cycling and making data‑driven decisions in infrastructure development and mobility policy. It also supports the implementation of Estonia's cycling strategy," Pihlak said.
Vehicle‑counting devices will be installed on international road sections, while pedestrian and cyclist counting points will be placed along state roads across Estonia, in both urban fringe and rural areas.
The densest concentration of counting points will be near Tallinn and Tartu — urban nodes in the TEN‑T transport network — where pedestrian and cyclist data play a key role in developing mandatory sustainable urban mobility plans.
According to Miller, the Transport Administration has previously counted road users at both permanent and temporary locations, but the new system uses different technology.

Red Cross says no access to Ukrainian POWs in two years
GENEVA, Sept 18 - The International Committee of the Red Cross has been denied access to Ukrainian prisoners of war held in Russian detention for two years, it told Reuters on Friday.
Thousands of Ukrainian prisoners of war are believed to be held in Russian detention centres where UN investigators have gathered evidence of systematic torture.
The 1949 Geneva Conventions, intended to limit the barbarity of war, provide for Swiss-based ICRC to visit prisoners of war to monitor their conditions, treatment, food and medical care.
Russia denies torture or other forms of maltreatment of POWs. The Russian diplomatic mission in Geneva did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"We can confirm the lack of access to POWs in Russia since 2024," an ICRC spokesperson said, adding that ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric raised the issue on a trip to Russia last month.
"If you want to uphold humanity, you have to talk about detention and what happens in prison," Spoljaric told the BBC earlier on Friday. REUTERS

Ukraine’s Inflation Reaches 8.1% as Fuel and Water Costs Rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:13:07 UTC
23:13:07 KST

Ukraine’s annual consumer inflation reached 8.1% in August, matching core inflation, as rising fuel and water costs offset a seasonal decline in food prices.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile prices and certain regulated prices, also remained above the National Bank of Ukraine’s (NBU) 5% target.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Fruit and vegetable prices fell sharply as the new harvest reached markets. Fuel and transport costs continued to rise, while higher tariffs pushed up water and sewerage bills.
The war in the Middle East has increased fuel and logistics costs, while labor shortages have added to pressure on service prices. Russian strikes on Ukrainian businesses are also raising repair and distribution costs.
Damage to civilian logistics and retail facilities could add 0.4–0.6 percentage points to annual inflation by the end of 2026, NBU Deputy Governor Volodymyr Lepushynskyi previously stated. The central bank expects most of that impact to emerge in the autumn.
The State Statistics Service published its latest report on Sept. 9.
Fuel prices rose 38.7% year-on-year in August, compared with 28% in July and 33% in June. Transport services cost 35.9% more than a year earlier, up from 28.9% in July. Road passenger transport prices rose 39.1% annually, while rail passenger fares increased 16%.
Water supply tariffs rose 16.8% in August and sewerage tariffs increased 16.7%, extending a run of double-digit monthly increases that began in June. Compared with a year earlier, water tariffs were up 77.6% and sewerage tariffs 73.6%.
Putin Transfers Russian Assets of Auchan, Nestlé to External Manager
                                                                                                                                                                         
Ukraine’s headline and core inflation both stood at 8.1% in August 2026, above the National Bank of Ukraine’s 5% target.
Food prices fall as harvest reaches markets
Food and nonalcoholic beverage prices fell 1.3% in August, their steepest monthly decline this year. Annual food inflation eased to 6% from 6.5% in July.
Vegetable prices fell 18.3% in August, while fruit prices dropped 12%. “This dynamic was primarily driven by a slowdown in the increase in vegetable prices for the borshch basket thanks to the new harvest,” the NBU wrote in its August 2026 Inflation Update.
Egg prices rose 4% in August but remained 24.1% lower than a year earlier. Sugar prices increased 2.2% during the month. Meat and meat products rose 0.9%, reversing July’s 0.6% decline. The NBU also pointed to increased investment in poultry farming, which had expanded the supply of chicken.
Fish and fish products rose 1.6% in August and 22.7% year-on-year, the largest annual increase among the food categories listed. Bread and pasta prices each rose 0.7% during the month, while butter fell 0.6%.
Utilities and services remain more expensive
Housing and utility costs rose 1.3% in August. Garbage collection fees increased 2.1% during the month and 18.5% year-on-year. Electricity, natural gas, hot water and heating tariffs remained unchanged, as they have throughout 2026.
Alcohol and tobacco prices rose 1.5% in August, matching July’s pace, while tobacco products alone increased 2.1%. Annual inflation for the combined category accelerated to 17% from 16.2% in July.
Annual service-price inflation slowed to 13.4%, according to the NBU. Price increases eased for mobile communications, health insurance and financial services.
Taxi and moving services became more expensive amid high fuel prices. Price increases also accelerated for housing rentals, cafes, hotels and boarding houses, dental and veterinary services, shoe repairs and dry cleaning, the central bank said.
Healthcare costs rose 0.7% in August, household goods and appliances increased 0.6%, and restaurant and hotel prices rose 1%. Recreation and culture prices were unchanged. Education costs increased 0.2% during the month and 14.6% year-on-year.
Lepushynskyi previously warned that inflation could remain above the NBU’s 5% target for an extended period.

A bitter inquest is under way among Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces as to how what was being billed as a decisive assault on Sana’a, the Houthi-controlled capital, suddenly collapsed into a military rout.
More than 15 brigades were defeated as the country’s entire west coast fell into Houthi hands. Efforts are now being made to reorganise the anti-Houthi forces representing the UN-recognised Yemeni government in order to capture the Kahbob mountains, a strategic point from which to restrict Houthi forces moving closer to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.
Some Yemeni politicians are claiming that billions of dollars were offered to persuade the forces defending the west coast to abandon their position. It is thought as many as 30,000 well-equipped fighters retreated, raising questions about coordination, readiness and morale.
The claim made by the governor of Hadramaut, one of Yemen’s largest governorates, did not identify the source of the payment, but others have tried to draw conclusions from the past links between the United Arab Emirates and the pro-government National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh. The UAE left Yemen in January, but remains bitter at the role played by Saudi Arabia in forcing it out and in the outlawing of the separatist Southern Transitional Council.
The Yemeni Nobel peace prize winner Tawakkol Karman has called for an investigation, while another political activist, the Mocha resident Abdu Mukabib, described the withdrawal of forces from the now Houthi-held port city in the early hours of 10 September as a great betrayal.
Saleh’s National Resistance Forces have said they made a necessary tactical retreat.
Hours before, the Houthis had captured the headquarters of the National Resistance Forces operating along Yemen’s western coast, situated on the high ground of Jabal al-Nar (Fire Mountain) and supposed to contain six military brigades and sophisticated weaponry provided by Saudi Arabia.
Mukabib said on his Facebook page that by the time the Houthis entered the city at 6am their forces numbered less than 20: two military vehicles, each carrying five people, and four motorcycles, each carrying two people.
He said that what happened, in his words, caused “humiliation” and betrayal to those who trusted the forces they fought alongside. “We are not accusing anyone, but they all participated in betraying us, conspiring against us, selling out our cause and abandoning us.
“It was not a withdrawal from weakness or lack of equipment and supplies, but rather a cowardly and shameful withdrawal.”
The National Resistance Forces said they had withdrawn after the death of 500 of their soldiers and to prevent encirclement. Saleh has said he is now forming the “Tihami Resistance”, a group that was entirely independent of Yemen national forces.
Others point to explanations for the reverse including poor command and control communications that led to slow decision-making, high-level Houthi intelligence and divisions within the anti-Houthi military forces, including the influence of Saudi commanders.
Alongside the inadequacies of the UN-backed forces, the Houthis have become an increasingly sophisticated army, bolstered by Iranian intelligence. They have benefited from the cut-price nature of modern warfare, using cheap drones to harass maritime traffic. But more than 10 years in control of many of Yemen’s key regions and the occasional payoff from Saudi Arabia have swelled their coffers enough to not only buy ballistic missiles, but develop their own indigenous weapon-making infrastructure, becoming less reliant on Iran in the process.
Iranian officials insist the Houthis are not a simple proxy force, but have their own unified command structure and set of priorities.
The inquest into what is widely regarded as a military catastrophe is not entirely retrospective. Both Yemen government and Saudi forces are urgently reviewing the lessons of defeat to better understand whether the Houthi gains can still be reversed.
It was claimed that a limited force from the Giants Brigades, a group once linked with the UAE-backed southern separatists, managed to repel the Houthi advance and recapture positions in the days before the fall of Mocha, which could have served as a springboard for regaining the initiative. However, the withdrawal of neighbouring National Resistance units weakened this advance and turned it into a series of retreats.
Prof Dr Abdulwahab al-Awaj at Taiz University in Yemen said: “The collapse of the western coastal fronts is not merely a conventional military defeat, but a warning sign of a breakdown in coordination and trust among the anti-Houthi forces. The Houthis exploited this breakdown more than any decisive military superiority.
“Regaining the initiative cannot be achieved simply by sending reinforcements. What is needed is a reorganisation of government forces and allied formations under a unified operational vision, addressing security gaps, and building genuine trust on the ground to prevent a recurrence of this scenario.”

20 municipalities around Brussels granted social housing exemption

23:11:33 KST

Twenty municipalities in the Flemish periphery around Brussels are to be granted a partial exemption for the construction of social housing. The mayors do not consider this to be their responsibility, as more and more people are moving from Brussels to the periphery.
20 municipalities around Brussels granted social housing exemption
The exemption has been granted by the Flemish Housing Minister, Melissa Depraetere of Vooruit. Municipalities that have built too little social housing in the past are being encouraged to clear their backlog. This is not possible for every municipality, partly due to spatial constraints.
“This is in the interests of vulnerable residents in their municipalities, who have often been on the waiting list for a long time,” Depraetere said. “At the same time, we are taking spatial realities into account. Municipalities that show they are making considerable efforts but lack sufficient space will be granted greater flexibility, without a single social housing unit being lost.”
This means we still have to build 496 social housing units. That is absolutely unrealistic
As a result, 20 municipalities including Drogenbos, Grimbergen, Halle, Kraainem, Overijse, Sint-Genesius-Rode, Sint-Pieters-Leeuw, Wemmel and Zaventem will be granted a full or partial exemption from the obligation to build social housing.
Halle is being granted a 75% exemption, but according to mayor Eva Demesmaeker of N-VA, this offers no added value.
“This means we still have to build 496 social housing units,” she said. “That is absolutely unrealistic. Our city’s future population growth is a major factor; for us, 80% of this growth consists of people from Brussels and abroad. That is why we will have to build so many social housing units in the future.”
As Halle and other cities and municipalities disagree with the decree, they are taking the matter to the Constitutional Court and the Council of State.
“On the one hand, there is the limited space we have here and the difficulties we face,” says Demesmaeker. “On top of that, there is also the issue of fines, whereby a city is fined, while ultimately it is the housing associations that are responsible for providing social housing. So there are a lot of issues at play here, but we will certainly not leave it at that.”

Cardiff pact: Is the UK heading for disintegration?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:10:52 UTC
23:10:52 KST

The heads of government from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland signed a document in the Welsh city of Cardiff early this week, declaring that the era of Westminster, the official seat of government for the United Kingdom, is “coming to an end”.
The declaration has sent shockwaves around the world, as the three countries, together with England, constitute the once-mighty British Empire, which stretched across all continents except Antarctica.
The first ministers of the three countries of the UK signed the document as “representatives of their parties” instead of heads of their respective governments, asserting that the three nations have the “right to self-determination”.
The declaration called on the British government to “prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change”, while recognising that each nation would proceed “in its own way and in its own time”.
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are all led by politicians committed to leaving the UK: John Swinney of the Scottish National Party (SNP), Rhun ap Iorwerth of the Welsh party Plaid Cymru, and Michelle O’Neill of the Sinn Fein’s party in Northern Ireland.
Experts say the declaration may not lead to a constitutional rupture within the UK, but they agree the optics are deliberate.
Laura McAllister, professor of public policy at Cardiff University’s Wales Governance Centre, tells TRT World that the September 14 meeting is “significant” for a number of reasons.
“It reflects the fact that there are now first ministers in each of the countries, all campaigning for greater autonomy and ultimately for independence,” she says.
“I think the wording around self-determination is important,” she says, adding that the asymmetry in terms of constitutional objectives is “quite different” in Scotland, Wales, and in Irish reunification.
Northern Ireland is part of the UK, while the Republic of Ireland is an independent country and EU member controlling five-sixths of the island.
An Irish reunification would end the partition, which has existed since 1921.
Disintegration: a low-probability outcome?
McAllister says the Plaid Cymru party of Wales won office in May after campaigning with a “heavy emphasis on avoiding the issue of independence this term,” following what she calls the SNP’s playbook for governing credibly first.
She also points out a bigger shift in the self-determination debate in the UK.
“This is the first time that the nations of the UK are attempting to drive the constitutional question rather than the centre,” she says.
But the anomaly is that England is not in the room.
“There would need to be England involved anyway because it would be the leftover part of the UK,” she adds.
James Mitchell, professor of public policy at the University of Edinburgh in Scotland, is far more dismissive of the Cardiff Agreement.
“(It) was little more than a photo-opportunity,” he tells TRT World.
Having nationalist first ministers in the three countries simultaneously is “novel”, but it does not alter the constitution, he says.
“None has been able to explain how this agreement will make any difference,” he says.
He doubts the public has even registered the supposedly important agreement.
“It is highly doubtful that many people in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland have taken much notice of this memorandum. The likelihood is that it will be forgotten about,” he says.
He describes the pact as “just another of numerous claims” that the UK's break-up is imminent.
He insists even some SNP supporters and advocates of Irish unity have been critical.
“Few in Wales are likely to take the prospect of Welsh independence as at all likely any time soon, if at all,” he says.
Timothy Ash, an associate fellow at Chatham House, tells TRT World that the probability of the UK’s disintegration is “low”.
He says the episode is “political theatre” set off by people in the US who “probably want to change the news cycle” from the months-old Iran war.
During a recent visit to Ireland, US President Donald Trump had said he would “love” to see Northern Ireland and the Republic unified and that “it may as well happen now”.
Ash cites opinion polls in Scotland showing no majority support for independence after the last referendum failed.
“The SNP government has struggled, and that has detracted from support for independence,” Ash says.
What would a UK breakup mean for England?
Northern Ireland is the most legally distinct case within the UK, analysts say.
Alan Whysall, a veteran of the Northern Ireland peace process now working at University College London’s Constitution Unit, tells TRT World that the issue is not independence, which nobody is seeking.
“It is whether Northern Ireland remains part of the UK, or joins a united Ireland,” he says.
The 1998 Belfast Agreement governs that question.
The British and Irish governments accepted at the time that it is a matter of consent “in each part of the island of Ireland, without external impediment”.
“Few people seriously suggest that there is at present a majority for unity in Northern Ireland. Neither opinion polls nor election results give any ground for suggesting that,” he says.
But a significant number of people think “it is coming soon”, he adds.
What a smaller UK would mean for England is a question that is less theatrical and more structural, analysts say.
England is the most populous of the UK's four constituent countries, with over 56 million people. Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland trail way behind with 5.5 million, 3.1 million, and 1.9 million people, respectively.
Ash calls the effect of disintegration “clearly negative,” even though he insists that the UK can “cope with the loss of Northern Ireland”.
Mitchell says much would depend on the inevitable successor agreements. The break-up of the political union between the four constituent countries would “diminish the status of what would be left of the UK”.
However, a breakup would also mean that England would no longer have to subsidise these other parts of the UK, he says.
The European dimension of the self-determination drive in the three countries is also complicated.
The text of the Cardiff agreement says that the future of the three nations “belongs in the European Union”.
Mitchell warns that Scotland and Wales would not meet the EU's eligibility criteria for membership.
That’s probably because of the EU’s benchmarks, such as an independent central bank, standalone regulatory bodies, and effective budgetary controls.
If England remained outside of the EU, both Scotland and Wales would suffer because England is by far their major trading partner, he says.
The case of Northern Ireland would be different, though, as it would be joining the Republic of Ireland, an existing EU member, he notes.
Ash says UK-wide polls show 60-40 support for rejoining Europe.
“But the Labour government seems reluctant to re-open the issue as it has been very divisive,” he says.

US attempts to militarize Moon threaten humanity — Chinese newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:10:13 UTC
23:10:13 KST

BEIJING, September 18. /TASS/. The US government’s attempts to militarize near-lunar space threaten the security of all countries, the Chinese newspaper Global Times writes.
"By explicitly bringing the lunar vicinity into its battlefield conceptualization, coupled with Washington's public acknowledgment that it has deployed on-orbit space weapons, senior US military officials are sending a highly aggressive and dangerous signal," the publication’s editorial states. "The old script of bloc-confrontation on Earth is now being played out on the Moon," it emphasizes.
The authors note that the US established the Space Force in 2019 and, in 2025, unveiled the Golden Dome space-based missile defense program. "As a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the US should uphold its spirit: Celestial objects such as the moon are to be used ‘exclusively for peaceful purposes,’ nuclear weapons cannot be placed in space and countries are ‘liable for damage caused by their space objects,’" the article says.
"Yet Washington has taken the lead in setting up an independent Space Force, publicly acknowledged the deployment of offensive space weapons, and continuously extended its operational concepts toward lunar orbit," the newspaper writes. "Such repeated crossing of regulatory red lines seriously undermines outer-space governance," it says.
The publication points out that Washington "seeks to justify such military buildup by pointing fingers at other countries: ‘maintaining unmatched space superiority is a top military priority, as adversaries such as China and Russia make massive investments in space weapons and other capabilities that can threaten American satellites.’" "Such logic of proactively stoking confrontation poses grave dangers for global security," the authors note.
Threat to humanity
The newspaper cites the opinion of an unnamed expert who believes that US officials are deliberately exaggerating external threats in order to increase defense spending. "Driven by dual strategic calculations both domestically and internationally, the US is seeking unrestrained space hegemony," the article emphasizes. "As it continues to expand its Space Force, Washington is planning to deploy various new weapons systems in space, aiming to transform the realm of deep-space exploration into a frontline of military rivalry among major powers; America's military adventurism is bound to fuel a global space arms race."
"Once the Earth-Moon space becomes a theater of confrontation, no country's space assets will be able to remain unscathed. Once the fuse of an arms race is lit, the destruction brought about by the risk of war will be borne by the entire world," the authors warn.
The article emphasizes that humanity's journey into space is driven by scientific progress. "It should not be reduced to a powder keg for great-power rivalry. The US is mired in numerous governance challenges," the article says. "Instead of working to resolve its own problems, it is inciting an arms race, going so far as to push the Earth-Moon space toward militarization. Such hysterical hegemonic impulses are spreading the risk of instability across the globe."
The authors note that, in the interests of all humanity, the US must "stop fueling fantasies of space warfare and return to the path of peaceful exploration in outer space." "Space is not the private property of any single country, and lunar orbit certainly should not become the next battlefield," they emphasize.
Earlier, General Dan Caine, Chairman of the US Joint Chiefs of Staff, stated that American troops need to prepare for combat not only in Earth's orbit but around the Moon.

Indian court grants bail to US national in terror training case – report

Indian court grants bail to US national in terror training case – report
A US national arrested along with six Ukrainians by India’s anti-terror agency for allegedly providing terror training to armed groups in neighboring Myanmar, was granted bail by a Delhi court on Friday.
The court granted the bail after the National Investigation Agency (NIA), which arrested them in March, failed to file a chargesheet on the terror charges within the mandatory 180-day period. The judge said that the agency’s chargesheet, which contained only sections relating to immigration, was a “piecemeal” job, according to the Bar and Bench website which reports on court proceedings.
That the agency is still investigating the offenses under the more stringent Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, or UAPA, does not mean that VanDyke is not entitled to default bail, Special NIA Judge Prashant Sharma said.
He added that all the other co-accused persons in the case are also entitled to default bail, if they apply for it.
VanDyke is the founder of Sons of Liberty International, which provides military training in conflict zones. He has reportedly been involved in conflicts in the past, including fighting with Libyan rebels in 2011.
The Ukrainians arrested with VanDyke are Viktor Kaminskyi, Petro Hurba, Taras Slyviak, Ivan Sukmanovskyi, Marian Stefankiv, and Maksim Honcharuk. The NIA had accused them of entering the restricted areas in India’s northeast without permits, and crossing over to Myanmar to impart terror training to ethnic groups there.
The agency had previously told the court it had found evidence that multiple consignments of drones from Europe were delivered by the accused to individuals and groups in the northeastern Indian state of Mizoram, and that they were involved in a drone strike on a Burmese civilian plane.
The seven were arrested from different cities while trying to fly out of India.
The court said that while on bail, VanDyke must stay in Delhi and appear before the NIA whenever required. He will be released on a personal bond of about $1,000 and a surety of the same amount.

Fact check: Zelensky's former press secretary says she speaks for Ukrainians. Her claims tell a different story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:09:35 UTC
23:09:35 KST

Fact check: Zelensky's former press secretary says she speaks for Ukrainians. Her claims tell a different story
Then-Press Secretary of the President Iuliia Mendel during a briefing at the Presidential Administration in Kyiv, Ukraine, on June 6, 2019. (Sergii Kharchenko / NurPhoto via Getty Images)
A Zelensky aide-turned-critic, Iuliia Mendel argues that the Kyiv leadership and its Western allies stand in the way of peace — and that she is the genuine Ukrainian voice to cut through the lies.
Since her controversial appearance on U.S. podcaster Tucker Carlson's show in May, Zelensky's former press secretary has been increasingly accused of echoing Kremlin narratives, dressed up as a persecuted call for peace.
She sought another chance to deliver her message to international audiences on Sept. 16, when she was set to speak at the European Parliament in Strasbourg at an event organized by the far-right Kremlin-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
The appearance was scheduled a few days after Zelensky imposed sanctions on Mendel. And things didn't go as planned for his former press secretary.
The European Parliament barred her from entering "without explanation," Mendel said. This didn't stop Zelensky's former ally from delivering her scathing indictment of her former boss in a video address instead.
Mendel has repeatedly rejected being "pro-Russian." Yet her address contains manipulations that distort the role of Russia, Ukraine, and the West in negotiations, and diminish Kyiv's efforts to end the war.
And while some of her criticism of Zelensky's governing style is rooted in legitimate grievances, it is also wrapped in distortion, hyperbole, and half-truths.
Who's the obstacle to peace?
While acknowledging Russia's role in starting the war, Mendel names two other culprits preventing peace — the West, with its ongoing military support, and, most importantly, Zelensky himself.
Casting herself as an insider — even though she left her position at Zelensky's side in 2021, before the full-scale war even started — Mendel vaguely alludes to behind-the-scenes "agreements" during peace talks that were allegedly rejected by the president.
Instead, Zelensky "promotes the most maximalist and unachievable way for victory as the only way to peace," Mendel alleged.
This account starkly differs from how the actual peace talks unfolded.
Zelensky acknowledged shortly after Trump's re-election in November 2024 that a cessation of hostilities might leave some territories temporarily under Russian control.
This stance further took shape during the U.S.-led peace talks when Ukraine called for a full, unconditional ceasefire along the current front lines as a precondition for further negotiations.
While Kyiv continues to maintain this position, Russia has repeatedly brushed it off, instead demanding that Ukraine cede Donbas, a partially occupied and strategically vital region in Ukraine's east.
Zelensky even recently voiced support for a U.S.-backed proposal for a neutral "free economic zone" in Donbas, an idea Moscow yet again rejected.
"What most people don't know is that there were…multiple legal interpretations of what is now simplistically reduced to the formula of 'cede land or not' — interpretations that could have helped Ukraine retain control with time," Mendel said.
Zelensky has publicly proposed exactly such solutions, where the occupied territories would remain under Russian control temporarily before being regained via diplomacy.
Only 32% of Ukrainians would agree to a peace deal that would require Ukraine to withdraw completely from Donbas, even in exchange for Western security guarantees.
In fact, Mendel contradicts her own claims about Zelensky's "uncompromising" attitude later in her speech.
"Today he changes the terms of peace by the week: now it is accession to NATO, now the return of Crimea, now the borders of 1991, now membership of the European Union — as though all of this were achievable in a single stroke — now the refusal to concede Donbas," she said — effectively listing various points in which Ukraine softened its position, while Russia has not.
Notably, Mendel stopped short of urging Ukraine to make territorial concessions, suggesting she "would be signing (her) own treason charge and (her) own 15-year or life sentence."
Next to Zelensky, Mendel also hurls accusations at Western governments that only "wish to destroy Russia no matter how many Ukrainian lives it costs" and refuse to talk to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
This comment seems to ignore various initiatives by Ukraine's leading allies in Europe to engage Russia diplomatically — though, so far, without any progress toward a settlement as Moscow refuses to compromise on its demands.
Mendel's other case against Zelensky
The second main point of Mendel's criticism toward Zelensky focuses on domestic matters — the president's authoritative governing style and the corruption scandals surrounding him.
And, indeed, Zelensky and his team have increasingly faced criticism from the Ukrainian public, activists, and the media on these points.
Some of Zelensky's closest allies were charged in a multi-million-dollar money-laundering scheme; the unexplained firing of popular Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov faced massive public backlash; and the president has been criticized for failing to communicate his decisions to the Ukrainian public and the media.
However, according to Mendel, the situation in Ukraine is so dire that it resembles Soviet-era repressions where people can be "convicted, sanctioned, or branded as traitors simply for calling for peace or criticizing the leadership."
Calling for peace is not illegal or persecuted in Ukraine — ending the war through negotiations is the stated goal of the Ukrainian government. And contrary to the second part of the claim, public criticism of Zelensky is active, legal, and loud, and it has achieved tangible results.
The President's Office backed away from its attempt to destroy the independence of Ukraine's anti-corruption agencies after public protests in the summer of 2025.
And while this year's protests did not achieve their goal of Fedorov's reinstatement, Zelensky gave in to at least one demand — firing Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi.
The independent media has indeed faced pressure from the authorities on several occasions, but the media have also successfully pushed back and continue to hold the administration accountable.
Such traits would be difficult to find in an autocracy, even though Mendel says that Ukraine's "democracy is now so fragile that it barely differs from any autocratic regime."
The voice of the Ukrainian people?
When Mendel explains the reason for her address, she says, "Someone must speak for the Ukrainian people."
This motif runs through her entire speech, in which she draws a line between regular Ukrainians suffering in the war and the Zelensky administration that helps perpetuate it.
As evidence, the ex-press secretary cites a Gallup poll published in June, which says that 66% of Ukrainians want a negotiated end to the war as soon as possible, while only 24% want to fight until complete victory.
The poll does not name the conditions under which Ukrainians would accept a negotiated peace — but other surveys do.
Only 32% of Ukrainians would agree to a peace deal that would require Ukraine to withdraw completely from Donbas, even in exchange for Western security guarantees, according to a survey published by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) in August.
The same poll shows that 59% of respondents would back a ceasefire along the current front lines, even if Russia maintains control over currently occupied territories, while Ukraine receives continued supplies of Western arms.
Effectively, these are the peace conditions presented by the Ukrainian leadership, showing there is little divide between the administration and the public on this issue.
Mendel's assertion that she speaks on behalf of the Ukrainians also contrasts with the fact that her visit was organized by the AfD — a party that not only wants to return to buying Russian energy and cut support for Ukraine, but also wants Kyiv to "repay" the assistance provided.
Speaking to the Kyiv Independent, Mendel defended her engagement with the AfD, rejecting what she called "superficial labeling" and stressing the need to engage with a party that "grows in popularity among Germans."
"(Mendel) is spreading Russian narratives mixed with truth — which only helps to discredit the truth."
The ex-press secretary also said she simply aims to open dialogue with "parties that want to make peace."
Despite finding common ground with Kremlin-sympathetic figures, Mendel has long rejected accusations of being pro-Russian, claiming her criticism is aimed simply at Zelensky's handling of the war.
But even Zelensky's critics inside Ukraine are not convinced.
"As a representative of the Ukrainian opposition, I consider her a traitor and an agent of Russia," Yaroslav Yurchyshyn, a lawmaker for the liberal opposition Holos party, told the Kyiv Independent.
The lawmaker called Mendel a "typical example of Zelensky's ill-conceived personnel policy, in which people are appointed to influential positions based on loyalty rather than professionalism."
"(Mendel) is spreading Russian narratives mixed with truth — which only helps to discredit the truth," concluded Volodymyr Ariev, a lawmaker from the opposition European Solidarity party.
"Cherry," a drone operator in Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, expressed frustration that figures like Mendel "feel so comfortable abroad and even have some kind of media platform."
"Yes, we need peace, but the main thing is what kind of peace it will be and for how long," Cherry remarked.
"If we just stop now and make concessions to Russia, then after a while they will attack again, and I will have to deal with this again as a 40-60 year-old for my children and grandchildren."
Francis Farrell contributed reporting.

Gallery: Tallinn opens city's first drone training classroom for kids
Tallinn opened its first drone training classroom on Friday, giving kids and teens in the Estonian capital a chance to learn hands-on skills in a fast-growing field.
The new city-funded classroom opened Friday at the Energy Discovery Center, where drone clubs for ages 8–11 and 12–16 started meeting earlier this month. Starting in October, Tallinn schools will also be able to book drone education classes at the center.
Energy Discovery Center CEO Darja Saar said drones can help spark kids' interest in engineering and technology.
"You can see young people's eyes light up the first time they fly a first-person view (FPV) drone or play drone soccer," Saar said, adding that the experience can lead to skills including 3D modeling and printing, programming, physics and math.
The center has been developing drone education for kids and teens in collaboration with the City of Tallinn and HOBIzone club since March. The initiative is part of the city's Test in Tallinn program.

Italian frigate escorts Italian merchant vessel in Bab el-Mandeb
Part of EU's Aspides op, 'concrete signal delivered with excellent timing'
ROME,
18 September 2026, 18:02
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
In the last few hours, the frigate Carlo Bergamini—deployed as part of the European Operation Aspides—escorted the Italian merchant vessel Jolly Oro, owned by the shipping company Ignazio Messina & C., during its northbound transit through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the Italian Navy announced Friday. "The activity falls within the tasks assigned to the naval forces of Operation Aspides," it said. According to the Navy, this represents "a concrete signal, delivered with excellent timing, regarding the importance of maintaining a high level of attention on the safety of commercial shipping in the area." Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said Thursday that Italy would not wait for the EU to protect its shipping in the strait.
He said Italy was willing to go it alone with military operations to ensure its ships can pass the Bab el-Mandeb - but as part of Aspides.
It will take the Bergamini two days to escort the Jolly Oro through the strategic waterway, the Navy said.

Speaking on the sidelines of the 70th General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in Vienna, Kamalvandi addressed the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, noting that Iran is making every effort to manage the situation and ensure the security of the strait.
Reacting to U.S. claims regarding maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, Kamalvandi added: “Regarding the number of ships, it is not what they claim. Currently, only a single-digit number of vessels are transiting in and out of the Strait of Hormuz.”
Commenting on the ongoing wartime conditions, Kamalvandi stated, “If you are under attack, you have all the cards at your disposal to defend yourself. Therefore, we have more than one card; of course, we have sufficient cards and options.”
He stressed: “But beyond these options, we have the resolve—a strong resolve to defend our country.” The senior Iranian nuclear official added, “And of course, regardless of how much pressure they exert on us, we will overcome this situation.”
Elsewhere in the interview, Kamalvandi addressed the absence of Mohammad Eslami, the Vice President and Head of the AEOI, at the conference in the Austrian capital, revealing that Austrian authorities “issued visas about two weeks ago, but suddenly, under American pressure, canceled them.”
“This is not just an issue concerning Iran; this is an international issue,” Kamalvandi said, concluding with the emphasis that “I think all countries must react to it.”

Caviar and champagne – how Air France’s luxury bet helped increase profits amid the war in Iran

Thanks to generous portions of caviar and champagne, Air France’s bold bet on luxury appears to be paying off, helping the Paris-based airline weather the fallout from the war in Iran. The company’s CEO, Ben Smith, told Reuters on Friday, UNN reports.
Details
Airlines around the world, including Air France-KLM’s parent group, are facing soaring jet fuel costs and disrupted flight schedules due to the war in Iran, which has been ongoing for nearly seven months; this is forcing some carriers to cut capacity and limit spending.
Meanwhile, Air France is successfully overcoming these challenges. The airline has capitalized on the popularity of the series "Emily in Paris" and tourists’ enduring interest in the French capital’s fashion, gastronomy and hotel industry. It has bet on premium services: updating its onboard menu with products from elite brands and investing heavily in outfitting its most profitable classes of service.
"All luxury brands are based in Paris. Paris has more Michelin-starred restaurants than any other city in the world," Smith said on the sidelines of an awards ceremony in London, where Air France received an award for the best first-class cabin.

Tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are spilling oil into the Persian Gulf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:05:00 UTC
23:05:00 KST

Strait of Hormuz attacks spill oil into Persian Gulf
September 18, 2026
A dark, muddied patch of blue, incongruent with the rest of the ocean; a winding thread of silvery white; a reflective metallic sheen — these are some of the telltale signs on a satellite image that oil may be leaking into the water.
Experts have identified these and many other visual signaturesin the Strait of Hormuz, leading them to conclude that there's an environmental crisis playing out amid the US-Iran war, as tankers are struck by missiles, set on fire or sunk.
One recent example: In June, a Russian tanker carrying about 800,000 barrels of oil stranded off the coast of Oman, causing a major spill.
Earlier in the war, there were as many as 85 large oil-laden tankers stuck in the Strait — that number has since dropped to 13, according to Greenpeace. Each stranded tanker, plus every other vessel trying to move through the waterway, poses a distinct risk for attack and thus a spill. Since the start of the war, the environmental organization has used satellite imagery to track more than 100 spills.
There are likely several other spills that we don't know of, amid widespread GPS spoofing in the region that causes ships to broadcast false positions. Greenpeace released a report this week calling the situation an "ecological catastrophe" and pinpointing a number of oil slicks that are extending into protected and fragile ecosystems.
"People should be concerned," Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief, told DW. The war has taken "a very, very heavy toll on the environment," she said, with the damage now reaching new scales.
Where is the oil spreading?
Greenpeace identified five major oil slicks earlier this week with a total visible area of 240 square kilometers (about 90 square miles) in the Strait of Hormuz. That's about four times the size of Manhattan.
These patches of oil floating on the ocean's surface are getting smaller — now about 80 square kilometers — according to more up-to-date satellite images, as weather conditions have likely made the slicks disperse. But that does not mean the ecological impact is any less severe, Noelle said. "Oil can also sink into the sediment and impact the ecosystems for years and years."
What's concerning is where the slicks were identified. One was found near Musandam National Park, a protected area in Oman that's home to coral reefs, sea life and important breeding grounds for sea birds. Another is close to Iran's Minab River Delta and its protected mudflats and mangrove forests. This kind of damage can take decades for ecosystems to recover from.
Tracking an unclear picture
It's hard to say exactly how far the oil has reached and how severe the damage is.
"What we have put out is the conservative estimate," Noelle said. "It might be worse. It's definitely not better."
Greenpeace and other environmental organizations are relying on satellite images provided by the Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellites. They're part of the European Union's Earth observation program and are publicly available.
There are also private satellite providers such as Planet Labs that tend to have higher-resolution images. But they've limited access to satellite imagery during the war to prevent their data from being used for military targeting. And there are limits to on-the-ground reports too.
"We don't have a lot of information coming from the country itself, both in Iran as well as the Gulf states," Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher who uses open-source methods at the Dutch peace organization Pax, told DW. "There is quite restrictive policies of people posting imagery from what's happening on the shore."
The toll on wildlife and people
Oil pooling into the Gulf poses a number of threats — both to biodiversity and to humans.
Oil can be deadly for seabirds. It coats their feathers, reducing their natural waterproofing and buoyancy, making it harder to stay afloat, fly, and hunt for food. Even small amounts of oil can damage eggs too, causing them not to hatch or to be born with deformities.
Mangrove habitats, which provide safe harbor for coastal species, are also hit hard.
"Mangroves have aerial roots, and the oil is covering these roots like a film and actually hindering the mangroves in exchanging gases," Noelle said. "They're kind of suffocated by the oil. Most of the time, it leads to the trees dying."
The risks extend to people, as well. Coastal communities rely on fish that die off after being exposed to oil. And oil spills contaminate water used for Gulf states' drinking supply. Desalination — or converting seawater into drinkable water — is where 90% of drinking water in Kuwait comes from, along with about 86% in Oman and 70% in Saudi Arabia.
Cleanup is no easy fix.
"It's unlikely that it will be addressed quickly, because of the war," Zwijnenburg said. "War in general makes it very difficult to respond fast to these kind of emergencies. There are a range of limitations because of the military movement, because of mines — so it's very difficult to get vessels and cleanup operations to start."
Environmental groups have pointed to the war in Iran — and the rising scale of oil spills it has caused — as further evidence that the world needs to move away from its dependence on fossil fuels.
"The most sustainable long-term damage prevention for things like that would be to reduce and ultimately end our dependency on oil and gas," Noelle said. "Because, as long as our energy systems and transport routes are centered around fossil fuels, there will be a continued environmental risk."

LONDON – British air traffic control operator NATS said on Sept 18 that a software defect caused last week’s outage, which affected hundreds of thousands of passengers.
The incident led to 2,000 flight cancellations and days of disruption, costing airlines millions of pounds as they scrambled to get crews and aircraft back into place and refund passengers.
NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe said the shutdown was not related to a problem in 2023, which also caused widespread disruption, nor was it linked to military intervention – as reported by some media outlets last week.
He added that safety was at no point compromised during the incident.
“This was a software issue in a specific part of our flight data system that we have traced to a small subsection of coding,” he said.
“The issue has been identified, and mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety tested and deployed.”
Transport Minister Heidi Alexander, who last week demanded that NATS produce a report on the matter and ordered an independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority, said the disruption was “completely unacceptable”.
“We need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos,” she said in a statement. “It is crucial that our national infrastructure is fit for the future.”
The incident followed a shutdown in August 2023, which caused travel chaos and cost airlines £100 million (S$170 million). A smaller technical issue involving NATS also caused 150 cancellations in July 2025.
Ryanair, Europe’s biggest airline, has repeatedly called on Rolfe to resign since the 2023 failure.
According to NATS’ report, the latest incident was triggered when a request for an identification code from an aircraft was followed by a request for a higher-priority activity, which paused the first request.
“Had the higher-priority request arrived even one millisecond earlier or later, the update would have completed normally,” the report said. REUTERS

Strait of Hormuz disruptions 'worst threat' to global trade in eight decades: WTO chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:03:50 UTC
23:03:50 KST

Global trade is facing its worst disruption in 80 years as supply chain bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz threaten global food and fertiliser prices, the World Trade Organization's (WTO) director-general warned.
Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, speaking on the sidelines of the WTO’s Public Forum in Geneva, told Anadolu on Friday that the global trading system remains resilient, but the ongoing Middle East conflict presents a major test for the organisation’s 166 member countries.
She noted that global trade in goods grew by an unexpectedly strong 4.6 percent this year despite geopolitical pressures, while 72 percent of all global commerce continued to operate under WTO rules.
The initial projection for overall goods trade growth was 1.9 percent for the entire year, but the first-quarter growth rate of 3.2 percent outpaced expectations.
Okonjo-Iweala stated that a significant portion of the momentum was driven by the surging trade in artificial intelligence, which it turn was driven by low- or zero-tariff agreements covering $3 trillion in global semiconductor and chip shipments.
She urged caution over the sustainability of the trend, while warning that the economic benefits of this booming trade remain concentrated in North America and East Asia, raising concerns about global market inclusivity.
Higher agricultural costs
Okonjo-Iweala said national reserves temporarily shielded markets from the shocks that the Strait of Hormuz disruptions have caused thus far, but prolonged blockades in the vital waterway will inevitably lead to higher agricultural costs.
The WTO’s previous estimates showed that crude oil prices reaching $90-a-barrel could drive down overall trade growth by 0.5 points, while current crude oil prices have exceeded that threshold.
Maritime shippers maintained trade volume by rerouting vessels via alternative routes, but these lengthy detours are adding steep premiums, calling into question the long-term stability of the current supply chain, Okonjo-Iweala warned.
Overhaul for global trade rules
Governments around the world are drafting contingency plans to protect their economies from future chokepoint failures, while the combination of supply chain instability and rapid shifts in technology has furthered internal WTO talks over the need to overhaul global trade rules for this century.
She noted that comprehensive institutional reform is key to equitable global development, and that the current framework of the WTO has frequently failed developing nations.
Okonjo-Iweala urged developing countries to participate in drafting modernised policies to ensure they can also seize economic opportunities, while the proposed reforms would target failing institutional mechanisms and help prevent these countries from being left behind.
A recent WTO report unveiled as part of its Public Forum estimated that a collapse in multilateral cooperation and a failure to modernise regulations could wipe out up to 10 percent of potential global economic growth by 2050.

Thailand to expand household solar power program to 10 GW
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:03:33 CST
23:03:33 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Thailand will expand its household solar power program to 10 gigawatts and buy surplus electricity from participants at 2.20 baht (about 0.07 U.S. dollars) per kilowatt-hour under 20-year contracts, a government official said on Friday.
The National Energy Policy Council raised the ceiling for the "people's solar" scheme to 10 gigawatts, enough for around one million households, from an initial proposal of 5 gigawatts, said deputy government spokesperson Lalida Periswiwatana.
Purchases will run on a net billing basis, with households consuming their own output first and selling only the excess, capped at 5 kilowatts per meter, Lalida said, adding that contracts were extended from 10 years to 20 to match the working life of panels, with the additional intake covering 2026 to 2028.
Households may now also mount panels on the ground and on water, not just rooftops, she said.
The council gave the energy and interior ministries and the three state electricity utilities one month to produce a grid readiness plan covering generation forecasting, real-time monitoring, transmission and distribution control, as well as battery storage.
Expanding to 10 gigawatts would give the public a greater role in producing clean energy, but it has to move in step with grid readiness, so the added capacity does not undermine the security of the power system, Lalida said.
The deputy spokesperson noted that agencies were also told to find a way to amend existing 10-year contracts so earlier participants need not cancel and reapply, and the industry ministry was assigned to draw up a recycling plan for panels and batteries. ■
