Japan's central bank lifts policy rate to 31-year high, signals more hikes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:03:25 CST
23:03:25 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Bank of Japan (BOJ) on Friday raised its key interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to a 31-year high of 1.25 percent, while signaling further rate hikes ahead.
The central bank lifted the rate again after bringing it up to 1.0 percent in June, marking the shortest interval between increases since the BOJ ended its negative interest rate policy in March 2024.
Seven of the BOJ's nine board members voted for the rate hike at its two-day policy meeting that concluded Friday.
The decision, widely anticipated, came as the prolonged Middle East conflict and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have sent crude oil prices surging, while the yen's slide to its lowest level in decades against the U.S. dollar has driven up import costs, though recent expectations of a September rate hike by the BOJ had helped the yen recover moderately.
BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said at a press conference after the meeting that the central bank had entered a phase in which it must pay greater attention to the possibility of higher-than-expected inflation, noting that the risk of inflation overshooting the BOJ's two-percent price stability target was becoming increasingly apparent.
Going forward, the BOJ said in a report explaining its latest monetary policy decision that it will continue to raise the policy interest rate and adjust the degree of monetary accommodation in response to developments in economic activity and prices as well as financial conditions.
The BOJ said it will pay particular attention to the impact of the situation in the Middle East, the effects of expanding global artificial intelligence-related demand, and developments in foreign exchange rates, among other factors, when determining the timing and pace of adjustment.
Rising interest rates would push up borrowing costs for both businesses and households, potentially weighing on economic activity and posing a challenge for the BOJ's efforts to contain inflation without hampering growth.
The BOJ has two policy meetings remaining this year, scheduled for October and December. ■

Slovakia records 3rd-warmest summer since 1931
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:03:13 CST
23:03:13 KST

BRATISLAVA, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- This summer was the third-warmest recorded in Slovakia since 1931, the Slovak Hydrometeorological Institute (SHMU) said on Friday.
According to SHMU, June was the fourth-warmest on record for that month, while August was the second-warmest.
The village of Muzla in the Nitra region recorded the highest number of summer days, at 87. The town of Hurbanovo, also in the Nitra region, recorded 56 tropical days, when the temperature reached at least 30 degrees Celsius. SHMU also recorded the country's longest heatwave this summer, lasting 22 days.
SHMU climatologist Peter Kajaba said the institute had never previously recorded such a long consecutive run of tropical days, noting that temperatures exceeding 42 degrees Celsius were recorded in Slovakia this summer.
The institute also assessed the country's precipitation and drought conditions. Drought reached its peak during the second 10-day period in August, with the soil moisture deficit in the Orava region reaching 100 millimeters.
Severe to extreme drought affected areas covering about 90 percent of Slovakia, according to the institute. The drought was more severe than that recorded in 2022, affecting both agriculture and forestry. ■

Xinhua Commentary: Remember history to safeguard peace
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:03:12 CST
23:03:12 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- As air-raid sirens wailed in Chinese cities on Friday to commemorate the September 18 Incident, alarm bells should toll for a dangerous rise of Japanese neo-militarism today.
On Sept. 18, 1931, Japanese troops blew up a section of the railway near China's Shenyang city and later that night launched surprise attacks against Chinese military barracks in the city, marking the start of the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War.
Japan's imperialist aggression during World War II inflicted untold suffering on the people of China and the rest of the world. Remembering history is all the more relevant and necessary to cherish and safeguard peace today, as rising neo-militarism in Japan is posing a threat to world peace and stability again.
Over the years, Japanese right-wing forces have tried to break free from the postwar international arrangements. They have been trying every possible means to deny and distort history, and even whitewash the crimes committed during Japan's war of aggression, including revising history textbooks and indoctrinating the Japanese people with a wrong perception of history.
Japan has been accelerating its remilitarisation, drastically readjusting its security policy, increasing its defense spending for 14 consecutive years, relaxing its restrictions on lethal arms exports, developing and deploying offensive weapons, and going farther down the wrong path of military buildup. Its ambitions were laid bare when Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made remarks that implied the possibility of Japan's armed intervention in the Taiwan Strait in November last year.
Only by learning lessons from history can one avoid repeating mistakes. What Japan should do is to face up to its history of aggression, reflect on its war crimes, and make a complete break with militarism. This is the correct choice that serves the fundamental interests of the Japanese people.
Today's China is no longer what it was 95 years ago. The country has bid farewell to its old era of poverty and weakness and is advancing on its unstoppable course toward national rejuvenation. Its economic aggregate has ranked second in the world for years, and its people's armed forces have achieved leapfrog development, giving the nation solid confidence to safeguard peace.
Adhering to peaceful development, China will stand together with peace-loving countries in the world to firmly hold back the malevolent emergence of Japanese neo-militarism and prevent the tragedies of history from being repeated. ■

Asian Games | China loses to Japan in men's basketball semifinals
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:03:09 CST

Wang Junjie (L) and Hu Jinqiu (R) of China compete during the men's semifinal basketball match between China and Japan at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Luo Yuan)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China lost to host Japan 97-77 in the men's basketball semifinals at the 2026 Asian Games on Friday, missing the final for the second consecutive Games.
Japan took control early, using a 9-0 run to build a 28-15 lead in the first quarter. Hu Mingxuan's 3-pointer helped China cut the deficit to eight points with 3:42 remaining in the second quarter, but Japan responded with an 11-0 run to take a 49-30 lead into halftime.
Japan repeatedly capitalized on fast-break opportunities and shot 14 of 19 from the field in a highly efficient third quarter, at one point stretching its lead to 35 points.
China narrowed the deficit in the fourth quarter but could not mount a full comeback, eventually falling by 20 points.
"We normally play good on the rebounds, but we lost on the rebounds today," Chinese forward Cui Yongxi said after the game. "And on defense, we did no good. We missed a lot of shots and they played a lot of transitions. They played hard on us, and we didn't play harder."
China captain Hu Mingxuan said defensive communication problems allowed Japan to dictate the game.
"We had issues on the defensive end, including communication breakdowns, which allowed our opponents to run their offense smoothly and made us have to follow their rhythm," Hu said. "When we tried to correct those problems in a timely way, we were already trailing by a large margin.
"It was clear today that we didn't match their intensity. Our in-game reactions probably weren't as sharp as theirs either. I think we didn't prepare adequately for the difficulties we would face, and that's what led to these issues."
Hu Jinqiu led China with 16 points. Cui Yongxi added 13 and Hu Mingxuan had 11.
For Japan, Ren Kanechika scored 19 points, while Alex Kirk, a U.S.-born player who was naturalized to represent Japan in 2024, recorded a double-double with 15 points and 11 rebounds. ■

China Focus: China's growing network of lifesaving stem cell donors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:03:06 CST
23:03:06 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- In May 2026, Wu Yuyang, a young college student working as an intern in east China's Jiangsu Province, traveled to Qingdao in the neighboring Shandong Province to donate hematopoietic stem cells. Meanwhile, a mother of a three-year-old child was waiting for cells that might give her a second chance at life.
About three months later, Wu received an unexpected piece of news: a fellow student at his alma mater, the Shandong Cultural Industry Vocational College, had made the same choice to become a stem cell donor. He, too, was named Wu Yuyang.
The two young men are the 296th and 309th hematopoietic stem cell donors in Qingdao, respectively, and two among more than 20,000 people in China who have made hematopoietic stem cell donations for unrelated recipients through China's national data bank of hematopoietic stem cell donors.
The China Marrow Donor Program (CMDP) announced on Friday that it has facilitated 24,000 hematopoietic stem cell donations from unrelated donors since its launch in 2001.
The program is now the world's fourth-largest bone marrow donor registry, with nearly 3.79 million registered potential stem cell donors.
Hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow are responsible for producing all types of blood cells. Donations from unrelated volunteers can be life-saving for individuals battling blood disorders such as leukemia and sickle cell anemia.
"To be honest, I was quite surprised -- pleasantly surprised," the elder Wu, now a staff member of the Shanghai Metro in east China, said after learning that his younger namesake had followed in his footsteps. "But more than anything, I was happy. To be connected by the same place and the same cause is a very special kind of bond."
Yang Yunxia, mother of the younger Wu, said she was worried about her son's health at first. "However, when my son told me, 'Mom, I am saving someone's life,' all those worries turned into pride. It is something meaningful, and I fully support him," she noted.
China reported its first case of a bone marrow transplant from an unrelated donor in 1996.
In recent years, as the CMDP has improved its capacity and as public awareness and understanding of hematopoietic stem cell donation have grown, more people are joining both the donor registry and the ranks of those willing to make an actual donation.
According to the CMDP, it took more than two decades for the program to go from its first unrelated hematopoietic stem cell donation to the 10,000th. But for the latest 1,000 cases, from the 23,000th donation to the 24,000th, the journey took only 112 days.
The CMDP's reach also extends beyond China's borders. It joined the World Marrow Donor Association in 2012, opening further channels for international donor matching.
A few months ago, a primary-level medical worker from the northern Chinese city of Tianjin underwent stem cell collection and donated 350 milliliters of hematopoietic stem cell suspension to a patient with a blood disorder overseas. She was this city's 16th donor to provide hematopoietic stem cells to a patient outside the Chinese mainland.
To date, the CMDP has facilitated 441 donations to patients in 35 overseas countries and regions.
World Marrow Donor Day falls on Sept. 22 this year. ■

Indonesia recovers 3 more bodies from sunken ship in Java Sea
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:03:04 CST
23:03:04 KST

JAKARTA, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- A joint search and rescue team on Friday recovered three more bodies from a ship that capsized and sank in the Java Sea, bringing the death toll to nine on the sixth day of the search, the Indonesian Navy said.
Indonesian Navy spokesperson First Admiral Tunggul said naval divers entered the sunken vessel and found the bodies of two men and a woman.
Divers also recovered 210 items from inside and around the wreckage, which will be handed over to Indonesia's National Transportation Safety Committee for investigation, said Galih Nurna Putra, commander of the Indonesian Navy base in Banjarmasin.
The Virgo Transport 8 was carrying 243 people from Surabaya in East Java province to Banjarmasin when it capsized in bad weather early Sunday.
According to the latest official data, 108 people have been rescued, nine have been confirmed dead and 126 remain missing. ■

Russian hybrid attacks against Europe intensifying, says Macron
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:02:09 BST
23:02:09 KST

Russian hybrid attacks against Europe intensifying, says Macron
- Published
French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France has intensified.
In a news conference at the Elysee Palace, Macron said he had ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites in the face of this threat.
He said France had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks which would not be left "without a response".
A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.
- War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready? 
  - Published22 hours ago
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
The French president was speaking to journalists after meeting party leaders to discuss the security impact of the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Macron mentioned last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany, blamed on Russia, and remarks by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggesting Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.
"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," he said.
"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."
On Thursday Tusk told Polish MPs that Russian plans included strikes by drones and missiles on countries supporting Ukraine. He said there was a "real risk" of such strikes on the territory of Nato countries, with Moscow then claiming that they were "accidental", in an attempt to split the alliance.
Last Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through along the same line.
Ukraine said all the passengers had been evacuated just minutes before the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine.
There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Russia does not plan to attack Europe, but Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned European nations against sending troops to Ukraine, which would be seen by Russia as a declaration of war.
"If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short," he said.
Meanwhile on Friday, Russia reiterated its warning to the UK that any British military facilities in Ukraine used to strike Russian territory were "legitimate targets".
It reserved the right to take "necessary counter-measures" in response to the UK's "fiercely confrontational stance regarding Ukraine", referring to its supply of drones and other weapon systems to Kyiv.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Macron also addressed the energy situation, saying that the government had been tasked with protecting critical infrastructure and the "most sensitive" defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks.
He announced that France would call a meeting of the G7 to discuss energy and raise the question of gas stocks with the European Commission.
"In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues, both to strengthen cooperation and to avoid unnecessary tensions between the G7 countries and our main partners," Macron said.
"It will also be an opportunity to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves."
In a domestic context, he called on candidates in next year's elections not to exploit public unease by blaming the government, but to acknowledge that fuel price inflation was the result of uncontrollable international circumstances.
The hard-right opposition National Rally candidate Marine le Pen is currently leading the polls for the April-May vote to replace Macron.

Ukraine’s Defense Demands Victory Over Corruption at the Top
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:02:00 UTC
23:02:00 KST

Ukraine is fighting two battles at once: one along a thousand-kilometer front line against Russia’s invasion and another in Kyiv against a culture of impunity linked to President Volodymyr Zelensky’s office, known as Bankova, after the name of street on which it sits.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
With Russian missiles hitting thermal plants and power grids, Kyiv’s pleas to Western partners get more urgent by the week: send more Patriot batteries; add interceptors; keep the direct aid that keeps the state running.
Yet in this crucial moment when Ukraine expects allied governments to justify to their taxpayers every dollar, euro, and pound they give in support, corruption allegations keep pointing to the inner sanctum of the presidential administration.
The general conclusion is that the ultra-centralized vertical forged for national survival has trumped institutional checks needed for mature rule-of-law democracy. While this benefits those who exploit the system, the downside is that this wartime model is both noxious and dangerous in the long term.
Russian bombs destroy concrete, steel, and lives, but unpunished corruption causes just as much harm – one that damages civilians’ morale, insults soldiers on the front lines, and damages Ukraine’s moral standing abroad. When public money and wartime contracts are treated like private spoils in an existential war, the damage to national resilience goes deeper than battlefield defeats.
Lithuania Prepares Vilnius Evacuation Routes in Case of Military Threat
Legal precision is crucial. None of the accusations swirling around Bankova have led to a criminal conviction, and Ukraine’s constitution provides for the presumption of innocence. But in wartime politics and diplomacy, public trust cannot wait for years of legal wrangling.
In the biggest scandal so far, anti-corruption detectives are looking into kickbacks linked to state nuclear operator Energoatom and contracts meant to protect critical energy infrastructure from Russian strikes.
At the heart of that probe is businessman Timur Mindich – a longtime friend of President Volodymyr Zelensky; Mindich denies all wrongdoing from his safe haven abroad. He has also been scrutinized by investigators after reports of an inquiry into luxury real estate surfaced around former Zelensky chief of staff and effective gray cardinal Andriy Yermak – allegations he has dismissed as completely baseless.
Defense procurement has also faced equally serious questions. Recently, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov publicly said that the sector was still under the thumb of entrenched middlemen and political favorites.
Such claims are subject to verification in formal proceedings, but they signal danger, which must be addressed urgently and credibly.
The justice system itself is now under an acute test. The current scandal involving former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko has added another blow to institutional integrity: after anti-corruption detectives searched his agency over suspected fraudulent schemes involving subordinates, he resigned; reports said he then left the country, and parliament approved his dismissal at the president’s embarrassed request.
Kravchenko has not been charged or convicted of any crime (the facts are still being investigated), but his sudden departure amid turmoil is a political disaster and an embarrassment for the state. The Prosecutor General’s Office cannot be a political shield for the executive or block independent inquiries.
Systemic corruption and prosecutorial manipulation are not unique to this administration – they existed under President Petro Poroshenko and his predecessors too. But practices that undermined peacetime governance are worse during an existential war.
Moreover, Ukraine is so reliant on foreign financial lifelines and air defenses, all the while trying to join the EU and NATO. Corruption scandals keep people home demoralized and undermine Ukraine’s cause abroad.
President Zelensky faces an unavoidable test of leadership. He cannot be an inspirational, Churchill-like champion of freedom abroad and run an insular, opaque, or lax administration at home. Inspirational rhetoric in allied capitals is not institutional integrity in Kyiv.
At the same time, parliament must stop being a wartime rubber stamp for Bankova. Lawmakers need to reclaim proper constitutional oversight: hold effective committee hearings, scrutinize defense and energy spending, defend NABU and SAPO from political interference, and call officials to account.
None of these failings justifies Western hesitation. Cutting off financial aid or withholding air defense systems would give Vladimir Putin a victory he cannot win on the battlefield and would also endanger European security. Foreign support must continue unabated, but it must be reinforced by rigorous joint audits, clear benchmarks, and sustained backing for Ukraine’s independent watchdogs.
Conditionality must be respected and applied – both as justified insurance for Ukraine’s allies and benefactors and, importantly, as a driver of improved governance and accountability so needed for democracy maturation in the country and preparation for big challenges that lie ahead after the war.
In short, Bankova (and especially the president himself) has to face up to an uncomfortable truth: tolerated corruption also endangers national survival – not just Russian bombardment. Missiles destroy physical infrastructure, but graft hollows out public morale, fractures national unity, and squanders international goodwill.
The time for action is now. Ukraine needs to break the cycle where high-profile scandals end in quiet resignations, bureaucratic evasions, or foreign departures; the Ukrainian public and allied nations need to see investigations tested in open, lawful courts and anyone convicted of exploiting a nation fighting for its survival punished.
At this critical moment in the country’s fight for survival, there can be no more excuses and delays. Zero tolerance for corruption, starting at the top, must be seen and enforced.

Saadet Gokce
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The Asian Games, hosted in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan this year, have been plagued by mishaps ahead of the opening ceremony on Saturday.
According to media reports, the organizing committee has opted for cruise ships, container unıts and hotels to accommodate athletes instead of building an athletes’ village, citing lower costs and environmental considerations.
However, despite these preparations, athletes have faced accommodation problems, including hours-long waits, mixed-gender room assignments, coaches being housed with athletes, and trainers with extensive medical equipment assigned to cramped, shared rooms.
“There have been cases where coaches, team officials, and athletes have been assigned to the same room. There are also situations where room assignments were made purely based on the numbers, such as assigning five twin rooms for a group of five men and five women,” Japan’s deputy Chef de Mission Hisashi Mizutori told a news conference on Thursday, according to The Japan Times.
The local organizing committee attributed the accommodation problems to an increase in the number of athletes and officials, saying it had initially expected 15,000 participants, but the figure increased as new sports were added.
Teams also faced difficulties upon landing at Nagoya Airport due to a technical glitch, leaving them unable to depart, according to the South China Morning Post.
Athletes and officials were stranded at the transport center after a data-entry error left many athletes missing from the airport's ground transportation database, resulting in staff being unable to authorize or dispatch their shuttle buses
Seating was scarce, with many officials, coaches and athletes from several countries and regions present. They were also left with only water to drink., according to the report.
China’s badminton team tried to use public transportation to leave, but only a few members could do so because of insufficient tickets.
The rest of the team was driven by Chinese residents living nearby after staff at the Chinese Consulate-General in Nagoya arranged assistance.
In another incident, the North Korean national anthem was mistakenly played for the South Korean team before a men’s hockey game between South Korea and Bangladesh on Friday, according to Kyodo News.
South Korea also said Thursday that it had filed an official complaint with the Games’ organizing committee over the highlighting of a Japanese warlord who invaded Korea during a recent ceremony.
The 2026 Asian Games will run for 16 days, from the opening ceremony at Paloma Mizuho Stadium on Saturday through Oct. 4.
The Games will be held under the slogan Imagine One Asia.
The event features 43 sports, 71 disciplines and a total of 469 medal events. Around 15,000 athletes from 45 countries and regions are expected to compete.

Dark personality traits predict support for violence by both Israel and Hamas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:00:24 UTC
23:00:24 KST

Recent psychology research indicates that while most people base their support for political violence on their personal ideological beliefs, individuals with high levels of psychopathy and sadism tend to endorse violence across the board. A new study examining attitudes toward the Israel-Hamas conflict suggests that these specific dark personality traits are linked to support for violent actions committed by both sides. The findings were published in Personality and Individual Differences.
In the study of political psychology, a common assumption is that people evaluate violence based on their group identity and political worldview. This means individuals usually justify violence when it is committed by a group they agree with, while firmly rejecting similar violent actions when committed by opposing groups. In highly polarized situations like the conflict between Israel and Hamas, this translates to an actor-specific view of violence. An individual might support the military actions of one side, but it is unusual for them to endorse violence from both sides simultaneously.
The author of the new study, Tobias Greitemeyer of the University of Innsbruck, wanted to explore whether certain personality characteristics override this partisan loyalty. He focused on the Dark Tetrad, a grouping of four socially aversive personality traits. These traits include narcissism, which involves grandiosity and entitlement; Machiavellianism, characterized by manipulative and cynical behavior; psychopathy, marked by callousness, low empathy, and impulsive thrill-seeking; and sadism, which involves deriving pleasure from the suffering of others.
Previous investigations have linked these traits to various forms of hostility. For instance, a 2024 study covered by PsyPost indicated that higher scores on dark personality traits were associated with higher levels of antisemitism, showing how these characteristics can shape views on Middle Eastern geopolitics. Other research, such as a 2015 study on consumer attitudes, has shown that dark personality traits are related to a concept called moral disengagement. Moral disengagement refers to the mental gymnastics people use to justify harmful behavior, allowing them to ignore their own moral standards without feeling guilty.
To test how these traits relate to attitudes toward the Israel-Hamas conflict, Greitemeyer conducted two separate online studies. The first study recruited 257 German-speaking participants, mostly from Austria and Germany. The participants completed a standardized questionnaire measuring their levels of the Dark Tetrad traits, as well as measures of their political orientation, their general attitudes toward war and peace, and their specific support for violent actions carried out by Israel and Hamas.
The results provided evidence for the traditional view that political violence is generally actor-specific. Support for violence by Israel and support for violence by Hamas were negatively correlated, indicating that participants who endorsed violence by one actor were less likely to endorse violence by the other. Older participants tended to show more support for Israeli actions and less support for Hamas actions. Men reported more support for Israeli military actions than women did, but there was no difference between men and women regarding support for Hamas.
When looking at personality, however, a different pattern emerged. Psychopathy and sadism were positively associated with support for violent actions by both Israel and Hamas. Individuals scoring higher in these two traits showed a generalized acceptance of violence, regardless of which side was responsible. This generalized support remained present even when the researcher accounted for the participants’ political ideologies. Narcissism and Machiavellianism, on the other hand, did not show this consistent, cross-actor support for violence.
A second study was conducted with 470 United Kingdom citizens to see if these findings would hold up in a larger sample and to explore potential psychological mechanisms. In addition to measuring the Dark Tetrad traits and support for violence by Israel and Hamas, participants completed assessments for two other variables. One was their interest in militarism, which captures a fascination with weapons, special forces, and martial arts. The other was their propensity for moral disengagement.
The second study mirrored the findings of the first. Once again, support for Israel and Hamas was negatively correlated overall, but psychopathy and sadism reliably predicted an endorsement of violence by both actors. Narcissism was only linked to support for Hamas, and Machiavellianism showed no reliable association with support for either side.
The data also indicated that interest in militarism and moral disengagement helped explain the connection between dark personality traits and support for violence, though only partially. Both militarism and moral disengagement acted as mediating factors for why psychopathy and sadism predicted support for Israeli violent actions. However, neither of these psychological mechanisms explained the link between the dark traits and support for Hamas’s violent actions, suggesting that different cognitive pathways might be at play depending on the specific actor involved.
“This confirms the work of earlier research and slightly extends it by explicitly showing that individuals scoring high on dark personality traits (especially on psychopathy and sadism) tend to exhibit support for political violence of multiple conflicted and even directly opposing groups,” said Tomislav Pavlović, a researcher working on the MOTIKA project, which focuses on understanding drivers and barriers to peaceful and violent collective action, who was not involved in the study.
“As earlier research demonstrated, individuals scoring high on dark personality traits also tend to exhibit more favorable attitudes toward violence in general,” Pavlović told PsyPost. “From this perspective, it is not surprising that individuals showing stronger support for violence as a general method of achieving goals also see it as a more acceptable method of achieving political goals.”
“The findings of this paper could be taken as an extension of existing research, indicating that endorsement of political violence is not related only to political beliefs and social identity (ideological partisanship), but also to individual differences in dark personality traits,” said Anja Wertag, a researcher at the Ivo Pilar Institute of Social Sciences in Croatia who was also not involved in the work. She told PsyPost the study highlights “the importance of integrating personality and political psychology perspectives in investigating violence endorsement.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in July 2024, which indicated that psychopathy strongly predicted support for military violence against civilians among Russian residents. The results also align with another 2024 study showing that higher psychopathy is associated with greater attitudinal support for politically motivated violence across multiple countries. Additionally, the conclusions echo a 2021 study that linked psychopathic traits to support for violent social change, regardless of whether that violence was endorsed by left-wing or right-wing groups.
But as with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding this study. The data rely on self-reported questionnaires, meaning participants might have altered their answers to appear more socially acceptable, especially on sensitive political topics. The samples were also non-representative groups of internet users from Europe, which limits how broadly the findings can be applied to the general public or to populations directly involved in the conflict.
“It is important to note that the Dark Tetrad traits explained only a modest amount of the variance in support for Israeli and Hamas violent actions – ranging from 5 to 8%,” Wertag noted. She added that because “all Dark Tetrad traits are multidimensional and the current study used only a brief measure to assess them, future research should include broader measures of dark traits to enable a clearer view of the relations between different aspects of the dark traits and violence endorsement.”
Pavlović pointed out another geographical limitation regarding the samples. “Finally, it is worth mentioning that none of the samples were from Israel or Gaza,” he said. “Therefore, (at least) the majority of participants perceive the conflict from the perspective of relatively neutral bystanders. We cannot tell whether these results would be replicated had the study been conducted on participants whose nations are involved in conflict.”
The cross-sectional design of the studies also means the research cannot determine cause and effect. It is possible that consuming media about political violence alters a person’s psychological state, rather than personality traits alone driving their political attitudes. Future research could investigate whether these patterns hold true in other geopolitical conflicts and explore other psychological mechanisms, such as a lack of empathic concern for victims, that might bridge the gap between dark personality traits and support for war.
“While dark personality traits and support for political violence are correlated, this relationship may reflect a third underlying variable (such as experience of violence),” Pavlović explained. “Furthermore, support for political violence should not be equated with actual participation in violent acts.”
Wertag agreed, warning against leaping to broad conclusions. “I am concerned about a possible overinterpretation of the results regarding the link between violence endorsement, regardless of the side, and psychopathy and sadism due to the above-mentioned methodological constraints,” she said. “The results also do not imply that personality traits are more important than political orientation; they simply highlight that both matter. Finally, the results say nothing about the actual tendency toward violent behavior.”
The study, “When darkness overrides partisanship: Psychopathy and sadism predict support for violence on both sides of the Israel–Hamas conflict,” was authored by Tobias Greitemeyer.

QinetiQ to build digital twin of UK vehicle test range
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:07 BST
23:00:07 KST

QinetiQ and AVL have agreed to create a digital twin of the Hurn Proving Ground in Hampshire, allowing defence and commercial vehicles to be tested virtually before entering physical trials, according to QinetiQ.
The partnership will combine AVL’s vehicle modelling and simulation technology with QinetiQ’s 632-acre test and evaluation site near Ringwood, with the aim of reducing development costs and speeding up the process of bringing new vehicles into service.
Under the memorandum of understanding, AVL will develop a digital representation of Hurn and provide modelling tools that allow vehicles to be assessed during design or down-selection before prototypes are fully built. QinetiQ said the approach would allow engineers to identify problems earlier, compare design options more quickly and reduce the amount of physical testing required before vehicles reach the proving ground.
Once digital testing is complete, vehicles can then be put through live trials across Hurn’s terrain, test tracks and specialist facilities, including what QinetiQ describes as the UK’s largest tilt platform.
Will Blamey, Chief Executive of QinetiQ’s UK Defence sector, said: “This new virtual offering will enable our customers to develop and test new capabilities more quickly, before being put through their final paces at our specialised test facility.”
He added: “The combined evidence from digital and live environments will bring greater insight and value for money, enabling issues to be identified earlier and better-informed decisions to be taken.”
The companies also intend to use the same digital engineering approach during the operational life of vehicles, supporting lifecycle management as platforms are upgraded, modified or maintained.
Tom Stone, Managing Director of AVL Powertrain UK, said: “We are incredibly proud to have formed a strategic partnership with QinetiQ and we are excited to see how our combined digital engineering approach can advance the development of future defence vehicles through faster design maturity, lifecycle optimisation and reduced physical testing costs.”
Hurn Proving Ground was originally constructed in the 1950s and has since been developed for a range of vehicle test and evaluation work. The site can support multiple vehicles at once and includes terrain intended to reproduce conditions ranging from battlefield environments to emergency and rescue operations.
QinetiQ said the agreement forms part of a broader effort to change how customers access UK test and evaluation infrastructure, combining virtual modelling with physical trials rather than treating them as separate stages of development.
The digital twin of Hurn is intended to let engineers run repeated simulations against the same terrain and test conditions before committing vehicles to live trials, with physical testing then used to validate and refine the digital results.

Are the doors to German universities closing for China’s STEM researchers?
As Berlin pursues de-risking, hundreds of visa applicants in China are rejected each year, an investigation finds
Chinese AI researcher “Joy” waited more than seven months to hear that his visa application for Germany had been rejected.
The 30-year-old had been offered a postdoctoral position at a German technical university but the rejection letter said there was an Ausweisungsinteresse, or public interest in denying him entry.
Citing Section 53 of Germany’s Residence Act, the letter said that for applications involving “study, research and similar employment”, particular attention had to be paid to the possibility that knowledge acquired in Germany could be misused in ways that harmed protected legal interests or other significant German interests.
The letter did not specify which aspect of his research, personal background or application materials amounted to a security risk. And Joy said he was not contacted by German authorities about his research, education or work history during the months of waiting.

How to Make the U.S.-China AI Race Less Dangerous
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

The timing could hardly be worse. Even as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent prepares to meet Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend to discuss AI, President Donald Trump has dismissed public warnings about runaway AI as a “hoax.” Meanwhile, an editorial in the state-owned China Daily accused America’s leading AI companies of using calls for a slowdown to “blunt China’s AI advance.”
Neither the United States nor China is ready to slow down. Neither trusts the other. And rapidly advancing AI systems will not wait for diplomacy to catch up. But these realities do not mean Trump and Xi can ignore the mounting calls for the U.S. and China to talk about AI. Any such dialogue must avoid the two most common pitfalls for U.S.-China diplomacy: setting the ambitions so low that the talks become meaningless or so high that agreement becomes impossible.
Aim too low, and the dialogue becomes a photo op followed by an anodyne communiqué about promoting innovation and reducing risks. Aim too high, chasing sweeping restrictions on frontier development that neither side has the political trust or the capacity to verify and enforce, and the meeting is set up for failure. The former path fails to meet the stakes of the moment; the latter fails to recognize its constraints.
The path to AI safety
A better near-term goal would be for the U.S. and China to pursue AI safety in parallel and demonstrate their progress in practice. That effort should be anchored in technical exchanges that make each country’s AI systems safer on their own terms. The two countries should also establish a protocol to communicate about emerging AI incidents before they spiral into international crises. These steps would represent meaningful progress, far more valuable than lofty statements or unverifiable commitments.
The Trump Administration should push for technical exchanges on how to actually test models for dangerous capabilities and behaviors that neither country wants to see released into the wild. These include AI systems capable of helping amateurs develop bioweapons, or evading human oversight and control. American AI companies have been studying these risks for years, and they have also begun to appear in Chinese technical standards related to safety testing. Exchanging best practices and new insights about how to test for and mitigate these risks could render the systems built in both countries meaningfully safer.
These proposed technical exchanges would not depend on “trust” or even strict “reciprocity” between the two superpowers, nor would they require identical conceptions of AI risk. They would be driven by self-interest. As the most advanced AI models grow even more powerful, both countries have an interest in ensuring that these systems remain controllable, regardless of where they are built or deployed. That will require both countries to improve their model testing, monitoring and safeguards, and share promising findings that could enhance safety without surrendering a competitive edge or undermining national security.
This diplomacy is less like negotiating a sweeping arms-control treaty than establishing shared safety practices and procedures for a technology neither government fully understands or controls. The premise is not that Washington should trust Beijing, or vice versa, but that neither country benefits if the other loses control of a powerful system.
For this approach to work, it must be accompanied by a government-to-government crisis-communication protocol. What if an American AI model escapes its company’s control and hacks the networks of a Chinese company or the Chinese government? What if a Chinese AI-powered drone attacks a U.S. Navy vessel, and neither side can immediately determine whether the incident was accidental or deliberate? What if Washington detects a Chinese model conducting a dangerous cyber operation but cannot tell whether Beijing authorized it or whether a company has lost control of it?
These are not the kind of existential risks President Trump has dismissed, but they are close cousins of incidents already unfolding in real time. The two countries need to lay the basic groundwork for dealing with them. Whether the communication channel succeeds or fails will depend on its operational design. What constitutes a notifiable incident? Who are the designated contacts? How do the two sides signal that an incident was unauthorized without revealing sensitive intelligence? Serious, technically-informed diplomacy will be required to reach even provisional answers to these questions.
One essential feature of the channel should be that information about an incident, at least initially, be transmitted in writing rather than solely by phone. Real-time calls are often poor vehicles for conveying technical information with a Chinese system that runs on committees and documents, increasing the risk of miscommunication and misunderstanding.
Sending a message in writing gives the relevant committees in China the ability to disseminate and analyze it and formulate a response that no individual official in China would feel empowered to give. It also reduces the recipient’s ability to shade or distort the message. Even this approach will be challenging, given China’s spotty record of suspending crisis-communication channels—or simply refusing to use them—precisely when tensions are highest. But it would eliminate one of the stumbling blocks: the refusal to pick up the phone.
How to talk to Beijing
The talks should begin without preconditions or concessions in the broader technology competition. If Beijing seeks to make any progress on AI safety conditional on relief from U.S. export controls on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment, Washington should keep the two issues separate. The goal of AI safety diplomacy is not to turn the United States and China from intense competitors into cooperative partners. It is to keep their competition from producing outcomes neither side wants.
The two sides are nowhere near the political conditions necessary for a sweeping agreement. Trump has rejected calls to slow American AI development, while Beijing increasingly interprets American pacing proposals through the lens of technological containment. Neither side seems prepared to accept broad restrictions on frontier development, and the United States has barely begun to regulate its own AI sector, which is a far more important step toward addressing AI risk than what diplomatic engagement can deliver. That is precisely why the two countries should begin with something narrower.
Starting modestly does not mean succumbing to fatalism. The politics of AI have shifted dramatically in just a few weeks, and advancing capabilities will continue to alter the calculations in both capitals. The upcoming U.S.-China talks will not be the last word. A limited start could build momentum over time, creating channels, expertise, and habits of interaction that will become more valuable if the trajectory of AI development increases Washington’s and Beijing’s levels of concern about severe risks.
Someday, as unlikely as it may seem now, the two countries may realize that they do not have to agree on who should win the AI race to agree that neither side can afford to lose control of it.

Project MACE: Air Mobility keeps moving as Brize Norton runway works progress
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:00 BST
23:00:00 KST

Forty aircraft operating from alternative locations, hundreds of personnel working across the UK, and the RAF's Air Mobility Force continuing to deliver around the clock.
RAF Brize Norton's runway is undergoing its major resurfacing programme, requiring aircraft, engineers, operations teams and support personnel to disperse across a network of airfields while flying operations continue elsewhere.
The undertaking, known as Project MACE (Mobility Agile Combat Employment), is enabling essential infrastructure work while also providing an opportunity to test how the Air Mobility Force can operate from multiple locations.
We sat down with Group Captain Andy McIntyre, Commander Air Wing, for an update on progress and the lessons already being learned.
Keeping Air Mobility moving
"Project MACE is all driven by the 20-year refurbishment, resurfacing of the Brize runway," Group Captain McIntyre explained. With the runway not available, we've had to continue operations by dispersing our fleets across other locations."
Prestwick Airport and Boscombe Down are among the principal operating locations, while East Midlands, Stansted and Bournemouth Airports are also supporting activity.
For the Air Mobility Force, however, the challenge extends far beyond relocating aircraft.
"The Air Mobility Force runs about 20 concurrent lines of activity at any given time. That's 24/7 global standby, activity, training. It's a huge endeavour."
Group Captain Andy McIntyre
Commander Air Wing
Despite the runway closure, that activity has continued uninterrupted.
Runway works remain on track
While operations continue elsewhere, significant engineering work is underway at RAF Brize Norton.
The runway is being resurfaced as part of its planned 20-year infrastructure cycle, with existing material removed before reconstruction begins.
By the end of August, much of the aggregate had been removed and work had moved into the reconstruction phase.
The force dispersed ahead of schedule, allowing contractors to begin work on time, while favourable weather throughout July and August has supported progress.
More than an infrastructure project
Although MACE was created to enable runway works, it has also provided a practical test of Agile Combat Employment (ACE), the RAF's ability to operate from dispersed locations rather than relying solely on established main operating bases.
The experience has focused attention on how the Air Mobility Force can continue generating operational output while working under pressure and from multiple locations.
The move has also strengthened relationships with partner airfields supporting the operation.
Personnel accustomed to operating from RAF Brize Norton have adapted to new infrastructure, processes and operating environments, while host airfields have gained a better understanding of Air Mobility requirements.
The people behind MACE
The Air Wing numbers around 1,600 personnel, with engineers, operations staff, movements specialists, medics, contractors and civilian partners all contributing to the effort.
One of the biggest challenges has been translating processes that normally happen instinctively at RAF Brize Norton into systems that work across multiple locations.
For Group Captain McIntyre, one measure of success is how little disruption others have noticed.
Activities normally coordinated from a single location are now being delivered across multiple sites seamlessly while aircraft and crews continue supporting Defence commitments worldwide.
The project has required new command-and-control arrangements, new relationships and new ways of working, while maintaining the same standards of safety and operational effectiveness.
Looking ahead
Project MACE has demonstrated that the Air Mobility Force can continue delivering global operations even when separated from its home runway.
Perhaps most significantly, the project has demonstrated the adaptability of the people delivering Air Mobility operations every day.
"It's down to every individual and the way that every individual has worked together as one whole team. I'm hugely grateful to everyone for that."
Group Captain Andy McIntyre
Commander Air Wing
For the Air Mobility Force, Project MACE is proving that even when its home runway closes, the mission continues.

Drones Offer Central Asian an Escape From Foreign Dependency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:59:00 UTC
22:59:00 KST

Drones are everywhere in the news and on the frontlines of the Iran-U.S. War and the Russia-Ukraine War, but their most recent use on a battlefield in Central Asia represents a long-term issue – continued dependency on foreign suppliers. The Central Asian states may just be replacing their long-term Russian security dependency with a Turkish one.
Central Asian leaders risk deepening this dependency and worsening security vulnerabilities as they announce deals with foreign suppliers that are often headquartered in a single state – Turkiye. However, developments in 2026 show that opportunities for local development and production that would benefit regional economies without offloading security responsibilities exist. Local politicians just need to invest locally.
In the 2022 border conflict between Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, Turkiye’s Baykar Bayraktar TB2 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) played a well-publicized role. After that conflict, Bishkek decided to deepen its Turkish dependency, ordering Aksungur and Akinci platforms, both from Turkish manufacturers, TAI and Baykar, respectively. It had already ordered additional TB2s and Anka (from TAI) as well.
Drones are certainly cheaper than manned aircraft, but these imported platforms weren’t without cost. Civil servants took a pay hit to fund the purchase of the new systems. And this doesn’t factor in the cost of operations and maintenance. To keep these aircraft flying with spare parts, ammunition, and sensors will require continual funding. When buying any big-ticket item, that platform is committing the state to long-term sustainment with certain suppliers.
Given Turkiye’s mercurial defense policy in recent years, can Bishkek rely on adequate sustainment in the event of another conflict? Turkiye, a NATO ally, hoped to procure F-35s, but acquired Russian S-400s, and is reportedly trying to resell those air defense system to the UAE, before aiming to rejoin F-35 talks. In addition to the initial procurement, depending on a foreign supplier means worrying about receiving additional parts and frames to replace losses from wear and tear or combat operations.
Russia and Ukraine initially looked to foreign support for their attritive war. Tehran supplied Moscow with propeller-driven one-way attack Shahed-136 drones within the first year of the conflict. Yet, Moscow soon realized that the battlefield demanded the systems evolve. Manufacturing facilities were set up inside Russia and improvements were applied to the platform including jet power, anti-radar materials, and better guidance (the latest Russian-made version is dubbed the Geran-4/5).
A similar learning process happened on Kyiv’s side. Chinese-made DJI Mavics, Turkish TB2s, and American Switchblades provided early inventory for Ukrainian forces. Yet, soon manufacturing was moved in country and development processes brought closer to the frontlines, to incorporate the daily lessons of countermeasures, deception, and the realities of a non-permissive battlespace.
While the support systems needed to keep UAVs aloft are simpler than those required for fighters, the current Iran-U.S. War – a much more permissive environment than that in eastern Ukraine – has shown how vulnerable drones are to anti-air capabilities. The U.S. has lost 45 MQ-9 Reaper tactical UAVs, 25 percent of its fleet, since the start of the campaign. Given the years and cost to replace its vehicles, the Pentagon may just switch over to different systems altogether.
Perhaps as a response to its competition and conflict with Bishkek, Dushanbe turned to its own foreign partner to develop a UAV capability. Around the same time, in 2022, it was reported that a program to produce, likely assemble, Iranian Ababil-2s in Tajikistan, was reached. At the signing were Iranian Major General Mohammad Bagheri and Tajik Defense Minister Sherali Mirzo. Bagheri was killed in Israeli air strikes in 2025 and Mirzo was shuffled out of office the same year.
It is unclear how much progress has been made with this facility, or if this was all just a smoke screen. Yet, even if this project had gotten off the ground, it is hard to see how that would not have resulted in significant risk. Manufacturing drones for Tehran could very quickly bring banking and dollar restrictions from Washington, making such a venture a real security risk and potential big money-loser. Ultimately, this appears to be four years with only minimal progress on UAV capabilities for Tajikistan.
Given the pitfalls of foreign dependency, Central Asia may look to develop its own systems, or at the very least license the full production process for its own domestically manufactured unmanned systems. First off, the costs are not prohibitive, unlike, say, developing an armored vehicle, ship, or manned aircraft. Second, the scale and security needs in the region are sufficient to support domestic UAV production.
Third, regional states already have a start on the research, development, and manufacturing needed to make such cooperation a success. Finally, the opportunities of joint drone research and production could lead to increased security cooperation along borders and against transnational threats. Doing so will help to escape the pitfalls of learned incapacity. What’s key though is that local leaders invest in R&D domestically – not outsource solutions.
Take for example the Kyrgyz company Nanospace that announced in May 2026 plans to open a UAV institute in Tash-Dobo, just outside Bishkek. This plan is still in its infancy, but training operators and developing technologies to network numerous small drones is an important step in developing domestic air defense, research, and surveillance, capabilities that are not dependent on foreign assistance.
Central Asia is already a regional education destination. This will continue, unless domestic actors eliminate academic freedom and quell basic research. Eurasian students have long come to Kyrgyzstan for higher education, whether at the University of Central Asia or the American University of Central Asia. Kazakhstan is a major international academic hub now as well, with some 30,000-plus foreign students attending branch institutions of Cardiff and Woosong, as well as attending homegrown universities like Al Farabi and Eurasian National. So, there are major opportunities to network skills and technologies that could benefit human capital and defense development for the entire region.
Meanwhile, an exhibit in the late summer of 2026 in Uzbekistan highlighted a new Shunqor-8 drone interceptor from the Center for Innovative Technologies that could serve as a cheap alternative to traditional missile defense. Usually, Russian exports have provided most of the region’s air defense. In recent years, for example, even amid a war that is demanding major stocks of air defenses, Kyrgyzstan demonstrated S-300PS and Tor-M2KM (long- and short-range) SAMs and Tajikistan took deliveries from Russia.
The region still connects to legacy CIS Joint Air Defense System (ADS), so this is another important step in terms of Central Asia states providing for their own defense. Boilerplate statements suggested “modernizing” the ADS and advancing cooperation in 2026, though there was a mention of AI being integrated. In addition, the quantities being delivered to the region are likely insufficient for any prolonged conflict. Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan already have experience with joint venture manufacturing lines. There’s no reason for Central Asian states to continue to procure UAVs from abroad rather than building them (even with licenses) at home.
Now, clearly the region won’t replace every imported component with a domestic analogue. Local manufacturers, for example, are unlikely to compete in the international market for electro-optical/infrared sensors. Yet, for smaller first-person view UAVs, and tactical UAVs, there’s plenty of room for choices in terms of cameras for reconnaissance or navigation systems that are mapped to the local environment and do not depend on one satellite network. Anticipating such payload flexibility can help Central Asian states avoid getting “locked in” to one new partner that just supplants the old one.
One-way attack (OWA) drones are another opportunity for Central Asian states to better, more effectively, target security threats. One of the issues in recent combat operations has been an employment of seemingly indiscriminate or inaccurate artillery fire and combat aircraft strikes. OWA drones offer a way to address this and safeguard civilian lives. For example, during the 2022 Tajik-Kyrgyz conflict, indiscriminate artillery shelling and automatic weapons fire contributed to significant civilian casualties in Khistevarz, Ovchi Kalacha, Ak-Sai, and Margun, among other locations.
In much earlier conflicts, manned aircraft with unguided weapons were ineffective, or suffered significant casualties, including in Rasht and the Ferghana Valley region. The cost of manned combat aircraft is such that most states in the region cannot afford such a fleet. And in any case, even if affordable, this still leads to foreign dependency. Training and education, parts and repairs, and operations even depended in large part on Russia. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are not unique in this, but surely this is an opportunity to reduce civilian casualties in conflict zones and limit reliance on a foreign power.
Finally, there are a host of interconnected challenges that drones can help the region address. Everything from detecting smuggling and trafficking across remote borders; to monitoring water flow from glaciers and water use downstream; or securing international events like the Nomad Games, there are huge opportunities for cooperative monitoring and security efforts with shared drone capabilities.
Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan don’t need Russia or China to address these challenges. They don’t need to depend on a foreign manufacturer for drones or the capabilities to produce many of the UAVs that have wide-ranging applications for the economy, environment, and defense of the region. And, to paraphrase some advice from Kenneth Waltz: they should be considering how to counterbalance new hegemonic threats, not swapping one vulnerability for another. Indeed, Astana is already headed in this direction.
The international order is being remade in real time, so regional governments need to look to their own security. Great powers might “ignore” their smaller neighbors for a time, but who’s to say when that benign neglect will come to an end. Investment in joint education, training, and production today can enable these states to address problems regionally, and sever dependencies at the same time, and make the whole region more secure from external threats over the long run. If they wait until the next regional conflict, it may be too late.

WHO flags growing health workforce gap as doctors and patients age
GENEVA – The World Health Organization (WHO) warned on Sept 18 of a gap in the medical workforce around the world in the 2030s, with a quarter of doctors set to retire in the next decade.
“In many countries, both our populations and health workers are ageing at the same time. This can intensify the projected global shortage of 11.1 million health workers by 2030,” the WHO said in a statement accompanying a major report on workforce trends based on data from over 100 countries.
By 2030, 67 countries are projected to lack sufficient staffing to maintain the standards of medical treatment they currently enjoy, it said.
To maintain the current density of medical staff to the population, an additional 832,000 health workers are needed, and this could increase reliance on foreign health care workers in poorer countries, the report said, potentially impacting healthcare standards there.
Higher income countries, including many in Europe, are set to be the hardest hit since they have a higher share of older healthcare workers, the report said.
In these countries, one in three doctors will retire in the next 10 years, it said. REUTERS

“I didn’t have any doubts,” Desronvil said in his first public statement to News Nation on Thursday, rejecting claims from fellow jurors that he had wavered during deliberations.
“Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned,” he added.
🇺🇸 A single juror blocked an insanity acquittal in the Lindsay Clancy case, and now defends that vote.
Michael Desronvil was the lone holdout after the 6-week, widely publicized Massachusetts trial.
He argues the evidence showed the mother PLANNED the 2023 killings of her 3…
Desronvil has also portrayed the furious reaction to his vote as ideological. According to a true-crime host who interviewed him at length off-camera, the juror said he was a conservative Republican on a panel dominated by Democrats and described some of the other jurors as liberal “activists.”
His newly hired lawyer, Edward Paltzik, has leaned into the political divide, describing Desronvil as an “American Hero and Champion of Justice,” a committed Christian and a supporter of President Donald Trump.
Clancy, meanwhile, has attracted an intensely mobilized following, particularly among women and advocates focused on postpartum mental illness, who view the killings as the catastrophic result of psychosis and failures in maternal mental healthcare.
Several fellow jurors have publicly criticized Desronvil since the mistrial, accusing him of refusing to accept their interpretation of the evidence and having “the hardest time getting off the fact that Lindsay viciously killed her children.”
Following the mistrial earlier this month, Clancy has further strengthened her legal team, bringing in high-profile Boston attorney Martin Weinberg to try to have the case thrown out before prosecutors can put her on trial again.
District Attorney Timothy Cruz has not publicly announced a final decision on a retrial, although Fox News has reported that prosecutors plan to pursue one. Meanwhile, legal experts note that a second trial would likely end in another deadlock as the prosecution would face a significant challenge in finding 12 jurors who would unanimously reject Clancy’s insanity defense.
Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington has meanwhile floated alternatives, including a judge-only trial on reduced charges, but says he would not accept any deal that sends her to prison. Her case is due back in court on September 29.
