To Succeed in AI, South Korea Is Reinventing Its Developmental State Model
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:56:00 UTC
22:56:00 KST

South Korea has embarked on an ambitious plan by launching the “AI for All” initiative, which aims to make artificial intelligence (AI) widely accessible to all its citizens. This initiative reflects a broader effort to integrate AI into almost every corner of Korean society. Rather than treating AI simply as another emerging technology, South Korea increasingly views it as a technology that will help realize its domestic economic development plans and geoeconomic objectives, retain its technological advantages in key strategic industries, and gain a strong foothold in emerging technologies amid intensifying technological competition.
The South Korean government plans to provide AI learning opportunities to approximately 5.14 million people in 2026. To support this initiative, it is developing AI services based on South Korea’s sovereign AI models, including a general-purpose AI chatbot that citizens will be able to use without charges or usage limits. More importantly, Seoul’s long-term ambition is to move toward an environment in which its citizens can have access to their own AI agents.
This plan can be understood as part of a broader trend among East Asian countries, particularly South Korea and China, toward emphasizing the rapid implementation and widespread application of AI. This approach reflects the distinction drawn by Kai-Fu Lee in his book “AI Superpowers: China, Silicon Valley, and the New World Order,” in which he contrasted China’s implementation-driven model with the innovation-first strategy associated with the United States. It also differs from the European approach, which places greater emphasis on AI governance, regulation, fundamental rights, and data privacy.
In many parts of the world, especially in liberal democracies, AI remains a subject of debate over safety concerns. In South Korea and other East Asian countries, however, the debate is different: it focuses on how rapidly AI can be deployed. The geoeconomic logic behind this approach is that rapid deployment will not only strengthen their positions in the AI ecosystem but also enable them to become future leaders.
South Korea views AI as one of the most promising next-generation growth engines and a strategic technology that will determine the country’s economic competitiveness. Seoul is learning from its historical experience, as the country’s growth has largely depended on technological upgrading and export-oriented manufacturing. Therefore, South Korea has linked AI to national survival, just as it did with semiconductors, which now form the backbone of the South Korean economy. South Korea’s strength in the semiconductor industry also supports its advancement in AI, as the expansion of AI is closely connected to growing demand in semiconductor-related sectors, including advanced memory, computing infrastructure, and AI chips.
A Shared National Commitment to AI
The continuing legacy of developmental state practices in South Korea has generated a unique level of commitment among the state, businesses, and society to realizing the country’s national ambitions. Historically, South Korea’s rapid technological advancement resulted from the state’s long-term planning, the establishment of national targets and industrial strategies, businesses’ active support and compliance, and, most importantly, society’s largely unopposed embrace of rapid, growth-oriented development. This national consensus prioritizes technological advancement and the fostering of key strategic industries over other considerations. The same pattern can clearly be observed in the case of AI.
In South Korea, political parties across the ideological spectrum support not only the rapid advancement of AI but also the goal of making the country a leading AI superpower. When the conservative government led by Yoon Suk-yeol was in power, South Korea set the ambitious goal of becoming one of the world’s top three AI powers, alongside the United States and China. The progressive government under Lee Jae-myung came to power in 2025 after Yoon was impeached, amid significant political conflict and turmoil involving conservative political forces. Nevertheless, one objective remained unchanged: South Korea’s national ambition to become a world-leading AI power. Therefore, a national consensus exists around realizing this ambition, regardless of changes in government and the high level of bipartisan political conflict within South Korea. That’s a consensus rarely seen in many liberal democracies.
The government’s ambition is also being reinforced by extensive business participation and, more importantly, growing societal demand for AI adoption. Frequent meetings between the government and business leaders are taking place in Seoul, with both sides agreeing that they must cooperate extensively to realize South Korea’s national ambitions.
Even more important is the growing social demand for AI implementation in South Korea. The general view is that rapid deployment will enable society to adopt AI more quickly, ultimately creating new opportunities for both the public and the country. According to a recent survey, almost seven out of ten South Koreans believe that AI services, deployed in collaboration with the government and corporations, will positively impact society.
This contrasts sharply with debates in Western liberal democracies, where AI adoption is often discussed in terms of privacy violations, job displacement, and other risks. Moreover, state-led AI planning is often viewed with greater suspicion in societies where anti-statist attitudes are more widespread. This does not mean that such concerns do not exist in South Korean society. However, many people appear to place these concerns within the broader context of the national priority of technological advancement and the belief that South Korea should not fall behind in the global AI race.
Deploying Developmental State Practices
In implementing its AI strategy, Seoul is deploying the practices of the developmental state, through which it previously achieved rapid technological advancement and built globally competitive strategic industries, including semiconductors and shipbuilding. Under this model, the state acts as a proactive planner, investor, and coordinator while collaborating closely with major domestic conglomerates.
Such practices are less common in neoliberal regulatory states, where proactive state intervention and close state–business collaboration – particularly with large corporations – are often viewed negatively. In South Korea, however, the state is actively fostering AI development in cooperation with major domestic companies. Meanwhile, many other countries, particularly liberal democracies, remain preoccupied with debates concerning AI regulation, oversight, and responsibility.
As a result, South Korea has moved far ahead in terms of large-scale investment in AI. While many parts of the world are waiting for, or heavily dependent on, private-sector investment in AI, the South Korean government is taking the lead in creating and expanding a substantial domestic AI market. One important example is South Korea’s decision to increase its national AI budget from 3.3 trillion won in 2025 to 10.1 trillion won in 2026 – almost three times the previous year’s allocation. This expansion occurred despite concerns about the country’s fiscal health. Such aggressive spending on a particular strategic industry also reflects South Korea’s developmental state philosophy of concentrating substantial resources on selected industries with high growth potential.
In addition to its investment role, the state is acting as a coordinator, which is another characteristic of developmental state practices. Under this model, state agencies play proactive roles as pilot agencies responsible for fostering strategic industries. For example, the Ministry of Science and ICT has been actively working with major conglomerates and other technology companies to establish consortia and accelerate AI development and implementation. This was evident in the ministry’s 2025 selection of five industry-led teams – Naver Cloud, Upstage, SK Telecom, NC AI, and LG AI Research – to develop sovereign foundation models.
More recently, the ministry selected three consortia, led respectively by SK Telecom, KT, and Kakao, to operate the “AI for All” project. In both initiatives, the ministry has acted as a pilot agency coordinating public and private actors around national strategic objectives.
This extensive collaboration is not limited to ministerial-level coordination. The government is also providing financial and material support to foster public–private partnerships. For example, to accelerate the implementation of “AI for All,” the South Korean government will provide the three selected consortia with access to up to 512 Nvidia B200 GPUs. Moreover, the government will subsidize part of the expenses involved in developing and operating these AI services.
The government will also finance public access by supporting the provision of AI chatbots to citizens without subscription fees or usage limits. Above all, participating companies will gain access to public service systems, enabling them to connect their chatbots with public AI agents that provide services related to taxation, healthcare appointments, education, and government support programs. Such access has generally remained restricted for private companies in many other parts of the world.
The Global Implications of South Korea’s AI Strategy
South Korea’s rapid deployment of AI across society offers several insights into the country’s political-economic approach to AI in particular and strategic industries more generally. By encouraging the widespread use of AI at an early stage, the government aims to create a large domestic market in which South Korean companies can develop, test, and improve their AI models, thereby supporting South Korea’s sovereign AI strategy. This approach strongly recalls the developmental state model that South Korea previously adopted to accelerate the growth of its strategic industries.
Indeed, South Korea’s lead in AI deployment is driven by a geoeconomic logic through which it seeks to maintain its technological advantages and become an AI superpower. More importantly, it reflects the deployment of developmental state practices, with the state playing a pivotal role and fostering collaboration with South Korea’s major technology companies to realize its national ambitions. Equally significant is the broad societal support for this state-business nexus in AI development. This is a distinctive feature carried over from South Korea’s developmental state era and is once again visible in its approach to AI deployment.
Nevertheless, a major challenge remains: how South Korea will address its shortage of AI talent. If South Korea is able to overcome this challenge, we may witness the emergence of a new technological power in the global AI race alongside the United States and China.
South Korea’s efforts to become one of the world’s top three AI powers also have global implications. If South Korea continues to compete with the U.S. and China for a leading position in AI, it would not be surprising to see a large number of South Korean AI companies, alongside American and Chinese firms, emerge as dominant players in the global market. As seen in today’s semiconductor industry, where companies from a small number of countries dominate and control key technologies, we may similarly witness the emergence of an AI landscape in which companies from only a few countries exercise extensive control, while the rest of the world remains primarily on the consumer side.
South Korea’s rapid deployment of AI across society is likely to place it among the first group of countries. The actions taken today are likely to produce results for countries actively developing AI, in contrast to the more passive approach currently adopted by many others. It should therefore not be surprising if South Korea emerges as a global AI leader in the near future.

What Are the Key Steps to Obtain a Crypto Exchange License in Poland?  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:54:22 UTC
22:54:22 KST

Setting up a crypto exchange platform in Poland means working through a defined registration path built around anti-money laundering compliance rather than a conventional banking-style license. Companies pursuing a Poland crypto exchange license need to establish a solid corporate structure, prepare compliance documentation, and submit their application to the appropriate authority. Each stage carries specific expectations, and skipping preparation typically results in delays or requests for corrections. This article walks through the key steps founders should follow to register a crypto exchange business in Poland.
Establishing the Corporate Foundation for an Exchange
A properly structured company is the starting point for any exchange platform seeking registration in Poland. The registering authority reviews the corporate setup closely, since it forms the basis for evaluating the applicant's legitimacy.
- register a limited liability company with a Polish registered address and a defined share capital structure;
- appoint management board members with no criminal record related to financial or economic offences;
- identify all beneficial owners and prepare documentation confirming their identity;
- define the exact scope of exchange services, including fiat-to-crypto and crypto-to-crypto operations;
- open a corporate bank account to support the platform's operational activities.
Completing these steps carefully reduces the likelihood of the tax administration requesting corrections during the review stage.
Preparing Compliance Documentation for the Application
Exchange platforms handle client funds directly, which means compliance documentation receives particularly scrutiny during the registration process. Polish regulators expect clear evidence that the applicant understands its obligations under anti-money laundering legislation.
1. Draft an internal AML policy covering client identification, transaction monitoring, and suspicious activity reporting.
2. Appoint a compliance officer with confirmed training in financial crime prevention.
3. Prepare a risk assessment procedure tailored to exchange operations specifically.
4. Establish record-keeping practices for client transactions and verification data.
5. Compile the full documentation package for submission to the Register of Activities in the Field of Virtual Currencies.
A thorough compliance package at this stage often determines how quickly the application moves through review.
Submitting the Application and Managing the Review Period
Once the corporate and compliance groundwork is complete, the application goes to the Polish tax administration for review. Authorities may request additional clarifications regarding the ownership structure or the AML procedures submitted. Responding to these requests promptly keeps the process on track and avoids unnecessary extensions to the review period. Polish VASP registration authorizes activity within Poland only. Offering services in other EEA markets requires CASP authorization under MiCA.
Adapting to the Upcoming MiCA Licensing Standard
Poland's current registration model is set to be replaced by the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, which introduces a unified authorization framework across the European Union. The transitional period ended 1 July 2026; national registration no longer authorizes crypto-asset services. Poland currently has no functioning CASP licensing pathway, since the implementing legislation designating KNF as competent authority has not been passed. Platforms must currently either wait for that legislation or obtain CASP authorization elsewhere in the EU and passport it into Poland.
Exchange platforms that begin aligning their internal structures with MiCA standards early typically face a far smoother transition when national registration is phased out.
Registering a crypto exchange in Poland involves careful corporate planning, thorough compliance preparation, and consistent communication with regulators throughout the review process. Companies entering this market should treat each step as part of a long-term compliance strategy rather than a one-time formality.

UTMA founder Viktoras Gecas eyes Baltic, and beyond, expansion after rapid growth in Lithuania  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:54:13 UTC
22:54:13 KST

Viktoras Gecas, founder and head of the martial arts organisation UTMA (Unique and Talented Martial Artists), and his team are preparing for the organisation’s biggest tournaments this autumn. UTMA 19 will take place at Kaunas’ Zalgirio Arena at 7pm on September 26, with star fighters Sergejus Maslobojevas and Dominykas Dirkstys meeting in the main event. On October 24 at 7pm, UTMA will welcome fans to Arena Vilnius. Gecas spoke to The Baltic Times about the organisation’s business model and its planned expansion beyond Lithuania.
The popularity of UTMA tournaments in Lithuania has grown very rapidly. How do you explain this success beyond the conventional answer that “a lot of work has gone into it”? Which figures are particularly important to you?
By believing that sport can grow in this country, because that is the global trend. Combat sport is one of the world’s most dynamic sports, and UTMA’s success merely demonstrates that we are engaging more and more people who are beginning to take an interest in combat sport.
How has UTMA’s business model evolved since you began operating in 2022?
When we started, we knew nothing – we just tried things. After every attempt, we identified our mistakes and tried to become better and correct them. Over time, we grew into a large organisation.
Could you give us a glimpse behind the scenes at UTMA? Where does its revenue come from? What proportion comes from participation fees, sponsorship, broadcasts and merchandise sales? Which revenue stream is growing fastest?
UTMA generates its principal revenue directly from people – ticket buyers and live-stream viewers. That is why I have repeatedly emphasised that UTMA is an organisation belonging to the people of Lithuania.
Who did you learn from and draw experience from when establishing UTMA Group? Which countries and organisations do you now look to for inspiration?
I have always admired ONE Championship for its order and meticulous precision, but over time I have become a fan of Dana White and the UFC because I increasingly understand that this sports business is impossible without showmanship.
Presumably, as the owner of a successful business – and its principal shareholder – you receive requests for advice and consultation from similar organisations elsewhere?
All sorts of things happen, but private conversations should remain private.
What types of brands do you work with, and what is the average value of a sponsorship package for one UTMA tournament?
The general sponsor of the UTMA organisation is TOPsport. We work with various brands, while our agreements with entities purchasing advertising are confidential.
Organising major tournaments is complicated. What are the largest cost items, and how do you manage to remain profitable? When we met, you said that only tournaments staged at Lithuania’s largest venues – Kaunas’ Zalgirio Arena and Vilnius’ Twinsbet Arena – are economically sustainable and profitable. Is that correct?
Fighters’ fees – which are the highest in Lithuania – event servicing costs, production costs and broadcast security costs. I could go on and on, while the answers concerning our success are, of course, a commercial secret.
What specifically did you offer Lithuania’s best-known fighters – Stanionis, Maslobojevas and Dirkstys – to persuade them to join UTMA? How much does the winner of a UTMA tournament at Kaunas’ Zalgirio Arena receive?
We can offer, and do offer, consistency. This is one of the most important conditions in combat sport because athletes’ careers are very short, while consistency and a clear plan are among the most important components of a combat-sport career.
Are you considering expansion into the other Baltic countries? What has already been done towards that goal?
We are considering it, and we will have some specific news very soon.
With geopolitical hotspots such as Russia, Ukraine and Israel, you presumably have to tread very carefully when selecting partners and planning your activities. What is your “golden rule” in this respect?
We have repeatedly stated publicly that we support Ukraine in every possible way. For this reason, we have made the categorical decision not to accept fighters who compete or have competed there. However, as sporting trends show, Russians and Belarusians are increasingly returning to the global sporting arena. That is regrettable, but I would like to take this opportunity to express our support for Ukraine once again.
Do you devote sufficient attention to the social dimension of UTMA as a business model? Outside the ring and on social media, viewers and readers see the glamorous side of fighters’ lives. I have not heard stories about UTMA helping a promising athlete find their place in life and get back on their feet. Do you not think such stories are needed?
That is a good idea, and I have already shared it with the team.
Some members of the public and young people dislike the way fighters trade insults and make demeaning gestures before tournaments – behaviour that would be unimaginable in basketball, for example. What is your view? What do UTMA’s rules say about it?
UTMA’s rules are an internal organisational matter and are intended exclusively for fighters. The rules provide for penalties for inappropriate conduct. Everything else is part of the show, and, as I have said, showmanship is essential in combat sport. However, the right balance must always be maintained.
Where do you see UTMA Group in five years?
Expanded across Europe, with deep roots in Lithuania.
How many UTMA-affiliated sports clubs do you have in the country? On what basis do they operate?
UTMA does not affiliate sports clubs.
What has this business given you personally – as an individual, a businessman and a young man?
Patience. This business has clearly taught me that patience is essential if you want to achieve results.

Source: Reuters, citing two people familiar with the plan, as reported by European Pravda

Possible locations for the summit include Israel, the United Arab Emirates and India, they added.

Dmitriev attended a meeting in Moscow this month with US representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

The AfD hopes the meeting will demonstrate its foreign policy credentials and expose the government's failure to tackle high energy prices, one of the sources said.

Europe to test secure satellite communications against disruption and cyberattacks  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:53:33 UTC
22:53:33 KST

TALLINN - Cybersecurity company CybExer is leading a ten-company European consortium developing an end-to-end capability to test and validate protected satellite communications linked to IRIS², the EU’s future secure satellite connectivity system.
Europe needs to know how secure satellite communications will perform under interference, disruption, and cyberattack before governments and critical operations depend on them. The new capability will make it possible to test this across the full communications chain, from the satellite link and ground infrastructure to the end user, under realistic disruption and adversarial conditions - without putting operational systems at risk.
Testing scenarios include satellite communications supporting drone operations and command and control in contested environments. Disruption to a satellite link can affect not only the aircraft but the wider communications chain through ground infrastructure to the operator.
The activity forms part of the IRIS² Low-LEO Pre-Operational and De-Risk Activities Consolidation Phase, within the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Programme Related to EU Secure Connectivity.
Laurent Jaffart, Director of ESA’s Resilience, Navigation and Connectivity, commented: “The future of secure connectivity will not be defined by a single technology or a single orbit. It will come from combining complementary capabilities and having the flexibility to adapt as Europe’s needs evolve. Through its Low-LEO activities, ESA looks forward to working hand-in-hand with the European Commission and European industry to explore what comes next for IRIS²; to shape the capabilities that will support Europe’s future connectivity needs.”
IRIS² is now moving into full-scale deployment, with a main constellation of 348 satellites and a 12-year concession valued at €15.6bn. It is intended to provide secure connectivity for governments and other critical users, including in situations where communications are disrupted or deliberately targeted.
Liina Vahtras, Minister of Economy and Industry of Estonia, said: “Estonia has established itself as both a cyber and a space nation, and CybExer’s project shows how these two strengths can reinforce each other. An Estonian company leading an international consortium on a European Space Agency project demonstrates that our companies can compete in major European technology programmes. Projects like this bring new expertise, high-value jobs and business opportunities to Estonia, while helping our companies grow internationally. The more we can develop technologies that Europe needs for its security and economy, the stronger both Estonia and Europe will be.”
Kristiina Omri, Vice President of Special Programmes at CybExer and Project Manager, said: “Once technology has been deployed in orbit, identifying weaknesses - and fixing them - becomes considerably more difficult. We need reliable evidence of how these systems behave under disruption and attack before they become part of critical operations. By bringing together expertise in space, telecommunications and cybersecurity, we can look beyond individual components and understand the resilience of the whole communications chain.”
The project formally launched on 17 September, when the parallel activities selected for ESA’s Low-LEO Consolidation Phase come together for a joint kick-off at the European Space Astronomy Centre (ESAC) in Madrid.
As prime contractor, CybExer is working with CGI Estonia, CR14, DamoTech, Hellas Sat, KrattWorks, M3S Italia, Magister Solutions, Rantelon and Spaceit, bringing together companies from Estonia, Finland, Greece and Italy.
About CybExer
CybExer develops cyber ranges and controlled digital environments that recreate real-world systems and infrastructure for testing, training and exercises. These environments allow organisations to test technologies, systems and operational responses under realistic conditions without exposing live infrastructure to risk. CybExer works across defence, government, critical infrastructure and space. CybExer’s wider ESA work in space cybersecurity spans satellite operations simulation, Space Cyber Range research and development, and cybersecurity testing for satellite and ground systems.
About IRIS²
IRIS² - Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite - is the European Union’s secure satellite connectivity system for governmental and other critical users. ESA’s Low-LEO Pre-Operational and De-Risk Activities are designed to mature and validate new governmental services and capabilities before potential operational integration. The main IRIS² constellation will comprise 348 satellites, with first launches planned for 2029.
About ESA Programme Related to EU Secure Connectivity
Under the overall responsibility of the European Commission, IRIS² is a bold endeavour to build a space-based secure and resilient connectivity network that elevates Europe’s strategic autonomy and competitiveness, where and when it matters most. ESA acts on behalf of the European Commission as the qualification and validation authority for the governmental infrastructure of the Union Secure Connectivity Programme. It manages development and validation contracts supporting the initial space and ground segments, verifies end-to-end system, service, and security performance against EC requirements, and coordinates these activities with ESA’s own programme.
Within this programme, the IRIS² Low-LEO Pre-Operational and De-Risk Activities components provide a rapid and recurrent mechanism for validating potential new governmental services and associated mission concepts in orbit up to a pre-operational level, subject to successful maturation and later programme level decisions of integration into the operational EU IRIS² baseline.
Ultimately, these activities aim at contributing to the continued evolution and enhancement of IRIS² services and capabilities, supporting Europe’s long-term leadership in space in an ever-changing world.

The 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026), scheduled for October 5-9 in Türkiye’s Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, has set records for research submissions and early registrations.
More than 10,000 participants from over 100 countries are expected at the NEST Convention Center, where the event’s loggerhead sea turtle mascot, Turquoise, will welcome guests.
The International Astronautical Congress is the world’s largest and most prestigious annual gathering for the global space and aviation community.
Organised annually by the International Astronautical Federation, the congress will be coordinated by Türkiye’s Industry and Technology Ministry.
The congress will be hosted by the Turkish Space Agency and co-hosted by SAHA Istanbul, Türkiye’s largest defence, aerospace and space industry cluster.
IAC organisers received 8,330 research abstracts from 108 countries, setting records for both the number of submissions and participating nations.
The figure surpassed about 7,000 abstracts submitted for the 2024 congress in Milan and 6,400 for the 2025 congress in Sydney.
Türkiye accounted for 1,810 abstracts, the highest number submitted by a single country in IAC history. Turkish researchers also recorded the highest number of accepted papers, with 674.
Following evaluation, 4,077 studies were accepted directly and 542 were placed on a waiting list. More than 4,000 presentations will be held across over 180 technical sessions.
The congress also received more than 3,000 early registrations from 83 countries, setting a record for early registrations.
Outreach activities at universities, Türkiye’s Sky Observation Event and TEKNOFEST encouraged students, academics and researchers across the country to submit their work to the congress.

Search expert: Wise to have a relative know your secret mushroom spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:53:00 UTC
22:53:00 KST

Search expert: Wise to have a relative know your secret mushroom spot
People heading into the woods should wear white clothing or a neon-colored reflective vest, determine their location before entering the woods and tell a family member or trusted friend where their secret mushroom-picking spot is, a PPA expert told ERR.
Every year, police have to search the woods for dozens of missing mushroom pickers. Last year, there were more than 170 such cases.
There are several ways to search for missing people. "The terrain has a major impact on which method we choose. Is it a patch of woodland surrounded on all sides by a highway, railway or settlement, meaning that whichever way you go, you'll eventually come out of the woods? Or is it a forest that starts near Rõngu and, figuratively speaking, you don't come out of it until after Riga?" said Kert Kotkas, head of the Police and Border Guard Board's (PPA) remote monitoring unit.
Whenever a drone can be used in a search, it is. "Even if we don't find the person, we can use a drone to rule out some places where we know they definitely aren't," Kotkas said, adding that no forest offers ideal conditions for a drone.
When the weather is overcast and even the tops of cell towers are shrouded in clouds, it is very difficult for a helicopter to fly to a location and begin operations. "Drones are also limited in how high they can fly and it's possible that the only thing that can help is a good dog," Kotkas said.
"If we know where the mushroom picker may have entered the woods, the person's scent may still be on the ground. The dog can pick up the scent and follow the trail. If the mushroom picker's vehicle has been left somewhere, it's better not to touch it and to call in a dog handler who can start from the scene and track down the missing person," dog handler Allan Kaljur said.
Mushroom pickers can also do quite a lot themselves to help rescuers find them quickly.
"Police ask what the person was wearing when they went into the woods. A white bucket and a white hat give us a better chance of finding someone quickly. In Estonian forests, one of the best things to wear is a neon-colored reflective vest, which is extremely visible regardless of the season," Kotkas said.
According to Kotkas, there are also times when the drone pilot and dog handler can be physically close to each other. "Estonian forests can be such dense thickets that it's entirely possible not to see a person in the brush just three meters away from you," Kotkas said.
"During the day, nothing beats white clothing and a white bucket; they are very easy to spot with a drone. Once a missing person has been found, a drone equipped with a loudspeaker can be used to call out to them and if they follow the drone, we can guide them out of the woods," Kotkas said, explaining the drone's role in the search process.
Police say people should get as clear an idea as possible of their location on a map before entering the woods and share it with a friend. "You don't have to tell the whole world about your secret mushroom-picking spots, but you should share them with a circle of trusted friends," Kotkas said.

The cost of Iran’s regional leverage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:52:49 UTC
22:52:49 KST

The cost of Iran’s regional leverage
Tehran’s use of pressure across the region is putting its rapprochement with Gulf states under increasing strain.
For more than two years, the 2023 Beijing-brokered agreement between Saudi Arabia and Iran seemed to mark a shift in Gulf politics: Away from confrontation and towards managed coexistence. The agreement neither ended strategic rivalry nor sought to do so. Its significance was more limited but still consequential: It created political space for competition to be managed without repeatedly spilling into direct regional escalation. That space came under severe strain earlier this year, when direct Iranian attacks on Saudi Arabia led Riyadh to expel Iran’s military attache and four other embassy staff. Renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi territory and the postponement of planned talks in Oman are now placing what remains of that diplomatic framework under further strain. Together, these developments expose a deeper contradiction at the heart of Tehran’s regional strategy: Can Iran sustain stable diplomatic relations with its Arab Gulf neighbours while continuing to draw strategic leverage from a regional network capable of directly threatening their security?
The attacks: When Yemen’s war crosses the border
The latest escalation marks an important shift in the trajectory of the conflict in Yemen. Fighting that had largely remained within Yemen’s borders has once again crossed into Saudi territory, drawing the consequences of the war directly into the Gulf security environment. On September 8, the Houthis launched a coordinated wave of drone and ballistic missile attacks against several Saudi cities and strategic sites, including Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran.
The significance of this escalation lies not only in the intensity of the attacks but also in their timing and geographic reach. The strikes coincided with renewed fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces around Bab al-Mandeb, one of the region’s most strategically important maritime chokepoints. By mid-September, the escalation had also produced serious humanitarian consequences, displacing tens of thousands of people within Yemen and pushing others across the Red Sea to Djibouti. The Houthi seizure of Mocha and strategic islands around Bab al-Mandeb further underscored the confrontation’s strategic dimension. The conflict, in other words, is no longer defined solely by control of territory within Yemen. It is increasingly tied to control of strategic geography and to the capacity to project pressure beyond Yemen’s borders.
Why now: Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the expanding geography of pressure
The timing matters because the escalation is unfolding alongside growing pressure elsewhere in the region. Since Israel and the United States launched their war on Iran in February, Tehran has severely restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, sharply increasing the importance of Saudi Arabia’s western export routes through the Red Sea. That shift has, in turn, increased the strategic importance of Bab al-Mandeb as an alternative gateway for energy flows.
These developments connect two maritime theatres that are often analysed separately. Hormuz is the Gulf’s principal eastern gateway; Bab al-Mandeb provides access to the Red Sea from the west. Simultaneous pressure around both creates a broader geography of strategic vulnerability, extending the consequences of confrontation well beyond the immediate battlefield. In that context, the Houthi position along Yemen’s western coast takes on significance beyond the internal dynamics of the Yemeni conflict. It becomes another point through which pressure can be exerted across the wider regional security system.
The central issue, then, is not whether Tehran directly determines every Houthi military decision. More important is whether developments in Yemen advance or complement Iran’s broader strategic objectives. When pressure around Hormuz coincides with instability around Bab al-Mandeb, two distinct maritime arenas can begin to operate as interconnected sources of leverage. The result is more than an expansion of the conflict itself: It is an expansion of the geography through which strategic pressure can be applied.
The Oman talks: When escalation narrows the space for diplomacy
The postponement of the Oman-hosted talks shows how quickly military escalation can constrict the political space available for diplomacy. Gulf states and Iran had been expected to meet in Salalah to discuss arrangements for managing navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, building on an existing understanding between Tehran and Muscat. The proposed talks were intended to focus on practical maritime security measures, including navigation arrangements and mechanisms for reducing risk around one of the world’s most strategically important waterways.
The regional environment, however, changed faster than the diplomatic process could absorb. Bahrain had already indicated that it would not participate, and Oman subsequently announced the postponement of the meeting, with no new date announced, concluding that the conditions required for productive negotiations were no longer in place. Iran acknowledged that the delay followed concerns raised by some regional states, while reports also pointed to disagreements over elements of the proposed framework.
The importance of the postponement therefore extends beyond the cancellation of a single meeting. It exposes a broader problem for regional diplomacy: Negotiations cannot easily be insulated from the security environment in which they occur. For Saudi Arabia, discussing maritime security with Tehran while simultaneously facing missile and drone attacks from an Iran-aligned actor created an increasingly difficult political contradiction. The question was no longer simply whether dialogue could continue, but whether enough strategic confidence remained for that dialogue to produce meaningful results.
The current escalation therefore raises a broader strategic question: Can Iran continue to extract leverage from regional pressure while preserving its longer-term objective of stable relations with its Arab Gulf neighbours? Since Saudi-Iranian diplomatic relations were restored in 2023, Tehran has sought to present regional dialogue as an alternative to permanent confrontation and to demonstrate that Gulf security can be managed through engagement rather than continual escalation. The durability of that approach, however, depends on more than keeping diplomatic channels open. It also requires convincing neighbouring states that rapprochement can provide a meaningful degree of strategic reassurance.
The current pattern of escalation puts that premise under increasing strain. When missile and drone attacks by an Iran-aligned actor reach Saudi territory at the same time that instability grows around Bab al-Mandeb and Hormuz, Gulf states may find it increasingly difficult to separate their diplomatic relationship with Tehran from their wider security concerns. Again, the decisive issue is not whether Iran directly controls every Houthi decision. Strategically, what matters is the perception that Tehran continues to benefit from a regional network capable of imposing costs on neighbouring states during periods of confrontation.
That dynamic creates a difficult paradox for Tehran. Iran has long sought to prevent the emergence of a more consolidated regional security architecture directed against it. Yet as the geography of pressure widens, Gulf states may have stronger incentives to deepen their external security partnerships and coordinate more closely with one another. An instrument intended to create strategic depth and bargaining leverage can therefore produce the opposite effect: Greater regional coordination around the very security concerns Iran is seeking to contain.
There is, however, another way to interpret Tehran’s calculation. Under direct military pressure and amid growing uncertainty about its regional position, Iran may view pressure generated across multiple fronts as a wartime source of leverage, rather than as the basis of its long-term relations with its neighbours. From that perspective, strategic pressure and regional diplomatic engagement need not be treated as mutually exclusive. They can instead be understood as different phases of the same strategy: Maximise leverage during confrontation, then return to diplomacy once the immediate balance of pressure has shifted.
That calculation carries a substantial strategic risk. It assumes that political trust can be suspended during confrontation and rebuilt afterwards. Yet diplomatic rapprochement involves more than restoring diplomatic representation or reopening channels of communication; its durability depends on expectations about future behaviour. Repeated cycles of escalation followed by diplomatic reset can gradually erode those expectations. Each cycle may therefore make the next attempt at reassurance more difficult and reduce the confidence on which future agreements depend.
The consequences extend beyond Saudi-Iranian relations. China’s role in brokering the 2023 agreement gave the rapprochement a wider international dimension, while the postponement of the Oman talks shows how quickly developments on the ground can narrow the space for regional diplomacy. The more often diplomatic arrangements are overtaken by renewed escalation, the harder it becomes for mediation and regional engagement frameworks to generate durable confidence. The damage is therefore not limited to a single negotiation; it can accumulate across the broader diplomatic architecture intended to contain regional rivalry.
This is ultimately the cost of leverage. Tactical pressure may broaden bargaining options in the short term, but its strategic value becomes harder to sustain when the same pressure begins to weaken the relationships needed for long-term regional stability. For Iran, the central challenge is therefore not simply how much pressure its regional network can generate. It is whether continuing to draw leverage from that network can remain compatible with the regional order Tehran says it wants to build.

A Ukrainian military member sitting next to Sting drone interceptors used to target Russian drones, during the monitoring of the sky for drone threats, at an undisclosed location in teh Dnipropetrovsk region on April 15, 2026. | Roman Pilipey/AFP via Getty Images
KYIV — Ukraine needs more air defenses, but allies are starting to doubt if they can help Kyiv withstand the growing scale of Russian attacks, Alyona Getmanchuk, Ukraine’s ambassador to NATO, told POLITICO on Friday.
“Their logic is straightforward: can we truly be effective against this level of terror when Ukraine’s most pressing need is Patriot interceptors, and we do not have enough of them, as stockpiles have been depleted and production rates remain insufficient?” Getmanchuk said in a written statement.
She said Kyiv’s allies should see that helping Ukraine is also in their interest.
Advertisement
“We need to stop viewing assistance that enables Ukraine to defend itself as purely a matter of supporting Ukraine. It is also in NATO’s own interest … the more drones and missiles Ukraine can destroy in its own airspace, the fewer will cross the borders of neighboring NATO countries,” the envoy added.
Getmanchuk underlined that Western countries still have stocks of interceptor missiles to donate, including missiles close to the end of their service lives.
“There is hardly a better way to decommission them than by using them in the Ukrainian sky,” Getmanchuk said.
Kyiv is proposing a workaround: allies hand over interceptors from their existing stocks now, and Ukraine replaces them later with missiles it has already ordered.
“It’s a swap — not a donation. What we need is to get through this winter,” Getmanchuk said.
Ukraine is placing substantial orders, using both partner funding and the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan. These contracts cover not only hundreds of Patriot interceptors — both PAC-2s and PAC-3s — but also European systems, including SAMP/T and Aster 30 missiles, IRIS-T and others.
Advertisement
Growing numbers of Russian ballistic missiles are passing through due to Ukraine’s shortage of interceptors. Kyiv also needs other air defenses to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones.
“Our short list of urgent air-defense needs therefore consists of three major categories, not one: Patriot interceptors, air-to-air missiles, and all types of MANPADS and missiles for them,” she said.
In addition to direct donations, Getmanchuk called on countries to boost their funding to the NATO-led PURL program, in which allies buy U.S. weapons to give to Ukraine. NATO says PURL now supplies 90% of Ukraine’s Patriot interceptors.
The ambassador underlined that helping Ukraine now will also save allies money once the war is over.
“The more we can protect today, the less we will have to rebuild tomorrow,” she said.

German diesel prices hit all-time high as pressure on Merz intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:51:36 UTC
22:51:36 KST

By Christof Rührmair, dpa.
Munich (dpa) – German diesel prices surged to a new record, reaching €2.453 ($2.81) per litre in the nationwide average on Wednesday, figures from the ADAC motoring organization showed on Thursday, increasing pressure on the government to come up with a plan to ease the burden on motorists.
Fuel prices in Germany have surged since the start of the Iran war and the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, with petrol costs also reaching another nationwide record high of €2.314 ($2.65) per litre on average on Wednesday, according to ADAC.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced on Tuesday that the government would “react to price gouging,” but he is yet to reveal any concrete measures.
The persistently high fuel price are adding to Merz’s woes, whose leadership has come under intense pressure due to his party’s poor showing in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany secured a landslide win with nearly 44%.
Two more state elections scheduled for Sunday could turn out to be the final straw for the beleaguered chancellor, with his CDU projected to post its worst ever state election result since World War II in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
SPD wants ‘quick decision’
The chancellor’s conservatives and their junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats (SPD), differ on how best to tackle the issue. While the SPD has called for a windfall tax on oil companies, Merz has rejected the idea.
But calls have been growing on the chancellor to act swiftly, including from within conservative ranks.
Thorsten Frei, a senior figure of Merz’s CDU, has said planned measures to tackle record-breaking fuel prices should be implemented by October 1.
“People don’t need the prospect of relief; they need relief,” he said.
Finance Minister Lars Kingbeil, who also serves as SPD co-leader, on Thursday also called for a “quick decision.”
“Fuel prices must come down, and commuters in particular need some relief.”
The government was currently weighing solutions, he added, asking motorists for patience and reiterating that he was in favour of imposing a windfall tax on oil companies.
Average motorist paying €34 more a month
Earlier this year, Berlin introduced a two-month fuel tax cut to relieve motorists that expired at the end of June. However, experts have warned against reintroducing a universal rebate, instead calling for targeted measures to support those with lower incomes.
Energy prices worldwide have surged worldwide after the US and Israel began attacking Iran on February 28, to which Tehran responded by disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key maritime route for the global oil and gas trade.
Despite repeated attempts at negotiating a settlement, there is currently no end to the war in sight, and fighting for control of the strait has escalated again recently.
Diesel prices in Germany reached their previous record high in April, which has now been exceeded by €0.06, according to ADAC.
A litre of diesel is currently some €0.71 more expensive than it was before the start of the war, while petrol costs some €0.54 more.
This means the average motorist driving a vehicle with average fuel consumption for some 800 kilometres per month spends around €34 more on petrol than they did before the war.
Those driving a diesel-fuelled vehicle for 1,400 kilometres a month with average consumption have to pay around €69 more.
Transport sector up in arms
But the price surges aren’t only affecting private consumers.
The longer energy prices stay high, the greater the risk that other prices will also rise because transport and refrigeration of food, among other things, become more expensive. Companies will, according to economists, be forced to pass the cost surge in energy on to their customers.
In an open letter to Merz, German hauliers on Thursday stressed that the situation in the transport sector – which is dominated by small and medium-sized enterprises – has worsened dramatically due to the rise in fuel costs, and called on the government to provide relief.
Since the start of the conflict in the Middle East, the price of diesel has risen by a net total of around €0.6 per litre, the BGL hauliers’ association said.
With a monthly mileage of 10,000 km, this results in additional costs of €1,800 per lorry, meaning additional costs of over €1 million a year for a fleet of 50 lorries, it said.
“These cost increases can hardly be borne by the companies alone any longer,” BGL board spokesman Dirk Engelhardt wrote
“The high diesel prices are jeopardizing numerous small and medium-sized enterprises and weakening the competitiveness of the German economy.”
Transport companies reject VAT cut
The hauliers rejected a proposal by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, of Merz’s CDU, to temporarily cut VAT on fuels, arguing that this would not result in any immediate relief for transport companies who are entitled to claim back VAT.
Instead, the association called for the removal of the double CO₂ burden on the German transport sector resulting from the national emissions trading scheme and the CO₂ surcharge on the lorry toll.
Hauliers also called for the introduction of a commercial diesel price, based on the example of other EU member states such as France, Spain and Italy, where the energy tax on diesel used for commercial purposes is reduced to the EU minimum.

Ground robotic system and FPV drones stop Russian assault in 20 minutes – video
Drone operators from the NC13 strike ground robotic systems unit of the Third Army Corps, working with FPV crews, have stopped a Russian assault using a Droid TW-12.7 ground robotic system and attack drones.
Source: Ukrainian defence company DevDroid
Details: During combat duty, NC13 drone operators detected a group of six Russian troops moving towards Ukrainian positions. To stop the assault, they deployed a Droid TW-12.7 ground drone equipped with a combat module fitted with a 12.7mm Browning machine gun.
"The ground robotic system opened fire on the group and stopped its advance. An unmanned systems battalion also joined the operation and used FPV drones to strike the assault group," the company said.
According to DevDroid, the six Russian troops were killed after approximately 20 minutes of joint work by the ground robotic system operators and FPV crews. The Ukrainian positions remained under the control of the defence forces.
NC13 commander, who goes by the alias "Makar", said the episode demonstrates how ground and aerial unmanned systems can work together to carry out a combat mission.
"The greatest value of this cooperation is that we do not need to send assault groups to clear positions and expose our service members to enemy fire. Technology allows us to operate at a distance and gain an advantage over the enemy, which helps us protect our personnel," Makar said.
DevDroid developed the Droid TW-12.7 as a ground robotic system for reconnaissance and fire missions on the battlefield. It is remotely controlled and equipped with a built-in ballistic computer and surveillance cameras. According to the developer, the system can engage personnel, unarmoured vehicles and lightly armoured equipment.
Background:
- Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that soldiers from the 44th Separate Mechanised Brigade had used a Droid TW-12.7 to remotely clear Russian troops from a building near Kostiantynivka.

How Zoe Kazan Made East of Eden Her Own
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:50:56 UTC
22:50:56 KST

In June 2024, Zoe Kazan boarded a flight to New Zealand. She was excited. For a mother of small children, a quiet solo flight is a vacation unto itself. She scrolled through the in-flight movies. “They had East of Eden, and I was like, ‘I guess the gods are conspiring,’” she says. She pressed play.
Until then she had been avoiding rewatching her grandfather Elia Kazan’s 1955 masterpiece. She was flying halfway across the world to scout locations for her own version of East of Eden, a seven-part adaptation of John Steinbeck’s novel that premieres on Netflix on Oct. 1. She hadn’t wanted the film to influence her. But her script, which she’d begun working on in 2020, was finally turned in.
As the end credits rolled, she sighed in relief. “It was less like the book than I remembered,” she says. The film, which introduced a brooding James Dean to cinema, is more inspired by the novel than a direct adaptation of it: It covers only the last third, crucial characters have been excised, and famous lines are missing. “For me,” says Kazan over cold brew, extra ice on the side, at a Brooklyn cafe on an August morning, “the power of the story is how, over 50 years, it shows history repeating itself—or not.”
Her faithful adaptation covers the entirety of the multi-generational saga, which reimagines the tale of Cain and Abel twice over. Cyrus (Tracy Letts in the new series), a self-mythologizing Civil War veteran, prefers his gentle son Adam (Christopher Abbott) to the violent one, Charles (Mike Faist). A generation later, Adam’s twin sons Aron and Cal (Joe Anders and Joseph Zada) vie for the affection of their emotionally absent father. Kazan wrangles with the novel’s central question: Whether those boys can escape the shadows of their family history and forge their own paths—and whether America, carrying the sins of slavery, campaigns of violence against Native Americans, and racism against immigrants building a future in the West, can do the same.
Both versions are, in Kazan’s estimation, self-portraits of the artists who made them. Renowned for directing A Streetcar Named Desire and On the Waterfront and co-founding the influential Actors Studio from which the school of “method acting” was born, Elia Kazan was called before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1952. The Hollywood blacklist was in effect and, Faced with the possibility of never being able to work in Hollywood again, he named names. His granddaughter has never read his autobiography, though she has tried. “There’s some very young part of me that’s like, I still want my grandpa to be my grandpa and not have access to all of this adult stuff,” she says. But she believes that Elia Kazan, who died in 2003 when she was 20, saw himself in the black sheep of the family: “He had this cold and demanding father, and I think he was projecting onto Cal.” Made during a period when the director was facing significant backlash, his version focuses on guilt, rejection, and alienation.
What most intrigued Zoe Kazan, a new mother when she started on the script, were characters her grandfather rewrote or omitted: Cathy (Florence Pugh), a mother who walks out on her infant sons and whom Kazan calls “irredeemable, irresistible, and so full of agency,” and Lee (Hoon Lee), a Chinese American servant who steps in to raise the boys.
Kazan may live closest to Cathy and Lee in her script. But perhaps the reason she was drawn to the project is the notion of living and working in her grandfather’s shadow. One cannot help but draw the parallel between her and the grandchildren in East of Eden, struggling with whether to embrace or break away from a burdensome legacy. “The irony was not lost on me. There’s a literal way that I’m following in my family’s footsteps,” Kazan admits. “I don’t think I’d be doing my job as an artist if I weren’t thinking about my family while making this family story.”
Zoe Kazan was a teenager when she fell hard for Steinbeck. At 15, the Los Angeles native embarked on a Steinbeck-themed road trip up the California coast with her parents, dog-eared East of Eden in hand. Years later, she asked her agents to contact her if anyone purchased the rights. The call came in December 2019, while Kazan was shooting in Australia. She emerged bleary-eyed from a flight back to L.A. with her 15-month-old to pitch her idea to the buyers. “I talked about America and the way that we don’t want to look at our shadow, and how the book argues that embracing your shadow, all of yourself, the good and the bad, is the only way to change,” she says.
By then she had built a career not just as an actor in The Big Sick and She Said but as a screenwriter with Ruby Sparks, a satirical take on the manic pixie dream girl, and Wildlife, a drama she co-wrote with her partner, Paul Dano. She landed the East of Eden job and spent the next six years in Steinbeck’s world, and much of that time in the head of one of literature’s most complicated female characters, Cathy.
Cathy appears mysteriously on Adam and Charles’ doorstep, badly beaten. From there, she vacillates between a mesmerizing seductress and evil incarnate. She’s a manipulator or a survivor, depending on your perspective. “I don’t think anything in her background excuses her behavior,” says Kazan, laughing. “At the same time, there’s something really compelling about her insistence on her autonomy and selfishness, especially as a woman. I was such a good girl, reading that felt very exciting.”
Cathy became the center of Kazan’s adaptation. Often accused by the narrator of being a liar, Cathy in fact often tells the truth. It’s just not a truth the men around her want to hear. She says she does not want to move to California. She says does not want kids. She says she does not want to stay once Cal and Aron are born. Today’s readers may be appalled by the way she earns her freedom, but we can also sympathize with a woman whose wishes are so blatantly ignored.
Not even Steinbeck could decide. In letters to his editor, “He starts out like, ‘You’ve never read a monster like this,’” says Kazan. “Then he starts referring to her like, ‘I’ll finally get back to my dear Cathy.’ He seems very seduced by her.” Kazan relied heavily on the book to flesh Cathy out. This is not some girlboss version of one of literature’s great antagonists. “I think the text supports my reading,” she says. “I don’t like historical fiction that imposes modern values on the past. I don’t think Cathy is a feminist. I don’t think she cares about other women. I think she cares about herself.”
Pugh was the only actor Kazan named in her script. She’s made an career of morally complex characters in Lady Macbeth, Midsommar, and even the Marvel movies. As Cathy, she’s transfixing. “Florence looks like a doll, but she has this steel rod inside,” says Kazan. “Cathy is all action, like a shark that always has to be moving forward.”
East of Eden has aged so well in some respects that Kazan might get accused of making modern updates by those who haven’t read the text. After Cathy leaves Adam, the story centers on two men, Adam and Lee, platonically raising a family and navigating the complicated gender-role implications of that arrangement.
Lee’s parents were brought from China to build the railroads. He spends his life being the smartest man in any room but feigning broken English to make the white men around him comfortable, only revealing his intellect to those he trusts. For a few chapters, Lee departs for San Francisco to pursue the dream of opening his own bookstore. He returns with little to say about what happened while he was gone. "Even though [Steinbeck] imagines things like Lee code-switching, which is such a shocking thing to read in this book from 1952, I felt like it was this mystery of what happens to Lee when he goes away,” says Kazan. “I wanted to give him a little bit more." Kazan brought in the novelist Alexander Chee to build out the scenes for Lee that Steinbeck left off the page.
She wrote eight episodes, including one exclusively following Lee on his San Francisco excursion. Netflix greenlit seven. "It was the obvious stuff that had to go, partially because it's off the main track of the story, but also because it's all new locations. It would have added a third to our budget,” she says. She had to weave the plot into another episode. “I was so sad to lose that episode, but I do think it's stronger for it, because he's not siloed. He's part of the cohesive story."
When Adam checks out psychologically for the better part of a decade, Lee raises Cal and Aron, deliberately trying to prevent in this new generation the fractures and violence of the previous one. Steinbeck’s narrator observes Lee’s domestic and emotional work with admiration and grants Lee an unexpected dignity given the time period. The Netflix series doubles down, lingering on Lee’s face to capture a flicker of resigned sorrow at moments when Adam claims ownership over the boys and their accomplishments.
“A lot of this caretaking, doing the invisible work, my experience of becoming a mother, is embedded in Lee,” Kazan says. But so, too, is she Cathy. “There’s also a part of me, as there is for many mothers, that’s like, ‘I love my children more than anything, and I wish I could disappear.’”
Early in our nearly two-hour conversation, Kazan asks a server to lower the music so we can dig our teeth into Lee’s famous monologue on timshel, a Hebrew word that translates to “thou mayest” in the Cain and Abel story. It offers Cain and others the choice to triumph over sin. It frees younger generations from repeating the mistakes of their forebears. One can guess why this may ring true for Zoe Kazan. We circle the question of the divide between an artist and their art as ice melts in her cup. I bring up a tweet she wrote over the summer.
When Taylor Swift got married in July and observers clocked the absence of a longtime friend from the wedding, Kazan posted her interpretation of the situation online: "I think she didn't invite her because she has come to the end of her marriage plot, thus cutting off access to her first great subject. Rather than root for her own divorce, she is generating the next chapter of interpersonal drama for herself via female friendship." The tweet read like a literary critic’s interpretation of a pop star’s public art. Swifties called it out of line. Kazan deleted it.
"When an artist makes her personal life the subject of her work, and has her wedding in one of our nation's foremost arenas with billboards outside saying ‘Just Married,’ I don't think it's a personal critique to talk about what they're doing in their personal life," she says. "I am very careful to be kind online. I never say anything mean about anyone's work. So I erased those tweets once I realized how upset people were by it. Should I have known better? Probably. But I had never been on the receiving end of Swifties before, so I didn't know."
I have spent much of the interview trying to divine how much of East of Eden is an extension of Kazan herself—she cites the timshel passage when referring to her relationship with her family’s legacy. Viewers familiar with her history may theorize about her connection to the material in the same way that Kazan offered up a theory about Swift. “[Swift] puts the names of her exes in her liner notes. There's a way that she has made her private life incredibly public and explicit,” she says. “The overlap with my personal history in this was all very conscious, and made more conscious the longer I worked on it. But it’s not the explicit subject of it.”
She hopes the story opens doors inside viewers, the way it did for her. “I think we have tendencies as humans to feel the weight of our nation’s original sins, or our family’s original sins, that they are so shameful and heavy that anything good we do is going to be insignificant,” she says. “And then I think we have this other, very Trumpian impulse, of whitewashing the past. I think the thing the book is arguing for, and that I find very moving, is this idea that we actually have to carry both things. The weight of our original sins, and the idea that we are not defined by them.”

Saudi oil pipeline closure puts Asia’s economic resilience to the test
Experts say the loss will hit Asian refiners first before feeding through to inflation, currencies and economic growth across the region
Asian economies heavily dependent on imported energy are facing an even sharper squeeze after the shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline removed a key escape route from the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, deepening an energy shock that has already pushed crude oil above US$100 a barrel.
Analysts said the loss of that bypass would hit Asian refiners first before feeding through to inflation, currencies and economic growth across the region.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, confirmed that the pipeline was shut as a precaution following an attack last week but did not disclose the extent of the damage, the number of affected pumping stations or a timetable for restarting operations, according to a Rystad Energy report on Monday.
The closure leaves Saudi Arabia with fewer ways to keep crude moving to Asian buyers, raising the risk of delayed or reduced deliveries if the outage drags on.

Nearly 3,000 flee Yemen to Djibouti in less than a week as violence escalates: UN refugee agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:47:39 UTC
22:47:39 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Nearly 3,000 people have fled Yemen for Djibouti in less than a week as escalating violence drives growing displacement within the country and across its borders, the UN refugee agency said Friday.
 
“Refugees continue to arrive by boat through Obock, Khor Angar, Moulhoule and Godoria after difficult journeys in small vessels,” UNHCR representative in Djibouti Sandrine Desamours told reporters in Geneva.
 
More than half of those crossing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait are women and children, while some families have been displaced for a second time after previously fleeing Yemen during the 2015 crisis and later returning.
 
UNHCR is preparing for at least 10,000 new arrivals but warned that capacity is rapidly diminishing. Markazi refugee village, designed for 5,000 people, was already hosting more than 2,700 Yemenis and 1,500 Eritreans.
 
More than 100,000 people have also been displaced inside Yemen as fighting intensifies, particularly along the western coast, Desamours said.
 
Health system under mounting pressure
 
Meanwhile, only 60% of 5,415 assessed health facilities in Yemen are fully functioning, WHO spokesperson Tarik Jasarevic told reporters in Geneva on Friday.
 
Only 6% provide a full package of trauma care, despite growing emergency needs.
 
More than 18,000 suspected measles cases and 106 deaths have been reported this year, alongside 390 diphtheria cases and 13 deaths.
 
Around 30,000 children experience severe acute malnutrition with complications annually, while some therapeutic feeding centers are operating at 120% bed capacity, he said.
 
According to the spokesperson, access remains particularly difficult in northern Yemen, where UN operations have been suspended in 90 priority districts.
 
To date, Jasarevic said, only $490,000 has been secured through WHO’s Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), leaving a “significant funding gap to sustain and scale up the required health response.”
ICRC delivers 22 tons of medical supplies
 
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said Friday it delivered 22 tons of life-saving medical supplies to Sanaa as intensified fighting left hospitals struggling with dwindling stocks and growing numbers of war-wounded patients.
 
"The recent escalation in hostilities has overwhelmed hospitals, which are grappling with critical shortages of medical supplies and an influx of war-wounded patients," Christine Cipolla, ICRC's head of delegation in Yemen, said in a statement.
 
The supplies will be distributed to priority hospitals and health facilities across the country, the ICRC said.
 
In Marib, an ICRC mobile surgical team has been working at Marib General Hospital since Aug. 23, assisting Yemeni medical personnel with emergency triage and surgical operations.
 
The organization said it is also bringing additional medical stocks into Yemen to bolster emergency capacity across front-line areas.
 
More than 50 ambulances operated by the Yemeni Red Crescent Society are now functioning on both sides of the front lines with ICRC support, according to the statement.
 
The ICRC warned that the scale of the crisis could quickly exceed existing response capacity, noting that in some areas it is the only international humanitarian organization operating on the ground.

US gives UN more time to end support for Somalia peacekeepers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:46:24 UTC
22:46:24 KST

The United States has agreed to give the UN another year to wind down its support for African peacekeepers in Somalia, a document showed - a move that gives some breathing space to a force that was fearing quicker cuts, but still leaves its future in peril.
Reuters reported in July that Washington - increasingly frustrated with the fragile administration in Mogadishu - said it would block the UN from supporting the African Union force which props up the government and helps it fight al-Qaeda-linked terrorists.
Analysts have warned that any weakening of the African Union peacekeepers would severely undermine the government there and could exacerbate the political turmoil in a combustible region bordering the Red Sea.
'A real risk of state fragmentation'
The peacekeepers, known as the AU Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia, rely heavily on UN support for essential logistics such as food, water, fuel, medical services and transportation of troops.
The administration of US President Donald Trump, which has pulled back from many international commitments, had told the African Union in a diplomatic note in July that it would use its clout to prevent the UN from supporting the peacekeepers from the start of next year.
In another diplomatic note seen by Reuters and shared with embassies last week, Washington said "the United States is willing to support a 12-month drawdown followed immediately by liquidation" of the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS).
Without that 12-month window, the funding could have stopped at the end of December, when the mandate of that UN office expires. Two diplomatic sources and a Somali government source said the new 12-month countdown would start in January.
A spokesperson for the US State Department told Reuters that Washington would no longer fund or support the UN office in Somalia, whose total budget is around $500 million.
"We would expect any drawdown processes and timelines to be discussed during UN Security Council deliberations in December," the spokesperson said in a statement. Five diplomatic sources and the Somali government source, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the 12-month deadline.
Somalia's defense ministry, UNSOS and the African Union Commission did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The move will buy Somalia and its partners some more time to find other backers, but does not lift the threat over the peacekeeping force's future.
"AUSSOM is a key pillar of Somalia's state," Afyare Elmi, professor at the City University of Mogadishu, said. "Without it, the country would face a real risk of state fragmentation and disintegration."
Samira Gaid, a regional security analyst, told Reuters the shutdown of UNSOS could spell the end for AUSSOM.
"The AU either needs to find alternative logistics arrangements or to draw down and exit," she said.
Financing for the AU mission has become increasingly precarious, leading to a huge funding shortfall.
Washington last year blocked a plan to shift to a financing model that would have seen UN funds cover three-quarters of the peacekeeping mission's $190 million annual budget.
Somalia has been mired in chaos and internal conflict since the fall of autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991. Islamists have strengthened their control of the countryside and, two decades ago, seized the capital before being forced out by a joint Ethiopian and Somali government force.
