100-meter shroud in New York displays names of over 20,000 Palestinian children killed in Gaza
TEHRAN - The handwritten names of more than 20,000 Palestinian children who have been killed in the Gaza Strip were displayed on a 100-meter-long shroud at the UN Church Center in New York.
The event was organized at the initiative of Doctors Against Genocide, Clergy Against Genocide in the United States, Justice for All, and several other groups.
The ceremony featured the recitation of the Holy Quran and an interfaith gathering coinciding with the opening of the UN General Assembly. The coalition honored victims as the UN General Assembly convenes in New York.
The initiative was part of a memorial project aimed at keeping alive the names and memories of Gaza’s martyred children and preventing them from being reduced to mere numbers and statistics, Palestine News reported.
"Not a number, but a name," organizers emphasized, explaining that the project aims to restore individual identity to every young person killed in the enclave, while demanding an end to Israeli military operations and establishing accountability for war crimes.
The initiative drew inspiration from an Italian memorial created in Rome by Pastors Against Genocide, which originated from the tragic practice in Gaza of parents writing children's names directly onto their bodies to ensure identification if their homes were bombed.

The Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition on Thursday held its 4th planning meeting in Saudi Arabia, the Saudi Defense Ministry said Friday.
The meeting in Jeddah was part of the coalition’s "ongoing transition from the founding stage to the actual operational stage, having reached Initial Operational Capability," the ministry said in a statement on US social media platform X.
It was attended by the representatives of "41 brotherly and friendly countries," the officials stated, adding that EU representatives also took part.
The coalition is a 14-country military alliance formed in July to ensure that vital waterways surrounding the Arabian Peninsula – the Gulf of Aden, Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and Red Sea – remain open to international traffic.
The coalition is currently integrating capabilities and preparing for operational execution and an actual presence in the maritime area of operations, the ministry highlighted.
It reviewed developments in the coalition’s work, achievements during the previous phase, and progress in countries joining the coalition, according to the statement.
The discussions also discussed requirements for joint operations and the capability contributions of participating countries to support coordinated and integrated multinational defensive operations and enhance the coalition’s operational readiness, it said.
The meeting marks an "advanced stage" in the coalition’s development, focusing on operational readiness under a unified command ahead of deployment and the launch of missions in the area of responsibility, the ministry added.

Mamata gets 'footballer', but can she win TMC 'khela'? Maharashtra has a red-card warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:31:19 UTC
22:31:19 KST

Mamata Banerjee faction got 'football player' as its symbol.
For 28 years, TMC has been Mamata Banerjee and Mamata Banerjee has been TMC in West Bengal; the two are almost synonymous with each other. And for voters, the political shorthand for Mamata Banerjee has been almost absurdly simple: two flowers on grass.Now, that shorthand has been taken away.The Election Commission on Friday allotted Mamata's faction a new name - 'Mamata All India Trinamool Congress', with a football player as its symbol. The rival Arup Roy faction will contest as 'Democratic Trinamool Congress', with an 'envelope' as its symbol. The decision follows the commission's September 17 order freezing the original All India Trinamool Congress name and its reserved 'flowers and grass' symbol for the upcoming bypolls.
Mamata Banerjee is now fighting to save her own party name and symbol.
But the EC's interim arrangement is only the first chapter. The substantive question of who gets the original TMC name and symbol will have to be decided under Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.And here, the story might look familiar.The same movie was played out twice in Maharashtra in recent years, first with the Shiv Sena and then with the Nationalist Congress Party.
They do not know that I cannot leave TMC. It will always be with me until I leave this world. Absolutely dirty game, but we are also ready to fight it out. I want the BJP to go from India. We want solidarity in INDIA alliance.
Mamata Banerjee
What Shiv Sena and NCP cases tell us
When Shiv Sena split between Uddhav Thackeray and Eknath Shinde in 2022, the EC first froze the party's 'bow and arrow' symbol and allotted separate interim identities to the two factions.
In its February 2023 decision, the commission eventually recognised the Shinde faction as the Shiv Sena and allowed it to use the original name and symbol.The NCP followed a similar path. After Ajit Pawar's rebellion in July 2023, the EC decided in February 2024 that the faction led by Sharad Pawar had a weaker numerical claim, while Ajit Pawar's group had superior support in the organisational and legislative wings. It consequently recognised Ajit Pawar's faction as the NCP and allowed it to use the party's 'clock' symbol. The EC order specifically recorded that the Ajit Pawar group had "far superior numerical support" in the organisational and legislative wings.That is a crucial part of the precedent for the ongoing TMC dispute.The conclusion from the Maharashtra cases may be that the EC followed the majority of legislators. The legal position is more nuanced. Paragraph 15 allows the election commission to examine rival claims through the party's organisational structure as well as its legislative strength.In its May 11, 2023 Constitution Bench judgment in Subhash Desai vs Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court held that the EC need not determine a party's identity solely through the numerical strength of its MLAs or MPs while adjudicating a dispute under Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order. The court said the EC could consider the majority in the organisational wing, the party constitution and, where appropriate, "any other appropriate test", underlining that a split among legislators is not necessarily the same as a split in the political party itself.
The timeline of TMC split.
The observation is particularly relevant to the TMC case, where the eventual contest could involve competing claims over the party's organisational structure and not just a headcount of elected representatives. The Supreme Court, however, did not itself decide which faction should receive the Shiv Sena's name and symbol, leaving the merits of that EC decision to separate proceedings.That distinction could matter considerably in the TMC case.The Shiv Sena and NCP rebels who ultimately secured the original party identities had substantial support among sitting legislators. The TMC's internal arithmetic, however, has to be examined on its own terms.The 2026 assembly election setback changed the party's internal arithmetic sharply. Its tally fell from 215 of 294 seats in 2021 to 80, and within weeks, 58 MLAs backed expelled leader Ritabrata Banerjee as their legislature party leader. He was subsequently recognised as leader of the opposition, while the rebel camp rejected Mamata's nominee, Sobhandeb Chattopadhyay.The revolt then spread to Parliament, with 20 Lok Sabha MPs led by Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar joining the NCPI and backing the BJP-led NDA. The TMC challenged their move before the Lok Sabha speaker and sought their disqualification. What began as a post-election leadership challenge had thus expanded into a contest over control of the party's legislative and parliamentary wings.Mamata Banerjee, however, remains the founder and central political figure of the organisation, and her camp's claim is not based only on her position as party leader but also on its organisational and electoral support.
The 'new' Mamata party
The names allotted on Friday were revealing because neither faction chose to abandon the Trinamool identity. Mamata's camp was given 'Mamata All India Trinamool Congress', while the rival Arup Roy camp became 'Democratic Trinamool Congress'. Both were, in different ways, laying claim to continuity with the party Mamata Banerjee founded on January 1, 1998.The distinction lies in the source of legitimacy each side is emphasising. The rebels' use of 'Democratic' fits their argument that the TMC's organisational functioning should be more representative and less centred around one leader. Mamata's faction, meanwhile, has effectively put the founder's name where the old party identity used to be, making 'Mamata' part of its temporary electoral brand. That is particularly striking for a party whose political identity has been inseparable from its founder for almost three decades.
They had said beforehand, 'naam bhi rakhne doonga, nishaan bhi nahi rakhne doonga' (Neither let you keep the name nor the symbol). Who are these people? They are in power today; they might not be in power tomorrow. They should understand their limitations.
Mamata Banerjee
The football-player symbol allotted to Mamata's faction also carries its own political resonance in Bengal. Football has long had a deep cultural presence in the state, but there is also a direct connection to the TMC's campaign vocabulary: 'Khela Hobe', the slogan that became a defining part of Mamata's 2021 assembly campaign against the BJP.
The symbol does not automatically recreate that campaign, but it gives the Mamata faction a ready-made visual association at a time when it has lost the party symbol voters have known for nearly three decades.The test, however, has now changed in a rather dramatic way for the Mamata faction.
Nandigram changes the bypoll test
Mamata faction's candidate, Sanchita Pradhan Dey, withdrew her nomination from the Nandigram contest altogether, a day before the deadline. Her withdrawal came minutes after she met West Bengal chief minister and BJP leader Suvendu Adhikari, although the circumstances surrounding the meeting and her decision remain a matter of political speculation.Mamata Banerjee later announced in a press conference that her party will now back the Congress candidate in Nandigram, and mentioned that the decision was taken "for the greater interest of the nation" and to strengthen the INDIA bloc."Rahul Gandhi rang me up yesterday, Arvind Kejriwal also expressed solidarity; we will all fight together against BJP. We will support Congress in the Nandigram bypoll to strengthen the INDIA bloc," Mamata said. The Congress candidate, however, was also arrested by the cops late in the evening in a land-grab case.That makes the October 6 bypolls a very different test from the one that appeared possible 24 hours earlier. The Mamata faction will now not be testing its new 'football-player' identity in Nandigram, but instead, ask its supporters to transfer their support to a Congress candidate, even as the rival TMC faction contests the seat under its own new identity.The political significance is difficult to miss. At precisely the moment when the EC has stripped Mamata's faction of the old TMC name and symbol and given it a new identity, the faction is now out of a direct fight in Nandigram, a constituency that carries an unusually strong personal history for both Mamata and Suvendu Adhikari.
Nandigram was where Mamata lost to Adhikari in the 2021 assembly election, after making the constituency the centrepiece of her campaign. Adhikari, who had moved from the TMC to the BJP before that election, defeated her by a narrow margin in a contest that became one of the defining episodes of Bengal politics. He subsequently retained Nandigram while also winning Bhowanipore, which he vacated to retain Nandigram, necessitating the October 6 bypoll.The EC may eventually decide who owns the TMC name and symbol, but the October 6 bypolls will offer the first test of how much of the old Trinamool identity survives without 'flowers and grass'. In Rejinagar, the football player and envelope will face each other directly; in Nandigram, Mamata's decision to back Congress will test whether her political support can travel even when her own new party name and symbol are not on the ballot.

Adopt This Data Center Plushie and Hear Its Piercing Scream
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Uh oh, we got a cute alert! It’s Bezzy, your adorable, cuddly, anthropomorphized server-rack and stuffed-animal friend! Give this soft lil’ doll a squeeze, and it shall sing you its telltale song: the piercing, grinding ambient squeals emitted from a real US data center.
The Bezzy doll is a stuffed plushie made in a satirical collaboration between the New York–based creative studio Basura and Big Data, the musical project of producer Alan Wilkis, best known for the song “Dangerous,” a 2013 collaboration with the band Joywave. The joint project, which is coming out the same day as a new Big Data single, is called Adopt a Data Center. The goal is to present people with a “cuddly introduction to life with a real data center.”
Data Centers are very un-vogue right now. Built out by all the big AI companies to power their increasingly power-hungry AI tools, data centers have spread across thousands of acres of land in the US. They have been heavily criticized for their energy consumption and expansion of gas power. They have also proven to be audibly annoying, stirring up complaints about noise pollution from those nearby.
The Adopt a Data Center stunt aims to make people think differently about how services produced by data centers fit into their lives. That manifests as a plush stuffie that looks like a server rack in a data center, albeit with long arms and legs and googly eyes. It’s cute in the way Don’t Hug Me I’m Scared is cute. Squeeze Bezzy’s torso and the sound bursts out. It’s a screeching few seconds of a recording taken by a neighbor of a data center in Virginia. The tag on the Bezzy plushie reads, “Hug me for ear-piercing forever hum.”
“We picked this recording as it was the clearest and most suitably irritating,” wrote Rajeev Basu, the founder of Basura, in an email to WIRED. In an interview with the person who recorded the audio, Basu says they described the sound as “like a car alarm going off nonstop. It's high-pitched, and it's all you can focus on.”
Basura has worked on other projects like making luxury wear for dogs and a partnership with Yerba Madre that made dirt shoes designed to break apart during a walk to spread wildflower seeds.
Along with Bezzy, the data centers project includes a collection of stickers that say things like “Every data center deserves a forever home” and “Open your heart. And your power grid.” Basu says the project is the result of dozens of interviews with people who live near data centers in the US. The website itself reads, “Adopt a data center: All they ask for is everything.”
Wilkis, whose band Big Data has “It’s giving Black Mirror, but make it music” in its Spotify description, says that the one upside of the data center debate is that the backlash is genuinely bipartisan.
“AI is a proxy for decades of widening wealth inequality in America, and data centers are its physical embodiment,” Wilkis wrote to WIRED. “With roughly 40 percent of the stock market's value riding on a handful of tech companies, the US economy is already a bet on AI's success.”
Sadly, only 20 Bezzy dolls are available for $99 from the Adopt a Data Center website and the Big Data storefront. Basura designed the toys, which are handmade in the US. But the physical toy isn’t the real point. The satire is meant to hook people into looking at the facts for themselves. When you click “adopt now” on the website, you’re taken to a statement with links to research and stories about how data centers fit into the world.
“It’s not about whether AI data centers should exist,” Basu says. “It’s about who gets to decide where they go, what resources they consume, and whether the communities living beside them actually benefit.”

South Africa secures nearly 24,000 polling stations
The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) has secured 23,696 voting stations ahead of the November 4 local government elections, including 33 mobile stations, as preparations for polling day continue.
IEC Chief Electoral Officer Sy Mamabolo said the figure could still change slightly as the commission finalises lease agreements for some sites. Of the 23,696 stations secured, 22,668 are permanent, 995 are temporary and 33 are mobile voting stations.
The IEC’s preparations come less than two months before South Africans head to the polls to elect new local government representatives. The commission said it was also making progress with the recruitment and training of election officials ahead of the elections. A total of 23,696 presiding officers and 29,964 deputy presiding officers are being recruited, with more than half recruited to date and training under way.
Mamabolo said the commission remained committed to ensuring that the elections were administered in a manner that was “credible, transparent, inclusive and compliant with the law”.
The IEC said the final list of voting stations would enable it to continue with its preparations for polling day, while the number of stations could be adjusted slightly as outstanding lease agreements were concluded.
The IEC is also continuing work on its election results system. It has engaged external independent auditors to validate key controls, processes and system functionality, while an independent quality assurance testing process is scheduled to run for three weeks.
Political parties would have access to the results system from October 5 to 12 to test it using their preferred experts.

Flight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software error
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:28:16 UTC
22:28:16 KST

A software defect in part of the UK’s air traffic control system corrupted flight data “in the space of a millisecond”, leading to a six-hour outage and mass airline cancellations and delays across the UK last week, National Air Traffic Services has said.
But ministers said the Nats report into the incident still left questions unanswered, saying they needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”.
According to the report, the error first occurred at 10am and was notified to engineers who investigated – but the system appeared to be working again, until 12.30pm when a repeat occurred and a major incident was declared.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) industry regulator would now “check their findings” and investigate Nats more widely.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers had their travel disrupted after the Nats failure on Tuesday 8 September, which ended up delaying and cancelling flights across the UK and beyond late into the next day.
Airlines have called for compensation and a “credible plan”, with Ryanair demanding the dismissal of the Nats chief executive officer, Martin Rolfe, after the third major air traffic control failure in the UK since summer 2023.
A government source said the CAA review would be “a chance to fundamentally investigate” if Nats was fit for purpose.
Rolfe said the incident was unrelated to the previous failures. He said he could “confirm that it was a software issue and not caused by any incorrect actions by either military or civil operators”.
The preliminary report said the failure was a “legacy and previously unknown software defect and a combination of very specific events occurring simultaneously” in part of the National Airspace System (NAS), which allocates codes to individual aircraft to identify flights on radar.
Nats said the software error occurred at 10am, with engineers first notified at 10.02am that the link between the NAS and London area control system had dropped. The engineers reported at 10.06am that the system had apparently recovered with no operational impact, but continued to investigate.
The report said the fault presented when a manual request for an aircraft code was being processed but paused for another, unspecified “higher priority activity” request. It said: “When processing of the aircraft code request resumed, the software defect meant it did not resume correctly and the resulting output was corrupted, and affected some subsequent flight data updates. This happened in the space of a millisecond.”
At 12.32pm the link between the national and London airspace management dropped again and a major incident was declared, with controllers having to conduct some tasks manually. By 12.45pm, Nats was restricting flights as the system continued to glitch, before failing completely at 1.32pm.
At 1.40pm airlines were advised of restrictions, and between 2.50pm and 4.09pm Nats rebooted the system, eventually resuming full operations at 7.30pm – but leaving mass congestion, displaced aircraft and hundreds of thousands of delayed passengers in its wake.
It took more than two days for the backlog of passenger disruption to be cleared, with more than 2,000 flights cancelled in total and hundreds of thousands of people’s travel plans disrupted.
Rolfe said: “The issue has been identified and mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety tested and deployed.”
He added: “I would like to apologise again, very sincerely, to everyone who was affected last week. It’s our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong. However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question.”
The transport secretary said: “The disruption we saw last week was completely unacceptable and I know how frustrating it was for passengers, airlines and airports.”
Alexander said she had received Nats’ report, adding: “It’s clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos.
“I have therefore tasked the CAA with conducting an independent review to check Nats’ findings and investigate their investment plans to enhance resilience in the future, along with regulatory accountability.”
The CAA’s review will be published within six months.
Tim Alderslade, the chief executive of Airlines UK, a lobby group representing the industry, said: “The CAA’s review must mandate real investment in Nats’ resilience so a single fault can never again descend into nationwide disruption.”
He said his members were writing to Nats to “demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience”.
The EasyJet chief executive, Kenton Jarvis, said: “Passengers deserve more than just another promise that lessons will be learned. Firm actions must be taken … and there must be a fair solution to ensure that airlines are not left to pick up the bill.”
The Ryanair chief operations officer, Neil McMahon, said: “‘The software ate my homework’ is not an acceptable explanation … How many times must the UK ATC system collapse before Martin Rolfe accepts responsibility and resigns.”

Blast hits military site in NATO state
Seven people have been injured in an explosion at a military shooting range in western Sweden, with five suffering serious injuries, according to local media reports. The incident near Karlsborg sparked alarm among parents, who feared that young conscripts may have been among the victims, before officials clarified that those injured were armed forces employees.
In a statement on Thursday, the Swedish Armed Forces said an explosion occurred at the Kraks shooting range shortly after 4:00 PM, injuring several people, some seriously, adding that the incident is being investigated.
National public broadcaster SVT reported that seven men in their 20s and 30s were taken to the hospital, including one by helicopter. Five were being treated for serious but non-life-threatening injuries, reportedly in intensive care, while the other two sustained minor injuries.
While the authorities would not say what caused the incident, Aftonbladet reported that an explosion occurred in connection with clearing old, unexploded ammunition.
The incident sparked alarm among parents before officials stressed that no conscripts were involved. “We have had some worried mothers and fathers calling, but it is not conscripts who were injured,” Armed Forces spokesman Mikael Agren told SVT.
An emergency department employee at a local hospital described the situation as “chaos,” with reports suggesting that the facility reinforced its emergency and operating departments but did not formally enter emergency mode.
Kroks range is administered by the local Skaraborg Regiment but is used by units from across Sweden.
The Karlsborg military hub hosts the Unmanned Aircraft System Center, which was opened last year to allow Sweden to catch up in drone warfare, which has become a staple of the Ukraine conflict.
This year, Ukrainian drone operators with frontline experience took part in the NATO-led Aurora 26 exercise in the wider Karlsborg area. However, there is no indication that drones or Ukrainian personnel were involved in the blast on Thursday.
The incident comes as Sweden, like many other NATO members, continues its military buildup; its defense budget has grown by 18% in 2026 alone. In 2017, Stockholm reactivated the draft, citing a deteriorating security environment and difficulties recruiting enough personnel voluntarily; in 2024, it joined NATO, citing the Ukraine conflict.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has criticized Sweden for taking steps to host NATO military infrastructure on its soil, stressing that Stockholm’s policies do not improve geopolitical stability. He also said Russia has no major disputes with Sweden.
Sweden has seen similar training accidents in the past. In March 2024, two conscripts and two instructors suffered shrapnel wounds after a hand grenade exploded near them during an exercise at the Mastocka range in the southwestern part of the country. The Work Environment Authority later found safety deficiencies in the training.

Without GPS and constant communication: how AI is changing the operation of drones and missiles
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:21:20 EEST
22:21:20 KST

Without GPS and constant communication: how AI is changing the operation of drones and missiles
Kyiv • UNN
AI helps drones and missiles navigate, recognize targets, and adjust their routes while electronic warfare is in effect. The technology cannot yet fully replace the operator.
Artificial intelligence is gradually becoming part of modern weaponry. It is used not only for data analysis but also directly in the operation of UAVs and missiles—for navigation, target recognition, and route adjustment. Such technologies are developing particularly rapidly amid the full-scale war in Ukraine. On the battlefield, satellite navigation can be jammed, while control channels can be disrupted. Under such conditions, software can take over some of the functions. UNN examined together with experts how AI is integrated into drones and missiles, what it provides in conditions of electronic warfare, and whether it can completely replace humans during the performance of a combat mission.
AI as a response to electronic warfare
One of the main drivers behind the development of autonomous systems has been electronic warfare. The enemy actively jams satellite navigation, control channels, and data transmission on the battlefield. As a result, a drone may lose contact with its operator or fail to receive the necessary navigation signals. AI could potentially solve this problem.
If artificial intelligence is capable of ensuring the operation of a weapon in the absence of the main communication or navigation channels, it can take over some control functions. Computer vision plays an important role here, enabling automatic target reacquisition. In such a case, electronic warfare may negatively affect the drone's operation for a certain period, but after communication is lost, control can be taken over by an autonomous control system, which will continue carrying out the programmed functions
However, he emphasized that it is still too early to talk about fully autonomous weapons.
I do not think that the operator will completely disappear from this process in the short term or even in the medium term. The operator will still be needed. Even if contact with the operator is lost, the operator can first guide the system to the area where the target is located, after which the drone begins searching for and identifying it independently. If, for example, a drone is tasked with flying 200 kilometers on its own, a system error may occur along the way. In such a case, the drone could potentially begin acting contrary to its intended purpose—including by creating a threat to friendly forces or civilians. Therefore, complete autonomy has serious limitations
Military analyst Oleksii Hetman, for his part, explained that modern AI in drones is primarily a complex computing system that can receive images from a camera, compare them with previously uploaded examples, and adjust the operation of the engines or control surfaces in order to direct its flight directly toward that target. At the same time, it does not "understand" the situation in the way an operator does.
How AI differs in drones and missiles
Ukrainian companies are currently actively working on implementing AI in both drones and missiles.
We see the use of AI for target selection and recognition practically every time Ukrainian unmanned systems units demonstrate drones striking Russian logistics at long range. When, due to the distance from the operator or the inability to respond to a situation in real time within fractions of a second, the operator can no longer fully control the process, artificial intelligence comes into play. It helps guide the weapon directly onto the target. Moreover, this is not limited to automatic target reacquisition. There is another interesting aspect—the possibility of a drone operating autonomously. It can have a database containing images of various types of equipment—tanks, armored combat vehicles, and specialized transport—and carry out its assigned task independently
Another application of AI in drones is computer vision. The camera transmits an image, and the algorithm compares it with data prepared in advance. For example, photographs of equipment, infrastructure facilities, vehicles, or other characteristics of the target.
This allows the drone not only to move according to predetermined coordinates, but also to уточнювати its position directly during flight. In particular, the system can compare images of the terrain with a map and use the result for the final correction of the route.
According to Irina Terekh, CEO of the leading defense company Fire Point, the company uses precisely this approach.
We use it for visual comparison with a map in order to make the final correction of the target. But I would not say that this significantly changes the approach to using drones, since I still believe that the final decision should be made by a human
Irina Terekh noted that the company uses both the "man-in-the-loop" and "man-on-the-loop" approaches. The difference between these approaches lies in the level of operator involvement. In the first case, a human directly participates in the critical decision. In the second, the system independently performs certain stages of the task, but the operator can monitor its actions and retains the ability to intervene.
There are several options for this type of terminal operation. At present, we are primarily at the stage of collecting more accurate data for inertial platforms such as ours. At the same time, this helps correct the course and control the aircraft in the event of a prolonged loss of communication, since the system is capable of recognizing the target and making a final approach toward it. But at this stage, a human still has to be involved — "human-in-the-loop"
In missiles, the operating principles are similar, but the requirements are significantly higher because they move much faster. According to the expert, the task of AI in missiles may be related to the operation of guidance systems and increasing the accuracy of striking targets at given coordinates.
For example, if a missile enters the area of effect of electronic warfare systems and its primary systems are affected, artificial intelligence could potentially support the operation of individual systems, continue along the designated course and route, and also adjust guidance for a more accurate strike on the specified target
russia is also integrating AI into its attacks
In the conditions of a full-scale war, it is not only Ukraine that is improving its weapons. The enemy is also trying to use artificial intelligence to increase the autonomy of drones and counter Ukrainian electronic warfare systems.
The president’s freelance adviser on the development of technological areas of defense, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, reported the use by russia of drones with elements of artificial intelligence. According to him, such systems can be used to make strike drones less visible to Ukrainian electronic intelligence.
At the same time, military experts note that there is no fundamental technological difference in the field of military artificial intelligence between Ukraine and russia.
Their drones with artificial intelligence operate according to similar principles. Artificial intelligence itself has no particular "national character" — its operating principle is the same regardless of whether the development is Japanese, Chinese, russian, European, or Ukrainian. The difference lies primarily in the speed of operation, memory capacity, computing power, and the component base on which the system is built. One board can be used, or another, but the operating principle remains the same
According to military expert Oleksandr Kovalenko, Ukraine is ahead of russia in creativity and high-tech development.
But this does not mean that Russia is significantly behind us. In certain areas, they may be approximately one or two steps behind. The difference is that Russia has more capabilities to counter such drones on its territory, in particular thanks to a greater number of air defense systems. They also have many problems and gaps in this system, but it works. We still have the problem of fully addressing the threat posed by jet-powered drones. And this issue should have been resolved not in an emergency mode over the course of a month, but as early as January 2024 — by preparing the appropriate range of means to be used after the enemy scaled up its use of jet-powered drones. Therefore, I would put it this way: technologically, we may be ahead of the enemy, but in practice, when it comes to responding to new threats, we often find ourselves behind
AI as part of the struggle for technological superiority
The war demonstrates that superiority increasingly depends not on a single specific technology, but on how quickly a country can develop, test, integrate, and use these technologies. Artificial intelligence is already being used to collect and analyze information, navigate without GPS, identify targets, and operate drones amid active electronic warfare. However, its main role at present is not to fully replace humans, but to transfer to the system certain functions that were previously performed by an operator.
For example, an operator can independently choose which vehicle to track or hunt for enemy servicemen. Artificial intelligence is not yet capable of making such decisions. It can identify an object that most closely matches an image or short video stored in its memory and head toward it. The main advantage here is that constant external control is not required. In a certain sense, a drone equipped with artificial intelligence cannot be confused by electronic warfare. It can continue carrying out the program embedded in it
That is why the struggle for technological superiority is increasingly turning into a struggle for data, computing power, and the ability to adapt to the new conditions of war.

The newspaper compared the ability to visit the island of Hainan without any entry documents to "a magnetic effect" that amplifies the benefits of the Hainan Free Trade Port. The publication noted that ahead of the national holidays of the Mid-Autumn Festival (September 25, 2026) and the National Day of the People’s Republic of China (October 1), Sanya’s tourism industry expects a major surge in visitors despite the end of the summer vacation season.

As a result, the resort city remains a popular tourist destination for travelers worldwide all year round, both in winter and summer.
The newspaper described the visa-free regime as a "golden key" that not only gives Hainan access to tourist flows but also unlocks the Chinese southernmost province’s potential for hosting exhibitions and conferences. For example, in early September, a delegation of around 100 representatives of travel agencies from Russian-speaking countries visited Sanya to exchange experience and to introduce new high-quality tourism products.
The Chinese resort city is attracting the attention of operators not only from Russia and its neighboring countries. Due to the strengthening of Sanya’s international status, the city has won the right to host an annual summit of the Pacific Asia Travel Association in 2027.

The publication also noted the rise in direct flights from Hainan to Russian cities, which should keep the flow of Russian tourists to the island active all year round.

Organizers seek way for signers to join expanded 2028 Song Celebration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

Organizers seek way for signers to join expanded 2028 Song Celebration
This week marked the official start of preparations for the XIV Youth Song and Dance Celebration and the XXIX Song and XXII Dance Celebration, taking place in summer 2028. Artistic director of the Song Celebration, Riivo Jõgi, said that some changes can be expected, and meetings are underway to find a suitable solution for sign‑language performers.
The 2028 festival will last a full week and a half, from June 30 to July 9. "This stems from the coronavirus pandemic. We decided to combine the youth festival tradition with the general Song Celebration tradition. That's why the festival is significantly longer than before," Jõgi explained.
The festival is titled "Olemise viis" ("Way of Being"). "The title was chosen to be multilayered and philosophical. One meaning could relate to what it means to be Estonian across time — a deeper underlying idea," Jõgi said.
"When writing the concept, I focused largely on time — who we have been in the past, who we are now, and what we leave to future generations. The Song Celebration will take place over three days, from Friday to Sunday. Previously it was held only on Saturday and Sunday. Spanning three days felt inspiring and compelling for expressing the passage of time," he noted.
Jõgi believes that this time the Sunday concert will not sell out far ahead of the others. "Each day has its own character. Friday is communal singing, Saturday features adult categories with wind orchestras under the arch, and Sunday is dedicated to children's categories. For the final combined choir, performers from the previous days join as well," he explained.
He emphasized that reaching the Song Celebration stage requires significant work. "But I'd even say that in the end, everyone can come to the Song Celebration. The real question is who gets under the arch and who listens. There is great magic in listening and being present at the festival. Sometimes it's even more wonderful to hear what is offered from under the arch," Jõgi said.
Jõgi noted that organizers have held meetings with sign‑language choirs, and discussions will continue in autumn. "We are trying to find a suitable way for them to participate in the Song Celebration," he said.
Among other changes, Jõgi highlighted the separation of mixed choirs and youth mixed choirs, as well as the separation of girls' and women's choirs.
"Since I'm more of an orchestra person and try to pay attention to those aspects, one difference compared to recent festivals is that on Friday we will use a wind orchestra as the accompanying ensemble. On Saturday and Sunday, a symphony orchestra. A lovely children's combined choir will also be formed — something we haven't done before — consisting of boys' choirs, young children's choirs, and children's choirs," Jõgi said.

South Sudanese migrant jailed in UK for piloting record Channel boat crossing
LONDON, Sept 18 - A South Sudanese man was jailed for two years and three months in an English court on Friday after he admitted piloting a small boat across the Channel from France, which carried a then-record 165 people.
Chan Mathok Atak, 19, previously pleaded guilty to endangering another during a July crossing to Britain in an inflatable dinghy.
The record for most migrants travelling to Britain across the Channel by small boat was broken again last month, when 230 people made the journey.
Atak's sentencing comes as the numbers of those arriving in Britain across the Channel have fallen, but the crossings remain a prominent political issue which successive British governments have struggled to tackle.
Earlier this month, hundreds of black-clad protesters gathered twice in two days on Britain's south coast, blocking streets in response to arrivals of small boats, which a government minister described as "thuggish".
Right-wing opposition parties and anti-migration activists have called for more action, but greater cooperation with French authorities and even repeated deaths have not deterred many people from seeking to make the perilous journey.
OVERCROWDED DINGHY CARRIED 165 PEOPLE
Atak was sentenced to 27 months in prison at Canterbury Crown Court. Prosecutor James Harrison said Atak piloted the dinghy for at least 90 minutes while it carried 164 other people, including 31 children aged 14 to 17.
He said there was no navigational or first aid equipment on the boat, which had only one of its two engines working and was slowly deflating and taking on sea water before it was intercepted by Britain's Border Force.
Atak's lawyer Audrey Cherryl Mogan said Atak was a young asylum seeker from South Sudan who did not have anything to do with the number of people or the conditions on board.
Judge Sarah Counsell accepted there was no evidence Atak organised the journey, but said that "those who chose to steer such vessels assume responsibility for the safety of those on board".
"This undermines public confidence in the immigration system and places considerable strain on already stretched public resources," she added.
The National Crime Agency's senior investigating officer John Turner said in a statement: "Chan Atak was unimaginably reckless and his actions could have easily resulted in many deaths had this boat not been intercepted." REUTERS

Smooth take off: Pilot handles Punjab turbulence with ‘no CM face’ formula; but can he carry Congress beyond winning line?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:18:01 UTC
22:18:01 KST

Sachin Pilot with Charanjit Singh Channi and Amrinder Singh Raja Warring during a protest to demand justice for the late Gulzar Singh in Chandigarh on Tuesday.
NEW DELHI: The Congress in Punjab has finally hit the ground running. Sachin Pilot, who replaced Bhupesh Baghel as the party’s state in-charge, successfully navigated the state unit out of months of internal turmoil and ensured the party’s campaign for the 2027 assembly elections could finally take off.With arch-rivals - former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi and state Congress chief Raja Warring - on board, Pilot led a mega protest demanding the resignation of Punjab finance minister Harpal Cheema, who faces charges of abetment of suicide of a Dalit, Gulzar Singh.The entire state leadership and thousands of party workers marched towards Cheema’s residence. Police used water cannons to stop the protesters’ march. But the point was made. The Congress was finally in action mode.Pilot ensured that Channi and Warring, whose open power tussle has derailed Congress’s Punjab campaign, not only shared the stage but also did a “tense” handshake.Putting up a huge show of unity during the protest, Channi said, "We will fight together." Warring reciprocated. The state Congress chief called Channi and other leaders his 'pagg da lar' (the fold of his turban).
Expressing gratitude to party workers for mobilising in such huge numbers at short notice, Pilot assured each one of them that the Congress will always stand by them. The Congress in-charge assured party workers that he was the representative of the high command and would not leave any stone unturned to restore the dignity and honour of every Congress worker.
But will Pilot’s truce hold?
That’s the big question. The Punjab Congress has seen a no-holds-barred battle between Channi and Warring ever since the high command announced on July 1 that Warring would continue as Punjab Congress chief, ignoring Channi’s claims.The announcement triggered immediate protests from Channi’s supporters. They demanded that Channi should be projected as the party’s CM face in the assembly elections. What followed left the Congress leadership red-faced. From war or words to slogan-shouting at party meetings, the wide split in the state unit was out in the open. The Congress sent Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhupesh Baghel to firefight, but he was also singed in the crossfire. Channi camp leaders accused him of siding with Warring.Pilot, who was then air-dashed to Punjab to set the house in order, has passed his maiden test. But assembly elections in the state are still at least 5 months away. Holding the rival factions together till then will indeed be a daunting challenge for the former Rajasthan deputy chief minister.
Well begun is half done
So, how did Pilot cross the first hurdle smoothly? What did he do differently, which Bhupesh Baghel couldn’t?Former Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhupesh Baghel was sent to Punjab in February this year. The Congress in Punjab then was a deeply divided house. Baghel worked hard on the ground to bridge differences between the state leaders. But on July 1, when the Congress high command announced to continue with Raja Warring as the state Congress president and made Channi the head of the campaign committee, the rebellion in the state unit came out in the open.Channi’s supporters openly opposed the decision. When Baghel reinforced the leadership structure and ruled out any change, the rebels openly protested and even raised slogans against him.Baghel tried to pacify the rebels by announcing that Punjab elections would be fought under the leadership of Rahul Gandhi and no state leader would be projected as CM face. But the rebels had lost his trust and refused to budge.With the rebels refusing to relent and their open infighting embarrassing the party leadership, the Congress high command decided to do a course correction to set its house in order.Baghel was shifted out, Pilot was brought in with a clear message: Congress would contest the 2027 assembly elections under collective leadership, and Rahul Gandhi would be the face of the campaign. This was a half-way compromise. The party leadership relented on Baghel but refused to budge on replacing Warring - at least for now.Warring was handpicked by the Congress high command to lead the Punjab unit after the party’s rout in the 2017 assembly elections - which saw the grand-old-party reduced to 17 assembly seats - its worst-ever performance in the state.
“No CM face” compromise
So, Pilot has crossed the first hurdle. But at what cost? Congress’s decision to fight the Punjab assembly elections under collective leadership, with Rahul Gandhi as the face of the campaign, may have at best delayed the inevitable power tussle.But it creates another challenge for the party. Much of the Congress’s success in the state till now has been driven by a strong local leadership - Captain Amarinder Singh, who is now with the BJP.The AAP has already announced to contest the upcoming assembly elections under the leadership of Bhagwant Singh Mann. Arvind Kejriwal, who is the face of AAP has largely worked from behind the scenes - planning and strategising for the Punjab challenge. For the Akalis, Sukhbir Singh Badal is the undisputed leader and the party’s campaign revolves around him.That leaves us with the BJP and the Congress.
PM Modi vs Rahul
The Congress decision to contest Punjab assembly elections with Rahul Gandhi as the party’s face makes the upcoming electoral contest interesting, and perhaps also challenging for the party.The BJP has already launched an aggressive campaign for Punjab with Prime Minister Narendra Modi leading the party’s campaign. PM Modi has already held two rallies in the poll-bound state and has announced a slew of development projects. As the campaign progresses, we will see the Prime Minister go all out against BJP’s political opponents. The BJP, which is in the process of building the party in the state, also has no visible local leadership. It has acquired quite a few prominent leaders from AAP and Congress, but it is unlikely any of them would be projected as the CM face. BJP’s campaigns in states are mostly centralised, with all top leaders campaigning for the party and PM Modi leading the charge. Punjab should be no exception.And that is what should worry the Congress. The fight to conquer Punjab could well become another PM Modi vs Rahul contest. In several such direct contests in the past, the Congress has struggled. However, Punjab could be different. The BJP, for a greater part of its existence in the state, has played second fiddle to the Akalis.
The BJP has announced a solo contest in 2027 elections.For the Congress, Punjab has been one of the happiest hunting grounds. Despite the haunting memories of Operation Blue Star and the anti-Sikh killings, Punjab has voted for the Congress. Now, it is over to Pilot to take the Congress beyond the winning line.

Social Democrats to form new government in Sweden

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:17:53 UTC
22:17:53 KST

An alliance of left-wing forces has won a fierce contest in Sweden’s parliamentary elections, and Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson will form the government, reports Politico.
Incumbent Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has stepped down following the election defeat, paving the way for the formation of a new center-left government. Andersson is now expected to begin formal negotiations with other parties in her bloc; if she succeeds in reaching an agreement, she will assume the role of Prime Minister in the coming weeks. In a social media address, Andersson stated that the Swedish people had voted for a new direction for the country. She noted that the election demonstrated a public desire for unity rather than division and pledged to achieve this as Prime Minister.
Andersson said she would prioritize a fair migration system that prevents unjust deportations, a climate policy focused on the transition to green technologies, improved healthcare and care for the elderly, and economic renewal to foster growth and reduce unemployment.
The election presented a choice between Andersson’s four-party alliance of center-left and socialist parties and Kristersson’s four-party right-wing group. The right-wing alliance also included the far-right, anti-immigration Sweden Democrats.
During the election campaign, Andersson—who had already served as prime minister prior to the 2022 election—warned voters against handing power to the Sweden Democrats. Kristersson had promised that the far-right party could secure ministerial posts in his future government. The results were not favorable for the Sweden Democrats;
the party had hoped to gain power for the first time but instead lost votes, seats, and influence.
Final results from the Swedish Election Authority show that Andersson’s bloc secured 176 seats, while Kristersson’s won 173. However, Andersson still requires support from three other left-wing parties to secure a majority. This could prove quite complicated, as two of her potential allies do not get along. The Left Party seeks ministerial posts in exchange for its support—a condition the liberal Centre Party is unwilling to accept. Andersson stated that a new era of cooperation among the parties would need to be established.
In his statement, Kristersson, the leader of the center-right forces, called for coalition talks involving all parties, noting that current “red lines” make forming a coalition difficult. Although he did not explicitly mention Andersson’s name or the rift between the Greens and the Left, that was most likely what he had in mind. Kristersson wrote that securing support now requires constructive and open cooperation among parliamentary parties. Talks must be held with all parties to break the deadlock and create the conditions for forming a stable and effective government.
One possibility sometimes cited by Swedish political commentators is for center-left and center-right parties—namely Andersson’s Social Democrats and Kristersson’s Moderates—to join forces and form a majority coalition that does not rely on support from parties at the fringes of the political spectrum. However, even if the two parties could reach an agreement (which is not considered a realistic prospect), they would still need the support of a third party to secure a majority.
Negotiations could drag on for weeks. The earliest date the new prime minister could be sworn in is the 29th of September.

Serial killer fears grow in South Africa after ninth woman found dead
South African police have found the body of a ninth woman near Johannesburg as they investigate a series of murders over the past two months.
The unidentified victim was found in Dawn Park in the Ekurhuleni municipality on Thursday morning. Her body was reportedly partially unclothed and appeared to have been dumped near a construction site. Gauteng’s Department of Community Safety said a multidisciplinary team has been mobilized to investigate the cases and identify those responsible. It has appealed to the public for information.
The latest discovery follows eight others in Kempton Park, Clayville, Olifantsfontein, Rhodesfield, and KwaThema. Most of the victims were women in their 20s and 30s whose bodies were found in open areas or near roads. Several were naked or partially clothed, while some showed signs of bruising or other injuries.
Police have not established that the women were killed by the same person or group. However, investigators have said similarities between the cases are sufficiently concerning to examine whether a serial killer could be responsible.
The first body was discovered near the R21 highway in Kempton Park in July. The 37-year-old victim was found naked and restrained with cable ties. A suspect reportedly identified as her partner was arrested in connection with the case but has not been linked to the other deaths.
Among the victims was 38-year-old Elizabeth ‘Tsontso’ Moselakgomo, whose disappearance after leaving home for a run prompted a widespread appeal. Her partially clothed and bruised body was discovered near the R21 highway on September 12.
The authorities have deployed additional officers, increased patrols, and offered a 400,000-rand ($25,000) reward for information leading to arrests.
In a message delivered at a memorial event on Thursday, President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killings have “disturbed our nation” and created fear in local communities. He directed police to “leave no stone unturned” and use all available means, including the latest surveillance technology, to track down those responsible.
The incidents have intensified public anger over violence against women in South Africa, where the female homicide rate is nearly six times the global average, according to UN data.

EU weighs windfall taxes on energy firms amid growing economic strain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:16:30 UTC
22:16:30 KST

EU ministers meeting in Dublin on Friday and Saturday are considering a windfall tax on energy companies, as price volatility continues to destabilise the economic outlook.
A windfall tax for firms profiting from energy price volatility is one of the ideas circulating among EU ministers meeting in Dublin on Friday and Saturday for the periodic meetings of the Eurogroup and Economic and Financial Council.
With the war in the Middle East continuing, Brent crude oil prices have surpassed $100 per barrel, and extreme volatility in energy prices is driving inflation higher across the bloc, which is not expected to return to the 2% target before the end of 2027.
While growth indicators are still performing well this year, the European Commission expects economic growth to slow down in 2027.
The EU is urging member states to pursue prudent fiscal policies and remain within the existing fiscal flexibility of 1.5% for defence spending, of which 0.3% can be used to contain energy prices.
Meanwhile, the European Central Bank (ECB) is gradually raising interest rates to contain inflation.
“There are several member states that put forward this initiative, it is part of our discussions," European Commissioner for Economy Valdis Dombrovskis said during a press conference on Friday, referring to the windfall tax.
"Member states can already implement windfall profit taxes at the national level if they decide to do so. From the Commission side, we are ready to support those member states by sharing best practices and finding a good way forward.”
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil is pressing the European Commission to present models for a windfall tax, asking to have something on the table by the next Economic and Finance Council meeting in October.
"You know that I have been fighting for this for a long time, together with other European finance ministers," Klingbeil said on the sidelines of Friday's meeting.
The Spanish Finance Minister Carlos Cuerpo also expressed his favour for the proposal on Friday.
“We are managing to lower the bill for homes, companies, industries, transport companies, and this at the expense of the taxpayer's money. We believe there may be fairer ways to distribute this cost,” Cuerpo said.
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure has been more cautious about the proposal.
“This [energy] shock can have a different impact on different countries. We do feel that whatever discussion we have, whatever work has been done, needs to take into account the specificities of each country," he said ahead of the meeting on Friday, specifying that France has a "bigger electricity mix".
To the direct question on whether he supports the proposal or not, Lescure said that he support any work that’s being done, but that "I can’t support something before I’ve seen it".
"I’ll see what the work comes out with, and then we’ll have a discussion.”
Energy taxes: the bulk of pricing
Although the energy crisis is affecting the bloc, not all member states are affected in the same way, with prices at the pump varying greatly.
Finland, Denmark and the Netherlands, the three EU countries currently paying the most for diesel, impose some of the highest fuel taxes in the world, pushing retail diesel prices much higher.
On the other hand, countries in Eastern Europe such as Bulgaria and Poland set excise duties far lower, keeping their pump prices down.
Yet according to EU official data published on Thursday, the EU country paying the least for diesel is Malta, with €1.20 per litre charged at the pump on 14 September.
The significant discrepancy in diesel prices across the EU is driven mainly by divergent national tax policies – excise duties and VAT – which make up the largest portion of the retail price of diesel.
However, the difference between diesel prices before and after taxes is staggering. Per the data released on Thursday, Finland’s diesel price stood €1.48 per litre before taxes and €2.50 after taxes.
Denmark also ranked high, with diesel at €1.43 before taxes and €2.50 per litre after taxes, while Dutch citizens would pay only €1.50 per litre of diesel without taxes and €2.49 with taxes.
France, which has the third-highest government debt in the EU, has chosen targeted to offer assistance for the sectors most exposed to the price shock rather than cutting fuel taxes.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asked ministers to extend support for sectors most exposed to higher energy costs until 31 December. Meanwhile, diesel prices at the French pump stood at €2.29 per litre on 14 September, against €1.30 before taxes.
Regional refining capacity also further amplifies energy pricing. All EU countries buy crude oil from the same volatile global markets, but the price motorists ultimately pay at the pump depends on whether there is sufficient refining capacity nearby, how easily fuel can be transported from other regions and how well local refineries can process the particular type of crude available.
During a supply shock like the one the EU is currently suffering, EU countries with spare refining capacity, diversified import routes and strong links to neighbouring fuel markets may be able to cushion the disruption more easily.

China Is Moving Toward a New Form of Coercion at Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:16:00 UTC
22:16:00 KST

Since Beijing announced special maritime operations on June 6, its forces have grown more assertive – pushing patrols into new waters, rotating formations to regularize presence, and deploying research vessels that can conduct military reconnaissance. This all points to a new form of coercion taking shape.
On July 4, the Global Times – a mouthpiece for the Chinese Communist Party – declared that China’s maritime patrols had entered “a new phase,” defined by a move towards “a more systematic, institutionalized, and long-term framework” and away from “isolated military exercises or patrols.”
Recent deployments bear this out. Between June 6 and June 10, China’s Ministry of Transport carried out its first special operation in waters east of Taiwan, halting commercial vessels and requesting information on their points of origin and destination.
While China has announced mandatory inspections during past exercises, it has never successfully enforced them. This time was different. Chinese Coast Guard ships conducted inspections en masse through radio communications with all transiting commercial vessels. Even foreign commercial vessels – including three vessels from Singapore, Benin, and Liberia – reported receiving radio messages from Chinese authorities to comply with requests.
According to Chinese state news agency Xinhua, across those four days, Chinese maritime authorities inspected 198 passing vessels, and even “rectified violations involving three ships.” The sheer quantity of reported inspections, followed by a public announcement of the results, demonstrates China’s ability to govern vessel traffic in Taiwan’s waters. Beijing uses that as grounds to assert jurisdiction over the island and to push the narrative that cross-strait dynamics are China’s internal affairs.
These operations may be testing grounds for an eventual quarantine, where China selectively permits commercial vessels to enter or leave, exerting immense pressure on Taiwan’s supply lines. If that is the case, the series of multi-day patrols serve two functions.
First, they test how foreign nations respond to maritime traffic controls. Knowing which nations elect to respond, and to what degree, gives Beijing some sense of what to expect. The United Kingdom, Germany, and France, for instance, issued a joint statement expressing alarm over the maritime activities. Australia raised concerns directly with Chinese officials. How forceful Beijing judges the pushback to be will affect the intensity of operations. In the event of an actual quarantine, though, responses are likely to be more pronounced.
Second, they normalize China’s vessel inspections, shortening the leap to a quarantine. In July, China’s Coast Guard began rotating its formations to regularize its law-enforcement presence. The Global Times has noted the advantages of maintaining a “constant presence” because “a normalized presence itself exerts pressure.” The longer Beijing can keep ships on station, the more quickly it can impose a quarantine.
The location of operations is unusual as well. Until June, China appeared to prioritize the Taiwan Strait, where conditions are most favorable for launching an amphibious invasion. Oddly enough, the maritime operations have been concentrated in waters opposite the strait, to the east of Taiwan. The island’s eastern coast has long been regarded as a low-priority zone as steep mountains make military landings difficult.
But choosing to operate in the east is not random. The move effectively shrinks the space that Taiwan can operate in, aligning with China’s broader boa-constrictor strategy to sever the island from international support. More telling is that these patrols, China claims, were initiated as a response to talks between Japan and the Philippines to delimit maritime boundaries east of Taiwan. Beijing hopes to deter strategic cooperation between two U.S. allies, one located north and the other to the south of the island, that may each play critical roles during a conflict over Taiwan.
A final novelty of the recent operations is the sharp increase in Chinese research vessels operating in waters around Taiwan. While Beijing maintains that these ships only conduct marine scientific research, their missions appear far less benign. Publicly available tracking data shows that these vessels could be systematically mapping the undersea terrain, presaging planning for naval operations. Since June 6, at least seven research vessels have been suspected of conducting research with military applications.
Taken together, these signs indicate that a more intrusive form of coercion is taking form. Regional nations would be unwise to dismiss this as more of the same.

“Nani mi, nani, Damyancho” – Lyubomir Pipkov’s poetry in music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:13:01 UTC
22:13:01 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
Article
Highlights of Bulgarian musical culture
“Nani mi, nani, Damyancho” – Lyubomir Pipkov’s poetry in music
Friday 18 September 2026 14:45
Friday, 18 September 2026, 14:45
PHOTO operasofia.bg
Font size
One of Bulgaria’s great composers of the 20th century, Lyubomir Pipkov holds an important place in both Bulgarian and European music. He was particularly gifted at turning words into music. Few figures in the Bulgarian school of composition could match his cultural and literary range or his poetic sensibility. Pipkov approached words both as a musician and as someone with a deep affinity for poetry.
This can be heard throughout his work, especially in his songs. Scholars have explored the different ways in which he interpreted a text and shaped the relationship between words and musical expression. Pipkov himself considered the choral song one of the central genres in his work. Among his masterpieces are Na nivata (In the Fields), Proleten vyatar (Spring Wind), Zhalta peperuda (Yellow Butterfly), Tsarevitsa ranna (Early Corn), and the cycles Four Madrigals and Muted Songs. They remain an important part of the Bulgarian choral repertoire today.
Among them, “Nani mi, nani, Damyancho” holds a special place. Written in 1948 for mixed choir to a traditional folk text, it brings together the directness of Bulgarian folk poetry and Pipkov’s skill as a composer to remarkable effect.
At the centre of the song is a mother trying to lull her child to sleep while working hard in the fields. Tenderness, exhaustion, anxiety and sorrow can all be heard in her soothing voice, against the reality of gruelling physical work. It is a lullaby that is both intimate and social, without a trace of pathos and with the natural simplicity of Bulgarian folk tradition.
“Nani mi, nani, Damyancho” also became a recurring musical idea in Pipkov’s work. He wrote a song for soprano and piano under the same title, and later gave the title to an instrumental piece in his 1973 piano cycle Spring Whims. His return to the same musical material suggests how close this subject was to him, revisited in different genres and through different forms of expression.
For Pipkov, folklore was not simply an outward sign of national identity. It was fundamental to the way he thought about music. As Prof. Ivan Hlebarov, one of the leading scholars of the composer’s work, wrote: “Pipkov is national not because of his subject matter, but because of the way he sees the world... And by drawing on folklore, he develops a harmony of consciousness that remains a defining feature of his worldview throughout his creative life.”
PHOTO operasofia.bg
“Nani mi, nani, Damyancho” is a vivid example of what Hlebarov describes. Pipkov does not quote a folk melody directly, yet there is no mistaking the Bulgarian character of the music. It is there in its intonation, in the treatment of the words, in the rhythm of the musical phrase and, above all, in the image at its heart: a mother’s voice, the closeness between mother and child, the burden of everyday life and the quiet human resilience that allows tenderness to survive even in the hardest circumstances.

Interview: Hong Kong's inaugural 5-year plan aligns with national strategy, targets economic diversification: HKSAR chief executive

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:11:27 CST
22:11:27 KST

HONG KONG, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The launch of Hong Kong's inaugural five-year plan represented a proactive push by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) to seize growth opportunities, HKSAR Chief Executive John Lee said on Thursday.
Lee made the remarks in an interview after unveiling the HKSAR's milestone five-year plan for economic and social development (2026-2030) earlier this week, adding that its rollout in tandem with the national 15th Five-Year Plan was "no coincidence."
The blueprint sets out 105 core development indicators through 2030, marking the first systematic medium-to-long-term development framework for the financial hub since its return to the motherland in 1997.
From industrial development to regional cooperation, the plan was grounded in national policies for Hong Kong, aligning directly with the country's overarching strategy.
Looking back on the drafting process, the chief executive said it had prompted reflections on the city's competitive standing.
"We conducted a self-assessment: Where are Hong Kong's strengths and weaknesses? What are our opportunities and risks? We must handle all four areas well," he said.
On strengths, the plan outlined measures to consolidate and enhance Hong Kong's status as an international financial, maritime and trade center, and to develop it into a global hub for high-caliber talent.
"What we do well, we must do even better," Lee stressed, vowing to beef up strengths in new areas such as international legal and dispute resolution, intellectual property trading and cultural and arts exchanges, further upgrading its international competitiveness.
The chief executive identified economic diversification as a key task in the coming five years, saying moving beyond service sectors such as finance and trade would help the city foster high-value industries and raise incomes.
A major driver of that shift is the Northern Metropolis. Covering around a third of Hong Kong's land area, the Northern Metropolis is expected to eventually house about a third of its population and become a key zone for economic growth and social well-being.
Lee underscored Hong Kong's unique advantages of enjoying the backing of the motherland and being open to the world under the "one country, two systems" framework.
The blueprint plans to better align Hong Kong with the development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area and deepen integration with the Chinese mainland.
So far, Hong Kong has set up regional cooperation mechanisms with nine areas in the Chinese mainland.
On global links, Lee stressed that Hong Kong will play its part as a "super-connector" to help Belt and Road participating countries and regions access the Chinese mainland market, thus contributing to the country's high-standard opening-up.
Indicators are vital to ensuring the delivery of the plan, Lee said, adding that the 105 indicators set out in the five-year plan are mapped directly to 284 concrete measures in the 2026 policy address, a ratio of roughly one target to three actionable steps.
The chief executive stressed that the plan "was not empty words," pledging strict accountability to turn the blueprint into concrete actions.
"If targets are not met, we will investigate the reasons and hold people accountable," he said.
From annual policy address to the systematic planning of the five-year blueprint, Hong Kong's governance model is undergoing a significant transition.
"The ultimate goal of governance is to improve people's livelihoods," Lee said, expressing confidence in meeting the targets in the blueprint. "We must pool our strength to make sure we get it done well." ■

Explainer: The battle for Bab al-Mandab in Yemen -- why it matters globally
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:11:20 CST
22:11:20 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The latest escalation in Yemen has thrust the Bab al-Mandab Strait into the global spotlight as a new flashpoint, following the Houthis' significant territorial gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast and around the strategic waterway.
Analysts say that, amid disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the Iran-U.S. conflict, the struggle for control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait is no longer simply about territorial gains inside Yemen. Rather, it is about gaining leverage in a shifting regional landscape by expanding its sway over global energy markets.
HOW IS THE ESCALATION UNFOLDING?
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. In recent days, fighting has intensified across western and northern Yemen, in one of the sharpest escalations since a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities.
On Sept. 10, the Houthi group seized the Red Sea port city of Mocha in southwestern Taiz province, forcing government troops to withdraw southward toward Dhubab, between Mocha and Bab al-Mandab. The capture brought the Houthis closer to the strait, marking a major battlefield shift along Yemen's western coast.
A day later, the group captured Dhubab and seized the Mayun Island at the heart of Bab al-Mandab after government forces pulled farther south into neighboring Lahj province. The capture of the island, which divides the waterway into two shipping channels, gave the group control of key positions overlooking the strait.
Following the developments, the government forces and the Houthis engaged in heavy clashes near the strait, with casualties reported on both sides.
According to military officials from both sides who spoke on condition of anonymity, fighting has raged fiercely since Wednesday across the Kahbub mountain area and surrounding heights in Lahj, where Houthi members launched a renewed push against government defensive positions.
The battle remained fluid on Thursday, with several commanding heights changing hands during attacks and counterattacks. Neither side had secured a decisive breakthrough, according to the officials. Both sides have sent additional fighters, weapons and military vehicles into the area, raising the prospect of further heavy fighting for control of positions overlooking approaches to Bab al-Mandab.
WHY DOES BAB AL-MANDAB MATTER?
Bab al-Mandab, between Yemen and the Horn of Africa, acts as a critical maritime chokepoint connecting the Gulf of Aden to the southern end of the Red Sea, forming an indispensable artery for global energy shipments and international trade moving to and from the Suez Canal.
"The battle for Bab al-Mandab is not simply about gaining territory inside Yemen," Aden-based political analyst Muqbil Naji told Xinhua. "Whoever can threaten this waterway acquires leverage that extends well beyond Yemen's borders."
Offering a similar assessment, Abdul-Salam Mohamed, chairman of the Yemeni think tank Abaad Studies and Research Center, said that the western coast is one of three fronts that could shape the course of the war.
The strategic importance of the western front lies largely in Bab al-Mandab, Mohamed said, noting that a Houthi advance toward the waterway would give the group "a potent new source of strategic leverage," while a major defeat could threaten its positions farther north along the Red Sea coast.
Assessing the broader regional dynamics, Yemeni political analyst Khalil Muthanna al-Omari said that with navigation through the Strait of Hormuz already severely disrupted, Houthi control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait would effectively create "a front parallel to the Strait of Hormuz," allowing Iran, through its Houthi allies, to exert influence on global energy shipping through two critical maritime chokepoints at the same time.
WHAT ARE THE IMPLICATIONS?
Abdulaziz Alshaabani, a Saudi researcher at Al Riyadh Center for Political and Strategic Studies, said that continued tensions around Bab al-Mandab could drive up insurance and shipping costs and prompt shipping companies to take longer and more expensive routes around the Cape of Good Hope.
Such disruptions would have a direct impact on the Suez Canal, as its security is closely linked to that of the southern maritime route, he said. If ships could not safely pass through Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea, some trade could shift to alternative routes, resulting in longer transit times, higher costs and added pressure on global trade.
The impact, however, would not be limited to shipping and trade. Alshaabani said the latest developments could make a political settlement of the Yemeni conflict more difficult.
He explained that control of coastal areas and strategic routes would give the Houthis more leverage and make the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab a lasting factor in the conflict. The Yemen crisis is therefore no longer only about power-sharing, but also about global maritime, energy and trade security.
The developments also raise broader regional security concerns, analysts say.
According to Yemeni political analyst Hamza al-Kamali, the "most dangerous" development would be the militarization of the strait and the involvement of different international powers in the confrontation in the Red Sea.
In that case, al-Kamali said, increased tensions and polarization along this important maritime route would further aggravate the maritime transport and supply chain crisis already stemming from the situation around the Strait of Hormuz. ■

Thailand tightens hospital birth records to curb nationality fraud
