Iraq Sentences Former Electricity Director General to Seven Years for illicit enrichment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:59:00 UTC
21:59:00 KST

Reported by
An Iraqi anti-corruption court has sentenced the former director general of a state electricity distribution firm to seven years in prison for illicit enrichment, ordering him to forfeit nearly $20 million in restitution and fines as part of a sweeping crackdown on graft in the country’s power sector.
The official, Alaa Samir Rashid Shukr Al-Jubouri, who headed the state-owned General Company of Electricity Distribution (Middle Region), was convicted by Iraq’s Central Criminal Court for Combating Corruption. According to the country’s Integrity Commission, Rashid amassed unexplained wealth exceeding 5.5 billion Iraqi dinars (about $4.2 million) along with an additional $5.5 million in U.S. currency.
The court ordered Rashid to return the illicit gains and levied an equivalent fine, bringing his total financial liability to approximately $19.4 million. Judges also upheld a freeze on his movable and immovable assets, paving the way for seizure.
Rashid’s prosecution followed an internal Ministry of Electricity audit in June that reviewed company contracting procedures from 2022 to 2025. Auditors uncovered 127 fraudulent procurement transactions valued at roughly $4.5 million. Citing "dangerous" misconduct that endangered the public interest, ministry officials stripped Rashid of his post on June 20. Two days later, judicial authorities froze his real estate holdings in Fallujah, leading to his arrest shortly thereafter.
Taha Al-Difai, chairman of the Iraqi Parliament’s Integrity Committee, told OCCRP that the case centers on wealth whose legitimate origin Rashid failed to demonstrate. Al-Difai warned that under Iraqi law, judicial asset recovery can extend to property transferred to officials' children and family members if tied to illicit enrichment.
Al-Difai added that graft in Iraq’s electricity sector is not isolated to distribution, noting that ongoing investigations and previous convictions have targeted systemic corruption across power generation, transmission, and regional government projects.
The ruling comes weeks after the same company’s financial director was sentenced to three years in prison on separate illicit enrichment charges.
Neither Rashid nor the Ministry of Electricity responded to requests for comment.

Sayyed al-Houthi pointed out that Saudi air strikes have targeted more than 2,000 mosques in Yemen, including historic mosques that were nowhere near the front lines. Call for an Islamic coalition against Israel

As Congress passes Russia sanctions, Trump weighs business deals with Moscow before the war ends
The Trump administration is weighing business deals with Russia even before the war in Ukraine ends, two sources close to the negotiations told The New York Times. One of the sources said such deals could show that the United States is serious about a “reset” in relations with Russia.
Since Trump began his second term, Russian officials have floated several cooperation options for Washington, including joint projects in the Arctic, development of rare earth metals, and aluminum production.
Washington had previously ruled out economic deals with Moscow before the war’s end. A year ago, during talks in Anchorage, possible energy projects were discussed, though Trump had said even before that meeting that he would not do business until “we get the war settled.” The current approach would mark a shift from Trump’s earlier stance, according to the Times.

Trump still has to sign the bill, and WSJ reports he intends to do so.

Belgium's federal government has approved a six-month extension of the military deployment at train and metro stations in the capital, Defense Minister Theo Francken said Friday.

US may lend more oil from strategic reserve amid price surge: Energy secretary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:55:38 UTC
21:55:38 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The US could lend additional crude oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve as higher prices and tight near-term supplies increase demand for prompt barrels, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said, according to energy-market information provider Argus Media.
The recent rise in crude prices has made another round of loans a “very real possibility” under the continuing 172-million-barrel drawdown authorized by President Donald Trump in March, Wright told reporters Thursday.
“The market right now is saying, ‘Hey, maybe we need that oil.’ So quite possibly we will respond to that,” he said.
Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude was trading near $101 per barrel, about 25% above the price of crude for delivery six months later.
The structure, known as backwardation, occurs when near-term crude prices exceed those for later delivery and can make borrowing oil from the reserve commercially attractive.
The Energy Department has already lent more than 130 million barrels, or over three-quarters of the authorized drawdown. Another 3 million barrels are scheduled for release in the coming weeks, while about 38.5 million barrels remain unallocated.
“We had stopped selling because the prices were flat,” Wright said. “The market today is pulling for it. If that remains, then it’s very possible we will finish the allocation of oil we originally agreed to trade.”
Under the program, companies borrow government-owned crude and later return the oil with an additional premium. Previous agreements are expected to result n the return of roughly 1.25 barrels to the reserve for every barrel borrowed.
The continuing drawdown has reduced the Strategic Petroleum Reserve's crude inventories to around 285 million barrels, the lowest level since 1982.
Wright has said the return of borrowed crude is expected to begin early next year and continue through 2029.

Ukraine’s snipers didn’t vanish in the drone war—their job changed beyond recognition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:54:41 UTC
21:54:41 KST

Drones get most of the attention in this war, and deservedly so—but the snipers are still out there, two Ukrainian marksmen told Army Inform, and the same drones have made their work far harder to survive. It now turns on watching, not shooting: long stretches at a hidden position, a thermal scope always running, and a constant fight to stay unseen.
Across the drone-saturated front, cheap cameras overhead have rewritten nearly every job—infantry, logistics crews, and now marksmen—so that surviving depends less on firepower than on never being seen.
The job is mostly watching
The men—a squad leader in a special-purpose sniper company, callsign Efiop, and his partner Maister—serve in the National Guard of Ukraine's 3rd Operational Purpose Brigade Spartan. Maister worked a factory milling machine before joining in 2022. He saw what Russian troops were doing, he said, and Ukrainian children started dying: he went to fight for the children, and he has a daughter of his own. A team takes a sector and holds it around the clock through a thermal scope.
"We can sit 40 days and never fire a shot. Or we go in, and in a single day we take down a lot of them," Efiop said.
His longest stint at one spot ran 48 days, and the greatest distance he has worked was 2,540 meters—more than a mile and a half.
Up to 154 pounds on your back, over 12 miles to cross
Reaching a position is often the hardest part. A sniper carries a vest, helmet, an assault rifle and the sniper rifle, and what supplies will fit—60 to 70 kilograms, or 132 to 154 pounds. They stay more than a month, and a month's worth will not go on one back. That load sometimes crosses more than 20 kilometers, over 12 miles, of open ground with no tree line to hide behind.
"You don't walk, you run," Maister said.
Lately it has eased a little: food can be dropped in by a heavy Vampire bomber drone.
Drones rewrote the rulebook
The biggest shift came from the sky. Russian drones with thermal cameras can see a bullet in flight because it is warm, Efiop said, and then burn out the position.
"They caught us like that once. We took out three, they saw where we fired from and burned the spot. We moved right away, and everyone lived," Efiop noted.
Now the snipers watch remotely from a safer place instead of lying behind the scope for hours. Once, that safer setup saved a life outright: a mortar round came in and pierced only the rifle scope.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy launched a new regional cooperation framework with seven neighbouring countries on Friday in an effort to stoke regional investment.

Member states will work together on security, energy, logistics, cross-border economic ties and support for local communities.

As Houthis grab Bab al-Mandeb, US appears willing to watch from sidelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:52:29 UTC
21:52:29 KST

As Houthis grab Bab al-Mandeb, US appears willing to watch from sidelines
Stretched by its war with Iran, Washington may have little choice but to trust Houthi assurances on shipping — rather than joining another war.
United States officials met Houthi representatives at the US embassy in the Omani capital, Muscat, over the weekend after the Iran-aligned movement seized thousands of square kilometres of territory in just a few days.
With strategically important islands and large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast now under Houthi control, the group has tightened its grip on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait – a crucial chokepoint for global shipping and energy supplies.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Bomb attack at Pakistan mosque kills at least 27 people
- list 2 of 4Ukraine fires drone barrage as Russia launches elections
- list 3 of 4Israel is killing the people who could end its wars
- list 4 of 4‘My children did not attack Iran’: 2bn South Asians suffer from distant war
During the talks, the Houthis assured US officials that they had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea, saying their restrictions would apply only to vessels linked to Saudi Arabia.
But that would still leave two of the world’s most important shipping routes facing serious disruption, with traffic through the Strait of Hormuz restricted for the past six months. Any further disruption could drive global oil and consumer prices even higher, creating another political headache for US President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections in November.
With the Houthis’ history of attacking commercial vessels, their ties to Iran and their deep ideological opposition to the US, some experts question how far their assurances can be trusted. But some analysts say Washington may have little choice but to take the group at its word, at least for now. US military resources are reportedly depleted and growing domestic opposition to the Iran war have all limited Washington’s ability – and willingness – to open another front in Yemen.
Pressure to intervene
As the Houthis seized territory in southwestern Yemen, the US publication Axios reported that Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Donald Trump twice last week, urging him to launch strikes against the group – but the US president refused.
Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of US Central Command, subsequently travelled to Riyadh for urgent coordination talks with the crown prince. The visit suggested Washington was seeking to intensify support for Saudi Arabia while avoiding direct military involvement.
Trump also attempted to reassure Riyadh, describing the crown prince as a “good friend” and promising that “everything will work out very well”.
But he offered no specific military commitment and the White House announced no explicit guarantee that the US would defend Saudi energy infrastructure or shipping routes.
Axios also reported that the military chiefs of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt attended a private gathering convened by the US.
While the US has avoided intervening, Israel, whose ships and territory have previously been targeted by the Houthis, has reportedly offered to intervene in Yemen on Saudi Arabia’s behalf. Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University, however, said any Israeli involvement would probably be limited.
“With elections coming up [in Israel], there comes a point when there is overreach,” Mabon told Al Jazeera. “In light of Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and the West Bank – as well as the question marks over Iran – Yemen could be a bridge too far.” Experts also say that the Saudis may be wary of being seen to rely on Israeli military support, particularly amid the war on Gaza, because doing so could damage Riyadh’s standing and legitimacy throughout the Arab and Muslim worlds.
Washington’s reluctance to act could deepen Saudi concerns about its longstanding security relationship with the US. “This is another instance of the United States failing to fulfil its role as a security guarantor,” Mabon said. “That will start to add up and create serious doubts in Saudi Arabia about whether it can rely on the United States.”
The kingdom began diversifying its relationships after attacks on its oil infrastructure in 2018 and 2019 exposed the limits of US security guarantees. Last September, it signed a mutual defence agreement with Pakistan, stipulating that an attack on either country would be treated as an attack on both. Riyadh expanded that emerging security arrangement last month by signing the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Pakistan and Turkiye, under which an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack against them all.
Mabon said the latest crisis was unlikely to produce a complete break with Washington, but could accelerate Riyadh’s efforts to build closer ties elsewhere.
“We are already seeing a diversification of security portfolios,” he said. “The Saudis are starting to believe that they cannot rely on the United States all the time, which is why we saw the agreement with Turkey and Pakistan.”
Why the US wants to stay out
Washington is already embroiled in an expensive and resource-intensive war with Iran, the Houthis’ principal regional backer. Trump entered that conflict expecting it to end within days. More than six months later, the war remains unresolved, oil prices are higher and the administration has yet to set out a clear route towards ending it.
Opening another front in Yemen would risk repeating that experience at a particularly difficult moment for Trump’s Republican Party. A new campaign in Yemen could complicate closely contested House and Senate races, especially after Trump built his presidential campaign around the promise to end US involvement in “forever wars”. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published last month found that just 31 percent of Americans supported US military action against Iran, down from 37 percent in March, while 83 percent expected the conflict to continue for an extended period.
“The elections in November are hugely significant,” Mabon said. “Republicans will be anxious about all of this. Opening a new front in what could potentially become another forever war would be deeply unpopular.”
It is questionable whether the US has the military resources required to sustain another operation. Reports emerged in July that supplies of some critical munitions, particularly long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors, were running low. Those concerns coincided with Washington halting attacks on Iran.
A Pentagon watchdog report published this week found that the first four months of the war cost $33bn, including $22bn in expended munitions. It also revealed that dozens of aircraft had been lost or damaged, hundreds of buildings and structures hit and Iranian attacks caused an estimated $184m in damage to US diplomatic facilities.
The Trump administration has denied that the US is running short of weapons, insisting that it retains “massive amounts” of weaponry.
But about 50 military officers and civilian officials working with the Joint Staff were ordered to take polygraph lie detector tests as the administration sought to identify the source of leaks about military readiness and weapons stocks.
“We know there are hugely depleted weapons stockpiles, which have prompted some US officials to urge a pause in the war on Iran,” Mabon said.
“When you put that together, it is probably the main reason Trump said no to MBS.”
Does China stand to lose more?
Washington’s response may also reflect the different strategic importance it places on the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb. Hormuz carries oil and gas from Gulf producers to a global market on which the US economy depends. Bab al-Mandeb has become particularly important for trade to Asia and China.
Some analysts have therefore argued that prolonged disruption could hurt Beijing more severely than the US. China remains somewhat dependent on imported energy via the Red Sea. Higher oil prices can also benefit US energy companies, some of which have donated millions of dollars to Trump and the Republican Party.
But Bab al-Mandeb disruption would not fall neatly along geopolitical lines, experts say. Attacks on Saudi infrastructure and shipping would directly harm one of Washington’s closest regional partners, while higher transport and energy costs would eventually feed into prices paid by US consumers.
Mabon rejected the suggestion that Trump was pursuing a calculated strategy of tolerating disruption to weaken China or reward his donors.
“The potential closure of Bab al-Mandeb and strikes on the Saudi pipeline will hit major US allies harder than China,” he said. Whatever benefits higher prices might bring US oil producers would be outweighed politically by the damage inflicted on consumers and the wider economy, he added.
With the US already stretched by war with Iran – which the Trump administration initially expected to end within days – Washington may now be confronting the reality that entering another war in the Middle East carries considerable military, economic and electoral risks.
“I don’t see any kind of grand strategy at play here,” Mabon said. “There is no off-ramp regarding Iran and I think that, in the case of Yemen, there is no easy off-ramp either.”

Canada seeks to join €90bn support loan for Ukraine, Brussels confirms
Unknown

2026-09-18

21:52:28 KST

Canada's inclusion will allow Ukraine to buy weapons from Canadian defence companies and bypass the "Made in Europe" requirements. In turn, Ottawa will have to pay a proportional share of the annual interest.
Canada is seeking to join the European Union's €90 billion support loan for Ukraine, the European Commission said on Friday.
"I can confirm that Canada has expressed an interest in joining the €90 billion Ukraine support loan," a Commission spokesperson told journalists. "We are working hard with Canada, and the respective technical talks are very much ongoing."
EU leaders set up the loan to meet two-thirds of Ukraine's financial and military needs for 2026 and 2027, with the other third covered by other Western allies.
So far, Brussels has disbursed nearly €15 billion, with more instalments expected soon.
The €90 billion is raised through joint borrowing and generates about €3 billion in annual interest payments, which will be paid proportionally by 24 member states. (Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic secured an opt-out from the scheme.)
Canada's inclusion, if successful, will allow Ukraine to procure weapons and ammunition from Canadian defence companies and bypass the "Made in Europe" requirements that govern the credit line. In turn, Ottawa will have to pay a share of the €3 billion in interest rates, depending on how much its firms benefit.
The specifics of the Canadian contribution are still under negotiation.
"The more countries involved, the better. That can ensure that Ukraine can get the best and most suitable equipment for its defence needs," the Commission spokesperson said.
The United Kingdom, a major donor to Ukraine, became the first non-EU country to join the support programme in July.
The news comes as Kyiv looks to allies to plug a growing budget deficit, which is being worsened by Russia's escalation and blockade in the Black Sea.
Brussels is trying to pin down the exact scope of Ukraine's additional needs and has asked other partners to step up. Norway recently announced $9 billion for 2027.
"It's important indeed that our like-minded partners also follow suit, including Canada and the UK," the Commission spokesperson said.
"That is a subject that we usually tend to take up with them regularly."
Canada's move to join the scheme is seen as part of a fast-moving impetus to expand and deepen ties between Ottawa and Brussels. This week, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the bloc's first "associate member".

Russian Elites Fear Covert Mobilization as Putin Eyes 300,000 New Troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:52:06 UTC
21:52:06 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Elites Fear Covert Mobilization as Putin Eyes 300,000 New Troops
Russian elites and Kremlin insiders are increasingly gripped by the fear of a looming military mobilization following the upcoming State Duma elections, Bloomberg reported on September 18.
This prompted a quiet scramble to move assets and relatives out of the country.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Internal documents obtained by Bloomberg reveal that Kremlin officials—and even workers at military recruitment centers—have been advising friends and family to leave Russia in the coming months while actively seeking ways to open foreign bank accounts.
The panic coincides with Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s recent directive to slash the number of regional officials by 15% to ease the burden on a deficit-ridden budget. However, according to the documents seen by Bloomberg, there are growing internal fears that the Kremlin intends to draft these newly unemployed bureaucrats into the military.
According to a European security official cited by Bloomberg, Russia is preparing to send an additional 300,000 men to the war in Ukraine. But unlike the chaotic partial mobilization of September 2022, which triggered a massive exodus of hundreds of thousands of Russians, the Kremlin may avoid a formal public announcement this time.
Instead, authorities have completely overhauled the conscription system to handle a silent draft. Paper summonses have been replaced with a unified digital registry that is now seamlessly integrated with the tax service, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, medical records, property databases, and border control.
Once an electronic summons is issued, the recipient is automatically barred from leaving the country.
While sources indicate that Putin has not yet made a final decision on whether to pull the trigger on a mass draft, the Russian army is facing severe manpower shortages. Russian leader continues to demand the full capture of Ukraine’s Donetsk and Luhansk regions, but the human cost remains staggering.
A source in Moscow familiar with the statistics told Bloomberg that frontline fatalities are reaching up to 1,000 soldiers every week.
Furthermore, the military is struggling to attract capable volunteers. The source noted that the overall “quality” of individuals currently signing contracts with the Ministry of Defense is extremely low.
To sustain the 700,000-strong force currently deployed in Ukraine—a figure cited by Putin himself—Russia must recruit approximately 400,000 new soldiers annually.
Yet, despite raising the average sign-on bonus to a record 1.8 million rubles ($19,000), the influx of recruits is noticeably shrinking. Janis Kluge, an expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, calculates that 234,000 people signed contracts in the first half of this year, down from 260,000 during the same period last year.
This manpower deficit has directly impacted battlefield progress. Territorial gains have practically stalled; Bloomberg analyst Alex Kokcharov estimates that Russia captured just 155 square kilometers during its summer offensive—13 times less than the 2,037 square kilometers seized during the same period a year earlier.
“The military situation in recent months indicates that Russia does not have enough manpower to concentrate troops on the main axis of attack and confidently cover the front line,” said Kirill Rogov, head of the Re: Russia analytical center. “In other words, mobilization is necessary if the goal is to reach the borders of the Donbas within the next six months.”
If a mobilization is initiated, the burden is unlikely to be shared equally across the country. Political scientist Ekaterina Schulmann told Bloomberg that the Kremlin will likely focus its drafting efforts on the regions that demonstrate the highest levels of support for Putin during the upcoming parliamentary elections.
“In places where loyalty, discipline, and administrative efficiency will be demonstrated, more people will be drafted,” Schulmann explained. In the eyes of the Kremlin, she noted, regional authorities who can successfully execute an election can equally execute a mobilization.
The Kremlin’s current reliance on shadow recruitment to avoid a formal mobilization has placed immense pressure on local authorities. According to recent reports, courts in 51 Russian regions have been fining municipal officials for missing their contract-soldier quotas.
This pressure has driven administrators to drastic measures, including attempts to draft hundreds of male orphans in the Irkutsk region. To enforce compliance, the State Duma is reviewing legislation to significantly increase these financial penalties and introduce suspensions of up to three years for noncompliant bureaucrats.

After tour dates were announced for 38 concerts in 2027, Oasis fans are already searching for travel to the host destinations – with Glasgow seeing the biggest surge, +2,400%, according to new data.
Oasis fans really are madferit, aren’t they? Even though tickets are yet to go on sale for the band’s 2027 tour, there’s already been a huge surge in online travel searches to cities set to host concerts.
After a sold-out reunion tour in 2025, Oasis will be back on the road next year with gigs in Glasgow, Manchester, Munich, Barcelona, Amsterdam, Paris, Rome, Boston and Las Vegas, before shows at Ireland’s Slane Castle and a landmark return to Knebworth.
Some might say that the confirmation of next year’s Oasis concert dates is great news for the bank balances of Noel, Liam and the rest of the band. However, judging by the frenzy surrounding the upcoming ticket sales, the tour could prove lucrative for the travel industry too.
According to data released by global online travel agency eDreams, searches for travel to Glasgow have seen the most dramatic uplift – rising by 2,400%. The Scottish city is hosting the opening five nights of the tour, with searches increasing 25-fold compared with the same period last year.
Huge increases in online searches – flight, rail, and dynamic packages – have also been recorded for Manchester (+846%), Rome (+659%), Barcelona (+655%), Dublin (+614%), Amsterdam (+592%) and Paris (+279%), eDreams said. In the US, searches for Las Vegas and Boston have risen by 692% and 487% respectively.
The Oasis reunion contributed to a record year for UK music tourism in 2025 – and the early surge in travel searches suggests next year’s tour could boost the trend yet again.
"Fans are no longer just buying a ticket; they're building entire trips around a single show, and that's reshaping demand in cities far beyond the venue itself,” Pablo Caspers, Chief Travel Officer at eDreams, told Euronews Travel.
“When Taylor Swift's Eras Tour moved through Europe, search interest in host cities like Edinburgh and Liverpool more than doubled almost overnight. We also see regular uplifts in searches for Eurovision host cities, and when festival lineups are announced for Coachella and Primavera Sound.
“With these new Oasis tour dates, we're seeing the pattern play out again: Glasgow searches are up 25-fold on last year, with Manchester up 846%, Dublin up 614%, and the ripple reaching as far as Las Vegas, up 692%, and Boston, up 487%, alongside Rome, Barcelona, Amsterdam and Paris.
"It shows that when an artist has enough cultural pull, they can move travel demand on a truly global scale."
The 2027 Oasis tour kicks off at Celtic Park in Glasgow, Scotland, on 21 May and concludes on 19 September at Knebworth in England. Ticket sales will take place across three days next week – Friday 25 September, Saturday 26 September and Sunday 27 September – with registered fans who receive an access code allocated an on-sale window.

Why does Canada want to join the Europe-led JEF military partnership?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:51:15 UTC
21:51:15 KST

Why does Canada want to join the Europe-led JEF military partnership?
This is the latest step in Canada’s bid to move closer to Europe amid bitter trade war with the US.
Canada has applied to join the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a European military coalition, as it seeks to diversify its diplomatic and security ties following a sharp downturn in relations with the United States.
Prime Minister Mark Carney made the request on Wednesday during an official trip to the United Kingdom, which he visited after meeting with European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels. She invited Canada to become the first-ever “associate member” of the bloc.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Canada’s Carney welcomes EU’s associated membership proposal
- list 2 of 4Trump says Canada becoming EU ‘associate member’ could be ‘hostile act’
- list 3 of 4Can ‘middle powers’ come together to build a new economic alliance?
- list 4 of 4UK’s Burnham, Canada’s Carney discuss AI risks, defence cooperation
In a statement, Carney called the UK-led JEF an “important initiative”.
Canada and the US have recently hit each other with tit-for-tat tariffs after trade talks failed. Ottawa has subsequently launched a transatlantic charm offensive to reduce its heavy reliance on the US on everything from trade to defence.
Here’s what we know about the military force and what Canadian membership might mean:
What is the JEF?
Formed in 2014, the coalition is made up of 10 European states and aims to be capable of rapid military deployments to deter threats from Russia in areas around the North Sea, the wider North Atlantic-Arctic region and the Baltic.
It is led by the UK and has its headquarters in Northwood, just north of London. Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden are its other members.
JEF states, among its conditions for membership: A common strategic interest in the security of Northern Europe, the High North, the North Atlantic, and the Baltic Sea region; shared values, including a belief in democracy, human rights and the rules-based international order; and NATO alignment.
The JEF acts independently of the NATO alliance, although it can support NATO or United Nations missions if needed.
Participation in exercises is voluntary, but members of the JEF should have “political will and trust” as it operates as a “coalition of the willing” rather than with a treaty, the organisation says.
The UK military envisaged it to function as a faster, more adaptable force with less bureaucratic drag. It is designed to take action “below the traditional threshold of war”, according to the UK parliament, meaning it can bypass issues NATO might hesitate to address because of its “an attack on one is an attack on all” policy, which carries a high risk of escalation.
Combined, the JEF’s rapid response forces number about 10,000 soldiers. The alliance has not been deployed yet on any high-stakes missions, so it remains untested.
There are, however, questions about how effective UK leadership might be, as London itself is viewed by MPs as not spending enough on defence at the moment.
A highly critical report by the parliamentary defence committee last year found that the UK is “nowhere near” where it needs to be to defend itself and allies. The report added that the UK is failing to meet its NATO obligations, and falling “far short of its claimed leadership position”.
The UK currently spends about 2.6 percent of its gross domestic product on defence, short of the NATO goal of 3.5 percent by 2035.
UK-based policy think tank, the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), called for Canada’s inclusion in the JEF last year, and recently urged London to ramp up investment and start deploying the force.
“It has been under-exploited because of the UK’s lack of capacity, so it’s in a position of far less strength than it could be … but changes to the membership structure might see new shifts,” defence analyst Keir Giles, of the Chatham House think tank, told Al Jazeera.
Why does Canada want to join the JEF?
Canada is seeking opportunities that will give the country more options beyond reliance on its traditional ally, the US, amid their ongoing trade war.
Like most other JEF countries, Giles said, Canada has in past decades run down its military forces because of reliance on external forces like the US and NATO, but is now rapidly rebuilding. Although the country’s military capabilities in the NATO alliance are often overlooked because of the US, Giles said Canada has always been a crucial part of NATO’s patrols in the North Atlantic and Baltic waters.
The JEF initially invited Canada to join in 2015, but Ottawa declined, citing the lack of an immediate threat. There are no reports of the US being invited. JEF invitations have so far only been extended to northern Europe and Baltic NATO countries.
But the coalition is concerned with securing areas in the North Atlantic where Canada is a neighbour, meaning there is now some geographical logic to the decision.
Security is only one aspect of the kind of integration Canada is seeking. Canada will likely agree to join the EU as an “associate member”, for example. Besides this, the UK and Canada share Commonwealth ties.
“Canada joining is a logical step because of the JEF’s purpose, because of the cultural affinity it shares with other members and because of a common understanding of how to deal with the threats in that shared area,” Giles noted, adding that the country “now fully understands the dangers of co-dependence with the US”.
Why is Canada having issues with the US?
Canada is locked in a trade war with the US. Back-and-forth retaliatory measures have resulted in both sides slapping new tariffs on each other. That’s especially painful for Canada, which exports 70 percent of all its goods to the US.
In August, trade talks between the two countries broke down, and US President Donald Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports, disrupting the long history of stable relations between the two North American neighbours.
Canada responded with tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
Trump has also previously suggested making Canada a 51st state, raising sovereignty concerns. He appeared to revisit this idea following news that trade talks had broken down when he wrote on his Truth Social platform: “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!” Trump recently renamed Lake Ontario to Lake America in a fit of pique over Ottawa’s refusal to bow down to his demands.
Canada, which has long remained in the shadow of the US in terms of defence, has since launched a strategy to bolster its domestic defence capabilities by ramping up military spending and reducing its reliance on US military suppliers.
Carney’s defence plan, launched earlier this year, will see defence spending increase from about 40 billion Canadian dollars ($28.6bn) to more than 60 billion Canadian dollars ($42.8bn) in the next five years.
This comes as Europe’s relations with Washington have frayed because of tensions over NATO funding. Trump has long claimed that the US shoulders an unfair share of this burden. His insistence on seizing control of Greenland also triggered a standoff.
More recently, European countries’ refusal to be dragged into the US and Israel’s war on Iran has irked the Trump administration.

Women dominate Europe's health workforce but earn 19% less per hour, WHO warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:50:47 UTC
21:50:47 KST

Despite dominating Europe's health and care sector, women hold just over half of its top-paying jobs, according to a new WHO report.
Women in healthcare in Europe — a sector where they dominate— earn 19% less per hour than men on average, the World Health Organization (WHO) warns in a new report.
The health and care sector is the fourth-largest employer and the single largest employer of women in the WHO European Region. Women account for 77% of the workforce in healthcare, compared with 45% in all other sectors combined. However, they make up only 55% of the sector’s top earners.
“Women make up the majority of the people who keep Europe’s health systems running, yet they’re paid less than their male counterparts, a gap that compounds over a lifelong career," said Natasha Azzopardi Muscat, director of the Division for Health Systems, at WHO Europe.
The gender pay gap — the difference in average wages between men and women who are engaged in paid employment — in hourly pay is widest at higher wage levels, ranging from a 2% gap among the lowest earners to over 22% at the top of the wage distribution.
The sector is especially important for women’s employment, the report found. It represents almost 17% of all women’s employment, compared with 5% for men.
These findings follow the same pattern documented across the wider labour market: heightened structural inequality that intensifies at higher wage and seniority levels.
Globally, the health sector mirrors Europe, with women earning on average 24% less than men — a wider gap than in many other industries.
What is behind this difference?
The authors noted that some of the healthcare sector’s pay gap can be explained by differences in work-related factors such as age, education, sector of employment — public versus private and employment type — full-time versus part-time.
Adjusting for those four factors brings the hourly pay gap down from 19% to 6% and the monthly pay gap down from 28% to 10%.
However, the remaining pay gap can’t be explained by anything measured in the data.
“Most of this gap isn’t down to women working fewer hours, being younger or working in different parts of the sector," Azzopardi Muscat explained. “It comes down to how the sector values women’s work. Age, education, working hours and public versus private sector employment only helps explain some of it.”
According to WHO, the report points to deeper structural factors, such as the undervaluation of care work, occupational segregation and potential discrimination in pay-setting practices.
The more feminised an occupational category is, the less it pays — a pattern that holds across managerial, professional and technical roles alike. Managerial jobs in health and care, for instance, employ more women than management roles in other sectors and pay less for it: €22 per hour on average, against €24.70 in comparable roles elsewhere.
The broader cost of the gap
The gender pay gap remains one of the most persistent forms of labour market inequality, the WHO noted.
Considering how many women work in health and care, this gap can have important economic and social consequences.
The report noted this inequality may lead to lower lifetime earnings and pension entitlements, increase women’s risk of poverty, reduce returns to education and undermine sustainable economic growth.
“It means lower pensions, less financial security in older age, and a higher risk of poverty for women who’ve spent their working lives caring for others,” said Azzopardi Muscat.
“This isn’t a coincidence, and it isn’t about qualifications. Women are being paid less for the same work and passed over for the roles that pay more.”
Closing gender pay gaps is therefore both an equity imperative and an investment in a stronger and more sustainable health workforce, the international health agency noted.
To that end, they suggest targeted actions, from ensuring salary transparency and facilitating female representation in decision-making positions to addressing gender norms and stereotypes.

An air raid alert does not mean the automatic cancellation of a remote lesson for schoolchildren — Kyiv City State Administration
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:50:19 EEST
21:50:19 KST

An air raid alert does not mean the automatic cancellation of a remote lesson for schoolchildren — Kyiv City State Administration
Kyiv • UNN
In Kyiv schools, lessons are suspended during an alert, not canceled. In-person classes continue in shelters or after the all-clear.
Kyiv’s schools operate according to individual adaptive algorithms that take into account various scenarios for the development of the security situation. In particular, during remote learning, an air raid alert does not mean the automatic end of a lesson—the class is suspended for the time students and the teacher need to move to a safer place, after which it can be resumed. This was stated by Valentyn Mondryivskyi, Deputy Head of the Kyiv City State Administration, reports the Official Portal of Kyiv, according to UNN.
Details
In the new academic year, Kyiv’s schools operate according to individual adaptive algorithms that take into account various scenarios for the development of the security situation. In particular, during remote learning, an air raid alert does not mean the end of a lesson: the class is suspended for the time students and the teacher need to move to a safer place, after which the lesson continues. This approach is provided for by the new recommendations of the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine and has been incorporated into the recommendations for general secondary education institutions in the capital
He noted that the action algorithm depends on the format in which children are studying. During an in-person lesson, after the “Air Raid Alert” signal, the class is stopped and students, together with their teachers, move to the shelter in an organized manner. If staying in the shelter is safe and appropriate conditions are available, learning may continue there directly. If such conditions are not available, the children remain in the shelter until the official all-clear signal is given and then return to their classrooms, where they continue their lessons.
During remote learning, the child and the teacher may be in different places, so the algorithm is different. If an alert is announced, everyone must move to a safer place. The online class is suspended for this time, and after moving and provided that safe conditions are available, the teacher continues the lesson. In other words, an alert does not mean the automatic cancellation of the entire lesson or school day, as was the case previously.
Reminder
The Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine recommends that schools determine in advance several scenarios for organizing education depending on the security situation, including in-person, blended, and remote formats.

Germany: Is it possible to replace the chancellor?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:49:00 UTC
21:49:00 KST

Germany: Is it possible to replace the chancellor?
September 18, 2026
It is the hot topic this week in Berlin: Does German Chancellor Friedrich Merz still have the backing of his own party, the Christian Democrats (CDU), and the coalition partners, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)? Will he be ousted? How would that work? Can he just step down?
Support for the chancellor has reached a record low: In the latest Deutschlandtrend representative survey, conducted by pollsters Infratest-Dimap for German public broadcaster ARD in early September, only 13% of respondents said Merz was doing a good job.
In early September, Merz's CDU suffered a resounding loss in the state of Saxony-Anhalt's parliamentary election, seeing the party's result halved from the 2021 election.
The election result has reinforced criticism of Merz, even from within his own ranks, and his communication style, which frequently alienates his audience.
But Merz remains chancellor. What are the options to change that? Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, grants the position a strong standing. German chancellors are not so easy to unseat.
- 
	Option 1: Resignation
Merz himself can decide to resign for any reason. That would not necessarily mean the end of the coalition government he leads. An example: In May 1974, then Chancellor Willy Brandt of the SPD resigned after a spy from the communist East Germany (DDR) was discovered to have been working in his inner circle. The governing parties, the SPD and the business-oriented Free Democrats (FDP), quickly agreed to continue their alliance.
Only 10 days later, Finance Minister Helmut Schmidt, also of the SPD, was elected as the new chancellor. To do this, an absolute majority of all lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, was needed (not only those present during the vote). This majority is called the "chancellor majority". Schmidt achieved this effortlessly, eventually got reelected and remained head of the German government for 8 years.
How likely is Merz to step down? Today's chancellor seems determined not to give up.
- 
	Option 2: A constructive vote of no-confidence
If a new majority were formed through alliances in the Bundestag or if a chancellor fell so far out of favor that their own supporters no longer believed in them, the instrument of a "constructive vote of no-confidence" could come into play. That means the majority of lawmakers vote in favor of a new candidate for chancellor.
An example: Helmut Schmidt of the SPD, lost the support of his junior coalition partner, the FDP, in 1982. The FDP wanted to push through changes to economic policy, which Schmidt rejected. They joined forces with the conservatives from the CDU and CSU, and jointly put CDU leader Helmut Kohl forward as a new chancellor. He won a majority in parliament, replaced Schmidt and moved into the chancellor's office where he remained for 16 years.
The probability of this happening in Merz's case is very remote. The conservatives and Social Democrats do not want to end their coalition. There is no clear rival candidate for Merz. North Rhine-Westphalia's State Premier Hendrik Wüst of the CDU is seen as a possible successor, but has not made a step forward. Besides: The CDU is usually very loyal toward its political leaders; ousting the chancellor via a vote of no confidence on the open stage of the Bundestag is simply unthinkable for most conservative lawmakers.
- 
	Option 3: A confidence vote
Germany's parliament cannot simply dissolve itself and call new elections. Lawmakers can, however, call a confidence vote on the chancellor and his government. Several chancellors have already used this mechanism, coupling it with a vote on a contentious issue.
As chancellor in November 2001, Gerhard Schröder (SPD) put forward a confidence vote in the Bundestag and linked it with the question of whether his government should deploy the German military to Afghanistan to support the NATO mission led by the United States following the September 11 attacks. Schröder won, remained in office and continued with his military policy.
Merz has already said he sees no point in calling for a confidence vote. There are also no signs of large breakaway movements from members of his coalition in Parliament.
If a chancellor loses a confidence vote, the Bundestag can be dissolved and fresh elections called. Following the defeat in the Bundestag, the chancellor can ask the German President to dissolve parliament and call voters to the polls. The president is not obliged to do so, but usually does.
It seems that Merz has ruled out this option. Neither the SPD nor the conservative Union (of CDU/CSU) are interested in calling new elections at a time when their approval ratings are low.
So will the government remain the same? Right now, it seems so. However, things have been so dynamic in recent days and weeks in Berlin political circles that nothing should be ruled out.
This article was originally written in German.

It is the hot topic this week in Berlin: Does German Chancellor Friedrich Merz still have the backing of his own party, the Christian Democrats (CDU), and the coalition partners, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)? Will he be ousted? How would that work? Can he just step down?
Support for the chancellor has reached a record low: In the latest Deutschlandtrend representative survey, conducted by pollsters Infratest-Dimap for German public broadcaster ARD in early September, only 13% of respondents said Merz was doing a good job.
In early September, Merz's CDU suffered a resounding loss in the state of Saxony-Anhalt's parliamentary election, seeing the party's result halved from the 2021 election.
The election result has reinforced criticism of Merz, even from within his own ranks, and his communication style, which frequently alienates his audience.
But Merz remains chancellor. What are the options to change that? Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, grants the position a strong standing. German chancellors are not so easy to unseat.
- 
	Option 1: Resignation
Merz himself can decide to resign for any reason. That would not necessarily mean the end of the coalition government he leads. An example: In May 1974, then Chancellor Willy Brandt of the SPD resigned after a spy from the communist East Germany (DDR) was discovered to have been working in his inner circle. The governing parties, the SPD and the business-oriented Free Democrats (FDP), quickly agreed to continue their alliance.
Only 10 days later, Finance Minister Helmut Schmidt, also of the SPD, was elected as the new chancellor. To do this, an absolute majority of all lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, was needed (not only those present during the vote). This majority is called the "chancellor majority". Schmidt achieved this effortlessly, eventually got reelected and remained head of the German government for 8 years.
How likely is Merz to step down? Today's chancellor seems determined not to give up.
- 
	Option 2: A constructive vote of no-confidence
If a new majority were formed through alliances in the Bundestag or if a chancellor fell so far out of favor that their own supporters no longer believed in them, the instrument of a "constructive vote of no-confidence" could come into play. That means the majority of lawmakers vote in favor of a new candidate for chancellor.
An example: Helmut Schmidt of the SPD, lost the support of his junior coalition partner, the FDP, in 1982. The FDP wanted to push through changes to economic policy, which Schmidt rejected. They joined forces with the conservatives from the CDU and CSU, and jointly put CDU leader Helmut Kohl forward as a new chancellor. He won a majority in parliament, replaced Schmidt and moved into the chancellor's office where he remained for 16 years.
The probability of this happening in Merz's case is very remote. The conservatives and Social Democrats do not want to end their coalition. There is no clear rival candidate for Merz. North Rhine-Westphalia's State Premier Hendrik Wüst of the CDU is seen as a possible successor, but has not made a step forward. Besides: The CDU is usually very loyal toward its political leaders; ousting the chancellor via a vote of no confidence on the open stage of the Bundestag is simply unthinkable for most conservative lawmakers.
- 
	Option 3: A confidence vote
Germany's parliament cannot simply dissolve itself and call new elections. Lawmakers can, however, call a confidence vote on the chancellor and his government. Several chancellors have already used this mechanism, coupling it with a vote on a contentious issue.
As chancellor in November 2001, Gerhard Schröder (SPD) put forward a confidence vote in the Bundestag and linked it with the question of whether his government should deploy the German military to Afghanistan to support the NATO mission led by the United States following the September 11 attacks. Schröder won, remained in office and continued with his military policy.
Merz has already said he sees no point in calling for a confidence vote. There are also no signs of large breakaway movements from members of his coalition in Parliament.
If a chancellor loses a confidence vote, the Bundestag can be dissolved and fresh elections called. Following the defeat in the Bundestag, the chancellor can ask the German President to dissolve parliament and call voters to the polls. The president is not obliged to do so, but usually does.
It seems that Merz has ruled out this option. Neither the SPD nor the conservative Union (of CDU/CSU) are interested in calling new elections at a time when their approval ratings are low.
So will the government remain the same? Right now, it seems so. However, things have been so dynamic in recent days and weeks in Berlin political circles that nothing should be ruled out.
This article was originally written in German.

Half of Germans expect Merz to be out by year-end – poll
Nearly half of Germans believe Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be out of office by the end of the year, a new survey has indicated, as his approval hits record lows and speculation over his future mounts ahead of crucial state elections.
The YouGov poll, published on Thursday, suggested that 48% expect Merz to leave the chancellery before the end of 2026, while only 31% believe he will remain in office and 21% were undecided. YouGov surveyed 1,611 German adults on September 17.
The findings come amid a sharp decline in support for Merz just 16 months into his chancellorship. He took office promising sweeping economic reforms and a stronger German leadership role in Europe, but his tenure has been marked by coalition disputes and battles over domestic policy. In August, just 13% of respondents told Forsa research institute they were satisfied with his performance, against 85% dissatisfied. Another poll this week put his approval at a record-low 10%, with 88% dissatisfied.
The discontent comes amid prolonged economic weakness, stalled reforms and criticism of Merz’s focus on foreign and defense policy. Germany endured three consecutive years of economic stagnation and recession before GDP grew 0.3% quarter-on-quarter in the second quarter of 2026. Despite modest gains, investment continued to fall and household consumption remained virtually flat.
After more than a year struggling to agree on key policies, Merz’s coalition in July approved a 34-point economic reform package including austerity measures, tax cuts, pension changes, and tighter sick-leave rules. The move, however, drew public criticism and added to pressure on the coalition. Merz has meanwhile prioritized defense, pledging to build the “strongest conventional army in Europe” in response to what he describes as a Russian threat – a claim Moscow rejects.
The political crisis deepened after Merz’s bloc suffered a major defeat to the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the Saxony-Anhalt state election earlier this month. With crucial elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania due on Sunday – where the AfD is also expected to make strong gains – German media have increasingly raised the prospect of a Kanzlertausch, or “chancellor swap,” if the CDU suffers further losses. ZDF reported that talk of replacing Merz has been circulating within his own political camp for months.
Politico and Der Spiegel this week outlined several scenarios for Merz, including a voluntary resignation, a constructive vote of no confidence, or the chancellor calling a confidence vote himself. The outlets noted, however, that removing him against his will would be difficult under Germany’s Basic Law, as the Bundestag can oust a chancellor only by simultaneously electing a successor. Media have floated several possible replacements, but none has emerged as a consensus candidate capable of securing support from both the CDU/CSU and its Social Democratic coalition partner.
Behind the scenes, senior CDU/CSU figures are already positioning themselves for a possible succession fight, according to Der Spiegel. The outlet reports that eastern CDU lawmakers tend to favor CSU leader Markus Soeder, while western members lean toward North Rhine-Westphalia’s Hendrik Wuest, with Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt also discussed as a possible compromise candidate.
Merz has, meanwhile, summoned the CDU leadership to Berlin on Sunday, where he is expected to face questions over his leadership as the election results come in. He has also canceled a planned trip to New York for next week’s UN General Assembly events, with a German official saying “his presence is required” in Berlin – a move some analysts say highlights the precariousness of his position at home.

Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Resident Evil' - How to resurrect a dead franchise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:46:29 UTC
21:46:29 KST

It's taken six attempts, one reboot and one doomed Netflix show... But now, after 24 years, we have a good Resident Evil film.
Being a video game fan is a tough gig when it comes to film adaptations. Unless you count recent TV series like The Last Of Us and Fallout, console-to-screen transformations have historically resulted in cinematic poison.
One video game franchise which has had a particularly rough time of it is Capcom's Resident Evil, which has been cursed with six live-action films, one dire 2021 reboot, and a failed Netflix series which was promptly cancelled because an actual viral infection would've been preferable to a second season.
When the news dropped that horror's indie darling Zach Cregger was helming a brand-new reboot of the maligned IP, there was every reason to be skeptical or depressed. Or both. After two critically acclaimed films (Barbarian and the Oscar-winning Weapons), it seemed like Cregger was cashing in already and happy to take some Playstation / Sony bucks in exchange for silencing his original voice.
We should have kept the faith, as it turns out the director knew what he was doing. It's taken 24 years, but thanks to Cregger, Resident Evil fans finally have an adaptation they can be proud to champion.
The 2026 premise discards the high-concept lore and events of the games, lets go of Milla Jovovich’s Alice, and takes things back to basics. We meet Bryan (Austin Abrams), a hapless medical courier who’s about to head home to his girlfriend, who has just informed him she's pregnant. Instead of clocking out, he accepts a double-pay gig that involves him transporting a high-priority package to Raccoon City General Hospital.
He believes he's dropping off a vital organ. It's not.
On the road, he hits a woman with his vehicle, who is alive but seems to be in shock. She's not.
Thus begins the longest night of Bryan's life, during which he'll battle a lack of phone service, struggle with guns he doesn't know how to reload, and contend with A LOT of pesky padlocks.
Oh yeah, and there's a virus that rewrites DNA, strips the infected of their humanity, and transforms them into flesh-craving zombies, cartwheeling multi-limbed monstrosities, tentacled mutants and kamikaze fleshbags. Those will all be a hindrance too.
Cregger gets so much right here, to the extent it's borderline heroic considering previous adaptations. He perfectly doses the gore, the nail-biting dread, some well-timed (and never gratuitous) jump scares, and adds a surprising amount of humour. This comedic element proves to be crucial, as Cregger and his co-writer Shay Hatten understood the merit of injecting some relatability into a mix which includes Brian Yuzna-levels of body horror and creatures which look like they've escaped from John Carpenter's The Thing.
This is made possible in large part thanks to Austin Abrams, who played the homeless drug addict in Weapons. His character is a squealing and bumbling everyman who possesses none of the heroic, action-savvy qualities you'd expect from a leading man. He's just an average guy on an A-to-B mission, trying to survive whatever is trying to kill him. Abrams understood the assignment and absolutely nails it.
The first half of Resident Evil is undeniably its strongest, as once Bryan runs into an Umbrella Corporation scientist and a security agent (Paul Walter Hauser and Kali Reis), the white-knuckle ride gradually starts to become a bit more repetitive. It's during this second half that you're reminded you're in a Resident Evil adaptation; the unavoidable inclusion of the nefarious biotech company and a few POV shots to keep gamers happy feel slightly jarring within the everyman fight for survival. It's never not deliriously entertaining though, all the way until an afterthought ending which does let the film down. Not in how bluntly and almost hilariously abrupt it is; that part feels in keeping with the film's increasingly loopy tone. It's the way it undercuts Brian's character arc and reduces it to a Society-shaped punchline which ends things on a bit of a bum note.
Still, for a large part of Resident Evil ’s runtime, Cregger pulls off not only the best Resident Evil film but the first great movie game adaptation. Granted, both very low bars to clear, but plaudits nonetheless go to a smartly handled reboot. Goes to show that when you hire the right talent behind and in front of the camera, even a doomed IP can be revived.
Resident Evil is out in cinemas now.
