A documentary, a deposition, a record: Why NAZA matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:53:47 UTC
20:53:47 KST

Breadcrumb
NAZA asks what happens when the people who carried out a war become its witnesses
The documentary NAZA is directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor — the same filmmakers behind the Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land — and produced by Jonathan Glazer, director of the Oscar-winning The Zone of Interest.
It won the Jury Award at the Mostra in Venice, where it premiered, and received one of the longest-standing ovations of any film festival.
The documentary, whose name is a Hebrew acronym for "collateral damage", has been caught in a spiral of controversy. On one side, people are calling out the attention it received compared to other pieces by Palestinian filmmakers, and on the other side, the Israeli government has put the filmmakers in the crosshairs, going as far as demanding the revocation of their nationalities.
The documentary breaks down the anatomy of a genocide from inside its machinery through a detached, almost omniscient third-eye point of view.
It weaves together footage from October 7, speeches, including one by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in which he defines terrorism, shots of Tel Aviv, and, most importantly, interviews with members of Israeli occupation forces. The filmmakers interviewed 24 Israeli officers, whose identities have been blurred.
The reactionary discourse fails to see this documentary for what it is.
Without discrediting all the journalistic and documentary work done by Palestinians themselves from the eye of the storm in Gaza, this investigative film sits in a different category because it is what we call in the legal world a "declaration against interest."
A declaration against interest is an out-of-court statement made by someone that goes against their own legal, financial, pecuniary, or penal interest at the time they made it.
Why does it matter? Because genocide is unique among international crimes in requiring proof of purpose. The death toll and the destruction, despite being undisputed, are not sufficient to meet the legal threshold.
Dolus specialis, i.e., the intent to destroy the group, is the hardest element to prove in international law because it requires access to a perpetrator's state of mind. If the perpetrator is an organised army, this entails having access to the administrative drill beyond the legal esquive of "collateral damage," "military necessity," and "proportionality".
Intent of this magnitude is not something an army documents for the record. Thus, having the officers themselves describe the intent as something they executed, and now, at personal and legal risk, admit to from inside the chain of command, is the very condition that makes a declaration against interest credible in the first place.
No one invents a confession that costs them this much.
Under Article 28 of the Rome Statute, a commander or superior can be held liable not only for what they ordered but also for what they knew or should have known was happening under their command and failed to stop.
The interviewees described a targeting and approval process, a calculated ratio of expected civilian deaths, and repeated authorisation up a chain. This is testimony that reaches upward, toward command liability, even though the people speaking are not the commanders.
What the film's own framing insists on is a "premeditated, calculated, and intentional act", and pre-empts both defences of human shields and proportionality simultaneously.
The Rwanda tribunal convicted largely on the statements of people who had participated in the killing and later spoke. Nuremberg relied heavily on internal military records and perpetrator admissions.
What sets NAZA apart from war journalism is that it is closer to a deposition than to a documentary. It falls under the lineage of what was admitted in the aforementioned tribunals.
The law does not ask whether the perpetrators felt remorse. The confessions of these officers were not wrung out under duress or delivered with the catharsis of guilt. The filmmakers asked about the facts and procedures.
The documentary's aesthetic is very sober. It reflects the coldness and eeriness of the topic at hand by letting the camera zoom in and out on a heartless, nonchalant Tel Aviv that goes on.
The apparent irony exacerbates the impact of said confessions. "It’s like a video game," says one officer.
The middle-class, self-proclaimed majority left-wing officers mentioned an AI programme that maps the calls from and to phones belonging to known Hamas members and transplants the pattern onto phones they have under surveillance.
The owners who verify the pattern are then attacked invariably at night. They also delve into the logistics involved in "cleansing" northern Gaza and in sniper attacks on Gazan civilians.
The accusation that this is nothing Palestinians haven't already said, and the charge of hypocrisy embedded in the attention it received, misreads what kind of object this documentary is.
We are not in the face of a narrative competing with other narratives for airtime. As a matter of fact, truth does not require a legitimacy card to be told.
Palestinians, despite being the primary victims of Israel's ongoing crimes, do not hold the monopoly of truth. If only victims ought to be allowed to narrate their own destruction, their testimonies will be perpetually contestable by anyone willing to claim the account is one-sided, biased, or unverifiable precisely because it comes from the aggrieved party.
What breaks that isolation is two accounts coming from two directions at once.
The clearest confirmation of this documentary's significance is not coming from critics or juries. It is coming from the Israeli government itself.
Miki Zohar, Israel's Minister of Culture and Sport, did not call the filmmakers liars. He called them traitors. What he is saying concretely is not "this isn't true," but "you shouldn't have said it."
Under such circumstances, the question of the legitimate messenger is quite sterile, both cinematically and legally.
The real question the discourse should focus on is whether the truth is finally on the record and being told exactly by those whose interest is to conceal it.
Chaima Gharsallaoui is a journalist and filmmaker from Paris
Follow her on Instagram: @chaimagharsallaoui

Anduril wins deal to help design future aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:52:31 UTC
20:52:31 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Anduril Industries an $85 million ceiling contract to build digital design tools for aircraft and thermal management systems.
- The 10-year VOLARE contract runs through 2036, with only $50,000 obligated so far on its first task order.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Anduril Industries a contract worth up to $85 million to develop computer-based design tools for future aircraft, part of a push to design and test new systems digitally before building physical hardware.
The Air Force Research Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, made the award under a program called VOLARE, short for Digital System-Level Mission-Driven Integrated Design Methods for Aerospace Systems.
The contract is structured as an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity agreement, meaning the $85 million is a ceiling rather than a guaranteed payout, and the Air Force will issue individual task orders against it as work is needed. Eight companies competed for the award. Anduril will do the work in Dayton, Ohio, and the contract runs through Sept. 17, 2036, giving it a 10-year window.
The program covers two related goals: building a software product that can model an aircraft’s overall vehicle systems, and developing methods for designing thermal management systems, the cooling architecture that keeps an aircraft’s engines, electronics and sensors from overheating. Modern military aircraft pack increasing amounts of high-power radar, computing and directed-energy equipment into the same airframe, and managing the heat that equipment generates has become a design challenge in its own right rather than an afterthought.
No money has been obligated on the base contract itself. The Air Force has funded only the first task order, worth $50,000 in fiscal 2026 research money, with additional funding expected to follow as later task orders are issued.
The award adds to Anduril’s growing work in digital engineering for military aircraft and missiles. The company won a Naval Postgraduate School and Office of Naval Research prize in April 2026 for a proposal that combined digital modeling, simulation and flight testing into a single development process for tactical missiles, an approach the judges described as a credible way to speed up how new weapons move from concept to prototype. AFRL’s Aerospace Systems Directorate, based at Wright-Patterson, has pursued similar digital modeling tools for aircraft thermal systems for more than a decade, including earlier government-funded research into software for simulating aircraft cooling systems.

U.S. Navy advances first new nuke since Cold War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:47:14 UTC
20:47:14 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded JRC Integrated Systems a $47.4 million contract modification for engineering support of its SLCM-N nuclear cruise missile program.
- The missile is also planned for the new Trump-class battleships Trump announced in December 2025, reviving a surface nuclear strike role after decades.
The U.S. Navy has awarded JRC Integrated Systems a $47.4 million contract modification to provide engineering and technical support for the Nuclear-Armed Sea-Launched Cruise Missile, or SLCM-N, the service’s effort to field its first new nuclear weapon since the Cold War.
The modification adds to a contract Strategic Systems Programs, the Navy office overseeing the program, awarded earlier and covers work through Nov. 30, 2030. Tasks include systems engineering and integration, test and flight test engineering, modeling and simulation, oversight of prototype work, system design documentation, and configuration management. The contract also covers nuclear command, control and communications support and both executive and tactical subject matter expertise on nuclear weapons, along with broader program management and acquisition support.
The Navy is obligating $10.1 million in fiscal 2025 research funds now, with the rest tied to optional line items. The work was awarded without competition under a legal provision allowing sole-source nuclear weapons contracts, after being posted publicly on the government’s contract announcement portal.
Work will be split mostly between Washington, D.C., where 80 percent of the effort will take place, with 15 percent at Naval Base Kitsap-Bangor in Washington state, home to the Navy’s Trident submarine fleet, and the remaining 5 percent in Norfolk, Virginia.
The award follows a separate, larger contract The Defence Blog reported earlier, when the Navy gave General Dynamics Missions Systems $194.1 million for engineering support on SLCM-N’s Fire Control Subsystem, with work split between Pittsfield, Massachusetts, and Manassas, Virginia. Rear Adm. Randy Wolfe, director of Strategic Systems Programs, told Congress in May 2025 that the prior year had been spent defining the missile’s overall system architecture, spanning the missile itself, its fire control and launcher systems, platform and warhead integration, and support equipment and training materials.
The SLCM-N traces back to 2018, when the first Trump administration proposed it in that year’s Nuclear Posture Review as a way to restore a low-yield, sea-based nuclear cruise missile option the Navy had given up when it withdrew the nuclear-armed Tomahawk Land Attack Missile from service in 2010. The Biden administration tried to cancel the program in its 2022 Nuclear Posture Review, arguing it was redundant given the submarine-launched W76-2 warhead, but Congress overruled that decision in the fiscal 2024 defense policy act, establishing SLCM-N as a formal program of record. Wolfe has said the Navy expects to deliver the capability in 2034, and Sandia National Laboratories announced in January 2026 that the missile would use a new W80-5 warhead variant.
The program’s surface-ship role became clearer in December 2025, when President Trump announced approval to build an initial pair of nuclear-armed “Trump-class” battleships, with the Navy eventually aiming for a fleet of 20 to 25 of the roughly 30,000- to 40,000-ton ships. As The Defence Blog reported at the time, the design includes Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic missile launchers, more than 100 vertical launch cells, and is expected to carry the SLCM-N, restoring a surface-based nuclear strike role the Navy has not fielded in decades. Navy Secretary John Phelan said the lead ship, the future USS Defiant, would serve as the Navy’s flagship.

In a video posted to Facebook, Abu Zaida says he served as a go-between and relayed a message from Yahya Sinwar to Israeli intelligence. According to his account, Sinwar, then Hamas’s leader in Gaza, threatened an “earthquake” if negotiations with Israel over a long-term arrangement failed.

As previously reported by i24NEWS, the Prime Minister’s Office subsequently said Netanyahu had instructed his lawyers to file a defamation lawsuit over the report. It said checks of telephone logs and entry records found no evidence of the alleged conversation or a visit by an Emirati representative carrying the secure telephone used for such calls.
The UAE declined to confirm or deny the reported conversation, saying relevant intelligence was shared with Israel through official channels when necessary. That statement did not substantiate Haaretz’s account.
Abu Zaida did not address the alleged UAE warning to Netanyahu in his video, The Times of Israel pointed out.
A former PA minister for prisoner affairs, Abu Zaida belongs to the Fatah faction aligned with Mohammed Dahlan, who broke with PA President Mahmoud Abbas and left the West Bank in 2011. Abu Zaida lived in Jabalia in northern Gaza before leaving for Egypt at the start of the war and now resides in Cairo, according to The Times of Israel.

According to him, the Carpathian Initiative could become an additional tool for European integration for EU candidate countries. “Romania is a firm supporter of the European path, and this format can also serve as an additional instrument for the European integration of candidate countries,” Romanian president said.

Türkiye cracks down on Israel-linked int'l fraud network, detains 175 suspects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:44:31 UTC
20:44:31 KST

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Türkiye on Friday launched simultaneous operations against an Israel-linked international fraud network accused of defrauding foreign nationals through fake forex and cryptocurrency investment schemes.
Authorities detained 175 of 239 suspects in raids at 286 addresses in Istanbul and the western province of Mugla, Türkiye's Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said.
Four separate investigations conducted by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office in 2026 uncovered evidence that some companies operating as call centers had used social media and the internet to advertise forex and cryptocurrency investments, promising high returns to foreign nationals, Gurlek said on US social media company X.
The investigation was coordinated by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office’s Bureau for Investigating Terror Financing and Money Laundering Crimes, in cooperation with the Istanbul Regional Directorate of the National Intelligence Organization, the Department of Combating Organized Crime and the Istanbul Police Department’s Cybercrime Branch, he noted.
Analyses by Türkiye’s Financial Crimes Investigation Board, findings by intelligence and police units, and hundreds of victim complaints obtained through Interpol revealed that people linked to Israel were predominant in the ownership and ultimate beneficiary structures of the companies, Gurlek added.
The findings led authorities to uncover an organized fraud network targeting victims in multiple countries, he said.
The network allegedly used multilingual customer representatives to recruit victims and directed them to investment platforms controlled by suspects, where fabricated profit figures were displayed to encourage them to deposit more money.
When victims attempted to withdraw their funds, they were allegedly asked to make additional payments under pretexts such as “account blockage” and “taxes.” The money deposited by victims was then transferred to bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets abroad.
The network targeted many countries, particularly in Europe, the Far East, and Africa, and reached a transaction volume of approximately 13 billion Turkish liras ($266.4 million) over two years in transactions believed to have been related to office expenses and salary payments, he said.
Based on the findings, authorities launched simultaneous operations at 5 am local time against 28 companies, 42 call centers, and 239 suspects at 286 addresses in Istanbul and Mugla, with Interpol units also participating.
By 10 am, raids had been carried out at the call centers and 175 suspects had been detained, while operations to apprehend the remaining suspects were ongoing, Gurlek said.

Albares sets measures in motion to firmly anchor Ceuta and Melilla in Europe
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:44:16 CEST
20:44:16 KST

The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, presented to the Council of Ministers on Tuesday a report on the measures promoted by the Foreign Ministry to make progress towards the full integration of the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla into the European Union. He also spoke personally on Wednesday about this European plan with the President of Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, and the President of Melilla, Juan José Imbroda, and today wrote to the ministries with which the various measures under the plan must be coordinated, ahead of its imminent formal presentation.
“First, dialogue with the Autonomous Cities, which is why I spoke with their Presidents; then with the Spanish institutions and the various ministries with which we need to coordinate and engage in dialogue; and immediately afterwards we will submit the formal proposal to the European Union without further delay, as I indicated to them during the meetings I held in Brussels last Tuesday and Wednesday,” the Minister said.
According to Albares, during the conversations both Presidents showed that they were “in agreement” with the approach, and he reiterated the need for unity among all political forces so that the plan can become a reality as soon as possible.
Ministerial coordination
To coordinate all the planned measures within the Government, the Minister has written to the Ministers responsible for Economy, Finance, Agriculture and Territorial Policy to take the necessary steps to enable Ceuta and Melilla to participate in the Customs Union, such as including the Autonomous Cities within the scope of the relevant EU directives and certain European Union policies.
The aim is to determine jointly, and in consultation with the authorities of Ceuta and Melilla, the most appropriate arrangements for addressing the geographical and socio-economic specificities of both cities.
European unity and solidarity
At the Council of Ministers, Albares also reported on the various meetings he held with senior officials from the European institutions last week, during which he stressed the need for the European Union to demonstrate unity and solidarity, as well as the importance of treating all European Union borders equally, both those in the east and those in the south.
The Minister stressed that these measures seek to ensure that both cities receive treatment appropriate to their geographical specificities, particularly taking into account that Ceuta and Melilla constitute the European Union’s only southern border on the African continent, with the resulting implications for migratory pressure on both cities.
European package
The measures announced to the Council of Ministers include establishing a permanent seat for Ceuta and another for Melilla on the Committee of the Regions; a greater Frontex presence in both Ceuta and Melilla—with an initial aid package announced last week—and steps towards integrating Ceuta and Melilla into the customs territory of the European Union.
The aim is to ensure that the European Union institutions take into account the “very special” geographical circumstances of Ceuta and Melilla, “which constitute the European Union’s only land border with Africa and the most unequal and, therefore, the most complex border we have”.
To promote recognition of their geographical specificities, the Minister detailed the steps required to ensure that, under the next Multiannual Financial Framework, Ceuta and Melilla receive treatment equivalent to that afforded to other land borders benefiting from specific funding, such as the European Union’s eastern borders.
In the words of Minister Albares, “the aim is to ensure that Ceuta and Melilla, both of which hold a special place in the hearts of all Spaniards, also hold a special place in the heart of Europe”.

Morocco's elections: Justice party seeks electoral comeback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:44:10 UTC

Breadcrumb
Morocco's elections: Justice and Development Party seeks new start by 'restoring trust'
The Justice and Development Party is entering Morocco's parliamentary elections, scheduled for 23 September, from a position different from that it occupied in at least the previous two elections.
It faces one of the most sensitive stages in its political and organisational trajectory, not only because of its electoral ambitions, but also because its leadership is seeking a new beginning for the Islamist-oriented party.
The party, which won just 13 seats in the 8 September 2021 elections after topping the 2016 elections with 125 seats, is working to regain its electoral appeal, overcome its setback and restore the trust of part of the base it lost.
Although the biggest decline in votes in the history of Moroccan elections for a party leading the government cast a dark shadow in recent years over the Islamists' internal affairs, as well as their future and position in the political scene, the Justice and Development Party, led by Abdelilah Benkirane, is contesting the 2026 legislative elections as a real test of its organisation's ability to overcome its electoral setback and, above all, "restore trust".
Hassan Hamouro, a member of the party's National Council, told The New Arab, "We view the 23 September elections as a key stage in rebuilding trust and restoring our electoral presence after the 2021 defeat."
"We have absorbed the lessons of that period and are entering these elections with a clear determination to renew party work, listen to citizens and defend their issues, based on our reference principles of credibility, integrity and reasonableness (seriousness). The party's stake is not limited to the number of seats, but rather to restoring citizens' trust and convincing them that politics can be a tool for serving the public good," Hamouro said.
"We will contest these elections with clear and responsible messaging that puts the government's record before citizens and opens the debate on possible alternatives, because in our view, opposition is not merely about criticism but a political responsibility that requires presenting an alternative," he added.
In his view, the 2021 elections were a difficult stage for the party, but they were also an opportunity to review and correct shortcomings. In this regard, he said, "Today, we want to turn that experience into a new starting point and prove that the Justice and Development Party is capable of renewing itself, maintaining its connection with society and continuing to play a role in political life with a spirit of responsibility and adherence to its principles."
Lazaar: a presumed rebirth for the party
Abdel Moneim Lazaar, a professor of political science and constitutional law at Mohammed V University in Rabat, remarked to TNA that "the party has gone through several critical turning points since its first participation in the 1997 legislative elections, whether linked to contexts outside electoral competition, like at the beginning of the third millennium because of the terrorist bombings that Morocco witnessed (16 May 2003), or those linked to electoral competition, such as in the 2021 legislative elections, which pushed the party to the bottom of the representational rankings with 13 seats".
Lazaar said that during the legislative elections expected on 23 September, the course of the electoral process is providing indications of the party's strong desire to return politically, electorally and representationally, driven by the personal ambitions and motivations of its secretary-general, Benkirane, to escape the curse of the 2021 legislative election results.
He further explained that the party's plan to achieve this is to bet on renewing its representative image by putting forward new elites in the electoral contest while focusing on tarnishing the record of its rivals' government and whitewashing the record of the party's government tenure from 2011 to 2021.
"This strategy may be aided by the circumstances in which the current legislative elections are being held, burdened by social questions, particularly rising prices, while the possibility of electoral abstention could give it momentum, potentially creating the conditions for a presumed second birth for the party and a return to the ranks of the major players within Morocco's party landscape," Lazaar said.
He added that the party "will not find the competitive field empty, and an electoral comeback will not be easy", further noting all political parties would defend their chances of survival and continuity with the same energy with which the Justice and Development Party will defend its bid to return.
Hammoudi: risk of organisational fragmentation has faded
Ismail Hammoudi, a professor of political science at Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University in Fez, believes that the Justice and Development Party "finds itself facing one of the most sensitive stages in its political and organisational trajectory, not because of the scale of the setback the party suffered in the 2021 elections, but because it is contesting these elections from a relatively different position".
"Over the past five years, it has managed to overcome a danger that appeared deeper than merely an electoral loss, the danger of organisational fragmentation, loss of identity and an inability to continue as a significant political force," the professor told TNA.
He argued that this transformation highlights Benkirane's role and importance, who has shown at this stage that he still has the qualities of a political leader capable of bringing the organisation back together and restoring the trust of most of its base.
Hammoudi further said that his return was not merely a personal return to leading the party but was, in a key respect, a mechanism for reunifying the party around its principles, identity and political discourse.
In his assessment, Benkirane turned the moment of defeat from an occasion for exchanging blame and accusations into an opportunity to rebuild internal cohesion.
This enabled the party to enter the current election with a degree of self-confidence that clearly differs from its position after the 2021 elections.
"More importantly, signs of recovery do not appear to be confined to the party's organisational structure. The scale of mobilisation accompanying the current electoral campaign, both within the organisation and in its political and social surroundings, suggests that the Justice and Development Party is not contesting these elections merely to overcome the threshold of its previous defeat but is entering them as a contender for an advanced position on the electoral map," he said.
"A distinction should be made between two things, returning to the scene and competing for the scene," he continued. "The party appears to have largely moved beyond the question of political survival; the question now is whether it can translate its organisational recovery and the mobilisation surrounding it into an electoral result that actually places it among the leading electoral ranks."
Hammoudi noted that the importance of this challenge is increasing because Benkirane has not limited himself to reorganising the internal ranks but has also recreated the party's image as a political force with a project for the government rather than merely a protest force against the government of Aziz Akhannouch.
Overall, he believes that the parliamentary elections next Wednesday will "clearly test for the first time whether the political capital that Benkirane has rebuilt within and around the party can be transformed into electoral strength".

Ukraine, Latvia and the United Kingdom plan to announce next week the signing of a memorandum to launch verification of the origin of Russian grain that may be transiting through Baltic ports, Agrarian Policy and Food Minister Taras Vysotsky said at a briefing on Friday.
"Together with Latvia and the United Kingdom, we are set to announce the signing of a memorandum next week to launch this kind of substantiated screening of all grain of Russian origin attempting to transit through Baltic ports," he said.

The grain origin verification system is already in use at the Lithuanian port of Klaipeda. Under an enhanced control procedure introduced in 2024, feed grain from Russia, Belarus and other high-risk countries is subject to geographic origin testing. In early September 2026, the Lithuanian service took its first samples of grain whose intended use — for food or feed — was not clearly stated in customs declarations, in order to verify its country of origin.
As previously reported, on Sept 17 the Latvian Saeima approved amendments to the railway transport law that allow for an expedited review of tariffs on grain transit from Russia, including cargo delivered to Latvian ports for further export. The special procedure will remain in effect until the end of 2026, and the government has called on LatRailNet to assess the possibility of raising fees for transiting Russian grain to up to 300% of the current level.

American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally.
Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide.
Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax

“I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.”
Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”.
“I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.”
Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”.
Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania.
During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter.
In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family.

There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it.
The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed.
Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland.
Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik.
Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US.
The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026
The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live.
The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship.
One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics.
Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago.
Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx

Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342.
However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty.
Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland.
Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage.

EU to ban metal scrap exports to India, Egypt on environmental grounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:42:50 UTC
20:42:50 KST

BRUSSELS — The EU has proposed banning metal waste exports to India and Egypt after both countries failed to prove they manage the waste in an “environmentally sound” manner.
The two countries, which are among the top importers of Europe’s recyclable materials, did not show they were applying the correct pollution controls on how the waste is treated, a European Commission assessment found.
The Waste Shipment Regulation — the bloc’s rules that restrict exports of certain types of trash to third countries to curb pollution — bans the export of non-hazardous waste to non-OECD countries from May next year, unless they are granted specific exemptions.
Advertisement
The EU exported nearly 19 million tonnes of scrap metal in 2025, accounting for over half the bloc’s total recyclable raw materials exports.
Egypt and India respectively bought over 1.3 million and 850,000 tonnes of scrap metal.
Last-minute concerns over the EU’s trade deal with India led the European Commission to withdraw planned export duties on aluminum scrap earlier this month.
India is a major importer of aluminum scrap. The country last year exported over 350,000 tons of aluminum scrap alone.
The executive was due to present an instrument to slow exports of cheap aluminum scrap to buyers outside the single market, keeping prices down for aluminum producers and users within the bloc. The European aluminum sector has pushed for priority access to local scrap.
EU industry chief Stéphane Séjourné said, however, that the EU would scrap the measure after it became clear it would only cover around half of the bloc’s aluminum scrap exports and decided to pursue a solution “entirely independent” of trade policy instruments.
Egypt and India will still be able to export other scrap materials, including paper, wood, rubber, and textile waste.
The Commission will consult on the suggested country exemptions until October 16, before adopting the final list in November, as required under the regulation.

INTERVIEW – EU ‘not afraid’ to confront tech giants over children’s online safety, commissioner says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:41:49 UTC
20:41:49 KST

- Social media platforms 'have the responsibility to make sure that these spaces are safe' for minors, commissioner adds
- Safer online spaces are only half the task, Micallef says, calling for investment in sports, parks, cultural spaces where children can spend time away from screens
 
The EU is ready to make technology giants take greater responsibility for children’s online safety through new legislation, European Commissioner Glenn Micallef told Anadolu.
Speaking in an exclusive interview, Micallef, the European commissioner for intergenerational fairness, youth, culture and sport, discussed the EU KIDS Act proposed this week.
“We're not afraid of sitting down around the table and making sure that they shoulder the responsibilities,” he said.
The proposed rules would place greater responsibility on platforms to make their services safer for minors, while introducing age-based restrictions, stronger age-assurance requirements and new obligations concerning potentially harmful or addictive design features.
Micallef said the shift represented a fundamental change in how responsibility for children's online safety is shared between parents, governments and technology companies.
"A parent can set a rule at home around the dinner table for their children, but you cannot expect parents to fight algorithms which are designed in a way to be addictive," he said.
"The biggest change is the shift towards greater responsibility for those companies, those corporations, those platforms that are designing spaces online where there are children.”
 
Age restrictions at heart of proposal
The commission's plans would establish a graduated system of access based on age.
"The younger you are, the stronger the protection,” Micallef said.
Under the proposal, children under 13 would not be allowed to access social media services.
For children aged 13 and 14, the proposal would introduce so-called "mini accounts," which would be linked to a parent's or legal guardian's account.
"This is age-based protection that we're talking about, with a responsibility on the platforms and on those designing these spaces to actually make sure that these spaces are designed in a way which is safe for who is using them," Micallef said.
Micallef pointed to enforcement of the Digital Services Act as evidence that the commission was already engaging with major technology companies over the safety of their services.
"We do this in a way where we converse, where we dialog, where we have an exchange with these platforms,” he said.
Under the commission's approach, platforms would be expected to demonstrate that services used by minors are safe by design, rather than simply responding after harm has occurred.
 
 
Aim is 'supporting parents'
Micallef rejected the idea that the commission's proposals were simply an attempt to restrict children's freedom online.
"This is supporting parents. A lot of parents out there are concerned about their children and their children growing up with all the risks associated to online environments," he said.
He said that parents increasingly face a challenge that cannot be addressed through household rules alone because digital platforms are designed around highly sophisticated recommendation and engagement systems.
The responsibility, he said, must therefore be distributed among parents, educators, policymakers and the companies that build and operate online services.
"We acknowledge that the parents have a responsibility,” Micallef said. 
 
“Us as legislators and policymakers, we have a responsibility. We're shouldering that by putting these rules on the table. Educators have responsibility, but then we're also ensuring that the companies, the platforms, they also have the responsibility to make sure that these spaces are safe.”
 
'We have to move fast'
The latest proposal still needs to go through the EU legislative process and is not yet law.
It will be examined by the European Parliament and the Council of the EU, with member states involved in the negotiations.
Micallef said he believed there was broad agreement on the need to strengthen protections for children.
"I trust and I have faith that there is a common understanding that we need to protect children and support parents," he said.
But he also warned that the EU could not afford to delay action.
"We are talking about safeguarding children, that's our responsibility. We have to show that, and we have to move fast on this."
Micallef stressed that tougher regulation of online platforms should be accompanied by greater investment in real-world opportunities for children.
"We need to make these online spaces safer and more secure, and this is the priority here," he said.
"But this is only half the youth and childhood policy that we need to work on, because we also need to make sure that there are healthy alternatives or interesting spaces for young people and children to be children in the real world."
He pointed to sports facilities, public parks, libraries and theaters as places where children can socialize and develop away from screens.
 
'Football should not be for sale'
The commissioner also spoke about the ongoing debate over football governance and the role of FIFA.
Several European national football federations, including those of Sweden, Scotland, Italy, Belgium and France, have withdrawn their support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino amid growing disagreements over the governing body's leadership and direction since the 2026 World Cup.
One of the most controversial issues has been a FIFA proposal to establish a commercial company that would allow private investors to acquire a 20% stake in the management of World Cup commercial rights.
The proposal was reportedly developed without consultation with FIFA's member associations and drew strong opposition before Infantino abandoned it several days later.
"I think that sport governing bodies should be there to protect and to safeguard sport, not to make profit out of it or not to make money out of it," Micallef stressed.
He referred to what he described as a "very controversial idea" that had been strongly rejected by parts of the football community.
"There's a shared feeling that football should not be for sale," the commissioner said.
He acknowledged that competition policy could potentially provide another avenue for action against FIFA but stressed that any competition case would require evidence and jurisdiction.
His preference, however, is to resolve disputes through dialogue.
"My preference would also always be to address these cases through dialog rather than through competition lawyers," he said.
"We continue to support also on a political level those federations, those fans, or those people who have strong voices, strong concerns, and we'll continue to work with them.”

Ukraine Launches Carpathian Eight Cooperation Format
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:41:11 UTC
20:41:11 KST

Ukraine launched the Carpathian Eight (C8), a new regional cooperation format bringing together eight European countries at a founding summit in Bukovel, on Friday, Sept. 18, in western Ukraine’s Ivano-Frankivsk region.
The initiative was announced during the first session of the three-day C8 Summit, which runs through Sunday. EU representatives, local authorities, businesses and investors are also taking part.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
What is the C8?
The C8 format includes Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary.
EU institutions are also participating in the initiative, which is designed to connect governments, regional administrations, businesses and communities across the wider Carpathian region.
The organizers present C8 as a platform for security cooperation, economic development, investment and cross-border projects rather than as a new military alliance.
The summit’s official program includes discussions on regional security, energy resilience, industrial cooperation, transport corridors, agriculture, tourism and cultural ties. More than 500 business representatives and international investors have been invited.
“Another strong element of EU interaction”
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the summit marked the first time that all Carpathian countries had gathered in Ukraine’s part of the region.
“We are launching a new C8 format – the Carpathian Eight – uniting us and our neighbors in Europe: Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary and, of course, the European Union as a whole,” Zelensky said in a statement published on his official Telegram channel.
‘Waiting for Death’: Russian-Occupied Oleshky Faces Starvation as Russia Blocks Aid and Evacuation
He said the initiative should create “another strong element of interaction at the EU level,” focusing on security, energy, expanded logistics, cross-border economic cooperation and support for local communities.
Zelensky welcomed the presidents of Romania and Serbia, the prime minister of Poland and representatives of Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Austria. Hungarian representatives were expected to join the summit later, according to state media Ukrinform.
Vucic highlights transport links
Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić attended the summit at Zelensky’s invitation. He said Serbia could cooperate with Romania, Hungary, Ukraine and Poland on transport and infrastructure.
“We have much to offer – from railway lines and roads to more open borders,” Vučić said.
He also said cooperation could include agriculture and other sectors, adding that his participation aimed to preserve stability and peace for Serbia and its citizens.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s participation comes amid growing concern over Russian hybrid threats against NATO’s eastern flank. Before traveling to Ukraine, Tusk warned that Russia could use drones or missiles in attacks designed to test the alliance’s unity.
$10.7B in projects presented
The summit’s investment program includes 90 projects totaling $10.7 billion, according to the official C8 Summit website.
The largest share consists of 33 energy projects worth about $7.28 billion. The proposed portfolio also includes transport and logistics projects worth about $1.05 billion, 17 industrial projects valued at about $782 million, and initiatives in infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare and technology.
The summit is scheduled to continue through Sunday, with further discussions on industrial cooperation, energy security, transport corridors, agricultural value chains and tourism.

Using a provision in the 2015 nuclear deal between Iran and major powers France, Germany and the United Kingdom triggered the "snapback" mechanism, which reimposed the sanctions on Sept. 27, 2025. U.S. to sell 48 F-35 Lightning fighter jets to Saudi Arabia

Both the Predator and Gray Eagle were designed for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions but they can also carry Hellfire missiles for striking targets. In the Strait of Hormuz, these unmanned aircraft can provide U.S. forces with persistent surveillance over the narrow waterway while also tracking Iranian military activity and monitoring threats to both American forces and commercial shipping.

Donbass, Novorossiya

New 120mm turret passes tests on Turkish medium tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:40:04 UTC
20:40:04 KST

- Otokar and Leonardo completed live-fire testing of the Tulpar medium tank fitted with Leonardo's HITFACT MkII 120mm turret at Italy's UTTAT Nettuno range.
- The Tulpar is one of four finalists to replace Brazil's Leopard 1A5 BR tanks, alongside the CV90, ASCOD and Lynx.
Turkish manufacturer Otokar and Italy’s Leonardo have completed integration and live-fire testing of a 120mm turret mounted on Otokar’s Tulpar medium tank platform, a combination now being pitched as a potential replacement for Brazil’s aging Leopard 1A5 tanks.
The companies ran the tests at Italy’s UTTAT Nettuno test range near Rome, fitting the Tulpar with Leonardo’s HITFACT MkII turret. Before any live firing, engineering teams from both companies worked through an extensive integration program covering the mechanical, electrical, electronic and software interfaces between the tracked platform and the turret. Once that phase was complete, the combined system went through live-fire trials in both static and moving conditions, testing the weapon system, fire control, stabilization and overall functionality across a range of operational scenarios. According to the companies, the system met all of its planned test objectives.
“The successful completion of this program demonstrates TULPAR’s ability to integrate advanced large-caliber turret systems, while delivering the mobility, survivability and firepower required by modern armed forces,” said Sedef Vehbi, head of Otokar’s military division.
“We are pleased with the outcome and proud to demonstrate the technological excellence of our systems,” said Luca Perazzo, deputy general manager of Leonardo’s Defence Systems Business Unit. “The HITFACT turret is currently the only system in the world equipped with a 120mm smoothbore gun that offers the same firepower as a main battle tank system, while being able to integrate onto light or medium platforms and use the new Vulcano 120 guided ammunition for precision engagements.”
The HITFACT MkII carries an OTO-Melara 120mm, 45-caliber gun capable of firing all NATO-standard 120mm ammunition under the STANAG 4385 specification. The same turret already arms the Centauro II wheeled cavalry vehicle, which Brazil’s army recently ordered and plans to produce domestically. For now, the Centauro II and the Tulpar are the only two platforms qualified to carry the HITFACT MkII. The Tulpar itself belongs to a modern medium armored vehicle family Otokar designed with weights ranging from 28 to 45 tonnes, built around cross-terrain mobility and a modular architecture that can accept different mission equipment.
Brazil’s interest stems from a program to replace its Leopard 1A5 BR tanks, whose availability has suffered as spare parts from Germany have become harder to obtain. The Brazilian Army’s Armored Forces Strategic Program is working toward a new family of tracked vehicles that would share components between a future main battle tank and a new infantry fighting vehicle, reducing logistics complexity as the force modernizes. Four platforms have been shortlisted for the tank requirement: BAE Systems’ CV90, General Dynamics European Land Systems’ ASCOD, Rheinmetall’s Lynx, and Otokar’s Tulpar. Brazil has held government-to-government talks with the supplying countries as part of its evaluation.
Otokar’s pitch to Brazil goes beyond building the vehicle locally with Brazilian components. The company has offered full technology transfer and the possibility of handing intellectual property for Brazilian versions of the vehicle to the Brazilian army, along with a supply chain the company describes as free of U.S. and German export-control restrictions, which it says would give Brazil complete logistical independence.
Turkey’s armored vehicle industry, which began with licensed production and adapted foreign designs in the early 1980s, has since grown into a major exporter, led by the Otokar-developed Altay main battle tank, a roughly 65-tonne design influenced by South Korea’s K2 Black Panther. Turkish officials have said the country exported roughly 2,000 armored vehicles over the past five years. Otokar signed a contract worth about 857 million euros with Romania in late 2024 for 1,059 Cobra II vehicles, most of them built locally with full technology transfer, and the company is preparing to produce the Tulpar, including the HITFACT-armed version, at a plant in Kazakhstan. Turkey’s overall defense exports reached $11.2 billion between July 2025 and July 2026, according to trade publication TurDef.
Brazil’s Senate has already approved a defense industry cooperation agreement with Turkey, adding to Brazil’s existing defense industrial relationship with Italy. No decision has been announced on which platform will replace the Leopard 1A5 BR.

Royan Institute achieves global milestone in regenerative medicine with WhartoCell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:39:15 UTC
20:39:15 KST

Royan Institute achieves global milestone in regenerative medicine with WhartoCell
TEHRAN – Iran has taken a major step forward in regenerative medicine with the approval of WhartoCell, an allogeneic stem cell therapy developed by researchers at Royan Institute to treat osteoarthritis.
The achievement was also highlighted by MedPath, an international platform specializing in medical information, clinical trials, and healthcare technologies, putting the spotlight on Royan Institute’s contribution to this scientific and technological breakthrough.
According to Mehdi Lotfipanah, Director of Public Relations and International Affairs at Royan Institute, the therapy is designed to reduce inflammation, support cartilage regeneration, and improve joint function in patients with osteoarthritis. “The introduction of innovative cell-based therapies requires a scientific and evidence-based approach to ensure their appropriate integration into clinical practice,” Lotfipanah said.
Technical Profile and Mechanism of Action
WhartoCell is derived from Wharton’s jelly of the neonatal umbilical cord, a rich source of mesenchymal stem cells. These cells possess anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties while supporting tissue repair and regeneration. A distinguishing feature of the product is that it does not require genetic matching, or human leukocyte antigen (HLA) matching, between donor and recipient.
This characteristic allows physicians to administer the treatment without lengthy preparation procedures, positioning WhartoCell as an off-the-shelf therapy expected to improve patient access to advanced regenerative treatments.
Manufacturing and Quality Standards
Royan Institute has emphasized that WhartoCell is manufactured under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, with quality and safety monitored throughout the production process. This adherence to internationally recognized manufacturing standards is intended to ensure consistent product quality and patient safety.
Broader Clinical Potential
Although WhartoCell was initially approved for osteoarthritis, researchers at Royan Institute suggest the technology may have broader applications in regenerative medicine. Potential future indications include cartilage repair, tendon and ligament injuries, bone fracture healing, avascular necrosis, and the management of inflammatory joint disorders.
Strategic Significance
Lotfipanah noted that the product represents an important achievement in developing indigenous biotechnology, reducing dependence on imported therapeutic products while expanding access for healthcare providers across the country. He added that greater awareness among physicians and healthcare providers would facilitate broader adoption of regenerative medicine technologies.
 
 Royan Institute plans to increase scientific communication around WhartoCell through specialized workshops, educational programs for physicians and patients, and scientific meetings, including activities tied to the upcoming 27th International Royan Congress. The institute, one of Iran’s leading centers for stem cell research and regenerative medicine, has developed several advanced cell-based therapeutic technologies over the past two decades as part of the country’s growing biotechnology sector.
Iran among top 10 countries in regenerative medicine
With the approval of six new advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs), Iran has showcased breakthroughs in regenerative medicine, improving the country’s global ranking from 12 to 7.
According to the latest global report, out of 148 ATMPs approved in 2025 under the supervision of 12 internationally recognized regulatory bodies, seven were made in Iran, placing it among the top 10 countries in the field, IRNA reported.
The number of licensed products in regenerative medicine has grown from one product in the Iranian year 1402 (March 2023-March 2024) to seven in Iranian year 1404 (March 2025 – March 2026.
These include cell therapy, tissue engineering, and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy products, which are used to treat different diseases such as vitiligo, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), cerebral palsy (CP), burns, diabetic foot ulcers, arthritis, and B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (B cell ALL). Some of these high-tech medical products have export potential.
In August 2026, the Royan Institute played host to the 17th International Summer School in Tehran to examine the growing role of the microbiome in regenerative medicine.
Bringing together researchers, physicians, faculty members and students, the event opened on August 15 and came to an end on 19.
Titled “The Symphony of Therapy: Unlocking Regenerative Potential through the Microbiome,” it focused on recent scientific advances and clinical applications of microbiome research, IRNA reported.
According to the Royan Institute, the program explored how the human microbiome influences immune regulation, chronic diseases, tissue repair and regeneration, while highlighting emerging therapeutic approaches and translational research.
The five-day event featured sessions on stem cells and the microbiome, intestinal stem cells and microbial ecology, reproductive health, inflammation and tissue repair, and microbiome-based therapies, including prebiotics and postbiotics.
Participants also discussed advanced research technologies such as organoids, omics platforms and co-culture systems, alongside the ethical and clinical challenges of translating laboratory discoveries into medical practice.

EU sanction deadlock deepens as Luxembourg complicates the picture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:38:34 UTC
20:38:34 KST

Luxembourg insists that if France is able to get a particular oligarch delisted, it should be able to do the same, raising fears of a domino effect among member states.
Luxembourg has deepened the deadlock over the EU's sanction list renewal, tying a French demand to delist Russian businessman Alisher Usmanov to the case of Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the Grand Duchy over his frozen assets.
Last week, Paris joined Slovakia in demanding the removal of Usmanov from the sanctions list pending renewal. Now Luxembourg says that if Usmanov comes off the list, Fridman should too.
"France risks setting off a race to the bottom, which is the absolute opposite of what the EU is signalling politically, given the Russian escalation in Ukraine but also against EU member states in recent weeks," an EU diplomat told Euronews on condition of anonymity.
Slovakia has long pushed to delist both Usmanov and Fridman, oligarchs whom Brussels placed on the sanctions list for being close to the Kremlin. Both men deny the allegations.
Under EU rules, the list of 1,600 sanctioned entities and individuals must be renewed with the unanimous support of the bloc's member states every six months. The deadline was set to expire on Tuesday, but was extended by one week to allow time for a diplomatic solution.
Earlier this week, it also emerged that France's request to delist Usmanov was intended as a trade for the release of French citizens detained in Azerbaijan, a revelation that caused frustration among other member states.
Luxembourg raised the stakes further on Friday, telling a meeting of EU ambassadors that if France succeeds in delisting Usmanov, Fridman should be delisted as well.
Fridman is locked in an ongoing legal battle with Luxembourg over its implementation of EU sanctions, seeking compensation for his frozen assets in the country, which are estimated to run to around $16bn. He has also sued the Council of the EU before the European General Court.
For other member states, Luxembourg's latest demand illustrates exactly why national interests should not be allowed to shape individual sanctions listings, since doing so risks a domino effect in which other capitals begin pushing their own agendas.
EU ambassadors will reconvene on Monday. A Luxembourg official did not reply to Euronews' request for comment.
"Putin only speaks the language of power. If Paris really wants to push this through, France risks making the EU look weak," the diplomat added.

Egyptian deported by US to Equatorial Guinea held incommunicado for a week, lawyer says
Sept 18 - An Egyptian man deported from the US to Equatorial Guinea who criticized the conduct of security forces there has been held for a week at a gendarmerie station, one of his lawyers said.
Ahmed Soliman was arrested on Friday last week and has not been able to see his attorneys, the lawyer, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters.
The spokesman for the central African nation's government and its embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.
VIDEO SHOWS ALTERCATION IN HOTEL
Earlier this month, Soliman said police officers pulled guns on him and other migrants during an altercation at a hotel in Malabo, the former capital, where he and other migrants deported by the US have been held.
Video of the incident and news of Soliman's subsequent arrest spurred fresh criticism from rights groups of the so-called third-country deportation deals that the Trump administration has struck with several African countries.
The deals enable Washington to deport migrants who cannot legally be sent to their home countries because they obtained protection from US immigration judges.
Washington has defended the third-country deals as lawful and said deportations are carried out in accordance with US immigration law.
Soliman was in custody at La Luna gendarmerie station in Malabo, his lawyer said.
The facility has been used in the past to hold human rights activists, according to rights groups including Amnesty International.
DETAINEES ACCUSED OF BREAKING MIRROR, AMNESTY SAYS
Soliman had been accused of breaking a mirror in an elevator in the hotel, though that was a pretext for his arrest, the lawyer said.
"We are certain that it was a retaliation for Ahmed speaking out and the videos leaked," said the lawyer, referring to footage of security forces pulling guns on deportees.
Amnesty International said in a statement on Friday that Soliman was being held with another deportee, Samson Birhane, and that they were both accused of breaking the mirror.
"Police officers covered the two men’s heads with a bag and beat them in their heads, backs and ribs," Amnesty said, describing how they were allegedly taken into custody.
"The authorities must immediately release them, inform them of any charges against them and allow them unimpeded access to counsel."
Equatorial Guinea's government spokesman and its US embassy have not released any statements on Soliman's case.
In a statement on Wednesday, US Representative Adelita Grijalva, a Democrat from Arizona, where Soliman has spent much of his life, criticized the third-country deportations.
"Our country is responsible for sending people out this way, period," she told Reuters.
"And so we should make sure that where they're going is somewhere safe. Just because a country accepts somebody does not mean that that's a good placement." REUTERS

Latvia's State Security Service (VDD) opened a criminal case on 9 September over threats of terrorism against Latvian companies that supply weapons to Ukraine, after a pro-Kremlin group issued the same demand to Latvia, Poland, and Portugal.
The threat comes amid a series of fires and explosions at European sites connected to Ukraine's war effort, at least four at ammunition facilities alone since 10 August. No common cause has been established, and authorities have not publicly linked any of them to Global Citizens Against War 1984.
VDD detained one person in Riga on 10 September, searched their home and vehicle, and seized data storage devices and other items, the service said on 17 September. The suspect has been remanded in custody, and the case runs under part two of article 79.6 of Latvia's criminal law.
The ultimatum and the group behind it
The group, calling itself Global Citizens Against War 1984, published its ultimatum on 8 September, demanding that Latvia, Poland, and Portugal stop supplying weapons and ammunition to Ukraine.
The seven companies are Latvia's Eraser, a military drone maker, and Unitrack, which develops all-terrain vehicle prototypes; Poland's PGZ, WB Electronics, JFG Composites, and Nitro-Chem; and Portugal's Tekever, according to inbox.lv. VDD did not name the companies in its statement.
The group said the companies would face operational shutdown "by any means necessary" if the demands were not met by 7 October. It also circulated photographs of graffiti bearing its abbreviation, which it says was sprayed in Riga, Warsaw, and Lisbon.
The group previously claimed responsibility for planning an arson attack on the Slovak plant of Skyeton, a Ukrainian drone maker. Slovak police announced the detention of three foreign suspects on 25 August. Authorities have not said whether the suspects are connected to the group.
An investigation by The Insider found evidence suggesting Russian origins for the group: Russian-language folder labels on its English-language Instagram account, an Orwell quotation on its website back-translated from a common Russian rendering rather than taken from the original, and a proprietary Yandex font left in the page code. The outlet did not establish which Russian organization, if any, operates the group.
European security services have also reported suspected sabotage targeting defense companies and infrastructure, including a fire at an Estonian military robotics company, fires at a Bulgarian ammunition facility, and an explosion at an ammunition plant in Italy. Authorities have not publicly linked those incidents to Global Citizens Against War 1984.

New species of wild cat discovered for first time in more than a century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:36:00 UTC
20:36:00 KST

New species of wild cat discovered for first time in more than a century, researcher says
Scientists have discovered a new species of wild cat for the first time in more than a century, a Bolivian researcher told AFP on Thursday.
The Tilcayo tiger cat, a small feline with a spotted, leopard-like coat, was identified in the mountainous Yungas region near the capital, La Paz.
Locals who saw the creature in the Bolivian Andes had mistaken it for an ordinary house cat, said biologist and National Geographic explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who was part of the research team that studied them.
The nickname "tilcayo" given to the animal by locals inspired its new scientific designation: Leopardus tilcayo.
Nogales-Ascarrunz lauded the discovery as a "remarkable event, because a new wild cat species hasn't been described in 100 years."
The cat is the first feline discovered since the Uruguayan pampas cat in 1923.
The tilcayo is slightly smaller than a domestic cat, measuring around 18 inches, with rounded ears.
A pair of tilcayos -- the only such creatures found so far -- have undergone whole genome sequencing, Nogales-Ascarrunz said, referring to a type of in-depth genetic testing.
A male tilcayo is living at an animal shelter in Yungas after it was handed over by a family who had taken it in.
A female was rescued and released into the wild after being attacked by locals.
Research on the species was published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology, capping off research that scientists began in 2021.
"So far, it's only been detected in Bolivia" and not "anywhere else on the planet," Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
She said the creatures were classified as vulnerable to extinction, but their small numbers meant they could soon be considered "at much greater risk" of dying out.

The life and death of the sun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:35:48 UTC
20:35:48 KST

The sun seems unchanging—a constant source of light and warmth for Earth and the most fundamental necessity for life as we know it.
But nothing in this universe is unending.
Eventually the sun will cease to be the nurturing star we know as it undergoes a series of dramatic—and, in some cases, cataclysmic—changes that will ultimately lead to its demise. These won’t happen for eons yet, but the seeds of those transformations have already been planted in our star’s heart and are slowly growing.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The key to the sun’s life (if I may call it that) is thermonuclear fusion—squeezing lighter elements so tightly together that their nuclei fuse to form heavier elements. This fusion process in the sun’s core is actually quite complex. Called the proton-proton chain, it involves a series of steps that, in the end, convert four hydrogen nuclei (that is, four protons) into a single helium nucleus.
This nets a meager trickle of energy per helium atom forged, but there are a rather large number of hydrogen atoms in the sun’s core: our star fuses about 600 million metric tons of hydrogen into 596 million metric tons of helium every second. The difference of four million metric tons is converted (via the equation E = mc2) into a staggering amount of power: 4 × 1026 watts. That means the sun emits more than 600,000 times as much energy in one second as all of humanity is estimated to use in a year.
That’s enough to power a star.
Fusing hydrogen requires very high temperatures, about 15 million degrees Celsius. But even at that scorching level, the newly formed helium nuclei are inert. They fall down to the center of the sun and settle there, like ash in a fireplace. Although millions of metric tons accumulate every second, the core of the sun is so huge that the amount of helium added to it is relatively small on human timescales.
But it does add up. Because four hydrogen atoms are needed to make one helium atom, over time, there are fewer atoms in the core to support the enormous pressure from the mass above them. Squeezed by the mounting pressure, the core shrinks and heats up, which, in turn, makes the sun shine brighter. This process is slow but inexorable. The sun is about 4.6 billion years old, and over that time, its luminosity—the rate at which it emits energy—has increased by about 30 percent.
In a billion years or so, the sun will be so much brighter that it will trigger a runaway greenhouse effect on Earth. The oceans will boil, and all the water will be lost to space. At that point, it’s very likely our planet will no longer be able to support life.
But the sun won’t be done yet.
It will continue to fuse hydrogen into helium—at least, for a while. When it reaches an age of about 10.9 billion years (a little more than six billion years from now), it will run out of available hydrogen fuel to fuse. By then, the inner core will be comprised of inert helium, which will continue to contract and get very hot—so hot that a thin shell of hydrogen outside the core will begin fusing.
That will pump even more energy into the sun’s overlying layers, which will expand as they heat up, causing the entire star to swell. At this point, the sun will be what astronomers call a subgiant, but the expansion will continue. After another 700 million years (when the sun is more than 11 billion years old) it will reach about twice its current size. Counterintuitively, this will also cause its surface temperature to drop. The surface area of the sun will increase so much as it swells that the amount of energy it radiates per square centimeter will actually decrease. The gas, once white-hot, will cool to red, and the sun will become a true red giant.
For the next 600 million years, the nascent red giant will continue to grow, peaking at around 170 times its current diameter and cooling all the while. Its luminosity, however, will grow enormously, peaking at more than 2,000 times its current level. This will cook the planets; in fact, our star will expand enough at that point to physically consume the planet Mercury.
As the sun swells, its surface gravity will drop: the force of gravity weakens with distance. Paired with the fierce luminosity, this weakened gravity will cause strong winds of gas to blow out from its surface. Over the time it will take to reach the peak of the red giant stage, the sun will lose more than a quarter of its total mass to these winds.
Meanwhile helium will still be accumulating in its core—and will be getting hotter. About 1.3 billion years after running out of hydrogen, the core’s temperature will reach about 100 million degrees C—high enough to begin fusing helium into carbon and oxygen. This will actually produce less energy than shell hydrogen fusion, so the sun will shrink to about 10 times its current size, and its surface will get hotter and bluer. Fusion will continue steadily for 100 million years, until the sun runs out of available helium in the core.
Then a semirepeat of previous events will unfold. This time, carbon and oxygen will accumulate in the core, where they will heat up and spark helium fusion in a surrounding shell (and hydrogen fusion in a shell around that). The sun will swell again, getting even bigger than before: almost 200 times its current diameter. It will blast out energy at 2,000 times its current rate, cooling and reddening yet again. This is called the asymptotic giant branch phase of the sun’s life, and this phase will also be accompanied by powerful stellar winds.
As those winds blow away even more mass, the sun’s gravitational pull will decrease, becoming so weak that the planets will start to move outward. This migration won’t save Venus, which, like Mercury, will get consumed. Earth may manage to avoid being eaten—the science on this isn’t clear—but it hardly matters: the giant sun will fill nearly half of Earth’s sky and will quite thoroughly broil our planet.
Amazingly, it gets worse. Shell helium fusion is extremely sensitive to temperature, and even tiny changes in the core will cause the rate of fusion to fluctuate wildly. Every time that happens, a huge pulse of energy will be emitted, swelling the sun and causing its luminosity to soar. After the fourth (and final) pulse, the sun will be well more than 200 times its current size and more than 5,000 times more luminous! These pulses will blast away the remaining outer layers, exposing the core: an ultradense, extremely hot ball of oxygen and carbon, only about the size of Earth but hundreds of thousands of times denser. Astronomers call this a white dwarf.
At that point, at an age of more than 12 billion years, the sun will be essentially dead. No longer generating energy, it will cool and darken over billions more years to fade away into a black dwarf.
I’ll admit this sounds bleak. But it’s eons away, so remote from now that, even if humanity survives into that far-off future, it’s impossible to know what our species’ existence will look like. Perhaps we’ll have long since found a different, younger star to make our home. Perhaps we won’t even need one by then.
Astrophysics shows us the inevitable timeline of the sun, but humans are a bit more complex. Our own future is much trickier to predict.
My thanks to astronomer Richard Pogge for conversations on this topic some years ago; the timings listed above are from his wonderful page outlining the sun’s future.
