This dolphin terrifies fish until they puke—and then it eats their upchuck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:35:34 UTC
20:35:34 KST

New videos reveal how a male dolphin has perfected a never-before-seen hunting technique for his species: he terrorizes fish until they vomit—and then feeds on their regurgitated food.
The observations, aside from being gross, offer some of the most compelling evidence of kleptoparasitism—the act of stealing food from other animals—in a cetacean.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
While diving off Lady Elliot Island in Australia’s southern Great Barrier Reef between 2021 and 2025, researchers and divers documented 20 occasions when this male individual—a common bottlenose dolphin nicknamed “Bubbles”— hunted for regurgitated food from bigeye trevallies. Bubbles succeeded in his quarry 11 times.
The nasty catch goes as follows: The dolphin approaches a school of fish and searches for a specific target. Once he has identified the unlucky fish, he starts chasing it, isolating it from the group. The chase continues until the fish vomits whatever food it has in its belly, and the dolphin quickly snaps up the regurgitated material.
Bubbles generally went through this process multiple times in a single sitting, performing up to 10 chases in 30 minutes. As Bubbles hunts, he makes vocalizations that the researchers believe might stress his targeted fish out even more and cause it to vomit—but the echolocations may also help the dolphin pinpoint which fish have the fullest bellies.
“Echolocation does allow dolphins to discriminate small differences in their targets’ shape, size and structure, so the dolphin potentially uses echolocation to decide which fish to target to get the best reward,” says Asia Armstrong, a marine scientist at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia and a co-author of the study. But more investigation is needed to confirm those hypotheses, she says. The findings were published on September 13 in Ecology and Evolution.
Seeing the same dolphin repeatedly perform the behavior over and over is interesting and “makes it compelling evidence that this was more than simply opportunistic feeding,” says Jason Bruck, a dolphin behavioral scientist at Stephen F. Austin State University, who wasn’t involved in the research. “I would be cautious, though, about assigning intention. We can’t yet say the dolphin is pursuing the fish because it expects it to regurgitate.’’
It’s also unclear whether Bubbles learned to hunt this way by himself or from other dolphins or whether this kind of kleptoparasitism is widespread among other cetaceans.
“It’s very possible that other species use this tactic,” Armstrong says. “Dolphins and whales use a variety of unique foraging tactics, which is reflective of their intelligence, adaptability and ability to learn and pass information to one another socially.”
Still, documenting these behaviors underwater is challenging, Bruck says. ‘’A dolphin can perform a complex feeding behavior several meters underwater, and we may never know exactly what happened,” he says.

Iranian physician wins 2025 Kuwait Prize for control of cancer
TEHRAN – Amir-Ali Hamidieh, an Iranian professor at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, has won the State of Kuwait Prize for the Control of Cancer, Cardiovascular Diseases, and Diabetes in the Eastern Mediterranean Region.
The Foundation for the State of Kuwait Prize for the Control of Cancer, Cardiovascular Diseases, and Diabetes in the Eastern Mediterranean Region was established in 2003. Based on the recommendation of the Foundation Committee at its 72nd session in October 2025, the Regional Committee decided to award the Prize to Hamidieh for his significant contribution in the field of cancer.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the prize consists of a bronze medal and a sum of money; it will be presented in October during the 73rd session of the Regional Committee.
A distinguished physician, academic and pioneer in paediatric haematology, oncology and stem cell transplantation, Hamidieh earned his M.D. from Islamic Azad University, Tehran, and pursued postgraduate training in paediatrics and paediatric haematology/ oncology at Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences. He later completed advanced fellowships in haematopoietic stem cell transplantation at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center and Baylor College of Medicine in Texas, United States of America.
Hamidieh currently serves as Professor of Pediatric Hematology/ Oncology and Stem Cell Transplantation at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, where he also directs the Pediatric Cell and Gene Therapy Research Center.
He is the founder of the Iranian paediatric stem cell transplantation programme and the national stem cell donor network, which established the country’s first human leukocyte antigen (HLA) registry.
 
  
 
 He chairs the National Council for Development of Stem Cell Sciences and Technologies under the Vice-Presidency for Science and Technology and is a member of the executive boards of the Asia-Pacific Blood and Marrow Transplantation Group and the Iranian Food and Drug Administration.
His leadership has enabled the development of seven paediatric transplant centres across the Islamic Republic of Iran and the successful completion of more than 2100 paediatric stem cell transplants.
 
 Hamidieh has authored more than 100 peer-reviewed articles on research spanning regenerative medicine, gene therapy, immunodeficiencies and paediatric cancers.
He has also led clinical innovations in CAR-T cell therapy and photopheresis across many countries. Through his academic leadership, clinical excellence and commitment to equitable care, Hamidieh has significantly advanced the field of paediatric stem cell transplantation in Iran and the broader Eastern Mediterranean Region.
Majid Ghayour Mobarhan, an Iranian professor at Mashhad University of Medical Sciences, Davood Khalili, an epidemiologist and professor at the Center for Research on the Prevention of Metabolic Diseases at the Institute of Glandular Sciences at Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, Afshin Ostovar, a professor at Tehran University of Medical Science, and Fereydoun Azizi, the director of Iran’s Institute for Endocrine Sciences, won the prize in 2024, 2023, 2022, and 2007, respectively.

The matter is being investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation.A re-test was conducted on June 21, with the results announced on July 16.Following allegations of a NEET-UG question paper leak in 2024, the Supreme Court had declined to cancel the examination but issued several directions to prevent paper leaks and laid down criteria for cancelling public examinations.

Emergency services were called to Banga National High School in South Cotabato province in Mindanao at about 1:30 p.m. local time (0530 GMT).

Incident under investigation
There was also no immediate information about a possible motive.

While school shootings are rare in the Philippines and gun ownership is tightly regulated, there have been a few shooting incidents at centers of learning in recent months.
In August, a high school student opened fire at a private university campus in the Philippines, killing a fellow student and wounding two others before turning the gun on himself.
Earlier, in June, three pupils were killed and around 20 others injured in another school shooting in an attack that took place in Tacloban City in the east of the country and resulted in the arrests of two suspects, aged 14 and 15.

Ryanair’s planned Baltic expansion is part of a broader strategy to increase its annual passenger traffic to 300 million by 2034, from 208 million in the financial year that ended in March.
However, the airline said it will cut its winter flight capacity in Lithuania and Estonia by 25% because of higher airport charges. It plans to move some of those flights to what it described as more competitive markets, including Slovakia, Poland, Italy and Sweden.

NASA’s Roman Space Telescope could last more than twice as long as planned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:31:56 UTC
20:31:56 KST

NASA’s Roman Space Telescope could last more than twice as long as planned
- Date:
- September 18, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Roman Space Telescope may now have enough fuel for at least 22 years of science, more than double its original 10 year design life. An extremely precise course correction, extra fuel at launch, and additional expected savings could keep the powerful observatory studying the universe for decades.
- Share:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope may be able to operate for far longer than originally expected. An exceptionally precise first mid-course correction, combined with other fuel savings, could more than double the observatory's potential lifetime in space.
"As a result of exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team, brilliant execution by the operations team, and a precise launch from SpaceX, Roman has fuel for at least 22 years of potential science operations," said Jamie Dunn, center director at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.
Several factors are behind that dramatic extension. Roman used far less fuel than expected during its first course correction, carried additional propellant at launch, and is projected to conserve even more during its second mid-course correction and orbital insertion.
Roman Was Originally Designed for 10 Years
Roman was built around a five-year primary mission and a five-year extended mission, giving it a total fuel budget intended to support 10 years of operations. Because propellant is the spacecraft's main consumable resource, every kilogram saved during its journey can potentially translate into additional years of scientific observations.
First Maneuver Could Add Four Years
Roman carried out its first burn on Aug. 31, adjusting its path toward the observatory's eventual orbit. Since then, the mission team has been studying how the maneuver affected Roman's long-term fuel outlook.
The results were better than expected. The maneuver was completed with more than 99% accuracy and consumed less than 10% of the fuel reserved for it. Roman used about 40 pounds (18 kilograms), compared with the planned allocation of 441 pounds (200 kilograms).
Those savings alone could provide roughly four additional years of potential science operations.
Extra Fuel at Launch Could Add Another Four Years
Roman also began its journey with more propellant available than planners originally expected to need.
Engineers calculated the spacecraft's fuel requirements using a conservative maximum weight of 21,605 pounds (9,800 kilograms). Roman ultimately weighed just 17,760 pounds (8,056 kilograms) at launch.
Because the spacecraft was lighter, it required less fuel for its mid-course correction. Its lower mass also allowed the team to fill Roman's propellant tanks to capacity rather than carrying only enough fuel for the original 10-year mission.
That additional fuel could support roughly four more years of operations.
"A spacecraft's mass changes throughout the design and build process, so we base the propellant budget on a set maximum value so we won't come up short," said Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard. "We track the propellant needed based on actual mass throughout integration and testing as well, to make sure we have wiggle room. Since Roman's was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed to for the 10-year requirement."
More Fuel Savings Expected Ahead
Roman's successful first mid-course correction is also expected to make its second correction much smaller, potentially conserving still more propellant.
Because the first maneuver was so accurate, mission controllers can wait longer before making the follow-up adjustment, which is now scheduled for later this month. That burn will provide the final amount of energy Roman needs to reach its targeted position before entering its permanent orbit around L2.
Roman is expected to arrive at L2 approximately 100 days after launch, around early December.
Current estimates indicate that the second correction and orbital insertion should both require less fuel than originally budgeted. Together, those savings could provide approximately four additional years of potential mission life and leave even more propellant available for future scientific work.
Once Roman settles into its orbit around L2, maintaining its position should require only periodic station-keeping burns about once every 28 days.

Courts asked to shut 130 farms for breaching nitrogen limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:31:37 UTC
20:31:37 KST

Courts asked to shut 130 farms for breaching nitrogen limits
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Around 130 farmers risk being forced to give up their businesses after environmental group Mobilisation for the Environment (MOB) petitioned regional courts to tear up their nature permits, according to an investigation by RTL.
The organisation has started legal action in 10 provinces since 2023, asking judges to withdraw the permits of farms that exceed the limits for nitrogen depositions near Natura 2000 conservation areas.
Provincial governments have so far rejected applications from MOB, arguing that the cabinet in The Hague is working on a voluntary buyout scheme and other measures to reduce cattle numbers and nitrogen pollution.
Farmers must reduce ammonia emissions by 42% to 46% by 2035, compared to 2019 levels, under the latest package announced by agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen in June. The measures still have to be put before parliament.
The failure of successive cabinets to come up with a definitive plan since the Council of State ruled the system for issuing nature permits illegal in 2019 has prompted MOB to take the provinces to court.
Concentration in south
The majority of requests were made in the southern provinces of Noord-Brabant, Limburg, Gelderland and Overijssel, where pig, poultry and cattle farming is concentrated.
Noord-Brabant decided to withdraw its permits in July after a deadline of a year to settle the issue with MOB expired.
Van Essen said earlier this month that court orders to shut down farms were “exactly what we’re trying to prevent” with the government’s package of measures, which include a 5% to 10% across the board cut to livestock numbers as a last resort.
But Chris Backes, professor of environmental law at Utrecht University, questioned whether the plans went far enough.
“Measures by the national government are only part of the solution,” he told RTL. “For some nature areas they are sufficient, according to research by the Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (PBL).
“But in most cases the provinces will have to implement additional measures.”

US weapons in space to trigger political, technical reaction — Russian expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:31:04 UTC
20:31:04 KST

BEIJING, September 18. /TASS/. An open admission by the US that it has deployed weapons in orbit will prompt a response at both the political and technical levels, Russian Academy of Sciences Center for International Security Research Fellow Dmitry Stefanovich told TASS on the sidelines of the 13th Beijing Xiangshan Forum on international security.
"I am confident that the reaction here will be both political and technical," the expert said.
Stefanovich noted that space surveillance assets had been in orbit for a long time. "Now, we're probably talking about systems capable of having a more active impact on other countries' satellites," he said.
He recalled that Russia and China had proposed a draft treaty to prevent the deployment of weapons in space, and that Russia, along with a number of other states, had been among the first to issue statements pledging against the deployment of such weapons.
On September 14, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink publicly announced that the country had space control assets deployed in orbit, referring to them as "weapons." "The United States has deployed weapons in space and will use them to defend American forces," he said.

IDV unveils upgraded British VIKING UGV with EW and strike roles
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:30:43 BST
20:30:43 KST

IDV has unveiled the latest generation of its British-built VIKING uncrewed ground vehicle in electronic warfare and precision-effects configurations, with the upgraded platform gaining an electric-only range of up to 30km.
The two variants were shown at DVD 2026 at Millbrook, demonstrating how the same vehicle architecture can carry significantly different payloads. One VIKING was equipped with precision effectors, while another carried Leonardo’s Guardian Vantage electronic warfare and signals intelligence system. The latest version of VIKING has been designed to improve range, usability and autonomous operation. Its electric-only range has been extended to as much as 30km, allowing the vehicle to move with a reduced acoustic and thermal signature.
The platform can be transported internally by Chinook helicopter or carried as an underslung load, and can also move under its own power or be towed.
Geoff Davis, Managing Director of IDV UK, said: “As demand for uncrewed capabilities accelerates across NATO, platforms such as VIKING are becoming an essential element of modern land operations.”
He added: “VIKING embodies this approach, offering a flexible and scalable platform that can be configured for a wide range of roles, from ISTAR, electronic warfare, counter-UAS and precision effects to logistics and casualty evacuation.”
The electronic warfare configuration pairs VIKING with Leonardo’s Guardian Vantage system, while a portable Guardian Shield unit can be carried aboard the vehicle and left in position separately. The systems are designed to passively detect transmissions, identify emitters and determine their direction before, when required, moving to active jamming.
IDV said the uncrewed vehicle could therefore carry out what it described as a “jam and scoot” role, operating away from the troops it is supporting, transmitting when required and then moving before the position can be targeted.
The VIKING’s series-hybrid powertrain is particularly relevant to that role. The electronic warfare payload can run from the vehicle’s battery while the engine is switched off, reducing both its thermal and acoustic signature while it listens passively. IDV argues that power generation is becoming an important distinction between different classes of uncrewed ground vehicle, particularly as increasingly demanding sensors, electronic warfare systems and other payloads are fitted to them.
Guardian Vantage and Guardian Shield are designed in the UK and manufactured at Leonardo’s Basildon plant. IDV said both use components and software supplied by British small and medium-sized companies and carry no US International Traffic in Arms Regulations restrictions.
VIKING itself is developed and built at IDV UK’s facility at MIRA Technology Park in Nuneaton, using a British supply chain. The company says the vehicle has undergone more than a decade of trials with armed forces in Britain, Europe and the United States, with initial orders now placed by allied armies. The vehicle’s modular architecture is intended to allow different mission systems to be fitted to the same basic platform, with IDV listing possible roles including reconnaissance, electronic warfare, counter-drone operations, precision effects, logistics and casualty evacuation.
IDV also displayed its MUV Military Utility Vehicle in an ambulance configuration and an 8×8 protected logistics vehicle from its Modular Military Range, but the upgraded VIKING represented the company’s clearest move towards higher-end autonomous battlefield roles.

World Patient Safety Day focuses on safe care for NCDs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:30:24 UTC
20:30:24 KST

World Patient Safety Day focuses on safe care for NCDs
TEHRAN – World Patient Safety Day is observed on September 17 every year and serves as an opportunity to raise public awareness, enhance collaborations among healthcare stakeholders, and expedite measures to reduce preventable harm associated with the delivery of health services.
Each year, the day is observed under a specific slogan. In 2026, it focuses on safe care for non-communicable diseases (NCDs), under the theme ‘Safe care for life!’.
NCDs such as cardiovascular diseases, cancers, diabetes, and chronic respiratory diseases are among the most significant global health challenges, accounting for 74 percent of deaths worldwide; they affect people of all ages and require constant, lifelong care. Patients' frequent interactions with the healthcare system can put their safety at risk. These risks are also influenced by health system challenges and the broader determinants of health.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 1 in 10 patients is harmed during health care, with around half of this harm being considered preventable. People living with NCDs are particularly vulnerable to harm due to the long-term nature of their conditions, ongoing treatment needs, and frequent interactions with health systems.
With some conditions, such as cancer, up to 1 in 3 patients experience adverse events during care. Many people also live with multiple chronic conditions, further increasing the risk of harm.
Addressing NCDs is a global priority, reflected in the United Nations political declaration on NCDs and mental health, which calls for strengthened prevention and long-term management of NCDs. Achieving these commitments requires access to safe and quality care.
Improving safety in NCD care requires addressing risks related to the complexity of care, strengthening health systems through a primary health care approach and tackling wider determinants that can increase the risk of harm. The day also highlights the importance of engaging people with lived experience in the design and delivery of NCD services and in their own care.
The main objectives of World Patient Safety Day 2026 are as follows:
 
 Raise global awareness of patient safety challenges associated with NCDs across the continuum of care through a primary health care approach while considering disease-related factors, health system challenges and determinants of health that may increase the risk of harm.
Promote the meaningful engagement of people living with NCDs and communities in identifying safety risks and co-developing solutions with health practitioners, organizational leaders and policy-makers.
Awareness of the condition, understanding treatment-related risks, participating in treatment decisions, and raising questions and safety-related concerns can help reduce harm and improve the quality of health services.
Encourage stakeholders to integrate patient safety principles across NCD-related legislation, policies, strategies and programs, with an emphasis on strengthening PHC-oriented health systems.
Support health workers in strengthening patient safety practices such as safer diagnosis, medication safety and meaningful patient engagement.
World Patient Safety Day was established in May 2019 when the 72nd World Health Assembly adopted resolution WHA 72.6 on ‘Global action on Patient safety’. This global campaign builds on a series of annual Global Ministerial Summits on Patient Safety initiated in 2016, as well as the high-level advocacy and commitment of major international and national stakeholders.

Germany news: Fuel costs dominate debate ahead of polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Germany news: Merz government approves fuel-price discount
Published September 18, 2026last updated September 18, 2026
What you need to know
- Germany's coalition government approves fuel price relief
- Poll: Nearly half of Germans expect Chancellor Merz to step down
- Two states gear up for elections this weekend
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday September 18, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Germany receives first F-35 warplane
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius attended a ceremony in the US to receive the first of nearly three dozen F-35 stealth warplanes it ordered four years ago.
Germany ordered 35 of the jets in a deal inked in 2022, with the aim of replacing Berlin's aging fleet of Tornado aircraft.
The F-35 has a shape and low-observability coating that make it very difficult to detect on radar.
The ceremony for Germany's new planes took place at manufacturer Lockheed Martin's production facility in Fort Worth, Texas.
In a statement, Pistorius hailed the plane as "the world's most advanced combat aircraft" and said the handover marked "the beginning of a new era for the German Air Force."
"It is characterized by its stealth capabilities, close integration with other platforms, and exceptionally powerful sensor technology," Pistorius added.
It all comes as US President Donald Trump has put pressure on European nations to spend more on their own defense and in the wake of Russia's war in Ukraine. Countries like Germany responding by ramping up military budgets and modernizing their armies.
German government to provide fuel discount
The German government reached an agreement to provide a fuel discount and fuel price cap for vehicles on Friday night.
The move comes as Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition seeks to help ease the burden of high fuel prices on motorists. The deal is the product of negotiations that took place on Sunday between the national and state governments over the fuel price crisis.
Government sources told Germany's DPA news agency that the tax on gasoline and diesel would be cut by 17 cents ($0.20) starting in October, while the fuel price cap would go into effect in January 2027.
Fuel prices in Germany have spiked due to the war in Iran, in which Tehran imposed a stranglehold on the vital Strait of Hormuz, restricting Gulf crude exports, and later by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis targeting an alternative export route on the Red Sea.
Merz had vowed earlier this week to provide solutions for motorists in his country "soon".
Germany's conservative chancellor is under intense political pressure after the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has surged in popularity, while his center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has struggled.
The fuel relief plan announcement comes just two days before key elections in the north-eastern German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pommerania and Berlin.
Wuppertal: Prosecutors see clear antisemitism signs from synagogue arsonist
Wuppertal's prosecutors office say the suspect in an arson attack on the western city's synagogue has made clear antisemitic comments.
The 37-year-old Afghan national is being investigated for attempted aggravated arson. He was set to appear before a judge at an arraignment hearing on Friday.
The man was caught near the synagogue on Thursday shortly after allegedly having thrown three bags of flammable liquid at a stairwell leading into the synagogue and an adjoining door and then set it alight
Authorities searched his apartment and are still evaluating the contents of his mobile phone, prosecutors said on Friday. They also located several knives and a machete positioned so as to be easy to reach.
Prosecutor Wolf-Tilman Baumert said the man had a prior criminal record for threatening a female neighbor.
The fire was quickly extinguished by a staff member and nobody was hurt. Police said the damage to the building was also minimal.
The Central Council of Jews in Germany condemned that attack in the build-up to the Yom Kippur religious holiday.
"Once again an attack on a synagogue has taken place at the time of Jewish high holidays," Council President Josef Schuster said. "What disturbs me most is how coolly the perpetrator in Wuppertal carried out this attack in broad daylight. There's no sign of a sense of shame or being conscious of wrongdoing."
WATCH — Rising fuel prices put pressure on German drivers
Fuel prices in Germany have risen sharply, increasing costs for motorists. Although forecasts vary, some experts warn that gasoline prices could soon approach €3 per liter ($13.50/gallon).
Though many drivers blame filling stations for higher prices, operators say they earn only a small commission on fuel sales and rely largely on shop revenue.
Germany's beer capital, Bavaria, expecting poor hops harvest
Bavaria's hop farmers are expecting a rather poor harvest in 2026.
According to initial estimates, they expect a yield of 29,244 metric tons, as reported by the Bavarian State Office for Statistics on Friday in the city of Furth.
That would be a good fifth less than in 2025 and the lowest amount in a decade.
The extreme heat waves and prolonged drought this summer are cited as the reasons.
Hops arre an essential ingredient for beer, adding balance, bitterness and variety to the flavor.
The news comes as the world's largest beer festival, Oktoberfest, kicks off Saturday in Munich.
Poll shows almost half of Germans expect Merz gone by next year
A poll released by YouGov on Friday provided another example of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's tanking approval ratings.
According to the survey, 48% of the 1,611 adults questioned expect that Merz will no longer be chancellor by the end of 2026. Another 31% said they expected Merz to remain, while 21% did not answer.
The low approval ratings come as Merz's conservative Christian Democrat (CDU) party performed very poorly in regional elections in the eastern state of Saxony Anhalt two weeks ago.
Having won the previous state election, the CDU got just 17% of the vote, while the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) dominated at over 44%.
Polls for the upcoming state elections in Mecklenburg Western Pomerania show the CDU coming in at 7%, which is perilously close to the 5% threshold needed to win seats in parliament. Polling currently shows the Social Democrats (SPD) neck and neck with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).
If these polls play out on election day, it would be the worst CDU election performance at any level since World War II.
For weeks, German media outlets have speculated over whether another election drubbing could cost Merz the chancellory.
Germany's government still undecided on fuel price relief
Germany's governing coalition is under pressure to show progress on bringing soaring gas prices under control ahead of elections this weekend in the northeastern states of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
On Friday, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's Social Democrat (SPD) state premier, Manuela Schwesig, told the public broadcaster ZDF that Friedrich Merz should quickly implement a price cap.
The SPD is junior coalition partner with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative bloc (CDU/CSU) at federal level, but the parties have diverging ideas on how to address the soaring prices brought on the by the Iran war.
Despite Merz's insistence on Tuesday that gas price relief is coming quickly, the ruling coalition has yet to agree on an approach.
Germany's conservatives have resisted the SPD's call for price caps and a windfall profit tax in favor of a fuel tax relief scheme.
Such a scheme was enacted in the first months of the Iran war and expired in June.
What the parties are saying about fuel prices in Germany
On Thursday evening, CDU General Secretary Franziska Hoppermann told a talk show that the coalition government was aiming for gas price relief of "around 22, 23, 25 cents per liter" by the beginning of October, without sharing concrete measures on how to reach that.
Germany's SPD Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has for months advocated a government-enforced price cap on gasoline and diesel, along with new taxes on heavy oil company profits.
"We are right now looking for solutions" said Klingbeil on Friday at a EU finance minister meeting in Dublin, Ireland.
"I want a clear, quick signal at the gas pumps right now," said Klingbeil, who is also vice chancellor. "I'm confident that we'll be able to get it done very quickly."
Klingbeil added he expects the European Commission to prepare proposals for a windfall profit tax by the next meeting of EU finance ministers in October.
Prices for gasoline and diesel have broke record highs several times over the past week. On Thursday, the ADAC motoring club reported diesel at a record-breaking €2.47 per liter ($10.72 per gallon) on average, and the lowest cost E-10 gasoline at over €2.30.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from Bonn as we kick off the weekend with everything Germany is talking about today.
Soaring gasoline and diesel prices are dominating political discussion this week, with Germany's ruling coalition still divided on how to best provide price relief.
The debate comes ahead of two key state elections on Sunday. Voters are heading to the polls in the city-state Berlin and in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania (MWP) in the former East Germany.
Both races are set to be close-run affairs. The Left Party and Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats are battling it out in Berlin, while the center-left Social Democrats and the far-right AfD are neck and neck in MWP.
This Friday, sees the final day of campaigning.

Prosecutors drop case against man who arranged break‑in to retrieve his cat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Prosecutors drop case against man who arranged break‑in to retrieve his cat
The Northern District Prosecutor's Office has closed a criminal case against a man who arranged a break‑in at a stranger's apartment to retrieve his missing cat.
The cat had ended up with the nonprofit Cats Help, which then placed it with a temporary caretaker who refused to return the animal and posted a misleading social‑media message claiming the cat had gone missing from her care, writes Postimees.
The owner recognized his cat and decided to retrieve the pet himself. Before acting, he called the emergency number 112 to ask what punishment he might face and explained his motives.
At the apartment, he pried open a window left ajar for ventilation but did not dare enter himself. Instead, he hired a random passerby, offering a bottle of vodka to persuade him to go inside.
Police opened a criminal investigation under the statute covering incitement and assistance in unlawfully entering a dwelling. Prosecutors later determined that continuing the case was not in the public interest and that the man's culpability was low.
Prosecutors considered the man's cooperation, his explanation of motives, and his willingness to compensate for the damage. He must pay €152.50 for the window repair and €475 for the procedural costs, both due by January 17.

Russia demands Japan remove US Typhon missile systems — Foreign Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:29:44 UTC
20:29:44 KST

MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. Russia urged Japan to take seriously the September 3 protest note over the deployment of US Typhon ground-based systems designed to launch intermediate-and shorter-range missiles, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"Russia sent a protest note to the Japanese side in Moscow and Tokyo on September 3 over the deployment on Kyushu (one of Japan’s four main islands, located in the country’s southwest – TASS) of US Typhon ground-based systems designed to launch intermediate-and shorter-range missiles," the diplomat said in a commentary. "The note specifically stressed that Tokyo had once again taken this step despite repeated Russian demarches expressing concern over threats to national security, regional peace and stability arising from the deployment of these weapons on the Japanese archipelago."
"Russia deemed Japan’s forward deployment of the above-mentioned systems on its territory unacceptable under any pretext, regardless of the duration or method of their deployment," the spokeswoman said. "Moscow urged Japan to stop this practice and remove the above-mentioned systems from its territory."
"We emphasized the need for the Japanese leadership to fully recognize the outcome of World War II, including its territorial aspects concerning the southern Kuril Islands, and to abandon its policy of remilitarization," the diplomat stated.
"On Wednesday, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko urged Japanese Ambassador to Moscow Akira Muto during a meeting to take the contents of the earlier submitted note very seriously," the commentary said. "Chinese partners delivered a similar note to the Japanese Foreign Ministry in recent days and also expressed concern over Tokyo’s policy of remilitarization, including the deployment of Typhon systems on the islands," she said.

====================================================================================================

World Insights: What is behind Takaichi's LDP executive, cabinet reshuffles?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
19:29:25 CST
20:29:25 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who also heads the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), revamped the party's executive team on Wednesday and reshuffled her cabinet on Thursday.
In the new lineups, most key posts were left unchanged, while a member of the right-wing Japan Innovation Party (JIP), the LDP's junior ruling partner, was named to the cabinet for the first time.
Analysts said Takaichi's latest personnel changes target next year's LDP presidential election, in which she seeks to secure another term as party leader, adding that the hawkish conservative leader is likely to accelerate her right-wing policy agenda. However, the reshuffles are seen as unlikely to address longstanding problems facing Japan and could bring new trouble.
TWO CHARACTERISTICS
Japanese public opinion holds that Takaichi's latest personnel arrangement has two main characteristics.
First, it preserved the "core framework" of the administration. In the LDP executive revamp, most key posts, including vice president, secretary general, and posts in charge of policy and election, remain unchanged.
The main change was Hiroshi Kajiyama, who replaced Haruko Arimura as head of the LDP's decision-making General Council, while Hideki Murai became Diet affairs committee chief.
In the cabinet, eight of the 18 ministers other than Takaichi herself remained in their posts, including core posts of chief cabinet secretary, foreign and defense ministers, as well as finance minister.
Masaya Inoue, a professor at Japan's Keio University, said that the retention of these key ministers indicates that there will be no major shift in the Takaichi government's foreign and security policies, and that she will continue pursuing an expansionary fiscal stance.
Second, cooperation between the LDP and the JIP moved from "outside the cabinet" to "within the cabinet."
The JIP had not sent any of its members to join the cabinet since forming a ruling coalition with the LDP last October, until the latest reshuffle, in which Hiroshi Nakatsuka, formerly secretary general of the JIP, assumed the post of minister in charge of regulatory reform.
Some analysts said the JIP's previous decision was to maintain flexibility and avoid being too closely tied to the LDP, which at the time was mired in a "double minority" in both houses of the Diet, Japan's parliament.
Over the past year or so, however, Takaichi has worked hard to win the JIP over, pushing ahead with a number of policies under the coalition agreement with the party.
She also led the LDP to win the House of Representatives election in February this year, consolidating the foundation of her administration. As a result, the JIP shifted its stance to in-cabinet cooperation.
Shigeaki Koga, a former official at Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, said the JIP holds largely the same position as Takaichi on foreign and security policies, and is even more hawkish than her in some respects, meaning it could step on the "accelerator" as Takaichi pushes ahead with hawkish policies.
Just as Takaichi was carrying out the latest personnel reshuffles, Japan's main opposition party, the Centrist Reform Alliance, which formed in January by lower house lawmakers from the major opposition Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan and the Komeito party, formally split on Wednesday.
Given the continuing divisions among the opposition parties, Hiroshi Shiratori, a professor at Japan's Hosei University, said that the opposition would struggle to effectively counter Takaichi's moves toward military expansion and constitutional revision, and that Takaichi would likely pursue tougher security policies going forward.
SEEKING RE-ELECTION
In Japanese politics, prime ministers often try to create "surprises" through cabinet and party personnel changes to boost their approval ratings.
However, Hiroshi Onishi, professor emeritus at Keio University, pointed out that experience suggests only sweeping shake-ups can achieve such an effect.
Given the limited scale of Takaichi's reshuffles, he said, they are unlikely to significantly budge her approval ratings.
Japanese media widely believe that Takaichi's latest move is primarily aimed at next autumn's LDP presidential election, intended to shore up her administration's power base and secure her re-election.
Generally speaking, an LDP politician holding a senior post within the current administration is seen as a supporter of that administration, with no reason to oppose the incumbent prime minister and party president seeking re-election.
The Asahi Shimbun reported that by retaining her rivals in key government positions, including the posts of foreign and defense ministers, Takaichi is seeking to nip any emerging "anti-Takaichi bloc" in the bud.
The newspaper quoted a senior LDP lawmaker as saying that Takaichi's top priority is to secure her re-election as party president, and that this latest personnel arrangement is meant to lay the groundwork for that goal.
A Yomiuri Shimbun analysis noted that as the sole remaining faction within the LDP, the faction of Taro Aso has about 60 lawmakers and remains one of the most organized intraparty political forces.
Aso's support was key to Takaichi's victory in last October's party leadership race. Her decision to retain Aso as LDP vice president and his brother-in-law as the party's secretary general clearly appears to be part of her preparations for next year's LDP presidential election, the newspaper said.
OLD PROBLEMS, NEW TROUBLE
Analysts said Takaichi's latest personnel reshuffles could create new challenges for her administration going forward.
The Asahi Shimbun reported that in this round of changes in the LDP executive lineup, Takaichi took into account, to some extent, the views of Aso, who is seen as the "guardian" of the administration, but did not accept his preferences in full.
Aso had hoped that Kajiyama would remain as Diet affairs chief, but Takaichi insisted on promoting Murai to the post instead.
The report said that for Takaichi, whose base within the party remains relatively weak, the discontent over this personnel arrangement could become a political liability for her administration in the future.
At the same time, the entry of a JIP member into the cabinet could deepen the party's friction with the LDP.
Although the two parties share much common ground on foreign and security policies, they also diverge on a range of other issues.
The JIP's push to cut the number of seats in the House of Representatives faced wide criticism from opposition parties because it is deemed disadvantageous to smaller parties. The proposal has also drawn considerable dissent within the LDP.
The JIP, however, remains firm on the issue and is seeking to have a bill to cut lower house seats passed during the extraordinary Diet session this autumn.
Shiratori said that the JIP's entry into the cabinet could give the administration a stronger JIP imprint, which could in turn spark a backlash within the LDP.
In addition, the latest personnel reshuffles signal that Takaichi will press ahead with military expansion while sticking to a proactive fiscal policy.
Whether procuring weapons and equipment or cutting the consumption tax, each requires substantial fiscal funding.
With the Japanese government already grappling with a mounting debt burden, market confidence in Japanese government bonds has notably weakened, sending bond yields sharply higher. This means Takaichi will continue to face the longstanding problem of insufficient fiscal resources.
Koga said that if Takaichi fails to address the country's fiscal and economic challenges effectively, she will not be able to sustain her current approval ratings. ■

Economic Watch: Growing competitiveness drives Chinese NEVs into spotlight at Sydney EV show
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
19:29:12 CST
20:29:12 KST

by Nie Xinyu, Li Xiaoyu, Qi Zijian
SYDNEY, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The three-day Everything Electric Sydney 2026 opened at Sydney Olympic Park on Friday, bringing together the latest electrified products from automakers around the world.
A number of Chinese new energy vehicle (NEV) makers showcased new models at the event, drawing strong interest from visitors. Their growing competitiveness and ability to adapt to local market needs are adding momentum to their expansion in Australia.
Chinese brands including Chery, GAC, MG, GWM, Zeekr and BYD displayed a range of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) at the show, drawing local visitors to their stands for enquiries and test-drive bookings.
Executives from several Chinese automakers told Xinhua that as Australia's electric vehicle market continues to grow, they are introducing more products while expanding their presence through technological innovation and greater localization.
Dan Caesar, CEO of Everything Electric, told Xinhua that Australia's EV market has grown markedly this year, as rising attention to vehicle running costs has prompted more consumers to consider the practical benefits of electric cars.
Caesar said Australians had previously been somewhat hesitant about EVs, partly because of the country's vast distances and concerns over driving range. But those perceptions are changing as more models become available and more people gain first-hand experience with electric vehicles.
"People are starting to understand that actually EVs can work as well in Australia as anywhere else," he said.
Market data also point to the shift. According to the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries (FCAI), 27,089 BEVs were sold in Australia in August, accounting for 24.9 percent of the new-vehicle market. Sales were up 171 percent year on year, setting a new monthly record.
Five Chinese brands -- BYD, GWM, MG, Geely and Chery -- ranked among Australia's top 10 auto brands by sales in August, according to the FCAI's new-vehicle sales figures.
Caesar said the arrival of Chinese auto brands had given Australian consumers more choice. He said Chinese vehicles were highly competitive in areas including technology, features and pricing, while the speed at which Chinese automakers adapt products to different markets had also impressed him.
The shift is also visible in consumer choices. Stan, an EV owner from Kangaroo Island in South Australia, told Xinhua that he had been driving a Chinese-brand electric vehicle for about eight months. After seeing a new model at the show, he said he was considering trading in his current car.
"I love Chinese cars," he said.
Lu Wen, chief executive officer of Chery Motor Australia and New Zealand, said Australian consumers were becoming increasingly receptive to Chinese EV brands.
"Ultimately, it comes down to the competitiveness of Chinese EVs -- not only in technology, but also in design, quality, value and the wide range of new-energy powertrain options," Lu said. "Competitiveness has never been just about price."
As more Chinese auto brands enter the Australian market, localization has also become an increasingly important part of their expansion.
Dimitri Andreatidis, marketing director of MG Australia and New Zealand, said Australian consumers have their own driving habits and product preferences, and MG adjusts vehicle tuning, specifications and even color choices accordingly.
Citing the MG U9 as an example, Andreatidis said feedback from the Australian market is passed directly to engineering and styling teams and incorporated into vehicle calibration and specifications.
Yuan Xikun, head of marketing at GAC International Australia, said the company has so far signed up 49 local dealers and plans to increase the number to 60 this year. It has also established a local parts warehouse in Australia to improve after-sales service and parts supply.
Yuan said GAC also plans to introduce two to three additional models next year based on the needs of Australian consumers.
Lu said Australia's roads, climate and driving conditions are highly distinctive, making a strong understanding of local consumers essential to product development.
"Only by truly understanding consumers here can we make the products right," he said, adding that feedback from Australian customers is important to the company's product development.
Caesar said Chinese auto brands had demonstrated strong capabilities in technology, product iteration and adapting to local markets, as more Australian consumers become familiar with and experience Chinese NEVs. ■

El Nino likely to shadow food prices, supply in Fiji, warns consumer watchdog
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
19:28:57 CST
20:28:57 KST

SUVA, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Food prices and the availability of essential goods could come under pressure in Fiji as El Nino brings drier-than-normal conditions to much of the country, according to Fiji's consumer watchdog.
The Fiji Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) said Friday that prolonged dry weather could reduce local food production while increasing reliance on imported goods, potentially pushing up procurement, freight and retail costs.
Fiji is experiencing an El Nino phase, with its weather agency forecasting below-normal rainfall across most parts of the country.
El Nino, associated with unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific, can disrupt normal rainfall patterns across Pacific Island countries.
The FCCC said sugarcane is particularly vulnerable to prolonged dry conditions, while rice, cassava, taro and other crops could also be affected.
Fiji's experience during the 1997-1998 drought highlighted the potential impact -- the country's sugarcane harvest fell by about half after two consecutive dry seasons, with some areas suffering complete crop losses.
The effects could extend beyond agriculture. Fiji imports a significant share of its food and raw materials, meaning reduced domestic production could increase demand for imported substitutes.
The FCCC said this could push up procurement, shipping and landed costs, particularly for goods not subject to price controls.
International prices, freight and logistics costs and fertilizer prices could add further pressure to imported food and groceries.
The FCCC said it would continue monitoring prices and supply conditions as the El Nino develops. ■

Iran joins global ‘100 Hours of Astronomy’ celebration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:28:35 UTC
20:28:35 KST

Iran joins global ‘100 Hours of Astronomy’ celebration
TEHRAN – As the global “100 Hours of Astronomy” celebration gets underway in countries around the world, Iran’s skies will also host a series of astronomical observation and public outreach programs from September 30 to October 3, coinciding with the event’s 2026 edition, which is being held under the theme “A New Perspective on the Solar System.”
Astronomy groups, enthusiasts, educational institutions and science communicators across the country have been invited to take part in the international event by organizing a variety of programs.
The 2026 edition of “100 Hours of Astronomy” will coincide with astronomy events being held in different countries, providing an opportunity for astronomy enthusiasts, educational centers and science outreach groups to engage the public through a range of activities.
The celebration aims to bring astronomy closer to the public and provide people with opportunities to experience and learn more about the night sky. Activities may include public stargazing sessions, educational workshops, lectures, hands-on and interactive programs, as well as other astronomy outreach initiatives.
According to the International Astronomical Union’s Office for Astronomy Outreach (OAO), the theme of “100 Hours of Astronomy” in 2026 highlights how observations, space missions, and new scientific discoveries have transformed and expanded humanity’s understanding of the solar system.
Under the theme, organizers can introduce audiences to the latest findings about the Sun, planets, moons, asteroids, and other solar system objects. Through observation and educational programs, they can also offer a fresh perspective on Earth’s cosmic neighbors.
Our understanding of the Solar System has never been static. Every new observation, mission, and discovery helps us refine our knowledge, challenge old ideas, and reveal a richer and more dynamic picture of our cosmic neighbourhood.
Throughout history, our view of the Solar System has transformed dramatically, from an Earth-centred universe to a heliocentric system filled with planets, moons, asteroids, comets, and countless other worlds. More recently, space missions have reshaped our understanding of the origins of water and the building blocks of life, the nature and diversity of Solar System bodies, and humanity's place within the cosmos.
100 Hours of Astronomy is a yearly global celebration organised by the Office for Astronomy Outreach that invites people of all ages and backgrounds to come together and connect with the night sky — and with the science that helps us understand it.
From vibrant cities to the most remote corners of the world, this event brings astronomy closer to communities everywhere. Through public stargazing, workshops, talks, and hands-on educational activities, 100 Hours of Astronomy sparks curiosity, encourages shared exploration of the cosmos, and invites us all to reflect on our place in the Universe.
The International Astronomical Union's Office for Astronomy Outreach was established in 2012 as a legacy of the International Year of Astronomy in 2009. This international year highlighted the profound impact that astronomy can have when shared with society, inspiring the creation of a dedicated office – the OAO – to strengthen the connection between the academic and scientific community and the public.
The OAO works to break down barriers between professional astronomers and society, fostering inclusive engagement and encouraging dialogue about the Universe and humanity's place within it. By opening the doors of the scientific community, we aim to make astronomy accessible to everyone, inspiring curiosity, discovery, and a sense of shared wonder.
Leveraging astronomy's capacity to inspire awe, the OAO is dedicated to empowering learners of all ages to engage with science through astronomy, building up global science capital through localising resources and opportunities, fostering trusting community relationships, and building an international coalition of astronomy communicators. Through its National Outreach Coordinator network that spans more than 120 nations, and with the support of the IAU membership, the OAO connects diverse communities, bridging professional and amateur astronomers, citizen scientists, communicators, and the public.

Zelenskyy: Norway provides Ukraine with over $100 mln in budget support via Ukraine Facility
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:27:44 EEST
20:27:44 KST

Ukraine has received over $100 million in budget support from Norway under the Ukraine Facility mechanism, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced.
"I am grateful to Norway for the more than $100 million in budget support for Ukraine provided through the Ukraine Facility mechanism. This is an important and very timely decision, which I discussed with Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre during our recent meetings," Zelenskyy emphasized in a message posted on his Telegram channel.
The President noted the importance of Norway's support for Ukraine, stating that the country "is always there to help."
As noted on the website of Ukraine's Ministry of Economy on Friday, the funds will be disbursed through the end of 2026 and will be used to support the state budget—specifically to ensure the functioning of government bodies and the provision of critical services, as well as to implement reforms outlined in the Ukraine Plan.
In addition, Norway is participating in the investment component of the Ukraine Facility (the Ukraine Investment Framework). Specifically, the country has allocated NOK 500 million through this channel to support energy supplies, and NOK 1.5 billion for the purchase of gas for electricity and heat generation.
As previously reported, on June 8, Ukraine received the seventh tranche of EU funding under the Ukraine Facility, totaling EUR 2.8 billion, of which EUR 2.6 billion was allocated to the state budget.
Under the Ukraine Facility program—which has a total budget of EUR 50 billion and runs from 2024 to 2027—funds for direct budget support (EUR 38.27 billion) are disbursed in quarterly tranches once the European Commission confirms that Ukraine has implemented the specific reforms and met the targets outlined in the Ukraine Plan. Delays in implementing reforms or achieving targets result in corresponding delays in funding.
As of August 31, 2026, according to monitoring by the RRRU4 consortium, 14 program targets remained unmet. However, in September, the Verkhovna Rada stepped up efforts to fulfill them. Specifically, bills were adopted at the first reading regarding the trade of commodities associated with deforestation and forest degradation (No. 15352), simplified insolvency procedures for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (No. 15024), and strengthening the independence of the National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission (No. 14282). Additionally, a law on implementing EU legislation in the renewable energy sector (Bill No. 14271) was adopted.
Furthermore, a tender has been announced to select a consultant to conduct an independent audit (assessment) of financial processes.

Armenia attempting to force Russian owners to divest assets — Russian Security Council
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:27:33 UTC
20:27:33 KST

MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. Armenian authorities are seeking to devalue Russian assets to force their owners to divest them, Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexey Shevtsov told reporters.
"We are seeing signs that Russian industrial and infrastructure enterprises in Armenia could become the next targets (of forcible takeovers - TASS)," he said.
"Arguments about them being underfunded, the negative impact on the investment climate, environmental damage caused by their operations, low employee wages are being put forward," Shevtsov said, adding that "this is being done to devalue Russian assets and force owners to get rid of them."
"Such a tactic is going to be a real 'shot in the foot' for the Armenian economy, considering that Russian businesses have created tens of thousands of jobs in the republic and effectively and legally manage their assets, making a significant contribution to Armenia’s GDP," he warned.
Secretary of the Russian Security Council Sergey Shoigu said earlier that a hostile stance and blatant double standards are appearing against Russian businesses operating in Armenia, adding that what is happening to enterprises and entire sectors, into which Russia has made investments amounting to billions, can be described as a forcible takeover.
"We state that official Yerevan is exerting pressure not only on Russian business but also on Armenian entrepreneurs who disagree with the policy of [Prime Minister Nikol] Pashinyan and belong to the opposition," Shevtsov said. "As we can see, the economic ‘stick’ and corporate raiding are becoming a fully functional tool for Armenian authorities pursuing a policy advantageous to themselves of worsening conditions for Russian companies and the citizens they employ, as well as eliminating the political landscape of their main rivals," he stressed.

Bulgaria's Radev: We Are Not Replacing One Oligarchic Model With Another

Israeli forces launch new incursion into southern Syria with 9 military vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:26:22 UTC
20:26:22 KST

Mohamed Majed
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The Israeli army shelled the outskirts of Beit Jinn in the western Damascus countryside on Friday after launching an incursion into southern Syria with nine military vehicles and detaining a shepherd in Daraa province, Syrian state media reported.
 
Israeli forces carried out artillery shelling on the outskirts of Beit Jinn in the western Damascus countryside, Alikhbariah TV said.
 
The broadcaster did not report the outcome of the shelling, and there was no immediate comment from the Syrian government, which has previously demanded an end to Israeli violations.
 
In an earlier development, Israeli military vehicles entered the Wadi al-Raqad area, Syria's Al-Ikhbariya television reported, without providing further details about the nature of their movements.
 
The broadcaster later said an Israeli force detained a shepherd during the incursion into Wadi al-Raqad, without identifying him.
 
Wadi al-Raqad is located in the Yarmouk Basin area of the Daraa countryside and has witnessed repeated Israeli incursions and military movements in recent months.
 
Southern Syria has witnessed repeated Israeli incursions since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime on Dec. 8, 2024, when Israel announced the collapse of the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement and occupied the Syrian buffer zone and other areas.
 
Damascus demands that Tel Aviv withdraw to the lines held before Dec. 8, 2024, and has reaffirmed its commitment to the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement.

Houthi attack damages an Italian fighter jet in Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:26:08 UTC
20:26:08 KST

An Italian Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet was hit during an overnight attack on King Fahd Air Base near Ta’if, Saudi Arabia, Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto confirmed Friday.
Crosetto said the aircraft, designated F-2000 by the Italian Air Force, was parked in a remote area of the base when it was struck. No Italian personnel were injured, and no other vehicles or infrastructure used by Italian forces sustained damage, he said. Crosetto said he had personally followed the situation overnight in contact with Gen. Luciano Portolano, Italy’s chief of defense staff.
King Fahd Air Base has hosted Task Force Air-Arabia since late March 2026, an Italian Air Force deployment of roughly 300 personnel formed in response to the Gulf crisis and a request for support from partner nations. The task force includes Task Group Typhoon, four Eurofighter jets tasked with helping defend the assigned airspace, and Task Group Argo, which operates an E-550A CAEW aircraft for airborne early warning, surveillance and command and control.
The base has come under repeated attack or alert in recent days. Saudi civil defense authorities issued a warning for the province on Sept. 11, later declaring the danger passed, and press reports at the time cited possible missiles directed at the King Fahd Air Base area, though Saudi officials never confirmed the target.
On Sept. 14, the Saudi-led coalition confirmed Houthi forces had launched multiple ballistic missiles and drones at Ta’if, Abha and Khamis Mushait.
Italian aircraft have been hit in the region before. In March 2026, during the U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran, an Italian MQ-9A Reaper drone was destroyed on the ground at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, where Italy also maintains a Eurofighter presence under a separate mission supporting operations against ISIS. Italian and international media reported at the time that two Italian Eurofighter Typhoons stationed there had also been damaged by shrapnel, though the Italian Ministry of Defense never officially confirmed that account.

India: Are food safety rules too much to swallow?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:26:00 UTC
20:26:00 KST

High-profile raids spotlight India's food-safety struggles
September 18, 2026
Over the past few months, inspectors from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) raided kitchens at five-star hotels in New Delhi's Aerocity — including the JW Marriott and Andaz.
The inspectors reported "several serious food safety and hygiene deficiencies" at the Andaz, including "improper segregation of vegetarian and non-vegetarian food, pest activity, poor sanitation, inadequate food handler hygiene and improper storage practices."
During their visit to the JW Marriott property, inspectors observed "serious hygiene and sanitation deficiencies" — including "unclean utensils and food-contact surfaces, visible particulate matter in the drinking water" and "inadequate pest control."
Both hotels said they were cooperating fully with regulators and reviewing or implementing corrective measures while reaffirming their commitment to food safety, hygiene and guest well-being.
Beyond hotel kitchens
The FSSAI crackdown is not limited to premium restaurants. The regulator has also issued more than 150 notices since July to leading food and beverage companies, primarily over misleading advertisements, health claims and labeling.
The concerns highlighted by the recent raids are reflected in the FSSAI's testing data.
In 2023-24 and 2024-25, authorities tested about 170,000 food samples each year — with roughly 1 in 5 found to be nonconforming. In 2025-26, the testing showed only a slight improvement: Out of 223,808 samples, 40,023 failed to meet safety or labeling standards, according to provisional data given to Parliament in July. "Non-conforming" includes adulterated, substandard, contaminated and misbranded food.
Sunil Ghadiok, a veteran hotelier with more than 45 years in the industry and founder of Enserve Hospitality and Management Services, told DW that the "lapses" do not reflect the industry as a whole.
"Lapses occur because food safety depends on execution at the operational level," Ghadiok said. "The bigger concern is not the existence of standards, but the commitment to overall hygiene and food safety." He said inspections needed to become more regular and go where the risk is.
"A complaint or a high-profile inspection should not be what brings food safety back into focus," Ghadiok said.
Rules versus reality
India seems to be struggling to routinely enforce its food rules.
FSSAI's Hygiene Rating Scheme for restaurants is voluntary. Businesses can apply for a rating, but they are not required to participate. Food-safety enforcement can therefore become highly visible when something goes wrong, while routine scrutiny is less apparent.
Yash Bhanage, founder and COO of Hunger Inc Hospitality, which runs The Bombay Canteen, O Pedro and Bombay Sweet Shop, told DW that food safety issues are not necessarily linked to the size or reputation of an establishment.
"Food safety cannot be treated as a checklist that you complete because an inspector is coming," Bhanage said. "It has to become part of the operating culture of a restaurant." The challenge, he said, is maintaining standards across changing staff, suppliers, multiple shifts and busy periods.
Bhanage said the current attention on food safety was "an opportunity for the industry to move from a culture of compliance to a culture of prevention."
Manu Chandra, chef and restaurateur, told DW that the industry's systems need to reach further.
"A robust ecosystem has to be built around the [food and beverage] sector, which in many ways remains disorganized," Chandra said. "There is a strong need for systems to be in place, and FSSAI's rules must trickle down, but right now they don't reach every corner of the industry. Better traceability and stronger checks across the supply chain will help the sector in a big way."
The crackdown is already prompting some businesses to strengthen their own systems.
Samir Kuckreja, of Tasanaya Hospitality, a Delhi-based hospitality consulting firm, told DW that restaurants and hotels are seeking more help with food-safety audits, operating procedures and staff training.
"We first assess how the kitchen functions and tailor training to address specific shortcomings," Kuckreja said. "Unannounced inspections followed by frequent audits usually offer better results than scheduled visits or self-assessment checklists."
India's food regulator also under scrutiny
The question of enforcement extends beyond restaurants.
FSSAI's action against major food and beverage companies has included labeling and violations related to misleading claims.
Separately, India's Supreme Court has questioned the regulator about its proposed front-of-pack warning labels for packaged foods high in sugar, salt or fat.
The court has asked FSSAI to provide greater clarity on the scientific basis and thresholds for the proposed warnings, with the case set to return later this month.
The two issues are separate, but both raise a broader question about how effectively food safety rules are translated into practice.
The recent raids have shown what inspectors can uncover. The question now is whether that scrutiny becomes routine.
"The real measure of a mature food-safety system is what happens on the 364 days when nobody is inspecting you," Bhanage said.
Edited by: Keith Walker

Hungary plans to completely abandon Russian gas
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:25:44 EEST
20:25:44 KST

Hungary plans to completely abandon Russian gas
Kyiv • UNN
Hungary aims to replace Russian gas and diversify oil supplies by October 2027. The Paks nuclear power plant project is also being reviewed.
Hungary plans to completely abandon Russian gas by October 2027. The government is also reviewing cooperation with Russia in nuclear energy and seeking alternative oil suppliers. Bloomberg reports this, citing Hungarian Economy Minister István Kapitány, UNN writes.
Details
Kapitány said that Hungary has sufficient pipeline connections to receive gas from other sources at competitive prices. The government is also reviewing the Russian-led expansion of Hungary’s only nuclear power plant and is negotiating with suppliers to diversify crude oil deliveries and reduce dependence on Russia.
"If the situation develops as it currently appears, gas supplies to Hungary can and will be secured from other sources" by October 2027
As the publication notes, these statements indicate Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s readiness to move away from Orbán’s approach to relations with Russia. During the 16 years of rule that ended after the April elections, Orbán strengthened Hungary’s energy dependence on Moscow, even as other EU countries began abandoning their own dependence following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Hungary reviewing Russian nuclear power plant project
The Orbán government’s decision in 2014 to cancel an international tender for the expansion of the Paks nuclear power plant and award the contract to the Russian corporation Rosatom was widely viewed as a key element in changing and subsequently bringing the country’s relations with Russia closer.
Kapitány said that the project, whose implementation is several years behind schedule, is also being reviewed. A decision is to be made by the end of the year on whether the 2,000-megawatt expansion of the power plant is needed at all.
He noted that technological progress could allow Hungary to extend the operating life of its four existing nuclear units, which would otherwise expire in 2032, by another 20 years.
The review is still ongoing; we will complete it by the end of the year, and then decide whether Hungary needs additional nuclear units in its energy mix
According to him, the review is being conducted "impartially and with complete objectivity."
In addition to diversifying its energy sources, Hungary also seeks to reduce imports, particularly electricity. The plans include increasing energy storage capacity and opening the country to large-scale investment in wind energy.

EU fails to agree on extending sanctions against Putin and Lavrov
The EU's Committee of Permanent Representatives (Coreper) has once again failed to reach agreement on extending the European Union's sanctions against Russia for its violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity. It will meet again on Monday 21 September.
Source: European Pravda's correspondent in Brussels, citing several European diplomats
Details: The decision on extending EU sanctions against Russia for its violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity has been postponed until 21 September.
"The ambassadors met at Coreper this morning but failed to reach an agreement on extending the sanctions. They agreed to continue the discussion on Monday," a source told European Pravda.
The sanctions are due to expire at midnight on Tuesday 22 September.
The EU sanctions regime in response to Russia's violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty covers almost 3,000 individuals and entities deemed responsible for Russia's war against Ukraine, including Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
Background:
- European Pravda reported that on 14 September the EU extended the sanctions regime for seven days, as Slovakia and France are continuing to insist that two Russian oligarchs be removed from the sanctions list.
- Earlier, European Pravda sources in French diplomatic circles explained why Paris wants sanctions against Alisher Usmanov to be lifted. It later emerged that France plans to "trade" Usmanov's removal from the sanctions list for the release of several French citizens currently imprisoned in Azerbaijan.
- The individual sanctions were last extended on 14 March, when Slovakia continued pushing until the last moment for Russian oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov to be dropped from the sanctions list.

India news: El Nino leading to driest monsoon in 17 years

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Friday, September 18:

ICC eyes China as next frontier in push to expand cricket's global fanbase
China is emerging as a key growth market for cricket as the International Cricket Council looks to expand the sport's global fanbase by 500 million, its chief executive told the AFP news agency.
While South Asia currently accounts for roughly 90% of cricket's billion-plus fans, the ICC sees China's 1.4 billion people as a major untapped audience, aided by the steady rise of its women's national team.
"The continued success of their women's team has provided a major boost to cricket in the country," ICC CEO Sanjog Gupta said.
China became a focus market after hosting cricket at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, and its women's team has climbed 10 places in the world T20 rankings over the past two years. It currently stands at the 36th spot, whereas the men's side stands 92nd.
The ICC has invested $1.5 million (~1.3 million euros) in the country over the past five years, helping build three top-level venues, including a new 1,500-seat stadium in Taicang meant to host matches and serve as a training base.
Moving beyond bigger teams like India, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, Asian cricket is expanding its influence. At their Asian Games 2026 fixture against India on Friday, Japan's women's team did not let their loss define the journey.
Japan's Ahilya Chandel, who is half-Indian, told AFP that facing India in person after watching them on television was a special moment, adding that home crowds in Nagoya included newcomers to the sport: "That's what we want as a women's cricket team, to attract Japanese people who don't know cricket."
India will now play Bangladesh in Sunday's semi-finals.
Electoral body strips Trinamool factions of party name, symbol ahead of West Bengal byelections
The Election Commission of India has barred both rival factions of the Trinamool Congress from using the party's name and its "flowers and grass" symbol ahead of byelections in West Bengal, assigning each faction a new interim identity instead.
The commission's order, issued late Thursday night, applies to the faction led by former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee and her nephew Abhishek Banerjee, as well as a rival group led by expelled legislator Ritabrata Banerjee.
On Friday, the commission allotted Mamata's faction the name "Mamata All India Trinamool Congress" with a football player as its symbol, while the rival group was named "Democratic Trinamool Congress" (or Ganatantrik Trinamool Congress) and given an envelope symbol.
Both groups will be treated as recognized parties in the states of West Bengal, Meghalaya and Tripura on an interim basis while the commission decides the underlying leadership dispute.
The ruling affects two upcoming byelections, in Nandigram and Rejinagar, scheduled for October 6.
Soon after the new symbols were announced, Sanchita Pradhan Dey, the Mamata faction's candidate in Nandigram, withdrew her nomination after meeting West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari. Adhikari, who was once a close aide of Mamta Banerjee,joined the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in 2020.
As nominations had already been scrutinized, her faction cannot field a replacement. Instead, Mamata Banerjee said she would back the Congress candidate to strengthen the opposition INDIA bloc.
Local media reported Mamata Banerjee referring to the Election Commission's decision as a "black day for democracy."
Opposition Congress leadership also slammed the polling body, calling it the commission's "late night birthday gift to Modi ji." Prime Minister Narendra Modi turned 76 on Thursday.
