India on track for driest monsoon in 17 years
India is expected to experience its weakest monsoon season since 2009, as a strengthening El Nino weather pattern curbs rainfall and raises concerns over crop yields and food inflation.
Cumulative rainfall during the June-to-September monsoon season is currently running 15% below the long-term average, according to the India Meteorological Department, local media reported. The initial forecast was just a 10% shortfall back in May.
If the deficit holds, this would be the weakest monsoon since 2009, when rainfall was 18% below normal.
A potential tropical cyclone could form in the Bay of Bengal in the final week of September, potentially easing the shortfall in eastern and northeastern India, Christian Werner of Global Weather Climate Analytics told Bloomberg.
He said the storm was unlikely to significantly shift the national picture, with the seasonal deficit expected to settle between 13% and 16%.
The lack of rain threatens both current harvests and the next planting cycle, adding pressure on food prices that have already risen for seven straight months, hitting 5.95% in August — the highest level this year, according to the Free Press Journal.
Rice, sugarcane and corn planting are running behind last year's pace, and the government has responded by permitting duty-free sugar imports and selling subsidized onions in some states.
READ — Smuggling suspected as more rare animals seen in India
Five infant orangutans, a species found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra and on Borneo, were found in a forest by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India's eastern Odisha state last week.
In recent years, orangutans, rare reptiles and other exotic animals are popping up in India, suggesting the country is becoming a major destination for trafficked wildlife.
iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max go on sale in India, prompting long queues
Long lines formed outside Apple Stores across India on Friday as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max went on sale — this year's most expensive Pro lineup to date, with prices roughly Rs 30,000 (€270, $310) higher than last year's equivalent models at launch.
The high prices were not a barrier for many buyers, whose wait began before dawn. In Bengaluru, a customer named Rahul told newswire ANI he arrived at the Apple Store around 5 a.m. local time and found people already in line.
Rahul, who said he has bought every iPhone since the iPhone 7, described the ritual as something bigger than a purchase: "I've been purchasing iPhones for a very long time ... But it's like a festival for me. iPhone launch is like a festival. Every year, I try to buy an iPhone."
At the Apple Store in the northern city of Noida, one buyer said he had traveled from the nearby state of Punjab and began his wait at 6 a.m. local time, just to be first through the door: "Mine was the very first booking; I am the first one who has got the phone."
This year's price increase — pushing the iPhone 18 Pro to Rs 164,900 (€1,500, $1,720) and the Pro Max to Rs 179,900 (€1,635, $1,900) at the base storage tier — breaks Apple's recent run of holding launch prices steady in India.
India's GDP per capita stood at $2,702.5 in 2025, according to World Bank figures. The numbers do not account for income inequality.

Protests sweep across Tunisia: is change coming?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:23:49 UTC
20:23:49 KST

Breadcrumb
From north to south, protests sweep across Tunisia: is change at hand?
Several Tunisian provinces are witnessing growing popular protests demanding development, jobs and dignity, the same slogans that drove the revolution that erupted on 14 January 2011.
For the first time since then, residents are joining unemployed people in protesting after becoming tired of unfulfilled promises and unenforced laws and conditions that are worsening day by day.
Several provinces took to the streets yesterday, Thursday, 17 September, after a large popular mobilisation was held in the town of Menzel Bouzaiane in Sidi Bouzid province, the birthplace of the Tunisian revolution, on Monday.
As part of the escalation, the same delegation witnessed a second mobilisation by unemployed people on Wednesday, under the slogan "Work, freedom, national dignity."
The province of Kasserine in central-western Tunisia witnessed unprecedented tensions on Tuesday, when unemployed university graduates, accompanied by their children and families, protested, demanding the implementation of Law No. 18 of 2025, which provides for their recruitment into the public sector.
Protests by unemployed university graduates are continuing in Gabes province in southern Tunisia and several other Tunisian provinces.
On 14 September, renewed calls were made to hold a regional protest outside the headquarters of the Gabes governorate.
In an effort to contain public anger, Tunisian President Kais Saied held a meeting with Prime Minister Sarra Zaafrani Zenzri and Economy and Planning Minister Samir Abdelhafidh on Tuesday evening to prepare the draft finance law for next year.
According to a statement from the presidency, Saied stressed the need to place the options contained in the draft finance law within the framework of the five-year plan that had been approved in a way that would ensure the desired regional balance, provide job opportunities and effectively achieve dignity within the framework of purely national choices.
Links between political, social and economic sectors
Wissem Sghayer, spokesman for the Republican Party, told The New Arab that "the social movement is, at its core, a political movement. The political issue is not only about rights and freedoms but also brings together and intersects with social and economic issues," adding that this movement therefore represents one of the major aspects of the political issue.
"The demands of elites across different fields intersect with everything social and economic, and as the crisis Tunisia is experiencing worsens, there will be an intersection between the sectoral social movement, whose demands are specific, and political action, which political and civil elites express and represent," he stressed.
"The moment will come when all these issues converge in the same arena", Sghayer said, further elaborating that "an important element has entered the overall scene, namely the Tunisian General Labour Union and its call for a general strike."
"These are all interconnected and complementary elements, as the union played a role in the national dialogue and is therefore a key component of the overall scene. Despite its declining role, its recent action last Thursday represents a message to the authorities that it stands against authoritarianism and injustice. All these components converge around the same message, and this bleak situation may change, as may the balance of power compared with what it was previously," he added.
Former foreign minister and Ennahda Movement leader Rafik Abdessalem said that "there is a growing protest movement with social demands in the capital and across the country."
"Some of these demands concern water and electricity cuts and the lack of necessities of life, while others relate to jobs, services, marginalisation and other issues," he said.
The former minister also said that with the Tunisian General Labour Union entering the scene through regional actions, in preparation for a general strike, the social arena is heading towards greater tension, indicating a major state of unrest similar to the atmosphere that preceded the Tunisian revolution.
This is particularly the case amid the authorities' inability to meet citizens' basic needs and their rejection of all forms of dialogue and social negotiations, as if their message to Tunisian society and its political and social forces is that there is no way to achieve change other than through popular protests.
"At the same time, despite the systematic repression carried out by the coup authorities through arrests, political trials and silencing voices by using Decree 54, which restricts freedom of expression, the political arena is witnessing growing mobilisation, represented by the formation of political and social initiatives and political fronts," Abdessalem remarked.
"However, what has been observed so far is that the social and political movements are moving along relatively parallel tracks, but over time they are heading towards convergence, particularly as everyone has come to realise that social demands, without political organisation and a political horizon, remain limited in their impact," he added.
Tunisia's head of state
The former minister also told TNA, "Social protests have begun to feature political slogans directed at the head of state, particularly after they hit a wall of indifference, manipulation and repression by the regime. Therefore, the scene is likely to move, through the accumulation of crises and the development of protests, towards greater overlap and convergence between the social and political tracks."
He noted that the Tunisian General Labour Union itself, which has clearly distanced itself from the authorities and saw a correction in its trade union line after its latest congress last Thursday, had included issues of freedoms, opposition to political trials and the use of the judiciary in its statements and trade union demands.
He also pointed out that "Tunisia is recovering its long-standing political traditions based on political and organised social action and on coordination and joint work in confronting an authority that seeks to undermine all intermediary bodies and destroy all the gains brought by the revolution under the slogan 'the people want', which has turned into the slogan 'the leader wants', without a people, safeguards or oversight."
"The most important lesson Tunisians have drawn from their revolution is that social demands, if they remain within their sectoral or local regional framework, remain limited in scope, while when they combine with political action, they become a key driver of change," he added.
He stressed that Tunisia is moving towards "the convergence of the various streams of political struggle and social protest based on restoring freedom and democracy, particularly as the promises of the coup authorities have faded and their failures have increased at all levels, while anger and tension have intensified and spread across different areas."
"This increases the possibility of the social movement converging with the political movement, and this may be one of the most prominent features of the next phase in Tunisia," he concluded.
For it's part, The National Democratic Socialist Party said in a statement on Monday: "The unemployed are facing promises that have not found a way to implementation and a reality that exposes the falsehood of the slogans raised by the Kais Saied authorities, which placed employment, social justice and the right to a dignified life at the forefront of its priorities. Employment therefore remains the main demand embodied by the revolutionary process, and the authorities must stop delaying and stalling and activate the law for those whose unemployment has lasted a long time."
The party stressed that "the struggle of the unemployed is part of the struggle against exploitation and injustice."
Unemployment fuels protests
According to researcher specialising in social movements Ramadhan Ben Omar, "protests by unemployed people are intensifying across the regions, and the geographical scope of the protests is expanding daily."
"We are facing a growing and escalating state of protest across the regions. The authorities will face a real test: either confronting these protests using traditional methods, namely security and repression, or attempting to discredit the protests through rhetoric about conspiracies, treason and the existence of external actors," he said. "This is the rhetoric the authorities resort to whenever there are movements linked to social and economic demands, and not only to discredit rights and civil society protests."
"The unemployed continue to put the authorities in an embarrassing position and hold them responsible. They will face two options: either submit and issue the implementing orders for Law No. 18 of 2025, which concerns exceptional provisions for recruiting higher education graduates who have been unemployed for a long time into the public sector and civil service, or the protests will take on other dimensions, as several parties with different demands may join them," he noted.
Wiam Othmani, a civil society activist and one of the unemployed people in Menzel Bouzaiane, told The New Arab that the movement in Menzel Bouzaiane is peaceful "but it is continuing to escalate because Law No. 18, published in the Official Gazette in 2025 and providing for the employment of those who have been unemployed for a long time, has not been implemented, and the promises made to the unemployed have not been fulfilled."
"14 years have passed without her being employed, while some people have been unemployed for 20 or 25 years, or even longer," she said, pointing out that "the situation in her area is extremely bad, indeed very dire", adding that "all the delegations in Sidi Bouzid will rise up, with residents taking part, not only because they are their children's biggest supporters, but because the cup has overflowed."
She continued, "There is no turning back," explaining that their protests have no leadership, "but they organise themselves to ensure that they remain peaceful until their demands for jobs and dignity are met."

Istanbul Archaeological Museums renewed after extensive restoration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:23:40 UTC
20:23:40 KST

Aise Humeyra Akgun
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
An extensive restoration and renovation project has revitalized the historic buildings and visitor areas of the Istanbul Archaeological Museums, Türkiye’s culture and tourism minister said.
The work covered the complex’s main neoclassical building, the Museum of the Ancient Orient, the Tiled Kiosk, the courtyard and nearby Gulhane Square, according to the Culture and Tourism Ministry.
Türkiye’s Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the project's main objective was to preserve the buildings’ original architectural character while introducing contemporary museum practices.
Restoration of the main museum building began in 2011 and was conducted in stages. Following structural reinforcement, conservation and exhibition work, the building reopened to visitors in 2021.
The latest phase, launched in January 2023, focused on the Museum of the Ancient Orient and the Tiled Kiosk.
At the Museum of the Ancient Orient, teams reinforced the building's concrete and vaulted ceilings and masonry walls, renewed the roof and conserved decorative elements and sculptures on the facade.
The museum's Assyrian, Sumerian, Sumerian-Akkadian, Arabian, Babylonian, Hittite, Urartian and Egyptian galleries were reorganized with updated exhibition and lighting systems. The museum reopened on July 6.
Conservation work at the Tiled Kiosk included removing later roof additions and replacing old lead coverings with materials compatible with the original structure.
Teams also cataloged approximately 54,000 tiles on the building’s exterior and prepared a separate conservation plan for each one. The tiles underwent cleaning, strengthening, repairs and color restoration.
Displays in the kiosk’s Iznik, Kutahya, Canakkale, Early Ottoman and Seljuk galleries were also updated.
The project extended beyond the museum buildings. The complex’s main entrance was moved to Gulhane Square, where a new visitor reception center was established.
A total of 38 archaeological artifacts are now displayed along Osman Hamdi Bey Slope, which connects the square to the museum, while approximately 140 artifacts have been placed outdoors in the redesigned courtyard.
“We regard this not simply as a museum complex where artifacts are exhibited, but as a living cultural space where visitors can engage with history, art, architecture and culture,” Ersoy said.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's (NCP) government survived a confidence vote in parliament on Friday by 96 votes to 82.
Twenty MPs were absent from the vote, while opposition Social Democratic MP Timo Harakka abstained.
The vote followed an interpellation debate into the government's agricultural policies, held after the opposition Centre Party submitted an interpellation question to parliament earlier this month.
Centre Party leader Antti Kaikkonen noted at the time that the Finnish agricultural sector is the least profitable in the EU. The interpellation therefore demanded that the government provide the struggling sector with emergency funding of between 100 and 150 million euros — a move recently proposed by Sweden's outgoing government.
According to Kaikkonen, the Finnish agricultural sector has slid even further into difficulties during the current government's term in office.
The Centre Party, a historically agrarian party with firm roots in the Finnish countryside, suggested the money needed to support the sector could be obtained by the government cancelling its proposed corporate tax cut, which is set to come into effect next year.
Finland's rate of corporate tax, the duty levied on a company's profits, will be reduced from 20 percent to 18 percent from next year, according to the government's proposal. This will mean a loss of some 850 million euros for the state coffers.
Farmers protested outside of parliament in the spring over growing concerns about the future of Finnish agriculture, in particular Finland's food supplies and agricultural policies.

Zelensky downplays rift as Hungary renews EU accession blockade over minority rights

Ukraine's progress toward membership has once again stalled after Hungary started blocking progress on additional accession clusters — to-do lists of reforms a candidate must undertake before joining the bloc.
Budapest first wants Kyiv to implement additional guarantees for the rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine, in accordance with an agreement concluded in the summer.
The Hungarian side now waits for the Ukrainian parliament to adopt a relevant law before moving forward, Zelensky said during a press conference at the first Carpathian 8 Summit in Ukraine's Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast when responding to a question by the Kyiv Independent.
"I don't see a real big problem with this between us," Zelensky added, voicing hope that the Hungarian government will unblock the remaining clusters once it sees "political will from our side."
Kyiv hopes to open at least two additional clusters before October, and the remaining two by the end of the year, Zelensky added.
Hungary's pro-European Prime Minister Peter Magyar has adopted a more flexible stance toward Kyiv's EU accession efforts than his Kremlin-friendly predecessor, Viktor Orban.
The new Hungarian government initially lifted its veto on Kyiv's EU bid after concluding an agreement with Ukraine on Hungarian minority rights, allowing Ukraine to open its first two accession clusters — focusing on the so-called fundamentals and external relations — over the summer.
Hungary's prime minister has nevertheless rejected any shortcuts for Kyiv's accession, stressing that Ukraine must implement all the necessary reforms to enter the bloc.
Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration Vsevolod Chentsov said in early September that Kyiv has made progress on minority rights reforms and that the government is preparing a relevant bill.
The timeline for the legislation's introduction and vote remains unclear, and the parliament has increasingly struggled to pass key reform legislation tied to Ukraine's EU accession and foreign aid.

Bangladesh and Pakistan hit by Gulf energy disruptions
Bangladesh’s export factories are cutting production and Pakistan has rolled out fuel subsidies as disruptions to Gulf energy supplies drive shortages and higher costs across South Asia.
The pressure follows disruptions to oil and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran. Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis has also threatened trade through the Red Sea, another key route for Gulf energy supplies.
Bangladesh has been particularly exposed. The country relies heavily on imported LNG for electricity, and disruptions to supplies from Qatar have forced Dhaka to seek more expensive cargoes on the spot market. The gas and power shortages have triggered blackouts and factory shutdowns.
Asian spot prices for liquefied natural gas (LNG) have climbed close to $30 per million British thermal units from around $10 before the conflict.
The pressure is now hitting Bangladesh’s garment industry, its biggest export sector. A survey by the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association found that 55% of factories have seen buyers cancel or reduce orders because of gas and power shortages since late August, while 78% partially halted production.

Subsequently, ICAO urged member states to strengthen measures protecting civil aircraft against risks arising in conflict zones, amid growing threats to civil aviation posed by modern military technologies.

A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.
Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.
Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.
A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.
Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.
Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”
Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.
The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank.
In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.
“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”
Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.
Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outlet Nyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”
Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.
Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.

Bakma: Purposeful grotesquerie or mere overstatement?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:21:20 UTC
20:21:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Bakma: A Tunisian nightmare of institutional violence, misogyny and urban abandonment
A woman’s dismembered body is discovered with a dog’s head sewn where her own should be. It is a typically blunt opening statement from Bakma, Abdelhamid Bouchnak’s fourth feature: a film with no interest in easing its audience into the brutality to come.
Premiered in Locarno’s out-of-competition sidebar, the 117-minute Tunisian thriller is lurid, abrasive and often grotesque. It is also more intriguing than its uneven execution initially suggests.
Police officers Ali and Khaled are assigned to investigate the ritualistic killing, whose perpetrator soon proves interested not only in murder but in staging a spectacle. His victims are drawn largely from the city’s margins, while dogs become both targets and symbols in his private war.
Khaled, played by Aziz Jebali, gradually emerges as the more developed of the two officers: damaged, volatile and struggling to keep his professional obsession from swallowing what remains of his family life. The killer, meanwhile, taunts the police through a menacing voiceover while constructing an increasingly elaborate mythology around his crimes.
The dog killings are not simply an imported horror device or a bid for easy provocation. Tunisian municipalities have long used shooting campaigns to reduce stray-dog populations, officially as a response to rabies and attacks on humans.
The policy remains current: authorities in Greater Tunis announced coordinated capture-and-shooting operations in late 2025, while the municipality of Kef launched another campaign in June 2026. Animal-welfare groups have pressed instead for vaccination and sterilisation, arguing that culling is both cruel and ineffective.
That reality gives Abdelhamid’s imagery a political charge, even when his screenplay cannot fully control it. Interestingly, the title refers to voicelessness, and the film aligns animals, unhoused people, sex workers and other social outcasts through their exposure to violence and their inability to shape the story told about them.
Its city is neither the photogenic Tunisia sold to tourists nor an exoticised vision of spectacular poverty. Chams Ghorab’s cinematography instead renders it as a recognisable urban environment hollowed out by night: dark streets, worn interiors and anonymous corners that become threatening without turning into a fantasy slum.
When the grotesque goes too far
Visually, Bakma is competent and occasionally striking. The low-key photography suits the genre, and the camera’s nocturnal movements build a sustained atmosphere of decay. Yet the approach is more functional than original, indebted to a familiar lineage of serial-killer procedurals.
More damagingly, the practical effects vary wildly in quality. Some wounds and mutilations carry the intended physical weight; others have a conspicuously plastic texture. A number of corpses and severed parts look manufactured enough to strain the viewer’s suspension of disbelief.
This inconsistency extends to the film’s tone. Abdelhamid embraces excess, but does not always distinguish between purposeful grotesquerie and mere overstatement. Scenes are held beyond the point at which their meaning is clear, as though the film does not trust either its images or its audience.
The violence itself is not necessarily the problem: this is, after all, a story about a merciless serial killer, and sanitising him would be dishonest. The weakness lies in how rarely the brutality acquires another dimension once its initial shock has landed.
The characters are similarly underworked. Khaled receives enough contradictions to suggest a life beyond the investigation, but much of the supporting cast remains sketched rather than developed. The performances are serviceable across the board, with no conspicuous failures but few memorable peaks.
At times, one senses that the actors are working in slightly different tonal registers, some leaning into pulp while others treat the material as unyielding social realism.
The killer’s psychology is the most serious limitation. His fury towards women and marginalised people could have become a study of punitive masculinity or of the way social disgust disguises itself as purification.
Instead, the explanation eventually leans too heavily on his relationship with a supposedly impure mother. That is too slight and schematic a foundation for such elaborate pathology.
Consequently, it remains unclear whether his contradictions are meant to expose a wider sickness or merely supply the film with lurid motivation. Ambiguity is not inherently a flaw, but here it often feels less like a deliberate refusal of answers than an idea insufficiently developed.
For most of its runtime, the investigation maintains reasonable momentum, though the film would benefit from a tighter edit. Its final revelation operates on the level of plot mechanics but is perhaps telegraphed too early to land the intended blow. A bolder structural decision might have matched the extremity of the imagery.
A filmmaker willing to take risks
Still, Abdelhamid’s willingness to take risks deserves recognition. Dachra explored horror, Golden Butterfly moved into drama and fantasy, and The Needle, screened in competition at the 2024 Torino Film Festival, confronted the pressures placed on parents after the birth of an intersex child.
In a Tunisian industry where resources are limited, and certain subjects carry genuine social sensitivity, this movement between genres is not negligible. He repeatedly chooses difficult material and refuses tasteful restraint.
That makes Bakma a logical selection for Locarno: it is precisely the kind of unruly genre piece whose audacity can generate a life beyond its premiere, particularly across horror and medium-sized international festivals. But daring subject matter is not the same as daring filmmaking.
Abdelhamid has found potent raw material in institutional violence, misogyny and urban abandonment; he has not yet shaped it into an equally rigorous work.
Had the film’s artistic choices matched its premise, Bakma might have been exceptional. As it stands, it is a flawed but arresting nightmare, more convincing as evidence of its helmer’s ambition than as a fully realised work.
Davide Abbatescianni is an Italian Film Critic and Journalist based in Rome
Follow him on X: @dabbatescianni

Biden also said in the interview that he did not currently intend to run for political office.
Instead, he said he preferred to use his public profile to reach people struggling with addiction.
Biden, who has spoken publicly for years about his addiction to drugs and alcohol, told LBC that he has been sober for more than seven years and that public exposure and shame had forced him to confront his condition openly.
That process, he said, "in many ways saved my life."

====================================================================================================

France loans Mexico rare Aztec manuscript as nations celebrate 200 years of diplomatic ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:21:10 UTC
20:21:10 KST

The Azcatitlan Codex, a rare manuscript that recounts the founding of the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan and the subsequent arrival of Spanish conquistadores, is back in Mexico for the first time since 1840.
The 16th-century artifact, considered one of the most important visual records of Aztec history, is on loan from France's Bibliotheque Nationale, where it has been held since 1898. The two nations are celebrating 200 years of diplomatic ties.
Combining Mesoamerican pictograms with European writing, the Azcatitlan Codex is divided into three sections. It traces the Mexicas' migration from Aztlan, the mythical birthplace of Aztec civilization, to the founding of Tenochtitlan (in present-day Mexico City).
It also recounts the succession of the city's tlatoanis, or rulers, and depicts the arrival of the Spanish, the conquest and the subsequent evangelization, according to Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History.
"These codices are extremely important to us because they continue to give us identity and value as human beings during these very special times we are experiencing," said Maria Eugenia Castañeda, representative of the Mexica peoples. "They elevate our morale, our customs, our culture, and our sense of who we are."
Codex to be displayed until December
More than five centuries have passed since the fall of Tenochtitlan to Hernan Cortes, the leader of the invading Spanish force. After defeating the Aztec leaders and the Mexica people who lived in Tenochtitlan, Cortes and his allies looted and razed the city, ushering in three centuries of Spanish domination.
An Indigenous craftsman from the Otomi people created the Azcatitlan Codex, according to Maria Castañeda de la Paz, historian at the Institute of Anthropological Research at Mexico's National Autonomous University (UNAM).
The codex will be on display until December at Mexico City's famed National Museum of Anthropology. As part of the exchange, Mexico will loan France another important historical document, the Codex Boturini.

The Venezuelan government and the opposition are close to an agreement to transfer the central bank's gold reserves, worth about $4 billion, from the Bank of England to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the Financial Times reported on Friday.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report, which cited four people familiar with the discussion.
Under the proposed deal, the interim government of Delcy Rodriguez would gain legal control of the gold but would be unable to sell the holdings immediately, the report said.
Instead, the reserve could be used as collateral for government borrowings, including for reconstruction following June’s twin earthquakes, the newspaper added.
A spokesperson for the British foreign office said the government was "not a party in the legal case to determine who should have control of Venezuelan gold held in the Bank of England."
UK Courts and the Bank of England are independent of government, the spokesperson added.
In response to a Reuters query, the Bank of England said it is not in a position to act until there is a further order from the UK Court on who has legal authority over the account.
"This requires the parties involved in the case to approach the UK Court to settle the dispute," the BoE said.
Gold could be used to try to counter inflation
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment outside regular business hours. The Venezuelan government and the opposition could not be reached for comment.
Last month, Venezuela's National Assembly chief Jorge Rodriguez said the country was working to recover gold reserves held in the Bank of England's underground vaults, in an effort to counter surging inflation.
The Bank of England has withheld about 31 metric tons of Venezuelan gold for years, citing its non-recognition of the legitimacy of then-president Nicolas Maduro's government.
The BoE's refusal to release the gold goes back to early 2019 when the British government joined dozens of nations in backing then Venezuelan opposition leader Juan Guaido on the basis that Maduro's election win the previous year had been rigged.
The bullion has since been the subject of a prolonged legal dispute in British courts, and has not been released despite Maduro's capture by the US in January and a request by acting President Delcy Rodriguez to King Charles.
“The UK maintains its longstanding position of support for a democratic transition of power in Venezuela which reflects the will of the Venezuelan people,” the spokesperson for the British foreign office said.

'Go die in your own country': Thai PM comes down on foreigners wanting private cemeteries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:21:02 UTC
20:21:02 KST

Thai Prime Minister and Interior Minister Anutin Charnvirakul issued unusually harsh remarks on Thursday against foreigners seeking to establish private cemeteries in the country, saying, "If you're going to die, go die in your own country. There's no need to come die here," during an Interior Ministry policy meeting in Bangkok, in which he instructed provincial governors to step up enforcement against foreigners who break the law.
Anutin did not explicitly mention Israel or a Jewish cemetery. However, his remarks came as he discussed foreigners establishing houses of worship and private cemeteries, just days after a highly publicized controversy surrounding a Jewish cemetery in Chachoengsao Province, east of Bangkok.
On Wednesday, Thai authorities removed four bodies from the site, those of three Israeli citizens and one British citizen, and transferred them for reburial at a licensed cemetery in Chonburi Province. The cemetery received a license in 2021, but the permit was subsequently not renewed. One of the Israelis was buried while the license was still valid, while the other three deceased were buried after it had expired.
"Establishing a place of worship is not something you can simply do on your own," Anutin said, according to reports in Thai media, adding that the establishment of religious institutions must take local society and culture into account.
He then turned to the issue of cemeteries. "I recently learned that an application had also been submitted to establish a private cemetery. This is already going too far," he said. "The fact that we allowed you to come here is more than enough. If you come, earn your living honestly. If you're going to die, go die at home; there's no need to come die here. And don't take advantage of others."
Thai PM says enforcement not aimed at any particular nationality
He made the remarks Thursday morning at the Interior Ministry headquarters in Bangkok during a meeting attended by senior ministry officials, with provincial governors joining by video conference. The prime minister ordered authorities to intensify enforcement against foreigners who, he said, exploit Thai citizens, operate businesses illegally, use nominees, or establish institutions without the necessary permits.
Anutin stressed that the enforcement measures he was discussing were not aimed at any particular nationality. He said authorities have encountered cases involving foreigners from various countries in Asia, the Middle East, Central Asia, Europe, and Africa. He added that foreigners who enter Thailand legally, earn an honest living, and respect the country's laws and culture are welcome to continue coming.
The remarks come amid growing public discussion in Thailand about the conduct of foreigners in the country, including Israelis. In recent months, local media have published allegations concerning inappropriate behavior at tourist sites, operating businesses without permits, using nominees, holding land in violation of the law, and breaching local customs.
A survey by the NIDA Poll Institute published this week also illustrates the role of media exposure in shaping the discussion. Some 76.38% of respondents in six provinces said they had heard through the media or social networks about inappropriate or illegal behavior attributed to Israelis in Thailand. By contrast, only 5.11% said they had personally experienced such an incident.
Among respondents who had been exposed to such reports or who reported direct experience, 77.49% said the authorities should enforce the law strictly. The survey was conducted from September 8 to 10 among 1,410 people in Bangkok and the provinces of Chachoengsao, Chonburi, Surat Thani, Phuket, and Mae Hong Son, meaning it does not constitute a fully representative nationwide sample.
Thai attitudes toward Israelis shifting
In recent weeks, attitudes toward Israelis have become a more prominent subject in Thai public discourse, against the backdrop of protests, media reports, and contacts between Thai officials and Israeli representatives. At the same time, the Thai government has continued to stress that enforcement measures against illegal activity by foreigners are not directed at Israelis alone.
Now, days after the bodies were removed from the Jewish cemetery, the prime minister's unusually sharp remarks about the establishment of private cemeteries add another layer to the discussion, even though Anutin himself did not explicitly connect his comments to Israelis or Jews.

Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire chair, becomes chairman emeritus

2026-09-18

20:20:54 KST

Berkshire Hathaway said on Friday that Warren Buffett will step down as the conglomerate's chairman and will become its chairman emeritus, effective immediately.
Earlier this year, Buffett had stepped down as CEO, handing the reins to longtime lieutenant Greg Abel.
"Father Time always wins. He has, however, been generous with me," Buffett, 96, wrote in a letter to shareholders.
The conglomerate named his son, Howard Buffett, a Berkshire director since 1993, as chairman.
"As Chairman Emeritus, Mr. Buffett will remain a member of the Board of Directors and will continue to offer his valued judgment and perspective," Berkshire said in a statement.
Buffett built Berkshire into an approximately $1.03 trillion conglomerate with dozens of businesses, including Geico car insurance, the BNSF railroad, Berkshire Hathaway Energy, Dairy Queen ice cream, Fruit of the Loom underwear and Squishmallows plush toys.
"The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian," Abel said in a statement on Friday.
Buffett's influence extended beyond Berkshire Hathaway
Buffett's influence has extended far beyond Berkshire, shaping generations of corporate leaders and investors with his emphasis on long-term thinking, disciplined capital allocation and straightforward management.
CEOs across Corporate America have looked to him as a sounding board on everything from acquisitions and succession to navigating periods of market turmoil, while his annual shareholder meetings became a gathering point for investors seeking insight into the broader business landscape.
Buffett first announced plans to step away from the conglomerate in May 2025, surprising shareholders and analysts despite his age. After decades at the helm, he had become synonymous with the company, making his succession one of the most closely watched in corporate America.
In August, Berkshire said it began reducing its enormous stockpile of cash in the second quarter, investing billions of dollars in stocks such as Alphabet and repurchasing billions of its own, as it reported higher-than-expected profit.
Its quarterly operating profit rose 16% to $12.98 billion, topping analyst forecasts, while net income more than doubled to $25.67 billion, including unrealized gains and losses on stocks that Omaha, Nebraska-based Berkshire still owns.

At least 112,000 people have been displaced inside Yemen within the last two weeks as fighting continues along the country's west coast amid a renewed conflict, while nearly 3,000 have fled by sea to Djibouti, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi terrorists have stepped up attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure while advancing along Yemen's Red Sea coast towards the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key shipping route. Responding to the Houthi offensive, the Saudi and Yemeni air forces have bombarded Houthi targets.
Nearly 3,000 people have crossed the Gulf of Aden to Djibouti in the Horn of Africa in less than a week as escalating violence has forced more families to flee, Sandrine Desamours, the representative for the UN’s refugee agency, UNHCR, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Djibouti.
The government of Djibouti is preparing for the arrival of up to 10,000 refugees - which will add acute pressure on the country’s health care and education services, she said.
The UN International Organization for Migration said people are fleeing on overcrowded boats and arriving with very limited food and water. Most fleeing are Yemeni families seeking refuge in Djibouti, but IOM is also beginning to see a small number of migrants, mainly from Ethiopia, heading in the same direction.
Additionally, authorities in Somaliland and Puntland have also reported increased arrivals from Yemen, including Yemeni refugees and Somali refugee returnees, though numbers remain in the hundreds for now, UNHCR said.
UN: Yemen escalation is crisis on top of multiple crises
UN agencies described the latest fighting as being a crisis on top of multiple crises, as the country’s health services and economy have been shattered amid a long civil war between forces of the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed administration and the Houthis, creating one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises.
The Houthi advance along Yemen's Red Sea coast is bolstering Tehran’s hand in its conflict with the US, as the group tightens its control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a strategic chokepoint for global oil and commodities shipping, more than six months after US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

OpenAI ‘ethically hacked’ with help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:20:44 UTC
20:20:44 KST

Cybersecurity researchers have hacked into OpenAI with the help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot, in the latest example of security issues at the company.
A team at a US-based startup compromised a number of OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts, starting a process that enabled them to access their target’s software cache – and potentially more.
“The scope of what we could theoretically access was huge,” said researchers at Hacktron AI.
Initially, the research team used Claude, which can generate code for hackers, to access ChatGPT accounts via an OpenAI staff discussion forum hosted by the Discourse platform. They then made a harmless “pull request” – an attempt to change the code in a file – to OpenAI’s service on the GitHub software repository.
Hacktron reported the hack to OpenAI, having carried out the operation under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers for testing its systems. The researchers stressed that they had access to, but did not download, the code from the GitHub repository.
Despite initial use of Claude, the researchers said they were largely using OpenAI’s own cutting edge GPT-5.6 Sol model to carry out the hack, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
An OpenAI spokesperson said: “We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings”, adding that the company had addressed the vulnerabilities that had been exploited.
Hacktron said AI tools had made a once-complex hacking task far easier and drastically shortened the time needed to plan and execute an attack. This is a common refrain from cybersecurity experts when discussing the impact of AI.
“Work that once required a well-resourced team and months of effort can now be compressed into days,” said Hacktron, which received a $6,500 payment from OpenAI under the company’s bug bounty programme.
The hack is the latest safety incident at OpenAI, which revealed in July that a “swarm” of agents – the term for AI tools capable of carrying out tasks autonomously – powered by its technology had hacked the AI startup Hugging Face during a cybersecurity test.
This week the San Francisco-based company revealed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” actions by its technology, and warned that the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer”.
Anthropic made a fresh call at the weekend for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk. Anthropic also repeated warnings that unrestrained AI development posed an existential threat, concerns that some experts are sceptical about.
Donald Trump has rejected calls for a slowdown, citing a need to stay ahead of China’s AI industry and dismissing “negative forces … bringing up things that won’t happen”.

TRAI cracks the whip on spam calls; robocalls &amp; pre-recorded messages to face action now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:19:22 UTC
20:19:22 KST

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has introduced fresh measures to strengthen regulations governing spam calls and commercial messages.
NEW DELHI: You may soon get some relief from the unending nuisance of unsolicited commercial communications (UCC) or spam calls including robo-calls and pre-recorded/artificial voice technologies. Now, commercial communications can be sent to a customer on the basis of an inquiry made in writing or through digital only for a week. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has tightened the rules to prevent misuse of telecom resources for sending UCC and will use AI for spam detection, automated calls, and will take strict action against repeat offenders into the regulatory net.Now action will be triggered against the sender if of UCC as soon as there are three or more unique complaints within 10 days and the concerned sender’s calling line identification (CLI) is also flagged by the AI/ML-based system as suspected of sending UCC. Consumers will now be able to appeal against the resolution of UCC complaints.Amending the Telecom Commercial Communications Customer Preference Regulations, 2018 (TCCCPR, 2018), TRAI has also cracked down on application-to-person (A2P) which are made without direct human dialling and include using autodialing, robo-calls and pre-recorded/artificial voice technologies. “Every entity using A2P calls must pre-declare such use to its telecom service provider (TSP) along with the details of calling line identification (CLIs) to be used for making such calls.
A2P calls made without the required prior declaration will be treated as UCC. To act as a deterrent, a termination charge of up to 5 paisa per minute has been introduced” on such catering entities, said a TRAI statement.TRAI has now mandated TSPs to identify the sender’s CLIs having a high probability of being used for sending UCC and share the information among the TSPs. “Where five or more CLIs associated with a sender are flagged within 10 days, further investigation and graded action will be initiated by the access providers, including KYC re-verification, physical verification, barring of outgoing services, and disconnection of telecom resource in cases of repeated violations and misuse of telecom resources,” said the statement.Special series designated for commercial communications, including the 140xx, 1600xx and 1601xx series will not be flagged as suspected spam for recipients, said TRAI on Friday while introducing the Telecom Commercial Communication Customer Preference (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2026.
TRAI has introduced a consumer appeal mechanism where the same can be made “through any of the modes available for lodging UCC complaints (like) TRAI DND App, TSPs App/Portal, and call or SMS to 1909 besides the modes specified under TCCRR, 2012.”TRAI has expanded the definition of consent to include legacy consents already available with the entities. The framework is being amended to enable the recognition and digitisation of such legacy consents. “However, the legacy consents shall be considered valid only where they have been obtained through verifiable means and are subsequently registered on the Digital Platform of the TSPs.”TRAI has introduced a new regulation where it can classify senders UCCd into different categories and may specify differentiated sets of enforcement measures applicable to such categories of senders for violations of the regulations.

US gives UN more time to end support for Somalia peacekeepers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:18:23 UTC
20:18:23 KST

US gives UN more time to end support for Somalia peacekeepers
MOGADISHU/NAIROBI, Sept 18 - The United States has agreed to give the UN another year to wind down its support for African peacekeepers in Somalia, a document showed - a move that gives some breathing space to a force that was fearing quicker cuts, but still leaves its future in peril.
Reuters reported in July that Washington - increasingly frustrated with the fragile administration in Mogadishu - said it would block the UN from supporting the African Union force which props up the government and helps it fight al Qaeda-linked militants.
Analysts have warned that any weakening of the African Union peacekeepers would severely undermine the government there and could exacerbate the political turmoil in a combustible region bordering the Red Sea.
'A REAL RISK OF STATE FRAGMENTATION'
The peacekeepers, known as the AU Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia, rely heavily on UN support for essential logistics such as food, water, fuel, medical services and transportation of troops.
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump, which has pulled back from many international commitments, had told the African Union in a diplomatic note in July that it would use its clout to prevent the UN supporting the peacekeepers from the start of next year.
In another diplomatic note seen by Reuters and shared with embassies last week, Washington said "the United States is willing to support a 12-month drawdown followed immediately by liquidation" of the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS).
Without that 12-month window, the funding could have stopped at the end of December, when the mandate of that UN office expires. Two diplomatic sources and a Somali government source said the new 12-month countdown would start in January.
A spokesperson for the US State Department told Reuters that Washington would no longer fund or support the UN office in Somalia, whose total budget is around $500 million.
"We would expect any drawdown processes and timelines to be discussed during UN Security Council deliberations in December," the spokesperson said in a statement. Five diplomatic sources and the Somali government source, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the 12-month deadline.
Somalia's defence ministry, UNSOS and the African Union Commission did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
FUNDING GAPS
The move will buy Somalia and its partners some more time to find other backers, but does not lift the threat over the peacekeeping force's future.
"AUSSOM is a key pillar of Somalia's state," Afyare Elmi, professor at the City University of Mogadishu, said. "Without it, the country would face a real risk of state fragmentation and disintegration."
Samira Gaid, a regional security analyst, told Reuters the shutdown of UNSOS could spell the end for AUSSOM.
"The AU either (needs) to find alternative logistics arrangements or to draw down and exit," she said.
Financing for the AU mission has become increasingly precarious, leading to a huge funding shortfall.
Washington last year blocked a plan to shift to a financing model that would have seen UN funds cover three-quarters of the peacekeeping mission's $190 million annual budget.
Somalia has been mired in chaos and internal conflict since the fall of autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991. Islamists have strengthened their control of the countryside and two decades ago, seized the capital before being forced out by a joint Ethiopian and Somali government force. REUTERS

Over the past week, the Russian Armed Forces disabled a number of infrastructure facilities at Ukrainian ports used by the Ukrainian military to receive and store cargo and fuel and lubricants.
A number of infrastructure facilities at Ukrainian ports that facilitated the receipt and storage of military-grade cargo, as well as fuel and lubricants intended for the Ukrainian military, have been disabled," the Defense Ministry stated.

"Battlegroup Dnepr units inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, and two territorial defense brigades. Over the week, more than 280 troops, an armored combat vehicle, 129 motor vehicles, a field artillery gun, and eleven electronic warfare and counterbattery radar stations were destroyed," the ministry said in a statement.

Meanwhile, troops from the Battlegroup North secured control of Chernyakov, Shirokoye, Shevchenkovo, Olkhovatka, and Malaya Volchya in the Kharkov Region.

"Over the week, 12 dry cargo ships, two Ro-Ro sea ferries, a tanker and a tugboat operating in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces were hit," the ministry said.
Russian army hits four dry-cargo ships in Ukrainian ports and Black Sea
Russian operators of Geran-4 Seeker UAVs have hit four additional dry-cargo ships in the ports of Chernomorsk and Odessa, as well as in the Black Sea.

All targets were hit," the Russian Defense Ministry said in a news release.

Intibint: The Yemeni-British artist turning heritage into music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:16:56 UTC
20:16:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen, grime and the search for home: Yemeni-British artist Intibint on finding her voice
For years, Yemeni-British singer, producer, and visual artist Intibint (the stage moniker of Noha Al Maghafi), who is also the sister of well-known BBC journalist Nawal Al-Maghafi, has always known she wanted to make music.
As a child in Yemen, she looked forward to traditional weddings and parties for the music, watching small bands perform as people socialised around her, more interested in listening than joining in.
But even as she enjoyed those moments, growing up in a conservative culture meant she never saw making music herself as something she was allowed to pursue, until completing her master’s at SOAS prompted her to stop ignoring that part of her life.
She began by messaging friends and looking for instrumentalists to work with before deciding to learn how to produce music herself. From there, she taught herself how to make and mix tracks, develop live sets and eventually perform them.
Learning those skills was important because she did not want to depend on others to turn her ideas into music, particularly after realising that, as a female vocalist, she was sometimes expected to wait for a producer or instrumentalist to shape the track.
"I always knew I wanted to pursue music. I always knew I loved music, and I was always very sensitive to it. It's something that's always been super important in my life," Intibint tells The New Arab.
That decision to learn the process herself has shaped Half Moon Eyes, her debut album, but the music on it comes from a much wider range of influences. Her earliest memories are tied to Yemeni folk music and musicians including Fuad al-Kibsi, Hamoud Al-Sama and Abu Bakr Salem, whose music she heard at weddings and family gatherings.
Growing up in London later introduced her to a completely different range of sounds, and she describes herself as someone who never really restricted what she listened to. Iron Maiden, Destiny's Child and grime are among the influences she names, with grime becoming particularly important during her teenage and university years. Its heavy bass and beats appealed to her, and that influence appears directly on the album.
Elsewhere, she takes a melody from a well-known Yemeni song and reworks it within a track that also draws on rock, metal and electronic music.
"I really am the definition of 'I listen to everything'," she says, laughing.
Those influences reflect the different places she has lived, but they also help explain why Yemeni music remains such an important part of the record.
Intibint has moved between Yemen, Egypt, Scotland, Slovakia and London, and says her experiences of growing up between Yemen and the UK have given her a particular perspective as a Yemeni woman and member of the diaspora.
Rather than treating that background as separate from her music, she has used it as part of how she writes, produces, and thinks about her work.
"My Yemeni heritage is a huge part of who I am as a person and a creative," she says, adding that her experiences as a woman growing up in Yemen and the UK have influenced both the sound of the album and the stories behind its songs.
That connection to her heritage is not limited to the musical references. Intibint also uses field recordings, conversations and other sounds taken from her own life throughout Half Moon Eyes.
She records things regularly on her phone and laptop, sometimes capturing a conversation, a voice or an interesting sound that she later finds a place for in a track. Even something as ordinary as a door closing can become part of the production.
For her, these recordings allow her to include personal experiences without having to explain them directly in the lyrics. They also reflect the freedom she has found in producing her own work, where she can experiment with sounds simply because she is interested in what they might become.
"I think it [the recordings] kind of makes it more personal, and it allows me to tell certain stories without having to be so literal or write exactly what happened in the lyrics," she explains.
Looking through the qamariya window
The idea of turning everyday experiences into part of the music also connects to the title Half Moon Eyes.
Intibint says she has always been interested in the moon and particularly likes the thought that people in different places can look up at it at the same time, sharing a moment without knowing anything about each other's lives.
She then connected that idea to the qamariya, a colourful stained-glass feature found in many Yemeni homes.
That being said, the qamariya is usually positioned above a window and takes a half-moon shape, with its name coming from 'qamar', meaning 'moon'.
Intibint was also drawn to the way the shape resembles an eye, which led her to the idea of eyes as windows into a person's feelings and inner life. The title therefore brings together the moon, Yemeni architecture and the album's wider interest in emotions that can be difficult to put into words.
"Qamariyas are always a half circle. They’re never a full circle, which I think is really beautiful," she says. "They kind of look like eyes."
While the title brings together ideas that were important to the finished record, the album itself was not planned from the beginning. Intibint started making the music in 2022 with a much simpler aim: she wanted to learn how to produce music in the way she wanted to hear it.
At the time, she was still working, mainly with refugees and asylum seekers, and was travelling whenever she had the opportunity. She spent time in Morocco and Slovakia, moved to East London and also lived in Glasgow, where some of the album's most personal songs began to take shape.
For much of that period, she was simply making music without thinking about whether it would eventually become a full project.
It was only in the last year, when she went back through the material she had accumulated, that she realised she could select the songs that meant the most to her and build an album from them. Some tracks changed considerably during that process, while others remained almost as they were when she first made them.
"I didn't know what I was doing," she says of the early stages of the project. "My main goal was to learn how to make music in the way that I wanted to make it."
Writing through anger, freedom and change
Looking back through four years of music also meant seeing how closely some of the songs were connected to particular periods of her life.
Hayati, for example, was written in 2022 after she arrived in Glasgow and found herself largely alone in a new city. She was working freelance from home and knew very few people, which gave her an unusual amount of space to think about what she wanted her life to look like.
That situation led her to think about the freedom that can come from being somewhere where nobody knows you or has expectations about who you should be. She connects that feeling to the guilt and shame she had experienced as a woman trying to live for herself, and Hayati became an expression of taking control over those decisions.
"I was kind of like, wait, I can literally do anything I want, like be whoever I want," she says of that period in Glasgow.
She hopes that feeling reaches other women who listen to the song, particularly Arab women and women in the diaspora.
That intention is part of a wider thread across the album, where personal experiences become starting points for songs about self-possession, protest and identity rather than being treated as isolated events.
That becomes more direct on Disrespectful, which Intibint says grew out of a frustrating encounter in which she was called 'disrespectful' after confronting someone over racist behaviour.
"I started making Disrespectful because I thought the beat was so thick. Then I had an interaction with someone who was being racist. I called them out on it, and they turned around and said I was being disrespectful. I remember thinking how funny it was that when people of colour, or Arabs, defend themselves, the blame can so quickly be turned back on them.
"I went home feeling annoyed, opened up my file and finished the whole song in about an hour. Then I thought, I'm going to call it Disrespectful too, because if you're going to call me disrespectful for calling out racism, then maybe we should just be even more disrespectful," she explains.
In sharing this, Intibint notes that the track also opens with a recording from a protest in Glasgow, where she later spoke to her mother about what had happened.
"It starts with a recording from when I was at a protest in Glasgow, and I was just telling my mum about it. I was like, 'Oh, the police showed up and stuff,' and she was like, 'You know, just be careful, look after yourself, don't get arrested again.' Because I got arrested in France once when I was working with refugees there. I think all of these kinds of situations have influenced how I see things and the world, and maybe they've influenced the direction of the sounds as well," Intibint notes.
Finding home, finding her voice
Alongside Disrespectful, other songs on the album address protest, migration, chosen family, unfinished conversations, and private grief, bringing different parts of her life into the same record.
These experiences also inform the album's recurring focus on home, although Intibint says her understanding of what home means has changed in recent years.
For a long time, she associated home with Yemen and with the loss of access to ordinary family experiences because of the war.
She describes hearing people talk about going home for Christmas, finding old childhood photographs or visiting their grandparents and thinking about how those experiences were no longer available to her in the same way.
Living in different places has gradually made that idea less fixed. Over the past year, she says she has started to realise that home does not necessarily have to mean one particular country or city, while still recognising how important Yemen is to her identity and how much it has shaped her.
"I think releasing this album is also part of me letting go of the old idea that home can only be in one place," she shares. "Regardless of where I am, it doesn't change who I am or where I came from."
With the album slated for release on 18 September, there is plenty for Intibint to look forward to as she moves into the next stage of her career.
For now, however, she is less focused on deciding exactly what her next project will sound like and more interested in performing.
She says she used to be extremely shy about playing gigs and had reached a point where she did not want to perform at all, but that changed over the past two years, particularly during the last year.
“I think now I’m at a point where I really want to perform and I really want to connect with people through the music,” she concludes.

Olympic medalists Henry Sildaru, Eileen Gu join X Games' Golden State
Estonian freestyle skier and Olympic silver medalist Henry Sildaru was drafted to XC Golden State, where he'll team up with gold medalist Eileen Gu in the new X Games league.
The X Games will consists of three stages this season, with 40 athletes selected for the league's new team format.
Golden State, led by 1998 Olympic moguls gold medalist Jonny Moseley, selected Sildaru in the fourth round of the 2026 winter draft in Los Angeles this week.
Among others, Sildaru will team up with Chinese-American freestyle skiing star and San Francisco native Eileen Gu, who competed against his sister Kelly Sildaru in Milano Cortina. Gu also had a say in assembling the California-based team.

Henry Sildaru will also compete in FIS World Cup events and the world championships this season.
"Now things are gonna get interesting," he said, describing the coming season as likely the busiest of his career. He still has several training camps and final preparations ahead before competition begins.
"Most likely the busiest season of my life and definitely one of the most challenging," he added.

A new wave of listings: Tashkent prepares companies for global markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:14:29 UTC
20:14:29 KST

Uzbekistan’s investment fund (UzNIF) is preparing major companies in telecoms, aviation, banking and energy for potential listings. Uztelecom is currently the most advanced candidate as governance reforms advance and efforts to attract new capital gather pace.
Uzbekistan is preparing to bring some of its biggest state-linked companies to public markets, with national telecommunications operator Uztelecom now the most advanced candidate for an international listing.
The programme extends across telecommunications, aviation, banking and energy and is designed to attract more private and international capital while bringing major companies under the transparency and governance requirements expected by public investors.
For international investors, that could open access to some of Uzbekistan’s largest corporate assets. For Uzbekistan, it is a test of whether its capital-market reforms can move beyond UzNIF’s London debut to a broader pipeline of publicly traded companies.
The process is being driven through the National Investment Fund of Uzbekistan (UzNIF), managed by Franklin Templeton, which holds stakes in 13 major Uzbek companies and made its own London market debut in May.
The next step: listing the companies
Uztelecom is furthest along in the potential IPO pipeline, according to Marius Dan, CEO for Central Asia at Templeton Global Investments.
The company is already listed on the Tashkent Stock Exchange. UzNIF is considering an international listing and an increase in the number of shares available on the domestic market.
An international offering could allow more investors to buy shares in the company and could also provide fresh capital for future investment.
Responding to questions from Euronews, Dan said preparations included assessing Uztelecom’s financial reporting, governance and operational readiness.
Five equity-adviser selection processes are also under way for Uzbekistan Airways, Uztelecom, Regional Electric Networks, the National Electric Grid of Uzbekistan and Sanoat Qurilish Bank (SQB).
“Over the next 24 to 36 months, roughly 78% of the net asset value of the fund will move from unlisted to listed companies,” Dan said.
That would mean most of UzNIF’s value would eventually be held in companies whose shares are publicly traded.
A presidential decree provides for six UzNIF portfolio companies to be listed by the end of 2028. The fund said no final decision has yet been taken on the timing or sequence of individual transactions.
Changing how companies are run
UzNIF and Franklin Templeton are also changing corporate governance across the portfolio, including the composition of supervisory boards and the way companies plan, manage finances and report performance.
“We've made changes across all 13 companies. We've appointed the members of our investment team and recruited 10 very reputable international directors that were appointed on the supervisory boards in certain cases of more than one company,” Dan explained.
Ten independent non-executive directors have been elected across the portfolio, while 11 of the 13 companies now have supervisory boards on which independent directors and Franklin Templeton representatives form a majority.
Nine transformation plans have been completed, with four more expected in the coming months.
At Uzbekistan Airways, for example, the fund has identified 120 initiatives covering growth, efficiency, profitability, customer experience and expansion.
Those changes are important because a stock-market listing involves more than selling shares. Companies also need reliable accounts, clearer decision-making and governance structures that can withstand outside scrutiny.
Inside UzNIF’s €2.28bn portfolio
UzNIF’s net asset value stood at around €2.28bn as of 31 July 2026.
For the first half of 2026, the fund reported €147mn in net profit, including a €156mn fair-value gain and €24mn in dividend income.
Energy-related holdings represented around 37% of the fund’s net asset value.
Dan said a new regulated asset base framework was among the factors affecting valuations at several energy companies. The system determines how regulated utilities can earn returns on infrastructure investment and how tariffs are calculated.
Initial tariff adjustments took effect on 1 August, with further details expected by the end of 2026 or in the first quarter of 2027.
IPOs could bring fresh capital
The potential listings could also bring money directly into the companies rather than simply allowing existing shareholders to sell stakes.
Dan said the government would have priority if it chose to sell shares, while UzNIF could also sell part of its own holdings if needed to ensure sufficient market liquidity.
“The companies will also have priority to raise capital as part of these IPOs because these are all incredibly exciting assets. They have significant capex programs, more investments that are needed,” he said.
The distinction is important: selling existing shares changes ownership, while issuing new shares can give companies money for aircraft, telecom networks, power infrastructure or other investment.
The final structure of each transaction will be decided later.
2026 is the first full year in which Franklin Templeton has managed UzNIF, after taking over in May 2025.
Dan said this year’s results should provide a fuller basis for assessing profitability and future dividend capacity. The first UzNIF dividend would be considered in 2028, based on the fund’s 2027 financial results.

Wine Production in Crimea Drops 25% Amid Fuel Shortages and Supply Line Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:13:00 UTC
20:13:00 KST

Wine production in annexed Crimea fell by one-quarter in the first eight months of 2026 due to fuel shortages and logistical bottlenecks triggered by intensifying Ukrainian attacks, the newspaper Kommersant reported Friday.
Data from Russia’s Federal Alcohol Market Regulation Service show Crimean still wine output dropped 24.7% year-on-year between January and August, while sparkling wine production fell 38%. In Russia, still wine output fell nearly 15% and sparkling wine dropped 14.5% over the same period.
Crimea, which Moscow annexed from Ukraine in 2014, is a major regional supplier, accounting for 20% of all still wine and 10% of sparkling wine sold in Russia.
Industry experts told Kommersant that the production slump was due to Ukraine ramping up its attacks on the peninsula this summer, triggering an acute fuel shortage and disrupting shipping between Crimea and the Russian mainland.
Transporting essential production materials — including glass bottles, corks and packaging — has become increasingly expensive and hazardous, the experts said. Rolling power outages caused by strikes on energy infrastructure have further strained winemaking operations.
At the same time, fewer tourists have been traveling to Crimea due to deadly Ukrainian attacks, leading to a decrease in people making wine purchases while on vacation there.
Despite the current drop in output, winemakers anticipate a recovery later this year, buoyed by forecasts of a strong grape harvest expected to be the best in a decade.

Russian e-commerce will lose $4.8 billion to the drone campaign against its warehouses, analysts estimate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:12:13 UTC
20:12:13 KST

Ukrainian drone strikes on the warehouses of Russia's biggest online marketplaces will cost the country's e-commerce 400 million orders and 400 billion rubles ($4.8 billion) in revenue this year, the research firm Data Insight estimates, The Moscow Times reported. It prices what the campaign has done to a whole consumer market, not only to the companies whose warehouses burned. Sellers are cutting back on the platform at the center of it, and Wildberries' payout delays are pushing some of them out.
The forecast, cut by a fifth
Data Insight lowered its growth forecast for Russian online retail by 20%, founder Fyodor Virin said. The market will now grow to 9.6 billion orders this year instead of 10 billion, and to 15 trillion rubles ($178 billion) in sales instead of 15.4 trillion.
That is exclusively the effect of the Ukrainian strikes on marketplace warehouses, Virin said, and most of the loss falls on Wildberries. The bombardment of the depots cut sales because goods were unavailable in a given city or entirely, and because delivery times grew as parcels had to travel further.
All of it lands in the second half of the year. Strikes on Wildberries warehouses began on 18 July and on Ozon's on 25 August, according to Virin. Euromaidan Press reported the first strike on an Ozon warehouse on 22 August.
About 30% of the orders that got stuck or disappeared from sale were cancelled outright, Virin estimates. The rest of the unmet demand went mostly to other online platforms and, to a lesser degree, to physical retail. Payout delays that began in mid-August have pushed some sellers to pull their stock, and Wildberries blamed the first missed round on a DDoS attack.
A warehouse built to hold up to 54 million items burned down in Tambov Oblast, Russia
What the companies lost
Damage to RWB, the company that runs Wildberries, from the loss of warehouses and infrastructure may reach 147 to 280 billion rubles ($1.7–3.3 billion), while sellers have provisionally lost 445 to 507 billion rubles ($5.3–6 billion), Data Insight's lead analyst Sergei Semko estimated. All of the marketplace's key logistics complexes have been hit, and it could lose a fifth of its network and over half its main hubs at once.
Much of what the sellers lost will not come back. On 22 July, Wildberries' founder said the warehouses were insured but that standard policies do not cover drone-strike risk, and Ozon has told sellers that losses from military action are an entrepreneurial risk neither it nor insurers will compensate.
Total losses for Ozon and its sellers are far lower, at around 100 billion rubles ($1.2 billion). Ozon has a much more branched warehouse network and rents most of its large complexes, Alfa-Bank analysts said. Its shares still fell as much as 29% in a single August session on a day when the Moscow exchange lost 2.9%.
