“Please observe safety precautions; the threat is currently being countered. Polling stations will resume operations as soon as it is safe to do so,” Proshunin said.
Air defenses were tracking and attempting to engage Ukrainian drones operating in regional airspace, and all citizens should remain calm, he said.
According to unconfirmed reports in local media, on Friday at least one Ukrainian drone struck and damaged a Sochi voting site, blowing out windows and breaking up fixtures and furniture inside a public building.
Authorities moved the polling station “to a reserve site,” and ballot-casting would continue once polling sites re-opened, Ella Pamfilova, Chairperson of the Central Election Commission, said in a briefing as reported by the news platform BFM.RU.
Russian national elections taking place between Sept. 18-20 will select representatives for all 450 seats in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament. Regional governors and legislature members will also be determined by around 111 million eligible voters.
Slovakia’s Fico Pours Cold Water on Fulfilling NATO’s Article 5 Mutual Defense
On Wednesday, on the eve of polls’ opening, a Ukrainian drone struck and killed Elena Astanina, a Ukrainian citizen collaborating with Russian occupation authorities in the Ukrainian city of Tokmak in southern Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, pro-Russia news sites reported.
Astanina had served as a Russian election council member since 2022 and was attacked by a drone while helping prepare a voting site, the news magazine Zhivaya Kuban reported.
The independent Russian news agency SOTA, and later Kremlin state media TASS, confirmed the strike and Astanina’s death. A statement from Zaporizhzhia region occupation authority chief Sergei Obertas praised Astanina as a Russian patriot and said the state would assist her family.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Thursday said that Ukraine was launching drone strikes with the intent of undermining “democratic elections” in her country, and spun the Ukrainian strike on Astanina as a terrorist attack against a peaceful Russian citizen.
In occupied districts of Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, voting was proceeding as planned on Friday, according to Ukrainian news agencies, but officials were using paper records to conduct voting and track ballots after Ukrainian drone strikes targeting electric transformers in the region cut off power.
A statement from the Russia-run local power utility Khersonenergo confirmed the loss of electricity deliveries to some 150,000 customers, but blamed the outage on “a technical problem.”
Russia’s defense ministry on Friday morning claimed its forces had shot down 629 Ukrainian drones in Russian airspace, making the night’s raids by shootdown claims one of the four or five most massive drone attacks of the entire Russo-Ukrainian War.
Ukrainian military sources and independent media said that the night’s attacks targeted port facilities in the city of Taganrog on the Azov Sea, and a nearby military airfield in Rostov-on-Don. Both air raids were follow-up attacks, with dozens of Ukrainian aircraft having hit and damaged a Taganrog aerospace factory and megawarehouse on Tuesday, and a power substation and military airfield near Rostov on Thursday.
Some Ukrainian drone sorties have reached 3,000 km (1,250 miles) deep into Russia, with massed drone attacks usually targeting Russian Federation military- or energy-linked infrastructure. Although initially scoffed at by authorities as pinpricks mighty Russia might ignore, actual or threatened Ukrainian drone attacks are now taken more seriously by local officials.
On the first day of national elections, which the Kremlin traditionally has used to pump up patriotism and state-manage an image of a stable and prosperous Russia under President Vladimir Putin’s leadership, Russia’s Central Election Commission published instructions to election officials about what to do if Ukrainian kamikaze aircraft seemed en route and potentially able to disrupt the voting process, a major Russian daily reported.
Officials at a voting site forced to shut down because of a potential or actual Ukrainian drone attack should turn over voter registers, voting boxes, and ballots to the election site boss for storage in a safe, while police and emergency response officials would supervise the orderly evacuation of the voting site, official step-by-step procedures at a voting site in the Volga region city of Kazan mandated, according to a Friday BiznesOnline report.
A policeman stationed by the safe until an all-clear was called would ensure a fair poll without fraud, the article says.
Although more than 1,200 km (750 miles) from probable Ukrainian launch sites, industrial sites in Kazan have been regularly hit by Ukrainian drones for more than a year. Probably the most frequently attacked facility has been the Nizhnekamsk oil refinery, which Ukrainian drones have hit at least seven times since November 2025, Kyiv Post’s records show.
United Russia, the ruling party backed by Putin, is widely expected to retain its dominant position and supermajority thanks to state-controlled media and state repression of opposition parties.
Sochi, with a permanent population of over 500,000 that rises to more than 3 million during the high season, is Russia’s wealthiest and most exclusive beach resort. Putin’s luxurious 40-hectare Bocharov Ruchei summer home, with a helipad, yacht mooring, tennis courts, orchards and fresh and seawater swimming pools, sits in Sochi’s elite northern district.
Ukraine, since launching a long-range drone bombardment of Russia in mid-2025, has hit port, oil refining and fuel storage structures around greater Sochi at least 10 times, but never attacked Putin’s residence, Kyiv Post’s strike records show.
The most recent confirmed Ukrainian attack in Sochi’s vicinity took place on Sept. 14, with at least four drones destroying an advanced Russian S-400 air defense system deployed to protect the city and Bocharev Ruchei from Ukrainian air strikes, those records show.

====================================================================================================

Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:55:00 UTC
19:55:00 KST

Germany's electric car boom cuts fuel tax revenue
September 18, 2026
"People are moving away from gasoline and diesel," Jens Boysen-Hogrefe, a tax and transportation expert at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW), told DW.
"The boom in electric cars triggered by high fuel prices is accelerating the transition in drive technologies that was already planned anyway," Boysen-Hogrefe said.
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), sales of electric vehicles in Europe rose by nearly 30% in the first quarter of 2025 compared with the same period last year.
Norway is leading the way, with electric cars accounting for as many as 95% of all newly registered passenger cars in the country.
The agency's "Global EV Outlook 2026" reveals that EV growth rates in Asia-Pacific countries, excluding China, were even more remarkable, with sales in some regions rising by up to 80%. In Latin America, that figure was about 75%.
Fossil fuels remain a tax windfall
In Berlin, the boom in electric mobility has not been met with universal enthusiasm. That's particularly the case at the Ministry of Finance, as charging an electric car does not incur energy taxes, but only minimal electricity taxes.
Currently, a liter of diesel in Germany is taxed at 47.04 cents (54 US cents per gallon), and a liter of gasoline at 65.45 cents. On top of that, there is a carbon levy and a 19% value-added tax.
With gasoline priced at €2.10 per liter, taxes account for €1.14 of the total, meaning that more than half of the pump price goes to the government, according to the ADAC motoring club.
The current fossil-fuel-based system, with its energy taxes, truck tolls and CO2 tax, is very lucrative for the government, Boysen-Hogrefe said. "The finance minister doesn't benefit much when people drive electric cars," he noted. "Quite the opposite."
Energy tax revenue in decline
"If the shift to electric cars takes place and nothing changes in the tax system, the road system will become a money-losing venture for the federal government," Boysen-Hogrefe said, predicting billions of euros in losses.
According to the Federal Statistical Office, revenue from the energy tax on diesel and gasoline fell from €37 billion in 2016 to €33 billion last year.
In 2022, a report by the scientific advisory committee to the German Transport Ministry projected that revenue from the energy tax would drop to as low as €5 billion by 2050.
Pressure to reform road funding
"The transition to electric vehicles has fiscal implications that have hardly been discussed so far," the report states. The expected tax shortfalls add to the costly subsidies for electric vehicles that are currently still necessary to drive the transition forward, it added.
In Germany, government incentives to purchase electric cars — amounting to several thousand euros per vehicle — were scrapped at the end of 2023.
Electric cars are still exempt from vehicle tax through 2035. And companies that invest in electric cars continue to enjoy tax benefits.
In their report, the transportation experts advised the government not to wait until the tax deficit becomes so large that it is forced to act.
That's because "the lead time for such measures spans several legislative terms," they argued.
Boysen-Hogrefe said fiscal pressure could now increase. If people continue to buy electric cars in droves, "the government can't just shrug it off," he said.
How other countries are responding
Countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have already come up with measures to deal with the new situation.
In the United Kingdom, for instance, a levy on electric cars is set to take effect in April 2028. The so-called "Electric Vehicle Excise Duty" charges 3 pence (3.5 euro cents) per mile (1.6 kilometers) on fully electric cars and 1.5 pence on plug-in hybrids.
Since 2024, New Zealand and Iceland have required annual odometer checks for electric vehicles to calculate mileage-based fees.
And in Switzerland electric vehicle owners will be required to pay a road-use charge from 2030, either through a weight-based fee per kilometer or a tax on electricity purchased at charging stations.
Meanwhile, Norway, a trailblazer for electric vehicles, has restricted the VAT exemption for electric cars starting this year. It has also introduced a weight-based purchase or registration tax and tolls.
Are road tolls the answer?
In Germany many experts are advocating for a passenger car toll to compensate for the shortfall in energy tax revenue while also taking road use more fully into account.
"The recommended policy option is a distance- and traffic-based toll," according to a recently published study by the University of Münster.
"If we realistically assume that policymakers will shy away from this step, the vignette solution is recommended," according to the report.
Under a vignette system, drivers pay a flat fee for road use over a defined period.
"If this, too, encounters insurmountable political resistance, the only solution left is to raise the motor vehicle tax," they concluded.
This article was originally written in German.

====================================================================================================

‘I crawled through a sea of flames’: remembering the fatal Sabena plane crash of 1946
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:52:06 UTC
19:52:06 KST

Eighty years ago, on the night of 18 September 1946, a plane operated by the Belgian airline Sabena crashed in forests in Newfoundland, today part of Canada. The crash killed 26 people, 20 of them Belgians. What followed was a historic rescue operation.
‘I crawled through a sea of flames’: remembering the fatal Sabena plane crash of 1946
Forty-four people were on board the Douglas DC-4 plane that night, which was travelling from Brussels to New York. Only 18 people survived. The rescue operation lasted two days and involved the use of a helicopter to evacuate the seriously injured – one of the first times this had ever been done. The wreckage still lies at the crash site, alongside a small cemetery for the victims.
“I and others spent the night in great fear, because the weather was exceptionally bad,” said Jef Deschuyffeleer. He was one of the survivors of the crash and spoke on the radio the day after he was evacuated to Belgium.
We heard a tremendous cracking sound; I think it was the plane first making contact with the treetops
“The descent was erratic, with sudden jolts. After a few minutes, everyone began to sense that something unusual had happened,” he said. “Then we heard a tremendous cracking sound; I think it was the aeroplane first making contact with the treetops. What followed was a whole series of explosions and noises.”
Deschuyffeleer describes how flames shot out of the plane from all sides after it came to a halt. “I crawled 15 to 20 metres away from the sea of flames and told people to crawl further away, because of the risk of explosions.”
This was one of the first transatlantic flights operated by Sabena, the predecessor of Brussels Airlines. Cynrik De Decker, author of the book Sabena: The Turbulent Story of an Aviation Pioneer, explains: “Before the Second World War, there were no transatlantic flights. But during the war, the Americans developed large bombers capable of covering great distances and carrying large payloads. After the war, transatlantic commercial air travel took off. Sabena was quick to jump on the bandwagon.”
Flights were carried out in several stages. From Brussels, they first flew to Shannon in Ireland to refuel. They then continued to Gander in Canada, where they refuelled again, before flying on to New York.
A small cemetery was laid out at the tail end of the aeroplane. The remains were never moved
That night 80 years ago, it took some time before people realised the plane had crashed. And once it was known, it took until midday the following day before the wreckage was spotted in the vast Canadian forests.
Water was gradually supplied via parachutes, a doctor arrived and the survivors were evacuated a day later. In total, the rescue lasted two days.
It was one of the first ever rescue operations to involve a helicopter. Men were dropped off and cleared a space where they laid planks so the helicopter could land. This enabled them to evacuate the seriously wounded by helicopter. They were then transported by seaplane via the nearest lake in what De Decker calls “a truly massive operation”.
The wreckage still lies where it crashed all those years ago. “A small cemetery was laid out at the tail end of the aeroplane. The remains were never moved,” De Decker says.
It was Sabena director Gilbert Périer who decided to bury the victims there. No one had been injured during the rescue operation, and he wanted to keep it that way. Among the graves are those of his ex-wife Marie Noblet and his daughter, also called Marie.
“It was a huge event at the time,” De Decker says. “The air disaster dominated the front pages for days on end, not only in Belgium but also abroad.”
National carrier
Sabena was Belgium’s national airline and was founded in 1923. Its first flight was from Belgium to the United Kingdom, but Sabena soon expanded its network, with the Congo – then a Belgian colony – also becoming an important destination.
In the decades that followed, Sabena grew into an internationally recognised brand. However, financial problems mounted and in 2001 the company went into administration.
Shortly after the bankruptcy, SN Brussels Airlines was established. It later merged with Virgin Express and continued as Brussels Airlines. Today, Brussels Airlines flight numbers begin with SN, in a nod to the company’s history.

Taiwan takes down 450,000 noncompliant machinery listings online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:51:21 UTC
19:51:21 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — More than 450,000 listings for noncompliant machinery and equipment from e-commerce platforms have been removed as of the end of August, the Ministry of Labor said Friday.
Government agencies began working with major e-commerce platforms in 2025 to prevent unsafe products from entering workplaces. The parties established procedures to screen regulated machinery before listings go live, audit products after they are listed, and remove those that violate regulations.
Regulated items include grinders, circular saws, band saws, planers, power presses and forklifts. Authorities previously identified more than 520 violations a year, but the number has fallen to around 15 cases per month since the new system was introduced, according to Taisounds.
Major domestic e-commerce platforms, including Shopee, Momo and Pchome, are taking part. Before a product is listed, platforms use data matching and keyword searches to identify machinery that may fall under regulated categories.
Sellers are then required to provide relevant safety documents before the products can be put up for sale. The platforms also conduct random checks after products are listed.
Regulated machinery must be properly registered or type-certified and carry the required safety labels or certification marks before being listed for sale. Sellers who violate the regulations can face fines of up to NT$2 million (US$62,892).

Digested week: BuzzBallz signed by Tory leader builds excitement for conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:51:20 UTC
19:51:20 KST

Monday
It’s funny, isn’t it, how many things we take for granted in life? How many things go wholly unmentioned, even wholly unconsidered in any even minutely conscious way – and yet, when they are suddenly kicked away you realise just how much of your internal organisation, your mental integrity, your structural soundness altogether, rested on these unexamined pillars.
One of mine, it turns out, is the belief – no, surely more than that? The sure and certain knowledge, in my bones if never alas vouchsafed by my mere mortal eyes – that Bruce Springsteen does not wear pyjamas.
This is fundamental, surely? The Boss sleeps naked. This is an eternal verity.
But no. According to what I can only describe as reports, he is a loyal customer of the venerable sleepwear shop Schostal in Rome, which was opened in 1870 by two brothers from Vienna. There’s a photo of Bruce hugging the manager, Shirley Braine – to whom he apparently sends regular postcards – and everything.
So. There you have it. The Boss sleeps in pyjamas. Acceptable province of 1950s boarding school boys, your worst boyfriend, and your dad. Please go carefully about your day and from the fragments of your shattered psyche may you rebuild better soon.
Tuesday
Party conference season is almost upon us – I know! Try to contain yourselves! – and the preparations for fun times are gathering pace. News breaks that Blue Beyond, a young Conservatives group (and I always like to know that they’ve found each other rather than roaming free and confused), is offering as a grand raffle prize a BuzzBallz signed by Kemi Badenoch! I said try to contain yourselves! And not only is it signed, but it is a large BuzzBallz! I SAID TRY TO CONTAIN YOURSELVES.
In case you are not as young as a youngster or as cool as a Conservative, I should explain: a BuzzBallz is a spherical plastic container that contains a cocktail, usually of a lurid hue and unsubtle flavour profile (the inscribed orb itself is Berry Cherry Limeade and whyever not?). They come in two sizes – small, which is a bit larger than a tennis ball, and large, which is a bit smaller than a football.
Tickets are available now. The winner will be drawn at the Tory conference and must be over 18 to collect. Rumours that Michael Heseltine will launch it at your head for a small further fee are popular but as yet unsubstantiated.
Wednesday
I find myself unaccountably drawn to the story of the Hyrox poo-er. Not because of any coprophiliac inclinations, you understand, but because the idea of exerting myself to the extent that I might lose control of my bowels is so out of my realm of personal possibility that I am increasingly intrigued by the question of whether Joanna Wietrzyk and I technically qualify as the same species at all.
Again, for the uninitiated/hitherto and possibly blissfully ignorant, a recap: Hyrox Beijing is an intense indoor fitness event and Wietrzyk one of its world record- holding contestants. About halfway through the insanely difficult competition, which comprises a series of horrendous things – I don’t know precisely what, I passed out after reading the word “burpees” – Wietrzyk suffered what was later termed “a severe faecal event”, which went down her leg but didn’t stop her progress round the course.
Cue a roar of outrage against her and the organisers, who didn’t disqualify her immediately before she touched any other equipment, and eventually an apology from Wietrzyk and a forfeit of her points.
To hell with the critics, say I. Biohazardry be damned! You push yourself so hard you crap yourself and keep on going, you’re a winner in my book. Now, someone unwrap this Mars bar for me. Typing is exhausting, you know.
Thursday
Not all heroes wear capes. Or a light coating of faeces down their legs. Some of them are headteachers who suspend 25 students in the first week back after the summer holidays, including one for the crime of zipping his bag too loudly. The head’s name is Dan Jeffries and, while he denies parents’ claims of suspension for minor infractions, it is clear that whatever measures he has indeed taken, he has no regrets about any of them.
Parents of some of those suspended from Frome college have compared the school to “a military base” and say the strictness demotivates pupils. Whatever, whatever. The world is made up of two types of people: those who want to hear the children’s side of things and those of us who just want Jeffries put in immediate charge of a new government department called The Whole of Modern Life, Starting With Quiet Coaches on the Train and After That I Have a List.
Friday
My mother summons me and my sister home. Apparently she needs to clear out the attic before she dies, but ideally before Sunday.
“What’s happening on Sunday?” I ask.
“Sunday,” she replies.
Deadlines by fiat were a mainstay of my childhood and so I ask no more.
My mother has lived in our house for 50 years. We brace ourselves for a hard 48 hours’ work and climb up into the loft.
Three small cardboard boxes of stuff await us.
“There are – there are just three small cardboard boxes of stuff up here.”
“Yes,” she says. “I can’t believe I’ve let it get this bad.”
We bring them down.
My wedding shoes and some papers – including my first book, The Story of Esmerelda, written when I was nine and some letters home from university – are in the first one. The second one contains my son’s baby clothes. The third has my sister’s childhood attempts at making a working model of Sizewell B and some postcards she wrote to Dad when he went on his first trip to America. “Come hom. Shez insane.” On reflection, she shouldn’t have given them to Mum to post.
“Excellent,” Mum says. “We can bin the lot.”
Ah, fiats. Ah, memories.

How did data on 1.2 million people leak from CSDD? Investigation reveals multiple failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:51:00 UTC
19:51:00 KST

The data breach at Latvia’s Road Traffic Safety Directorate (CSDD) was facilitated by several shortcomings in cybersecurity management, including inadequate security testing, insufficient network protection, a lack of multi-factor authentication and flaws in software development, according to an assessment carried out by a commission established by the Ministry of Transport.
The Ministry of Transport commission, acting on an order from Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis (JV), has completed its assessment of the CSDD cyber incident. Its task was to establish the circumstances surrounding the causes of the incident, assess the effectiveness of its detection and response, and evaluate whether the technical and organisational measures implemented by CSDD were adequate.
The commission has prepared a report summarising its conclusions and recommendations for addressing technical vulnerabilities and strengthening cybersecurity.
Kozlovskis said the assessment shows that several mistakes and failures occurred in CSDD’s cybersecurity management, including, at times, an overly formal approach, which meant that opportunities for a cyberattack were not fully eliminated.
Shortcomings were identified in the procedures
followed both by the organisation’s employees and by external service providers. At the same time, assessing the responsibility of individual officials falls within the competence of law enforcement authorities.
“The task of the internal investigation was to establish the situation and its circumstances and to prepare recommendations for specific measures so that similar risks can be prevented in the future and the data of Latvia’s residents can be kept secure,” Kozlovskis explained.
The commission established by the Ministry of Transport concluded that the incident was made possible by a vulnerability in the CSDD-operated web application “med.csdd.lv”, which allowed the attacker to gain initial access to information systems.
Several technical and organisational shortcomings prevented the vulnerability from being addressed earlier,
including inadequate security testing, insufficient network protection, the absence of multi-factor authentication and flaws in software development.
The investigation also identified the long-term storage of historical personal data, an issue that will be assessed by the Data State Inspectorate.
A cybersecurity control system had been established, but in practice it repeatedly failed to achieve its intended purpose. The commission identified several shortcomings in risk management and cybersecurity governance, including insufficient specialist capacity, an inadequate scope of security testing and audits, and incomplete documentation.
After gaining initial access, the attacker was able to extract large volumes of data over an extended period because
there were insufficient mechanisms for controlling the volume of requests and identifying anomalous activity.
The commission concluded that, regardless of the reason the initial vulnerability emerged, a professional security monitoring service provider would normally be expected to identify and restrict unusual, prolonged data activity in a timely manner in order to prevent large-scale data extraction over an extended period.
After detecting the incident, CSDD fulfilled its statutory reporting obligations to the relevant state authorities within the required deadlines.
The commission’s report lists several recommendations for strengthening CSDD’s cybersecurity. These include addressing the identified cybersecurity and data protection risks, reviewing data retention periods, ensuring sufficient capacity for cybersecurity functions, reviewing and improving the contract with Tet, and introducing a system for managing such outsourced services.
The commission did not assess the possible responsibility of individual CSDD officials,
as this falls within the competence of law enforcement authorities. The assessment report and related materials will be forwarded to law enforcement institutions.
As previously reported, a cyberattack on CSDD in early August resulted in the theft of personal data belonging to 1.2 million people, as well as data relating to approximately 200,000 legal entities. The information was obtained from payments made to the Directorate over the past 18 years.
Following calls from several officials for those responsible to step down, both the CSDD Management Board and Supervisory Board resigned.
Kozlovskis ordered an expedited internal investigation to establish all the circumstances and determine responsibility in connection with the cyberattack and the large-scale data breach. Among other issues, the investigation was also tasked with assessing CSDD’s contract with Tet for the provision of cybersecurity services.
Meanwhile, the Prosecutor General’s Office has launched a prosecutor’s review into possible violations or negligence that may have resulted in the data breach from CSDD information systems.
The State Police have also opened criminal proceedings over the cyberattack on CSDD.

how the situationists turned spectators into participants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:50:44 UTC
19:50:44 KST

the city as a field of possibility
What if the city wasn’t something to consume but something to play? For the Situationists, this was a way of challenging the passive role assigned to people in modern society. Instead of simply following the routes, functions, images, and routines laid out for them, they imagined inhabitants who could wander, interfere, improvise, and collectively reshape the environments around them. The city, in other words, could become a field of possibility.
This ambition runs through the work of the Situationist International, the group of artists, writers, and theorists formed in Europe in 1957. Their critique extended from advertising and mass media to architecture, urban planning, art, and everyday life, all of which they saw as contributing to a culture in which people would experience the world as spectators. Guy Debord gave this condition its most influential name: the spectacle. But the Situationists’ response was not to produce better images. They wanted to change the relationship between people and the world those images represented, proposing wandering through cities without predetermined destinations, hijacking existing cultural material, constructing temporary situations, and imagining entirely new environments organized around play.
More than half a century later, their ideas have become strangely familiar. We move through immersive installations, interact with responsive architecture, participate in temporary urban interventions, and constantly produce and circulate our own images. Yet this raises a question the Situationists would probably have recognized immediately: when a space asks us to participate, are we actually given agency or are we being offered a more sophisticated way to perform within the spectacle?
New Babylon-Barcelona, 1963, original dimensions | image via @constant.101
the problem with being a spectator
The Situationist International emerged in postwar Europe amid economic growth, expanding consumer culture, mass media, and the reconstruction of cities. Everyday life was becoming more and more mediated by advertising and images of consumption. Urban space was being reorganized around specialized functions: housing here, work there, shopping somewhere else, with movement between them structured by roads, schedules, and infrastructure.
Guy Debord gave this condition its most influential formulation in The Society of the Spectacle, published in 1967. For Debord, the spectacle did not mean television, advertising, cinema, or visual entertainment, but it described a social condition in which relationships between people take place through representations and images. As he writes, the spectacle is ‘a social relation between people that is mediated by an accumulation of images that serve to alienate us from a genuinely lived life.’
The distinction matters because the Situationists were not simply opposed to images. Their criticism was directed at the relationship produced by the image, the distance between the person watching and the reality being watched.
Asger Jorn and Guy Debord, The Naked City, 1957, published in Guide psychogéographique de Paris
leave the map behind
One of the Situationists’ most concrete attempts to create that activity was the dérive, or drift. Instead of moving through the city according to practical objectives like going to work or buying something, the dérive asked participants to abandon their usual reasons for moving and allow the attractions of the terrain and unexpected encounters to influence their route. The practice grew out of psychogeography, which the Situationists used to describe the effects of geographical environments on emotions and behavior. A street could feel inviting or hostile. A familiar route could produce a completely different experience depending on the person moving through it. The city was psychological.
The Situationists responded by trying to read it differently. Their maps and diagrams did not describe streets according to geography but attempted to represent zones of attraction, movement, and atmosphere. Guy Debord’s The Naked City, produced in 1957, fragments a map of Paris into separate pieces connected by arrows, presenting the city through psychogeographical relationships. The dérive changes the relationship between an existing environment and the person moving through it, and architecture becomes more about the behaviors it permits, discourages, or makes imaginable.
If the dérive attempted to disrupt the way people moved through the city, détournement attempted to disrupt the way they read culture. The Situationists used détournement (rerouting) to describe the reuse of existing cultural material within a new context. Images, texts, advertisements, comics, films, and other familiar forms could be appropriated and reorganized so that their original meanings were altered or contradicted. The Situationists hijacked the language that already surrounded them. Asger Jorn’s Modifications, for example, intervened in existing paintings with new painted elements, transforming the source material. The gesture reflected a broader Situationist interest in taking existing cultural forms and putting them to different uses.
For design, the interesting part is the shift from making to using, as a cultural object is no longer understood as a finished message passed from an author to an audience, but as something whose meaning can change through the way it is picked up, reused, and reinterpreted by the people who encounter it. In this sense, the spectator is no longer just receiving meaning but interfering with the work and helping to shape what it becomes.
Untitled (unfinished dis-figuration), 1962, Oil on canvas, 122 × 97 cm, Museum Jorn Collection
build a situation, not an object
This idea comes into focus with the Situationist concept of the constructed situation, which treated everyday experience as something that could be deliberately set in motion. The Situationists were interested in creating temporary environments, events, and encounters that people could enter and influence, with the outcome left open to what happened between them.
The distinction becomes particularly interesting when we look at experience design today. An installation might invite visitors to move, touch, trigger sounds or lights, and follow different paths, while every possible response has already been anticipated by its designer. It can feel highly interactive while leaving the structure of the experience untouched. For the Situationists, participation depended on the possibility of changing what was happening and introducing something that had not been planned in advance. Play offered one way to make this possible. It loosened the fixed functions of everyday spaces and opened them to experimentation. A street could become a place to wander, a building could take on an unexpected use, and a gathering could develop according to the people involved.
These moments gave people a chance to test the limits of their surroundings and discover forms of activity that ordinary routines tended to suppress. The ambition was to bring that sense of possibility into everyday life, where people could have a greater hand in shaping the experiences and environments they moved through.
Espencat, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
constant imagines a city without fixed uses
No project brings this ambition into architecture more clearly than Constant Nieuwenhuys’ New Babylon, the vast urban vision he developed from the mid-1950s through 1974 around the idea of homo ludens, the playing human. Constant imagined a city made up of interconnected sectors where living, working, moving, and leisure could overlap, giving inhabitants the freedom to continually alter the spaces around them. Light, climate, color, and atmosphere could all become part of this changing environment, with the configuration of spaces responding to the activities taking place within them. Constant was interested in what might happen when a city could accommodate a society that was constantly changing, with its inhabitants shaping their surroundings through everyday use.
The project was deeply utopian, but its focus was less on what the perfect city might look like and more on how people might live within it. Constant gave considerable attention to models, drawings, maps, and other studies that allowed him to explore an environment without a fixed final form. The city remained open because its inhabitants were expected to give it meaning through the way they occupied it.
Freedom in New Babylon was never completely without structure. Constant was designing the spaces, systems, and conditions within which people would be able to change their surroundings, so the question of how much an architect could determine and how much could be left to the people living there was built into the project from the beginning. The architecture had to provide enough structure to hold the city together while leaving enough open for its inhabitants to take over, adapt it, and give it new uses.
Constant’s time with the Situationist International was relatively short. He joined in 1958 and left in 1960, after which New Babylon continued to develop as an independent project. He worked on it until 1974, producing an extensive body of models, drawings, maps, texts, and paintings around the idea of a city shaped by the people who inhabit it.
New Babylon-Paris, 1963 | image via @constant.101
when the ideas reached the street
By 1968, Situationist ideas about everyday life, participation, and the use of public space had begun to circulate beyond the group itself. When students and workers occupied universities, factories, and streets across France in May, the city became a place for collective action, with familiar spaces taken over and put to new uses.
The Situationists were not responsible for the uprising, but their criticism of institutions and passive social roles had already found an audience through texts such as On the Poverty of Student Life, published in Strasbourg in 1966 and principally written by Situationist member Mustapha Khayati. Two years later, the distinction between watching and taking part had become physical as people occupied the spaces around them and disrupted their usual functions.
The same period also exposed a problem that had always been present in the Situationist project: recuperation, the process through which radical ideas could be absorbed into the culture they were meant to challenge. Images, slogans, publications, and gestures could circulate as forms of resistance before eventually becoming things to reproduce, collect, exhibit, and consume. The Situationists’ own afterlife carries this contradiction, with their once-radical publications, maps, and images now preserved and displayed as cultural artifacts. Their critique was built around escaping the spectacle, but the spectacle proved capable of turning even that escape into an image.
Constant, Portfolio New Babylon, nr. 5, 1963, 37 x 36 cm, lithograph, multiple collections incl. Collection Kunstmuseen Krefeld, Germany and collection Boijmans van Beuningen, NL | image via @constant.101
are we participants now?
Today, participation is almost everywhere. We move through immersive installations, interact with responsive environments, occupy public spaces for temporary events, and spend much of our time making and sharing images online. The figure of the passive spectator seems, at first, to have disappeared. Look a little closer and the picture becomes less clear. A visitor can trigger a light, choose a route through an installation, or change something on a screen, while the experience remains tightly controlled. The visitor is active, but only within the limits of what has already been designed.
This is where the Situationists’ ideas feel current. They were interested in what people could do with a space once its usual rules were loosened: wandering without a destination, taking over an existing environment, giving a place an unexpected use, or seeing the city differently. Much of the pleasure came from not knowing exactly where the experience would lead. Contemporary interactive spaces often work in the opposite direction. They are carefully programmed to anticipate what a visitor might do, with every response, movement, sound, and image accounted for. Even the photograph taken at the end can become part of the experience, ready to be shared and circulated.
None of this makes these spaces uninteresting, and interactivity can certainly change how we experience architecture and art. The Situationists set the bar somewhere else, as for them, participation became meaningful when people could affect what happened around them, introduce their own uses, and leave the experience different from how they found it. That idea reaches beyond museums and installations, raising questions about public space, architecture, and the increasingly designed environments of everyday life: who decides what a place is for, how easily can people change it, and what happens when they use it in a way nobody anticipated?
We live with a different version of that problem now, surrounded by spaces that promise interaction and platforms that invite constant participation. The difference between taking part and having a say can be surprisingly small on the surface, and enormous underneath. When we enter a space designed to respond to us, how much of it can we actually change?
Eric Koch for Anefo, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Number of medical residents hits record high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18

19:50:00 KST

Number of medical residents hits record high
This fall, 187 new medical residents began specialist training at the University of Tartu, bringing the total number of residents to a record 891. In recent years, interest and competition have intensified in critical specialties such as family medicine and emergency medicine, the university said.
Of the students who graduated from the basic medical program this year, 78 percent applied for specialist training at the University of Tartu. The residency admissions competition received 318 applications — significantly more than in previous years.
Family medicine received the highest number of applications, while the tightest competition was in oral and maxillofacial surgery, with nine candidates per training spot. Dermatovenerology, pediatric surgery, and otorhinolaryngology (ear‑nose‑throat) also saw high demand.
Forty‑six residents entered family medicine this year — the highest number ever.
As the number of residents grows, the university is expanding its training offerings. To support residents, the University of Tartu is launching a mentorship system and developing a digital e‑portfolio learning environment.

North Korean hackers attacked IT engineers in 100 countries and stole nearly $11 million in cryptocurrency
Kyiv • UNN
North Korean hackers infected more than 30,000 devices through fake job postings and stole $10.9 million in cryptocurrency. The funds were transferred to North Korea.
Hackers linked to North Korea attacked engineers in more than 100 countries and regions, including Japan, stealing cryptocurrency assets worth at least 1.7 billion yen (more than $10.9 million) and illegally transferring the funds to the DPRK. Kyodo News reports, according to UNN.
Details
Japanese authorities said they had uncovered a method that allows hackers to remotely control devices belonging to supporters in Japan in order to obtain foreign currency.
The statement was intended to expose and condemn countries or organizations suspected of being involved in cyberattacks, as well as warn them and deter them from carrying out further attacks. The statement was issued jointly with the relevant authorities of the United States, Australia, and Germany.
According to the Japanese agency, the hackers likely posted fake job vacancies on job-search websites and other resources from December 2025 until approximately July of this year.
The attacks infected more than 30,000 devices used by IT engineers who applied for the fake vacancies. This resulted in the theft of more than 7,000 cryptocurrency assets.

‘Waiting for Death’: Russian-Occupied Oleshky Faces Starvation as Russia Blocks Aid and Evacuation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:47:04 UTC
19:47:04 KST

By Friday, Sept. 18, Russian-occupied Oleshky had gone almost four months without a confirmed delivery of food or medicine, leaving thousands of civilians to survive on garden produce, preserves and barter while minefields and drone attacks made evacuation nearly impossible.
According to Oleshky Military Administration head Tetiana Hasanenko, the last successful supply and evacuation mission reached the city on May 26. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission independently confirmed that no food had reached Oleshky between that date and June 24, while Hasanenko told Suspilne on Sept. 11 that deliveries had still not resumed.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv Post reported in July that Oleshky had already been cut off from food and medicine deliveries for more than a month.
Reports from residents, volunteers, Ukrainian officials and international monitors indicate critical shortages of food, drinking water, medicine, electricity and gas. However, Russia’s information blockade and the danger of contacting people inside the city make the precise number of residents and deaths impossible to establish independently.
Estimates for Oleshky itself range from around 2,000 to 4,000 people. Hasanenko said her administration previously counted about 2,000 residents, including 45 to 47 children, but recent evacuees told her that between 3,000 and 4,000 could remain.
The higher figure of more than 6,000 people, including about 200 children, cited by Lubinets, covers Oleshky and surrounding settlements on the occupied left bank of the Dnipro.
Trump Administration Weighs Russia Business Deals Before Ukraine War Ends – NYT
Four kilometers from food
Oleshky lies only a few kilometers across the Dnipro from Ukrainian-controlled Kherson. In practice, the river, destroyed bridges, frontline fighting, minefields and drone surveillance have made that short distance impassable.
“Only four kilometers from us, there is life with food, but there is physically no way to leave the city,” resident Alla Lykhman-Malysh said on Facebook.
Lykhman-Malysh said that during the summer residents survived largely on cucumbers, tomatoes, zucchini and eggplants grown in gardens. As autumn approaches, that source of food is disappearing.
By early August, the local market reportedly offered little beyond vegetables, herbs, watermelons and margarine left in storage at a former dairy plant. Flour, cereals, potatoes, tea and coffee were available mainly through barter rather than for money.
A kilogram of sugar and a packet of the common painkiller Citramon each cost about 1,000 rubles, she said. The reported prices and shortages were also detailed in local accounts.
Hasanenko told Suspilne that money had effectively lost its value because there was almost nothing left to buy.
“No matter how much money you have, nobody is selling anything,” she said.
Residents interviewed by the German newspaper Bild said Russian soldiers had turned vehicles carrying food away at checkpoints. One resident claimed soldiers told people attempting to leave: “Go back and die there.” Kyiv Post could not independently verify the reported exchange.
A diary of disappearing food
A first-person diary from inside Oleshky, published by The Ukrainians in April, documented how the city’s food supply gradually collapsed during the winter.
The diary’s author wrote that deliveries stopped after heavy snow on Jan. 10. A small shipment arrived eight days later, but bread was taken as it was unloaded and the supplies quickly ran out. The city’s remaining stores subsequently closed.
By late January, residents were selling their own preserves and the last packages of pasta, tea and condiments. One pharmacy was clearing its remaining stock because neither medicine nor fuel was arriving.
The diarist described finding dried carrots and cereal bought years earlier, rationing flour and baking bread in a frying pan. Gas cylinders could no longer be refilled, forcing residents to cook on wood-burning stoves or small camping burners.
A limited Russian-controlled aid distribution was held in February, the diary said, but supplies were reportedly available only to pensioners holding Russian documents, with an exception for people over 80 who still had Ukrainian pension certificates.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty separately collected accounts from residents and volunteers who said people hunted pheasants and caught pigeons during the winter. Volunteer Ksenia Arkhipova said relatives frequently contacted her with messages such as: “Dad is at this address. There is no food.”
More recent testimony published in a Kyiv Post opinion article described the same pattern. One woman, identified by the pseudonym Oksana for security reasons, said her parents exchanged vegetables for eggs and dried their remaining bread for winter. Another resident, Alya, said she had survived at times by drinking water with honey.
Aid missions end in mines and drone attacks
Regular deliveries reportedly became unreliable in December 2025. By the end of February, only one shipment had reached Oleshky since mid-January, according to the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group.
The UN said the last grocery store ended regular operations in January. Residents then depended on preserved food and sporadic deliveries by private suppliers, which were often inaccessible to elderly or disabled people.
A convoy carrying food and humanitarian aid struck a mine at the city’s entrance on June 2. The UN recorded one person killed and three injured. Hasanenko later told Suspilne that two people were killed and two severely wounded. The discrepancy could not be independently resolved.
Accounts of another attempted delivery on Sept. 1 also differ.
Hasanenko told Suspilne that vehicles encountered mines and tripwires and were forced to turn around. Lykhman-Malysh and Arkhipova separately reported that vehicles were attacked by drones despite carrying signs identifying them as civilian, according to Vgoru reporting. Kyiv Post could not determine whether the accounts referred to the same vehicles or separate attempts.
Lykhman-Malysh said desperate residents later walked approximately seven kilometers along the mined route to collect whatever remained around damaged vehicles, including scorched potatoes, onions and rain-soaked flatbread.
UN monitors stressed that responsibility for individual drone attacks in the frontline area cannot always be conclusively established. Oleshky and neighboring settlements are under Russian control but are also within range of Ukrainian short-range drones.
The UN nevertheless confirmed that drones and landmines have effectively prevented food deliveries, medical transfers and organized evacuation.
“People can’t get out, food can’t get in, and sick and injured are not getting the medical assistance they need,” said Danielle Bell, head of the UN monitoring mission.
Residents cross minefields to escape
Lubinets said Ukraine and Russia had previously developed procedures for a humanitarian evacuation. A list of evacuees was compiled, Ukrainian forces prepared to observe a local ceasefire, and the International Committee of the Red Cross said it was prepared to participate within its mandate.
Russia has since failed to reconfirm its readiness to proceed with the mission, Lubinets said on Sept. 16.
Kyiv Post reported on Sept. 16 that Russian authorities had failed to uphold the previously agreed arrangements for the humanitarian mission.
His office has received 176 appeals concerning the humanitarian situation in occupied Kherson Oblast and verified information about 358 people who urgently need assistance leaving.
“The most terrible thing is that people are already walking through mined fields because they see no other way out,” Lubinets wrote.
Speaking separately on Ukrainian television, the ombudsman said many residents had reportedly died after stepping on mines during independent escape attempts. No verified casualty count was provided. He also discussed the blocked evacuation in an Espreso interview.
Some evacuees have described walking ahead of vehicles to locate mines and guide drivers along damaged roads. Others traveled through occupied southern Ukraine, Russia and Belarus before returning to Ukrainian-controlled territory through Europe.
A woman interviewed by Novynarnia said she escaped with her husband and 84-year-old mother after surviving largely on potatoes and pasta recovered from abandoned cellars. The journey took four days.
The UN said volunteers had helped approximately 180 people leave Oleshky and neighboring communities through improvised arrangements by late June. The largest operation evacuated 32 people during a three-day easing of hostilities in May.
Such private missions are far too small for the remaining population and are particularly difficult for older people, people with disabilities and bedridden residents.
The hospital has no medicine or evacuation route
Oleshky’s remaining clinic reportedly operates without reliable electricity, diagnostic equipment, antibiotics, painkillers or basic supplies for treating wounds, according to the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group.
Ambulances have stopped visiting homes, while critically ill or injured patients cannot be transferred to hospitals elsewhere in occupied territory.
The UN documented one patient dying while waiting to be transferred to Skadovsk. Residents and local officials have also reported deaths from strokes, heart attacks, sepsis, hypothermia and possible starvation, although no independently verified breakdown exists.
Bodies can remain uncollected because going outside risks mine explosions and drone attacks. The city’s morgue has been destroyed and there is no refrigeration, according to Hasanenko, whose account was also documented by KHPG.
The EU’s External Action Service published an estimate, attributed to local officials and volunteers, that more than 300 residents had died from cold or hunger by spring. No underlying list or independent verification was provided, and Kyiv Post could not confirm the figure.
The UN has recorded reports of at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan during 2026, many of them in drone attacks. It said many of those cases had been verified but that responsibility could not be conclusively established in every incident.
Russia acknowledges crisis but blames Ukraine
Russian-installed Kherson regional chief Volodymyr Saldo denied in May that a humanitarian crisis existed and claimed Russia was supplying Oleshky with essential goods. He also rejected a proposed ceasefire for an evacuation, citing alleged fears of a Ukrainian “provocation.”
On June 20, Russian Foreign Ministry representative Rodion Miroshnik acknowledged a humanitarian crisis in Oleshky but blamed Ukraine and Western countries.
Moscow and its occupation administration have not presented independently verifiable evidence of regular food or medicine deliveries since May.
Ukraine’s National Resistance Center said Russian occupation authorities were using the crisis for propaganda by blaming Ukrainian forces for the blockade and attempting to shift responsibility for conditions in territory controlled by Russia.
Under international humanitarian law, an occupying power must ensure food and medical supplies for the population and facilitate humanitarian relief when local resources are inadequate, the UN monitoring mission noted.
Ukrainian officials have accused Russian forces of deliberately keeping civilians in Oleshky as human shields. The allegation has been raised publicly by Ukrainian lawmakers. That specific motive cannot be independently verified, but Russia’s refusal to confirm the negotiated evacuation has also prevented the planned transfer of residents to other Russian-held areas such as Skadovsk or Crimea.
Oleshky has been occupied since the first days of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
The city was devastated again in June 2023 when the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam caused catastrophic flooding across the Kherson region, destroying homes, documents and infrastructure.
The city, which had a prewar population of more than 24,000, is now largely ruined, cut off from utilities and surrounded by an expanding frontline minefield.
“People are no longer living,” Hasanenko said. “They are waiting for death.”

This is what an out-of-control measles outbreak looks like
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:46:32 UTC
19:46:32 KST

In Bangladesh, hospitals and community health workers are facing an unrelenting battle against measles. Despite increased vaccination rates, cases have surged into the deadliest outbreak the South Asian country has seen since 2005.
The viral disease causes a blotchy rash and flulike symptoms but can develop into severe, life-threatening illnesses, such as pneumonia and brain swelling. Between March 15 and September 16, Bangladesh’s Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) reported at least 175,198 suspected cases and 1,044 confirmed and suspected deaths, with the majority of infections occurring among unvaccinated children younger than age two. Experts say these numbers are likely an underestimate, particularly in rural areas that have struggled to obtain resources and vaccines.
“These viruses are not merciful,” says Sakil Faizullah, a health communications researcher at Texas A&M University and a former communications specialist at UNICEF Bangladesh. “If there is a break in the regular vaccination process, they will just attack, and that is what happened in Bangladesh.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
DGHS did not respond to Scientific American’s request for comment.
Measles rates in the country hovered around 100 to 300 cases total between 2021 and 2025. What’s happening now is a “stunningly big outbreak that is clearly tied to an unusual drop in the vaccination coverage,” says Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University. It underscores a grim global resurgence of measles, a vaccine-preventable disease that was once on the path toward worldwide eradication.
Several countries, including Canada, Mexico and the U.S. have recently experienced an uptick in cases and flurries of outbreaks. Confirmed cases in the U.S. this year have already reached 3,294; just this week Pennsylvania reported its fourth measles-related death. The exact circumstances in each nation differ, but vaccination gaps are a common thread, leading some experts to question if more catastrophic measles outbreaks are around the corner.
“We don’t want hundreds of deaths to get people involved,” says Walter Orenstein, an epidemiologist and expert in measles epidemics. “Measles vaccines are very safe, very effective, and getting vaccinated not only helps you but helps your community.”
For measles, populations need vaccination rates of 95 percent or higher to achieve herd immunity—the level of protection required to prevent disease spread. This helps protect groups who are ineligible for the two recommended vaccine doses, such as very young infants, Orenstein says. And because measles is so infectious, even a small slip in vaccine coverage can allow the virus to run rampant.
A Perfect Storm
For decades, Bangladesh was a “poster boy for vaccination,” Faizullah says. In the 1970s the country rolled out a national immunization program that bolstered uptake nationwide. Community-based organizations helped keep people up to date with routine vaccinations.
“When I was growing up in Bangladesh, you trusted the community health workers,” says Ayesha Mahmud, a demographer at the University of California, Berkeley, who has previously studied population dynamics and infectious disease spread in Bangladesh. “The country has a really strong history of using community health workers and local clinics to get messaging across and ensure that the reach of these vaccination campaigns was widespread.”
In 2019 national measles vaccine coverage in Bangladesh sat around 97 percent for the first dose and 93 percent for the second, according to the World Health Organization and UNICEF. The nation was on its way to becoming a measles-free country, but then “things fell through the cracks,” Faizullah says.
Like many other countries, Bangladesh saw routine childhood vaccination rates drop in 2020, during the COVID pandemic. As public health workers tried to boost rates, vaccine access took another dramatic turn in 2024. An interim government overhaul of long-standing vaccine procurement processes may have limited stockpiles, Faizullah says. Political unrest may have delayed supplemental measles immunization programs, and cuts to funding for the U.S. Agency for International Development, or USAID, may have affected health care staffing and distribution chains, he adds.
In 2025 measles vaccination rates in Bangladesh fell to 86 percent. A UNICEF assessment estimated that around 400,000 children hadn’t received all of their recommended vaccines and that 70,000 did not receive any vaccine. Low inoculation rates mixed with undernutrition, overcrowding in urban areas and an overwhelmed health care system.
“It was really kind of a perfect storm of different things,” says William Moss, an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University, who studies global measles epidemics. “It just spiraled out of control.”
Vulnerable Pockets, Shadowed
Measles has no specific treatment; care is entirely supportive, Nuzzo says. The fastest, most effective way to combat a measles outbreak, she says, is widespread vaccination. After a first dose, people gain protective antibodies quickly and immunity levels peak within about two weeks.
In April Bangladesh health officials initiated a large-scale measles vaccination campaign, targeting some 18 million children. The outbreak has shown signs of slowing since, but experts caution that the recovery may be patchwork.
“One big story here in Bangladesh is that national-level coverage estimates can be very deceiving because you can have reasonably high coverage but have large pockets of susceptibles that can ignite outbreaks,” Moss says.
We’ve seen this in the U.S., he says. Recent major outbreaks in Texas, South Carolina and Pennsylvania reveal the threat of measles in undervaccinated, insular communities. For example, in Gaines County, Texas, the epicenter of the 2025 West Texas outbreak, kindergarteners’ measles vaccination rate was 82 percent compared with about 93 percent nationally. In the past, most outbreaks in the U.S. were imported—someone would catch the disease while traveling and introduce it to a community with low vaccination rates. Now the disease seems to be circulating on its own, sparking mass infections more frequently, Orenstein says. That means targeted vaccination efforts in hard-to-reach, undervaccinated groups are particularly important to stopping a larger epidemic, Mahmud says.
The U.S. and Bangladesh both have immunity gaps, but the reason behind those gaps is very different. “For Bangladesh, it is the supply and health system disruption,” Faizullah says. “In the U.S., I would say it’s localized undervaccination and obviously vaccine refusal or vaccine hesitancy.”
This distinction is important, Nuzzo says.
“Anyone who wants a measles vaccine [in the U.S.] can go get one,” she says. “What we’re seeing in Bangladesh is not the consequence of anti-vax.”
Nuzzo and Moss say that a widescale disruption in U.S. vaccine availability, as has happened in Bangladesh, is very unlikely. But recent actions by the Trump administration have raised concerns of reduced access. Officials rolled back the number of recommended shots in the childhood vaccine schedule in January. (The action was later blocked by a court.) And in August President Donald Trump announced an executive order that seeks to split the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three separate shots. Medical societies and public health experts have denounced these decisions for lacking evidence.
If the administration were to make it easier to sue vaccine manufacturers over unsubstantiated harms, some makers could drop out, Moss says. That could drastically reduce vaccine availability. “I don’t think that’s going to happen,” he says, “but that’s kind of how I could see this whole thing really spiral down.”
The situation in Bangladesh highlights the dangers of disrupting vaccine supplies, Nuzzo says. But she cautions against making too many direct comparisons between the U.S. and Bangladesh.
“I think you have to compare a country to itself,” she says, “and the diagnosis is that the U.S. is very sick in a way that we haven’t been in 30 years.”

How heat makes it harder for students to learn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:46:30 UTC
19:46:30 KST

The end of the 2025–2026 school year was plagued with heat waves across the country, with strings of 90-plus-degree Fahrenheit days in late March through June forcing early school dismissals and lost days due to extreme heat. The lengthening heat wave season is subjecting more students to more extreme heat—and research shows that besides just missed days of class, it means they’re having a harder time learning.
Studies consistently show higher temperatures are associated with lower academic performance, including standardized test scores in math, science and reading, according to a systematic review published this past July. The analysis folded together 14 studies from around the world, including four from the U.S. And lower scores can have major consequences: for example, one study found that higher temperatures on test days were associated with a lower probability of passing the New York State Regents exams, a series of standardized tests that has been required to graduate high school in the state.
Beyond the effect of one or two scorching days, cumulative temperature exposures over an entire school year also take a toll. In just one example, a study published in the American Economic Journal: Economic Policy that pooled data from 10 million U.S. students from 2001 to 2014 found that students who took the PSAT multiple times had lower scores in years with hotter school days than in cooler years.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But why does heat slow down learning? “There are several potential mechanisms,” says Emory University epidemiologist Christine Ekenga, senior author of last July’s review. “The most straightforward one is this physiological strain that’s associated with heat fatigue that can make it harder to focus and maintain attention, which can interfere with cognitive function.” Ekenga says thermal discomfort—the physical uncomfortableness of being exposed to heat—can also make it difficult for students to pay attention.
Those mechanisms highlight where schools can step in to mitigate the problem. “In our review, the most important finding was about air conditioning,” Ekenga says. In one study, “the schools that had full air conditioning experienced about one fifth the learning loss that was observed in schools without air conditioning.”
Schools in some regions, particularly the Northeast and Pacific Northwest, haven’t historically needed air conditioning as classes typically began and ended outside the summer heat season. But as temperatures continue to rise and heat waves bleed into spring and fall, there have been efforts in some cities and towns to install air conditioning in schools without it. In 2017, New York City launched an “AC for All” initiative to bring air conditioners to every public school room, but the Department of Education is not required to make sure the units are properly functioning, and the effort didn’t extend to areas such as cafeterias. A 2025 report showed that one fifth of NYC classrooms still lacked air conditioning.
Some people are looking at other measures, too—for example, towns and school districts around Boston have advocated for a later start date to the year to avoid summer heat.
Putting air conditioning into older school buildings isn’t cheap, which can make it more difficult for some cities and school districts to implement. Ekenga’s work, as well as previous reporting, shows that students who experienced the greatest learning loss were from low-income families as well as from racially marginalized groups. Many people in these groups may also struggle to afford air conditioning at home, which can mean that outside of the classroom, students also experience the consequences of heat exposure, particularly poor or lost sleep.
Fixing the problem of heat’s effect on learning will go beyond the classroom walls. “This is really going to be a community effort,” Ekenga says. “Thermal comfort in school is just as important as what’s happening outside of the schools and in the neighborhoods as well.”
