Listening to a forest before it changes forever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:46:15 UTC
19:46:15 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. This week we’re diving into what we like to call a Friday Fascination—a story that uses sound to transport you into the heart of the narrative.
Today’s episode takes us all the way to Indonesia, where the capital of Jakarta is sinking, possibly faster than any other city in the world. To adapt, the country has started building a new capital on the densely forested island of Borneo. The hope is that this city, called Nusantara, will be green and walkable—but even as a beacon of sustainability, it will still have a dramatic impact on the local habitat. As construction is beginning to transform one of the world’s most biodiverse rainforest areas, scientists and their Indigenous collaborators are racing to record the sounds of the forest—and preserve generations of ecological knowledge before it’s lost forever.
Our guide for this story is Leah Varjacques, a two-time Emmy-Award-winning video journalist, producer and cinematographer. Here she is now.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Leah Varjacques: I’m hiking up a steep hillside called Mount Tembinus in the Bornean rainforest, weaving through waist-high ferns and giant elephant ears. I’m sweating from every pore in my body, trying to keep up with my guide, Abidin, a short man in his late 40s wearing a traditional beaded hat, a cigarette perpetually hanging from his lips.
Abidin: This is the land of my ancestors from long ago. We are people who love farming in the mountains. I feel at peace being here because the atmosphere is calm and safe.
Varjacques: Abidin machetes a path to a tree with a white metal box strapped to it. It says Swift on the side, just above a cage protecting a small black microphone. This is a terrestrial passive acoustic recording unit. It’s a cheap, sturdy and weatherproof recorder used for research and conservation. Abidin is here to swap its batteries and SD card.
Abidin: So with these wildlife recording devices, we are preserving the knowledge of our ancestors. Then from us, if possible, we’ll pass it down to our children and, and grandchildren.
Varjacques: This recorder has been here for 18 months already, continuously monitoring the sound of the forest and its inhabitants, because this forest is going through a major transition. The Indonesian government is building a new capital city here.
The current capital of Indonesia, Jakarta, is perhaps the fastest-sinking city in the world. That’s because most of Jakarta’s drinking water comes from pumped groundwater, a colonial legacy from when the Dutch controlled the country and created a segregated pipe system. The piped water served only elite areas, leaving most people and businesses to pump their water directly from wells, draining the aquifers literally holding up the city.
Even after the Dutch left, this water system remained, and centuries of pumping groundwater faster than it can be replenished have compacted the soft, watery sediment that the city is built on. In some neighborhoods, the ground sinks one foot per year. Sea-level rise made a bad situation worse. Indonesia has been building sea walls higher and higher for years to buy time.
[CLIPS: DW: “By 2050, 90 percent of North Jakarta could be permanently flooded.” PBS News Hour: “About 40 percent of Jakarta is below sea level, and it’s estimated nearly half of the city could be inundated and uninhabitable by 2050.”]
Varjacques: In the face of such dire predictions, then president Joko Widodo, known as Jokowi, announced a plan to move the capital city in 2019.
[CLIP: Widodo: “Indonesia as a great nation must dare to take steps. We must be brave to have a big agenda, and this is for the advancement of our country, for the progress of the nation.”]
Varjacques: The Indonesian government chose a 256,000-hectare site in the hills of Eastern Borneo. That’s like three times the size of New York City. It’s situated on an industrial eucalyptus forest, far from the coast, and designed as a forest city: all-electric, renewable-energy-powered and with lots of green open space—basically the anti-Jakarta, which is known for its density, record-breaking air pollution and traffic.
They’re naming it Nusantara, which means archipelago, and it’s smack-dab in the geographic center of Indonesia, symbolizing that its future will distribute opportunity across all the islands, unlike the country’s current Java-centric economy.
The city is being pitched as the perfect balance between nature and the 21st century.
[CLIP: Nusantara marketing: “Smart forest city.”]
Varjacques: The promotional video for Nusantara shows futuristic renderings of nature-inspired architecture—all greens, crystal blues and cream—elevated infrastructure to allow for natural water flows and wildlife corridors, and lots of space. That’s because the city, projected to be completed by 2045, is really only meant to house a quarter of Jakarta’s population, two and a half million people, and most of the residents will be government workers.
As for the rest of Jakarta, the plan is to build an $80-billion, 575-kilometer sea wall along the north coast of Java, which is Indonesia’s most populous island. Construction is expected to begin this month.
Wendy Erb: We heard that Indonesia was moving the capital to Kalimantan. I knew immediately building a new capital city there has the potential to have a huge impact on forest and animals there.
Varjacques: That’s Wendy Erb. She’s a primatologist and bioacoustic scientist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. She’s worked in Indonesia for 20 years. When she says Kalimantan, she means the Indonesian portion of the island of Borneo, which is also home to Brunei and a region of Malaysia.
Erb: We’re interested in documenting what’s here before all of this big change happens, and we’re trying to do that all through sound work.
Varjacques: Bioacoustics is a scientific discipline that is the study of the sounds of the natural world. It brings together ecology, biology and animal communication, engineering, and machine learning.
Erb: So we have, uh, recorders, like, on top of mountains. We have recorders in mangrove areas. We have recorders right next to caves in the middle of eucalyptus forests. We ended up sampling 20 different sites. And then from there, we could do comparisons over time as we recorded across 18 months as the capital was being built, as this environmental change is happening, as the social change is happening, economic growth is happening. And could we see places where wildlife were sort of being displaced. Maybe those are places where more investment could be made in conservation and management efforts.
Giant squirrel—they sound like bubblegum lasers.
Varjacques: East Kalimantan is a place of incredibly high biodiversity with endangered species like the proboscis monkey, Bornean orangutan, Southern Bornean gibbon, gray gibbon, red langur and long-tailed macaque.
A more well-known method of wildlife monitoring is camera traps. But camera traps only capture what’s in their field of vision. With audio, species that are making sounds from far away can still be tracked. That means you can get a much more comprehensive picture of the wildlife’s health and movement.
At the lab, Wendy’s computer is open to a software with a bunch of sound waves on a track. The audio appears like turquoise dust on an indigo continuum called a spectrogram. Wendy selects a cluster that repeats in a pattern, labeling it the Rhinoceros Hornbill. Each species has its own sonic fingerprint.
Erb: I mean, it’s the best feeling scanning through these spectrograms and just waiting for, like, some discovery to pop up. Like, you just don’t know. Like, maybe there’s going to be an orangutan there, or maybe you will record a clouded leopard or a sun bear. Like, you never know, like, what’s coming on that next pass of the screen.
It’s so exhilarating. I love it.
Varjacques: With the help of AI, Erb sifts through thousands of hours of recordings and identifies which species are where as a baseline. The idea is that as the city is built, scientists can use this baseline to understand how construction is impacting the ecosystem. The government has set clear environmental impact goals, and the sounds of the forest are one way to measure the true effects.
Erb: You don’t know what you’re losing if you haven’t figured out what was there before you started.
Varjacques: What Wendy’s learning is telling, but many questions still remain.
Erb: So our big question is really to understand, what is here now in Nusantara? What came before Nusantara was a twinkle in the president’s eye? And what can we anticipate in the future? What should we worry about for the future? What can we mitigate?
Varjacques: That’s where Abidin comes in. Abidin is from Pemaluan, a village at the periphery of Nusantara’s footprint. He’s part of the Balik people, an Indigenous group in Kalimantan that’s lived in harmony with the forest for generations. Certain animal sounds are culturally significant to the Balik.
Abidin: The most distinct sound is the sound of monkeys or gibbons. Back then, our ancestors used their sound as a sign.
Usually gibbons at dawn, just before morning, they would call. If they call at around nine or 10 in the morning and everything feels eerily quiet, that’s usually a sign indicating that someone will pass away in the village. In the past, the most dominant sound came from the White-breasted Waterhen, then hornbills with their loud calls.
The most iconic one is the Great Argus.
Now we can hear other sounds. Our people say that usually the chainsaw is the loudest.
Varjacques: We take an electric bus past the major construction zones and the nearly finished state-of-the-art hospital and Swiss-Belhotel to a boulevard lined with gray and white buildings, all curved lines and living roofs. Construction crews are putting glass windows on the balconies. These are the ministry buildings surrounding a sort of national mall.
At one end, a bottle-green structure made of hundreds of steel lines comes together in the shape of a giant Garuda or eagle, the national emblem. This is the presidential palace. At the other end stands a Statue of Liberty–like Garuda monument. In the middle, a large organically shaped pond with zigzagging bridges snakes around lush greenery, offering unobstructed viewpoints of both structures.
People are taking selfies. We’re in the center of Nusantara, which the government is showing off to locals, tourists and, it hopes, foreign investors. Indonesia committed 20 percent of the city’s budget but has planned for 80 percent of it to be financed through foreign investment. Despite offering long-term corporate tax breaks and unprecedented land and ownership rights to potential investors, momentum has stalled.
Potential backers are hesitant because of construction delays, a presidential transition and major doubts about the commercial viability of a city that doesn’t yet exist and is located in a remote jungle area. Abedin finds some shade on a bench and lights a cigarette. A security guard immediately comes up and tells him that smoking is not allowed in Nusantara.
Abedin puts out his smoke and mutters, “Fuck this place.”
The government has already evicted some Balik people from their homes and warned others that they will have to relocate. Abidin’s home, which houses his wife and 12 kids, is safe for now, but everything around him is forever transformed.
Abedin: I’m worried about my children’s future.
In terms of education, they are far behind compared to our brothers and sisters from Sumatra, from Java. Especially in city life, you have to be smart, right? Meanwhile they, so to speak, are still relying on the lifestyle of the past. What can we do in the city? I myself can’t live in the city. I don’t understand what I can do.
If we become scavengers in our own hometown, it’s better to just die.
Varjacques: Erb’s acoustic monitoring project can seem like too little too late in the face of such irrevocable change.
Erb: Maybe this work, like we can’t actually stop anything from happening, and sometimes that feels really sad and hard to sit with, ’cause maybe you're like, “But we, we could do something. Things could be different.”
But maybe they can’t. Or maybe, like, it’s also not really our place to do that.
Varjacques: Erb’s collaborative research process has engaged the community at every step of the way to determine what the local people want out of the bioacoustic recordings. The community asked Erb and her team to create an illustrated children’s book about the animals traditionally found in and around the forest and a platform or app to easily be able to play and access the sounds.
Erb’s funding ran out after 18 months of recording, and she and her lab are still sifting through the data. She’s not the only one to have lost funding
In January 2025 a new president, Prabowo Subianto, took office and in his first year slashed the budget for Nusantara, raising major questions about its future.
The government maintains it is committed to finishing the city, but it’s delayed the president’s planned move-in date to the new palace. Erb’s endeavor is a reminder to listen to the voices of not only the local people but also the forest and the more-than-human world.
Erb: The question is, can we tune our ears? Can we pay attention? Can we notice when the natural world is feeling a little sick?
Abidin: I can teach my children the sounds of animals in the forest. Even though there are changes now, I still feel this is my home.

EDF intel chief: Russian losses at over 10,000 soldiers for third consecutive week

Unknown Publisher

EDF intel chief: Russian losses at over 10,000 soldiers for third consecutive week
Russian armed forces losses in the war of aggression against Ukraine have remained above 10,000 troops for the third consecutive week, exceeding the number of new soldiers being recruited, said Col. Ants Kiviselg, head of the EDF Intelligence Center.
"For the third week in a row, Russia has lost more than 10,000 troops, including both wounded and killed. This week's average daily losses are around 1,600 troops, meaning that just over 11,000 were lost over the course of the week," Col. Kiviselg said at the Defense Ministry's regular Friday briefing, giving an overview of the 238th week of the war.
"The trend therefore continues, with Russia losing more troops on the battlefield than it is able to recruit," he added.
The head of the Estonian Defense Forces Intelligence Center also noted that Ukraine had for the first time released figures on its counteroffensive toward Lyman in Donetsk Oblast where around 85 square kilometers were liberated and cleared during the counteroffensive. "Ukrainian operations in Donetsk Oblast are currently continuing," Kiviselg added.
Turning to other Ukrainian successes, Kiviselg listed continued airstrikes against Russian oil facilities in Krasnodar Krai, Saratov and Samara oblasts and the Republic of Tatarstan, a strike on the port of Makhachkala on the Caspian Sea, attacks on chemical plants in Perm Krai and Volgograd and a strike on a drone factory in Rostov Oblast.
"Among military targets, there have been attacks on airfields in Rostov Oblast, as well as air defense systems and launch sites used to store long-range drones in Rostov and Oryol oblasts. The damage is still being assessed, but the Ukrainians have probably managed to either put some aircraft out of action or damage them and the same applies to helicopters," the colonel added.
Kiviselg also cited a report by the International Energy Agency (IEA), according to which the condition of Russia's oil refineries has deteriorated as a result of Ukrainian long-range strikes, while sanctions are hampering efforts to repair damage caused by the airstrikes. The IEA estimates that Russia's oil refining capacity will remain 30 percent below its prewar level for the next 18 months.
Russian continues hitting civilian infrastructure
Although Russia has stepped up pressure on Ukraine by attacking its civilian infrastructure, surveys show that Ukrainians are unwilling to give in despite the hardships caused, Kiviselg said.
"Russian long-range strikes have continued to hit critical and strategic infrastructure in Ukraine this week, as well as residential buildings, potential warehouses, shopping centers, gas stations, vehicles and businesses in at least 17 Ukrainian oblasts. In approximately half of those oblasts, the attacks have also caused disruptions to energy supplies," he said.
Russia has once again begun using relay stations in Belarus to carry out such attacks after they had been out of operation for a period, meaning Russian strikes can now reach western Ukraine and are likely to be more accurate and effective, Kiviselg added.
The head of the EDF Intelligence Center also noted that Russia has attacked around 500 locomotives in Ukraine over the course of the full-scale war. This year, around 10 warehouses holding U.N. humanitarian supplies have been attacked, along with four pharmaceutical warehouses in September.
"So it is very clear that the Russians continue to target civilian sites," he said. "The Russian Federation is doing everything it can to make the coming winter and getting through it as difficult as possible for Ukrainians."
At the same time, recent polls in Ukraine show that around 77 percent of the Ukrainian population do not want to give in to Russia's demands or accept Ukraine's defeat and believe resistance should continue even if they have to cope for periods this winter without electricity, hot water or sewage services, Col. Kiviselg said.
The intelligence chief also highlighted a Russian drone strike on September 13 against a train at Yahodyn station near the Ukrainian-Polish border. Foreign guests who had attended the Yalta European Strategy forum and were traveling to Poland were also nearby. "The guests included many former heads of state and government, former and current senior government officials, lawmakers and experts. The good news is that none of the foreign guests were injured in the attack," he said.
Russia has said it attacks only military targets and logistics infrastructure used for military purposes and has previously warned Ukrainians and Western countries about similar attacks, saying it cannot guarantee the safety of foreign visitors in Ukraine and advising foreign nationals to leave the country, Kiviselg recalled. He said this latest incident was another Russian attempt to influence Western policymakers to withdraw their support for Ukraine.
"In response, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has said that Russia's hopes of undermining unity among Ukraine's supporters and bringing support for Ukraine to an end will not be realized and that assistance to Kyiv will instead be increased," the colonel said.
Commenting on an idea raised last week for both sides to halt attacks on energy infrastructure, Kiviselg noted that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has proposed ending attacks on Russian oil refineries and other fuel infrastructure on the condition that Russia stops attacking Ukraine's electricity grid and gas infrastructure.
"Ukraine wants an agreement banning all attacks on all energy infrastructure and is waiting for Russia to provide a list of facilities that would be exempt from attack under a potential ceasefire covering energy infrastructure," he added.

Druskininkai mayor loses office after corruption conviction – but plans political comeback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:44:00 UTC
19:44:00 KST

Ričardas Malinauskas has lost his position as mayor of Druskininkai after a corruption conviction, ending more than two decades at the helm of the Lithuanian resort town.
But his political career may not be over.
Lithuania’s Central Electoral Commission voted unanimously Thursday to terminate Malinauskas’ mayoral powers after the Court of Appeal upheld his conviction in a corruption case linked to the notorious “Vijūnėlė mansion” affair.
The affair, which unfolded in the mid-to-late 2010s, concerned an illegally constructed residence by a lake in Druskininkai with the involvement of town officials.
Under Lithuanian election law, a mayor must lose office once a criminal conviction takes effect.
Because less than a year remains before the next regular municipal elections, Druskininkai will not hold a special mayoral election. Instead, the town council is due to appoint an interim mayor Monday to serve until next spring’s elections.
Malinauskas, however, will be eligible to seek the office again if he fulfils the court-imposed punishment. The courts did not ban him from holding public office for a specified period.
That prospect is already dividing opinion in the resort town.
Malinauskas said on Facebook that losing his office was not the end of his political path.
“This is definitely not the end of my road,” he wrote. “With such support from the people and such a great team, I am moving forward with my head held high. For Druskininkai and with Druskininkai.”
Malinauskas has served as Druskininkai’s mayor since 2000 and won more than 72% of the vote in the 2023 mayoral election.
A conviction he still rejects
The Court of Appeal on Monday upheld Malinauskas’ conviction in the case involving alleged influence peddling in the Vijūnėlė mansion affair. The ruling took effect immediately, although it can still be appealed to Lithuania’s Supreme Court.
Malinauskas was sentenced to a €60,000 fine, with €30,000 ordered to be confiscated.
The case involved allegations that money was offered to influence a judge in an effort to prevent the demolition of the Vijūnėlė mansion, a long-running controversy in Druskininkai.
Appeal court judges said there was extensive evidence supporting the conviction, including recordings made by Lithuania’s Special Investigation Service of conversations about transferring money in exchange for influence in the case.
Malinauskas has consistently denied wrongdoing.
“A hundred and fifty volumes of the case. Not a single piece of evidence of guilt. Yet I was found guilty,” he said after the ruling. “No. I do not respect such a court decision and I do not trust such law enforcement officials as those I encountered.”
Support remains strong
In Druskininkai, reactions to Malinauskas’ removal reflect the deep support he has maintained among some residents, as well as criticism from political opponents.
“I think this is some kind of settling of scores,” resident Bronius said.
“It is a shame for his reputation. Yes, although those trials have been going on for a long time, he fought all the way, but in the end he lost. Personally, I feel sorry for him,” resident Vaclovas said.
Another resident, Zita, said Malinauskas had impressed her both as a person and as mayor.
Albina said she believed residents would elect him again.
“It is unfair to treat such a hardworking person this way,” she said, pointing to what she described as Malinauskas’ accomplishments in Druskininkai. “We will elect him. He will be mayor again.”
Others were more critical.
“I would, of course, like the mayor not to have been convicted of corruption-related crimes,” resident Sandra said.
Antanas Balkė, a Druskininkai town council member and opposition representative, said the possibility of Malinauskas returning to the mayor’s office could shape the next election.
“There remains a possibility that next year he could return to the mayor’s position and, accordingly, seek revenge in an even sharper form,” Balkė said.
A town facing a political transition
The opposition’s Right faction on the town council issued a statement saying the time had come for Druskininkai to change. It argued that fear had prevailed in municipal institutions and that Malinauskas’ views had effectively been the only accepted position.
Balkė acknowledged that changing the political culture of the town could be difficult after Malinauskas’ long tenure.
“Getting Druskininkai out of that state and into democratic governance will be difficult,” he said. “Love for Malinauskas will not fade so easily.”

TMC's Nandigram bypoll candidate withdraws nomination after meeting Suvendu Adhikari

NEW DELHI: In a significant blow to the Mamata Banerjee-led faction of the Trinamool Congress (TMC), the party's candidate for the upcoming Nandigram assembly bypoll, Sanchita Dey Pradhan, withdrew her nomination on Friday.Pradhan’s sudden departure from the race came after she met West Bengal chief minister and senior BJP leader Suvendu Adhikari in Kolkata. Her withdrawal also came just a day ahead of the deadline for withdrawing nominations. A photograph purportedly showing Adhikari and Pradhan together went viral on social media, the authenticity of which could not be confirmed.
The October 6 bypoll was necessitated after Adhikari vacated the Nandigram seat to retain Bhowanipore—Mamata Banerjee's traditional bastion—where he had defeated the then chief minister in the West Bengal assembly elections held in April.That election marked the end of the TMC's 15-year rule, and the BJP formed its maiden government in West Bengal.
Mamata extends support to Congress
Addressing a press conference, Mamata Banerjee announced that her party would support the Congress candidate in Nandigram.Opposition leaders, including Congress' Rahul Gandhi, had called her up to express solidarity, she added."We are extending our support to Congress in Nandigram and in Assam. We are doing this for the greater interest of the nation...
Rahul Gandhi rang me up yesterday, Arvind Kejriwal also expressed solidarity; we will all fight together against BJP," the former chief minister said.She also strongly criticised the Election Commission over its decision to freeze the TMC's original "flowers and grass" symbol on Thursday. Following the split in the party, the poll panel on Friday assigned the name "Mamata All India Trinamool Congress" with the "football player" symbol to Mamata Banerjee's faction, while recognising the rebel camp led by Arup Roy as the "Democratic Trinamool Congress" with the "envelope" symbol.
The political turmoil follows massive internal rebellion after the TMC's assembly election loss, with over 60 of its 80 MLAs revolting against the leadership. In the Lok Sabha, 20 of the party's 27 MPs recently merged with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India to extend support to the BJP-led NDA government at the Centre.

United Nations says US may have committed war crimes in Iran: What it means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:43:18 UTC
19:43:18 KST

United Nations says US may have committed war crimes in Iran: What it means
UN-mandated probe finds the US unlawfully struck an Iranian school and sports centre, killing children; White House rejects findings.
A United Nations-mandated fact-finding mission has concluded that the United States may have committed war crimes when it carried out two strikes on Iran in February 2026 – one on a primary school in Minab, the other on a sports complex in Lamerd.
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Islamic Republic of Iran submitted its findings to the UN Human Rights Council after months of investigation into the February strikes, when the US and Israel began the war on Iran amid stalled nuclear negotiations. It concluded that there were reasonable grounds to believe the US acted “recklessly” in the strikes.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3UN fact-finding mission says US committed possible war crimes in Iran
- list 2 of 3US approves visas for top Iranian leaders to attend UN General Assembly
- list 3 of 3Iran expels Swedish diplomat in retaliatory move
Neither Washington nor Israel granted the mission access to personnel or responded to its requests for information, so investigators relied, instead, on satellite imagery, verified video, weapons analysis and witness accounts from Iranian sources and independent organisations.
“The Mission concluded that when identifying and directing its attack against the primary school in Minab, whose civilian nature is apparent, the US failed in its obligation to do everything feasible to verify that it was a military objective,” the report stated.
Here’s what we know.
What happened in Minab and Lamerd?
On February 28, during the opening hours of the joint US-Israeli assault on Iran, missiles hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab, Hormozgan province in southern Iran, at about 10:30am local time (07:00 GMT).
The school was roughly 72 metres from an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) naval facility but was separated from it by a wall, had its own entrance, and was visible in satellite imagery as a functioning school, with children’s murals, a playground and classrooms.
Investigators found that the school had been struck twice. The first strike hit the lower floor; as staff moved children to a prayer room upstairs, a second hit the upper floor, killing many of them.
Local officials put the death toll at 156, including 120 schoolchildren and 26 female teachers. Independent sources cited by the UN mission put the toll at 157, including 15 children aged six.
While the Trump administration initially tried to place the blame on Iranian forces, weapons analysts identified a missile used in the strike as a US Tomahawk Land Attack Missile, which Iran does not possess, from fragments at the site.
At about 5:10pm (13:40 GMT) on February 28, the same day as the Minab strike, there was an air strike on the Shahid Haj Khalil Naimi Cultural and Sports Complex in Lamerd, Fars province – also in the south of the country – a facility the UN-mandated mission said had no military use.
Verified video showed one missile exploding over a nearby residential area, then a second directly above the centre. Local officials reported 22 deaths, including four children, and more than 100 injuries. An adjacent school was also damaged.
What has the US said about these strikes?
Since evidence emerged of the Tomahawk missile at the site of the Minab school strike, the US has not disputed responsibility.
On May 19, CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said preliminary Pentagon findings “correlated” the strike with US forces. In June, US President Donald Trump said that “nobody” purposefully attacked the school.
The mission also cited reporting by The New York Times and Reuters revealing that a preliminary Pentagon investigation attributed the strike to outdated intelligence that had wrongly identified the school as part of the adjacent military site.
Washington, however, does dispute responsibility for the Lamerd strike.
CENTCOM has claimed the damage is consistent with an Iranian Hoveyzeh cruise missile.
However, the mission rejected that finding, citing weapons experts who identified design differences ruling out the use of a Hoveyzeh and pointing, instead, to a US-made Precision Strike Missile, a weapon the US has publicly confirmed using in Iran for the first time.
What is the White House saying about the UN mission report?
The Trump administration disputes its findings.
White House Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly told Al Jazeera: “The UN Human Rights Council has accomplished nothing for human rights, spouting unserious nonsense for decades.”
“The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbours in the region,” she added.
“The president is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable.”
What is Iran saying about this?
Iran has publicly rejected the US denials of the Lamerd strike, insisting the missile responsible was American, not Iranian, and has cited the strikes on Minab and Lamerd as evidence of what it calls indiscriminate attacks by Washington against civilians.
Iranian officials, including Minab Prosecutor Ebrahim Taheri and the Lamerd County Sports and Youth Department, have published their own casualty figures for both sites, putting the Minab toll at 156 and the Lamerd toll at 22.
Iran has previously accused the US and Israel of committing crimes against humanity throughout the war, and has called for international accountability over the strikes.
What does ‘war crime’ mean here, legally?
International humanitarian law requires parties to distinguish military from civilian targets and take “all feasible” precautions before launching strikes.
Reed Brody, a human rights lawyer and member of the International Commission of Jurists, told Al Jazeera that not every violation of the laws of war meets the threshold for a war crime, however.
“For any crime, there has to be an intent element,” he said, adding that no one is alleging the US intended to hit a girls’ school. The relevant standard, he said, is recklessness. Recklessness means acting with awareness of a substantial risk of an unlawful outcome and proceeding regardless. The mission’s report describes this as acting with “dolus eventualis”, a mental state that, under international humanitarian law, is legally sufficient to establish the specific war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack.
Brody said the mission’s “recklessness” finding rests on three factors: outdated targeting data, a building “readily identifiable” as a school, and a US administration he said had made “a practice of weakening and dismantling the systems intended to minimise collateral damage”.
He cited cuts to the Pentagon’s civilian harm mitigation office and remarks by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth favouring “maximum lethality, not tepid legality over stupid rules of engagement”.
The mission concluded the US acted “willfully” with “the requisite mental element of recklessness”, and that its failure to update targeting information “went beyond mere negligence”.
Both incidents could meet the legal threshold for the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack.
Brody said the US has, at minimum, committed an “internationally wrongful act” by striking civilian sites, drawing a comparison with Nicaragua’s 1980s case against the US over the mining of its harbours after which Washington withdrew its acceptance of the ICJ’s general jurisdiction.
Will there be any consequences for the US?
Brody said the report carries no automatic legal consequences.
“It doesn’t by itself generate any consequences,” he said, adding that such findings can nonetheless “form the basis for other proceedings”, as UN reports have in The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar and South Africa’s case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague.
However, the US has withdrawn from the ICJ and, Brody said, Iran is unlikely to join the International Criminal Court (ICC), which pursues cases against individuals rather than countries, since doing so would expose its own record to scrutiny.
Brody said accountability ultimately depends on political will rather than legal mechanics. “It means what people make of it,” he said, noting Congress has grown more willing to press the administration as midterm elections approach, which could increase demands for the Pentagon’s internal findings to be made public. “It gives them a hook,” he said – not a binding legal tool, but “more ammunition”.
The UN-mandated mission urged an immediate end to US-Iran hostilities, calling for victim reparations and diplomatic paths towards lasting peace.

Spanish police launch operation to clear Ceuta migrants off beach

Spanish police launch operation to clear Ceuta migrants off beach
MADRID, Sept 18 - Spanish riot police fired rubber bullets into the air and struck people with batons on Friday as they began an operation to clear thousands of migrants off beaches in the North African enclave of Ceuta and move some of them into temporary housing.
Spain estimates 10,000 migrants remain in the tiny territory. More than 72,000 crossed into the enclave from Morocco at the end of July in an unprecedented border rush, although most later left.
The authorities have built new temporary housing inside the enclave's port to hold 1,700 people. NGOs say thousands remain unhoused and have been sleeping rough in camps.
Friday's operation to clear the beaches began shortly before 7 a.m. local time (0500 GMT) and involved both riot police and the Spanish military.
Migrants who had spent the night waiting on the beach in hope of a place in temporary shelter initially applauded as the march got under way, but tussles later broke out as they competed for the limited number of places available.
Footage from state broadcaster TVE showed crowding and jostling as people struggled to enter the designated route. Police fired rubber bullets into the air and struck several migrants with batons before the situation calmed down and the operation resumed.
Later footage showed mostly adult men carrying belongings, walking in small groups under police escort along a route of just over 1 km (0.6 miles) from the El Trampolin beach to the port.
The vast majority of the migrants are men and boys. The temporary housing is built only for adult men, so minors are being separated and housed separately.
Three NGO leaders told Reuters that authorities had been too slow to provide migrants with minimum shelter required under the European migration pact, and that reception centres opened so far could not accommodate those still sleeping on the streets.
One NGO estimated that about 4,000 migrants remained outdoors on Ceuta's beaches and pavements, meaning the new centre would not be sufficient to clear makeshift camps in public areas. Two NGO leaders said officials probably expect most migrants to return voluntarily to Morocco. REUTERS

Skat-350M UAV has significant upgrade potential — Kalashnikov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:42:59 UTC
19:42:59 KST

PRETORIA, September 18. /TASS/. Russia’s leading unmanned reconnaissance system, the Skat-350M, has considerable potential for modernization and is continuously being improved based on the results of its use in the special military operation in Ukraine, Director of the Kalashnikov Group Division for the Export of Drones and Loitering Munitions Leonid Rokeakh told TASS at the Africa Aerospace and Defense (AAD) exhibition in South Africa.
"In 2025 alone, the Skat-350M underwent more than 40 modifications. The system has proven highly successful. We are constantly working to improve it. We are in constant contact with troops on the line of contact and receive feedback from them, which helps us understand what needs to be improved or refined. The Skat-350M is constantly evolving and has great potential for modernization. We will soon reveal the drone’s new capabilities," said Rokeakh.
As part of Rosoboronexport’s joint exhibit in South Africa, Kalashnikov showcased a system that includes the Skat-350M reconnaissance drone and the Kub-2ME loitering munition. The company is also demonstrating its latest reconnaissance and strike system featuring the Rus-PE guided munition.
The Africa Aerospace and Defense international exhibition is taking place from September 16 to 20 in Pretoria at the Waterkloof Centurion Air Force Base.

- Emergency authorities confirmed the death after searching from the air and on the water.
- Sorrento Beach, in Perth's north, is a popular swimming spot known for its calm waters.
A swimmer is dead after being attacked by a shark off a popular Western Australian beach.
Emergency services attended Perth's Sorrento Beach about 10.30am on Friday after reports a male had been bitten by a shark while swimming along the coast.
Authorities searched for the swimmer from the air and sea, but he died from the attack, with his remains found in the water, WA Police said.
The Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development is investigating the incident, the second shark attack off WA's coast in five days.
A witness told ABC News she was alerted to the attack when she was walking along the beach and saw a pool of blood in the water.

The City of Joondalup has closed all beaches in the area, from Burns Beach in the north to Marmion in the south, until midday on Saturday as a precaution.
The fatality follows a shark attack on a surfer at a remote WA beach on Monday.

He was taken to the nearby Geraldton Health Campus and is now in a stable condition.
Surf Lifesaving WA's helicopter shark patrols began for summer last week.
They will operate initially on weekends before increasing to a daily frequency between Mandurah and Yanchep, and Rottnest Island to the west, from 26 September until the end of April.

British MPs to tackle UK crisis — why it does so badly in Eurovision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:41:02 UTC
19:41:02 KST

LOOK MUM NO COMPUTER representing the U.K. with the song 'Eins, Zwei, Drei' performs on stage during the Grand Final of the 70th Eurovision Song Contest at Wiener Stadthalle on May 16, 2026 in Vienna. | Christian Bruna/Getty Images
Lawmakers in the United Kingdom, the country that gifted the world The Beatles and S Club 7, will seek answers on how to make the nation’s pop music more competitive on Europe’s biggest stage.
The House of Commons’ Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee will hold an evidence session in the coming months to discuss the process to select the U.K.’s Eurovision Song Contest entry, its chair, Dame Caroline Dinenage, told the BBC.
MPs will examine what Dinenage called a “dismal record of achievement in recent years.” At this year’s Eurovision in Vienna, ‘Eins, Zwei, Drei,’ a synth-pop song from the British YouTuber ‘Look Mum No Computer,’ finished in last place with just one point.
Advertisement
The British entry is currently selected internally by the BBC, one of the world’s largest public broadcasters, and chosen from the third biggest record industry on the planet, behind the U.S. and Japan. It also automatically qualifies for the contest’s final because the BBC is one of the largest contributors to the event’s organizer, the European Broadcasting Union.
Despite this, the U.K. has repeatedly finished in the bottom half of the leaderboard over the past 15 years, with only one exception: Sam Ryder, who claimed second place in 2022 with ‘Space Man.’
The committee is expected to hear from figures from the BBC and the music industry to establish whether the U.K.’s track record is “the result of bad song choice, weak performance … or something else,” Dinenage told the BBC.
The British broadcaster has yet to announce its entry for next year’s event, which will take place in May 2027 in Burgas, Bulgaria.
The contest has been overshadowed in recent years by boycotts from multiple nations over Israel’s participation, following the Oct. 7 2023 Hamas attack and subsequent Israeli military offensive in Gaza. Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS and Ireland’s RTÉ have already announced that they will not be taking part in next year’s contest.

Security Council sets out measures to protect Bulgaria’s strategic sites

Unknown Publisher

News
Security Council sets out measures to protect Bulgaria’s strategic sites
Friday 18 September 2026 12:58
Friday, 18 September 2026, 12:58
PHOTO Council of Ministers
Font size
Bulgaria has set out measures to strengthen security at strategic and critical infrastructure sites, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov and Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said after a meeting of the Security Council under the Prime Minister. The measures include plans for additional counter-drone systems and improved video surveillance, as well as increased police patrols and inspections of facilities where explosives and ammunition are produced or stored.
Stoyanov said additional funding was needed to purchase counter-drone systems and upgrade security systems at Defence Ministry facilities. Measures to modernise their protection had been identified, he added.
Demerdzhiev said police and security services would inspect facilities producing or storing explosives and ammunition and issue recommendations on improving their protection. Police patrols around the sites will also be stepped up.

"We are such stuff as dreams are made on," Shakespeare wrote. Directed by Viviana di Bert, it is original and energetic and keeps the audience constantly engaged. "Since September 15, the production has been part of the repertoire at Teatro Tordinona in Rome - a stage where Shakespeare’s world continues to connect with contemporary audiences in a vivid, immediate, and impactful way," Veneta Nenkova, head of Parallel 43 Association in Rome, told Radio Bulgaria.
The role of Miranda is played by Bulgarian actress and playwright
Silviya Stanoeva - an artist whose name has been associated with
terms like "theatrical discovery" and "undeniable
talent" since her student days. Early in her professional
career, she attracted critical attention and earned acclaim for her
striking stage presence.

Russia Foreign Ministry reaffirms Arctic peace priority, readiness for dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:40:29 UTC
19:40:29 KST

MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. Maintaining peace and security in the Arctic is a priority for Russia, which is ready for constructive cooperation, Director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department of European Problems Vladislav Maslennikov said at a briefing.
"Regardless of external factors, maintaining peace and stability in the North and ensuring safe conditions for effective social, economic and technological development of Russia’s Arctic Zone remain an absolute priority for Russia," he said.
Maslennikov noted that as the largest Arctic power, Russia has all the capabilities needed to independently develop and ensure the security of its Arctic Zone and accomplish national objectives in the Arctic but this does not rule out the development of international cooperation.
"This does not mean that we will deliberately reject mutually beneficial international cooperation if it is based on a desire for honest dialogue and the search for joint solutions to common problems in the Arctic, as well as respect for the rights and interests of our country. We remain consistently open to cooperation with all foreign partners that show a reciprocal willingness to engage in constructive joint work," he added.

Early voting begins in midterms as campaign shifts focus to cost of living and Iran war – US politics live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:40:27 UTC
19:40:27 KST

In chaotic news conference, Trump refers to barring CNN, Politico and MS Now as his 'ban on the free press'
Near the end of a chaotic news conference in the Oval Office on Friday, when a reporter tried to bring Donald Trump back to the subject of his move to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House, over unflattering coverage he referred to as “fake”, the president seemed to admit that what he is attempting to do is a violation of the freedom of the press enshrined in the US constitution.
“On the ban, what does that mean in practice?” the reporter asked. “Are you taking away their badges? Are you banning them from the pool? What does this actually mean?”
“When you say ‘the ban’, which ban?” Trump replied. “Do you know how many bans I’m involved in? I’ve got more bans going than any human being!”
“On the three news outlets, sir, what does that mean in practice?” the reporter clarified.
Looking genuinely confused, Trump said: “Wh- I still don’t know what she’s”, before turning for help to those around him.
NBC News correspondent Kelly O’Donnell then rephrased the question, asking: “What do you envision the bans would look like on the media outlets?” Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?”
“Uh”, Trump said, “a very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can. And if they could straighten themselves out, you know, if they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it. Look, they’re very dishonest people. They write in a very dishonest way.”
He then went on to give an inaccurate account of the settlements he extracted from ABC News and CBS News after suing them over coverage he objected to, and, not for the first time, falsely claimed that the BBC documentary on the January 6 2021 Capitol riot he has sued the corporation over used technology to put words in his mouth that he never actually said. “They put horrible fighting words into my mouth,” Trump claimed, incorrectly. “BBC actually changed my language and they put words in my mouth.”
“We’ll be suing these people too,” he added, in apparent reference to the three outlets he banned from the White House on Friday.
Trump and leaders of Denmark and Greenland announce security pact to be signed next week
Donald Trump’s threatened annexation of Greenland appears to be off the table, as the US president, and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland announced on Friday that they expect to sign an Arctic security pact next week during the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Trump cast the deal as a personal triumph, claiming on social media that the agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns.”
“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” the president added without mentioning that the US already has a presence on the island, and the right to expand bases, through Nato.
Statements from Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and the leader of Greenland’s government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, posted online late Friday, emphasized that the agreement would fall far short of Trump’s stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States.” The island is a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark.
Frederiksen said that the agreement “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination.”
Nielsen said the agreement “ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance,” suggesting that the deal might possibly just reiterate the existing US rights through Nato to use the island as a security base.
In chaotic news conference, Trump refers to barring CNN, Politico and MS Now as his 'ban on the free press'
Near the end of a chaotic news conference in the Oval Office on Friday, when a reporter tried to bring Donald Trump back to the subject of his move to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House, over unflattering coverage he referred to as “fake”, the president seemed to admit that what he is attempting to do is a violation of the freedom of the press enshrined in the US constitution.
“On the ban, what does that mean in practice?” the reporter asked. “Are you taking away their badges? Are you banning them from the pool? What does this actually mean?”
“When you say ‘the ban’, which ban?” Trump replied. “Do you know how many bans I’m involved in? I’ve got more bans going than any human being!”
“On the three news outlets, sir, what does that mean in practice?” the reporter clarified.
Looking genuinely confused, Trump said: “Wh- I still don’t know what she’s”, before turning for help to those around him.
NBC News correspondent Kelly O’Donnell then rephrased the question, asking: “What do you envision the bans would look like on the media outlets?” Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?”
“Uh”, Trump said, “a very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can. And if they could straighten themselves out, you know, if they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it. Look, they’re very dishonest people. They write in a very dishonest way.”
He then went on to give an inaccurate account of the settlements he extracted from ABC News and CBS News after suing them over coverage he objected to, and, not for the first time, falsely claimed that the BBC documentary on the January 6 2021 Capitol riot he has sued the corporation over used technology to put words in his mouth that he never actually said. “They put horrible fighting words into my mouth,” Trump claimed, incorrectly. “BBC actually changed my language and they put words in my mouth.”
“We’ll be suing these people too,” he added, in apparent reference to the three outlets he banned from the White House on Friday.
Here is a statement from Jameel Jaffer, the executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, on Donald Trump’s move to bar CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House for unflattering coverage of his work as president:
The First Amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage, just as it prohibits him from punishing universities because he doesn’t like the courses they offer, or from punishing law firms because he doesn’t like the clients they represent. With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you’d think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now. If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a ‘public forum’ under the First Amendment, which means the president can’t exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints.
“Donald Trump just did what dictators throughout history have done,” Chuck Schumer, the leader of the Senate Democrats posted in response to Trump’s move to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.
Directly addressing Trump on social media, Schumer added: “this is a democracy. You will not be able to manipulate the news or hide the truth.”

Report: Trump's FBI chief halted cooperation with Canadian authorities over broadcaster's guidelines on 9/11
After news outlets reported in August that Canada’s national public broadcaster had issued internal guidance not to refer to the September 11 attacks as terrorist attacks without outside attribution, Kash Patel, Donald Trump’s FBI director, voiced his outrage on social media.
“Any agency in Canada that doesn’t publicly reject this bastardization of history, and an insult to the souls lost during our largest terrorist attack in US history will no longer have friend in this FBI… Not to mention our heroes that responded in the aftermath 🇺🇸,” Patel tweeted.
Patel, it turned out, made good on his threat. But it wasn’t the broadcaster, CBC – which is editorially independent from the Canadian government – that Patel retaliated against. Rather, Patel responded by cutting off cooperation with the FBI’s counterpart in Canada, the Royal Canadian Mounted police, the New York Times reported Friday.
The CBC revised its policies soon after they came to public attention, the Times reported, but that didn’t stop the FBI from canceling meetings with the RCMP, and halting parts (but not all) of the cooperation between two law enforcement agencies that typically work closely together.
The unusual move to retaliate against a domestic law enforcement agency over the policies of a public broadcaster came amid escalating US-Canada tensions, and in the shadow of a growing trade war stoked by the US president.

The poll by the The Washington Post and Schar School found that most likely voters it surveyed in Michigan, including a majority of independents, weren’t a fan of the tariffs on Canada. Support largely broke down along party lines, with 89 percent of Democrats against them, but only a slim majority – 56 percent – of Republicans in favor.
Michigan hosts one of this year’s most closely-watched Senates races, between Republican congressman Mike Rogers, a Republican, and his progressive Democrat challenger Abdul El-Sayed. Unlike other Republicans in northern border states, who have spoken out against the escalating US/Canada trade war, Rogers has largely voiced support for Trump’s tariffs.
The latest round of US tariffs against Canada snapped into effect in late August, after negotiations between the two countries broke down in the eleventh hour. Canada retaliated with new tariffs on US goods, disrupting a flow of trade vital to the economies of border states like Michigan.

Ukraine has opened a new border crossing with Romania
Kyiv • UNN
The government has opened the Bila Tserkva–Sighetu Marmației border crossing in Zakarpattia. It will operate around the clock for vehicles weighing up to 3.5 tonnes.
The Cabinet of Ministers has decided to launch a new road border crossing with Romania, "Bila Tserkva – Sighetu Marmației," in Zakarpattia region. This is stated in government resolution No. 1130, reports UNN.
Details
To open the international border crossing point for road traffic, "Bila Tserkva - Sighetu Marmației," using temporary infrastructure to facilitate the passage of passenger vehicles with a maximum permissible weight of up to 3.5 tonnes, with a permanent operating regime and round-the-clock working hours
Until construction of the border crossing point is completed, it will operate within the framework of the construction project "Construction of an international border crossing point on the Ukrainian-Romanian state border between the settlements of Bila Tserkva (Ukraine) and Sighetu Marmației (Romania), with access roads to the road border bridge in Zakarpattia region."
The Administration of the State Border Guard Service and the State Customs Service have been instructed to ensure the operation of the relevant units of those services at the international border crossing point "Bila Tserkva - Sighetu Marmației."
We remind you
Ukraine and Romania discussed the construction of a bridge across the Danube between Orlivka and Isaccea, which could become an important transport corridor between Ukraine and the European Union.

TOKYO, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The 23rd round of ocean discharge of nuclear-contaminated wastewater from Japan's crippled Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant was completed on Friday, with 7,863 tons of such wastewater released, local media reported.
The newly discharged wastewater contained approximately 1.2 trillion becquerels of radioactive tritium, according to Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings (TEPCO), the plant's operator.
The latest release began on Aug. 31. As of its completion, the cumulative volume released has reached about 181,000 tons.
Despite concerns and opposition from the international community, Japan unilaterally launched the discharge of nuclear-contaminated water from the Fukushima Daiichi plant into the ocean in August 2023.
According to data from TEPCO, as of Sept. 3, storage tanks at the plant still held about 1.232 million tons of nuclear-contaminated water. ■

Family of man who died during arrest file manslaughter complaint
Unknown

Family of man who died during arrest file manslaughter complaint
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The family of a man who died after being arrested when police wrongly suspected him of stealing a fatbike have formally accused the force of manslaughter.
Alfredo Goeloe, 51, collapsed as officers restrained him after he was stopped on the bike in Rotterdam on Saturday evening. Police tried unsuccessfully to resuscitate him at the scene using a defibrilator.
In a video clip shot by a passer-by, Mr Goeloe could be heard screaming in pain and protesting that he had diabetes. His family said he had gone out on his sister’s fatbike to fetch diabetes medication while he was attending her baby shower party.
Around 1,000 people took part in a silent vigil on Monday evening and a march to the police station on Zuidplein.
A police spokesman later admitted that the bike had not been stolen. Mr Goeloe was pinned to the ground after he allegedly resisted arrest when police tried to detain him for failing to show ID papers.
The lawyer for the family, Gerard Roethof, said a formal complaint of manslaughter had been filed against the police force, which independent investigators will now have to assess.
“Too fast”
“The family say this is about much more than the order to use force,” Roethof told NOS. “We think this is a case of manslaughter, or in any event severe assault with fatal consequences.”
The prosecution department said on Friday that initial investigations showed he had been stopped by police on suspicion of riding too fast on the fatbike rather than because the vehicle was stolen.
At the time police in the area were looking out for a man and woman described as around 40 years old who had allegedly stolen a fatbike.
The internal police investigations division Rijksrecherche is examining the circumstances of Mr Goeloe’s death, including video footage, and the family’s complaint.

Europe’s most popular castles and palaces revealed – according to traveller reviews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:38:14 UTC
19:38:14 KST

From Prague Castle to Dracula’s fortress in Romania, these are the European palaces and castles attracting the most attention from travellers in 2026.
As we ease into autumn, many European travellers say that culture and heritage are among their main travel motivations.
When the weather starts to cool down in October and November, people are increasingly planning trips around these activities, according to the European Travel Commission.
That research is backed up by data from travel company TUI Musement, too.
Its findings show that 94% of people say they are interested – or very interested – in enjoying experiences related to history, culture and heritage during their next city break. Eight out of 10 respondents also say they have visited a monument or landmark close to where they live.
With that in mind, TUI Musement has revealed a new ranking of the 30 most popular castles and palaces in Europe for 2026, using accumulated Google reviews to back it up.
Its analysis compared the volume of reviews recorded in 2023 and 2026 to show how the ranking of attractions has changed over the past few years.
The list shows that Spain is the country with the greatest representation, with six of the 30 castles and palaces located in the country. Both the Alhambra in Granada and the Royal Palace of Madrid are in the top 10.
Ever-popular Prague Castle manages to retain its first-place spot, while Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna enters the top three. Buda Castle in Budapest was the only new entry into the list, thanks to a 65% increase in the number of accumulated Google reviews compared with 2023.
These are the top 10 castles you may want to consider visiting this autumn.
Top 10 shows a wide geographic spread
Few who have visited Prague Castle will be surprised to see it in the top spot.
Boasting 199,000 reviews – 31% more than in 2023 – it’s one of the largest palace complexes in the world.
A visit offers travellers the chance to discover centuries of history in one place, as a ticket includes the chance to see landmarks including St Vitus Cathedral, the Old Royal Palace and the picturesque Golden Lane.
Next up on the list is Buckingham Palace, arguably London’s most famous monument. One of the three official residences of the British monarchy, it’s an enormously popular tourist attraction.
Thousands of visitors annually watch the daily Changing of the Guard and, in the summer, they can opt to enter the building and tour its iconic state rooms.
Climbing two places from its 2023 ranking to third is Schönbrunn Palace in Austria’s capital, Vienna.
This year, it’s celebrating the 30th anniversary of its designation as a World Heritage Site, and offers a rich history and insight into the world of the imperial legacy that shaped centuries of Austrian history.
In fourth place is the Palace of Versailles, an integral part of French history, and the former residence of the kings of France.
The beautiful structure houses the Hall of Mirrors, royal apartments and extensive, manicured gardens. Here, you can explore everything from the absolutism of Louis XIV and the fall of the monarchy to the signing of the Treaty of Versailles that brought the First World War to an end.
Although it’s dropped two places since 2023, Wawel Castle in Kraków still ranks fifth and remains one of Europe’s major cultural attractions.
The former residence – and coronation site – of Poland’s kings also houses the famous Dragon’s Den statue at its foot, which remains one of the city’s best-known symbols.
Castles in Spain take the sixth and seventh places in the ranking.
Granada’s Alhambra is in sixth, and its complex of palaces, gardens and fortresses is nothing short of breathtaking.
Once home to the Nasrid sultans and then the kings of Castile, the Nasrid Palaces, Generalife, Alcazaba and Palace of Charles V are among its most iconic spaces.
In seventh spot is the Royal Palace of Madrid, which is up one position after increasing its number of accumulated Google reviews by 47% since 2023.
The vast space actually continues to host receptions and official events of the royal household, but members of the public can visit highlights including the throne room, Gasparini room and royal chapel.
For eighth place, it’s back to London and the iconic Tower of London.
This ancient building saw events which shaped England’s destiny, including the execution of Anne Boleyn and the disappearance of brothers Prince Edward V and the Duke of York.
Today, it’s home to the legendary Crown Jewels and is guarded by traditional Yeoman Warders as well as ravens, who some consider the guardians of the fortress.
Neuschwanstein Castle, in the Bavarian Alps, has risen to ninth place in the ranking, thanks to a significant increase in reviews.
The palace, which looks like something out of a fairy tale, invites visitors into the world of King Ludwig II of Bavaria, known as the “Mad King” or “Swan King”, and his fascination with art, architecture and medieval legends.
Rounding out the top 10 is Bran Castle in Romania. Also known as “Dracula’s Castle”, it makes a visit to Transylvania a must for fans of all things spooky.
Beyond the Dracula myth, it also lays bare centuries of Romanian history, from its role as a frontier fortress to its period as a royal residence.

The Economic Security Bureau cannot independently expand the concepts of the Tax Code or establish new taxation rules — lawyer
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:36:27 EEST
19:36:27 KST

The Economic Security Bureau cannot independently expand the concepts of the Tax Code or establish new taxation rules — lawyer
Kyiv • UNN
The Economic Security Bureau may assess payments within the framework of criminal proceedings, but it does not have the authority to independently expand the concepts of the Tax Code or establish new taxation rules. Against the backdrop of criminal cases against airlines due to the interpretation of leasing payments as royalties, the issue requires a unified approach by the state.
The Bureau of Economic Security may provide a legal assessment of payments during criminal investigations, but it does not have the authority to independently expand the concepts defined by the Tax Code or establish new tax legislation norms. This was stated in an exclusive comment to UNN by Oleksandr Latenko, a lawyer and head of the tax law practice at Prikhodko & Partners Law Firm.
BES interprets aircraft leasing as royalties
As UNN previously reported, since 2024 the Bureau of Economic Security has begun interpreting transactions involving the leasing of air transport from nonresidents of Ukraine as the use of equipment. According to the investigation, Ukrainian air carriers were supposed to pay royalties for leasing aircraft and helicopters. Based on this approach, the BES opened criminal proceedings against at least five air carriers, including MAU, Constanta Airlines, Windrose, H3Operations and Skyline Express. According to UNN, another airline—Urga—may also be involved in a similar case.
The criminal cases were opened despite the fact that almost all of the air carriers had successfully passed tax inspections, and the tax authorities' only leasing-related objections concerned one company.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of the legislation and requires the establishment of a unified state approach.
In response to a request from UNN, the Ministry of Finance stated that the taxation of transactions involving the leasing of aircraft is carried out in accordance with the Tax Code and Ukraine's international treaties. At the same time, the Tax Code of Ukraine does not provide for the taxation of aircraft leasing as royalties. Therefore, the Bureau's approach to interpreting aircraft leasing without changing the tax legislation is described as pressure that could destroy the entire passenger and freight transport industry. After all, according to data from the State Register of Civil Aircraft of Ukraine, 86% of the aircraft fleet of Ukrainian companies is leased.
That is why the issue of aircraft leasing was submitted for consideration by the tax committee of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the creation of a working group under the Ministry of Finance, which is to develop a draft generalized tax consultation on the taxation of leasing payments made to nonresidents.
The BES does not have the authority to expand the concepts of the Tax Code
According to lawyer Oleksandr Latenko, it is fundamentally important what the legislation itself means by the concept of "royalties." This refers to a regular monetary payment (remuneration) that a user (licensee) pays to an owner (licensor) for the right to use intellectual property or natural resources.
The Bureau of Economic Security of Ukraine may provide its own legal assessment of payments within criminal proceedings, but it cannot "create" a new category of royalties beyond the definition established by law
He recalled that subparagraph 14.1.225 of the Tax Code of Ukraine defines royalties regardless of what the parties called the relevant payment in the contract, based on its legal and economic substance. In particular, this concerns payments for the use of, or the granting of the right to use, specified intellectual property objects—trademarks, patents, copyrights, software and other objects.
At the same time, the Tax Code also establishes a list of payments that are not considered royalties.
The Bureau of Economic Security of Ukraine does not have the authority to independently establish tax legislation norms
Thus, the Bureau may examine the actual substance of a specific monetary transaction and verify whether other legal relations are concealed behind its formal documentation. However, such an assessment must be carried out within the framework of definitions already established by law, rather than by BES investigators formulating their own tax rules.
What powers does the BES have during an investigation
At the same time, as Oleksandr Latenko explained, the Criminal Procedure Code provides the BEB with a broad range of tools for collecting evidence as part of criminal proceedings.
In particular, detectives may question witnesses, conduct searches and inspections, obtain temporary access to items and documents pursuant to a ruling by an investigating judge, obtain information constituting bank secrecy, and examine payments and their purpose. Covert investigative (detective) actions may also be conducted in cases provided for by law.
According to the lawyer, such measures may make it possible to establish, for example, whether certain monetary transactions were fictitious and whether the actual substance of the payments corresponds to how they are documented.
At the same time, Oleksandr Latenko draws attention to the delineation of the competences of tax and law enforcement authorities.
In particular, the State Tax Service is the direct regulatory authority in the field of taxation. It is the STS that has powers defined by the Tax Code regarding tax administration and the provision of individual tax consultations.
The BEB of Ukraine is not a tax administration body and is not vested with the authority to establish generally binding rules for interpreting the Tax Code of Ukraine; the task of the BEB of Ukraine is different – to detect and investigate criminal offenses in the economic sphere, including criminal offenses related to tax evasion
In this context, it is important to understand that, according to the State Tax Service, the airlines against which the BEB raised claims over its interpretation of aircraft leasing as royalties successfully passed tax audits. The tax authorities' remarks regarding leasing concerned only one company.
As a result of one audit of companies in the aviation sector, lease payments were reclassified as royalties. Only one audit
The situation with aircraft leasing shows that the BEB's legal assessment cannot substitute for the provisions of the Tax Code and the position of the regulatory authority. Criminal proceedings cannot be used as a tool for establishing a new taxation practice not provided for by law. In the case of aircraft leasing, the Ministry of Finance should put an end to the divergent approaches to interpretation by ensuring uniform rules for tax authorities, law enforcement agencies, and businesses.
