Russia seizes control over assets of Nestle, French firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:18:33 UTC
19:18:33 KST

Russia has placed the local businesses of Nestlé, Auchan and other Western-linked companies under temporary administration. Nestlé is weighing its options, while Auchan and Lemana Pro say their Russian operations continue as normal.
A little-known Russian company called L.E.V. Management has been handed temporary control of 16 businesses linked to Nestlé, Auchan and several other Western groups.
President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on Thursday placing the management of stakes and shares in the 16 Russian companies under the control of the firm.
The move tightens Moscow’s control over Western-owned assets amid its confrontation with Western countries over sanctions imposed following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
"Of course, one of the factors taken into account when making this decision was that these are unfriendly countries, which are currently most actively involved in military operations against our country," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said at a press conference on Friday.
The businesses concerned include Nestlé Russia, Nestlé Kuban, French retailer Auchan’s Russian subsidiary, two local FM Logistic entities and Le Monlid, which operates the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain under the Lemana Pro brand.
The measure does not formally confiscate the businesses or change their ownership, according to Russian lawyers cited by business newspaper Kommersant. However, temporary administration has previously preceded the sale or transfer of Western-owned assets to Russian buyers.
L.E.V. Management was registered in Moscow in October 2024, and its shareholders are not publicly disclosed. According to Kommersant, the company showed no active business operations in its publicly available 2025 accounts.
Andrei Krayushkin was appointed its general director on 10 September, one week before the decree was issued. Independent outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe reported that his name and date of birth match those of a Russian interior ministry major general. This has not been independently confirmed.
Most Western companies quickly sold or ring-fenced their Russian businesses after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia has since made it increasingly difficult for foreign companies to leave, requiring presidential approval for deals and placing some assets under temporary administration.
In a statement, Nestlé said it was “assessing the situation and its options”.
“Nestlé is committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees,” it said.
Nestlé has around 7,000 employees and six factories in Russia. It has suspended most non-essential sales, imports and exports, as well as advertising and capital investment, while continuing to supply products it considers essential.
Jean-Philippe Bertschy of Swiss investment bank Vontobel said the financial impact was expected to be limited because Russia now accounts for around 1% of Nestlé’s group sales, down from approximately 2% before the war.
Auchan Retail Russia told Russian business news outlet RBC that it had asked the authorities to clarify the decree and would comment further after receiving more information. It said its stores and other facilities continued to operate normally.
Auchan employs around 30,000 people and operates approximately 230 stores and an online business in Russia.
Lemana Pro told Kommersant that it had not yet received official information from the authorities and continued to operate normally.
Leroy Merlin’s French parent company, Adeo, transferred control of its Russian business to local management in 2023. The operation was subsequently rebranded as Lemana Pro and now has 112 stores.
FM Logistic had not publicly commented at the time of publication.
The move echoes Moscow’s 2023 takeover of Danone’s Russian business. It was initially placed under the management of Yakub Zakriev, a nephew of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov, before Danone sold the operation at a substantial discount in 2024.

Radical changes to agriculture needed for Belgium to be carbon-neutral by 2050, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:18:09 UTC
19:18:09 KST

If Belgium is to become carbon-neutral by 2050, in addition to a significant reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, there is a need for reforestation and a radical transformation of land use, agricultural practices and forest management. This is according to a study by the Climate Change Department of the FPS Public Health.
Radical changes to agriculture needed for Belgium to be carbon-neutral by 2050, study finds
Belgium will have to drastically cut its greenhouse gas emissions across the board to become carbon-neutral. Certain remaining emissions must be offset by natural carbon sinks, such as forests or permanent grassland. These are, however, being depleted by urbanisation, the conversion of permanent grassland into arable land, and a reduced capacity of forests and natural ecosystems to absorb CO2, against the backdrop of global warming.
“Our absorption capacity has decreased by a factor of six since 1990,” says Camille Reyniers of the Climate Change Department. “We are at risk of ending up in a situation where our natural ecosystems would become a net source of emissions.”
The study, carried out by researchers from Vito, Sytra (UCLouvain) and Gembloux Agro-Bio Tech (ULiège), analyses three land-use scenarios: one based on current trends, one that takes into account approved or planned policy measures, and one of radical change.
It concludes that only the radical change scenario makes it possible to meet climate neutrality targets by 2050.
One of the key measures in that scenario concerns livestock farming and involves a significant reduction in livestock numbers (45% for dairy cows, 70% for pigs and 71% for cattle compared with 2022 levels), freeing up a great deal of land currently used for animal feed.
We are at risk of ending up in a situation where our natural ecosystems would become a net source of emissions
As a result, 278,000 hectares of agricultural land – more than a fifth of Belgium’s total agricultural area – could be repurposed for other uses: reforestation, the reflooding of drained peatlands, or the conversion of nearly 10,000 hectares of drained meadows into wetlands.
This scenario, alongside people changing to a more plant-based diet, provides for a greater scale of agroforestry and organic farming. It also entails greater diversity in forests, particularly in terms of tree species and their age, as a younger tree absorbs more CO2 than an older one.
The authors of the study highlight the co-benefits that the most ambitious scenario would bring, such as greater resilience of ecosystems to extreme weather conditions or enhanced biodiversity.
Finally, they highlight the need for a “coherent and stable” policy framework and close coordination between the various levels of government to successfully bring about a transition, which must be accompanied by support for the agricultural sector.

PRESS REVIEW: Early voting is underway in Russia, which is holding its first parliamentary election since the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The result is a foregone conclusion – Vladimir Putin’s party is all but guaranteed to win given that only parties supporting Putin have been registered to run. In its analysis today, the Moscow Times details how Russia has barred opposition candidates from running. Other candidates have been disqualified for posting photos or references to the late Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny. The paper explains that these widespread disqualifications reflect efforts by regional officials to show their loyalty to the Kremlin.
Novaya Gazeta, a Kremlin-critical media calls the election a "listless affair." Any discussion of the Ukraine war is pretty much illegal. It sounds idyllic except the river is home to 500 saltwater crocodiles!

The publication says the discovery is "monumental" – because it could redraw the cat family tree and could lead to more discoveries of new species.

The Leftist Split Over AI Doom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

On September 10, two days after researcher Jacob Coxon, who had recently quit his job at Anthropic, sounded the alarm about the industry potentially bringing about the end of humanity, the New York City Democratic Socialists of America posted a carousel of images on Instagram. The first slide was a drawing of an ouroboros—a dragon eating its own tail—set against a hot pink background. “AI alarmism and AI hype are the same story: both keep your attention on a science-fiction future to distract you from the real harms experienced in the present,” the image reads.
The post was authored by the NYC DSA’s Tech Action Working Group, which focuses on tech regulation issues for the chapter, the largest in the country. It garnered more than 25,000 likes on Instagram. But not everyone agreed with the post: “Horrible and dangerous take,” one comment reads. “Sometimes sounding the alarm is justified.”
As politicians scramble to understand AI safety, an ideological split is opening on the American left. Among the questions it’s centered on is whether to believe tech companies’ claims that their products are so powerful that they could end the world.
Some on the left question the value in elevating theoretical concerns about AI over actual harms. They believe repeating claims promoted by the frontier labs about the dangers of AI empowers the AI companies, turning attention away from regulating the current harms of the technology and toward an impossible future.
“AI has become the latest tool of capitalist exploitation. The damage that unregulated and misused AI is already causing is clear across the country,” Alan Dang, a member of Tech Action, tells WIRED. “As socialists, we don’t trust these corporations to craft their own regulations.”
But others are following the direction of Senator Bernie Sanders, the unofficial leader of the American left, who has enthusiastically taken up the AI safety issue, asserting that AI has the potential to eliminate humanity. They say that it’s possible to address all harms from AI—both those happening now and those that could happen in the future—at once.
“The same people concerned about frontier governance and the development of superintelligence are also addressing those current harms,” says Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI issues. “We should address all these other important factors. Those frontier AI abilities are true and increasing in power. They are not fake or hype.”
Over the past year, Sanders dove head-first into the world of AI safety, bringing conversations that were previously happening in Bay Area circles to Washington and his large populist base. The 85-year-old was early to both opposing data centers—a massive organizing pole for the left this year—and speaking out about AI’s potential harms, from job loss to existential dangers. His data center moratorium bill, released in March, explicitly linked pausing construction with the need to pass federal regulation to protect “the future of humanity.”
Sanders’s positioning on this issue has put him in some unusual alliances, most notably with Steve Bannon, President Donald Trump’s former adviser and a right-wing populist podcast host. It has also seemingly inspired a raft of messaging from left-wing candidates running for office across the country, many of whom have been tying broader concerns around AI to the furor over data centers. On September 9, a day before the New York DSA post, six candidates affiliated with the Working Families Party, including four backed by Sanders, released statements on the need for Washington to regulate AI to prevent existential threats to humanity.
This has come with both public and private criticism. AI researcher and tech industry critic Timnit Gebru has accused Sanders and others on the left of “taking their cues from literal doomsday eugenicist cults,” referring to the effective altruist and rationalist philosophies, which underpin AI safety conversations in Silicon Valley. And Sanders’s moves have inspired some private agita within certain left-wing circles.
“Some of us are looking at Bernie and saying, what happened?” one NYC DSA member with a tech background tells WIRED.
Rumman Chowdhury, CEO and founder of the nonprofit Humane Intelligence, understands the concerns expressed by the DSA working group. Chowdhury, who formerly led the machine learning ethics, transparency, and accountability team at Twitter, thinks that all the attention that the AI safety discourse is generating will ultimately be beneficial to frontier labs.
“[The companies] grab all the attention, time, energy, and money by spouting really extreme perspectives. But then they actually backtrack to where we sit, all while they discount all of our expertise,” she says. “I think it's hard for normal people to think of how the mind of a venture capitalist works and these investors work. The scarier and more fantastic these CEOs make these companies seem, the more investors want in on it.”
For AI companies—particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, which aim to go public in the coming years—the attention and scrutiny on their products now could also be a boon in the long run. “Part of IPOing is sharing a lot of diligence documentation on risks and how risks have been addressed,” says Chowdhury. “This way, they can say, there is a full regulatory regime that they are part of establishing in this industry to guard against the worst risks, and that we have all established exactly what the ‘worst risks’ are.”
Pragathi Balasubramanian is a member of the NYC DSA’s Tech Action working group and a leader in the group’s anti-data center organizing, which netted a major win earlier this year by helping New York pass a one-year moratorium. Balasubramanian feels there may be a disconnect in the conversation around what exactly constitutes the most pressing AI-related harms to regulate. “When it comes down to what's happening on the ground,” they say, the conversation about existential risk “doesn’t come up at all.” Instead, they say, “there's an understanding that AI and data center companies don't have our interests at heart.”
McCoy, who is advising several Congressional candidates on AI, asserts that there is no real divide between actual leaders on the left on the issue. McCoy noted that several members of the DSA, including New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, have come out with recent statements about Coxon’s warnings and the Hugging Face hack.
McCoy says Gebru and similarly-minded critics are “marginal, unrepresentative, and also, frankly, picking an unnecessary distinction. It’s yes and. We should address harms like surveillance and Flock cameras, and other important factors. These do not come in any way at the expense of governing frontier AI capabilities.”
Phil Aroneanu, executive director of Irreplaceable, a left-leaning pro-AI safety organization, says that his time working as a climate activist has informed his approach to the AI regulation question. He believes that addressing both AI’s immediate and existing harms as well as future threats is both needed and possible. (McCoy helped found Irreplaceable with an initial seed fund from the Center for AI Safety.)
“This very similar intersection between the direct impact of fossil fuel extraction, people's homes getting flooded out because of climate-change-fueled storms, and then the broader movement focusing on the longer-term issue of risks and emissions,” he says.
Sanders and New York representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez don’t appear to be on the exact same page, either. While she cosponsored Sanders’ data center moratorium legislation, including the language around AI threatening humanity in her own House version of the bill, she has not participated in the high-profile AI safety discussions that he has been present for. While Sanders has called AI “the most transformational technology in the history of the world,” much of Ocasio-Cortez’s language around AI thus far has focused on data centers and the harms to jobs the technology could create, and worries that the industry is creating a bubble.
When asked by a reporter about AI safety last week, Ocasio-Cortez threaded a careful line, saying that “two things can be true at once,” noting AI “can be very dangerous when pursued without any guardrails,” and warning that “we could be seeing an economic bubble collide with a technological frontier.”
As the safety conversation quickly coalesces in Washington and in statehouses around the country, the ultimate question for the left is not whether to support AI regulation, but what regulations the movement should put its time and resources behind. Dang told WIRED that the DSA Tech Working Group supports “comprehensive AI and tech regulation at the federal, state, and city level, addressing frontier model regulation while also fighting back against the ways that corporate AI is already being used.”
A convention resolution currently before the DSA, meanwhile, proposes organizational support for Sanders and representative Greg Casar’s bill to ban superintelligence altogether—hardly something the frontier labs would agree on. And any ideological concerns within the DSA itself may not matter too much when voters get a say. A Politico poll released Wednesday shows that two in three Americans think that there is at least some risk that AI could “destroy humanity.”
Balasubramanian says that, if nothing else, they’re “happy that everyone is talking about AI now.”

Türkiye’s net international investment position deficit narrowed to $398.7 billion in July from $407.2 billion in June, Central Bank data released on Sept. 18 showed.
The net position measures the difference between residents’ financial assets abroad and liabilities to non-residents. A deficit means liabilities exceed assets.
External assets rose 4.2 percent month-on-month to $419.6 billion, while liabilities to non-residents increased 1 percent to $818.3 billion.
The Central Bank’s reserve assets rose by $17 billion to $164.4 billion, from $147.4 billion in June.
Direct investment assets abroad increased 0.8 percent to $81.8 billion, while other investment assets fell 0.5 percent to $161.7 billion. Banks’ foreign currency deposits abroad declined 6.9 percent to $44.7 billion.
Financial derivative assets rose 0.7 percent to $2.5 billion.
On the liabilities side, portfolio investment rose 3.5 percent to $160.2 billion. This included $50.2 billion in equities and investment fund shares, up 1 percent from June.
Direct investment liabilities fell 0.3 percent to $232.5 billion, while other investment liabilities increased 1.6 percent to $421.6 billion.
Financial derivative liabilities declined 43 percent to $4 billion.

Harri Tiido: Geopolitics in an era when rules no longer work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:10:00 UTC
19:10:00 KST

Harri Tiido: Geopolitics in an era when rules no longer work
In his commentary series, Harri Tiido this time examines survival in chaos with the help of Mark Leonard. Leonard writes that today's global divide is not so much between democracies and autocracies or East and West, but between different approaches to the very idea of order, Tiido notes.
Chaos seems to be one of the favorite themes among observers of international affairs. The basis for this discussion is the book Surviving Chaos: Geopolitics When the Rules Fail (2026) by Mark Leonard, director of the European Council on Foreign Relations.
The title may sound like a self‑help manual, but the book is an interesting work largely devoted to China as an example of how to navigate contemporary chaos. It includes a chapter of recommendations for European leaders and has even been described as Leonard's manifesto. The ideas are useful, and when combined with the recommendations in Mario Draghi's report on modernizing the European Union, the book is worth recommending to observers, practitioners, and decision‑makers alike.
A good starting point is the understanding that the old world order is gone, rule‑based life is a thing of the past, and we must adapt to a new world.
Leonard divides approaches to order into two types. One is the "architects'" approach — the effort to build structures and institutions capable of protecting us. This fits a world based on order.
The other is the "craftsmen's" approach. Craftsmen, in Leonard's sense, are people who, instead of thinking in terms of large structures, try to understand where the world is heading and find their place within that movement. One group tries to build a new rigid structure; the other tries to turn emerging conditions to its advantage.
Most of the West, especially Europe, fits the first category. China, Leonard argues, represents the second.
In his opinion, a new era requires a new language, and he suggests that the current state of the world should be called not disorder or chaos, but unorder. His explanation: unorder is a state in which order nominally exists but rules are broken. Disorder would be a state in which rules are irrelevant and simply ignored. It may sound like linguistic acrobatics, but the author is entitled to his terminology.
As noted, the old liberal, rules‑based world order is already gone. Today's global divide is not primarily between democracies and autocracies or East and West, but between different attitudes toward the concept of order — between architects and craftsmen.
Leonard argues that instead of trying to build new structures, it would be more useful to adapt old ones, give them new functions, and improvise. Try different approaches; if something works, continue. If it doesn't, try something else. A somewhat start‑up‑like mindset.
While Europeans talk about the need to preserve the existing order, the Chinese see the world as chaotic and look for ways to find a suitable place within it — and perhaps even benefit from the changes.
Leonard has studied China extensively and argues that the assumption that Beijing sees itself as the leader of a Western‑style global architecture designed to solve the world's problems is wrong. China is not trying to create a new world order; it is preparing for a world without a shared order. In the movement of the world through confusion, the Chinese see opportunity. Their thinking responds to how the world changes — a core idea in Confucian teaching.
Europe views change with fear, assuming things can only get worse. Europeans tend to favor grand plans or alternative orders. The opposite mindset is the Chinese approach: endurance and benefiting from chaos.
This instinct can also be found in other rising states, from India and Turkey to Saudi Arabia and South Africa. Mindset is what distinguishes the camps in today's changing world.
Europe will be ready for the new era of unorder when governments prove capable of adapting. Leonard summarizes the biggest upcoming changes with four keywords: capital, climate, chips, and civilizations — the "4C," which also happens to be the short variant of the plastic explosive Semtex. Another wordplay, but why not.
There is no need to unpack these changes here, but in each of them we can find differences between Chinese and Western approaches. In any case, the world is moving toward a heavily unpredictable unorder characterized by fragmented power, a multitude of actors, and a blurring line between war and crime.
We live in an era where there is no longer a shared understanding of what is right or wrong — not even a shared understanding of what truth is. And if we accept unorder as the new normal, we must get used to constant interconnected crises. Leonard offers the term "polycrisis" where the whole is more overwhelming than the sum of its parts.
We live in a time of continual rebirth, and it is too late to mourn what has been lost. Global politics is becoming different and more chaotic than before. For the Chinese, none of this is new; they have encountered such situations repeatedly throughout history, and that is their advantage.
Chinese thinkers have compared Western thinking to stone tablets, while China's approach resembles flowing water — endlessly flexible. China has also developed effective tools to protect its interests, and Leonard argues Europe should learn from them in both economics and foreign policy.
Europe's understanding of multilateralism is based on rules; China's is based on relationships with other states. A country's influence is determined by the number of its connections and its position within the network of relationships. Europe must understand that it does not have a monopoly on truth, and while it must defend its values, it must also accept that others think differently.
Bulgarian political scientist Ivan Krastev has said that Europe should abandon the role of missionary and instead become a monastery. It should not impose its views on others, but should declare: in our monastery, our rules apply, and anyone who comes here must follow them.
Europe must act according to its own interests, stop outsourcing its security to the United States, and mitigate risks in accessible ways — in economics, technology, politics, and security. It must create a unified capital market and invest money in Europe so companies do not have to seek investment in the U.S. And it must bring talent back to Europe. Europe's greatest challenge is to rediscover its political imagination.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Yemen conflict displaces 112,000 people inside country, thousands flee to Djibouti, UN migration agency says
GENEVA, Sept 18 - At least 112,000 people have been displaced inside Yemen within the last two weeks as fighting continues along the country's west coast amid a renewed conflict, while nearly 3,000 have fled by sea to Djibouti, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure while advancing along Yemen's Red Sea coast towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route. Responding to the Houthi offensive, the Saudi and Yemeni air forces have bombarded Houthi targets.
Nearly 3,000 people have crossed the Gulf of Aden to Djibouti in the Horn of Africa in less than a week as escalating violence have forced more families to flee, Sandrine Desamours, the representative for the UN’s refugee agency, UNHCR, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Djibouti.
The government of Djibouti is preparing for the arrival of up to 10,000 refugees - which will add acute pressure on the country’s health care and education services, she said.
The UN International Organization for Migration said people are fleeing on overcrowded boats and arriving with very limited food and water. Most fleeing are Yemeni families seeking refuge in Djibouti, but IOM is also beginning to see a small number of migrants, mainly from Ethiopia, heading in the same direction.
Additionally, authorities in Somaliland and Puntland have also reported increased arrivals from Yemen, including Yemeni refugees and Somali refugee returnees, though numbers remain in the hundreds for now, UNHCR said.
UN agencies described the latest fighting as being a crisis on top of multiple crises as the country’s health services and economy have been shattered amid a long civil war between forces of the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed administration and the Houthis created one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises.
The Houthi advance along Yemen's Red Sea coast is bolstering Tehran’s hand in its conflict with the US, as the group tightens its control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic chokepoint for global oil and commodities shipping, more than six months after US and Israeli attacks on Iran. REUTERS

Russia showcases Zhnets anti-UAV system at exhibition in South Africa

PRETORIA, September 18. /TASS/. Components of Russia’s Zhnets UAV countermeasure system, developed by Rosel Holding (part of Rostec), were showcased by Russia for the first time at the Africa Aerospace and Defense (AAD) 2026 international exhibition in South Africa, Stanislav Volsky, the development and digital transformation director at the Vektor Research Institute, told TASS.
The products are being presented as part of the joint exhibit of the state arms exporter Rosoboronexport (a subsidiary of Rostec). Rosel presented components of the Zhnets anti-UAV system for the first time at the exhibition in South Africa. The system includes UAV detection radio frequency and radar systems, as well as radio frequency jamming capabilities. The system is controlled by special Vector-HUB software. "This is a situation center that displays the air situation and allows for the control of detection and jamming equipment. The system can operate in manual, semi-automatic, and fully automatic modes," said Volsky.
According to him, the detection systems showcased at the exhibition are the Ogonyok and Rucheyok products. Ogonyok analyzes the radio spectrum in the frequency range from 250 MHz to 12 GHz and detects signals emitted by UAVs. It analyzes these signals and identifies the specific UAVs in the air. The Rucheyok system is capable of intercepting video streams from FPV drone cameras. "In other words, to see through the intruder’s eyes," Volsky noted.
Jamming systems that are part of the Zhnets complex are also on display in Pretoria. "The jamming systems featured at the exhibition are the Serp-VS6 and Press. The Serp family jamming systems are designed on a modular principle. Serp-VS6 and Serp-VS7 together form the Serp-VS13 system, which generates jamming across 13 bands simultaneously. But that’s not the limit. A system capable of operating simultaneously across 40 bands has been put into production," the expert added.
Volsky noted that mobile protection against FPV drones is an important achievement. "It is essential for supporting mobile armed units, special services, protection of convoys, and repair crews. Modern threats require powerful countermeasures. Therefore, portable systems and anti-drone guns can no longer provide the required level of protection. Rosel presented the Press-VM system for countering FPV drones mounted on a wheeled chassis at the exhibition," he added.
The expert specified that Press-VM includes the Ogonyok and Rucheyok detection systems, as well as a vehicle-mounted version of the Serp jammer--the Press. Press specializes in countering FPV drones. Press-VM is based on a pickup truck, with a powerful power unit hidden in its cargo bed," Volsky said.

Forum on Mobility in Europe 2030: EU’s future mobility must be sustainable, resilient and competitive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:06:33 UTC
19:06:33 KST

At a high-level event held in Riga, the European Economic and Social Committee (EESC), in cooperation with the Latvian association ‘Sustainability Cluster’, stressed the need for substantial progress on delivering the EU’s vision for an improved system of mobility.
In the rapidly changing international geopolitical landscape, the European Union must step up its efforts towards climate-neutral, resilient and competitive mobility systems and military mobility capabilities. This was the clear message that emerged from a forum on Mobility in Europe 2030– serving sustainability and military purposes, held in Riga on 17 September 2026.
Organised by the EESC’s Section for Transport, Energy, Infrastructure and the Information Society (TEN) in cooperation with the Latvian association ‘Sustainability Cluster’, the event brought together representatives from the European institutions, national authorities, business, academia and civil society.
The high-level forum served as a space for strategic dialogue to assess progress, share best practices, and set out practical pathways for both achieving sustainable mobility and boosting military mobility capabilities across Europe.
Focus on the mobility value chain
European mobility is being asked to deliver more than ever before – for Europe’s economy, citizens, climate and increasingly also for its security. The objective is that by 2030 it will connect Europe better and make it genuinely sustainable and more resilient, while ensuring that no one is left behind.
More specifically:
- Mobility is becoming a strategic European issue – Europe is asking more and more of its transport system. Mobility has to be cleaner and more sustainable; infrastructure must strengthen the EU’s competitiveness and single market; transport must remain accessible and affordable for citizens; and, in today’s geopolitical landscape, networks must be resilient and capable of supporting Europe’s security.
- Sustainability and resilience have to reinforce each other – Reducing the dependence on imported fossil fuels can strengthen both the EU’s climate objectives and its strategic autonomy.
- Infrastructure can serve several European objectives at once – Europe’s future mobility system must invest in dual-use civilian-military infrastructure (railways, roads and technologies) and at the same time in people and skills.
- Europe needs to invest seriously in connectivity – The EU needs to invest to remove bottlenecks from its infrastructure, complete cross-border connections and modernise its transport networks. On this matter, the EESC has called for at least EUR 100 billion to be allocated to transport in the Connecting Europe Facility 2028-2034, underlining that investment must deliver European added value and respect social and environmental criteria.
- Sustainability has to reach people’s everyday mobility – European mobility is also about people’s everyday lives. The green mobility transition will only succeed if citizens experience it as better mobility – not simply as more restrictions or higher costs. The mobility transition must also not create new inequalities between urban and rural areas or between people with different levels of access to transport services.
- Competitiveness, sustainability and social responsibility – The EU needs a transport system that is economically strong, environmentally sustainable and socially responsible. Digitalisation and interoperability should reduce unnecessary administrative burdens. At the same time, simplification must support enforcement, safety, workers’ rights and the single market.
Quotes from high-level speakers
‘Europe in 2030 must be able to move – sustainably, competitively, fairly and securely. Our task is to design a European mobility system in which these objectives do not compete with one another, but reinforce one another.’
Marcin Nowacki, President of the Section for Transport, Energy, Infrastructure and the Information Society, European Economic and Social Committee (EESC)
‘Mobility is no longer simply a transport issue – it is a strategic issue. Europe needs infrastructure that serves citizens and economies while strengthening resilience, security and military readiness across borders.’
Baiba Miltoviča, President of EESC’s Permanent Group on Transport
‘A sustainable future will not be built by vision alone – it requires decisive action today. Sustainability has become a strategic imperative, shaping our economy, security, mobility and quality of life. The challenge before us is to move beyond isolated projects and short-term solutions and build resilient, interconnected systems capable of meeting the needs of future generations.’
Armands Gūtmanis, Chairman of the Latvian association ‘Sustainability Cluster’
‘Most of the issues for military mobility are low hanging fruit – they don’t need a lot of money or time to be solved. I am certain we can find solutions with our Council and Commission colleagues. We have to learn lessons from Ukraine’s experiences and improve our own mobility and security.’
Roberts Zīle, Vice-President of the European Parliament
‘European transport mobility has become a fundamental pillar of safety, security and competitiveness, requiring infrastructure to facilitate economic movement while enabling rapid military deployments. Addressing these challenges requires strong EU funding support and cross‑sector cooperation to integrate regional projects, expand energy resilience and build a connected, dual-use transport network.’
Rihards Kozlovskis, Latvian Minister for Transport

Beijing and Manila on Friday issued conflicting claims over a fresh vessel “collision” in the disputed South China Sea, blaming each other, according to statements from both sides.
The China Coast Guard (CCG) said a Philippine vessel “ignored repeated warnings and suddenly cut across a CCG boat’s bow near Xianbin Jiao, causing a collision,” Beijing-based daily Global Times reported.
Sabina Shoal (known as Xianbin Jiao in China and Escoda Shoal in the Philippines), is a disputed low-tide elevation in the Spratly Islands.
China accused the Philippines of being “fully responsible for the actions, which seriously violated international law and threatened the safety of CCG vessels”.
However, Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) spokesperson Jay Tarriela said it was the Chinese vessel CCG-21585 that “rammed BRP Datu Magat Salamat (MMOV 3015) … as it carried out its maritime patrol to deliver fuel subsidies to our fishermen”.
“Even after the collision, CCG-21585 conducted yet another dangerous manoeuvre, passing dead astern at a distance of only about 5 metres (16 feet),” he claimed in a statement posted on X.
Tarriela said the incident happened off the coast of the Philippine province of Palawan, “well within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone”.
“Let us be clear about what this vessel was doing: it was bringing fuel to Filipino fishermen so they can keep fishing in our own waters and keep food on Filipino tables. The China Coast Guard deliberately rammed a civilian government vessel on a humanitarian and livelihood mission, endangering the lives of its Filipino crew,” he said.
However, the CCG urged the Philippine side to “stop all acts of infringement and provocation”, warning that Manila “would bear the consequences”.
The latest incident comes amid persistent tensions between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea, where the two countries have repeatedly confronted each other over competing territorial claims.

Notorious ex-Assad prison chief gets 60 years for torture in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:05:56 UTC
19:05:56 KST

Samir Ousman Alsheikh, a former senior official in the government of Syrian President Bashar Assad, was sentenced Thursday in the United States to 60 years in prison for torturing political prisoners at Syria’s notorious Adra prison and defrauding U.S. immigration authorities by concealing his past.
Alsheikh, 74, is the highest-ranking official from the Assad government to have been prosecuted and convicted outside Syria. Given his age, the sentence means he is likely to spend the rest of his life in prison.
“The message is clear: human rights violators who come to the United States will receive no safe harbor here,” the U.S. Justice Department said after the sentencing. “We will find them, and they will be prosecuted and punished for their heinous crimes.”
The federal judge in Los Angeles described Alsheikh’s conduct as “despicable,” unimaginably cruel and so violent that it was almost beyond description.
Prosecutors had sought a sentence of at least 80 years. Alsheikh’s attorneys asked for five years, citing his age and medical and cognitive condition. His lawyers said after the hearing that they planned to appeal.
A jury convicted Alsheikh on all six counts against him: conspiracy to commit torture, three counts of torture, one count of visa fraud and one count of attempted naturalization fraud. The trial lasted nine days, and jurors took only several hours to return guilty verdicts on every count.
Torture inside Adra prison
Alsheikh, a retired brigadier general, held a series of senior positions in Syria’s police and internal security apparatus and was affiliated with the ruling Baath Party.
From 2005 to 2008, he headed Damascus Central Prison, commonly known as Adra prison, one of Syria’s most notorious detention facilities.
The prison contained an underground punishment section known as “Wing 13,” which included cramped isolation cells and interrogation rooms. According to evidence presented at trial, Alsheikh ordered prisoners sent to the wing, monitored their torture from his office through surveillance cameras and at times personally participated in their abuse.
Three of his victims testified against him. Two said they were sent to Wing 13 after refusing to abuse political prisoners. A third was punished after guards intercepted a letter of support he had written to a political prisoner.
They described cold, damp cells infested with insects and prisoners being shackled to pipes in the ceiling and suspended by their arms for hours or even days. They said detainees were beaten with cables while hanging in the air. One witness testified that he felt as though his arms were about to be torn from his body.
A central focus of the trial was a torture device known as the “flying carpet” or “magic carpet.” It consisted of two hinged wooden boards onto which a prisoner was strapped on his back. Closing the boards folded the victim’s body at the waist, inflicting extreme pain and sometimes causing spinal fractures.
One witness testified that Alsheikh personally stepped on the device while it was being used.
Another prisoner said that after being tortured he was forced to put on a red jumpsuit reserved for prisoners facing execution, leaving him convinced he was about to be killed.
Other testimony described detainees being forced inside automobile tires and beaten while unable to move.
‘He still lives in my memory’
Alsheikh continued rising through the Assad government after leaving his prison post.
In 2011, as the uprising against Assad began and Syria descended into civil war, Assad appointed Alsheikh governor of Deir el-Zour and head of the province’s security committee.
Syrian documentation groups have accused forces operating under his authority during that period of firing on protesters, carrying out arbitrary arrests and committing torture. Those allegations were not part of the charges on which he was convicted in the United States.
Alsheikh applied for a U.S. immigrant visa in 2018 and entered the United States in March 2020. Prosecutors said he concealed his work at Adra prison, his ties to the Baath Party and his involvement in political persecution and violence on immigration documents.
He obtained permanent resident status, commonly known as a green card, and later applied for U.S. citizenship while continuing to conceal his past, according to prosecutors.
His presence in the United States came to light after a Syrian woman recognized him in a photograph circulated on social media in 2022 and contacted human rights activist Omar Alshogre, himself a survivor of detention and torture in Assad government prisons.
Syrian activists gathered testimony and passed information to U.S. authorities.
Alsheikh was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport in July 2024 as he prepared to board a one-way flight to Beirut.
He was initially charged only with immigration offenses. In December 2024, four days after the fall of Assad’s government, prosecutors filed a superseding indictment adding the torture charges.
Alsheikh became only the fifth person prosecuted under a U.S. law enacted in 1994 that allows authorities to prosecute people found in the United States for torture committed abroad.
German police assisted U.S. investigators in locating and interviewing Syrian witnesses living in Germany.
More than 50 relatives and acquaintances submitted letters to the court describing Alsheikh as generous and compassionate, while his children appealed to the judge for leniency.
His victims offered a starkly different account.
Sultan Abd al-Malik, who was tortured at Adra prison, said that even after 20 years, he still “lives in the prison of memory.”
His brother, Khaled, said he continues to suffer chronic back pain and restricted movement as a result of the abuse. When his son asks to ride on his back, Khaled said, he has to tell him, “I’m no longer strong enough to carry you.”
Assad sentenced to death in absentia
The sentencing comes about a month after a Syrian court sentenced former president Bashar Assad to death for war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by his forces during the country’s 13-year civil war, which began with the 2011 uprising.
Assad’s conviction and death sentence were handed down in absentia. He remains in Russia, where he fled as the collapse of his government became inevitable and where he has been granted asylum by the government of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

19:04:47 KST

The number of electric cars registered in Türkiye rose 53.2 percent year-on-year to 472,157 at the end of August 2026, according to Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) data compiled by Anadolu Agency.
Electric cars accounted for 2.62 percent of the country’s 18.04 million registered cars. Their number stood at 308,217 in August last year.
The electric car fleet numbered just 565 in 2015, reaching 183,776 at the end of 2024 and 370,591 by the end of 2025.
The net increase over the first eight months of 2026 was 101,566 cars.
An expanding charging network and changing consumer preferences have supported the increase.
Domestic carmaker Togg’s growing market share and new model launches have also contributed.
The number of registered hybrid cars reached 896,270 in August, up from 697,027 at the end of 2025 and 391,296 at the end of 2024.
Hybrids accounted for 4.97 percent of registered cars, up from 4 percent at the end of last year.
Hybrid cars first appeared in Türkiye’s registration statistics in 2011, when there were 23. Their number rose to 13,877 in 2019 and 222,328 by the end of 2023.
Together, electric and hybrid cars numbered about 1.37 million at the end of August, accounting for approximately 7.6 percent of the country’s registered car fleet.

Companies to need average wage of UAH 28,600 or more to defer employees – 2027 draft state budget
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:02:26 EEST
19:02:26 KST

Companies will need to have an average wage of at least UAH 28,638 to defer employees from military conscription, following the planned increase in the minimum wage under the 2027 draft state budget.
According to bill No. 16000, dated Sept 15, the 2027 draft state budget provides for the minimum wage to rise from Jan 1, 2027, to UAH 9,546 from the current UAH 8,647.
Under resolution No. 692, dated May 30, 2026, companies currently need an average wage of at least three times the minimum wage (currently UAH 25,941 per month) to defer employees from conscription, and the employees being considered for deferral must also earn that wage throughout the deferral period.
If the state budget is adopted with the planned minimum wage increase, companies will need an average wage of at least UAH 28,638 per month starting Jan 1, 2027, and employees being considered for deferral will need to earn that wage throughout the deferral period.

Barcelona has a bold plan to protect its vulnerable coastline – and it could be prize-winning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:01:58 UTC
19:01:58 KST

The Spanish city has been selected as a finalist for The Earthshot Prize.
This summer, Barcelona recorded its highest temperature in more than a century.
It’s part of a worrying trend: the Mediterranean is warming around 20 per cent faster than the global average, while record-warm waters are fuelling stronger storms, sea level rise and coastal erosion.
The collapse of a stretch of a storm-hit promenade on Barcelona’s northeast coast in 2023 underlined the need for climate resilient infrastructure. Around 70 per cent of the artificial sand added in 2010 has since disappeared.
“Cities like ours must learn to live with climate change while protecting the places and communities that define them,” says Jaume Collboni, Mayor of Barcelona.
The Spanish city’s ambitious coastal resilience project is now in the running for a prestigious environmental award.
Barcelona is a finalist for The Earthshot Prize
Barcelona has been announced as a finalist for The Earthshot Prize in the Revive Our Oceans category. First launched in 2020 by Prince William, the awards recognise environmental solutions to “repair” the planet.
The Spanish city is pouring €150 million into restoring one of Europe’s most intensively used urban coastlines. The project will create 22 hectares – roughly the size of 31 football pitches – of climate- and heat-adapted public space along the Sant Martí seafront, integrating restored marine habitats, natural coastal protection and waterfront access.
It is hoped that it will become a blueprint for coastal cities around the world facing increasingly severe sea-level rise, stronger storms, flooding, biodiversity loss and extreme heat – something The Earthshot Prize will help with by boosting visibility and knowledge-sharing opportunities.
“Every year, our Finalists give me renewed optimism,” says Prince William, President and Founder of The Earthshot Prize. “They show us that, even as the environmental challenges remain urgent, extraordinary people around the world are already proving that progress is possible.”
‘Climate-resilient infrastructure designed for everyone to enjoy’
Instead of repeatedly rebuilding its vulnerable northeast shoreline, Barcelona is intentionally moving parts of the waterfront inland, including relocating a popular seafront football pitch, and moving the sea walls back.
This will allow for wider beaches that act as natural buffers, absorbing wave energy and creating more space for storms, erosion and rising sea levels, as well as providing a vital refuge during increasingly severe heatwaves.
Scheduled for completion in spring 2027, Passeig Marítim de la Mar Bella will encourage sustainable use of the coastline while boosting air quality and biodiversity with a 15,000-square-metre linear park.
Visitors will be able to stroll along a 12-metre-wide pedestrian path or cycle down bike lanes – stretching all the way to the Fòrum – resting at energy-producing solar pergolas along the way.
“The choice facing coastal cities is no longer whether to adapt, but how,” says María Buhigas, Chief City Architect of Barcelona. “This is not a defensive structure added to the edge of the city; it is a new piece of climate-resilient public infrastructure designed for everyone to enjoy.”
Who else is in the running for The Earthshot Prize 2026?
From nearly 7,000 nominations across 169 countries, 15 finalists have been selected for The Earthshot Prize.
Each is aligned with one of the five ‘Earthshots’: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate – with winners in each category poised to receive a £1 million (€1.17m) prize.
For the first time, positive tipping points were part of the selection process, rewarding innovations where progress builds on itself, costs fall with scale and recovery becomes self-propelling.
Other European finalists include Ørsted (Fix Our Climate) – the Danish renewable energy company behind some of the world’s largest offshore wind projects – and PFAS-Free France (Build a Waste-Free World), the policy and civil-society campaign that helped securing, and is now implementing, France’s ‘forever chemical’ phaseout in everyday products.
Further afield, Argentina’s Satellites on Fire is being recognised for its AI-powered wildfire detection and alert platform, alongside zero-emission shipping alliance ZEMBA, and India’s electric three-wheeler pioneer Mahindra Last Mile Mobility.
Reconnecting a vast mountain landscape across Canada and the US so wildlife can move freely once again, conservation collaboration Yellowstone to Yukon is among the contenders for the Protect and Restore Nature prize.
“Seeing solutions work gives us all confidence to act. When they succeed, they inspire others and accelerate change,” says Prince William.
The five winners of The Earthshot Prize 2026 will be announced at an awards night in Mumbai, India, on 17 November.

Dame Caroline Dinenage, who heads the digital, culture, media and sport committee, told the BBC: “We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant, on what basis and whether our dismal record of achievement in recent years is the result of bad song choice, weak performance … or something else.”
Prior to 2000, the UK could be proud of its efforts: it finished in the top 10 every year except 1978, 1987 and 1999, and won with Love Shine a Light by Katrina and the Waves in 1997.
But since then it has reached the top 10 only three times and finished in last place six times – in 2003, 2008, 2010, 2019, 2021 and 2026 – with Jemini and James Newman scoring nul points in 2003 and 2021 respectively. The exception was Sam Ryder’s Space Man in 2022, which came second.
The act that represents the UK is selected by the BBC with support from a record label or music management company.
The Commons committee is reportedly expected to hear evidence from BBC bosses as well as music industry experts over the coming months.
In 2026, Bulgaria won the contest when Dara swept to victory with the song Bangaranga. The 27-year-old singer’s triumph was the first victory for Bulgaria, which joined Eurovision in 2005 and had sat out the past three editions.
The UK finished last with Look Mum No Computer, AKA Sam Battle. The YouTuber, who makes his own synthesisers, failed to win over neutral voters with the song Eins, Zwei, Drei. The song received zero points in the public vote, meaning it did not make it into the top 10 in any of the voting countries.
The contest has become increasingly political, primarily over the inclusion of Israel, which has been participating since 1973. Ireland is to boycott the contest for the second year running over the Gaza war. It was one of five countries, along with Iceland, the Netherlands, Spain and Slovenia, that refused to take part in the competition this year in protest against Israel’s participation.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — US Representative Young Kim on Tuesday urged Washington to support Taiwan's bid to join the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
During a House Financial Services Committee hearing, Kim discussed the Taiwan Non-Discrimination Act, legislation she introduced that was incorporated into the National Defense Authorization Act last year, per UDN. "This legislation directs the IMF representative to use the US voice and vote to support Taiwan's membership in the IMF," said Kim.
Kim said the US has been discussing the issue with Taiwanese government officials and is preparing to submit an application. “I hope the US will use our voice to support their petition to join, or encourage them to do so as soon as possible,” said Kim.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent responded, "We are aware of your bill," without commenting on the White House's stance on Taiwan's IMF application. Kim said economic security equates to national security, adding, "A strong Taiwan is our best tool to counter Chinese economic coercion."
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs thanked Kim and other members of the US Congress for supporting Taiwan's IMF participation, UDN reported. The ministry said it is consulting with relevant agencies, diplomatic allies, and like-minded countries, including the US, to develop a feasible strategy, and will provide updates on progress.
Taiwan was a founding IMF member, but its representation was transferred from Taipei to Beijing in 1980. Former IMF historian James M. Boughton said, “Its 1980 decision involved neither the admission of a new member nor the termination of an existing membership, but only the recognition of a different government to represent the member.”
Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research Director Liu Da-nien (劉大年) told UDN that Taiwan's biggest obstacle to joining the IMF would be recognition of its status as a state. He noted that Taiwan joined the World Trade Organization as the Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen, and Matsu, a designation available to territories with autonomy over their external trade policies.
The IMF presents additional challenges because applicants must meet requirements concerning their financial systems and membership obligations, Liu said. Although the IMF operates independently of the UN, it could still draw on the UN's definition of statehood when assessing Taiwan's eligibility, he added.

NATO drills new layered air defence over Romania
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:00:55 BST
19:00:55 KST

NATO has carried out a multinational air and missile defence exercise over Romania as the Alliance shifts from traditional air policing towards a broader system designed to counter aircraft, drones and cruise and ballistic missiles, according to Allied Air Command.
The Flexible Deterrent Option training on 9 September brought together fighter and tanker aircraft from France, Greece, Romania, Spain and Türkiye, alongside NATO Airborne Warning and Control System aircraft and a tanker from the Multinational MRTT Unit.
The main focus was Integrated Air and Missile Defence, with the participating forces also conducting Close Air Support training with Romanian ground forces. Aircraft taking part included French Rafales, Romanian and Greek F-16 Fighting Falcons, Spanish F/A-18 Hornets and Turkish F-16s. Spain also deployed an A400M Atlas tanker, while Turkey contributed a KC-135 Stratotanker.
NATO said the activity formed part of a wider move away from an Air Policing framework primarily concerned with safeguarding Alliance airspace against aircraft and uncrewed systems, towards a multi-layered air defence posture capable of dealing with a wider range of threats.
The new framework is intended to cover threats including conventional aircraft, uncrewed aerial systems, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, using sensors, command-and-control systems, fighters and other capabilities as parts of a single integrated network.
Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Alberto B. Calvo López, commander of the Spanish detachment conducting NATO Air Defence duties at Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base, said: “The evolving threat also reminds us of the importance of collective, layered air defence, in which sensors, command and control systems, fighters and other Allied capabilities must be able to operate as a single, integrated system.”
The exercise used a “Red” versus “Blue” scenario focused on Integrated Air and Missile Defence.
NATO AWACS aircraft acted as the principal command-and-control element for the “Red” force, directing tanker aircraft and coordinating with Romanian forces on the ground. The training was designed to test how airborne and ground-based systems could be brought together in real time, with information shared between participants and command procedures rehearsed against a simulated air threat.
NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre at Torrejón in Spain oversaw the activity, providing operational-level command and control while coordinating aircraft and supporting capabilities across the exercise. AIRCOM said the new Air Defence framework brings the Alliance’s air and missile defence activities under common rules, guidelines and command procedures regardless of the type of threat being faced.
The intention is to give NATO commanders greater flexibility to move and combine forces supplied by different member states, synchronising sensors, aircraft and other assets across several domains. The Romanian exercise was also intended to test how quickly allied forces could be assembled and integrated under a Flexible Deterrent Option, with those activities used to rehearse collective defence arrangements before they might be required during a crisis.

====================================================================================================

Taiwan must weigh military AI’s benefits against escalation risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:49 UTC
19:00:49 KST

Taiwan should carefully weigh its military AI applications as they offer opportunities to strengthen deterrence and national resilience, but their integration must account for escalation risks and vulnerabilities.
In recent months, Taiwan has accelerated efforts to integrate artificial intelligence into military systems. In October, President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) announced T-Dome, a multi-layered air-and-missile defense system that will use AI to improve real-time decision-making.
At the same time, the Ministry of National Defense established a pilot AI office within its Defense Innovation Division to explore military AI applications, starting with image recognition, cyber defense and anti-hacking. Yet while the government has identified militarized AI as a way to enhance national defense, it has not received attention comparable to that given to unmanned vehicles.
Military AI applications offer new opportunities to raise deterrence in the Taiwan Strait and enhance monitoring and data-gathering on Chinese operations, and therefore deserve serious consideration. At the same time, they carry risks of escalation, deception and exploitation.
As the environment evolves, Taiwan needs to evaluate military AI applications according to their military value, their reliability under disruption, and the degree of authority delegated to them.
Taiwan currently faces multi-sectoral threats, from disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks to blockade rehearsals. Growing tensions in the strait require Taipei to enhance both its military capabilities and defense resilience. In that context, the benefits of integrating autonomous weapon systems and AI-enabled decision support systems cannot be neglected.
Deterrence and preparedness
First, AI can help counter several aspects of China’s gray-zone tactics. China has leveraged its coast guard as a form of hybrid warfare to create uncertainty and normalize intrusions into Taiwan’s waters.
To raise deterrence and preparedness, Taiwan could integrate AI into maritime patrols. A fleet of autonomous unmanned surface vessels could provide constant, real-time monitoring and data-gathering on Chinese operations. AI systems could then digest that data to identify behavioral patterns, key zones of intrusion and timing characteristics.
The defense ministry has identified coastal surveillance drones as crucial systems to meet operational requirements for national defense, and new funds have been requested for the acquisition of such maritime drones in 2027. By reinforcing intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities, it can strengthen its decision-making and early-warning processes, accelerate vessel detection and reduce response times.
AI can also enhance unmanned vehicle operations through drone swarms and a faster kill chain, increasing deterrence in the strait.
Since February, the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology has partnered with Shield AI, a US defense-tech company, to integrate Hivemind, an end-to-end AI pilot, into Taiwan’s unmanned systems.
AI pilots
These AI pilots can decide and act autonomously, without human intervention, allowing Taiwan’s unmanned systems to remain effective in GPS- and GNSS-denied environments. Keeping unmanned systems operational under constant communications and GPS jamming would be essential should China invade.
Moreover, by allowing one operator to supervise multiple unmanned systems, AI could help Taiwan expand drone operations without a corresponding increase in the number of pilots. Overall, AI can accelerate the targeting cycle — identifying, selecting and engaging targets — reducing the time between detecting a threat and responding to it.
These developments would enhance Taiwan’s defense capabilities and support the island’s capacity to deny the People’s Liberation Army passage across the strait.
Beyond the military, AI’s contribution to Taiwan’s defense can extend to civilian capabilities that help society withstand coercion and information manipulation. The 2024 presidential election illustrated how China uses AI-generated content to shape narratives in its favor through disinformation.
This information warfare requires constant, high-quality fact-checking, which AI systems can support. Taiwan FactCheck Center and Cofacts, two key actors in Taiwan’s fact-checking environment, are using AI to collect and analyze data to ensure quicker and stronger fact-checking.
Together, these applications offer tangible benefits for Taiwan’s military capabilities and national resilience.
Escalation and exploitation
However, these benefits should not eclipse the risks that military AI applications carry. The Taiwan Strait is a tense, fast-paced environment in which one wrong decision could inflame the situation.
Taiwan’s armed forces and the Coast Guard Administration do a remarkable job protecting the nation — a task that requires judging when to respond, how strongly to respond and when to exercise restraint. In this environment, removing humans from the loop could drastically increase the risks of escalation. In 2025 alone, China’s air incursions across Taiwan’s median line amounted to 3,764 intrusions.
Because autonomous weapon systems do not possess the same contextual understanding as humans, each of those 3,764 events could have become a moment in which a deployed autonomous weapon system mistakenly decided that a PLA aircraft represented an imminent threat and opened fire without prior human approval.
Unintended escalation is not tied to strikes alone and can also arise from flying too close to an aircraft or crossing into China’s territory. Moreover, through their indications, predictions and recommendations, AI-enabled decision support systems can alter the process of making a decision to use force by influencing human judgment.
AI-enabled decision support systems could, for example, deceive commanders or wrongly assess a situation, prompting an escalatory response. Biases in the data and lack of transparency compound the risks.
Finally, integrating AI into military systems also carries risks related to cyberattacks and adversarial machine learning. Through data poisoning, an adversary could manipulate the data used to train these systems, undermining their reliability or causing them to misidentify threats.
In the strait, the consequences of a military AI failure could be used as justification for an invasion. Taiwan therefore needs a dedicated framework to assess these applications and establish the safeguards required before deployment.
Framework for AI adoption
Finding the right balance between military AI integration and AI safety is complex. Tensions in the strait push Taiwan to accelerate adoption of new technologies that could offer a military advantage. Conversely, adopting immature technologies too quickly could undermine its own military capabilities.
As Taiwan plans to deploy AI across military systems, it will need robust control architectures that ensure risk mitigation. Testing and evaluation will be key to establishing how systems behave under disruption and when human intervention is required.
Currently, Taiwan does not possess a clear framework to assess the inherent risks of military AI applications. The Ministry of Digital Affairs’ recent AI Risk Taxonomy and Assessment Framework excluded military uses from its classification.
The defense ministry could, for example, define clear conditions for military AI deployment, including which decisions must remain under human authority. The central objective should remain reinforcing Taiwan’s defense without increasing the risks of a conflict it seeks to prevent.
These safeguards should be developed alongside Taiwan’s military AI capabilities, as any failure would carry a cost Taiwan cannot afford to pay.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei’s interim Dongmen Market began a trial run on Wednesday and will officially open on Oct. 9, allowing vendors to continue operating while the century-old original market is redeveloped.
CNA reported that all 45 vendors from the original Dongmen Market have moved to the temporary site. Taipei’s Market Administration Office said the facility has air conditioning, improved lighting and ventilation, and wider walkways for shoppers.
Dongmen Market was established in 1928 during the Japanese colonial era (1895-1945) and later became known for its high-quality fresh food. Older generations of Taipei residents called it the “aristocratic market” because it was near government offices and official residences.
The city built the interim market to keep vendors in business during redevelopment. The temporary site also provides cleaner and more spacious shopping areas than the original market, per Liberty Times.
Some vendors said they are still adjusting to the new equipment and layout. They said longtime customers returned on the first day of the trial run, while residents welcomed the cooler and less humid environment.
The market is divided into three sections for prepared food, fresh produce and meat, and general merchandise. Vendors sell items including rice noodle soup, vegetables, meat, seafood, imported goods, religious supplies, hardware, and clothing, per FTV News.
The market office said the city plans to begin demolishing the original Dongmen Market on Feb. 1, 2027. It said that the interim market’s official opening on Oct. 9 will include promotional offers and other activities.

‘minimalism feels cold when empty of narrative’: how aarke shapes its brand identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:25 UTC
19:00:25 KST

AARKE TRANSFORMS HIDDEN APPLIANCES INTO COUNTERTOP ARTIFACTS
For the sixth feature of Navigators of Design, a 10-part interview series produced with Most Studios, designboom connects with Malin Gäfvert, Creative Director at premium kitchen appliance brand Aarke. Stepping into the digital and physical frontier of contemporary brand building, Malin explores how creative direction transforms everyday objects from functional utilities into elevated lifestyle artifacts. Rather than viewing kitchen appliances as disposable tools to conceal in cabinets, her approach injects worth into mundane daily moments, turning routine tasks into quiet rituals of understated design.
‘Kitchen appliances have traditionally been purely utilitarian and transactional. Aarke started with a simple insight: the kitchen category was overlooked by design, in both form and function,’ opens Malin Gäfvert in the interview. ‘Sparkling water makers used to be bulky plastic pieces you’d rather hide in a cabinet. Our mission was to replace the disposable with the desirable, by making things people really want to have visible in their kitchen — pieces that stand the test of time and withstand the wear and tear of the eye for many years to come.’
portrait of Malin Gäfvert, Creative Director at premium kitchen appliance brand Aarke | all images © Petter Bäcklund, Frida-M, Malin Gäfvert
INTERSECTION OF PRODUCT DESIGN, INTERIORS, AND FASHION
Founded in 2013 by industrial designers Carl Ljungh and Jonas Groth, Aarke — derived from the Southern Sami word for everyday — was built to refine forgotten home essentials. While the founding team leads the industrial design and product engineering, Malin Gäfvert shapes the intangible ecosystem surrounding the objects, establishing a distinct brand identity that bridges product design, interior space, and fashion imagery.
‘Our visual identity doesn’t have to look like a typical appliance brand. It shouldn’t. I think we are more at the intersection of product design, lifestyle, interior, and fashion,’ Gäfvert notes. ‘One defining decision was building a distinctive identity — an identity with a few cues, repeated consistently, that carry the brand and build recognition. In our storytelling, that shows up as Everyday Engineering: celebrating how Aarke integrates into daily life, not just talking about what the products do and perform, but how they improve your everyday, your lifestyle, your kitchen.’
founded in 2013, Aarke was built to refine forgotten home essentials
HOW AARKE BALANCES FORM, FUNCTION AND CULTURAL RESONANCE
Driven by a clear strategic vision, Aarke’s creative direction shifts focus from functionality to deeper meaning. Placing the emphasis on what objects represent rather than just what they do allows the brand to establish a consistent narrative across its entire product collection.
‘We treat the product like a piece of design from day one, rather than as an accessory that gets shoved in a cupboard between uses. In our branding, function became the entry point, not the whole story. We really emphasize how we can inject a sense of worth into the everyday, mundane tasks you do, turning those moments from ordinary to extraordinary by transforming them into small rituals,’ says Malin.
the brand’s identity bridges product design, interior space, and fashion imagery
Aarke’s visuals balance precise product close-ups that highlight materiality and form with dynamic lifestyle imagery. Physical evidence of human interaction brings warmth and context to the design narrative, allowing the brand to create a grounded visual identity free from cold minimalism.
‘Minimalism only feels cold when it’s empty of narrative. Our fix is to balance the more product-close visuals we do, where we focus on design and tactile material, and mix them with visuals that bring in the physical evidence that a human being is present and using the thing,’ declares the creative director. ‘In art direction, that means we favour authentic settings, capturing real moments, shot in ambient light, often on analogue film. It creates a nice contrast between the two visual worlds we’re in: from the precise product-focused engineering to the real everyday moments in the home. That tension, between the engineered and the everyday, is what makes the brand interesting and recognisable.’
Aarke’s creative direction shifts focus from functionality to deeper meaning
Focusing on daily routines, the brand creates products designed to eliminate minor frustrations and clutter. This user-centered perspective steps away from fast-moving trends, elevating everyday objects through thoughtful storytelling that adapts to seasonal shifts by relying on deliberate tone and timing rather than altering its core identity to fit brief fads. Beyond the physical objects themselves, internal filters ensure that packaging, unboxing, and retail environments mirror this exact design standard, establishing a unified identity across every brand touchpoint.
‘Moments that happen every day deserve better design, because those are the moments people actually live in, repeatedly. They should be free from mess, errors, and bumps,’ concludes Malin Gäfvert. ‘Aarke’s product philosophy: durability, longevity, quality materials, considered design – doesn’t move with trend cycles. But the way we talk about it can flex and adapt: seasonal content, cultural moments, platform-native formats, etc. We can jump on a craze if we think it’s interesting and has something to do with us. And if we do, it happens at the edges, never in the object or the core message.’
