“Mankeeping” takes a toll on women’s mental health and relationship satisfaction, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:19 UTC
19:00:19 KST

A newly developed psychological survey provides a way to measure the unpaid, emotional labor that women perform to manage and maintain the social lives of their romantic partners. The research, published in Sex Roles, details the creation of a scale that captures how women experience the effects of men’s shrinking friendships. The tool offers a standardized way to study this dynamic and its impacts on relationship satisfaction and individual well-being.
The survey centers on a concept called mankeeping. This term describes the effort women exert to compensate for the decline in their male partners’ social networks. It involves behaviors like organizing social events, encouraging men to reconnect with friends, and serving as a primary or sole source of emotional support to prevent the men from becoming isolated.
The concept builds on a long history of sociological research into household and emotional labor. For instance, a 1985 study established the idea of kinkeeping, which refers to the everyday, invisible work that women typically perform to keep family members connected and preserve relational harmony.
At the same time, recent public health data indicates that men are facing a widespread decline in close friendships. A 2022 study observed that men generally face greater social isolation than women across most of their adult lives. This vulnerability is also reflected in a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, which showed that psychological distress tends to shrink men’s support networks much more severely than it does for women.
Recognizing the intersection of these two trends, researchers Angelica P. Ferrara and Dylan P. Vergara formally theorized mankeeping in a 2024 paper. They proposed that the ongoing decline in men’s friendships shifts a heavy, unreciprocated social burden onto their female partners, who act to shield the men and the relationship from the negative consequences of isolation.
“‘Mankeeping’ is something many women express that they have been doing for their partners for quite some time,” lead researcher Vincent Mancini told PsyPost. Mancini is an adjunct senior research fellow at the UWA Medical School and a senior research fellow at the UWA Centre for Child Health Research. “With loneliness being a population health crisis that has gendered features, the aim of this work was to better understand how women may engage in additional effort to help maintain their male partner’s social needs.”
Prior to this work, scientists lacked a validated survey to actually quantify the extent of mankeeping and its psychological toll. By developing a specialized scale, Mancini and his colleagues aimed to provide a reliable way to investigate how men’s loneliness reshapes the daily lives of the women who care for them. To build the scale, the researchers first drafted a large pool of questions based on the initial theory of mankeeping.
They recruited 402 women residing in the United States who had been in a heterosexual romantic relationship for at least six months. The participants rated their agreement with 62 potential scale items using a seven-point rating system. They also completed several established psychological questionnaires measuring depression, anxiety, stress, relationship burnout, relationship burden, and overall relationship satisfaction.
Through a statistical process that groups related questions together based on how participants respond, the researchers refined the survey down to 46 items spanning six distinct categories. These six factors include the actual behaviors women perform to manage their partner’s social life, the emotional impact of that labor, and a recognition that their emotional support is often unequal or unappreciated. The remaining three factors capture the woman’s appraisal of her partner’s social network status, a desire for her partner to expand his friendships, and the extent to which the partner depends on her for emotional support.
The results indicated that the survey accurately captured theoretical predictions about mankeeping. Higher scores across the mankeeping dimensions strongly correlated with lower relationship satisfaction and higher levels of relationship burden and burnout. In addition, five of the six dimensions positively correlated with women’s self-reported depression, anxiety, and stress.
“There is now a validated and useful measure that can help to assess how women engage in this effortful process to help address their partner’s unmet social needs,” Mancini said. “Women who engage in these behaviors more tended to show poorer relationship satisfaction, which may signal the importance of social connections outside the romantic relationship that can help to more widely distribute social needs.” He added that “these results, whilst preliminary, indicate fairly robust and strong effects.”
Interestingly, simply appraising that a partner lacked friends was not strongly linked to psychological distress; rather, it was the active behaviors and the resulting emotional impact that were associated with poorer mental health. The data also showed that women who held more traditional beliefs about gender roles were more likely to report engaging in mankeeping behaviors.
Next, the team sought to verify that their newly developed survey, titled the Mankeeping Scale – Partner Report, operated consistently across different populations. They administered the 46-item survey to a second group of 395 romantically partnered cisgender women living in the United Kingdom. Statistical analyses confirmed that the original six-category structure fit the UK data just as well as the US data. This suggests that the survey measures the same underlying concepts regardless of which of these two countries the women reside in, establishing what researchers call measurement invariance.
Recognizing that a 46-item questionnaire can be overly long for many research or clinical settings, the scientists combined the data from both the US and UK participants, totaling 797 women. They identified the three most mathematically and theoretically strong questions from each of the six categories to create an 18-item brief version. Testing showed that this shortened survey maintained excellent reliability and produced similar associations with relationship satisfaction and psychological distress as the full-length version, offering a practical alternative for future studies.
“It is incredibly useful to have validated measures of concepts such as mankeeping, so that research can move from theory to actually testing associations with possible outcomes,” said Sara B. Chadwick, an assistant professor of Gender and Women’s Studies and Psychology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. “Having a validated measure of mankeeping will allow researchers to better understand how women’s efforts to support and maintain their men partners’ social networks and emotional health are connected to a variety of outcomes for both women and men in these partnerships,” she told PsyPost.
“The development of this measure offers a clear extension of research theorizing ‘mankeeping,’ and builds on previous feminist scholarship that has aimed to conceptualize the many ways that gender norms shape women’s romantic relationships with men,” Chadwick added.
She noted that earlier research has highlighted how gender norms often position women as caregivers for their male partners in ways that mimic a parent-child dynamic. “Overall, I would say this offers an important contribution to feminist research by specifically naming the kinds of behaviors that women engage in for the sake of supporting their men partners and by creating a way for researchers to measure and thus further explore it.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind about these findings. The survey relies entirely on self-reported data from one partner, meaning it captures a woman’s perception of her partner’s social life rather than an objective measure of his actual friendships. A man might feel his social needs are adequately met, even if his partner appraises his network as lacking. Future studies would benefit from surveying both members of a couple simultaneously to get a complete picture of the relationship dynamics.
“It is absolutely crucial to recognize that these results at the population level might not apply in the same way to the individual/couple level,” Mancini cautioned. “Romantic couples are incredibly diverse, not every man is lonely, nor does every woman need to engage in this process. This paper should also not take away from the importance of understanding loneliness as a population health issue, that all genders can experience.”
Chadwick agreed that context is crucial, noting that emotionally supporting a partner or helping them maintain social networks can sometimes be a consensual arrangement or a necessity based on temporary life circumstances, such as moving to a new city or dealing with a period of depression.
“The behaviors listed are not in themselves problematic, even when they may be burdensome,” Chadwick explained. “The key here is consent and mutuality, or in other words, it is essential that women either have consented to an arrangement where they take on the majority of social networking and emotional labor, or that this labor is offered to women in their times of need from their men partners.”
The current data is also a single snapshot in time, which makes it impossible to determine a strict chain of cause and effect between mankeeping behaviors and declining mental health. In addition, women’s responses to the survey might be influenced by internalized societal expectations about how a romantic partner is supposed to act.
Because the study focused on populations in the US and the UK with similar cultural norms, the survey might perform differently in other cultures. Expanding the research to include non-Western populations, as well as developing a companion survey to capture how men experience and perceive this social labor, will help clarify the full scope of this dynamic.
The issue arises, she pointed out, when women are automatically expected to take on this labor. “Unfortunately of course, with the way that gender norms function, the majority of mankeeping is indeed likely to be nonconsensual and non-mutual and thus have a disproportionately negative impact on women,” Chadwick said. In future research, she hopes to see investigations into whether this support is reciprocated, noting that the labor might not have a negative impact “if women feel they are offered the same types of labor from their partner in their own time periods of loneliness or need.”
“Our team is looking to engage in some longitudinal work that can allow us to follow couples over time, so that we can better understand how the phenomenon of mankeeping unfolds over time,” Mancini explained. “Being able to also capture the experiences of male partners, and develop interventions that can bolster the relationship quality between partners are our key future priorities.” He noted that the researchers are “always happy to chat to clinicians, researchers, and communities who have thoughts and ideas about the utility of this work!”
The study, “Measuring Mankeeping: Development and Validation of a Scale Assessing How Women Experience the Impact of Men’s Declining Social Networks,” was authored by Vincent O. Mancini, Briana N. Guerrini, James J. Clarke, Dylan P. Vergara, Zac E. Seidler, and Angelica P. Ferrara.

Trump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:16 UTC
19:00:16 KST

The Trump administration has started sending a majority of undocumented children who came to the US alone and have new immigration court cases to Texas, where government facilities for them are unlicensed, their chances of getting a lawyer are low and advocates fear that “a deportation churn-out factory” awaits them, the Guardian has learned.
Almost 80% of children in federal custody who arrived unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian and who were placed in immigration court proceedings in July – and over 90% in August – have been funneled into shelter networks somewhere in Texas, a dramatic upswing from the months prior, according to analysis shared exclusively with the Guardian from researchers at the immigration data insights platform bklg.org.
This is understood to amount to a total of 925 children in the care of the Health and Human Services (HHS) department’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR) and in open immigration court proceedings based in Texas, with 651 sent there in July and August alone.
Federal officials’ sudden shift toward ushering these vulnerable kids to the Republican-controlled, deeply conservative state for no publicly stated reason has alarmed immigrants’ rights advocates amid concerns about their treatment and access to due process under US laws.
Experts who spoke to the Guardian fear the advent of a mass apprehension campaign – forcing immigrant children from their communities within the country’s interior to gather them in Texas to ultimately pack them onto repatriation flights, which often leave from areas along the US’s southern border.
“We’re thinking about congregating children in facilities in Texas, where there are less attorneys, where it’s one of the harshest jurisdictions, you know, in the country with regard to immigration judges and how they handle cases. And it’s close to the border, where they can just get planes,” said Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, deputy director at the Arizona-based legal service non-profit, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project.
She added that these facilities could be “a deportation churn out factory that has attorneys in name but not real representation”.
Unaccompanied immigrant kids, who often come to the US fleeing abuse, neglect, abandonment, trafficking or other harms, regularly cross the US-Mexico border and enter the custody of ORR, which is legally tasked with their welfare, not the Department of Homeland Security’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency.
There were more than 1,800 kids in ORR’s care nationally at the end of July, scattered among shelters, foster care and secure facilities across the country. Yet already, more than 60% of those still detained with ongoing immigration court proceedings are now believed to be living in Texas, compared with fewer than half in June.
ORR did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.
The processing to Texas is occurring despite the state’s GOP-dominated government refusing to provide state licensing for ORR care providers, a policy that hasn’t stopped the facilities from operating there, but has meant less child welfare oversight and protections for kids.
“Texas is very sympathetic to the Trump administration, at least the governor and the Republican legislature. And so I think the Trump administration knows that not only will there be no pushback from the state government and from the governor, but that people like Governor Greg Abbott are willing accomplices,” Veronica Escobar, a Democratic congresswoman from west Texas, told the Guardian in a phone interview this week.
Meanwhile, many of the kids – from toddlers to teenagers – are navigating the US’s byzantine immigration laws mostly without attorneys. Already, only 31.7% of children in ORR custody with active immigration court proceedings nationally have had a notice of legal representation filed in their cases. Kids held in Texas are faring even worse, with 17.2% in Houston, 18.6% in El Paso and just 8.7% in San Antonio having a legal representation form filed on their behalf, bklg.org’s research found.
“There needs to be far more oversight and representation, for children especially. These kids deserve lawyers,” Escobar said.
At the same time, ORR officials have alarmed advocates by seeking multiple contracts for “emergency influx facilities” of up to 3,000 beds – despite the fact that such facilities can only open when the agency’s operational capacity reaches 85% or higher for multiple days, and ORR’s shelter and foster care network, by its own count, is operating at about 27% capacity.
“Who are they planning to fill those facilities with?” Avila-Cimpeanu asked. “Our fear is huge mass internal apprehension of children.”
Plans for such facilities were first reported by the Independent last month.
At a recent roundtable presentation for roughly 120 stakeholders, ORR officials said the contracts would potentially give the administration “the capability to rapidly respond to any surges at the border of unaccompanied alien children”, according to a transcript of the meeting shared with the Guardian.
But encounters with unaccompanied children at the south-west border have been exceptionally low over the last year and a half. Still, officials pushed for an aggressive timeline, with only 90 days for a facility to become fully operational after a contract is awarded.
“That’s fast and you’re like: ‘I don’t know if I can do that.’ I think it’s very feasible. That is the intent of where we need to be,” said Tony Canales, a branch chief at ORR’s division of acquisition requirements, according to the transcript.
“We’re looking to see whatever you got. I mean, if it’s a permanent facility, if it’s temporary buildings, if it’s a site that is blank that you plan on building on, whatever the case may be. We will definitely look at it and take [it] into consideration,” Canales told the attendees.
The presentation specified that any shelter would require an 8-ft high perimeter fence.
Although officials did not specify a location for such emergency influx facilities, many of the stakeholders closed in on Texas while asking questions.
Officials also said the chosen contractors would be responsible for providing legal services, which could present a serious conflict of interest given that attorneys tasked with representing kids would now be dependent on ORR.
For critics of the second Trump administration, the emergency influx facilities raise the spectre of a worst case scenario, with large-scale detentions for immigrant children in communities across the country, given that there is no apparent current need for the massive shelters otherwise.
“The way that a country and a government treats its children and children in their custody is a direct representation of the level of morality or immorality of that government and those individuals,” Escobar said. “And so it is shameful the way that this administration has chosen to treat children.”
José Olivares contributed reporting

Dolly Parton, Gloria Steinem, and Why Grieving a Celebrity Feels So Personal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Recently, the world has collectively mourned the unexpected losses of several well-known public figures, from Dolly Parton and Gloria Steinem to Bob Mackie and Tim Curry. Their deaths have hit fans, followers, and industry colleagues hard, and their tributes are going viral online.
Although these celebrities primarily appear to us on screen or on stage, many people feel as though they know them personally because of the meaningful impact they’ve had on their lives. These are known as parasocial relationships or “nonreciprocal social-emotional connections” with public figures and celebrities, per the journal of Current Opinion in Psychology.
When a public figure or celebrity dies, we grieve collectively. According to Gina Moffa, grief therapist and author of the book, Moving on Doesn’t Mean Letting Go, this happens when a large group of people mourns at the same time. “This can be felt even if they never knew the person or community, or weren’t directly affected by the event,” says Moffa. And it isn’t limited to the passing of public figures and celebrities. Many people also experienced shared loss after 9/11, Sandy Hook, COVID-19, and the Nepal floods.
In this current cultural moment, we’re seeing collective grief intersect with a psychological phenomenon called parasocial grief. According to psychotherapist and NYU adjunct professor Olivia Verhulst, this can occur when there’s a one-sided sense of familiarity with a public figure after they die. “Relationships don’t need to be reciprocal for feelings to be real,” Verhulst says. “Loss brings up a lot for all of us no matter what form it takes, whether it’s shock, disbelief, or confrontation with our own mortality.”
A small study in 2025 from the journal Acta Psychologica found that parasocial grief can negatively impact mental health and can lead to unhealthy coping mechanisms like substance use.
In comparison with individual grief, shared bereavement is more diffuse. “It doesn’t have the built-in rituals we rely on, like experiences of a funeral and traditional closure,” Moffa explains. Therefore, when celebrities or public figures die, it’s now common practice to post online and engage in comments sections with other grievers. In this way, the comment sections become public memorials.
After Steinem’s passing, people expressed their gratitude and heartbreak by leaving flowers and cards outside her home. When Parton died, fans held up their iPhones with the flashlight on during Harry Styles concert at Madison Square Garden while her song, “I Will Always Love You,” played. Both of these in-person tributes circulated on social media and were widely shared.
Verhulst argues that the most significant difference in mutual sorrow is its “being witnessed” and it can offer more validation than individualized grief. “Given that human beings are fundamentally wired for connection, this broader sense of communal loss can feel comforting in many ways,” she says.
Shared bereavement isn’t a new idea; it dates back for centuries. Some of the most visible representations in recent decades have been the outpouring of support after the deaths of President John F. Kennedy, the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., and Princess Diana. At her funeral, there were an estimated one million people in-person and roughly 2.5 billion viewers who watched it on television.
Society often pushes individual grievers to move on from their losses, rushing them to heal before they’re ready, which can lead to more people struggling alone. But in our current culture, shared bereavement has become more widely accepted. “Social media has become a kind of ‘modern funeral,’ a space where people can come together online, without the barriers of physical geography getting in the way,” Moffa says. “For a lot of people, it’s become the primary place mourning happens now.”
Research has found grieving together is more beneficial than doing it without help. A meta-review from 2022 in the journal Frontiers in Psychology discusses the theory of collective effervescence, a phrase coined by sociologist Émilie Durkheim, as it relates to mourning practices, public memorials, and communal storytelling like after the loss of a public figure. This “intense state of shared emotional activation and sense of unity” can help people feel connected in the long term to others who understand their pain.
“When Steinem and Parton passed within days of each other, comment sections turned into genuine gathering places, telling each other how these women shaped their lives. It made the feeling less isolating and more like something they were carrying alongside a whole community instead of alone,” Moffa says.
Working with a therapist, especially for cognitive behavioral therapy, can also be effective. Treatment can give people a safe space to talk about discomfort and divulge feelings of loss over someone they didn’t know personally, with validation and without shame. It can provide more insight into a person’s emotional state, to see if there’s any unresolved or prolonged grief.
Integration is another useful method. Moffa suggests creating a small ritual in honor of that person, like playing their music, reading their books, or rewatching a favorite video clip. Then, write down what that person meant to you, rather than what they meant to the world, and talk about it with someone. “This can provide validation and connection, instead of having to carry it alone,” she adds. In fact, a recent study from the Death Studies journal in 2026 found sharing emotions, ceremonies, and rituals offer “sense making, solidarity and healing” in shared mourning.
While these are effective ways to navigate the pain, they aren’t the only ones. It’s key to adapt them to meet your needs and determine what works for you.
Verhulst noted there’s an outdated idea that grief occurs in fixed stages which is somehow linear. But, she says, there are truly no universal stages to heal from loss and no right way to grieve.
Sometimes, the best way to mourn is together.

The Earthshot Prize Is Embracing the Idea of Positive Tipping Points
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

At a time when companies are racing to deliver commercial fusion energy and promising a new generation of geothermal wells across the U.S., three-wheel electric vehicles may not seem like the most exciting clean energy technology. But in India, three-wheel vehicles are an essential part of daily transportation and account for up to a quarter of motorized trips in many cities.
The majority of new full-size passenger auto rickshaws sold in India are now electric, according to registration data, a striking milestone given that 10 years ago they were barely off the ground. Initially, scaling took a mix of policy, infrastructure build out, and innovative financing; now, the market has taken on a life of its own. “Once you cross 50%, electric becomes the dominant technology,” says Suman Mishra, the CEO of Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a key player in the market.
The development underscores an idea that is gaining currency in some climate circles: sometimes technologies that matter most are not the futuristic breakthroughs waiting to scale but the familiar ones where adoption begins to reinforce itself.
That shift sits at the heart of a new framework the Earthshot Prize is using this year to evaluate climate solutions. Rather than simply picking the climate solution with the most impressive technology, the judges looked for ways to recognize and advance “positive tipping points” that will unlock transformative changes beyond any individual company or project. “We know exactly the things that we’re looking for to try to tip these global systems in the right direction,” says Jason Knauf, CEO of the Earthshot Prize.
The pattern is visible across the finalist list. Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, one of this year’s Earthshot finalists announced on Sept. 18, has not just built affordable electric three-wheelers but also helped facilitate the infrastructure and policy necessary for them to take off. Another finalist, the Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance, or ZEMBA for short, has sought to coordinate demand for low-carbon shipping fuel from customers that ship goods. And Yellowstone to Yukon restores habitat corridors across North America, which then unlocks feedbacks that restore the underlying ecological ecosystem.
The concept of climate tipping points entered the vernacular nearly two decades ago to describe some of the most alarming risks posed by climate change. At the time, tipping points referred to the thresholds that, when crossed, would trigger a chain reaction of often irreversible damage—think of Antarctic ice sheet collapse leading to sea level rise or the destruction of the Amazon releasing stored carbon dioxide.
More recently, scientists have sought to reframe tipping points, showing that positive developments can have tipping points, too. Cheap energy leads to a rewiring of economies. Social movements unlock widespread policy changes. “The tipping point is where you have strong amplification within the system,” says Tim Lenton, a professor of the University of Exeter who has written seminal papers on the tipping points concept.
The reframe comes at an important moment for the climate narrative. With increasingly bleak climate news, positive tipping points offer grounded optimism about how things may change. That was a key logic for Earthshot’s embrace of tipping points.
“We don’t think you can just leave people with the negatives and the warnings,” says Knauf. “We think we have a responsibility to show them” where positive action is possible.
But the positive tipping point framework is also useful from a capital allocation perspective. As companies cut costs and governments look for ways to trim public spending, tipping points offer a way to identify what Lenton describes as the best “bang for your buck” for climate investment dollars.
In some cases, that means supporting initiatives outside the typical wheelhouse of climate technology startups. ZEMBA, for example, works with the customers who would like to reduce their shipping footprint with low-carbon fuel but cannot afford to do so on their own, thereby helping create a demand signal. That’s a coordinated effort that competitors rarely engage in. “Once those markets are spinning, we will fade into the mist,” says Ingrid Irigoyen, the organization’s CEO.
Such an approach makes sense for governments evaluating how they spend their public dollars. It also makes sense for pension funds and institutional investors concerned with the long-term economic implications of climate change. With relatively few dollars, certain investments will generate a long-tail of positive climate outcomes.
In a future world where climate impact is an important investment metric, tipping points may be a useful tool. For those interested, the Earthshot finalists may offer a useful place to start.

Press review: US sanctions bill may hamper Ukraine talks as Russian parliament vote opens

2026-09-18

MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. The sweeping US sanctions may hinder Ukraine talks, the Kremlin warned as Russian voters go to polls. Meanwhile, the EU is putting forward Ukraine for a proposed European Security Council. These stories topped Friday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: US bill on 'sanctions from hell' on Russia may hamper Ukraine talks
The White House will use the latest bill on additional sanctions on Russia passed by the US Congress as an instrument of pressure, experts say. However, using it in the context of a spike in oil prices could further destabilize energy markets. The largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, such as India, have displayed no willingness to follow Washington's instructions. Meanwhile, preparations for a new trilateral meeting on Ukraine are ongoing: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres supports holding talks at the UN General Assembly High-level Week 2026 in New York City.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which the US House of Representatives approved on September 16 with 262 to 159 lawmakers voting in favor of the measure, would only hamper the Ukrainian settlement process if introduced, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned on Thursday. The upper chamber of parliament voted for the document last month, and the vote at Congress has now sent it to President Donald Trump for his signature.
Against the backdrop of rising oil prices due to the Middle East conflict, Washington will act cautiously so as not to further destabilize energy markets, Tigran Meloyan, an analyst at the HSE Center for Mediterranean Studies, told Izvestia. In his opinion, the Trump administration may use the measure as a pretext to impose tariffs on countries that have nothing to do with trade with Russia. In addition, the document provides for the expansion of powers to impose sanctions on Iran's energy and weapons sectors - these provisions were proposed by Trump himself.
Trump will use the threat of tariff imposition as a political lever to pressure the sides to engage in active talks, Yegor Toropov, an analyst at the Higher School of Economics, argued. Even if the latest US trade restrictions on Russia are actually imposed, certain trade categories will probably be excluded from the sanctions regime under the pretext of their critical importance for the American economy, the expert believes.
Meanwhile, UN chief Guterres voiced his backing for holding trilateral talks during the UNGA High-level Week between September 22 and 28. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is planning to meet with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at this venue. Russia’s top diplomat stressed earlier that Moscow is ready for another round of talks on Ukraine and that it "has something to say."
A new potential round of talks will enable the parties to coordinate their positions and make their positions clear, said Oleg Karpovich, department head at the Diplomatic Academy of the Moscow State Institute of International Relations.
Izvestia: Parliamentary election opens in Russia
This weekend, from September 18 to 20, 450 State Duma seats will be contested, eight governors and members of parliaments of various levels will be elected nationwide. Residents of Kamchatka and Chukotka have already cast their first ballots. Ten parties which have nominated more than 4,300 candidates, including participants in the special military operation, will vie for seats in the lower house of the Federal Assembly. For the first time ever, the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR), the Lugansk People’s Republic (LPR), and the Kherson and Zaporozhye Regions, where martial law is in effect, will take part in the parliamentary election. Also, as many as 333 polling stations will be open abroad.
Ten parties are running in the Duma election, namely the ruling United Russia party, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), the Liberal Democratic Party of the Russian Federation (LDPR), New People, A Just Russia - For Truth, the Party of Pensioners for Social Justice, the Communists of Russia, Rodina, the Party of Direct Democracy, as well as the Greens Ecological Party. A total of 4,300 candidates from these parties, including more than 180 participants in the special military operation, have been registered.
In an address to the nation ahead of the election, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that everyone’s vote will be a small contribution to the protection of national interests. On July 1, the number of eligible Russian voters stood at 111 million, of them over 4 million have chosen to vote online. This time around, online voting will take place in 33 regions.
By restricting the voting of Russians, a number of European countries plan to demonstrate their negative attitude toward Russian politics and elections, Yegor Sergeyev, a senior researcher at the Institute of International Studies at MGIMO University, told Izvestia. According to him, European authorities understand that the votes cast by Russians abroad are unlikely to significantly affect the overall election result.
At that, unfriendly European countries treat Russia and its citizens differently, the expert added. In France, for one, four polling stations will be open - in Paris, Strasbourg, Marseille and Villefranche-sur-Mer. The Fifth Republic takes a softer stand on some of the anti-Russian measures discussed at the EU, Yegorov noted.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: EU seen pitching Ukraine up for new NATO
The European Union will involve Ukraine in a planned European Security Council, a certain analogue of NATO that doesn’t perhaps include the United States, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her State of the EU address on Wednesday. Some US politicians and military leaders, too, view Ukraine as a flagship asset of the North Atlantic Alliance. Former CIA director David Petraeus, who recently visited Kiev, called Russia a "shared threat" to the alliance as he stated that Ukraine is essentially fighting a war on behalf of NATO and that the West must support it.
His remark runs counter to the policy line being pursued by US President Donald Trump who has been pushing for ending the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Trump’s peace push in no way overrides the opinion of a range of US military leaders that Russia is an enemy of NATO.
Finland, for one, is building a TNT production facility with US support. The new plant will produce explosives to serve the needs of Finland and NATO as it will also provide long-term support to Ukraine, the Nordic country’s defense chief, Antti Hakkanen said.
"The Americans share intelligence data with Kiev and supply IT technology to its armed forces. Washington is ready to continue to sell Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine at the request from Europe and the EU, AI-powered drones among other modern weapons. Therefore, Trump’s rhetoric about putting an end to the conflict is empty words. The US earns as it encourages the EU to support Ukraine and works to reduce Russia’s defense capabilities," military expert and retired Colonel Nikolay Shulgin told Nezavisimaya Gazeta.
Ukrainian Finance Minister Sergey Marchenko has acknowledged that Kiev will need more than $52 billion in international financial assistance in 2027. According to Vladimir Zelensky, Ukraine has secured approximately $20 billion in financial commitments from its Western partners and is in talks to bridge the remaining deficit.
Amid the financial issues facing Ukraine, its army is struggling to hold the front, Shulgin continued. "Kiev is trying to deliver long-range strikes inside Russia. But these attacks cannot cause substantial damage to Russia’s military capabilities thanks to effective air defenses," he concluded.
Kommersant: Arctic Council increasingly losing form
September 19 will mark the 30th anniversary of the Arctic Council, once a powerful regional structure that was even considered a de facto "shadow Arctic government." The organization is not in its best form ahead of the anniversary: since seven of its Western member countries refused to cooperate with Russia, the group’s previously rigorous activities have largely ground to a halt, and the Council itself is increasingly viewed globally as a mechanism lacking an exclusive mandate.
Before, member countries of the Arctic Council were wary of claims against the Arctic from countries outside the region as they considered it their exclusive zone of influence. Players outside the region, such as China and India, could only seek the role of observer countries with quite modest rights and powers. Against the background of the Ukraine conflict and a major diplomatic freeze, Russia has increasingly embraced cooperation with extra-regional countries, including BRICS nations, in the polar realm.
Countries outside the region themselves, including China and India, have been more active in expressing their interest in participating in affairs in the region which they are eying for logistics, among other reasons. The situation in the Strait of Hormuz and broader instability regarding southern deep-sea transit are driving interest in trans-Arctic routes among many nations.
At the same time, amid confrontation between Western Arctic states, all seven of which are now NATO members, and Russia in the region, once called an area of cooperation, is increasingly transforming into a hotbed of tensions.
For the time being, the Arctic Council remains relevant to all its member countries, including Russia, Irina Strelnikova, an associate professor of the School of International Regional Studies at HSE University and a member of the Valdai International Discussion Club, told Kommersant.

On September 16, the US Federal Reserve increased its benchmark interest rates by 0.25 percentage points to 3.75-4% for the first time since 2023, and the market expects at least one more hike later this year and continued monetary tightening in 2027. The Fed’s new forecast sees rates returning to where it stood before the latest meeting, or 3.6%, only in 2029. Experts interviewed by Vedomosti said that global regulators are embracing the era of high rates.
Dmitry Kulikov, senior director of the regional ratings group at ACRA, expects the Fed to almost certainly raise its rates once more and said two more are highly likely to come by the year-end. The combination of effects from rising energy prices and utility tariffs as well as labor market conditions and the frenzy of investment in AI, which will only increase its productivity later on, points to more monetary tightening, the expert told Vedomosti. Wednesday’s rate hike is unlikely to be the last, Olga Belenkaya, head of Macroeconomic Analysis at Finam Financial Group, said in agreement. In her view, there is a high probability of at least one or two more rate hikes before the end of this year and in the first quarter of 2027.
The era of zero or low rates in key global economies has come to an end, economist Yegor Sunin, the author of the TruEcon channel on Telegram, argued. And it happened about two years ago, post COVID-19 and large-scale fiscal stimulus. In the next few years, global central banks will gradually tighten monetary policy, the expert believes. "Many global central banks will feel the pressure from dollar rates, and other markets too will likely embrace monetary tightening," Kulikov agrees.
However, even this may not be enough, Susin warned, as global regulators will not act too aggressively to mitigate the consequences of the war in the Middle East, the fuel crisis and rising inflation.

Izvestia: US bill on 'sanctions from hell' on Russia may hamper Ukraine talks
The White House will use the latest bill on additional sanctions on Russia passed by the US Congress as an instrument of pressure, experts say. However, using it in the context of a spike in oil prices could further destabilize energy markets. The Lindsey O. The upper chamber of parliament voted for the document last month, and the vote at Congress has now sent it to President Donald Trump for his signature.
Against the backdrop of rising oil prices due to the Middle East conflict, Washington will act cautiously so as not to further destabilize energy markets, Tigran Meloyan, an analyst at the HSE Center for Mediterranean Studies, told Izvestia. In his opinion, the Trump administration may use the measure as a pretext to impose tariffs on countries that have nothing to do with trade with Russia. This weekend, from September 18 to 20, 450 State Duma seats will be contested, eight governors and members of parliaments of various levels will be elected nationwide. Ten parties which have nominated more than 4,300 candidates, including participants in the special military operation, will vie for seats in the lower house of the Federal Assembly. For the first time ever, the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR), the Lugansk People’s Republic (LPR), and the Kherson and Zaporozhye Regions, where martial law is in effect, will take part in the parliamentary election. Also, as many as 333 polling stations will be open abroad.
Ten parties are running in the Duma election, namely the ruling United Russia party, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), the Liberal Democratic Party of the Russian Federation (LDPR), New People, A Just Russia - For Truth, the Party of Pensioners for Social Justice, the Communists of Russia, Rodina, the Party of Direct Democracy, as well as the Greens Ecological Party. A total of 4,300 candidates from these parties, including more than 180 participants in the special military operation, have been registered.
In an address to the nation ahead of the election, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that everyone’s vote will be a small contribution to the protection of national interests. On July 1, the number of eligible Russian voters stood at 111 million, of them over 4 million have chosen to vote online. This time around, online voting will take place in 33 regions.

It Still Feels Like Summer in Parts of the US. Blame El Niño
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

A summer that started early across the US has no intention of quitting, even as the calendar turns to autumn.
The culprits? El Niño and climate change, which contributed to this summer’s record-breaking warmth and are delaying pumpkin spice season.
Forecasters with the US Climate Prediction Center continue to see increased odds for hotter-than-normal temperatures across much of the country through at least the end of September.
Computer models show a pronounced ridge pattern, an atmospheric arrangement that can lock in sustained spells of warmer-than-normal conditions. This setup will feature widespread unseasonable warmth throughout the country, a pattern consistent with a strong El Niño. The greatest odds of above-normal temperatures exist around the Upper Midwest and the Deep South. Some models suggest temperatures could run 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit above normal for the latter half of September.
The blast of unseasonably warm air comes after the hottest summer in US history in a year in which tens of thousands of heat records have fallen across the US. That includes nearly 44,000 record daytime highs and more than 53,000 record-high overnight minimum temperatures recorded at weather stations across the country. Thousands more monthly and all-time heat records have fallen since the start of 2026. Over the same period of time, only about 21,500 low-temperature records fell, or around one cold record for every four heat records.
Many of the busted records date back more than a century. Salt Lake City hit 109 degrees Fahrenheit on July 12, for example, marking its hottest-ever temperature since records began in 1874. Washington, DC, tied its all-time warmest overnight low of 84 degrees Fahrenheit on July 3, where daily observations date back to 1871.
The heat hasn’t relented, despite the calendar turning to September. Even areas that typically escape countrywide heat waves have suffered. Much of Southern California endured excessive heat warnings during the second week of September as hot conditions and soupy air made Rodeo Drive feel more like Bourbon Street.
Why Has Fall Started So Hot?
Climate change is far and away the primary driver of the extreme heat baking the US. Rising average temperatures raise the baseline for extreme heat, making very hot days even steamier now than they would’ve been just a few decades ago.
That trend has been especially notable at night: Many communities across the country have also seen a precipitous increase in overnight temperatures during the warm months as both temperatures and mugginess increase. The lack of relief is what makes heat waves particularly deadly; without beneficial overnight cooling, heat stress becomes too much for many people to withstand.
A warmer climate is also altering upper-level patterns in a way that’s more favorable to extreme heat events. Strong centers of high pressure aloft force air to sink toward the ground. This air heats up as it compresses, combining with intense sunshine and dry soils to ratchet the heat well above normal. These ridges, often called heat domes, are more common in a warming world.
When Will the Heat End?
While overall highs for the remainder of September won’t be as extreme as they are in July, many areas will continue to endure summer-like heat.
El Niño is also lurking in the background. This pattern of warmer-than-normal waters in the Pacific Ocean affects weather patterns around the world.
We typically feel El Niño’s greatest effects during the cold months as these abnormally warm ocean temperatures alter the jet stream, which are responsible for weather patterns during the autumn and winter months.
This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be a record-setting event. Each El Niño is different, but the patterns during previous strong El Niños suggest that a vast swath of the US is in for overall warmer-than-normal temperatures through the fall and winter. In other words, we’re likely not done breaking heat records yet this year.

In December 2025, singer Aleyna Tilki, actor İrem Sak and influencer Danla Bilic were among those taken into custody and later released after biological samples were collected.
In May of this year, authorities detained 20 people from a list of 25 suspects that included actors Serenay Sarıkaya and Onur Tuna, singer Mabel Matiz, and television presenter Mirgün Cabas.
In July, searches and biological sampling were carried out on a further 25 suspects including singers Sıla Gençoğlu and İlyas Yalçıntaş and producer Fatih Aksoy. Yalçıntaş was subsequently arrested.

Eurozone consumers raise inflation expectations across all horizons: ECB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:55:30 UTC
18:55:30 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Eurozone consumers raised their inflation expectations across all time horizons in August, according to a European Central Bank (ECB) survey released Friday.
Median inflation expectations for the next 12 months increased to 3% from 2.9% in July, the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey showed.
Expectations for inflation three years ahead rose more sharply to 2.9% from 2.7%, while the five-year outlook climbed to 2.5% from 2.4%.
The median rate of inflation perceived by consumers over the previous 12 months, meanwhile, remained unchanged at 3.5%.
Uncertainty surrounding expectations for inflation over the next year declined but remained above the level recorded before the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, the bank said.
Respondents in the lowest income group continued to report higher inflation perceptions and expectations than those in the highest income group. Consumers aged 18 to 34 also reported lower expectations than older respondents.
Expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months remained unchanged at 1%, while anticipated spending growth held at 3.6%.
Consumers’ assessment of their spending growth over the previous year edged up to 5.2% from 5.1%.
Economic growth expectations for the coming 12 months remained at minus 1.2%, while the expected unemployment rate declined to 11% from 11.2%.
The survey also showed that consumers expected home prices to increase by 3.4% over the next year, while anticipated mortgage rates remained unchanged at 4.9%.
The ECB conducted the survey between Aug. 6 and 24 among approximately 19,000 adults in 11 euro-area countries.

Slovakia’s Fico casts doubt over NATO mutual defense clause
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:51:48 UTC
18:51:48 KST

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said he does not want to see his country dragged into war over NATO's Article 5 mutual defense clause, raising fresh questions about the populist leader’s commitment to the alliance.
“I don’t want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5,” Fico said on Thursday in the Slovak city of Prešov. “We are part of NATO, we value that, and we are committed to cooperation and fulfilling our obligations. But as prime minister, I will do everything in my power to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a military conflict.”
“The situation has never been as serious and tense as it is now, in terms of the possibility of a pan-European military conflict,” he added.
Advertisement
Under NATO’s Article 5, an armed attack against one ally is seen as an attack against all 32 members. If that ally requests or consents to a collective response, others must come to its defense, triggering a political process that can end with military action. Article 5 has only been activated once, after the Sept. 11, 2001 terror attacks in the U.S.
The comments underscore growing anxiety in Europe as tensions with Russia soar amid an escalating campaign of sabotage attempts, airspace violations and cyberattacks across the continent.
Fico, seen as one of Europe’s most Kremlin-friendly leaders, has also long argued that Western countries’ approach to Russia and continued support for Ukraine risks war with Moscow.
“Sometimes there’s a tendency to mask our inability to solve problems such as illegal migration, competitiveness, and high energy prices by resorting to this bellicose talk: ‘Come on, let’s fight.’ For heaven’s sake, who do we want to fight? Who?” Fico told students at a university hospital in a ceremony marking the start of the academic year.
“Can you imagine, ladies and gentlemen, that Article 5 of the NATO treaty would be invoked?” he said. “Can anyone imagine that they would tell us: ‘Prepare 5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers,’ and they will go to war somewhere? And we will not even know with whom, why and for what.”
Fico is set to join leaders including Poland’s Donald Tusk and representatives from Austria, the Czech Republic, Romania, Serbia and Hungary in western Ukraine on Friday for a regional economic summit dubbed the Carpathian Integration Initiative.

Police move hundreds of migrants still in Ceuta off beaches in Spanish enclave
Spanish police in Ceuta on Friday morning started moving hundreds of migrants from the beaches of the Spanish enclave to a new tented area. Several thousand migrants remain in Ceuta after tens of thousands of people crossed the border with Morocco in late July.
Police on Friday began moving hundreds of migrants from the beaches of Ceuta to the Spanish enclave's port area.
During the transfer, the police struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a spot at the new tented site after weeks of living on the beaches. Authorities say there are enough tents for 1,700 people.
Read moreThe Ceuta effect: how far will Europe's anti-migrant backlash go?
Tens of thousands of migrants flooded across the border from Morocco in late July and though most quickly returned, several thousand have remained with many now sleeping rough on the territory's beaches.
Police started rounding up the migrants at 6:30am (04:30 GMT), according to a Spanish government source in Ceuta.
The tent city in the port has showers and beds, the source added.
Ceuta authorities estimate that 13,000 migrants have remained in the 18.5 square kilometre (7.2 square mile) territory. The central government says the figure is lower.

Portugal prepares for rising temperatures and likely heatwave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:48:50 UTC
18:48:50 KST

In Portugal, temperatures could climb close to 38°C in the Alentejo and the Tagus Valley, driven by an anticyclone positioned north of the Azores.
Portugal is set to see a gradual rise in temperatures from this Saturday. The Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA) has raised a yellow warning for nine districts (source in Portuguese).
For this Saturday three districts are under a yellow warning: Coimbra, Leiria and Lisbon. On Sunday, the warning is extended to Setúbal, Santarém, Aveiro, Porto, Braga and Viana do Castelo. The alert will remain in force in these nine districts at least until eight o'clock on Monday evening.
The yellow warning is the lowest level of risk on a scale that also includes orange and red alerts. According to the institute's website, it indicates a "situation of risk for certain activities".
The IPMA says there is a likelihood of a heatwave:
"This spell of hot weather will be defined mainly by its duration, with a high probability of meeting the criteria for a heatwave across much of the territory", the institute said in a statement (source in Portuguese).
The document explains that a heatwave occurs when "over a period of six consecutive days, the maximum air temperature is 5 °C above the average value of the daily maximum temperatures".
Temperatures are therefore expected to reach above 30 °C on the mainland. In some areas, such as Lisbon and the Tagus Valley, they could even approach 38 °C.
Minimum temperatures will also rise, staying above 20 °C in some parts of Alto Alentejo, Beira Baixa, the Tagus Valley and the eastern Algarve.
"Although the forecast maximum temperatures are lower than those recorded in some episodes this summer, they will be substantially above the average values for the second half of September", the statement adds.
The hot weather is due to "the influence of an anticyclone located to the north of the Azores, extending in a ridge as far as the Bay of Biscay". This will bring "a mass of air of continental origin (hot and dry) over the Iberian Peninsula".
In July, Portugal had already experienced anomalous temperatures, with red warnings in most of the country and the government declaring an alert situation. That situation extended to the rest of continental Europe during July.
A report by the non-profit organisation Climate Central concluded that the continent was "the most abnormally warm region on the planet". Almost nine in ten Europeans lived through an entire month of "dangerous heat".

These blood thinners may have an unexpected benefit for Alzheimer’s patients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:48:31 UTC
18:48:31 KST

These blood thinners may have an unexpected benefit for Alzheimer’s patients
- Date:
- September 18, 2026
- Source:
- Karolinska Institutet
- Summary:
- Newer blood thinners may do more than prevent strokes in people with Alzheimer’s disease and atrial fibrillation. Researchers found that patients taking NOACs experienced a slower decline in cognitive function than those using warfarin or no blood thinners. The effect was modest each year but could add up over time.
- Share:
People who have both atrial fibrillation and Alzheimer's disease may experience slower cognitive decline when treated with newer NOAC blood thinners, according to research from Karolinska Institutet published in the European Heart Journal.
Atrial fibrillation is a common heart rhythm condition in older adults and also affects many people living with Alzheimer's disease. Doctors often prescribe blood thinners to these patients to reduce the chance of blood clots and stroke. Earlier research has suggested that anticoagulant treatment may lower the risk of developing dementia, but far less is known about whether these drugs influence cognitive decline after Alzheimer's disease has already been diagnosed.
"There are reasons to believe that the treatment could have a positive effect on cognition, for example by improving blood flow and reducing small-scale damage in the brain," says Maria Eriksdotter, professor at the Department of Neurobiology, Care Sciences and Society, Karolinska Institutet, and senior consultant in geriatric medicine at Karolinska University Hospital, who led the study.
Comparing Newer and Older Blood Thinners
Researchers analyzed information from SveDem (Swedish Register for Cognitive Disorders/Dementia), a national quality registry, and included 7,308 people diagnosed with both atrial fibrillation and Alzheimer's disease.
Participants were placed into three matched groups. One group received newer anticoagulants known as NOACs, another was treated with the older blood thinner warfarin (Waran), and the third did not receive any anticoagulant medication.
To track changes in thinking and memory over time, researchers used the standardized Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE).
Slower Cognitive Decline With NOACs
People taking NOACs showed a significantly slower decline in cognitive function than those treated with warfarin or those who received no anticoagulant medication.
The difference amounted to slightly more than 0.2 MMSE points per year. While that change is relatively small over a single year, the researchers say it could become more meaningful if it continues over a longer period.
"The difference is modest for an individual patient from one year to the next, but over a longer period even such an effect could influence how cognitive function develops. Our findings suggest that NOAC treatment may also be significant for cognition in this patient group," says Nanbo Zhu, researcher at the Department of Neurobiology, Care Sciences and Society, Karolinska Institutet.
Lower Risks of Stroke and Other Complications
The potential benefits were not limited to cognition. Compared with people who did not receive anticoagulants, those treated with NOACs also had lower risks of death, stroke, blood clots and fractures.
Warfarin was also associated with lower risks of death, stroke, and blood clots. However, people taking warfarin had a higher risk of major bleeding.
Why the Findings Need Caution
The researchers emphasize that the study has important limitations. Because it was observational, the results cannot prove that NOACs directly caused the slower cognitive decline or the other health benefits seen in the data.
Some factors that could affect both which treatment a patient received and how their health changed over time could not be fully evaluated. The researchers also note that some participants may have switched from one medication to another during the follow-up period.
The study was funded by, amongst others, the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish Brain Foundation, CIMED, ALF project funding and Karolinska Institutet funds. Maria Eriksdotter has participated as a consultant in one-off meetings with BioArctic AB, Roche, Eli Lilly, Biogen/Eisai and Novo Nordisk, and has given lectures at symposia sponsored by Roche and BioArctic/Eisai. No other conflicts of interest are reported.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Karolinska Institutet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Nanbo Zhu, Hong Xu, Sara Garcia-Ptacek, Sumonto Mitra, Maria Eriksdotter. Oral anticoagulants, cognition, and clinical outcomes in atrial fibrillation and Alzheimer’s disease: a Swedish nationwide study. European Heart Journal, 2026; DOI: 10.1093/eurheartj/ehag584

'Coal Eyes' revealed: Ex-Fatah official says he passed on Sinwar's pre-Oct. 7 warning to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:46:08 UTC
18:46:08 KST

Sofian Abu Zaida, a former senior Fatah official, revealed in a video posted to his Facebook account that he is the figure known as "Coal Eyes," the channel through which then-Hamas leader in the Gaza Strip Yahya Sinwar conveyed direct warnings shortly before the October 7 massacre.
As previously reported by Haaretz, Sinwar held a one-on-one meeting with Abu Zaida ("Coal Eyes") in September 2023, several weeks before the attack.
During the conversation, Sinwar demanded that a firm message be conveyed to Israel: "Tell the Israelis that if they do not move forward, I am preparing a huge surprise for them." At the time, Sinwar used the keyword "zilzal" ("earthquake"), an unusual reference that was meant to raise red flags among the intelligence community.
According to Haaretz, Abu Zaida left the conversation shaken and consulted with a close friend, a Palestinian who had emigrated from Gaza to Abu Dhabi and served as an adviser to UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Abu Zaida feared reporting directly to the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), worried he would be accused of cooperating with Sinwar, but at the same time feared for his life if the information was not passed on. As a result, it was decided to convey the message directly to the UAE leader.
UAE president warned Netanyahu about October 7
In mid-September 2023, they held another meeting in Gaza. According to Eldar's report, Sinwar asked Abu Zaida whether the message had been passed on. When he was told that it had not, he calmly said: "Send them a message that I am preparing a surprise from the land of surprises. A terrifying operation. Something unusual," again repeating the word "zilzal."
Abu Zaida quickly left the Gaza Strip and held a private meeting with the adviser in Abu Dhabi. After an in-depth analysis of Sinwar's body language, tone of voice, and the context of his remarks, the two reached a clear conclusion: Sinwar was not making empty threats, but intended to launch a full-scale war.
Following this, the UAE president called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and warned him of the expected attack.
Israel, Hamas negotiated for release of hostages in exchange for prisoners
In a video Abu Zaida published Thursday night, he also noted that lengthy contacts had taken place between Israel and Hamas before October 7 in an effort to reach a deal.
The agreement was intended to secure the release of the four Israeli hostages Hamas was holding at the time, Hadar Goldin, Oron Shaul, Avera Mengistu, and Hisham al-Sayed. In exchange, Israel would release hundreds of Palestinian prisoners, lift the blockade on Gaza, and work to resolve electricity and water issues, basic needs for life in Gaza, which Israel had conditioned on the release of the bodies and prisoners held by the organization.
Abu Zaida also promised to publish additional details in the coming days about the message Sinwar asked him to deliver to the Israeli side in mid-September 2023, just weeks before the October 7 attack.

‘This is a war’: South Africa battles femicide as women’s bodies pile up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:43:43 UTC
18:43:43 KST

‘This is a war’: South Africa battles femicide as women’s bodies pile up
Bodies of nine women have been found in a Johannesburg neighbourhood in two months. Police say there is no clear link between them. But rights groups question the government’s response to gender-based violence.
A ninth woman has been found dead in South Africa’s Ekurhuleni municipality in about two months, intensifying concerns over violence against women and prompting renewed scrutiny of the government’s response to the country’s femicide crisis.
The latest victim was found on Thursday morning in Dawn Park, a residential area of Boksburg, east of Johannesburg. The woman is believed to be in her thirties and was found half-naked and wrapped in a sheet. Police are investigating the deaths but have not established that all nine cases are connected.
“We are still investigating whether we are dealing with one perpetrator or a group of men that are behind the murders of these women,” South African Police Service spokesperson Athlenda Mathe told the Reuters news agency on September 15.
Mathe said investigators were also examining whether copycat crimes could be involved, but stressed that police had so far found no links between the cases.
“This is not an investigation that you can rush, because it is quite complex,” she said. “It may at this stage involve multiple perpetrators. But let’s leave it to the detectives.”
‘It feels like individuals are being hunted’
Princess Eurika Mogane, a commissioner at South Africa’s Commission for Gender Equality, told Al Jazeera the killings reflected a broader crisis facing women across the country.
“This is a war. It feels like individuals are being hunted,” Mogane said. “When someone is the hunter, [the] best thing that you can do is to ensure that the prey are protected.”
The National Shelter Movement of South Africa (NSMSA) says its 24-hour helpline and affiliated shelters are seeing women arrive with increasingly severe experiences of abuse, including death threats, stalking, strangulation, coercive control and repeated violations of protection orders.
“These are not isolated incidents,” the organisation told Al Jazeera in an emailed statement. “They are indicators of a broader crisis in which violence against women has become deeply normalised in many communities.”
‘Adjust our lives to perpetrators’
Police advice urging women not to walk or run alone and to avoid isolated areas following the killings has prompted criticism.
“A lot of the women in South Africa right now are saying, ‘You are basically telling us to adjust our lives to perpetrators,’” Mogane said.
The NSMSA said women alter their routes, avoid travelling at specific times, share their locations with loved ones and restrict their movements to try to stay safe.
“Safety messaging should not imply that women can prevent violence simply by making different choices,” the organisation told Al Jazeera. “The responsibility for violence lies with perpetrators, while the responsibility for protection lies with society and the state.”
Among the women discovered dead was Elizabeth Moselakgomo, a 38-year-old mother and runner who disappeared after leaving home in the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg, for her usual run about 5:30 pm on September 9.
Her eight-year-old daughter raised the alarm when her mother did not return. Moselakgomo was found dead three days later on September 12.
Nokukhanya Khanyile-Lenake, a specialist paediatrician and mental health advocate, told Al Jazeera that women, as it is, take multiple precautions to protect themselves “from the dangers of gender-based violence”.
What particularly struck her, Khanyile-Lenake said, was that Moselakgomo’s eight-year-old daughter “knew the danger signs and did the right thing”, realising her mother had not returned and notifying other family members.
“And that still wasn’t enough,” she said. “As women, we’ve done the maximum to the point where we’re even teaching our young children what to do, and it’s still not enough.
“What I saw was a woman who chose to take care of herself and make a decision she’s probably made a thousand times before, which is just to go for a run,” Khanyile-Lenake added.
‘If I leave today, can I survive?’
The killings come less than a year after South Africa classified gender-based violence and femicide as a national disaster in November 2025. South Africa’s parliament says the country’s femicide rate is five times the global average.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has pledged that perpetrators will face justice, while authorities say police patrols and deployments have been increased in high-risk areas.
But Mogane questioned what had materially changed since the national disaster classification.
“The declaration is there. But what progress has there been?” she said, pointing to the need for more forensic facilities and shelters for survivors.
The NSMSA said shelters continue to face inadequate and inconsistent funding, rising demand and capacity constraints, while survivors report delays in police responses and difficulties obtaining or enforcing protection orders.
Leaving an abusive relationship can itself be one of the most dangerous periods for a woman, the organisation said, with survivors often simultaneously needing police protection, emergency accommodation, transport, healthcare, childcare and financial support.
“For many women, the fundamental question remains unchanged: ‘If I leave today, can I survive financially, find safe accommodation, and remain protected from my abuser?’” the NSMSA said.
Al Jazeera asked the South African government what measures it has taken since the national disaster classification and for its response to criticism of its handling of violence against women, but had not received a response by the time of publication.

Anthropic says AI systems moving towards building themselves

Anthropic says AI systems moving towards building themselves
- Anthropic revealed its AI system Claude now leads 26% of its research and development, working on over 90% of tasks with human supervision but not fully autonomously yet.
- Concerns rise as AI models increasingly self-improve, potentially making human control harder and sparking calls for slowing AI development due to risks like job loss and environmental impact.
- Anthropic aims to provide transparency on AI progress amid fears of losing control, with about 30,000 AI agents active and plans for a major IPO in 2026, despite regulatory worries.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic said on Sept 17 that AI systems are increasingly capable of building future versions of themselves, adding to mounting concerns about the dangers of the powerful technology.
The debate over the risks of AI has intensified in recent months, fuelled by several incidents and apocalyptic warnings from industry professionals.
Anthropic said its Claude chatbot now leads more than a quarter of its research and development work, and collaborates with human staff on more than 90 per cent of tasks.
The company said it was publishing the information to give the public, third parties and governments “better visibility into the pace of AI development” as the world “considers slowing” its pace.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called in September for AI development to slow down, with rapid advances in the technology fuelling concerns over job losses and the soaring energy demand and environmental impact of data centres.
Fears that designers of AI agents could lose control of their creations also mounted after several models from Anthropic and rival OpenAI reportedly broke out of their confined environments on their own, accessed the internet and intruded on websites and platforms.
“Models accelerating their own development could make it more challenging for humans to understand or control these systems,” Anthropic said in a report.
“It is therefore important to share these metrics to understand how close the world is to reaching recursive self-improvement (a model fully autonomously building its successor).”
As of August, Claude leads 26 per cent of Anthropic’s research and development, meaning it can complete most of a task from start to finish with human supervision.
Anthropic said Claude could not yet operate “fully autonomously”.
The firm said it had about 30,000 AI agents doing research and engineering work, referring to bots that have the potential to carry out tasks.
Anthropic is expected to beat OpenAI to the public markets with a blockbuster IPO later in 2026, despite concerns around industry regulation. AFP

Asian Games | OCA explains absence of traditional athletes' village at Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:41:59 CST
18:41:59 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) on Friday explained the decision not to build a traditional athletes' village for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, saying that while such a facility would be preferable, organizers also needed flexibility.
"We wish that we have an athlete village, number one. But, number two, we also have to be flexible," OCA Director General Husain A H Z Al-Musallam said at a press conference.
He said organizers needed to consider the circumstances of the host country and plans for facilities after the Games, rather than automatically constructing a dedicated village.
Nagoya is instead using existing hotels and other accommodation, along with temporary container-style housing at Garden Pier and a cruise ship at Kinjo Pier. The arrangement was adopted after organizers decided against building a purpose-built athletes' village, with the cruise ship serving as floating accommodation.
"Every host, we have to look to what is the actual situation inside the host country. What is their plan for after the Games?" Al-Musallam said, noting that the approach could differ from one Games to another.
He cited previous Asian Games as examples of how dedicated athletes' villages can be repurposed after an event. The village built for the 2006 Doha Asian Games, he said, was converted into a medical center, while the athletes' village for the Hangzhou Asian Games was later sold to the public.
He pointed to Nagoya's existing residential infrastructure, saying the priority was to provide athletes with suitable accommodation rather than follow a fixed model.
Mohammad Tayyab Ikram, chairman of the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games Coordination Committee, said organizers did not want to leave a "white elephant" after the Games.
"It was not easy discussions, but it was also not a compromise because then we found very unique alternatives," Ikram said, defending the use of container accommodation.
"We are gathering for sport," Al-Musallam said, stressing that athletes should be able to compete in a safe and suitable environment.
On preparations for a possible typhoon affecting the region next Monday, Ikram said disaster management, particularly typhoon preparedness, had been discussed at coordination meetings throughout the past three to four years. He said every competition and non-competition venue had its own emergency plan, with large shelters prepared near Garden Pier, where some 3,000 to 4,000 athletes are staying, as well as for those accommodated on the cruise ship.
Al-Musallam also said six nations had expressed interest in hosting the 23rd Asian Games, including India and the Philippines. The OCA Executive Board will establish an evaluation committee to visit the interested countries next year before drawing up a shortlist and conducting a further evaluation closer to those Games. ■
