Xinhua Commentary: History warns against Japan's return to militarism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:41:57 CST
18:41:57 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Ninety-five years ago, on Sept. 18, 1931, Japan launched an act of aggression in northeast China that marked the start of Japan's 14-year invasion of China, one of the darkest chapters in modern Chinese history.
The smoke of war has long dissipated, but the lessons of that history remain relevant. Remembering the September 18 Incident today is not about perpetuating hatred. It is about understanding how militarism once led Japan down the path of aggression, and why any sign of that path being revisited deserves vigilance.
History shows that Japanese militarists repeatedly invoked so-called "existential crises" to justify expansion. The occupation of northeast China was presented as necessary for Japan's survival.
Now, Japan's incumbent leader has wantonly claimed that a so-called "Taiwan contingency" could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, and has even threatened the use of force against China. The gimmick of invoking an "existential crisis" to justify military intervention is reminiscent of the logic once used by Japanese militarists to pursue aggression in the past.
In fact, the resurgence of militaristic tendencies in Japan in recent years deserves close attention.
After World War II, Japan adopted a pacifist constitution and committed itself to a peaceful path. Yet some forces within Japan have failed to genuinely reflect on the country's history of aggression and have expressed dissatisfaction with the postwar international arrangements. In recent years, Japan has taken a series of steps to expand its military role and capabilities.
Japan has significantly increased defense spending, strengthened its military-industrial capabilities, deployed intermediate and long-range missiles and expanded the scope of the Self-Defense Forces' activities. It has also eased restrictions on arms exports and sought to revise its security doctrines. These moves have raised concerns about Japan's departure from its postwar security framework and the principle of an exclusively defense-oriented policy.
Japan has become increasingly involved in matters concerning the Taiwan Strait and the South China Sea. Under the pretext of building a "free and open" region, it has strengthened security cooperation with other countries and sought to bring external military forces and mechanisms into the Asia-Pacific. Such moves risk increasing confrontation and adding uncertainty that threatens regional peace and stability.
At the same time, efforts to distort or downplay wartime history remain a concern. Visits by Japanese politicians to the Yasukuni Shrine, revisions to history textbooks and changes to historical public narratives have drawn criticism for downplaying or distorting Japan's wartime aggression. Such practices can mislead the public and make it more difficult for Japan to face its history and build trust with neighboring countries that suffered from Japan's aggression.
The failure of the international community at that time to effectively restrain Japan's aggression offers a lasting lesson: threats to peace must be taken seriously before they become irreversible.
For Japan, the choice is ultimately about what kind of role it wants to play in the region. The Japanese people once witnessed their country being transformed into a war machine under militarism and suffered the consequences of war. Recent anti-war protests in Japan have also reflected strong opposition among the public to sliding back to the militarist path.
If Japan's policymakers ignore concerns at home and abroad, disregard the concerns of neighboring countries and move away from their international obligations, they will only plunge Japan into an abyss.
History moves forward, but its lessons remain. Any attempt to whitewash aggression, deny wartime crimes or revive militarism runs against the hard-won lessons of the past. Remembering Sept. 18 means ensuring that those lessons are not forgotten, and that the tragedies of history are never repeated. ■

China Focus: China aims to cement its place at forefront of biomedical innovation with new 5-year plan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:41:57 CST
18:41:57 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China on Friday released a five-year plan for its pharmaceutical industry, outlining targets such as keeping biomedical research, development and application at the global forefront by 2030. This move signals the country's resolve to turn drug innovation into a strategic strength.
The plan, jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and nine other authorities, calls for a major leap in the core competitiveness and international influence of China's pharmaceutical industry from 2026 to 2030. It is hoped that core technologies in key fields will see systematic breakthroughs during this period.
Specifically, first-in-class drugs developed in China should account for at least 25 percent of the global total, with the number of innovative drugs approved for market ranking among the world leaders. The plan expects the innovative drug sector to grow at an average annual rate of at least 20 percent.
China also expects the biomedical sector to take shape as an emerging pillar industry at an accelerated pace.
The combined revenue of pharmaceutical enterprises above a designated scale threshold -- an annual main business revenue of 20 million yuan (about 2.96 million U.S. dollars) -- should reach at least 3.5 trillion yuan by 2030, the plan says.
The number of companies with an annual revenue exceeding 10 billion yuan should grow to 50. At least five Chinese drugs should achieve global annual sales exceeding 1 billion U.S. dollars, according to the plan.
The biomedical sector is one of six emerging pillar industries China has identified for strategic development, alongside integrated circuits, aerospace, low-altitude economy, new energy storage and intelligent robotics. The combined output of these sectors, which stood at nearly 6 trillion yuan in 2025, is expected to surpass 10 trillion yuan by 2030.
The plan arrives at a pivotal moment as China's pharmaceutical industry shifts rapidly from its traditional identity as a supplier of active pharmaceutical ingredients and a large consumption market toward a new phase defined by the export of innovative drugs.
In the first half of this year, 38 innovative drugs were approved in China, of which 31, or more than 80 percent, were domestically developed. As of the end of 2025, China had 4,751 innovative drugs in the pipeline, accounting for one third of the global total and placing it first in the world for drugs under development.
Moreover, China's innovative drugs have gained wider global reach. The total value of overseas licensing deals for innovative Chinese drugs has surpassed 120 billion U.S. dollars this year, up 36 percent year on year.
The broader industry also showed great vitality. Value-added output of China's pharmaceutical enterprises above the 20-million-yuan revenue threshold grew 6.4 percent year on year in the first half of this year.
When interpreting the plan, the MIIT said China's aging population and growing demand for whole-lifecycle health management are placing new and higher demands on the pharmaceutical industry, underscoring the urgency of stronger top-level planning to accelerate innovation-driven development.
The plan lays out 25 priority tasks across eight areas, including strengthening original innovation capacity and accelerating the development of frontier technologies and products.
Efforts will be made to deepen AI-driven upgrades and advance digital and intelligent transformation, and international industrial cooperation will also expand to build an open and mutually beneficial new pattern, according to the plan.
The 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) will be pivotal five years in which China's biomedical industry makes the leap from quantitative to qualitative growth, Li Yan, a researcher with the Development Research Center of the State Council, said.
Accelerating shifts in global biomedical technology paradigms, a maturing multi-tiered domestic healthcare system and steadily improving homegrown research and development capabilities are converging to create a historic opportunity for the industry, Li said. ■

SHANGHAI, September 18. /TASS Correspondent Andrey Popov/. The Russian Maritime Register of Shipping has the professional expertise to cooperate actively with Chinese companies on the Northern Sea Route, the classification society's CEO Sergey Kulikov said in an interview with TASS.
"The Register is a recognized expert and a global leader in classification and technical monitoring of vessels designed to operate in difficult ice conditions, including the Northern Sea Route," he said. "The prospects for cooperation with Chinese companies are quite wide - from classification and technical support of projects for the new Arctic fleet to capabilities assessment of ships that are already in operation."
The Register's ice classes regulations are based on the unique practical experience of the Russian Arctic shipping, he continued. "The company has also announced plans to expand transportation along NSR and to use Arctic-class container ships."
"As cargo traffic increases, the demand for specialized fleet of high ice classes will be growing like the demand in the efficient use of existing vessels," the Register's CEO said. "Here, the Registry has specific technical solutions."
The Northern Sea Route is a shipping route and the main transportation link in the Russian Arctic. It runs along Russia's northern shores through the Arctic Ocean seas from the Kara Gate Strait to Providence Bay. The route is 5,600 km long.
About the Register
The Russian Maritime Register of Shipping has been successfully operating in China since 2003. The city of Tianjin was the entry point to the Chinese market. During repair of ships, the Register carries out technical supervision: it reviews technical solutions, monitors repair operations and equipment replacement, participates in necessary inspections and tests. In 2014, the classification society established a branch office in Shanghai. On September 16, an office was opened in Zhoushan City (eastern Zhejiang Province).

Peace is precious: China marks start of war against Japanese aggression
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:41:42 CST
18:41:42 KST

A ceremony to commemorate the September 18 Incident is held at the square of the 9.18 Historical Museum in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, Sept. 18, 2026. A bell tolled at the square of the 9.18 Historical Museum in Shenyang on Friday to commemorate the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident, which marked the start of the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. (Xinhua/Han He)
SHENYANG, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Air-raid sirens wailed. Traffic halted. Pedestrians stood still. At 9:18 a.m. on Friday, the city of Shenyang paused in a three-minute silence to mourn those killed in the Japanese invasion of China and to cherish the hard-won peace.
Friday marks the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident, the start of China's 14-year war of resistance against Japanese aggression. On Sept. 18, 1931, Japanese troops blew up a section of railway near Shenyang under their control and accused Chinese troops of sabotage, using this as a pretext for their later attack that night on barracks near Shenyang, launching the premeditated invasion of China.
Since 1995, Shenyang, the capital city of northeast China's Liaoning Province, has sounded air-raid sirens annually on this day to commemorate the incident.
"Those few minutes when everything stopped for the sirens reminded me that our everyday life is built on hard-won peace," said Li Xuyang, an employee of Brilliance Auto based in Shenyang.
At a ceremony held Friday morning at the 9.18 Historical Museum, which was built near the site of the explosion, 14 representatives from all walks of life solemnly tolled the Bell of Warning. The 14 chimes echoed through the air, symbolizing the 14 arduous years of the Chinese people's fight against Japanese invaders.
Li Hongzhong, vice chairman of the National People's Congress Standing Committee and a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, attended the ceremony and delivered a speech.
The Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression marked China's first complete victory against foreign aggression in modern times, Li said. He called for drawing lessons from history to light the way forward, stressing the importance of upholding the Party's overall leadership, advancing Chinese modernization, and contributing to building a community with a shared future for mankind.
"I learned about the September 18 Incident in textbooks. Hearing the bell today, I want to know even more about what children of my age went through back then," said Ma Zihao, a sixth grader in Shenyang.
"Seeing today's children able to go to school without a worry makes me feel that the sacrifices back then were not in vain," said Yang Huafeng, a 93-year-old veteran of the war who attended the event. "I hope they remember the martyrs who laid down their lives for this country and understand how precious peace is."
The commemorations in Shenyang anchored nationwide events marking the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident. The Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-1945) broke out first and lasted the longest in the World Anti-Fascist War. Over 14 years, some 35 million Chinese were killed or wounded.
"The annual observances give the younger generation a chance to rethink the relationship between war and their own lives. Only by remembering the suffering war brought to ordinary people can we truly appreciate how precious peace is and what it takes to protect it," said Gao Jian, a researcher at the 9.18 Historical Museum. ■

Russia shares AI-generated Putin selfie as use of artificial content spreads among Europe's politicians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:41:41 UTC
18:41:41 KST

The Russian embassy in South Africa recently shared an AI-generated image of BRICS leaders. It's part of a growing trend of public figures and institutions using AI in their communication, which researchers say can undermine public trust.
The Russian embassy in South Africa has shared a picture that appears to show Russian President Vladimir Putin taking a group selfie with the 10 BRICS world leaders during September's summit.
The 18th BRICS Summit took place in New Delhi, India, on 12 and 13 September.
The verified X account posted the picture, which garnered more than 2 million views, alongside the caption "BRICS is a superpower".
However, this selfie is not real.
No credible news organisation has published the image as real, and the official website of the summit did not share it either.
The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, has also run it through image detectors, which revealed it to be AI-generated.
For instance, after running the image through OpenAI, the tool revealed to have found "a SynthID watermark that originated from OpenAI".
Furthermore, the official logo and slogan of BRICS India 2026 do not match those portrayed in the AI-generated picture.
This summit's theme was "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability", while the AI-generated picture states "Stronger together for a brighter tomorrow".
At no moment does the Russian embassy in South Africa disclose that the picture was generated using AI.
A rising phenomenon among politicians
While the image appears harmless, it is becoming increasingly common for European politicians and public institutions to publish AI-generated images without labelling them as such.
Sometimes they are used for disingenuous purposes, and often they can erode trust among the public.
Recently, the leader of the Portuguese far-right Chega party, André Ventura, posted an AI-generated video of a woman with six fingers, seemingly to push an anti-immigration narrative.
The video depicts a hijabi woman supposedly looking up and down at a white, non-hijabi woman wearing a short dress, alongside the caption "if it were the other way around, it'd be racist and xenophobic. They come to our countries... Why do they not get used to respecting our values?"
Despite many comments from users stating the video was clearly AI, Ventura didn't disclose that the video was AI-generated, and it remains active on his profile as of the time of publication.
The phenomenon of politicians using AI-generated content to publicise their policies isn't confined to Europe: high-profile figures such as US President Donald Trump are infamously using more and more AI-generated images and videos in their communications and on their social media channels.
What are the consequences of politicians' AI use?
A 2026 study from the European non-profit AI Forensics showed that AI is being used not only to create photorealistic images "but also for stylised, cartoonish imagery to reinforce key campaign messages, including anti-immigrant narratives".
The research, which focused on the French municipal elections, found that the use of AI remains most pronounced among right and far-right parties, and that the lack of disclosure could put public trust in the electoral process in danger.
Most of the material looked at by researchers carried no explicit AI disclaimer, even when watermarks were present.
Since August of this year, the EU's AI Act has generally required realistic AI-generated or manipulated material to be clearly disclosed as such.
"Providers of generative AI have to ensure that AI-generated content is identifiable," the Act states. "On top of that, certain AI-generated content should be clearly and visibly labelled, namely deepfakes and text published with the purpose to inform the public on matters of public interest."

Russian scientists identify earlier unknown warm surface current in Arctic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:40:01 UTC
18:40:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. Russian scientists identified an earlier unknown current of more than 1,000 kilometers long in waters of the Barents and the Kara Seas, which transports eastbound big amounts of warm and salty water from the Atlantic Ocean into the Russian Arctic. The newly identified water stream was named the Keldysh current after the Russian scientific vessel, the Russian Science Foundation's press service said.
"The main surprise is that part of the Atlantic water, unlike it was believed earlier, does not sink into the depths north of Novaya Zemlya. It remains at the surface and forms an extended current that crosses the Kara Sea's north. We have managed to see a unified picture only after merging results of numerous expeditions over almost 30 years," the Russian Science Foundation's press service quoted MIPT's chief researcher Alexander Osadchiev as saying.
The scientist and his colleagues discovered the phenomenon while analyzing data collected over recent three decades off the Akademik Mstislav Keldysh Russian research vessel and other scientific vessels in the Barents and the Kara Seas. During those expeditions, scientists repeatedly reported areas with abnormally warm and salty surface water, while its origin remained unclear.
To find that water's source, the scientists merged data, obtained during 25 marine expeditions in the Russian Arctic between 1995 and 2024. While analyzing the data, they studied how water temperatures and salinity were changing at different depths in waters between Novaya Zemlya and Franz Josef Land, in the St. Anna Trench, and at the Kara Sea's continental slope.
The calculations, carried out by the scientists, indicated the existence of a near-surface current some 50-100 meters thick, which transports warm Atlantic waters to the Barents and the Kara Seas. It emerges at approximately 77-78 degrees north latitude north of Novaya Zemlya and then moves along the archipelago's northern coast towards the northeast. After that, it turns passing north of the St. Anna Trench eastern slope and approaches the continental slope, moving on towards the Laptev Sea.
The scientists say that this current's length is about 1,000 kilometers, and it is 50-100 kilometers wide. Thus, the Keldysh current has a strong influence on the seasonal growth and thawing of sea ice, which is specifically true in the St. Anna Trench's northern part. Noteworthy, related anomalies are observed throughout the year, the scientists say. This needs to be taken into account in assessing changing conditions of the Russian Arctic ice cover, they said in conclusion.

Bolivia: New cat species discovered by scientists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

Bolivia: New cat species discovered by scientists
September 18, 2026
Scientists in Bolivia have identified a small wild cat with a leopard-like coat as a previously unknown species.
Local communities call the feline "tilcayo," a nickname that inspired the cat's new scientific designation: Leopardus tilcayo.
Biologist and National Geographic explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz described the discovery as a "remarkable event, because a new wild cat species hasn't been described in 100 years."
The last feline species to be discovered was the Uruguayan pampas cat in 1923.
What do we know about Leopardus tilcayo?
The cat was found in Bolivia's Yungas forest, a remote region on the eastern slope of the Andes mountains.
The animal measures around 18 inches (46 centimeters) long and weighs around 3 pounds (1.4 kilograms), making it smaller than the average domestic cat.
"Its fur is light brown ... with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body," Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
According to National Geographic, Nogales-Ascarrunz first came upon the animal in 2016 after receiving a call from a local wildlife sanctuary.
The organization said at the time that it had been handed "a weird cat."
"I took a hundred pictures of it," Nogales-Ascarrunz told National Geographic. "I was so fascinated."
It was a few years later that she realized the cat she had photographed was unlike any previously seen.
Species finds its place in cat family tree
Research on the new species was published this week in the journal Current Biology.
Using genetic analysis in collaboration with geneticist Eduardo Eizirik, co-lead authors Nogales-Ascarrunz and the University of Antwerp's Jonas Lescroart were able to place the feline in its specific category in the cat family tree.
Nogales-Ascarrunz said that a pair of tilcayos have undergone whole-genome sequencing and are the only such creatures found so far.
"So far, it's only been detected in Bolivia" and not "anywhere else on the planet," Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
"Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats ... there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message," said Eizirik, who is an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.
"There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them."

Subsidy for the 2026/27 heating season: who needs to contact the Pension Fund and when
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:39:57 EEST
18:39:57 KST

Subsidy for the 2026/27 heating season: who needs to contact the Pension Fund and when
Kyiv • UNN
For most recipients, the subsidy will be recalculated automatically, but certain categories must submit an application by November 30.
At the start of the 2026/27 heating season, the Pension Fund of Ukraine (PFU) will recalculate housing subsidies. Most households that are already receiving assistance will not need to submit documents again: the payment amount will be determined automatically. This also applies to those who were granted a subsidy of UAH 0 for the non-heating season. At the same time, some citizens will need to contact the PFU themselves before winter.
What is needed for this and how to do it is explained by UNN.
A housing subsidy is targeted state assistance for households whose income is insufficient to pay for housing and utility services independently. Its amount is not fixed: the PFU calculates the payment separately for each family, depending on income, household composition, the set of utility services, and the established social standards.
Who is eligible to apply to the PFU for a subsidy
A new application must be submitted by those applying for a subsidy for the first time, those who were denied a subsidy for the non-heating season, and households in which the composition or social status of family members has changed, or other circumstances affecting eligibility for assistance have arisen. Tenants, households where fewer people actually live than are registered, internally displaced persons (IDPs) in the event of a change in their actual place of residence, and those seeking a subsidy to purchase liquefied gas or solid or liquid stove fuel must also apply separately.
For those seeking a payment from the beginning of the season, the deadlines are important. If the documents are submitted during the first two months of the heating season, that is, by November 30 inclusive, the subsidy may be granted from the beginning of the season, but not earlier than the date on which the right to assistance arose. If the application is submitted later, the subsidy will be granted starting from the month in which the application was submitted.
What documents are needed to apply for subsidies
The basic package consists of an application for a housing subsidy and a declaration of household income and expenses. Other documents depend on the specific situation.
For rented housing, a lease agreement may be required; for IDPs applying for assistance at their actual place of residence, an IDP certificate may be required. If there is a debt for utility services, applicants may provide an agreement on its restructuring, a document confirming repayment of the debt, or a court ruling on opening proceedings to challenge the debt. An income certificate is submitted if the relevant information is not available in state information resources.
An application can be submitted at a PFU service center, through a ЦНАП or an authorized representative of a territorial community, by mail, or online via the Pension Fund's web portal or mobile application and the Diia portal.
How the subsidy amount is calculated
The amount of assistance is the difference between the cost of housing and utility services within the established social norms and standards and the mandatory payment of the specific household. In other words, the state does not compensate the entire amount shown on the bill: normative consumption is used in the calculation, while the family must pay part of the expenses independently.
The mandatory payment percentage depends on per-person income. To determine it, the household's average monthly income is divided by the number of its members. The resulting amount is compared with the subsistence minimum per person as of January 1, 2026, which is UAH 3,209. The result is divided by two and multiplied by 15%. Accordingly, the lower the per-person income, the smaller the share of the mandatory payment.
For a subsidy from the beginning of the 2026/27 heating season, the PFU takes into account household income for the first and second quarters of 2026. For pensioners, the pension accrued for August 2026 is taken into account.
Why a subsidy may not be granted
One of the typical problems is incorrect or incomplete information in the application and declaration. If data on household composition, income, property, or actual place of residence does not match the information in the registers, the applicant may be asked to clarify it. If some documents are missing, they must be submitted within the specified time limit.
A separate reason is utility debt. A subsidy may not be granted if overdue debt of more than three months exceeds 40 non-taxable minimum incomes, i.e. UAH 680. At the same time, this is not a hopeless situation: the debt can be repaid, restructured, or challenged in court, with supporting documents submitted to the PFU.
Eligibility for a subsidy is also affected by the applicant’s financial situation. Among the criteria checked by the PFU are purchases and other transactions defined by law totaling more than UAH 100,000 over a 12-month period, a deposit exceeding UAH 100,000, transactions involving the purchase of foreign currency or bank metals totaling more than UAH 50,000, as well as ownership of a certain number of residential properties or a relatively new vehicle. Exceptions are provided for a number of these restrictions.
Another mistake is failing to notify the PFU about changes that may affect the payment. A subsidy recipient must inform the Fund of circumstances specified by law within 30 days. Therefore, before the heating season, it is worth checking whether the information about registered persons and those actually living in the house or apartment, information about property, and other circumstances is up to date. Those who have already been granted a subsidy and have no grounds for submitting a new application do not need to apply again before winter.

Anthropic's Claude helped cybersecurity researchers breach OpenAI: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:39:21 UTC
18:39:21 KST

Dilara Hamit
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
A three-person cybersecurity research team used Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 to exploit vulnerabilities in an OpenAI community forum, take control of employee accounts and demonstrate access to the company’s private code repository.
The operation began on July 23 and was carried out by researchers from Hacktron AI, who disclosed the vulnerabilities to OpenAI and stopped testing without examining the company’s source code.
The Wall Street Journal, which interviewed the researchers and first reported the incident, said OpenAI paid the team $6,500 for its discovery.
The researchers reported the OpenAI-side vulnerability through the company’s bug-bounty programme. Testing of the third-party forum software itself, however, was outside the scope of OpenAI’s bounty programme.
The researchers, Harsh Jaiswal, Mohan Pedhapati and Rahul Maini, published a detailed technical account explaining how they combined a flaw in the software behind OpenAI’s community forum with a separate problem in the company’s sign-on system.
The attack began at community.openai.com, a help forum powered by the third-party discussion platform Discourse.
Hacktron found that certain uploaded image formats were processed through ImageMagick and a vulnerable version of the image-decoding library libheif. The vulnerability allowed specially prepared image data to trigger remote code execution, meaning an attacker could potentially run commands on the forum’s server.
A separate identity-management flaw then allowed the researchers to move from a compromised forum session to ChatGPT and Codex accounts belonging to active forum members, including OpenAI employees.
Because those accounts could be connected to other services, the potential reach extended to platforms including GitHub, Slack and Outlook, according to Hacktron.
To demonstrate the impact without reading confidential material, the researchers instructed a compromised employee’s Codex account, which was connected to OpenAI’s GitHub organization, to open a harmless pull request in the company’s private “openai/openai” monorepo, the central digital vault housing the core source code for all its AI systems
The team said it stopped testing immediately afterward and updated its report to OpenAI.

Harris was positive on the pitch, calling it “really exciting” and pointing to climate and cybersecurity as two issues where the EU and Canada could cooperate.

“I'm less concerned about what you call it, and more enthused by the idea that Canada and the European Union want to work together on a program of substance,” he said.

Anthropic and OpenAI hunt for smaller data center deals, sources tell CNBC, in race to deploy AI capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:38:17 UTC
18:38:17 KST

Anthropic and OpenAI are hunting for smaller AI data center deals, sources told CNBC, as the race to access the infrastructure needed to deploy workloads ramps up.
The two AI labs have both inked huge deals for AI data centers in the past year for facilities of multi-hundred-megawatt and gigawatt capacity, but sources have said those companies are now also looking for compute capacity deals for much smaller deployments of 20-30 MW.
Anthropic has sounded out agreements within that range across the U.K. and the Nordics, four people familiar with the conversations, who asked to remain anonymous when discussing private business dealings, told CNBC. OpenAI had been exploring opportunities for those smaller capacity deployments in the Nordics, two of the sources said.
One source said they were also familiar with talks involving Anthropic and OpenAI about U.S. capacity deployments at that scale.
Both companies have announced a flurry of AI infrastructure deals over the past year as they've looked to train and serve their models to end users. Deals to secure smaller allocations of compute allow companies to deploy workloads faster amid the AI boom.
"We're building a diversified compute portfolio to meet growing demand for AI around the world," an OpenAI spokesperson told CNBC.
"Different workloads need different infrastructure, so we have conversations with a range of partners and assess opportunities based on our requirements, performance, reliability, timing and cost," they added. "We don't comment on specific commercial discussions."
Anthropic did not comment when approached by CNBC.
'Speed to usable capacity'
Both AI labs typically rent compute capacity from data center operators and neoclouds and have sought large-scale, long-term agreements.
Anthropic inked a roughly $45 billion cloud deal with Nscale, which will see the AI lab rent around 460 MW of compute capacity at a data center development in West Virginia, two people familiar with the matter told CNBC in August.
OpenAI has said it surpassed the original commitment of 10 GW to its Stargate AI infrastructure project in April and has since committed to developing a further 3 GW in Georgia and 8 GW in Ohio.
Huge data center projects in the U.S. and further afield are increasingly facing pushback from local communities. The sector is also under pressure in much of Europe, where available land and power are in short supply.
Smaller capacity deals are often attractive because of "speed to usable capacity," Jabez Tan, head of research at Structure Research, told CNBC.
"Securing a few megawatts at an existing powered site can be more practical than waiting for a much larger block in one location," he said. "For workloads that can operate across separate sites, a collection of smaller deployments can add up to substantial capacity."
Shift to inference
Training AI models requires large amounts of computing power to process huge quantities of data, but deploying those systems day-to-day — a process known as inference — can be done with smaller clusters of chips.
"Training a large model typically requires many chips working closely together," Tan said. "Many inference workloads can instead serve separate requests across multiple smaller clusters, opening up more locations."
The shift matters as more AI compute moves from training models to serving them in production. The amount of capacity being used to serve inference is therefore expected to rise.
The proportion of total data center capacity used for inference workloads is expected to overtake training workloads in 2027, according to a report by real estate company JLL. In 2025, inference made up 9% of global workloads in data centers compared to 14% for training, the report said. By 2030, inference is projected to use 37% of that capacity, compared to just 13% for training.
In February, it was announced that Nvidia would collaborate with several data center stakeholders to study smaller-scale data centers designed for distributed inference.
U.S. company Crusoe, which built a huge data center complex in Texas used by OpenAI, is now investing in smaller data centers, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday. Those facilities will be faster and cheaper than larger builds, which are facing delays across the U.S., the Journal said. Crusoe did not respond to a request for comment.
Crusoe is one of several neoclouds that have seen business boom amid the AI buildout. The company announced on Thursday it had raised a $3.9 billion funding round at a $30.9 billion post-money valuation.

Authorities had offered a reward of 30 million Malawian kwacha, about $17,000, for information leading to her rescue and the arrest and conviction of those responsible.
Police have not disclosed a possible motive for the kidnapping or whether anyone else was involved.

Nestlé Weighing All Options After Kremlin Takes Control of Its Russian Business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:36:15 UTC
18:36:15 KST

The Kremlin said on Friday that hostile actions by "unfriendly" countries played a role in its decision to take control of the Russian assets of Swiss food giant Nestlé and French retailer Auchan.
The move, announced in a decree signed by President Vladimir Putin, is the most significant action against Western firms since the seizure of the Russian assets of French dairy company Danone and Danish brewer Carlsberg in 2023.
"We are talking about European companies from unfriendly countries," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters, adding that these states were "currently involved in the most active manner in military actions against our country."
Peskov did not name France or Switzerland specifically, but Russia says Western countries that supply weapons to Ukraine, including France, are effectively parties to the conflict.
Switzerland does not provide arms to Ukraine but has angered Russia by imposing sanctions against it. The Swiss government expressed concern about the seizure of Nestlé and said it was supporting the company in its efforts to reverse the decision.
Nestlé, maker of Nescafé coffee and KitKat chocolate bars, said it was assessing the situation.
"Nestle is committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees," the company said in a statement.
It declined to comment further on what action it was considering. Nestle shares were down 2.4%.
Russia has steadily tightened its grip on foreign-owned assets since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. A 2023 decree signed by Putin allows assets from countries Moscow deems "unfriendly" to be placed under temporary administration.
Moscow has also used the framework to raise funds through forced sales, exit taxes and discounts, while rewarding Kremlin-linked insiders.
According to a 2025 estimate by Moscow law firm NSP, the Russian state has seized more than $50 billion of private property, including assets belonging to foreign companies that exited Russia, since the start of the war.
The Russian assets of Nestlé and Auchan were transferred to temporary control by L.E.V. Management, a little-known company with no public profile.
Auchan, which runs 230 stores and an online business in Russia, employing about 30,000 people, declined to comment.
Nestlé has six factories in Russia producing coffee, pet care and infant formula products. It generated sales of about 2 billion Swiss francs ($2.4 billion) in Russia in 2021, the last year it released figures, and has about 7,000 employees there.
That amounted to about 2% of group sales, although analysts estimate the contribution has declined since Nestlé scaled back operations in Russia.
Nestlé has suspended most sales, non-essential imports and exports, advertising and capital investment in Russia, said Bank Vontobel analyst Jean-Philippe Bertschy, who estimates the country now accounts for around 1% of group sales.
"While negative for sentiment and raising the prospect of an asset impairment or unfavourable disposal, we expect a marginal financial impact, given Russia's limited contribution to group sales," he said.
The newspaper Kommersant previously reported that a company called KS Logistika asked Putin to place Nestlé's assets under temporary administration, arguing that existing management was preventing expansion.
In previous cases, temporary administration has often been followed by state expropriation, with assets later transferred to Kremlin-linked individuals or companies. Peskov said only temporary administration was under consideration for now.
Other Western companies have sold Russian assets or handed them to local managers in response to sanctions or the threat of state intervention.
Nestlé has defended its continued presence in Russia by arguing that it supplies essential food products.
Kepler Cheuvreux analyst Jon Cox said the development did not bode well for Nestlé.
"Ultimately, Nestlé may end up losing those assets — around 2% of its sales and cash tied up in Russia — for the foreseeable future and any compensation is unlikely to be an offset," he said.

Russia’s First Duma Election Since the Full-Scale Invasion: What’s the Significance?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:33:06 UTC
18:33:06 KST

Voting opened Sept. 18 in Russia’s first State Duma election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has explicitly framed the ballot as a national demonstration of unity and unwavering support for his war effort. Yet the country’s sole registered party openly campaigning against that war has been banned from the nationwide party-list ballot.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russia is asking its citizens to endorse an invasion while systematically denying them any legal, nationwide option to vote against it. Worse for Kremlin optics, the vote arrives as Ukrainian deep strikes aggressively bring the war home, paralyzing oil refineries, triggering fuel shortages, and shattering the illusion that everyday Russian life can be isolated from the front lines.
What are Russians electing?
Russians are electing 450 State Duma members for five-year terms, split equally between party lists and single-member constituencies.
Putin’s United Russia party needs 300 seats to hold its constitutional supermajority, the exact threshold required to rewrite the constitution without minority votes. Moscow flatly declined to invite election observers from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE).
Putin’s presidency is not on the ballot, nor will this vote produce a parliamentary opposition capable of ending the war.
But the Duma remains critical: It approves military budgets, wartime taxes, conscription drives, and an ever-expanding body of repressive laws. A compliant parliament gives the Kremlin seamless legislative cover for a prolonged war of attrition.
Trump Administration Weighs Russia Business Deals Before Ukraine War Ends – NYT
Why Yabloko’s exclusion matters
On Aug. 10, Russia’s Supreme Court disqualified Yabloko’s national party-list registration following a lawsuit by the pro-Kremlin Rodina party. The court cited manufactured campaign-finance violations and alleged threats to Russia’s “territorial integrity.”
While a few Yabloko candidates can still compete in isolated single-member constituencies, Russians are strictly barred from casting a nationwide party-list vote for its ceasefire platform.
Yabloko posed no threat of taking power – it held zero seats in the outgoing Duma. Its threat was purely symbolic: It offered a legal, recognized vehicle to register anti-war dissent. Viral clips showed young Russians holding apples (yabloko meaning “apple” in Russian) when asked how they intended to vote, while prominent exiled opposition figures – including Yulia Navalnaya, Ilya Yashin, and Vladimir Kara-Murza – urged supporters to rally behind the party.
As Kyiv Post previously examined, Yabloko’s anti-war stance does not automatically make its leaders champions of Ukraine’s interests. The Russian liberal opposition carries a complex, troubling record on Crimea, Russian imperialism, and state responsibility for the invasion. But banning even this cautious opposition strips the election of its last legal anti-war choice.
11 years for advocating a ceasefire
The crackdown extends far beyond barring candidates.
On Aug. 17, a Pskov court sentenced Yabloko deputy chairman Lev Shlosberg to 11 years and one month in a penal colony for “discrediting the military” and spreading “false information.”
His “crime” was calling for an immediate ceasefire during an online debate and sharing a British newspaper cover depicting Putin beside a wounded Ukrainian woman.
While many Ukrainians strongly criticized Shlosberg’s ceasefire proposal for risking the freeze and consolidation of Russian territorial gains, the Kremlin did not imprison him for being soft on Kyiv. It jailed him simply for publicly opposing the war.
In June, fellow Yabloko deputy chairman Maxim Kruglov also received a seven-year sentence over social media posts documenting Ukrainian civilian casualties.
Can Russian polling tell us what Russians actually think?
The Kremlin’s crackdown makes claims of overwhelming public support for the war impossible to verify.
State-linked polling routinely claims massive approval ratings for Putin and the invasion. However, Russian anti-war activist Daniil Chebykin explained to Kyiv Post that polling in an authoritarian state is hopelessly distorted by fear, selective participation, and coercive methodologies.
VTsIOM, for instance, conducts a portion of its political polling via in-person “route sampling,” where state interviewers visit citizens directly in their homes.
“The respondent understands that the people asking the questions have his home address and personal data,” Chebykin told Kyiv Post. “Of course he won’t say: ‘No, I am against Putin. I am against the war.’”
Government critics simply refuse to participate or give the safest possible answer. These in-person polls also disproportionately reach pensioners and habitual state-television viewers. Official polling cannot be treated as a clean metric of political consensus, and this election suffers from the exact same structural lie.
Ukraine is making the war harder to ignore
The vote is unfolding as the physical and economic consequences of the war bleed directly into Russian cities.
Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign against Russian energy infrastructure has expanded dramatically, striking refineries, ports, and logistics hubs hundreds of kilometers inside Russia. International Energy Agency (IEA) data cited by Reuters indicates a Russian oil refinery was successfully struck on average once every three days during the first eight months of 2026.
On Sept. 17, Ukrainian drones struck the massive Yaroslavl refinery – roughly 250 kilometers (155 miles) northeast of Moscow – paralyzing crude processing by destroying a primary unit handling 40% of the plant’s capacity. Another unit representing a third of capacity was already offline following a prior strike. The facility processes roughly 300,000 barrels of oil per day.
This campaign has crippled Russian fuel distribution. Moscow was forced to enact sweeping export bans to protect domestic supplies, driving August seaborne fuel exports down roughly 50% year-over-year. Widespread fuel shortages and rationing at the pump have now been reported across dozens of Russian regions.
While Russia retains substantial offensive capacity and continues launching heavy missile attacks against Ukraine, it can no longer insulate its civilian population from the war’s economic fallout.
Why remove Yabloko now?
The Kremlin’s pre-election panic stems from its own internal polling.
In July, the state-linked Public Opinion Foundation (FOM) recorded Putin’s sharpest weekly approval drop since the 2022 mobilization. VTsIOM noted similar declines, while independent Levada Center polling placed public support for the military’s actions at its lowest point since the full-scale invasion began.
Fuel rationing, economic anxiety, and relentless drone strikes have made political detachment impossible. In an autocracy, the Kremlin does not fear an opposition party winning an election – it fears a visible, quantifiable protest vote that shatters its illusion of total control.
Who can scrutinize the vote?
Independent monitoring has been thoroughly erased.
Golos, Russia’s premier election watchdog, was shuttered in July 2025 after co-chair Grigory Melkonyants was sentenced to five years in prison for involvement with an “undesirable organization.” The group warned that continued activity placed anyone seeking basic legal advice at risk of criminal prosecution.
Barring opposition candidates dictates who can run; destroying independent watchdogs obscures how the ballots are counted. Together, they ensure the final tally cannot answer the one question the Kremlin wants it to answer: Whether Russians freely support the war.
Putin wants a mandate for a war he has not won
Putin has explicitly linked this election to securing victory in Ukraine and resisting Western pressure.
The message targets Western capitals as much as domestic voters. A manufactured supermajority allows Moscow to claim that Russian society remains solidly behind the invasion, making Western hopes of political collapse futile.
Yet the battlefield contradicts Moscow’s propaganda. Before meeting US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in early September, Putin reportedly insisted Russia would capture the entire Donbas by late 2026 – a timeline Western military analysts dismiss as delusional.
As Kyiv Post also reported, Ukrainian lawmaker Anna Skorokhod sharply criticized the US mission, noting the delegation merely returned with even harsher Russian demands while Ukraine continues to hold key territory Moscow claims to own.
What should Ukraine watch?
Moscow is also staging this election across occupied Ukrainian territory, using forced voting to fabricate an illusion of permanent annexation.
For Kyiv, the official United Russia percentage is meaningless. The critical metrics to watch post-election are further expansions of the Russian military budget and wartime taxation, new conscription or mobilization decrees, harsher statutory crackdowns on domestic dissent, and any sudden shifts in Russia’s diplomatic posture.
As Ukrainian strikes continue to degrade Russian refining capacity and choke domestic fuel markets, the Kremlin will be forced to make agonizing choices between military logistics, export revenues, and civilian stability.
Putin wants this election to project a nation united in endless war. But Ukraine is proving it can make the price of that war unpayable.

Officers fire warning shots as thousands of migrants moved to new facility in Ceuta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:31:11 UTC
18:31:11 KST

Migrants are being moved to a fifth temporary reception space set up to deal with the crisis, which began in late July when more than 70,000 people crossed into Ceuta from Morocco.
On Friday, Spanish authorities began moving thousands of migrants to a new facility in Ceuta, with police struggling to maintain order as people fought to secure a spot at the new site after weeks of living on the beaches and streets.
The operation, which saw migrants moved from the Trampolín and Benítez beaches to the port of Ceuta, got underway shortly after 6:30 am, with several Civil Guard patrols deployed to gather people and escort them on foot to the new settlement, around two kilometres away.
The transfer quickly became difficult to manage.
As the first groups from Trampolín beach reached the area of Benítez beach, the number of migrants sharply increased as they joined up with those staying there, with some breaking into a run as officers worked to contain the crowd.
The tented facility - which reportedly has beds and showers - in Ceuta's port has capacity for around 1,700 people, while it is estimated that there were more than 4,000 migrants coming from the two beaches. An exact figure will not be known until all transfers have been completed and all the migrants have been registered.
It is the fifth temporary reception space set up by the Spanish government to deal with the crisis, which began in late July when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta from Morocco.
The port camp
The new camp has been surrounded by controversy and has also faced legal challenges.
On Thursday, Spain's National Court rejected a request from the Unified Police Union (SUP) for an interim injunction that had sought to halt the installation of tents at the port, which is considered critical infrastructure for the city.
Ana Alarcón, a spokesperson for SUP, said on Friday that "the port is not a safe place."
"It is not a solution in terms of security (…). If anything happens, we are going to demand that people be held responsible," she told Antena 3.
For his part, the vice-president of Ceuta, Alejandro Ramírez, accused the government of improvising and said everything had been "done in a rush."
"The number of incidents in the port has gone from 80 to more than 1,000 in 50 days," he told Onda Cero.
Foreign Minister seeks to 'anchor' Ceuta and Melilla to the EU
It comes after Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares presented a package of measures to the Committee of Ministers this week aimed at moving towards the full integration of Ceuta and Melilla into the European Union - a plan that he has already outlined to the presidents of both autonomous cities.
The measures include establishing a permanent seat for Ceuta and another for Melilla in the European Committee of the Regions, as well as increasing Frontex's presence in both territories, according to a statement from the Foreign Ministry.
The government is also working to ensure specific treatment for Ceuta and Melilla in the EU's next Multiannual Financial Framework.
In addition, the Foreign Ministry has begun coordinating with the ministries of Economy, Finance, Agriculture and Territorial Policy to advance the integration of Ceuta and Melilla into the EU Customs Union and to determine the most appropriate arrangements given their particular geographical and socio-economic circumstances.

Estonian sumo wrestler joins Japan's professional league
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:31:00 UTC
18:31:00 KST

Estonian sumo wrestler joins Japan's professional league
Estonian sumo wrestler Anatoli Zadorožnõi has officially joined Japan's professional sumo league, the Estonian Sumo Association announced.
Zadorožnõi passed his Japanese-language exam, and his first tournament will take place in November. He will begin competing in the lowest division, jonokuchi, and his ring name will be chosen by his coach.
Zadorožnõi joined Japan's newest sumo stable, Hidenoyama, last summer. It is run by Kotoshogiku, a former rival of Estonia's famous Baruto, Kaido Höövelson, who also reached the rank of ozeki.
Professional sumo has six divisions. The highest is makuuchi, followed by juryo and makushita, and then sandanme, jonidan and jonokuchi. According to the Japan Sumo Association, the Hidenoyama stable currently has one wrestler in jonokuchi, five in jonidan, and two in sandanme.
Six major tournaments are held each year: Hatsu-basho in January, Haru-basho in March, Natsu-basho in May, Nagoya-basho in July, Aki-basho in September and Kyushu-basho in November. This year's November tournament runs from November 8 to 22.
Born in Tallinn in 2006, Zadorožnõi is a five-time Estonian sumo champion. While living in Estonia, he trained at the Eesti Karud sumo club, run by Höövelson aka Baruto — together with his sister Tiina and half-brother Meelis. In addition to sumo, Zadorožnõi has also practised judo and Greco-Roman wrestling.
After retiring from Sumo in 2013, Höövelson came home to Estonia and won a Riigikogu seat with the Center Party at the 2019 elections.

Türkiye’s sports economy hits 181 billion liras
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:30:53 UTC
18:30:53 KST

Türkiye women's national volleyball team (AA Photo)
Türkiye’s sports economy reached 181 billion Turkish Liras ($3.7 billion), driven by massive public investments and direct sector expenditures, a joint report revealed.
The National Olympic Committee of Türkiye (TMOK) and Deloitte Türkiye prepared the study. Public investments in sports facilities account for 100 billion liras ($2 billion). Direct expenditures make up the remaining 81 billion liras ($1.6 billion).
The professional club and athlete economy hit 54.2 billion liras ($1.1 billion), dominated by football at 41.4 billion liras ($849 million). Direct fan spending generated 18.5 billion liras ($379 million) in the football sector. Broadcasting revenues contributed 8.8 billion liras ($181 million).
Basketball followed with 7.3 billion liras ($150 million), ahead of volleyball at 4.6 billion liras ($94 million). Women’s volleyball constitutes 60 percent of the volleyball economy. The top-tier Sultanlar Ligi accounts for 45 percent, becoming a strong international sports brand.
The amateur sports economy reached 10 billion liras ($205 million). Football claimed 4.7 billion liras ($96 million). School and university sports generated 1.2 billion liras ($25 million). The Paralympic ecosystem recorded 761 million liras ($16 million) following Türkiye’s 28-medal haul at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games.
Sports tourism contributed between 45 billion and 55 billion liras ($923 million and $1.1 billion) to the economy. International visitors provided 50 to 60 percent of this revenue. Golf tourism in the southern province of Antalya’s Belek resort area and team training camps stood out.
“This study, revealing the size of the sports economy, allows us to see the economic activity in the sector in a data-driven way,” Deloitte Türkiye Strategy and Business Design Leader Elif Düşmez Tek said. “We believe the obtained data will form an important reference for future work.”
TMOK President Professor Veli Ozan Çakır said revealing the current state of the sports economy carries great importance for tracking the sector’s development. “We aim for this report to shed light on efforts for the development of the sports economy,” he said.
The Turkish government subsidizes sports infrastructure across the country, building stadiums and training facilities in nearly all 81 provinces over the past two decades. Private sponsorship deals and broadcasting rights continue to shape the financial landscape of top-tier professional leagues.

Vodafone Ukraine (VF Ukraine PrJSC, Kyiv), Ukraine's second-largest mobile operator, fully owned by the NEQSOL holding, could receive up to $350 million in direct financing from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and use it to refinance existing debt, according to DFC materials.
"Support will be provided through the refinancing of existing debt, which will allow the borrower to redirect cash that would otherwise be reserved for debt repayment toward the procurement of equipment from vetted suppliers worth at least $350 million over the first five years of the loan term," the materials state.
The project, approved by the DFC's board of directors on Sept 16 this year, is meant to support the uninterrupted operation and resilience of Ukraine's telecommunications infrastructure, as well as enable Vodafone Ukraine to continue operations, meet its foreign debt obligations, and make capital investments amid the full-scale invasion.
The company itself has so far only confirmed that the DFC has approved the loan.
"The financing is expected to allow Vodafone Ukraine to redirect its own spending toward capital investment. The loan remains subject to approval and the signing of the relevant documentation. The company will separately announce the conclusion of binding contractual documents and the receipt of the loan funds," the company said in a statement on its website.
As previously reported, Vodafone Ukraine agreed with holders of its nearly $400 million in eurobonds in February 2025 to postpone repayment by two years, to Feb 11, 2027, offering to partially repay nearly $100 million plus accrued interest, raise the coupon rate from 6.2% to 9.625%, and pay a fee of 2% of face value.
Since the end of May 2025, in connection with dividend payments for 2024-2025, the company has been buying back eurobonds in a volume equivalent to about EUR 1 million per month. After the completion of the 12th such buyback, the volume of bonds outstanding will fall to approximately $270 million.
VF Ukraine PrJSC increased its consolidated net profit by 14.2% year-on-year in January-June 2026 to UAH 1.9 billion, while revenue rose 10.6% to UAH 14.9 billion.
The mobile operator's customer base stood at 15.1 million in the second quarter of 2026, with the number of contract subscribers growing to 3.3 million.
The company said it invested more than UAH 3.5 billion in restoring and developing telecom infrastructure in the first half of 2026, matching the level seen in the first half of 2025. Among other results, the operator highlighted continued testing of 5G technology, with initial coverage zones available in Kyiv, Lviv, Kharkiv and Boro dianka, and recently announced open 5G testing in Odesa as well.

The Shin Bet domestic security agency and police said Friday they recently arrested a 32-year-old Israeli man suspected of maintaining contact with a foreign agent from Lebanon and carrying out security-related assignments at her direction.
Hamdan Hamdan, a resident of Majd al-Krum, an Arab town in northern Israel, was arrested on suspicion of offenses including contact with a foreign agent and carrying out security-related tasks on the agent’s behalf, the agencies said.
According to the investigation, Hamdan was in contact with the foreign agent for several months and was asked to carry out a series of assignments at her direction.
Investigators said Hamdan knew he was communicating with a foreign agent based in Lebanon, a country that remains technically at war with Israel.
Authorities said attempts were made to compensate Hamdan for completing the assignments through an unusual payment method: The foreign handler allegedly arranged for products to be purchased in Israel and transferred to him.
The investigation was conducted jointly by the Shin Bet and the Israel Police’s Lahav 433 national crime-fighting unit, including its division responsible for investigating international and serious crimes. The case was overseen by the Haifa District Prosecutor’s Office.
Prosecutors are expected to file an indictment against Hamdan on Sunday.
Police and the Shin Bet renewed their warning to Israelis against communicating with foreign actors from enemy states or unidentified individuals, particularly when they are asked to perform assignments in exchange for payment or other benefits.
“We again warn the citizens and residents of the State of Israel against maintaining contact with foreign elements from enemy states and/or unidentified parties, and all the more so against carrying out tasks for them in exchange for payment or for any other reason,” the agencies said in a joint statement.
Security authorities said intelligence and militant organizations from enemy states continue attempting to recruit Israelis to carry out security-related, espionage and terrorist activities inside Israel, including during the current war.
The agencies said such recruitment efforts have also included approaches to Israelis through social media.

South Korea Set to Approve Abortion Pills Next Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

South Korea this week announced that it plans to approve abortion medication, with restrictions, for the first time in a nation that used to have one of the strictest policies against abortion among developed countries.
Government officials are looking to authorize such medication seven years after the country’s Constitutional Court ruled a longstanding ban on most abortions unconstitutional. While abortion was decriminalized, the South Korean parliament has yet to enact new regulations.
President Lee Jae-myung recognized this legal vacuum on social media and said the government’s decision to introduce abortion drugs in phases can improve protections for women who need access to medically safe procedures.
“During that time, women have been unable to obtain safe abortion drugs and have had to rely on overseas direct purchases or illegal transactions, taking risks in the process,” Lee said Thursday. “Even while fixing a leaking roof, the floor gets wet. I believe that doing what we can now, rather than waiting for a perfect solution, is a slightly better decision.”
Won Min-kyong, Minister of Gender Equality and Family, said Wednesday that under the proposal, women up to nine weeks pregnant could acquire the drug with a prescription and only through hospitals or clinics. The first rollout, starting in the first quarter of 2027, will span at least two years, and Won added that they will use this period to monitor for safety issues or side effects.
“We expect this to serve as an opportunity to strengthen the policy foundation for overall women’s health, including pregnancy, childbirth, and contraception,” Won said.
Before the 2019 ruling, abortion was strictly banned save for a few exceptions, including for pregnancies resulting from rape or incest. Estimates from South Korea’s Institute for Health and Social Affairs suggest that the number of abortions in the country had fallen from an estimated 241,411 in 2008 to just 32,063 in 2020, the last year for which statistics are available. In 2011, the health ministry director at the time attributed the downward trend to “a combination of factors including easier accessibility and use of contraceptives, broadening anti-abortion campaigns, and an improved social environment for childbirth and childcare.”
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook responded to critics and conservatives who are against the abortion medication plan, saying the government is also taking “concerns regarding the value of life” seriously. “This measure is aimed at protecting the people’s health rather than encouraging abortion,” Han said.
What drug will be used?
The Ministry of Food and Drug Safety has been reviewing an application for approving the import of a drug combination of mifepristone and misoprostol—the most common regimen for abortion medication in the U.S.
Misoprostol and its combination with mifepristone are included on the World Health Organization’s Model List of Essential Medicines and are used for the management of medical abortion. Mifepristone blocks progesterone, the hormone that keeps pregnancies going, while misoprostol, taken 24 to 48 hours later, empties the uterus. But misoprostol is also used to treat stomach ulcers.
The WHO has recommended that women less than 12 weeks pregnant could use the drug combination to induce abortions. But South Korean officials said that the limit was set to 9 weeks since the product seeking approval in the country was tested on women that long into their pregnancies.
How is abortion medication used globally?
France and China became the first countries to approve mifepristone in 1988.
According to the WHO’s Global Abortion Policies Database, 84 nations have country-recognized approval of mifepristone or a mix of mifepristone and misoprostol, which means that the drug is either included on the national Essential Medicines List or any other official national list. Of the 84, 32 are in Europe, 23 in Africa, and 18 in Asia. However, dispensing regulations and prescription requirements widely vary.
The database also lists that 123 nations have country-recognized approval of misoprostol, with 41 in Africa, 28 in Asia, and 23 in Europe. Some countries, however, have only approved misoprostol for non-gynecological use.
The U.S. approved mifepristone in 2000. In the U.S., medication abortions accounted for 63% of abortions in states without total abortion bans in 2023, according to the sexual health research and advocacy organization Guttmacher Institute, with higher proportions recorded in rural states like Wyoming (95%) and Montana (84%). As of August, 28 states have policies restricting access to medication abortion.
What have been the reactions in South Korea?
The Korea Women’s Political Network welcomed the plan, saying in a Wednesday statement that it was “a significant step forward in that it establishes an institutional foundation to enable women seeking abortions to access safe and verified medical services, amidst the legislative and institutional vacuum.”
But the women’s advocacy group also raised several concerns about the plan, such as the prescription requirement. It said that requiring a prescription and dispensing only in hospitals and clinics “excessively restricts women’s access to medication” and could act as a barrier for those having difficulty accessing ob-gyn services. It also urged increasing the covered period up to 10 weeks into a woman’s pregnancy. Most women find out they’re pregnant around the four-week mark or later.
The Catholic Bishops' Conference of Korea, meanwhile, said the government should move away from expanding access to abortion pills and instead build “a roadmap of support to help women in crisis not give up on life.”
Representatives of South Korea’s medical community called for protections for medical professionals who could “risk criminal punishment” for administering abortion medication or for refusing to administer it, given the lack of legislation around abortion’s legality.
“Our organization is not opposed to the introduction itself in principle (of Mifepristone),” the Korean Association of Obstetricians and Gynecologists said in its statement. “We will not accept any introduction that does not guarantee patient safety and the legal protection of medical professionals.”

Where Can Russian Athletes Compete After the IOC’s Provisional Ban Lift?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Russia’s return to international sports competition was already well underway long before the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifted its ban on the Russian and Belarusian Olympic Committees this July.
The shift began in September 2025, when the International Paralympic Committee voted against maintaining its ban on Russian and Belarusian athletes, paving the way for them to compete at the 2026 Milano-Cortina Paralympic Games, where Russian competitors won eight gold medals.
By December, the IOC recommended that international federations lift their bans on Russian and Belarusian youth athletes.
However, some individual governing bodies acted even earlier. The International Judo Federation became the first to restore full participation rights to senior Russian athletes in November of last year. World Taekwondo followed this January by approving the full return of both junior and senior athletes from Russia and Belarus.
Since then, eight additional Olympic sports federations have restored full participation rights to Russian athletes and teams, allowing the use of the Russian flag, national anthem and team uniforms.
Below is a list compiled by The Moscow Times detailing where and how Russian athletes can currently compete on the international stage:
Federations that allow full senior and youth participation
Archery: On August 14, World Archery reinstated Russian athletes, allowing them to compete under their national flag and bringing their status in line with Belarusian athletes, who were reinstated in May.
Aquatics: The World Aquatics Bureau lifted its ban on senior Russian and Belarusian athletes on April 13, 2026, two months after it lifted its ban on Junior athletes.
In its statement, World Aquatics President Husain Al Musallam said, “Over the last three years, World Aquatics and the AQIU have successfully helped ensure that conflict can be kept outside the sporting competition venues. We are determined to ensure that pools and open water remain places where athletes from all nations can come together in peaceful competition.”
Boxing: On July 30, World Boxing announced that it was restoring full participation rights to all Russian athletes.
"The Executive Committee accepted that Russian athletes would now take part in World Boxing competitions like boxers from any other national federation. However, World Boxing will strictly monitor the behaviour of Russian delegations during events as well as compliance with anti-doping protocols," the statement read.
World Boxing previously lifted its restrictions on Belarusian athletes on May 12.
Equestrian: The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) will lift restrictions on Russian riders and officials starting Oct. 5 and once again allow international competitions to be held in Russia, the governing body has said.
FEI had already approved a return to competition for junior athletes from Russia and Belarus on May 19, 2026, but did not change its stance that senior athletes should compete with neutral status at that time.
Fencing: The International Fencing Federation (FIE) reinstated Russian and Belarusian athletes on June 2, 2026.
“The decision reflects the FIE’s commitment to the fundamental principles of the Olympic Charter, including non-discrimination, equal treatment and the universality of sport, as well as the objectives and principles set out in the FIE Statutes,” FIE’s statement read.
On July 28, Russian fencer Pavel Graudyn won gold in the Men's individual sabre at the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong, marking Russia's first gold at a major championship since the International Fencing Federation lifted its restrictions.
Field Hockey: On Sept. 17, the Russian Field Hockey Federation announced that it had received a letter from the International Hockey Federation (FIH) lifting all restrictions against its athletes and national teams.
Gymnastics: The Executive Committee of World Gymnastics released a statement on May 18, 2026, that it had decided to lift all restrictions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts.
On July 28, 2026, European Gymnastics voted to bring itself in line with World Gymnastics in allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete with their national symbols.
Handball: On July 15, 2026, the International Handball Federation (IHF) lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian teams and officials, citing the IOC’s recommendation.
“The IHF reiterates its longstanding commitment to the Ukraine Handball Federation and continues to stand in solidarity with Ukraine. It strongly condemns the ongoing war in Ukraine and its devastating consequences. It is the IHF’s sincere hope that the conflict will soon come to an end, paving the way for a return to peace, the restoration of normal sporting relations and the resumption of peaceful international cooperation,” the IHF statement said.
“At the same time, the IHF remains committed to safeguarding the values of sport, promoting dialogue within the international handball family, and ensuring that its decisions continue to reflect the recommendations of the IOC and the interests of the global handball community”
Judo: The International Judo Federation, calling sport the “last bridge for reconciliation and peace,” was the first to allow Russian and Belarusian senior athletes back, doing so on Nov. 27, 2025.
“Athletes have no responsibility for the decisions of governments or other national institutions, and it is our duty to protect the sport and our athletes,” the federation’s statement said.
“Sport must remain neutral, independent and free from political influence. Judo, rooted in the values of peace, unity and friendship, cannot allow itself to become a platform for geopolitical agendas. The decision to reinstate full national representation reflects the IJF’s confidence in its ethical safeguards, as well as in the strength and integrity of the sport,” it continued.
Modern Pentathlon: The International Union of Modern Pentathlon lifted its ban on Russian athletes on July 13, 2026, citing the IOC’s recommendation.
Taekwondo: The World Taekwondo Council allowed Russian and Belarusian athletes back into the fold on Jan. 31, 2026, at a meeting in the United Arab Emirates.
Triathlon: Mikhail Degtyarev, head of the Russian Olympic Committee and the Russian Minister of Sport, said on Aug. 21 that World Triathlon had granted Russian athletes full participation rights.
World Triathlon lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian junior athletes in April 2026, while senior athletes continue to compete as neutral athletes.
"This was made possible by the restoration of the Russian Olympic Committee's status. Earlier in April, World Triathlon already admitted Russian junior and para-athletes," Degtyarev said.
Volleyball: The International Volleyball Federation (FIVB) announced on July 8, 2026, that Russian teams and athletes would be restored to the World Ranking with the same World Ranking points they had at the time of the initial ban.
“The FIVB remains deeply concerned about the ongoing war in Ukraine and strongly condemns all forms of violence. We continue to hope for a peaceful resolution as soon as possible and remain committed to supporting the Ukrainian volleyball community through the FIVB Volleyball Empowerment programme,” FIVB added.
Weightlifting: The International Weightlifting Federation decided on June 26, 2026, to reinstate Russian and Belarusian athletes.
“The IWF remains committed to promoting fair competition, safeguarding the integrity of the sport and ensuring that athletes have the opportunity to compete in an environment that respects the principles of neutrality, inclusion and excellence,” the decision read.
Wrestling: United World Wrestling announced on May 15, 2026, that Russian and Belarusian wrestlers would be able to compete without restrictions starting with immediate effect.
Federations that allow full youth participation
Baseball/Softball: On Jan. 19, 2026, the World Baseball Softball Confederation (WBSC) reinstated Russian and Belarusian youth athletes. However, senior athletes remain banned.
Chess: The International Chess Federation (FIDE) lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian youth chess players on Dec. 14, 2025. Senior athletes may compete under a neutral designation.
Curling: World Curling announced on Jan. 30, 2026, that, following the IOC’s recommendation, Russian and Belarusian junior athletes would be able to compete in international competition. Senior athletes remain unable to compete.
Sailing: The Russian Sailing Federation published a statement on June 9, 2026, announcing that the World Sailing Federation had approved a return to competition for Russian junior athletes.
Ski Mountaineering: The International Ski Mountaineering Federation (ISMF) reinstated Russian and Belarusian youth athletes.
