Canadian cycling experts: The car still feels like king in Tallinn and Tartu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:08:00 UTC
18:08:00 KST

Canadian cycling experts: The car still feels like king in Tallinn and Tartu
Although cycling and pedestrian infrastructure in Tallinn and Tartu has improved in recent years, there is no common standard, sustainable mobility experts Melissa and Chris Bruntlett noted
The Bruntletts say better options would ease congestion and make Estonia's cities more accessible to all, and not just to drivers.
"Both Tallinn and Tartu have a lot going for them, especially when it comes to recent developments. At the same time, there is plenty of room for improvement in both cities," Chris says. Together with his wife Melissa, he visited Estonia's two largest cities earlier on this month, and they tried for themselves getting around both cities by bicycle.
"It feels very inconsistent. It feels like something only the most dedicated people, or people who are really committed to using these modes of transportation, will do," Chris Bruntlett says.
Originally from Canada but now already in their seventh year living in Delft, in the famously cycling-friendly Netherlands, the married couple assess cities around the world through the prism of the transport culture of their adopted home country. Based on their experiences in Tallinn and Tartu, they say that the different modes of transport have been developed unevenly here. "If you want mass walking and cycling in your city, you really have to make it enticing, attractive," Chris points out.
From the Bruntletts' perspective, the ideal urban environment is one like Delft's. "The ideal city is one where you see public life being enjoyed by everyone, all different ages, abilities, genders," Melissa says. In an ideal city, she says, the environment is more social and lively streets encourage people to spend more time outdoors.
Walking and cycling are thus an integral part of life in the Bruntletts' ideal town. "People can make their own choices about what mode of transport they want to use and the route they want to choose, instead of the city making that choice for them," Chris explains. According to the couple, transport should be seen as a tool for making the city a better place for everyone to live. In other words, the broader goal is livability, rather than mobility for the sake of itself.
While getting around Tartu, the experts did catch glimpses of their ideal. Tartu's two official bicycle streets, Tähtvere and Õnne, felt different to them from the rest of the urban environment. "Thanks to the greenery, flowers and trees, they were much more inviting. They were pleasant places where people genuinely want to spend time and feel proud of and connected to their neighborhood," Chris says.
While cycling in Tallinn, however, Melissa encountered somemore uncomfortable situations. "There were a lot more situations where I felt really uncomfortable, and that can also be because of the size of the city and the number of people moving around," she says. She also noticed more children, adults and elderly people using active modes of transport in Tartu than in the capital. This showed that despite the patchy development, Tartu has made greater progress in diversifying its transport landscape. "The challenge now is to keep going with that momentum, and it sounds like things have gotten a little bit stalled here," Melissa points out.
Despite these developments, both Tartu and Tallinn still appear car-centric to the Bruntletts. "In full direct Dutch mode, the car still feels like king in both Tallinn and Tartu," Chris says. At the same time, any city must take into account that not everyone can drive because of their age or health. "If we say that the car is freedom, then we're saying that only people that can drive can enjoy that freedom," Melissa says.
According to the couple, not everyone has the same choices. Chris notes that about a third of the population does not have the physical or financial means to drive a car, and that this group is often left out of the conversation. "They're not part of the conversation. Many of them can't vote, and the politicians aren't necessarily listening to them," he says. "A city should not cater only to that one third for whom the car is the only way of getting around," Melissa adds.
At the same time, the experts stress that they are not asking everyone to give up their cars. If driving is essential because a person lives far from the city center, the Bruntletts say that is entirely understandable. However, they do not recommend planning cities solely around the needs of people living in the suburbs. "We're not saying no. We're saying if it's needs must, then yes. But not everyone lives on the outside of the city, some people live on the inside," Melissa says.
According to the couple, the issue ultimately comes down to social justice: does everyone have the opportunity to participate in society and access services? An elderly person in poor health or someone with a visual impairment, for example, cannot independently get around the city by car. "If we start from that when planning cities and think about how to provide alternatives for those who cannot drive, we also turn sidewalks into a genuine option," Melissa points out.
Chris says people are accustomed to thinking of transport as a zero-sum game in which creating opportunities for one group of road users means that others lose something. In reality, if there were attractive alternatives to driving, drivers themselves would also benefit, because fewer cars on the roads would mean less congestion. "Drivers in the Netherlands, which has really high rates of walking and cycling and public transport, are among the most satisfied in the world. They have the best driving conditions, they have the lowest levels of traffic congestion because they have less competition on the street with other drivers," Chris says.
According to the couple, national infrastructure design standards would help improve the situation in Tallinn and Tartu. In many countries, such standards specify how wide sidewalks or cycle paths must be. They also prescribe the materials to be used in construction. "If cycle paths are built piecemeal and without a broader vision for a coherent network, cycling is not treated as a serious mode of transport. Then only 5–10 percent of the population will use it," Chris says.
He recommends setting high standards, committing to investment in infrastructure and then building it out. Cities must also be prepared for change to take decades. "It took the Netherlands 50 years to get where it is today," Chris points out. "When you design a system for one mode of transportation, it doesn't work for anybody, including the car drivers."
During their time in Estonia, Melissa and Chris Bruntlett also presented their new book "Women Changing Cities". In it, they examined why women in city leadership had succeeded in 11 significant cities where previous leaders had failed.
"We concluded that there are five leadership qualities that each of the women we talked to exemplified that helped make their approach different," Melissa recalls. For example, the female leaders studied were empathetic in their work, understanding that their own lived experience was not the only lived experience. They also listened to different stakeholders and trusted community members' knowledge of what worked and what did not in their neighborhoods.
However, there is a long way to go. "The problem is that there are currently too few women in leadership positions. As we mentioned at the presentation, when we were writing the book, only 25 of the world's 300 largest cities had female mayors, or fewer than nine percent," Chris says. Although male leaders by all means can also display all the qualities highlighted in the book, he says women are accustomed to being criticized regardless. As a result, they are often more prepared to make difficult decisions and bring about change.
Melissa says that, more broadly, it is important for the people who lead and shape cities to better reflect their communities. "If half of your population is women, half of the people running your cities should probably also be women, but they should also be of varying ages, varying backgrounds, because we are informed in the way that we approach our work by our lived experience," she says.
At the end of the day, Melissa says, it is easy to feel frustrated. "But we see the potential here, and I think a lot of people see that potential in themselves and in their cities. It's not always easy and it can get very frustrating, but that community is there," she says. "Everything is not all lost. There is that hope at the end of the day."
ITALIXS Melissa and Chris Bruntlett were invited to Estonia by landscape architect Aljona Galazan to explore the country's towns and to give presentations. In addition to presenting their book, the Bruntletts held a communications workshop in Tallinn for local advocates, experts and representatives of local governments. In Tartu, they met members of the Tartu cyclists' association and city government representatives and familiarized themselves with Tartu's bike-sharing system. ITALIXS

Warwickshire man jailed after promoting far-right violence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:07:54 BST
18:07:54 KST

A Warwickshire man has been jailed for two years after admitting offences involving threatening online material intended to stir up hatred on the grounds of religion and sexual orientation, according to Counter Terrorism Policing.
Thomas Webster, 29, of Yew Tree Close in Lapworth, came to the attention of investigators after appearing in a BBC Wales documentary broadcast in January 2025.
The programme followed an undercover journalist who had spent a year with a far-right group and included footage of Webster discussing extreme views and talking about making video guides concerning different racial groups. Information following the broadcast was passed to Counter Terrorism Police in the West Midlands, which opened an investigation focusing particularly on material Webster had posted to social media.
He was arrested in September 2025 and later charged with 12 public order offences relating to racial hatred, religious hatred and hatred based on sexual orientation. The charges concerned material posted across six social media accounts between September 2024 and September 2025.
Counter Terrorism Policing said investigators examined a large volume of material before a selection of charges was presented to the Crown Prosecution Service to represent the offending identified during the investigation. Webster pleaded guilty at Coventry Magistrates’ Court on 5 August to posting online material using threatening words or behaviour intended to stir up hatred on the grounds of sexual orientation, together with a further offence involving material intended to stir up religious hatred.
Further material was shown to the court during sentencing, with police saying it demonstrated that the views behind the offences were not confined to individual social media posts.
Detective Chief Superintendent Alison Hurst, head of Counter Terrorism Policing West Midlands, said: “I hope the fact that he is now serving a prison sentence sends a clear message that extreme racist views and promoting serious violence is completely unacceptable in our society and it simply will not be tolerated.”
She also thanked the BBC for the documentary, which she said had assisted the subsequent police investigation. Webster was sentenced to two years in prison.

West seeking ‘pretext’ for major Russia-NATO war – Fico

NATO member warns bloc seeking pretext for war with Russia
Europe is moving dangerously close to a direct clash between NATO and Russia, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has warned, accusing the West of seeking a “pretext” for a major conflict between the two sides.
Fico made the comment in a Facebook post on Thursday, which accompanied the remarks he delivered before traveling to Ukraine for a meeting with Vladimir Zelensky and several European leaders.
“I am deeply concerned that they are merely looking for a pretext for a major conflict between NATO and Russia,” he wrote.
Reflecting on the Ukraine conflict, Fico said that the hostilities had “gotten out of control,” while accusing European nations of engaging in increasingly bellicose rhetoric which he said risked dragging the continent into a broader war. “The situation has never been as serious and tense regarding the possibility of a pan-European war conflict as it is now,” he said.
Fico also warned that Bratislava could face pressure from NATO to commit troops if the bloc’s Article 5 – a collective defense clause applied if a member state is attacked – is invoked. “Can anyone imagine being told to prepare 5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers, and that they would go somewhere to fight? We don’t know with whom, why, or for what reason,” Fico said.
“I don’t want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5,” he stressed, adding that, though his country still “cares about collaboration and fulfilling obligations”. “As prime minister, I will do everything to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a war,” Fico stressed.
Fico has consistently opposed military support for Ukraine since returning to office in 2023 while halting government weapons shipments to Kiev. He has also opposed Kiev’s accession to NATO, and insisted that Ukraine’s EU membership is only possible if it meets all the requirements.
He has also argued that the West’s strategy to “bring Russia to its knees” had “completely failed.” “The European Union does not need more weapons and Russophobia. The European Union needs more diplomacy and concrete plans to help the economy,” Fico said last month.
Russia has accused the EU of rapid militarization, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying the bloc is directing increasing military capabilities against Moscow while portraying it as an enemy.
President Vladimir Putin has consistently rejected claims that Moscow intends to attack NATO countries, but warned last week that deploying European forces to Ukraine “would mean war with Russia.” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov also stressed that Russia has no intention of attacking the West but warned that if Europe attacked first, the resulting conflict would be “very short.”

Doctors in Hong Kong have been urged to arrange blood tests for patients with symptoms of chikungunya fever, regardless of their travel history, after the city recorded its first local case of the mosquito-borne disease this year.
The Centre for Health Protection issued a reminder to doctors on Thursday after a 55-year-old woman with no recent travel history was reported as Hong Kong’s first locally acquired chikungunya fever case in 2026.
“To facilitate early diagnosis and timely public health intervention, please consider arranging diagnostic testing for any patient presenting with symptoms suggestive of chikungunya fever, regardless of their travel history,” the centre wrote in a letter to doctors.
Testing for the mosquito-borne disease is free of charge at the public health laboratory service under the centre.

ICC eyes China as next frontier in push to expand cricket's global fanbase
China is emerging as a key growth market for cricket as the International Cricket Council looks to expand the sport's global fanbase by 500 million, its chief executive told the AFP news agency.
While South Asia currently accounts for roughly 90% of cricket's billion-plus fans, the ICC sees China's 1.4 billion people as a major untapped audience, aided by the steady rise of its women's national team.
"The continued success of their women's team has provided a major boost to cricket in the country," ICC CEO Sanjog Gupta said.
China became a focus market after hosting cricket at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, and its women's team has climbed 10 places in the world T20 rankings over the past two years. It currently stands at the 36th spot, whereas the men's side stands 92nd.
The ICC has invested $1.5 million (~1.3 million euros) in the country over the past five years, helping build three top-level venues, including a new 1,500-seat stadium in Taicang meant to host matches and serve as a training base.
Moving beyond bigger teams like India, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, Asian cricket is expanding its influence. At their Asian Games 2026 fixture against India on Friday, Japan's women's team did not let their loss define the journey.
Japan's Ahilya Chandel, who is half-Indian, told AFP that facing India in person after watching them on television was a special moment, adding that home crowds in Nagoya included newcomers to the sport: "That's what we want as a women's cricket team, to attract Japanese people who don't know cricket."
India will now play Bangladesh in Sunday's semi-finals.
Electoral body strips Trinamool factions of party name, symbol ahead of West Bengal byelections
The Election Commission of India has barred both rival factions of the Trinamool Congress from using the party's name and its "flowers and grass" symbol ahead of byelections in West Bengal, assigning each faction a new interim identity instead.
The commission's order, issued late Thursday night, applies to the faction led by former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee and her nephew Abhishek Banerjee, as well as a rival group led by expelled legislator Ritabrata Banerjee.
On Friday, the commission allotted Mamata's faction the name "Mamata All India Trinamool Congress" with a football player as its symbol, while the rival group was named "Democratic Trinamool Congress" (or Ganatantrik Trinamool Congress) and given an envelope symbol.
Both groups will be treated as recognized parties in the states of West Bengal, Meghalaya and Tripura on an interim basis while the commission decides the underlying leadership dispute.
The ruling affects two upcoming byelections, in Nandigram and Rejinagar, scheduled for October 6.
Soon after the new symbols were announced, Sanchita Pradhan Dey, the Mamata faction's candidate in Nandigram, withdrew her nomination after meeting West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari. Adhikari, who was once a close aide of Mamta Banerjee,joined the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in 2020.
As nominations had already been scrutinized, her faction cannot field a replacement. Instead, Mamata Banerjee said she would back the Congress candidate to strengthen the opposition INDIA bloc.
Local media reported Mamata Banerjee referring to the Election Commission's decision as a "black day for democracy."
Opposition Congress leadership also slammed the polling body, calling it the commission's "late night birthday gift to Modi ji." Prime Minister Narendra Modi turned 76 on Thursday.

From traditional indigenous spices in Kerala to the threatened Himalayan salamander, communities are finding ways to protect India's abundant natural heritage.

India on track for driest monsoon in 17 years
India is expected to experience its weakest monsoon season since 2009, as a strengthening El Nino weather pattern curbs rainfall and raises concerns over crop yields and food inflation.
Cumulative rainfall during the June-to-September monsoon season is currently running 15% below the long-term average, according to the India Meteorological Department, local media reported. The initial forecast was just a 10% shortfall back in May.
If the deficit holds, this would be the weakest monsoon since 2009, when rainfall was 18% below normal.
A potential tropical cyclone could form in the Bay of Bengal in the final week of September, potentially easing the shortfall in eastern and northeastern India, Christian Werner of Global Weather Climate Analytics told Bloomberg.
He said the storm was unlikely to significantly shift the national picture, with the seasonal deficit expected to settle between 13% and 16%.
The lack of rain threatens both current harvests and the next planting cycle, adding pressure on food prices that have already risen for seven straight months, hitting 5.95% in August — the highest level this year, according to the Free Press Journal.
Rice, sugarcane and corn planting are running behind last year's pace, and the government has responded by permitting duty-free sugar imports and selling subsidized onions in some states.
READ — Smuggling suspected as more rare animals seen in India
Five infant orangutans, a species found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra and on Borneo, were found in a forest by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India's eastern Odisha state last week.
In recent years, orangutans, rare reptiles and other exotic animals are popping up in India, suggesting the country is becoming a major destination for trafficked wildlife.
iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max go on sale in India, prompting long queues
Long lines formed outside Apple Stores across India on Friday as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max went on sale — this year's most expensive Pro lineup to date, with prices roughly Rs 30,000 (€270, $310) higher than last year's equivalent models at launch.
The high prices were not a barrier for many buyers, whose wait began before dawn. In Bengaluru, a customer named Rahul told newswire ANI he arrived at the Apple Store around 5 a.m. local time and found people already in line.
Rahul, who said he has bought every iPhone since the iPhone 7, described the ritual as something bigger than a purchase: "I've been purchasing iPhones for a very long time ... But it's like a festival for me. iPhone launch is like a festival. Every year, I try to buy an iPhone."
At the Apple Store in the northern city of Noida, one buyer said he had traveled from the nearby state of Punjab and began his wait at 6 a.m. local time, just to be first through the door: "Mine was the very first booking; I am the first one who has got the phone."
This year's price increase — pushing the iPhone 18 Pro to Rs 164,900 (€1,500, $1,720) and the Pro Max to Rs 179,900 (€1,635, $1,900) at the base storage tier — breaks Apple's recent run of holding launch prices steady in India.
India's GDP per capita stood at $2,702.5 in 2025, according to World Bank figures. The numbers do not account for income inequality.

Teenager jailed over Islamic terrorism offences
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:05:37 BST
18:05:37 KST

A 19-year-old man has been jailed for nine and a half years after being convicted of possessing articles for a terrorist purpose and disseminating terrorist publications, according to Counter Terrorism Policing North East.
Mohammed Khalil Nadir, of Clough Close, was sentenced at Leeds Crown Court on 1 September following his conviction at trial in June. The court heard that Nadir had accumulated terrorist material and shared a video showing himself wearing an imitation suicide vest which he had modified with a fake wire and trigger. An explosion sound was added to the recording before it was shared on Telegram.
Investigators said Nadir had researched the mock explosive vest used during the Heaton Park Synagogue attack and ordered a similar vest several hours later. On the day it was delivered, he added 500 steel ball bearings to an online shopping basket.
Counter-terrorism officers arrested Nadir in October 2025. Searches subsequently found the weighted vest in his wardrobe alongside handwritten material promoting martyrdom operations. Police also recovered what they described as a large quantity of terrorist material from his mobile devices, including Daesh propaganda videos and texts calling for the killing of people described as “disbelievers”.
The investigation also examined Nadir’s activity in online chat rooms and voice messages. Police said he regularly sought out people who shared his views, promoted violence and circulated terrorist guides and propaganda.
Detective Chief Superintendent James Dunkerley, head of Counter Terrorism Policing North East, said the evidence showed that Nadir’s views had developed over a period of around two years.
He said: “Nadir wasn’t simply in possession of high volumes of material which encouraged acts of terrorism. He deliberately shared terrorism guides and propaganda online and regularly used chat rooms to promote violence and justify martyrdom to others.”
Dunkerley said the combination of the weighted vest, Nadir’s interest in obtaining ball bearings and his online activity had caused particular concern during the investigation.
He added: “There is no telling what harm this information could do in the hands of the wrong person.”
Alongside the nine-and-a-half-year prison sentence, Nadir will be subject to an extended licence period of three years following his release. He will also be subject to a Serious Crime Prevention Order for five years and terrorism notification requirements for 30 years.

Swiss lawmakers back stricter asylum measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:04:55 UTC
18:04:55 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The Swiss House of Representatives voted in favor of stricter measures on asylum on Thursday, broadcaster Swissinfo reported.
The House adopted a motion put forward by the right-wing Swiss People’s Party parliamentary group, urging the government to oppose any proposed changes to EU rules on compensation for unemployed cross-border workers.
A separate motion called on the federal government to revoke the Swiss citizenship of dual nationals convicted of the most serious crimes and deport them.
The House also called on the government to change its practice in handling asylum applications from Afghan women, so they would no longer be automatically granted asylum but instead receive provisional admission status.
The majority further backed legislative changes to introduce targeted sanctions against countries of origin that refuse to cooperate.
The federal government had previously rejected all nine motions debated by the House. The Senate will now consider the motions approved by the lower house during an extraordinary session focused on “the EU and asylum.”

Taiwan migrant fishers union calls for better working conditions in tuna supply chain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:04:22 UTC
18:04:22 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – A labor union representing Indonesian migrant fishers has called on StarKist to improve working conditions on Taiwan-flagged vessels supplying tuna to the US seafood brand.
The Forum Silaturahmi Pelaut Indonesia–Pingtung Migrant Fishers Union (FOSPI-PMFU) and its allies launched a global campaign Thursday calling on StarKist to negotiate a binding agreement over working conditions and guarantee five fundamental rights for migrant fishers. These include the rights to communicate via guaranteed access to Wi-Fi on fishing vessels and to a transparent and fair grievance mechanism, according to a press release.
As part of the campaign, Global Labor Justice published a report documenting three years of forced labor conditions in StarKist’s Pacific albacore tuna supply chain.
“Fishers in StarKist’s supply chain can spend months at sea isolated without independent access to Wi-Fi or other means of external communication, effectively turning vessels into ‘union-free zones’ where workers cannot contact unions, report abuses, seek help, or exercise freedom of association,” the report said.
The other demands include the right to a healthy and safe workplace, fair wages and employment contracts, and the right to organize a union without intimidation or retaliation.
Taiwan’s distant-water fishing industry has long faced criticism over the treatment of migrant workers, who are largely excluded from local labor protections. Since 2020, the US Department of Labor has flagged the industry for indicators of forced labor, citing issues including excessive working hours and deceptive recruitment, per CNN.
The campaign focuses on StarKist but highlights the prevalence of forced labor across the tuna supply chain, according to the press statement.
FOSPI-PMFU General Secretary Achmed Mudzakir was quoted as saying in the press release, “When (workers) are at sea, they are often cut off from the world and have little recourse to the captain’s decisions.
“That’s why we are calling on StarKist to negotiate directly with our union for an enforceable brand agreement that we can ensure is enforced by everyone in the supply chain: StarKist, vessel owners, captains and fishers. We want StarKist to come to the bargaining table in good faith, hear our demands, and come to a fair agreement.”
“A more equitable global economy requires that multinational corporations buy from supply chains where workers have unions and labor rights at work,” said Jennifer Rosenbaum, executive director of Global Labor Justice. “Today FOSPI- PFMU sets the direction for the seafood sector to end forced labor and advance freedom of association and more dignified work for fishers.

‘I am back’ – Julian Assange
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:03:01 UTC
18:03:01 KST

‘I am back’ – Julian Assange
WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange has suggested that he is returning to public life, following a hiatus after his release from British custody in 2024.
The transparency activist spent five years behind bars while fighting a US extradition request that could have resulted in a lengthy sentence in a high-security US prison. He eventually struck a deal that secured his freedom amid a global campaign urging Washington to drop the case against him.
The WikiLeaks account on X announced on Thursday that Assange is “back,” posting a photo in which he is posing in front of a mural depicting him in Sydney, Australia.
Assange reposted the message, confirming his return and saying it is the first post in eight years that he has personally written.
I'm back. https://t.co/2e58azeJkt
— Julian Assange (@JulianAssange) September 17, 2026
His wife Stella said more news will follow next week.
WikiLeaks became a global phenomenon in 2010 after publishing a leaked video showing a US military airstrike in Baghdad in 2007 that killed at least a dozen people.
Chelsea Manning was arrested and later convicted in 2013 for providing WikiLeaks with the footage and other classified US military materials.
The US espionage case against Assange centered on obtaining the files from Manning, while Britain’s initial efforts to detain him arose from an unrelated case that his supporters said was fabricated.
Assange was granted political asylum by Ecuador in 2012 and spent years inside the South American country’s embassy in London. A change of government in Quito eventually led Ecuador to revoke his asylum and allow British police to arrest him in 2019.
Under the deal reached with the US in 2024, Assange pleaded guilty to a single felony charge of conspiring to obtain and disclose classified US documents. He was sentenced to time already served in London’s high-security Belmarsh Prison. In Britain, he was convicted of violating bail conditions.
Since regaining his freedom, Assange has made several public appearances. Months after his release, he addressed the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe in Strasbourg, France, speaking about the ordeal he endured.
In 2025, he took part in a pro-Palestinian march in Sydney with an estimated 100,000 people.

Gaza rescuers recover 12 more bodies from rubble, total hits 75
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:01:00 UTC
18:01:00 KST

Gaza Civil Defense teams recovered the bodies and remains of 12 Palestinians from beneath the rubble of homes destroyed in Gaza City, bringing the number recovered from the site to 75, the agency said Thursday.
The latest recoveries were made in the Al-Taj Square area as search teams continued operations beneath collapsed homes in the Yarmouk neighborhood for a 12th consecutive day.
The operation is being conducted by Civil Defense teams in Gaza governorate in cooperation with an Egyptian committee as part of the second phase of the agency’s “Recovery of Martyrs’ Bodies” project, launched July 19 to locate and recover Palestinians believed to be buried beneath buildings destroyed during the war.
The second phase covers destroyed homes in Gaza, northern Gaza and central Gaza governorates and is scheduled to involve about 800 working hours. Civil Defense figures indicate that teams are searching 147 destroyed homes where the remains of an estimated 1,072 people are believed to be buried.
The recovery effort has been slowed by severe shortages of heavy machinery and other equipment needed to clear the vast quantities of rubble. Palestinian authorities have said the cease-fire agreement that took effect in October 2025 provided for heavy equipment to enter Gaza to support debris removal and the recovery of bodies, but the machinery available to rescue teams has remained limited.
The latest operation is part of a broader effort to account for thousands of Palestinians who remain missing. Gaza’s Government Media Office said in October 2025 that about 9,500 people had been reported missing since the war began, including people believed to be trapped beneath destroyed buildings and others whose whereabouts remained unknown.
The first phase of the recovery project began in late November 2025. Civil Defense teams recovered about 333 bodies and sets of remains belonging to an estimated 559 missing people beneath 54 homes and buildings, according to figures released by the agency.
The scale of the task remains immense. In recent weeks, Civil Defense teams have continued to recover groups of remains from destroyed residential buildings across Gaza, while a shortage of excavators, bulldozers, trucks and other specialized equipment has restricted the pace of operations. Earlier in the second phase, Civil Defense officials said teams had only very limited machinery available for the work.
The continuing recovery effort has also highlighted the dangers posed by Gaza’s war-damaged buildings.
A separate seven-story residential building in Gaza City collapsed this week, killing at least 20 people and injuring others, according to Palestinian authorities and Reuters. Rescue teams worked with limited equipment as people remained trapped beneath the debris.
Gaza’s Health Ministry said Thursday that 73,821 Palestinians had been killed and 174,897 injured since Oct. 7, 2023.
It said 1,386 people had been killed and 4,784 injured since the cease-fire took effect, while 831 bodies had been recovered during that period. The ministry also said some victims remained beneath rubble and on roads that rescue teams could not reach.
The figures are issued by Gaza health authorities and cannot be independently verified in real time because of the conditions in the enclave.

Royal Navy records £8m loss after sensor programme axed
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:39 BST
18:00:39 KST

The Royal Navy recorded an £8.332 million constructive loss after terminating a programme to replace thermal imaging cameras and laser range finders, with the funding redirected to other projects across the service.
The figure appeared in the Ministry of Defence annual report and accounts for 2025-26 and was raised in a written parliamentary question by Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty. He asked for further information on the £8.332 million constructive loss associated with termination of the Thermal Imaging camera and Laser Range Finder replacement programme.
Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard said the decision formed part of the Navy’s continuing review of its spending priorities.
He said: “The Royal Navy continues to review all its programmes and to allocate funding appropriately based on operational requirements and value for money.”
Pollard confirmed that money associated with the programme had instead been directed elsewhere in the service. He said: “Funding for some initiatives, such as the Thermal Imaging camera and Laser Range Finder replacement programme, has been repurposed to prioritise other projects across the service.”
The termination resulted in the £8.332 million figure being recorded in the department’s accounts as a constructive loss.

DONETSK, September 18. /TASS/. All 633 polling stations for the State Duma elections have opened in the Donetsk People’s Republic, with operations proceeding as normal, regional Election Commission Chairman Vladimir Vysotsky told TASS on Friday.
"All 633 polling stations have opened in the DPR. Operations are proceeding as normal. Mobile teams are also working," Vysotsky said.
Early voting took place in the region from August 30 to September 17. Military personnel were the first to vote, followed by civilians starting September 8. According to preliminary data as of September 17, at least 1 million people had already cast their vote, accounting for around 75% of eligible voters.

‘I spend a bagful of money and don’t fill a bag’: the energy crisis hits Bangladesh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:00:14 UTC
18:00:14 KST

At 1am, Halder’s alarm goes off and the 34-year-old Bangladeshi bank employee rises and heads to her kitchen. She is up at this time not for work but to cook for her family. An energy crisis paralysing the capital, Dhaka, a city of almost 40 million people, means this has become the only time when the piped gas supply is strong enough to allow cooking.
The city now operates in darkness, as people try to continue their lives with power even in public areas shut off early in the evening to preserve energy.
It is a crisis created by the US war on Iran but exacerbated by Bangladesh’s reliance on imported energy. It is also a challenge that a government elected only weeks before the war began has struggled to meet.
“I don’t want anything extraordinary from the government; I want to turn on the stove and find gas, I want to switch on the light and find electricity, I want clean water from the tap,” says Halder. “These are not luxuries.
“Some nights I’m sleeping three hours, sometimes less. Then I’m expected to be a mother, run a household and do a full day at the office as if everything is normal.”
The Bangladesh Nationalist party government was elected in February, following protests in 2024 that overthrew the previous government of the Awami League, which had been in power for 15 years and was accused of political repression, corruption and economic mismanagement.
After a period of interim government, the BNP was tasked with forging a new path for the country but within weeks, war had broken out in Iran and the closure of the strait of Hormuz meant crucial gas shipments from the Middle East were disrupted.
The government responded by rationing energy, and ordered shops, markets and shopping centres to close by 8pm – an hour earlier than previously permitted. Illuminated billboards must be switched off by 7pm, with exemptions only for hospitals, pharmacies, food shops and emergency services.
The situation is worse in rural Bangladesh, where in August people were going without electricity for up to 16 hours a day. National load-shedding, or cuts in output, exceeded 3,000MW during the worst of the shortage, according to government data.
But it is in Dhaka, a city usually in constant motion, that the change appears most dramatic. Long stretches of roads in areas packed with offices, businesses and shops, such as Mohammadpur, Kawran Bazar and Dhanmondi, are now eerily dark.
The crisis has forced local residents to make calculations constantly, such as when the gas might be strong enough to cook with, how long a fan can be run during the humid summer, and how long the queue might stretch at the petrol station.
As a result, almost 3 million more people are expected to be facing food insecurity in the final months of this year, a rise of 18% from the summer figure of 15.3 million, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a global malnutrition monitor.
Ahmed, 50, who wished to give only his last name, runs an electrical workshop in the central area of Mohammadpur but lives in Keraniganj, on the outskirts of Dhaka, where housing is cheaper.
A commute he managed for years now fills him with dread. Once Ahmed has closed his shop, transport is hard to find and more expensive, and he fears being mugged in streets now left in darkness.
“By the time I close the shop, it is already dark,” he says. “Then you are thinking all the way home about whether someone will stop you, rob you or take your phone and money.
“Sometimes I think I should just leave the country and try somewhere else,” he says. “But I am 50; I don’t have the money needed to go. So I think about it, and then I feel there is nowhere to go.”
Daily gas demand in Bangladesh is about 107-113m cubic metres (3.8-4bn cubic ft), far outstripping the available supply of roughly 74m cubic metres.
The country produces little energy domestically, so it is reliant on gas from the Middle East, which provides almost half of Bangladesh’s energy supply. The US war with Iran has hit Bangladesh’s liquid natural gas (LNG) imports particularly hard – between July and August, imports fell by 83%.
The situation was made worse on 21 July, when a fire put one of Bangladesh’s two floating LNG terminals out of action, temporarily adding to disruptions that have forced factories to run costly generators, cut production or even close down, raising manufacturing and transport costs.
Khondaker Golam Moazzem, research director at the Centre for Policy Dialogue, a Dhaka thinktank, says the disruption added to longstanding frailties in Bangladesh’s energy system, caused by mismanagement of public utilities. As well as leaving households struggling, energy-intensive sectors of the economy such as textiles, ceramics, glass and steel, transport, agriculture, fisheries and general commercial activity were all affected.
“Almost all economic activities have been operating at significantly lower levels of their usable capacity because of the energy crisis,” Moazzem says.
At Krishi vegetable market in Dhaka, 41-year-old Aleya Begum struggles to run her roadside stall selling tea and street food. It is her family’s main source of income and pays for her son’s education; she had also been saving for her daughter’s marriage.
Begum says the price of vegetables has risen so much that she can afford barely enough for her family. “I used to be able to fill a bag with vegetables without spending very much,” she says. “Now I can spend a bagful of money and still not fill the bag.”
She has cut back on fish and chicken, and has to think twice about whether she buys eggs.
Begum does not pay much attention to statistics on lost megawatts of energy or debates over the extent to which the government inherited an economic crisis or if it was caused by events abroad.
“Governments can say many things, but we look at the market,” she says. “If prices don’t come down and our lives don’t get easier, how are we supposed to understand that anything has changed?
“I don’t need big promises,” she adds. “I need to be able to go to the market, feed my family and come home without worrying about how I will manage tomorrow.”

Best Open Earbuds (2026): Shokz, Bose, Soundcore, and More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Open earbuds are the big new thing in headphone land. Unlike in-ear variants, open earbuds are like tiny speakers that rest on the ear and let outside sound in naturally, so you can fully hear the world around you. Some use a hook style that wraps around the back of your ear, while others are clip-ons that look more like statement-piece earrings. Style aside, they are excellent for anyone who finds traditional earbuds uncomfortable or wants full environmental awareness for activities like running, biking, or even just doing chores around the house.
I've tested dozens of models since 2022, and while I still recommend having a pair of noise-canceling earbuds, I also love open earbuds for specific use cases.
For more headphone recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Earbuds, Best Workout Headphones, and Best Wireless Headphones.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Open Earbuds Overall
Specs
The Shokz OpenDots 2 are everything I want open earbuds to be. These are truly take-everywhere, do-anything headphones. That's partly thanks to extremely long battery life—10 hours on a single charge, and 40 hours total with the charging case. They also have an IP57 dust and waterproof rating, the same as premium, flagship earbuds like Apple AirPods Pro 3 and Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro. I've worn them in the rain, on the beach, and fully submerged them in water multiple times without issue.
They're clip-ons that wrap around the earlobe, with the speaker end resting at the ear canal opening and the other end behind the ear. Importantly, the top of your ear is free for glasses, sunglasses, or hats. Like nearly all open earbuds, they let in sound from your surroundings, so don't expect them to be a great companion for long-haul flights or daily gym sessions.
They are a bit pricey, though. Shokz recently launched the lower-priced Shokz OpenDots Air and Shokz OpenFit Air 2—I may update this recommendation depending on how my testing goes.
Runner-Up
Specs
Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata is a huge fan of the Soundcore Aeroclip for a lot of the same reasons I love the OpenDots 2. The Aeroclip buds are light, comfortable, and stable on your ear, plus they have stellar battery life and strong water and dust resistance (not waterproof). Waniata used them for daily life: walking the dog, strolling with the baby, riding bikes, making dinner, and hanging out at home—any situation where you want your music but also want to be aware or talk to people. The Soundcore app is easy to use and offers plenty of customization for controls, EQ, and multipoint pairing.
The brand recently announced the Soundcore Aeroclip 2 and Aeroclip 2 Pro, which I will be testing soon. Look out for deals on these original Aeroclips as a result.
Best Premium Open Earbuds
Specs
The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds were a big deal when they launched in 2024—a brand-new design from Bose and one of the biggest swings from a major brand in clip-on open earbuds. Two years later, they are still a solid, if expensive, option. That's mainly because of sound quality—these earbuds have a clearer, more defined sound than most competitors. Another differentiator is physical button controls on each bud, which I find easier to use than touch alternatives, especially when running or biking.
Like the Shokz and Soundcore, they are supremely comfortable, so much so that I sometimes forgot I was wearing them. But they are much pricier by comparison, and only worth it if you want the best sound quality in this clip-on form factor.
Best Cheap Open Earbuds
Specs
It can be a little nerve-wracking to spend big bucks on a concept (open earbuds) you aren't totally convinced by. That's one reason I love this $50 option—the PearClip Pros aren't super pricey and are a great way to find out if you even like open earbuds in the first place, especially the kind that clip onto the outside of your ear.
They are far less refined than Shokz or Soundcore. Things like the app and touch controls can be a little finicky. But that's common at this super-low price point, and you can always upgrade to a more premium earbud if you fall in love with the clip-on form factor.
Best Open Ear Headphones
Specs
The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are more headphones than earbuds—they have a wraparound headband styling, long battery life, great sound quality (for open headphones), and no charging case. They use a combination of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver sound that's clearer than most smaller open earbuds, especially in noisy environments. That combination of technologies is why these are some of my favorite earbuds for outdoor fitness activities like running and biking.
I do wish these headphones were a little cheaper. I'm currently testing the recently released, more affordable Shokz OpenRun Air 2, and hopeful they can be a budget-friendly alternative.
Honorable Mentions
Nothing Ear (Open) for $99: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So loves these earbuds and uses them for almost all her outdoor activities. They are very slim (19-mm wide) and lightweight. They fit slightly inside your ear and, like most Nothing headphones, have a distinct transparent design. The case doesn't clamp shut very firmly, so be careful, but at this price, that's forgivable.
JLab Epic Open Sport for $100: JLab’s Epic Open Sport stands out for its controls: the JLab emblem is a touch sensor, and each earbud also has physical buttons on top, making it a breeze to control. What holds the Epic Open Sport back is audio quality—the sound isn't very detailed, and it's generally boring to listen to.
Other Open Earbuds I’ve Tested
EarFun Clip for $70: For around $70, these are a solid pick for anyone on a budget. Waniata found the overall package punching above its price point, with a snappy, compact case, comfortable fit, push-button controls, and reliable multiple Bluetooth connections. The problem is our budget pick, the Soundpeats PearlClip Pro, is often on sale for less and offers a similar overall experience. Don't dismiss these earbuds if you find them heavily discounted.
Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro has a great premise: open earbuds with noise canceling. Hear the world around you as you would without headphones, and turn on noise-canceling when you don't, just like regular earbuds. And while they do cancel some noise, it's not much. The bigger issue is price: for $250, you could get open earbuds and great noise-canceling earbuds that do a better job for each task.
Suunto Wing 2 for $179: These open-ear headphones are designed for endurance athletes—they have a long 12-hour battery life but also come with a wireless power bank you can take on the go. Dock the headphones in the power bank for up to 36 hours of battery life total. There's nothing inherently wrong with these headphones, but I don't see a world where I would recommend them over the Shokz Openrun Pro 2, which retail for the same amount and offer more comfort, a sleeker design, better sound, and a more robust app.
Suunto Spark for $179: The Suunto Spark has a similar story to the Suunto Wing 2: with athletes in mind, it has features that sync with Suunto fitness watches, but it is outclassed in the areas that matter (comfort, sound quality, battery) by the similarly priced Shokz Openfit 2.
What Are Open Earbuds and How Do They Sound?
At a glance, open earbuds seem a lot like typical wireless earbuds. The big difference is that, instead of going inside your ear canal, they rest somewhere on the outside of your ear, leaving it open so you can easily hear the world around you. I use them all the time for outdoor exercise like running or biking, where I want my music but also need to hear other runners, bikers, and cars to stay safe.
Because they leave your ears open and the sound comes from farther away (outside your ear rather than inside), audio performance isn't as clear, intimate, or bassy as regular earbuds. They also typically don't have noise-canceling features, so they are not a great fit for the office or air travel.
When or Where Would I Use Open Earbuds?
Open earbuds are perfect for outdoor activities, or when you want to talk to other people without taking off your headphones. When I run or go for a bike ride, I only use open earbuds so I can hear my surroundings and stay safe. I also like using them around the house when I am cooking or doing laundry.
What About Semi-Open Earbuds?
Semi-open earbuds, like Apple's AirPods, sit inside the ear but don't have eartips that create a sound seal. They can offer better audio quality than other open earbuds because the speakers and microphones are closer to your ear and mouth. Semi-open earbuds are comfortable, but they're usually pretty loose—they can fall out easily and may be a poor option for fitness activities.
How Do I Test Open Earbuds?
I test open earbuds like I test any pair of headphones: in the real world, in my daily life. I wear each pair for at least a few weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I listen to podcasts, watch TV shows, jam out to my favorite playlists, and call friends.
With open earbuds in particular, I also wear them on jogs, bike rides, and errand runs to get a better feel for how stable they are on my ears. I do not expect them to cancel any noise, so I don't make a point of testing them on airplanes or loud commutes—they aren't really made for that. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, but, when possible, I test other formats and codecs as well.

Why AI Isn’t Likely to Wipe Out Humanity With Bioweapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Concerns about an AI-induced apocalypse are reaching a fever pitch, from Silicon Valley to Washington, DC.
One of the top theories about how a rogue AI will wipe us out? Biological weapons.
Earlier this summer, AI CEOs called for new laws to control the manufacturing of synthetic DNA. Then last month, researchers at Stanford University and the Arc Institute showed that AI can design new viral genomes. The idea gained steam last week after Anthropic released a report indicating that there had been efforts to use Claude in ways that “could support biological weapons development. “The report authors cite biological misuse as “one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models.” Shortly thereafter, chief executive officer Dario Amodei urged the government to help AI labs “pace the frontier.”
Despite the alarm around an AI-created killer plague, many scientists say the risk is fairly low on the list of the world’s concerns.
David Bellamy, a research scientist at the Institute of Foundation Models in Sunnyvale, California, does not see AI as a fundamentally new threat when it comes to the creation of bioweapons. The scientific community has grappled for decades with the question of whether to publish potentially dangerous biological research—known as the dual-use dilemma.
Before large language models, the internet itself, open-access science journals, and translation services like Google Translate made it easier for people to access biological information, including lab protocols, Bellamy says.
“AI is essentially a tool that can help both good actors, like scientists, and also threat actors to peruse information more quickly and define and source those protocols more quickly,” he adds. “But those capabilities are not really the bottleneck in the production of bioweapons.”
The real bottleneck, he says, is the process of assembling a virus or other biological agent and the raw materials, equipment, and knowledge that would be needed to do so. A bad actor would need to obtain the necessary gene fragments and build a whole genome from scratch, then verify that the virus can infect humans, cause the desired illness, and be transmissible from person to person. Robotic lab assistants can automate some tasks and speed up workflows to a point, but a person would still need the know-how to run those experiments and the resources to carry them out.
Jason Kelly, the CEO of the biotech startup Ginkgo Bioworks, thinks it’s unlikely an artificial general intelligence could commandeer and disseminate existing pathogens, let alone engineer new ones and deploy them. Ginkgo Bioworks specializes in creating autonomous labs and recently ran a project with OpenAI where its GPT-5 model ran a lab.
“The AI could not take over the lab,” he says, in part because the humans who worked inside could simply decline to get the bot whatever substances and equipment it was requesting to physically produce a bioweapon. All those pesky humans acting as checks mean “you’d have to have dramatically more robots all over the place,” he says, for an AGI to be able to deploy machines to do the often-delicate virology work required.
Immunologist Derya Unutmaz likewise says humans would be able to thwart any attempts by AGI to develop a deadly disease. Even if a nefarious super intelligence did somehow manage to unleash a supervirus, he argues that scientists would be able to use other AI systems to swiftly develop a vaccine.
Still, even some people who don’t think that AGI independently siccing a bioweapon on us right now is a real threat are concerned about bad actors using the technology as well as what might happen down the line.
“It is impossible for AI to access a fully autonomous lab and autonomously build a virus today because fully autonomous labs do not exist yet,” says Olivia Scharfman, a biotechnology fellow at the technology think tank Institute for Progress. “But I do think that an AI could pay someone to do it for them.”
She thinks AI-assisted bioterrorism is an immediate threat and that there are some groups that might be nihilistic enough to do so, including “transhumanist AI successionists,” people who buy into a fringe ideology who hope to supplant humans with bots.
Other experts aren’t so worried about an AI bioweapon because they don’t think that biological warfare makes much sense methodologically. “The risks tend to be somewhat misunderstood,” genetic biologist and professor of computational biology Francois Belloux tells WIRED, noting that people tend to “overestimate the value of pathogens as weapons.”
Setting aside the AGI of it all, Belloux says that bioweapons are simply not an especially attractive choice for aspiring genocidaires, especially as it’s difficult to target certain groups and spare others, and mass-producing and distributing pathogens is logistically complicated versus, say, launching a bomb. “If you want to kill people, there are much, much, much better ways to kill them than to try to engineer some virus or bacterium and then release it,” he says—whether you’re the most sophisticated artificial mind ever created or just a regular human.
With AI bringing the threat of bioweapons into focus, Scharfman says this is the right moment to push for better protections against all biological threats, including existing pathogens like H1N1. That could include high-level actions like passing legislation to enhance security protocols around DNA synthesis technology, but she also advocates for changes to mitigate risk from all viruses, like upgrading air purification systems in buildings.
Whether AI demonstrably raises the risk of bioweapon development is a hard question to answer, says Steph Guerra, head of AI and bio at Rand Corporation, a policy think tank. “AI has been shown to be very good at integrating information together and being motivational to people for doing good and bad things,” she says.
Even if the risk is low, Guerra says, there are still ways that society can protect against potential misuse. One is that governments can adopt laws requiring firms that sell synthetic DNA and RNA to screen customers and orders to prevent the misuse of genetic material. Many companies already use software to screen orders for so-called “sequences of concern,” but the practice is not universal or mandated.
Before a bad actor could get to that point, though, most everyone agrees that models should have appropriate safeguards in place so that they don’t provide actionable, dangerous information to people.
Guerra says the risk of an AI-developed biothreat can also be mitigated by strengthening global surveillance systems to detect outbreaks of new diseases and circulating pathogens to researchers as early as possible. She says data-sharing protocols across AI companies, gene synthesis providers, and the government could also help prevent misuse.
“With pretty much almost any biosecurity control, there are going to be ways that they can be circumvented,” she says. “That's why we need layered approaches that provide friction across the entire pathway, from ideation to intention of a bad actor, all the way to the release of a bioweapon.”
Unutmaz says there’s an even more pressing worry: that all the AI doom conversations are diverting attention from how cutting-edge systems can assist humans in vaccine development and other medical breakthroughs.
“We really need to focus on the positive aspect of it,” he says.

Drone Attacks Disrupt First Day of Voting in Southern Russia and Occupied Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:59:56 UTC
17:59:56 KST

Ukrainian drone strikes disrupted the work of election workers at polling stations in southern Russia and parts of occupied Ukraine, Russian authorities said Friday, the first day of a three-day voting period for parliamentary and regional races.
“There are small incidents I can’t fail to mention,” Russia’s Central Election Commission (CEC) chief Ella Pamfilova told reporters during a morning press conference. “In the Krasnodar region, one polling station had to be moved to an alternative location because the windows were broken due to damage from a drone.”
Fourteen polling stations in the occupied Luhansk region of eastern Ukraine briefly lost power after drones damaged energy infrastructure, Pamfilova said, though the sites eventually switched to backup power supplies.
Andrei Proshunin, the mayor of the southern resort city of Sochi, said election workers and voters were forced to seek shelter Friday morning due to an air raid alert. He did not say whether any additional safety measures had been introduced across the city’s more than 240 polling stations amid near-daily drone attacks.
Russia is holding elections for the lower-house State Duma for the first time since President Vladimir Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Alongside parliamentary races, gubernatorial elections and votes for local legislative assemblies are taking place in several regions.
Earlier this week, the CEC said one of its members was killed in a drone attack in the occupied Zaporizhzhia region. Voting is also taking place in parts of occupied Ukraine, which Russia claims to have annexed in September 2022.
Russian election officials also reported cyberattacks on the country’s remote electronic voting system, with the head of Moscow’s election commission assuring that “an army” of IT specialists was working around the clock to repel the intrusions.
On the eve of the first election day, Pamfilova warned of mobile internet disruptions across Russia, a common tactic used by the Russian military to disrupt the guidance systems of drones. “For us, this is no reason to cancel the vote,” she said.
The independent news outlets RusNews and Sotavision, citing election observers in Moscow, reported widespread failures of electronic voting terminals. The Moscow Times could not independently verify those reports.
Despite the anti-drone measures, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported more than 350 incoming Ukrainian drones between Thursday night and Friday morning. He claimed at least 64 unmanned aircraft were destroyed on their approach to the capital.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 629 Ukrainian drones overnight across Russia and annexed Crimea.
In Ukraine, authorities said two people were killed when the Russian military struck a business in the northwestern Zhytomyr region. Separate attacks wounded multiple people near Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, with authorities reporting damage to infrastructure, schools, clinics and residential buildings.

The government has established new requirements for the &quot;Air Raid Alert&quot; signal
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:59:30 EEST
17:59:30 KST

The government has established new requirements for the "Air Raid Alert" signal
Kyiv • UNN
The signal will last one minute at the red level and 30 seconds at the yellow level. The yellow threat will be announced differentially by district.
The Cabinet of Ministers has established new rules for issuing the "Air Raid Alert" signal. From now on, its duration will depend on the level of threat, while the yellow level will be issued differentially by district. UNN reports this with reference to government resolution No. 1128.
The "Air Raid Alert" signal consists of the "Attention everyone" audible signal and a voice announcement about the threat level from means of air attack: "red level," "yellow level
The duration of the "Air Raid Alert" signal is, when the following is established:
-  red level - 1 minute;  
-  yellow level - 30 seconds.  
If a yellow threat level is established, the "Air Raid Alert" signal is issued differentially by district. The "All Clear" signal is issued by broadcasting the corresponding voice announcement without sounding the "Attention everyone" audible signal.
The government also established that business entities (shopping centers, stores, and so on) must inform personnel and visitors about the availability of a shelter and a safe space by placing signs at the entrances to premises, buildings, structures, or territories, and on their exterior walls, bearing the wording "The facility is equipped with a shelter," or "The facility is equipped with a safe space," or "The facility is not equipped with a shelter," as well as establish procedures for personnel to follow in the event of an "Air Raid Alert" signal.
As a reminder
The Cabinet of Ministers defined the procedure for railway transport operations during yellow and red levels of air raid alert. In particular, at the yellow level, train movement and passenger boarding and disembarking are permitted, whereas at the red level, boarding and disembarking are suspended, and passengers and employees must proceed to shelters.

At least two killed in Philippines school shooting

17:55:00 KST

The shooting is the third at a Philippines school in recent months. (AFP File Photo)
At least two people were killed in a school shooting in the southern Philippines on Sept. 18, a regional disaster agency worker told AFP, the country’s third deadly campus incident since June.
Local rescuers received a call about gunfire on the campus of Banga National High School in South Cotabato province in Mindanao at about 1:30 p.m.
“From what I know, they are both students. There’s really no complete details as of now,” disaster agency worker Rolly Aquino said of the two victims, adding that at least seven people were being treated in hospital.
“For now, we are trying to let our fellow citizens know that the situation is stable and the case is contained,” said South Cotabato provincial governor Reynaldo Tamayo.
“We never thought that this would happen.”
In a video posted to Facebook and confirmed by AFP, a man can be seen carrying what appears to be a wounded child from the school, rushing him into the sidecar of a waiting motorbike.
In another, a teacher speaking in a local dialect can be heard saying that there were two shooters, with a student insisting they were outsiders.
Nationwide live shooter drills were conducted this month to strengthen security following two rare school shootings that shook the Philippines in the past few months.

Russia Claims Bucha Massacre Was a Western Fabrication – But Why?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:54:00 UTC
17:54:00 KST

Ever since responsibility for the deaths of more than 450 civilians during the 2022 occupation of the town of Bucha in the Kyiv region was attributed to Russian forces, Moscow has protested its innocence. The latest attempt to prove its troops were not guilty of those atrocities is in the publication of a report by the self-styled “International Public Tribunal on Crimes by Ukrainian Neo-Nazis.”
The tribunal is an unofficial, Russian-instigated public organization that was founded days after the start of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine to “investigate, document and prosecute Ukrainian war crimes against captured Russian servicemen and civilians.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It is chaired by Maxim Grigoryev and claims representation by civil society from 33 countries.
This latest 21-page report is entitled, apparently without any irony, “Heirs of Goebbels: falsification of the events in Bucha and bloody staged performances of the Kiev [sic] regime,” mirroring the Kremlin’s attempts to portray the Ukraine invasion as a continuation of its WWII fight against Nazi Germany.
A press conference, sponsored by the Russian state news agency TASS and chaired by Russia’s Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Maria Zakharova, was held on Sept. 17 to present Grigoryev’s report, which says it shows that the 2022 Bucha massacre was a poorly executed hoax conducted by Ukraine and Western intelligence agencies.
Meloni: Putin Seeks European Escalation to Mask Ukraine Failures
Various investigations – including those by the New York Times (NYT) – have identified the victims and full circumstances of their deaths, so how is Russia “debunking” it?
More importantly, why?
What evidence does Russia have, and where is it?
The press conference restated the Kremlin’s oft-stated view, as represented in the report, that indisputable facts show how Ukraine, the European Union, and European nations positioned deceased Ukrainian military personnel who had died in combat, along with elderly Ukrainian citizens who had died of natural causes, as civilians killed in Bucha. These were then passed off as victims of Russian occupiers in the town.
They say the report also presents indisputable evidence of a widespread practice conducted by the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) of the deliberate killing of their own citizens – including women, children and the elderly – to support Kyiv’s claims of outrages conducted by Russia, during the latter’s so-called “special military operation.”
But the majority of the killing took place on Yablunska Street in occupied Bucha, where Russian troops were stationed, when the town was under occupation, and not under Ukrainian control.
The bulk of Grigoryev’s “evidence” is also to compare the names of several of those who died in Bucha with open-source images and reports of Ukrainian servicemen, some of whom are known to have died elsewhere or civilians who died trying to defend the town from Russian attack, which, in the report’s view, makes them combatants, not “innocent civilians.”
An NYT investigation identified 36 of the victims on Yablunska Street, including mothers, fathers, children and grandparents, and pieced together their final moments via eyewitness accounts, text messages, and satellite imagery.
A video from occupied Bucha, contained in another 2022 NYT report, shows a line of Ukrainian men being marched by a Russian soldier at gunpoint to a base, with eyewitness accounts noting that gunshots were heard and the men never returned. Some bodies, including those of men and women, were found strewn across the streets of Bucha following the town’s liberation, while further examinations discovered mass graves in nearby forests containing remains of residents.
But Grigoryev’s report also gives its view, after Russian forces withdrew from Bucha, that no time passed before the Western media were allowed to descend on the town, where they bore witness to the bodies that lay strewn about the town, which it suggests were pre-positioned by Ukrainian forces as part of an anti-Kremlin propaganda onslaught.
It then seeks to underline the veracity of its hypothesis of what happened in Bucha by recording eyewitness testimony – not from Bucha, but from other towns and cities where it alleges Ukraine staged Russian war crimes or hid its own.
However, the premise is undermined by the lack of any truly impartial evidence or corroboration of the evidence presented by any neutral parties.
Who is the report for?
It is unclear who exactly the report is aimed at, but the claim, long echoed by the Kremlin and its propaganda machine, is often echoed by skeptics of the West.
But sometimes, they also coincide with attempts at peace talks.
Zakharova said during the press conference that Russia had identified the claims of a massacre in Bucha as a falsification at the time. She asserted that on March 30, 2022, Russian Armed Forces had withdrawn from the area around Kyiv, including Bucha, as a gesture of goodwill amidst the aborted peace negotiations with Ukraine in Istanbul.
She then said the reports of what had been an obviously orchestrated information campaign following Moscow’s withdrawal, the town had become a “place of pilgrimage” for Western leaders, heads of international organizations and Western journalists. – a claim also echoed by US Vice President JD Vance.
For Moscow’s fellow-travelers, it will reinforce the view that the Russian invasion was an unfortunate necessity because of the threat from the West and that accusations against its armed forces are simply propaganda designed to undermine its “righteous cause.”
The timing of the release on the eve of the elections of the ninth convocation of the State Duma is also unlikely to be coincidental and again needed to shore up ordinary Russians’ view of the war.
From the viewpoint not only of Ukraine and its allies, but also from the numerous inquiries and investigations that were carried out after Russian withdrawals, there is no doubt that Bucha, along with several towns that were previously and are still occupied, did indeed suffer from the outrageous and barbaric behavior of Russian servicemen – from looting and theft, rape, torture and murder.
This latest report will do nothing to assuage that view.
