Trump faces skeptical UN audience as Iran war enters 7th month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:54:00 UTC
17:54:00 KST

President Donald Trump returns to the United Nations next week facing a Middle East conflict that has proved far more complicated and prolonged than he predicted, with Iran still resisting U.S. pressure and its Houthi allies threatening another critical global shipping route.
When Trump addressed the U.N. a year ago, he portrayed the U.S. bombing of Iran's nuclear facilities as a decisive success, saying American strikes had "totally obliterated everything" and claiming he had helped bring peace between Israel and Iran.
Six months into the latest U.S.-Iran war, those declarations face a much more skeptical international audience.
Iran has been weakened militarily and economically, but it has continued to challenge Washington, restricting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz while its Iran-aligned Houthi allies in Yemen have rapidly expanded their control along the Red Sea coast. The Houthi advance toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has created a second threat to a vital global shipping corridor and pushed energy prices higher.
The developments have left Trump confronting a difficult strategic choice. Washington wants to keep both waterways open and reassure Gulf allies, but the U.S. military is already heavily committed to the Iran conflict and Trump has shown little appetite for opening another major front in Yemen.
The Houthi gains have also exposed vulnerabilities among U.S. partners. Saudi Arabia has requested greater American military support as the group attacks Saudi cities and energy infrastructure, but Washington has so far emphasized intelligence and targeting assistance rather than direct U.S. strikes.
"The US clearly has (military) capacity challenges but even so the cost of inaction here is likely to intensify tensions among Gulf allies," said Jonathan Panikoff, a former deputy national intelligence officer on the Middle East.
Trump entered the conflict after campaigning on avoiding prolonged foreign military engagements. He has since repeatedly suggested that the war could end soon, while offering shifting objectives and timelines.
On Wednesday, he again said he hoped the conflict was nearing its end.
"Well, hopefully we are towards the end of the war," Trump told reporters.
But the war that began Feb. 28, when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, has entered its seventh month. Iran responded with strikes against Israel and Gulf countries hosting U.S. military bases, while negotiations aimed at ending the fighting have repeatedly stalled.
The conflict has also placed pressure on U.S. military resources, including missile stockpiles, while creating economic consequences that have spread well beyond the battlefield.
Oil prices have remained above $100 a barrel amid disruptions to regional energy infrastructure and shipping. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen sharply, while the Bab el-Mandeb is also facing growing disruption because of the Houthi advance.
For Trump, the economic fallout carries an additional political dimension. Higher energy costs are emerging as an issue ahead of November's midterm elections, when Republicans will defend their control of Congress.
"We are seeing what happens when a president launches a war of choice without anticipating the unintended consequences," said Aaron David Miller, a former Middle East adviser to both Republican and Democratic administrations.
Iran's nuclear program was central to Trump's justification for military action, but questions remain over the extent to which the strikes achieved the administration's stated objectives.
During his U.N. speech last year, Trump recalled the U.S. deployment of B-2 bombers and the use of 30,000-pound bombs against Iranian nuclear facilities. He described the strikes as having demolished Iran's uranium-enrichment capacity.
Experts subsequently assessed that the attacks had severely damaged the program but had not eliminated it.
Trump has continued to argue that the campaign successfully weakened Iran's nuclear capabilities. The administration has also intensified sanctions and economic pressure on Tehran.
Iran, meanwhile, has maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful and has denied seeking nuclear weapons.
The disagreement over the nuclear issue remains one of the central obstacles to diplomacy. Negotiations earlier this year produced competing accounts over inspections, Iran's frozen assets and the future of its nuclear activities.
The United Nations has also added fresh scrutiny of the war. A U.N. fact-finding mission said Thursday that there were reasonable grounds to believe the U.S. was responsible for strikes on a school and a sports facility in Iran in February that constituted war crimes. The mission separately accused Iranian authorities of crimes against humanity during a crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings are expected to further complicate Trump's appearance before world leaders.
Trump's approach has also raised concerns among Gulf states that rely heavily on U.S. security guarantees.
Those concerns have grown because the U.S. entered the war without consulting several allies and has since resisted Saudi requests for direct intervention against the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia is particularly vulnerable because the Strait of Hormuz has been heavily disrupted, increasing the importance of alternative routes through the Red Sea. The Houthi advance toward the Bab el-Mandeb now threatens that option as well.
The crisis has also strained Washington's relationships with European and Asian allies, many of which have resisted Trump's calls for greater involvement in a conflict they did not help initiate.
At the same time, the humanitarian consequences in Yemen are mounting. More than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed fighting, while thousands more have fled by sea to Djibouti, according to the U.N. refugee agency.
The Houthi offensive has complicated Trump's search for an exit strategy.
A major U.S. intervention in Yemen could further stretch American forces and expose U.S. personnel and bases to retaliation. But allowing the Houthis to gain control over the Bab el-Mandeb would give Iran-aligned forces leverage over another major international shipping route.
U.S. officials met Houthi representatives in Oman last weekend in an apparent effort to contain the situation. The Houthis indicated they were targeting Saudi shipping but did not intend to attack American vessels, according to people familiar with the discussions.
Meanwhile, Washington continues to pursue economic pressure against Tehran.
The Trump administration has described its campaign as an effort to cripple Iran's economy and force concessions, while Iranian officials have rejected the pressure and continued to resist U.S. demands.
Trump will also encounter Iranian officials at the U.N. gathering. The U.S. has agreed to allow Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi to attend the General Assembly despite the ongoing conflict, although the delegation will face restrictions while in New York.

Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) has extended the application deadline until the end of September for its social entrepreneurship and veteran business schools, specifically for applicants from Vinnytsia and Mykolaiv regions.
"The Ukrainian Red Cross continues to accept applications for the Social Entrepreneurship School and the Veteran Business School for veterans and their family members from Vinnytsia and Mykolaiv regions. Applications can be submitted up to and including September 30," the URCS announced on Facebook on Friday.
According to the URCS, both schools will help participants gain practical knowledge to launch or grow their own businesses, work with mentors, and prepare a business plan.

The Social Entrepreneurship School is designed for those wishing to start or grow a business that has a positive impact on the community or helps address social issues. Participants will gain knowledge on building a sustainable business model, finance, and communications, and will work with mentors on their business plans and financial models. Upon completion of the training, there is an opportunity to receive a grant of up to EUR 12,500 to implement a social business project.
The training schools are conducted as part of the Support for Veteran Reintegration in Ukraine program, implemented by the Ukrainian Red Cross with the support of the Danish Red Cross and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Denmark. The educational component of the program is delivered by the International Management Institute.

North Korea’s nuclear tests awaken fault lines pointing to huge volcano at China border
Researchers find evidence of persistent earthquake activity that has also steadily intensified along two distinct paths
The joint Chinese and South Korean study, which appeared on Thursday, found that the five nuclear explosions conducted between 2013 and 2017 at the Punggye-ri test site beneath Mount Mantap fundamentally altered the region’s geological stability.
Instead of fading quickly, the earthquake activity had not only persisted for nearly a decade, it had also steadily intensified, the researchers found. It is now propagating along two distinct parallel fault zones heading directly towards the China-North Korea border.
At the end of those fault lines is Changbai Mountain, known on the Korean peninsula as Mount Paektu, a dormant but restless volcano that had its last major eruption in AD946 – one of the largest on the planet in the past 2,000 years.

The Italian Embassy in Morocco is participating in the first edition of “Morocco Design,” opening the Teatro Italia construction site in Casablanca for three days. From October 5 to 7, the space currently undergoing restoration, adjacent to the Consulate General of Italy in Casablanca, will host “L’Axe Invisible,” a solo exhibition by Moroccan artist and designer Hamza Kadiri, curated by Amine Amharech. During Morocco Design—the two-day event that will fill Casablanca with exhibitions, initiatives, and discussions on the theme of international industrial design—visitors will be able to enter the theater’s spaces while they are still undergoing transformation and experience them in a state that will no longer exist once the restoration is complete. “The construction site will not be hidden,” explains the Embassy in a press release. “The still-raw surfaces, the traces of the work, and the theater’s architecture will become part of the exhibition and interact with Kadiri’s works.” After all, the exhibition “L’Axe Invisible” stems precisely from its relationship with this space and its current condition. The press release further explains: “The artist’s exploration of materials, woodworking, and the relationship between form, craftsmanship, and sculpture thus finds in the Teatro Italia a context that is unlikely to be replicated.” Hamza Kadiri is one of the leading figures in Morocco’s new creative scene, and this year he is also among the Moroccan artists featured at “Homo Faber” at the Giorgio Cini Foundation in Venice, where one of his works is on display. “We wanted to open the Teatro Italia right now, before the renovations give it its new look,” emphasizes Pasquale Salzano, the Italian Ambassador to Morocco. “For three days, the public will be able to enter a historic site in the city and discover it as it changes. I am particularly pleased that it is the work of a Moroccan artist that is bringing it to life at this moment and that the theater itself is becoming part of the exhibition. It is a tribute from Italy to contemporary Moroccan creativity, but also a concrete way to provide space and visibility to a new generation of creatives, capable of drawing on a great tradition of craftsmanship and bringing it to life through new forms of expression.” ‘L’Axe Invisible’ will be open to the public at the Teatro Italia, located at the Consulate General of Italy in Casablanca, 43 avenue Hassan Souktani, on Monday, October 5, and Tuesday, October 6, from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., and on Wednesday, October 7, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.

Israel would rather not watch NAZA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:49:16 UTC
17:49:16 KST

Israel would rather not watch NAZA
The backlash against the Gaza documentary is part of a broader refusal to confront the reality of the genocide.
NAZA (Hebrew acronym for “collateral damage”), the documentary made by Yuval Avraham and Rachel Szor, has yet to secure an Israeli distributor or a public screening, despite its creators’ stated intention to show it widely in the country. Various senior executives, from the Israeli military chief of staff to the minister of culture, promised that they were about to “take steps” against the creators of the film. Other than stripping them of their Israeli citizenship (considered a remarkably rare measure), what those “steps” could be was unclear. However, one refrain dominated the outrage directed at Avraham and Szor: Those condemning the film had no intention of watching it.
It is important to emphasise that this oath to refrain from watching the film was authentic. In a way, it is a variation on a theme that became prevalent throughout the first months of the “war”. When images of devastation began to emerge from Gaza, many Israelis wrote that they could feel no pity for the children of Gaza (at the end of 2023, the number of children killed and orphaned was already known and difficult to grasp, as were military “procedures”). These Israelis said they had “closed their hearts” in response to the huge, intentional death toll in the Israeli towns and villages surrounding Gaza. They claimed they would not and could not feel pity for anyone who had committed such atrocities, or for anyone related to them. Activists on the Israeli left believed that if Israelis were exposed to images from the already nearly deleted Gaza, they would head for the streets and call for a stop to the war. These activists were soundly rebuffed.
NAZA was, itself, a rebuttal of the position actively taken by the Israeli media – “Yes, the Israeli military had made mistakes but these should be investigated by the military and the Israeli legal system, both very much capable of carrying out the task.” Raviv Drucker, perhaps Israel’s most prominent investigative journalist, when asked by Yuval Avraham (during an interview of Avraham himself conducted by Drucker) why Israeli media had done nothing to expose the methods of killing documented by NAZA, said with visible embarrassment that doing so was “difficult” for a host of reasons. However, Drucker was also quick to add that if it were up to him, he would not have aired the film because he believed it lacked journalistic professionalism, relying as it does on anonymous testimony. This line of criticism was quickly taken up by other journalists considered a part of the Israeli left. They attacked the film and its creators, accusing them of everything from seeking money and attention to actively working for Israel’s downfall in the service of Netanyahu and Qatar. They were called “useful idiots”, meaning people who work for a worthy cause but are unwittingly used in the service of another. Journalists like Uri Misgav acknowledged the importance of criticism but implied that NAZA served the goals of Israel’s enemies. They suggested that its disregard for journalistic standards showed that the creators had already reached their conclusion: That Israel was the root of all evil and solely responsible for the state of Gaza.
For Israelis, not watching NAZA is a point of pride. Some will cite the lack of journalistic standards (this from a country that assassinated more than 200 journalists over the course of its genocide in Gaza). Other Israelis will suggest that they recognise “treason” when they see it. Many Israelis will apply the following wondrous excuse: “Even if some of this is true, you wash your dirty laundry at home; you don’t entertain others by using that dirty laundry to demonstrate that Israel really is responsible for the killing of 20,000 children and more than 70,000 Palestinians in Gaza.” The fact that the military and the Israeli legal system have proven themselves to be incompetent at best (and thoroughly politicised at worst) when investigating war crimes and crimes against humanity is beside the point for many Israelis. After all, one could offer up such incompetence as an excuse for the strategies exposed by NAZA. Israelis wouldn’t hear of it. This is yet another example of the world’s hatred for Israel (“anti-Semitism”, if you like) that makes international accusations levelled against Israel completely irrelevant. No matter what we do, we will emerge at fault, so why encourage this state of affairs by having lengthy discussions about a critical movie? We’ve heard the criticism countless times. We know there is a web of detractors all over the world (perhaps funded by Qatar, perhaps by the Red-Green alliance between the woke left and radical Islam). It doesn’t matter.
Just as Israelis “closed their hearts” when the genocide began, so they are shutting their eyes and ears now. They take pride in their ignorance of the film’s content. They feel it misrepresents them. How do they know? They don’t, but that only makes them even more convinced of the one-sidedness of the whole episode. It is enough to hear that the directors received an unprecedented 25-minute standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival, where they won a special jury prize. Special, eh? Everything about Israel is special. A special prize can simply be invented on the spot to present Israel negatively. It isn’t as though Avraham and Szor walked away from the podium with the Silver Lion, one of the festival’s major awards, is it? Their film is not art. Nor is it a documentary because it doesn’t observe the codes of documentary filmmaking. Its only purpose is to discredit Israel, isn’t it? If that is the case, why should an Israeli with any sense of identity do the enemy’s work: The ultimate destruction of Israel as a Jewish state (democracy was abandoned right at the start), for them? Better to deny and reject reality. It isn’t just that we do what we want – we are the ones who define the very nature of reality itself. When we don’t like it, we close our eyes and wait for the threat to pass. It always does.

Interview: China-ASEAN cooperation can play key role in haze prevention, management: think tank
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:48:21 CST
17:48:21 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Worsening air quality has reached hazardous levels in Southeast Asia in recent weeks. Indonesia's Kalimantan and Sumatra regions have faced widespread forest and land fires this year, with haze disrupting flights, forcing school closures and causing hazardous air quality in parts of the country.
The transboundary haze problem in particular is a wide-ranging issue that affects public health, education, transport, and tourism across Malaysia, Singapore, and the Philippines, presenting a challenge that cannot be ignored and must be overcome, said Kat W. Wong, executive director and chief strategist at the Center for Advanced Studies and Research.
While existing regional frameworks, such as the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, have served as constructive platforms for dialogue and technical coordination, current mechanisms primarily focus on monitoring and response after fires occur rather than addressing root causes.
"The current approach, which focuses on monitoring and responding to haze once it occurs instead of preventing fires at the source, leaves out the crucial responsibility of every country to ensure peatland protection and restoration, stronger land-use management," she said.
According to her, closer coordination and cooperation between the ASEAN grouping and China could lay the groundwork for effective disaster prevention and management, particularly on regional haze.
"China's advanced capabilities in satellite remote sensing, weather forecasting, early-warning digital platforms, drones, and emergency equipment align directly with ASEAN's operational needs," she said.
Both sides "could further strengthen cooperation in disaster early warning, emergency response training and post-disaster reconstruction. This could include the exchange of meteorological and disaster-related data, the application of early-warning technologies and digital platforms, as well as joint training and emergency response exercises," said Wong.
This pragmatic cooperation will offset the continued disruption caused by climate events that have exacerbated conditions leading to regional forest fires and the resulting transboundary haze, and build long-term disaster resilience and environmental security, she told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Wong noted that practical steps have already been taken with the launch of the ASEAN-China Disaster Management Cooperation Project in April, which establishes a concrete channel for collaborative action while respecting ASEAN centrality. Joint training initiatives involving Malaysia and China have already significantly enhanced local disaster management and response capabilities.
"Disaster prevention and mitigation is an important area in which China and ASEAN can further deepen cooperation. It directly concerns the safety of people and property across the region and is closely linked to regional development and people's well-being," she said, adding that as extensive operations require significant funding, ASEAN must remain open to external assistance to ensure comprehensive, long-term environmental and regional security. ■

China's property market sees major changes in supply and demand: official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:47:54 CST
17:47:54 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China's property market has seen major changes in supply and demand and entered a new phase increasingly centered on existing housing stock, an official said Friday.
The share of second-hand home transactions in total housing transactions rose from 27 percent in 2020 to 46 percent in 2025, and 52 percent in the first eight months of this year, said Zhang Xuetao, an official with the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, at a press conference.
A share exceeding 50 percent marks the property market's transition into the new phase, according to Zhang.
To adapt to these changes, China is accelerating efforts to foster a new development model for the real estate sector, Zhang said. The country will press ahead with reforms to three key systems governing property development, financing and sales to promote the sector's sound development.
In property development, each real estate project will operate through a dedicated project company that is an independent legal entity, while corporate headquarters will be barred from improperly diverting project funds, Zhang said.
In property financing, each project will have one lead bank or banking consortium to manage project funds and meet reasonable financing needs, with the bank and project company sharing benefits and risks, Zhang said.
In commercial housing sales, China will promote sales of completed homes to allow buyers to "get what they see" and reduce delivery risks, Zhang said, adding that the share of completed homes in total new-home sales by floor area has risen year by year in recent years.
Meanwhile, China will strengthen housing support for low-income urban families, new urban residents and young people, providing rental housing or homes for purchase as appropriate to meet basic housing needs, Zhang said.
Efforts to foster a new real estate development model have gathered pace this year. In August, authorities deepened reforms to the housing provident fund system and refined regulations on commercial housing sales and property financing as part of broader efforts to chart a new path for real estate development.
Data released earlier this week showed narrower year-on-year declines in home prices across major Chinese cities in August, pointing to further signs of stabilization as China continues city-specific policy adjustments, inventory reduction and urban renewal.
Meanwhile, overall property transaction volumes have improved, with second-hand home transactions by floor area rising 10.6 percent year on year in the first eight months, while the total floor area of unsold new commercial housing fell 1.1 percent year on year at the end of August, the sixth straight monthly decline. ■

====================================================================================================

Scientists have discovered a new species of wild cat in Bolivia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:47:26 EEST
17:47:26 KST

Scientists have discovered a new species of wild cat in Bolivia
Kyiv • UNN
Scientists discovered Leopardus tilcayo, which diverged from other tiger cats 1.4 million years ago. The population size of the species is unknown.
For the first time in 100 years, scientists have discovered the first new species of felid in Bolivia, naming it Leopardus tilcayo. National Geographic reports this, citing a study published in the journal Current Biology, according to UNN.
Details
The animal was brought to the Senda Verde reserve in Bolivia in 2016. A local man found the kitten near a forest and initially thought it was a domestic cat, but about a year later realized that it was a wild animal.
Biologist, scientist, and founder of the Bolivian Cat Research Program Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz noticed the cat’s unusual appearance. It was significantly smaller than an ordinary domestic cat, had long whiskers, short, rounded ears, and leopard-like spots.
I took a hundred photographs of it. I was so fascinated
According to available data, it became the first new species of the cat family discovered in more than 100 years.
What is interesting is that this discovery is not a confirmation of a species proposed in the distant past, nor of a previously recognized subspecies elevated to species status, which are more common and significant findings. No, this cat was something completely new to science
At first, the researcher thought it was Leopardus tigrinus, a species that was described as early as 1775. However, in 2019 she noticed that the rosettes on its fur differed from those of tiger cats in Brazil.
Together with geneticists from Brazil and Belgium, the scientist studied the animal’s genome. A comparison of the complete genomes of 38 representatives of the genus Leopardus showed that L. tilcayo is a separate species and diverged from other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago.
It took several more years for Nogales-Ascarrunz to develop her genetic analysis skills to the point where she could study the genome of the mysterious cat with any degree of accuracy. Then, working with Eduardo Eizirik, a geneticist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil, and study co-author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp, the team was able to determine its distinct place on the cat family tree. In their paper, the researchers propose calling the cat Leopardus tilcayo ( Leopardova tilkayo ) after the word by which it is known to local residents
At the same time, very little is known about the lifestyle of the new felid species. The researchers note that the discovery could also affect the conservation of these animals, since after one species is divided into several separate populations, the populations must be assessed individually. At present, scientists do not know how many L. tilcayo tiger cats live in the wild.

====================================================================================================

Gingerbread mines and petrol-flavoured Snickers: how Mala Tokmachka became the centre of the universe for 48 days
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:47:00 EEST
17:47:00 KST

Gingerbread mines and petrol-flavoured Snickers: how Mala Tokmachka became the centre of the universe for 48 days
"He who controls Mala Tokmachka controls the world," Otto von Bismarck once declared.
"I don't know where World War III will be fought, but World War IV will be fought in Mala Tokmachka," Albert Einstein warned.
"I conquered the Gallic tribes, subdued Gaul and defeated Pompey in the civil war, but I never made it to Mala Tokmachka," Julius Caesar lamented.
This eight-square-kilometre village in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, home to around 3,000 people before the full-scale war, has been the subject of memes, jokes and made-up quotes like those above for several months now. But behind the jokes lies a real story of resistance. Back in April this year, United24 calculated that Mala Tokmachka had already held out for 1,500 days – longer than Carthage during the Third Punic War or Leningrad during World War II.
Control of the village is tactically important for the defence of the city of Orikhiv, which in turn plays a crucial role in the defence of Zaporizhzhia.
The Russians have claimed in their reports to have "taken" Mala Tokmachka several times already. In November 2025, Russian Defence Minister Andrei Belousov even officially congratulated the troops on capturing the village. However, according to the latest DeepState battlefield monitoring data, the Russians have only managed to reach its south-eastern part.
In April 2026, soldiers from the 3rd Detachment of the 144th Special Operations Forces Centre were tasked with reinforcing troops from the 118th Separate Mechanised Brigade, who were holding the defence of Mala Tokmachka. For three weeks, the detachment cleared basements and houses and reached the eastern outskirts of the village, where the special forces set up observation posts. They left their positions at the end of May after spending 48 days there.
Mala Tokmachka is a symbol of Ukrainian resistance and at the same time an illustration of what war can look like today: all the work is carried out by small groups, and the main tactic is to advance a little, dig in, and avoid getting hit by a Russian drone.
Ukrainska Pravda invites our readers to immerse themselves in the 48-day defence of Mala Tokmachka alongside the soldiers of the 144th Special Operations Forces Centre.
"I didn't like the infiltration"
They had been told the operation would last two weeks, but Fizruk expected it to take at least a month. It wasn't as though he was a seasoned soldier – this was his first combat mission. But you didn't need to be a genius to anticipate the unpredictability of war.
The task was this: reach Mala Tokmachka, where Ground Forces troops were already holding positions, set up a patrol base and, when the weather allowed, clear the eastern part of the village of Russian troops and reach its outskirts.
The special forces split into two groups of five. They decided on a bold approach: nip in in two Kozak armoured vehicles, get out and immediately take cover.
It was mid-April. A dry, fresh spring night.
"Anyone in their right mind goes in when there's fog or rain, but we just went in on a clear night. I didn't like the infiltration," admits one of the group commanders, whose alias is Pravyi.
This is the same Pravyi who two years earlier was seriously wounded during an operation near Chasiv Yar, was taken prisoner by the Russians, and later captured the same Russian soldier who had taken him prisoner.
Of course you're unlikely to enjoy an infiltration when a Russian drone spots your group as you get out of your vehicle and starts to hunt you. Weapons in your hands, heavy bags on your backs – hardly the best conditions for racing against an FPV drone.
Still, Pravyi's group managed to reach cover.
The Russian drone exploded three metres away from a soldier who goes by the alias Mahon. He'll remember that moment for a long time: Mala Tokmachka was his first combat mission, and the attack was an entirely new experience.
"That's how, in the very first hour, I learnt what a combat mission is, what drones are and what war is," he reflects.
Fortunately, no one was hit. The soldiers managed to run into a basement. Just in time – seconds later another FPV exploded nearby.
Looking back on that day, Pravyi admits that it was lucky that the drones had focused on the first group. The men knew the route and quickly reached shelter, unlike the second group, who spent long minutes circling around, trying to find the entrance to the basement they needed.
Having realised that reinforcements had entered the village, the Russians began heavily shelling the position with artillery, mortars and drones.
"Thank God they weren't guided aerial bombs," Fizruk sighs. "The position was already torn apart as it was. If a guided bomb had hit it, that would've been really bad."
The Russians continued to fire on the area for roughly another week.
Mop-up
What does "mopping up" actually mean? Essentially, it involves checking houses, basements, sheds and other shelters where the enemy might be hiding. But what does that look like in practice?
Mala Tokmachka stretches from north-west to south-east, with two 7-km-long main streets and several smaller ones. A map of the village showing its buildings was divided into sectors, each one a different colour.
The soldiers went out on mop-up operations at dawn or dusk, when there was less chance of being spotted by drones. They moved in two pairs, with another two men following behind in case their brothers-in-arms needed assistance.
They advanced from ruin to ruin, basement to basement. Some entrances were blocked by rubble as though they had been blown up from inside. The soldiers tried to make as little noise as possible: if a Russian soldier was hiding somewhere, he must not know they were approaching.
The weather dictated their pace. When it was windy, they could cover about a kilometre. One day it poured with rain and the skies became safer than usual. That was when the clearing group made its greatest advance.
"Today we cleared the orange zone, tomorrow we'll get the red one done," recalls Lev, a special forces soldier. "One pair moved along one street, the other along another. We mopped up the green zone last. And gradually we made it all the way to the end."
They encountered no living Russian soldiers inside the buildings – only bodies. They also found large quantities of items capable of exploding: 50kg high-explosive aerial bombs, remnants of cluster munitions, drones, anti-tank mines…
Sector by sector, the soldiers reached the outskirts of Mala Tokmachka – four days ahead of plan. The next stage was to set up observation posts and take turns manning them.
During the day, they listened out for any signs of Russians approaching. At night, they tried to work out where the artillery fire was coming from.
"There weren't any major mood swings or anything like that. It was constant jokes and funny stories all the time. We played chess and cards," Lev says, describing everyday life in the shelter.
And from time to time they ventured out in search of food, because the supplies they had managed to bring with them to the position did not last long.
Gingerbread and Snickers
The first prianyky – traditional gingerbread-like biscuits – appeared in Kyivan Rus in the ninth century, when they were known as "honey bread". But when Mahon hears the word "prianyk", he doesn't think of a sweet treat with a centuries-old history. Instead, he assumes someone is talking about a new type of anti-personnel mine. The Pryanik (the Russian transliteration of the Russian-made mine) is half the size of a Lepestok ("petal") mine, resembles a prianyk in appearance and comes in various colours. The Russians scatter these mines from drones.
"It's their innovation, so to speak. They're very difficult to spot. And if you're walking along a road and see one 'prianyk', you have no idea how many more are hidden in the grass. Because the bastards scatter 15 or 20 of them at a time. It's a very dangerous thing," Mahon explains.
Mahon and his brothers-in-arms once had to walk down a street littered with Pryanik mines to retrieve supplies. It was one of the moments from the operation that has stayed with him most vividly.
Here is what happened. For about two weeks, the men lived on whatever food could be delivered by UAV or whatever they could find in the village themselves. But it's hard to keep an entire group supplied by drone: a drone can't carry much, and some of what does reach the positions just smashes into the ground when dropped. The drone can't descend too low either, because of the risk of it becoming entangled in fibre-optic cable.
"Feeding ten people with a Nemesis [the UAV used to drop supplies to the soldiers – ed.] is extremely challenging," Pravyi says. "If we hadn't looted [gathered/found – ed.] a sack of tinned meat during that time, if the infantry hadn't shown us where we could get water for boiling, we'd have been screwed. And even then we were really hungry until the unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) showed up."
But the unmanned ground vehicle brought adventures of its own. About a kilometre short of its destination, it drove into a water-filled crater left by a mortar round and got stuck. So at around 02:00, Mahon and his brothers-in-arms donned anti-thermal-imaging cloaks and set off to unload it. That was when they had to manoeuvre between the Pryanik mines. No drones spotted them, and the soldiers returned to their shelter laden with useful supplies. Once freed, the UGV headed back in the opposite direction.
There was an almost comical incident with another UGV: it arrived at the position with its light still on.
"I don't know what kind of genius engineer designed a machine where you can't turn the light off. We're looking through the thermal imager and it's lit up like a Christmas tree – you can see it from miles away," says a soldier who goes by the alias Venom.
Venom generally takes a philosophical view of life. Asked about his role in the group, he says it's to do whatever the commander orders, whether the soldier likes it or not, despite his fear and regardless of his emotions. But when recounting the story of the UGV that gave away its own position, even Venom struggles to remain stoical.
A Russian drone spotted the UGV, but it didn't attack immediately. It loitered, waiting to see whether any of the soldiers would come out to unload it. Only after realising that nobody was going to emerge and the battery was running down did it strike.
The first hit disabled the UGV, but much of its cargo remained intact. And it was real treasure: tinned meat, sugar, coffee, cereals, petrol for the generator, cigarettes and chocolate.
But in situations like this, the Russians try to destroy the entire delivery, knowing how important it is to the soldiers in their shelters. If the weather prevents them from finishing it off with drones, they use mortar fire instead. So they didn't stop at a single attack. After all the strikes, all that was left of the cargo were three packets of cigarettes, a few Snickers bars, and a couple of packets of porridge.
The surviving chocolate tasted of smoke and petrol, but they ate it anyway.
"It's fine. Tastes good," Mahon says, squinting.
Listening to him, you realise that perhaps nowhere do you learn to appreciate the taste of ordinary things quite as much as you do on the front line.
It was in Mala Tokmachka, while savouring bread from one of the deliveries, that Mahon remembered – and understood for the first time – something his grandad used to say: bread is the staff of life. He had never eaten anything so delicious. Soldiers normally have rusks or crispbread dropped to them – they are lighter and more compact and keep for a long time. So when an actual loaf of bread makes it all the way to a position, it's a cause for celebration.
***
Was the Special Operations Forces' mission in Mala Tokmachka a success? Absolutely, the special forces soldiers say. And not merely because they completed their task four days ahead of plan. Most importantly, they suffered no casualties either entering or leaving the positions.
Several attempts were made to evacuate the soldiers by vehicle, but the weather would not permit it. So they left on foot, in two groups of five. Even within each group they split up: three men set off first, followed by another two 15 minutes later.
The first group took 14 hours to reach the evacuation point. They crossed the village in grey, overcast conditions, but spotted a cluster of drones along the way and had to hide and wait. The other group set out a day later. They were luckier and made it in four hours.
When the conversation turns to Mala Tokmachka memes, the special forces soldiers recall that it felt oddly surreal. Not because the Russian army was claiming successes in the village while Ukrainian soldiers had it under full control – that part didn't surprise them.
What did surprise them was how much attention had suddenly become focused on a tiny village of which little more than the name remained. It was as though Mala Tokmachka were not simply one of many points along the front line, but, in a way, the centre of the universe.
For these soldiers, though, for 48 days it was exactly that.
One day, Lev – by then, perhaps, he will no longer be using his alias – would like to get into a car, sit his son beside him and bring him to a free Mala Tokmachka. He wants to show him the places where he and his brothers-in-arms sheltered and tell him the stories of what they went through.
And he wants to experience for himself what it feels like to walk down the main street without running from cover to cover, without hiding in bushes. Not to be scanning the sky, listening for the buzz of a drone. Just to walk with his son, look around – the scenery there is beautiful, Lev says – and listen to the song of the wind.
Rustem Khalilov, Ukrainska Pravda
With a serviceman from the 144th Special Operations Forces Centre with the alias Producer

Russia damaged 310 locomotives in 2026 – infrastructure ministry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:46:35 EEST
17:46:35 KST

Russian attacks have damaged 310 locomotives since the start of 2026, compared with 227 damaged over the entire preceding period since the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukraine's Minister for Reconstruction, Infrastructure and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk has said.
"So the issue here is the rapid resumption of procurement of used [locomotives], and there are also preliminary agreements and plans to purchase new ones," Kalashnyk said at a meeting of the Verkhovna Rada's transport and infrastructure committee this week.
The strategic plan presented for 2026-2027 envisages restoring 70% of locomotives and 10% of rolling stock, as well as converting 25 railway stations into inclusive facilities.
The minister said railway infrastructure and logistics hubs in frontline regions are being protected from drones, including through the installation of modular shelters. He added that Ukrzaliznytsia has already built 150 such structures this year.
"This is much cheaper than buying from private companies. Ukrzaliznytsia has also licensed this production," Kalashnyk added.
He said plans call for scaling up this production by the end of the year, with the goal for next year being to fully equip all railway stations, including intermediate ones, with the corresponding protection.
The minister also said the experimental public service obligation (PSO) model for rail passenger transport — a state order for which UAH 16 billion was allocated in the budget for the first time this year — will continue next year.
Kalashnyk also confirmed plans to complete the electrification of the Chop-Uzhhorod section this year and to begin reconstruction of the Mostyska-Sknyliv rail line.
Among other strategic plans, the minister cited the modernization of five checkpoints and the creation of one new checkpoint.
In road transport, the minister said plans call for introducing electronic waybills, as well as reforming the taxi market and transportation via digital platforms.
Kalashnyk said bringing the taxi market out of the shadow economy could generate about UAH 10 billion in additional revenue for the state budget.
The minister also announced plans to prepare a bill on the principles of infrastructure reconstruction by the first quarter of 2027.

Tbilisi City Court Judge Nino Tarashvili on Wednesday found Liluashvili guilty of “accepting bribes on an especially large scale,” said the Prosecutor's Office of Georgia’s press release announcing the verdict.

This unfounded, unlawful, and unjust decision will be challenged in the Court of Appeals.”
The Tbilisi City Court accepted prosecutor evidence alleging four instances of bribery, including one in which he took $1,365,000 between 2021 and 2022 in exchange for using his official authority to protect a scam call center operated by an organized crime group in Tbilisi.

In the fourth and final alleged instance of bribery, prosecutors indicted Liluashvili for taking a share of 5,325,943 lari (roughly $2million) in kickbacks collected on procurement contracts between 2018 and 2023.
The case adds to a wider unraveling of senior Georgian Dream members. Since late last year, the government has pursued 10 major cases against former high-ranking ruling party officials, including former Prime Minister Garibashvili, who is serving a five-year sentence for money laundering in a January plea deal.

Tallinn to evaluate condition of trees from photos in new tree-felling rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:45:00 UTC
17:45:00 KST

Tallinn to evaluate condition of trees from photos in new tree-felling rules
Tallinn is preparing changes to its tree-felling regulations aimed at simplifying permit requirements, reducing bureaucracy and expanding the use of digital tools while protecting the city's trees.
Tallinn's Environment and Public Works Department is preparing amendments to the city's tree-felling regulations aimed at making the rules clearer, reducing the administrative burden and introducing more digital solutions.
According to Kaili Lemberg, head of direct services at the department, the city is not creating an entirely new set of regulations but addressing issues that have emerged in day-to-day work.
Lemberg said the main aim of the changes is to strike a balance between protecting nature, carrying out work using modern solutions and ensuring people do not get lost in a maze of bureaucracy.
"To clarify, tree-felling regulations already exist and are currently in force, but in carrying out this work every day, we realized that the current rules do not ensure that the requirements are very clear to people. At the same time, the existing rules make it difficult to protect nature. Thirdly, we should also be doing our work intelligently, as one should in the 21st century," Lemberg said.
Condition of trees to be determined from photos
The amendments are intended to define more clearly when a tree-felling permit or a pruning permit is required.
"From a person's perspective, it is important to strike a balance between when a tree-felling permit is required and when a pruning permit is needed — for example, whether a permit is necessary for every tree branch," Lemberg said.
The Environment and Public Works Department also wants to reduce the need for officials to visit sites in person to inspect trees listed in tree-felling permit applications.
"We will certainly set out the rules and requirements for replacement planting more clearly in the regulation. We will also try to make greater use of photographs in our work to reduce our footprint — we should not have to constantly drive around the city and should instead be able to assess a tree's condition using photographs and mapping applications," Lemberg said.
She said, for example, that in the case of an obviously dead tree, a tree-felling specialist is sufficiently qualified to make an assessment based on photographs and mapping applications.
Lemberg acknowledged that this also creates a risk of fraud, meaning officials will still have to make sure that the tree shown in a photograph is the same tree that is subsequently felled.
In addition to amending the regulation itself, the department is updating its internal working procedures and an information system that has been in use for a year and a half, with the aim of making the process easier both for property owners and developers seeking to remove trees from construction sites.
"If all three of these things — a user-centered information system, tree-felling regulations that enable more modern ways of working and our own working procedures — are successfully implemented, then I believe [removing trees from construction sites] will become easier," Lemberg said.
According to Lemberg, in cases involving trees on construction sites, for example, it should be clear at an early stage whether replacement planting will be required and, if so, to what extent.
Another important issue under consideration is the procedure for challenging tree-felling permits and the possible introduction of a waiting period between the issuance of a permit and the felling itself. Currently, a tree covered by an approved felling permit can be cut down on the same day the permit is issued, even though there is formally a 30-day period for challenging the permit.
"The tree-felling regulations are currently being updated and I hope a complete draft will be ready this fall, after which we can begin broader discussions. We have considered whether a waiting period should be introduced," Lemberg said.
At the same time, she stressed that anyone challenging a permit must still have the necessary legal connection to the matter, for example by owning a neighboring property or living in the area.
Lemberg said the Environment and Public Works Department values mature trees in the city.
"Absolutely! We have a great many people working toward that goal. Of course, we need to preserve and protect what we already have. But arborists have pointed out that, in many Scandinavian countries, for example, it is accepted that mature trees have somewhat shorter lifespans in cities than they do in actual forests because the conditions are different," Lemberg said.
Lemberg added that the department may also need to give more thought to periodically renewing and replacing mature trees.
"It is difficult for trees to live forever in an urban environment. This is certainly very important because we are the Environment and Public Works Department — we don't just build roads. We create and maintain a much broader environment around people's homes than infrastructure alone," she said.

Merz faces new state polls after far-right thrashing
Unknown

2026-09-18
08:44:59 UTC
17:44:59 KST

Election campaign poster depicting top candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party Kristin Brinker is seen in front of the headquarters of Germany's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party depicting top candidate of the CDU party Stefan Evers for the upcoming Berlin state elections in Berlin on September 17 2026. (AFP Photo)
Two German state elections on Sept. 20 could deal a double blow to embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz, two weeks after his party suffered a stunning defeat at the hands of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).
Tight races for power, each with their own unique electoral dynamics, are expected in the city-state of Berlin and the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The AfD is expected to make strong gains in both, a fortnight after it trounced Merz’s center-right CDU by a margin of almost 44 to 17 percent in the ex-communist eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD triumph badly rattled Merz and fueled speculation that the 70-year-old leader, who took power in May last year, may not sit out the end of his four-year term as leader of Europe’s top economy.
Amid speculation about a potential change at the top, eight CDU state premiers closed ranks on Sept. 16 and declared jointly that Germany needs “stability now more than ever” rather than “discussions about personnel.”
Merz has vowed to reboot Germany’s flagging economy, rearm the country to deter a hostile Russia and contain irregular immigration to soothe voters’ fears and lure them away from the AfD.
Speaking at a campaign appearance in Berlin on Sept. 17, Merz touted improved growth forecasts despite the war in the Middle East as evidence the economy was slowly improving.
“We’re on the way out of crisis,” he said. “We’re on a rather good path. I say rather good, and not very good. There’s a lot still to do.”
But the AfD now leads nationwide polls, Merz’s personal approval ratings hover around 10 percent, and his coalition with the center-left SPD is increasingly torn by infighting.
In one election on Sept. 20, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Merz’s party is an onlooker to the main battle between the SPD of popular state premier Manuela Schwesig and the AfD.
While the AfD was polling at 37 percent against the SPD’s 35 in the latest INSA survey, Merz’s CDU, at just 7 percent, may drop dangerously close to the 5-per cent hurdle needed to stay in the state parliament.
A CDU crash below that line would be a historic first and heap enormous pressure on Merz.
If the CDU “were indeed to fail to clear the 5-percent threshold, I consider it quite likely that Mr. Merz would be pressured by his party to step down,” said Ursula Muench of the Academy for Political Education in Tutzing.
“Barring such a drastic turning point, I do not foresee this happening for the time being.”
In Berlin, the ruling CDU is running a neck-and-neck race against the far-left Die Linke, which is popular with many young people and promises drastic steps to solve a dire housing crisis.
A CDU defeat in the capital would be another black eye for Merz.
The AfD is, meanwhile, expected also to do well in Berlin, although it is set to remain shut out of power in both states because all other main parties have agreed on a “firewall” of non-cooperation with it.

EXPLAINER - Canada-EU 'associate membership': What it means for Ottawa and Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:44:27 UTC
17:44:27 KST

- Prime Minister Mark Carney frames closer EU ties as a way to build economic resilience as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on the US
- US President Donald Trump warns emerging Canada-EU arrangement could trigger heavy tariffs if he views it as hostile, while Ottawa insists it will choose its own partners
 
Amid fraying ties with the US, Canada's push to move closer to Europe is taking shape around a new idea: an "associate member" relationship with the EU that would stop short of full membership but deepen ties across trade, defense and technology.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen put the idea on the table Wednesday, telling Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney that she wanted to work with him on "opening the door on Canada being the first associate member of the EU."
The proposal, made at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, would break new ground. 
The EU currently has no formal category of "associate membership," meaning its precise legal structure, rights and obligations would have to be worked out.
Carney embraced the broader ambition Thursday in his own address to European lawmakers, calling for what he described as an "alliance for the future" spanning critical minerals, defense, artificial intelligence, energy, research, financial services and digital trade.
 
What is being proposed?
Neither side is proposing that Canada become the EU's next full member.
Carney said after his speech that Ottawa is neither in a position nor seeking to become a full EU member, stressing that the substance of the relationship would matter more than whatever label is ultimately attached to it.
Instead, von der Leyen has proposed building on the Canada-EU Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) to create what she called a "common prosperity and economic security space."
CETA has been provisionally applied since September 2017, eliminating tariffs on the vast majority of goods traded between the two sides. But it has still not fully entered into force because 10 EU member states have yet to complete national ratification.
Carney's proposals suggest the new relationship could go considerably further.
He called for Canada and Europe to work together on critical mineral supply chains, defense industrial capacity, artificial intelligence and computing infrastructure, energy security, space and payment systems.
He also proposed moving toward "seamless, digital trade" in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services, while also exploring a more integrated market for financial services.
Carney also said Canada could participate in the EU's Erasmus+ student exchange program and the next generation of its Horizon research program, arguing that young Canadians and Europeans should have greater opportunities to live, work and study on either side of the Atlantic.
Canada has already moved closer to the EU in defense, becoming the first non-European country to participate in the bloc's SAFE defense procurement initiative.
 
Why now?
The push comes as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy economic dependence on the US amid a sharp deterioration in relations with Washington.
The US accounted for 71.7% of Canadian merchandise exports in 2025, according to Statistics Canada, leaving Ottawa particularly exposed to changes in American trade policy.
Washington and Ottawa are now engaged in an escalating tariff dispute, with each side imposing 50% duties on roughly $20 billion worth of selected goods.
President Donald Trump has also repeatedly suggested Canada should become the 51st US state, an idea Carney and most Canadians vehemently reject.
Without naming the US in his European Parliament speech, Carney said economic integration was increasingly being used as a weapon, tariffs as leverage and supply chains as vulnerabilities that could be exploited.
He argued that sovereignty now requires countries to have secure access not only to food, energy and defense but also to artificial intelligence, semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean-energy technology, vaccines and space-based communications.
"The objective is not self-sufficiency. It is collective resilience," he said.
Carney also sought to distinguish the proposal from an attempt to create another geopolitical power center.
"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners," he said, adding that the objective was to build enough resilience to prevent other powers from controlling open markets or dictating national choices.
 
How has Washington responded?
Trump has directly warned against the emerging arrangement.
Speaking in North Carolina on Wednesday, he said the EU's effort to bring Canada closer could be considered a "hostile act" if it was undertaken with what he described as bad intentions.
"If it's a good intention, that's fine," Trump said. He warned, however, that the US could impose heavy tariffs on Europe or restrict trade in certain sectors if he concluded otherwise.
Carney responded Thursday that Canada would decide for itself which international partnerships to pursue.
"Nobody is going to dictate our culture, or with whom we can strike agreements," he told reporters in Strasbourg.
The European Commission has also rejected the suggestion that the initiative is aimed at Washington, saying closer Canada-EU ties are intended to strengthen the two partners rather than target another country.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins has separately cautioned that Canada's move toward Europe could make it harder to repair its relationship with Washington and resolve the tariff dispute, while Democratic Sen. Chris Coons has said he is seeking to organize a bipartisan congressional visit to Canada.
 
What comes next?
For now, "associate membership" remains a political proposal rather than a defined EU status.
Carney said Canada welcomed von der Leyen's ambition but stopped short of endorsing a particular institutional model, saying the two sides would define the relationship together. 
Some EU diplomats have also expressed reservations about creating a new membership category, even as there is broad interest in expanding cooperation with Canada.
The next major milestone is the Canada-EU summit scheduled for Oct. 29-30 in Montreal, where officials are expected to develop the proposed relationship further.
The eventual arrangement could therefore look less like conventional EU membership and more like a customized framework tying Canada more closely to European markets, defense programs, research networks and strategic industries.
Exactly how far that integration would go — and what either side would have to give up or change in return — remains to be negotiated.

Iranians rally by the hundreds of thousands in biggest show of defiance since US-Israeli war began
Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied Friday in a government-organized show of defiance after months of war, pledging their readiness to take up arms in the biggest such demonstration since the United States and Israel launched the war in February.
Iran's government has sought to rally the people and stress national unity, even as the economy worsens under a US naval blockade of Iranian ports and new US sanctions meant to increase Tehran's economic pain.
Estimates varied of the number of people volunteering to receive limited military training and defend the country in an effort described as "Janfaday-e Iran," or the "ones who sacrifice their lives for Iran." They marched through downtown Tehran in combat uniform, carrying flags, as onlookers cheered.
For days, state media have encouraged Iranians to join the campaign, saying training with assault rifles would begin soon. The volunteers would be an additional layer of security to the powerful Revolutionary Guard paramilitary and its all-volunteer arm, the Basij.
Tehran’s Guard chief, Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, told the state broadcaster that over 600,000 people had registered to participate, with over 1 million expected to take part in the training. On Friday morning, the broadcaster estimated over 300,000 people were on the streets.
The new head of the Basij, Hossein Taeb, declared in a speech as the rally began that the volunteers will be ready for “full-fledged defense” and similar rallies will take place in other cities soon.
The new trainees will make a “nightmare” for Iran's enemies, Taeb added, as President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders and other senior officials watched the march.
Some participants trampled flags of the U.S. and Israel. Others chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
"I am here to tell Trump that we Iranians have no fear about his threats against our homeland," said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her toddler and husband. "No one in history could invade Iran and remain there."
The rally was also a chance for Iran to show off military hardware. Anti-aircraft batteries were on display, while female Guard members in black headscarves sat with truck-mounted machine guns.
The Guard displayed drones that have been widely used against ships in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has asserted control since the war began, severely affecting the Gulf region’s shipments of oil and natural gas to the rest of the world.
Friday's events also suggested that hardliners like Taeb among Iran's leadership will be more prepared to suppress any future demonstration against the theocracy.
In January, shortly before the war, Iran saw some of its largest nationwide protests in history, which began over the struggling economy and turned to wider grievances. Activists have said a crackdown killed over 7,000 people and saw tens of thousands detained.
In May, government officials said more than 30 million people in Iran—home to a population of some 90 million—had volunteered via an online form or at public gatherings to lay down their lives for the theocracy.

Europeans still believe in the European dream. They just don't think it's within reach, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:41:43 UTC
17:41:43 KST

A new ECFR study finds most Europeans still want a stronger, united Europe, but doubt it's achievable: around 68% see decline, not renewal.
In her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen warned of a "battle of narratives" seeking to weaken confidence in Europe.
A new study, 'Future Nostalgia: Europe's Unfinished Song', published by the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) and the European Cultural Foundation (ECF), suggests that the confidence problem is real, and its authors call it an "imagination gap": most Europeans still want a stronger, more united continent, but a majority doubt it will ever get there
The findings, based on nearly 6,000 interviews across six countries, paint a picture of a public that hasn't abandoned the European project, but has largely lost confidence in its ability to deliver.
A continent bracing for decline
On average, 68% of respondents describe Europe's current situation in terms of "general deterioration or loss of normality." Just 12% see it as a moment of "awakening or renewal." The gloom varies by country: it's most pronounced in France, at over 80%, and least widespread in the UK, where it still affects a majority, but by a narrower margin.
Asked to name Europe's biggest challenges, war and security topped the list at 43%, rising to 47% in Poland and the UK, where the war on Europe's borders and its consequences weigh most heavily on public opinion.
Economic pressure follows at 33%, but its weight differs sharply from country to country: 41% of Italians call it Europe's main challenge, compared with just 23% in Poland and the Netherlands.
The verdict on Europe's response, whatever the concern, is blunt: 74% say the bloc is handling its challenges poorly, and 56% believe its future is genuinely "in danger," against just 21% who disagree.
The dream isn't dead
Despite the pessimism, the study finds little appetite for retreat. Some 73% of respondents still hold what researchers classify as a "positive vision" for Europe's future, against 14% with a negative outlook and 13% who express no clear vision at all.
Asked to describe their hopes for Europe two decades from now, respondents most often pointed to greater unity and political integration, followed by peace and security, and prosperity and shared wellbeing.
That's the paradox at the heart of the report: Europeans haven't given up on the idea of a stronger, more unified Europe.
Even those who feel most anxious about where the continent is heading tend to remain attached to the European project rather than turning against it. What they've lost faith in isn't the vision itself, but whether it can actually happen.
Why trust is eroding
The study identifies specific, recurring reasons behind that doubt.
Nearly a third of respondents (32%) describe Europe as too slow to act, a complaint that rises above 40% in Germany and the Netherlands, where the issue has become a fixture of domestic political debate.
It's a criticism von der Leyen herself seemed to anticipate in her address, telling MEPs that "in today's economy, speed is of the essence" as she pushed her simplification agenda to cut administrative burden.
Almost as many (30%) see Europe as inconsistent, failing to live up to the values it claims to represent.
Perhaps most tellingly, 44% of respondents, nearly half, could not name a single recent example of European action going right. Researchers say this absence of visible "wins" is central to why the public struggles to imagine a credible path from today's Europe to the one it wants.
An imagination gap, not a legitimacy crisis
According to ECFR senior fellow Pawel Zerka, the study's lead author, the findings shouldn't be mistaken for rising euroscepticism. Even among the most anxious segments of the public, attachment to the European project remains strong. The problem is one of credibility, not commitment.
"For many of the people we spoke to, the problem is not that they have stopped wanting a stronger Europe, but that they no longer believe it is achievable," Zerka said. "People can picture the kind of Europe they want to see, but struggle to imagine a credible path from where it is today to where they want it to be."
The report argues that closing this gap will require less emphasis on grand promises and more visible proof that European cooperation can deliver results people notice in their daily lives.
In her address, von der Leyen called on Europeans to "fight back" against forces seeking to divide the bloc and undermine confidence in the European project. The study suggests that the fight will be won less with rhetoric than with evidence.

Russia Is Holding an ‘Election,’ Ukraine Is Defending Democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:41:23 UTC
17:41:23 KST

This weekend, Russia will hold elections to the State Duma, including in parts of Ukraine it occupies and claims to have annexed. The Kremlin will present the spectacle of voting as evidence of constitutional normality. Yet the contrast with the debate unfolding in Ukraine reveals the difference between holding a ballot and preserving democracy.
In Russia, meaningful competition has been extinguished. The Supreme Court removed Yabloko’s federal list from the ballot, excluding the only registered party that opposed the war. The remaining parliamentary parties largely operate within boundaries set by the Kremlin. Russia has not invited observers from the OSCE, whose independent scrutiny it has again chosen to avoid.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Voting will also be organized on sovereign Ukrainian territory under military occupation. The European Union has already said it will not recognize such “elections” or their results. A ballot does not acquire legitimacy merely because boxes are opened and votes are counted –especially when it is imposed by an occupying power.
Ukraine presents a very different picture. Elections remain suspended under martial law because the country is fighting for survival. After his dismissal as defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov called for voting during the war. His proposal was publicly debated and rejected even by organizers of protests that had supported him.
Canada-Ukraine 100-Year Partnership: What Does It Mean for Both Countries?
That disagreement is not evidence of democratic failure. It is evidence that democratic politics persists under extraordinary pressure. A prominent former minister can challenge the president. Civil society can support him on one issue and oppose him on another. Election authorities, parliamentarians and experts can openly examine how voting should eventually resume.
It would be tempting to conclude that, because Russia is staging an election, Ukraine should quickly hold one too – if only to deny Moscow a propaganda argument. That would be the wrong lesson. Democracy is not a contest over who can announce an election date first. A credible election requires security, political pluralism, independent media, meaningful competition, impartial administration, public scrutiny and the sovereign participation of citizens. Russia is violating these principles while using the rituals of elections to legitimize its war.
Ukraine would risk undermining those same principles if it rushed to vote. Millions of citizens are displaced inside the country or abroad. Many are serving in the armed forces. Others live under occupation. Missile and drone attacks would threaten voters and election workers, while campaigning and media access would be profoundly unequal.
But postponing elections cannot mean postponing democratic preparation. Emergency powers derive their legitimacy from being exceptional and temporary. Those who exercise them must preserve the conditions for full political competition to return as soon as circumstances genuinely permit.
Ukraine’s Central Election Commission and a parliamentary working group have already developed proposals for the first post-war elections. Their technical work should now become part of a broader national discussion involving government and opposition, civil society, the armed forces, local authorities and independent media.
That discussion should address the security conditions for voting, the participation of soldiers and citizens abroad, the voter register, campaign finance, media pluralism, voting in territories emerging from occupation and safeguards against Russian interference. Agreement should be sought before an election date is fixed – and before political actors know which arrangements may favor them.
Russia’s objective in a future Ukrainian election may not be to secure victory for a preferred candidate. After years of aggression, that may be impossible. It may instead seek to convince different parts of Ukrainian society that the process was manipulated or stolen. Building broad agreement in advance is therefore not simply electoral housekeeping; it is a matter of national security.
Europe should reinforce this distinction. It should reject Russia’s illegal voting in occupied Ukraine and support Ukraine in building the conditions for a credible democratic return. EU accession is not only a legislative or economic process. It is also a security project centered on political pluralism, accountable institutions and citizens’ right to choose their leaders freely.
Russia is trying to show that an election can legitimize conquest. Ukraine must show that a lawful and temporary postponement, combined with open preparation, can protect democratic sovereignty.
The democratic frontline does not begin when an election date is announced. It is already visible today: in Ukraine, through argument, scrutiny and preparation; in Russia, through polling stations opened as political choice is closed.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Russia confirms rocket launch behind viral sky “jellyfish”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:40:14 UTC
17:40:14 KST

- Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed on Sept. 18 that a Soyuz-2.1b rocket launched a classified satellite from Plesetsk the previous evening.
- The glowing shape that fueled online missile-launch claims was a documented "space jellyfish" effect caused by sunlight hitting the rocket's exhaust plume.
Social media users shared widespread footage Thursday evening of a glowing, tentacled shape in the night sky, with some posts claiming it showed a missile launched toward Ukraine. Within hours, astrophysicist and satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell offered a more mundane explanation, and Russia’s Ministry of Defense confirmed it the next day.
“Russia appears to have launched a Soyuz from Plesetsk at around 1650 UTC Sep 17, probably with another Glonass navigation satellite, but no official confirmation yet,” McDowell wrote on X on Thursday.
By Friday, Sept. 18, Russia’s Ministry of Defense released video of the launch, identifying the rocket as a Soyuz-2.1b lifting off from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome carrying a satellite for the ministry’s own use. The ministry did not name the satellite or describe its mission, following its usual practice of keeping military payload details classified.
The glowing shape that alarmed observers is a well-documented optical effect known as a “space jellyfish.” It happens when a rocket climbs high enough into the atmosphere to catch direct sunlight during evening or morning twilight, while observers on the ground remain in darkness. The rocket’s exhaust plume expands rapidly in the thin upper atmosphere, and the illuminated, billowing gas cloud can resemble a glowing jellyfish trailing tentacles across the sky. The same phenomenon has accompanied SpaceX Falcon 9 launches over Florida and California this year, as well as previous Soyuz launches from Russian and Kazakh spaceports.
Plesetsk, located in Russia’s Arkhangelsk region roughly 800 km (500 miles) north of Moscow, is the country’s primary military launch site and has hosted a steady stream of Soyuz-2.1b missions carrying Defense Ministry satellites throughout 2026, including launches in February and April. Those earlier missions were also witnessed and photographed across Finland and Scandinavia, consistent with the rocket’s typical flight path toward high-inclination orbits to the north. That trajectory runs opposite the direction claims about a strike on Ukraine would require, since Ukraine lies south of Plesetsk rather than along the rocket’s ascent path.
McDowell’s guess that the payload was another Glonass navigation satellite has not been confirmed by Russian officials, who described the cargo only in general terms as serving the Ministry of Defense’s interests. Russia has not disclosed the satellite’s orbit, designation, or intended function.
