‘Just ask Grok’: How ISIL is using Big Tech’s AI to build bombs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:39:59 UTC
17:39:59 KST

‘Just ask Grok’: How ISIL is using Big Tech’s AI to build bombs
Evidence shared exclusively with Al Jazeera shows ISIL supporters sharing ways to bypass AI safeguards.
Boko Haram fighters are using the artificial intelligence chatbots of Big Tech companies to help build more powerful bombs, plan attacks and solve problems during combat, according to research by the University of Cambridge.
Researchers interviewed 27 former members of Boko Haram’s two factions – the ISIL affiliate in West Africa Province (ISWAP) and Jama’at Ahl as-Sunnah lid-Da’wah wa’l-Jihad (JAS). A number of members described using Sam Altman-led OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, Elon Musk’s Grok, Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI and China’s DeepSeek as a routine source of technical and military advice before, during and after attacks.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Real Madrid stars appear to hide Ceuta solidarity message
- list 2 of 4Israeli double-tap strike kills 15-year-old and paramedic in Gaza
- list 3 of 4India summons Pakistani diplomat after incident in Arabian Sea
- list 4 of 4Moment Kash Patel’s senate hearing takes bizarre turn
Meanwhile, exclusive material obtained by Al Jazeera reveals how supporters of the wider ISIL (ISIS) movement are sharing instructions on bypassing AI safety controls and obtaining weapons-related information. Researchers at Tech Against Terrorism infiltrated a pro-ISIL technical forum where supporters instructed one another on how to use AI and circumvent its safety restrictions.
The findings come amid growing concern over ISIL’s adoption of emerging technologies. In February, United Nations officials warned the Security Council of increased use of advanced AI by ISIL and its affiliates. At the same time, researchers and several of the technology industry’s most prominent figures have warned that increasingly powerful AI systems are advancing faster than safeguards, raising concerns that unchecked advances in AI are making it easier for armed groups to exploit the technology.
“There is nothing we haven’t received an answer on,” a former ISWAP commander told the researchers.
From a projector to the battlefield
Deep inside a rebel stronghold in northeastern Nigeria, former fighters described a strikingly organised and sophisticated system for putting the technology to use.
According to the Cambridge research, operatives travelled to ISWAP-controlled territory to teach senior members how to use AI. Fighters were selected and assembled in rooms around laptops and projectors and shown how to query chatbots and circumvent the safeguards designed to prevent them from answering dangerous requests.
“The white guys came and taught us,” one former commander recalled. “They assembled the top people in a room and used a projector to show how it works on a big screen.”
The trainers supplied laptops equipped with privacy and encryption tools, while accounts and paid subscriptions to multiple AI platforms were set up for members, according to former fighters cited in the study. Respondents repeatedly identified the wider ISIL movement as the source of their AI training.
What followed, the research suggests, went far beyond occasional use of ChatGPT by individual fighters. Both ISWAP and JAS established dedicated AI units staffed by people with specialist operational knowledge, including engineers, weapons specialists and bomb-makers. One former JAS commander described a specialised unit of 23 people working from a solar-powered room, where its members answered questions, analysed information and trained senior commanders gathered around a laptop.
“‘[Ask] how can I build a bomb?’ and then it tells you how,” explained a former Boko Haram commander. “It is like a human robot. We used it a lot.” Another former member was similarly enthusiastic: “God has helped us, and so will AI.”
Often, according to the study, bomb-makers would keep laptops beside them, each time returning to the chatbot when they encountered a problem while they assembled explosive devices.
Building bombs with AI
Antonia Juelich, who authored the Cambridge study, told Al Jazeera roughly 10 of the 27 people interviewed discussed the use of AI in relation to explosives, including attempts to make bombs more powerful and recover explosive material from military ordnance.
But what Juelich found most concerning was not simply that fighters could obtain information about weapons – much of that has long been available in manuals and online. AI could instead respond to the specific problem in front of them.
She pointed to accounts of fighters asking AI how to improve explosives using the limited materials they already had available. Rather than searching for generic instructions, they could tell the chatbot what materials they had, ask questions and return with follow-ups when they encountered problems. This gave them something closer to a technical expert available 24 hours a day, tailoring its answers to the materials they had and the bomb they were trying to build.
Some of the other striking accounts concern unexploded military ordnance, where ISWAP had sought to recover explosive material from bombs and other munitions that failed to detonate, according to the Cambridge research. During one earlier incident described in the report, fighters disagreed over how to deal with an unexploded bomb. After they approached and handled it, the device exploded, reportedly killing 40 people. Former members said AI was now being consulted for guidance on recovering military-grade explosives from unexploded ordnance dropped or fired by opposing forces, which could then be repurposed in the group’s own devices.
AI was also reportedly used to adapt commercially available drones to carry and drop explosives onto targets.
‘Just ask Grok’
The bomb-making accounts were only one part of the story, with former fighters describing AI reaching into almost every stage of combat. In one account, a fighter entered combat with a camera strapped to his chest, transmitting images back to camp. A commander uploaded them to ChatGPT, used it to analyse the situation and relayed new instructions to fighters on the front line.
AI was also reportedly consulted when fighters encountered unfamiliar weapons. In one instance, commanders asked one of the group’s so-called AI specialists how to operate newly acquired firearms. His response suggested how routine the technology had become: “Just ask Grok,” referring to Elon Musk’s AI chatbot.
In another account, fighters turned to AI after government forces dug trenches around bases to stop motorcycle assaults. A former commander said fighters had seen motorcycles jumping obstacles in films and consulted AI as they tried to replicate the idea. He claimed 18 fighters died during repeated attempts to master the technique, before eight eventually succeeded and later crossed the trenches during an attack following a consultation with AI.
AI was also used to rethink how many fighters were sent into battle. One former ISWAP fighter said the group lost 60 men after deploying about 200 in one operation. He said commanders subsequently asked AI if smaller, more coordinated groups could be more effective in battle.
The technology was still being consulted after the fighting ended. Former members described returning from unsuccessful operations, telling AI what tactics they had used and asking why they had failed. Footage was also reportedly uploaded for analysis as fighters sought ways to change their approach for the next attack.
‘Removing the speed limiter’
Evidence reviewed exclusively by Al Jazeera suggests attempts to exploit AI extend into the wider ecosystem of ISIL supporters around the world.
Tech Against Terrorism researchers, who gained access to a pro-ISIL online technical forum, found users discussing how to obtain weapons-related information and circumvent AI safety guardrails – restrictions designed to stop chatbots from providing dangerous information.
One supporter compared the process to modifying a car. “It’s like removing the speed limiter of the car,” the user wrote. “The car still works but now it’s become more useful and it can go way faster than the manufacturer intended.”
Lucas Webber of Tech Against Terrorism said researchers were seeing increasing discussion of how to “jailbreak” AI systems – the term commonly used for attempts to make models ignore their safeguards.
“This is the tip of the iceberg,” he said.
Juelich acknowledged the difficulty of regulating AI when many questions can have legitimate uses. Researchers and journalists, for example, may ask about military tactics. But requests for help making bombs, she said, fall much more clearly outside companies’ rules and should be caught by their safety guardrails. “They are jailbreaking, circumventing the restrictions,” she said, adding that as AI becomes more powerful, the industry needs to be more heavily regulated.
Major AI companies say they have safeguards designed to prevent such misuse. OpenAI prohibits its systems from being used for terrorism, violence and weapons development, while Anthropic and Meta say they use classifiers and other safeguards to identify and block dangerous requests. xAI also prohibits attempts to circumvent its safeguards. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, Meta and DeepSeek have been contacted by Al Jazeera for comment on the findings.
The new evidence and research come as Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has urged AI companies to slow the development of their most advanced models to give safety checks time to catch up, while calling for independent evaluations and common safety standards.
But the administration of United States President Donald Trump has taken a markedly different approach, claiming that US AI companies must be free to innovate without “cumbersome regulation” and pursuing what it calls a “minimally burdensome” national framework.
That leaves the companies themselves playing a significant role in deciding where their systems draw the line – even as researchers and many within the industry warn about the risks posed by increasingly capable models.
The Cambridge interviews with former Boko Haram members largely describe AI use during 2023 and 2024, and Juelich believes this makes the findings more concerning given how rapidly the technology has advanced since then.
She told Al Jazeera she was concerned about what the same fighters might now be capable of achieving with the more advanced AI systems available in 2026.
“I worry about where this is heading,” Juelich said.

The administration of US President Donald Trump has announced the approval of the sale of nearly 50 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, a policy shift that has raised concerns among some members of Congress, the BBC reports.

The proposed sale of military equipment would not alter the military balance in the region.

Putin’s wartime test as Russians vote in 'controlled' election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:36:00 UTC
17:36:00 KST

Russians began voting Friday in a three-day parliamentary election that is widely expected to preserve President Vladimir Putin’s political dominance, with the Kremlin using the first State Duma vote since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine as a measure of public support for the war and a test of domestic stability.
The election will determine all 450 seats in Russia’s lower house, with voting continuing through Sunday and initial results expected after polls close at 6:00 p.m. GMT.
United Russia, Putin’s ruling party, currently controls about two-thirds of the Duma and is expected to retain its dominant position.
The vote comes as the war enters its fifth year and its effects are increasingly felt inside Russia. Ukrainian drone strikes have reached targets far from the front line, while fuel shortages, high interest rates, labor shortages and Western sanctions have added pressure to an economy that has continued functioning despite the restrictions.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said Friday that Ukraine launched more than 350 drones at the Moscow region overnight, adding that most were destroyed. The strikes underscored how the war has increasingly reached Russian territory as voters head to the polls.
Putin has framed the election as a demonstration of national unity and support for Russia's war effort. In a televised address ahead of voting, he urged Russians to cast ballots as a way of helping secure victory in Ukraine and showing resolve against what the Kremlin describes as external threats.
For many voters, however, the election offers little genuine choice.
Russia's political landscape has narrowed sharply since the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Major parties contesting the election, including the Communist Party, the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party, A Just Russia and New People, broadly support Putin's policies and the war.
The liberal Yabloko party, which has called for an end to the fighting, was removed from the nationwide party-list contest after Russia's Supreme Court ruled that it had violated electoral rules. Some Yabloko candidates are still competing in individual constituencies.
Russia has also intensified restrictions on dissent since the invasion. Critics of the war have faced imprisonment, exile or other forms of pressure, while former opposition leader Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
The result has been an election in which United Russia faces no major anti-war force capable of challenging its dominance nationally.
Despite the limited political competition, the vote could offer the Kremlin clues about how Russians are responding to a war that has lasted far longer than many initially expected.
The conflict has brought casualties, economic disruption and growing security concerns. Ukrainian attacks have struck infrastructure and industrial facilities deep inside Russia, while businesses have faced higher borrowing costs and shortages of workers.
Some Russians remain firmly behind Putin and his military campaign.
At a Moscow polling station, rail worker Sergei Korenets, 41, said he planned to vote for United Russia because he wanted "stability." He also said he wanted the war to end as quickly as possible but did not want political change at home, saying he was satisfied with his financial situation.
Lyubov, 55, expressed support for the Kremlin's justification for the war, saying NATO should not be near Russia's borders. But she also criticized domestic policies, including Putin's decision several years ago to raise the retirement age.
Such views reflect the complicated picture facing the Kremlin. Support for the government and its military campaign does not necessarily translate into satisfaction with every aspect of Russian life.
One of the biggest concerns among some Russians is what could happen after the election.
The 2022 mobilization of 300,000 reservists was deeply unpopular and prompted a large exodus of draft-age men from the country. As the war continues, some Russians fear another call-up could follow the parliamentary vote.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the Kremlin of preparing a new mobilization campaign this autumn, a claim Putin has denied.
The Kremlin has not announced a new mass mobilization, but concerns about further recruitment have added to anxiety surrounding the election.
Russia's exiled opposition has urged anti-Kremlin voters not to boycott the election. Instead, it has called on them to use their ballots against United Russia.
Navalny's widow, Yulia Navalnaya, has urged anti-war Russians to gather at polling stations at noon Sunday as part of a protest strategy.
Yabloko has taken a different position, arguing that participating in an election with such limited political competition would simply strengthen the system it opposes.
The disagreement highlights the difficult choices facing Russians who oppose the war or the Kremlin but have few avenues for expressing that opposition through the formal political system.
Voting is also taking place in Ukrainian territories that Russia claims to have annexed, a move Ukraine and its international partners have rejected.
With United Russia expected to retain control of the Duma, the most closely watched question may not be whether Putin's party wins, but what the vote reveals about turnout, economic frustration and the public's willingness to continue supporting a war that has increasingly affected daily life inside Russia.
Partial results are expected to begin coming in Sunday evening, with near-complete results expected Monday.

Citizens' initiative demanding restrictions on data centers reaches 50,000 signatures
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:35:38 EEST
17:35:38 KST

A citizens' initiative calling for tighter legislative control of data centres in Finland has reached the required 50,000 signatures within three days of starting, and it will now proceed to parliament to be debated by MPs.
The petition, entitled 'Datakeskukset kuriin' (roughly translated as 'Rein in the data centres') was launched on Tuesday in the wake of search engine giant Google's announcement last week that it will significantly expand its data centre operations in Finland over the coming years.
The signatories want the government to set conditions on how data centres connect to Finland's electricity grid and operate their business "taking into account the electricity grid's capacity, mandatory backup power, and the utilisation of waste heat".
In addition, the initiative calls for the introduction of a separate data centre fee, which should be calculated based on the "environmental harm caused by operations and the resources used (including electricity, water, land use)".
This would ensure that energy prices remain affordable for households and other industries, the initiative adds.
Finland has become a magnet for data centres in recent years, with companies such as Microsoft and TikTok owner ByteDance recently announcing planned investments.
Finland is an attractive destination for such investment because of the country's climate — which helps reduce the costs associated with the heat produced by data centres — as well as Finland's large supply of low-carbon electricity.

Trump Administration Weighs Russia Business Deals Before Ukraine War Ends – NYT

A US official told the newspaper that such deals could move forward because they would “show that the United States is serious about a reset relationship with Russia.”
The administration also wants to create additional economic incentives for Russian elites to push Moscow toward peace, according to the official.
The thinking is that business agreements with the US could “help convince anti-American hawks around Mr. Putin that Mr. Trump really does want to create a new relationship with Russia,” the official said.
The reported shift comes as US efforts to broker an end to the war have stalled, including over Russia’s demands for control of Ukrainian territory in Donbas.
It would mark a departure from Trump’s position last year that economic cooperation with Russia would come only after the war was resolved.
Ahead of his meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Alaska in August 2025, Trump said Russia wanted economic cooperation but that there would be none of that “until we get the war settled.” A year later, reports said his treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, conveyed the same stance to his Russian counterpart on the sidelines of the G20 summit in August.
Trump Says ‘Major Progress’ Being Made on Potential US Army Base in Poland
Trump has repeatedly highlighted Russia’s economic potential and expressed interest in restoring business ties with Moscow.
The specific agreements now under consideration remain unclear. Potential areas of cooperation previously discussed by Moscow and Washington have included energy, investment, Arctic projects and the involvement of US companies in Russian industries.
After Putin met with Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said the talks covered “economic issues and potential major mutually beneficial Russian-American projects.”
The reported approach comes as Washington simultaneously pursues additional economic pressure on Moscow. The US Congress has advanced legislation that would expand sanctions on Russia and allow tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy.
For now, any new business agreements remain under discussion and have not been announced as official US policy.

Yemen fighting spreads as Houthis, Saudi Arabia exchange strikes

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:34:00 UTC
17:34:00 KST

Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen traded fresh cross-border strikes Thursday as civilians fled fighting by boat across the Red Sea, adding to concerns over global oil supplies as the Middle East conflict widens.
Houthi-controlled television reported Saudi airstrikes in Yemen’s Hajjah province near the Saudi border and Red Sea coast, as well as around Taiz farther south and inland.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense said a Yemeni resident was killed by debris from a drone intercepted over the western city of Taif. It was the first death Riyadh has reported from repeated Houthi attacks since fighting intensified last week. Saudi authorities have previously said more than 80 people were wounded.
Separately, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy said a Togo-flagged oil tanker caught fire after being struck while attempting what it described as an “illegal passage” through the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported.
The tanker stopped after the fire broke out, the Guards Navy said, adding to concerns over the security of a waterway critical to global energy supplies.
The spread of the war to Yemen and Saudi Arabia has raised new concerns about oil supplies by jeopardizing the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains constrained. Shipping data showed only four commodity vessels transited the strait Thursday, well below the 10-day average of 16.
U.S. President Donald Trump has rebuffed Saudi appeals for military support against the Houthis, who agreed to a ceasefire with the U.S. last year after Washington bombed the group for two months.
Trump said Thursday that he was approaching a critical juncture over whether to restart large-scale attacks on Iran.
“I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them or do I not? It’s a big decision. Anything could happen with me,” Trump said in an interview with Axios.
Trump has previously threatened major new attacks that did not materialize.
Global crude prices eased Thursday but remained above $100 a barrel after reaching their highest levels since May. Brent crude fell $2.14 to $102.68 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude fell $1.83 to $100.08.
The average U.S. retail diesel price hit a record high Thursday, just shy of $6.40 a gallon.
The U.S. and Iran have held no negotiations to end the war since an interim agreement reached in June collapsed within weeks. The war is expected to come up for discussion at the United Nations General Assembly next week, with an Iranian delegation able to attend, according to the U.S. State Department.
The fighting has driven Yemeni civilians to flee across the Bab el-Mandeb, Arabic for “Gate of Tears,” the narrow strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
In Djibouti, on the African shore of the Red Sea, Wahida Omer, 50, reached land after crossing from Yemen on a small boat when her village of Dhubab came under attack as the Houthis swept into the area. Her husband was left behind, and she had no idea whether he was alive, dead or had been captured by the Houthis.
“The sea was frightening, difficult,” she said in an interview filmed by the International Organization for Migration. Those on the boat were “crying the whole way, and we arrived still crying” with nothing to eat.
The IOM says more than 100,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the latest fighting. The United Nations has put the number at about 125,000.
The Houthis, who have seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a lightning advance since last week, say the Saudi air force has carried out hundreds of airstrikes in recent days. On Wednesday, the Houthis said they had shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet.
“We want the Saudis to cease their blockade and occupation of our country, and to stop their aggression against us. This is our demand!” Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi said in a televised speech, seated with a traditional dagger in his belt. Slogans on the wall behind him read: “Death to America, death to Israel, a curse upon the Jews, victory for Islam.”
The U.S. Navy is trying to guide ships through the Strait of Hormuz, the outlet to the Gulf along Iran’s coast, where about one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas previously passed before the war. The U.S. is also imposing a blockade on Iranian ports.
Iran says the strait is closed and will remain shut until Washington lifts the blockade. It is seeking an agreement with neighboring Gulf states that would allow it to collect fees from ships passing through the strait.

Poland’s prime minister says Russia is preparing ‘accidental’ drone and missile strikes on NATO countries that support Ukraine

Poland’s prime minister says Russia is preparing ‘accidental’ drone and missile strikes on NATO countries that support Ukraine
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament that Russia is planning “hybrid” strikes using missiles and drones against countries that support Ukraine.
Tusk cited intelligence assessments, the Reuters news agency reports. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles may fly into the territory of one or more NATO countries on the eastern flank, even cause destruction,” he said.
“These potential strikes would be quote-unquote ‘accidental’ in nature, intended to paralyze or at least weaken the resolve of NATO states to invoke the relevant NATO provisions in the event of aggression against a member country,” Tusk said.
According to Tusk, these Russian attacks could coincide with “political changes in certain European countries granting power […] to those who, increasingly invoking noble slogans of peace, pacifism and needless casualties, will call for peace,” but which in fact call for ”the total capitulation of Ukraine.”
Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Estonia, Lithuania, and Latvia in recent months. Authorities in those countries said the drones were Ukrainian and had strayed into their airspace because of Russian electronic warfare.
NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight on September 15, the first time a drone has been destroyed in the country’s history. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda later said the drone was Russian.
Russian forces also used drones to attack a gas station near the Yahodyn border crossing on the Polish–Ukrainian border and a passenger train on the Kyiv–Warsaw railway line overnight on September 13. Another train carrying Western politicians returning from Ukraine was traveling nearby when the drone struck. Tusk said the incident showed that “escalation by the Russian Federation is becoming a fact, and examples of it are getting closer and closer to our border.”

Elections to the State Duma have begun in Russia amid reports of violations

Elections to the State Duma have begun in Russia amid reports of violations
Kyiv • UNN
On September 18–20, Russia is electing 450 State Duma deputies, including in the occupied territories of Ukraine. Pressure on observers and public-sector employees has been reported.
A three-day vote in the elections to Russia’s State Duma has begun. Voting will take place from September 18 to 20, including in the occupied territories of Ukraine, amid pressure on observers and coercion of public-sector employees. Russian media report this, UNN writes.
Details
Following the elections, 450 State Duma deputies are to be elected: 225 in single-member constituencies and another 225 from party lists. Ten parties are participating in the federal list after the Yabloko party was removed from the elections. At the same time, individual candidates from this party are running in single-member constituencies.
The elections are taking place amid reports by Russian media outlets and human rights organizations of pressure on opposition observers and candidates. In particular, in Voronezh Oblast, according to Russian media, about 400 observers from the Communist Party of the Russian Federation were barred from working due to alleged deficiencies in their documents.
There are also separate reports of possible pressure on voters. In a number of regions, according to local opposition groups and media outlets, public-sector employees are allegedly being forced to report that they voted for United Russia. Such reports have come, in particular, from Altai Krai and the Novosibirsk, Sverdlovsk, Belgorod, and Samara oblasts.
It is noted that ahead of the elections, Russian CEC Chair Ella Pamfilova also warned of possible disruptions to mobile communications and data transmission. According to her, such problems may occur due to "security measures," but will not constitute grounds for canceling the vote.
Additional information
The 2026 State Duma elections are the first parliamentary elections in Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Voting is also being held in the territories of Ukraine occupied by Russia, which constitutes a violation of Ukrainian legislation and international law.

New light armored vehicle debuts at Africa’s top defense show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:31:14 UTC
17:31:14 KST

- Paramount and India's Kalyani Strategic Systems unveiled the Mbada, a new 4x4 light armored vehicle, at AAD 2026 in Pretoria on Sept. 17.
- The roughly 10-tonne vehicle offers STANAG 4569 Level 2 ballistic protection and can survive a 6-kilogram mine blast beneath the hull.
Paramount and India’s Kalyani Strategic Systems Limited unveiled a new 4×4 light armored modular vehicle (LAMV) called the Mbada at the Africa Aerospace and Defence exhibition in Pretoria on Sept. 17, marking the vehicle’s first public showing at an international defense show.
The Mbada is built as a modular platform that customers can configure for reconnaissance, border protection, troop transport, logistics runs, command and control, surveillance, or weapons carriage, among other roles. Paramount and KSSL, the defense arm of India’s Bharat Forge, jointly developed the vehicle from the start rather than adapting an existing design, and the companies are targeting militaries across Africa, India and South Asia. The vehicle isn’t entirely new to the public: it debuted at Eurosatory 2026 in Paris in June under the name Simha, the version aimed at Indian and other global markets, with Mbada serving as the name for Africa and additional international customers.
At roughly 10 tonnes, the Mbada runs on a 450-horsepower, six-cylinder turbo-diesel engine producing 1,627 newton-meters of torque, paired with a six-speed automatic transmission and a two-speed transfer case that can lock for off-road driving. It reaches a top road speed of 110 km/h (68 mph). The vehicle’s fully welded hull, built as a single monocoque structure rather than a frame with separate armor panels, meets STANAG 4569 Level 1 and Level 2 ballistic protection standards and Level 2a and 2b blast protection, a NATO classification system for how much explosive force a vehicle’s armor can withstand. Paramount says the hull can survive a 6-kilogram (13-pound) TNT-equivalent mine detonating beneath a wheel or the hull itself.
The Mbada carries a crew of four, a driver, commander and two additional crew members, with four side doors and a turret ring for mounting a weapon station. It comes in left- and right-hand-drive configurations and can operate from -20°C to 45°C (-4°F to 113°F) without special preparation. Customers can add extras including a remote weapon mount, communications and C4I equipment, a central tire inflation system, run-flat tires, shooting ports, a winch, a wading snorkel and FLIR night-driving cameras.
“As military forces across Africa and around the world adapt to increasingly complex, dispersed and unpredictable operational environments, demand is growing for lighter and more agile armoured vehicles that combine mobility and survivability with the flexibility to rapidly integrate new technologies, weapons and mission systems,” said Lindiwe Tshabalala, CEO of Paramount South Africa.
“By combining KSSL’s advanced engineering and manufacturing strengths with Paramount’s proven expertise in protected mobility, we have created a versatile and future-ready platform designed to meet the evolving operational requirements of modern armed forces,” said Neelesh Tungar, CEO of Kalyani Strategic Systems Limited.
KSSL has been expanding its defense manufacturing footprint beyond the Mbada program. The company also showed a 155mm, 39-caliber truck-mounted howitzer called the MArG 39 at Eurosatory in June, part of a planned family of artillery systems built on a shared 4×4 chassis. Paramount and KSSL have positioned both the vehicle and artillery lines around sovereign production, an arrangement that lets a buying country manufacture and maintain the equipment domestically rather than depend on continued foreign supply.

Swiss apprenticeship market remains bouyant
Some 76,000 new apprentices have signed contracts in Switzerland, meaning that the model will remain stable in 2026.
Vocational training remains the most important educational pathway for young people after compulsory schooling.
+ Why the world should take notice of the Swiss apprenticeship model
At the end of August, the number of apprenticeship contracts stood at around 76,000, in line with previous years, according to the State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI).
This shows that companies are investing in the next generation of skilled workers and that vocational training is on a solid footing.
More
Apprenticeships in Switzerland
The fact that vocational apprenticeships are the most important educational pathway after completing compulsory schooling had already become apparent in SERI’s Transition Barometer. In June, 63% of around 98,000 young people stated that they were considering basic vocational training.
Some 43% were interested in the Matura academic qualification or specialist secondary school, whilst bridging programmes and gap years were mentioned less frequently.
Basic commercial training and careers in the health and social sectors were particularly in demand.

Chinese paint cuts wall temperature by 25 degrees Celsius in summer test: report
The super-coating, which can help cool buildings, goes into mass production, making the leap from lab to industry
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Dannie Pengin Beijing
China has begun mass production of a super-coating that can cut wall temperatures by 25 degrees Celsius in summer, according to the state-run Science and Technology Daily.
The material, which has undergone six months of real-world testing at a petrochemical plant in the southern island province of Hainan, uses the principles of radiative cooling. It requires neither electricity nor cooling agents and its overall performance is reportedly the highest among known global competitors, according to the report published on September 7.
The coating may also have potential for broader use in public infrastructure and homes.
The need to reduce the effects of heat on buildings was apparent in Europe this summer when record heatwaves left many residents sweltering in homes without air conditioning.

Less than half of Brussels police officers are bilingual
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:27:12 UTC
17:27:12 KST

Bilingualism within the Brussels police force is falling, with less than half of officers able to communicate in both French and Dutch. The figures come from Interior Minister Bernard Quintin in response to a parliamentary question from Barbara Pas, leader of the Vlaams Belang parliamentary group in the Chamber of Representatives.
“For a Flemish person who needs to call on the police in our bilingual capital, there is now a greater chance that they will not be able to be helped in Dutch,” says Pas. Figures On 1 January, 3,008 of the 6,672 police officers in Brussels were bilingual, or 45.1%. In 2021, the figure was 51.6%.
98.1% of police staff are proficient in French, while 46.9% know Dutch. “For Dutch speakers, receiving service in their own language is increasingly a matter of luck,” says Pas. Forty of the 292 new officers recruited in Brussels in 2025 were Dutch-speaking. Only 8% of the new recruits held the required language certificate.
“If more than 9 out of 10 new recruits are hired without a language certificate, it is hardly surprising that bilingualism is continuing to erode,” says Pas, who points out that communication can be of vital importance, particularly within the police and security services.
Vlaams Belang believes a structural federal approach is needed, in particular effective monitoring of compliance with the language law in recruitment and appointments. “The figures show that a few optional language courses are not making any difference,” says Pas.

Contracts in technology, research and development with the MOD
A list of places to find Defence contracts and funding in the technology, research and development (R&D) space.
Every year the Ministry of Defence (MOD) works with companies and researchers to develop next-generation innovation, technology and digital solutions to support our frontline troops. You can find some of the places we advertise those opportunities on this page. This is not an exhaustive list.
Opportunities outside the technology and innovation space can be found at Procurement at MOD.
To get notified every time this page gets updated sign up for email updates.
To give feedback on this page, please contact the Commercial X team at defcomrcl-comrclx@mod.gov.uk.
Guidance for new suppliers
A common way for suppliers to bid for contracts is via online platforms known as frameworks. These are usually set up to help government buy a specific type of product or service, and have standard terms and processes which make it easier to contract with us. Once you are on a framework you can apply for any advertised opportunities until the framework ends.
Some frameworks are ‘open’, which means they can be joined at any time, while others are only open during certain periods. There are also Dynamic markets which are continuously open for new suppliers to join, making it simpler and faster to access contract opportunities.

Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA). NATO DIANA stands for the Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic. It is a NATO organisation designed to find and accelerate “dual-use” deep tech technologies cutting-edge civilian innovations with potential defence and security applications across Alliance member nations. DIANA supports selected start-ups and innovators by providing contractual funding and access to a vast network of accelerator sites and over 200 test centres. These programmes focus on deep tech areas like artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, biotechnology, autonomy, and energy. Themed Challenges are published periodically for applications. President Lee Jae Myung has drawn a firm line against sending troops or assets to the Middle East, defying pressure from Washington
The stance comes amid mounting public opposition to any military deployment and growing pressure from Washington for Seoul to contribute to efforts to secure freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Lee’s government faces the difficult task of balancing its security alliance with the United States against the risks of becoming entangled in a distant conflict that could expose South Korean forces, citizens and commercial interests to Iranian retaliation.
“There will be no dispatch of troops or military assets that would lead to involvement in a conflict. There will be no engagement or involvement in war. I can say that clearly,” Lee said during a televised press conference on Friday. “We’ve been sticking to this principle, and this principle won’t change.”

Fear and broken families: Inside a Texas ICE detention centre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18

Fear and broken families: Inside a Texas ICE detention centre
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
Since Donald Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025, migrant arrests have surged in the United States. More than 610,000 people have passed through detention centres run by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the federal immigration agency in under two years. The pace only continues to accelerate: in August 2026, nearly 51,000 arrests were made in a single month – a record for Trump’s second term. Who are the people being held in these centres? What are their living conditions like? And how is Trump’s mass deportation policy upending the lives of families settled in the United States? In this report, Valérie Defert and Pierrick Leurent investigate the issue in Texas – the heart of the new US immigration detention system.
In Texas, a state where a significant portion of the detention system is concentrated, our reporters spent several weeks investigating what happens after an ICE arrest. They went to Dilley, just south of San Antonio, where the country’s largest family detention centre is located. It holds up to 2,400 people – both parents and children. ICE bars journalists from entering the facility. Since Donald Trump returned to power, more than 6,200 minors have been detained by ICE, including at least 500 infants and children three years old or younger.
Our team interviewed a Venezuelan family whose mother, Maria Betania, and two children were arrested while on their way to the school bus stop. They spent 17 days in Dilley before a federal judge ordered their release.
In San Antonio, a pastor meets with the families of detainees every week. She estimates that about one in four families in her congregation has had a loved one arrested and then deported.
Among these detainees is Jefferson, a Venezuelan asylum seeker and father of two. From inside the details Don Hutto detention centre, he describes the months he has spent separated from his family and condemns the living conditions and lack of access to healthcare inside the facility. Deaths in detention have risen sharply. At least 57 people have died in ICE custody since Trump’s return to the White House. According to Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights, the mortality rate had already more than doubled during the first 500 days of his second term.
This policy also represents a significant market for private companies tasked with managing some of the centres. In Dilley, a contract awarded to the Houston Chronicle provides for a monthly payment of $13.1 million to maintain the centre’s capacity to house up to 2,400 people. And the system is set to expand further: $45 billion has been allocated to increase detention capacity through 2029.

Nestlé responds to seizure of its business in Russia
Nestlé said on Friday 18 September that it was considering all options to protect its rights after the Kremlin decided to take control of the Swiss food manufacturer's Russian business.
Source: press release from Nestlé
Details: The manufacturer of Nescafé coffee and KitKat chocolate bars has said it has taken note of the decision, announced on Thursday 17 September in a decree by Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, and is currently assessing the situation.
Quote: "Nestlé is committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees."
Details: Russia has tightened its control over foreign-owned assets since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. A 2023 decree signed by Russian ruler Vladimir Putin gives Moscow the power to place assets belonging to companies from countries it considers "unfriendly" under temporary administration.
Moscow has also used the legislation to raise funds through forced sales, exit taxes and mandatory discounts, while rewarding insiders loyal to the Kremlin.
Nestlé has six factories in Russia producing coffee, pet care products and baby food. In 2021, the latest year for which figures have been disclosed, its turnover in Russia was around CHF 2 billion (about US$2.2 billion), and it employed about 7,000 people there.
This accounted for around 2% of Nestlé's total sales, although analysts estimate that this contribution has fallen since the company scaled back its operations in the country.
Since 2022, Nestlé has suspended the vast majority of sales, imports and exports of non-essential products, as well as its advertising activities and capital investment.
Reuters reported that French supermarket group Auchan, whose assets have also been frozen in Russia, declined to comment on the situation. The company still has around 230 stores operating in Russia and employs about 30,000 people there.
In previous cases, temporary administration has often preceded state expropriation, after which assets were transferred to individuals or companies with ties to the Kremlin.
Background: On 18 September, Russian ruler Vladimir Putin signed a decree nationalising the Russian assets of Auchan, Nestlé and the retail chain formerly known in Russia under the name Leroy Merlin.

Commemorative activities have been held across the country on the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident which marked the start of Japan's 14-year invasion of China.
During the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression which lasted until 1945, China suffered a total of 35 million military and non-military casualties, accounting for a third of the total casualties of all the countries in World War II.
On Friday, a bell tolled at the square of the 9.18 Historical Museum in Shenyang.
About 1,000 people from around the world attended the commemorative event.
In the city of Yangquan in Shanxi province, university students and faculty members gathered at the Monument to the Hundred-Regiment Campaign, presenting flower baskets and paying respects to the revolutionary martyrs.
And a themed exhibition commemorating the martyrs was on display in Harbin in Heilongjiang province. It featured a curated selection of cultural relics, historical archives and literature. 
On September 18, 1931, Japanese troops blew up a section of the railway near Shenyang, then under their control, and accused Chinese troops of sabotage as a pretext for subsequent aggression. (Reporting by Xinhua)

Poland Assembles Largest Military Aid Package Yet for Ukraine
Poland is preparing its largest and most comprehensive military aid package for Ukraine since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski announced the upcoming assistance package on Polskie Radio, emphasizing that Warsaw will not reduce its support for Kyiv despite ongoing Russian attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Polish Foreign Minister stated that increased Russian bombardments will only result in stronger solidarity with Ukraine.
He emphasized that Warsaw does not expect Russian behavior to change through diplomatic statements alone and is actively preparing for further escalation, noting that Russia’s hybrid warfare actions—including sabotage attempts, arson, drone attacks, and airspace violations—have already taken on a kinetic character.
"Russian generals have been threatening us with nuclear war for 20 years now," he recalled. He noted that Kremlin propagandists do this constantly. "This is an area where Russia obviously has an advantage, but, as it discovered in the case of Ukraine, this advantage is difficult to convert into use," Sikorski analyzed. "After all, if Russia could end this war through nuclear blackmail, it would have already done so," he argued.
When asked on Polskie Radio about potential Polish involvement in accelerating the delivery of Patriot air defense missile systems to Ukraine, a measure previously mentioned by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the minister noted that specific defense deliveries remain under the purview of the Ministry of National Defense.
To further reinforce Ukraine’s air defense, the European Union has recently approved $7.1 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan, explicitly clearing the way for Kyiv to procure American PAC-3 missiles for its Patriot systems via NATO mechanisms.
Announced by EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius, the package includes special exemptions allowing Ukraine to acquire critical US interceptors alongside domestic long-range drones, missiles, and potential Gripen fighter jets.
On September 13, a Russian drone strike targeted a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train in Ukraine’s Volyn region, occurring just two kilometers from the Polish border.
While no injuries were reported aboard the train, the attack also hit infrastructure near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing, damaging several parked trucks and a nearby gas station.
Following the strike, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called for a full trade embargo and comprehensive sanctions against Moscow, stating that Russian strikes near the border showed Moscow’s terror was knocking on the doors of the EU and NATO.

Kyiv Joins Ukraine’s High-Risk Zone as War Insurance Coverage Expands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Kyiv Joins Ukraine’s High-Risk Zone as War Insurance Coverage Expands
Kyiv and the Kyiv region have been designated as high-risk areas under Ukraine’s updated war risk framework, following persistent Russian strikes targeting civilian businesses, storage facilities, and critical logistics hubs. 
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi highlighted on September 17 the urgency of the change, emphasizing that Russian forces continue to attack civilian infrastructure daily, causing significant financial losses and creating a severe need for rapid recovery tools.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
To address these vulnerabilities, the Ukrainian government expanded its existing war risk insurance program for businesses while streamlining the application process for compensation.
The decision, implemented immediately rather than waiting for the upcoming budget draft, increases maximum insurance premium coverage from $67,000 to $112,000 annually per enterprise.
The updated rules also lower strict compliance requirements for insurance agreements, extend coverage to leased assets, and offer preferential loans with a 5.5% state-subsidized interest rate cap for major enterprise projects.
Under the new terms, eligible property now includes fuel alongside the vehicles used to transport and store it. The coverage expansion also extends to agricultural equipment, trucks, and trailers.
During the same week, state support was broadened to cover large-scale initiatives in fuel delivery, logistics, trade, and processing industries.
Businesses can access preferential loans to rebuild fuel and storage facilities, update processing plants, and top up working capital for wholesale and retail trade operations.
Funding for these updates comes amid limited state financial resources, with the government focusing on keeping local enterprises operating, preserving jobs, and collecting tax revenue during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, Russian strikes damaged 3,578 buildings across Kyiv, with 71 suffering severe destruction.
In response, municipal authorities restored 30 of the most heavily damaged structures, allocating roughly $56 million from the city budget toward housing recovery while providing temporary apartments and monthly rental subsidies to displaced residents.
The destruction continued to escalate through major aerial assaults, such as the combined barrage on May 24, 2026, when Russian forces launched 690 missiles and drones at the capital; despite Ukrainian air defenses intercepting 604 targets, direct strikes and falling debris impacted over 40 locations, resulting in two fatalities, 77 injuries, and damage to more than 500 properties.

Swiss airport Lugano get green light to operate until 2056
The Swiss transport ministry has renewed the operating licence for Lugano airport for a further 30 years.
The new licence came into force on September 16, 2026 and is valid until September 15, 2056.
This decision provides the airport with a long-term outlook and enables Lugano to further develop this “strategic infrastructure that serves mobility, the economy and the attractiveness of the Lugano region and the whole of the canton of Ticino”, the southern Swiss city authorities said.
The renewal of the concession comes during “a phase of gradual consolidation” of Lugano airport’s operations. The first half of 2026 closed with an operating profit of over CHF200,000, representing a significant improvement on the deficit of just under CHF100,000 in the same period last year.
Revenue exceeded CHF7 million, whilst total costs were slightly below forecasts.
The airport’s prospects have also been bolstered by the positive decision of the Senate, which aims to allow European airlines to operate domestic flights within Switzerland under certain conditions.
The change is an important step towards the future resumption of the Lugano–Geneva route.
During the Covid pandemic, the then operating company, Lugano Airport, had slipped into insolvency and liquidation.
To save flight operations, the city of Lugano took the reins, continued to run the airport itself as a temporary solution and launched a new tender process.
However, the planned privatisation failed in 2021 after the selected private consortium was unable to provide the financial guarantees by the deadline.

Arrests and Court Appearances Heighten Political Tensions in the Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:21:00 UTC
17:21:00 KST

Philippine politics was anything but dull in the past two weeks.
During this time, an arrest warrant was issued against Vice President Sara Duterte, who immediately posted bail and called for the resignation of her erstwhile ally, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez was arrested for plunder while recovering in a hospital before being transferred to a regular jail facility.
And lastly, former President Rodrigo Duterte made his first trial in-court appearance after more than a year of being under the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC).
These high-profile events will continue to unfold and affect not just the Marcos presidency but also the narratives of the 2028 elections.
Sara Duterte’s arrest warrant was issued in relation to the grave threats complaint filed against her after she said in an online video in late 2024 that she hired someone to kill Marcos and his wife. She posted bail to avoid arrest and called out Marcos for being ungrateful and betraying those who voted for him.
Duterte minced no words against Marcos in a speech delivered in front of her supporters outside a local court: “You’re a liar, abusive. He has no debt of gratitude to our people and everyone who went to the precincts to put him in power. He has no shame.”
The case is distinct from the current impeachment trial against Duterte, although the first article presented by the prosecution also related to the threats made by the vice president against the First Family.
After the drama surrounding Duterte’s posting of bail, an anti-graft court ordered the arrest of Romualdez in connection with his role in the flood control kickback scandal. The arrest was cited by Palace supporters as proof that Marcos is seriously pursuing accountability, since Romualdez is his close ally and first cousin. Romualdez spent a few days in the hospital before being placed in a regular prison cell.
The arrest was also seen as a move to counter the claim of Duterte’s camp that the vice president, her family, and allies were being unfairly targeted by the Marcos government.
It was also timed a few weeks before the first anniversary of the massive anti-corruption protests that demanded accountability against all those implicated in the flood control controversy.
Arresting Romualdez was therefore a political necessity for Marcos to dispute the allegations that he was persecuting the Dutertes, boost the credibility of his government’s anti-corruption drive, and assure the public that there’s no let-up in pursuing cases against corrupt officials.
As a former House speaker, Romualdez was the highest official tagged in the corruption scandal. It could ease the pressure on Marcos, who is also accused of masterminding the anomalous budget insertions. It could divert attention toward Romualdez and his accomplices in Congress, and weaken the clamor to scrutinize the culpability of Marcos and other Palace officials in the rollout of corruption-tainted pork barrel projects.
Meanwhile, Duterte’s appearance at the ICC coincided with the presentation of evidence concerning his daughter’s alleged unexplained wealth in the ongoing impeachment trial.
What are the political implications of Sara Duterte’s case, Romualdez’s arrest, and Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC appearance?
Sara Duterte’s fiery speech after posting bail may be intended to consolidate her base, portray herself and her family as victims of political persecution, and enhance the prospects of her presidential candidacy. On the other hand, the case reflects their eroded political influence and signals to senator-judges sitting in the impeachment trial that the Marcos government is mobilizing all remedies to remove the vice president from her position.
Romualdez appears to be the Marcos government’s sacrificial lamb amid the continuing uproar against the unresolved corruption mess. Public vigilance is crucial to reverse the impunity that has plagued the country’s political system. A former Cabinet member of Marcos who was also charged with plunder was recently released after agreeing to be a witness. Imelda Marcos, the president’s mother, was acquitted this month by the Supreme Court in a 1991 case involving a portion of their alleged ill-gotten wealth. This is the reason why Romualdez’s arrest could not totally appease the public, who have become skeptical about the real agenda behind the decision to finally charge the president’s first cousin with a non-bailable plunder complaint.
Rodrigo Duterte’s surprise appearance at the ICC, after months of waving his right to attend the trial, has agitated his loyal following and could strengthen his family’s clout. But it also made it clear that he is finally being held to account for the bloody “war on drugs” during his term.
The recent political developments should not be reduced to a mere maneuver among political factions competing for dominance ahead of the 2028 elections. Marcos is evading accountability and desperately denying his lame duck status. Sara Duterte wants to survive the crisis that she herself created, but could not muster enough political support to hit back at Marcos. It is the people speaking out against corruption and protesting in the flooded communities that could sway the political balance and determine how the Marcos presidency will end in 2028. This is the crowd that embodied the anger against the corrupt budget system and demanded an end to political dynasties. They are not easily swayed by spectacles staged by political parties, and they can certainly make Philippine politics more interesting in the lead-up to the 2028 elections and beyond.

Could the EU Kids Act unwittingly widen the transatlantic AI divide?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:19:10 UTC
17:19:10 KST

Europe must prepare for the potential consequences of implementing further digital rules that could make it more difficult for smaller European developers to compete, warns an industry insider.
Brussels wants to shield children from Big Tech. It may end up handing Silicon Valley an even bigger competitive edge.
The EU Kids Act, unveiled this week, promises age limits, parental controls and a crackdown on the "addictive" features baked into social media, video platforms and AI chatbots alike.
But as the bloc moves to police the tech giants, a harder question looms: can Europe regulate its way to child safety without regulating itself out of the AI race it is already losing?
The stakes could hardly be higher. Europe has just one significant AI company to speak of, Mistral, dwarfed by its US rivals OpenAI and Anthropic in both valuation and investment.
The bloc has never really left the starting blocks when it comes to scaling digital platforms to rival America's, relying instead on the strength of its single market and its power to regulate.
Now, as AI becomes the defining technology of the decade, that trade-off — rules versus growth — is seen as a "make or break" moment for the bloc.
What the Kids Act actually proposes
The legislation includes a number of measures aimed at protecting children online, including age restrictions, parental controls and limits on potentially addictive features.
The proposals have been welcomed by some in the tech industry, but Stanislas Marchand, a former mobile gaming lead at French unicorn Voodoo, says Europe must also consider the potential consequences for its own digital sector.
He argues that Europe "must prepare for the potential consequences by investing more urgently than ever in its homegrown AI capabilities".
The European Commission's proposals come amid growing pressure on governments to protect children from the risks posed by social media and other online platforms.
In the last couple of years, though, Big Tech has come under increasing scrutiny for its failure to protect children online, from cyberbullying, harassment and grooming to exploitation, extortion and misinformation.
Australia famously implemented the world's first social media ban for under-16s in December last year, a move that was watched keenly by governments around the world, prompting many to follow suit in implementing their own bans or exploring the possibility of doing so.
France, Greece, Austria, Denmark, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Germany, Poland and the Netherlands have all been considering or advancing national legislation on social media bans, piling pressure on Brussels to present an EU-wide measure and avoid fragmentation.
Meanwhile in the US this year, social media companies have faced and lost landmark liability cases, with many choosing to settle instead — such as Meta's recent $17bn (€14.9bn) deal to end a lawsuit brought by 47 US states.
Beyond social media
The EU Kids Act calls for a total, blanket social media ban for under-13s, while those up to 15 years old would be able to make "mini accounts" — limited, highly supervised profiles linked to a parent's profile.
Not only that, these accounts would also come with mandatory one-hour daily limits and a complete ban on "toxic or addictive features" like infinite scroll, endless autoplay and engagement rewards.
Marchand welcomed the proposed ban for under-13s, but said the proposal "should have been extended to everyone under 16" rather than permitting mini accounts for teens.
He argues the message from the Commission should have been that the platforms in question are "unsuitable for children" because they are "engineered to maximise attention".
The Kids Act goes well beyond social media.
It encompasses video-sharing platforms such as YouTube and Twitch, online video games like Roblox, Fortnite and Minecraft, and more recent entrants like AI chatbots and companions such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.
It would also require app stores and operating systems to integrate strict age-assurance filters to prevent underage users from downloading restricted apps and software in the first place.
And implementation, for Marchand, is where the problem lies, because the EU is asking platforms to "verify children's ages, operate parent-controlled accounts, enforce daily limits, restrict contacts and features, and prove that the resulting product is safe."
These requirements altogether could increase the cost and complexity of launching a product in Europe.
"Every one of those responsibilities creates another potential point of failure, and history gives us little reason to trust social media companies to execute them properly."
That concern is particularly relevant given that Europe's digital sector is dominated by American firms, and the continent has somewhat failed to make sure Big Tech follows the rules.
Meta has been fined twice for illegally transferring European user data to US servers, breaching GDPR in 2023 and the Digital Markets Act in 2025.
TikTok was fined €530m last year for failing to protect children's data and illegally transferring it to Chinese servers.
Elon Musk's X, which has had the most acrimonious relationship with EU lawmakers, was fined €120m last December over its deceptive "blue checkmark" verification and for denying researchers access to data.
Google, too, has been fined repeatedly for breaching antitrust rules, amounting to €10.38bn so far.
A patchy enforcement record
All of these fines are pocket change for Big Tech, and with the arrival of potentially even larger firms in the shape of AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic — again based in the US — it could become even more difficult for Europe to shape and enforce its own digital rules.
Marchand fears the Act could also make the EU a less attractive market to launch new products, while doing little to support European alternatives.
"If the Kids Act requires separate European products and costly ongoing assessments, US labs may delay launches here while smaller European developers struggle to compete," he warns.
He also points out that frontier AI companies already face enormous computing costs and uncertain paths to profitability, while some advanced Anthropic models have already been restricted outside the US and withheld from the UK's AI Security Institute.
For Marchand, the result could be an unintended consequence of the EU's attempt to protect children online.
"My feeling is this will further add to the transatlantic AI divide."

European stock markets also posted gains on Thursday, driven by surging auto, telecom and retail shares, while optimism that geopolitical tensions may ease contributed to the trend.

The Bank of Japan (BoJ) raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 1.25% on Friday, reaching its highest level in 31 years in a decision made by a vote of seven to two.
The bank said the economy is growing moderately and that this trend will continue, but the situation in the Middle East and rising demand for artificial intelligence (AI) continue to pose inflationary risks.
The BoJ also signaled that rate hikes will continue depending on economic activity and financial conditions. The recent decision was not unanimous, fueling uncertainty over whether the bank will continue on its tightening path, which led to a further depreciation of the yen.
The US dollar/Japanese yen exchange rate rose 0.2% to 157.2, while Japan’s inflation came in slightly below estimates at 1.9% in August.
Near Friday’s close, South Korea’s Kospi rose 2.6%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 gained 1.8%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.7% and China’s Shanghai Composite was up 1%.

Latvian fintech companies present solutions to German investors in Berlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:18:26 UTC
17:18:26 KST

Latvian financial technology companies met with representatives of German institutional investors, family offices, banks, and the FinTech industry during a trade mission to Berlin organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA). The Latvian companies presented their solutions and discussed investment opportunities, cooperation with the German financial sector, and opportunities to expand their operations in Europe’s largest economy. On Thursday, 17 September, the participating companies will continue individual business meetings with potential partners.
The FinTech programme was developed in cooperation with the Fintech Latvia Association and the House of Finance & Tech Berlin (HoFT). Participants included Latvia’s Minister of Economics Viktors Valainis, executives of Latvian FinTech companies, German investors, and other industry representatives.
“Eight investment platforms regulated in Latvia serve more than 800,000 investors abroad, while investments made through these platforms have already exceeded €13 billion. This demonstrates that Latvia has developed an internationally competitive FinTech industry, rather than merely a handful of successful companies. Our task now is to transform these technological and regulatory advantages into even stronger positions for Latvian companies in the European financial market,” said Minister of Economics Viktors Valainis.
Investors Explore Latvia’s FinTech Offering
During a roundtable discussion held on 16 September, Latvian FinTech companies introduced German investors to their solutions and the development of the sector in Latvia. Participants included German institutional investors, family-office representatives, and other members of the investment community.
Latvia’s FinTech sector was represented by Mintos, Debitum, Magnetiq Bank, TWINO, VIAINVEST, LANDE, and other companies. The discussions aimed to establish direct contacts with German investors, explore funding opportunities, and present Latvia as an attractive environment for the operation and growth of FinTech companies.
“German investors account for approximately 30% of demand on Latvian investment platforms. This means that our companies already have a market and customers in Germany, but further growth requires broader cooperation with banks, institutional investors, and other financial-market participants. We designed the FinTech programme in Berlin around precisely these opportunities—bringing companies together with partners who can help them significantly scale up their operations in Germany,” said Vita Balode-Andrūsa, Director of LIAA’s Export and Innovation Services Department.
Berlin is the centre of Germany’s FinTech industry. According to Germany’s federal Digital Hub Initiative, the city is home to more than two-thirds of Germany’s FinTech companies and attracts 90% of the venture capital invested in the sector.
“Germany is one of Europe’s most demanding yet attractive FinTech markets. Latvian companies, including Mintos, have demonstrated that it is possible to earn the trust of German investors by offering regulated, transparent, and practically useful investment products. This trade mission is an important step towards establishing closer and more sustainable economic ties between the Latvian and German FinTech ecosystems,” said Mārtiņš Šulte, CEO and co-founder of Mintos.
From Licensing to Cooperation with Germany’s Financial Sector
The Berlin–Riga FinTech Exchange and Networking event, dedicated to cooperation between the Berlin and Riga FinTech ecosystems, addressed the opportunities provided by the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), the licensing of FinTech companies in Latvia, access to the German market and capital, technological partnerships, and the cross-border growth of companies.
Tīna Lūse, head of the Fintech Latvia Association, introduced participants to Latvia’s FinTech ecosystem. Atrya representative Lorian Qorraj shared the company’s experience of the licensing process and launching operations in Latvia, while Latvia’s Magnetiq Bank and German company Vexcash presented their cooperation model in the lending-services sector.
The event allowed Latvian companies to connect with investors, financial institutions, technology companies, and industry organisations in one place. German partners, meanwhile, learned about the solutions offered by Latvian companies and their experience of operating within the regulated European Union financial market.
The FinTech programme concluded with a reception hosted by Ilze Rūse, Latvia’s Ambassador to Germany, where representatives of the Latvian delegation continued their discussions with German entrepreneurs, investors, and industry organisations.
Trade Mission Continues with Individual Business Meetings
On 17 September, companies from the Latvian delegation are scheduled to hold individual business meetings with potential German clients, investors, and cooperation partners. The meetings have been arranged according to each company’s field of activity and interests in the German market.
On the first day of the trade mission, the Latvian delegation also participated in an information session on Germany’s economic and political environment. Minister of Economics Viktors Valainis met Thomas Steffen, State Secretary at Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy, to discuss expanding economic cooperation between the two countries and opportunities for Latvian companies in the German market.
A memorandum of understanding was also signed in Berlin between LIAA, the Association of German Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHK), and the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce (AHK). It will provide Latvian companies with access to the expertise, contacts, and services of Germany’s network of chambers of commerce abroad, which operates at 150 locations in more than 90 countries.
The trade mission of Latvian companies to Germany, organised by LIAA, takes place from 14 to 17 September. It includes companies operating in information and communication technologies, financial technologies, life sciences, smart energy, defence, and dual-use technologies. The programme includes visits to companies and innovation centres, participation in international industry events, meetings with investors, and individual business discussions.
Germany is Latvia’s largest export market outside the Baltic states. Since 2020, Latvia’s exports of goods and services to Germany have increased by more than 40%, from €1.47 billion to approximately €2.1 billion in 2025. Last year, Latvia exported more to Germany alone than to the United States, France, and China combined.
Growth has continued this year: during the first half of 2026, exports to Germany increased by 11%, compared with 6% growth in Latvia’s overall exports. Germany is also Latvia’s largest market for services exports, which reached €779 million in 2025. More than 1,000 companies with German capital operate in Latvia, with their combined investment in share capital exceeding €800 million.
Participation in international trade missions is organised by LIAA under the European Union co-financed programme for the development of innovative entrepreneurship among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), supported by the European Regional Development Fund and national funding. Companies may participate in trade missions either by paying a participation fee or by receiving support to cover eligible costs.

Overcrowded buses leaving Tartu suburb students behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:16:00 UTC
17:16:00 KST

Overcrowded buses leaving Tartu suburb students behind
Students catching buses from Kõrveküla Basic School toward Tartu are increasingly being left behind by overcrowding, with no relief in sight before 2028.
Parents raised the issue with Tartu Municipality at the start of the school year, citing buses that are too full to accommodate all students, particularly on afternoon routes toward the rapidly growing Raadi area.
"The bus was so full that I tried to squeeze myself in, but everyone squeezed me back out," said Kevin, adding that this happens pretty frequently.
"I most often catch the bus to make it to practice," said Mirko, another student. "One time I missed the bus too, because it was so crowded."
Tartu Municipal Mayor Jarno Laur admitted there is no quick fix to the issue because both city and county buses are already operating at their maximum contracted capacity.
"There is absolutely no way for us to add departures under the existing contracts," Laur said.
The situation is further complicated by schools' ministry-imposed change to a 9 a.m. start, which the mayor said will require the municipality to arrange separate school bus routes starting next school year.
Most commuters travel to work in Tartu for 8 a.m., he said, making it difficult to use the same buses efficiently for both groups.
"Regional public transport centers have told us they cannot provide school bus transport with state subsidies because their role is to provide transport for working people," Laur said.
"For us, that means we'll have to set up separate school bus routes, even though we currently serve three schools with one bus route and the next two with another," he continued. "Meaning we'll have to rework what I'd say is a fairly efficient transportation system."
Articulated buses, extra capacity
Until additional capacity becomes available, the municipal mayor said students could be spread out by adjusting school schedules or using county buses, although some county bus stops are located further from home.
Tartu Municipality plans to address the problem in future transportation procurements by including larger articulated buses for rush hour departures and reserving some city-route capacity for necessary additional service.
"These issues will be easier to address in the next upcoming procurements," Laur noted.

Surinder Koli, acquitted in 2006 Nithari serial killings case, dies by suicide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
