Could AI really end humanity? Post your questions for our tech reporters now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:14:11 UTC
16:14:11 KST

That's all, folks!
Thanks everyone for the great questions. This is a difficult subject to negotiate and interacting with you always helps shape our thinking - and hopefully yours. Aisha, Blake and Dan
After a week of alarming warnings about artificial intelligence’s potential to destroy the world as we know it, our technology reporters answered your questions on the reality of the AI threat
Alberichthenibelung asks: What, if anything, can individuals like me do about it?
 Blake: There is, unfortunately, not much that comes to mind. Everyday people confronted with declarations of a coming AI apocalypse find themselves in a position similar to the cold war, with doom hovering over their heads and little say in it. We may all have to accept the faint tinnitus of paranoia buzzing in the background. You can stop using AI if you feel so moved, though I have found that unfeasible, and your job may require it. You can vote for politicians that endorse AI regulation. I myself don’t put much stock in the reality of an AI-made doomsday because a genuine belief in it would demand drastic, life-changing actions today, ones that I don’t want to take. A bit of inductive reasoning from how I’d like to situate my own life within the world.
Fulgrim asks: What would legislation look like? We only just passed the Online Safety Act and it is ineffectual, restrictive and late. Given the complexity, fast changes and its international nature, what kind of legislation would you like to see and how do we educate politicians on the issue?
Trentwarrior asks: Regulation, oversight and accountability for huge companies that appear unable or unwilling to eliminate the harms their products inflict - and that seem incapable of conducting safe experiments to ensure that AI does not leak into the wider internet - seem to be urgent and vital. What are the prospects for a global regulatory framework that is enforceable, particularly when the genie may already be out of the bottle, and when the US and China have very different objectives and applications for their AI technologies?
 Blake: It’s a tough question. One way to hinder the general development of AI could be restricting access to computing power, which is a vital resource that underpins the success of an AI model. In the absence of legislation that applies to all types of AI development, measures that target certain aspects of AI like housing allotment or children’s access to chatbots seem like the path lawmakers will take.
There are two big question marks hovering over a possible global regulatory framework. The first is whether Donald Trump will revise his “Drill, baby, drill” stance towards AI development. He has rejected any calls for a voluntary slowdown. In my opinion, he is not likely to change that position: He loves to post AI slop, and he loves AI has done for the US stock market.
The second question mark is Beijing, which has rejected US CEOs’ calls for a slowdown. Without China’s cooperation, an intentional slowdown would likely not succeed. Xi Jinping also seems unlikely to back down. A slowdown of AI development led by the US would offer China few obvious benefits.
Trump and Xi Jinping are also set to meet next week in Washington. AI will be high on the agenda.
The UN General Assembly is taking place now, with discussions of AI large and small on the schedule. It is possible that an initial version of a global regulatory framework emerges from there.
MacDuke asks: Do tech reporters feel responsibility for allowing tech bros to accumulate so much wealth without holding them to account for destroying the climate, society, and the economy (when the bubble bursts)?
 Blake: Sometimes! I rarely, if ever, write flattering pieces about them. Our job as journalists is to hold them to account. Our work does often change the perception of tech oligarchs; however, we have less power to compel changes in user behavior. Facebook, for all the reporting on the harms it has inflicted upon the world, has more than two billion daily users. Instagram has three billion monthly users. Those vast numbers are growing. By contrast, we are extremely happy if our stories reach one million readers, a rare outcome. The Washington Post summed this dynamic up quite well: “AI is just another technology Americans don’t like but can’t stop using.”
We do our best.
LlivracNhoJ asks: Why do some journalists persist in spreading the myth that “nobody understands how these technologies work” when we know it’s basically pattern recognition and inference?
 Aisha: In defense of my journalist brethren, there is an element of a “black box” in how ChatGPT or Claude answer specific prompts. The area of “AI interpretability” is an active field of study. In broad terms, yes we do know how an LLM is trained and built. But for example, no one can do a forensic A to B to C mapping of how an AI system might select a face from a lineup, pick one CV over another, or target one individual and not another in a conflict. That seems to be likely what they mean.
Davidabsalom asks: Is the recent desire for a slowdown by the tech bros more about their fear their money will run out and their businesses collapse rather than a genuine belief in the dangers?
Seaspray asks: Is this recent narrative push of the AI apocalypse an inventive way of preparing the public for the market crash and wipeout of AI shares? The companies seem overvalued and their borrowing and input costs have gone up.
 Aisha: The finances of the AI buildout are certainly shaky. Hundreds of billions of dollars are being ploughed into massive, unpopular infrastructure projects that our reporting has shown are not necessarily getting built. Nvidia appears to be the only company making a profit, and investigations I have done with Ed Zitron raise some questions about whether all its very expensive GPUs are actually, currently, getting plugged into datacentres. (Perhaps they are mouldering in warehouses instead.) There are some unsettling financial instruments being used to raise money to build yet more datacentres, such as GPU-backed debt.
Is that why tech bros want a slowdown? Perhaps. It looks like OpenAI just pushed back its IPO until 2027. This might be because, as we reported, things did not look amazing for them earlier this year in terms of floating on the market - they seemed to be struggling to monetise ads and erotic chatbots. Their valuation will depend a lot on vibes, and maybe the doomy vibes will help a potential share offering.
Westkent1023 asks: Milton Mueller, professor and program Director of Science in Cybersecurity Policy at Georgia Tech in the US has argued in a peer-reviewed paper in the Journal of Cyber Policy that the idea of AGI posing an existential risk to humans is an ‘unscientific myth’ that defies ‘economic constraints and even basic laws of physics’. Such claims he suggests distract and distort proper digital governance of risks from AI in its current form. What do you think of these arguments? And if the AI developers believe their claims about an existential risk to humanity, why don’t they provide scientific evidence to back this up?
JibbyJames asks: When experts discuss existential risk from AI, what specific mechanisms or scenarios are they actually concerned about, beyond the sensational doom mongering headlines?
 Blake: It’s a reasonable critique to ask whether these companies are using their own predictions of human extinction as a smokescreen to obfuscate the current ills of AI, of which there are many. Causing the apocalypse does not offer a flattering portrayal, but it does capture the imagination and shift the discussion. It’s harder to craft regulation to prevent the total annihilation of humanity than it is to prevent children from using chatbots in schools. AI CEOs seem shocked to learn the public doesn’t have a high opinion of them, to which I would say, you painted this portrait of yourself.
Critics of the AI industry say that the focus on a potential apocalypse distracts from elements of AI that are already inflicting widespread harm like algorithmic discrimination in housing allotment.
I asked Max Tegmark, head of the AI-safety-focused Future of Life Institute, whether discussion of the existential distracts from the immediate. He hosted a “pro-human” summit Tuesday in Washington, DC that featured both the progressive Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, former chief of staff to Donald Trump. Strange bedfellows, indeed.
   “It’s like saying we shouldn’t talk about climate change because there’s a forest fire blazing somewhere. It’s a ridiculous criticism,” he said. “It’s very patronizing to assume human beings are just a bunch of dummies. We can deal with challenges in parallel.”
As for specific mechanisms of the end of our species, they do seem far off, but nearer to us than before OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face. A former Google Deepmind researcher wrote in The Guardian that he worries about swarms of AI agents—autonomous software—taking over drones and critical infrastructure. I found his description quite evocative:
Suppose the Hugging Face swarm had been truly “superintelligent”: far more capable than any living person at key tasks like hacking and strategic reasoning. A superintelligent swarm could inflict many harms via blackmail, hacking, engineered plagues, and AI-pilotable weapons like drones. The AI would have a lot of drones to work with: this year, the Pentagon asked for more money for drone warfare than it requested for the entire Marine Corps in 2025.
   For the swarm to achieve its misaligned priorities, it might take control of key infrastructure and government functions to ensure humans didn’t get in the way. In other words, AI takeover: a superintelligent AI swarm could wrest control of human civilization. Knowing we would try to stop it from achieving its priorities, the swarm would likely wait until it’s too late to shut it off. There would be no going back.
I myself would guess AI takeover chances at roughly one-in-three–not a coin flip, but high enough to justify urgent action.
TooTrueMate asks: People (ie the tech-bros) bang on about the “benefits”: just what are they? We don’t need this rubbish!!
 Dan: Anyone who has used a chatbot to parse a lengthy document, argue against a parking fine or spitball ideas for a speech can point to the benefits of the technology - although this is very basic level stuff that people have been doing for a while now. There is also the everyday use of the technology from facial recognition to open your iPhone to asking Alexa to play an Oasis track or driving around in a Tesla. With those latter examples, you’d notice if AI wasn’t involved.
In science there are many examples of benefits, from Google’s AlphaFold model - which can predict how proteins behave and thus help us study the biological machinery that underpins living organisms (thanks Ian Sample) - to making weather forecasting more accurate, which is sadly necessary in this climate crisis era.
But there is an element of banging on about the benefits for the wider global economy, which have yet to reveal themselves on the scale predicted by the AI industry. For instance, these benefits require AI agents - tools that carry out tasks on your behalf while you’re at the water cooler or have clocked off - to be a lot more active in the workforce. We are not at that stage yet even if they are making inroads into areas like software programming.
Tintenfische asks: Does Europe need a sovereign internet to quarantine us from the mad house that is the US? Russia and China have pretty much their own to stop ideas of democracy spreading. Shouldn’t we have similar to stop the ideas of bellends and idiots from spreading?
 Aisha: I have written extensively about the ongoing trend – pushed by authoritarian regimes – to splinter the internet, and my answer here is no. The internet is a technology that sprung up organically, over time, and is a glorious, decentralised commons which enables democracy and free information flows worldwide. The US may be a madhouse but quarantining the internet somehow will not stop the spread of bad ideas; Europe is capable of inventing those on its own too.
It might be useful, though, to consider other forms of sovereignty. Europe would have more control over its information space if its own, homegrown social media companies, cloud providers and AI developers had more market share and were not throttled by the monopolies of US tech companies. The power of these companies is hard to challenge, but ultimately the better aim might be a resilient internet ecosystem, as opposed to a splinternet.
El_Awrens asks: Why is there not more scrutiny of the strange and terrifying beliefs shared by many of the key figures in the AI movement? It is impossible to understand these companies – or objectively assess their wild claims – without understanding the transhumanist, extropian, effective altruism and rationalist movements which shaped so many of them.
 Aisha
There is already a lot of scrutiny of these beliefs and there should be more. I suggest books like Tech Agnostic, by Greg Epstein, and More Everything Forever, by Adam Becker. The Guardian has written Long Reads on transhumanism and accelerationism. It is an area of continued interest.
Bratticus asks: What is behind the apparent reluctance to hold companies responsible for crimes committed by their researchers using “AI” tooling? We already have laws around holding individuals responsible for what autonomous agents (Ie, animals) do. Why is AI treated differently? Is it money? Lobbying?
 Aisha:
Money and a collection of sort of quasi-mystical narratives around the technology, which confound regulators and politicians, and prevent them from divining who has power and what they are trying to achieve. Many people buy into hype put forward by large tech companies because they are afraid of looking ignorant otherwise.

They beat detainees for smiling: two Russian prison officers who tortured Ukrainians identified
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18

16:14:00 KST

They beat detainees for smiling: two Russian prison officers who tortured Ukrainians identified
Ukrainian law enforcement officers have served notices of suspicion on two Russian prison officers from Penal Colony No. 1 operated by the Federal Prison Service Directorate for Tula Oblast who tortured Ukrainians.
Source: Russian Torturers project
Details: The suspects were identified with the assistance of analysts from Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
They are:
- Alexei Kochetov (born 28 February 1988), a native of Donskoy, Tula Oblast, Russia.
- Yevgeny Myasnikov (born 29 January 2000), a native of Donskoy, Tula Oblast, Russia.
At the time of the crimes in 2022, both men held posts as junior inspectors at the maximum-security Penal Colony No. 1 in Tula Oblast, located in Donskoy, 240 km from Moscow and 640 km from Kharkiv. Russia is holding Ukrainian citizens, both prisoners of war and civilians, in this prison.
Investigators say Kochetov and Myasnikov, together with other prison staff and special forces officers, systematically subjected civilian detainees to physical and psychological violence motivated by hatred towards Ukrainians.
At least four men detained in Kyiv Oblast in March 2022 were among their victims.
The torture began as soon as the detainees arrived at the prison. During the so-called admission procedure, they were forced to run past a line of prison officers, each of whom tried to hit them with their hands, feet, rubber batons, plastic pipes or stun guns.
The beatings continued even whilst the detainees were subsequently escorted to their cells.
Prison officers forced their victims to adopt uncomfortable positions – facing a wall with their legs spread wide apart, their heads pressed against the wall and their palms turned outwards – and then punched and kicked them wherever they could. The victims would lose their balance and consciousness from the blows and fall to the floor, after which they were forced to get back up and the beatings continued.
Kochetov also forced detainees into a push-up position, slapped them across the face, kicked them in the torso and stood on the back of a victim lying on the floor.
Myasnikov forced one of the victims to hang from a metal grille and punched him in the stomach. After the man jumped down, Myasnikov shocked him with a stun gun on the leg and neck.
The detainees were beaten for the slightest perceived offence or for no reason at all. Myasnikov beat one man with a baton and shocked him with a stun gun after seeing on CCTV that he was smiling. He beat another for getting dressed too slowly while leaving the shower room to go outside.
Kochetov and Myasnikov are being charged under Article 438.1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine for cruel treatment of civilians.
Their actions constitute serious violations of the Geneva Convention relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War and Additional Protocol I and, under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, are considered a war crime.
The criminal proceedings were entered in Ukraine's Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations under No. 42023000000000055 on 23 January 2023.

Oktoberfest in Munich 2026: when the festival will open, traditions, and how much a visit will cost
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:12:07 EEST
16:12:07 KST

Oktoberfest in Munich 2026: when the festival will open, traditions, and how much a visit will cost
Kyiv • UNN
Oktoberfest 2026 will take place in Munich from September 19 to October 4; admission is free. A liter of beer will cost €14.80–15.90.
On September 19, the 191st Oktoberfest — Germany’s largest folk festival and one of the world’s best-known festivals — will begin in Munich. For 16 days, Theresienwiese will be transformed into a huge festival site with beer tents, dozens of rides, orchestras, traditional Bavarian cuisine, and guests wearing traditional attire. Oktoberfest will end on October 4.
UNN has compiled interesting facts about the history, traditions, and present day of Oktoberfest.
When Oktoberfest begins and how long it will last
Oktoberfest 2026 will run from Saturday, September 19, through Sunday, October 4. The celebrations will last 16 days. The festival’s name may be somewhat misleading, as most of the modern Oktoberfest takes place not in October, but in September. However, this was not always the case. The first festival, in 1810, did indeed take place in October. Over time, organizers began moving it to an earlier period because of the warmer September weather and longer daylight hours. Since 1872, the festival’s start has been fixed in September, although it was decided not to change its historic name.
In 2026, the main Wiesn grounds will be open from Monday to Thursday from 10:00 a.m. to 11:30 p.m., on Friday from 10:00 a.m. to midnight, on Saturday from 9:00 a.m. to midnight, and on Sunday from 9:00 a.m. to 11:30 p.m. The rides will open at noon on the festival’s opening day. On subsequent days, their schedule will generally correspond to the opening hours of the festival grounds.
The beer tents have their own schedules. In most large tents, the last beer is served at 10:30 p.m., when the music program also ends. Some smaller establishments stay open a little longer. Exceptions include Käfer Wiesn-Schänke and Kufflers Weinzelt, which may receive guests until 1:00 a.m.; the last drinks there are served at around 12:30 a.m.
This year, the festival grounds cover 34.5 hectares. The organizers have admitted 478 businesses and establishments to participate: these include 36 food-service operators, 243 amusement and entertainment operators, 182 vendors, as well as service companies. Guests can look forward to 14 large and 21 small festival tents, with several more operating in the historic Oide Wiesn area.
Where the festival takes place and how Oktoberfest is opened
The location of Oktoberfest has remained practically unchanged since its founding. The festival takes place at Theresienwiese — a large open area in the Ludwigsvorstadt-Isarvorstadt district, not far from central Munich. The name Theresienwiese literally means “Theresa’s meadow.” The area was named after Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen, whose wedding to Ludwig, the Bavarian crown prince, in 1810 provided the occasion for the first major public celebration. Munich residents themselves often simply call Oktoberfest Wiesn — after the local form of the word Wiese, meaning “meadow.”
The official opening of the 191st Oktoberfest will take place on September 19 at exactly 12:00 p.m. in Festhalle Schottenhamel — the oldest and largest traditional beer tent. According to a long-standing tradition, the mayor of Munich (currently Dominik Krause) must tap the first barrel of festival beer and proclaim the famous “O'zapft is!” — a Bavarian expression meaning that the barrel has been tapped. After that, beer may begin to be served in the other tents. The first one-liter mug is handed to the Bavarian minister-president. This custom has existed since 1980.
It should be noted that the tradition of opening the festival by tapping a barrel is considerably younger than Oktoberfest itself: it was introduced in 1950 by Munich’s then-incumbent mayor, Thomas Wimmer.
Before the ceremony, a procession of festival-tent hosts and representatives of Munich breweries makes its way through the city streets. Decorated horse-drawn wagons, orchestras, and staff from the establishments head to Theresienwiese, after which the opening ceremony begins.
The following day, September 20, one of the festival’s main traditions is scheduled to take place — a grand parade of participants in traditional costumes and shooting associations. On September 27, a concert by the festival orchestras will be held near the Bavaria monument, while on October 4, the end of Wiesn will traditionally be marked by a cannon salute.
Beer, Bavarian dishes, and entertainment
The most famous gastronomic symbol of Oktoberfest is a one-liter mug of festival beer, which the Germans call a Maß. It should be noted that you cannot simply bring any beer to the “Theresienwiese” and sell it under the name Oktoberfestbier. Only products from six traditional Munich breweries are admitted to the festival: Augustiner, Hacker-Pschorr, Hofbräu, Löwenbräu, Paulaner and Spaten.
Since 2022, the name Oktoberfestbier has had a special status in the European Union. The European Commission approved it to guarantee the authenticity and quality of the product. Under the established rules, beer bearing this name may be brewed exclusively within the city of Munich and must comply with Munich’s 1487 Beer Purity Law. Brewers must also use only water from deep local wells during the brewing process.
However, the festival’s traditional menu is not limited to beer. Guests are offered roast chicken (Hendl), pork knuckle (Schweinshaxe), sausages, large pretzels, roast meat, potato and bread dumplings, a cheese spread (Obatzda), and the Bavarian version of cheese noodles (Kässpatzen). In recent years, establishments have been increasingly adding vegetarian and vegan dishes.
According to the organizers, food sales at the Wiesn increased in 2025, while among the meat-free dishes, cheese spaetzle (small dumplings with hot, stringy cheese and caramelized onions, – ed.) and mushrooms in cream sauce with dumplings were especially popular.
An important part of the festive atmosphere is traditional clothing. Many women come in dirndls (an outfit consisting of an apron, bodice and blouse), while men wear lederhosen. However, this is not a mandatory requirement for visitors, as the festival has no official dress code.
Oktoberfest is also known as a huge amusement park. In 2026, 243 operators of rides and other entertainment facilities were admitted to participate. The Theresienwiese traditionally features a Ferris wheel, roller coasters, carousels, haunted houses, free-fall towers and dozens of other attractions.
This year, special family days will be held on September 22 and 29 for families with children. Until 7:00 p.m., many rides, vendors and food establishments will offer reduced prices, while the large beer tents will provide special children’s meals. In addition, among the new features of 2026 is expanded access to free drinking water (ten drinking fountains will operate across the festival grounds). Cashless payments are also gradually becoming more widespread—the organizers note that cards are already accepted at approximately half of the kiosks and rides.
How much it will cost to visit Oktoberfest in 2026
Admission to the main Oktoberfest grounds remains free. You do not need to purchase a separate ticket to visit the Theresienwiese. Admission to both the large and small festival tents is also free.
Reserving a table is not mandatory: some seats in the large tents will be available to guests without reservations. However, during evening hours, on weekends and for large groups, making a reservation in advance significantly increases the chances of getting inside. The reservation itself is generally not sold as a separate ticket, but establishments may require guests to purchase vouchers in advance for a certain amount to cover food and drinks.
For many guests, the main expense is beer. In 2026, a one-liter mug costs between 14.80 and 15.90 euros, depending on the establishment. Compared with the previous year, the average price increased by 2.38%. In the large Augustiner-Festhalle, a liter costs 14.90 euros; at Schottenhamel, 15.80 euros; while at Armbrustschützen-Festzelt, Bräurosl and Löwenbräu-Festzelt, the price reaches 15.90 euros. Soft drinks are also difficult to call cheap. The average price of a liter of bottled water is 11.13 euros, lemonade costs 12.35 euros, and Spezi costs 12.84 euros. Prices are set by the establishment owners themselves, while the city authorities check the stated rates for reasonableness.
There is no single rate for the attractions—carousels and roller coasters—on the main grounds. Each operator sets their own price, and tickets are purchased directly at the attraction.
How to get to Oktoberfest and how much transportation costs
Theresienwiese is located near central Munich, so the organizers recommend using public transportation. The Theresienwiese U-Bahn station on lines U4 and U5 is located directly next to the festival. Alternatives are Goetheplatz or Poccistraße stations on lines U3 and U6. In 2026, a single ticket for an adult in Munich's central M fare zone costs €4.20. A day ticket, which allows unlimited travel in zone M until 6:00 a.m. the following morning, costs €10.10.
Those planning to fly to Munich should bear in mind that the airport is already located in fare zone 5, so a regular zone M city ticket is not sufficient for this journey.
Separate expenses include travel to Germany and accommodation in Munich. They do not have a fixed cost and depend on the booking dates, mode of transport, and area of accommodation.
Safety rules should also be taken into account. Large bags and backpacks are not allowed onto the grounds. Bags with a capacity of up to three liters and measuring no more than 20×15×10 cm are permitted. Large items can be left in the luggage lockers near the entrances; the service costs €5. Glass bottles and objects that could be used as weapons are prohibited.
From a royal wedding to a celebration for millions of visitors from around the world
The history of Oktoberfest began on October 12, 1810, when Bavarian Crown Prince Ludwig, the future King Ludwig I, married Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen. The city celebrations lasted several days, and on October 17, major horse races were organized in a meadow beyond the then boundaries of Munich. They were proposed by Andreas Michael Dall'Armi, an officer in the Bavarian National Guard. The celebration proved so popular that it was decided to repeat it the following year. The meadow was named Theresienwiese in honor of the bride.
At first, the giant beer tents familiar to modern tourists were not there. In 1818, the festival featured its first carousel and two swings, while by the end of the 19th century the entertainment area began to expand rapidly. In 1881, the first special rotisserie opened at Wiesn, selling roast chicken—one of the dishes without which it is now difficult to imagine modern Oktoberfest.
From 1819, responsibility for organizing the celebration was assumed by the Munich city authorities. At the same time, Oktoberfest was held far from every year: during various periods, it was canceled because of wars, epidemics, and other crises.
Over two centuries, the small horse races have transformed into an event with an audience of millions. In 2025, approximately 6.5 million people attended Oktoberfest. According to the organizers' estimates, they drank about 6.5 million liters of beer. In 2023, the festival welcomed approximately 7.2 million guests, a record attendance figure.

MSI-DS debuts a new gun mount made for the drone fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:11:57 UTC
16:11:57 KST

- MSI-Defence Systems unveiled the TERRAHAWK RAPTOR remote weapon station at DVD 2026, calling it its lightest counter-drone gun mount yet.
- The 7.62mm or 12.7mm system can add a 40mm grenade launcher and uses AI-enabled tracking to counter both drones and ground targets.
British manufacturer MSI-Defence Systems unveiled a new remote weapon station called TERRAHAWK RAPTOR at the DVD 2026 exhibition in Millbrook, calling it the lightest gun mount in its counter-drone product line.
RAPTOR is a remote weapon station, a gun turret a soldier can aim and fire from inside a vehicle rather than exposing themselves on top of it. The system comes fitted with a 7.62mm or 12.7mm machine gun, with an option to add a 40mm automatic grenade launcher, and MSI-DS built it specifically for countering drones rather than the ground-suppression role most remote weapon stations were originally designed for. Its compact size is meant to let it mount on tactical ground vehicles and uncrewed ground vehicles alike, using an open standard called Generic Vehicle Architecture that lets different vehicle systems share data without custom wiring for each installation.
The weapon station carries a multispectral sensor suite paired with an AI-enabled fire control system, which MSI-DS says can track, classify and engage both drones and ground targets while filtering out visual clutter that might otherwise confuse the system. RAPTOR is built to plug into multiple command-and-control systems, letting it operate as part of a larger, layered air defense network rather than only as a standalone gun.
“Conventionally speaking, RWS have been designed and deployed primarily for ground suppressive fire,” said David Codling, Business Development Director at MSI Defence Systems. “RAPTOR is different; we have designed and built an RWS optimised for the C-UAS fight in addition to class leading ground suppression and point fire.”
MSI-DS said it built RAPTOR in response to demand for specialist counter-drone systems roughly doubling across the UK, US and European markets. “The proliferation of explosive FPV and reconnaissance drones has necessitated armed forces to either retrofit legacy armoured vehicles or introduce new tactical units into the formation with lighter RWS,” said John Meldrum, Managing Director at MSI Defence Systems. “TERRAHAWK RAPTOR was designed to meet this need, and transform vehicle platforms into highly effective mobile air defence units capable of rapid response against swarming threats.”
RAPTOR extends a product family MSI-DS has built over more than 40 years of gunfire and remote weapon system work, spanning its Seahawk naval systems and its Terrahawk land line, which the company says is now used by more than 40 armed forces. An earlier Terrahawk variant, the Paladin, has already seen combat, with footage released in November 2025 showing Ukraine’s 156th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment operating the system against drone threats.
MSI-DS said future development will expand the RAPTOR architecture into a small modular launcher capable of firing interceptors, rockets and small missiles alongside its gun options.

Russia, China veto US resolution about Iran sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:09:31 UTC
16:09:31 KST

The meeting was held under France’s rotating presidency of the Security Council. The draft resolution received 11 votes in favor among the council’s 15 members, but failed to pass after Russia and China voted against it, while Pakistan and Somalia abstained.
China’s representative to the Security Council, Fu Cong, opposed the draft and called for “responsible action” by the council on issues related to Iran’s nuclear program. He also described US attacks on Iran as the “root of the current crisis” and said sanctions would contribute to escalating tensions.
Fu also referred to the expiration of Resolution 2231 on October 18, 2025, stressing that the Security Council’s consideration of Iran’s nuclear issue had come to an end. Beijing also opposed turning the Security Council into a platform for advancing unilateral objectives and called on all parties to play a constructive role in preserving the credibility of multilateralism and creating conditions for a political resolution to the Iranian nuclear issue.
Russia’s representative to the Security Council, Vasily Nebenzia, also described the 1737 Committee as “illegitimate,” stressing that the snapback mechanism had not been activated and that previous UN Security Council resolutions against Iran had not been reinstated.
Referring to the expiration of Resolution 2231 on October 18, 2025, Nebenzia reiterated Moscow’s position that the resolution had expired and was no longer on the council’s agenda. He said the meeting on the issue lacked legal and procedural grounds and rejected attempts to establish legitimacy by invoking the snapback mechanism.
Nebenzia also said Russia voted against extending the mandate of the panel of experts because it considers the 1737 Committee illegitimate. According to him, neither the snapback mechanism nor the reinstatement of the old resolutions 1737 and 1929 against Iran had taken place.
The Russian envoy added that Moscow had warned the sponsors of the draft resolution ahead of the vote about the consequences of such a move, but said the United States had chosen a path of political confrontation by insisting on extending the panel’s mandate. He described the move as part of what he called the Western countries’ “escalatory steps” over Iran’s nuclear issue.
Pakistan’s representative, who abstained from the vote, stressed the importance of diplomatic tools and the role of the International Atomic Energy Agency in addressing Iran’s compliance.
The UN Security Council’s 1737 Committee was established in 2006, before the implementation of the nuclear deal known as the JCPOA, following the adoption of Resolution 1737 against Iran. The committee was tasked with responsibilities related to implementing sanctions and restrictions imposed on Iran.
Following efforts by three European countries to activate the snapback mechanism, Russia and China repeatedly stressed, citing Iran’s commitments under the JCPOA, that they would oppose the restoration of the mechanism and the 1737 Committee. The two countries used their veto power on Thursday to block the US-drafted resolution.

NYT: Trump considers "appeasing" Russia with business deals before hostilities end
The White House is reportedly considering signing certain business deals with Russia even before Moscow ends its war against Ukraine, as a way of demonstrating its good intentions.
Source: The New York Times, citing anonymous sources
Details: According to two people familiar with the details of negotiations involving Trump's special envoys, the administration is already considering signing certain economic agreements with Russia without making it a precondition that hostilities in the war against Ukraine cease.
One of the sources, a US official, said deals before the end of the war were considered possible because they would "show that the United States is serious about a reset relationship with Russia".
Last year, Trump said economic cooperation with Russia could only resume once the Russia-Ukraine war had ended. In particular, ahead of his meeting with the Russian leader in Alaska, he said Russia wanted economic cooperation but that there would be none of that "until we get the war settled".
Trump's negotiators are now reportedly looking for new ways to encourage Moscow to end the war, as it has become clear that Ukraine is not prepared to surrender the unoccupied part of Donetsk Oblast without a fight.
The US official said the administration wanted to create more incentives for Russia's elite to push the country's leadership towards peace. The thinking is that economic deals with the US that appeal to Russia could "help convince anti-American hawks around Mr Putin that Mr Trump really does want to create a new relationship with Russia".
It is not yet known what specific agreements are under consideration. After special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner travelled to Moscow, Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said their discussions had touched on "economic issues and potential major mutually beneficial Russian-American projects".
Background:
- Russia has previously tried to entice Trump with the potential benefits of economic cooperation, discussing joint projects involving rare-earth mineral and aluminium extraction, projects in the Arctic and the involvement of US companies in selling Russian natural gas to Europe.
- Following Trump's recent proposal for an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, the Kremlin said it would also like Ukrainian strikes on its tankers in the Black Sea to stop and Western sanctions on Russian energy resources to be lifted.

Hanwha, General Atomics test runway-free drone in South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:06:21 UTC
16:06:21 KST

- Hanwha Aerospace and General Atomics flew the Mojave STOL drone from a South Korean Army airfield to a tank maneuver route and back at a Pocheon exhibition.
- The companies are developing a production version called the Gray Eagle STOL, targeting first flight in 2027 and deliveries in 2028.
Hanwha Aerospace and General Atomics Aeronautical Systems flew the Mojave short-takeoff-and-landing (STOL) drone from a South Korean Army airfield, landed it on a tank maneuver route, and flew it back again during a demonstration at the 2026 Defense Drone Technology Exhibition in Pocheon.
The maneuver was meant to show the aircraft can operate from short, unimproved sites rather than depend on a conventional runway. Mojave uses a 450-horsepower turboprop engine paired with high-lift wing systems to shorten its takeoff and landing distances, and the companies say the design supports surveillance and reconnaissance, ground attack, logistics runs and communications relay missions.
Hanwha Aerospace said in a statement that it plans to build research, development and production infrastructure for the aircraft in South Korea, with a goal of sourcing more than 70 percent of the components domestically once the program reaches mass production.
“The successful demonstration marks another step forward in our collaboration with GA-ASI and our efforts to advance next-generation unmanned capabilities in Korea,” Hanwha Aerospace said.
Mojave is General Atomics’ short-takeoff variant of its MQ-1C Gray Eagle drone, built around the same avionics and flight control systems but fitted with enlarged wings and a rugged undercarriage for rough-field operations. The company unveiled the concept in December 2021 and has since put it through a series of unusual tests: a 2023 demonstration on a dirt strip near El Mirage, California, where it took off in as little as 586 ft (179 m) and landed in 335 ft (102 m); a launch and recovery from the deck of the Royal Navy carrier HMS Prince of Wales that same November; and live-fire tests in 2024 in which the aircraft destroyed stationary targets. In November 2024, Hanwha and General Atomics launched and recovered Mojave from the South Korean Navy’s amphibious ship ROKS Dokdo off the coast of Pohang, the first time the aircraft had operated from a Korean warship.
That partnership became a formal program in October 2025, when the two companies signed an agreement at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference to jointly develop a production version of the aircraft, renamed the Gray Eagle STOL. Hanwha is investing more than 750 billion won, roughly $517 million, in Korean development and production facilities for the airframe and its engines. Under the deal, Hanwha will supply engines, landing gear, fuel systems, avionics and mission equipment, while General Atomics handles final systems integration and continues building its other Gray Eagle models in San Diego. The companies are targeting a first flight in early 2027 and initial deliveries in 2028, with South Korea’s Ministry of National Defense and the U.S. Department of War identified as the program’s first likely customers.
The production aircraft is expected to carry a payload of roughly 1.6 tons, including up to 16 Hellfire missiles, and to fly at speeds around 140 knots (161 mph) with an endurance of about 25 hours, according to General Atomics.

What's next?
The NFL has signed a multi-year deal to play two games in Australia with an option for a third, but it is not known which teams will be involved.
Los Angeles Rams coach Sean McVay hopes his NFL team never has to play in Australia again after a dismal loss to bitter rivals in Melbourne.

But the country will host more games in the future as the NFL has struck a multi-year deal with Victoria to play two matches with an option for a third.
It remains unclear whether the Rams will feature in the next edition, although the Seattle Seahawks, Las Vegas Raiders and Philadelphia Eagles are likely to take the field, as they share marketing rights with the Los Angeles team in Australia.
McVay's side also made a last-ditch journey, touching down in Melbourne about 24 hours before the game, unlike the 49ers who had been there all week interacting with fans and taking in the local atmosphere.
By game time, Los Angeles did not live up to their Super Bowl contender status at all, looking sluggish as they only scored one touchdown.

Sydneysider Jordan Mailata, who plays for Philadelphia and was part of the 2025 Super Bowl-winning team, had some advice for the next club that plays Down Under.
"I would have recommended going out early," the offensive lineman said earlier in the week.
"The flight is so long that I don't think 24 hours is enough to wash out that flight itself."

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Along the Long March route, remembrance endures amid change
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:05:38 CST
16:05:38 KST

NANNING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Every so often, Jiang Shilin leaves his home in a village in south China and walks about 10 minutes up a mountain path to visit a grave.
The 82-year-old has made the journey for as long as he can remember. Sometimes he carries a sickle to clear away the weeds. Other times, he brings a brush and paint to retrace the fading characters on the gravestone.
Seven people are buried there. Jiang never knew them. He does not even know their names.
But he knows how they died.
REMEMBRANCE
More than 90 years ago, the hills around Caiwan Village in Quanzhou County, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, became a battlefield. The seven were soldiers of the Red Army, the armed forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC).
They were taking part in the Long March, a 1934-1936 military maneuver that helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the CPC. Red Army soldiers braved raging rivers, snow-covered mountains and vast grasslands, with some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers -- a trek later described by American journalist Harrison Salisbury as "a great human epic."
In the winter of 1934 during the Long March, the Red Army fought its way across the Xiangjiang River in Guangxi and broke through the Kuomintang troops' blockade, but suffered tens of thousands of casualties in the battle.
For families such as Jiang's, however, memories of the Red Army were shaped not only by the fighting, but also by their encounters with the soldiers.
Jiang grew up hearing stories of those days from his father.
"My father told us that when the Red Army came to the village, the soldiers helped villagers carry water and do chores. The villagers, in turn, showed them the way, cooked sweet potatoes for them and brought them water," Jiang said.
Not long after the Red Army moved on, Jiang's grandfather, Jiang Zhongtai, and Jiang's father found the bodies of seven soldiers while collecting firewood on a nearby hill. They buried the bodies where they found them and marked the site with three small bricks.
Before Jiang Zhongtai died, he left his son with a request: Don't forget the grave.
For over nine decades, the family has kept that promise.
As a boy, Jiang would follow his father up the hill before festivals. He once asked why they returned year after year to honor men whose names they did not even know.
"My father said the Red Army fought for ordinary people," Jiang recalled. "We may not know who these men were, but we must not forget them."
Traces of the Battle of the Xiangjiang River can still be found along the river and in the surrounding hills. Old ferry crossings remain, along with graves of fallen Red Army soldiers. Some bear names. Others do not.
Jiang's family is not alone in caring for them. In nearby Xing'an County, generations of Li Guida's family have tended the graves of 12 Red Army soldiers.
Li, an ethnic Yao villager, said his grandfather once guided Red Army troops through the area. After the fighting, he joined other villagers in recovering and burying fallen soldiers under the cover of darkness.
"My grandfather used to say that the Red Army helped farmers have enough to eat, so we should always remember what they did for us," Li said.
Similar memories of the ties between Red Army soldiers and local residents have been passed down elsewhere along the route of the Long March. In Rucheng, central China's Hunan Province, three female soldiers are remembered for sharing their only quilt with a villager who had given them shelter. Before leaving, they cut the quilt in two and left half behind.
CHANGE
In Quanzhou, Guanyang and Xing'an counties, where the Battle of the Xiangjiang River was fought, rugged terrain and poor transport links long constrained local development. Today, roads wind through mountains that Red Army soldiers once crossed on foot, connecting once-isolated villages with the outside world.
Economic development accelerated in the decades after China launched its reform and opening-up drive in the late 1970s. By 2020, more than 100 impoverished villages across the three counties had been lifted out of poverty following years of targeted poverty alleviation efforts.
This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March and the start of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The plan calls for developing county economies with distinctive local strengths and fostering counties that excel in agriculture, industry or tourism.
Today, the three counties are developing specialty agriculture, rural tourism and traditional industries as part of their rural revitalization efforts.
Citrus farming, for example, has become an important source of income in Xing'an, where more than 40,000 farming households benefit from citrus exports. The citrus industry there generates over 1.1 billion yuan (163 million U.S. dollars) in annual output.
Near the Xiangjiang River, Guilin Jolly Cool Fruit Agricultural Products Co., Ltd. ships locally grown mandarins to markets in Central and Southeast Asia. Some local farming households now earn 50,000 to 60,000 yuan a year from growing the fruit and working at the company's factory.
"Our goal is not simply to sell the fruit, but to make sure more local people benefit from the industry," said Sun Kai, a sales manager at the company.
The area's wartime history has also become a resource for tourism and local development.
Not far from a memorial hall dedicated to the Battle of the Xiangjiang River in Quanzhou County, entrepreneur You Wei runs a study tour center that receives about 40,000 students a year. Through activities such as learning battlefield first aid, making stretchers and transporting supplies, students gain a better understanding of what happened there more than nine decades ago.
"The hardships endured by the Red Army on the Long March helped pave the way for the better lives we have today," You said. "We hope young people can also learn from their courage and draw strength from it when facing challenges of their own."
The changes are visible within Jiang's own family.
His father attended night school after the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, while the family's thatched home was eventually replaced by the two-story house where Jiang lives today. One of his granddaughters now works at a company in design and cost estimation; another is in high school and hopes to study in Beijing and pursue a career in technology.
Jiang himself has traveled across much of China and visited Vietnam, Singapore and Malaysia. Yet one journey has remained unchanged.
Around traditional festivals, Jiang still walks up the familiar mountain path, bringing offerings such as liquor, candies, biscuits, zongzi (sticky rice dumplings), and mooncakes. When fruit from the family's trees ripens, he brings plums, loquats or peaches.
These days, his children and grandchildren sometimes make the walk with him. At the grave, they bow three times.
"Thank you," Jiang silently told them. "You gave us the life we have today." ■

Column: BRICS and the evolving global financial system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:05:36 CST
16:05:36 KST

by Maya Majueran
The 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi highlighted a transformation that once seemed largely theoretical but is becoming increasingly tangible: the emergence of a more diversified global financial architecture.
For BRICS and much of the Global South, the objective is not necessarily to replace one dominant currency or financial center with another. It is to create more choices -- more currencies for trade, more payment channels, more sources of development finance, and greater protection from external financial shocks.
These are not luxury demands. They are fundamental elements of financial sovereignty and economic resilience.
Nor should the Global South's search for alternatives automatically be interpreted as hostility toward the dollar or aggression against the existing financial system. Wanting more choices does not mean wanting to destroy what already exists. It means becoming less vulnerable to any single part of it.
What is taking shape in the BRICS framework is arguably more pragmatic and potentially more consequential: a financial architecture built around choice rather than replacement.
Greater use of national currencies, interoperable cross-border payment systems, diversified development finance, and stronger alternative institutions do not require dismantling the existing financial system. They create additional pathways alongside it.
The most practical driver of this transformation is the growing push to settle more intra-BRICS trade in national currencies.
The logic is straightforward. If two countries trade extensively with each other, not every transaction necessarily needs to pass through a third currency. Direct settlement can, where sufficient liquidity and financial infrastructure exist, reduce conversion costs, diversify currency exposure, and provide additional channels for trade when traditional payment systems face disruption.
The significance lies in accumulation. One local-currency transaction will not change global finance. Millions of them might.
Financial multipolarity therefore does not require the dramatic creation of a single BRICS currency. It can emerge gradually as countries trade more frequently in national currencies, connect payment networks, and develop alternative settlement mechanisms.
The new financial architecture may not be declared into existence. It may simply be built, transaction by transaction. This is where BRICS Pay becomes significant. It is being developed as a cross-border payment framework intended to improve interoperability among national payment systems and provide businesses and consumers with additional ways to settle transactions.
Payment networks must communicate. Currencies must be exchangeable efficiently. Settlement mechanisms must function reliably. Regulatory systems must be compatible enough for transactions to move securely across borders.
Financial multipolarity may ultimately be built not through political spectacle, but through financial plumbing -- the payment networks, settlement systems, currencies, and institutions that quietly give countries more choices.
If BRICS Pay represents the payment infrastructure of financial multipolarity, the New Development Bank (NDB) represents its institutional dimension.
Created by the BRICS countries, the NDB provides an additional source of financing for infrastructure and sustainable development beyond traditional multilateral institutions.
Its founding governance structure is particularly significant. The NDB's original five BRICS members began with equal shareholding and voting power, in contrast to the weighted voting structures of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, where influence reflects shareholding and remains concentrated among major advanced economies.
But the NDB's significance lies not simply in lending money. It is also about how development finance can be structured.
Its growing emphasis on local-currency financing speaks directly to one of the Global South's most persistent vulnerabilities: earning in one currency while owing in another.
A government or business may operate a perfectly viable project and generate revenues domestically. But if its debt is denominated in dollars, a sharp appreciation of the dollar can make that debt substantially more expensive to service in local-currency terms.
U.S. monetary policy provides a clear example. When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates in response to domestic American economic conditions, the consequences can extend far beyond U.S. borders through a stronger dollar, tighter global financial conditions, capital movements, and higher debt-servicing costs for developing economies.
The Federal Reserve is understandably mandated to manage the U.S. economy. But developing countries also have a legitimate interest in reducing their vulnerability to monetary decisions over which they have no control.
With tens of billions of dollars approved for infrastructure and sustainable development, the NDB demonstrates such institutions can finance transport, clean energy, water systems and other productive investments.
Progress toward financial multipolarity may come through technical agreements: payment systems becoming more interoperable, national currencies being used more frequently in trade, alternative sources of development finance expanding, and emerging economies gaining a stronger voice in global financial governance.
Every transaction settled through an additional currency, every payment network successfully connected, and every development project financed through an alternative institution adds another pathway to the global financial system.
For the Global South, that is ultimately what financial sovereignty means: not replacing one dependency with another, but having enough credible choices that dependence itself begins to diminish.
Editor's note: Maya Majueran serves as the director of the Belt and Road Initiative Sri Lanka, an independent and pioneering organization with strong expertise in Belt and Road Initiative advice and support.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

Estonia considers delaying Rail Baltica completion to 2034
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:05:00 UTC
16:05:00 KST

Estonia’s government is considering delaying completion of its section of the Rail Baltica railway project until 2034 to make better use of European Union funding.
The issue is being considered as part of negotiations over Estonia’s 2027 state budget. The government is weighing whether to complete the Estonian section by 2030 or spread construction over a longer period, Estonian public broadcaster ERR reported.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Estonia is technically capable of completing its section by 2030, but doing so could require significantly more domestic funding.
“That could mean that we would have to invest more of our own taxpayers’ money in the project,” Michal said.
By slowing construction on some sections, Estonia could make greater use of EU funding, he said.
The EU’s current funding period runs through 2034. Michal said the project would nevertheless have to be completed by then.
The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – are currently coordinating a common position on the project. The Estonian government is expected to clarify its plans next week.
“Next Thursday, we will set out exactly what position we have taken. It will be a common position of all three Baltic states,” Michal said.
Estonia has made the most progress of the three Baltic countries in building its section of the railway, according to the prime minister. The country now faces a choice between completing construction more quickly at a higher cost or extending the timeline to make greater use of EU funding.
“We are the most advanced and can complete our section by 2030,” Michal said. “But if we build faster, we will spend more of our own money. If we build somewhat more slowly, we will be able to use significantly more EU funds.”

RAF test autonomy projects against US Air Force architecture
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:00:36 BST
16:00:36 KST

The RAF Rapid Capabilities Office is assessing whether its autonomy projects are compatible with the US Air Force’s Autonomy Government Reference Architecture, with Britain’s PYRAMID open avionics standard already shown to work with the American framework.
The work was confirmed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what steps had been taken to ensure the RAF Rapid Capabilities Office was aligned with the USAF Autonomy Government Reference Architecture, known as A-GRA.
Defence Minister Louise Sandher-Jones said: “Work is being conducted to assess the compatibility of relevant projects/activities in the RAF Rapid Capabilities Office with the USAF Autonomy Government Reference Architecture (A-GRA).”
She added: “For example, the UK’s PYRAMID Technical Standard open avionics system reference architecture developed by the Ministry of Defence has been shown to be compatible with the A-GRA.”
A-GRA is a US government-owned modular architecture intended to provide common interfaces between autonomous mission software and the aircraft or other platforms carrying it. The approach is designed to make autonomy software less dependent on a particular airframe and allow different compliant systems to be integrated more readily.
That has become increasingly important as the United States develops Collaborative Combat Aircraft and other uncrewed systems expected to operate alongside crewed combat aircraft. Rather than treating the autonomy package, mission software and aircraft as a single tightly integrated product, the architecture is intended to establish common technical boundaries between them. In principle, that makes it easier to update software, introduce new suppliers and move autonomy capabilities between compatible platforms.
The British PYRAMID standard follows a similar open-architecture philosophy. Developed for military avionics, it is intended to provide common interfaces that allow aircraft mission systems and individual applications to be introduced or replaced without redesigning an entire avionics architecture around them.
The work comes as both countries put greater emphasis on autonomous aircraft, collaborative systems and software-defined combat air capabilities, where the ability to integrate different sensors, mission applications and autonomy packages quickly is increasingly important.
Compatibility between the two architectures could also make future UK-US experimentation easier by reducing the amount of bespoke integration required when British and American systems are brought together.

Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK | Simon Jenkins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:00:11 UTC
16:00:11 KST

Monday must have been a historical first. Never before have three of the four “nations” of the United Kingdom jointly demanded freedom to vote for its dissolution. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have lost confidence in England. They declared in Cardiff that the unionist government at Westminster is “coming to an end”.
There was no such Celtic alliance against the Normans, Edward I or Cromwell. Celtic MPs have never formed a voting coalition in parliament. The Victorian Liberal party advanced “home rule for all”, but that was not independence and it got nowhere. Ireland rebelled, but it did so alone. When this eventually succeeded, Britain said good riddance, kept hold of Belfast and continued to centralise power in London.
So this is serious stuff. Yet London politics this week treated the declaration as on a par with the Oxfordshire village of Piddington voting to go it alone to ward off the possibility of asylum seekers being housed nearby.
The UK’s only serious geographical devolution came in 1999. It was half-hearted, mostly decentralising the running of the welfare state. But it surged the vote for Scottish and Welsh separatism and fed rather than abated the cause of independence. We can only imagine if ruling parties in Bavaria or Provence or Sicily had opted for independence from Germany, France or Italy – or if California said it had enough of Donald Trump’s US. The result would be political eruption.
What does the Cardiff “memorandum of understanding” actually mean? The answer is not much in detail. There was advocacy of policy collaboration, as on childcare and economic growth. There were hints of moves towards further devolution, of the sort promised by Andy Burnham. But there was no suggestion of a new Celtic state, a British Celtica. The talks seemed to concentrate on self-determination, which Burnham had described as “off limits”, at least in the case of Scotland. Yet this was a man who declared self-determination for the Falklands would be defended even at the cost of tens of millions of pounds a year.
The reality is that these three nations of the union have markedly different relations with England. Northern Ireland’s bipartisan government, a legacy of civil war and the Good Friday agreement, is clearly dysfunctional. As Donald Trump remarked last week, it really should advance toward Irish union.
As interfaith relations slowly improve, a possible majority in favour of reunion also becomes more plausible. Support for union in Northern Ireland is now around one-third, with a majority among the young. Self-determination is not in Burnham’s gift but is written into Northern Ireland’s constitution. Observers accept that it must and will happen one day.
Wales may also have a majority of its under-35s in favour of independence. But only a bare Welsh majority voted for even mild devolution in 1997 and support for independence hovers at 32%. The poor performance of the Welsh health and education services makes self-government ever more alarming, and the generosity of the London Exchequer ever more essential. Perhaps the novelty of the new Plaid Cymru government can transform things, but Welsh independence is at best a distant fantasy.
This leaves Scotland. Here independence is an active issue. The population of 5.5 million puts the country in the 5-10 million band of Europe’s medium-sized states, such as Denmark, Norway, Finland, Austria and Switzerland. “Small is beautiful” appears to suit Europe’s distinctive welfare economies and keeps them ahead of their larger neighbours.
Scottish unionists keep pointing to Scotland’s £25bn fiscal deficit, financed by London’s Treasury and sustaining the country’s struggling health service. But independence is a dynamic not static state. In 1922 Ireland was among the poorest countries in Europe, far behind Scotland. Its economic self-sufficiency seemed hopeless, and for some 30 years it was indeed in desperate straits. Yet by the 1990s Irish membership of the EU and the adoption of a fierce fiscal autonomy had utterly transformed it into the celebrated “Celtic Tiger”. From limping behind Scotland and other poorer European regions, Dublin raced ahead. It has become one of Europe’s richest nations per capita, albeit partly thanks to its status as a base for corporate tax avoidance.
Ireland’s burst of economic vitality in the late 20th century could never have taken place had it remained an adjunct of Britain. Income per head is now ahead of Scotland’s, having once lagged far behind. It grew between 2012 and 2022 by 9% on average, against Scotland’s 1%. Whether Ireland is richer than Denmark is much debated, but the performance of an autonomous Ireland cannot be gainsaid. It is a lighthouse for the macro-economics of smallness.
There is every reason why Scotland could feel held back by longstanding English dominance. Its economy, like the rest of Britain’s, has always been down the queue from London and the south-east. It has long felt cheated of its maritime oil and gas reserves. Trade has been crippled by Brexit. Unionists argue that the Barnett formula subsidy of £50bn a year is fair compensation. But Ireland’s experience suggests that dependence on foreign subsidy is a curse, not a blessing. The most glaring comparative statistic is that health outcomes in both Ireland and Denmark are now well ahead of Scotland’s. The scale of Glasgow’s drug deaths are a horror story.
British loyalist though I may be, if I were a Scot I would have no hesitation. This is a real nation, and has been throughout history. Scotland has a personality and a culture recognised worldwide. Its capital, Edinburgh, is among Europe’s finest cities. Its “Silicon Glen” should be leading Europe’s AI revolution. Tourism is an obvious attraction. That the country should stumble behind its Nordic neighbours is absurd.
Scotland would have a tough transition to self-reliance, as did Ireland. But experience everywhere suggests that small autonomous democracies fare well, witness other relative newcomers such as Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia and the Baltics. Their governments can concentrate on their own priorities and promote their own virtues.
An independent Scotland would be bespoke. It could retain its royal figurehead and Commonwealth membership. It could even honour a “united kingdom” and the king could stay in Balmoral. Relations with other states, EU and non-EU, would be complicated, as they are at borders across the continent. That is for diplomacy to resolve. The issue is self-determination, not convenience.
Burnham is the first British prime minister to appear sincere in decentralising political power. How far he understands its significance is moot. His beloved “metro mayors” are accountable regionally, not representatives of truly local loyalties. They appear as his agents, enacting his policies and enforcing his planning quotas on subordinate councils. He has shown he will stamp the Piddingtons of England into the ground.
That is why Burnham should welcome any Scottish desire for “independence”. It would be the most exciting constitutional reform of the UK in centuries and one that, on current figures, would save the Treasury around £25bn a year – the cost of the Scottish fiscal deficit. It would also release the Tartan Tiger.
- 
  Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

====================================================================================================

Rachel Griffiths to return to Aussie stages for first time in 25 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Rachel Griffiths returns to Australian stage after 25 years for Clarice Beckett play
Rachel Griffiths will return to the Australian stage for the first time in 25 years in a new play about artist Clarice Beckett.
Next year, the Total Control and Muriel's Wedding actor will star as the artist, considered a visionary of Australian modernism, in the play Clarice at Melbourne Theatre Company (MTC).
It's Griffiths's first stage role since 2012, when she made her Broadway debut in the play Other Desert Cities. At home, her last stage role was in the modern classic Proof at MTC in 2002.
"When Other Desert Cities finished, I swore I'd never do theatre again," Griffiths says.
For the play's six-month run, Griffith juggled her emotionally charged role with raising her three kids.
Now they are mostly grown, she feels ready to return to the stage, to tell the kind of distinctly Australian story that motivated her to move home after 20 years in the US.
"This is a snapshot of 30s Melbourne and how hard it was for women artists of the time to practise and be collected," she says.
Still, she admits to finding making theatre exhausting, which has kept her away from the stage.
"I haven't come across something I've wanted to bleed for until now," she says.
"The pull for me is the times we live in. There's a desperate desire to connect in a world where we are increasingly alone on our own screens.
"This will be a chance to collectively share something very tender, ephemeral and human — something only theatre can do."
But it's not a case of Griffiths being convinced to return to theatre. It was the actor who brought Clarice — by actor-turned-writer-director Trudy Hellier (Round the Twist) — to MTC's artistic director Anne-Louise Sarks.
Originally pitched as a movie, Griffiths had a sense the story could be "sublime" for a theatre audience that could be "perhaps more abstract and ephemeral than a film".
For Sarks, it was a no-brainer.
"[I love] telling stories about who we are and our history and shining a light particularly on brilliant women and stories audiences may know but not as deeply as they could," she says.
Clarice is one of 11 plays in MTC's 2027 season, which also includes a new Indigenous-led adaptation of sci-fi classic The War of the Worlds and a play exploring how then-prime minister Bob Hawke's reaction to a "rebel" cricket tour to South Africa was one of the catalysts for greater sanctions against the apartheid regime.
An overlooked artist
Beckett all but disappeared from Australian art history after her death in 1935, at the age of 48.
For decades, almost 2,000 of her works were stored — and neglected — in an open-sided farm shed near Benalla in rural Victoria before they were uncovered by curator and art historian Rosalind Hollinrake in 1970. Only 359 were salvageable.
In recent years, Beckett has been celebrated with retrospectives in Geelong in 2023 and Adelaide in 2021. A touring exhibition of Beckett works collected by the National Gallery of Australia opens in Goulburn on September 25.
She's an artist Griffiths has long been interested in. In 2022, she hosted an episode of ABC TV's Great Southern Landscapes where she tried to find the exact spot from which the artist painted Melbourne's Luna Park.
Beckett painted Luna Park when it was closed due to the Spanish flu pandemic.
The painting gained greater resonance for Griffiths over the course of the COVID-19 pandemic.
"It's magnificent," she says. "I walked past it every day during our lockdowns."
One of the starting points for bringing Beckett's story to the stage was the spate of interactive digital exhibitions coming to Australia, featuring artworks by the likes of Frida Kahlo, Claude Monet and Vincent van Gogh.
"They offered an insight into art through accessible and immersive experiences," Griffiths says.
"At the end of them though, I didn't really come out understanding the process of the artists.
"With Clarice, we have a chance to do both."
It's also an opportunity to challenge the idea "dying infamous or unrecognised is a tragedy", she says.
Instead, she thinks there's much we can learn from the artist about how to connect with the world around us.
"Clarice died unknown but she got to sit and observe nature every day she practised her craft," Griffiths says. "Her life was lived on her terms."
Griffiths is also interested in Hollinrake's role ensuring Beckett's place in the canon.
"It speaks to the theme of women hunting history to make sure great women are not forgotten," she says.
New Australian writing
MTC's 2027 season features six new Australian works, including Clarice; the cricket play, titled Rebels; and a new play by Andrew Bovell (Lantana) about the loved ones of people with substance use disorders.
Phar Lap: The Electro-Swing Musical, which premiered at Hayes Theatre in Sydney in 2025, also transfers to MTC as part of a national tour.
The focus on new Australian work is deliberate.
"I wanted to continue the mission to put new work at the centre of everything we do," Sarks says.
Kate Mulvany (My Brilliant Career) has drawn upon her experience of severe scoliosis (a sideways curvature of the spine) and related chronic pain to adapt William Shakespeare's Richard III as a one-woman show.
"To play multiple characters or tell a whole story alone on stage, you have to employ very clever, quite virtuosic theatre-making techniques," Sarks says.
"The audience is almost constantly aware they are in a theatre being told a story … It couldn't be television. It's capital-T theatre."
Two new Australian works are by Indigenous writers: road-trip comedy Dirty Diamonds by Abbie-lee Lewis, a co-production with Belvoir in Sydney, starring Lila McGuire and Ruby Henaway; and a new War of the Worlds by Claire G Coleman.
Researching the story while she was living in London before the pandemic, Sarks learned English writer HG Wells was partly inspired by the Black War between settlers and Indigenous people in Tasmania, which ran from 1824 to 1831.
Sarks recalls thinking: "This is a story about us and we need to own that."
Reading Coleman's speculative fiction novel Terra Nullius, which draws on Australia's colonial history, Sarks decided she might be the right person to make a new Australian version of The War of the Worlds.
After its Melbourne season, Coleman's The War of the Worlds is expected to tour regional Victoria.
"It's incredibly exciting to be able to champion First Nations work in the way that we are, and to place these stories front and centre in the season," Sarks says.
It's also a kind of course correction, the artistic director boasting the company has presented and collaborated on more work by Indigenous artists since she joined in 2021 than the 70 years prior.
"The increase is enormous, but it's vital if we want to talk about understanding who we are and our history," Sarks says.
"[We] learn and benefit so much from the artistry and the making practices of these brilliant artists."
Unexpected dangers
Dirty Diamonds and Phar Lap aren't the only shows that will see MTC collaborate with other companies in 2027.
Stereophonic by David Adjmi is a co-production with Belvoir and Queensland Theatre Company (QTC), while John Proctor is the Villain by Kimberly Belflower is a co-production with Sydney Theatre Company (STC).
Both are buzzy American plays making their Australian debuts.
"It's wonderful for us to be able to hold up the quality of our new work next to these international works and for audiences to be able to see and appreciate both," Sarks says.
The artistic director praises how companies working together increases how many people get to see a show, which becomes "richer, deeper and stronger over time" and keeps cast and crew employed for sustained periods.
"It is something companies are needing to do more," Sarks says. "It has really helped us stay large in our season, because we really want to be able to make a very ambitious big offer for audiences."
But Sarks is frank about the potential consequences of that increased collaboration.
"The danger is that over time there will be fewer shows," she says.
"I want us to be cautious as an industry and sure that we are still providing opportunities for artists — and that's why new work development is still at the core of everything we do."
It's a mission that has been successful this year, with the three Australian shows that opened the season — the return of the My Brilliant Career musical, Jean Tong's Do Not Pass Go, and Dennis McIntosh's West Gate, about the 1970 bridge disaster — selling out in their final weeks.
"They're works we created and developed here and audiences were hungry for them," Sarks says.
"That gives me so much hope for the future of Australian storytelling and theatre."
