'Software issue to blame' for UK flight disruption
Newsflash: British air traffic control operator Nats has reveale that the outage which affected hundreds of thousands of passengers last week was due to a software defect.
“This was a software issue in a specific part of our flight data system, that we have traced to a small subsection of coding.
The issue has been identified and mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety tested and deployed.”
The Financial Times reported last week that four people briefed on the incident claimed that the shutdown was caused by a flight plan submitted by a UK military aircraft.
NATS, though, is blaming “a software defect” in a small part of the National Airspace System (NAS), which is used to manage of UK airspace.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers were caught up in the disruption which began on Tuesday 8 September.
The software in question allocates codes to individual aircraft when manual requests are made; these are usually allocated automatically. These codes are used to identify flights on radar when they are airborne.
This glitch led to restrictions being put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety. Although the software issue only affected flights in the London Area Control centre – higher level flights operating mainly above 24,500ft – the restrictions had to be placed across the UK so that the NAS could be restarted and flight data reloaded, it says.
A software defect in part of the UK’s air traffic control system corrupted flight data “in the space of a millisecond”, leading to a six-hour outage and mass airline cancellations and delays across the UK last week, National Air Traffic Services has said.
But ministers said the Nats report into the incident still left questions unanswered, saying they needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”.
According to the report, the error first occurred at 10am and was notified to engineers who investigated – but the system appeared to be working again, until 12.30pm when a repeat occurred and a major incident was declared.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said the industry regulator the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) would now “check their findings” and investigate Nats’ plans.
The London stock market has recorded its biggest one-day drop since early July.
Japan’s central bank has increased interest rates to a fresh 31-year high as it attempts to combat global inflation linked to the war in Iran.
The Bank of Japan (BoJ) voted to raise its target interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level since 1995.
The move meant the BoJ joined the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in tightening monetary policy this month, as central banks attempt to curb the impact of rising prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
Retail sales across Great Britain unexpectedly rose last month, the latest economic indicator to defy gloomy forecasts as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to present next month’s budget.
Newsflash: German carmaker Volkswagen has slashed its outlook, and warned that it faces a €10bn hit due to challenges at its Porsche division and in China, and the cost of job cuts.
Volkswagen has cut its forecast for Operating Return on Sales to ‘up to 1%’, down from a previous forecast 4.0 to 5.5%.
It is taking a €6bn non-cash impairment against goodwill allocated to Porsche.
Additional restructuring expenses from the expansion of early retirement schemes, the planned sale of its Osnabrück site, and “the development in the Chinese automotive market” will knock another €2bn off profits.
The news came before the Frankfurt market closed, so there was time for Volkswagen’s shares to fall by 5.5%.
Back in the financial markets, UK and US government debt is continuing to sell off.
This has pushed the yield, or interest rate, on US two-year Treasury yields up to 4.7475%, the highest since July 2024. That’s a rise of 5.5 basis points (0.055 of a percentage point).
UK two-year gilts are selling off faster – pushing up their yield by 13 basis points (a rather chunky move), to 4.85%.
Traders may be disappointed that the early fall in the oil price has now all-but reversed, following reports that Saudi Aramco told at least two oil refining customers in Europe that they will be allocated no crude next month.
Premium sportswear brand On has signed a sponsorship deal with Kylian Mbappé- thereby ending the French sensation’s long-standing partnership with Nike - in a bid to break into the football market, my colleague Amee Joshi writes.
The Swiss company, founded in 2010 by ex-McKinsey consultants David Allemann and Caspar Coppetti, alongside world champion triathlete Olivier Bernhard, became known for its ‘Cloutec’ technology which Bernhard described as imitating the feeling of “running on clouds”.
Losing Mbappé, the star footballer many believe is poised to win this year’s Ballon D’or, only adds to Nike’s growing list of woes. Over the last five years, the sportswear giant’s shares have fallen by 75%, cast down by decreasing revenues in the lucrative Chinese market. Their persistent struggles culminated in last week’s announcement that it will crash out of the S&P 100.
Part of Nike’s decline has been attributed to their loss of focus on innovation, allowing smaller rivals, like On and Hoka, to attract top athletes and celebrities (like world champion marathon runner Hellen Obiri and actress Zendaya), and grow their global market share.
The “High Level Timeline” into the software glitch on 8 September shows there was a gap of almost two and a half hours before the initial problem, and the start of a major incident.
Initially, air traffic controllers and system engineers receive a system error notification at 10.02am that morning, related to the squawk code request explained in our earlier post.
That notification swiftly vanished, though, suggesting the system had recovered.
Between 10.06am and 12.32pm, health checks were carried out on infrastructure with no evidence found of any hardware fault.
But then at 12.32pm, the link between the London Area Control (LAC) system and the NAS was automatically dropped and the LAC system enters “a period of link instability”.
At 12.45pm, flight restrictions were imposed, and departures from UK airfields were temporarily stopped, so that air traffic controllers could operate safely under fallback arrangements.
Further restrictions were imposed through the day, before all airspace restrictions were lifted at 7.30pm.
Today’s report from Nats is only the provisional probe into this month’s disruption – the full inquiry will take longer.
Nats CEO Martin Wolfe says:
Our full investigation into the circumstances is under way and our major incident report will be completed within 60 days. At this early stage, however, I can confirm that this incident is not related to either the 2023 NATS FPRSA system failure or the radar issue in July last year.
I can also confirm that it was a software issue and not caused by any incorrect actions by either military or civil operators.
The software error which brought UK airspace to a standstill was due to a problem handling squawk codes - an identification code transmitted (squawked) by the aircraft during flight.
Nats’s report explains that the incident was triggered by a valid manual request for a squawk code.
While this request was being processed, the National Airspace System received a message for a higher priority activity to be undertaken which resulted in the squawk code allocation being paused while the system processed the higher priority message.
So far, so normal. But, when the processing of the squawk allocation request resumed, the software defect meant it did not resume correctly and the resulting output was corrupted.
Nats says there was a very narrow window for things to go wrong in:
The defect existed in a specific subsection of code within a software module, with an exposure window estimated as approximately one millisecond.
For the fault to occur, a higher-priority request had to arrive during that exact millisecond while the original request was part-way through updating a value.
Had the higher-priority request arrived even one millisecond earlier or later, the update would have completed normally.
The full scale of disruption will take time to confirm; but at this stage more than two thousand flights were delayed, cancelled or diverted, Nats says.
The air traffic controller adds that it handled some 1,800 fewer flights than forecast over the course of the day but we appreciate that does not reflect the full scale of the disruption experienced.

Russia opened polling stations in its Far East early Friday, launching a three-day parliamentary election that is expected to hand President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party another sweeping victory.
The vote is Russia’s first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. With meaningful opposition largely excluded, the election is less a contest for power than a Kremlin test of public support for Putin and his war.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Only parties broadly aligned with the Kremlin and its policies are allowed to compete. Moscow has also organized voting in occupied Ukrainian territories, a move condemned by Ukraine and Western governments.
The 450 seats in Russia’s State Duma, the lower house of parliament, are up for election. Voting will continue until Sunday evening, with Russia’s Pacific regions of Kamchatka and Chukotka among the first to cast ballots.
United Russia dominates Russian politics and is widely expected to retain control of the Duma. It faces four other parliamentary parties – the Communist Party, LDPR, A Just Russia and New People – all of which support most of Putin’s policies.
Anti-war parties and opposition figures have been pushed out of the political system. The liberal Yabloko party was barred from competing shortly before the election, while one of its prominent figures, Lev Shlosberg, has been imprisoned after criticizing the war.
Tusk: Intelligence Warns Russia Plans ‘Accidental’ Hybrid Strikes Against Ukraine’s Allies
The Kremlin is closely watching how the war affects public sentiment, particularly as Ukrainian strikes have reached areas far from the battlefield and Russia faces mounting economic and military costs.
Putin, who has ruled Russia since 1999, urged Russians to vote, saying participation would demonstrate that millions of people support Russian troops and oppose efforts to weaken the country.
Opposition sidelined
With protests and public criticism of the war heavily restricted, the election offers few avenues for Russians to openly challenge the Kremlin.
Much of Russia’s organized opposition has been driven into exile or imprisoned. Opposition leader Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
Russia’s exiled opposition has urged anti-Kremlin voters to participate and vote against United Russia. Navalny’s widow, Yulia Navalnaya, has called on anti-war Russians to coordinate their voting at noon Sunday.
Yabloko has taken a different position, arguing that participating would legitimize a political system it considers controlled by the Kremlin.
The election could also provide clues about public reaction to the possibility of further military mobilization.
Putin ordered a call-up of 300,000 reservists in September 2022, triggering widespread protests and an exodus of draft-age men from Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused the Kremlin of preparing another mobilization campaign this autumn. Putin has denied the claim.

Russia seizes control of Nestlé subsidiaries

Russia seizes control of Nestlé subsidiaries
Swiss food giant Nestlé is losing control of part of its Russian business. Russian president Vladimir Putin has placed two Nestlé companies under Russian control.
A decree issued on Thursday stated that shares in Nestlé Russia and Nestlé Kuban would now be managed by the Russian firm LEV Management. The presidential order also applies to French supermarket chain Auchan.
Although Nestlé remains the owner of its subsidiaries, it cannot make decisions regarding these holdings for the time being.
+ Russian supermarket shelves ‘full of Nestlé products’
When asked by the AWP news agency, a Nestlé spokesperson was initially unable to provide any details on the exact consequences.
In August, the Russian company KS Logistika had called on Putin to place five Russian Nestlé subsidiaries under external administration. At the time, Nestlé stated that it had not been contacted by state authorities.
The company added that a withdrawal from Russia was not on the cards.
Nestlé generates around 2% of its group turnover in Russia. The company operates six production sites in Russia, where it manufactures, amongst other things, coffee, confectionery, baby food and pet food.
More
Swiss pharma exports to Russia continue despite war
Following Russia’s military invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Nestlé decided not to completely cease its operations in Russia, despite criticism. The group justified this at the time by stating that, as a food manufacturer, it wished to continue supplying the population with essential foodstuffs, even in conflict regions.
Danone and Carlsberg as role models
Russia has been using the instrument of temporary administration since 2023 to take control of foreign companies’ assets. Nestlé is by no means an isolated case.
For instance, the French food group Danone lost control of its Russian operations as early as 2023. Danone eventually sold them in 2024 for around 180 million euros and recorded a total loss of 1.2 billion euros.
The Danish brewing group Carlsberg faced a similar fate. Its Russian operations were also placed under Russian state administration in 2023. At the end of 2024, Carlsberg completed its withdrawal through a management buy-out worth 320 million dollars. The Dutch brewer Heineken, for its part, sold its Russian subsidiary for the symbolic price of one euro and recorded a total loss of 300 million euros.

Lithuania’s foreign minister, currently on a visit to the US, said Thursday that he received assurances from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that a reduction in the number of American troops stationed in Lithuania will not last long.
Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys made the comments after meeting with Rubio in Washington.
“We received assurances that this gap, when we have a reduction in US troops, will not last long,” Budrys said in comments distributed by the Foreign Ministry in response to questions from LRT. “All decisions are being coordinated with the Department of War [Department of Defense], the Pentagon, but we expect to hear about them in the near future.”
He later said the decision may come within days.
“We’re probably talking about days, perhaps the coming weeks; I won’t speculate – they [the US] will make the announcement, but work is proceeding at a rapid pace,” Budrys said on the LRT TV programme Topic of the Day (Dienos tema).
Security issues dominated the meeting, Budrys said, but the two officials also discussed the broader regional situation and the war in Ukraine.
“We talked about the situation in the region, about US efforts to achieve peace in the war against Ukraine, and about Russia’s intentions and capabilities in the near future,” he said.
They also discussed “hybrid” and “kinetic” attacks and incidents in the region, as well as the conditions Lithuania has provided for US troops and decisions expected about their future deployment, Budrys said.
The United States is currently reviewing its military presence in Europe. More than 1,000 American troops completed a rotation in Lithuania this summer. While some US personnel remained in the country, Lithuania has not received a clear decision on the arrival of a new rotation.
The US has regularly deployed battalion-sized units to Lithuania since 2019. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Washington shifted its military presence in Lithuania to continuous rotational deployments.
The reinforced US battalions typically include 1,000 or more troops along with various types of combat equipment.
Lithuania has said it is prepared to host as many as 1,500 Americans.
Critical minerals deal
During the meeting, Budrys and Rubio signed a bilateral framework agreement on cooperation in the field of critical minerals.
“We already hold a huge share of the US market for femtosecond lasers, and we can expand it significantly. And what Secretary Rubio described today – that Lithuania is a ‘photon superpower’ – is something we could be and must be. And this is where we will play a major role in future technological developments in the United States,” said Budrys in a video comment released by the Foreign Ministry.
According to the ministry, the agreement aims to strengthen cooperation between the two countries by ensuring a secure and diversified supply of critical raw materials, promoting investment in their extraction and processing, increasing the resilience of supply chains and reducing strategic dependencies.
Lithuania intends to contribute to the agreement’s objectives by leveraging its expertise in high-tech manufacturing, advanced technologies, the processing of critical materials and logistics, according to the ministry.

RSHP and ERRE Selected to Design New Valencia Central Station in Spain

15:30:00 KST

The team led by engineering and technology group Sener, in collaboration with UK-based architecture practice RSHP and Valencia-based ERRE, has been selected to design the new Valencia Central Station in Spain. The proposal was chosen by Adif Alta Velocidad's Evaluation Committee following a competition for a new intermodal rail hub integrating high-speed, commuter, metro, tram, bus, taxi, and active mobility connections. The new infrastructure will be coordinated with the planned Central Park, the Access Canal project, and the future through tunnel. The scope also includes the refurbishment of the historic Valencia Nord Station, a designated Site of Cultural Interest, while preserving its architectural and urban heritage.
The new station is planned as an underground infrastructure connecting the Central Station with Valencia Nord Station and the future Central Park. A landscape axis will link these areas through pedestrian routes and cycle lanes, converging at a proposed Station Square. The railway infrastructure will also shift from the existing terminus configuration to through services, allowing trains to travel across Valencia from north to south without reversing direction.
According to the design team, the proposal is structured around five principles: railway functionality, urban integration, architectural identity, constructability, and operational safety. The scheme incorporates a modular construction system with a high degree of prefabrication and is designed to maintain railway operations throughout construction. In relation to Valencia Nord Station, the proposal will preserve the historic building's existing façades while integrating the new infrastructure into the surrounding urban space.

The project will involve the functional studies and design work for relocating the station and its tracks underground, as well as developing entrances, concourses, waiting areas, platforms, retail spaces, and an underground car park. The design also brings natural light and fresh air into the underground station, with daylight reaching the platforms and open spaces visually connecting the different levels. The proposal incorporates measures to reduce reliance on energy-intensive mechanical systems and improve material efficiency, with the aim of reducing the station's carbon footprint.

US approves $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia
The United States on Thursday said it had approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth warplanes to Saudi Arabia. Israel has previously voiced concerns about Riyadh buying F-35s, despite a push to normalise relations.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The United States has approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth warplanes to Saudi Arabia, the State Department said Thursday, the kingdom's latest major arms purchase since the start of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia has long sought to buy F-35s, but officials from Israel – currently the only country in the Middle East to operate the jets – have voiced concern about their sale to Riyadh despite a push for the kingdom to normalise relations.
Read moreTrump says Saudi nuclear deal contingent on Riyadh normalising relations with Israel
"The proposed sale will improve Saudi Arabia's capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defence, and improving interoperability with US forces," the State Department said in a statement.
It "will also augment Saudi Arabia's operational aircraft and enhance its air-to-air, and air-to-ground self-defence capability", the statement said.
The Saudi embassy in Washington praised the transaction, saying it "reflects the strength and enduring nature" of the relationship with the United States.
It added that the security cooperation between the two countries "has contributed to regional stability, strengthened our collective defence capabilities, and advanced our shared security interests".
Saudi Arabia has been repeatedly targeted with drone and missile strikes by Tehran's forces since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February, and has also been hit by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Read moreSaudi Arabia accuses Houthis of targeting Mecca, calls it a 'red line'
Yemen's civil war had been dormant for years, but fighting between Houthis and the internationally recognised, Riyadh-backed government reignited in July, with the rebels declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
Washington has not directly entered the conflict, but a US official said earlier this week that an American military task force is working to enhance intelligence sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces.
Congressional approval pending
The State Department has notified Congress about the proposed sale, which would require the approval of US lawmakers. It did not provide a time frame for the delivery of the jets.
The F-35 sale "will not alter the military balance in the region", the State Department said, in keeping with longstanding US policy that Israel must have a military edge over potential regional adversaries.
The United States has so far only allowed the sales of F-35s to its closest allies, including a number of European NATO allies and Israel.
Washington kicked NATO member Turkey out of the F-35 programme in 2019 because Ankara's purchase of a Russian air defence system sparked fears that Moscow could acquire the plane's technology.
Billions in arms sales
Washington also has concerns about potential Chinese espionage related to the jets.
The New York Times reported this week that US intelligence analysts have raised the possibility that Beijing could acquire F-35 technology through its partnerships with Riyadh.
US Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democratic member of the House Intelligence Committee, expressed opposition to the sale on those grounds.
It should not go ahead "when our own intelligence community is warning that it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party", Krishnamoorthi said in a statement.
The F-35 sale is the latest in a series of major arms buys by Saudi Arabia this year.
The State Department announced the approval of a $5 billion sale of more than 10,000 bombs – including highly destructive 2,000-pound weapons – to Riyadh earlier in September.
Washington also signed off on the sale of 60 tank engines and related equipment to Saudi Arabia at a cost of $750 million this month, and a $1.96 billion deal in July for the kingdom to buy guidance sections that can convert rockets into precision weapons.

Before the skyscrapers: Dubai’s oldest building, Al Fahidi Fort, set to reopen with new museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:26:46 UTC
15:26:46 KST

After a five-year closure for an extensive restoration project, the historic Al Fahidi Fort in Old Dubai will welcome back visitors in the ‘coming weeks or months’.
Think of Dubai and many people will imagine a metropolis of gleaming skyscrapers, mega shopping malls, palm-shaped islands and some of the world’s top luxury hotel and hospitality brands.
But away from all the glitz and glamour, which often dominate the headlines, there’s another side to the city that doesn’t always get the attention it deserves: Old Dubai, and in particular the historic Al Fahidi area.
Located on the southern side of the Creek, in this neighbourhood you’ll find traditional houses, cultural attractions, as well as Al Fahidi Fort, Dubai’s oldest standing building at more than 230 years old.
Originally built as a defensive stronghold around 1787, over the centuries the fort has also been a residence for the ruler, a centre of governance and administration, and a prison before it became Dubai’s first museum in 1971, the same year that the United Arab Emirates was formed.
‘A witness to Dubai’s history’
Al Fahidi Fort has been closed since 2021 as part of an extensive restoration project. Five years later, it is set to welcome back visitors “in the coming weeks or months”, according to Ayisha Khansaheb, Director of Al Fahidi Fort and Specialised Museums at the Dubai Culture & Arts Authority.
Speaking to Euronews Travel at Arabian Travel Market, Khansaheb believes the contemporary museum experience is going to be a “gateway into the story of Dubai itself” and a great starting place for visitors to truly understand the history of the city.
For a destination that’s known for its futuristic skylines and modern infrastructure, Dubai’s cultural heritage has sometimes been overlooked as a key attraction for international visitors. However, the reopening of the fort marks a new chapter in the city’s story.
“I think cultural heritage is important as an ecosystem for cultural tourism, but also for residents, for locals, and for schools to educate the students on the cultural history and heritage of the city itself,” said Khansaheb.
“I think we need to have offerings for everyone and I think this is something that you've been seeing more of in Dubai and in the wider region as well. It addresses a growing need to emphasise that there is a soul, there is a culture, and there is history here.”
What can visitors see at Al Fahidi Fort?
The revitalised museum combines the historic architecture of the fort with artefacts, archival material, and interactive technology to tell the story of the building and its place in Dubai’s development.
Visitors begin their experience in a new underground extension, where contemporary galleries explore themes including defence, leadership and craftsmanship, before moving into the historic fort itself.
Among the highlights is “The Vault”, a light and sound experience that follows the evolution of Dubai’s defence capabilities.
Another gallery, “A Landmark Across the Ages”, explores the fort’s changing role over more than 230 years, while visitors can also see a major collection of Islamic arms and armour. Interactive learning experiences designed for children have also been incorporated into the museum.
But one of the most important exhibits is the fort itself, where visitors can walk through its historic walls and explore its watchtowers, gates and courtyard. “You experience history through architecture,” Khansaheb said.

The “New Services Opportunities for MSMEs by Digital Empowerment” seminar took place Thursday. Academics from universities in Taiwan and Geneva spoke at the event, while WTO delegates from Thailand, Peru, Paraguay, Mexico, Poland, Lithuania, Australia, and the EU were present in the audience.
The speakers and the public exchanged views about the problems of small enterprises, the ministry said. They called on the WTO to strengthen its support for the businesses, assisting them to join international supply chains and develop even more thorough services.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Institute for Information Industry said on Tuesday that it has developed a digital notebook for long-term care.
Seniors can misplace their medical instructions when traveling, making it difficult for caretakers to keep track. The institute's AI department developed the service to streamline treatment records, per a press release.
The logbook exports data to the social media app Line. It lists data such as blood pressure and temperature, allowing the patient’s family members to compare and identify issues.
The institute spoke with NCKU physician Yang Yi-ching (楊宜青) about how to describe conditions such as hypertension. His input has made health issues easier to understand.
Users can upload photos for AI recognition instead of handwriting, freeing up time. The system can automatically generate a one-page summary during hospital visits, giving nurses a quick overview.
The institute has tested the program at many nursing homes. It collected user feedback from nurses, patients, and family members to improve accessibility.

Japan raises interest rate to 31-year high over inflation risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:23:52 UTC
15:23:52 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The Bank of Japan raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 1.25% on Friday, its highest level since 1995, citing the risk of inflation exceeding its target.
The hike, widely expected by economists, accelerated the central bank’s monetary policy normalization cycle. It came three months after the previous increase, compared with the six-month interval preceding that move.
The decision was approved by a 7-2 majority, with board members Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato voting to keep the rate unchanged.
The central bank said it decided to tighten policy because of the risk that inflation could deviate upward beyond its 2% target.
It added that it aims to stabilize underlying inflation at around 2%, preventing price increases from overshooting the target and subsequently hurting the Japanese economy.
The decision came as Japan grapples with persistent price pressures and a weak yen.
Japan’s annual consumer inflation rate stood at 1.9% in August, while core inflation, which excludes fresh food prices, eased to 1.7% from 1.8% in July.
Asada argued that the economy might not be sufficiently strong because core inflation remained below the central bank’s target, while Sato said economic activity and price developments had not accelerated substantially compared with earlier conditions.
The Japanese yen weakened following the decision, with the dollar gaining about 0.5% to trade above 156.6 yen. The yield on Japan’s benchmark 10-year government bond fell around 5 basis points to approximately 2.95%.
The hike extended the bank's shift away from years of ultra-loose monetary policy, which began when the bank ended its negative interest-rate policy in March 2024.

====================================================================================================

Mobilization 2.0: Is it inevitable, and what can Putin actually achieve?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:23:45 UTC
15:23:45 KST

Rumors are spreading across Russia that a new wave of mobilization will begin sometime after the State Duma elections conclude on Sept. 20. There is no shortage of cause for such speculation: regions are holding mobilization exercises, employers are being reminded of their obligations regarding military registration of employees, and an electronic register of people who can legally be called up for military service has been compiled. The developments come at the same time the recruitment of voluntary contract soldiers is becoming increasingly expensive. Even if mobilization does take place, however, it is unlikely to significantly alter the situation on the battlefield in Donbas in the near term or to resolve Russia’s financial problems — particularly given that mobilization itself would require substantial funding.
New recruits are getting more expensive
The debate over a new mobilization comes down to a simple question: does the Russian army actually lack manpower? Different methods of counting produce very different estimates of both the potential number of new soldiers and they extent to which they would actually expand the armed forces rather than simply replacing losses.
According to calculations by IStories based on federal budget expenditures for one-time enlistment bonuses, 71,200 people signed contracts with Russia’s Defense Ministry in the first quarter of 2026 and another 60,100 in the second. That puts the six-month total at 131,300 recruits, or an average of about 720 a day. This is almost the same as in the first half of 2025 (127,500), but it is roughly 20% below the 2024 figure. After falling in late 2025 and early 2026, the flow of contract recruits therefore appears to have stabilized.
However, economist Janis Kluge, who tracks regional budget spending, arrived at significantly higher figures: around 79,000 new contract soldiers in the first quarter of 2026 and about 93,000 in the second, or roughly 172,000 over six months — around 1,000 new contract soldiers a day in the second quarter. Deputy Security Council Chairman Dmitry Medvedev, meanwhile, cited an even higher figure: more than 200,000 contracts in the first half of the year.
The discrepancy between official statements and budget-based estimates has of course been seen before, and it is true that federal data on one-time payments probably do not capture the full scale of recruitment. For the calculations that follow, it therefore makes more sense to use a range rather than a single precise figure: roughly 700–1,000 new contract soldiers a day, or 20,000–30,000 a month.
The current rate of recruitment into the Russian armed forces is between 20,000 and 30,000 people a month
New calculations by Kluge published in September confirm this general estimate. According to regional budget data, approximately 234,000 contracts had been signed by the end of August 2026, compared with 260,000 over the same period in 2025. In August, the recruitment rate remained at around 1,000 people a day — a figure that was about 20% lower than a year earlier, despite higher payments and an increase in coercive recruitment.
Actual recruitment rates are probably still below the target set for regional authorities. As the Financial Times reported, the regions have been tasked with securing 409,000 new contracts by the end of 2026. Meeting that target would require an average of about 34,000 new contract soldiers a month, or 1,120 a day.
By itself, the current pace of recruitment is no longer enough to sustain the growth in the size of the Russian armed forces that was seen during the first years of the full-scale war. As military analysts Michael Kofman and Greg Wehner note, in 2023 the Russian military managed to replace its losses while significantly expanding its force, forming two new combined-arms armies, two motor-rifle divisions, and 27 new brigades and regiments. However, in 2024 the growth slowed, and by 2025 it had virtually stopped.
In September and December 2025, Vladimir Putin gave the same figure for the size of the force in the combat zone – around 700,000 troops. According to Kofman and Wehner, this suggests that the force had barely grown over the roughly 18 months since mid-2024. In June 2026, Putin again put the size of the Joint Grouping of Forces at 700,000.
It is difficult to assess the balance between reinforcements and departures more precisely. While estimates of the number of new contract soldiers differ by tens of thousands, estimates of Russian military casualties vary even more widely.
Using budgetary spending on compensation for the families of fallen soldiers, Kluge estimated Russian battlefield deaths in 2026 at roughly 9,000 a month — when compared with recruitment of 20,000–30,000 people a month, that would suggest no manpower shortfall at all.
However, fatalities account for only part of Russia's irreversible losses. They must be supplemented by severely wounded soldiers, those who are no longer medically fit to return to the front, and troops who are missing, captured, deserting, or otherwise removed from active service. Simply adding the numbers of dead and wounded would also be misleading, since a significant share of wounded soldiers return to duty after treatment.
According to The Guardian the number of Russian killed and wounded reached around 30,000 in April 2026. At a recruitment rate of roughly 1,000 people a day, a substantial share of new recruits would go towards simply maintaining the existing strength of military units. The figures cannot, however, be compared directly without accounting for the proportion of wounded soldiers who return to duty.
The Ukrainian General Staff, for its part, puts the Russian army's personnel losses over the summer at 124,200 — 39,300 in June, 42,900 in July, and 42,000 in August – about 26% more than during the three months of the spring and significantly above the current rate of contract recruitment. However, Ukrainian statistics count all personnel losses, not just irreversible ones, meaning the 124,200 figure cannot be directly compared with the number of new contract soldiers either.
The Financial Times reports that the Russian military command is sending most new contract recruits to existing units rather than using them to build a trained reserve. The current pace of contract recruitment is therefore probably somewhat below the target set for the regions.
There is another constraint that gets lost in the aggregate statistics: 30,000 recruits do not equal 30,000 soldiers with the skills the military needs. This is particularly evident in the Unmanned Systems Forces, established in late 2025. According to IStories, the Defense Ministry planned to recruit around 78,800 people for the new branch by the end of 2026. Most were not expected to come from ordinary contract recruits, with a target of 58,000 to be recruited from among students, graduates of DOSAAFtraining courses, former aviation personnel, and “women” with the necessary training. Another 10,800 were to be conscripts transferred to contract service, while only around 10,000 were to be transferred from other military units.
However, on July 17, 2026, Deputy Defense Minister Alexey Krivoruchko said that just over 8,000 specialists had been trained for the Unmanned Systems Forces in the first half of the year. The Conflict Intelligence Team noted that, if the annual target were being met evenly, the figure should have been roughly four times higher by that point. Analysts attribute part of the shortfall to the failure of the campaign to recruit students despite reports from Novaya Gazeta Europe that at least 47 of Russia’s 50 leading universities had campaigned to persuade students to sign such contracts.
After the mass call-up in the fall of 2022, the Russian authorities effectively built an alternative system of continuous military recruitment. The state tried dozens of methods for recruiting people, from advertising contract service and offering large bonuses to using paid intermediaries, conducting raids, targeting men with debts and financial problems, recruiting foreigners, and pressuring conscripts, prisoners, and defendants to sign up for contract service. This system has so far allowed the Russian military command to avoid a second wave of mass mobilization.
Nevertheless, maintaining the previous flow of recruits has become increasingly expensive. Higher payments can indeed temporarily boost recruitment, and after Tyumen region raised its one-time enlistment bonus to 3 million rubles ($35,600), a local military recruitment official reported that the number of inquiries had doubled. However, the need to keep raising both enlistment bonuses and payments to recruiters suggests that the previous level of financial incentives is no longer sufficient to meet recruitment targets. In Moscow, for example, according to sources cited by IStories and Verstka, the flow of recruits fell by roughly a third in the spring compared with the previous year.
The pool of potential recruits is also expanding. In September 2026, Irkutsk region cut the enlistment bonus for Russian citizens from 2.1 million ($24,850) to 1.8 million rubles ($21,300), while introducing a 900,000-ruble ($10,650) payment for foreign citizens and stateless people.
In August, authorities in Zabaykalsky Krai raised the regional payment for foreign citizens and stateless people from 400,000 rubles to 900,000 rubles ($4,750 to $10,650). However, at the same time, they cut the payment for mobilized soldiers who sign contracts from 2 million rubles to 400,000 rubles ($23,650 to $4,750). The contrast illustrates the logic of the current system: regional authorities have little reason to pay as much for someone already serving in the Russian armed forces as they do to bring in a new recruit.
At the same time, the Russian authorities are removing legal barriers to another source of manpower. In August, Putin signed a law expanding the categories of convicts who can sign contracts with the Defense Ministry during periods of mobilization, martial law, or wartime. During the bill’s consideration, Deputy Defense Minister Viktor Goremykin explicitly linked the change to the need to meet the military’s 2026 recruitment target. Kluge views such measures as an additional way to sustain the current recruitment rate.
Here it is important to distinguish between having enough people to replenish infantry units and having enough young, healthy, and trainable recruits for more specialized roles. According to sources cited by Important Stories and Verstka, the share of older recruits and men with serious health problems is growing.
In spring 2026, a source in one military unit claimed that contract recruits had “literally been scraped out of all the villages around here,” forcing recruiters to look for people in other regions. Such accounts cannot be extrapolated to the Russian army as a whole, but they point to another possible limit of the current model: not a shortage of people in general, but a dwindling pool of suitable recruits.
Russian statistics make it possible to count debtors, unemployed people, and those with criminal records, but they cannot show how many are actually fit for military service. It is therefore impossible to calculate mechanically how many months of war Russia can sustain by recruiting from among the poor and indebted.
The extent to which this pool is being depleted can, however, be assessed indirectly by looking at the cost of each next recruit and the effort required to find him. If maintaining roughly the same recruitment rate requires higher payments, more paid intermediaries, searches outside the region, and lower age and health requirements, that suggests the marginal cost of each additional recruit is rising.
That alone, however, does not prove that potential contract soldiers are running out: bonuses of several million rubles remain an enormous incentive for many Russian families.
Why might Putin need mobilization?
What matters is not so much the number of soldiers as the task the Russian military command expects them to perform. Replacing losses may be enough to sustain the current slow advance, but significantly accelerating the offensive, creating an operational reserve, or forming new force groupings would require a much larger pool of troops.
Over the past two years, the Russian military has adapted its offensive tactics in order to fit its limited capabilities. As early as 2024, Russian forces had already largely abandoned attempts to launch repeated attacks with large mechanized formations, instead shifting to small infantry assaults. In 2025, this tactic evolved further — into what has been described as “infiltration,” allowing Russian forces to maintain continuous pressure along a broad front using extremely slow advances that are difficult to turn into an operational breakthrough.
Kofman and Wehner note a paradox: as the Russian force grew, the size of the force the command could deploy simultaneously in direct attacks actually declined. The reason is the battlefield’s saturation with minefields, artillery, prepared defensive positions, and drones of both the reconnaissance and strike variety, all of which combine to make large concentrations of troops highly visible and extremely vulnerable.
As a result, brigades numbering several thousand troops can spend months advancing along a single ravine or toward one or two villages, even as very few of them can take part simultaneously in assaults. The Russian command has numerical superiority across the theater but cannot fully translate it into local superiority on the battlefield.
This is particularly important when assessing the prospects of an offensive against the Ukrainian-held cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, which form the northern part of a larger fortified belt of cities that also includes Druzhkivka and Kostiantynivka. The towns are separated by rivers, high ground, and wooded areas.
As of early September, the nearest Russian positions on the Lyman axis were 7–10 kilometers from Sloviansk — close enough for Russian artillery to shell the city. According to an officer with the 11th Army Corps of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, the Russian command has reinforced the sector with the 123rd Motor Rifle Brigade (which was previously involved in fighting around the Siversk salient), giving it the ability to threaten Ukrainian logistics. The Russian army has therefore moved closer to direct fighting for the Sloviansk–Kramatorsk urban area, while Ukraine’s new commander-in-chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, is effectively restructuring the defense command system around the expected battle for the area.
Ukraine’s military command system is being reshaped for the coming battle for Sloviansk and Kramatorsk
If the current model remains in place, the most likely first scenario is a continuation of the slow advance without a new mobilization. The Russian command could continue sending reinforcements directly to active units, replenishing assault infantry and gradually attempting to encircle the urban area from several directions while simultaneously degrading Ukrainian logistics and positions with drones, artillery, and airstrikes.
Kofman, however, described the 2026 campaign as significantly less successful for the Russian military than those of previous years. He stressed that the current rate of advance cannot simply be extrapolated to a date when the entire Donetsk region would be captured, as the outcome depends not only on Russian resources but also on the effectiveness of Ukrainian defenses.
Additional mobilization is not a prerequisite for continuing the offensive. The Russian army has sustained its advance for several years with virtually no operational pauses: newly formed or rebuilt units are generally not held in reserve but sent directly to different sectors of the front. Even Russia’s airborne forces and naval infantry are typically pulled from one sector, rapidly replenished, and redeployed to another rather than being kept as a permanent operational reserve. This system allows the Russian command to maintain pressure, but also makes it difficult to accumulate forces for a separate large-scale operation.
The second scenario is an attempt to sharply accelerate the capture of the remaining part of the Donetsk region by deploying a larger mass of infantry. At first glance, a new mobilization might seem the most obvious solution.
Kofman, however, considers this approach unlikely to be effective. In his assessment, if the Russian command simply adds several regiments or divisions to sectors already crowded with troops and continues to use them in the same way, the result will be higher casualties more than anything else. Even 100,000 additional troops would not automatically translate into 100,000 assault troops who could be deployed simultaneously to capture Sloviansk and Kramatorsk quickly.
A radical acceleration of the offensive would require not just more troops, but the ability to conduct larger, coordinated operations. This means a sufficient numbers of trained junior commanders and specialists, engineering support and logistics, and the ability to concentrate forces without allowing Ukrainian reconnaissance and drones to destroy them before they enter the fight.
Linear growth in troop numbers will not work without changes in tactics and organizational support
The third scenario better explains why the Russian leadership might need mobilization: not to reinforce existing assault units, but to form new ones and thereby change the geography of the war.
Kofman considers the most dangerous option to be the creation of additional regiments and several new corps that could be deployed, for example, in the Kharkiv, Sumy, or Chernihiv directions. Even without an immediate objective of capturing major cities, the emergence of substantial Russian troops there would force the Ukrainian command to keep additional brigades in the north and northeast instead of deploying them in Donbas or Zaporizhzhia. In this scenario, mobilization would not be about sending another 100,000 troops toward Kramatorsk, but about creating a shortage of reserves for the Ukrainian Armed Forces across several fronts at once.
This may be the purpose behind the 300,000–500,000 additional troops discussed, among other places, in an analytical memo published by the Black Mirror hacker group. The memo describes a mobilization on this scale as being potentially part of a much more ambitious scenario aimed at achieving a “decisive military advantage” that would allow Russia to establish control over the entire territory of the four annexed regions and Kharkiv region before forcing the Ukrainian authorities into negotiations. The authors consider 300,000–500,000 mobilized troops insufficient on their own, however, as the Russian military would also need to expand air support, strengthen defenses in the rear, and develop its drone capabilities.
Even if a mobilization decision is made, it will not determine the outcome of the 2026 campaign. Mobilized troops have to be assembled, assigned to units, given at least basic training, provided with commanders and equipment, and deployed to the front. And forming new units takes even longer.
Kofman estimates the minimum cycle for building such forces at roughly three months and notes that, in order to significantly accelerate the offensive in 2026, mobilization would have had to begin around May. An autumn mobilization – if it happens at all – would therefore primarily be a decision focused on influencing the 2027 campaign.
What could Putin achieve by expanding the army in 2027?
There is no definitive answer to where Putin’s war aims end. His territorial demands have shifted with the negotiating context. In summer 2024, Putin demanded that Ukrainian forces withdraw from the entire territory of the four Ukrainian regions claimed by Russia — Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia — as a condition for a ceasefire (while Russian-annexed Crimea remained non-negotiable).
During U.S.-mediated negotiations in 2025, according to Reuters, he was reportedly prepared to halt fighting along the existing front line in the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions but continued to demand the entire Donbas. This did not, however, mean that he had abandoned his claims to the other territories: in late June 2026, Putin again publicly described full control of Donbas, plus Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, as the goal of the “special military operation.”
After capturing the remaining part of Donetsk region, the Russian military would therefore face a much more difficult task in the south. To fully occupy Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, Russian forces would have to capture the major city of Zaporizhzhia, cross the Dnipro, and retake Kherson (which Russian troops abandoned in fall 2022). These would be operations on an entirely different scale from the current advance by small assault groups in Donbas.
So far, there are no clear signs that such operations are being prepared. In summer 2026, the pace of the Russian advance remained slow. Russian forces are positioned south of Zaporizhzhia, but Ukrainian defenses have so far prevented them from advancing toward the city. There are even fewer signs of preparations for a major operation across the Dnipro to retake Kherson. Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces have stepped up strikes on Russian logistics in the south, including on the port of Mariupol and the Chongar Bridge linking the occupied territories with Crimea.
If Putin intends to use military force to gain full control over all the Ukrainian territories he has incorporated into Russia’s constitution, the Russian military would have to continue its offensive in the south while holding a front more than 1,000 kilometers long. This would seem difficult without recruiting hundreds of thousands of additional troops for next year’s campaign.
But the Russian military’s potential objectives do not end with the territories incorporated into the constitution. Putin also seeks to expand a “security zone” along the Russian-Ukrainian border. Initially, Russian authorities linked the creation of such a zone to protecting the Belgorod region, and later, they invoked Ukraine’s 2024-2025 operation in the Kursk region as justification.
In June 2026, Putin stated explicitly that the Russian military’s objective in the Sumy and Vovchansk sectors was to seize Ukrainian territory along the border, presenting the loss of this territory as Ukraine’s price for its incursion into the Kursk region. In July, following an intensification of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, Putin again said that additional territory beyond Donbas needed to be seized in order to expand Russia's “buffer zone.”
There is no predetermined geographic boundary to such an objective. The greater the range of Ukrainian drones and other strike capabilities, the less realistic it becomes to secure Russia’s border regions simply by pushing the front line farther away. Nevertheless, the concept of a “security zone” provides the Russian authorities with a rationale for military operations in Ukraine's Kharkiv and Sumy regions, which Moscow has not formally declared part of Russia.
Still, this does not mean that Putin has decided to pursue such a widespread campaign. For now, the most concrete near-term territorial objective remains the part of Donetsk region that Russia does not yet control, and the timeline for achieving it remains unclear, even if Ukrainian officials have repeatedly claimed that the Russian command aims to do so by the end of 2026. In August, Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate, said that this deadline was included in the Russian General Staff’s plans, and in late August, Deputy Head of the Presidential Office Pavlo Palisa made a similar claim. However, there is no independent confirmation that such an order exists.
The Institute for the Study of War contends that the Russian command has repeatedly missed projected deadlines for capturing Donetsk region. The Conflict Intelligence Team, neverthless, argues that reports of yet another deadline allegedly set by Putin for the capture of Donbas should not be taken too seriously. In their analysts’ view, Putin is satisfied with the current pace of fighting, meaning a new mobilization is unlikely to be necessary.
The cost of avoiding mobilization – and the cost of carrying it out
Avoiding mobilization is becoming increasingly expensive for the Russian authorities. In addition to the federal payment of 400,000 rubles ($4,750), new contract recruits receive a regional bonus. According to economist Janis Kluge’s estimate, its average size reached a record 1.65 million rubles ($19,500) by August, up from 1.47 million ($17,400) in March, while the regions’ actual spending on such payments rose by about 30%. Including payments to intermediaries, the regional cost of recruiting a single contract soldier increased from roughly 1.4 million rubles ($16,550) in mid-2025 to 1.8–1.9 million ($21,900) in 2026. Including the federal payment, the state is therefore paying roughly 2.2–2.3 million rubles ($26,600) to recruit each new contract soldier.
At least 11 Russian regions (plus occupied Sevastopol) raised their enlistment bonuses over the summer. In early fall, a number of southern Russian regions followed suit. As Kluge notes, some regions are funding the higher bonuses by cutting other areas of spending, from pay increases for public-sector workers to regional payments to the families of fallen soldiers.
The increase in payments to recruits has been accompanied by an expansion of the recruitment machinery itself. By August 2026, 56 Russian regions were offering rewards for bringing in a new contract soldier, compared with 31 in fall 2025. According to The Moscow Times, at least 38 regions have formally established such payments through regional or municipal regulations. The state has effectively created a market of intermediaries that are paid to find new soldiers.
IStories calculated that in 2026, the regions’ average monthly spending on recruiter bonuses had more than doubled, from 358 million rubles ($4.2 million) to 802 million ($9.5 million). By mid-May, regional authorities had spent at least 7.7 billion rubles ($91.1 million) on such payments. In some regions, recruiters receive 100,000 rubles or more for each contract recruit they bring in.
At current payment levels, recruiting an additional 100,000 people would require roughly 220–230 billion rubles ($2.7 billion) in one-time bonuses; 300,000 would cost 660–690 billion ($8.0 billion), and 500,000 would cost 1.1–1.15 trillion rubles ($13.6 billion). This is a rough estimate: payments vary widely between regions and are frequently changed. But the scale makes the key point clear: building an additional force of 300,000–500,000 contract soldiers would cost around a trillion rubles before the state even begins paying them their regular salaries.
Mobilization saves money specifically on buying people’s consent. The state does not have to offer a conscript several million rubles to sign a contract, and it does not have to pay recruiters to find them. However, that is where the savings end. Mobilized soldiers must be trained, clothed, armed, housed, transported to the front, and then paid and maintained like other service members. Simply paying 300,000 mobilized soldiers the minimum monthly allowance of around 195,000 ($2,300) rubles would cost more than 700 billion rubles ($8.3 billion) a year.
Mobilization saves money on buying people’s consent
Finally, mobilization carries a cost that cannot be captured in any budget line. The first wave turned out to be one of the Russian government’s most unpopular decisions since the start of the war and triggered a mass exodus of men from the country numbering in the hundreds of thousands. A new mobilization would exacerbate labor shortages in two ways: several hundred thousand more men would be taken into the army, while countless others would try to evade the draft.
Additional spending would come at a time when the budget is in significantly worse shape than it was in 2022. Beginning in 2026, the government raised VAT from 20% to 22%, with the Finance Ministry explicitly citing the need to finance defense and security, including military pay and support for soldiers’ families, as a reason for the additional trillion rubles in revenue. In the first eight months of 2026, the federal budget deficit reached 5.8 trillion rubles ($68.6 billion), while the government’s ability to cover it with reserves and cheap borrowing has diminished.
The contract system, by contrast, allows the economic and social cost of drawing people into the military to be spread over time. Instead of drafting several hundred thousand people simultaneously, the state recruits hundreds of volunteers every day, many of them from groups for whom several million rubles is worth more than the income they would otherwise earn.
In other words, contract recruitment does not necessarily remove every new recruit from an already tight labor market. Russian authorities can continue recruiting among homeless people, people with alcohol or drug dependencies, and other socially disadvantaged groups, some of whom have no regular employment. The size of this pool, however, is unknown. The official 2020 census counted only 11,000 homeless people, while experts in 2024 estimated the actual number at around 2 million, including roughly 1.1 million men. In 2024, about 980,000 Russians were registered as having alcohol dependence and 208,000 as having drug dependence. It is not known, however, what proportion of these people are fit for military service, have not already been recruited, and are willing to sign a contract.
Notably, the threat of mobilization itself helps sustain the contract recruitment system. As The Guardian reports, recruiters use it as an argument: it is better to sign a contract now and get paid than risk being drafted into the army later without receiving a bonus. The result is a paradox: fear of a new mobilization helps the Russian authorities recruit more people than they otherwise would have, thereby allowing them to postpone mobilization.
What is known about preparations for mobilization
The Russian authorities are far better prepared technically for a new mobilization than they were in the fall of 2022. The clearest example is the Unified Register of Military Registration, created after the first wave.
As IStories found in a leak of documents from Mikord, one of the companies that developed the system, mobilization was built into it from the outset as a separate scenario. The register allows authorities to identify people liable for military service, send out draft notices (without any limit on their number), track the potential number of mobilized troops, and transmit information for imposing travel bans and other restrictions. The system’s capacity is currently designed to send up to one million draft notices a year.
In summer 2026, more explicit signs of mobilization-readiness testing emerged. In June, officials from the administrations of neighboring regions took part in mass-mobilization exercises in Volzhsky, Volgograd region. They practiced setting up a preliminary assembly point, notifying citizens, receiving military equipment, and operating a mobilization headquarters. In July, according to The Wall Street Journal (citing Western intelligence agencies), the military conducted a similar exercise in Kaliningrad region, practicing the accommodation, feeding, and arming of mobilized troops. The newspaper’s sources claim that similar exercises are being held in other regions.
The organizers of the Volzhsky exercises, however, offered a more prosaic explanation: mobilization preparedness is a “peacetime process,” and such drills are held every year.
At the same time, mobilization has become more prominent in the government’s dealings with employers. In July, three professional publications for accountants, HR specialists, and business executives published or updated guidelines on what employers should do in the event of mobilization. According to a source at the Alabuga industrial complex, the management there also received mobilization instructions in August. There were reports that major companies were compiling lists of employees exempt from mobilization, as well as an alleged order for a mobilization drill at a Gazprom facility. The Alabuga account and the authenticity of the document attributed to Gazprom could not be independently verified.
At the same time, the surge in guidance for employers does not in itself prove that a new mobilization is being prepared. Since 2022, requirements for military registration and the liability of organizations have been steadily tightened.
On September 4, Sberbank held an internal meeting on reserving employees against mobilization, according to sources at the state-owned bank cited by Mozhem Obyasnit. According to the sources, beginning September 10, Sberbank would begin cross-checking the military-registration records of all its employees. Notably, this was the first time the bank had held such a meeting.
The Russian authorities are also continuing to build out the administrative infrastructure that could be used in a mobilization. In August, the government introduced Bill No. 1322096-8, which would establish administrative penalties for failing to comply with decisions by regional governors and operational headquarters. The bill’s explanatory note explicitly lists mobilization measures and meeting the needs of the armed forces among the tasks of these bodies.
Earlier, the Prosecutor General’s Office updated its procedures for overseeing military registration, including the transfer of information on people liable for military service, employee exemptions, and deferments. None of these measures necessarily points to preparations for a new wave of mobilization on its own. Taken together, however, they show that the state continues to keep the mobilization machinery operational.
Russia is steadily strengthening its administrative infrastructure for mobilization
This is the main difference from September 2022. Back then, the authorities first announced the call-up of 300,000 people, but many of the mechanisms for registration, notification, and oversight had to be created or reworked after mobilization had already begun. Military recruitment office databases were incomplete, businesses and regional authorities often had to work out the rules as the campaign unfolded, and there was no electronic draft-notice register. Now, by contrast, much of this infrastructure exists on a permanent basis.
Still, this does not mean that a decision on a new mobilization has already been made, and as The Wall Street Journal's intelligence sources say, no such decision has yet been made. The Guardian reached the same conclusion: in mid-August, two people familiar with discussions in Moscow, plus a Western official, saw no sign that Putin had decided to launch a new mass call-up. For now, the Russian authorities’ actions can be interpreted equally plausibly as preparations for creating the option of future mobilization, or as an effort to put everything in place in order to avoid actually having to mobilize.
In recent months, Russian officials have conspicuously denied that a new call-up is being considered. In July, Deputy Security Council Chairman Dmitry Medvedev called reports of mobilization a “lying provocation.” On Aug. 20, Russia’s UN ambassador Vasily Nebenzya said that it was “neither planned nor expected.” On August 25, presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the reports as “information hoaxes,” while three days later Medvedev again said that mobilization was unnecessary because there were enough contract soldiers. Then, on Sept. 1 and 3, Putin joined them, calling the mobilization rumors (1, 2) “complete crap” and an “information attack.” For now, however, these repeated denials are the strongest public indication that the authorities are concerned enough about the mobilization issue to address it repeatedly.
In any case, the state is maintaining and refining the infrastructure needed to carry out a mass call-up quickly while simultaneously spending ever more money and resources to replenishing the army without one.
So, are the Russian authorities preparing for a new mobilization? The answer is: they are preparing for the possibility. The electronic register, system of restrictions, mobilization exercises, work with employers, and legal framework make a repeat of the organizational chaos of September 2022 less likely. The decision will depend primarily on whether Putin wants to expand military operations in 2027 or if he limit his aims to eventually capturing Donbas. In other words, it will depend on whether he has a military objective important enough to justify the political and economic cost of forcibly recruiting several hundred thousand more Russians quickly.

Nearly half of Germans expect Chancellor Merz gone by year's end

2026-09-18

15:18:43 KST

Ayhan Simsek
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Nearly half of German voters expect Chancellor Friedrich Merz to leave office by December, a YouGov poll showed, raising the stakes ahead of Sunday's state elections.
Published late Thursday, the representative survey found 48% of respondents said they did not expect Merz to remain chancellor through the end of the year. About 31% said they expected him to stay in office, while 21% were undecided.
The poll landed ahead of elections in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and the city-state of Berlin on Sunday, where surveys show Merz’s CDU heading for heavy losses.
The conservatives have already taken a sharp blow this month in Saxony-Anhalt, where the right-wing AfD finished first with 43.8%, ahead of the CDU on 17.2%. The result was a major defeat for the party, which had governed the state for decades with changing coalition partners.
In the latest ZDF poll for Berlin, the CDU is at about 20%, down from 28.2% in the 2023 election, and risks losing power in the capital. The socialist Left Party leads with 22%, opening the way for a three-party government without the CDU.
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU is heading for another setback, polling at 6% in the latest surveys, close to the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament. The latest ZDF poll put the center-left SPD at 37% in the eastern state and the anti-immigration AfD at 36%.
Local issues still shape the regional races, but many observers say the party’s slide across three state contests this month has been compounded by Merz’s weak performance in office, increasing pressure within his party for him to step aside.
Senior CDU leaders plan an internal meeting on Monday. Lawmakers from the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the CSU, are due to meet two days later.
A potential leadership change in the CDU would not automatically dissolve parliament or trigger a national election. If pressure within the party forces Merz to step aside, the Bundestag could elect a new chancellor without a nationwide vote.

Berlin's acute housing shortage and soaring rents dominate city election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:18:21 UTC
15:18:21 KST

Berlin's acute housing shortage and soaring rents dominate city election
BERLIN, Sept 18 - Berliners cycle, picnic and fly kites on the city's vast former Tempelhof airfield that opened as a park in 2010, yet developers are circling and whether to build homes on the historic site has dominated debate ahead of an election on Sunday.
While immigration has featured prominently in other German state elections and driven a surge in support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, in Berlin, where 85% of households rent their homes, housing and rents are voters' top concerns.
The city will need 211,000 more homes by 2040 and advertised rents have nearly doubled since 2014, stoking deep frustration at the city government, which mirrors Germany's national coalition in its alliance of centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU) and centre-left Social Democrats (SPD).
The vote on September 20 therefore marks another test of support for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's struggling government two weeks after the AfD swept to victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Neighbouring Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania also votes on September 20.
The far-left Left Party stands at 23% in Berlin, Merz's CDU on 21% and the AfD at around 17%, ahead of the SPD and the environmental Greens, according to the latest poll on September 11 by Forschungsgruppe Wahlen.
For the AfD, Berlin's housing crisis has fed into its argument for restricting immigration. The Left Party meanwhile is pledging to build affordable new homes, freeze rents for one year then limit increases to 1%, forcibly reduce rents that are 20% over the local average, curb holiday rentals in housing blocks, and offer flats that become vacant in the centre to those with a right to social housing.
Both it and the AfD have roughly doubled their support since Berlin's last election in 2023.
FROM NAZI AIRPORT TO MUCH-LOVED PARK
The fate of the Tempelhofer Feld - which is almost twice the size of London's Hyde Park and one of the largest urban open spaces in the world - reflects a broader conflict between the need for more housing and desire to protect public green space.
The original 1920s airport was expanded by the Nazis and after World War Two became a lifeline for the city during the 1948-49 Berlin Airlift, when Western allies supplied the blockaded city by air. The airport closed in 2008. Four years after opening as a park, nearly two-thirds of Berliners voted to keep the site largely free of development in a referendum.
"Open space is not land for development. It is social and ecological infrastructure — and Tempelhofer Feld is Berlin's open space," said Anita Moeller, a member of the 100% Tempelhofer Feld initiative, which opposes development.
The CDU, Free Democrats (FDP) and AfD support limited housing development on parts of Tempelhofer Feld. The SPD, Greens and Left Party oppose construction there and favour developing other sites.
"The referendum was 12 years ago, the need was nowhere near as great then as it is today," said Stefan Evers, the Berlin CDU's lead candidate, in an interview with Tagesspiegel.
GROWTH HAS A DOWNSIDE
For the past decade, Berlin's economic growth has outpaced Germany's sluggish economy, mainly due to its services sector, which generates almost 90% of the city's economic output.
Berlin is Germany's startup capital, with more than 600 companies founded in 2025 alone. E-commerce group Zalando and fintech N26 are among the digital consumer-services companies headquartered in the capital.
But that growth has come at a cost, pushing up rents as the population has grown. Would-be developers of Tempelhof say it will help ease the shortage of homes, but many struggling to pay their rent say more needs to be done to make housing affordable.
Others say that the German capital, once a global symbol of rough-edged urban cool and dubbed "poor but sexy" by former mayor Klaus Wowereit, simply now resembles Europe's other major cities in costs.
On September 5, thousands of demonstrators gathered in Berlin to protest against high rents. Among them was Mareen Harant. In Berlin you can easily end up paying €1,500 ($1,720) or more a month for a one- or two-room apartment, she said. "Who on earth is supposed to be able to afford that?"
The election campaign has been anything but a triumph for the ruling CDU and SPD. In July, CDU Mayor Kai Wegner withdrew as lead candidate amid criticism of his handling of a January power outage that left large parts of the capital without electricity for four days.
The SPD has also faced turbulence after police raided the home and offices of its lead candidate Steffen Krach as part of an investigation into a tender process in the health sector. He denies any wrongdoing.
"Growth also has a downside: prices rise and, above all, land prices rise, so space becomes scarce," said Martin Gornig, a researcher at the German Institute for Economic Research, DIW Berlin.
Berlin's legendary nightclub scene has also been hit.
"We had to move because we simply could no longer afford the rent," said Jakob Turtur, managing director of Jonny Knueppel, a collectively run club. REUTERS

Australian research finds severe mental illness linked to shorter life expectancy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:17:19 CST
15:17:19 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- People with severe mental illness die more than 10 years earlier than the general population, according to research led by Australia's University of Queensland (UQ).
Researchers analyzed hospital mortality data from about 255,000 patients in the Australian state of Queensland over 14 years to assess the mortality rates of those with severe mental illness, such as depressive, neurotic and stress disorders, alcohol and drug use, and schizophrenia, according to a UQ statement released on Friday.
The study, published in Lancet Regional Health -- Western Pacific, found that while mortality rates had improved, inequality is still prevalent, with males with mental health disorders dying 12 years earlier and females 10 years earlier than the general population.
"The mortality gap is improving, and people with severe mental illnesses are living longer than they were 14 years ago, which shows the health care system is on the right track," said lead author Mike Trott from UQ's Faculty of Health, Medicine and Behavioral Sciences.
However, mortality rates for patients with psychoses such as schizophrenia had "flatlined," highlighting that the sickest patients were not benefiting from better care, Trott said.
The research also shows patients are dying younger from preventable physical health conditions, such as cardiovascular disease, and physical illness is the principal driver of excess mortality.
"Patients with severe mental illness tend to require more complex care, and often medication side effects such as weight gain and reduction in physical activity can lead to poorer physical health," Trott said. ■
