Interview: China's 2027 BRICS chairmanship to further deepen cooperation, says expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:17:00 CST
15:17:00 KST

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China's assumption of the BRICS chairmanship in 2027 will provide new opportunities to further deepen practical cooperation among member countries and advance collaboration in innovation, green development and other areas, a South African expert has said.
"BRICS has evolved from a high-level dialogue forum into a platform for practical cooperation," Farhana Paruk, a Cape Town-based China-Africa expert, told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Paruk said the mechanism has developed a number of practical cooperation platforms and programs, including the New Development Bank (NDB), the Contingent Reserve Arrangement and initiatives in trade, finance, food and energy security, digital public infrastructure and people-to-people exchanges.
"Yet significant room remains to deepen collaboration, particularly in local-currency settlement and cross-border payment interoperability, supply-chain resilience, scaled-up NDB project financing and structured cooperation on AI governance, standards and skills development," she said.
"Under China's 2027 chairmanship, there is scope to deepen traditional cooperation through joint agri-tech platforms, affordable irrigation and food-storage systems and pooled expertise in solar, batteries, grids and green hydrogen," she said.
Paruk expected China to further advance cooperation in AI, the digital economy and green development through closer collaboration on governance, standards, finance and technology.
This could be achieved "by accelerating BRICS for innovation by scaling AI governance dialogues, shared testbeds, startup funds and digital economy standards, and delivering green BRICS through biodiversity, climate, green finance and environmental technology and research initiatives," she said.
Paruk also expected China's chairmanship to strengthen people-to-people exchanges among BRICS countries, particularly through greater interaction among young people, academics, cultural institutions and media organizations, helping make BRICS more visible and relatable to citizens.
On global governance, Paruk said China is expected to work with other BRICS countries to advance reforms that would give developing countries a greater voice in international institutions and promote more inclusive development.
"In parallel, China is expected to work with other BRICS members to promote a more just and equitable global governance system by advocating multilateral reform, greater representation for the Global South in financial and political institutions and rules that support development financing, climate action and digital inclusion," she said. ■

Early voting begins in US midterms that could see Republicans lose control of Congress
In-person early voting for the US midterm elections begins Friday, six weeks ahead of the final November 3 vote, which will determine whether Republicans will maintain their majority in the US House and Senate. Some of the main issues American voters are deciding on are how to navigate the cost-of-living crisis, the war in Iran and President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement campaign.
In-person voting for this year’s midterm elections begins Friday, ushering in the final six weeks for Americans to decide who they trust to lead Congress through a cost-of-living crisis, a prolonged war in Iran and other pressing issues.
Election administrators say they’re prepared and confident the vote will be accurate and secure. Nevertheless, President Donald Trump has continued with efforts to denigrate certain voting methods and reshape how US elections are run, through court challenges, an expansive federal hunt for noncitizen voters and a pressure campaign to force election officials to share sensitive voter data.
Friday marks the start of early voting in Virginia. Voters in a handful of other states, including Idaho, Minnesota and South Dakota, are able to cast absentee ballots in person, typically at a local election office or voting centre. More expansive early voting is scheduled to begin in those and other states in the coming weeks.

The November 3 election includes votes for governor and state legislature in most states and will determine whether the US House and Senate maintain their Republican majorities. If Democrats retake Congress, it will alter the trajectory of the final two years of Trump’s term, likely leading to investigations and other oversight efforts.
The start of early voting comes at a time of deep angst among many Americans about issues including rising gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran, the looming risks of artificial intelligence technology and Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement campaign.
It also follows an unprecedented spate of mid-decade redistricting for the US House that began when Trump urged the Republican-controlled legislature in Texas to redraw its congressional map to help the party. California and other states followed.
The changes affect millions of people: Research shows 1 in 10 Americans this fall are residents of a different congressional district than in 2024.
Those partisan efforts are expected to continue ahead of the 2028 elections after a landmark ruling earlier this year from the Supreme Court weakened the federal Voting Rights Act’s protections against racially discriminatory redistricting.
As the start of early voting approached, Trump was focused on efforts to assert federal control over election administration, even as the Constitution bestows the power to run elections on the states and, in some cases, Congress. The Supreme Court rejected Trump's bid to restrict mail ballots this week, but several of his administration's other efforts to influence the voting process and mine state voter lists for illegitimate voters are ongoing.

Trump for years has raised the spectre of widespread noncitizen voting in US elections, and this year is no exception. But despite his administration's insistence that hundreds of thousands of people are illegally on voting rolls across the country, research continues to show noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare.
David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said he wouldn’t be surprised if the president continues “his disinformation campaign and his attack on election officials”. But he said he thinks despite that and other challenges, “ultimately the process will hold as it has in past years”.
Voting rights advocates have encouraged voters this year to cast mail ballots early, in part because of concerns about recent changes in US Postal Service operations that could delay the application of postmarks to ballots.
“Voting early, whether in person or by mail, is good for all of our communities because it gives voters options, eases lines on Election Day and can even mean faster results,” said Hannah Fried, co-founder and CEO of the voting rights group All Voting Is Local.
In a press briefing Thursday, Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon urged people not to be swayed by stories they might have seen or read that cast doubt on election operations. They would be able to vote “just like they always have”, he said.
“I just want to reaffirm that Minnesota’s elections are fundamentally free, fair, accurate, honest and secure,” he said.

The conflict has also added economic pressure, with Russia facing rising military spending, fuel disruptions and other costs linked to the war.
The vote is being closely watched for signs of public sentiment towards the war, although the restricted political environment limits the range of choices available to voters.
Some Russian opposition figures have also raised concerns about a possible new military mobilisation after the election.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Moscow of preparing for a new call-up, while Putin has denied plans for another mobilisation.

Pellet prices begin to fall in Latvia – producers predict what will happen next
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:13:40 UTC
15:13:40 KST

Demand for wood pellets is beginning to decline both in export markets and domestically, according to Didzis Palejs, Chairman of the Board of the Latvian Biomass Association LATbio.
Assessing trends over the past month, Palejs said the situation in the pellet market is improving, although not as quickly as he had previously expected. A month ago, he anticipated a more substantial decline in pellet prices than has occurred so far.
Palejs expects pellet prices to continue falling steadily, but slowly. He said pellet producers located closer to Riga expect a more significant price decline around mid-October.
Pellets currently cost between 290 and 320 euros per tonne excluding value added tax (VAT) when purchased directly from producers, the LATbio chairman said.
He noted that
pellet prices are falling both at producers and in shops,
while availability from producers has improved compared with this summer. Palejs acknowledged that some producers still have waiting lists, but said pellet manufacturers generally report that consumers have begun buying less.
Demand for Latvian pellets is also declining in the Polish market, and this is being reflected in prices.
While Latvian pellets were previously exported to Poland at around 350 euros per tonne excluding VAT, the price for Polish buyers has now fallen to approximately 300 euros per tonne excluding VAT. Palejs stressed that these figures are approximate and prices may vary between producers.
Palejs said not all pellet producers have sufficient raw materials, with most facing difficulties securing adequate supplies.
He explained that
problems with raw material availability are primarily linked to raw material prices rising faster than pellet prices.
As a result, producers cannot afford to purchase raw materials at prices that would force them to manufacture pellets at a loss. Raw material prices remain very high, while pellet prices are declining.
Weather conditions are also making it more difficult to secure raw materials by hampering timber harvesting in forests. According to Palejs, this has a particularly significant impact on producers that manufacture more industrial pellets and use low-quality roundwood, such as timber that has deteriorated or is of an unsuitable species.
Palejs also noted that many pellet producers are concerned about a possible increase in electricity prices. He explained that a sharp rise in electricity prices would have a significant impact on production by increasing costs.
At the same time,
when electricity prices are high, cogeneration plants in export markets tend to increase production,
which in turn raises their pellet consumption. If consumption at cogeneration plants increases unexpectedly, this creates additional demand.
Higher demand from cogeneration plants could affect the distribution of available pellet supplies. If pellet supplies became insufficient while new demand emerged, this could create complications in the market, Palejs said.
In his view, there should be no pellet shortage this winter, as most people purchased the supplies they needed during the summer, leaving Latvian consumers in a relatively secure position.
“Even if the export market explodes, most Latvian consumers have already secured everything they need,” Palejs said.
LATbio was established in 2008. Its main objectives include promoting the use of biofuels, including wood, in the energy sector, supporting biofuel production and representing the interests of biofuel producers, thereby contributing to Latvia’s energy independence through the use of locally available resources.

Russia adapts a training missile to lead its ballistic onslaught of Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:08:21 UTC
15:08:21 KST

Russia adapts a training missile to lead its ballistic onslaught of Ukraine
- Russia uses repurposed RM48U training missiles in large numbers to sustain its missile attacks on Ukraine without depleting more accurate Iskander missiles.
- The less precise RM48Us cause significant civilian casualties, such as the deadly August strike on a Kyiv suburban railway platform.
- Ukraine faces critical defence shortages, urgently seeking US Patriot interceptors to counter Russia's escalating ballistic missile campaign this winter.
AI generated
LONDON/KYIV – The bodies of passengers strewn across a bloodied suburban railway platform near Kyiv in August bore grim testament to the escalating air war dominating the conflict in Ukraine.
They were among eight people killed in a barrage of Russian missiles that was mainly focused on industrial facilities in the Brovary district, where the station is located, according to local officials.
The attack that hit the railway wasn’t carried out by Russia’s main Iskander strike missile, Ukrainian investigators said, but by a less accurate weapon originally designed to serve as target practice for air defence crews.
Russia’s mass deployment of these repurposed training missiles, or RM48Us, has driven its aerial onslaught to record levels in recent months, official Ukrainian data seen by Reuters shows.
RM48Us made up more than half of the 228 ballistic and hypersonic missiles fired at Ukraine in July and early August, according to the figures compiled by military analysts at the General Prosecutor’s Office.
The scale of the RM48U deployment, which hasn’t been previously reported, helps show how Russia has been able to expand its attacks over the summer without running down its stocks of Iskanders and other primary strike missiles.
Moscow has been able to keep up a daily air barrage during a critical window in which Ukraine finds itself highly exposed: It has virtually exhausted its stocks of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapons in its arsenal capable of downing Russian ballistic missiles.
There is little clarity on when fresh supplies might arrive, with more Patriots being funnelled to the US military and its allies in the Gulf than to Ukraine.
Russia’s defence ministry didn’t respond to questions about its use of RM48Us and other missiles in Ukraine.
Moscow has denied intentionally harming civilians, saying it only targets military infrastructure.
On Aug 5, the day of the railway deaths, the defence ministry said it struck a logistics centre in Brovary that was being used to store drone components.
Firing large numbers of RM48Us serves as a way for Russia to drain any remaining Ukrainian interceptor stocks and attack lower-value targets without using up its precision strike missiles, according to Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at RUSI, a London-based defence think-tank.
“Their use allows the Russians to husband the more capable missiles they have, the Iskanders, but also the KN-23s and the Zircons, for winter when they would want to really lean into their ballistic missile campaign,” he said.
Indeed, as the RM48U attacks surged in July, the number of Iskanders fired fell to 38 from more than 100 the previous month, the Ukrainian data showed.
The war in Ukraine has entered yet a new phase.
With battle lines on the ground locked across a ferocious “kill zone”, both sides have launched intensifying air campaigns.
Russia has fired hundreds of ballistic missiles over the summer and is widely expected to pound critical infrastructure including heating and power sites this winter.
Ukraine, which has a far smaller arsenal of missiles, has unleashed hundreds of long-range drone attacks on Russian refineries, ships and ports.
July saw the deaths of at least 437 civilians in Ukraine, the largest toll recorded in a single month since the early months of the invasion, according to the United Nations, which pointed to missile and drone strikes as a key factor.
Russian civilian casualties, while far lower than in Ukraine, are also at record highs.
The Conflict Intelligence Team, an independent open-source investigation group, said 327 civilians were killed in Russia in the first seven months of 2026, compared with 145 in the same period in 2025.
Ballistic trajectory, high speeds
The RM48U – RM for “raketa mishen” or “missile target” – flies on a ballistic trajectory at high speeds, Ukraine’s prosecutor’s office and the country’s GUR military intelligence agency told Reuters.
But it is less powerful and accurate than the Iskander, Russia’s primary short-range ballistic missile, the prosecutor’s office said.
The Ukrainian missiles data shows this summer was the first confirmed time the munitions, which are fired from Russia’s S-400 air-defence systems, have been deployed in large numbers.
The prosecutors linked the RM48U and its lower precision to several strikes that have caused high civilian casualties in the last few months, including the Brovary district railway platform.
They said their military experts found that RM48Us deviate from their intended targets by around 300m on average and that their exploding warheads can unleash metal fragments over a large area.
Forensic investigators concluded the railway strike was conducted with an RM48U after analysing the crater near the rail line beside the platform, metal fragments and damage to the platform, trees and bodies, the office said.
Reuters couldn’t independently verify the Ukrainian findings.
Volodymyr Bihun, head of Brovary’s military administration, said the rail attack happened shortly after midnight.
Russia also fired a number of missiles that hit logistics facilities in the district, he said.
Overhead imagery obtained from commercial satellite company Planet Labs showed that a warehouse complex near the Kvitnevyi railway platform had been damaged.
Two plumes of smoke could be seen rising into the air.
In July, Russia fired the largest number of ballistic and hypersonic missiles in a single month since its 2022 full-scale invasion, according to the official Ukrainian data, which only includes strikes confirmed by on-the-ground analysis.
Of those 158 strikes, 87 were from RM48Us, the data showed.
The pace of the aerial assault has only intensified; there were 70 Russian ballistic and hypersonic strikes in the first eight days of August, the Ukrainian data showed, with 36 of them from RM48Us.
In August, the Ukrainian air force stopped publishing regular readouts of the number of missiles fired and shot down during enemy attacks.
It said the decision was taken to prevent Russia parading reports about the poor performance of Ukrainian air defences for propaganda purposes.
Russia strives to overwhelm depleted defences
Russia has a stockpile of about 100 Iskanders available, compared with 400 RM48Us, the US-based Institute for the Study of War estimated in August.
According to Ukraine’s GUR, the country also has smaller stocks of KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles and Zircon and Kinzhal hypersonic missiles, which can travel faster than five times the speed of sound.
RUSI’s Kaushal put Russia’s Iskander production at around 750 missiles a year. The solid rocket motors are a limiting factor, pushing Moscow to use the weapons judiciously, he said.
Kaushal said Russia could use the cheaper RM48U to attack lower-value and more easily struck targets such as food warehouses, which Ukrainian officials say have been systematically targeted and heavily damaged in recent weeks.
The GUR said Russia plans to more than double production of the RM48U to 480 missiles this year from 200 last year.
Ukraine has been urging the US and other Western allies to supply Patriots to replenish its defences, although production of the munition has failed to keep pace with spiking demand during the Iran war.
A senior US administration official said Washington has more than enough munitions to meet its strategic goals, adding that it must prioritise protecting its critical weapons systems and expanding production.
The US is exploring potential pathways for future defence industrial cooperation with Ukraine, although nothing has been decided, the official added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stressed his country’s dire need for Patriots just hours after the Aug 5 attacks, which struck Brovary and other targets in the Kyiv area and involved both Russian missiles and drones.
“Ballistic missile interceptors could have saved the lives of those killed today,” he said. REUTERS

SPK sets payment rules for 131 funds in liquidation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:06:51 UTC
15:06:51 KST

Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek (AA Photo)
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said measures to contain Türkiye’s fund market problems were sufficient, as regulators outlined how investors in 131 funds ordered into liquidation would be repaid.
“There is no widespread systemic risk,” Şimşek said on Sept. 18, adding that 90 percent of the market was functioning normally.
“We have quarantined the troubled segment,” he said.
The Capital Markets Board (SPK) assigned İşbank to oversee the six affected Tera Portföy funds. Ziraat Bank will handle funds run by A1 Capital Portföy, Atlas Portföy, Bulls Portföy, Hedef Portföy, Pardus Portföy and Pusula Portföy.
Media reports said the original 130 funds held more than 800 billion Turkish Liras and had over 500,000 investors. An additional Tera equity fund was later added to the liquidation list.
The intervention followed redemption defaults disclosed by Pusula and Tera, while Atlas reported payment delays at a money market fund.
Cash from asset sales and maturing investments will be paid to investors in proportion to their holdings, at intervals set by the banks. The banks will set the pace of sales according to investors’ interests, market depth and liquidity.
Amounts due from unfulfilled redemption orders through TEFAS, Türkiye’s electronic fund trading platform, will be recorded as fund debts and paid first.
Investor holdings must be reconciled with custody records within two business days of the rules taking effect. Reconciliation of the funds’ debts, receivables and permitted expenses must be completed within 10 business days of the SPK decision.
Liquidation must end by the first business day following three months from the announcement, unless the SPK extends the deadline.
The affected funds are closed to purchases and redemptions both on TEFAS and through other distribution channels.
Existing management fees will be payable to the banks after custody is transferred, and other permitted expenses will continue. Available cash may be invested in money market instruments pending payments.
The liquidation rules will be published on each fund’s page on the Public Disclosure Platform (KAP).
Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said four suspects, including fund executives, had been remanded in custody in an investigation into alleged fund and share-market manipulation following an SPK criminal complaint.
He said 51 people were barred from leaving the country and bank accounts and other assets linked to the case had been frozen.
In a separate case in Bakırköy, 16 suspects were remanded over alleged efforts to manipulate markets through social media, he said.
He also reported a separate order blocking access to 246 social media accounts.
The Financial Stability Committee, chaired by Şimşek, described the fund problems as “temporary and manageable” on Sept. 17.
The Central Bank pledged more funding through one-week repo auctions and lower collateral haircuts, while the banking regulator temporarily eased capital rules for listed banks’ share buybacks.
Şimşek said the banking system had no liquidity or asset-quality problems.
Emlak Katılım’s savings finance subsidiary has begun talks to acquire Katılımevim and Birevim, according to a stock exchange filing.
Şimşek said the process was intended to protect investors.
He also called for closer oversight of the growing nonbank financial sector and said the 10 million Turkish Lira threshold for qualified investor status could be reviewed.

Finance ministry sees no way to lower diesel excise duty despite soaring prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:05:00 UTC
15:05:00 KST

Finance ministry sees no way to lower diesel excise duty despite soaring prices
Diesel prices have risen 36 cents per liter in two weeks. Fuel retailers and hauliers are calling for a cut in excise duty, but the Ministry of Finance says the tight state budget rules this out.
Tiit Parik, head of Haanpaa, which is owned by French logistics group Samat, said rising diesel prices have made freight transport more expensive.
"For our company, fuel accounts for a third of all costs and when fuel prices change by as much as they have risen over the past six months, it is clear that no fuel company or transport company can absorb those costs. They have to be passed on to the end consumer through a fuel surcharge," Parik said.
Global fuel demand exceeded supply by 2.8 million barrels per day in August, while inventories remain low. In just two weeks, diesel prices on the global market have risen by 36 cents per liter due to the Strait of Hormuz crisis and the war in Ukraine.
Competition in Estonia is so strong that fuel stations have been unable to raise prices by the same amount.
"Excise duty rates are higher in Estonia than in Latvia and Lithuania, but prices are lower. That speaks for itself — prices should be much higher," said Alan Vaht, a member of Terminal's management board.
Vaht said excise duty should be cut to prevent higher diesel prices from feeding through to consumer prices.
"It should be cut to the minimum level, which would reduce the pump price by around 12.2 cents including VAT. The question is not whether cutting diesel excise duty would create additional demand in an already difficult fuel market. The question is whether the Estonian state wants to protect the competitiveness of Estonian companies," Vaht said.
Parik said that while Estonia suspended this year's planned excise duty increase in the spring, Sweden cut its rate.
"Our trucks operating in Sweden refuel there, so the excise duty and VAT go to Sweden and those liters do not generate revenue for the Estonian state budget," Parik said.
The government, however, says it cannot cut fuel excise duty.
"Over three months, that would amount to more than €50 million if we factor in gasoline. Our budget — and I think everyone is aware of the situation — simply does not allow for tax breaks like that at the moment," said Evelyn Liivamägi, deputy secretary general at the Ministry of Finance.
Higher fuel prices have also not resulted in additional VAT revenue.
"If you compare the first half of 2025 with the first half of 2026, in both cases around €60 million in VAT was collected from fuel. Ultimately, households have a limited number of euros to spend. If they spend more on fuel, they spend less somewhere else," Liivamägi said.
Situation difficult for farmers
Diesel is also a major input cost in agriculture, with high prices particularly noticeable during spring and fall fieldwork.
Although agricultural businesses registered with Estonia's Agricultural Registers and Information Board (PRIA) can use specially marked blue diesel, which is 50 cents per liter cheaper due to lower excise duty, steadily rising prices over the past year have left farmers concerned about the future.
The Sargvere agricultural cooperative uses diesel to cultivate land and produce feed for its 400 dairy cows.
"The average price delivered to us has been around 60 cents per liter. The latest order will probably be around €1.30. So the price has more than doubled," said Toomas Uusmaa, a member of the cooperative's management board.
"We still try to get everything done and keep land cultivation to a minimum. But grain drying and producing feed have to be done and there's no way around it. You just keep going as long as you can and as long as you can afford it," he added.

Tallinn Zoo's binturongs attempted multiple escapes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:04:00 UTC
15:04:00 KST

Tallinn Zoo's binturongs attempted multiple escapes
Young binturongs at Tallinn Zoo staged several successful escape attempts from their enclosure, forcing the Tropical House to close to visitors. The pair, Maru and Maimu, have now been moved to a new location where slipping away won't be nearly as easy.
Over the span of a couple of weeks, Maru and Maimu managed to break out of their enclosure four times.
Their first escape came at the end of August, when an Ironman event was taking place in Tallinn's Rocca al Mare district and a large stage had been set up near the zoo.
"It was a very noisy weekend, and quite a few animals were disturbed by it. I don't know whether it was because conditions were somehow unfavorable — the stage was pointed toward us, the wind carried the sound our way," said Tiiu Ramst, senior wildlife keeper at Tallinn Zoo.
"In any case, it was an unfortunate coincidence that the noise was much louder than expected. And so, for the first time, they decided to escape at night, which is when they're most active. The event also ran late into the night. Most likely they went looking for a quieter place."
The first time, the animals were quickly retrieved. The next attempts were far more troublesome.
"The worst was the second escape. One of them — Maru — decided to climb onto the end of a ventilation pipe high up near the ceiling. And it's above an enclosure with a roof slanted at 45 degrees, where no one was willing to climb," Ramst said.
With no other options, the Tropical House was closed and staff waited for the animal to change its mind. On the third day, hunger finally coaxed the bearcat down. To curb the siblings' escape drive, an extra barrier was added to the enclosure and the electric fence was given more charge. But even that didn't help.
"Possibly because of stress, they were very determined to escape and took the risk — jumping onto the rock ledge so that their bellies touched the electric fence. They have very thick fur, and it seems the fence didn't affect them through it," Ramst explained.
After the fourth successful escape, the decision was made to move the siblings into an empty adjacent enclosure covered with mesh. The animals have tried to break out from there as well, but so far without success. Accustomed to sleeping cuddled up with their parents, the youngsters are deeply offended by the change.
"They're very sad. At first they sat inside for several days and didn't want to come into the enclosure at all. And when they finally did, they only climbed along the edge of the rock, tried to push themselves through the mesh, and got stuck between the rock and the net," Ramst said.
According to the keeper, the teenage binturongs are now beginning to accept their new home — and since they are about to reach adulthood, they would have had to move out from their parents sooner or later anyway.
The binturong (Arctictis binturong), also known as the bearcat, is a medium-sized, tree-dwelling mammal native to the tropical rainforests of South and Southeast Asia.

Burning the bard: 'Macbeth' defies fiery curse as Lisbon's Teatro D. Maria II reopens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:02:46 UTC
15:02:46 KST

The D. Maria II theatre reopens with "Macbeth", the Shakespearean tragedy being performed when a 1964 fire destroyed the building. Now the Bard of Avon's "cursed play" is being revived by Pedro Penim, this time with real flames on stage.
After almost four years closed, the National Theatre D. Maria II, on Rossio in Lisbon, is finally reopening its doors after the biggest renovation in decades. It is doing so with a "cursed play" and with tickets almost sold out.
"Macbeth" by William Shakespeare, which was on stage at the National Theatre D. Maria II when a fire destroyed the building in 1964, is the production chosen for the reopening.
It is a deliberate choice by artistic director and director Pedro Penim and serves as a provocation in the face of the many productions that have been plagued by accidents. In the show he signs, real fire is used on stage in a symbolic gesture, recalling the tragedy that reduced the theatre to ashes.
"It was a kind of trauma in the theatre's history, it was a very defining moment, and this play, which is believed to be a cursed play, full of superstitions, was never staged again," says Pedro Penim, director and artistic director of the National Theatre D. Maria II, in an interview with Euronews.
The Shakespearean tragedy has, over the centuries, accumulated stories of disasters backstage: injured actors, props swapped for real weapons, spectacular falls and deaths on stage.
"Whenever this play is staged, some misfortune seems to happen. So I decided to challenge not only fate but also to draw a parallel with the theatre's own history, given that we are reopening as the National Theatre D. Maria II celebrates its 180th anniversary," the director adds.
But putting together a production of this scale did not come without setbacks. The initial intention was to use the translation by Brazilian poet Manuel Bandeira, the same used by the Rey Colaço-Robles Monteiro company in the ill-fated 1964 staging. However, the holders of the poet's rights never responded to the requests and Pedro Penim found himself 'cornered' into translating Shakespeare's text himself.
The translation signed by Penim will now be published as a book. "The idea was to find a Portuguese that retained the decasyllabic verse while at the same time looking for words that would not be inaccessible to a contemporary Portuguese audience and, in that way, to find something that did not lose the poetry."
As for the staging, it seeks to leave the work open to interpretation by audiences. "It is a work that allows thousands of readings." However, there is an inevitable parallel that connects this tragedy to the 21st century. "There is a dimension linked to the idea of fascination with evil, the way evil shows itself off, struts around our society; it is present in our lives when we turn on the television, look at our mobile phone, in people's conversations. Suddenly, evil is no longer ashamed to show itself," Penim explains.
"The seductive language Macbeth uses is a kind of poetry that enchants, but which at the same time carries a very significant weight in terms of the execution and the imagining of the crime," reflects the director.
This production also pays tribute to the theatre itself: Joana Sousa's set reproduces the façade of the emblematic building on Rossio, and one of the characters is Queen Maria II herself.
The refurbishment work on the building has also improved the technical and artistic conditions of the main auditorium, breathing new life into "Macbeth". The stage now rotates and can be raised. There have also been upgrades to lighting, sound and stage machinery.
"It is a play that has been staged many times with many different visions, many different casts and very diverse directors, as well as very different set designs. In this case, we wanted to bring this proposal right to the heart of the National Theatre D. Maria II and turn the theatre itself into the set after so many years in which this play was, in fact, not staged or not presented on this stage," Pedro Penim explains.
To give substance to this two-and-a-half-hour curse, Pedro Penim has opted for a cast he has worked with before, with particular emphasis on the leading pair. In the role of Macbeth is José Raposo, "one of the country's most beloved actors", as the director is keen to point out, who plays one of the greatest villains in drama.
"It is a production that carries a lot of weight, also because of the symbolism of this whole bridge that Pedro Penim has built with the fact that the theatre burned down in 1964. And now, after these works, it has that charge that makes us feel an even greater sense of responsibility," the actor tells Euronews.
Taking on the role of Lady Macbeth is actor Bárbara Branco, who drives the plot. "Technically, it is a hugely ambitious production. Pedro [Penim] is making full use of all the features the theatre has, the platforms, fire, water, etc. We are making use of everything, and I think that technical difficulty means the responsibility goes beyond the play itself, beyond these characters. Beyond the reopening of the theatre."
The cast also includes Ana Coimbra, Ana Tang, Bernardo de Lacerda, Hugo Van Der Ding, João Grosso, José Neves, June João, Sandro Feliciano, Stela and Vítor Silva Costa.
The anticipation surrounding the return to the Garret auditorium at the D. Maria II is already visible at the box office: with a season longer than usual, tickets have sold out quickly, leaving only seats with restricted visibility.
"Macbeth" premieres on Friday 18 September and will run until 31 October.

Oman oil escape route: How ship-to-ship transfers work — despite big risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:02:08 UTC
15:02:08 KST

Oman oil escape route: How ship-to-ship transfers work — despite big risks
Oman’s Sohar port is becoming a popular spot for ship-to-ship oil transfers amid continued Hormuz blockade.
Saudi Arabia’s oil exports have been disrupted after Iran-aligned Houthis damaged its key East-West pipeline, which helped circumvent the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz – a global oil chokepoint.
With the strait in effect closed and Bab al-Mandeb falling under Houthi control, Riyadh has been forced to find ways to export its oil. It is now increasingly offering crude to buyers through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman.
As commercial ships are increasingly refusing to pass through the strait due to the conflict, Saudi Arabia is transporting the crude to Oman’s Sohar port, located just outside the strait, where the oil is transferred from Saudi tankers to others.
Iran closed the strait, through which nearly a fifth of pre-war global energy passed, in response to the United States-Israeli war, and has used the waterway as leverage in the talks.
Media reports suggest that the Hormuz closure and rising oil prices have pushed the US and its allies in the region to adopt shadow tactics, much like what Iran has been doing for years to export its own crude.
So, what are ship-to-ship transfers, and are they safe?
Where are these ports?
Two ports that have become central to bypassing the Strait of Hormuz are Sohar and another off the coast of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.
Sohar is a major deepwater industrial hub that handles substantial bulk cargo, petrochemicals and container traffic. Its strategic position has allowed international shipping lines to bypass the narrow Gulf bottleneck while maintaining direct overland connectivity to Arabian Peninsula markets.
The UAE’s Port of Fujairah is situated on the country’s eastern coast and serves as one of the world’s largest bunkering and crude oil storage hubs. Its open-ocean anchorage provides a crucial offshore staging area for ship-to-ship transfers and energy exports outside the Strait of Hormuz.
These ports are close to the boundaries drawn by the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, the new Iranian body established to manage the Strait of Hormuz.
The Iranian authorities have attacked ships that they say use unauthorised routes – the southern route of the strait, closer to Omani waters – to transit the waterway.
The US military has reportedly been assisting scores of these secretive ship-to-ship oil transfers to keep Gulf energy exports flowing, starting from early May this year.
What are ship-to-ship transfers and how do they happen?
Ship-to-ship (STS) transfers are maritime exchanges where cargo — read crude oil or liquefied natural gas (LNG) here — is transferred directly between two vessels at sea.
STS transfers serve as a critical logistical bridge when direct port access is blocked or restricted.
The companies need to undertake meticulous coordination amid favourable sea conditions to prevent spills and collisions.
One vessel, often the larger ship, maintains a steady course or anchors. The manoeuvring ship approaches slowly, followed by hulls brought parallel, protected by pneumatic rubber fenders deployed along the ship sides to absorb impacts.
Their trackers are turned off to maintain secrecy and avoid detection. After some mandatory safety checks, the discharging ship’s pumps move the oil through the connected hoses while monitoring pressure and weather.
Who is engaging in ship-to-ship transfers and why?
Riyadh relied on the East-West 1,200km (746-mile) pipeline, which connects the kingdom’s main oil-producing fields in the east of the country with Yanbu port on the Red Sea coast in the west, to export oil.
With its closure after recent drone attacks, Riyadh’s first option becomes “shipping more crude from its Gulf terminals through the Strait of Hormuz, including ship-to-ship transfers outside the strait, such as Sohar in Oman,” said Rishi Rajanala, research specialist in Oil Americas at LSEG Data & Analytics.
“Gulf producers have already been moving part of their exports this way, but volumes depend on tanker availability, insurance and freight costs, and remain well below pre-war levels,” he added.
Starting this month, Hormuz-route exports have “edged higher, over 2 mb/d [million barrels per day] in the first two weeks, roughly 1 mb/d above August,” said Rahul Choudhary, VP Upstream Research, Rystad Energy.
He added that the uptick is expected to rise further this month as “already evident in Aramco offering additional loadings to Asian refiners out of Sohar”.
“Saudi Arabia can lean further on dark tanker activity in the coming days to offset Yanbu losses,” he added, referring to Saudi Arabia losing access to the Red Sea for shipping.
But it isn’t only Saudi Arabia. Reports from independent trackers and the media have also identified Kuwait and Qatar as relying on similar tactics at times to transit cargoes past the Strait of Hormuz.
Are ship-to-ship transfers safe?
Ship-to-ship transfers are relatively dangerous, especially when being taken up in shadows — and also inefficient compared with standard shipping by vessels.
Experts note that unregulated STS transfers often rely on ageing vessels with poor hull maintenance, uninspected hoses, and turned-off AIS tracking without insurance coverage.
TankerTrackers, a platform that monitors global oil shipments, said last week that ship-to-ship transfers are rising. “Over the past 14 days, there were 7.15 million barrels per day being exchanged,” the monitor said, quoting AIS numbers and satellite imagery.
The monitor added that it represents an increase of 56 percent compared with the previous month.
What’s the advantage of ship-to-ship transfers?
Despite the risks, ship-to-ship transfers also carry an upside in a volatile landscape like the Middle East today.
Ships and tankers belonging to major transport companies are unwilling to enter the Strait of Hormuz because of the threat of attacks from either Iran or the US. At the same time, countries in the Gulf need to get as much oil and gas out through the Strait of Hormuz as possible.
So these countries, in effect, bear the risk, sending their tankers and ships, often with trackers switched off, just across the Strait of Hormuz, where traditional oil and gas carriers wait in safer waters. These carriers then ferry the oil and gas to markets in China, India, South Korea, Japan and elsewhere.
Who provides insurance for such ship-to-ship transfers?
For traditional insurers, ship-to-ship transfers can be “particularly complicated”, said Oscar Seikaly, CEO of the NSI Insurance Group.
Any loss could involve the physical vessels and their cargo, but also “pollution and collision liabilities, cargo insurance, war-risk cover,” and other factors, he said. “Underwriters may also impose navigational warranties, security conditions, additional war premiums or restrictions,” he told Al Jazeera.
However, he pointed out, “most of the oil that is being moved belongs to the national oil companies of the respective country”. Therefore, Seikaly said, many rely on sovereign-backed self-insurance arrangements and private insurance markets.
“During wartime or other high-risk disruptions, insurers are unlikely to provide broad cover to include ship-to-ship transfers,” he said. “As a result, a significant share of the risk may ultimately remain with the producing country rather than being transferred fully to commercial insurers.”

Could Chinese explorers have settled New Zealand before the Maori?
Mainstream academics and Maori groups voice scepticism, but researchers say acknowledging lesser-known history could alter national identity
For generations, the narrative of New Zealand’s human settlement has held that Polynesian voyagers – the ancestors of the Maori – arrived and settled the islands in the 13th century, followed by European explorers in the 17th century.
This timeline underpins New Zealand’s history and its political model. The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between the British Crown and about 540 Maori chiefs, served as New Zealand’s founding document, paving the way for Britain to claim sovereignty and incorporate the country into the British Empire.
Outside the halls of universities and government institutions, two independent researchers are on a quest to discover pre-Maori Chinese presence in New Zealand.

UK NATO interoperability roadmap will remain secret
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:00:25 BST
15:00:25 KST

The UK’s NATO Interoperability Roadmap has been completed and is already being implemented, but the Government says it will not be published because it contains information on defence planning and capability development.
The status of the document was confirmed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked when the roadmap would be made public.
Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard said the document had in fact been completed at the beginning of the year and approved by the then Minister for the Armed Forces, Al Carns.
Pollard said: “The UK’s NATO Interoperability Roadmap was completed in January 2026 and approved by the then Minister for the Armed Forces, Al Carns MP. Implementation commenced immediately thereafter.”
The roadmap stems from the Strategic Defence Review, which directed Defence to establish a plan for deeper interoperability with NATO allies and to develop shared approaches and standards.
According to Pollard, the UK document is aligned with NATO’s own Interoperability Plan and is intended to provide a framework for improving the ability of British forces to operate alongside allied militaries.
He said: “It provides Defence with a framework to improve the Armed Forces’ ability to operate effectively alongside NATO Allies through common standards, digital integration, training, exercises and capability development.”
The Government has, however, ruled out publishing the document.
Pollard said: “The UK’s NATO Interoperability Roadmap contains information relating to Defence planning and capability development and will therefore not be published.”
He added: “The House may be assured, however, that the SDR’s ‘NATO First’ principle remains central to both the Roadmap and its implementation.”
The answer clarifies that the roadmap is not awaiting completion or approval, but has been in implementation since January. Its work covers areas including common standards, digital systems, training, exercises and the development of military capabilities intended to make British forces more readily interoperable with other NATO members.

Revealed: How Russia use mobile ‘super-app’ Max to spy on its citizens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:00:13 UTC
15:00:13 KST

Over the past 18 months, tens of millions of Russians have been forced to install a new app on their phones – a violet-blue button designed for messaging and payments, called Max.
Authorities have touted it as a patriotic alternative to Telegram and WhatsApp; Russian glitterati have promoted it in rap videos and comic routines. This summer, it became the country’s most-used messaging app.
It is a product of VKontakte, the Russian social media company, which is deeply entangled with the Russian state. The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, reportedly owns an indirect stake in Max.
Max is Russia’s version of a “super-app,” combining an ecosystem of services into a single platform. It is a container for a number of “mini-apps” that now facilitate everyday life in Russia – banking apps, a messaging service that aims to replace Telegram, and apps for essential government services. The best-known super-app in the world is WeChat, China’s everything platform which facilitates the state’s social controls.
But while WeChat was developed over decades, in step with China’s other internet controls, Max has been imposed on a population that once had mostly-free internet access.
Now, forensic research has revealed a fuller picture of Max’s powerful surveillance capabilities. These amount to a “backdoor” into its entire mini-app ecosystem on every user’s device, said Roya Ensafi, an associate professor of computer science at the University of Michigan.
“We have studied Russia’s escalation of internet control for the past decade,” said Ensafi. “What Max provides is the cleverest and also the scariest tactic by authoritarian governments” to surveil their citizens.
Max is “a blueprint any government can follow” towards digital authoritarianism, said Ensafi.
It represents the cutting edge of what governments such as Iran, Kazakhstan and India may soon try to achieve.
Ensafi’s team were able to download the version of the app used in Russia. They found that Max can screenshot users’ devices – and the contents of its mini-apps – without their knowledge. It can access all the information stored in these mini-apps, their messages and payments. It can impersonate its users without them knowing.
It can even inject code into mini-apps – which would mean, said Ensafi, that the Russian government could use Max to launch cyberattacks.
Their research adds new clarity into an ongoing debate on Max’s surveillance capabilities. Crucially, said Ensafi, it cannot break into apps like Telegram and WhatsApp, if users have these installed. However, Russia has banned both.
Many Russians working in or around state institutions have in effect been forced to use Max. Officials and public-sector employees, university students, teachers and even schoolchildren have all faced pressure to move their communications on to the platform.
One schoolteacher in Moscow said staff at their school were ordered to switch to Max after instructions from the city authorities.
“The school director called us in last March and told us directly: from now on, everything is on Max. That included chats with parents, sending out homework and other school communication,” the teacher said.
“There isn’t really an option to say no, so in the end you just use the app,” they added.
Daniil, a university student in St Petersburg, said he reluctantly downloaded Max shortly before the start of the academic year after being told students would be denied access to university buildings or dormitories without a QR code generated through the app.
He said he had concerns about the app’s security and privacy, but felt he had little choice if he wanted to continue accessing campus.
Among Russia’s elite, use of Max often appears to be largely performative, with Telegram and Signal still widely used for day-to-day communication, according to several well-connected figures and prominent businesspeople.
One person in the Kremlin’s inner circle said he and several friends had bought second phones solely to install Max, while continuing to use their main devices and preferred messaging apps as before.
“It’s all for show. No one in politics really uses it,” the person said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Max has yet to replace Telegram as a major source of news for Russians. Public channels – used by media outlets, bloggers and officials to broadcast news and commentary to large audiences – remain far less developed on Max, where only a small number have built audiences comparable to the biggest channels on Telegram.
Several Max users contacted by the Guardian said the app closely resembles Telegram, long Russia’s most popular messaging platform, in its design and functionality, but concerns about privacy and surveillance were widespread.
“Using Max feels like you never quite know who else might be watching,” said Nikolai, a 34-year-old consultant in Moscow.
While the app looked modern and slick, Nikolai said there was always something slightly sinister about using it.
“You end up using it more and more because the alternatives are becoming harder to access. But it still doesn’t feel right.”
Russia’s success in rapidly pushing out Max should be a “wake-up call”, said Ensafi. China reached its current state of digital authoritarianism over the course of 35 years. But Russia has imposed these sweeping restrictions – shepherding people on to a state-controlled internet – in just a decade.
“The world is changing, the infrastructure of private communication is changing – and the assault by authoritarian governments is very aggressive,” she said.
Max and VKontakte were approached for comment.

Global leaders urged to join initiative to fight extreme inequality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:00:11 UTC
15:00:11 KST

More than 1,500 academics and economists from 100-plus countries are urging global leaders to join an initiative against extreme inequality, calling current unfairness “a policy choice that can be reversed”.
Before the UN general assembly in New York next week, the experts have signed an open letter backing the International Panel on Inequality (IPI).
High-profile signatories include the former US Treasury secretary Janet Yellen, the Nobel prize-winner Daron Acemoglu, and a slew of other prominent economists, including Thomas Piketty, Mariana Mazzucato and Jayati Ghosh.
In the letter, they say: “Extreme concentrations of income and wealth translate into undemocratic concentrations of power, unravelling trust in our societies and polarising our politics.”
Set up with the support of Spain, South Africa, Brazil and Norway and championed by the UN secretary general, António Guterres, the IPI aims to mirror the International Panel on Climate Change, which assesses the state of the climate emergency and makes recommendations.
It will be chaired by the Nobel-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz, who said he hoped it could become “the world’s leading authority on the issue”.
He said: “It is news to no one that the gap between the richest and the poorest in most countries is large and growing. The interrelated impacts of the inequality crisis are affecting the lives of many, with significant political, economic, social and environmental consequences playing out across the globe.”
The signatories of the letter suggest the IPI could work towards a “shared scientific consensus” on the nature and scale of international inequality, as well as pointing the way to potential policy solutions.
It would bring together leading experts, partner governments and multilateral institutions to produce regular reports and seek to raise the profile of inequality as a global issue.
Experts are concerned about the gap between wealthy and poor countries, and inequalities within individual economies.
Ghosh, a professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts Amherst in the US, said: “India’s experience tells us everything we need to know about why an International Panel on Inequality is needed. One of the world’s fastest-growing economies is also one of its most unequal and its extraordinary wealth sits alongside profound deprivation.”
The World Bank said recently that “barring a miracle” the 2020s would be a “lost decade” for many developing countries, which – aside from India and China – had failed to narrow the gap with the industrialised world.
Former global leaders including Germany’s Olaf Scholz, Ireland’s Leo Varadkar and New Zealand’s Helen Clark also backed the idea of the IPI in a separate statement this week.
In the UK, the government has not yet said whether it is prepared to join the IPI, but the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has indicated a willingness to work with other countries on shared international challenges – notwithstanding the reluctance of Donald Trump’s US to participate in such initiatives.
Andy Burnham will attend the UN general assembly next week, marking one of his most significant appearances on the global stage since arriving in Downing Street in July. The prime minister is expected to meet Trump on the sidelines of the New York gathering.
Stewart Wood of the Foreign Office, said: “Changing the way our economy works so that it is fairer and more productive is not just about what we do at home. It also requires that we work in partnership with other countries and international institutions to strengthen the global economy.
“That’s why this government will work with allies to build the coalition we need for economic change – to boost global growth, combat inequality, make our international financial institutions more effective, and back more coordinated development support and climate action.”
The government also recently reaffirmed Labour’s promise to restore the UK’s aid spending to 0.7% of national income, although no timetable has yet been given. The pledge was in the party’s 2024 manifesto but Keir Starmer subsequently cut aid sharply to fund the rising defence budget.

Watson said he was “terrifically excited” by the new role as Palantir’s senior vice-president and highlighted two of the contracts that are in dispute when he said he wanted to help Palantir speed up NHS diagnosis, treatment and discharge from hospitals and enable “our police to crack crimes and root out corruption”. ‘Like a Bond villain’s lair’: I climbed the Dolomites to the world’s most spectacular mountain hut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:00:10 UTC
15:00:10 KST

‘I think my boots are falling apart!” shouts Nigel just as we hit the pinnacles, a whole range of them jutting up and out from the mountainside, all thrillingly tall, spiky and knobbled. Through them we painstakingly step, fingers aching in gloves, heads sweating in helmets – squashing up narrow chimneys, squeezing through mighty boulders and inching along slender ledges on a twisting path that’s only just discernible through swathes of sharp white scree.
I know how Nigel’s boots are feeling: the going is far harder than I was expecting. This is only the first day of our annual trip to the Dolomites, a vast range of breathtaking sawtooth peaks in northern Italy, but my head’s already full of the thought I have every year as we start out: “If only you’d got fitter.”
But it should be worth all the scrapes, bumps, scares and sweat. Somewhere up ahead, hopefully not too far, is Rifugio Passo Santner, or Santnerpass Hut, a spectacular mountain refuge that, as everyone who sits near my desk at work knows, has been obsessing me ever since I first saw a picture of it eight months ago.
Allowing you to stay deep in the mountains for days on end, the high-altitude Dolomites huts we overnight at all have their charms, from hearty food to giddying views to a generous way with the grappa. But in terms of appearance, they tend to fall into two not particularly pulse-quickening camps: stone block or cuckoo clock. Although you’re almost always overjoyed to see them, none could ever pass for a Bond villain’s lair, however much grappa you’ve had.
Yet that is exactly what Santnerpass Hut resembles. Perched on top of a sheer cliff, this elongated triangle encased in a gleaming wrapper of galvanised steel looks like a giant Toblerone still in its foil – an eyepopping hit of modernity, originality and innovation in a place where tradition usually dictates more of the same.
After one final push, the five of us scramble up on to the summit and there it is just ahead, side on and glowing silver in the late afternoon sun, like a star that has touched down on Earth to enjoy the stunning views of the surrounding peaks with the rest of us, up at the bracing height of 2,734m.
“Welcome!” says the bartender as we enter. “You made it. Well done!” With the customary relief – if not actual jubilation – that follows a tough climb finally ending, we ease off our backpacks, gloves and boots then look around, slowly realising that Santnerpass Hut isn’t just a treat for the eyes from the outside.
Inside, what you first notice is the unbroken parade of huge windows wrapping around the refuge’s front and flanks. This doesn’t just turn every spot of the roomy ground floor into a light-filled observation point. It also means the hut achieves passive heating since it’s effectively one big solar collector. So there’s no need for log-devouring stoves. That’s quite an achievement at ground level; at more than 2km up, with no road access, it’s verging on miraculous.
Then there’s the wood. It’s blond and everywhere. Guests are basically cocooned within a spellbinding timber tapestry that casts everything in a warm yellow glow, quite a novelty to anyone used to the dingy two-watt corridors and bedrooms of most refuges.
The flooring is larch, the restaurant furnishings maple and the load-bearing A-frame spruce, its hefty angular joists exposed on the sundeck, where we soon find ourselves sinking well-earned ice-cold drinks and marvelling at this beacon of sustainable architecture.
There are other things to marvel at. Off in the distance, piercing up through an immense blanket of cloud, the lofty peaks of the Latemar group are catching the last rays of the sun, turning pink, orange and purple in a ravishing Dolomites phenomenon known as the enrosadira, triggered by calcium and magnesium in the rock. “This place is incredible,” says Donnie, sipping an Aperol spritz. “I’ve never been anywhere like it in my life.”
Santnerpass Hut was built in 1956 but in the last decade or so was taken over, closed and rebuilt, finally opening its generous glass doors in 2023. Designed by alpine specialists Senoner Tammerle Architects, the new refuge is not just meant to please the eye: the shape lets it shed thick snow and deflect howling winds.
There are more surprises when we take our pre-dinner showers. Not only does the wood here give way to zesty yellow laminated panels that wouldn’t look out of place in a chic nightclub, the showerheads also actually stay pointing at your body for the full three minutes of hot water a token gets you.
Dinner, however, may have been the biggest surprise of all. It was completely vegetarian – a shock for all of us and a treat for veggies Sam and Nigel. No goulash, no ragu, no pork chops. Instead, out of the kitchen came herb-sprinkled lentils with asparagus, radish and onion, pea and mint soup, then beetroot dumplings on a rich bean, tomato and yellow pepper broth, washed down with superb local wine in actual wine glasses and finished off with creme brulee.
“A delicious and nutritious meal,” said Sam, running his spoon round his plate. “What an eye-opener. A win-win for hiker and planet.”
Curfew was at 10pm but the restaurant was clearing out anyway. This may have been due to the fact that, in high spirits after our action-packed day, we had taken the hut’s guitar off the wall and treated everyone to that Proclaimers Alpine classic Sunshine on Leith, managing to get a singalong going with the very up-for-it, very international audience.
The refuge sleeps 4o in 16 rooms. Ours was a spacious affair with bunkbeds, a dainty dormer window and two large cubbyholes each, one for your bag, the other for your stuff – so much more useful than the usual pointless wardrobes and drawers that no one ever unpacks into, since you’ll be gone in a hurry at the crack of dawn.
We reached Santnerpass Hut via the König Laurin cable car, 22 miles (35km) from Bolzano, gateway to the Dolomites. After that, it’s a rising, fairly straight line to the refuge, a two-to-three-hour hike through loose scree, then boulders and pinnacles. But be warned: the last section is a via ferrata, meaning there’s a metal cable for you to clip your harness to, and grab hold of as you reach trickier, more treacherous passages. It’s not for beginners.
I’d heard, though, that there was another route and, keen to take it back down to the cable car, asked at reception. “Yes, there’s another way,” said Romina Huber, who co-owns and runs the hut with her husband (and chef) Michel Perathoner. “It’s not a via ferrata and it’s super beautiful.”
She wasn’t kidding. First it took us past the Vajolet towers, dramatic spires that lure climbers from all over the world. Then we swung right on to a winding path of fine white scree that rises sharply through meadows full of edelweiss, saxifrage, dwarf pine and boulders, leading to bulging cliffs and eventually the Coronelle Pass, an astonishing vantage point at 2,360m.
“Well, that was a walk and a half,” said Mac as we descended in the cable car 30 minutes later, exhausted after the final knee-popping trudge down from the pass on timber-pinned switchbacks. “My boots,” said Nigel, lifting his feet to let us see a rip in one and a sole flapping off the other, “have completely had it.”
Santnerpass Hut starts at €105pp per night, including breakfast and four-course vegetarian dinner
Hutiquette: the mountain hut code
Mountain huts may occasionally be rather luxurious these days, but their original function, still relevant, is survival. There are, as you might expect, several very sensible codes that make great use of words like “respect”, “other users”, and “environment”. My own code is no less worthy and comes from hard-won experience.
No complaining
Huts are not hotels. If there’s a problem, go sort it out. Certainly, never complain about snoring, even when you are convinced it is about to trigger an avalanche. I once did, only to be informed, rather too forcefully, that is was me doing the snoring, an outrageous lie that triggered grunts of approval from other grumpy insomniacs. Gel ear plugs work well.
Share
It’s sometimes hard to drop the urban habit of self-assertion to ensure survival. One night in a Corsican hut with a shared sleeping platform, an obnoxious Brit in a down bag shoved all the other sleepers into a pile at one end of the bench, claiming later that he was “dreaming of being pushed”. I pray never to run into him again.
Clean up after yourself
… and take your rubbish home. The British Mountain Bothy Code has a good reminder on this point. I’d go even further and say, try to leave absolutely no trace at all. Visiting one treasured wild swimming spot recently, I found the scorch mark of a campfire. Whoever it was had not left any rubbish, and there was nothing to mark their visit, except that dreaded black spot, as if Blind Pew had delivered a death sentence.
The hut is for everyone
I once cycled to a remote Icelandic hut and found it blissfully empty of people. Lighting the fire, I prepared my simple meal, and apart from wishing I had packed a beer, looked forward to a night of splendid isolation. Then a large group of locals arrived. I felt my heart sink. My solitary bliss was gone. They sat down, gave me a beer, and two hours later, after helping to eat their huge delicious feast, I felt like I’d joined a tribe. When a hut generates that kind of gang conviviality, it’s uplifting.
Look after others
In Scandinavia, this is a social habit that is deeply embedded. You turn up in a hut in winter and there are logs because the last visitors left them for you. You cut your finger and they all have the plaster that you forgot to bring. The Norwegian Mountain Code has a list of essential reminders.
Kevin Rushby

‘Gateways to heaven’: readers’ favourite trips in Europe’s mountains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:00:10 UTC
15:00:10 KST

All the fun of the funicular in Switzerland
No doubt your first thought on hearing the words “double-decker” is of a bus. But in the Swiss village of Stans, an old wooden funicular carriage ascends to the station, where a double-decker cable car awaits. Inside, a spiral staircase leads you to an open upper viewing deck. At the summit, the views back to Lucerne are superb, and there are alpine marmots to spot too. There was a wedding ceremony going on at the summit on our trip! 
Martin
Liechtenstein’s Route 66
Steinbock, marmot and elderflower jam are in abundance on Liechtenstein’s Route 66 track – a  multi-day hike that is popular with locals, but little known to others. The route traverses the Drei Schwestern (the Three Sisters), where you’ll experience white knuckles and lush valley views. After an easy 5km hike, you land at the first mountain hut, where a succulent homemade three-course dinner awaits you. Befriend the other walkers over a game of cards, as golden hour lights up the mountains.
Inez
Picturesque French Pyrenees
Luz Saint Sauveur in the French Pyrenees is the gateway to heaven. Whether it be by bike, car, motorbike or on foot, stunning surroundings, wildlife-a-plenty and quaint French shops await you at this picturesque market town. Eat the local saucisson, drink the jurançon white wine, marvel at the blue skies in the shadows of the legendary Tour de France Cols, jump in canyons and be merry with the surroundings. Simply beautiful and fun for all ages.
Will
High on the hog in Donegal
For mountain scenery without Alpine crowds, head to north-west Donegal. Errigal gets the attention, but don’t overlook flat-topped Muckish, whose name comes from the Irish for “pig’s back”. Drive the small roads around the Poisoned Glen and through Glenveagh national park, where each bend reveals another reason to stop. Allow far longer than the satnav suggests: our best moments came from pulling over for an unexpected view rather than racing between sights. Pack walking shoes and a picnic, then reward yourself afterwards in a cosy pub. Here, a mountain day can include Atlantic beaches and a well-earned pint.
Niamh Kerr
The quiet side of Italy’s Dolomites
The Brenta Dolomites seem to go strangely unnoticed, while the main Dolomites heave with Instagrammers. We based ourselves in Pinzolo, an alpine town an hour north of Lake Garda, then took the lift from Madonna di Campiglio for a three-day hut-to-hut trek, tackling two via ferrata routes across knife-edge ridges and limestone spires. Rifugio Agostini was the highlight: a warm welcome and hearty mountain food after a hard day’s climbing, with jagged peaks filling every window. We descended into the town of Molveno for a well-earned aperitivo by the lake.
Ben Bryant
A spectacular climb in Kosovo
After exploring Kosovo’s historic monasteries and wartime memorials, we escaped to the Sharr mountains national park, a 40-minute drive south of Prizren. The road winds through the spectacular Zhupa valley and follows the bubbling Lumbardhi river through its steep-sided gorge. At Prevallë, we left the car and began what turned out to be a strenuous climb over rocky paths and grassy slopes. We kept expecting the summit to appear, but every turn revealed another, until we finally reached our destination and were met with spectacular mountain views. Afterwards, we rewarded ourselves at Hotel Krojet with coffee and a reviving glass of raki. 
Roy Messenger
Peaceful paths above Lake Como
This spring, my partner and I hiked the Via dei Monti Lariani, a 78-mile (125km) trail through the mountains on the western shore of Lake Como between Cernobbio and Sorico. Skirting the border between Italy and the Swiss canton of Ticino, the route passes through mountain pastures with views towards the Alps, and remote villages shaped by a history of cross-border smuggling. The accommodation is a highlight, ranging from Alpine rifugios to agriturismi, where we sampled regional specialities, including polenta uncia, polenta with local cheese and butter, and pizzoccheri, buckwheat pasta with cabbage and potatoes. Quiet trails, excellent food and complex history made it an especially rewarding route.
Ross Cameron
Grand canyons of the Spanish Pyrenees
This summer my family and I stayed at Fox House in the tiny village of Santa Engràcia in the Tremp valley, in the foothills of the Spanish Pyrenees. Perched on a cliff edge, the beautifully renovated guest house has panoramic views, eclectic art and a warm homely feel. Laura and Carl were excellent hosts, creating a relaxed atmosphere and serving delicious evening meals. Days were a mix of poolside downtime and outdoor adventure, including rafting, mountain biking, canyon kayaking and swimming in crystal blue lakes. 
Maria
Campsite with a view in Austria
Camping Grubhof, in the small town of Lofer between Salzburg and Zell am See, is simply beautiful. It’s an immaculate campsite, surrounded by mountains. Lofer (and the campsite) have direct access to a huge network of cycle trails as well as to the beautiful village swimming pool (free with the local access pass). Walking high in the mountains, surrounded by cows with bells is simply beautiful. Come the afternoon, there’s time for an apple strudel at a mountain hut and a glass of radler low alcohol beer. There is a camping meadow where you can pitch a tent and cabins to rent, as well as the best shower blocks I’ve come across. 
Mark
Winning tip: Stars, sunsets and glaciers in Italy
The views over Mont Blanc from Rifugio Bertone in Italy are incredible, but it’s the whole experience that makes it special – great food, proper mountain atmosphere, and the Balconata Val Ferret has some of the best walking in the area. It’s also near Courmayeur, which is a lovely town. Arrive for sunset, watch the light move across the glaciers, then look up at the stars as Mont Blanc disappears into the darkness. A brilliant place to eat, walk, breathe and simply take in the mountains. And it’s very affordable.
Eddie Campbell

Text description provided by the architects. The Gisor cultural center stands on a site that for many years remained at the margin of the town center. New cat species identified in Bolivia, first in over a century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:59:00 UTC
14:59:00 KST

New cat species identified in Bolivia, first in over a century
- A new wild cat species, Leopardus tilcayo, has been identified in Bolivia's cloud-covered Yungas forest, the first new living cat species named in over a century.
- Genetic studies revealed tiger cats are five distinct species, with Tilcayo diverging about 1.4 million years ago, highlighting previously unknown biodiversity.
- The species faces threats from habitat loss due to deforestation, fires, and mining, prompting calls for urgent conservation efforts in the vulnerable Yungas ecosystem.
AI generated
LA PAZ – A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.
The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America.
It was found in Bolivia’s lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers.
It measures about 46 cm long and weighs around 1.4kg, making it smaller than the average domestic cat.
Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.
“Its fur is light brown... with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Sept 17 in the journal Current Biology.
Little is yet known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle.
Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
Tiger cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.
Referring to the new species, Lescroart said: “Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.”
One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives in Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.
‘A different animal’
Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: What tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?”
The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South American countries, including eight museum specimens.
The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.
“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said.
Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago.
“The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.
The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas, naming it Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca Empire that included the area it inhabits.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, Red List tracking the status of species currently treats tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species with declining populations.
The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess the five lineages separately.
That could give a more accurate picture of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could potentially be considered endangered when assessed on their own.
The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute in the Yungas, one of the region’s most threatened ecosystems.
The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales-Ascarrunz added.
“Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats... there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study.
“There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.” REUTERS
