‘Run! Get away!’: witnesses recount Israeli ‘double tap’ strike that killed child and medic in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

Mohammad Abdul Zinati was walking home from school through the rubble of Salah Khalaf Street, in northern Gaza City, when he stopped at a supermarket where a group of classmates and friends had gathered.
Shortly before 3:30pm, an explosion tore through the air. Along with several others, Mohammad rushed into the street to see what had happened.
When the smoke and dust cleared, they saw a man lying bleeding on the dusty road. He was badly wounded, but still alive. The man was calling for help, and Mohammad ran towards him.
He did not hear the shouts of his cousin, who had spotted an approaching Israeli drone. Within seconds, the drone released a glide bomb, designed to allow operators to identify and strike targets with a high degree of accuracy.
The munition plunged towards the street, detonating just metres from the teenager. Mohammad did not have time to react before a second blast killed him.
The Guardian verified footage of the attack, and spoke to witnesses and weapons experts in an effort to shed light on the latest Israeli strike to kill a child in Gaza.
“We heard a loud explosion and tried to make our way to the scene to find out what had happened,” said Tamer Lubbad, a witness who filmed the attack. “We found a man lying on the ground. He was still alive and calling for help.”
The man injured in the initial strike was later identified by Gaza’s civil defense as the paramedic Sharif Shadi Labad. The Israeli military said that Labad was targeted because he was a Hamas militant.
Several other civilians approached Labad, as he lay injured in the street. Among them was Mohammad Zinati’s cousin, Mohammed Rajeh Zinati, 26.
“I ran from the house towards the street to find out what had happened,” he said.
“On my way, I saw my cousin coming out of the supermarket. He was running towards the site of the strike. I started shouting at him: ‘Mohammad, stop!’ but he didn’t hear me and kept going. Then I saw a drone in the sky.
“I started shouting: ‘Run! Get away!’ At that moment, Mohammad had reached the injured man. As soon as he got there, the drone struck him.”
“Mohammad was hit directly in the chest and abdomen and was killed almost instantly. I couldn’t do anything to rescue him,” said Zinati.
Video filmed later showed Mohammad’s body lying under a white shroud outside al-Shifa hospital after the attack, as his father bid him an emotional farewell, reciting verses from the Qur’an.
People who knew Mohammad said he was a much-loved figure in the neighbourhood.
“He was a kind, helpful, polite and respectful boy,” his cousin said. ‘‘He would help elderly to collect water from the water trucks. When he was killed, people from the neighbourhood came out into the street, crying for him.”
The IDF has repeatedly rejected allegations that it deliberately targets civilians, saying it assesses and takes into account the risk of civilian harm when carrying out strikes.
However, weapons experts who reviewed the video said the teenager’s death may have been avoidable.
‘‘The bomb that is visible before impact is a Mikholit, which is deployed by Israeli unmanned vehicles (UAVs) or drones, said Trevor Ball, a conflict researcher and trainer at Bellingcat and drone expert. ‘‘These UAVs have high-quality cameras that would have been able to see the teenager and the man approaching the body. Some variants of the Mikholit at least are capable of being redirected to a different target/point while in flight.’’
The strike that killed the teenager and the paramedic appears to fit the pattern commonly described as a “double-tap” attack: an initial strike followed by a second on the same location after rescuers or bystanders have arrived to help the wounded.
In a statement to the Guardian, the Israeli military said Sharif Shadi Ibrahim Labad was a Hamas terrorist who belonged to the elite Nukhba forces. The IDF stated that Labad had participated in the 7 October attacks in 2023 at the Erez border crossing and was targeted because he was planning new operations.
Asked why the second attack went ahead when its target was visibly a minor, the military did not respond, but said it ‘‘is aware of reports indicating that an uninvolved individual was harmed as a result of the strike targeting the terrorist, regrets any harm to uninvolved individuals and makes every effort to minimise such harm”.
The Israeli military said the incident was under review.
On Tuesday, medical sources in Gaza reported an Israeli strike on al-Bureij refugee camp that killed an adult and a five-year-old child, identified as Udai al-Muridi.
A pregnant Palestinian woman died on Saturday from injuries sustained after being shot in the head by Israeli forces south of Khan Younis, according to her family and medical workers.
The woman, named as Iman Shalouf, 27, who was nearly eight months pregnant, was sitting inside her family’s tent in the Mawasi area when Israeli gunfire struck her, according to paramedics and witnesses.
The Israeli military said it had no information about the killing of the pregnant woman.
According to Unicef, several other children have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza in recent days, including two sisters aged six and 12, who were killed with their parents in an airstrike on Beit Lahia while they slept, and three other girls aged, three, eight and nine, who were killed by gunfire.
According to the territory’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. Since Israel’s war in Gaza began on 7 October 2023, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to health officials.

Helen Goh’s recipe for blackcurrant and vanilla finger buns | The sweet spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

Soft, feather-light and topped with a thick strip of icing: few things are as irresistible to me as an iced finger bun. Here, I’ve flavoured the fondant with blackcurrant jam, which lends a gentle tartness to balance the sweetness, though almost any good-quality jam will work. A simple tanzhong (a cooked flour-and-milk paste) gives the buns their wonderfully fluffy crumb and keeps them soft for longer. For a more indulgent version, split the buns along the top and fill with whipped cream and a spoonful of jam instead. They’re best assembled just before serving, and make a particularly lovely afternoon treat.
Blackcurrant and vanilla finger buns
Prep 10 min
 Prove 2 hr+
 Cook 1 hr 15 min
 Makes 12
For the dough
  270ml whole milk 
  7g dried instant yeast
  400g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
  50g caster sugar
  1 large egg, lightly whisked
¾ tsp fine sea salt
  1 tsp vanilla paste
  60g unsalted butter, cut into small cubes and softened, plus a little extra for greasing
For the blackcurrant fondant
  70g blackcurrant (or other) jam
  180g icing sugar, sifted
2 tsp lemon juice
1 tiny pinch fine sea salt
  1-2 tsp hot water, as needed
Pour the milk into a small saucepan and heat gently until just lukewarm. Measure 140ml into the bowl of a stand mixer, stir in the yeast and leave until bubbly.
Meanwhile, whisk the remaining milk in the pan with 25g of the flour, then cook, whisking constantly, on a medium heat for about five minutes, until it thickens into a smooth paste. Set aside to cool until just warm.
Whisk the milk and yeast mix, then add the remaining 375g flour, the sugar, egg, salt, vanilla and the cooled milk/flour mix. Attach the dough hook and mix on low speed for about three minutes, until it turns into a rough dough. Turn up the speed to medium, add the butter a few cubes at a time and mix for eight to 10 minutes in total, scraping the base and sides of the bowl occasionally, until the dough is smooth and elastic. The dough should start to pull away from the sides of the bowl while still feeling soft and slightly tacky. Transfer the dough to a large, lightly greased bowl, cover and leave in a warm place for one to two hours, until doubled in size.
Line a large baking tray with baking paper. Turn out the dough on to a lightly floured work surface and weigh it. Divide the total by 12, then cut the dough into 12 equal 60g pieces. Shape each one into a tight ball by pulling the edges into the centre and pinching to seal underneath. Put the balls seam-side down on your worktop and, using lightly cupped hands, roll until smooth. Gently roll each ball back and forth to form neat, 12cm-long logs; if you like, taper the ends slightly.
Arrange the buns on the lined tray, leaving about 3cm between them (they’ll expand and just meet as they bake, which helps keep the sides soft). Cover loosely and leave to prove for an hour, until risen and puffy.
Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5, then bake the buns for 15 minutes, rotating the tray once halfway, until lightly golden. Transfer to a rack to cool completely.
Meanwhile, make the fondant. Warm the jam gently until loosened, then pass it through a fine sieve – you should have about 50g. Whisk in the sifted icing sugar, lemon juice and salt, until smooth, then add just enough water to make a thick, spreadable fondant. Transfer to a shallow bowl wide enough to dip the buns into.
Dip the top of each cooled bun into the fondant, allowing any excess to drip back into the bowl, then put on a rack for the icing to set before serving.

Improved air quality linked to better mental development in toddlers, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

Improvements in air pollution are leading to brighter, smarter toddlers, according to a new study from Columbia University in New York.
For more than two decades, Prof Frederica Perera and a team from the Columbia Center for Children’s Environmental Health measured the air pollution exposure of pregnant women and the development of their children in the disadvantaged communities of northern Manhattan and the South Bronx. More than 1,100 children were assessed when they were one, two and three years old.
Perera said: “We tested cognitive processing including memory and sensory perception, problem-solving such as matching shapes, stacking blocks and communication, both speech and language comprehension. In the early years of the study, we reported significant associations between prenatal exposure to air pollution and neurodevelopment effects in the children. That was bad news.”
Over the course of the study, air pollution in central New York improved massively. Clean-air legislation reduced some pollutants from the city’s yellow taxis by as much as 80%. Heavy fuel oils are being phased out for heating the city’s buildings and cleaner fuels are being used in the city’s buses. Fine particle pollution and levels of nitrogen dioxide halved between 1998 and 2016.
Perera continued: “Would we see an association between improved air quality and improved mental development scores in the toddlers over time?”
The good news is that the toddlers’ scores improved as the air pollution improved. This was especially clear when the children were two and three years old, and during times of sharper falls in air pollution. The researchers were also able to take into account the effects of other factors that may have affected the children’s development. These included rapid declines in the proportion of children who lived with a tobacco smoker, which fell from 34% to 18%, and increases in maternal education, with a nine percentage-point increase in the proportion of mothers who had successfully graduated from high school.
The New York study adds to the growing evidence that air pollution is a fixable problem and that health improves when air pollution is reduced.
In the UK, the introduction of London’s ultra-low emission zone was accompanied by an improvement in children’s lung health and fewer children with clinically impaired lung function. For adults in central London, there was a 3% reduction in annual trends for emergency admissions, including an 8% reduction for heart problems and a 6% reduction for breathing problems. A reduction of about 25% in GP visits for heart and breathing problems followed the implementation of a clean-air zone in Bradford, West Yorkshire.
Despite the improvements in New York, Perera emphasised: “We cannot conclude that contemporary levels of air pollution are safe for the neurodevelopment of all children.”
Action on air pollution requires bold political leadership. It is often controversial and can be made into a divisive political issue, but it can work. Perera said: “We need more studies such as ours to increase public awareness of the value of clean air and climate policies and motivate policymakers.”
A recent report by the UN Environment programme found that integrated action on air pollution and climate change emissions makes economic sense too, with an average return of $15 in economic benefits for every $1 invested.

MPs urge ministers to break off Thames Water talks with US hedge funds
Unknown

2026-09-18

14:00:09 KST

Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a cross-party group of MPs who are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds who are effectively running the company.
Adding their voices to demands that the prime minister takes public control of the company, which has debts of £20bn and is being controlled by a group of 100 hedge funds and distressed-debt investors, the MPs said in a report that ministers should consider emergency legislation to take control of its financial affairs to stabilise the company.
Alistair Carmichael, the chair of the environment, food and rural affairs committee (Efra), said it was unbelievable that the special administration regime (SAR) for insolvent or failing water companies could not be triggered for Thames Water on performance grounds alone.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has suggested that an SAR – effectively temporary public control – cannot be triggered under the current law because of the way the US hedge funds that bought Thames Water’s debt have kept it running while seeking a deal to renegotiate its liabilities.
The report said Ofwat and the government should withdraw from negotiating with the consortium of distressed-debt specialists who lacked the proper expertise to turn around a vital public service.
Carmichael said the creditors were operating in an opaque way, seeking relief from environmental penalties and dragging out negotiations while reaping millions of pounds in debt interest.
“Thames Water’s 16 million customers have largely lost faith in it,” he said. “They are sick of seeing their waterways polluted, their bills going up, and drinking water gush through broken pavements while supplies run low. We believe Thames Water can be turned around, but not by giving the keys back to the people who have been joy-riding in the family car.
“The government should reject offers from the company’s creditors in return for relief from fines for pollution and poor service. We do not believe this opaque consortium of 100 hedge funds and others has the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart.”
The report said ministers should explore all potential alternative options, including an SAR or using fresh legislation to draw a line under the debacle and restore stability to the sector by putting Thames Water on a sound footing for new buyers.
Carmichael said putting the company into special administration once its money ran out could be the only way to reset its fortunes. “Liabilities that the government will face in the short term may be offset by a future sale of Thames Water once a new buyer can be found,” he said.
The intervention comes after 64 MPs debated a 200,000-strong petition, set up by the campaigner Ash Smith of Windrush Against Sewage Pollution, to hold a referendum on putting the privatised water industry back into public ownership.
MPs on the Efra committee said they were concerned that not enough regulatory due diligence had been carried out on the US-led consortium that bought Thames Water’s debt.
Elliott Investment Management is one of the leading creditors in the group that includes Silver Point Capital, BlackRock and M&G. Elliott’s founder and co-chief executive is Paul Singer, a Trump donor whom Bloomberg has described as “the most feared investor in the world”.
The consortium of hedge funds – known as London & Valley Water – is attempting to take over Thames in a multibillion-pound restructuring. It is seeking relief from environmental fines which could be worth up to £1bn, requesting leniency on environmental measures including pollution, leakage and other performance targets imposed a year ago.
MPs said: “Their demands demonstrate that they will not prioritise the swift turnaround in performance that Thames Water so desperately needs.
“Whilst keeping the company in limbo by drawing out negotiations, these creditors are simultaneously reaping millions in debt interest and fees. We have grave concerns … L&VW is an opaque consortium which is failing to live up to the transparency the public expects of the water sector.”
The committee said it was difficult to see why SAR had not already been instigated for Thames Water. “Thames Water is at the end of the road. The company’s performance and the behaviour of its creditors are unacceptable. Their investment strategies are based on extracting value through debt rather than ensuring long-term success.”
A spokesperson for the London & Valley Water consortium said: “Our enhanced proposal will address all feedback from Ofwat and ministers and is the fastest route to fix Thames Water’s complex problems.
“The plan will write off billions of pounds of debt to achieve an investment grade rating and provide £10bn of new capital from experienced investors to improve and upgrade Thames Water’s infrastructure and clean up local rivers.
“All fines Thames Water faces will be paid, all profits will be reinvested, and no dividends will be taken until the company is turned around and returned to the public markets. There will be no cost to the government or taxpayers, and customers will be protected from the costs of Thames Water’s restructuring.
 “A new board with specialist expertise will oversee Thames Water’s transformation and work tirelessly to drive the turnaround and rebuild trust. We are committed to ensuring Thames Water provides the service that customers and local communities deserve. This group of investors has never been in control of the company and has never received a dividend from Thames Water. They have stepped in to fund a significant revenue shortfall to ensure Thames Water’s record capital investment programme can continue without disruption.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “Thames has been failing the public for a long time, and this government has been clear that nothing’s off the table when it comes to a solution that delivers for customers and the environment.”
A Thames Water spokesperson said: “Turning Thames Water around will take a decade and require significant and sustained investment in our infrastructure, but we are already making progress and this is a different business from the one it was two years ago.
“To sustain that turnaround, Thames Water needs to be recapitalised and put on a firm financial footing, including returning to an investment-grade credit rating, so we can continue investing for our customers and the environment over the long term. Anything that delays the recapitalisation risks slowing the turnaround, disrupting investment and increasing the cost of delivering the improvements our customers and the environment need.”

Children and mature adults we know about, but why is society so clueless about young people in between? | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:09 UTC
14:00:09 KST

When did you realise you had finally grown up? It’s a trick question, obviously: maturity is just realising that life is full of things you don’t feel old enough for but somehow manage anyway, while getting better at pretending to know what you’re doing. But the question is worth asking nonetheless, because for gen Z the goalposts of grownup life are clearly shifting.
It’s a truism that adulting now comes later than it did to generations who still don’t consider adulting a verb, with 43% of 25-year-olds still living at home and plenty more jobless university graduates boomeranging back there this summer, thanks to a grim labour market. Since they’ll probably be working longer into what were once retirement years, perhaps it’s only natural that they’re taking longer to get started. But there’s a fine line between choosing to grow up more slowly and becoming trapped into a kind of limbo between childhood and adulthood, with nobody to pull you out of the morass beyond parents who aren’t sure how to handle this new life stage either.
If your unemployed 22-year-old is getting rejection after rejection, should you rewrite their job applications for them, or let them figure it out for themselves? What do you do with an 18-year-old too depressed to leave their bedroom, now they’re old enough to make their own GP appointments but not mature enough to know they need one? Kidulthood can be a minefield.
The idea that the state should recognise the years roughly between 18 and 25 as a phase distinct from either childhood or full adulthood, which needs its own tailored policies, is catching on around Westminster. The Nuffield Foundation charitable trust, which has spent two years researching changing journeys to adulthood, held a seminar this week drawing together threads from academia to Alan Milburn’s genuinely thoughtful review of what is causing so many young people to be Neet (not in education, employment or training). As Milburn put it to the Nuffield Foundation’s Carey Oppenheim, councils have to ensure that teenagers are studying or training up to 18, but what happens after that is not their problem. Yet in the Netherlands, the state’s responsibilities extend up to 24 or, in some cases, 27. Guess which country has fewer Neets.
More broadly, he suggested, the British state may be too quick to shrug off responsibility for young people struggling with the transition to adulthood. “We haven’t aligned now with the reality of the transitions that young people are going through in their lives,” he said.
In Australia, Oppenheim points out, the equivalent of Britain’s children and adolescent mental health services runs from age 12 right up to age 25, recognising a growing argument within medicine that adolescence doesn’t end neatly at 19. But in Britain, teenagers still hit a cliff edge, tumbling abruptly out of children’s mental health services into adult ones where the threshold for intervention can be far higher. Even the new social media ban for under-16s assumes teenagers are mature enough at 17 to handle what they couldn’t the day before.
Meanwhile the IPPR thinktank’s State of A Generation project, another deep dive into the coming of age process, warns of a society where “transitions to adulthood are blocked” and young people are increasingly nihilistic about their future.
There’s much we still don’t understand about this evolving life stage, including how far to accept it and how far to push back. If a quarter of 18- to 34-year-olds living with their parents say they’re genuinely happy at home or not ready to leave, rather than feeling stuck, does that imply a worrying failure to launch? Or, as the demographer Prof Ann Berrington argues, a new form of “privileged dependence”, where some young people enjoy a financial and emotional security that ultimately boosts them into adult life, and it’s the young people who can’t go home in a crisis we should worry about?
There’s an obvious danger here of over-babying young people, potentially making them even more anxious in the process, or of the state intruding too far into the lives of twentysomethings who are coping fine. As the parent of a 19-year-old, I’m well aware that gen Z are often far more resilient and competent than they get credit for.
But a significant minority do seem to be falling into a gap between childhood and adulthood, and in a chilly economic climate they look increasingly exposed. Maybe the real mark of having finally grown up is feeling ready to help someone else do the same.
This article was amended on 18 September 2026. An earlier version described the Nuffield Foundation as a “thinktank”. In fact it is constituted as a charitable trust.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Is the tie dead? Fashion connoisseurs hope not as House of Lords relaxes rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:08 UTC
14:00:08 KST

The House of Lords has long been derided as a stuffy relic of the past. But now its benches, usually filled with haughtily dressed men, could soon resemble something more akin to “dress-down Friday”.
One of the nation’s most storied chambers of power has enacted a rule change: men are no longer required to wear a tie in the House of Lords. Instead, they should opt for “business attire”.
Ties have long been a knotty item of neckwear. For some, they are a nuisance: too tight and they are uncomfortable, too loose and they look a bit shabby. For others, such as Stephen Fry, who professed his love for ties in a 256-page book, they can add a touch of undeniable class.
Peter York, a writer and style commentator, is firmly on the traditional side of the debate, saying the dumbed-down dress code will “end in tears”.
“Lords are not famous for being well-dressed at the best of times. If they can go without ties, they can also wear plimsolls and stuff like that. They will look silly,” said York, who owns hundreds of ties.
He called them “little works of art”, and decried those who shunned them while dressing formally. “It looks as if you’re not completely dressed, or you’ve forgotten something,” he said.
On Savile Row, views on ties were mixed. “I don’t think ties are completely dead, they’re just having a down moment,” said Guy Hills, 58, a fashion photographer and owner of Dashing Tweed, who was sauntering down the street in a green tweed suit. Something else was also green: his moustache.
He said his dyed facial hair might be allowed in the House of Lords, and is in support of the relaxed dress code, believing that members have a responsibility to keep up with fashion trends.
“They used to be the driving force of fashion, especially around Savile Row. They would go to their tailors and try to outdo each other. When you stop all that, and it becomes like a living museum, then the whole menswear fashion world stops,” he said.
Hills usually has something around his neck. “I can’t go out without a scarf because it looks too slovenly,” he said. But Thursday afternoon was, unluckily, one of the rare occasions he was without a silk scarf or cravat.
While ties aren’t totally “in”, Hills thinks they could make a comeback. “The younger generation is now getting more interested in sustainability and proper clothing. A tie really finishes a whole outfit off,” he said.
Among the few wearing a tie on Savile Row was Chaand Singh. The 25-year-old, who works in marketing, had decided to wear a navy tie from Next because of an important work meeting. “Dressing up and adding a tie elevates the look,” he said – so much so that he had received compliments from people. “Someone said that I look a bit more sharp today.”
Ties were no longer an office must, said Singh – but he thinks they still have their place. “I’ve got some from the 80s with cool patterns. They’re usually wider and designed when fashion was a bit more experimental,” he said. “I would wear them at work for the right scenario, but casually as well. Some girls even wear ties as belts.”
What do tailors on the Row think? “The House of Lords should be a mirror of society. What better way of doing it than reflecting current trends?” said James Sleater, 45, the owner of Norton & Sons. “Women don’t have to wear ties, and if men have the option, it’s OK by me.”
Sleater said that in the “post-Covid era, there has been a huge decline in neckwear and the number of people wearing ties to the office”, adding that the “relaxation of dress codes is symptomatic of people working several days a week at home”.
Norton & Sons sees people from all walks of life. “Yesterday we had an ex-prime minister and today we’ve got a Hollywood star having a fitting. We also see people wanting a suit for their first job and people celebrating a wedding,” he says. Have these customers shunned ties and other neckwear in droves? Actually, no. “We’re seeing the reversal of this trend,” says Sleater. “We’re selling more neckwear this year than we did in previous years.
“If you’re no longer forced to do something, it almost becomes a pleasure to it,” he adds. “To wear a suit to work when you don’t have to is a joy. When you’re told to do it, you’re almost feeling rebellious and you don’t want to do it.”
People have opted for “more characterful textures rather than just plain silks or bright brash colours”, though Slater sees a limit to a potential neckwear revival. “I don’t see cravats or bow ties coming back,” he said.
As for Lords who can keep their ties at home, some are in favour of the new rules. “In truth, the only people now wearing ties for business purposes are estate agents and funeral directors,” Lord Davies of Brixton, a Labour peer, told the Telegraph. “The tie is disappearing.”
It remains to be seen if Davies’ fellow Lords will heed the message.

Saudi Arabia faces a “humiliating dilemma” after the United States refused to militarily intervene to prevent the Iran-aligned Houthi militia from tightening its blockade of the kingdom’s key backup maritime trade route with Asia, according to analysts.
US President Donald Trump on September 12 dismissed the Houthi seizure of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast as a problem that “only affects one country”. Iran has already blockaded the Straits of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia’s main oil and petrochemicals export lane from the Gulf.

France selects THUNDART for long-range land strike
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
06:00:00 BST
14:00:00 KST

France has selected the THUNDART system from MBDA and Safran Electronics & Defense to provide the French Army with a new sovereign long-range land strike capability and replace the existing Unitary Rocket Launcher, according to the companies.
The French Defence Procurement Agency, the DGA, has notified the programme following an initial development phase which included a successful demonstration firing in April 2026. THUNDART is intended to provide precision strike at long range in high-intensity and heavily contested environments, with the system designed, developed and produced in France.
MBDA and Safran say the programme is also intended to give the French Armed Forces full autonomy of use by 2030, reducing reliance on foreign-controlled technologies for a capability regarded as increasingly important in European land warfare. The two companies will establish a 50/50 joint venture in the Paris region to take the programme forward. It will oversee development, production and in-service support, as well as future upgrades and potential adaptation of the system for other environments and export customers.
Safran’s contribution includes navigation and optronics technology intended to allow the weapon to retain accuracy where access to satellite navigation is disrupted or denied.
Alexandre Ziegler, Head of the Defense Global Business Unit at Safran Electronics & Defense, said: “This selection reflects the complementarity of our expertise with MBDA. Faced with the critical challenges of interference and denial of access to GNSS signals, Safran Electronics & Defense provides its proven leadership in inertial navigation and optronics technologies to ensure accuracy in all circumstances.”
He added: “I would like to thank the DGA for their renewed confidence. THUNDART will provide our armed forces with a decisive and sovereign tactical advantage.”
The programme is intended to replace France’s LRU, or Lance-Roquettes Unitaire, as the Army moves to restore and expand its ability to conduct tactical deep strikes from land.
MBDA said the project would draw on mature subsystems while industrial preparations were already being put in place ahead of production.
Stéphane Reb, Executive Vice President Programmes and Managing Director of MBDA France, said: “The notification of the THUNDART programme marks a decisive step for French sovereignty in terms of long-range land strikes.”
He added: “By leveraging mature subsystems and an industrial ramp-up that is already underway, we are able to respond with agility to the Army’s most specific needs. The close partnership with Safran Electronics & Defense, embodied in the creation of a joint venture, allows us to mobilise all the skills of our teams and our production capabilities to deliver a complete solution within optimised deadlines.”

LRT English Newsletter: Drones and pigs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

LRT English Newsletter – September 18, 2026
What a week it has been! On Sunday afternoon, people in and around Vilnius received air alert warnings about a possible drone sighting. Well, that turned out to be just a flock of birds. However, it turned out that an actual drone had flown across southern Lithuania a little earlier. No alert was issued in that case (the military said the drone posed no immediate danger – and perhaps the sighting occurring at the ungodly hour of 4 AM made them conclude the alert would not be appreciated), which gave the defence minister occasion to voice concerns about public safety and security alert protocols. He later said he was satisfied with the military’s reasoning for not sending out the alert.
But then came Tuesday and, right after midnight, another drone was spotted flying from Belarus westwards. NATO fighter jets were scrambled from the air base near Šiauliai to shoot it down just south-east of Kaunas, the first such case in Lithuania (it happened in Latvia this summer). No one was hurt and no property was damaged, although nearby residents reported being seriously frightened.
What was the drone and what was its target? Russia hawks issued the predictable “we will not be intimidated” statements and calls to up the ante, while the defence minister cautioned that it might take some time before investigators can give reliable answers. Still, the president came forward after a State Defence Council meeting to say it was probably a Russian Gerbera launched towards Ukraine but knocked off course by Ukrainian electronic warfare.
As if that was not enough dronefare, Vilnius Airport suspended traffic for half an hour on Tuesday over a suspicious airborne object and foresters discovered a crashed drone in the woods of northern Lithuania. This one, however, appeared to have been used by smugglers and fallen down several months ago.
ANTI-MUSLIM ACTION
Last Friday, several biker groups decided to show Lithuania’s Muslims – many of them recent migrants – that they are not welcome. They disturbed prayers at a mosque in Kaunas with loud music, revving their bikes, chanting nationalist slogans – and even displaying a pig’s head.
The incident brought to the fore developments that have been brewing for quite some time. Besides the usual anti-migrant sentiment, there have been tensions within Lithuania’s Muslim community: the country’s indigenous Muslims, mostly of Tatar descent, have been feeling outnumbered and overwhelmed by the newcomers (this has been used by some right-wing politicians to present their positions as defence of historic Muslims rather than Islamophobia). Moreover, residents around the Kaunas mosque have complained about traffic problems during prayers – a point that has also been invoked in discussions about the bikers’ action.
Relatively few political leaders have censured the incident as hate speech, although on Wednesday, around sixty public figures and former politicians published a letter condemning it. Reportedly, police officers were present during the action but refrained from interfering. Under some public pressure, the police have opened an investigation into possible incitement of hatred – having initially treated it as simply an unsanctioned rally.
KAUNAS PRIDE
So it’s been an eventful week for Kaunas. On Saturday, it held its second-ever Pride March (the first one happened in 2021), attracting around 500 participants who demanded legal regulation of same-sex partnerships, trans-inclusive healthcare, and LGBTQ+ representation in school curricula. Moreover, Palestinian flags featured prominently at Kaunas Pride, with many participants chanting “no pride in genocide”. This has led to accusations, even from within the LGBTQ+ community, that the organisers veered too far from the traditional focus of pride events and might have alienated parts of the community.
ANOTHER BELARUS DEAL
This week, US President Donald Trump’s special envoy for Belarus John Coale made another trip to Minsk – with a stop in Vilnius – brokering a deal exchanging political prisoners for sanctions relief. This time, 25 prisoners were brought to Lithuania on Wednesday, while the US lifted sanctions on two Belarusian companies. This is a significantly smaller batch than before – in March, a similar deal saw the release of ten times as many political prisoners – but Coale said he hoped another one will be concluded soon.
Lithuanian leaders, who are notoriously sceptical about any sanctions relief for Belarus, nevertheless thanked Coale for his efforts – while making clear they still didn’t like Lukashenko.
CORRUPTION WITH EU MONEY
This week, Lithuania’s anti-fraud agency carried out several high-profile searches at the National Paying Agency, the main body that disburses the EU’s generous agricultural subsidies. According to reports, the investigation extents to the agency’s director and his deputy, the latter already facing charges of directing EU funds towards his relations.
EDITOR’S PICKS
– A Cuban dance teacher allegedly helped organise a terrorist attack in Lithuania on the orders of Russia’s military intelligence agency. LRT Investigation Team reports.
– Art unites, art divides. This time, it’s two gilded skulls representing a sixteenth-century love story between the King of Poland and his Lithuanian wife.
– The UK’s University of Cambridge is considering establishing a professorship in Lithuanian studies.
– Is Lithuania losing its grip on the national sport, basketball?
– Kaunas may beat Vilnius to (re)introducing a new mode of public transit, the tram.

‘Once-in-a-century’ crater discovered on Moon (PHOTOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:53:06 UTC
13:53:06 KST

‘Once-in-a-century’ crater discovered on Moon (PHOTOS)
The largest newly formed crater ever discovered in the solar system has been found on the Moon, in what scientists have described as a once-in-a-century impact event.
The crater, measuring 222 meters (728 feet) across and 43 meters deep, was identified using images from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC), according to a study published in Science Advances on Wednesday.
Researcher Robert Wagner first spotted the feature during a routine check of images taken by LROC’s Wide-Angle Camera in October 2025. Scientists then used higher-resolution observations over the following months to measure the crater and examine the surrounding terrain.
According to NASA, the crater formed between April 11 and May 22, 2024, when a comet or asteroid roughly the size of a three- to six-story building slammed into the lunar surface.
The Moon’s got a big new crater! 🕳️
Spotted by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, the McGetchin crater formed when a rock as big as a six-story building crashed into the Moon. It’s 141 feet deep and wider than the length of two football fields.🪨💥🌕https://t.co/I2fX7bPts1pic.twitter.com/Zft4mKUv1Z
The collision hurled debris across the surrounding terrain and created a “cold spot” about seven kilometers (four miles) wide, where nighttime temperatures are up to nine degrees Celsius (16 degrees Fahrenheit) lower than in nearby areas.
Researchers believe the impact loosened, or “fluffed up,” the regolith – the layer of loose rock and dust covering the Moon – making it less dense and therefore less able to retain heat.
Officially named McGetchin after pioneering lunar scientist Tom McGetchin, the crater dwarfs previously detected recent impacts. Before its discovery, the largest contemporary impact crater identified on the Moon measured about 70 meters across.
The discovery comes as the Moon becomes an increasingly important focus of international space exploration.
The US is “very much in a space race” with China, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told CBS News in July. NASA’s Artemis program is targeting 2028 for its first crewed lunar landing since the Apollo era, with the longer-term goal of establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.
Russia and China, meanwhile, announced plans in 2021 to jointly develop the International Lunar Research Station.
As part of the project, Russia plans to deploy a power station on the Moon within the next decade. During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Moscow last May, Russia and China signed an agreement on building a nuclear power plant on the Moon to provide energy for the planned research station, which is expected to become operational in the mid-2030s.

NATO 3.0 marches into Copenhagen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:51:26 UTC
13:51:26 KST

NATO 3.0 marches into Copenhagen
At NATO’s first high-level summit since Ankara, the bloc’s new, Europe-centric incarnation is taking shape. But it’s ordinary Europeans who stand to lose their future, and potentially their lives.
NATO’s Military Committee is meeting in Copenhagen on Friday and Saturday. Chaired by Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the Military Committee, which is NATO’s highest military authority, is tasked with turning the bloc’s strategic goals into executable plans. When NATO orders a battlegroup to Lithuania, for example, the Military Committee ensures its tanks will be able to get there across multiple countries’ rail networks, its troops will be supplied and housed, and the deployment will not leave another sector of the bloc’s so-called ‘eastern flank’ unmanned.
Accordingly, NATO is keeping the meeting’s agenda under wraps. The organization’s website simply states that the defense chiefs will take part in a “Session 1” and “Session 2” of talks, followed by a press conference, a photo opportunity, and then a “Session 3” of discussions.
Looking at the political decisions made since the bloc’s headline summit in Ankara in July, the broad aim of the conference becomes clearer: flesh out NATO’s plan to militarize Europe and prepare the continent for war with Russia, all while insulating the US from the consequences of the conflict.
What is NATO 3.0?
Coined by US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, ‘NATO 3.0’ is an America-first reworking of the Cold War pact. In a speech to NATO defense ministers in February, Colby explained that the US will, going forward, focus on preparing for a potential clash with China in the Indo-Pacific, leaving NATO’s European members to “assume primary responsibility for the conventional defense of Europe.”
Under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth’s visionary leadership, we are driving toward a NATO 3.0 in which Europe takes primary responsibility for its conventional defense. Many said that it could not be done – that Europe couldn’t or wouldn’t step up. That is being disproved… https://t.co/svqGBLPIdE
— Under Secretary of War Elbridge Colby (@USWPColby) July 2, 2026
Europe will increase its military spending to NATO’s current target of 5% of GDP and shift to wartime levels of defense production, Colby explained, all while the US retains control over the bloc’s nuclear weapons. The Europeans will also be expected, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth stated in June, to guarantee “access, basing and overflight” for American forces.
At Ankara in July, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte sold this one-sided deal as a win for Europe. “We are rebalancing our security for the better, that is what NATO 3.0 is all about,” he said.
We’re rebalancing our Alliance: a stronger #NATO with Europe & Canada spending more, producing more and doing more for their security
Building for our future
This is NATO 3.0 pic.twitter.com/pgmvA4CcAW
In light of US President Donald Trump’s threats to withdraw US forces from Germany and annex Greenland, a more Europe-centric NATO was an easy sell for Rutte at the time. Trump’s threats toward Greenland were likely a key factor in the choice of Copenhagen for this weekend’s meeting. However, in the months since Ankara, Rutte and NATO’s European leaders have revealed what the shift actually means for the continent.
Europe steps up and pays
NATO 3.0 means the death of the European welfare state. In the UK, where living standards have already suffered their worst decline since the Second World War, meeting the bloc’s pre-Ankara 3.5% spending target will involve “eye-watering” cuts to education, transport, and justice budgets, George Robertson, who co-wrote the country’s defense strategy, warned in June. Even before the spending target was hiked to 5%, Robertson claimed that the British public was “too comfortable,” and must accept the “pain and great difficulty” of “preparing for war.”
In Germany, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s plan to rebuild the Bundeswehr as “the strongest conventional army in Europe” has already precipitated social security cuts and a planned three-year hike in the retirement age. “The welfare state that we have today can no longer be financed,” Merz announced last August, before increasing Germany’s defense budget by almost 40% in a single year and telling Germans to “work harder.”
The Netherlands and Sweden have introduced emergency taxes to fund rearmament, with the Dutch levy branded as the “freedom contribution.” Estonia has increased income tax, Belgium and Finland have cut social spending, and 18 of NATO’s EU members have borrowed money from Brussels to build out their militaries since last May.
“On average, European countries easily spend up to a quarter of their national income on pensions, health, and social security systems, and we need only a small fraction of that money to make defense much stronger,” Rutte told the European Parliament last year. The “small fraction” demanded by Rutte has since almost doubled.
Serving American interests
In return, the Europeans are not getting the strategic autonomy that some, such as France, want. NATO’s “interoperability” standards mean weapons manufactured in Europe are built to American standards, and the AI and cloud computing technology that guides them is provided almost solely by American companies.
The Ankara Summit Declaration states that “we are developing an interoperable transatlantic warfighting cloud and adopting powerful AI models.” With the EU relying on the US for 80% of its digital infrastructure, American companies such as Palantir, Anduril, and SpaceX will be the beneficiaries of this development.
Furthermore, while the US handed control of three operational commands – Norfolk in the UK, Naples in Italy, and Brunssum in the Netherlands – to European commanders earlier this year, Washington took over management of NATO’s highest Land, Air, and Maritime commands in exchange, and maintains the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) post.
Although NATO 3.0 envisions Europe alone deterring Russia, the bloc’s European members are still expected to go along with American wars far beyond their borders. Speaking in the UK this week, Rutte called it “essential” that Britain’s “armed forces continue to provide the hard power NATO needs” to tackle “Russia and its war against Ukraine, terrorism, Iran and the tectonic shifts of global geopolitical competition.”
NATO was not formed to counter Iran, but the US still punished its European members who refused to aid the US-Israeli war on Iran earlier this year, threatening a complete trade embargo on Spain after Madrid denied overflight and basing to American aircraft taking part in the war, and pulling troops from other countries seen as insufficiently supportive of the war.
Bleeding for NATO
In addition to handing over their money and autonomy, Europeans risk handing over their lives, if NATO’s proxy war in Ukraine degenerates into open conflict with Russia. Having dangled the prospect of NATO membership in front of Ukraine since 2008, fomented the pro-Western Maidan coup in 2014, and juiced Ukraine with weapons and training over the next decade, the US has finally succeeded in dumping the resulting conflict on Europe’s lap, with the eager participation of the continent’s Atlantacist leaders.
NATO 3.0 makes it explicit that Europe now owns this conflict, and it is the possibility of escalation that will likely occupy the bloc’s Military Committee in Copenhagen this weekend. Managing the grim minutiae of war – predicting casualty rates in an open confrontation with Russia and preparing hospitals and morgues, for example – is the committee’s remit, and NATO’s European members are already thinking in this direction.
Germany is currently assessing whether its civilian hospitals could handle an influx of 1,000 wounded soldiers per day, and considering reopening a massive subterranean medical bunker in the city of Ulm. The German military practiced moving casualties from field hospitals in Lithuania to operating theaters in Germany during its largest-ever medical exercises in March.
Norway has trained its surgeons in treating combat injuries and ordered that 7,000 hospital beds be made available for wartime casualties. France is preparing for what Paris calls a “major engagement scenario” by equipping civilian hospitals to absorb military casualties. Sweden and Lithuania have begun stockpiling blood.
A short war
NATO’s Military Committee planned for these eventualities throughout the Cold War. However, the bloc’s European members understood that if the war went hot, only US intervention would save them. Charles de Gaulle was famously skeptical of this promise, asking John F. Kennedy whether the Americans would be willing to “trade New York for Paris” in a nuclear war with the Soviets. With NATO 3.0, the US has openly told Europe that Washington’s contribution to its security will be more “limited and focused,” in Colby’s words.
Nevertheless, NATO’s European leaders, from Rutte down to the generals and admirals on the Military Committee, continue to march toward war with Russia, against all logic and self-interest. These preparations have a momentum of their own, which can be accelerated by miscalculation and political commitments; Europe’s leaders learned this lesson the hard way in the opening months of the First World War.
This time around, the potential consequences are even greater. Russia possesses the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, and in a stark warning on Wednesday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov declared that “if Europe, which talks daily about preparing for war against Russia, attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short.”

125 years of Ivan Tabakov - the forgotten classic of Bulgarian painting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:36:10 UTC
13:36:10 KST

Author
Diana Tsankova
News
125 years of Ivan Tabakov - the forgotten classic of Bulgarian painting
“The artist had a remarkable gift for rendering light, bringing greater vitality to his subjects,” says Hristo Bozhkov, curator at the Vratsa Art Gallery
Friday 18 September 2026 07:05
Friday, 18 September 2026, 07:05
Ivan Tabakov (self-portrait)
PHOTO artzona.bg
Font size
September 18, 1901, is the birthdate of Ivan Tabakov, one of Bulgaria’s major painters. His refined sensibility and distinctive ability to recreate the visible world were nurtured from an early age in an atmosphere steeped in classical art. This combination of artistic sensitivity and musical culture would go on to shape his perception of colour, light and the human figure.
PHOTO galleryloran.com
Born in Sofia, from an early age Ivan Tabakov showed an interest in the violin, while his sister, Tsvetana Tabakova, would later become one of Bulgaria’s celebrated opera singers. Despite the musical milieu in which he grew up, he gradually discovered his true vocation in painting. At the Sofia Academy of Art, he studied under the distinguished artists Professors Nikola Danushev and Nikola Marinov before leaving for Paris.
Hristo Bozhkov, curator at the Ivan Funev Art Gallery in Vratsa
PHOTO Regional History Museum in Vratsa
“He remained in the French capital until 1932, where he continued his artistic training and exhibited actively,” says Hristo Bozhkov, curator at the Ivan Funev Art Gallery in Vratsa.
“With his well-known portraits of women from 1930 and 1931, he took part in the Salon d’Automne, and a year later he exhibited his paintings at the Salon des Indépendants. After returning to Bulgaria, he began painting seascapes, probably influenced by his friendship with the celebrated Bulgarian marine painters Alexander Mutafov and Mario Zhekov.
In 1933, he held his first solo exhibition in Bulgaria, presenting mainly works from his Paris period, alongside portraits and paintings depicting scenes of rural life. In addition to drawing inspiration from countless subjects encountered in his native land, the artist travelled extensively throughout the world, and his work was well received. At the 1942 Venice Biennale, he exhibited a portrait of the writer Georgi Raichev, attracting the attention of the Italian press. The Milan Academy of Fine Arts subsequently named him an honorary member.”
Paris on the Seine, 1960s
PHOTO galleryloran.com
The Vratsa Art Gallery holds 12 works by Ivan Tabakov. Among them are Morning on the Seine, with its radiant light playing across the river, and Boats for Repair, inspired by the Bulgarian marine painting tradition, as well as his depictions of the cathedrals of Saint-Séverin and Sainte-Geneviève, the large portrait of opera singer Tsvetana Tabakova and My Wife, along with Autumn, a landscape rendered in an impressionistic manner.
Tsvetana Tabakova, 1930s
PHOTO galleryloran.com
“Ivan Tabakov left a lasting mark primarily as a portraitist and landscape painter, although art historians also place him among the artists strongly influenced by Impressionism,” the gallery curator adds. “At the Académie Julian in Paris, his professors Albert Besnard and Marcel Baschet encouraged him to engage with the high academic tradition of European art, where he rediscovered his interest in portraiture, landscape and still life. Baschet was one of the leading portraitists of his time, while Besnard was a passionate adherent of Impressionism.
“Ivan Tabakov had a remarkable ability to render light, which gives his figures greater vitality, and in this respect he clearly absorbed something of Albert Besnard. This makes him a particularly interesting artist, trained at prestigious European academies as well as at the Bulgarian Academy, which laid the foundations of his academic education.”
1960s
PHOTO galleryloran.com
“Unfortunately, even during his lifetime he remained undeservedly in the shadow of the more prominent names of his generation, and after his death his name gradually fell into oblivion,” art historian Lyudmil Veselinov notes. In recent years, several galleries have sought to bring back into the light one of the forgotten classics of Bulgarian painting.
"Vasil Levski creates a secret revolutionary committee", 1973
PHOTO galleryloran.com
Text: Diana Tsankova (based on an interview of Sonya Valeriva from BNR's Radio Vidin)
Photos: artzona.bg, galleryloran.com, Regional History Museum - Vratsa

Hungarian chess great Judit Polgar: Make your own moves
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:35:49 CST
13:35:49 KST

Hungarian chess legend Judit Polgar speaks during a press conference for the 12th Judit Polgar Global Chess Festival in Budapest, capital of Hungary, Sept. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Hu Zhixuan)
by sportswriters Zhou Xin, Chen Hao
BUDAPEST, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- For Judit Polgar, one of the greatest female chess players in history, the game has always been about making decisions and taking responsibility for them.
Across more than two decades at the highest level, the Hungarian grandmaster studied opponents, prepared with computers and faced some of the strongest players of her generation. But once she sat down at the board, nobody else could make the move for her.
"In chess, you are responsible for every move," Polgar told Xinhua on Thursday at a press conference for the 12th Judit Polgar Global Chess Festival in Budapest. "You make mistakes, but you also learn that mistakes can be corrected."
The youngest of the famous Polgar sisters, she helped Hungary win the Women's Chess Olympiad at 12 and became a grandmaster at 15 years and four months, breaking Bobby Fischer's then-record as the youngest titleholder.
She later reached the world's top 10 and built her career largely in open competition, defeating a number of leading male players, including world champions.
For Polgar, elite chess demanded far more than calculation. "What does my opponent want to do? What do I want to do? If I make this move, how will my opponent react?" she said.
A wrong move cannot be taken back. The player must accept the new position, reassess the situation and decide what comes next.
That experience also shaped her attitude toward technology. Polgar was part of a generation of top players that saw computer analysis become an important part of professional preparation. She used engines to study positions and review games, but also learned not to rely on them blindly.
"There was a period when I trusted it, and then I trusted it too much," she said. "I paid a price for that, and even lost games."
The lesson remains relevant today: technology can help, but it cannot replace human judgment.
That idea was also reflected at Thursday's press conference, where a magician used a card trick to introduce a discussion about artificial intelligence.
"Magic is a carefully constructed illusion, and sometimes AI can feel like that too," Polgar said.
An answer may look convincing, she added, but people still need to question, verify and understand how it was reached.
Since retiring from competitive chess in 2014, Polgar has devoted more time to education and promoting the game among young people. She believes chess can help develop concentration, problem-solving skills, emotional control and the ability to take responsibility for decisions.
"The process of finding the solution and eventually reaching the answer is the most important thing," she said.
The 12th Judit Polgar Global Chess Festival will be held on Sept. 26 at the Hungarian National Gallery in Budapest, with "critical thinking in the age of artificial intelligence" among its main themes.
For Polgar, the link between chess and the AI era goes back to what she learned as a competitor: players may prepare with coaches, databases and powerful engines, but when the clock is running and the position is on the board, responsibility lies with the player.
"Technology may offer more answers than ever before, but you still have to make your own moves," Polgar said. ■

Across China: Geotourism gains ground as travelers seek more than scenery
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:35:43 CST
13:35:43 KST

LANZHOU, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- At the Zhangye Colorful Danxia Scenic Spot in northwest China, middle school student Xu Yan held up an English textbook and watched as the image on its cover aligned almost perfectly with the colorful, layered hills before him.
"Seeing it in person gave me a much deeper understanding of this kind of Danxia landform," said Xu, who had traveled from south China's Guangdong Province.
He was one of many visitors who arrived at the scenic spot in Gansu Province during the summer vacation with the same textbook in hand. Matching the textbook's cover image with real-life landmarks has become popular on Chinese social media, but at geological sites, the exercise is also taking on an educational dimension.
Across China, dramatic landforms are increasingly being treated as places to explore and understand, rather than simply photograph. Hiking, field study, camping and science courses are being added to conventional sightseeing, giving rise to a form of travel that asks visitors to "read" the landscape.
The scale is considerable. China has 51 UNESCO Global Geoparks, the largest number in the world. A national report on tourist attractions counted 2,047 A-rated scenic areas centered on geological and geomorphological resources, or 13 percent of all such attractions in the country.
Travel data point to the same trend. Online travel platform Trip.com Group's 2026 summer travel report found growing interest in experiential study tours, while nature exploration ranked among the leading choices for family trips.
At Zhangye, this change can be seen in the form of guided tours that take small groups closer to geological formations, where visitors examine tilted strata and the layers that give the hills their distinctive appearance.
Children on study tours go a step further. Equipped with geological hammers and guided by instructors, they learn how minerals containing iron and manganese contribute to different colors in the landscape. In 2025, Zhangye UNESCO Global Geopark, where the Zhangye Colorful Danxia Scenic Spot is located, received 216 study-tour groups involving 170,000 student visits.
"Visitors are no longer satisfied with conventional sightseeing," said Li Junling, deputy head of the general management department of the scenic spot.
Elsewhere in China, geological attractions are bringing more science into the visitor experience.
At Danxia Mountain in Guangdong, from which the Danxia landform takes its name, geological field routes have been combined with science interpretation. The scenic area works with universities and research institutions to train guides and science-education volunteers, while courses on landform evolution and environmental protection take schoolchildren into the field.
In Chishui, southwest China's Guizhou Province, meanwhile, geological education is paired with hiking and immersive experiences. Visitors can explore red Danxia cliffs, waterfalls and forests, while light-and-sound installations illustrate how the landform evolved over hundreds of millions of years.
Gao Hongshan, a professor at the College of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Lanzhou University, in Gansu, said the significance of such experiences lies in changing how knowledge is acquired.
Allowing visitors to use geological compasses, microscopes and other tools turns abstract concepts into something they can observe and test themselves, he said. Virtual and augmented reality can also be applied to make geological processes easier to grasp.
For geological destinations, however, richer visitor experiences must be balanced with the protection of sensitive geological heritage.
At Danxia Mountain, key field-study routes are confined to controlled areas and separated from sensitive geological formations, while Zhangye limits access to some core areas through small-group tours with designated vehicles and guides.
This is where science education can become part of conservation itself.
Cheng Hongyi, an associate professor at Lanzhou University, said that when visitors understand the scientific value and fragility of geological heritage, conservation can become a voluntary act, rather than a mandate imposed on them, and that is a key value of geological tourism. "Science communication is the soul of geological tourism."
Local people are increasingly benefiting from the geological tourism. Nantai Village, about a 10-minute drive from the Zhangye Colorful Danxia Scenic Spot, now has 128 households engaged in tourism-related businesses. Their per capita annual income stands at approximately 27,400 yuan (roughly 4,054 U.S. dollars), and around 80 percent of that comes from tourism. ■

"There will be three great matches in three great stadiums capable of hosting a total of over 150,000 spectators," said RFEF President Rafael Louzan. "Istanbul has hosted the Champions League finals in 2005 and 2023, as well as the 2026 Europa League final."
"It boasts the necessary infrastructure, stadiums, and a passionate fan base. We are certain that Istanbul will fully embrace the Supercup."
The RFEF said Istanbul was chosen from seven candidate cities. Saudi Arabia, which had hosted the Supercopa since 2020 except for 2021, was unavailable this year as it will stage the AFC Asian Cup in early 2027.
Louzan said the event would be "an extraordinary occasion that will also boost the city's tourism and international profile." ■

TOKYO, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Bank of Japan (BOJ) on Friday raised its policy interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to 1.25 percent, the highest in about 31 years, following a two-day board meeting.
The central bank lifted the rate again after increasing it to 1.0 percent at its June policy meeting, the shortest interval between increases since the BOJ began the current rate hike cycle in March 2024.
The decision came amid mounting concerns that Japan's inflation could overshoot the BOJ's expectations, as the yen's slide to its lowest level in decades against the U.S. dollar has driven up import costs, while the prolonged Middle East conflict and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have sent crude oil prices surging.
Two of the BOJ's nine policymakers voted against the rate hike.
Rising interest rates would push up borrowing costs for both businesses and households, potentially weighing on economic activity and posing a challenge for the BOJ's efforts to contain inflation without hampering growth. ■

Markets bet 95pc chance of September rate hike after latest RBA comments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:31:51 UTC
13:31:51 KST

RBA leaders warn that interest rates are just back to 'sensible level'
In short:
RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser said, "We're probably rather closer now to a more sensible level of long-term global real interest rates than we were a year or two ago."
More economists have joined financial markets in tipping a September rate hike, with the possibility of another in November.
What's next?
The RBA's Monetary Policy Board will meet on September 28-29 to determine the next move in the cash rate target.
Economists believe that the Reserve Bank's senior officials have decided that interest rates need to be hiked in September, and they expect the RBA's board to rubber stamp an increase in the cash rate to 4.6 per cent.
This view was already developing following public appearances by deputy governor Andrew Hauser on the ABC's 7.30 program last week and the bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter at two conferences over the past fortnight.
"We think tactically November's a better choice but certainly the internal members of the board are making noises that they want to go," former RBA assistant governor and current Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis told ABC News yesterday.
"You can see that they're trying to signal to the market that they want to raise rates. So September is a genuine possibility as well."
However, an appearance in front of the federal parliament today by RBA governor Michele Bullock, deputy governor Andrew Hauser, and assistant governors Sarah Hunter and Brad Jones has many economists firmly convinced the bank will hike at the end of its next two-day meeting on September 29.
RBC's head of economics and rates strategy Robert Thompson was previously expecting a rate rise in November, but is now forecasting one at the September meeting as well which, if correct, would take the cash rate to a peak of 4.85 per cent — the highest level since before rates plunged in the wake of the 2008 global financial crisis.
"September now seems all but a lock, with November becoming the more contentious decision-point. On the other side of the cycle, we keep a first cut in November 2027," he wrote in a note this afternoon.
"RBA communication has tipped us over.
"The barrage of recent RBA communication (capped off by a lengthy House Economics Committee appearance today) has left us with little doubt that bank insiders have already made up their minds — a hike in September is the necessary course of action."
Marcel Thieliant from Capital Economics agrees that a September rate hike "now looks like a done deal".
However, he thinks that will be the RBA's last move higher.
"Monetary policy is already quite restrictive and we think the bank will be wary of causing a sharp rise in the unemployment rate," he argued.
"Accordingly, we don't expect any further tightening after September."
Financial markets are now pricing in a 95 per cent chance of a rate rise in September, according to LSEG data, with a 37 per cent chance of a follow-up hike in November.
What did the RBA officials say about interest rates?
The clearest indication that interest rates are likely to move even higher, and potentially stay there, came from RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser.
He backed a view that had been recently expressed by leading US economist Kenneth Rogoff that the decline in long-term interest rates between the GFC (2007-2009) and COVID-19 (2020) was an anomaly, rather than the norm, and that we're now returning to a more normal period in which long-term interest rates will be higher.
"Interest rates were never going to be zero or near zero for a long while," Mr Hauser observed.
"We all thought maybe they normalised a year ago.
"I think my personal view — as a personal view — is that we're probably rather closer now to a more sensible level of long-term global real interest rates than we were a year or two ago."
He wondered aloud whether the angst about current levels of interest rates might be related to people coming to terms with that.
"I think the interesting question is, have borrowers adjusted to that new reality?"
RBA governor Michele Bullock gave indications that the bank's ability to "look through" higher oil and fuel prices might be wearing thin, noting they have been elevated for much longer than people were originally anticipating.
"I think there's much more of an inclination [from businesses] to think that we need to pass through these cost increases because it's going to be much more persistent," she said.
"So they're the sorts of things that are shaping our views, I think, and shaping the views of overseas central banks."
While the bank has repeatedly and recently reiterated its desire to protect as many of the employment gains post-COVID as it can, Ms Bullock said that is also becoming more difficult.
"And the other point I would make is that these supply shocks, the Middle East in particular, it has worsened the trade-off between inflation and employment," she told the committee.
"And a typical textbook response people say is, 'Well, it's a transitory shock. You look through it, and then it will come back.'
"But … it's much harder to look through when there are persistent shocks, because of the risk that will flow through to inflation expectations.
"I think we have to acknowledge that the trade-off has got worse, that this particular Middle East shock has made us poorer, and we can't respond to that by letting inflation get out of control."
Both Ms Bullock and Mr Hauser get a vote on the nine-person Monetary Policy Board that will meet on September 28-29 to determine the cash rate.
RBA still sanguine about housing downturn
While the RBA governor acknowledged that "conditions in the housing market have softened, and a larger-than expected easing could be a downside risk to economic activity," she also played down the degree of the decline.
"These falls follow a period of strong growth — housing prices are still around 50 per cent higher than they were in early 2020," Ms Bullock observed.
Brad Jones, the RBA's assistant governor (financial system), who is in charge of safeguarding financial stability, said the surge in Australian house prices were far larger than in other comparable countries.
"If your starting point for that comparison is prior to COVID, the run-up in Australian housing prices exceeds that of large advanced economies, also smaller open economies," he commented.
"It's been a very material run-up, and so we've seen 5 per cent to 6 per cent declines in Sydney and Melbourne, 1 per cent to 2 per cent in the other states."
He said, in that context, the property price declines in Australia this year have "not been overly material".

Country diary: Dinner time for the buzzard family is not a dignified affair | Kate Blincoe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:30:07 UTC
13:30:07 KST

I’m out on the farm most days, but I miss so much. It took a few days to notice a mother mallard with her late brood of 12 ducklings until they were all dabbling in a yard puddle. Dad sees more than me. He told me of the lazy adult buzzard that waited in a tree, then dive-bombed a peregrine that had caught a pigeon. The peregrine dropped its prey, which the buzzard then delivered to a hay bale already strewn with feathers. A pair of juvenile buzzards swiftly followed, ready for a meal.
Later, Dad placed the trail camera at the bale. The young buzzards were soon back in position with yet another dead pigeon. The footage tells a story that many parents will recognise after the long summer holidays.
One young buzzard claims the pigeon, turns its back on the other and opens its wings around the food. Known as “mantling”, it creates a share-proof barrier. The other bird looks disgruntled, shifting around, head down, trying to work out a plan. It sticks a leg out under its sibling’s defensive wings and is told off with a shrill screech.
Opting instead for being persistently annoying, it eventually provokes the pigeon-possessor to rise in attack. There’s a funny moment when both birds overbalance and plummet off the side of the bale. Another high-pitch squeak arises, off-camera. I shouldn’t anthropomorphise, but the expressions of the birds throughout this little drama do seem very familiar.
There are three pairs of buzzards that nest on the farm, each wood has its couple. Usually seen soaring on thermals above the farm, or loafing around in the woodland canopy, they are in turn majestic and clumsy. Despite centuries of persecution, followed by the myxomatosis outbreak in the 1950s that reduced their favourite rabbit prey, buzzards somehow persisted, and more recently increased in numbers.
The bales have now been cleared from the fields and this next generation of buzzards must fend for themselves.
Meanwhile, back in the yard, each night there is a diminishing of ducklings. We’re down to eight now. Still an impressive amount in the numbers game of reproduction, but they have a long way to go until they too are independent.
