No hope, no vote … how most of Delhi’s sex workers are being struck off electoral rolls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
03:00:06 UTC
12:00:06 KST

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

Can the new Pinglu Canal become China’s Yangtze of the southwest?
The 134.2km waterway promises shorter routes to the sea and lower transport costs, potentially reshaping the fortunes of landlocked regions
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Frank Chenin Nanning, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region
The opening of China’s first new river-to-sea canal since 1949 – which will boost trade links with Southeast Asia – could transform the economy of the country’s landlocked southwestern interior in ways comparable to the Yangtze’s role in Shanghai’s rise, according to its operator.
The 134.2km (83.4 mile) Pinglu Canal, which opened on Wednesday, links a major tributary of the Pearl River in the southern Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region with the Gulf of Tonkin, known as the Beibu Gulf in China, serving as a short cut for cargo moving between western China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).
The project was prioritised to ease severe congestion at traditional logistics hubs and additional projects were already under way to maximise the waterway’s economic potential, the operator said.

Taiwan bank lending to small and medium-sized businesses tops full-year target by July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:58:50 UTC
11:58:50 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Demand for financing among small and medium-sized enterprises remained strong in Taiwan, with domestic bank lending to these firms exceeding the government’s full-year target by the end of July.
The Financial Supervisory Commission set a target of NT$500 billion (US$15.7 billion) in SME lending for the year. Domestic banks’ outstanding SME loans increased by NT$535.4 billion in the first seven months of the year, marking the largest increase for the period in nearly a decade, according to CTEE.
As of the end of July, outstanding SME loans totaled NT$11.42 trillion, up NT$132.7 billion from June. The increase was the second-highest for July, after NT$148.85 billion recorded in 2020.
Banking Bureau Deputy Director General Chang Chia-kuei (張嘉魁) said the increase was mainly driven by steady domestic economic growth and continued expansion in business activity. Strong activity in the technology sector, particularly among related supply chains, also boosted financing needs, along with companies’ spending on new operating facilities, he said.
Chang said SME financing needs are expected to remain stable if the domestic economy continues to grow steadily. Lending to small and medium-sized businesses is expected to remain stable in the second half of the year, he added.
The five domestic banks with the largest outstanding SME loan balances as of the end of July were First Commercial Bank at NT$1.44 trillion, Taiwan Cooperative Bank at NT$881.2 billion, Taiwan Business Bank at NT$832.8 billion, Hua Nan Commercial Bank at NT$807.2 billion, and Mega International Commercial Bank at NT$784.9 billion.
Under the Ministry of Economic Affairs’ definition, an SME is a business with paid-in capital of no more than NT$100 million or fewer than 200 employees, according to UDN Money.
According to the ministry’s latest survey, Taiwan had 1.715 million SMEs in 2024, accounting for 98.8% of all businesses in the country. The number increased by 41,000, or 2.4%, from a year earlier. SMEs provided 9.19 million jobs in 2024, accounting for nearly 80% of Taiwan’s total employment.

Interview: Pinglu Canal, win-win economic artery linking China and ASEAN: expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:55:05 CST
11:55:05 KST

MANILA, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Pinglu Canal is not simply an important waterway; it is an economic artery and a bridge between inland China and ASEAN, holding potential to deliver win-win results, said a Filipino expert who visited the canal in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region in southern China in early September.
"The canal's opening is good news not only for Southeast Asia and China, but for broader Asian connectivity, trade, tourism, cultural exchange and technological cooperation," Wilson Lee Flores, a columnist for The Philippine Star, a Filipino media outlet, told Xinhua in an interview.
Built at a cost of 72.7 billion yuan (about 10.75 billion U.S. dollars), the 134.2-km canal runs from Hengzhou, a county-level city in Guangxi, to the Beibu Gulf.
Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal shortens the inland waterway journey for goods from southwest China to the sea by more than 560 km compared with traditional routes through ports in Guangdong Province.
"I was deeply impressed by its scale, engineering, high technology, environmental safeguards and strategic significance," said Flores. He added that southwest Chinese provinces and cities including Guizhou, Yunnan and Sichuan could particularly benefit from the shortcut.
"As the physical foundation of economic cooperation, better connectivity makes it easier and less costly to move goods, people, capital, technology and ideas," said Flores.
He pointed out that ASEAN and China are not only two of the world's most economically dynamic and fast-growing regions; they also share an exceptionally robust economic relationship. China has been ASEAN's largest trading partner since 2009, while ASEAN has been China's largest trading partner since 2019.
Flores said the Pinglu Canal can add an important physical link to this bilateral economic architecture and become an important new link in the ASEAN-China economic relationship.
"Benefiting from the canal, ASEAN companies can gain easier access to China's vast inland market and diversify their supply chains," he said.
He noted that the canal also makes investment in areas of inland China more attractive. For Chinese enterprises, "they can deepen their engagement with the dynamic economies of resource-rich Southeast Asia."
The canal opens in the first year of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), as the world's second-largest economy seeks to promote more coordinated regional development and further expand high-standard opening up -- priorities outlined in the plan.
Flores believed the canal's significance goes beyond cargo. It is a potential corridor of opportunity not only for the business sector, but also for workers, farmers, students, scientists and beyond.
"Infrastructure such as the Pinglu Canal can turn geographic proximity into practical economic opportunity and inclusive development," said Flores, adding that it should be efficiently operated and complemented by sustainable policies. ■

WELLINGTON, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's goods exports rose 15 percent in August from a year earlier, while imports increased 13 percent, according to data released by Stats NZ on Friday.
Goods exports grew by 888 million NZ dollars (about 508 million U.S. dollars) to 6.7 billion NZ dollars, while imports gained by 924 million NZ dollars to 8 billion NZ dollars, the statistics department said in a statement.
The monthly trade balance was a deficit of 1.3 billion NZ dollars, it noted.
Among major export commodities, meat and edible offal rose 144 million NZ dollars, or 23 percent. Fruit increased 100 million NZ dollars, or 12 percent, and milk powder, butter and cheese rose 84 million NZ dollars, or 7.6 percent, statistics showed.
Stats NZ said exports to China increased by 191 million NZ dollars in August, or 16 percent. The largest increases were in logs, wood and wood articles, milk powder, butter and cheese, and fruit.
Goods imports to New Zealand grew 13 percent to 8 billion NZ dollars in August from a year earlier, boosted by a 43-percent increase in petroleum and products, the department said.
In the year ending in August, goods exports rose 7.7 billion NZ dollars to 85.3 billion NZ dollars, while imports increased 10 billion NZ dollars to 90.8 billion NZ dollars, resulting in an annual trade deficit of 5.4 billion NZ dollars, a rise from 3.2 billion NZ dollars a year earlier, it said. Brazil's Lula rejects U.S. critical minerals proposal

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:54:28 CST
11:54:28 KST

BRASILIA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Thursday that he outright rejected a U.S. proposal seeking priority access to Brazil's critical minerals, without even waiting for the negotiations to begin.
In an interview with radio network Radio Itatiaia, Lula said that the terms proposed by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration were "unacceptable," and that the document was consigned to the Brazilian administration's "dead files."
"It was the first communication we received, and we rejected it. We didn't even discuss the document, because it was unacceptable for a country to have priority over our nation's mineral wealth," he said.
Under the proposal, Washington reportedly sought, among other things, advance notice of the sale of Brazil's strategic mineral assets before deals were finalized, as well as priority access for U.S. companies.
Lula noted the exploration, processing and industrialization of Brazilian mineral resources must remain subject to rules established by the South American country itself.
According to the Brazilian president, his government's strategy encourages the establishment of processing and manufacturing stages in Brazil that add value to minerals prior to export.
"We now want to extract here and sell the finished product here in order to create quality jobs and develop production within Brazil," he said.
This policy is not intended to block foreign capital, but to encourage foreign companies to integrate into a supply chain that keeps the processing and manufacturing stages, and a larger share of the added value, inside Brazil, "so that we export value-added goods rather than raw materials," he stressed.
He dismissed the possibility of revisiting the terms presented by Washington in 2025, describing the document as "obsolete."
On Wednesday, Lula signed a law establishing the National Policy on Critical and Strategic Minerals, and creating the National Council for the Industrialization of Critical and Strategic Minerals, which is linked to the President's Office. ■

In July, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative imposed a 25 percent surcharge on several Brazilian products after nearly a year of review. An additional 12.5 percent surcharge was later applied to more Brazilian goods.

Italy to deploy warships to protect shipping through Bab al-Mandeb
Italy’s defence minister warns of severe economic fallout if Bab al-Mandeb becomes impassable, bypassing EU delays.
Italy will deploy warships to ensure safe passage for its commercial vessels through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said, adding that Rome would not wait for a joint decision from the European Union.
“We have the capabilities to protect the passage,” Crosetto said, warning that if the waterway became impassable, the economic consequences would be severe.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Djibouti calls for assistance as thousands of Yemenis flee to country
- list 2 of 3Yemeni forces target Houthis as US rules out direct role
- list 3 of 3‘They called us’: Has Trump abandoned Bab al-Mandeb to the Houthis?
The Italian defence minister said that Rome “must not allow bureaucratic delays in decision-making to exacerbate an already complex situation”.
Bab al-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, forming one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors between Europe and Asia and a critical route for oil, gas and container traffic heading to and from the Suez Canal.
Roughly 12 to 15 percent of global trade has historically passed through the narrow waterway, which separates Yemen from Djibouti and Eritrea on the African side and is only about 30km (19 miles) wide at its narrowest point.
The strait’s importance has grown sharply since Iran effectively seized control of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year amid its war with the United States and Israel, choking off the world’s most important oil chokepoint and pushing much of the Gulf’s crude exports towards alternative routes.
Saudi Arabia, in particular, has increasingly relied on pipelines and Red Sea shipping to bypass Hormuz altogether, making the Bab al-Mandeb strait one of the last major arteries still open to Gulf oil reaching global markets.
Control of the strait has been contested for years, as Yemen’s government, Houthi rebels and, at times, forces in the region have held stretches of its coastline at different points since the war in Yemen began in 2015.
The significance of the strait has been hit dramatically in the past few weeks, when the Iran-backed Houthi movement launched a rapid offensive that brought the entirety of Yemen’s western Red Sea coast under its control, including several strategically located islands.
The advance has given the Houthis effectively unrestricted access to the waterway, a development seen as a major setback for international shipping, given the group’s history of attacking vessels it associates with the US or its allies in the region.
The US and the European Union have already carried out military operations aimed at better protecting merchant ships from Houthi attacks in the area, though those efforts have struggled to fully secure the route as fighting in Yemen has escalated.

Drone attacks by armed groups in Colombia surged 146 percent in the first five months of this year compared with the same period in 2025, according to the country’s Ombudsman’s Office.

Ombudsman Iris Marin warned that the drones inflict fear well beyond the immediate casualties, with their recurring buzz terrorising communities in conflict-affected areas.
Drones are part of the escalating war between armed groups and government forces, leaving civilians caught in between.
Homes, educational institutions, petrol stations and infrastructure were also hit.

Council of Europe launches tool to detect AI-driven discrimination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:30:27 UTC
11:30:27 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The Council of Europe on Thursday published a practical guide to help equality bodies determine whether an artificial intelligence system has contributed to discrimination and what steps should follow if it has.
The European assessment methodology on algorithmic discrimination was presented in Brussels at the closing event of a two-year project co-funded by the EU and carried out by the Council of Europe with the European Commission.
The Council of Europe said the publication “translates standards and legal and technical expertise into a practical, step-by-step approach for practitioners.” It explains how equality bodies can identify discrimination caused by an algorithm or AI system and what remedial steps to take.
The guide is designed to help equality bodies and other actors identify the algorithmic system involved in a case, collect the information needed to assess possible discrimination, examine the issue from legal and technical angles, and map possible remedies when discrimination is found.
The publication is initially available in English, Dutch, French, Swedish, Finnish, and Portuguese, according to the statement.

Germany’s Merz says US friendship since war ‘probably over’ for now

“This era of unconditional transatlantic friendship is probably over for the foreseeable future,” Merz told party members in Berlin on Sept 17. “On the other side of the Atlantic, we are seeing a change in political attitudes, a change in the assessment of the transatlantic alliance, which we might not have thought possible.”

Trump lauded a shock victory by Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany in a state election earlier in September, an event that has shaken the country’s political establishment and raised calls for Merz to step aside.

AI companies would need to report 'rogue' incidents under proposed laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:13:35 UTC
11:13:35 KST

AI companies would need to report 'rogue' incidents under proposed national standards
In short:
The government has released a consultation paper with proposals for its anticipated national standards for AI and data centres.
It comes amid a time of global concern around the use and safety of AI.
What's next?
Responses to the consultation paper are open until October 9.
AI companies could be legally required to report rogue incidents such as the hacking of another company, under a proposal from the Albanese government as part of its plans for new safety, environmental and industrial rules for the technology.
Data centres already in development but not yet built may also be retrospectively required to comply with a raft of new rules being considered by the government, which includes prioritising the use of recycled water and forcing AI companies to reserve computing capacity for Australian businesses and researchers.
These options have been floated in a new paper from the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet on the proposed national "AI standards", which the federal government hopes to legislate in early 2027.
It sets out the goal of attracting major investment from top AI companies here in a "sustainable" way.
"The Australian Government has been clear about the important objective of growing AI capability in Australia. We welcome investment, but on Australia's terms," assistant science minister Andrew Charlton said in a statement.
New rules for 'reportable incidents'
In July, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced his government would create a set of national laws and rules about the development of AI and its infrastructure, such as data centres, in Australia.
A discussion paper published today for feedback, said companies authorised to undertake large-scale AI training in Australia would face minimum safety and security requirements, including "disclosing defined reportable AI incidents to relevant Australian authorities".
It did not define what a "reportable incident" would be, but the paper asked for feedback on whether developers should have to provide information proactively, on request, or through public disclosures.
Australia currently has no such rule.
It comes during a period of heightened global scrutiny on AI safety, with leaders of frontier AI companies recently coming out in favour of a coordinated slowing of development.
Over the past few months, several major AI companies and some individuals have disclosed incidents of AI models taking potentially malicious actions without being asked, starting with OpenAI's disclosure that two of its models had gone "rogue" and broken into the systems of AI company Hugging Face.
This week, OpenAI, one of the world's biggest AI companies, reported six incidents of unexpected or concerning behaviour observed during the training or evaluation of its models over the past six months.
Projects already approved could face requirements
The consultation paper also provided more detail about which data centres the standards could apply.
This included opening discussion on whether they should retrospectively apply to projects not yet operational when the rules commence, including those already moving through approvals and development.
The ABC last week identified 27 approved-but-unbuilt data centres, following the prime minister's earlier comments the rules would not apply retrospectively to projects already approved or under construction.
Larger facilities would face tougher requirements under proposed capacity tiers, while small centres with electricity connection capacity below 30 megawatts could be excluded.
Projects above a capacity threshold could have to submit compliance plans and confirm they had the necessary building and electricity connection approval.
The discussion paper shows the government also wants large data centres to bring forward enough new renewable energy generation to offset their electricity demand, which can be backed by gas, batteries or hydro to keep supply reliable.
Centres could also have to adjust their electricity demand to support the grid and operate in ways that minimise costs for households and businesses.
Whether electricity use should be matched with renewable generation during particular periods has also been floated, including the idea of requiring matching consumption annually and during some periods with renewable energy certificates.
For water, the proposed standards would require centres to minimise consumption, prioritise efficient cooling and recycled or non-drinking water, and pay their share of infrastructure and servicing costs.
Data centre providers would also have to prepare for drought and water disruptions, meet efficiency standards and report water use.
Companies training advanced AI here would also be expected to support Australian research, including by paying directly or by reserving computing capacity for their work.
Advocacy group Data Centres Australia chief executive Belinda Dennett welcomed the paper, saying it supported a national framework rather than a patchwork of other regulations.
"The paper asks the right questions, on energy, water, costs and community, and it rightly recognises that this infrastructure has to be built on terms that work for Australians," Ms Dennett said.
Anthropic, one of the world's biggest AI companies, and which this week signed a deal with the Queensland government to use part of a proposed $32 billion data centre in the state, welcomed the paper.
"We believe that Australia should have agency in how AI is used and developed. This includes clear rules on how the associated infrastructure is built out. We intend to build to meet these standards and look forward to engaging constructively in this process," the company's ANZ head of policy David Masters said.
Speaking at an AI parliamentary hearing this morning, Department of Industry, Science and Resources deputy secretary Helen Wilson said hosting AI training would give Australia greater influence over the technology.
"By having training here, that does give us the ability to help shape the development and deployment of AI," she said.
Responses to the AI standards consultation paper are due by October 9.
OpenAI, Google and Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index on Thursday rebounded above 46,000 points despite a sell-off in US stocks following the US Federal Reserve’s first rate hike in three years.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index, or TAIEX, rose more than 1,000 points at one point to an intraday high of 46,874.84. It closed up 439.1 points, or 0.96%, at 46,288, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
Turnover totaled NT$819.4 billion (US$25.7 billion), up from NT$643.8 billion in the previous session. Total market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$151.4 trillion, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
The index’s most heavily weighted stocks were mixed. TSMC gained 1.89% to close at NT$2,425.
MediaTek fell 0.66% to NT$4,500. Foxconn rose 1.01% to NT$250.5, Delta Electronics dropped 1.46% to NT$1,685, and ASE added 1.49% to NT$614, according to Yahoo Stocks.
Buying shifted noticeably toward traditional industries, with polyester fiber stocks among the strongest performers. Oriental Union Chemical gained 6.05%, while Lealea Enterprise, and Tainan Spinning both rose more than 4%, according to Sinotrade.
The sector’s strength came as inventories across the global apparel and clothing supply chain returned to healthier levels after more than a year of adjustment. European and US brands have become more active in stocking up ahead of the fall and winter peak season, helping orders for upstream polyester fiber materials recover.
Plastic and general-purpose resin stocks, which had remained weak for an extended period, also attracted buying. Industry leader Formosa Plastics rose 3.53%, Taiwan Styrene Monomer gained 6.36%, and Nan Ya Plastics rose 5.36% on heavy trading of more than 90,000 lots, or 90 million shares.
Meanwhile, copper-clad laminate stocks came under pressure following market speculation about the impact of co-packaged optics (CPO), a packaging technology that uses light-based signals to transmit data through silicon chips instead of relying solely on electrical signals, according to National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University.
CPO could eventually reduce the need for repeated upgrades to high-speed materials used in server motherboards, raising concerns about long-term demand for high-end CCL. Key suppliers Co-Tech Development, Elite Material, and Taiwan Union Technology all fell more than 6%.
Shares of glass fiber cloth producers, whose products are key upstream materials for CCL, also fell. Glotech Industrial Corp. fell 5.77%, Fulltech Fiber Glass declined 5.49%, and Baotek Industrial Materials lost 2.98%.
Printed circuit board makers, which use CCL as a core material, came under pressure. Iteq hit its daily limit-down, while Gold Circuit Electronics, Unimicron Technology, Kinsus Interconnect Technology, Cheer Time Enterprise, Zhen Ding Technology, and Nan Ya PCB posted significant losses.
Senior analyst Chien Po-yi (簡伯儀) said the Fed’s rate decision was in line with market expectations, while the easing of some uncertainty helped the market rebound. Chien said trading volume also recovered, pointing to renewed investor participation, according to CTEE.
Chien suggested investors watch whether turnover continues to increase and whether the TAIEX can hold above its five-day moving average. If those signs persist, the market could see further gains as investors adjust their portfolios for the third quarter, he added.

Taiwan doctors debunk COVID-19 vaccine rumors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:06:54 UTC
11:06:54 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Concerns about COVID-19 vaccine side effects and long-term health effects are circulating on Taiwanese social media, with some users linking the vaccines to cancer despite a lack of evidence for such a connection.
The findings come from Taiwan-based data platform DailyView, which analyzed COVID-related discussions on Threads over one year to identify the topics that garnered the most attention.
Physicians have weighed in on the concerns raised in the discussions and debunked several rumors about COVID-19 vaccines, per CNA.
Huang Li-min (黃立民), a distinguished professor at NTU College of Medicine, said COVID vaccines have improved, and reports of adverse events have declined, adding that the reporting rate per 100,000 cases is now comparable to that of the flu vaccines.
Huang also rejected claims that the mRNA vaccines alter human DNA or cause cancer. He explained that mRNA uses ribosomes in the cytoplasm to produce proteins that trigger an immune response; it does not enter the cell nucleus or alter DNA.
Chiu Nan-chang (邱南昌), a pediatrician and infectious disease specialist at Mackay Memorial Hospital, told Taiwan FactCheck Center last year that COVID vaccines use genetic instructions to produce the virus’s spike protein, triggering an immune response. He said there is no evidence that the spike protein produced through vaccination causes cancer.
Doctors have also urged people to consider the health risks associated with COVID infection, particularly among older adults and those with chronic conditions.
Since October 2025, 675 COVID cases have been reported in Taiwan, with people aged 65 and older accounting for 73% and those with chronic conditions making up 83%, according to the latest CDC data. About 84% had not received the vaccine this season.
Chen Hung-lin (陳宏麟), a physician and chair of the Taiwan Association of Clinical Diabetes, said many patients with chronic conditions take their medications regularly and keep their blood sugar or kidney function under control, but fail to get vaccinated.
He said COVID not only affects the lungs but can also trigger systemic inflammation involving the heart, kidneys, brain, muscles, and blood vessels.

ACCRA, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Ghana is ready for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, the Ghana Olympic Committee (GOC) said in a statement on Thursday.
The GOC announced that 13 young athletes will represent the West African country at the Games, competing across eight disciplines.
The athletes, aged between 13 and 17, qualified through international federation pathways and will represent Ghana at the first Youth Olympic Games to be held on African soil.
The Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games will be held from Oct. 31 to Nov. 13, bringing together around 2,700 athletes competing in 25 sports.
Ghana has competed at every edition of the summer Youth Olympic Games since the event was first held in Singapore in 2010, followed by Nanjing in 2014 and Buenos Aires in 2018. ■

Germany and Spain go head-to-head in EU budget fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:04:02 UTC
11:04:02 KST

Germany and Spain go head-to-head in EU budget fight
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and four other leaders compete with Spanish finance minister in POLITICO articles signaling EU budget deal is still far off.
DUBLIN ― Germany and Spain used separate POLITICO opinion pieces to clash over the total size of the EU’s next approximately €2 trillion seven-year budget, setting the scene for tough negotiations to strike a deal before an informal end-of-year deadline.
With talks entering what officials hope will be their final few months, capitals are fighting against each other to save their pet projects and spare their taxpayers from sending more money to Brussels.
But after almost a year of painstaking negotiations, countries still seem far away from a landing zone — with disagreements growing stronger by the day, as underscored by the two articles from rival camps. One is penned by Spanish economy minister Carlos Cuerpo, the other by the leaders of Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Austria and Finland.
Advertisement
Governments are under heavy pressure to finalize a deal before elections in France, Italy, Spain and Poland next year threaten to derail negotiations and delay payouts to farmers and researchers.
Spain’s Cuerpo broke ranks to demand hundreds of billions of euros extra for the EU’s common cash pot, and a delay in repayments of post-Covid debt to free up €11 billion a year to spend on agriculture, defense and competitiveness.
“The next long-term budget should be set at 2% of EU GNI [gross national income), a level commensurate with the challenge of supporting both the economy and social cohesion,” Cuerpo wrote.
Send taxpayers the bill
But in the other article, Germany’s Friedrich Merz, Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen, the Netherlands’ Rob Jetten, Austria’s Christian Stocker and Finland’s Petteri Orpo — whose countries contribute to around 40 percent of the total budget — rejected both of Spain’s ideas.
They argued that more money and debt are not the solution but the problem.
“We cannot just add every new priority to every old one and send taxpayers the bill,” they wrote.
Advertisement
They are pressuring Ireland, in its position at the helm of the six-month rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, to cut hundreds of billions of euros in their next negotiating document due in October.
Officials involved in the negotiations who spoke to POLITICO and were granted anonymity because the discussions are confidential see more moderate cuts as the most likely outcome.
Debt time bomb
The EU’s seven-year budget, the multiannual financial framework, which governs EU spending from farmers’ subsidies to student exchange programs, is the subject of some of the fiercest negotiations in Brussels and pits different groups of countries against one another.
To try to bring their positions closer together, European Council President António Costa toured 25 EU countries in the past month to sound out leaders on the most sensitive questions facing the negotiations. He continued the trip in Dublin on Thursday.
In his bid to free up more budget funding, Cuerpo said he wants to delay repayment of joint debt issued in 2021 to tackle the economic fallout from the Covid-19 pandemic.
Around €300 billion must be repaid from 2028 to 2058. While interest repayments are set in stone, governments have more leeway to set the timeline for repaying the principal.
The current plan compels EU governments to front-load repayments and cough up €25 billion a year over the next budget cycle. Critics say this limits the funds available for other areas of spending and further constrains negotiations.
Advertisement
As a workaround, Cuerpo suggested pushing back the repayment schedule to free up an additional €11 billion per year.
“The result remains unchanged: a steady and predictable reduction of liabilities on time,” Cuerpo wrote in the POLITICO article.
His idea is backed by the European Commission and a growing number of EU countries including Italy, France, Portugal and Poland.
Several officials privately say that this option can be a last-minute workaround to smooth a deal in December.
However, supporters will have to overcome resistance from Germany and its allies, who have traditionally opposed joint EU debt.
They wrote in their op-ed that the post-Covid spending spree has “already burden[ed] the next MFF by almost €170bn. That money is no longer available for our new priorities.”
Advertisement
Their argument is that postponing the repayment of the principal will lead to small savings — and is therefore no alternative to slashing the overall size of the budget.
“The EU budget is ultimately paid for by European citizens,” they said. “That remains true whatever financing mechanism we invent. So, there is no avoiding the difficult question of the overall volume.”

Everyday physical activity is linked to a major boost in energy and mood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:00:50 UTC
11:00:50 KST

People tended to feel more energetic and positive when they were more physically active than usual, and they were also more likely to become active after reporting better well-being, according to a large analysis published in Nature Human Behaviour.
Physical activity includes more than organized exercise. It can involve walking, household movement, commuting and other everyday activities. Affective well-being refers to a person’s momentary emotional state, including whether they feel happy or unhappy, energized or tired, calm or tense, and generally good or bad.
Earlier research has often linked exercise with improved mood, but studies conducted in laboratories or through occasional questionnaires may not accurately reflect people’s ordinary lives. Researchers have increasingly used wearable movement monitors and smartphone surveys to record what people are doing and how they feel throughout the day. However, these studies have used different methods and have produced mixed results.
The current researchers aimed to combine this evidence and determine whether physical activity and well-being were related in both directions. They also wanted to distinguish changes within individuals from differences between individuals. This distinction matters because a person who is generally active may also be happier for other reasons, such as better health, social support or living conditions.
Led by Johanna Rehder of the University of Salzburg in Austria, the team analyzed 67 datasets from 14 countries. The study included 8,223 participants, with an average age of 36.33 years. Sex or gender information was available for 8,190 participants: 54.93% were female and 0.06% were nonbinary.
Participants wore accelerometers, small devices that objectively record movement, for periods ranging from one to 100 days. They also received smartphone prompts asking them to report their current well-being. Across the datasets, participants provided 321,345 well-being ratings linked to nearly 1 million hours of movement measurements.
The researchers examined five aspects of well-being: positive feelings, negative feelings, overall pleasantness, energy and calmness. They assessed both whether physical activity came before later changes in well-being and whether well-being came before later physical activity.
Within individuals, physical activity was consistently associated with greater energy, more positive feelings and better overall pleasantness. The strongest relationship involved energetic arousal—the feeling of being awake, alert and energized. In practical terms, moving from sitting to walking was associated with a 0.62-point increase in energetic arousal on a 1-to-4 scale. The same comparison was associated with a 0.24-point increase in positive feelings and a 0.16-point increase in pleasantness. Physical activity did not, however, show a consistent relationship with negative feelings such as sadness or anxiety.
Physical activity was also linked with feeling less calm. This does not necessarily mean that movement made people distressed. It may reflect the fact that being active is associated with feeling more alert and stimulated rather than relaxed.
The relationship also operated in the opposite direction. When people reported feeling better and more energetic than their own average, they tended to be more physically active afterward, whereas feeling calmer was associated with less subsequent activity. Negative feelings, however, did not show a consistent relationship with later activity. At the level of differences between people, physical activity was most consistently associated with positive feelings and pleasantness.
The strength of the associations varied substantially among individuals. Age, body mass index, sex or gender and whether measurements were taken on a weekday or weekend explained some of this variation. For instance, younger adults and those with a lower body mass index showed stronger positive emotional responses linked to physical activity. Additionally, the energy boost from being active was more pronounced on weekends than on weekdays, and women felt more energized after activity than men.
The authors concluded that “the results document the critical relevance of [physical activity]–[affective well-being] relations in everyday life.”
Important limitations remain. For example, the datasets were observational, so they cannot establish that physical activity directly improves well-being or that positive feelings cause later activity. The studies also differed in the devices they used, how often participants reported their feelings and how well-being was defined.
The study, “An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis of How Physical Activity Relates to Affective Well-being in Daily Life,” was authored by Johanna Rehder, Irina Timm, Gesa Berretz, Iris Reinhard, Andreas B. Neubauer, Onur Güntürkün, Keisuke Takano, Walter Bierbauer, Miriam Cabrita, Matthew Bourke, Joshua Smyth, Jinhyuk Kim, Johannes Michalak, Joshua Curtiss, Björn Pannicke, Jacob B. Gallagher, Ana M. Abrantes, Toru Nakamura, Yoshiharu Yamamoto, Paul Cook, Lena M. Wieland, Birte von Haaren-Mack, Bryan McCormick, Justin Hachenberger, Tomas Vetrovsky, Benjamin Henwood, Louise Poppe, Gorden Sudeck, Laura Hollands, Andrea B. Goldschmidt, Lynn Martire, Martina Kanning, Jaclyn P. Maher, Yu-Mei Li, Ulrich Reininghaus, Corina Berli, Caroline Seiferth, Derek J. Hevel, Kate Leger, Amanda E. Staiano, Almut Zeeck, Stefano Calza, Yue Liao, Geralyn R. Ruissen, the CoCA Consortium, Andreas R. Schwerdtfeger, Matthias Haucke, Loree T. Pham, Siwei Liu, Mark C. Thomas, Andreas Meyer-Lindenberg, Genevieve F. Dunton, Steriani Elavsky, Ulrich W. Ebner-Priemer, Marco Giurgiu, Julian Packheiser and Markus Reichert.

The need for speed as Hong Kong plugs in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:00:17 UTC
11:00:17 KST

The need for speed as Hong Kong plugs in
- As Hong Kong prepares for a much larger EV population, a new Gold Coast pilot shows where ultra-fast charging could fit into the city’s expanding network
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Hong Kong is preparing for many more electric vehicles on its roads. The city’s First Five-Year Plan, announced alongside the Policy Address, calls for the steady electrification of vehicles and safe, efficient charging networks, with around 10,000 fast chargers expected by 2035 to support about 500,000 EVs.
That longer-term target follows an updated EV roadmap released in February, which calls for fast chargers to become the backbone of Hong Kong’s public charging network. An interim target of at least 4,000 fast chargers has been set for 2030, supporting about 200,000 EVs.
Industry is responding with different initiatives, from expanding charging networks to introducing technology designed to get motorists back on the road more quickly.
At Gold Coast Piazza in Tuen Mun, a new ultra-fast charging station can compress charging times to as little as five minutes for compatible EVs. The system can charge a compatible EV battery from 10 to 70 per cent in five minutes, or from 10 to 97 per cent in nine minutes.
The pilot project is a collaboration between Sino Group, BYD, CR EVIVA and iCar, with each contributing to its development and operation.
The technology is also being made available to EVs from other manufacturers. Vehicles equipped with the compatible European-standard CCS2 charging interface can use the station, with charging performance depending on the capabilities of each vehicle.
“Sino Group has, in fact, continued to expand EV charging facilities across its managed properties over the years, with more than 2,200 charging points currently available across its portfolio,” said Bella Chhoa, Chief Commercial Officer of Sino Group.
Charging away from home
Speed, however, is only one consideration in meeting Hong Kong’s charging needs.
Research published by HKU Business School found that private cars in Hong Kong travel about 30km a day on average, meaning a full charge in most mainstream private EVs can cover more than a week of usual commuting.
Away from home, faster charging provides another option for motorists who want to replenish their batteries and continue their journeys with minimal delay. For commercial vehicles such as taxis and light goods vehicles, spending less time charging also means getting back to work sooner.
CR EVIVA brings experience from operating one of Hong Kong’s largest charging networks. According to the company, its network covers more than 1,700 contracted charging spaces, including around 400 DC fast and ultra-fast charging spaces. It introduced 500kW fully liquid-cooled charging technology in 2024 and is now working with partners on the latest ultra-fast charging technology at Gold Coast.
Delivering ultra-fast charging presents a technical challenge since higher charging power requires more electricity to be available at a charging site.
This is addressed at the EVIVA ultra-fast charging station at Gold Coast through energy storage. Fully liquid-cooled charging equipment is used in conjunction with an energy-storage battery system, allowing electricity to be stored and released at high power when a vehicle plugs in.
Safety and compatibility have also been considered. The station uses the European CCS2 charging standard and has undergone the necessary approval procedures in Hong Kong.
The road ahead
EV technology is advancing in parallel with charging infrastructure. BYD’s Flash Charging technology is designed to work with vehicles equipped to support higher charging speeds, including models using its second-generation Blade Battery technology.
Ouyang Xiaocheng, BYD Hong Kong Sales Director, said the Gold Coast station represented an important development for the company’s Flash Charging technology as it expands its use outside the mainland market.
At the launch, BYD and iCar Group also announced the establishment of Hedi Flash Charging Technology, a joint venture intended to support the development and operation of charging infrastructure in Hong Kong.
“We will continue working with local partners to provide drivers with more efficient and safer ultra-fast charging,” he said.
“We believe our collaboration with EVIVA, BYD and iCar will give drivers a more efficient and convenient charging option and support greater EV adoption,” said Chhoa.

Russians go to polls against backdrop of Ukraine war and Putin’s tightening grip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:00:05 UTC
11:00:05 KST

Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly controlled vote stripped of meaningful competition and with little doubt about the result.
Vladimir Putin’s United Russia is expected to extend the grip on parliament it has held for 23 years, alongside a handful of nominal opposition parties that reliably vote with the Kremlin on the issues that matter. The three-day vote begins on Friday, with results expected after polls close on Sunday.
For all the predictability of the outcome, the first Duma election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is taking place against the backdrop of a war that, once distant for many Russians, is increasingly intruding into everyday life.
Swarms of Ukrainian drones have struck oil refineries, factories and logistics hubs across Russia over the summer, while polling has pointed to growing anxiety about the course of the fighting and what may still lie ahead.
Against that backdrop, the Kremlin has tightened its grip further.
Last month, the authorities barred Yabloko, the liberal anti-war party, from the ballot, removing the only political force remaining in Russia that was openly challenging the invasion of Ukraine.
That leaves a handful of other parties, from the Communists to the far-right Liberal Democrats, which together form what is known in Russia as the “systemic opposition”: groups permitted to criticise the authorities at the margins, but which fall into line with United Russia on issues that matter to the Kremlin.
For years, they have served as a political safety valve, giving voters somewhere to register discontent without posing a serious threat to the ruling party’s dominance. But even by the diminished standards of Russian politics, these parliamentary campaigns have been strikingly lifeless.
“In most elections, candidates compete for attention. In Russia this year, many are doing the opposite,” said Farida Rustamova, a political analyst and founder of the independent Vlast newsletter. “No one wants to come into the spotlight or discuss anything sensitive.”
Most candidates have barely campaigned at all, she noted.
Televised debates have at times taken place in half-empty studios because politicians failed to turn up, producing awkward clips that quickly became memes online.
United Russia’s campaign videos have leaned heavily on low-budget AI, with few memorable slogans or promises. None of the parties has dared to address the growing questions surrounding the continuing war that increasingly dominate private conversations.
“The Kremlin is deliberately keeping the election low-key, as greater interest would not benefit them. They don’t want to discuss difficult issues and just [want to] get it over with,” said a person close to the Kremlin, speaking on condition of anonymity.
By keeping the election subdued, Moscow hoped to depress turnout among disaffected and independent-minded voters while ensuring its own supporters made it to the polls, said Rustamova.
Yabloko’s exclusion followed the same logic.
Several observers believe that officials had initially expected the party to receive a negligible result, demonstrating how little support remained for an explicitly anti-war platform. But when polling instead suggested growing support for the party, the authorities removed it from the ballot rather than risk an unscripted result.
Vladimir Gelman, a professor of Russian politics at the University of Helsinki, said another purpose of the elections was to provide the Kremlin with a continuing source of legitimacy and reinforce the impression that there was broad public consent behind the political system and the war.
“Even though these elections are neither free nor fair, they are still the only source of legitimacy,” he said.
In a televised address before the vote this week, Putin explicitly linked participation in the election to the war in Ukraine, presenting voting as a demonstration of unity in the face of outside pressure.
“Your choice and your will will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory and love for our homeland,” Putin said.
Putin himself secured another six-year term in the 2024 presidential election, with genuine opposition barred from the ballot, extending his rule until at least 2030.
For many Russians, however, the election’s greater significance lies not in the result, but in what follows.
With Moscow’s troops making little progress at high cost in Ukraine, rumours of another large-scale mobilisation have spread across the country. The fear is that once the election is safely out of the way and a compliant new Duma is installed, the Kremlin will have greater freedom to pursue unpopular measures it has so far avoided.
The anxiety has already prompted some young men to leave the country, hoping to wait out any new mobilisation – scenes that carry echoes of September 2022, when hundreds of thousands of Russians fled after Putin announced the first wartime draft.
The person close to the Kremlin said several friends had sent their sons abroad in recent weeks, a sign, he said, that even among those with access to the system, few are certain what will happen after the voting.
Putin has sought to calm those fears. In recent weeks, he has twice dismissed suggestions that a new mobilisation is imminent.
But those reassurances have not been enough for some men, including Dmitry, who flew to Yerevan, Armenia last week. “I’ll just wait a few weeks after the elections,” he said, adding that he felt the risk of a new mobilisation was too high to ignore. “Let’s see if anything changes after the vote.”

Germany’s Merz girds for a post-election fight for political survival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Germany’s Merz girds for a post-election fight for political survival
One conservative official predicts “all hell breaks loose” if the ruling CDU fails to win any seats in the regional election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Embattled German Chancellor and leader of the Christian Democratic Union Friedrich Merz speaks at a campaign event ahead of state elections in Berlin on Sept. 17, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
BERLIN — Chancellor Friedrich Merz is bracing for a fresh barrage of bad news that is expected to intensify questions about his capacity to remain Germany’s leader when results of two regional elections come in on Sunday.
Merz already appears to be preparing for a fight for his political survival ahead of the votes, knowing full well that his chancellorship could rapidly unravel should he fail to rally the increasingly restive rank-and-file of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) behind him.
That will be no small task following the CDU’s crushing defeat to the far-right Alternative for Germany party in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month. The CDU risks another major loss this Sunday in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where according to polls the conservative party is set to suffer its worst defeat in a state or national election in Germany’s post-World War II history.
Advertisement
It’s for this reason that Merz has arranged a meeting with CDU leaders to take place Sunday, just before polls close, at which he’s expected to gauge their support and attempt to convince them that he has a plan to turn things around. Merz has also canceled a planned speech at the United Nations General Assembly scheduled for Wednesday to remain in Berlin and address the domestic fallout from the CDU’s performance.
In an effort to rally support, Merz is emphasizing the importance of avoiding turbulence in Berlin during volatile times for Europe.
“All eyes are on Germany, on Berlin, on our role in the world,” Merz said at a CDU campaign event in Berlin on Thursday evening. “Expectations are placed on us to contribute to keeping this European continent stable.”
‘Hell breaks loose’
Despite his efforts to remain at the helm, Merz’s fate could be sealed by as little as a few percentage point shifts on Sunday in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Polls show Merz’s conservatives collapsing to just 7% in the state, as its center-left premier takes on the leading AfD in an increasingly two-way contest between the strongest centrist force and the far right.
Hendrik Wüst, Minister President of North Rhine-Westphalia and seen as Merz’s most likely replacement, speaking during the 2026 Digital X at Rheinauhafen in Cologne on Sept. 8, 2026. | Thomas Lohnes/Getty Images
Should the CDU fall further, it would put the party at risk of failing to meet the 5% vote threshold required to enter the state parliament — a result that one conservative official, speaking on condition of anonymity to frankly discuss the mood inside the party, said would mean “all hell breaks loose.”
In Berlin, where the other regional election will be held this Sunday, the chancellor’s party is polling better — but things could still go poorly. The CDU is narrowly trailing the far-left Die Linke, or Left Party, at around 20% support, according to polls. That is still 8 percentage points below the CDU’s result in the last Berlin election — a decline that could see the conservatives ousted from the city government they currently lead and replaced by a coalition of left-wing parties.
Advertisement
In an effort to quell open rebellion in his party that could come with these bad outcomes, Merz has pushed to line up support in advance of the elections, with some success.
On Wednesday, all eight CDU state premiers released a public letter backing the chancellor and emphasizing, like Merz, the need for a stable German government given Europe’s increasingly volatile politics. Among the signatories was Hendrik Wüst, the premier of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia and the politician who has emerged as Merz’s most likely replacement.
“Our country will continue to need a stable and effective federal government with its own majority in the Bundestag,” the statement read. “Parliamentary elections will be held next year in Poland, Italy, Spain, and Greece, and presidential elections will take place in France. The outcomes are uncertain. This makes a stable and strong Germany in a united Europe all the more crucial.”
‘Connect more deeply with people’
Merz has already begun to show some nascent signs of how he will attempt to address his core problem: improving his approval ratings with voters, which at this point in his tenure are some of the lowest for any chancellor in Germany’s postwar history.
Merz, in short, appears to be giving in to more of what voters want even as he calls on them to sacrifice benefits as part of his reform drive to make pension, health insurance and long-term care schemes more sustainable.
Merz this week suggested he’s ready to yield to long-standing demands from state premiers to address soaring fuel costs — with diesel reaching a record €2.453 per liter on Thursday, up more than 50% from a year ago — after long opposing measures to bring down prices as too expensive. He has also softened his position on restricting early retirement for people who have worked and paid into the pension system for 45 years.
Advertisement
Merz, who has often taken a scolding tone with voters, has already admitted he needs to sound less like a taskmaster. “We must try — myself included — to connect more deeply with people, including their full range of emotions,” he said the day after his party’s defeat in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month.
The shift is slight, and in no way represents a retreat from Merz’s reform drive, which Merz, during the CDU campaign event on Thursday evening, compared in its importance to the effort to rebuild Germany after World War II.
For many conservatives, Merz’s minor change of tack hardly constitutes a bold vision for how he can save himself. Still, until now, conservative politicians and leaders have largely kept their deep concerns about the chancellor out of the public eye.
That can’t be said for some members of the youth wing of the Merz conservative bloc, who have been far more vocal in their criticism of the chancellor, but whose views are likely to reflect a much broader swath of the CDU.
“This isn’t just about Friedrich Merz, but he is part of the problem,” Clara von Nathusius, one of the leaders of the conservative bloc’s youth wing, told German public television on Sunday. “And that’s why, unfortunately, I believe we can’t win any more elections with this chancellor.”

What Andy Burnham needs from Donald Trump at their New York meet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

What Andy Burnham needs from Donald Trump at their New York meet
Britain’s new prime minister is set for his first meeting with the U.S. president next Tuesday. Unlike Keir Starmer, he won’t be angling for a second helping.
LONDON — When Keir Starmer had his first dinner with Donald Trump, he strained so hard to impress the U.S. president that his host offered the British team a second helping of chicken.
Andy Burnham’s face-to-face introduction next Tuesday will look very different. Instead of the two-hour Trump Tower rendezvous that Starmer enjoyed in September 2024, British officials expect their new prime minister to sit down with his U.S. counterpart on relatively neutral ground in the United Nations headquarters at the far edge of Manhattan.
Their meeting is currently penciled in for Tuesday afternoon, sandwiched between Burnham’s 15-minute address to the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday evening and Trump’s morning speech to the same hall — which given his past form, may drown out other headlines with whatever he says there.
Advertisement
That may prove convenient for Burnham.
“There will be so much going on that it reduces the intensity and scrutiny,” said Claire Ainsley, a former aide to Starmer who is now at the center-left Progressive Policy Institute think tank.
POLITICO spoke to a dozen current and former senior U.K. officials, ministers and MPs, many of them granted anonymity to speak frankly, about Burnham’s likely handling of the visit. Almost all predicted he would opt for a middle road somewhere between Starmer’s initial charm and the more combative approach of Canadian PM Mark Carney: Get in, smile, press the case for Ukraine, and try to leave without a major upset.
Downing Street’s overwhelming priority for the New York visit has been to squeeze in an IRL meeting with Trump, with whom Burnham has now spoken to by phone twice, according to a person familiar with the preparations. It will allow the two men to engage but with far lower stakes than a one-to-one visit in Washington or London, just one of a series of leader meetings that blend into the noise of a multilateral summit.
The hope, one U.K. government official said, is to “get the Trump meeting done and dusted in a relatively safe environment.”
That was then
The shift away from Starmer’s more high-pressure encounters is driven not so much by Burnham’s laid-back style — the new PM said last month he will “say what I feel” to Trump while also trying to “find a connection” — as by a profound change in the balance of risk since 2024.
Advertisement
Burnham has less to prove. Starmer, who took office shortly before Trump’s second election victory, signed deals on tech, trade and pharmaceuticals from scratch. Warming to Trump was the “medicine required at that period,” said a U.K. diplomat.
His successor’s job is to fix the mess of unresolved threads left behind.
Burnham also has the benefit of hindsight, having watched Starmer’s efforts to praise Trump lead to embarrassment when the president lambasted the PM over the Iran conflict, oil drilling and tech taxes. Trump at one point even dissed Starmer as “no Winston Churchill.”
Donald Trump shakes hands with Britain’s former prime minister Keir Starmer at a joint press conference at the White House on February 27, 2025. | Carl Court/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
The new PM won’t “bend the knee in the way Starmer did,” predicted the same U.K. diplomat. He won’t be going to “kiss the ring,” added the first U.K. government official quoted above. “It’s completely different this time. There’s no drama about having to stay in his good books.”
Yet Trump still has two years left in office, and a smooth relationship will be vital for the U.K. leader who has tried to keep his focus on domestic issues — but is watching his promises to ease living costs be buffeted by rising defense pressures and inflation from the Iran war.
The two men will also meet at a point where Britain and its allies are turning their heads away from the U.S.
Advertisement
Two years ago “Trump was at the height of his powers,” said one Starmer Cabinet minister. “The reality is different now.”
While November’s looming midterm elections threaten to dent Trump’s authority at home, abroad his approaches to NATO and the Middle East have led European allies to find solace elsewhere. Britain and its allies are forming groups of so-called middle powers, while Carney pushes closer ties between Canada and the EU that will still be in negotiation long after Trump’s departure. And Burnham has repeatedly talked about strengthening ties with Brussels — seeing through a reset in relations that Starmer initiated.
Olivia O’Sullivan, director of the U.K. in the World Programme at the Chatham House think tank, said the country is now “testing the waters” of loosening its strategic alignment with the U.S. — even as it continues to rely on America’s security and nuclear weapons architecture. (And even as Burnham continues to let the U.S. use Britain’s air bases for limited strikes on Iran.)
Emily Thornberry, the Labour MP who chairs the House of Commons’ foreign affairs committee, said there’s a reason for that: “I think a couple of years ago, the hopes were high that Trump would help with Ukraine, we would have a proper trade deal, and so on. He hasn’t delivered on those things, so we’re getting used to the disappointment. We don’t expect as much.”
One former senior official under Starmer put it more starkly: “The world is just viewing the United States differently. He is doing enormous long-term damage to the U.S.’s relationship with all of its allies. Institutions that have stood for decades can no longer do the jobs that they used to be able to do, because America is proving to be an unreliable ally. This is hugely significant in the long term.”
No list of deliverables
Burnham, whose two calls with Trump since July have both run far over their allotted time, is at least looking to keep things friendly.
Advertisement
The new prime minister is not expected to take a big list of deliverables or policy goals into his meeting, two people familiar with the planning said.
Burnham is expected to press Trump on U.S. support for Ukraine after paying his first overseas trip there last month. British officials hope there is now a more pro-Ukraine atmosphere on Capitol Hill after the House of Representatives passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill long championed by the late Senator Lindsay Graham.
Thornberry said the PM should urge Trump to speed up supplies of Patriot missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter. Ukraine’s forces are “winning without the Americans, but they could actually win if the Americans did help,” she added.
Andy Burnham visits the scene of Russian strikes on Lukanivska Market in Kyiv, Ukraine on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Britain’s wider activities at UNGA — which Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will also attend — could be dominated by a clash over the hardening stance of the U.K., France and Canada against Israel. The three countries issued joint sanctions against West Bank settlements earlier in September, after what one U.K. official described as a “tag team” coordination effort between Miliband, Burnham and the leaders and foreign ministers of allied countries.
The U.K. is hoping to use UNGA to work on the next steps in the humanitarian response for Gaza. British officials are privately hopeful that the U.S. response will continue to be muted; two U.K. government officials said they believed Secretary of State Marco Rubio viewed the intervention as helpful, given it applies pressure to Israel without it coming from the U.S.
Burnham faces a choice about how hard to lean into the issue of the Middle East in his own speech to UNGA. His closest No. 10 aides have kept a “tight hold” on the thinking around his remarks, said the person with knowledge of the planning quoted above.
Advertisement
Whatever he chooses, plenty of dangers lie in wait — not least Trump’s views on oil and gas in the North Sea. Industry figures believe Burnham’s government has delayed a decision on whether to drill at two fields until after an Oct. 8 special election to replace Starmer, where Labour is battling the Green Party. Trump has long been perplexed by the delay.
Burnham’s government has also delayed a key decision on defense spending until 2027, despite pressure from the U.S. to set out a clearer timetable.
And Britain is stuck over how to proceed with its deal giving up sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically crucial archipelago in the Indian Ocean, after Trump disowned the pact earlier this year. Mauritius — the beneficiary — could agitate at UNGA to unfreeze the deal.
But it’s the issue of artificial intelligence that has lately rocketed up the news agenda. Here, Burnham faces a conundrum.
On the one hand, Britain can sell a “third way” in AI development between Trump’s free-for-all and burdensome regulation in the EU, argued Emily Darlington, a Labour MP and member of the Commons Science and Technology Committee.
“There are things that [U.S. tech firms] need from us, not least some of the really advanced stuff that we’re doing around quantum, and in the future neuromorphic computing,” she said. “We’re a huge market for them. Large language models are desperate to train on British material that goes back centuries. The BBC archive, all of these sorts of things, are what they’re desperate for. There’s a bit of a fight over whether there is a British advantage to allowing them access to that material, and so there is a bit of a negotiation.”
Advertisement
Yet the U.K.’s digital services tax has drawn Trump’s repeated ire, while PoliticsHome reported this week that U.S. officials warned Britain at the London embassy against its online safety restrictions and plans to ban under-16s from social media. One minister said Burnham’s conversation “can’t be on the digital services tax or regulation like the Online Safety Act, because there’s a tangible risk Trump will go ballistic.”
‘Andy has been a lucky general’
The same minister suggested Burnham will want the sort of relationship that Tony Blair had with George Bush — respectful, even if not as equals.
It is a tall order for a president as mercurial as Trump, yet old allies of Starmer insist he paved the way for it. They point to Starmer’s decision to push back against Trump to defend Greenland’s sovereignty, to bring together a “coalition of the willing” for Ukraine and to welcome Kyiv’s leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy after Trump hectored him in the Oval Office.
Volodymyr Zelensky shakes hands with Andy Burnham ahead of their bilateral meeting at Horodetskyi House in Kyiv, Ukraine, on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Starmer was not being nice to Trump because he liked him, argued the Starmer Cabinet minister quoted earlier in this story, but because he had to bring him back from the brink on NATO and Ukraine.
It means Burnham has inherited an established relationship in which he has no need to lavish the president with praise. All he has to do, argue some, is avoid a barrage of abuse on Truth Social.
“Andy has been a lucky general in the calming of Trump,” argued one U.K. official who worked under Starmer. “Keir was dealing with a completely different beast.”
And yet, this person added: “It could all change in the space of two weeks.”
