A common budget that makes common sense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

With Spain for the first time set to become a net contributor to the next EU budget, we are more than willing to pay our fair share to make it a global powerhouse, writes Madrid’s finance minister.
Carlos Cuerpo is Spain’s deputy prime minister and minister of economy, trade and business.
Europe’s existential challenges keep piling up. From rising energy bills and defense spending to a dizzying race for AI leadership, the €1.2 trillion in annual investment the continent needs to stay competitive looks increasingly like an underestimate.
Addressing these challenges cannot come at the expense of the resources needed to strengthen integration, solidarity and a robust welfare state — core elements of the European project and our safest bet for securing the EU’s place on the world stage.
Advertisement
As Europe rushes to unify its capital markets and mobilize trillions of euros in idle household savings, it should also pursue a long-term financial framework that breaks with its reactive past. Instead, we are moving in the opposite direction.
Louder calls to slash the EU’s 2028–2034 financial framework will prevent Europe from acting on its own terms in a hostile world. The European Commission’s original proposal of almost €2 trillion varies little from the current spending plan once repayments of the post-pandemic recovery grants are excluded. That amounts to roughly 1.15% of the EU’s gross national income (GNI).
To get the debate back on track, Spain has proposed freeing up to €11 billion a year in resources that make both financial and political sense.
Instead of repaying the debt associated with the grant component of NextGenerationEU faster than required, the EU should link its service to its long-term economic capacity. An annual payment of about 0.06% of EU GDP would retire the debt by 2058, the deadline agreed by member states. Under the current plan, repayments would amount to between 0.09% and 0.11% a year over the next seven years.
Reprofiling the debt payment would free up nearly €70 billion over that period, which is equivalent to about one-fifth of the proposed European Competitiveness Fund that would channel investment into strategic sectors. It also amounts to roughly one-third of the aid the EU has sent to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.
This approach would not only release extra resources but keep the stock of EU debt broadly stable in the medium term while sending a strong signal to investors who are demanding more euro-denominated assets.
Advertisement
The proposal can also be seen as part of a more ambitious strategy to develop a European safe asset that drags down the liquidity premium that investors are asking for. Separately, Spain has proposed allowing the Commission to issue a portion of member countries’ debt on their behalf, helping to create a deeper common market for European debt. This could generate €25 billion in annual interest savings.
With Spain for the first time set to become a net contributor to the next long-term budget, we are more than willing to pay our fair share to help make the EU a global powerhouse that creates opportunities for its citizens.
The next framework should have a ceiling equivalent to 2% of EU GNI — enough to support both the economy and society.
That figure would still fall well short of the investment gap identified by Mario Draghi and Enrico Letta. But it would at least begin to address the concerns of investors and citizens.
The size of the next budget will send an important message to voters ahead of elections next year that will take more than half of the EU population to the polls. Populist far-right parties are making political gains by offering simple answers to complicated problems — and blaming the EU in the process.
Europeans need economic security. They need reassurance that their energy bills will not soar again and that their factories will stay open. In the most challenging decade since the Cold War, this is not the time for Europe to make itself smaller. Doing so would play into the hands of populists intent on dismantling the European project.
Through initiatives such as NextGenerationEU, Europe came together to provide much-needed economic security. It took a crisis to get us there. The task now is to build on that progress and get back on track before the next one.

Donald Trump shakes hands with Britain’s former prime minister Keir Starmer at a joint press conference at the White House on February 27, 2025. | Carl Court/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
The new PM won’t “bend the knee in the way Starmer did,” predicted the same U.K. diplomat. He won’t be going to “kiss the ring,” added the first U.K. government official quoted above. “It’s completely different this time. There’s no drama about having to stay in his good books.”
Yet Trump still has two years left in office, and a smooth relationship will be vital for the U.K. leader who has tried to keep his focus on domestic issues — but is watching his promises to ease living costs be buffeted by rising defense pressures and inflation from the Iran war.
The two men will also meet at a point where Britain and its allies are turning their heads away from the U.S.
Advertisement
Two years ago “Trump was at the height of his powers,” said one Starmer Cabinet minister. “The reality is different now.”
While November’s looming midterm elections threaten to dent Trump’s authority at home, abroad his approaches to NATO and the Middle East have led European allies to find solace elsewhere. Britain and its allies are forming groups of so-called middle powers, while Carney pushes closer ties between Canada and the EU that will still be in negotiation long after Trump’s departure. And Burnham has repeatedly talked about strengthening ties with Brussels — seeing through a reset in relations that Starmer initiated.
Olivia O’Sullivan, director of the U.K. in the World Programme at the Chatham House think tank, said the country is now “testing the waters” of loosening its strategic alignment with the U.S. — even as it continues to rely on America’s security and nuclear weapons architecture. (And even as Burnham continues to let the U.S. use Britain’s air bases for limited strikes on Iran.)
Emily Thornberry, the Labour MP who chairs the House of Commons’ foreign affairs committee, said there’s a reason for that: “I think a couple of years ago, the hopes were high that Trump would help with Ukraine, we would have a proper trade deal, and so on. He hasn’t delivered on those things, so we’re getting used to the disappointment. We don’t expect as much.”
One former senior official under Starmer put it more starkly: “The world is just viewing the United States differently. He is doing enormous long-term damage to the U.S.’s relationship with all of its allies. Institutions that have stood for decades can no longer do the jobs that they used to be able to do, because America is proving to be an unreliable ally. This is hugely significant in the long term.”
No list of deliverables
Burnham, whose two calls with Trump since July have both run far over their allotted time, is at least looking to keep things friendly.
Advertisement
The new prime minister is not expected to take a big list of deliverables or policy goals into his meeting, two people familiar with the planning said.
Burnham is expected to press Trump on U.S. support for Ukraine after paying his first overseas trip there last month. British officials hope there is now a more pro-Ukraine atmosphere on Capitol Hill after the House of Representatives passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill long championed by the late Senator Lindsay Graham.
Thornberry said the PM should urge Trump to speed up supplies of Patriot missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter. Ukraine’s forces are “winning without the Americans, but they could actually win if the Americans did help,” she added.
Andy Burnham visits the scene of Russian strikes on Lukanivska Market in Kyiv, Ukraine on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Britain’s wider activities at UNGA — which Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will also attend — could be dominated by a clash over the hardening stance of the U.K., France and Canada against Israel. The three countries issued joint sanctions against West Bank settlements earlier in September, after what one U.K. official described as a “tag team” coordination effort between Miliband, Burnham and the leaders and foreign ministers of allied countries.
The U.K. is hoping to use UNGA to work on the next steps in the humanitarian response for Gaza. British officials are privately hopeful that the U.S. response will continue to be muted; two U.K. government officials said they believed Secretary of State Marco Rubio viewed the intervention as helpful, given it applies pressure to Israel without it coming from the U.S.
Burnham faces a choice about how hard to lean into the issue of the Middle East in his own speech to UNGA. His closest No. 10 aides have kept a “tight hold” on the thinking around his remarks, said the person with knowledge of the planning quoted above.
Advertisement
Whatever he chooses, plenty of dangers lie in wait — not least Trump’s views on oil and gas in the North Sea. Industry figures believe Burnham’s government has delayed a decision on whether to drill at two fields until after an Oct. 8 special election to replace Starmer, where Labour is battling the Green Party. Trump has long been perplexed by the delay.
Burnham’s government has also delayed a key decision on defense spending until 2027, despite pressure from the U.S. to set out a clearer timetable.
And Britain is stuck over how to proceed with its deal giving up sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically crucial archipelago in the Indian Ocean, after Trump disowned the pact earlier this year. Mauritius — the beneficiary — could agitate at UNGA to unfreeze the deal.
But it’s the issue of artificial intelligence that has lately rocketed up the news agenda. Here, Burnham faces a conundrum.
On the one hand, Britain can sell a “third way” in AI development between Trump’s free-for-all and burdensome regulation in the EU, argued Emily Darlington, a Labour MP and member of the Commons Science and Technology Committee.
“There are things that [U.S. tech firms] need from us, not least some of the really advanced stuff that we’re doing around quantum, and in the future neuromorphic computing,” she said. “We’re a huge market for them. Large language models are desperate to train on British material that goes back centuries. The BBC archive, all of these sorts of things, are what they’re desperate for. There’s a bit of a fight over whether there is a British advantage to allowing them access to that material, and so there is a bit of a negotiation.”
Advertisement
Yet the U.K.’s digital services tax has drawn Trump’s repeated ire, while PoliticsHome reported this week that U.S. officials warned Britain at the London embassy against its online safety restrictions and plans to ban under-16s from social media. One minister said Burnham’s conversation “can’t be on the digital services tax or regulation like the Online Safety Act, because there’s a tangible risk Trump will go ballistic.”
‘Andy has been a lucky general’
The same minister suggested Burnham will want the sort of relationship that Tony Blair had with George Bush — respectful, even if not as equals.
It is a tall order for a president as mercurial as Trump, yet old allies of Starmer insist he paved the way for it. They point to Starmer’s decision to push back against Trump to defend Greenland’s sovereignty, to bring together a “coalition of the willing” for Ukraine and to welcome Kyiv’s leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy after Trump hectored him in the Oval Office.
Volodymyr Zelensky shakes hands with Andy Burnham ahead of their bilateral meeting at Horodetskyi House in Kyiv, Ukraine, on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Starmer was not being nice to Trump because he liked him, argued the Starmer Cabinet minister quoted earlier in this story, but because he had to bring him back from the brink on NATO and Ukraine.
It means Burnham has inherited an established relationship in which he has no need to lavish the president with praise. All he has to do, argue some, is avoid a barrage of abuse on Truth Social.
“Andy has been a lucky general in the calming of Trump,” argued one U.K. official who worked under Starmer. “Keir was dealing with a completely different beast.”
And yet, this person added: “It could all change in the space of two weeks.”

I Make Claude Interview Me Before Every New Project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
01:59:54 UTC
10:59:54 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
AI as a very impressive intern
My favorite way to think about AI is that it’s like a very, very educated but somewhat incompetent intern.
Interns are great. When I worked in corporate, I had a few interns that I really enjoyed working with. But interns, like every new employee, don’t come with any context.
They can’t just jump in and start producing quality work right out of the gate. But, unlike new employees, managers must get them up to speed quickly. Most interns are only around for six to eight weeks. That’s how long we give most new employees to get acclimated.
So like a new intern, any time we start something new with AI, we must provide context. Sometimes context is just a few lines in your prompt.
”This student analysis report is for my manager, make sure not to use any profanity”
That sort of thing.
But what about when you’re using AI to work on bigger projects. You want AI to help you build a new course. Or to update an established learning program after a product release changes what customers need to do.
That’s where putting your context into a prompt just isn’t going to cut it.
This is where setting up a project becomes really important, and setting up that project with the right context is even more important.
Introducing the context map:
Context comes in many forms and it can be hard to know exactly where to put everything.
Here is how I think about context:
- 
Project instructions — Writing rules, learning-design standards, accessibility expectations, handling of uncertain claims
- 
Context documents — Project goal, customer profile, learner starting point, target performance, scope
- 
Reference documents — Product documentation, screenshots, demo transcripts, feature notes, existing customer questions
- 
Current request — Create the outline, lesson, practice activity, or job aid
- 
Skill — A repeatable method for turning product sources into customer enablement
- 
Memory — Decisions and discoveries accumulated while developing the project
Not every project needs all of the layers of context, or needs everything that belongs in each layer.
But the map is a helpful place to start, particularly if your work will involve several related conversations that need access to the same context.
Enough context. Let’s set this thing up.
Let’s say I need to create a short onboarding experience that helps an instructional designer new to Sage Studio add their existing source files.
I’d set up my project in three easy steps:
The Intake → The Foundation → The Craft
The Intake
Start by creating a new Claude project. Give it a name and description that will help you recognize it later.
These fields are for you. Claude does not receive the project name or description as context, so we’ll give it the actual project goal in a chat.
Once you’re inside, you’ll see the project instructions and context areas on the right.
This is where most people start adding things. I don’t. Not yet.
First, I ask Claude to interview me.
I started doing this because writing project instructions from a blank page is weirdly difficult. I either add too little, try to anticipate every possible need, or write instructions for some imaginary version of the project.
The interview gives Claude enough information to help me build the setup. More importantly, it forces me to think through the engagement before I start dropping client information into the project.
Here’s the prompt I use:
I'm starting a new project and this workspace will be used for its full duration. Your job right now is to interview me, then draft the workspace's setup artifacts. Do not start any project work until setup is done.
## Project goal
[One to three sentences: what I'm making or doing, for whom, and any links or tools involved.]
## Step 1: Read the goal back
Before asking anything, tell me in a few lines:
- What kind of project you think this is
- The dimensions that matter most for this kind of project (e.g., audience, scope, constraints, deliverables, stakeholders, tools, success criteria)
- What the goal statement already answers, so you don't ask it again
If the goal includes links, open them first. If you can't access one, say so and ask me what's there.
Wait for my correction or confirmation.
## Step 2: Interview
- Use the question tool for anything with bounded answers (formats, phase, cadence, experience level). Ask open-ended questions in plain text where multiple choice would flatten the answer (the situation, the audience, what success looks like, risks).
- Ask in rounds of up to 3 questions, grouped by theme. Later rounds should follow from my answers, not from a fixed script.
- Always cover these, whatever the project type: who the output is for, what's in scope and explicitly out of scope, deliverables and deadlines, constraints, my own role and experience level with this kind of work, and the recurring tasks I'll use this workspace for.
- The last item matters most: the instructions should be built around the work I'll actually do here, so get specific about task types.
- If I say "don't know yet," log it as an open question and move on.
- Stop when another round wouldn't change the artifacts. Target 3-6 rounds, fewer for small projects. Tell me when you have enough and what you'd still be guessing at.
## Step 3: Draft
Deliverables:
1. Project instructions: standing instructions for this workspace. Cover my role, the project, how you should behave here, output standards, and what to never do.
2. Context documents: separate files for the project knowledge base. Propose the set that fits this project. Typical candidates: a project brief, an audience or stakeholder profile, working agreements, and a decisions/open-questions log. Merge, split, or drop as needed. A small project may need only one.
Rules:
- First give me a short outline of the proposed artifacts and what goes in each. Wait for my confirmation.
- Write the instructions as direct guidance to the model working in this project, not as a summary of our conversation.
- Mark every assumption I didn't state, inline, so I can correct it.
- Put volatile information (dates, status, current phase) in the context docs, not the instructions.
- Scale the setup to the project. A two-week project doesn't need four documents.
- Deliver each artifact as its own file.
Start with Step 1.
For this project, I’d replace the placeholder under Project goal with:
Create a short onboarding experience that helps an instructional designer who is new to Sage Studio add their existing source files.
Claude starts by telling me what it thinks the project is and what information will matter. This gives me a chance to correct its interpretation before the interview begins.
Once the goal looks right, I approve it and move on to the interview.
Claude asks its questions in small rounds. I answer what I know, correct anything it has misunderstood, and say “I don’t know yet” when I haven’t made a decision.
That last part is important. The goal isn’t to manufacture an answer for every question. An unanswered question is useful information about the project’s state.
When Claude has enough information, it proposes the project instructions and context documents it thinks the workspace needs.
I review that list before asking it to create anything. A small project doesn’t need four documents and an administrative system that requires its own administrative system.
The Foundation
Once I’m happy with the proposed setup, I tell Claude to create the instructions and context documents.
This is where my judgment becomes more important, not less.
Claude marks the assumptions it made while drafting. I review every one of them.
I replace assumptions with real information when I have it. I remove details the project doesn’t need. If the project is for a client, I also decide whether each piece of client information is appropriate to include in Claude at all.
Once the documents are accurate and appropriate, I save local copies.
I like owning the files separately from the Claude project. I can update them, share them when appropriate, or use the same context in another approved tool without recreating everything.
Project instructions work a little differently from the other files. I copy the final instructions into Claude’s project-instructions field.
Then I add the remaining approved documents to the project context.
At this point, Claude has the engagement-specific foundation: what I’m creating, who it’s for, what matters, what constraints exist, and how I want it to work with me.
The Craft
The foundation tells Claude about this project.
The final layer tells Claude what good work looks like for our team.
I keep reusable guidance in Markdown files so I don’t have to explain the same standards during every project. Depending on the work, I might add:
- 
Brand design guidelines
- 
Copy and voice guidance
- 
Instructional-design principles
- 
Production and accessibility standards
- 
Examples of previous work
- 
Other methods or requirements that remain consistent across projects
I keep ours in a folder called Sagecraft Shared Standards for AI.
I don’t automatically add every file in the folder. I choose the guidance that applies to this project.
A short onboarding experience may need our writing, instructional-design, and accessibility standards. It probably doesn’t need every framework, template, and example we’ve ever created.
Now the project is ready for its first real assignment.
I haven’t tried to fit the entire engagement into one enormous prompt. I’ve worked out what Claude needs, decided what belongs in the project, and added the standards that make the work ours.
That’s the setup:
The Intake → The Foundation → The Craft
The work can start from there.
Intelligence by Design is for people who help customers, partners, channel members, or sales teams perform.
We write about instructional design, AI, and the systems behind good learning. You don’t need deep technical knowledge to follow along. We’re all figuring out what these tools can do, where they fall short, and where they belong in the work.
We don’t gatekeep what we learn, including the tools and practical workflows we use on real enablement and learning projects.
We’re building a community of people who care about helping others perform and want a meaningful voice in deciding how AI belongs in that work. If you want to be part of it, subscribe.
I’m curious: what’s one thing you find yourself explaining to AI over and over? Tell me in the comments. I suspect a lot of us are rebuilding the same context every time we open a new chat.

The United Nations Security Council’s monthly meeting on Syria’s post-Assad transition has seen Syria, Israel and Turkiye trade accusations over who can rightfully have a military presence on Syrian soil.
Syria’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ibrahim Olabi, told council members on Thursday that he had hoped to focus on the country’s progress but was compelled to address Israel’s actions in Syria, according to a UN summary of the meeting.

Thailand eyes strategic partnership with Türkiye by 2028: Ambassador
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
01:55:38 UTC
10:55:38 KST

Thailand's newly appointed ambassador to Ankara, Chaturont Chaiyakam, said he hopes 2028 will mark the establishment of a strategic partnership between Thailand and Türkiye, identifying defense industry cooperation as a key priority.
Chaiyakam, who began his posting after presenting his credentials to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Sept. 8, spoke to Anadolu about his impressions of Türkiye, his experiences in the country and bilateral relations.
He first visited Türkiye 15 years ago to attend the third summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia, held in Istanbul. He said his exposure to the country had been limited until recently.
After exploring Ankara, Chaiyakam said he was surprised by Türkiye's development, particularly in the automotive and electronics sectors.
Although interaction between the Turkish and Thai peoples remains limited, he said the two countries are tourism destinations for each other. 
Türkiye's culture, cuisine
Chaiyakam said he was excited to learn he would be posted to Türkiye, having visited the country only once before. He added that he was familiar with Ottoman history.
The ambassador said he had not yet had an opportunity to learn Turkish. For now, he knows only the phrase "merhaba asker," which he heard while presenting his credentials to Erdogan.
He said he was trying to learn about Turkish culture.
"I tried to learn as much as possible. Because Türkiye is a big country, (there is) so much to learn. It's exciting," he said.
Chaiyakam said he particularly enjoyed kebabs and hummus among Turkish dishes. He also expressed surprise that access to Thai cuisine was limited in Türkiye.
He said he had visited Cappadocia and Antalya so far, describing Cappadocia as a destination with significant potential. However, he noted that the number of visitors from Thailand remains low and that the region needs greater promotion. 
Cultural similarities unite Thai, Turkish traditions
Despite their different geographical locations, Thailand and Türkiye share cultural similarities, Chaiyakam said, recalling that he had seen the Turkish tradition of escorting a bride from her family home, which reminded him of a custom in Thailand.
He explained that in Thailand, the bride is accompanied in a procession to the groom's home.
"I saw this in Türkiye, and the wedding is full of fun, same as in Thailand. Your hospitality, your family values are also very similar to Thai people. Even the food sharing, that's also very unique for our culture," he said. 
Diplomatic ties date back to 1958
Diplomatic relations between Türkiye and Thailand were established in 1958, and the two countries will mark their 70th anniversary in 2028, Chaiyakam said.
He noted that relations between the Thai and Turkish peoples, as well as trade, remain below their potential.
"Trade volume is only around $2 billion, the two-way trade, annually. So I think there would be room for improvement," he said.
Chaiyakam emphasized the need to expand two-way trade, adding that tourism also offers significant room for growth. 
Strategic partnership targeted for 2028
The ambassador said numerous programs and events could be organized in 2028 to mark the anniversary of diplomatic relations.
"At the moment, we have a joint economic and trade commission meeting between ministers. But we want to upgrade it to foreign minister level, so the ministers can discuss a wide range of issues, political, economic, and other geopolitical issues or other cooperation," he said.
Chaiyakam said he expected the joint commission to be established soon, possibly in early 2027, and that efforts were underway to arrange high-level visits between the two countries.
He also recalled that a decision was made on July 21 at the ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting to establish a Dialogue Partnership between Türkiye and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
He said high-level contacts could be organized both on that occasion and to mark the anniversary of Türkiye-Thailand diplomatic relations.
Regarding Türkiye's designation as an ASEAN Dialogue Partner, Chaiyakam said: "For Thailand, I think it will give the impetus for both countries to strengthen the relationship."
"We target that Thailand and Türkiye to be strategic partnership," he said. 
Defense industry cooperation a priority
Chaiyakam highlighted Istanbul Airport's position as a major aviation hub in Europe and said Thailand also serves as a hub on mainland Southeast Asia.
He recalled that Turkish Airlines and Thai Airways had signed a strategic cooperation agreement. Thai Airways operates one or two flights a day to Istanbul, while Turkish Airlines operates at least four daily flights to Bangkok, he said.
The ambassador said such initiatives could help the peoples of both countries become better acquainted and gain a deeper understanding of each other, adding that he would do his best to support these efforts.
Turning to defense industry cooperation, Chaiyakam said: "For the defense industry, that's also top on our agenda."
He said Thailand would encourage visits by senior officials to meet with defense industry companies in Türkiye.
"In November, we plan to have high-level (officials) from Navy of Thailand to come to Türkiye to look at various industries in Türkiye. And then I'm in talks with a few companies for a joint project," he said.

The European Union will disburse €3.3 billion ($3.8 billion) to Ukraine for missiles and drones, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday after a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
“Tomorrow, we will disburse another €3.3 billion to Ukraine,” von der Leyen said in an official readout of the call.
She said the payment comes as Russian strikes continue to hit the Ukrainian capital.
“Russia is relentlessly targeting Kyiv, trying to make daily life impossible for its inhabitants,” she said. “We stand with them. And with all Ukrainians.”
The funds are part of the €28.3 billion set aside for Ukraine’s defense this year under the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan.
Von der Leyen said the bloc last week approved EU funding for Patriot systems through the same loan, a step that also opened the way for Ukraine to buy US-made Patriot interceptors used against ballistic missiles.
“But clearly more is needed,” she said.
She said Brussels was ready to use remaining funds from SAFE — Security Action for Europe, the EU’s defense financing instrument for member-state investment and joint purchases — to start a new program for joint EU-Ukraine defense projects.
“We want to develop together a European air and missile defense system, building on our joint anti-ballistic Freya system,” said von der Leyen, “so that we can combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience and innovation with Europe’s technology and industrial strength.”

A-League season start under threat with referees on strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
01:35:39 UTC
10:35:39 KST

A-League referees are on strike, with the season start just one month away
It is seemingly a rare occurrence indeed that Australian football does not find itself in some degree of turmoil.
So it is perhaps of little surprise that as the A-League Men's and Women's seasons fast approach, the code is once again lurching towards another crisis.
The nations top referees have been on strike since September 4, citing "significant changes to the elite refereeing structure" proposed by Football Australia (FA).
The change would see the referees contracted directly by the league, instead of FA.
The Professional Football Referees Association (PFRA) says those changes would be "detrimental to individual referees and represent a drastic step backwards for the professional refereeing program".
The A-League seasons begin in four weeks. And the parties are, as things stand, at something of a stalemate.
The APL and FA have all told ABC Sport they are continuing to work together with the aim of reaching a resolution.
The referee's body said in a statement earlier this month that it would "continue to engage with Football Australia with the aim of resolving the outstanding matters and returning its members to the field as soon as an acceptable outcome can be reached".
As players and supporters at all levels know, without referees there can be no game, so how have we got here?
Who runs the A-Leagues?
To get into the weeds of this dispute, we can go back to the 2020 decision to decouple the A-League from Football Australia.
FA relinquished full control to a newly formed body, the Australian Professional Leagues, after a long period of agitation from both the clubs and world body FIFA about governance issues within the game.
In practice, this meant handing over the commercial reins of the A-Leagues to the clubs, in line with many other professional football leagues around the world, such as the Premier League, Bundesliga and J-League, among others.
The reality has been somewhat different.
In 2024, half of A-League Men players said they were "dissatisfied" with how the competition had been managed by the APL, and close to half said they had "low trust" in whether it could improve the league.
That same year, APL slashed the annual distribution to the clubs from close to $2 million to just $530,000 on account of an increasingly worrying financial outlook.
That followed a frankly disastrous plan to sell off grand finals to Sydney and rapidly declining interest and attendances.
Since then, the stalled expansion drive and the removal of failed club Western United and last month's breakdown of talks between the league and the players over the collective bargaining agreement have added to an environment of intense distrust.
Why are the referees on strike?
Since the league unbundled from Football Australia, the sport's governing body has still provided the referees to the league, with the APL reimbursing FA for those costs.
Now, Football Australia has proposed that it will only pay for matches that come under their jurisdiction: the Australia Cup and Australian Championship.
That means the APL has to pay the referees to officiate its competitions directly, which FA says is the APL's responsibility under the contract it has signed with the league.
However, this is one of the issues that the PFRA has railed against, arguing in essence it would be a conflict of interest to officiate the clubs, who are in effect their employers.
"Such an arrangement would place referees in an unacceptable position of potential conflict and raise serious concerns regarding the integrity and impartiality of the refereeing program," the PFRA said in a statement.
The referees would prefer the formation of an independent referees body, as is the case in England with Pro Ref, formerly known as PGMOL.
The PFRA added that the proposed structure was "untenable" and that referees "cannot grow without trust [or] succeed without independence".
Football Australia said there were no issues around the integrity with their proposal, and that it was consistent with FIFA regulations.
The PFRA also said match officials who officiated in trial matches involving A-League clubs had not been paid their outstanding match fees by FA, which was refuted by FA, which said there were no outstanding debts owed.
Have games been affected?
Football Australia was forced to fly in four Singaporean referees for the Australia Cup semifinal clash between Sydney FC and Melbourne Victory on September 9.
Young Australian referee Rowan Fisher, who does not have any A-League experience, took charge of the second semifinal between South Melbourne and Lions FC earlier this week.
It is understood that there is no risk of the Australia Cup final between South Melbourne and Melbourne Victory on October 10 not being played.
This is due to a group of referees that have signed a contract with FA despite the stand-off.
The second season of the second-tier Australian Championship, which kicks off on Thursday October 15, is also not expected to be at risk.
Both those competitions are administered by FA.
However, no assurances have been given about the A-Leagues, Men and Women, which both start that same weekend.
'Nobody becomes a referee because they want to withdraw their services'
The nation's referees are clear they want to get back to the business of refereeing.
But they feel their voices need to be heard.
"Our members have delivered an overwhelmingly clear message. They are seeking certainty around their employment, payment of outstanding amounts, and a clear and sustainable structure for professional refereeing in Australia," PFRA president Evgeny Vizelman said in a statement.
"We do not take the decision to stop officiating matches lightly. Our members want to officiate football, prepare for the upcoming season and positively contribute to the success of football in Australia.
"Nobody becomes a referee because they want to withdraw their services.
"Taking ourselves off the field hurts. There comes a point where people have to stand together and say the way they are being treated is not good enough."

Observers abducted, public-sector workers coerced and communications cut: how Russia's elections have begun
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
04:35:00 EEST
10:35:00 KST

Observers abducted, public-sector workers coerced and communications cut: how Russia's elections have begun
Mobile networks and internet access may be shut down in Russia during the three days of voting for the State Duma (lower chamber of the Russian parliament) and regional parliament elections on 18-21 September due to what authorities describe as "security measures". Meanwhile, systematic pressure on election observers, coercion of public-sector employees and widespread electoral fraud are being reported across the country.
Source: Russian independent media outlets Vazhnye Istorii (Important Stories) and Astra; human rights organisations; media outlets 7x7 and Verstka, and regional Telegram channels
Details: Ella Pamfilova, head of Russia's Central Election Commission, warned of possible restrictions on communications. She said network disruptions would not prevent the voting process from going ahead.
"There may be some, shall we say, unintentional disruptions to mobile communications and data transmission. For us, this is not a reason to cancel the vote," Pamfilova said.
Although the three-day voting period began on 18 September, numerous violations and cases of intimidation of independent observers and opposition representatives began well in advance.
In Altai Krai, local election commissions have reportedly been falsifying lists for home voting on a large scale, adding citizens without their consent. Local activists conducted telephone surveys of people at addresses on the lists, and residents confirmed that they had not submitted any applications and were not expecting election commission members to visit them.
In addition, voters in the region are being forced to register for remote e-voting. More than 250,000 Altai Krai residents have so far applied to vote online, accounting for almost 15% of the region's electorate.
The Russian authorities are forcing public-sector employees to report individually on votes cast for Vladimir Putin's United Russia party. Reports of this have emerged from Altai Krai and Novosibirsk, Sverdlovsk, Belgorod and Samara oblasts.
Representatives of the anti-war Yabloko party have also faced pressure. In Kazan, candidate Sofia Fedorova and her team are facing attempts to force them out of their offices: immediately after a meeting with voters on 16 September, the electricity to the premises was cut off and the landlord demanded that they vacate the office immediately.
In Sverdlovsk Oblast, five Yabloko candidates were abruptly removed from the State Duma election race.
In Tambov Oblast, law enforcement officers have begun systematically pressuring election observers, demanding face-to-face meetings. Human rights advocate Vladimir Zhilkin said police officers were working from extensive, pre-prepared lists of independent observers and that their actions appeared to be coordinated across different districts of the oblast.
Other parties are also facing obstruction. In Voronezh Oblast, for instance, around 400 observers from the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF) were barred from polling stations on the grounds of alleged "errors in the paperwork".
The situation is particularly critical in Russian regions bordering Ukraine, where Russia's Central Election Commission authorised early voting to take place 12 days before the nationwide election day.
In Rostov Oblast, unidentified masked individuals abducted Boris Mikliukov, an observer representing Yabloko. Three unidentified people forced the activist into an unmarked car and drove him towards one of the police stations in Rostov-on-Don. Contact with him has since been lost.
In Belgorod Oblast, widespread ballot stuffing was recorded on the very first day of early voting during home voting, with election commission members casting votes on behalf of voters.
"They're voting for everyone en masse. My mother called me and happily told me that I didn't need to go anywhere because someone had already voted for me," a Belgorod resident said.
The previous day, investigative journalists published leaked internal documents concerning the State Automated System Vybory 2.0 (Elections 2.0), which is being used fully for the first time in Russian federal elections in 2026. According to the developer's technical documentation, the updated system contains tools that allow final vote-count protocols to be directly substituted, electoral rolls to be altered and unverified electronic voting results to be uploaded.
Background:
- On 17 September, the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) called on the parliaments and governments of foreign states, international organisations and parliamentary assemblies to condemn the holding of sham elections to the Russian State Duma in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine and not to recognise their results.
- Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs stressed that Russia's organisation and conduct of the sham vote in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine constitute a gross violation of Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, Ukrainian law and international law, including the UN Charter.

White House withdraws Lance Schroyer’s nomination to lead ICE
Unknown

White House withdraws Lance Schroyer’s nomination to lead ICE
The ex-Oklahoma state trooper’s nomination had stalled in the Senate as ICE faced growing scrutiny over its operations.
The White House has withdrawn the nomination of former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to lead United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), without giving a reason for the decision.
The withdrawal was announced on Thursday. Schroyer, a senior adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, was nominated by President Donald Trump in June but had yet to receive a hearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
Recommended Stories
list of 1 itemend of list
Republican Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who chairs the committee, had refused to hold a hearing until the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) provided information he had requested about civilian deaths during ICE enforcement operations.
“I don’t have a concern with who the nominee was. I had asked them to give me an update on the internal investigation into civilian deaths,” Paul told The Associated Press news agency.
Paul said he had intended to hold a hearing on Schroyer’s nomination but learned that it had been withdrawn when the White House made the decision public.
ICE remains under scrutiny
Schroyer had little experience in immigration and had not previously worked at ICE or led a major law enforcement agency. Two US officials told the Reuters news agency when he was nominated that he had been a surprise choice for the position.
When announcing Schroyer’s nomination in June, Trump said on Truth Social that he had “firsthand experience getting Illegal Aliens OFF our streets” and called on the Senate to confirm him “IMMEDIATELY”.
The withdrawal comes as ICE remains under scrutiny over its enforcement operations as the Trump administration carries out its immigration crackdown.
Critics have raised questions about how the agency has recruited and trained officers as it rapidly expanded its workforce. Federal immigration officers have also shot and killed multiple people during enforcement operations, including two US citizens in Minneapolis earlier this year.
ICE arrests have continued to increase, reaching nearly 51,000 in August, the highest monthly total of Trump’s second administration.
ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed director since 2017. David Venturella is serving as acting director after Todd Lyons resigned earlier this year.
The White House has not indicated when it might announce another nominee to lead the agency.

Robert Kraft was right about Macklemore, the explanation was all wrong - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
01:23:32 UTC
10:23:32 KST

The problem was not Robert Kraft’s decision. The problem is how we explain it.
We removed the messenger from the stage without confronting the lie he was spreading. We focused on Macklemore–his rhetoric, his history, the hurt his words cause–when the far greater threat is the message itself. And in doing so, we inadvertently helped create precisely the narrative Macklemore and his defenders wanted.
Now the story practically writes itself: Macklemore dared to “speak truth to power.” He said what others supposedly do not want Americans to hear, and for his courage, a Jewish billionaire and other venue owners took away his microphone. Macklemore becomes the martyr. His cancellation becomes evidence of his righteousness. And Jews assume precisely the role his rhetoric already assigns us: morally compromised and willing to use our influence to suppress anyone brave enough to expose an uncomfortable truth.
We should stop defending ourselves against the accusation and start challenging the accusation itself.
Macklemore did not belong on that stage because he was using it to spread hateful lies about the Jewish state. He was telling an audience that the world’s only Jewish state is committing “genocide” and practicing “apartheid,” presenting those accusations not as arguments to defend, but as settled truths.
That is not the same as supporting Palestinians or criticizing Israel. Macklemore remains free to say what he believes. But freedom of speech does not entitle anyone to someone else’s microphone, particularly an entertainment stage before thousands who bought tickets for a concert rather than to hear a political polemic.
There is also a bitter irony in the outrage over Macklemore being “canceled.” Where was this defense of artistic freedom when American Jewish musician Matisyahu had concerts canceled after activists targeted venues over his support for Israel, creating security and staffing concerns? Macklemore did not lose his place because of his identity. He lost that stage because of what he chose to do with it.
The accusations coming from more than Macklemore
And this is much bigger than Macklemore. He did not invent these accusations. He is simply their latest celebrity messenger.
“Genocide.” “Apartheid.” “Ethnic cleansing.” “War criminal.” We hear these charges on college campuses, across social media, in newsrooms, entertainment, politics, and our institutions. Repeated often enough, they enter our discourse not as extraordinary accusations requiring proof, but as established facts requiring allegiance.
That is where the Jewish community has missed something fundamental. We have become very good at identifying antisemitism and condemning those who traffic in it. We have been far less willing to confront the lies that make the antisemitism possible.
Dara Horn has articulated something essential about antisemitism: it does not operate simply as hatred or intolerance toward Jews. It operates through a recurring lie–that Jews are responsible for destroying whatever a society holds most dear.
That distinction changes the prescription. If we treat antisemitism primarily as intolerance, we answer it with tolerance: more education, dialogue, and opportunities to understand Jews. Those things have value. But you cannot cure a lie by teaching people to become more tolerant of the people being lied about. You have to challenge the lie.
And we must confront the genocide lie more boldly. Israel is not committing genocide. The accusation is false and outrageous.
Genocide is not a synonym for a terrible war, a high civilian death toll, or even violations of the laws of war. It is a specific crime requiring intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group as such. Intent is not incidental to the definition. It is essential.
Israel’s conduct matters too. John Spencer, chair of urban warfare studies at West Point’s Modern War Institute, has argued after studying the Gaza campaign that Israel has implemented more measures to prevent civilian harm than any military he has studied. That does not mean every Israeli decision was correct or every strike justified. But warnings, evacuations, and extensive civilian-harm precautions are evidence that must be confronted before accusing a country of intending to destroy a people.
The genocide accusation is a modern blood libel.
The original blood libel accused Jews of deliberately murdering Christian children. Its power came from transforming hatred into righteousness. Those who believed it did not imagine themselves persecuting innocent Jews. They imagined themselves protecting innocent children from evil.
The moral vocabulary changes. The mechanism remains hauntingly familiar. Today, someone can accuse the Jewish state of deliberately destroying a people and still sincerely insist–as Macklemore has–that he has nothing against Jews. He may genuinely believe he is standing against evil. That is precisely what makes the libel so dangerous.
Concern for Palestinian human rights, advocacy for Palestinians and criticism of Israel are not antisemitic. Palestinian suffering is real. Innocent civilians have died, and where individuals commit crimes, they should be held accountable.
But none of that establishes genocide. And compassion does not demand self-flagellation or self-erasure.
Jews should not have to accept the lie that Israel is committing genocide to prove that we care about Palestinian lives. We should not have to sever our connection to Israel to establish our moral credibility or repeat a blood libel against the Jewish state to demonstrate our decency.
Yet that is increasingly the moral test imposed upon us.
Accept that the world’s only Jewish state is committing one of humanity’s gravest crimes, and you can remain among the righteous. Challenge that premise, defend Israel against the charge, or refuse to distance yourself from the Jewish state, and suddenly your disagreement becomes complicity–and your connection to Israel becomes evidence against you.
That is not incidental to the antisemitism. It is how the antisemitism works.
Some argue that Netanyahu’s government or particular Israeli policies have made defending Israel more difficult. But difficulty does not turn an accusation into a fact. We do not have to support Netanyahu or defend every Israeli action. And distancing ourselves from Israel will not make American Jews safer; it only reinforces the dangerous fiction that Jewish safety depends on Jewish behavior.
We can defend Palestinian humanity without surrendering our own. We should not disavow Israel to demonstrate our decency or accept collective guilt for a crime Israel did not commit.
The answer to a blood libel is not to prove that Jews are good people. It is to expose the blood libel as a lie.
Robert Kraft is a hero for standing up. Now it is our job to stand with him–and fight the lies.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked 28 Chinese military aircraft, seven naval vessels, and two official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Thursday and 6 a.m. on Friday.
Twenty-four of the 28 People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern, central, southwestern, and eastern air defense identification zone, according to the MND.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems to monitor PLA activity.
So far this month, the MND has tracked Chinese aircraft 155 times and ships 172 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

Former Assad officer sentenced to 60 years in US for torture
Former Syrian official sentenced to 60 years in US prison for torturing prisoners under al-Assad’s regime.
A former Syrian military official convicted of torturing prisoners during the rule of former President Bashar al-Assad has been sentenced to 60 years in a United States prison.
A federal judge in Los Angeles sentenced Samir Ousman Alsheikh on Thursday. A jury found him guilty in March of one count of conspiracy to commit torture and three counts of torture while in charge of Syria‘s infamous Adra Prison from roughly 2005 to 2008.

“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel, and almost unspeakably violent and brutal,” the judge said before announcing the sentence.
Human rights groups and the United Nations have accused the Syrian government officials of widespread abuses in detention facilities, including torture and arbitrary detention of thousands of people, in many cases without informing their families.
US prosecutors said Alsheikh, seeking to quash political dissent, sent certain prisoners to a wing of Adra where they were held in small isolation cells and tortured.
At the two-week trial, three victims recounted beatings while suspended from pipes on the ceiling for hours or days and the use of a device that folded their bodies in half at the waist, according to a press release from the US Department of Justice. One person testified that Alsheikh stomped on the device with his foot, according to the department.
“Defendant knew that what he was doing was wrong,” Justice Department prosecutors said in a sentencing memo filed this month. “Nonetheless, he ordered and participated in the torture of his victims because he had the power to do so and because he thought he would never be held accountable.”
The memo included statements from several victims, one of whom, Nidal Shikhani, said he can “still hear the screams of others begging for mercy, repeating, ‘Leave me, leave me.’”
The prosecutors asked US District Judge Hernan D Vera for a minimum sentence of 80 years. Alsheikh’s lawyers, Nina Marino and Collin Cate, called for a five-year sentence, noting that he is 74 years old and has “significant medical and cognitive conditions”. They also said he was willing to be deported to Syria, where a new government has sought to hold Assad-era security officials accountable.
“Whatever moral weight this case carries in the broader arc of history — however much the world, or the victims, or the public might wish the sentence to ‘send a message’ — that desire cannot be the foundation of a just sentence,” Marino and Cate wrote in their September 3 memo.
Alsheikh came to the US in 2020 and applied for citizenship, but the Justice Department said he lied about his past. Federal authorities arrested him at Los Angeles international airport in July 2024.
Jurors also convicted him in March of lying to US immigration authorities and fraudulently obtaining a green card and attempting to naturalise as a US citizen.
“The acts Alsheikh ordered and directly participated in are gruesome and disturbing. We would like to offer our gratitude to the brave victims who testified leading to today’s sentencing,” Heith Janke, assistant director of the FBI’s criminal division, said in a press release Thursday.
Al-Assad was ousted in a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024, bringing a 14-year civil war to an end, but the country has continued to suffer from sporadic outbreaks of violence.
In March 2025, armed groups aligned with al-Assad ambushed the new government’s security forces on Syria’s coast. A government counteroffensive then spiralled into sectarian revenge attacks and the massacre of hundreds of civilians from the Alawite religious minority, to which al-Assad belongs.
On Thursday, three people were sentenced in the Syrian city of Aleppo in connection with the violence. One member of the pro-Assad groups was sentenced to death and another to life in prison, while a member of the government security forces who took part in the revenge attacks was convicted of murder and sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Guizhou's "Hundred-Time Champion" jockey rides village horse-racing wave
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:13:06 CST
10:13:06 KST

GUIYANG, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The starting gun cracked and the brown horse burst forward, hooves pounding the dirt as dust billowed behind. On its back, jockey Lu Guo leaned low, his red helmet and yellow shirt flashing against the September sky.
When "Meteor Warrior" crossed the finish line first at the 2026 Guizhou Village Horse (GVH) village-level league final in Sandu Shui Autonomous County, southwest China's Guizhou Province, the crowd erupted. "'Hundred-Time Champion' wins!" they shouted.
Lu straightened up, patted his horse's neck and broke into a wide grin. The brown horse gave a low whinny, as if answering the cheers.
"Hundred-Time Champion" is a nickname Lu has long lived up to. Since he began competing at the age of eight, he has won well over 100 titles. But the 37-year-old from Yongkang Village in Sandu is not one to dwell on past success.
"'Hundred-Time Champion' belongs to the past," he said modestly. Looking ahead, he hopes to continue competing on the fast-growing GVH circuit and eventually raise his own racehorse and win more titles.
At the 2026 GVH village-level league final, held at Guwen Hill in Sandong Community, Zhonghe Town, Lu won two gold medals and one silver, making him the event's most successful rider.
"In recent years, as the GVH has gained popularity far beyond local circles, races are held throughout the year in Sandu, which is perfect for a jockey," said Lu, his face bronzed by the sun.
Lu is a native of Sandu, home to the Shui people, who have a long tradition of breeding, riding and racing horses, earning them the nickname "an ethnic group on horseback." From September to November, during the Shui New Year festival known as the Duan Festival, villagers hold horse races on open, gently sloping hills accessible to people of all ages.
The youngest of seven siblings in a Shui family, Lu was influenced by his father, a horse breeder and jockey, as well as his eldest sister, now in her 60s, who still enjoys riding. He first rode a horse at six and began competing at eight. At the time, there were no age or horse classifications and no saddles. Courage was often the only requirement for taking part.
From watching races with his father to competing himself, Lu grew familiar with the roar of thousands of spectators. His favorite mount was a white horse named "Little White Dragon," raised by his cousin, and he won many titles riding it.
With limited entertainment options at the time, Duan Festival horse races drew crowds from miles around, and Lu went wherever races were held. He won prizes ranging from 15 yuan to 250 yuan, as well as goods including quilts and refrigerators. Those carefree racing days lasted throughout his nine years of schooling.
Then life took a different turn. A year after his father died in 2004, 16-year-old Lu finished middle school and left home to earn a living. As more people left the area for work, participation in Duan Festival horse races declined. After two years in factories, Lu, longing for the freedom of racing, returned to jockeying and competed in places such as Anhui, Hebei, Beijing, Jiangsu and Wuhan.
Although Lu won many titles over more than a decade, the itinerant lifestyle eventually took its toll. "There were few races in those years. I was like an apprentice drifting from place to place with no stable job," Lu said.
Injuries sustained in competitions in 2017 and 2019 added to the strain, and Lu often returned home to decompress through farm work such as rice transplanting and harvesting. In 2022, he returned home permanently. Employed by a local horse owner in Sandu as a trainer and jockey, he also competed in several major events outside the province, with limited success.
His fortunes changed with the rise of the GVH, a grassroots horse racing event that grew out of Sandu's traditional Duan Festival races. Featuring local villagers as jockeys, it has developed into a popular sporting and cultural event.
In 2023, inspired by the Village Basketball Association, dubbed "Cun BA," and the Village Super League, known as "Cun Chao," Zhonghe Town and Colorful Guizhou Cultural and Art Co., Ltd. began organizing local horse racing events.
During the 2024 National Day holiday, the company launched the GVH Racing Invitational at Sandu Western Racecourse. Videos of the races gained widespread attention online and drew visitors from across the country, helping the GVH gain popularity.
The expansion created new opportunities for Lu. Over the years, the GVH has staged more than 180 events and attracted nearly 3,000 riders nationwide. The Duan Festival races have also made a comeback, growing from just nine race sites three years ago to 34 today and contributing to local cultural, sports and tourism development.
Competing year-round, Lu now earns more than 100,000 yuan (about 14,904 U.S. dollars) annually in prize money. He also cares for horses for several owners, earning more than 10,000 yuan (about 1,490 U.S. dollars) a month. "Since the 'Village Horse' went viral, races are held all year round. My income and quality of life have improved," Lu said.
The GVH has also given Lu a renewed sense of purpose. Over the past year, he has won more than 10 titles in GVH events. At the 2026 May Day National GVH Invitational, he claimed four gold medals and one bronze across five races in a single day.
"In hometown races, family and friends come to cheer me on, which brings me great joy," Lu said, adding that he has also mentored many children who want to learn from him, something he finds equally rewarding.
With the GVH continuing to grow, Lu's life has become increasingly stable. His biggest wish now is to own a racehorse again. "I used to have one, but had to sell it due to injury and financial constraints," he said, adding that he is determined to work hard to buy another and further develop his racing career.
"My fate is now closely intertwined with the GVH," Lu said, emphasizing that he hopes the GVH will carry his dreams even further into the future. ■

RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- New Botafogo manager Tite said Thursday his immediate priority is survival as a tightly contested league leaves mid-table teams at risk of relegation.

"Being at this club allows you to have ambition, to set goals," the former Brazil head coach said in his first press conference as Botafogo manager on Thursday.

Tite replaces Rodrigo Bellao, who had filled the role on an interim basis after Franclim Carvalho was sacked on August 18.

"In my opinion, the Brazilian championship has flattened out," the 65-year-old said. "Everyone's level is very similar, very close. The teams at the top stand out a bit more, but those lower down have grown significantly, to the point where you see teams at the bottom winning extremely important games against top teams."
Tite, who had been out of work since leaving Cruzeiro in March, agreed to a deal that ties him to Botafogo until December 2028.
He said the offer of a long-term deal had been crucial in his decision to accept the job.
"The chance to develop a squad over the mid to long term is what I think is required to achieve success in football," he added. ■

The Cafeteros will play Mexico in Baltimore on September 26, Paraguay in New Jersey on October 2 and Peru in Miami on October 6.
The matches will mark the team's first outings since a penalty shootout loss to Switzerland in the World Cup round of 16 in July.
Lorenzo paid tribute to Rodriguez, who is Colombia's most capped player with 131 international appearances and its second-highest scorer with 31 goals.
"I didn't intervene in his decision [to retire]," Lorenzo said. "I listened to him and respected his timeline. I had known since the match against Switzerland, and I respected his decision regarding how and when to announce it."
"James has given an enormous amount to the national team. He was a cornerstone of our project. We must thank him for everything he did and hope that the shirt continues to shine."
FIFA's extended international window, which combines the previously separate September and October dates, allows teams to play up to four fixtures over a 16-day period.
Lorenzo has said that he will use the friendlies to test new players ahead of South America's 2030 World Cup qualifiers. ■

Trump says 'major progress' made towards US military base in Poland
US President Donald Trump said that Washington and Warsaw were making "major progress" towards establishing a US military base in Poland, potentially giving the United States a permanent military foothold on NATO's eastern flank even as his administration reviews its broader troop presence in Europe.
US President Donald Trump said Thursday there had been "major progress" towards establishing an American military base in Poland, after Warsaw said it was holding talks with Washington on the issue.
"Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made towards establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said on social media.
"If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance."
Trump's announcement comes despite his administration launching a formal review of its military presence in Europe, raising fears among allies that it could cut back its forces in European nations.
But Poland, which borders both Ukraine and Russia on NATO's eastern flank and spends around five percent of its GDP on defense, is working to strengthen the US presence on its soil.
"We are ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defence cooperation: seriously, responsibly, and always together," Nawrocki said on X.
"I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base."
Nawrocki is a conservative ally of Trump, and he visited the White House last year. During that visit Trump offered to send more US troops to Poland.
Polish deputy defence minister Pawel Zalewski said in August that his country was discussing with the United States whether to set up a permanent US base on its territory.
"We have already completed the initial stage (of the process), not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago," Zalewski told public broadcaster TVP.
Almost 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland – which is also an EU member state – but almost exclusively on a rotational basis.
Washington has levied heavy criticism against a number of European countries that refused to allow US forces to use NATO bases on their territory in their war with Iran.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had also threatened to reduce his country's contribution to the alliance's budget if certain states refused to honour the commitments made last year at the NATO summit in The Hague.
At that summit, NATO allies pledged to devote by 2035 at least five percent of their GDP to security spending, including 3.5 percent devoted strictly to military expenditures.

Scientists trace half the DNA in Xinjiang’s oldest tombs to Yellow River farmers
Study of Bronze Age remains uncovers a population with roots in both Yellow River farmers and Eurasian steppe groups
2-MIN READ2-MIN
1
 Listen
Nestled between the Tianshan Mountains and the Gobi Desert, the Hami oasis in Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region is a land of little rain, battered by wind and sand year-round.
It is also home to the region’s oldest known burial site, the Tianshanbeilu cemetery, located around 500km (310 miles) east of Urumqi, the regional capital. More than 700 Bronze Age tombs have been unearthed here, long assumed to belong to Eurasian nomads who migrated eastward from the steppes.
But a study published on Friday in the journal Science upends that view, revealing a previously unknown, genetically mixed population that lived in the eastern Tianshan region 3,600 years ago, during China’s Shang dynasty (1600-1050BC).

Former Philippine President Duterte Makes First In-person Appearance at ICC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:56:00 UTC
09:56:00 KST

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appeared in person at the International Criminal Court (ICC) for the first time on Wednesday, ahead of his trial for atrocities committed during his violent “war on drugs” campaign.
Duterte, 81, has been in the court’s custody since his arrest in the Philippines in March 2025. He faces three charges of crimes against humanity for extrajudicial killings carried out during the anti-drug campaign, a flagship policy of his administration between 2016 and 2022.
For all of the pre-trial hearings so far, including his initial appearance in March 2025, Duterte has appeared via video link from the ICC’s detention unit.
He appeared yesterday before the ICC’s Trial Chamber III, which held a third status conference to discuss how to manage the sprawling case against Duterte. The Inquirer.net reported that the case involves “hundreds of thousands of pages of documents, more than 1,000 audio and video files, and an estimated 193 hours of direct examination by prosecution witnesses.”
During the proceedings, Duterte sat quietly sipping water and at one point stood and waved to family members in the public gallery, Reuters reported.
However, the physical condition of the former president, who appeared thin and haggard, raised the question of whether he will live to see a verdict – and whether he is even fit to stand trial.
Duterte’s attorneys claimed last year that he was in frail health and that his condition was deteriorating in the ICC’s detention unit. In one filing in June, they argued that the ex-president’s illness and “advanced age” created “compelling humanitarian grounds” for judges to grant his interim release. In September 2025, they claimed that he was unfit to stand trial due to “cognitive impairment in multiple domains.”
In January, judges rejected the defense claims, arguing that Duterte “is able effectively to exercise his procedural rights and is therefore fit to take part in the pre-trial proceedings.” They also requested his physical presence in court.
However, the defendant’s advanced age and apparent ill-health are likely to remain pressing issues as the court moves toward the beginning of his trial on November 30.
At Wednesday’s hearing, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner expressed concerns about the volume of evidence and the length of the prosecution case. She said the chamber was “very anxious” that the prosecution case should conclude “as swiftly as possible in the circumstances,” due to Duterte’s age and health. The trial is set to begin on November 30.
“It’s important this trial goes ahead as quickly as possible,” she said, pressing parties to limit the number of witnesses and focus on key evidence.
Duterte’s attorney, Peter Haynes, said that his team did not have the time to examine the tens of thousands of pieces of evidence submitted by prosecutors, calling the task “enormous and impossible.”
“If I had a younger and healthier client, I would request pushing back the trial by six months,” he said, as per Reuters.
Duterte is charged with the murders of at least 76 people and the attempted murder of two others. Nineteen of the alleged murders were carried out between 2013 and 2016, when Duterte was mayor of Davao City. The remainder were committed during the “war on drugs” campaign, which Duterte launched upon becoming president in 2016. The campaign resulted in a death toll of at least 6,000 – the official estimate of the Philippine police – but independent estimates run as high as 30,000.
In April of this year, the ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed the charges against Duterte and ordered the case to go to trial. The chamber’s judges concluded that “there are substantial grounds to believe that Mr. Duterte is responsible for the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder.” These crimes “were committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population on the territory of the Republic of the Philippines.”
The alleged crimes took place between November 1, 2011, and March 16, 2019, the date on which Duterte withdrew the Philippines from the ICC’s Rome Statute.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday took strong exception to 31 unnatural deaths in Manipur's relief camps - set up after the eruption of Kuki-Meitei ethnic clashes in 2023 to shelter internally displaced persons (IDPs) - including one due to sexual assault.A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the state govt to file an affidavit giving details of the causes of death as ascertained through postmortem reports and the investigations to identify the culprits. It also questioned the state for giving a meagre Rs 30,000 as compensation to the next of kin even though the state had paid Rs 4 lakh-5 lakh to relatives of victims of the ethnic clashes.This order was passed after perusing Justice Gita Mittal Committee's report. Only after prodding did govt provide the required information. Jiribam and Churachandpur relief camps recorded nine unnatural deaths each; six were reported in Bishnupur, four in Imphal West, two in Imphal East and one in Kakching.The bench directed the state chief secretary to submit what remedial measures would be taken to prevent such incidents. It also asked the state to detail the steps taken to expedite investigations into the FIRs.
Justice Mittal Committee informed the court that the mother of the sexual assault victim in Churachandpur relief camp was given Rs 2.5 lakh as compensation but in most cases, the next of kin got only Rs 30,000. In Kangpokpi relief camp, where 128 IDPs died natural deaths, no compensation was paid to their kin, it said.

Trump to offer Putin economic deals before the end of Russia’s war against Ukraine - NYT
Kyiv • UNN
The Trump administration is considering deals with Russia before the end of the war to encourage the Kremlin to pursue peace. This contradicts the position of Congress and Kyiv.
The White House is considering signing economic agreements with Russia before it ends the war in Ukraine. The New York Times reports this, citing "two people close to the talks," UNN reports.
Details
According to one of the publication's sources, agreements with Russia before the end of the war are possible because they would show that the United States is serious about resetting relations with the Kremlin.
This approach represents a departure from Mr. Trump's promise last year that economic agreements with Russia would not be concluded "until we resolve the war." It indicates that Mr. Trump's envoys on ending the war, Steve Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, are looking for new ways to persuade Russia to stop hostilities, now that it has become clear that Ukraine will not give up part of its own territory, which, at Mr. Putin's insistence, he must control before the end of the war
The authors point out that this contrasts with the approach advocated by both Republicans and Democrats in Congress, not to mention Kyiv's European allies and Ukraine itself, that only increased economic and military pressure on Putin can force him to compromise.
"But since the Trump administration is pursuing a carrot-and-stick approach with Mr. Putin, the carrot appears to be the focus. According to a U.S. official, the administration wants to create more incentives for members of the Russian elite to seek peace. Concluding some business agreements before the end of the war could help convince the anti-American hawks around Mr. Putin that Mr. Trump really wants to establish new relations with Russia," the publication writes.
Context
The U.S. House of Representatives supported the Senate version of H.R. 5334, a bill that provides for a major strengthening of sanctions against Russia and the possibility of imposing tariffs of up to 100% on countries that purchase Russian energy resources.
Later, Russian dictator's press secretary Dmitry Peskov said that the adoption in the United States of a law on "hellish sanctions" was an unfriendly step.
