Tunisia floods disrupt capital as heavy rain traps motorists and residents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:49:24 UTC
09:49:24 KST

Tunisia floods disrupt capital as heavy rain traps motorists and residents
Recurring floods disrupt daily life in Tunis, raising questions about drainage, transport and flood preparedness.
Tunis, Tunisia – Heavy rain brought parts of Tunisia’s capital to a standstill on Thursday, flooding roads and homes, trapping people in cars and disrupting electricity and internet services.
Home to nearly three million people, the Greater Tunis region has faced repeated flooding in recent years. Thursday’s flooding came only months after severe January rains caused widespread disruption across the capital and other parts of the country, leaving several people dead and causing significant damage.
Weather warnings had been issued in advance, but the decision to suspend classes in Tunis was announced only shortly before it took effect. Parents rushed to schools to collect their children as the rain intensified and traffic backed up across the capital.
Videos shared online showed flooded streets, cars stranded in rising water and what appeared to be power lines catching fire. Residents also reported power and internet cuts and water entering homes.
‘The road became almost unrecognisable’
Fatma, a 35-year-old employee in Tunis, said the situation deteriorated quickly as she struggled to get home safely.
“At about 4pm, the road became almost unrecognisable. The tunnel leading to Bab Saadoun was completely closed because of the rain,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Most people were stranded by the roadside for hours, waiting for public transport that never came. I saw three cars that filled with water and broke down, and people carrying their children on their shoulders.”
“Every season, the same thing happens. Roads close and traffic comes to a complete standstill. All the drains start overflowing with waste,” she said.
The National Institute of Meteorology had warned of locally heavy thunderstorms on Thursday, including heavy rain over short periods that could cause flooding, disrupt traffic and overwhelm drainage networks. It also warned of potential power cuts.
Residents question flood preparedness
“Tunisia has become used to these disasters. Every year, we end up flooded even when there is little rain,” said Intissar, 33, from the Lafayette area of Tunis.
She blamed local authorities for failing to carry out preventive work before the rainy season.
“This is work that should have been done during the summer,” she said.
But she also acknowledged the role of residents.
“We cannot deny the responsibility of citizens who dump waste that blocks drainage channels,” she said.
At a government meeting in August, officials called for drainage networks and waterways to be cleaned and flood-protection work to be accelerated. The government said 29 flood-protection projects were under way across the country.
The flooding comes as Tunisia prepares for a national march in Tunis on Saturday, with organisers calling for the release of four activists detained in connection with the Al-Soumoud Flotilla. The march is scheduled for 5pm, as rain is forecast to continue through Saturday.
A struggle to get home
Fatma said the lack of reliable public transport, combined with repeated flooding, was making it increasingly difficult for people to manage without cars.
“The problem makes people look for their own solutions. That is why most people are trying to find a way to buy a car, because it has become difficult to live without one with these recurring problems,” she said.
The flooding also came as students returned to schools and universities this week, adding pressure to roads and public transport.
For Fatma, the disruption is becoming a familiar pattern.
“This shows that the state has no vision. It is caught off-guard just like citizens are,” she said.

It proposed the round "be conducted strictly in accordance with the existing principles or rules applicable to a stray vacancy round, with no provision for upgradation of candidates who are already holding/joined a seat", govt said.After the second round of NEET-SS counselling, 1,857 super specialty seats - including 1,094 DM/MCh seats and 763 DNB-SS seats - were vacant. A substantial number of these pertain to highly specialised medical and surgical disciplines.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday told Tamil Nadu govt that it needed to change its mindset towards teaching Hindi in schools and should thrash out issues with Centre on setting up Navodaya Vidyalayas in every district.As Vijay-led TN govt took the same stand taken by the previous DMK govt, a bench of Justices B V Nagarathna and A G Masih said individual states could not act like countries. "You have to change your mindset, it can't be that Hindi will not be taught on the soil of TN," the bench said.TN has been opposing the setting up of these schools as they follow a three-language policy, including Hindi, which is against the state's two-language policy.
"We are saying in addition to all the good things you're doing in your state, having something in addition will not bring down your standards... People in Chennai should not alienate Delhi and vice versa," SC said.Senior advocate Jaideep Gupta, appearing for the state, submitted it was against the federal structure to impose Centre's decision on a state. "It is against the state policy. It supersedes Tamil. This kind of unification is not the purport of Constitution.
It is not a central govt school. It is a school run by a society. There is an adamancy that Hindi must predominate," he said.Gupta submitted that cooperative federalism would never work in only one direction and such a policy should not be enforced by the court.
The bench asked the state to comply with its order and posted the case for further hearing in Dec. SC had last Dec directed TN to identify land required for establishing Navodaya Vidyalayas in each district within six weeks."We are not asking you to acquire land. We are only asking you to identify it... There is a need for dialogue. You can't say I won't accept a policy. Today it is education, tomorrow it will be something else. You have to relax this rigidity in your mind," SC said.The court was hearing TN's plea challenging a Madras HC judgement directing it to set up Navodaya Vidyalayas in every district. HC had ruled that Navodaya Vidyalayas did not violate Tamil Nadu Tamil Learning Act and the state's blanket refusal to set up such schools curtailed students' right to choose educational institutions.

The US state department said on Wednesday that it had again denied entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead next week’s United Nations general assembly gathering in New York.
The state department said in a statement the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) had “failed to live up to their commitments”, accusing the groups of “taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ)” and of “glorifying terrorism” among other allegations.
“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the department said.
The move marks the second year in a row the Trump administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from traveling to New York to attend the UN general assembly in person.
The foreign ministry of the Palestinian Authority denied the allegations made against it in a statement on Thursday, describing the visa sanctions as an “unjustified measure” that “contradicts the efforts being made to restore trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and prepare the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability in the region”.
Among the Palestinian officials barred from entering the US is Mahmoud Abbas, the longtime president of the Palestinian Authority, according to reports.
The UN general assembly voted on Thursday to allow Abbas to address the gathering via video, for the second year in a row.
This year’s UN general assembly general debate begins on 22 September.

US court sentences ex-Syrian official who ran notorious ‘punishment wing’ to 60 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:37:22 UTC
09:37:22 KST

- 
  This article contains descriptions of torture.
A US federal court in Los Angeles sentenced a former Syrian government official who ran one of the country’s most infamous prisons to 60 years in prison on Thursday – the most significant punishment handed to an official of ousted president Bashar al-Assad’s regime by a foreign court and to a defendant present in person.
Samir Ousman al-Sheikh was the head of the Adra prison, on the outskirts of Damascus, between 2005 and 2008, when he oversaw an underground “punishment wing”, known as “Wing 13”, in which prisoners and regime opponents were interrogated and tortured as he watched through surveillance cameras. A federal jury convicted al-Sheikh last March of having tortured prisoners and then lying about it in US immigration forms.
“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and almost unspeakably violent and brutal,” said Hernan D Vera, a US district judge, before delivering the sentence.
Al-Sheikh’s legal did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Assistant attorney general A Tysen Duva of the justice department’s criminal division said in a statement the sentence sends a clear message: “Human rights violators who come to the United States will receive no safe harbor here. We will find them, and they will be prosecuted and punished for their heinous crimes.”
Al-Sheikh, 74, who also served as governor of Syria’s Deir Ez-Zour province in 2011, at a time of violent regime crackdowns against protesters, moved to the United States in 2020, obtained a green card and applied for US citizenship. He was arrested in July 2024 at Los Angeles international airport on immigration fraud charges and prosecutors later added four-torture related charges.
He is the first al-Assad regime official to go to trial in the US and the highest ranking regime official to be tried anywhere in the world in person. Al-Assad was ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the regime in just 11 days.
Since then, Syria’s new government has held a number of in absentia trials for former regime officials in connection to crimes committed during the country’s years-long civil war, which killed about half a million people and displaced half the country’s prewar population of 23 million. In August, a court sentenced al-Assad and his brother Maher to death for crimes against humanity and war crimes, but the two men have been in Moscow since the regime’s collapse.
Other factions in Syria’s civil war have also been accused of abuse of detainees, including insurgent groups and the US-backed, Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces.
During al-Sheikh’s nine-day trial, several victims and witnesses testified. They described guards folding prisoners into car tires, restraining and beating them. Some they said, were cuffed by their wrists to pipes on the ceiling, beaten with cables, and left suspended for extended periods of time.
Others testified that they were placed on a device known as a “magic carpet” or “flying carpet” which consisted of two large wooden panels with hinges in the middle onto which guards strapped prisoners, forcing the panels together to cause excruciating pain. One victim recalled al-Sheikh himself stomping on the device. Another testified he was subjected to the “magic carpet” or “flying carpet” as punishment for writing a letter of support to a political prisoner and also forced to wear a red jumpsuit assigned to prisoners designated for execution, leading him to believe he was going to die.
“[Al-Sheikh] chose to serve the ruthless, repressive Assad regime in Syria throughout his professional life, including for four years as the warden of Syria’s largest prison,” prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memo. “[He] knew that what he was doing was wrong. Nonetheless he ordered and participated in the torture of his victims because he had the power to do so and because he thought he would never be held accountable.”
Several victims and witnesses also submitted written and video testimonies to the court ahead of the sentencing, in which they spoke of being haunted and traumatized by their experiences two decades later.
“I still hear the screams of others begging for mercy,” said one of the men, Nidal Shikhani.
“Even though 20 years have passed, I still live in the prison of my memory,” said another, Sultan Abdul Malek. “I suffer from sudden panic attacks and constant anxiety.”
His brother, Khaled Abdul Malek, who was taken to “Wing 13” twice during his four years at Adra prison, spoke of the physical and psychological scars he was left with, including chronic back pain and mobility problems.
“My son Battal asks if he could ride my back and with a heart wrung with pain, I am forced to tell him I [am] no longer strong enough to carry him,” he said.
Several witnesses also submitted testimony on al-Sheikh’s behalf, speaking about his age and frailty as they asked the court for leniency. More than 50 people sent letters of support to the court, describing him as “a person of integrity, compassion, and generosity to his family and community”, his attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors had asked the court for a minimum sentence of 80 years; al-Sheikh’s attorneys had called for a five-year sentence, citing his poor health and noting that he was willing to be deported to Syria.
“Whatever moral weight this case carries in the broader arc of history – however much the world, or the victims, or the public might wish the sentence to ‘send a message’ – that desire cannot be the foundation of a just sentence,” the defense team wrote in a memo to the court.
Al-Sheikh is one of only five people to be prosecuted under the extraterritorial Torture Act, which allows the US government to prosecute individuals physically present in the US over acts of torture committed abroad.
“This case sends a message both to the new government of Syria and to other victims that justice is possible,” said Ela Matthews, an attorney at the Center for Justice and Accountability, which represented several victims. “The transitional justice process that is happening in Syria needs to continue to evolve and bring individuals like this to account, but in the US this sends a message that the rule of law is still functioning and that these types of cases are possible.”

Carney: The EU and Canada must strengthen their ties  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:33:45 UTC
09:33:45 KST

TALLINN - The European Union and Canada must strengthen their relations, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said at the European Parliament's plenary session on Thursday.
"Canada and Europe are not geographical neighbours, but like-minded friends," Mark Carney said.
In her introduction to Mark Carney's speech, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said: "Europe and Canada both know that we are stronger when we work together. Canada has stood by Europe during difficult moments in history, and we will never forget what they have sacrificed. Today, however, we look to the future together, and both sides have much to gain from cooperation in the fields of defence, trade, energy, education, and research."
Mark Carney stressed that the current geopolitical shift requires a new approach. "Europe and Canada have a long shared history, and we are both equally committed to the rule of law, the unwavering protection of human dignity, freedoms, and democracy."
"A strong economy is not an end in itself, but a means to achieve a just society. We all prosper more when we share our success," he added.
In Carney's view, Europe and Canada each have their own strengths, allowing them to support and complement one another. A closer partnership between Canada and Europe is therefore in the interest of both sides.
The Prime Minister also responded to Ursula von der Leyen's proposal from yesterday to grant Canada the status of an associated country of the European Union: "Such a direction is very welcome. To protect their strategic autonomy, Canada and Europe should cooperate closely on all strategic issues, including critical minerals, the defence industry, artificial intelligence, energy security, space, and payment solutions."
Carney also highlighted how beneficial it would be to create a single market for financial services and for Canada to participate in the Erasmus+ programme and the EU's next framework programme for research and innovation.
"Deepening and expanding our relations will strengthen our sovereignty, lower prices, improve opportunities and security for Europeans and Canadians, and allow us to live the lives we want," Carney said.
The Prime Minister stressed that he does not want to create a new bloc to compete with world powers, just more politely. "Our goal is not power and domination over others. On the contrary. Our goal is stability, ensuring that no one can influence our open markets, limit our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or restrict our freedom, democracy, and the rule of law," Carney explained.
"We must create an alliance so strong that no one else can make decisions for us. An alliance so open that others can join it. And an alliance so principled that its strength supports the international legal order, rather than overriding it," he said.

Russia to open voting booths at border with Poland, Baltic states  - The Baltic Times

MOSCOW - Russia said Thursday it would open voting stations at its border points with Poland and the three Baltic states.
Moscow is holding a three-day parliamentary election across its 11 time zones starting on Friday, with President Vladimir Putin's party facing no real opposition and guaranteed to win.
Russia's ties with EU members Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia -- already historically fragile -- are de-facto frozen, with embassies open but many diplomats expelled and most Russian consulates closed.
The head of Russia's electoral commission, Ella Pamfilova, said Moscow would open "10 voting points near border crossings" for Russians living in those countries to cast their ballots.
Four of them, she said, will be in the Kaliningrad exclave, which borders Poland and Lithuania.
Another five will be in the Pskov region -- which shares a border with Latvia and Estonia -- and one more will be opened in the Leningrad region on the border with Estonia, Pamfilova said.
Russian diplomatic missions will open polling stations in other EU countries, Moscow has said.

Baltic Pitching Forum unveils industry names and events that will make up its 14th edition  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:33:37 UTC
09:33:37 KST

Leading industry professionals head to Lithuania for four days of pitching, masterclasses, lectures and film screening at the 14th Baltic Pitching Forum
Returning to Lithuania’s capital city of Vilnius between 6 and 9 October, the 14th edition of the Baltic Pitching Forum (BPF) will reaffirm its status as the leading short film industry event in the Baltic region. Celebrating the best short film projects from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – alongside this year’s guest country Italy – the BPF will provide talented filmmakers and industry professionals a space to network, collaborate and celebrate the breadth and depth of the short film industry in the Baltics and beyond.
The main focus of the forum will be the pitching of the 12 selected projects, which will take place on the 8th of October. Different lectures, presentations and keynotes will be part of the forum’s program, open not only to participants, but also to observers. Pitching sessions and other public events will be accessible to all registered professionals.
On October 6th, the first day of the Baltic Pitching Forum, German pitching expert and longtime BPF collaborator Gabriele Brunnenmeyer will give a presentation titled Creating a “Good” Pitch. The talk will focus on what convinces people during the pitch, and how preparation and a structured presentation can resonate with an audience.
On October 7th, Italian marketing strategist and audience designer, Nicolò Gallio will present Short Films, Big Stakes: What AI Can and Cannot Do for Filmmakers. The lecture will examine key implications of working with Generative AI: its ethical and ecological costs, the cognitive risks of uncritical adoption, and the strategic question of where human judgement remains irreplaceable. This lecture is organised in partnership with Creative Europe MEDIA Desk Lithuania.
Later the same day, producer Anne-Laure Guégan – from Belgian production company Need Production – will present Building a Sustainable Relationship Between Director and Producer. She will be talking about building a long-term, trust-based partnership between director and producer, identifying the right creative partner for your project, and balancing creative ambitions with the reality of production.
With October 8th being dedicated to the pitching sessions of the 12 selected short film projects from Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Italy, the Forum will invite participants of the Baltic emerging producers training program UP! to introduce themselves to the international audience.
The final day of the Forum, October 9th, will start with Let’s Stop Whispering, The Baltic Moment (Your Moment) Is Now, where Simona Inta and Viktorija Cook, co-founders of the Baltic Talents Agency, explore how creatives in the Baltics have been making world-class creative work for decades and how they want to amplify those creative voices so the world knows what the Baltics have to offer.
Later on, Jacopo Chessa, president of the Italian Film Commission, will invite the forum's audience to a presentation: Why Italy? Your Next Co-Production Destination. Following it, the manager of the Italian Short Film Center, Elena Ciofalo, will present key opportunities available at the Italian Short Film Center and ShorTO Film Market.
The second half of October 9th will place the focus on successful BPF alumni. Gintė Regina and Akvilė Žilionytė (director and producer of “On Conductor Street”, BPF 2023, Lithuania) will talk about their experiences with the journey of their films and discuss some of the challenges that they have faced along the way.
This will be followed by the traditional Who is Taking Care of Short Films? which brings together European short film sales, distribution and television companies to give filmmakers a practical insight into how they work and what they are looking for. Featuring contributions from many of the BPF’s industry guests, this is a crucial event for those wanting to take the pulse of the short film world.
As a tradition, the Forum will be rounded out by a short film screening from the guest country, Italy, “Contemporary Italian Animated Short Cinema”, curated by the Italian Short Film Center. The programme will showcase acclaimed Italian animated short films that reflect the creativity of contemporary Italian animators and their growing presence on the international festival circuit. The screening will take place at Muzeoteka and will be open to everyone.
This year’s BPF Panel will consist of Anne-Laure Guégan (producer at Need Productions, Belgium), Elena Ciofalo (manager of ShorTO Film Market, Italy), Eva Schweizer (TV distributor at SRF TV, Switzerland), Olivier Berlemont (producer at oriGine Films, France), Sari Volanen (buyer at Yle, Finland), Simone Bardoni (distributor at Lights On, Italy), Stine Wangler (sales agent at Kurzfilm Agentur Hamburg, Germany), Vanya Rainova (producer at Portokal, Bulgaria), and Laurent Crouzeix (coordinator at Euro Connection, France).
Aside from giving immediate feedback to the pitches, the BPF Panel will award two short film projects (from the Baltic States) with participant rights to the European Short Film Co-production Forum Euro Connection (part of the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival), and the ShorTO Film Market and its Pitching Session ‘You Only Pitch Twice’.
The Producers’ Jury will have four members: Dagnė Vildžiūnaitė (Just a Moment, Lithuania), Maie Rosmann (Estonia), Antra Cilinska (Juris Podnieks Studio) and Enrica Capra (Graffiti, Italy). One of the projects will receive the Producers MEDIA Award (€1,000), initiated by the Creative Europe MEDIA Desks in Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and Italy.
Projects will also be eligible to win awards established by other BPF partners. One project will receive The RIGA IFF Award, which allows the film to participate in the SHORT RIGA Test Screenings event in 2026 or 2027. Another project will get The UP Records Sound Post-Production Award, which provides sound post-production services valued at €2,000. The Baltic Talent Digital Strategy Award – open to Baltic projects – will award one project a consultancy session to sharpen its digital presence ahead of its festival launch, covering EPK development, social media strategy, and positioning materials for the market and press. Finally, students from Lithuanian, Latvian and Estonian National Film Schools will select their favourite project and award it with the Baltic Film Schools Student Choice Award.
The 14th Baltic Pitching Forum will take place from 6 to 9 October at the National Gallery of Art in Vilnius. The event is open to the general public and free of charge.

Latvian MEPs express concern about prominence of security issues in EC President's Speech  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:33:30 UTC
09:33:30 KST

RIGA - Members of the European Parliament (EP) representing Latvia have mixed views on European Commission (EC) President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union address (EU) - some welcome the plan to cooperate more closely with Canada and the expressed support for Ukraine, while others express concerns about the funding of new initiatives and the direction of European security policy.
MEP Inese Vaidere (New Unity) highlighted the large number of new initiatives as a positive aspect, but she expressed doubts about how all of these plans could be implemented. In her view, it is also important to assess what has not been accomplished from previous commitments. As one example, the MEP cited defense against drones, criticizing the situation in which relatively inexpensive drones are shot down using disproportionately expensive military assets.
The MEP also criticized the fact that a solution regarding the use of Russia’s frozen assets has still not been reached. She questioned whether Belgium’s objections should hinder the achievement of such a solution, emphasizing that the funds are needed both to support Ukraine and for Europe’s own defense.
Vaidere, however, viewed von der Leyen’s proposal to establish a European Security Council positively, particularly highlighting the plan to involve Ukraine, the United Kingdom, and Canada in this format. She acknowledged that it is not yet clear how this council will function, adding that it should not be established as an alternative to NATO. In the MEP’s view, NATO and the collective defense guarantees enshrined in its Article 5 remain the foundation of security.
MEP Martins Stakis (P) highlighted von der Leyen’s proposal for Canada to become the EU’s first associated member state as a significant development. He emphasized that Canada is a particularly important security partner for Latvia and that bringing it closer to the EU is of strategic importance.
Stakis suggested that a similar status could, in the future, serve as an alternative even in situations where objections from individual member states might hinder the full admission of an EU candidate country.
"This is an alternative status through which we could move forward without closing the door on that country," said Stakis, adding that von der Leyen’s plan to first offer such status to Canada is a far-sighted step.
Meanwhile, MEP Sandra Kalniete (New Unity) urged caution in drawing conclusions about the specifics of the associate member status offered to Canada, since von der Leyen announced this initiative during her speech and it is not yet clear exactly what such status would entail.
The MEP noted that the EU already has association agreements with many countries, so it remains to be clarified whether the EC President intended associated member state status to denote a new and closer model of partnership.
She also explained that this would be a serious decision requiring a resolution by the Council of the European Union, but, depending on the chosen legal form, the matter could also be brought before the European Parliament. Kalniete considers closer cooperation between Canada and the EU to be significant in the context of both security and Arctic policy. She pointed to Russia’s and China’s interest in the Arctic and emphasized that Europe, too, must pay greater attention to this region.
The MEP also reminded Canada’s military presence in Latvia and its investments at the Adazi base, and therefore, in her view, security and military cooperation could become a significant part of closer EU-Canada relations.
MEP Ivars Ijabs (For Latvia's Development) described von der Leyen’s annual address as a ritual event in which the EC President attempts to address various audiences, though he assessed this year’s speech critically overall. He noted that the speech covered a wide range of issues, including climate, migration, competitiveness, and technology, but that it lacked discussion of the defense of the eastern border and investment.
Ijabs reminded that initiatives to strengthen the EU’s eastern border had been proposed previously, including measures related to protection against drones, but this time these issues were not among the main points of the speech. He viewed positively von der Leyen’s remarks on EU competitiveness and technological development, including the need to focus more on industrial and manufacturing solutions in the field of artificial intelligence, rather than attempting to replicate the development path of large language models taken by the US and China.
He also emphasized that von der Leyen’s remarks demonstrate that there is still a consensus within EU institutions on the issue of support for Ukraine. In the MEP’s view, the speech did not address certain issues that deserve greater attention, such as Russia’s frozen assets.
MEP Reinis Poznaks (United List) highlighted as the most significant positive message the fact that security and defense remain among the EU’s priorities and that support for Ukraine is set to be strengthened. He also welcomed the plan to build closer relations with Canada, emphasizing that as Europe strives for greater autonomy, it simultaneously needs partners. The MEP highlighted Canada’s technological capabilities and natural resources.
MEP Roberts Zile (National Alliance), however, was critical of von der Leyen’s proposals on security. He emphasized that some of these threats are already having a direct impact on people’s daily lives, citing examples such as school closures, disruptions to train service, or difficulties accessing healthcare.
Zile reminded the previously announced initiatives to strengthen the EU’s eastern flank and defense against drones, expressing dissatisfaction with the pace of their implementation and the level of funding. In his view, von der Leyen’s speech also lacked an assessment of which of the initiatives to date have been successful and which have not.
Zile also took a critical view of the plan to establish a European Security Council and new security mechanisms. He is not convinced by the idea of creating new structures parallel to NATO, as this, in his view, could take a long time without providing an immediate practical contribution to the security of the Baltic states. However, the EP Vice President acknowledged that closer cooperation with Canada is beneficial for both Europe and Canada in the current situation.
MEP Nils Usakovs (Harmony) emphasized that von der Leyen’s speech contained several symbolic messages-and ones of regional significance-regarding security and the economy; but for him, the most important issue is the financial coverage of these plans. In his view, the new taxes mentioned in the EC President’s speech will not be sufficient to provide additional funding for the EU’s current ambitions, let alone new initiatives.
According to the MEP, the question of where the EU will obtain the funds to both strengthen security and support border regions remains unanswered. He emphasized that in border regions, it is necessary not only to fund military infrastructure but also to support the people living there.

Announcement regarding Canada as a potential EU associate member is political and vague - expert  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:33:21 UTC
09:33:21 KST

RIGA - The announcement regarding Canada’s possible status as an associate member of the European Union (EU) is currently only political in nature, and it is unclear what that would entail, Maris Andzans, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies and associate professor at Riga Stradins University, told LETA, commenting on remarks made by European Commission (EC) President Ursula von der Leyen on the matter.
He emphasized that von der Leyen’s remarks were purely political, since there is currently no such legal status as an EU associate member state, and it is unclear what that would entail.
In Andzans’ view, this can be explained solely by the trade war between the U.S. and Canada - specifically, the trade tariffs imposed by the U.S. on Canada and Canada’s retaliatory measures. The expert noted that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has also made no secret of his desire to strengthen ties with the EU wherever possible.
Following von der Leyen’s statement, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to impose new tariffs on the EU if it allowed Canada to become an associate member of the EU. Andzans notes that Trump has always been vocal in his statements against his allies, especially Canada, which is why Canada must find ways to diversify its trade relations. The EU is clearly one of the most like-minded partners at the moment, said Andzans.
He added that Canada is also a NATO member and shares security and defense interests with the EU.
The expert believes that such a statement could have been a signal to Trump that Canada is welcome in the EU, although this does not immediately imply membership.
At present, there are questions about what will happen to the European Economic Area, as well as questions regarding EU candidate countries, including Ukraine, he noted.
Andzans emphasized that in order to legally establish a specific status for Canada within the EU, the founding treaties would need to be amended, and this would most likely take several years.
Overall, the expert believes that during the Trump presidency, Canada will only grow closer to the EU and drift further away from the U.S. Canada will also become more involved in the EU’s political and security processes, but this will not be on a legal basis, Andzans said.
As previously reported, von der Leyen stated on Wednesday that Canada could become the EU’s first associate member, although such a status does not yet exist.
The EC President noted that Europe can no longer rely on a rules-based international system as the sole means of safeguarding its interests or assume that its rules will protect Europe from threats. She emphasized that Europe must rebuild its partnerships and form global coalitions to strengthen resilience and democracy.

BirdyChat rebrands as Balsio, and launches in Latvian  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:33:14 UTC
09:33:14 KST

The Latvia-founded European work messenger is sharpening its focus on small teams that need structured professional communication without the complexity of larger collaboration platforms.
Riga, Latvia — September 16, 2026 — BirdyChat, the European messenger for professional communication, becomes Balsio as it sharpens its focus on small professional teams. Alongside the new identity, the company is expanding its localization across Europe, with the app now available in Latvian and eight other European languages.
The rebrand reflects Balsio’s growing focus on an underserved space between personal messaging apps and enterprise collaboration platforms like Slack and MS Teams. Small teams often reach a point where personal messaging apps become difficult to manage for work, while enterprise collaboration platforms introduce more complexity than they need. The problem is particularly acute for agencies and other client-facing teams, whose communication often extends beyond their own organization to customers, freelancers, and external collaborators. The app is already used by teams such as SPRING PR & Communications, startup community project Shipyard, and Riga Investment and Tourism Agency.
Balsio is designed around professional messaging rather than a broad suite of workplace tools. Threads and lists help users organize conversations by client, project, or topic, while work-email registration allows people to keep their private phone numbers separate from professional communication.
“Small teams run a surprising amount of their work through personal messaging apps, especially when they communicate regularly with clients and external partners,” said Rolands Mesters, co-founder and CEO of Balsio. “At the same time, moving everyone into a large collaboration platform can feel like overkill. We are building Balsio for that space in between: professional communication that is structured and manageable, while still feeling as straightforward as the messaging apps people already know.”
Balsio, formerly BirdyChat, was the first app to use the Digital Markets Act’s WhatsApp interoperability framework. Balsio users can message participating WhatsApp contacts without requiring them to install Balsio, provided they have enabled third-party chats in WhatsApp. The company launched across Europe in May 2026 after attracting a waiting list of more than 50,000 people.
As part of the rebrand, BirdyChat becomes Balsio in the App Store and on Google Play, while the website moves to balsio.com. Existing accounts, chats, and message history remain unchanged, with no action required from users.
With Latvian now added, Balsio is currently available in eight other languages: English, French, German, Dutch, Spanish, Italian, Lithuanian, and Estonian. The app is available on iOS, Android and Mac, with a Windows application scheduled for release in early October.
Balsio also provides an API and Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, allowing companies to connect the messenger with existing business tools and AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude. Balsio is developed in Europe, where its user data is also hosted.

The autumn season at the Lithuanian National Museum of Art: returning masterpieces, new names, and unexpected ways to engage with art  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:33:13 UTC
09:33:13 KST

As the days get cooler, the Lithuanian National Museum of Art (LNMA) invites visitors to brighten up the season across its exhibition venues. As fall foliage fades, the LNMA museums and galleries will launch 13 new exhibitions, spanning diverse periods and forms of art. Beyond promising a cozy refuge from capricious autumn showers, the upcoming season promises an inspiring cultural calendar. Among the first events of the season is EDUFEST, a festival of art and education, showcasing the museum’s approach to public engagement, complemented by the latest LNMA publications to deepen visitor experience of the exhibitions.
‘Though autumn is often perceived as monotonous and gloomy, inside the LNMA exhibition venues it will be vibrant and bursting with colour, spanning diverse periods and geographies, and exploring the breadth of human experience,’ says Dr Arūnas Gelūnas, Director General of the LNMA. ‘This season’s exhibitions invite visitors to reflect on personal and collective memory, society-shaping shifts, human connection to places, nature, and material. I hope that each visitor will find their own shade of autumn here and connect to works of art not only through visual contemplation, but also actually touching them.’
September: time for the young artists’ ideas; the return of masterpieces; woven happiness, and the EDUFEST
On 10 September, the 16th edition of the Young Designer Prize exhibition – organized by the Vilnius Academy of Art – kick starts the autumn season. Creative explorations by 15 most promising design graduates go on show for public appraisal until 4 October at the Museum of Applied Arts and Design in Vilnius.
On 17 September, the Museum of Applied Arts and Design opens an exhibition titled Feliksas Jakubauskas (1949–2025): The Happiness of Weaving, spanning over four decades of the celebrated textile artist’s career. The tapestries on display will feature compositions of the artist’s favourite geometrical shapes – squares, triangles, pyramids, fans, alongside straight and diagonal lines – structured rhythmically and harmoniously like music or poetry. Included views from the workshop will evoke moments of weaving the way they were captured by the artist.
On 19 – 20 September, the courtyard of the Chodkevičius Palace becomes an open ground for artistic creativity as the museum hosts the 2nd edition of a free educational event titled EDUFEST. Visitors across all ages all invited to take part in its hands-on workshops and artistic experiments, and to find out about education programmes run by the different branches of the LNMA. Participants of the festival will encounter the museum as a vibrant, welcoming cultural space where they can explore multiple, sometimes not readily apparent, ways to engage with art.
On 22 September, the Radvila Palace Museum of Art brings back the Masterpiece Room, a project that has previously enjoyed immense viewer acclaim. Conceived by an interdisciplinary group of art historians and artists, the immersive environment will surround visitors with rich historical context while enabling a quiet, undisturbed moment with the art. The initiative once again features The Evangelist Luke and The Evangelist Matthew by Dutch Golden Age master portraitist Frans Hals. The masterpieces were brought to Lithuania from the Odesa Museum of Western and Eastern Art following the start of a full-scale war against Ukraine.
The Memory Chapel and never-ending summer in coastal Lithuania; Bauhaus-inspired ideas and echoes of New York in Vilnius
On 23 September, the Palanga Amber Museum launches Andrius Erminas’s solo exhibition titled The Memory Chapel. The Sun Above a Cabbage Field. His conceptual sculpture pieces going on show in Palanga carry on the artist’s explorations on the themes of personal and collective memory, place and identity. Casts from cabbage heads made specially for the museum space will reference the myth of birth and genesis. By transforming the dull industrial materials into sculptural symbols, the artist pairs the historical context of the building and his childhood memories into a unique archive of memory.
The very palette-intensity of Andy Sweet’s (1953 – 1982) expressive colour photography exhibition, opening on 8 October at the Pranas Domšaitis Gallery, can be trusted to brighten up the gloom of autumn. The American photographer from Miami Beach evokes in his pictures the life of seemingly careless ‘capital of sun and fun’, yet his photographic chronicles reflect some deeper and unsettling aspects of the social change among the residents of Miami Beach – Jewish traditions permeating American daily life, the emerging LGBTQ+* community, alongside racial and ethnic segregation. In his ironic pictures, hidden themes emerge from behind the sun-tanned bodies, such as the desire to belong to a community or the fear of the passage of time. Observing his protagonists with tenderness, Sweet created an ode to his beloved town – the place where summer apparently never ends.
On 9 October, the National Gallery of Art opens an exhibition spanning the life and career of the architect Vladas Švipas (1900-1965). The one and only Lithuanian who had studied at the Bauhaus and afterwards applied the ideas of rational planning in Kaunas, was also dealt a war-refugee fate in a German DP camp, followed by the hardships of integration as an immigrant to New York City. The exhibition tells Vladas Švipas’ personal story, yet alongside, it traces a transnational trajectory of a modernist architect whose career evolved against a backdrop of the changing political regimes and major historical shifts.
On 14 – 16 October, the Vilnius Picture Gallery holds an international conference titled Same, but Different: Copy, Pastiche, and Forgery in Visual Art. The event explores the phenomenon of the artistic copy across cultural, social, and political contexts, ranging from historical workshop practice of learning under a master, to contemporary challenges in attribution, examination, the art market, and legal regulation.
The alchemical transmutations and tactile art at the Radvila Palace
On 15 October, the Radvila Palace Museum of Art opens an exhibition titled Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury structured around the principles of alchemical thought.
The Middle Ages and Renaissance saw alchemy flourish in royal and aristocratic courts where the practitioners sought to turn base metals into silver and gold or to create an elixir of eternity. At its core, alchemy was about spiritual and psychological transformation, using physical matter as a symbolic mirror. Rather than presenting sulphur, salt, and mercury as chemical substances, the exhibition framing uses them as metaphors for the fundamental potential to change. Alchemy will become a lens to explore the transformations across matter, nature, the human body, and consciousness.
On 22 October, the Radvila Palace Museum of Art opens an exhibition designed for both visual and tactile appreciation of the work by Leonas Strioga, one of Lithuania’s most prominent artists, a recipient of the Lithuanian National Prize for Culture and Arts. Strioga’s works are uniquely suited for hands-on engagement. Throughout his long career, he worked across diverse mediums, including stone, marble, granite, gypsum, metal, terracotta, and wood. By inviting visitors to explore texture, temperature, and form through touch, the exhibition highlights how material properties shape our perception of art.
Festival exhibitions will introduce variety into the season’s programme at the Radvila Palace Museum of Art. NK-INTERACTIVE by the Inconvenient Films festival invites viewers to immerse themselves into extended- reality works by Lithuanian and foreign artists. Ryšiai (Bonds), Art Festival of Mental Health, opens its exhibition on 5 November.
The magic of the sea; fragility as a parallel between ceramics and memory
On 29 October, the Vytautas Kasiulis Museum of Art opens the first retrospective of Irena and Joana Karpińska’s creative legacy, a symbolic artist sisters’ homecoming to the places of their formative years in the interwar Vilnius. The artists never forgot the city nor the people they became friends with in Vilnius as students of art. This comprehensive presentation of the work by the Karpińska sisters will add some lesser-known names, facts, and works to the history of women’s art.
On 12 November, the Museum of Applied Arts and Design opens Sober Boys, a ceramics exhibition by Rokas Dovydėnas. Two-hundred-vase installation is conceived as a commentary on vulnerability, fragility, and the muscle of society (and ceramics). Clay is a paradoxical medium: under suitable conditions it can reach us through millennia as archaeological testimony, yet a slightest impact may break a fired ceramic item. This oscillation between stability and vulnerability becomes an overarching metaphor for humans, society, and the world we inhabit – unstable, constantly changing, and undefined.
On 19 November, the Pranas Domšaitis Gallery opens an exhibition curated by Dr Arūnas Gelūnas that explores the multifaceted relationship with the sea across different eras. It traces how European art depicted the sea from a mythological, chaotic force violently tossing ships – to an idyllic heaven for rest, physical renewal, light, and personal experience. The exhibition features Lithuanian and Western European paintings from the collections by the LNMA and other Lithuanian museums, paired with prints, photography, sculpture, contemporary art, design objects, and historical nautical instruments from the collections of the Lithuanian Sea Museum.
On 26 November, the Clock and Watch Museum opens Echoes of Time. Lithuanian Memory Portraits, a photographic exhibition by Gianluca Sodaro that brings into focus faces of Lithuania’s elderly – the true guardians of the country’s history. Though most of them are reduced to the margins of the grand historical narratives, their experience stands witness to the major society-shaping shifts, trauma, and daily routines. The likenesses immortalized by the photographer remind us that history is made not only by the prominent personalities, but also by the multitudes of its apparently invisible participants.
The coming autumn months present last opportunities to see the LNMA and international partners’ exhibitions abroad. Aleksandra Kasuba’s Shelters for the Senses is on at Tate St Ives until 4 October. Eglė Budvydytė’s Animism Sings Anarchy at the Lithuanian Pavilion of Venice Biennale and Fires over the Tiber: Rome Through the Eyes of Kanutas Ruseckas at Castel Sant’Angelo Rome run through 22 November.
The exhibitions opening this autumn can be explored beyond the exhibition rooms. The new publications by the LNMA, guided tours, educational programmes, and hands-on workshops for visitors of all ages expand the scope of the themes they dwell on beyond the walls of exhibition venues. For more information on the museum’s exhibitions and the accompanying events please visit the LNMA website and social media.

F-16 Crashes During Training Exercise in Michigan; Pilot Ejects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:25:21 UTC
09:25:21 KST

An F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the Texas Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Wing crashed during a training mission in Michigan on Sept. 17.
The fighter’s sole pilot ejected safely. The Michigan State Police said in a social media post the pilot is in stable condition at a local hospital and there are no other known injuries related to the crash.
In a statement, the wing said the aircraft was conducting a “routine training mission” in the afternoon at Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center, a Michigan Air National Guard facility in the northern part of the state near Traverse City. The F-16 is based at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas.
The 149th is participating in an exercise called “Operation Northern Cactus” as part of training for deployment to an “austere environment,” according to information the wing released earlier this week.
The wing said the crash is under investigation.
The stricken F-16’s wingman told air traffic control that the crashed aircraft may have suffered a bird strike and said the pilot planned to bail out of the fighter before ultimately ejecting, according to audio recorded by the website LiveATC. The audio indicates the two planes were flying together on the mission as call sign BUCK 11 flight.
Imagery posted to social media showed a large plume of black smoke rising from the area. Buildings within a one-mile radius of the crash were evacuated due to a “hazardous chemical spill,” according to the State Police. F-16s carry hydrazine, a highly toxic chemical that fuels the plane’s emergency power unit, which powers the jet’s flight controls and other critical systems in the event of an engine failure.

Almost 50 dead in Nigeria after drinking alcohol suspected to contain methanol
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:23:31 UTC
09:23:31 KST

At least 48 people have died and about 100 others are receiving treatment in southern Nigeria after consuming a locally brewed alcoholic concoction suspected to contain methanol, officials said on Thursday.
Banji Ajaka, Ondo state’s commissioner for health, said the cases had been reported in the Odigbo and Irele local government areas. A total of 182 people are believed to have been affected and some are being treated in the hospital, he said.
“I took like two shots and I went out on Friday. On Saturday, I noticed that I could not see,” 32-year-old Sola Adebayo told the local TVC News channel from a hospital bed.
Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated.
“This thing happened rapidly. Once they consume, depending on the quantity, the kidneys will pack up, the eyes will go, the brain will be damaged,” Ajaka told The Associated Press, speaking about the drink.
Ondo state police spokesperson Abayomi Jimoh said in a statement that 15 people were arrested in connection with the incident, including one allegedly “involved in the production of substances suspected to contain methanol and is currently assisting the police with investigations.”
Locals told the AP they suspected a popular herbal drink with high alcohol content, known as “Monkey Tail,” was mixed with methanol, causing the deaths.
A trader who sells the concoction in Odigbo, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of being arrested, told the AP there are two versions of Monkey Tail: an original, safe version, and another version which is unsafe.
Local media reports said the first death was reported nearly two weeks ago.
Nigeria’s National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control is now enforcing a nationwide ban on alcohol in sachets and small plastic containers, which it said are easily accessible to children and young people.

Assad-era Syrian official jailed for 60 years by US court

Assad-era Syrian official jailed for 60 years by US court
WASHINGTON, Sept 17 - A former Syrian government official who headed the Damascus Central Prison under ousted President Bashar al-Assad and was convicted of torture by a US federal jury has been sentenced to 60 years in prison by a US judge, federal prosecutors said.
Samir Ousman Alsheikh, 74, was charged in 2024 and convicted in March this year on three counts of torture and one count of conspiracy to commit torture for his involvement in the abuse of prisoners at Adra Prison in Damascus.
Alsheikh was also convicted of lying to US immigration authorities about his commission of the crimes, fraudulently obtaining a green card and attempting to naturalize as a US citizen, the US Department of Justice said.
Thursday's sentence was handed down by US District Judge Hernan Vera in Los Angeles.
Prosecutors said Alsheikh ordered subordinates to inflict physical and mental pain on prisoners to deter opposition to Assad's government and was sometimes personally involved in such incidents.
The US Justice Department said Alsheikh, who held positions in the state security apparatus, was the highest-ranking former member of Assad's government to be tried and convicted in person outside Syria so far.
Alsheikh's legal team had asked for a five-year sentence. In March, they said they were "disappointed" by his conviction. Alsheikh, who headed Adra Prison from 2005 to 2008, had previously pleaded not guilty.
Khaled Abdul Malek, a witness in the case who was detained and tortured at Adra prison, said in a written statement shared with reporters that the sentencing showed that "even when justice is delayed, it will always come".
"This trial is not the end, but the first step on the road toward accountability and justice for everyone whose hands have been stained with the blood of innocent people," he said.
Syrian rebels put an end to more than 50 years of rule by the Assad family in late 2024 following a lightning advance. Hundreds of thousands died in a civil war that lasted more than a decade, unleashed a global refugee crisis and left cities across the country in ruins.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former al Qaeda commander, took over after Assad's ouster and has worked to improve ties with the West.
Last month, a Syrian court sentenced Assad, who resides in Russia, in absentia to death after convicting him of crimes including killings, torture, and arbitrary arrest during the country's war. REUTERS

Egyptian teen's murder sparks debate over police's social media use
An Egyptian teenager was murdered this week, allegedly by her brother, after authorities posted information about retrieving her from a young man's home, sparking a debate around the appropriateness of the police force's use of social media.
Local media reported on Wednesday that Aya Radwan, 16, was killed in her hometown of Al-Saf, south of Cairo, and that her brother was in custody after allegedly murdering her "for fear of disgrace".
On Tuesday night, the Ministry of Interior had published slightly blurred photos of Radwan, including one of her standing next to a man after they were detained together.
The ministry's post mentioned Radwan's area of residence and said police had received a missing persons report from her mother.
"Investigations led to locating the missing girl... and she was apprehended. Upon questioning, she admitted to leaving her home of her own will and staying with an acquaintance," adding that "legal measures have been taken".
The post sparked criticism on social media, with users accusing the ministry's social media account of effectively stoking an "honour killing" in a patriarchal, conservative society.
On the ministry's post, one user commented that "a one-line statement would have been enough to reassure people without going into details that tarnish the girl's personality and bring shame to her family".
Mostafa Kassem, a Cairo-based lawyer, told AFP he was filing a complaint with the public prosecutor against the administrator of the ministry's account.
He accused the page of being complicit in Radwan's killing, and said Egypt's Criminal Procedure Code "prohibits the publication of any information regarding minors or cases of sexual violence".
The interior ministry's social media accounts post several times a day about the arrests of suspects, including minors, detailing their places of residence and the charges against them, and showing their slightly blurred faces.
Many posts say authorities launched investigations based on videos circulating on social media platforms.
Last year, Egypt's top media authority celebrated the Ministry of Interior's Facebook page being named the world's second highest-performing government account, after the White House.
"It was the police's responsibility to protect her upon her return to her family," Lobna Darwish, advocacy lead at the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), told AFP.
"What happened to her after her photo was published next to a man, in a statement announcing her arrest, was not unexpected."
According to Kassem, Egypt's child protection laws should have seen Radwan placed in a government shelter before being returned to her family.
Violence against women is rampant in Egypt. The most recent state figures from 2021 show nearly a third of women have faced domestic abuse at the hands of their husbands, though data on violence by other family members is not recorded.
According to the same state survey, published in 2022, only 2 percent of familial abuse cases are recorded.

Turkey's Erdogan to run again in early 2028 vote: top adviser
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:04:29 UTC
09:04:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Turkey's Erdogan to run again in early 2028 vote, top adviser says
A top adviser to Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the Turkish leader would run again in an early election likely to be held in April 2028, media outlets reported on Thursday.
It was the first official confirmation that the 72-year-old leader would run again for president.
"If 360 lawmakers back a decision to call a new election, it will be held on April 16, 2028," Mehmet Ucum said in remarks cited by private NTV broadcaster and Cumhuriyet newspaper.
Under Turkish law, an election would normally be held in May that year.
By bringing the election forward by one month however, the Turkish leader is able to sidestep a constitutional provision limiting a president from serving more than two five-year terms in office.
Under the constitution, parliament can trigger early elections if such a move has the support of 360 of the chamber's 600 lawmakers.
Erdogan's ruling Islamo-conservative AKP and its nationalist ally MHP hold 326 seats in parliament, meaning to trigger the election, they will need the support of at least 34 other lawmakers.
Erdogan, who came to power as prime minister in 2003, served three terms as premier before being elected president in 2014.
Following a referendum three years later, Turkey switched to an executive presidential system, which took effect when Erdogan was re-elected in 2018.
He was re-elected for the third time in 2023.
'I won't run again'
Until now, the government has repeatedly insisted elections will be held on schedule.
During a weekend visit to his Black Sea home province of Rize, Erdogan spoke to supporters of "the upcoming elections" in remarks seen by observers as signalling an early vote.
"Within this unity and solidarity, I renew my belief that we will, God willing, successfully get through the upcoming elections," he said.
But party spokesman Omer Celik dismissed the suggestion, telling reporters: "It was not a signal of an early election. There is no election on our agenda."
After he was re-elected in May 2023 following a devastating earthquake and as concerns grew over Turkey's economic outlook, Erdogan said it would be his final term in office.
And last year, during discussions about updating Turkey's constitution, Erdogan said: "I have no intention of being re-elected or running for president again."
Opposition leader Ozgur Ozel has repeatedly called for an early election since the March 2025 jailing of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, widely regarded as Erdogan's main rival, over what critics have said is a politically motivated graft probe.
Imamoglu was jailed on the same day he was named the 2028 presidential candidate for the main opposition CHP.
But following a court ruling that reshaped the CHP leadership earlier this year, Ozel left to set up the Yeni Parti (New Party) drawing support from enough MPs to take over as Turkey's main opposition force.
It remains unclear who would be the main opposition's challenger to Erdogan, with Imamoglu unlikely to be able to run from behind bars.
Erdogan has been frequently accused by critics of authoritarian tendencies, particularly after the failed July 2016 coup and the sweeping purges that followed.
But he remains popular among his supporters, who see him as the only leader capable of resisting Western pressure and steering Turkey through regional and international crises.

====================================================================================================

Brain waves predict sexual side effects of common depression medications
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
00:00:48 UTC
09:00:48 KST

Measuring brain activity before starting depression medication might help doctors predict which patients will experience sexual side effects. A recent study shows that a specific brain wave pattern related to serotonin can forecast whether a patient will struggle to reach orgasm after taking common antidepressants. The research was published in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.
Depression often brings a host of challenging symptoms, with sexual difficulties being highly prevalent. Between 40 and 60 percent of people with major depressive disorder experience sexual disturbances as part of their condition. While treating depression can sometimes improve a person’s sex life as their mood lifts, the medications themselves frequently cause new problems.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, usually referred to as SSRIs, are the most common medications prescribed for depression. SSRIs work by increasing the availability of serotonin, a chemical messenger in the brain. Higher serotonin levels help alleviate depressive symptoms but also inhibit sexual function in many individuals.
Between 40 and 70 percent of patients taking SSRIs report adverse reactions such as diminished sexual desire, difficulty becoming aroused, or trouble reaching orgasm. These side effects can drastically affect a person’s quality of life and relationships. As a result, many patients stop taking their antidepressants altogether.
The study was conducted by researchers at the Copenhagen University Hospital and the University of Copenhagen. Gudrun Dilja Ketilsdottir and Kristian H. Reveles Jensen led the research team. They wanted to find a way to predict individual susceptibility to these side effects before a prescription is written.
The researchers focused on a biological marker called the loudness dependence of auditory evoked potentials. This marker is measured using an electroencephalogram, or EEG, which records electrical activity in the brain through sensors placed on the scalp. The measure tracks how the brain reacts to sounds of increasing volume.
Previous research suggests that this auditory brain response acts as an inverse indicator of serotonin activity in the central nervous system. A weaker brain response to louder sounds indicates higher baseline serotonin activity. The researchers hypothesized that people who already have high serotonin activity before starting medication might be pushed over a threshold by SSRIs, triggering sexual side effects.
The research team analyzed data from 90 unmedicated patients diagnosed with major depressive disorder. The participants were between the ages of 18 and 57, and roughly three-quarters of the group were women. None of the patients had taken antidepressant medication for at least two months prior to the study.
Before starting any treatment, each participant underwent an EEG recording. During this session, they listened to a series of tones at five different volume levels, ranging from 60 to 100 decibels. The researchers calculated the auditory brain response for each patient based on how their brain waves changed as the tones grew louder.
Alongside the brain scans, the researchers assessed each patient’s baseline sexual function using clinical questionnaires. They also measured blood levels of testosterone. Afterward, 86 of the participants began treatment with the SSRI escitalopram for eight weeks.
During the treatment period, clinicians monitored the patients for changes in their depression symptoms and the emergence of side effects. If a patient did not respond well to escitalopram or experienced intolerable side effects by week four, they were offered a switch to a different type of antidepressant called duloxetine. Seven patients made this switch.
At the end of the eight weeks, the clinicians formally rated the severity of any medication-induced sexual side effects. The researchers then ran statistical models to see if the pretreatment brain wave measurements corresponded to the side effects observed at the end of the trial.
The analysis revealed a robust link between baseline brain activity and later sexual difficulties. Patients who displayed a weaker brain response to increasing sound volume prior to treatment experienced higher rates of SSRI-induced orgasmic dysfunction. This specific brain wave pattern accurately predicted distressing orgasmic dysfunction 87 percent of the time.
The researchers also looked at whether the brain marker could predict a loss of sexual desire. They found a marginal association between the brain response and decreased libido, though it was not as strong as the link to orgasmic dysfunction. The brain marker was entirely unrelated to the occurrence of erectile dysfunction in the male participants.
When the team incorporated pretreatment blood testosterone levels into their predictive models, the changes in accuracy were not statistically significant. The auditory brain response alone, combined with basic demographic information and the patient’s baseline sexual function, was sufficient for predicting the side effects.
The researchers also examined the participants’ sexual function before any medication was introduced. They found that the auditory brain response was not associated with the level of sexual dysfunction caused directly by the depression itself. The brain marker appears specifically linked to how the body reacts to the introduction of the SSRI medication.
Because the biological mechanism for orgasm relies heavily on specific serotonin receptors, the researchers suggest that the brain marker is capturing the precise neurological pathway disrupted by SSRIs. In contrast, sexual desire involves a wider network of brain chemicals, which might explain why the brain marker was less predictive of decreased libido.
The study relied on an open-label design, meaning both the patients and the clinicians knew which medication was being administered. Without a placebo control group, some of the observed changes in sexual function could be related to natural fluctuations in the illness rather than the medication alone. The study participants were also relatively young, with an average age of 27.5 years, which may limit how well the findings apply to older adults.
Because a small portion of the group switched from escitalopram to duloxetine halfway through the trial, the results capture the effects of two different antidepressants. The researchers did perform a secondary analysis isolating only the patients on escitalopram, which produced the same outcome. Even so, testing the brain marker against a single medication in a more standardized protocol would provide firmer conclusions.
Moving forward, the research team aims to test this biological marker in more diverse groups of patients in standard clinical settings. If the auditory brain response proves reliable across broader populations, it could eventually serve as a routine screening tool. Doctors could use the test to identify patients at high risk for sexual side effects and prescribe alternative antidepressants that act on different brain chemicals.
The study, “Serotonergic activity estimated by EEG loudness-dependent auditory evoked potentials as a predictor of sexual SSRI side effects,” was authored by Gudrun Dilja Ketilsdottir, Cheng-Teng Ip, Vibe G. Frokjaer, Annamaria Giraldi, Martin Balslev Jørgensen, and Kristian H. Reveles Jensen.

WASHINGTON - The United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved a Paramount Skydance request to allow foreign investors to back its US$110 billion (S$140 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, but said they could not hold voting stock.
A group of Democratic senators had raised concerns about Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds taking stakes.
In a decision released by the FCC’s media bureau on Sept 17, the commission said it was waiving the 25 per cent cap on foreign equity ownership and said individual investors could own up to 20 per cent of the equity.
It also said foreign investors can have no voting stock and “will not have any influence, direction, or control over or provide any commentary or guidance on Paramount’s content decisions, company management”, or access to non-public data on US citizens.
Paramount praised the approval and said it followed a review by a US government committee of national security officials known as “Team Telecom” after ensuring that foreign investors will not have access to personal data of US citizens.
“A combined Paramount-WBD will have the scale and resources necessary to compete, invest, innovate, and deliver premium content to audiences worldwide,” the company said.
A US judge has temporarily blocked the takeover pending a trial in March on a legal challenge filed by a dozen US states. The US Justice Department and FCC previously approved the merger.
Paramount said when the deal closes, the family headed by billionaire and Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison and RedBird Capital Partners will collectively hold the largest equity stake in the combined company and 100 per cent of the voting shares, with no other equity participant having any governance rights.
The FCC said Middle Eastern investors would own about 85 per cent of the equity in Paramount after the deal closed, including 15.1 per cent for the Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund.
Paramount said sovereign wealth funds would own 38.5 per cent after the deal closed.
Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez said on Sept 17, “The FCC just let some of the most repressive governments in the world indirectly control nearly all of a combined Paramount-Warner Bros. An investment this large in one of America’s biggest media companies doesn’t just buy equity, it secures influence over what gets said and what gets made.” REUTERS

Campus in a Village-Town — Xinzhou, located on the south side of Futian Central Area in Shenzhen, is an important residential and living district. Over the years, it has developed a unique blend of commercial, residential, and urban village spaces. This rich urban fabric has fostered diverse communities and vibrant street life. Having settled in Shenzhen early on, I once lived in Xinzhou for seven years. It may not be the most "aesthetic" or "efficient" area, yet it offers something increasingly rare in standardized urban development: the unpredictability of life, social diversity, spatial inclusivity, and organic growth. It serves as an honest mirror, reflecting the delicate yet resilient daily life pulsating beneath the grand narrative of a megacity. To the southwest of the site, Fuqiang Road is an urban trunk road that generates significant noise. Northwest Xinzhou Fifth Street and northeast Xinzhou Seventh Street, as urban branch roads, serve as the primary access interfaces for the building complex. With a total floor area ratio (FAR) of 2.26, the project is a typical high-density campus in Shenzhen. To mitigate noise impact and explore spatial potential both vertically and underground, a rational overall layout was efficiently developed through comparative evaluation of multiple schemes, followed by the detailed architectural design.

Mbappe draws political fire over Ceuta t-shirt controversy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-17
23:57:00 UTC
08:57:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Mbappe draws political fire over Ceuta t-shirt controversy
Kylian Mbappe has come under mounting criticism from conservative and far-right politicians in Spain and France after the Real Madrid forward declined to fully wear a t-shirt supporting residents of Ceuta, Spain's north African exclave grappling with a migration crisis.
Immigration has emerged as one of Spain's dominant political issues in recent months following July's influx to Ceuta, and the debate has increasingly spilled into football ahead of next year's parliamentary elections.
The dispute erupted before Real Madrid's La Liga match on Tuesday when Mbappe, alongside Vinicius Junior and fellow Frenchman Ibrahima Konate, partially rolled up t-shirts bearing the words "We are all Ceutans", which was intended to be a message of support for people in the Spanish territory bordering Morocco.
Images of the three players quickly spread on social media and prompted political reactions in Madrid.
A spokesperson for the mainstream conservative Popular Party (PP) said she felt "deep shame" over the incident, while a lawmaker from the far-right Vox party said Spaniards were "perfectly free to feel outraged by three millionaires who live in Spain and then do not support Spaniards".
Ultras Sur, a Real Madrid supporters' group linked to the far right and banned from the Santiago Bernabeu, described the players' actions as "unacceptable" and called for public apologies.
Last week, AFP news agency reported that several hundred ultras gathered outside the stadium chanting "Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta must be defended!" before the 2-1 Champions League win over Inter Milan.
More than 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta from Morocco on July 30 and 31 in an unprecedented, chaotic surge that left scores dead and sparked European Union infighting over the sensitive topic of immigration.
'Complete solidarity'
Most returned in the following hours, but thousands remained in precarious conditions in the small, overwhelmed city, sleeping rough or in makeshift tents. Deteriorating conditions have fuelled tensions with local residents and regular protests, some of which have been embraced by far-right groups.
Responding to the criticism, Mbappe told sports daily AS he was in "complete solidarity with Ceuta and all the victims".
"But I also wanted to make a gesture and express my thoughts for all the immigrants who have lost their lives and who are also living in difficult conditions," he said.
Mbappe has previously spoken out on issues beyond football, including racism and opposition to France's far-right National Rally (RN).
French far-right figures also criticised the France captain's gesture, with RN spokesperson Julien Odoul condemning his behaviour, while European Parliament member Marion Marechal questioned why public figures showed solidarity with migrants but not Europeans affected by the crisis.
The row has become entwined with Spain's broader political debate over migration, with the PP and Vox accusing Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's government of failing to protect Spanish sovereignty in Ceuta.
Sanchez has defended a more open approach to irregular immigration in contrast with tougher policies promoted by European peers.
This year his government launched a scheme to grant legal status to irregular migrants already living in Spain that is expected to benefit around 500,000 people, mostly Latin Americans.
