Putting conversation first: Jerusalem ulpan founder reflects on 18 years of teaching Hebrew to olim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:10:22 UTC
07:10:22 KST

Any immigrant who ever struggled to become conversant in Hebrew could rightfully feel a bit jealous of Ami Steinberger.
He grew up in a bilingual home in Los Angeles, speaking English with his mother and Hebrew with his Israeli father. That gave him a huge advantage when he relocated to Israel.
Steinberger felt he could help those without prior Hebrew fluency reach a conversational level that most could not achieve in existing ulpan classes. (“Ulpan” means “studio” but is also used to describe an intensive school for learning Hebrew.)
On August 18, 2008, he held his first ulpan class in his living room in Katamon. He had four students. Two months later, he was asked to hold two simultaneous classes at AACI and had to hire another teacher.
Today, Steinberger’s Ulpan La-Inyan (ulpan.com) employs 80 to 90 teachers in a variety of time zones, teaching private lessons and group courses to roughly 2,000 students annually, online and in person. Companies, embassies, and gap-year programs are among its clients.
In celebration of Ulpan La-Inyan’s 18th anniversary, Steinberger talked with the Magazine about the history of his ulpan, current trends and methodologies for teaching Hebrew, and how Hebrew is increasingly pivotal to Jewish identity outside of Israel.
A new kind of ulpan
Although he officially made aliyah in 1994 at age 14, when his family lived in Ra’anana for a year, and came back for a year after high school and two years after college, Steinberger permanently relocated in 2007. He had earned an undergraduate degree in English literature from Yeshiva University and a master’s degree in clinical psychology.
Ulpan La-Inyan was born of his interest in languages – he had searched for an effective method for mastering Arabic, French, and Spanish as a hobby – combined with his realization that the free ulpan courses offered by the government for new immigrants weren’t always successful.
“I noticed that although some English-speakers would come out of a traditional government ulpan with strong Hebrew, many of them would come out understanding the difference between verb forms but not being able to open their mouths and speak,” he said. “These ulpan classes are too large for the teachers to engage each student, so they rely more on theory than on practice. They’re teaching language as if it’s an academic discipline rather than a social skill.”
He saw this as a gap that needed filling.
“I decided to open my own language school based on the method that had helped me learn foreign languages. And it turned out that the need was real. People would come to me and say, ‘I’ve been to five ulpanim, and this was the first one that worked.’
“Traditional ulpan, for many people, is like taking a horse and buggy to your destination; our ulpan gets you there in a car.”
Grammar drills vs speaking skills
Steinberger creates scripted lessons based on research into how the brain absorbs and processes language. Without going into detail, this method teaches words by repeating them at very specific intervals.
“All of this takes place in a conversation which is relevant and useful, where you feel as if you’re actually participating. We don’t teach words with flashcards but through natural conversation.”
In the past decade, additional private ulpanim in Israel have followed suit, radically shifting the emphasis from grammar drills to speaking skills.
“I like to think we started that trend,” Steinberger said. “However, none of them use our exact method, our secret sauce.”
Along with online quizzes and games, ulpan homework these days might include watching a contemporary Israeli TV show and discussing it in the next class, or meeting up in a Hebrew-speaking environment like a café.
Another trend is online learning. Ulpan La-Inyan is still headquartered in Jerusalem with a branch in Tel Aviv, but the physical location doesn’t matter as much anymore.
“Before corona, we offered only private lessons online, not group lessons, and that segment constituted no more than 10% of our clientele. Since corona, 50% of our students participate online, in private and group classes,” Steinberger said.
Students come from North America, South America, Mexico, and Europe. Not all students are Jewish. For example, clientele includes Jerusalem Arabs seeking to improve their Hebrew for easier integration into academia or the workplace.
Hebrew via AI?
The growing preference for long-distance learning comes in tandem with many options for language acquisition – for example, the popular Duolingo digital language-learning platform and app. Steinberger said Duolingo is fun but not very effective for Hebrew, Arabic, and other non-European languages.
“Then there are AI language-training apps with an avatar acting like a language coach; the learner speaks, and the avatar corrects them.
“However, if someone really wants to progress in a language, it requires discipline. If you have good self-discipline to engage with the app on a consistent basis, AI is great. If you’re somebody who needs a structured learning environment where you feel accountable to the teacher and classmates to show up, that is what will help you progress,” he said.
“Either way, AI is not human, and it’s the human element in conversation that really drives communication.”
Ulpan La-Inyan is developing a hybrid option: a digital course combined with human interaction in real time.
“This enables you to experience fadihot, those embarrassing mistakes, together and get past them,” Steinberger said. “AI can be helpful, but people will always need a sense of human connection because language is ultimately a social activity.”
Pitfalls, pet words, and identity
What are the most common difficulties for new Hebrew-speakers?
“Pronunciation can be difficult to master,” said Steinberger. “English-speakers often confuse the pronunciation of the Hebrew letters hay and het, while French-speakers often confuse raish and het.”
Aside from that, he said, “mostly it’s the verb conjugations that trip people up.”
Steinberger noted that shaky Hebrew skills lead many a new immigrant to feel a frustrating loss of self-esteem. “They may have a PhD, but their Hebrew is on a first-grade level.”
It helps to inject some basic everyday expressions into your vocabulary from day one. Handy exclamations such as sababa, ahla, and yalla – all of which, ironically enough, are borrowed from Arabic – lend ease to daily interactions even if your ability to put a full sentence together isn’t yet up to speed.
Steinberger believes that the ability to interact with Israelis in their own tongue is increasingly essential to Jewish identity formation in the Diaspora, particularly in non-Orthodox streams.
It’s true that many graduates of Orthodox and ultra-Orthodox schools lack conversational Hebrew fluency because Hebrew is often taught as a subject and not a language, he says. But their Jewish identity is tied to Torah values and lifestyle rather than spoken Hebrew.
“However, in the non-Orthodox world, the educational emphasis is on creating a link with peers in Israel. Hebrew could be that bridge, especially in times when Israel’s reputation is in question and Jewish identity becomes complex,” Steinberger said.
“If someone opts to say ‘I stand with Israel,’ then learning the language becomes their opportunity to connect with Israelis. Many people with a strong feeling of Jewish identity abroad feel they don’t belong at all when they’re in Israel because they can’t really have a conversation.”
And that brings us back to the question of how best to acquire a comfortable command of Hebrew.
Studies back up Steinberger’s contention that the old-style approach of memorizing grammatical rules and vocabulary word lists is not nearly as effective as the way babies learn to talk, by listening and speaking.
So, if you haven’t progressed as well as you’d like in a public or traditional ulpan, don’t despair – Ulpan La-Inyan or similar programs may be just the ticket for a faster ride to fluency.■

‘Checkout,' ‘Fauda’ test the appetite for Israeli spy stories after October 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:10:13 UTC
07:10:13 KST

Is there still an appetite for Israeli spy stories?
Two productions arriving in the United States this month are testing that question: Checkout, a dark Israeli comedy about an aging Mossad operative, and the fifth season of Fauda, the Israeli action thriller about undercover counterterrorism agents.
One is an indie film that spent years getting to the screen; the other is a global Netflix hit whose new season plunges directly into the trauma of the October 7 massacre.
The two projects are seeking audiences in a challenging climate. A Pew Research Center survey conducted in March found that 60% of Americans had an unfavorable view of Israel, compared with 37% who viewed the country favorably. And Israeli cultural exports have faced increasing scrutiny abroad over the country’s conduct since October 7.
Yet Fauda has returned to Netflix with considerable international attention, while Checkout opened in Manhattan to a sold-out audience.
“It’s hard for Israeli movies right now to find an audience because everything translates to, you know, the ‘P’ [Palestinian] problem,” Jonathan Dekel, the writer, director and executive producer of Checkout, said in an interview. “It’s problematic.”
Checkout premieres to sold-out theater
Checkout opened September 17 to a sold-out audience at the Quad Cinema in Greenwich Village, which Dekel described as a “stalwart of indie cinema.”
Dekel has said the film’s six-year production was almost as difficult as the journey of its protagonist. They shot in Ukraine in November 2020, at the height of the pandemic, and barely escaped with the film’s hard drive after the set was bombed when Russia invaded. They had just finished editing when October 7, 2023, arrived, and Dekel was called up for military service.
Dekel knew that the movie would debut in a world transformed by the war and its aftermath.
“Trying to find a good time to put out a movie, a satire - a dark comedy about the Israeli special forces - was very, very touch and go until we finally decided to go for it,” he told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
Checkout is not a conventional spy thriller. Its protagonist, Dov, is an American-born New Yorker who moved to Israel and is now about to retire from the Mossad.
“The day he checks out of his hotel to retire, someone else checks in, and it turns out it’s Mossad’s number one target - an arch terrorist [code-]named Gilgamesh,” Dekel said. “The entire movie is this weird weekend in a hotel where these two middle-aged men, spy-versus-spy, try to figure out who they are. They’re trying to find out about each other, but they find themselves.”
Josh Pais, who plays Dov, said his character is a man searching for meaning in his life - and comes to believe he can find it by tracking down and stopping a terrorist.
“He is possibly stepping into delusion,” said Pais. “What was appealing to me was that this is a story of what really happens to spies. So many movies tap into, you know, the James Bond of being a spy. Those movies are awesome, but this movie is about what it’s really like to be sent to a distant land, to be on location and to pretend that you’re someone else. Over a certain amount of time these guys start to lose touch with reality because, in truth, the vast majority of time as a spy nothing happens.”
Shai Satran, the movie’s co-writer, said he believes this is the “perfect moment for a movie about the Israeli intelligence community and an operation gone bad.”
“His driving force is not really to catch that guy - he doesn’t care about that guy. The driving force is to be accepted by his peers, the people who sent him - that’s at the core,” said Satran. “I don’t want to be crude about this, but there was something pre-October 7 about the Israeli security forces, maybe the special forces: There’s a certain arrogance in being only worried about your peers and not being aware of” the wider mission. In the lead-up to the Hamas attacks of October 7, “Israel, in a sense, thought that they were more in control of the situation than they were,” he said
Fauda's international success rewarded with fifth season
That idea - of intelligence work as something more complicated than heroic missions and exotic adventures - also runs through Fauda, though in a much more conventional action-thriller format.
The Israeli series has been an international success since its Netflix debut in 2016, and its fifth season, which arrived on Netflix September 8, is now testing whether audiences will follow its characters into a story shaped directly by and set two years after October 7.
Lior Raz, the show’s creator, co-writer and star, said last month at a fundraiser in Lenox, Massachusetts, for Israel’s Magen David Adom emergency service that he was genuinely surprised by the show’s reception in unlikely places: Previous seasons of the show hit No. 1 in popularity in Lebanon and the United Arab Emirates, and it was No. 2 in Qatar.
Season four ran in 2022 in Israel and early the next year on Netflix. The show’s creators had originally begun writing a different fifth season. But after the October 7 Hamas attack, Raz said those scripts were discarded. The new season deals directly with the aftermath of the attack and what Raz described as the nature of revenge. One reviewer called it “gripping, emotionally exhausting and often deeply difficult to watch,” particularly because of its depiction, in flashbacks, of October 7.
Raz, in his MDA talk, said the backlash against Israel was a campaign orchestrated by radical activists and Israel’s enemies. The latest season of Fauda is in part an attempt to depict the Israeli perspective for those open to nuance. “I want them to look in my character’s eyes, and to see what we felt on those days,” he told the New York Times. “If it would happen in their countries, they would feel exactly like we felt and how we feel about the world. So I hope it would open people’s eyes to see what happened on October 7.”
Although its reception abroad is hard to gauge, the latest season was a hit in Israel: The Times reported that it had already been the most-watched season of any show in the history of Israel’s Yes network.
Lacking the backing of a streaming giant, Checkout will have to work harder to find an audience. The Sundance Screenwriters Lab supported the Checkout script, Dekel said, but that was before October 7. Since then, “finding a distributor, finding a Netflix, Amazon or Hulu was pretty much crickets [silence] all over. It might be our movie, but looking around [at] movies from my colleagues - Israelis - I think it’s pretty much a broad phenomenon.”
Asked if he believed the difficulty he faced was because it is an Israeli movie or because it involved Jews, Dekel replied, “Is there a difference?”

The Archbishop of Canterbury withdrew on Thursday an award given to a Muslim cleric who praised Osama bin Laden in comments he made in 2007.
Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi, a Muslim cleric from Pakistan, received the Hubert Walter Award for Reconciliation and Interfaith Cooperation at Lambeth Palace, the residence of the Archbishop of Canterbury, last Friday.
Ashrafi serves as the chairman of the Pakistan Ulema Council, an Islamic umbrella group composed of Islamic scholars from a wide spectrum of Islamic traditions.
The Archbishop’s office said that Ashrafi was being honored for “his outstanding work as an ambassador of interfaith harmony in Pakistan, known for his commitment to promoting religious tolerance.”
The statement continued to praise Ashrafi’s role in supporting “religious minorities in Pakistan, particularly the Christian community.”
Bin Laden was 'fighting for Islam'
The ceremony coincided with the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in New York City. Lambeth Palace announced the withdrawal of the award after Ashrafi's comments resurfaced.
Comments made by Ashrafi emerged from 2007, in which he praised bin Laden, the architect of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, as someone who had “been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans, and British,” and in a different instance said he would give bin Laden the title “Saifullah,” meaning “sword of God.”
Lambeth Palace faced backlash over the resurfaced comments and announced it would withdraw the award.
“It is a longstanding principle of interfaith dialogue and co-operation that we must engage with one another across deeply held differences, and that remains the case,” Lambeth Palace announced.
“However, previous comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light that have led Lambeth Palace to reconsider this award, and we can now confirm today that the award has been withdrawn. We have contacted Imam Ashrafi to make him aware of this decision,” the statement continued.
'An unfair campaign' against him
In a statement to the BBC, Ashrafi told reporters that his comments from 2007 had been “totally taken out of context” and the subsequent outcry was “an unfair campaign” aimed at smearing him.
Ashrafi said he made the comments in response to “the hurt felt by many Muslims” after the British government’s decision to knight the “Satanic Verses” author Salman Rushdie.
Ashrafi has also been criticized since the award was first announced for his support of the Pakistani blasphemy laws, which have been criticized by human rights groups.
Ashrafi claimed the laws actually “save lives” by stopping people from taking matters of religious offenses into their own hands.
Human Rights Watch said last year that “the laws perpetuate religious discrimination and are used to target the poor and minorities in unlawful evictions and land grabs.”
The group also called on Pakistan’s government to reform the laws to prevent them from “being weaponized” against any of Pakistan's minority communities.

US granted permanent control over all security needs in Greenland, Trump announces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:09:54 UTC
07:09:54 KST

WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump announced that the United States has reached what he described as a permanent agreement with Denmark and Greenland, granting Washington sweeping and indefinite security rights in Greenland, including the ability to expand its military presence and prevent adversaries from establishing bases, deploying forces, or making sensitive investments there.
Trump said the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” while fully addressing what he described as longstanding American concerns in the strategically important territory.
“There will be NO COST to the United States!” Trump wrote in announcing the agreement.
“At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America,” he said.
Trump also said that under the agreement, no US adversary would be permitted to establish a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without express written American approval.
“For over 100 years, Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it,” Trump said. “I am proud to be the President that permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation.”
He described the arrangement as an “Infinite Life” agreement, declaring that “there is no end.”
Permanent access, bases, and overflight rights
A US State Department official provided additional details on the agreement, describing it as an unprecedented arrangement that permanently guarantees US security interests in the Arctic at no cost to the American taxpayer.
According to the official, the deal gives the United States permanent security control over Greenland and ensures that the territory will remain part of what Washington describes as the strategic defense area of North America.
The agreement explicitly guarantees the United States “the complete ability to do what it deems is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the American continent,” the official said.
Those authorities include permanent access, basing and overflight rights.
The agreement also allows the US military to increase the number of bases in Greenland as necessary, according to the State Department official.
Trump said the United States would “immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” adding that Washington would work with the people of Greenland on development and construction.
“This solution is a great one for the United States of America, Denmark, Greenland, and all of our Allies,” Trump said.
Non-NATO countries prohibited from building bases in Greenland
The State Department official said the agreement explicitly prohibits any non-NATO country from building a military base in Greenland or maintaining a troop presence there.
The official contrasted that with what the administration described as the previous status quo, under which countries outside NATO could potentially have been allowed to establish military facilities or send forces to Greenland.
The official singled out China and Russia, saying the agreement guarantees that neither country can establish a base in Greenland or deploy troops there.
It also creates mechanisms designed to prevent adversaries from investing in sensitive sectors.
According to the official, only the United States and its allies will be able to make sensitive investments in Greenland under the agreement, replacing what the administration described as a previous system under which adversaries could invest in sensitive areas without investment screening.
The deal, the official said, is intended to remain fully in force even if Greenland one day becomes a fully independent country.
Rubio: ‘A huge win’
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the agreement “a huge win for the United States and the American people.”
“Thanks to President Trump’s vision and leadership, this historic agreement permanently guarantees US security interests in the Arctic at zero cost to the US taxpayer,” Rubio said.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” he added.
Rubio said the agreement “permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.”
Trump framed the deal in similarly sweeping terms, calling it “a dream come true for the United States of America” and describing it as “very important, historic, and special.”
“We look forward to working with the wonderful people of Denmark and Greenland toward a magnificent future with respect to this large, and highly strategic, parcel of land,” Trump said. “We will be very protective of it.”

====================================================================================================

Screen time isn’t linked to language delays in autistic children, large U.S. study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:00:57 UTC
07:00:57 KST

A recent study suggests that reading books together at home is associated with better language abilities in young autistic children. The research provides evidence that this shared reading time helps explain why children from higher-income families tend to have stronger communication skills, but finds that screen time does not have a negative impact on these abilities. The findings were published in Autism Research.
Language skills vary widely among children on the autism spectrum. Autism is a developmental condition characterized by differences in social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviors. Some autistic children experience challenges producing or understanding spoken language, whereas others develop abilities similar to or exceeding those of their neurotypical peers. To understand this variation, scientists are increasingly looking at environmental influences that shape early development.
Human development is shaped by different layers of a child’s environment. Broad, distant factors include a family’s socioeconomic status, which generally refers to household income and the parents’ education levels. Closer, everyday factors include the specific activities a child experiences at home, such as shared book reading and screen time. Shared book reading involves an adult caregiver looking at and reading a story with a child, encouraging them to actively participate.
Screen time refers to the hours a child spends in front of televisions, tablets, computers, or smartphones. In the general population, researchers have observed that reading together provides benefits for communication skills. For example, a 2026 study of early childhood development indicated that interactive home literacy routines, like reading books and discussing past events, directly promote language growth over time.
However, reading with an autistic child might look different. In fact, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that autistic children tend to focus their attention differently during shared reading than neurotypical children, looking less at the reader’s face and more at background objects. Because autistic children might engage with their environment in unique ways, scientists wanted to see if the typical patterns seen in other children hold true for them.
“Children with autism are likely to experience language delays and other challenges using and/or understanding spoken language that emerge early in childhood and sometimes persist into adulthood,” said lead author Meredith Pecukonis, an assistant professor in the Department of Psychology at Smith College and director of the Autism & Neurodevelopment (AND) Lab. “Identifying how certain aspects of the home environment relate to language abilities in autistic children is an important first step towards understanding how children’s experiences at home are shaping their language development, and developing interventions that lead to stronger language outcomes for autistic children.”
“Prior to publication of our study, only three studies had looked at the association between screen time and language abilities in autistic children,” Pecukonis told PsyPost. “All of these studies were conducted in China, and therefore no studies had been done in the U.S. on this topic. This gap in the literature was surprising to us, given that several studies have linked excessive screen time to language delays in neurotypical children, and autistic children engage in more screen time than their neurotypical peers.”
To address this gap, the researchers aimed to map out how socioeconomic status, reading habits, and screen use connect to language development. They wanted to see if the broader impact of a family’s income and education might operate through the daily routines children experience at home. To investigate this, the researchers analyzed data from the National Survey of Children’s Health collected between 2018 and 2022.
They focused on a nationally representative group of 1,217 autistic children living in the United States. The children in the sample were between the ages of two and five. Data was collected through surveys completed by parents or adult caregivers who lived with the children.
The survey assessed socioeconomic status by recording the highest level of parent education and calculating the family’s poverty ratio based on their income. It also tracked daily habits, asking parents how many days per week they read to their child and how many hours per weekday the child spent on electronic devices. To measure language, the researchers looked at both expressive and receptive skills.
Expressive language included abilities like speaking single words, asking questions, and telling a story. Receptive language involved understanding instructions, pointing to objects, and recognizing the beginning sounds of words. The statistical models accounted for both the age and sex of the children.
The results showed that autistic children from households with a higher socioeconomic status tended to have higher expressive and receptive language skills. These children were also read to more often and spent less time using screens. The researchers found a direct association between reading frequency and communication abilities. Autistic children who experienced more shared book reading at home demonstrated better language skills across the board.
When analyzing the connections between these variables, the researchers found that shared book reading partially explained the link between socioeconomic status and language skills. This suggests that children from higher-income families experience more frequent shared reading, which in turn helps build their communication abilities. The daily habit of reading acts as a bridge connecting a family’s broader resources to a child’s specific developmental gains.
“Effect sizes are small, meaning that the environment has a small yet significant impact on language development in autism,” Pecukonis said. “Parents raising children in lower SES households may have less time and energy to devote to shared book reading if they are working multiple jobs to pay their bills. Lower SES households may also have reduced access to books in the home.”
“If we want to support autistic children’s language development, we need to acknowledge that children are shaped by various aspects of their environments,” she continued. While some aspects can be addressed through direct family interventions, she noted that others “will likely require systemic change through public policy (e.g., providing greater financial support and services to lower SES families).”
The study found that screen time was not statistically associated with expressive or receptive language skills in autistic children. This means that the amount of time these children spent on devices did not predict better or worse communication abilities. This lack of an association stood out to the researchers, as previous studies of neurotypical children frequently link heavy screen use to developmental delays.
“We were really surprised that the association between amount of screen time and children’s language abilities was non-significant,” Pecukonis said. “This contradicts with what has been reported in the literature on neurotypical children.”
“The non-significant association between screen time and language abilities doesn’t suggest that screen time is ‘good’ or ‘bad’ for autistic children… it just shows that there is no association,” she added.
The results are in tension with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that replacing shared reading with screen time was linked to lower developmental scores. However, that earlier study looked at neurotypical preschoolers, whereas the new study focused exclusively on autistic children. Similarly, a 2024 study linked higher screen time to poorer language skills in the general population, which contrasts with the neutral effect observed here for autistic children.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study relied on parent surveys, which can sometimes be subject to reporting biases, such as overestimating reading time or underestimating screen use. The data also captured a single snapshot in time rather than tracking the children over many years. Because of this, it is not possible to declare that reading directly causes better language skills in this group.
“We only looked at two household activities (shared book reading and screen time) as our measures of the environment when in reality there are probably hundreds, if not thousands, of other aspects of the environment that are shaping language development in autism that we just didn’t measure here,” Pecukonis explained.
“The purpose of this work isn’t to ‘blame’ parents for their children’s language delays, but rather to document trends, show that the environment does matter for language development, and find ways to support autistic children through modifications to their environment,” she emphasized. “Our hope is that these findings will ultimately help autistic children and their families by showing that there is a need for greater support for those from lower SES households.”
The study also measured the sheer quantity of screen time and reading without looking at the quality of those activities. It is entirely possible that autistic children with stronger language skills are more likely to request story time, leading to more frequent reading sessions. Future studies could use direct observation to see how the types of digital media and the specific reading strategies parents use shape language development.
“We just applied for funding to run a longitudinal study to see how screen time measured early in development relates to language abilities measured later in development,” Pecukonis noted. “This study will also measure both the quantity and quality of screen time.”
The study, “Socioeconomic Status and Quantity of Shared Book Reading, But Not Screen Time, are Positively Associated With Language Skills in a Nationally Representative Sample of Autistic Children,” was authored by M. Pecukonis and A. Geffin.

Trump claims deal with Denmark gives US ‘permanent control’ over Greenland
Denmark and Greenland plan to sign a US defence pact next week, pending approval from both parliaments.
United States President Donald Trump claimed on Friday that Washington has entered into an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other needs”.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said, “At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the US will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump threatens Spain trade, demands US take over Greenland at NATO summit
- list 2 of 3Russia warns Denmark after near miss in Baltic Sea
- list 3 of 3EU pledges more than $200m to Greenland amid Trump annexation threats
He added that US adversaries will be barred from establishing military bases or personnel in Greenland unless they receive written authorisation from the United States.
Trump alleged that plans will begin immediately to build a significant US military footprint in suitable areas across Greenland, noting there are numerous potential locations.
Denmark and Greenland released a joint statement on Friday indicating that a pact with the US is set to be signed during next week’s high-level United Nations General Assembly summit.
The statement added that the agreement remains subject to formal parliamentary approval in both Nuuk and Copenhagen.
Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the agreement “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination.”
